chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS)
About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS)
About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS)
Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Governed Space: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary
Canonical Definition
Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) governs what simulation-derived information may legitimately become evidence, what evidential meaning and weight that evidence may carry, how far reliance upon it may extend, which uses must remain limited, and how simulation evidence must interface with broader validation governance.
SERBS addresses a fundamental simulation problem:
A simulation can produce technically precise, repeatable, and convincing results without those results necessarily providing equally strong evidence about reality.
The Standard creates the governance layer between simulation results and reliance upon simulation results.
Why SERBS Matters
Organizations increasingly use simulation to support decisions that cannot be tested easily, safely, economically, or repeatedly in the real world.
This creates a methodological risk.

A simulation may contain millions of executions, high-fidelity models, sophisticated physics, realistic environments, and highly precise outputs while still depending upon assumptions, abstractions, scenario limitations, incomplete reality representation, uncertain correlations, or conditions that do not fully transfer to the real world.
SERBS prevents simulation sophistication from being mistaken for evidential certainty.
It requires organizations to establish:
What is evidence? What does that evidence actually support? How much evidential weight may it carry? Under which conditions does that meaning remain valid? Where does legitimate reliance stop? What additional validation is required before broader conclusions are made?
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Outputs + Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence Qualification → Simulation Evidence Weight → Simulation Reliance Boundary → Simulation Use Limitation → Simulation Validation Interface → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record
Where broader validation is required:
Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → VALIDOS® Validation Governance
What SERBS Helps Organizations Govern
SERBS provides a structured method for determining whether simulation-derived information can legitimately support a particular engineering, scientific, safety, mission, operational, or deployment proposition.
It helps organizations distinguish between:
Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence

Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination
Evidence Volume ≠ Evidential Strength
Correlation ≠ Reality Equivalence
Repeated Runs ≠ Independent Evidence
Technical Precision ≠ Evidential Certainty
The result is not less reliance on simulation.
It is better-governed reliance on simulation.
Reliance Boundary
SERBS requires simulation evidence to remain bounded by the conditions that created its meaning.
Those boundaries may include: Simulation Object and configuration; simulation purpose and scope; represented reality; assumptions; model applicability; input basis; scenario coverage; execution conditions; output classification; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; temporal relevance; known limitations.
Evidence may therefore be highly useful while still being legitimately narrow.
SERBS prevents narrow evidence from silently becoming a broad claim.
Boundary with VALIDOS®
SERBS does not determine whether an entire system, object, claim, or operational proposition has been validated.
The architectural boundary is explicit:
SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean.
VALIDOS® determines whether that evidence, alone or together with other evidence, is sufficient to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance.

This allows simulation evidence to enter broader validation without losing the conditions, uncertainty, provenance, and limitations that define its legitimate meaning. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Evidence Before Reality Exists
A space organization is preparing a future lunar landing mission.
Large simulation programs reproduce spacecraft dynamics, navigation, landing trajectories, crew interaction, surface operations, failure conditions, environmental effects, and mission contingencies.
Thousands or millions of simulation executions may demonstrate apparently stable mission performance.
But a fundamental problem remains:
the operational reality being predicted may not yet have been experienced in the exact mission configuration being simulated.
Some environmental effects can only be approximated. Real mission data may be sparse. Crew behavior under actual lunar conditions may not yet exist. A highly sophisticated simulator may therefore provide powerful evidence without providing complete real-world proof.
Without SERBS, an organization could gradually transform:
“The mission architecture performed successfully across these governed simulations.”
into:
“The mission architecture is proven to perform successfully in lunar operations.”
Those statements are not methodologically equivalent.
SERBS requires the simulation evidence to carry its actual basis:

tested mission configuration → represented lunar conditions → assumptions → scenario coverage → executions → observed outputs → available reality correlation → remaining uncertainty → permitted reliance.
The resulting evidence may legitimately support mission design, contingency planning, crew preparation, engineering decisions, or a broader validation program while still carrying an explicit boundary against claims that the simulation alone cannot establish.
The value of SERBS is not to weaken the simulation evidence. It is to prevent that evidence from being asked to prove more than the simulation actually tested. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: Simulation Success Before
Real-World Transfer
An organization develops an autonomous vehicle, mobile robot, delivery robot, industrial robot, or other autonomous system primarily through large-scale simulation.
The system completes millions of simulated scenarios involving traffic, pedestrians, obstacles, sensor conditions, failures, environmental variation, unusual events, and behavioral edge cases.
The simulation campaign reports extremely high success rates.
The organization now considers the system ready for broader real-world deployment.
But another fundamental problem appears:
success inside a simulated environment does not automatically establish equivalent behavior after transfer into physical reality.

Real sensors may respond differently. Friction and dynamics may vary. Lighting, weather, surfaces, object appearance, human behavior, sensor noise, actuator behavior, latency, hardware faults, and combinations of rare conditions may differ from the simulated representation.
Even millions of successful executions can share the same underlying model assumptions or representation gaps.
SERBS therefore asks a different question from:
“How many simulated scenarios did the system pass?”
It asks:
“What real-world proposition may those passed simulations legitimately support?”
SERBS qualifies the evidence, evaluates its simulation-specific weight, identifies common dependencies across the simulation campaign, establishes the permitted reliance boundary, and preserves use limitations before the results enter broader validation or deployment decisions.
The organization may conclude that the evidence strongly supports:
performance across the represented scenario space
while not yet supporting:
equivalent performance across unrestricted operational reality.
Additional real-world testing, observation, correlation, or other validation evidence can then be added through VALIDOS®.
A million successful simulations can increase confidence. They cannot eliminate an ungoverned reality gap.
Enterprise Value
SERBS gives organizations a repeatable governance structure for turning simulation results into decision-usable evidence without overstating what that evidence proves.

It is particularly valuable where: real-world testing is expensive; failure is dangerous; physical testing cannot cover enough scenarios; the operational environment does not yet exist; simulations operate at enormous scale; simulation is used to support safety or deployment decisions; simulation outputs feed regulatory or validation processes; sim-to-real transfer remains uncertain.
SERBS therefore provides the missing boundary between what simulation can show and what an organization may legitimately conclude from what simulation has shown.
Foundational Principle
Simulation-derived evidence must not travel farther than its governed meaning can legitimately support.

OOF™ About Simulation Execution Standard - (SES)
About Simulation Execution Standard - (SES)
About Simulation Execution Standard (SES)
Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Governed Space: Simulation Execution Operational Space: Simulation Execution Governance Governance Flow Position: 8 of 12 — Simulation Scenario → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance
Canonical Definition
Simulation Execution Standard (SES) defines the governance conditions under which a governed simulation is instantiated, executed, controlled, observed, repeated where required, and documented so that the actual execution remains traceable to the Simulation Object, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, configuration, runtime conditions, interventions, deviations, and outputs that formed the execution event.
SES governs the point at which a designed simulation becomes an actual simulation execution.
It ensures that organizations can distinguish between:
what was intended to run
and:
what actually ran.
Why SES Matters
Modern organizations may execute thousands or millions of simulations across AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering environments, and mission systems.
The challenge is therefore not only whether simulation capability exists.
The governance question becomes:

Can the organization reconstruct exactly what happened during a materially relevant simulation execution?
SES provides the structure for answering:
Which configuration actually ran?
Which model and environment versions were used?
Which scenario, inputs, and parameters were instantiated?
What happened during execution?
Were there interventions, interruptions, failures, or deviations?
Was the simulation repeated under comparable conditions?
Can the resulting outputs be traced to the execution that produced them?
What SES Governs
SES governs five connected execution spaces:
Simulation Instantiation Establishes the exact executable simulation instance and binds it to its relevant configuration.
Simulation Execution Control Governs how execution is initiated, progressed, controlled, interrupted, modified where permitted, terminated, and completed.
Simulation Observation Preserves materially relevant states, events, transitions, anomalies, interventions, and runtime conditions.
Simulation Repetition Governs repeated runs, randomization, repeatability, reproducibility conditions, execution variance, and comparability.
Simulation Execution Documentation Creates the traceable record needed to reconstruct what actually occurred.
Governance Flow
Governed Scenario & Simulation Configuration
↓
Simulation Instantiation
↓
Execution Control
↓
Simulation Observation
↓
Simulation Repetition
↓
Execution Documentation
↓
Governed Simulation Execution Record
↓

Simulation Output Governance What SES Does Not Determine
SES does not determine whether: the Simulation Object was correctly selected, the representation perfectly reflects reality, the simulation assumptions are universally valid, the simulation output is correct, an inference from the output is justified, the simulated system is safe, or the system should be deployed.
Those questions belong to other SIMULOS® spaces or compatible OOF® architectures.
SES governs specifically:
the execution event and its reconstructability.
Enterprise Application
SES can operate above an organization's existing simulation infrastructure.
A company does not need to replace its: simulation engine, robotics simulator, digital twin, Monte Carlo environment, HPC infrastructure, AI evaluation environment, engineering simulator, or proprietary simulation platform.
SES provides a governance layer for examining whether simulation execution remains identifiable, controlled, observable, repeatable where required, documented, and traceable.
This makes SES applicable both as an execution governance framework and as a diagnostic structure for identifying execution-governance gaps in existing simulation environments. Use Case 1 — Autonomous System SimulationScenario
A company performs thousands of simulations before deploying an autonomous robotic system.

Several runs show unexpected collision-avoidance behavior, but engineers cannot reliably determine whether the difference originated from: model version, environment configuration, sensor inputs, randomization, parameter changes, runtime intervention, or actual autonomous behavior.
SES Application
SES binds each material execution to its:
Execution ID → Model → Environment → Scenario → Inputs → Parameters → Runtime Conditions → Observations → Outputs
Repeated runs remain distinguishable, while material execution deviations and interventions remain visible. Result
The organization can reconstruct the simulation conditions associated with the anomalous behavior and determine which executions are legitimately comparable before downstream interpretation or validation begins. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation CampaignScenario
A space organization executes a large mission-simulation campaign covering combinations of: navigation uncertainty, communication loss, sensor degradation, power limitations, subsystem failures, autonomous recovery, and changing environmental conditions.
A critical mission decision depends upon results generated across a very large population of simulation runs.
SES Application
SES establishes execution and campaign traceability so that materially relevant results remain connected to:
Scenario → Configuration → Execution Conditions → Runtime Events → Repetition → Completion Status → Output

Interrupted, failed, modified, or anomalous runs remain visible rather than disappearing from the analytical record. Result
Decision-makers can determine not merely that simulations were performed, but which configurations actually executed, under which conditions, whether execution remained complete and controlled, and which exact executions produced the outputs being relied upon.
Business Value
SES can help organizations identify potential governance gaps such as:
Execution Traceability Gaps
Configuration-to-Run Gaps
Observation Gaps
Intervention Traceability Gaps
Execution Drift
Repetition Comparability Gaps
Failed-Run Visibility Gaps
Execution-to-Output Lineage Gaps
These findings can then be investigated before conclusions are drawn about simulation quality, validity, safety, or operational readiness.
Relationship to Adjacent SIMULOS® Standards
Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) asks:
What scenarios must be simulated?
Simulation Execution Standard (SES) asks:
What actually happened when those simulations were executed?
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) then asks:
What exactly did those executions produce, and what may legitimately be inferred from those outputs?
The architectural transition is therefore:
Scenario → Execution → Output
Foundational Principle
A simulation result cannot be fully understood from its output alone; it must remain connected to the execution conditions and execution history that produced it.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Execution Standard (SES) provides the governance structure through which simulation intent becomes traceable simulation activity. By governing instantiation, execution control, observation, repetition, and execution documentation, SES enables organizations to reconstruct what actually ran, distinguish intended configuration from executed configuration, preserve material deviations and failures, compare repeated executions appropriately, and maintain lineage between simulation executions and the outputs they produce.

resources.title: OOF™ About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
resources.parent_standard: OOF™ About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
Simulation
Every simulation depends on inputs.
Those inputs may come from sensors, historical records, operational systems, scientific measurements, external models, human operators, AI systems, synthetic generators, or previous simulations.
But information does not become suitable simulation input merely because it exists or because a simulation can technically ingest it.
Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) governs the conditions under which information may legitimately enter and influence a simulation.
Canonical Definition
Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) defines the governance conditions under which data, values, signals, measurements, states, distributions, synthetic inputs, and other information may enter a simulation and influence its behavior, requiring material inputs to remain sufficiently identifiable, representative, transformation-governed, temporally appropriate, uncertainty-aware, and traceable to their simulation use.
Why SIDS Exists
A strong simulation model can still produce weak or misleading results when the information entering it is: unrepresentative, stale, temporally misaligned, transformed incorrectly, based on the wrong population, missing important variation, synthetically generated without disclosure, uncertain, incomplete, or incompatible with the simulation context.
SIDS therefore separates:
Data Availability
from:

Simulation Input Suitability
The key question is not:
Do we have data?
It is:
Is this the right information to enter this simulation under these conditions?
Governed Space
Simulation Inputs & Data
SIDS governs data specifically at the point where it becomes capable of influencing simulation behavior.
It does not attempt to govern the entire organizational data lifecycle.
Its focus is the simulation-input boundary.
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Model & Environment
↓
Input Need
↓
Simulation Input Identification
↓
Representativeness Assessment
↓
Transformation Governance
↓
Temporal Qualification
↓
Input Uncertainty
↓
Acceptance / Restriction / Exclusion
↓
Governed Simulation Input & Data Basis
↓
Simulation Scenario Design What SIDS Governs
SIDS establishes whether material Simulation Inputs are:
Identifiable — what exactly entered the simulation?
Representative — do the inputs sufficiently represent the conditions the simulation is intended to model?
Transformation-Governed — what happened to the data before simulation use?
Temporally Appropriate — does the data represent the right point, sequence, period, or system state?
Uncertainty-Aware — what measurement, estimation, sampling, transformation, or representativeness uncertainty remains?
Traceable — which inputs influenced which simulation configuration and execution?
Representativeness Matters
Data can be accurate and still be inappropriate for a simulation.
For example:

data collected during normal operation may accurately describe normal behavior while being unsuitable for a simulation of emergency failure.
Likewise:
data from one population, climate, geographic region, system generation, or operating state may not represent another.
SIDS therefore treats representativeness as a simulation-specific governance question.
Representative for what?
must always remain connected to:
Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Scenario Context Transformation Must Remain Visible
Simulation inputs are frequently transformed before use.
They may be: normalized, aggregated, filtered, interpolated, extrapolated, encoded, converted, cleaned, derived, imputed, or synthetically generated.
These transformations may materially change the information entering the simulation.
SIDS therefore preserves the chain:
Source Data → Transformation → Simulation Input
A transformed input should not silently be represented as identical to the original source information.
Synthetic Inputs
Synthetic data can be essential to simulation.
It may enable testing of: rare failures, extreme environments, unavailable populations, hypothetical systems, future conditions, edge cases, or dangerous scenarios that cannot reasonably be reproduced in reality.
SIDS does not treat synthetic data as inferior by default.
It requires one essential distinction:
Synthetic Input ≠ Observed Reality

The synthetic origin and the conditions under which that input may be used must remain visible.
Temporal Context Matters
Simulation data always has a relationship to time.
SIDS therefore asks:
When was this information observed?
Which period does it represent?
Is it sufficiently current for this simulation?
Do multiple inputs represent the same point in time?
Does sequence matter?
Has temporal aggregation hidden material events?
This becomes especially important for fast-changing systems such as: AI, autonomous systems, financial systems, infrastructure, transportation, digital twins, or live operational simulations.
Uncertainty Must Travel With the Input
Measured or estimated inputs are rarely perfectly certain.
A sensor may have tolerance.
Historical data may have sampling limitations.
Synthetic data may depend upon generation assumptions.
Interpolated values may not have been directly observed.
SIDS requires material uncertainty to remain connected to the input rather than disappearing when the data enters the simulation.
The simulation therefore should not imply greater certainty than its input basis supports.
Missing Data
Missing information is itself a governance condition.
SIDS prevents missing values from silently becoming:
zero
average
default
or:
synthetic replacement
without an identifiable treatment.
Possible responses may include substitution, imputation, scenario restriction, conditional use, or exclusion.
The important requirement is visibility.

Conflicting Inputs
Different sources may disagree.
For example:
Sensor A = 50
while:
Sensor B = 75
SIDS requires material conflict to remain identifiable and the treatment of that conflict to remain governable.
A simulation should not simply choose the more convenient value without preserving why that choice was made.
Input Sets
A simulation execution rarely depends on one input.
It consumes a complete Simulation Input Set.
SIDS allows each execution to remain connected to the exact set of materially relevant information that entered it.
This enables later reconstruction:
Which inputs produced this result?
Which were measured?
Which were synthetic?
Which had been transformed?
Which were estimated or uncertain?
Which represented an older system state?
Business Value
For organizations using simulation, SIDS provides direct operational value.
It helps detect situations where expensive simulation capability is being fed with information that is unsuitable for the question being simulated.
This may reveal: weak datasets, hidden population gaps, temporal mismatch, synthetic-data dependence, transformation loss, stale inputs, incompatible data sources, missing information, and outputs that appear precise despite uncertain input conditions.
SIDS therefore improves the ability to: compare simulation runs, explain outputs, reproduce results, challenge simulation conclusions, update simulations, trace failures, and prepare simulation outputs for downstream validation.

Relationship to Simulation Assumptions
SAS governs what the simulation assumes.
SIDS governs what information the simulation consumes.
An assumption may influence how an input is interpreted, but the two remain distinct.
For example:
Assumption: Weather remains stable.
Input: Measured temperature at simulation start.
Relationship to Model & Environment
SMES establishes the controlled model and environment.
SIDS determines what information may enter that governed structure.
The relationship is:
Model & Environment → Input Requirements → Governed Input & Data Basis Relationship to Scenario Design
SIDS does not determine which scenarios should be run.
It determines which information is available and suitable to support those scenarios.
The next Parent Standard, Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS), governs:
Which combinations of conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, and alternatives should actually be simulated?
Relationship to VALIDOS®
SIDS does not perform universal data validation.
VALIDOS® may separately validate: an input dataset, a source, an evidence object, a simulation output, or the simulation itself.
The boundary is:
SIDS governs whether information may function as simulation input.
VALIDOS® governs formal validation of the relevant Validation Object.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
Simulation Inputs may originate from that reality.
SIDS governs the transformation from:
Operational information
into:
governed simulation input

without redefining Operational Reality itself.
Relationship to INTEGROS® and ADIT®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity of input objects, records, transformations, and preserved states.
ADIT® may preserve evidence of input acquisition, transformation, substitution, and execution use.
SIDS remains focused on the simulation-specific suitability and use of the input.
Architectural Position
SIDS is the sixth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The progression is:
Simulation Object
↓
Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model & Environment
↓
Simulation Inputs & Data
↓
Simulation Scenario Design
SIDS therefore marks a critical transition.
Before SIDS, SIMULOS® establishes:
what the simulation is, what it represents, what it assumes, and through which structure it will operate.
SIDS then establishes:
what information may legitimately enter that structure.
Only after that foundation exists can scenario governance meaningfully determine what conditions the simulation should be asked to explore.
Foundational Principle
Information becomes legitimate simulation input only when what it represents, how it was transformed, when it applies, what uncertainty it carries, and where it may influence the simulation remain sufficiently governed.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) governs the information boundary of SIMULOS® by ensuring that material inputs remain identifiable, sufficiently representative, transformation-governed, temporally appropriate, uncertainty-aware, and traceable to the simulation activity they influence. By distinguishing technical ingestibility from methodological suitability, observed information from synthetic input, current information from temporally mismatched data, and raw information from transformed input, SIDS provides the governed Input & Data Basis required before simulation conditions can be intentionally organized into scenarios and executed.

resources.title: OOF™ About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS)
resources.parent_standard: OOF™ About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS)

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS)
About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS)
About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS)
Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation
Canonical Definition
Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) governs how the continuing relevance of a simulation is monitored after its creation and use, how material divergence between the governed simulation basis and changing reality is recognized, and when change requires simulation update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement.
SLRS addresses a fundamental lifecycle problem:
A simulation that was appropriate when created may become progressively less representative as the object, environment, assumptions, data, operational conditions, or reality itself changes.
The Standard prevents historical simulation results from retaining unchanged authority after the conditions that gave them meaning have materially changed.
Why SLRS Matters
Simulation governance does not end when a simulation campaign finishes.
Systems evolve. Environments change. New operational data appears. Previously unknown failure modes emerge. Models improve. Assumptions become obsolete. Inputs shift. New scenarios become relevant.

SLRS establishes a governed mechanism for asking:
Is this simulation still relevant to the reality for which it is being relied upon?
Where the answer changes materially, SLRS determines whether the appropriate response is:
continued use → review → update → partial resimulation → broader resimulation → replacement → retirement.
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Basis → Lifecycle Monitoring → Simulation Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope Determination → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement → Updated Governed Simulation Lifecycle
This creates the recursive lifecycle:
Simulation → Operational Use → Reality Change → Simulation Drift → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement What SLRS Helps Organizations Govern
SLRS helps organizations prevent simulation results from becoming methodologically stale while remaining operationally influential.
It provides a structured basis for monitoring changes in: the Simulation Object; object configuration and version; represented reality; environmental conditions; assumptions; models; inputs and data; scenarios; observed operational behavior; simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence relevance; known limitations.
Not every change requires complete resimulation.
SLRS exists partly to determine which changes are material enough to require action and how much of the simulation lifecycle must be reopened. Use Case 1 — Space Mission: Mission Reality Changes After Simulation

A space mission has undergone extensive simulation covering trajectory, spacecraft behavior, navigation, landing conditions, environmental effects, system failures, crew procedures, and mission contingencies.
Months later, new information becomes available.
The spacecraft configuration has changed. Updated environmental observations alter expected surface conditions. A component behaves differently during physical testing. New mission constraints modify the landing profile.
The original simulations may still be technically correct representations of the conditions under which they were executed.
But those conditions are no longer identical to the mission now being prepared.
The critical governance question becomes:
Which previous simulation results remain relevant, which have materially drifted from the current mission basis, and what must be simulated again?
SLRS provides the lifecycle mechanism for identifying those changes, determining their materiality, activating appropriate resimulation triggers, and defining whether resimulation must cover one affected scenario, one subsystem, a scenario family, or a much larger part of the mission simulation campaign.
This prevents two opposite failures:
continuing to rely on obsolete simulations
and
unnecessarily repeating an entire simulation program whenever anything changes.
Resimulation should follow material change, not merely the passage of time. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: Operational Reality Evolves

An autonomous vehicle or robot is developed through millions of simulated scenarios and subsequently enters real-world operation.
Operational experience begins producing conditions that were absent or materially different in the original simulation environment.
New road layouts appear. Sensor hardware changes. Software behavior evolves. Human interaction patterns differ from those represented during development. Previously rare edge cases become observable. Weather, lighting, surfaces, obstacles, or environmental distributions change.
The original simulation campaign does not suddenly become useless.
But neither should its relevance be assumed to remain unchanged.
SLRS establishes continuous lifecycle governance between:
the simulation basis that existed when evidence was produced
and
the operational reality that exists now.
Material differences become Simulation Drift Candidates.
Where drift becomes significant, SLRS can trigger targeted resimulation of the affected conditions rather than automatically rebuilding the entire simulation campaign.
If the underlying model or representation has become fundamentally unsuitable, the appropriate outcome may instead be replacement or retirement.
This creates a feedback loop:
Real-World Operation → New Reality Evidence → Drift Recognition → Resimulation → Updated Simulation Basis
The simulation therefore becomes a governed evolving representation rather than a static artifact frozen at development time.

A simulation should not remain authoritative merely because it was once representative.
Enterprise Value
SLRS enables organizations to maintain simulation relevance across long operational lifecycles without treating every change as either irrelevant or grounds for complete resimulation.
It supports:
change-sensitive simulation governance → proportionate resimulation → preserved relevance → controlled retirement.
For organizations operating large simulation programs, this can reduce unnecessary computational and engineering repetition while making material simulation drift visible before outdated simulation evidence continues influencing important decisions.
Foundational Principle
A simulation remains governably relevant only while the conditions that support its meaning remain materially applicable; when those conditions change, continued reliance requires governed reassessment.

resources.title: OOF™ About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES)
resources.parent_standard: OOF™ About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES)

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES)
About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES)
About Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES)
Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) is the fifth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
It governs the point at which a defined Reality Representation and governed Simulation Assumptions are transformed into the actual model and environment through which simulation activity can occur.
Canonical Definition
Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) defines the governance conditions under which a simulation model and its simulation environment are constructed, structured, configured, parameterized, bounded, versioned, controlled, and maintained as an identifiable execution context capable of supporting governed simulation activity.
Why This Standard Exists
A simulation can have a clearly defined object, purpose, representation of reality, and assumptions and still produce misleading results if the model or environment implementing them is incorrectly structured or configured.
SMES therefore creates a governed bridge between:
what the simulation intends to represent
and:
the executable structure through which that representation is simulated.
It makes model structure, environment configuration, parameters, boundaries, dependencies, versions, and material changes visible and governable rather than leaving them as hidden technical implementation details.
What SMES Governs

SMES governs the simulation-specific relationship between:
Simulation Model → Simulation Environment → Boundaries → Parameters → Configuration → Versions → Controlled Execution Context
It establishes whether the model and environment being used are actually the governed model and environment intended for the simulation.
This includes governance of model structure, environment configuration, boundary interactions, parameterization, model-environment compatibility, configuration control, version continuity, material changes, configuration drift, and reconstruction.
Governance Flow
Governed Reality Representation
↓
Governed Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model Structure
↓
Simulation Environment Configuration
↓
Boundary & Interaction Definition
↓
Parameterization
↓
Model–Environment Compatibility
↓
Configuration & Version Binding
↓
Controlled Simulation Execution Context
Governance Boundary
SMES begins when the governed Reality Representation and Simulation Assumptions must be converted into an executable simulation structure.
It ends when the model, environment, parameters, boundaries, configuration, and versions are sufficiently established and controlled for the next stage of the SIMULOS® lifecycle.
It does not determine whether the resulting simulation is universally valid, whether its outputs justify operational reliance, or whether the simulated environment is equivalent to actual Operational Reality.
Architectural Position

Within the 12-Parent-Standard SIMULOS® lifecycle:
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → [Simulation Model & Environment] → downstream simulation governance
SMES therefore occupies the transition between conceptual simulation design and the controlled technical structure required for simulation execution.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality; SMES governs the constructed simulation environment.
VALIDOS® governs validation questions and resulting validation claims; SMES governs how the simulation model and environment themselves are established and controlled.
INTEGROS® governs integrity as a distinct governance space; SMES does not duplicate general integrity governance.
ADIT® may provide evidence and audit governance for model, configuration, version, and change records.
Why It Matters
Two simulations can appear to test the same problem while actually using different models, environments, parameter sets, boundaries, or versions.
Without explicit governance of those differences, their outputs may appear comparable even when their underlying execution contexts are materially different.
SMES makes those differences governable and traceable.

A simulation becomes structurally governable only when the model and environment through which it operates remain identifiable, bounded, configured, parameterized, versioned, controlled, and traceably connected to the reality representation and assumptions they implement.

resources.title: OOF™ About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS)
topics: Defining What the Simulation Actually Represents

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS)
About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS)
Defining What the Simulation Actually Represents
Actually Represents
Every simulation begins with an object.
That object may be a machine, system, process, environment, behavior, population, mission, infrastructure, autonomous system, AI-enabled system, or another target intended to be represented through simulation.
Before anything can be simulated, one question must be answered:
What exactly are we simulating?
Simulation Object Standard (SOS) establishes the governance conditions required to answer that question consistently.
SOS is the first Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
It governs the Simulation Object before simulation purpose, representation, assumptions, models, scenarios, execution, outputs, or reality correlation begin.
Why SOS Exists
Simulation can produce highly precise outputs while still representing the wrong object.
This may occur when: the object is poorly defined, the wrong version is simulated, configurations are mixed, important components are excluded, system boundaries are unclear, a proxy is treated as the real target, or the object changes while the simulation continues to rely on an older definition.
SOS prevents these problems by establishing a stable object foundation for the complete simulation lifecycle.
What Is a Simulation Object?
A Simulation Object is the governed target that a simulation intends to represent.
It defines:

what belongs to the simulation target,
what remains outside it,
which version applies,
which configuration applies,
which state applies,
and:
which object the resulting simulation outputs actually concern.
A Simulation Object may be simple or highly complex.
It may represent one component or an entire system-of-systems.
The key requirement is that its identity and boundaries remain explicit.
Object Before Representation
SOS separates the real or intended simulation target from the mechanisms used to simulate it.
Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Model
Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Representation
Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Environment
The Simulation Object is what is being simulated.
The model, representation, and environment are mechanisms through which the object is later represented and examined.
This distinction prevents simulation technology from redefining the object merely because a particular model is easier to construct.
Object Identity and Boundary
A governed Simulation Object must be sufficiently distinguishable from materially different objects.
Depending on the context, this may require identification of: system identity, version, configuration, relevant components, operational state, dependencies, temporal condition, and object boundaries.
The object boundary establishes what the simulation claim can legitimately refer to.
If only part of a system is included, the resulting simulation must not be represented as though the entire system was simulated.

Versions, Configurations, and Change
Simulation relevance may depend on the exact object version and configuration.
A simulation of:
Version A
does not automatically apply to:
Version B.
A simulation of:
Configuration X
does not automatically apply to:
Configuration Y.
SOS therefore keeps simulation results connected to the object state they actually represent.
When the object materially changes, that change must remain visible to downstream SIMULOS® governance.
Complex Simulation Objects
SIMULOS® may govern simulations involving: autonomous vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft, robot fleets, AI systems, industrial facilities, digital twins, infrastructure networks, organizations, populations, environmental systems, and complete system-of-systems environments.
SOS allows complex objects to be decomposed into identifiable components while preserving their relationship to the overall Simulation Object.
This makes it possible to understand whether a simulation conclusion applies to:
a component,
a subsystem,
a complete system,
or:
an interconnected operational environment.
Preventing Object Inflation
One of the central functions of SOS is to prevent a narrow simulation from becoming a broader claim than the object definition supports.
SOS therefore protects against:
component → whole-system inflation
single-version → product-family inflation
single-configuration → all-configurations inflation
and:
proxy-object → target-object substitution

The simulation claim must remain anchored to the object actually simulated.
Governance Flow
SOS progresses through:
Candidate Simulation Target → Simulation Object Identification → Object Boundary → Object Structure → Object Version → Object Configuration → Object State → Object Documentation → Governed Simulation Object
Once the Simulation Object is sufficiently established, SIMULOS® can proceed to the next question:
Why is this object being simulated, and what must the simulation cover?
Relationship to SIMULOS®
SOS establishes the first governance foundation of the complete SIMULOS® lifecycle.
The architecture then progresses into:
Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Lifecycle & Resimulation
Every downstream stage depends upon the object established by SOS.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
SOS governs specifically the Simulation Object.
ORA™ governs operational reality.
OBIDENITY® may govern broader identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and authority.
INTEGROS® governs integrity.
VALIDOS® governs validation.
ADIT® governs continuous audit and evidence.
These architectures may interact with SOS, but they do not replace its simulation-specific function.
Why It Matters
A sophisticated simulation cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined object.

If the object is wrong, outdated, incomplete, or ambiguous, downstream simulation precision may create only precise answers about the wrong target.
SOS therefore establishes a simple but fundamental rule:
Define the object before simulating the object.
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot legitimately claim to represent an object more precisely than that object has been identified, bounded, versioned, configured, and documented.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Object Standard (SOS) establishes the object foundation of SIMULOS® by ensuring that every simulation begins with a clearly identified, bounded, versioned, configured, state-aware, and traceable Simulation Object. By separating the simulation target from its model, representation, and environment, SOS ensures that every downstream simulation activity remains connected to the exact object it claims to represent.

resources.title: OOF™ About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)
resources.parent_standard: OOF™ About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)
About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)
Simulation Results Actually Mean
A simulation may produce enormous amounts of data.
But producing an output is not the same as understanding what that output legitimately establishes.
A Simulation Output may be: direct, derived, aggregated, statistical, execution-specific, scenario-specific, or generated across millions of repeated runs.
The output may also be transformed, filtered, summarized, compared, or interpreted before someone eventually uses it to support a decision.
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) governs this transition.
Canonical Definition
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) defines the governance conditions under which outputs produced by Simulation Execution are identified, classified, bounded, interpreted, limitation-aware, documented, and connected to the execution basis that produced them so that direct Simulation Outputs remain distinguishable from derived results, aggregation, subsequent inference, and claims extending beyond the simulation itself.
Why SOGS Exists
Simulation programs often focus heavily on:
building the model
and:
running the simulation.
But a critical governance problem begins after execution:
What exactly does the result mean?
For example:
18 failures occurred in 250,000 simulation runs.
That is an output.
From that output, someone may conclude:
The system has a failure probability of 0.0072%.

That may already involve aggregation and interpretation.
Another person may then conclude:
The real system is 99.9928% reliable.
That is a much stronger claim.
These three statements are not methodologically equivalent.
SOGS exists to keep them separate.
Governed Space
Simulation Output Governance
SOGS governs Simulation Outputs after governed execution and before claims about Operational Reality, validation, or operational reliance are made.
The central question is:
What did the simulation actually produce, and how far may interpretation legitimately extend from that result?
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output
↓
Output Identification
↓
Output Classification
↓
Execution & Scenario Binding
↓
Simulation Inference
↓
Output Limitations
↓
Output Documentation
↓
Governed Simulation Output
↓
Reality Correlation Output Is Not Inference
One of the most important distinctions in SOGS is:
Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Inference
For example:
Output: The simulated spacecraft entered Safe Mode in 14 executions.
Inference: Safe Mode activation appears associated with a specific simulated power and communication condition.
The inference may be supported by the output.
But it is still an inference.
SOGS keeps that interpretive step visible.
Simulation Inference Is Not Operational Reality
An even more important boundary is:
Simulation Inference ≠ Real-World Fact
A simulation may demonstrate:
Under these modeled conditions, this behavior occurred.

That does not automatically establish:
The real system will behave the same way.
SOGS therefore prevents a direct methodological leap from:
simulated behavior
to:
Operational Reality.
That next step requires downstream Reality Correlation and, where applicable, VALIDOS®.
Direct and Derived Outputs
SOGS distinguishes between:
Direct Simulation Output
and:
Derived Simulation Output.
A Direct Output may include: state reached, event occurred, trajectory produced, action selected, temperature exceeded, collision occurred, system recovered, or failure occurred.
A Derived Output may include: average, percentile, failure rate, distribution, ranking, comparison, aggregated metric, or post-processed result.
Derived Outputs remain legitimate.
But their relationship to the original executions must remain visible.
Aggregation Must Not Hide the Story
Large simulation programs often reduce millions of executions into a small set of numbers.
For example:
Mission Success Rate: 99.98%
That figure may be useful.
But SOGS asks:
Which executions were included?
Which failed?
Which were excluded?
Which Scenario Space was represented?
Did one rare but critical failure mode disappear inside the aggregate?
Was the output produced from nominal scenarios, stress scenarios, or the complete governed Scenario Set?
This protects organizations from allowing a convenient aggregate to conceal the conditions that produced it.
Outputs Must Remain Connected to Execution

A Simulation Output should remain traceable to:
Simulation Object
↓
Model & Environment
↓
Inputs
↓
Scenario
↓
Execution
↓
Output
Without this relationship, a result may later be interpreted outside the conditions under which it was generated.
SOGS therefore works directly with the execution lineage produced under SES.
Limitations Travel With the Output
A Simulation Output may inherit limitations from: assumptions, abstraction, fidelity, Input Data, scenario coverage, execution conditions, observation limitations, repetition sufficiency, model boundaries, or unresolved uncertainty.
These limitations do not disappear when an attractive chart or precise percentage is generated.
SOGS establishes:
Output processing does not erase upstream limitations.
Precision Does Not Equal Certainty
Simulation systems can produce extremely precise numbers.
For example:
0.00481763
The numerical precision may be mathematically correct.
But the result may depend upon: uncertain inputs, incomplete scenario coverage, simplified reality representation, assumptions, or limited execution conditions.
SOGS therefore distinguishes:
Computational Precision
from:
Strength of Interpretation.
Unexpected Outputs Matter
Simulation Outputs do not always confirm what was expected.
Unexpected behavior may reveal: a new interaction, a hidden dependency, an Edge Case, a Scenario Coverage Gap, an unstable model region, an execution anomaly, or a new simulation question.

SOGS therefore does not treat unexpected outputs as disposable noise by default.
They may create a feedback path:
Unexpected Output
↓
New Question
↓
Scenario Reassessment
↓
Additional Simulation Output Classification
Classification helps downstream users understand what type of result they are seeing.
A Simulation Output may be:
Direct
Derived
Aggregated
Intermediate
Final
Deterministic
Stochastic
Execution-Specific
Repetition-Based
Scenario-Level
Campaign-Level
or another governed class.
This becomes especially important when simulation outputs move between engineering teams, management, regulators, customers, or external partners.
Output Population Matters
An output should identify what population it represents.
For example:
Failure rate = 0.2%
means little unless it is known whether that represents: one scenario, one system configuration, one environment, one Repetition Set, an entire Scenario Set, or a complete simulation campaign.
SOGS keeps that population boundary visible.
Inference Boundary
A Simulation Inference should remain bounded by the simulation conditions that support it.
If a simulation examined:
Environment A
the output should not silently become evidence about:
Environments A, B, C, and D.
If a simulation represented:
one software version
the inference should not automatically extend to:
all future versions.
If the Scenario Set covered:
normal and moderate stress conditions
the conclusion should not automatically extend to:
extreme failure conditions.

Business Value
SOGS helps organizations answer questions that often become difficult after large simulation programs produce enormous amounts of results:
Which result came from which execution?
What is direct output and what is interpretation?
Which executions contributed to this aggregate?
Which results were excluded?
What limitations remain attached?
What can legitimately be claimed?
Where does the simulation stop and a reality claim begin?
This makes SOGS useful as both:
a Simulation Output governance framework
and:
a diagnostic layer for existing simulation programs. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation OutputScenario
A space organization runs millions of simulations for autonomous spacecraft recovery.
The resulting dashboard reports:
Mission Recovery Success: 99.96%. Application
SOGS separates:
Direct Outputs — individual recovery outcomes.
Aggregated Output — 99.96% simulated recovery success.
Inference — recovery performs strongly across the simulated campaign.
The standard also preserves: which scenarios contributed, which runs failed, which executions were excluded, applicable power and communication conditions, scenario coverage limitations, and the execution lineage behind the aggregate.
Result
The organization can legitimately state what the simulation campaign demonstrated without converting:
99.96% simulated recovery success
into an unsupported claim that:

the real spacecraft has a 99.96% recovery probability. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle Safety SimulationScenario
An autonomous vehicle simulation reports:
99.99% successful collision avoidance
across a large simulation campaign. Application
SOGS examines whether the result represents: all Scenario Families, only nominal traffic, Edge Cases, degraded perception, adverse weather, combined conditions, and stress scenarios.
It also separates:
Observed Simulation Performance
from:
Inference about system safety. Result
The organization may conclude:
The system achieved 99.99% collision avoidance within the defined governed simulation population.
It may not automatically conclude:
The autonomous vehicle is 99.99% safe in Operational Reality.
That stronger claim requires downstream correlation and validation.
Relationship to SES
SES — Simulation Execution Standard governs what actually ran.
SOGS governs what those executions produced.
The handoff is:
Governed Simulation Execution Record
↓
Governed Simulation Output Relationship to SSS
SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard establishes the Scenario Space and Scenario Coverage.
SOGS ensures that output interpretation remains bounded by the scenarios actually represented.
Therefore:
Broad Output Volume ≠ Broad Scenario Meaning.
Relationship to Reality Correlation
SOGS deliberately stops before establishing whether simulated behavior corresponds to Operational Reality.
That next governance question is:

How strongly does the governed Simulation Output correlate with actual reality?
This belongs to the next SIMULOS® lifecycle space.
Relationship to VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may subsequently evaluate whether a Simulation Output, Simulation Inference, reality-correlation claim, or simulation process can support a formal validation conclusion.
SOGS prepares the Simulation Output for that downstream assessment.
Relationship to INTEGROS®
SOGS deliberately does not create a separate Simulation Output Integrity governance space.
General integrity remains governed under INTEGROS®.
SOGS focuses specifically on:
Output Identification
Output Classification
Inference
Output Limitations
and:
Output Documentation.
Architectural Position
SOGS is the ninth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The progression is:
Simulation Scenario Design
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output Governance
↓
Reality Correlation
SOGS therefore marks the transition from:
what happened inside the simulation
to:
what that result may legitimately support as an interpretation.
Why It Matters
Modern organizations increasingly have no shortage of Simulation Outputs.
They may have: millions of runs, enormous datasets, dashboards, distributions, AI-generated summaries, automated anomaly detection, and highly precise numerical results.
The real bottleneck can become:
meaning.
SOGS provides a governance layer for determining:

what the simulation actually produced, what was subsequently inferred, what remains limited, and where the claim must stop.
Foundational Principle
A Simulation Output becomes governable only when what the simulation directly produced remains distinguishable from how that output was processed, interpreted, limited, aggregated, and ultimately used to support claims beyond the execution that produced it.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) governs the transition from executed simulation to interpretable simulation result by ensuring that Simulation Outputs remain identifiable, classified, execution-bound, inference-bounded, limitation-aware, and documented. By separating direct output from derived output, aggregation from individual execution behavior, computational precision from interpretive certainty, and simulated behavior from claims about Operational Reality, SOGS enables organizations to use large and complex simulation outputs without allowing the meaning of those outputs to exceed the simulation conditions that actually produced them.
