OOF™ About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS)
About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS)
Governing Why a Simulation Exists Before Deciding How It Should Represent Reality
Simulation Exists Before Deciding How It Should Represent Reality
A simulation may be technically sophisticated and still be unsuitable for the question it is being used to answer.
Before models, environments, assumptions, scenarios, inputs, or execution methods are selected, the simulation must establish why it is being performed and what it is legitimately intended to cover.
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) provides this governance layer within SIMULOS®.
Canonical Definition
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a simulation, the questions it is intended to address, its governed scope, material inclusions and exclusions, applicability context, required simulation depth, and appropriate simulation precision are formally established before downstream simulation representation begins.
Why SPSS Exists
Organizations use simulations for different purposes: system design, engineering analysis, safety assessment, operational planning, autonomous-system testing, AI evaluation, infrastructure planning, scenario exploration, scientific investigation, training, decision support, and pre-deployment testing.
These purposes are not interchangeable.

A simulation designed to explore possible behavior may not provide sufficient basis for a safety-critical decision.
A simulation covering one operating environment cannot automatically support conclusions about another.
A simulation examining one configuration cannot silently become evidence for every configuration of the system.
SPSS prevents this purpose and scope inflation.
Governed Space
Simulation Purpose & Scope
SPSS governs the transition from:
Defined Simulation Object
to:
Governed Simulation Inquiry
It establishes what the simulation is expected to investigate before downstream simulation architecture is constructed around that objective.
Governance Flow
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Question → Simulation Scope → Inclusions & Exclusions → Applicability Context → Simulation Depth → Simulation Precision → Governed Simulation Purpose & Scope
This governed basis then becomes an input to the next SIMULOS® space:
Reality Representation
What SPSS Establishes
A governed simulation should establish:
Purpose — why the simulation is being performed.
Simulation Question — what the simulation is expected to investigate or demonstrate.
Scope — which parts of the Simulation Object, system, process, environment, behavior, or interaction are included.
Exclusions — what the simulation explicitly does not represent or evaluate.
Applicability — the environments, configurations, populations, operating conditions, or contexts to which the simulation relates.

Simulation Depth — how extensively the simulation must investigate the defined problem.
Simulation Precision — what level of representational and analytical precision is appropriate for the intended purpose.
Business Value
For organizations using simulation, SPSS creates a clear governance basis before significant resources are committed to simulation design and execution.
It helps organizations determine whether: the simulation being built actually addresses the business or engineering question, simulation expenditure is aligned with the intended decision, critical operating conditions have been excluded, simulation conclusions are being used beyond their legitimate scope, different simulation projects are addressing comparable questions, and downstream teams understand exactly what the simulation is and is not intended to establish.
This becomes increasingly important when simulation results influence investment, engineering, deployment, safety, regulatory, autonomous-system, or high-consequence operational decisions.
Governance Boundary
SPSS begins when a sufficiently identified Simulation Object requires a defined simulation purpose and governed operational scope.
It ends when the simulation purpose, questions, scope, exclusions, applicability context, required depth, and appropriate precision have been sufficiently established to support governed Reality Representation.

SPSS does not determine whether the simulation is valid, whether its evidence is sufficient for external validation, or whether operational reliance should ultimately be authorized.
Those questions belong to their appropriate downstream SIMULOS® spaces or complementary OOF® architectures.
Practical Governance Test
Before simulation development proceeds, an organization should be able to answer:
What exactly are we trying to learn, test, examine, or demonstrate through this simulation?
Which reality does that question concern?
What is inside the simulation scope?
What is explicitly outside it?
Under which conditions will the resulting simulation remain applicable?
How much simulation depth and precision does the intended purpose actually require?
If these questions cannot be answered, downstream simulation sophistication cannot compensate for the missing governance foundation.
Relationship to SIMULOS®
SPSS is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
It follows:
Simulation Object Standard
and precedes:
Reality Representation governance.
Its architectural role is fundamental:
The Simulation Object establishes what is being simulated.
SPSS establishes why it is being simulated and what the simulation is allowed to cover.
Only after both are established should the architecture begin governing how relevant reality will be represented.
Foundational Principle

A simulation cannot legitimately answer a broader question than the purpose and scope for which it was actually designed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard establishes the governed inquiry boundary of SIMULOS® by defining why a simulation is performed, what questions it is intended to address, what it includes and excludes, where its applicability begins and ends, and what level of depth and precision its purpose requires. By establishing these conditions before reality representation, model construction, scenario design, and execution, SPSS prevents simulation results from acquiring broader meaning, authority, or applicability than the simulation was actually designed to support.

OOF™ About Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
About Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
Simulation Must Actually Examine
A simulation can be technically sophisticated and still miss the conditions that matter most.
A model may be correct.
The environment may be controlled.
The input data may be suitable.
Yet the simulation may still provide weak insight if it examines only convenient, expected, or easily modeled conditions.
Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) governs this problem.
It determines how materially relevant scenarios are identified, varied, combined, stressed, bounded, prioritized, and assessed for sufficient coverage before simulation execution begins.
Canonical Definition
Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation scenarios are identified, selected, varied, stressed, combined, bounded, and assessed for sufficient coverage so that the simulation examines expected conditions, materially relevant variations, edge cases, failures, uncertainty, stresses, transitions, and plausible alternative conditions capable of affecting simulation outcomes.
Why SSS Exists
Simulation quality is not determined only by how many simulation runs are performed.

A simulation may execute thousands or millions of times while still missing: critical edge cases, combined failures, degraded operating states, rare but severe events, transition failures, uncertainty ranges, environmental extremes, dependency failures, cascading events, or combinations that were never deliberately examined.
SSS therefore separates:
Simulation Volume
from:
Scenario Coverage
More simulation does not automatically mean better examination.
Governed Space
Simulation Scenario Design
SSS governs the condition space that exists between a prepared simulation basis and actual Simulation Execution.
It asks:
What must the simulation be asked to examine before its outputs can meaningfully represent the declared simulation inquiry?
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Basis
↓
Scenario Requirements
↓
Baseline & Expected Conditions
↓
Scenario Variation
↓
Edge Cases
↓
Stress & Failure Conditions
↓
Scenario Combinations
↓
Scenario Coverage Assessment
↓
Coverage Gaps & Prioritization
↓
Governed Simulation Scenario Set
↓
Simulation Execution From Simulation Capability to Simulation Examination
Before SSS, SIMULOS® establishes whether the simulation has a governed foundation.
SSS then converts that capability into an intentional examination plan.
The distinction is important:
The fact that a model can simulate a condition does not mean that condition was actually tested.
SSS therefore makes the Scenario Set itself a governed object.
Expected Conditions Are Only the Beginning

Nominal and expected operating conditions remain necessary.
They establish: baseline behavior, routine performance, expected operating states, and controlled comparison points.
But they are not sufficient where the Simulation Purpose includes materially relevant non-nominal behavior.
SSS therefore expands scenario design beyond the expected state.
Scenario Variation
Systems operate under variation.
Inputs change.
Environments change.
People behave differently.
Resources fluctuate.
Dependencies degrade.
Autonomous systems encounter situations not present in their nominal operating assumptions.
SSS governs deliberate variation across those conditions so that simulation behavior is examined across a meaningful condition space rather than at one convenient point.
Edge Cases
Some of the most important simulation failures occur outside the center of the operating distribution.
An autonomous vehicle may perform well in ordinary traffic but fail when: visibility is partially obstructed, multiple road users interact unexpectedly, lane markings degrade, sensor confidence conflicts, or several individually manageable conditions occur together.
A spacecraft may behave correctly during nominal mission phases while a critical issue emerges only during: communication loss, degraded navigation, partial power availability, unusual thermal conditions, or a transition between mission modes.
SSS makes these conditions governable as Scenario Requirements rather than optional afterthoughts.

Stress Conditions
Stress scenarios intentionally push the simulation beyond normal conditions.
The objective is not to create arbitrary extreme tests.
The objective is to understand:
Where does behavior materially change?
Where do margins disappear?
Where do dependencies become critical?
Where does one degradation trigger another?
This is especially important for complex autonomous, aerospace, industrial, infrastructure, and mission systems.
Combined Conditions
Real failures are often not isolated.
A system may tolerate:
communication delay
and separately tolerate:
sensor degradation
while failing when:
communication delay + sensor degradation + reduced power
occur together.
SSS therefore governs materially relevant combinations rather than assuming that individual-condition testing establishes combined-condition coverage.
Transition Scenarios
Some systems are most vulnerable not in stable states but during transitions.
Examples include: launch, landing, docking, shutdown, restart, handover, human-to-autonomy control transfer, autonomy escalation, failover, recovery, or operational-mode change.
SSS explicitly recognizes transition scenarios because:
safe State A + safe State B does not automatically mean a safe transition between A and B.
Failure and Degraded-State Scenarios
A simulation should not examine only complete success and complete failure.
Many operational problems occur in degraded states where the system still functions but under reduced capability.

Examples include: partial sensing, limited communication, degraded power, reduced computation, incomplete navigation, restricted human support, partial actuator capability, or weakened infrastructure.
These conditions are particularly important for autonomous and mission-critical systems because the system may continue operating while its decision environment has materially changed.
Rare but High-Consequence Conditions
Frequency alone does not determine scenario importance.
A condition may be rare but capable of producing catastrophic consequences.
SSS therefore supports consequence-aware scenario design.
The question is not only:
How often might this happen?
It is also:
What happens if it does?
Uncertainty Must Become Scenario Coverage
Upstream SIMULOS® standards may identify uncertainty in: assumptions, inputs, environment, parameters, or representation.
SSS converts materially relevant uncertainty into scenarios where necessary.
For example:
uncertain parameter range
may require:
low / central / high conditions
rather than one point estimate.
This prevents uncertainty from being documented upstream but ignored during actual simulation.
Scenario Coverage
Scenario Coverage is one of the central outputs of SSS.
It asks whether the Scenario Set sufficiently examines the materially relevant dimensions of the simulation inquiry.

Coverage may include: nominal operation, variation, environments, populations, uncertainty, failures, transitions, stress, boundary conditions, rare events, dependencies, combinations, and recovery.
Coverage Is Not Scenario Count
Ten thousand scenarios may still provide poor coverage.
A smaller set may provide much stronger coverage if it deliberately spans the materially relevant condition space.
SSS therefore establishes:
Scenario Count ≠ Scenario Coverage
This is one of the most important practical distinctions in the standard.
Scenario Coverage Gaps
If a materially relevant condition cannot be simulated, SSS does not allow that absence to disappear.
The architecture records a:
Scenario Coverage Gap
or, where the simulation itself cannot represent the condition:
Scenario Capability Gap
This is valuable because it turns an unknown weakness into an explicit governance object.
Scenario Prioritization
For complex systems, exhaustive scenario enumeration may be impossible.
The number of possible combinations can become enormous.
SSS therefore allows governed prioritization based on: consequence, plausibility, uncertainty, system sensitivity, dependency concentration, boundary proximity, failure history, novelty, and Simulation Purpose.
The objective is not brute-force scenario generation.
It is governed selection of materially relevant scenario space.
Space and Mission Systems

Scenario governance has particularly strong application in space systems because many important conditions: cannot be reproduced economically in reality, may occur only once during a mission, are difficult or impossible to reproduce after deployment, involve interacting subsystem failures, depend upon changing environments, or occur during short but high-consequence mission phases.
A mission simulation may therefore need to examine not only:
nominal trajectory
but combinations such as:
communication degradation + navigation uncertainty + reduced power + thermal constraint during a mission transition.
SSS provides a structure through which such conditions can be identified, separated, combined, prioritized, and traced to actual simulation execution.
Autonomous Systems
Autonomous systems create a similar challenge.
Their behavior can depend upon combinations of: environment, sensor state, incomplete information, other agents, human behavior, communication, timing, uncertainty, and internal decision state.
SSS provides the scenario-governance layer through which these combinations can be deliberately examined rather than discovered only after real-world deployment.
Scenario Discovery
Simulation itself may reveal new scenarios.
An unexpected behavior may expose: a previously unknown dependency, a new failure sequence, a new interaction, or a previously unrecognized edge case.
SSS therefore treats Scenario Design as capable of evolving.
The lifecycle may become:

Scenario → Execution → Unexpected Behavior → New Scenario Requirement → Scenario Set Expansion
The original Scenario Set remains historically preserved.
No Outcome-Seeking Scenario Design
Scenario design can become biased if it focuses only on conditions likely to produce favorable outcomes.
SSS establishes a simple boundary:
Scenario design must remain capable of exposing unfavorable, contradictory, or unexpected system behavior where such behavior is materially relevant to the Simulation Purpose.
Relationship to SIDS
SIDS — Simulation Input & Data Standard establishes which information may enter the simulation.
SSS determines which combinations of those inputs, parameters, environmental states, and other conditions should actually be assembled into scenarios.
Therefore:
SIDS governs the information basis.
SSS governs the condition space examined.
Relationship to SMES
SMES — Simulation Model & Environment Standard establishes the model, environment, boundaries, parameters, and versioned simulation structure.
SSS configures that governed structure into deliberate scenario conditions.
Relationship to Simulation Assumptions
Scenario design may specifically test: assumption boundaries, uncertain assumptions, high-dependency assumptions, or conditions where assumptions may cease to remain applicable.
SSS does not govern assumptions themselves.
It determines when those assumptions should become the subject of deliberate simulated conditions.
Relationship to VALIDOS®

SSS does not determine whether scenario coverage is sufficient for a formal validation claim.
VALIDOS® may later consume scenario design, execution, and resulting evidence when evaluating validation requirements.
The boundary remains:
SSS governs what the simulation examines.
VALIDOS® governs what the resulting validation record can legitimately demonstrate.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SSS may use real operational conditions, incidents, environments, or failure states as inputs to Scenario Requirements.
But the scenario remains a simulation object.
It is not Operational Reality itself.
Relationship to ASGA™ and AIG®
ASGA™ and AIG® may identify governance conditions relevant to autonomous-system or AI behavior.
Those conditions may become Scenario Requirements when the governed system is simulated.
For example:
autonomous escalation condition
may become:
simulation scenario requirement
without transferring autonomous-system governance into SSS.
Architectural Position
SSS is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The progression is:
Simulation Object
↓
Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model & Environment
↓
Simulation Inputs & Data
↓
Simulation Scenario Design
↓
Simulation Execution
SSS therefore marks the transition from:
a simulation that is prepared
to:
a simulation that knows what it must actually examine.
Why It Matters

A simulation program can invest heavily in: better models, larger computing infrastructure, more data, higher fidelity, faster execution, and more simulation runs
while still leaving the most important conditions unexamined.
SSS provides a governance structure for identifying that gap.
That makes the standard useful not only for designing simulations but also for diagnosing existing simulation programs.
An organization may discover that its key bottleneck is not:
simulation capability
but:
scenario selection and scenario coverage.
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot claim meaningful coverage merely because it executes successfully; it must deliberately examine the materially relevant conditions, variations, boundaries, uncertainties, failures, stresses, interactions, and alternatives capable of changing the behavior or conclusions of the simulation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) governs the condition space that a simulation must deliberately examine before execution can meaningfully support broader interpretation. By separating simulation volume from scenario coverage and governing expected conditions, variations, edge cases, boundaries, failures, degraded states, transitions, uncertainty, stress, combinations, prioritization, coverage gaps, scenario discovery, and scenario-to-execution traceability, SSS establishes a technology-neutral methodology for ensuring that simulation capability is converted into deliberate examination of the conditions most capable of changing system behavior or simulation conclusions.

OOF™ About SIMULOS®
About SIMULOS®
Simulation Governance Architecture
Reality is increasingly simulated before it is entered.
Systems are tested before they are built.
Autonomous systems are exposed to conditions before they encounter them.
Missions are evaluated before they are launched.
Infrastructure is stressed before it fails.
Future conditions are explored before they exist.
Simulation is becoming part of how organizations understand, design, test, compare, prepare, validate, and make decisions about reality.
SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture was created to provide a stable governance architecture for this expanding simulation domain.
SIMULOS® does not define simulation software, numerical solvers, physics engines, digital-twin platforms, modeling languages, computing infrastructure, or implementation technologies.
SIMULOS® governs simulation. Why SIMULOS® Exists
Simulation can generate enormous amounts of information.
But the existence of simulation does not itself answer fundamental governance questions:
What exactly is being simulated?
Why is it being simulated?
Which parts of reality are represented?
Which assumptions make that representation possible?
Which models, environments, inputs, and scenarios define the simulation?
How was the simulation executed?
What do its outputs actually mean?
How closely do those outputs correspond to reality?
What may simulation-derived evidence legitimately support?
When does changing reality require resimulation?

SIMULOS® addresses these questions by defining the governable spaces that exist throughout the complete simulation lifecycle.
Rather than standardizing one simulation technology, SIMULOS® standardizes the governance conditions under which simulation can be identified, scoped, represented, executed, interpreted, correlated with reality, converted into bounded evidence, relied upon, monitored, and resimulated. Simulation Before Reliance
The objective of SIMULOS® is not to prescribe how a simulation must be technically built.
The objective is to define how simulation must remain governable.
Every simulation has an object.
Every Simulation Object requires a purpose and scope.
Every scope determines what reality must be represented.
Every representation depends upon explicit or implicit assumptions.
Every simulation requires a model and environment.
Every model operates upon inputs and data.
Every meaningful simulation requires relevant scenarios.
Every scenario must be executed under governed conditions.
Every execution produces outputs.
Every output requires interpretation before broader meaning can be attributed to it.
Claims about reality require a governed simulation-to-reality relationship.
Simulation-derived evidence requires qualification before reliance.
Continuing reliance requires lifecycle monitoring and, where material change occurs, resimulation.
SIMULOS® therefore treats simulation as an independent governance domain. The Simulation Governance Architecture

SIMULOS® consists of twelve independent simulation governance spaces.
Each space answers one architectural question.
Each space governs one distinct part of the simulation lifecycle.
Each space has a defined beginning, operational purpose, and governance boundary.
Each space begins where the preceding simulation governance requirement has been sufficiently established.
Together, these spaces form the complete Simulation Governance Architecture.
The architecture progresses through:
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Simulation Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation
This progression represents the governance journey from identifying what is being simulated to determining whether simulation-derived evidence remains legitimate enough to support continuing reliance as reality changes . Simulation Spaces Rather Than Technical Components
SIMULOS® does not organize simulation governance around software packages, simulation engines, computing architectures, vendors, departments, or technical components.
Instead, it organizes governance around distinct simulation governance spaces.
Each space represents an independent governance responsibility that exists regardless of the simulation technology used.

A digital twin, autonomous-driving simulator, spacecraft mission simulator, engineering model, scientific simulation, physical test simulation, AI training environment, or future simulation technology may be technically very different.
Yet each may still require governance of:
object → purpose → representation → assumptions → model → inputs → scenarios → execution → outputs → reality correlation → evidence → lifecycle.
Because these spaces are technology-neutral, SIMULOS® can remain applicable while simulation technologies continue to evolve. A Methodology Rather Than an Implementation
SIMULOS® is a governance methodology.
It is not a simulation implementation framework.
The architecture defines which simulation governance conditions must exist, how they relate to one another, where their boundaries lie, and what must remain explicit before simulation results acquire broader meaning or reliance.
Organizations remain free to select their own: simulation platforms, modeling methods, numerical methods, physics engines, digital-twin technologies, AI models, computing infrastructure, scenario-generation systems, verification tools, data systems, engineering processes.
SIMULOS® governs the methodological structure surrounding those implementations rather than replacing them.
This separation allows the architecture to remain stable while simulation technology changes. From Simulation Object to Governed Evidence
Simulation cannot be governed as a single computational event.

Before a simulation can be scoped, the Simulation Object must be identified.
Before reality can be represented, the purpose and scope must be known.
Before models can legitimately represent reality, assumptions and representation boundaries must be explicit.
Before execution, models, environments, inputs, data, and scenarios must be sufficiently governed.
Before outputs can become evidence, their meaning must be established.
Before simulation-derived evidence can support broader claims, the relationship between simulation and reality must be understood.
Before evidence can support reliance, its qualification, weight, applicability, uncertainty, and limitations must be bounded.
And before historical simulation evidence can continue to be relied upon, the simulation basis must remain relevant as reality changes.
SIMULOS® transforms these dependencies into a structured and navigable simulation governance lifecycle. Simulation Is Not Reality
One of the most important distinctions within SIMULOS® is:
Simulation ≠ Reality
A simulation may reproduce aspects of reality with extraordinary precision.
It may execute billions of scenarios.
It may demonstrate behavior that appears stable across enormous parameter spaces.
It may correlate strongly with observed reality.
None of these facts alone makes the simulation equivalent to reality.
SIMULOS® therefore preserves the distinction between:
Represented Reality
and
Operational Reality.

This distinction enables simulation to be used powerfully without allowing computational representation to acquire greater authority than its governed basis can support. Simulation Output Is Not Automatically Evidence
SIMULOS® also establishes another fundamental distinction:
Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence
A simulation engine may produce millions or billions of outputs.
Those outputs do not automatically become evidence merely because they were computationally generated.
Simulation-derived information must first acquire a defined evidential purpose, remain traceable to its simulation basis, and retain the assumptions, scenarios, conditions, correlations, uncertainties, and limitations that determine its legitimate meaning.
Only then can simulation-derived information enter governed evidential reliance.
This creates a methodological boundary between:
what a simulation produced
and
what an organization may legitimately conclude from what the simulation produced. Simulation Evidence Is Not Validation
SIMULOS® deliberately separates simulation evidence governance from broader validation governance.
SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean.
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture determines whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient to support a Validation Determination and intended reliance.
This distinction prevents simulation success from automatically becoming a claim of real-world validity.

A simulation may provide strong evidence.
It may provide decisive evidence for a narrowly defined question.
It may substantially reduce uncertainty.
But simulation-derived evidence remains one governed evidential source whose broader validation significance must be determined within the appropriate validation architecture. The Simulation-to-Reality Boundary
The transition from simulation to reality is one of the most consequential points in the architecture.
A simulated autonomous vehicle may perform successfully across millions of scenarios.
A simulated spacecraft may survive thousands of modeled failure conditions.
A digital twin may reproduce observed industrial behavior with high accuracy.
A scientific model may repeatedly predict known outcomes.
These results matter.
But the governance question is not simply:
Did the simulation succeed?
The stronger question is:
What relationship has actually been established between the simulated result and the reality to which that result is being applied?
SIMULOS® therefore treats Simulation-to-Reality Correlation as an independent governable space rather than assuming that simulation performance automatically transfers into operational reality. Lifecycle Governance and Resimulation
Simulation does not end when execution stops.
Reality changes.
Simulation Objects change.
Models change.
Inputs change.
Assumptions become obsolete.
Operating environments evolve.
New evidence appears.
Previously unknown scenarios become relevant.

A simulation that legitimately supported a conclusion yesterday may no longer provide the same evidential basis tomorrow.
SIMULOS® therefore extends governance beyond execution and evidence into Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation.
Where material change affects the simulation basis, the architecture supports governed re-entry into the earliest materially affected simulation space.
The result is not uncontrolled repetition of the complete lifecycle.
It is targeted governed resimulation. Who May Benefit
SIMULOS® may support: AI developers and operators, autonomous-system developers, robotics organizations, digital-twin environments, engineering organizations, scientific institutions, research laboratories, aerospace and space organizations, automotive and transportation organizations, healthcare and medical simulation environments, financial and economic modeling environments, industrial operators, infrastructure planners, safety and reliability teams, public institutions, regulators, assurance and validation organizations, critical infrastructure providers, organizations using simulation to support material decisions.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
SIMULOS® governs simulation.
It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures.
GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance structure, authority, scope, delegation, accountability, continuity, and interoperability.

ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs Operational Reality and provides the methodological distinction between what actually exists or occurs and what is represented through simulation.
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs Validation Objects, validation purpose and scope, criteria, methods, evidence fitness, source reliability, execution, determination, Validation States, reliance, and revalidation.
INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across the complete integrity lifecycle.
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin, identity, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability.
AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability, responsibility, attribution, delegation, and accountable relationships.
AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs AI behavior.
ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous systems, autonomous agents, autonomous authority, constraints, execution, and operational autonomy.
CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture governs cognition, reasoning, interpretation, and cognitive integrity.
MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture governs memory, memory continuity, and memory integrity.
ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture governs continuous auditability and evidential observation across operational lifecycles.

Together, these architectures allow simulation to interact with operational reality, validation, integrity, accountability, AI, autonomy, cognition, memory, and auditability without collapsing those independent governance domains into one architecture. Use Case 1 — Autonomous System Before Real-World Deployment
An organization develops an autonomous robot intended to operate in complex physical environments.
Before deployment, the robot is exposed to millions of simulated scenarios involving obstacles, people, environmental variation, sensor degradation, unusual events, system failures, and behavioral edge cases.
A conventional analysis may report:
99.97% simulation success.
SIMULOS® asks a much larger set of questions.
What robot configuration was actually simulated?
Which operational reality was represented?
Which physical effects were simplified?
Which assumptions were required?
Were the inputs representative?
Which scenarios were absent?
Were repeated executions genuinely diverse?
What did the outputs actually demonstrate?
How strongly did simulated behavior correlate with physical tests?
What proposition can the resulting evidence legitimately support?
Where does reliance upon that evidence stop?
The result may be that simulation provides substantial evidence for performance across the represented scenario space while still requiring physical evidence before unrestricted operational deployment.
SIMULOS® does not make simulation less useful.

Simulation is moving from a specialized engineering technique toward a foundational infrastructure for understanding and acting upon reality.
AI systems may learn inside simulated worlds.
Autonomous systems may experience millions of synthetic situations before encountering physical ones.
Digital twins may continuously mirror infrastructure, factories, cities, biological systems, economies, and operational environments.
Scientific simulations may explore conditions humans cannot directly observe.
Organizations may increasingly make consequential decisions about real systems based upon events that occurred only inside simulated environments.
As this transition accelerates, the central question will no longer be only whether organizations can build more powerful simulations.
It will also be:
How can society know what those simulations legitimately mean?
The long-term objective of SIMULOS® is to provide a common simulation governance language through which organizations can identify, structure, compare, govern, evaluate, rely upon, monitor, and resimulate representations of reality without confusing simulation capability with reality itself.
SIMULOS® is intended to make simulation governable before execution, during execution, after execution, at the boundary with reality, at the boundary with evidence, and throughout continuing reliance. Canonical Principle

Simulation technologies, models, environments, computational capabilities, and represented realities will continue to change. Simulation governance must remain stable. SIMULOS® therefore governs the methodological conditions that determine what is being simulated, why it is being simulated, how reality is represented, what simulation results legitimately mean, how those results relate to reality, how far simulation-derived evidence may be relied upon, and when material change requires governed resimulation. Canonical Closing Statement

SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture provides the governance foundation through which simulation can be formally identified, purpose-bounded, reality-represented, assumption-governed, model-structured, input-controlled, scenario-designed, execution-governed, output-interpreted, reality-correlated, evidentially bounded, and continuously maintained through lifecycle governance and resimulation. By defining the independent governable spaces of the complete simulation lifecycle, SIMULOS® establishes a technology-neutral methodology for ensuring that simulation-derived knowledge remains traceable to the object, purpose, representation, assumptions, models, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, uncertainties, limitations, and changing reality from which its legitimate meaning originates. SIMULOS® therefore enables simulation to become more powerful without allowing computational representation to become indistinguishable from Operational Reality, and provides the methodological infrastructure required for simulation-derived evidence to support engineering, science, AI, autonomy, safety, validation, mission planning, critical infrastructure, and future operational environments with explicitly governed meaning and reliance.

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS)
About Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS)
Architecture: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Standard Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary ------------------------------ Understanding the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard
Real-world and digital activity rarely arrives as perfectly separated events.
A commercial transaction may contain multiple operational steps. A digital service may involve several systems, settlements, infrastructure operations, and machine-generated actions. An autonomous process may execute hundreds or thousands of technical operations while contributing to only one or several meaningful governed events.
Before such activity can progress through tax-relevant event governance, the system must establish where one governed event ends, what belongs within it, what remains outside it, and where separation from surrounding activity is required.
The Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) establishes the governance layer for making that distinction.
TREBS does not determine whether the event is taxable.
It determines the legitimate structural extent of the governed event that may later be evaluated by taxation systems. ------------------------------ What Is the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard?
TREBS is the fourth Parent Standard within TREGA™.

It receives a sufficiently formed event from the Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) and governs the establishment of its structural boundary.
Its purpose is to prevent operational systems, transaction identifiers, database structures, platform conventions, machine processes, or technical workflows from automatically defining what constitutes the governed extent of an event.
TREBS therefore addresses a fundamental question:
What actually belongs to this governed event, and what does not?
This distinction becomes increasingly important when economic activity spans multiple organizations, platforms, systems, jurisdictions, digital environments, autonomous agents, or machine operations. ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard governs how a sufficiently formed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is bounded as a distinct governed event by establishing its legitimate structural extent, including what belongs within the event, what remains outside it, and where separation from adjacent or overlapping activity is required.
TREBS preserves the distinction between Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Event Determination, and jurisdiction-specific taxation.
Event Formation ≠ Event Boundary.

A structurally formed event does not automatically possess a legitimate final boundary. ------------------------------ Why TREBS Exists
Operational reality does not naturally divide itself according to database rows, invoice numbers, transaction IDs, API calls, machine instructions, accounting records, or tax categories.
The same underlying activity may appear differently across different systems.
A marketplace may organize activity around an order.
A payment provider may organize it around settlements.
A logistics system may organize it around shipments.
An ERP system may organize it around invoices.
An autonomous system may organize it around objectives, tasks, executions, or machine actions.
None of those representations should automatically determine the governed Event Boundary.
Without explicit Event Boundary governance, the same operational reality can be artificially aggregated into one oversized event or fragmented into numerous artificial events.
TREBS provides the methodology for preventing both conditions. ------------------------------ TREGA™ Architecture Governance Flow
TREGA™ governs the Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle through twelve sequential Parent Standards.
1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard Event Context
↓
2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard Event Recognition
↓
3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard Event Formation & Root Association
↓
↓
4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard ←Event Boundary — CURRENT STANDARD
↓

5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard Event Timing
↓
6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard Event Location
↓
7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Event Participation
↓
8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Event-to-Value Association
↓
9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Event Relationships
↓
10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Governed Event Determination
↓
11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
↓
12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Event Lifecycle & Continuity
↓
Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event
↓
Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine
↓
Tax Determination
↓
Reporting / Compliance TREBS Position
Event Formation
↓
EVENT BOUNDARY
↓
Event Timing
TREBS therefore occupies the governance layer immediately after an event has been structurally formed and before its governed temporal position is established. ------------------------------ What TREBS Governs
TREBS governs the structural extent of a formed event.

This includes governance of: Event Boundary identification Event Boundary scope inclusion within the governed event exclusion from the governed event separation from adjacent activity separation of potentially independent event structures overlapping boundary conditions boundary ambiguity boundary revision prevention of artificial event aggregation prevention of artificial event fragmentation traceability of boundary decisions
The result is a Governed Bounded Event capable of progressing into Event Timing governance. ------------------------------ What TREBS Does Not Determine
TREBS does not determine: whether the event is legally taxable which jurisdiction may tax the event when a legal tax point occurs the applicable tax period who is legally the taxpayer the applicable tax base tax rate exemptions or deductions reporting obligations payment obligations tax liability enforcement consequences
It also does not replace the responsibilities of later TREGA™ Parent Standards.
TREBS establishes the event boundary.
It does not determine the legal tax consequence of that boundary. ------------------------------ Why the Distinction Matters
A boundary is a representation of the governed event.
It is not a tax conclusion.
For example, an activity may span Switzerland, Germany, and France and still require one coherent governed event representation.

Conversely, a single commercial contract or platform order may contain several operationally distinct events that should not automatically be collapsed into one governed event.
TREBS must therefore establish the event structure independently of the tax interpretation subsequently applied.
This supports the broader TREGA™ principle:
One Event
↓
One Governed Event Layer
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
The governed event should remain stable even when different jurisdictions interpret its tax consequences differently. ------------------------------ Event Inclusion and Exclusion
A boundary becomes meaningful only when the system can distinguish between what belongs to the event and what does not.
TREBS therefore requires a governed basis for inclusion and exclusion.
An operational action should not become part of an event merely because it: occurred in the same system shares a transaction identifier belongs to the same customer account occurred within the same workflow was executed by the same machine belongs to the same commercial contract occurred within the same accounting period
Each relationship must be evaluated according to the governed structure of the event.
Technical Association ≠ Event Membership. ------------------------------ Event Separation
TREBS also governs when activity must remain structurally separated.
Two occurrences may be closely connected while still representing distinct governed events.

Separation may become necessary where independent operational structures, materially different purposes, distinct formation structures, or other governed characteristics demonstrate that treating the activity as one event would distort operational reality.
TREBS therefore protects against artificial aggregation.
At the same time, it protects against the opposite problem: artificial fragmentation.
Multiple technical operations do not automatically represent multiple governed events. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision
Event boundaries may require reconsideration when materially relevant information becomes available.
TREBS allows a governed boundary to be revised while preserving the historical traceability of the previous boundary state.
A revision must not silently rewrite the historical event representation.
Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure.
Where new information demonstrates that the original boundary was incomplete, excessive, or structurally incorrect, the boundary may be reconsidered through governed revision.
Whether the change instead requires formation of a new event remains subject to the wider TREGA™ lifecycle. ------------------------------ Machine and Autonomous Activity
TREBS is actor-neutral.
Its governance applies whether the underlying activity was produced by: a human an organization a software platform an API an AI agent an autonomous system a robot a machine network a distributed digital system

Machine activity creates a particularly important boundary problem because one economically meaningful activity may generate thousands or millions of technical operations.
Those operations must not automatically become thousands or millions of governed tax-relevant events.
Likewise, a single autonomous objective must not automatically collapse all resulting activity into one event.
TREBS provides the boundary governance necessary between these extremes. ------------------------------
Architectural Position
TREBS receives its principal upstream governed object from:
TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard
Input:
Governed Formed Event
TREBS governs:
Event Boundary
Output:
Governed Bounded Event
The output progresses to:
TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard
Therefore:
Governed Formed Event
↓
TREBS
↓
Governed Bounded Event
↓
TRETS
TREBS does not reopen Event Recognition or reconstruct Event Formation unless a legitimate governance issue requires upstream reconsideration.
It also does not prematurely perform the responsibilities of Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Event Record Governance, or Event Lifecycle & Continuity. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Global Digital Marketplace Activity
A customer places one order through a global marketplace.

The order produces: three shipments two payment settlements one partial refund multiple platform fees logistics operations payment-provider records merchant records marketplace records automated accounting entries
Different systems represent the activity differently.
Using the order ID as the Event Boundary could incorrectly aggregate activity that should remain structurally distinguishable.
Using every settlement, shipment, or system record as a separate event could create the opposite problem and fragment one coherent activity into artificial events.
TREBS establishes the governed boundary independently of those technical representations.
The resulting event structure can then progress into timing, location, participation, value association, relationship, and determination governance.
The system identifier does not decide the Event Boundary. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Production Network
An autonomous manufacturing environment receives a production objective.
AI-controlled systems coordinate material movement, robotic welding, quality checks, machine scheduling, energy allocation, inventory movements, logistics preparation, and automated settlement.
Thousands of machine actions may occur.
Treating every machine action as an independent tax-relevant event would create extreme artificial fragmentation.
Treating the entire autonomous production objective as one event could hide materially distinct operational events.

TREBS establishes governed boundaries between the relevant event structures without determining their tax consequences.
Those bounded events can subsequently be evaluated by different jurisdictions or tax systems without requiring the underlying operational reality to be reconstructed.
Machine topology does not define the governed Event Boundary. ------------------------------
Canonical Closing Statement
The Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard establishes the governed structural perimeter of a formed event before timing, location, participation, value association, relationships, determination, and jurisdiction-specific taxation are applied.
It prevents databases, transaction identifiers, commercial labels, workflows, platform structures, autonomous objectives, and machine operations from becoming accidental substitutes for governed Event Boundaries.
TREBS governs where the event begins and ends as a governed structure — not what tax law ultimately decides that event means.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

chunks.text:
OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard - (TRECS)
About Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard - (TRECS)
Context Before the Tax-Relevant Event
An observed occurrence does not become meaningful merely because a transaction record, machine signal, payment instruction, asset movement, platform interaction, autonomous action, or digital operation exists.
Governance first requires an understanding of the environment within which that occurrence took place.
The same technical action may represent materially different economic or operational realities depending on the surrounding organizational, transactional, technological, digital, infrastructural, value-related, or autonomous context.
Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) establishes the governed contextual layer required before an occurrence can legitimately proceed through the TREGA™ event lifecycle.
It ensures that downstream event governance begins from a sufficiently structured representation of the surrounding reality rather than from an isolated data point. What Is Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard?
Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) is the first Parent Standard of TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™.
It establishes the governance conditions required to identify, scope, relate, maintain, and revise the materially relevant context surrounding an observed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence.

TRECS creates the contextual basis upon which the next TREGA™ stage — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition — can operate.
It does not determine whether the occurrence is legally taxable.
It does not determine tax jurisdiction, tax nexus, taxpayer status, tax base, tax liability, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
Its role is more fundamental:
TRECS governs the environment necessary to understand an occurrence before TREGA™ determines what governed event, if any, that occurrence becomes.
Canonical Definition
Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) defines the governance conditions required to establish and maintain the economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, and value-related context materially relevant to an observed occurrence entering tax-relevant event governance, while preserving the distinction between contextual understanding, event recognition, event formation, and jurisdiction-specific taxation determination.
Why TRECS Exists
Operational and digital systems continuously produce enormous numbers of records.
A payment exists.
A machine executes an instruction.
A digital platform moves an asset.
An autonomous agent purchases a service.
A product crosses an infrastructure boundary.
An API triggers an economic action.
A distributed system creates multiple technical records around one economic activity.

None of these observations necessarily explains, by itself, what actually occurred in a form suitable for tax-event governance.
A record may show that something happened without establishing the context necessary to understand what that occurrence represented.
Without governed context, downstream systems may incorrectly: treat technical operations as independent economic events; combine unrelated actions into one event; interpret machine activity without understanding the underlying operational process; rely on current organizational conditions to reconstruct historical activity; infer jurisdiction from location information prematurely; confuse a transactional environment with legal taxability; interpret value-related signals without understanding their governed value context; process incomplete or ambiguous records as if their meaning were certain.
TRECS exists to prevent these failures at the first stage of the architecture.
It establishes the contextual foundation before recognition, formation, boundary determination, timing, location, participation, value association, event relationships, event determination, and canonical recording take place.
What TRECS Governs

TRECS governs the contextual representation surrounding an occurrence, including where materially relevant: economic context; operational context; organizational context; transactional context; commercial context; digital context; technological context; platform context; system context; infrastructural context; autonomous-system context; machine-generated context; value-related context; process context; business-model context; distributed operational context; contextual dependencies and relationships; contextual scope; contextual relevance; contextual uncertainty; contextual change; contextual continuity; historical context; multi-context occurrences.
The Standard does not require every surrounding fact to be collected.
It requires the materially relevant contextual conditions necessary for legitimate downstream event governance to be sufficiently governed.
This distinction is essential.
More information does not automatically produce better governance.
The objective is not unlimited context.
The objective is sufficient, relevant, structured, and maintainable context.
What TRECS Does Not Determine

TRECS deliberately does not determine: whether an occurrence is ultimately recognized as a candidate Tax-Relevant Event; how an event is formally assembled; where the final Event Boundary lies; the legal tax point; tax jurisdiction; tax nexus; taxpayer status; legal taxability; taxable value; tax base; applicable tax rate; exemption or deduction eligibility; tax liability; reporting or filing obligations; tax payment; enforcement.
This separation protects the central architecture principle:
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
TRECS may establish that an occurrence took place within a particular economic, digital, operational, organizational, or cross-border environment.
It may not transform those contextual facts directly into a legal taxation conclusion.
Why the Distinction Matters
The distinction between Event Context and Tax Determination becomes increasingly important as economic activity becomes distributed across systems, platforms, infrastructures, organizations, machines, and jurisdictions.
A conventional transaction may already involve several technical and organizational layers.
An autonomous or machine-generated transaction may involve many more.
For example, one economic activity may involve:
an AI agent
↓
a digital platform
↓
an API
↓
a payment infrastructure
↓
a cloud service
↓
a physical service provider
↓
multiple geographic locations.
Each layer may produce its own records.

Those records do not necessarily represent separate economic events.
Nor does the physical or digital location of one technical component automatically establish taxation rights.
TRECS provides the methodological contextual layer required to preserve these distinctions before downstream tax rules are applied.
This allows operational reality to remain governed independently from the jurisdiction-specific interpretation subsequently imposed upon it.
Context Before Recognition
Within TREGA™, context must precede formal Event Recognition.
The sequence begins:
Real-World / Digital Occurrence
↓
Event Context
↓
Event Recognition
TRECS answers:
What surrounding environment is necessary to understand this occurrence?
The next Parent Standard, TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard, answers a different question:
Is this occurrence sufficiently established as a candidate Tax-Relevant Event?
This separation prevents TREGA™ from treating contextual relevance itself as proof that a tax-relevant event exists.
Therefore:
Context-Ready ≠ Event-Recognized. Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary
TRECS also preserves an important distinction between the contextual environment surrounding an occurrence and the governed event itself.
The context may be wider than the eventual event.
A supply-chain event, for example, may require knowledge of a larger operational process even though only part of that process belongs to the eventual governed event.
TRECS therefore governs:

what surrounding information is materially relevant to understanding the occurrence.
TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard later governs:
what actually belongs inside the governed event.
Therefore:
Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary.
Cross-Border and Multi-System Relevance
TRECS is designed to operate across heterogeneous environments.
A single occurrence may simultaneously exist within: a physical operational context; a digital platform context; an organizational context; a contractual context; an economic context; a machine-execution context; a distributed infrastructure context; a cross-border context.
TRECS permits those contexts to coexist without forcing the occurrence into one artificial representation.
This is particularly important for modern tax infrastructure because:
Multiple Contexts ≠ Multiple Events.
A single governed occurrence may later support one event, several events, or no tax-relevant event at all.
That determination belongs to subsequent TREGA™ governance.
Machine and Autonomous Economy Relevance
TRECS does not assume that economic activity originates exclusively from human action.
Context may be required for occurrences generated by: autonomous agents; AI systems; machine-to-machine transactions; robots; automated marketplaces; software services; algorithmic execution; autonomous infrastructure; distributed systems.
A machine-generated action may be technically clear while remaining economically ambiguous.

TRECS provides the contextual governance necessary to understand where that action sits within the surrounding operation before TREGA™ evaluates it further.
The Standard therefore supports future taxation infrastructures without embedding assumptions about whether the underlying actor is human, corporate, digital, or autonomous.
Architectural Position
Within TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™, TRECS is the first Parent Standard in the governance flow:
Event Context
↓
Event Recognition
↓
Event Formation
↓
Event Boundary
↓
Event Timing
↓
Event Location
↓
Event Participation
↓
Value Association
↓
Event Relationships
↓
Event Determination
↓
Governed Event Record
↓
Event Lifecycle & Continuity
TRECS establishes the first governed interpretation layer between an observed occurrence and the remaining tax-relevant event lifecycle.
Its output is not a tax decision.
Its output is a sufficiently governed contextual foundation from which legitimate event governance can proceed. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Cross-Border Service Execution
An autonomous software agent purchases and activates a digital service through a platform.
The agent operates from infrastructure distributed across several countries, payment is executed through another jurisdiction, the service provider is established elsewhere, and several APIs generate separate technical records.

TRECS governs the relevant operational, digital, platform, organizational, machine-execution, and cross-border context surrounding the occurrence.
It does not determine which country has taxation rights or whether the activity is legally taxable.
The governed context can subsequently proceed through TREGA™ and may later be presented to multiple jurisdiction-specific taxation systems. Use Case 2 — Industrial Transaction Across Integrated Systems
A manufacturer produces, transfers, stores, and delivers an industrial component through an integrated ERP, warehouse, logistics, and automated production environment.
Each system generates multiple operational records.
A technical transfer between systems may not represent a separate economic transaction, while a later physical delivery may form part of a materially different governed event.
TRECS establishes the relevant production, organizational, transactional, logistics, system, and economic context so that subsequent TREGA™ standards can distinguish the surrounding operational reality from the event structures that ultimately require taxation evaluation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard establishes the foundational contextual governance layer of TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ by ensuring that real-world, digital, economic, transactional, machine-generated, and autonomous occurrences enter tax-relevant event governance within a sufficiently identified, scoped, related, and maintainable representation of their surrounding reality. By separating contextual understanding from Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, tax jurisdiction, legal taxability, and downstream tax determination, TRECS prevents isolated technical records, incomplete operational information, cross-border complexity, machine activity, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules from prematurely defining what an occurrence means. The Standard therefore provides the governed contextual foundation upon which the entire TREGA™ lifecycle can operate while preserving the core principle that TREGA™ governs the event and the jurisdiction governs the tax.

resources.title: OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard - (TREDS)
