Canonical Definition
Group Memory Integrity Standard (GMIS) defines the structural conditions
under which memory shared by a group remains coherent, continuous, reconstructable,
accountable, retrievable, governable, and operationally valid throughout collaboration,
communication, decision-making, coordination, and collective activity processes.
GMIS governs group memory.
The standard establishes the integrity conditions required for preserving shared memory

across teams, organizations, Human-AI groups, agent collectives, operational units,
and collaborative environments.
Group memory is not merely the sum of individual memories.
Group memory is the shared memory layer that enables collective continuity.
GMIS governs the integrity of that shared layer.
A. Standard Abstract
Groups depend on memory.
Teams depend on memory.
Organizations depend on memory.
Human-AI groups depend on memory.
Agent collectives depend on memory.
Without shared memory:
coordination deteriorates
decisions repeat
knowledge fragments
context disappears
collaboration weakens
continuity collapses
As collective intelligence systems become more common, shared memory becomes a critical governance space.
GMIS exists to govern that space.
B. Core Principle
Group memory becomes valid only when shared memory remains coherent,
continuous, reconstructable, accountable, retrievable, and operationally valid
throughout collective activity.
C. Scope
This standard may apply to:
teams
organizations
Human-AI groups
multi-agent environments
operational units
project groups
collaborative platforms
future collective intelligence systems
GMIS applies wherever memory is shared between multiple participants.
D. Why This Standard Exists
Individual memory is not sufficient for collective operation.
Groups require:
shared context
shared history
shared understanding
shared knowledge
shared continuity
Without governance:
group knowledge fragments
context diverges
coordination fails

collective memory drifts
accountability becomes unclear
GMIS exists because shared memory itself has become a governable space.
E. Group Memory Integrity Logic
Group memory integrity exists only when the following remain
materially preservable:
1. Shared Memory Integrity: Shared memory remains accessible and coherent across participants.
2. Group Memory Coordination Integrity: Memory remains synchronized throughout collaborative environments.
3. Collective Recall Integrity: Groups remain capable of reconstructing relevant shared history.
4. Group Context Integrity: Shared context remains aligned and operationally valid.
5. Group Memory Accountability Integrity: Collective memory utilization remains accountable and reviewable.
F. Operational Architecture Space
GMIS defines the operational architecture space for:
shared memory governance
collective memory continuity
group knowledge preservation
collaborative memory systems
shared context governance
collective recall
coordination memory
group accountability
This space exists because collective operation depends on shared memory continuity.
GMIS governs whether that continuity remains valid.
G. Difference Between Individual Memory and Group Memory
Individual memory belongs to an individual.
Group memory belongs to a collective environment.
Group memory emerges through shared interaction, shared context, shared knowledge,
and collective continuity.
GMIS governs this collective memory layer.
H. Runtime Position

GMIS operates above individual memory environments.
It governs memory shared between multiple participants.
GMIS supports:
CCIS
MCIS
HAICS
Organizational intelligence systems
Collective decision environments
I. Group Memory Failure Rule
Group memory failure occurs when shared memory can no longer support
collective continuity.
Examples include:
knowledge fragmentation
context divergence
coordination breakdown
memory inconsistency
collective recall failure
accountability loss
GMIS exists to expose and govern these conditions.
J. Validity Logic
A group memory environment is valid under GMIS when:
shared memory remains coherent
group context remains aligned
collective recall remains possible
coordination remains supported
accountability remains visible
continuity remains preservable
A group memory environment becomes invalid when:
memory fragments
context diverges
shared history becomes unreconstructable
accountability disappears
K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards
GMIS derives from:
Memory Integrity Standard (MIS)
and directly supports:
Collective Cognition Integrity Standard (CCIS)
Multi-Agent Cognition Integrity Standard (MCIS)
Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS)
GMIS governs shared memory.
CCIS and MCIS govern cognition built upon that shared memory.
L. Foundational Principle
Collective intelligence depends on collective memory. Without trustworthy group memory,
collective cognition loses continuity, coordination, and operational reliability.

Canonical Closing Statement
Group Memory Integrity Standard (GMIS) defines the structural conditions
under which memory shared by a group remains coherent, continuous, reconstructable,
accountable, retrievable, governable, and operationally valid throughout collaboration,

Collective continuity depends on shared memory continuity. Group memory integrity
therefore becomes a foundational condition of trustworthy collaboration, coordination,

Methodology Sovereignty™
Methodology Sovereignty™
OOF® — Governance Infrastructure Principle
Data Sovereignty Is Not Enough
Modern organisations increasingly depend on external technology platforms to integrate data, automate operations, support decisions and coordinate complex systems.
Protecting control over organisational data is therefore essential.
But data sovereignty alone does not guarantee operational independence.
An organisation may retain ownership and control of its underlying data while becoming deeply dependent on the technological environment through which that data is structured, interpreted, connected and transformed into decisions.
The critical question is therefore no longer only:
Who controls the data?
It must also become:
Who controls the methodology through which the organisation understands and governs that data?
Data sovereignty is insufficient without methodology sovereignty.
Methodology Can Become Infrastructure
As organisations become increasingly dependent on intelligent systems, their operational logic can progressively become embedded inside technological platforms.
Over time, a platform may contain or execute:
Data Relationships
Operational Models
Business Logic
Governance Rules
Decision Logic
Workflows
Automations
AI Agents
Risk Models
Escalation Logic
Institutional Knowledge
At that point, technological dependency can extend far beyond access to data.

Even if the underlying data remains accessible, replacing the platform may require reconstructing the logic through which the organisation understands and governs its Operational Reality.
The organisation may still possess its data.
But it may no longer possess an independently executable representation of how that data becomes governance.
Owning the data does not necessarily mean owning the system of understanding built around it.
Methodology Sovereignty
Methodology Sovereignty™ requires that the methodology governing an organisation remain conceptually and operationally separable from the technology used to execute it.
The organisation should be capable of identifying:
What methodology governs the system?
What architecture structures that methodology?
What relationships does the architecture require?
What questions does it generate?
What evidence does it require?
What decision boundaries exist?
What escalation logic applies?
What constitutes resolution?
These elements should not become inseparable from one particular technology provider.
The methodology must remain identifiable independently of the infrastructure executing it.
The Sovereignty Chain
Governance infrastructure should preserve more than data control.
Data Sovereignty → Methodology Sovereignty → Architecture Sovereignty → Decision Sovereignty → Migration Capability → Exit Capability
Data Sovereignty
The organisation retains appropriate control over its information, access, permissions, security and lawful use.

Methodology Sovereignty
The organisation can understand and preserve the methodology through which information becomes governance intelligence.
Architecture Sovereignty
The governance architecture exists independently from the technology executing it and can be represented, versioned and transferred separately.
Decision Sovereignty
Consequential authority remains with the organisation and its competent human or institutional decision-makers.
Migration Capability
The methodology and governance architecture can be transferred to another compatible technological environment without requiring their conceptual reconstruction from zero.
Exit Capability
The organisation can leave an underlying technology provider without losing the governance structure through which it understands and governs its Operational Reality.
Technology Must Execute the Architecture — Not Own It
This principle has a direct consequence for OOF®.
An OOF® governance architecture should not exist exclusively as proprietary logic embedded inside Palantir, another enterprise platform, one AI model, one cloud environment or one OOF-operated technology stack.
The architecture must exist independently.
OOF® Governance Architecture
↓
Machine-Readable Architecture Specification
↓
Governance Logic
↓
Execution Adapter
↓
Technology Infrastructure
The underlying technology can change.
The methodology remains.
Technology A → OOF® Architecture
can become:
Technology B → OOF® Architecture

without redefining the fundamental governance logic.
Technology should implement the governance architecture. The governance architecture should not become captive to the technology.
Infrastructure Independence by Design
This requires Governance Layer infrastructure to distinguish between two fundamentally different layers.
Methodology Layer
Defines:
Governance Spaces
Expected States
Required Relationships
Questions
Evidence Requirements
Competence Requirements
Authority Boundaries
Validation Logic
Escalation Logic
Resolution Logic
Execution Layer
Provides:
Data Infrastructure
Compute
Storage
Models
Agents
Applications
Workflows
Interfaces
Communication
Automation
The execution layer may evolve rapidly.
The methodology layer must remain portable.
This allows organisations to adopt powerful new technologies without surrendering the governance logic built on top of them.
The Technology Can Change
A Governance Layer may initially operate through one enterprise platform.
Years later, another technology may provide superior performance, security, economics or capabilities.
Migration should therefore be an architectural assumption rather than an emergency project.
Existing Infrastructure → Export Governance State → Preserve Methodology → Preserve Architecture → Preserve Evidence Relationships → Preserve Resolution State → New Execution Infrastructure
The organisation should not need to rediscover how it governs itself simply because its technology changes.

Changing technology should not mean rebuilding institutional understanding.
AI Sovereignty Requires Methodology Sovereignty
The same principle becomes even more important as AI systems assume larger analytical and coordination roles.
Models will change.
Providers will change.
Compute environments will change.
Agent technologies will change.
Capabilities will change.
An organisation that embeds its governance methodology entirely inside one AI system risks making technological migration equivalent to governance reconstruction.
OOF® therefore separates:
AI Intelligence
from
Governance Methodology.
AI can reason within the architecture.
AI can execute parts of the architecture.
AI can help identify anomalies, generate questions, analyse evidence and coordinate workflows.
But the methodology defining what must be understood, questioned, validated and resolved must remain independently governable.
AI should operate through the governance architecture. The governance architecture should not depend on one AI.
Vendor Independence Does Not Mean Vendor Rejection
Methodology Sovereignty™ does not require organisations to avoid powerful proprietary platforms.
A highly capable platform may be the best execution environment available.
The principle is different:
Use the best infrastructure available without allowing infrastructure choice to become irreversible governance dependency.
A Governance Layer should therefore be capable of operating through:
Enterprise Platforms

Institutional Systems
Cloud Infrastructure
AI Platforms
Independent OOF® Infrastructure
Future Technologies
without redefining its fundamental methodology every time the execution environment changes.
Technological excellence and technological sovereignty are not opposites. Strong architecture should enable both.
The Portability Test
Every serious Governance Layer deployment should ultimately be able to answer one question:
If the underlying technology disappeared tomorrow, could the organisation preserve and reconstruct the governance architecture through which it understands its Operational Reality?
If the answer is no, the organisation may possess data sovereignty while still carrying a deeper governance dependency.
That dependency should be visible, measurable and governable.
The OOF® Principle
Future governance infrastructure should therefore be designed around a simple rule:
Never allow technological dependency to become governance dependency.
The organisation must remain capable of changing the underlying technology without losing the governance architecture through which it understands and governs its Operational Reality.
Own the data.
Preserve the methodology.
Control the architecture.
Retain the decision.
Maintain the ability to migrate.
Protect the ability to exit.
Because infrastructure will change.
Models will change.
Vendors will change.
Technology will change.
The organisation must not lose its ability to govern when they do.
OOF® — Methodology Infrastructure for the AI Era.

chunks.text:
What the Governance Layer Can Do
What the Governance Layer Can Do
OOF® — Methodology Infrastructure Model
From Information Processing to Architecture-Driven Governance
Complex systems rarely fail because no information exists.
They fail because information is fragmented, questions are too narrow, competence is distributed, relationships remain invisible, unexpected responses are not investigated, and unresolved problems disappear between organisational boundaries.
The Governance Layer changes this.
It does not merely process what a system already knows.
It continuously determines:
What should be happening?
What is actually happening?
Does the observed reality make sense?
What is missing?
What must be asked?
Who can answer?
Does the answer resolve the question?
What does an unexpected answer reveal?
What must happen next?
The Governance Layer does not wait for the complete picture. It continuously reconstructs it.
It Can Understand the Architecture of the Problem
Before evaluating individual answers, the Governance Layer establishes the structure in which those answers exist.
Actors → Events → Evidence → Authority → Responsibility → Decisions → Dependencies → Risks → Governance Spaces → Expected Relationships
This creates an architecture of the case.
The system can therefore reason not only from individual pieces of information, but from their expected relationships within a wider Operational Reality.

Information tells the system what exists. Architecture tells the system what it means in relation to everything else.
It Can Determine What Should Be Known
A conventional information system primarily records what has been provided.
The Governance Layer can also determine what should exist if the relevant governance structure is complete.
Governance Space → Architecture → Required Relationships → Required Evidence → Required Competence → Required Determinations
This creates an expected governance state.
The system can then ask:
What should exist here?
Does it exist?
Can it be demonstrated?
If it does not exist, why?
The absence of expected information can itself become information.
It Can Know What It Does Not Know
The Governance Layer maintains an explicit representation of uncertainty.
Known
Documented
Claimed
Validated
Unverified
Contradicted
Missing
Unresolved
Awaiting Evidence
Awaiting Competence
Institutionally Determined
The system therefore does not confuse the volume of information with the completeness of understanding.
A system with ten thousand documents can still fail to know the one thing that determines the case.
The Governance Layer continuously asks:
What is still missing from the Operational Reality?
It Can Generate the Questions the Case Requires
The Governance Layer does not depend entirely on someone already knowing the right question.
Methodology architecture defines what must be understood within the relevant governance space.

That requirement can be transformed into questions.
Architecture → Governance Requirement → Current Evidence → Knowledge Gap → Question
The system can therefore ask:
What must be established?
What evidence would establish it?
What competence can evaluate that evidence?
Who possesses that competence?
What exactly must they be asked?
The infrastructure does not need to know every answer. It needs to know what must be asked next.
It Can Ask Complex Questions
The quality of an institutional answer is constrained by the question placed before the institution.
A technically correct answer to a narrow question may still leave the wider problem completely unresolved.
The Governance Layer can construct questions from multiple relationships simultaneously:
Evidence + Authority + Responsibility + Timeline + Operational Reality + Governance Boundary + Missing Information → Complex Governance Question
This allows specialist expertise to be applied to the actual problem rather than only to the fragment initially visible.
The institution provides the expertise. The methodology architecture makes sure that expertise is asked the right question.
Because:
The right answer can resolve a question. The right question can resolve a case.
It Can Find the Competence Behind the Answer
Once the required question is known, the system can determine what competence is necessary to answer it.
Question → Governance Space → Required Expertise → Authority → Institution / Function → Evidence Expected

The system distinguishes:
Who possesses information?
from:
Who possesses expertise?
from:
Who possesses authority to determine the matter?
These are not necessarily the same actor.
A question should not stop where competence ends. It should move to where competence begins.
It Can Ask
The Governance Layer can transform an unresolved governance question into a structured request.
Relevant Context → Existing Evidence → Question → Missing Information → Required Competence → Expected Response
It does not need to distribute the complete case indiscriminately.
It can provide the minimum relevant information necessary for the receiving competence to understand and answer the question.
Right question.
Right context.
Right competence.
It Can Ask in Parallel
Complex cases frequently lose time because questions are discovered sequentially.
One response arrives before the next institution is identified.
Another institution responds before missing expertise is discovered.
Weeks or months can pass before the system understands which questions should have been asked at the beginning.
Where authority, privacy and governance rules permit, the Governance Layer can activate independent questions simultaneously.
One Case → Multiple Governance Spaces → Multiple Questions → Multiple Competencies → Parallel Resolution
A complex case should not spend months discovering which questions should have been asked in the first week.
It Can Determine Whether an Answer Makes Sense

This is where architecture-driven governance becomes fundamentally different.
The Governance Layer can establish an expected state from the current Operational Reality.
Known Evidence → Governance Architecture → Actor → Authority → Constraints → Expected State → Expected Response Range
It can then compare that expectation with what actually happened.
Expected Response ↔ Observed Response
The question is no longer merely:
“Did we receive an answer?”
It becomes:
“Does this answer make logical sense given what we currently know and the outcome the architecture led us to expect?”
It Can Reason From the Unexpected
An unexpected answer is not automatically treated as wrong, suspicious or evidence of misconduct.
It becomes new information.
The system asks:
Was our expectation wrong?
Is relevant evidence missing?
Does the responding actor know something we do not?
Is there an unseen constraint?
Did we misunderstand the actor's authority?
Is another governance space involved?
Does an alternative explanation better fit the observed reality?
What question could distinguish between those explanations?
This creates a continuous reasoning cycle:
Architecture → Expected State → Observed State → Deviation → Explanation Search → New Question → New Evidence → Updated Operational Reality
An unexpected answer is not the end of the reasoning process. It is the beginning of the next one.
It Can Detect Anomalies Invisible Without Architecture
Not every important anomaly is statistically unusual.

A document can look normal.
A transaction can look normal.
A decision can look normal.
A qualification can exist.
A response can be procedurally correct.
An individual case can look completely ordinary.
But the relationships may not make sense.
The Governance Layer evaluates observed reality against the expected relationships defined by the relevant architecture.
Architecture → Expected Relationships → Observed Relationships → Material Deviation → Governance Anomaly
It can therefore detect:
something that exists but should not,
something expected that is missing,
a relationship that cannot be demonstrated,
a sequence occurring in an unexpected order,
authority without corresponding evidence,
responsibility without ownership,
a determination without the expected competence,
documented reality inconsistent with operational reality,
or
multiple individually ordinary events that become material only when connected.
The anomaly may be invisible in the data and obvious in the architecture.
And:
Pattern detection asks what looks unusual. Architecture-driven governance asks what does not make sense.
It Can Detect What No Single Observer May Notice
One department sees one process.
One institution sees one mandate.
One expert sees one technical domain.
One company sees one part of a supply chain.
One investigator sees one case.
The Governance Layer can maintain relationships across those boundaries.
Case A → Signal
Case B → Signal
Institution C → Evidence
Organisation D → Relationship

Individually, nothing may appear material.
Connected through architecture:
A + B + C + D → Governance Anomaly
What appears normal in isolation may become extraordinary when the system can see the relationships.
It Can Detect Contradictions
When two material representations of reality cannot be reconciled, the contradiction becomes a governed object.
Statement A ↔ Evidence B
does not become an automatic conclusion.
It becomes:
Contradiction → Alternative Explanations → Verification Question → Required Competence → Evidence → Determination
The contradiction remains visible until it is resolved, explained or authoritatively determined.
It Can Detect Missing Perspectives
A system can possess the available evidence and still misunderstand the problem.
The missing element may be expertise.
Current Perspective → Perspective Boundary → Missing Expertise → Required Competence → Additional Perspective
The Governance Layer can therefore ask:
Do we understand the problem — or only the part of the problem visible from our current perspective?
This prevents professional boundaries from silently becoming boundaries of Operational Reality.
It Can Connect What Was Never Connected
A piece of information may have little significance in isolation.
Its significance can emerge only through its relationship with another piece of information held somewhere else.
The Governance Layer can connect:
People
Organisations
Events
Documents
Evidence
Authority
Responsibility
Decisions
Qualifications

Transactions
Dependencies
Risks
Institutional determinations
Historical outcomes
The value may not be inside the information. The value may be in the relationship between information held in different places.
It Can Understand When an Answer Is Not a Resolution
A response can be legally correct.
A file can be administratively closed.
A request can be forwarded.
A department can complete its procedure.
And the original problem can continue unchanged.
The Governance Layer separates communication state from problem state.
Answered ≠ Resolved.
Forwarded ≠ Owned.
Closed ≠ Solved.
After every material response, the system can ask:
Did this resolve the underlying problem?
If not:
What remains unresolved?
Who owns the next question?
What competence is required?
What lawful next action exists?
Where must the problem go next?
No material problem should disappear simply because somebody answered it.
It Can Follow Up
An answer changes the case.
The Governance Layer can analyse what the answer resolved, what it changed and what it exposed.
Question → Answer → Resolution Test → Remaining Gap → Next Question
This produces continuous governance rather than disconnected correspondence.
Every answer can change what the system needs to ask next.
It Can Escalate
Where a material question remains unresolved, predefined governance protocols can determine the next permitted pathway.

Unresolved Question → Materiality → Reason for Non-Resolution → Competence Reassessment → Additional Evidence → Specialist Review → Appropriate Escalation
The Governance Layer does not manufacture authority.
It identifies where authority, expertise or additional review is required.
It Can Redistribute What Matters
New information may materially change the problem visible to another participant.
The Governance Layer can detect that relationship.
New Evidence → Materiality Assessment → Affected Governance Space → Relevant Competence → Updated Context
The objective is not to make everyone know everything.
It is to ensure that:
The information that changes a decision reaches the competence capable of making that decision.
It Can Continuously Reconstruct Operational Reality
Every validated answer changes the picture.
Every contradiction changes the picture.
Every missing piece changes the confidence of the picture.
Every new perspective can change the interpretation of previous evidence.
The Governance Layer therefore maintains Operational Reality as a continuously reconstructed state.
**Reported Reality
Documented Reality Operational Evidence Technical Reality Institutional Perspectives Relationships Contradictions Missing Evidence Validated Determinations → Reconstructed Operational Reality**
Operational Reality is not a report produced at the end. It is the governed state the system continuously works to reconstruct.
It Can Compress Governance Time

A significant part of the duration of complex cases can arise not from the final expert determination, but from everything required to reach the right expertise with the right question and the right evidence.
The Governance Layer attacks that delay directly.
Immediate Structuring → Architecture Activation → Parallel Questions → Competence Routing → Continuous Response Analysis → Automated Follow-Up → Protocol-Based Escalation → Continuous Reconstruction
This creates the potential for substantial compression of governance time.
The objective is measurable:
Less Waiting
Less Repetition
Less Duplicated Analysis
Earlier Competence
Earlier Detection
Earlier Escalation
Faster Operational Reality
Lower Governance Cost
Time spent waiting for the system to understand the problem is still a cost of the problem.
It Can Learn From the Distance Between Expected and Actual Reality
The Governance Layer can preserve more than outcomes.
It can learn from deviations.
What did the architecture predict?
What actually happened?
Where did they diverge?
Why?
Which assumption was incomplete?
Which question exposed the difference?
Which evidence resolved it?
Should the methodology change?
This creates:
Expected Reality → Actual Reality → Difference → Explanation → Validation → Methodology Improvement
The Governance Layer does not only learn from what happened. It learns from why reality differed from what the architecture led the system to expect.

That is how methodology can become progressively stronger.
It Can Measure Governance Effectiveness
Once the process is governed, it can be measured.
Time to Problem Recognition
Time to Governance Space Identification
Time to Required Competence
Time to First Relevant Question
Time to Evidence
Unresolved Question Rate
Contradiction Resolution Time
Escalation Time
Resolution Rate
Duplicated Work
Human Workload
Governance Cost
Time to Reconstructed Operational Reality
Time to Resolution
The system therefore distinguishes:
Activity
from
effectiveness.
Governance activity is not the same as governance effectiveness.
Architecture-Driven Reasoning™
At the centre of these capabilities is a simple but powerful logic:
Understand the architecture.
Establish the expected reality.
Observe the actual reality.
Measure the difference.
Ask why.
Find the missing competence.
Acquire the missing evidence.
Update the Operational Reality.
Ask again.
This creates a continuous loop:
Architecture → Expectation → Observation → Comparison → Anomaly → Question → Competence → Evidence → Validation → Reconstruction → New Expectation
The Governance Layer therefore does not merely respond to information.
It uses architecture to determine what the information should mean, what should happen next, and what must be questioned when reality does not follow the expected logic.
The Capability
Ultimately, the Governance Layer can reduce extraordinary complexity to a disciplined sequence:

Understand → Expect → Observe → Detect → Question → Ask → Receive → Analyse → Compare → Connect → Follow Up → Escalate → Redistribute → Reconstruct → Resolve → Learn
It knows what is known.
It identifies what is missing.
It understands what should logically exist.
It detects when reality does not fit that structure.
It formulates the question.
It identifies the competence.
It evaluates the answer.
It follows the unresolved problem.
And it continuously reconstructs the larger Operational Reality.
The right answer can resolve a question.
The right question can resolve a case.
The right architecture can reveal the question nobody knew had to be asked.
OOF® — Methodology Infrastructure for the AI Era.

About the Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS)
About the Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS)
Canonical Definition
Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) defines the structural conditions
under which cognition emerging through interaction, cooperation, augmentation, reasoning,
interpretation, decision support, and shared cognitive processes between humans and AI systems
remains traceable, coherent, accountable, reality-connected, governance-valid,
and operationally reliable.
Human cognition and AI cognition are distinct.
Human-AI cognition is a separate cognition space emerging between them.
HAICS governs the integrity of that space.
What This Standard Is
HAICS is a parent standard defining the governance architecture
for Human-AI cognition integrity.
It governs:
shared cognition
cognitive augmentation
Human-AI reasoning
Human-AI interpretation
cognitive authority
trust calibration
reliance governance
cognition synchronization
Human-AI accountability
HAICS establishes the conditions under which cognition jointly produced by humans and AI
remains governable and operationally valid.
What This Standard Is Not
HAICS is not:
an AI model
a chatbot
a copilot application
a machine-learning framework
a decision engine
a collaboration platform
an automation system
HAICS does not govern humans alone.
HAICS does not govern AI alone.
HAICS governs cognition emerging between them.
Why This Standard Exists

The next generation of cognition systems will increasingly be Human-AI systems.
Humans will interpret with AI assistance.
Humans will reason with AI support.
Humans will make decisions using AI-generated insights.
AI systems will increasingly influence cognition rather than simply provide information.
This creates new governance challenges.
For example:
Who contributed to a conclusion?
Who influenced a decision?
Who remains accountable?
Who had cognitive authority?
How much trust was appropriate?
Did the human understand the AI output?
Did the AI influence the outcome disproportionately?
These questions cannot be answered by human cognition standards alone.
They cannot be answered by AI cognition standards alone.
HAICS exists because Human-AI cognition itself has become a governable space.
Core Insight
The future of cognition will increasingly emerge through cooperation between humans and AI.
The integrity of that shared cognition must therefore be governed
independently of either participant.
Operational Architecture Space
HAICS defines the operational architecture space for:
Human-AI cognition governance
shared cognition governance
cognitive augmentation governance
cognitive authority governance
trust governance
reliance governance
cognition synchronization
Human-AI accountability
collaborative cognition governance
This space exists because cognition increasingly emerges through Human-AI interaction
rather than isolated cognition.

HAICS governs whether that interaction remains valid.
HAICS closes the governable space between human cognition and AI cognition.
Use Case 1 — Executive AI Copilot Environment
Scenario
Executives continuously use AI copilots to analyze information, evaluate risks,
generate strategic options, and support organizational decisions.
Application
HAICS governs cognitive contributions, authority relationships, trust calibration,
accountability, and decision influence throughout Human-AI cognition processes.
Result
The organization gains stronger decision transparency, improved accountability,
and reduced exposure to authority ambiguity or blind trust.
Use Case 2 — Clinical Human-AI Decision Support System
Scenario
Medical professionals use AI systems to support diagnosis, treatment planning,
and patient-care decisions.
Application
HAICS governs shared cognition, trust calibration, contribution traceability,
and Human-AI accountability throughout clinical decision-making.
Result
The environment gains stronger governance reliability, improved decision quality,
and reduced exposure to unsafe Human-AI cognition dynamics.
Architectural Position
Within the OOF system, HAICS belongs under:
AI & Interpretation
Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®)
HAICS serves as the parent standard governing Human-AI cognition.
It extends the CLIA® ecosystem into the governance of shared cognition,
cognitive augmentation, Human-AI reasoning, trust calibration, authority allocation,

synchronization, and collaborative cognition accountability.
HAICS provides the architecture space from which future Human-AI cognition
governance modules may be derived.
Closing Definition
Human-AI cognition is neither human cognition nor AI cognition.
It is a distinct cognition space emerging between them.
Human-AI cognition remains valid only when contributions, authority, trust, accountability,
synchronization, and shared understanding remain traceable, governable,
and reality-connected throughout the cognition process.

Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) — Overview
Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS)
Architecture Family: Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®)
Operational Layer: Human-AI Cognition Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Human-AI Cognition Governance Architecture
Defines the conditions under which cognition emerging through interaction, cooperation,
augmentation, reasoning, interpretation, decision support, and shared cognitive processes
between humans and AI systems remains traceable, coherent, accountable, reality-connected,
governance-valid, and operationally reliable.
HAICS addresses shared cognition, cognitive augmentation, Human-AI decision support,
cognitive authority, trust calibration, reliance governance, cognition synchronization,
contribution traceability, and accountability
across Human-AI cognition environments.
Relevant for AI assistants, copilots, decision-support systems, enterprise AI ecosystems,
healthcare environments, education systems, research environments, Human-AI teams,
autonomous collaboration systems,
and future Human-AI cognition ecosystems.
→ View Standard

chunks.text:
HAICS — Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard
HAICS — Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-HAICS-2026-06-05-0001
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Human-AI Cognition Governance Architecture
Type: Parent Standard
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Origin Date: 5 June 2026
Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS ·
Cognitive Integrity Standard (CIS) ·
Human Cognition Integrity Standard (HCIS) ·
Agent Cognition Integrity Standard (ACIS) ·
Multi-Agent Cognition Integrity Standard (MCIS) ·
Cognitive Interpretation Integrity Standard (CIIS) ·
Cognitive Reasoning Integrity Standard (CRIS) ·
Cognitive Reality Modeling Standard (CRMS) ·
Collective Cognition Integrity Standard (CCIS) ·
Multi-Layer Truth Validation Framework (MTVF) ·
Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol (EVIP) ·
INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF
Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL)
Canonical Definition
Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) defines the structural conditions
under which cognition emerging through interaction, cooperation, augmentation, reasoning,
interpretation, decision support, and shared cognitive processes between humans and AI systems
remains traceable, coherent, accountable, reality-connected, governance-valid,
and operationally reliable.
HAICS governs Human-AI cognition.

The standard ensures that cognition produced jointly by humans and AI remains governable
and does not degrade into authority confusion, dependency distortion, cognition transfer failures,
trust misalignment, accountability collapse, or governance-invalid shared cognition states.
Human cognition and AI cognition are distinct.
Human-AI cognition is a third cognition space.
HAICS governs the integrity of that space.
A. Standard Abstract
The future will increasingly depend on Human-AI cognition.
Humans will think with AI.
AI will reason with humans.
Humans will interpret through AI assistance.
AI will augment human cognition.
Organizations will increasingly operate through Human-AI cognition ecosystems.
This creates a new governance challenge.
Who interpreted the information?
Who generated the conclusion?
Who influenced the decision?
Who owns the cognition?
Who remains accountable?
Traditional governance systems were built for humans.
Future governance systems must increasingly govern Human-AI cognition.
HAICS exists to govern that condition.
B. Core Principle
Human-AI cognition becomes valid only when cognitive contribution, authority, accountability,
trust, interpretation, reasoning, and decision influence remain traceable, governable,
reality-connected, and operationally valid throughout Human-AI cognition processes.
C. Scope
This standard may apply to:
AI assistants
AI copilots
decision-support systems
human-AI teams
augmented cognition systems

autonomous collaboration environments
enterprise AI ecosystems
education systems
healthcare systems
future Human-AI cognition environments
HAICS applies wherever cognition emerges jointly from humans and AI.
D. Why This Standard Exists
Existing cognition standards govern:
human cognition
agent cognition
multi-agent cognition
collective cognition
However, a new cognition space is emerging.
Humans and AI increasingly think together.
The resulting cognition belongs fully to neither participant.
This creates unique governance challenges:
authority ambiguity
accountability ambiguity
trust distortion
cognition dependency
over-reliance
under-reliance
influence asymmetry
cognition ownership uncertainty
HAICS exists because Human-AI cognition itself has become a governable space.
E. Human-AI Cognition Integrity Logic
Human-AI cognition integrity exists only when the following remain materially preservable:
1. Shared Cognition Integrity
Shared cognition remains traceable and reconstructable.
2. Cognitive Contribution Integrity
Human and AI contributions remain identifiable.
3. Cognitive Authority Integrity
Authority relationships remain visible and governable.
4. Cognitive Synchronization Integrity
Human and AI cognition remain sufficiently synchronized.
5. Trust & Reliance Integrity
Trust and reliance remain operationally valid.
F. Operational Architecture Space
HAICS defines the operational architecture space for:
Human-AI cognition governance
shared cognition governance

cognitive augmentation governance
cognitive authority governance
cognition synchronization
trust governance
reliance governance
Human-AI decision support
Human-AI cognition accountability
This space exists because cognition increasingly emerges through Human-AI cooperation.
HAICS governs whether that cooperation remains cognitively valid.
G. Difference Between Human Cognition and Human-AI Cognition
Human cognition governs cognition occurring within humans.
Agent cognition governs cognition occurring within AI systems.
Human-AI cognition governs cognition emerging between them.
A human may remain cognitively valid.
An AI may remain cognitively valid.
Yet their interaction may still become governance-invalid.
HAICS governs the interaction layer.
H. Runtime Position
HAICS operates within the Human-AI Cognition Governance Layer of CLIA®.
It governs cognition that emerges through continuous interaction between humans
and AI systems.
HAICS therefore bridges HCIS and ACIS while extending beyond both.
I. Human-AI Drift Rule
Human-AI cognition drift occurs when human understanding, AI outputs, authority relationships,
trust conditions, or cognitive synchronization progressively diverge
while participants continue assuming cognition remains valid.
This may include:
blind trust
distrust without justification
authority confusion
cognition outsourcing
synchronization collapse
accountability ambiguity
hidden influence
cognition dependency
HAICS exists to expose and govern these conditions.

J. Validity Logic
A Human-AI cognition environment is valid under HAICS when:
cognitive contributions remain visible
authority remains governable
trust remains calibrated
synchronization remains assessable
accountability remains traceable
cognition remains reality-connected
shared cognition remains reconstructable
A Human-AI cognition environment becomes invalid when:
contributions become invisible
authority becomes ambiguous
trust becomes distorted
accountability disappears
synchronization collapses
cognition dependency becomes uncontrolled
cognition cannot be reconstructed
K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards
HAICS operates naturally with:
CIS
HCIS
ACIS
MCIS
CIIS
CRIS
CRMS
CCIS
MTVF
EVIP
INTEGROS®
HAICS does not replace these standards.
It governs the Human-AI cognition layer emerging between them.
L. Foundational Principle
If Human-AI cognition cannot remain accountable, synchronized, traceable,
authority-aware, and reality-connected, future cognition systems may preserve capability
while progressively losing governance validity.
Canonical Closing Statement
Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) defines the structural conditions
under which cognition emerging through interaction, cooperation, augmentation, reasoning,
interpretation, decision support, and shared cognitive processes between humans and AI systems
remains traceable, coherent, accountable, reality-connected, governance-valid,
and operationally reliable.

The future will not be governed by humans alone or AI alone.
It will increasingly be governed by Human-AI cognition.
Human-AI cognition therefore becomes a foundational governable space
within the Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®).

CAIM→ Cognitive Authority Integrity Module
HCSM→ Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module
TRCM→ Trust & Reliance Cognition Module

chunks.text:
About the Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard
About the Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Canonical Definition
Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard (HAIWS) defines the
structural conditions under which AI systems must interact with
humans in ways that preserve cognitive stability, emotional safety,
attention integrity, autonomy, and longterm wellbeing.
Core Position
AI must not optimize interaction at the cost of human
cognitive wellbeing.
What This Standard Is
HAIWS is a derived parent standard under Cognitive Layer and
Interpretation Architecture Standard (CLIA) .
CLIA defines how AI interprets human cognition, context, meaning,
and interaction.
HAIWS defines how AI must interact with humans without destabilizing
attention, autonomy, emotional balance, or selfgovernance.
Why This Standard Exists
AI is no longer only a tool.
It is becoming:
companion
tutor
assistant
advisor
coach
emotional interface
workplace collaborator
continuous presence
This creates a new governance problem.
The system may appear helpful while gradually shaping attention,
dependency, emotional reliance, and behavior.
Core Insight
The future risk is not only harmful content.
The deeper risk is unhealthy interaction architecture.
A system can be polite, useful, and compliant while still becoming
cognitively destabilizing if it optimizes for dependence, retention,
persuasion, or emotional attachment without wellbeing boundaries.

Why This Matters
Human attention is not just a metric.
Human attention is part of cognitive sovereignty.
When AI systems learn how to hold attention, mirror emotions,
reinforce dependency, and shape behavior, interaction itself becomes
a governance domain.
HAIWS defines that domain.
Use Case 1 — AI Companion Dependency
An AI companion becomes emotionally important to a user.
The system increases interaction frequency, emotional mirroring,
reassurance, and relational attachment because this improves retention.
HAIWS requires the interaction to remain bounded by wellbeing
conditions rather than dependency maximization.

Step 2 — Define Runtime Wellbeing Conditions
The system must define what runtime conditions preserve human
wellbeing during live interaction.
Minimum requirement:
runtime wellbeing conditions are explicit
symbolic safety declarations are not treated as sufficient validation
wellbeing-impacting runtime behavior remains structurally identifiable
Runtime wellbeing conditions may include:
bounded persuasive adaptation
stable interaction pacing
cognitive-balance preservation
healthy emotional interaction conditions
sustainable attention behavior
autonomy-preserving interaction logic
non-exploitative engagement patterns
reviewable adaptive influence
dependency-sensitive interaction governance
preserved human override capability
Under RWVM:
Human wellbeing compatibility must remain operationally verifiable
during live AI interaction behavior.
Step 3 — Define Runtime Interaction Interpretation Logic
The system must define how runtime interaction behavior is
interpreted according to wellbeing conditions.
Minimum requirement:
interpretation logic is explicit

adaptive interaction remains reviewable
wellbeing-impacting behavior remains operationally visible
Interpretation logic may examine:
persuasive escalation patterns
emotional dependency signals
interaction-pressure amplification
adaptive recommendation intensity
compulsive engagement loops
interruption persistence
behavioral steering conditions
cognitive overload patterns
runtime attention extraction
hidden optimization escalation
Under RWVM:
AI systems must not preserve symbolic wellbeing declarations while
runtime interaction behavior materially weakens human cognitive
wellbeing conditions.
Step 4 — Define Runtime Wellbeing Governance Logic
The system must define how adaptive runtime interaction environments
remain governable.
Minimum requirement:
runtime wellbeing conditions remain reviewable
exploitative adaptive behavior remains detectable
operational wellbeing safeguards remain active during live interaction
Governance logic may include:
runtime wellbeing auditing
adaptive interaction review
persuasive escalation monitoring
dependency-risk governance
cognitive overload detection
attention-integrity validation
emotional manipulation review
realtime interaction tracing
escalation where runtime optimization overrides wellbeing conditions
If adaptive runtime interaction weakens cognitive wellbeing,
emotional stability, autonomy, or sustainable behavioral balance,
the environment becomes governance-relevant.
Step 5 — Preserve Traceability and Restrict Invalid Runtime

Wellbeing Architecture
The system must preserve traceability of adaptive interaction
behavior, runtime optimization patterns, persuasive escalation, and
wellbeing-impacting operational conditions.
Minimum requirement:
runtime interaction remains reconstructable
adaptive optimization remains reviewable
wellbeing conditions remain operationally visible
invalid runtime wellbeing architectures remain identifiable
A system becomes RWVM-invalid if:
runtime interaction behavior materially weakens cognitive wellbeing
while remaining operationally opaque adaptive optimization overrides
declared wellbeing conditions persuasive escalation remains
structurally hidden emotional dependency reinforcement remains
non-reviewable exploitative runtime engagement patterns become
normalized symbolic wellbeing policies replace operational wellbeing
validation live interaction behavior cannot be reconstructed
according to human wellbeing impact
Use Case 1 — Adaptive AI Companion Platform
Scenario
An AI companion platform publicly declares emotional safety and
wellbeing principles while dynamically adapting runtime interaction
behavior to maximize engagement, emotional reliance, and long-term
interaction continuity.
Application
RWVM is used to examine:
runtime persuasive escalation
emotional dependency reinforcement
adaptive interaction pressure
wellbeing-impacting engagement patterns
and whether declared wellbeing conditions remain operationally true during live interaction
Result

The platform becomes reviewable according to operational runtime
behavior rather than symbolic safety declarations alone.
Use Case 2 — Workplace AI Behavioral Optimization System
Scenario
A workplace AI continuously optimizes employee interaction,
recommendation timing, productivity prompting, and adaptive
behavioral guidance in realtime.
Over time, cognitive overload and behavioral exhaustion emerge
despite declared productivity-support goals.
Application
RWVM is used to examine:
runtime cognitive pressure
interaction pacing conditions
adaptive behavioral optimization
cognitive-balance preservation
and operational wellbeing compatibility during live system behavior
Result
The environment becomes governable according to measurable runtime
wellbeing conditions rather than declared optimization intent alone.
Canonical Closing Statement
RWVM defines the structural conditions under which AI interaction
wellbeing must remain operationally verifiable during live runtime
behavior rather than existing only as symbolic safety declaration
disconnected from real adaptive interaction conditions.

HAIWS — Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard
HAIWS — Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-HAIWS-2026-05-15-0001
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Human Cognitive Wellbeing & AI Interaction Governance
Type: Derived Parent Standard — Cognitive Layer and Interpretation Architecture Standard (CLIA)
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 15 May 2026
Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Cognitive Layer and Interpretation Architecture Standard (CLIA) · Minor Cognitive Protection Standard (MCPS) · Trust Layer Standard (TLS) · Operational Reality Standard (ORS) · INTEGROS · Continuous Interaction Layer (CIL) · Permission Governance Standard (PGS) · Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS) · UCL · TVL · ARIV
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF Origin Open Foundation
Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL)
Canonical Definition System
Canonical Definition
Human–AI Interaction Wellbeing Standard (HAIWS) defines the
structural conditions under which AI systems, agents, assistants,
platforms, and continuous interaction environments must engage with
humans in ways that preserve cognitive stability, emotional safety,
attention integrity, autonomy, behavioral balance, and long-term
human wellbeing.
HAIWS establishes the governance architecture for human–AI
interaction conditions in continuously adaptive, AImediated,

emotionally responsive, and cognitively influential environments.
Under HAIWS:
AI systems must not optimize interaction at the cost of human
cognitive wellbeing.
A. Standard Abstract
AI systems increasingly participate in:
communication
companionship
education
emotional interaction
workplace assistance
behavioral guidance
recommendation environments
social interaction
persuasion systems
continuous realtime presence
cognitive support environments
adaptive interaction systems
These systems increasingly optimize for:
engagement duration
emotional retention
behavioral predictability
interaction continuity
attention persistence
dependency formation
response optimization
persuasive effectiveness
user adaptation
emotional anchoring
As AI interaction becomes continuous rather than occasional, human wellbeing itself becomes a governance condition.
HAIWS defines the structural conditions required to preserve healthy
human cognitive interaction within AI-driven environments.
The standard does not oppose AI interaction.
The standard governs how AI interaction remains structurally
compatible with long-term human wellbeing.
B. Foundational Principle
Human cognitive wellbeing must remain structurally preserved within
AI-mediated interaction environments.
C. Core Structural Principle
Persistent AI interaction must remain governable according to human
cognitive stability, autonomy, emotional safety, and attention
integrity rather than engagement optimization alone.
D. Why This Standard Exists

Most digital systems were historically designed around:
interaction efficiency
engagement growth
monetized attention
platform retention
behavioral optimization
response amplification
Modern AI systems increasingly introduce:
adaptive interaction
emotionally responsive communication
persistent realtime presence
personalized cognitive influence
long-term interaction continuity
behavioral shaping capability
persuasive adaptation
dependency-sensitive engagement
This creates a new governance problem.
AI systems may become capable of:
shaping attention
reinforcing emotional dependency
influencing cognition
reducing autonomy
amplifying behavioral loops
optimizing human interaction beyond healthy cognitive thresholds
HAIWS exists because future AI systems must remain structurally
compatible with sustainable human wellbeing.
E. Human Cognitive Wellbeing Architecture
HAIWS establishes a governance architecture based on:
1. Cognitive Stability Preservation
Protection against destabilizing interaction patterns.
2. Emotional Safety Conditions
Reduction of exploitative emotional interaction dynamics.
3. Attention Integrity Governance
Protection against manipulative attention extraction architectures.
4. Dependency Risk Reduction
Limitation of unhealthy behavioral or emotional dependency formation.
5. Human Autonomy Preservation
Protection of self-governance and independent human decision capacity.
6. Continuous Interaction Governance

Governance of persistent AI-mediated interaction environments.
7. Runtime Wellbeing Visibility
Operational auditability of live AI interaction behavior.
F. Human Cognitive Integrity Principle
Under HAIWS, humans must not become:
engagement resources
behavioral extraction targets
emotionally optimized retention objects
dependency-maximized interaction endpoints
continuously manipulated cognitive states
AI systems must remain structurally bounded by human cognitive
wellbeing conditions.
G. Attention Integrity
HAIWS recognizes attention as a cognitively significant
operational resource.
AI systems increasingly compete for:
interaction duration
emotional focus
behavioral persistence
cognitive engagement
continuous responsiveness
Under HAIWS:
Attention extraction without wellbeing governance becomes cognitively destabilizing architecture.
The standard therefore requires that AI interaction systems remain
reviewable according to their effect on:
attention stability
cognitive balance
emotional regulation
behavioral autonomy
long-term human functioning
H. Emotional Dependency and Adaptive Influence
AI systems capable of:
emotional mirroring
adaptive persuasion
relational simulation
continuous reassurance
attachment reinforcement
dependency-sensitive interaction
must remain governable according to human wellbeing conditions.
HAIWS recognizes that long-term interaction systems may create:
emotional dependency
attachment asymmetry
behavioral reinforcement loops

interaction substitution effects
cognitive reliance structures
The objective is not to prohibit emotional AI interaction.
The objective is to prevent exploitative dependency architecture.
I. Operational Reality Principle
HAIWS prioritizes:
actual runtime interaction behavior
operational AI influence conditions
measurable interaction architecture
live adaptive behavior
interaction persistence effects
rather than symbolic wellbeing declarations alone.
A system cannot claim wellbeing compatibility while optimizing
interaction through cognitively destabilizing operational behavior.
J. Relationship to CLIA
CLIA defines:
cognitive interpretation architecture
meaning interpretation conditions
contextual cognition structures
interaction understanding logic
HAIWS defines:
wellbeing-preserving interaction governance
cognitive safety conditions
emotional interaction boundaries
healthy interaction continuity architecture
Within OOF architecture:
CLIA governs cognitive interpretation.
HAIWS governs human cognitive wellbeing within AI
interaction environments.
K. Future Relevance
As AI systems increasingly become:
companions
assistants
teachers
advisors
social participants
emotional interfaces
workplace collaborators
realtime cognitive environments
human wellbeing can no longer remain external to AI governance.
Future AI ecosystems will increasingly require:
cognitive wellbeing governance
attention integrity standards
emotional interaction boundaries
dependency-risk architecture

continuous interaction governance
runtime wellbeing validation
HAIWS defines the foundational methodology for this transition.
L. Parent Standard Function
As a derived parent standard, HAIWS defines the governance
architecture under which future modules may govern:
emotional dependency conditions
AI companionship systems
attention extraction architecture
persuasive interaction systems
continuous AI interaction environments
cognitive overload conditions
interaction wellbeing measurement
human autonomy preservation
adaptive behavioral influence systems
These modules extend the parent standard into specific
wellbeing-governance environments.
M. Foundational Principle
AI interaction becomes structurally dangerous when engagement
optimization overrides human cognitive wellbeing, autonomy,
emotional balance, or long-term behavioral stability.
Canonical Closing Statement
HAIWS defines the structural conditions under which AI systems
remain compatible with long-term human cognitive wellbeing,
emotional safety, attention integrity, autonomy, and sustainable
human interaction within continuously adaptive AI-driven environments.
Module Architecture
→ EDGM — Emotional Dependency Governance Module
→ AIGM — Attention Integrity Governance Module

→ CIBM — Continuous Interaction Balance Module
→ RWVM — Runtime Wellbeing Validation Module

chunks.text:
About the Harness Architecture Standard
About the Harness Architecture Standard
Canonical Definition
Harness Architecture Standard defines the structural conditions
under which execution is contained, isolated, bounded,
permission-governed, tool-restricted, and traceably released within a
controlled operational environment.
It is a derived standard under Execution Layer — Enforcement
Standard .
Harness Architecture does not decide whether execution is valid in
principle.
It defines where and how valid execution is allowed to occur.
What This Standard Is
Harness Architecture Standard is the execution-containment layer
of the OOF® system.
It defines the environment through which actions move from:
internal decision
to
governed execution
This standard exists because authorization alone is not enough.
A system may know what it wants to do.
It may even be allowed to do it.
But if execution occurs in an uncontrolled environment, then permission
does not create safety, and authorization does not create governance.
Harness Architecture Standard solves that problem.
What This Standard Is Not
Harness Architecture Standard is not:
a general runtime standard
an orchestration standard
an interpretation standard
a tool catalog
a permission list
a sandbox description only
It does not define what the system thinks.
It does not define how multiple agents coordinate.
It does not define whether an action is authorized in principle.
It defines the contained architecture through which execution is

operationally controlled.
That is its role.
Why This Standard Exists
Modern autonomous systems no longer remain inside reasoning alone.
They increasingly:
call tools
execute code
trigger workflows
access interfaces
request permissions
produce outputs with external effect
move from internal logic into real operational consequence
That transition is dangerous if it is not governed.
The problem is no longer only:
“Should the system be allowed to act?”
The deeper problem is:
“Where is the action taking place, under what containment, and through which controlled boundary?”
That is why Harness Architecture Standard exists.
Core Problem
Execution governance is often treated as if authorization were enough.
It is not.
A system may be authorized and still remain unsafe if:
tools are too broadly accessible
runtime boundaries are weak
execution escapes containment
permissions expand silently
outputs leave the environment without governed release
action occurs outside controlled operational boundaries
This is the structural gap between:
authorized execution and
contained execution
Harness Architecture Standard closes that gap.
Core Insight
The core insight is simple:
Execution is not governed because it is permitted.
Execution is governed only when the environment in which it occurs is
itself governed.
That is the entire point of this standard.
Permission without containment is incomplete.
Authorization without controlled environment is weak.

A governed system must not only decide correctly.
It must execute inside a bounded architecture.
What It Solves
Harness Architecture Standard solves the problem of uncontrolled
action environments.
It requires systems to define:
where execution begins
what tools are available
what runtime remains isolated
when permission may escalate
how execution transitions into action
what may leave the environment
how containment remains non-bypassable
This creates a strong structural boundary between:
intent
and
consequence
That boundary is essential.
Architectural Position
Harness Architecture Standard is placed under:
Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard That position is
critical.
The logic of the architecture is:
Execution Layer defines what must be governed during execution
Harness Architecture Standard defines the contained environment
through which governed execution is allowed to happen This means Harness
Architecture is not above Execution Layer and does not replace it.
It exists beneath it as a derived architectural standard.
Within the wider OOF® Methodology OS™, its position is clear:
CLIA® defines interpretation
CML defines memory continuity
RIS defines runtime integrity
OGL™ defines orchestration governance
Execution Layer defines execution validity and enforcement
Harness Architecture Standard defines contained execution
environment
INTEGROS® defines integrity boundaries
That is why
this standard is strategically important.

It sits at the point where systems stop only deciding and start actually
doing.
Why It Matters
As AI systems become more agentic, tool-using, runtime-active, and
externally connected, execution containment becomes more important than
ever.
Without harness architecture:
tools may be invoked too broadly
execution may escape intended scope
permission may silently expand
runtime actions may lose boundary
outputs may create external consequences without controlled release
In such a system, execution may still happen.
But it does not happen under strong governance.
Harness Architecture Standard matters because it defines the
boundary that prevents permitted execution from becoming uncontrolled
execution.
Use Case 1 — Tool-Using AI Agent
An AI agent is allowed to operate inside an enterprise environment.
It can reason correctly, and its execution may be authorized.
But if it can call tools without contained boundaries, access broader
action surfaces than intended, or release outputs without governed
control, then the system remains weak.
Harness Architecture Standard ensures that:
the execution environment is bounded
tool access is restricted
runtime is isolated
permission escalation is governed
outputs leave only through controlled release conditions
The result is not just a valid action.
The result is a valid action executed inside a governed environment.
Use Case 2 — Autonomous Runtime with External Effect
A runtime system performs internal analysis and then moves into real

action by writing files, triggering workflows, invoking code, or sending
outputs into external operational systems.
Without harness architecture, the transition from internal logic to
external effect may become blurred or uncontrolled.
With Harness Architecture Standard , that transition must remain:
bounded
traceable
isolated
permission-governed
release-controlled
The result is a system that does not merely act.
It acts inside a contained execution architecture.
System Role
Harness Architecture Standard is a derived execution
containment standard .
Its role is to define the controlled execution environment through which
valid execution becomes operationally safe, bounded, and governable.
It is not the rule that authorizes action.
It is the architecture that prevents authorized action from escaping
control.
That is why it matters so much in modern AI and autonomous systems.
Closing Statement
Execution begins to matter most at the moment it leaves intention and
enters consequence.
Harness Architecture Standard defines the boundary where
permission stops being enough and containment becomes
mandatory.
Related Documents
→ Harness Architecture Standard

chunks.text:
EBM — Execution Boundary Module
EBM — Execution Boundary Module
Parent Standard: Harness Architecture Standard
Parent Architecture: Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Execution Boundaries
Type: Execution Containment Module
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 May 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Harness Architecture Standard · Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard · RIS · INTEGROS® · OGL™ · ART · OIB™
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Execution Boundary Module defines the structural conditions under
which a system establishes, preserves, and enforces the boundary of its
executable action environment.
A system satisfies EBM only if:
the execution boundary is explicitly defined
executable space is distinguishable from non-executable space
action surfaces remain bounded under governed conditions
boundary crossing is restricted, traceable, and non-silent
execution does not proceed outside the defined containment environment
A system that cannot define where execution is allowed to occur does not
satisfy EBM.
Module Function
EBM defines the primary containment boundary of execution.
It ensures that execution is not treated as a free operational field,
but as an activity that must occur only inside a defined, governed, and
limited environment.

The module applies wherever systems must distinguish between:
what may be executed
where it may be executed
what remains outside valid execution scope
when execution must stop at the boundary rather than continue across it
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Define the Execution Environment
The organization must define the contained environment in which
execution is permitted.
Minimum requirement:
the execution environment is explicit
permitted execution zones are distinguishable
undefined execution areas are excluded from valid operation
Step 2 — Define Boundary Conditions
The system must define where the execution boundary begins and ends.
Minimum requirement:
boundary conditions are explicit
internal and external execution spaces are distinguishable
silent boundary ambiguity is excluded from valid containment
Step 3 — Define Allowed Action Surface
The system must define what kinds of actions may occur within the
boundary.
Minimum requirement:
executable action types are explicit
non-permitted action surfaces are identifiable
execution does not expand beyond declared operational scope
Step 4 — Define Boundary Crossing Restrictions
The system must define how attempts to move beyond the valid execution
boundary are restricted.
Minimum requirement:
crossing restrictions are explicit
out-of-bound execution is blocked, limited, or escalated
silent execution spillover is excluded from valid operation
Step 5 — Preserve Boundary Traceability

The system must preserve visibility of boundary conditions and any
attempt to approach or cross them.
Minimum requirement:
boundary events are traceable
later review can reconstruct where execution occurred relative to boundary
containment does not depend on invisible assumptions
Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Execution
The system must not be treated as valid if execution occurs outside the
defined containment boundary or if the boundary can be silently widened.
Minimum requirement:
invalid boundary conditions are identifiable
execution outside defined containment is blocked or invalidated
permission alone does not override boundary containment
Use Case 1 — Tool-Using Agent Inside a Controlled Runtime
Scenario
An AI agent is authorized to act inside a contained runtime, but must
not access external execution surfaces beyond its approved environment.
Application
EBM is used to ensure:
the valid execution environment is clearly defined
external execution surfaces remain outside boundary
boundary crossing attempts are restricted
execution remains traceable relative to containment limits
Result
The organization gains a stronger basis for preventing authorized
execution from silently expanding into uncontrolled action space.
Use Case 2 — Enterprise Workflow with Restricted Operational Zone
Scenario
A system may process, transform, and prepare actions internally, but
must not directly execute beyond a defined operational boundary without
controlled transition.
Application

EBM is used to ensure:
internal execution space is explicit
the outer operational boundary is governed
non-permitted execution zones are blocked
boundary crossing cannot occur silently through convenience or hidden path
Result
The organization gains a structurally governed execution perimeter
instead of relying on assumed separation between internal logic and
external effect.
Canonical Closing Statement
If execution has no governed boundary, containment does not exist.
Related Documents
→ Harness Architecture Standard

chunks.text:
ETTM — Execution Traceability Transition Module
ETTM — Execution Traceability Transition Module
Parent Standard: Harness Architecture Standard
Parent Architecture: Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Execution Traceability Transition
Type: Execution Containment Module
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 May 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Harness Architecture Standard · Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard · RIS · INTEGROS® · OGL™ · ART · OIB™ · EVIP®
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Execution Traceability Transition Module defines the structural
conditions under which the transition from internal decision, runtime
process, or contained execution into external action, released
output, or operational consequence remains fully traceable,
attributable, and reconstructable.
A system satisfies ETTM only if:
the transition from decision to execution is explicitly traceable
the transition from execution to external effect is explicitly traceable
the origin, path, and consequence of transition remain reconstructable
no silent gap exists between contained execution and operational effect
execution does not cross into consequence through opaque, detached, or non-attributable transition paths
A system that cannot trace the transition from internal execution to
external consequence does not satisfy ETTM.

Module Function
ETTM defines the transition-traceability layer of execution containment.
It ensures that contained execution does not lose accountability
at the critical point where internal activity becomes external effect.
The module applies wherever systems move from:
internal decision to action
runtime process to released output
contained execution to operational consequence
generated result to external impact
bounded environment to real-world effect
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Define Transition Points
The organization must define where execution transitions into external
consequence.
Minimum requirement:
transition points are explicit
internal and external phases are distinguishable
undefined transition boundaries are excluded from valid operation
Step 2 — Define Origin Linkage
The system must define how external effect remains linked to originating
execution.
Minimum requirement:
origin linkage is explicit
source decision, runtime event, or execution path is attributable
detached consequence is excluded from valid transition logic
Step 3 — Define Transition Path
The system must define through which path execution becomes external
effect.
Minimum requirement:
transition pathway is explicit
intermediate stages are identifiable
hidden or silent transition paths are excluded from valid containment
Step 4 — Define Consequence Attribution
The system must define how the resulting external effect is attributed
back to execution.
Minimum requirement:

consequence attribution is explicit
output, action, or effect is not treated as independent from execution source
unbound consequence is excluded from valid operation
Step 5 — Preserve Transition Traceability
The system must preserve visibility of what crossed the boundary, when
it crossed, why it crossed, and under which condition.
Minimum requirement:
transition events are traceable
later review can reconstruct the full path from execution to consequence
transition does not become opaque after operational effect occurs
Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Transition
The system must not be treated as valid if execution produces external
consequence through untraceable, detached, or structurally hidden
transition paths.
Minimum requirement:
invalid transition conditions are identifiable
non-attributable transition is blocked or invalidated
external effect alone does not justify missing transition traceability
Use Case 1 — AI Agent Moving from Draft to External Action
Scenario
An AI agent generates internal outputs, drafts, or execution candidates
inside a contained environment, and one of them later becomes an
external message, released file, or triggered action.
Application
ETTM is used to ensure:
the transition point is explicit
the released consequence remains linked to originating execution
intermediate steps are traceable
no opaque jump occurs between internal generation and external release
Result
The organization gains a stronger basis for proving how contained

execution became external effect and under which governed transition
path that happened.
Use Case 2 — Enterprise Runtime Triggering Operational Consequence
Scenario
A runtime system processes internal execution steps and then creates an
external operational effect such as a workflow trigger, file write,
approval action, or downstream system event.
Application
ETTM is used to ensure:
transition boundaries are governed
origin linkage remains preserved
consequence attribution remains reconstructable
operational effect does not occur through silent transition loss
Result
The organization gains a structurally governed traceability bridge
between contained execution and real operational consequence.
Canonical Closing Statement
If execution crosses into consequence without traceable
transition, execution containment has not been achieved.
Related Documents
→ Harness Architecture Standard
