About Authority Integrity Standard (AIS)
About Authority Integrity Standard (AIS)
Governing Identity Authority
Authority Integrity Standard (AIS) defines the governance conditions
under which authority over a governed identity remains legitimate,
attributable, verifiable, delegated, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
A governed identity may have an owner.
It may also have one or more authorized authorities acting on
its behalf.
AIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Identity Authority?
Identity authority is the governed relationship that determines who
may legitimately control, administer, represent, manage, or exercise
governance rights over a governed identity while preserving governance
integrity, accountability, and trust.
It enables organizations to establish legitimate authority, delegate
governance rights, validate authority relationships, preserve
authority boundaries, and ensure that every governance action remains
authorized throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Canonical Definition
Authority Integrity Standard (AIS) defines the structural conditions
under which authority over a governed identity remains legitimate,
attributable, verifiable, delegated, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why AIS Exists
Ownership alone does not determine who may legitimately act.
Organizations delegate authority.
Individuals authorize representatives.

Digital identities may be governed by designated administrators.
Without governed authority, governance actions become ambiguous,
permissions lose legitimacy, accountability weakens, and
trust deteriorates.
AIS exists because Identity Authority represents the fourth governable
space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
What AIS Governs
AIS governs the structural conditions under which identity
authority remains:
legitimate,
attributable,
verifiable,
delegated,
bounded,
governable.
Rather than governing organizational hierarchies or legal
authorization frameworks, AIS governs the governance conditions
required for trustworthy identity authority.
Architectural Position
Authority Integrity Standard serves as the fourth governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that determines who may
legitimately exercise governance over a governed identity before
permissions are granted, responsibilities are assigned, provenance is
established, transfers occur, continuity is preserved, and
auditability is achieved.
Without governed authority, trustworthy identity governance cannot
be sustained.
Canonical Closing Statement
Ownership answers who possesses a governed identity. Authority answers
who may legitimately govern it. Authority Integrity preserves this
distinction by ensuring that every exercise of authority remains
legitimate throughout the complete identity lifecycle.

Core Question
Can every governance aspect of a governed identity be
independently verified?
Canonical Definition
Auditability Integrity Standard (AUDIS) defines the structural
conditions under which every governance aspect of a governed identity
remains independently reviewable, verifiable, evidence-supported,
traceable, and continuously governable throughout the complete
identity lifecycle.
AUDIS governs identity auditability.

The standard establishes the governance conditions required to ensure
that every governance decision, relationship, responsibility,
transfer, continuity event, and supporting evidence associated with a
governed identity can be independently examined and verified.
Governance creates trust.
Auditability proves that trust.
AUDIS governs that proof.
Governance Flow Position
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
Standard Abstract
Trustworthy governance requires independent verification.
Every governed identity should be capable of demonstrating how it was
created, governed, modified, transferred, and preserved throughout
its lifecycle.
Without governed auditability:
governance cannot be independently verified,
evidence loses operational value,
accountability weakens,
compliance becomes uncertain,
long-term governance trust declines.
AUDIS establishes the governance conditions required for transparent,
evidence-based, and continuously verifiable identity governance.
Operational Role
Auditability Integrity Standard provides the governance layer
responsible for governing how the complete governance lifecycle of a
governed identity remains independently reviewable and
continuously verifiable.
Its role is to ensure that every governance element remains supported
by authentic evidence, complete traceability, and transparent
governance records.
Operational Space
AUDIS governs:
audit trails,

evidence verification,
relationship auditing,
compliance auditing,
integrity verification,
governance review,
lifecycle auditability,
identity auditability.
This governed space ensures that identity governance remains
continuously transparent, independently verifiable, and trustworthy
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why This Standard Exists
Governance without verification depends on trust alone.
Trustworthy governance requires evidence.
Auditability transforms governance claims into independently
verifiable governance reality.
AUDIS exists because Identity Auditability represents the tenth
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.

AI identities,

Together these architectures ensure that every governed identity
remains independently verifiable, evidence-supported, transparent, and

continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle.

Trustworthy identity requires trustworthy auditability. Every governed
identity must remain independently verifiable through authentic
evidence, complete traceability, and transparent governance throughout
its complete identity lifecycle.

verification. Auditability Integrity ensures that every governed
identity can demonstrate—not merely claim—its authenticity, governance
history, and integrity throughout the complete identity lifecycle.

About Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS)
About Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS)
Governing Continuity Integrity
Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS) defines the governance conditions
under which a governed identity preserves its continuity, legitimacy,
traceability, provenance, governance relationships, and continuous
governability throughout the complete identity lifecycle despite
legitimate lifecycle changes.
Governed identities may evolve.
They may be inherited, merged, replaced, or transferred.
CIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Continuity Integrity?
Continuity integrity is the governed condition in which a governed
identity remains continuously recognizable, attributable, traceable,
and governance-valid despite legitimate lifecycle transitions.
It enables organizations to preserve identity continuity across
succession, inheritance, mergers, replacements, platform changes, and
other governance-approved lifecycle events without compromising
governance trust.
Canonical Definition

traceability, provenance, governance relationships, and continuous
governability throughout the complete identity lifecycle despite
legitimate lifecycle changes.
Why CIS Exists
Governed identities are expected to exist beyond individual owners,
organizations, technologies, and operational environments.

Without governed continuity, governance relationships become
fragmented, provenance loses meaning, long-term accountability
weakens, and identity trust cannot be sustained.
CIS exists because Continuity Integrity represents the ninth
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.
What CIS Governs
CIS governs the structural conditions under which identity
continuity remains:
continuous,
legitimate,
traceable,
attributable,
verifiable,
governable.
Rather than governing backup systems, synchronization technologies, or
technical migration processes, CIS governs the governance conditions
required for trustworthy continuity integrity.
Architectural Position
Continuity Integrity Standard serves as the ninth governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that preserves the identity
itself across legitimate lifecycle transitions before complete
governance auditability is established.
Without governed continuity, trustworthy identity governance cannot
survive the passage of time.
Canonical Closing Statement
Time changes identities, but governance must preserve their
continuity. Continuity Integrity ensures that every governed identity
remains continuously recognizable, trustworthy, and governable
throughout its complete identity lifecycle.

Governing Identity Integrity
Identity Integrity Standard (IIS) defines the governance conditions
under which governed identity remains unique, authentic, verifiable,
distinguishable, and continuously governable throughout the complete
identity lifecycle.
Origin determines where identity begins.
Identity determines what the governed entity is.
IIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Identity Integrity?

remains uniquely identifiable, authentic, classifiable, verifiable,
and protected from ambiguity, duplication, substitution, or identity
corruption throughout its complete lifecycle.

identity continuity, validate identity authenticity, and ensure that
every governed identity remains consistently recognizable across
systems, organizations, platforms, and future
operational environments.

under which a governed identity remains unique, authentic,
distinguishable, classifiable, verifiable, and continuously governable
throughout its complete lifecycle.

governance cannot reliably operate.

space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.

unique,
authentic,

under which a governed identity remains unique, authentic,
distinguishable, classifiable, verifiable, and continuously governable
throughout its complete lifecycle.

Origin establishes where a governed identity begins.
Identity establishes what the governed entity is.

uniqueness cannot be guaranteed,
attribution becomes unreliable,
ownership cannot be established,
authority becomes ambiguous,
governance loses precision.
IIS establishes the governance conditions required for trustworthy
identity integrity throughout the complete identity lifecycle.

Identity Integrity Standard provides the governance layer responsible
for preserving the uniqueness, authenticity, classification,
verification, and lifecycle integrity of governed identities.
Its role is to ensure that every governed identity remains
consistently identifiable throughout its complete lifecycle.

identity uniqueness,
identity validation,

governed identity integrity,
identity authenticity,
trustworthy identity management.
This governed space ensures that every identity remains unique,

verifiable, and continuously governable throughout its
complete lifecycle.

Governed identity cannot exist without a trustworthy identity.
Origin establishes where identity begins.
Identity establishes what exists.
IIS exists because Identity Integrity represents the second governable
space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.

AI identities,
autonomous agents,
robotics,
digital assets,
organizations,

critical infrastructure,
future intelligent ecosystems.

ASGA™ for autonomous operational governance.
Together these architectures ensure that governed identities remain
unique, authentic, attributable, and continuously governable
throughout their complete lifecycle.
Foundational Principle
Trustworthy governance requires trustworthy identity. Every governed
identity must remain unique, authentic, verifiable, and continuously
governable throughout its complete lifecycle.
Canonical Closing Statement
Identity transforms origin into a governable entity. By preserving
identity integrity, IIS ensures that every governed identity remains

unique, distinguishable, authentic, and trustworthy as it progresses

About Origin Integrity Standard (OIS)
Governing Origin Integrity
Origin Integrity Standard (OIS) defines the governance conditions
under which the origin of a governed identity remains authentic,
verifiable, attributable, traceable, and continuously governable
throughout its complete lifecycle.
Every governed identity begins with an origin.
That origin establishes the governance foundation upon which identity,
ownership, authority, responsibility, and trust are built.
OIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Origin Integrity?
Origin integrity is the governed condition under which the origin of
an identity can be established, verified, attributed, and continuously
preserved throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
It enables organizations to establish trustworthy identity
foundations, preserve attribution, validate origin authenticity,
maintain governance continuity, and ensure that every governed
identity remains connected to its legitimate origin.
Canonical Definition
Origin Integrity Standard (OIS) defines the structural conditions
under which the origin of a governed identity remains authentic,
verifiable, attributable, traceable, and continuously governable
throughout its complete lifecycle.
Why OIS Exists
Governed identity cannot begin with ownership, authority, permission,
or responsibility.
It must begin with a trustworthy origin.
OIS exists because origin represents the first governable space of

OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.

OIS governs the structural conditions under which identity
origin remains:
authentic,
verifiable,
attributable,
traceable,
trustworthy,
governable.
Rather than governing identity technologies or identity management
platforms, OIS governs the governance conditions required for
establishing trustworthy identity origin.

Origin Integrity Standard serves as the first governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation upon which identity,
ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance,
transfer, continuity, and auditability are built.
Without governed origin, trustworthy governed identity cannot exist.
Canonical Closing Statement
Trustworthy identity begins with trustworthy origin. Origin Integrity
establishes the governance foundation that enables every governed
identity to remain authentic, verifiable, attributable, and
continuously connected to its legitimate origin throughout its
complete lifecycle.

Core Question
Where did the governed identity originate?
Canonical Definition
Origin Integrity Standard (OIS) defines the structural conditions
under which the origin of a governed identity remains authentic,
attributable, verifiable, traceable, and continuously governable
throughout its complete lifecycle.
OIS governs origin integrity.
The standard establishes the governance conditions required to ensure
that every governed identity begins from a legitimate, verifiable, and

attributable origin before identity, ownership, authority, permission,
responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, or auditability can
be established.
Every governed identity begins with origin.
Governance preserves trust in that origin.
OIS governs that origin.
Governance Flow Position
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
Standard Abstract
Every governed identity begins somewhere.
Without a trustworthy origin:
identity cannot be reliably established,
ownership cannot be confidently assigned,
authority cannot be legitimately delegated,
provenance cannot be continuously reconstructed,
long-term trust becomes difficult to preserve.
OIS establishes the governance conditions required for trustworthy,
attributable, and continuously governable identity origin.
Operational Role
Origin Integrity Standard provides the governance layer responsible
for establishing the legitimate beginning of every governed identity.
Its role is to ensure that identity origin remains authentic,
verifiable, attributable, and continuously governable throughout the
complete identity lifecycle.
Operational Space

origin creation,
origin verification,
origin attribution,
origin traceability,
origin continuity,
origin evidence,
origin legitimacy,
trustworthy identity origin.
This governed space ensures that every governed identity begins from a
trustworthy governance foundation.
Why This Standard Exists

Governed identity cannot begin with ownership, authority,
or responsibility.
It must begin with origin.
OIS exists because origin represents the first governable space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
Scope
This standard may be applied across:
AI identities,
autonomous agents,
robotics,
digital assets,
organizations,
human identities,
digital twins,
enterprise identity systems,
public-sector identity infrastructures,
future intelligent ecosystems.

It interoperates with:

CLIA® for cognition,
MGIA™ for memory governance,
ASGA™ for autonomous operational governance.
Together these architectures ensure that governed identities begin
from a trustworthy, attributable, and continuously governable origin.

Trustworthy identity begins with trustworthy origin. Every governed
identity must remain continuously connected to its legitimate origin
throughout its complete lifecycle.

Origin is the first governance anchor of identity. By governing origin
itself, OIS establishes the trusted foundation upon which identity,
ownership, authority, responsibility, provenance, continuity, and
auditability can exist throughout the complete lifecycle of a
governed identity.

About Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS)
About Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS)
Governing Ownership Integrity
Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS) defines the governance conditions
under which ownership of a governed identity remains legitimate,
attributable, verifiable, transferable, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Origin establishes where identity begins.
Identity establishes what exists.
Ownership establishes to whom the governed identity
legitimately belongs.
OWIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Ownership Integrity?
Ownership integrity is the governed condition in which ownership of a
governed identity remains legitimate, continuously attributable,
independently verifiable, protected from unauthorized claims, and
preserved throughout its complete lifecycle.
It enables organizations to establish lawful ownership, validate
ownership claims, resolve ownership conflicts, preserve ownership
continuity, and ensure that every governed identity remains under
legitimate governance.
Canonical Definition
Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS) defines the structural conditions
under which ownership of a governed identity remains legitimate,
attributable, verifiable, transferable, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why OWIS Exists
A governed identity cannot participate in trusted governance unless
its legitimate owner is known.
Without governed ownership, authority cannot be legitimately

exercised, permissions cannot be reliably granted, responsibility
cannot be fairly assigned, and governance disputes become difficult
to resolve.
OWIS exists because Ownership Integrity represents the third
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.
What OWIS Governs
OWIS governs the structural conditions under which ownership remains:
legitimate,
attributable,
verifiable,
transferable,
continuous,
governable.
Rather than governing legal property systems or contractual ownership
mechanisms, OWIS governs the governance conditions required for
trustworthy ownership integrity.
Architectural Position
Ownership Integrity Standard serves as the third governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that connects a governed
identity with its legitimate owner before authority, permissions,
responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability can
be governed.
Without governed ownership, the remaining governance relationships
cannot be established with confidence.
Canonical Closing Statement
Origin creates identity. Identity enables ownership. Ownership
Integrity establishes the trusted governance relationship that
connects every governed identity to its legitimate owner throughout
its complete lifecycle.

About Permission Integrity Standard (PIS)
Governing Permission Integrity
Permission Integrity Standard (PIS) defines the governance conditions
under which permissions associated with a governed identity remain
legitimate, attributable, verifiable, enforceable, revocable, and

Authority establishes who may govern.

What Is Permission Integrity?
Permission integrity is the governed condition in which every
permission associated with a governed identity remains explicitly
authorized, appropriately limited, independently verifiable,
continuously enforceable, and compatible with governance throughout
the complete identity lifecycle.
It enables organizations to grant permissions, control access,
regulate identity usage, authorize modifications, revoke privileges,
and ensure that every permitted action remains legitimate
and governance-approved.
Canonical Definition

under which permissions associated with a governed identity remain
legitimate, attributable, verifiable, enforceable, revocable, and
continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why PIS Exists
Legitimate authority does not automatically grant unlimited rights.
Every governance action requires appropriate permission.

Without governed permissions, authority may be misused, excessive
privileges may emerge, governance boundaries become unclear, and
identity integrity may be compromised.
PIS exists because Permission Integrity represents the fifth
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.
What PIS Governs
PIS governs the structural conditions under which permissions remain:
legitimate,
attributable,
verifiable,
enforceable,
revocable,
governable.
Rather than governing authentication technologies or access-control
implementations, PIS governs the governance conditions required for
trustworthy permission integrity.

Permission Integrity Standard serves as the fifth governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that determines what
legitimate authorities may actually do before responsibility is
assigned, provenance is established, transfers occur, continuity is
preserved, and auditability is achieved.
Without governed permissions, trustworthy identity governance cannot
be sustained.
Canonical Closing Statement
Authority determines who may govern. Permission determines what may be
done. Permission Integrity preserves governance trust by ensuring that
every authorized action remains legitimate throughout the complete
identity lifecycle.

About Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS)
Governing Responsibility Integrity
Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS) defines the governance
conditions under which responsibility associated with a governed
identity remains legitimate, attributable, verifiable, continuous, and
continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Authority determines who may act.
Permissions determine what actions are permitted.
Responsibility determines who remains answerable for those actions.
RIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Responsibility Integrity?
Responsibility integrity is the governed condition in which
responsibility associated with a governed identity remains clearly
assigned, continuously attributable, independently verifiable,
preserved across governance changes, and compatible with governance
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
It enables organizations to assign responsibility, coordinate shared
responsibilities, preserve responsibility continuity, attribute
governance consequences, and ensure that every governed identity
remains connected to accountable participants.
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibility associated with a governed
identity remains legitimate, attributable, verifiable, continuous, and
continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why RIS Exists

Governance cannot exist without responsibility.
Every governance action produces accountable participants.
Without governed responsibility, accountability becomes fragmented,
governance obligations become unclear, and identity governance loses
trust and continuity.
RIS exists because Responsibility Integrity represents the sixth
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.

RIS governs the structural conditions under which
responsibility remains:
legitimate,
attributable,
verifiable,
continuous,
traceable,
governable.
Rather than governing legal liability or organizational reporting
structures, RIS governs the governance conditions required for
trustworthy responsibility integrity.

Responsibility Integrity Standard serves as the sixth governance space
of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that connects every governed
identity with accountable participants before provenance is
established, transfers occur, continuity is preserved, and
auditability is achieved.
Without governed responsibility, trustworthy identity governance
cannot be sustained.
Canonical Closing Statement
Authority enables governance. Permissions enable action.
Responsibility preserves accountability. Responsibility Integrity
ensures that every governed identity remains continuously connected to
those responsible for its governance throughout the complete

identity lifecycle.

Governed Space
Identity Responsibility
Core Question
Who remains responsible for a governed identity and its
governed actions?
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibility associated with a governed
identity remains legitimate, attributable, verifiable, continuous, and
continuously governable throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
RIS governs identity responsibility.

The standard establishes the governance conditions required to ensure
that every governed identity has clearly attributable, continuously
traceable, and governance-valid responsibility throughout its
complete lifecycle.
Authority determines who may act.
Responsibility determines who remains accountable for those actions.
RIS governs that responsibility.
Governance Flow Position
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
Standard Abstract
Every governed action produces responsibility.
Every governance decision creates accountable participants.
Without governed responsibility:
accountability becomes fragmented,
responsibility may become ambiguous,
governance obligations may be avoided,
operational trust declines,
governance reconstruction becomes difficult.
RIS establishes the governance conditions required for legitimate,
attributable, and continuously governable responsibility.
Operational Role
Responsibility Integrity Standard provides the governance layer
responsible for governing how responsibility is assigned, shared,
transferred, preserved, and continuously governed throughout the
complete identity lifecycle.
Its role is to ensure that every governance responsibility remains
legitimate, attributable, traceable, and governance- approved.
Operational Space
RIS governs:
responsibility assignment,
shared responsibility,
responsibility escalation,
responsibility continuity,

consequence attribution,
governance responsibility,
accountable participation,
identity responsibility.
This governed space ensures that responsibility remains continuously
compatible with trustworthy identity governance.
Why This Standard Exists
A governed identity cannot exist without clearly
defined responsibility.
Ownership identifies who possesses the identity.
Authority determines who may govern it.
Permissions determine what may be done.
Responsibility determines who remains answerable for
governance outcomes.
RIS exists because Identity Responsibility represents the sixth
governable space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity
Governance Architecture.
Scope
This standard may be applied across:
AI identities,
digital identities,
human identities,
enterprise identity platforms,
autonomous agents,
robotics,
digital assets,
organizational identity systems,
public-sector identity infrastructures,
cross-platform identity ecosystems.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
RIS governs identity responsibility.
It interoperates with:
GOA™ for governance responsibility,
ORA™ for operational responsibility,
AGA™ for accountability,
AIG® for behavioral governance,
CLIA® for cognition,
MGIA™ for memory governance,
ASGA™ for autonomous operational responsibility.
Together these architectures ensure that responsibility remains
legitimate, attributable, continuous, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Foundational Principle

Trustworthy identity requires trustworthy responsibility. Every
governed identity must remain connected to clearly attributable
responsibility throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Canonical Closing Statement
Authority enables action. Responsibility preserves accountability.
Responsibility Integrity ensures that every governed identity remains
connected to those responsible for its governance, decisions, and
consequences throughout the complete identity lifecycle.

About Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS)
About Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS)
Governing Transfer Integrity
Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS) defines the governance conditions
under which a governed identity and its associated governance
relationships may be transferred while preserving legitimacy,
continuity, traceability, accountability, and continuous governability
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Governed identities may change owners.
They may change authorities, platforms, organizations,
or jurisdictions.
TIS governs this identity governance space.
What Is Transfer Integrity?
Transfer integrity is the governed condition in which a governed
identity and its associated governance relationships are transferred
without compromising identity integrity, provenance, accountability,
continuity, or governance trust.
It enables organizations to transfer ownership, authority,
permissions, responsibilities, and governed identities while
preserving complete governance continuity and independently verifiable
lifecycle history.
Canonical Definition
Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS) defines the structural conditions
under which a governed identity and its associated governance
relationships may be transferred while preserving legitimacy,
continuity, traceability, accountability, and continuous governability
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Why TIS Exists
Governed identities are not permanently tied to one owner, platform,
organization, or generation.

Without governed transfer, governance continuity may be interrupted,
provenance becomes fragmented, authority becomes unclear, and identity
trust may be lost.
TIS exists because Transfer Integrity represents the eighth governable
space of OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
What TIS Governs
TIS governs the structural conditions under which identity
transfer remains:
legitimate,
traceable,
continuous,
accountable,
verifiable,
governable.
Rather than governing technical migration tools or data transfer
technologies, TIS governs the governance conditions required for
trustworthy transfer integrity.
Architectural Position
Transfer Integrity Standard serves as the eighth governance space of
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
It establishes the governance foundation that enables governed
identities to move across ownership, authority, organizations,
platforms, and jurisdictions without breaking governance continuity
before long-term continuity and auditability are established.
Without governed transfer, trustworthy identity governance cannot
survive legitimate change.
Canonical Closing Statement
Identity may move, but governance trust must move with it. Transfer
Integrity ensures that every legitimate transfer preserves the
complete governance relationship of a governed identity throughout the
complete identity lifecycle.

→ Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS)

Ownership Transfer Module (OTRM) defines the structural conditions
under which ownership of a governed identity is transferred while
preserving legitimacy, provenance, accountability, continuity, and
continuous governability throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
OTRM governs ownership transfer.
The module establishes the governance conditions required to ensure
that every ownership transfer remains authorized, verifiable,
traceable, and governance-approved before ownership changes
become effective.
Ownership may change.
Identity integrity must not.
OTRM governs that transfer.
Module Operational Role
OTRM defines the ownership transfer layer of TIS.

Its role is to govern the legitimate transfer of ownership while
preserving the complete governance history of the governed identity.
Module Operational Space
OTRM governs:
ownership transfer,
ownership succession,
ownership reassignment,
governance-approved ownership change,
ownership verification,
ownership continuity,
transfer authorization,
ownership governance.
Module Function
The module applies wherever ownership of a governed identity must be
transferred between legitimate participants.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Define the Ownership Transfer Object
Identify the governed identity and the ownership relationship
requiring transfer.
2. Define Transfer Conditions
Establish governance conditions governing ownership authorization,
verification, acceptance, traceability, and governance approval.
3. Define Transfer Failure Logic
Identify conditions where ownership transfer becomes unauthorized,
disputed, incomplete, unverifiable, or governance- invalid.
4. Define Governance Response
Define governance actions for approval, rejection, suspension,
investigation, correction, or governance escalation.
5. Preserve Transfer Records
Preserve ownership transfer records, governance decisions, supporting
evidence, provenance updates, and transfer history.
Use Case 1 — Enterprise Digital Identity
Scenario
A strategic enterprise identity is transferred to a new legal owner
following a corporate acquisition.
Application

OTRM governs the ownership transition and preserves the complete
governance history.
Result
Ownership changes without compromising identity integrity or
governance continuity.
Use Case 2 — AI Identity Governance
Scenario
Ownership of a governed AI identity is transferred from one
organization to another.
Application
OTRM verifies the legitimacy of the transfer and preserves the
complete provenance chain.
Result
The AI identity retains continuous governance integrity throughout the
ownership transition.
Canonical Closing Statement
Ownership may legitimately change, but governance trust must never
restart. Ownership Transfer preserves identity integrity by ensuring
that every new owner inherits a governed identity with its complete
history, legitimacy, and continuity intact throughout the complete
identity lifecycle.

About Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®)
About Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®)
Governing Identity
Identity exists everywhere.
Every person, organization, AI system, autonomous agent, digital
asset, robotic system, and governed object depends upon identity.
Technology evolves.
Platforms change.
Identity providers change.
Implementation models change.
Identity governance must remain stable.
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®) was created
to provide a stable identity governance architecture that remains
applicable regardless of how identity technologies continue to evolve.
OBIDENITY® does not govern identity providers, authentication systems,
credentials, registries, software platforms, or
implementation technologies.
OBIDENITY® governs identity.
Why OBIDENITY® Exists
Most identity initiatives focus on authentication, authorization,
access management, digital credentials, identity providers, security,
or technical implementation.
These perspectives are essential, but they do not fully answer a more
fundamental question:
How should identity itself be governed?
OBIDENITY® addresses this question by defining the governable identity
spaces that exist throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Rather than standardizing identity technology, OBIDENITY® standardizes
the governance conditions that enable identity to remain uniquely
identifiable, attributable, ownable, governable, transferable,

continuous, and independently verifiable.
Identity Before Technology
The objective of OBIDENITY® is not to define how identities
are implemented.
The objective is to define how identity remains governable.
Every identifiable entity possesses identity.
Every identity creates governance relationships.
Every governance relationship requires trustworthy identity.
OBIDENITY® therefore treats identity as an independent
governance domain.
The Identity Governance Architecture
OBIDENITY® consists of ten independent identity governance spaces.
Each space answers one architectural question.
Each space governs one identity condition.
Each space begins where the previous space ends.
Together these spaces form the complete identity
governance architecture.
The architecture progresses through:
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
This progression represents the complete governance journey of
identity—from establishing legitimate origin to independently
verifying the complete identity lifecycle.
Identity Governance Spaces Rather Than Technical Components
OBIDENITY® does not organize identity governance around
software components.
Instead, it organizes governance around identity spaces.
Each identity governance space represents a distinct governance
responsibility that exists independently of any specific identity
platform, authentication mechanism, identity provider, registry,

vendor, or implementation technology.
Because identity governance spaces are technology-neutral, the
architecture remains applicable even as identity technologies continue
to evolve.
A Methodology Rather Than an Implementation
OBIDENITY® is a governance methodology.
It is not an implementation framework.
The architecture defines what identity governance conditions must
remain true.
Organizations remain free to determine how those conditions are
implemented within their own operational, regulatory, organizational,
and technical environments.
This separation allows OBIDENITY® to remain stable while
implementation methods continue to evolve.
Who May Benefit
OBIDENITY® may support:
organizations,
public institutions,
identity governance teams,
enterprise architects,
AI developers,
autonomous system developers,
digital identity providers,
digital asset platforms,
auditors,
regulators,
cross-platform ecosystems,
future intelligent environments.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
OBIDENITY® governs identity.
It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures.
GOA™ governs governance itself.
ORA™ governs operational reality.
AGA™ governs accountability relationships.
AIG® governs AI behavior.
CLIA® governs cognition and reasoning.
MGIA™ governs memory and memory continuity.
ASGA™ governs autonomous systems.
Together these architectures create a structured methodology for
governing increasingly complex digital, organizational, autonomous,
and intelligent environments.

The Long-Term Vision
As identities increasingly move across organizations, platforms,
autonomous systems, AI ecosystems, digital assets, and future
intelligent infrastructures, identity governance will become as
fundamental as identity itself.
The long-term objective of OBIDENITY® is to provide a common identity
governance language that enables organizations to identify, classify,
govern, transfer, preserve, audit, and continuously protect identity
regardless of future technological change.
Canonical Principle
Identity technologies will continue to evolve. Identity governance
must remain stable. OBIDENITY® therefore governs the structural
conditions that remain valid regardless of future identity
technologies, platforms, and implementation models.
Canonical Closing Statement
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®) provides
the identity governance foundation through which identity can be
established, governed, attributed, transferred, preserved, audited,
and continuously verified. By defining the governable spaces of
identity, OBIDENITY® establishes a technology-neutral methodology for
ensuring that identity remains trustworthy, attributable, governable,
and continuous throughout its complete lifecycle.

OBIDENITY® Architecture Map
OBIDENITY® Architecture Map
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture
Official Identity Governance Reference Map for AI Systems, Autonomous
Agents, Human Identities, Digital Assets, Organizations, Robotics,
Cross-Platform Environments, and Future Governed Identity Ecosystems
OBIDENITY® serves as the official identity governance reference map
used to identify, classify, navigate, validate, and understand
identity governance spaces across AI systems, autonomous agents, human
identities, organizations, digital assets, robotics, cross-platform
environments, and future governed identity ecosystems.
The purpose of OBIDENITY® is not to govern identity technology.
The purpose of OBIDENITY® is to identify, define, and map the
governable spaces of identity throughout its complete lifecycle.
OBIDENITY® serves as the official identity governance reference
map for:
AI Systems
Autonomous Agents
Human Identities
Organizations
Digital Assets
Enterprise Identity
Public Identity Infrastructures
Robotics
Cross-Platform Identity
Future Governed Identity Ecosystems
Core Architectural Principle
Every identity governance space answers one primary question.
No identity governance space duplicates the purpose of another
identity governance space.
Every identity governance space begins where the previous identity
governance space ends.
Together these identity governance spaces form the official identity
governance reference map of OBIDENITY®.

Official Identity Governance Flow
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
1. Origin Integrity Standard (OIS)
Governed Space: Origin Integrity
Core Question
Where did the governed identity originate?
Canonical Definition
OIS defines the structural conditions under which the origin of a
governed identity remains authentic, verifiable, attributable,
traceable, and governance-valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when a governed identity is created or recognized.
Ends when its legitimate origin has been established.
2. Identity Integrity Standard (IIS)
Governed Space: Identity Integrity
Core Question
What exactly is the governed identity?
Canonical Definition
IIS defines the structural conditions under which a governed identity
remains uniquely identifiable, authentic, distinguishable, consistent,
and continuously governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when an identity requires unique recognition.
Ends when identity integrity has been established.
3. Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS)
Governed Space: Ownership Integrity
Core Question
Who legitimately owns the governed identity?
Canonical Definition
OWIS defines the structural conditions under which ownership of a
governed identity remains legitimate, verifiable, attributable,
transferable, and governance-valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when ownership must be established.
Ends when legitimate ownership has been verified.

4. Authority Integrity Standard (AIS)
Governed Space: Identity Authority
Core Question
Who has legitimate authority over the governed identity?
Canonical Definition
AIS defines the structural conditions under which governance authority
over a governed identity remains legitimate, accountable, delegated,
verifiable, and continuously governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when governance authority must be assigned.
Ends when legitimate authority has been established.
5. Permission Integrity Standard (PIS)
Governed Space: Permission Integrity
Core Question
Who may legitimately access, use, modify, or interact with the
governed identity?
Canonical Definition
PIS defines the structural conditions under which permissions
associated with a governed identity remain authorized, validated,
governed, enforceable, and continuously manageable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when governed access or interaction requires authorization.
Ends when permissions have been legitimately established.
6. Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS)
Governed Space: Identity Responsibility
Core Question
Who remains responsible for the governed identity and its
governed actions?
Canonical Definition
RIS defines the structural conditions under which responsibility
associated with a governed identity remains attributable, accountable,
traceable, governable, and continuously verifiable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when a governed identity performs or influences
governed activities.

Ends when responsibility has been legitimately established
and maintained.
7. Provenance Integrity Standard (PRIS)
Governed Space: Identity Provenance
Core Question
Can the complete history of the governed identity be proven?
Canonical Definition
PRIS defines the structural conditions under which the provenance of a
governed identity remains authentic, traceable, evidence-supported,
historically verifiable, and continuously governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when governance-relevant events become part of the
identity lifecycle.
Ends when complete provenance has been preserved and can be
independently verified.
8. Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS)
Governed Space: Identity Transfer
Core Question
How can the governed identity be transferred while preserving
governance integrity?
Canonical Definition
TIS defines the structural conditions under which a governed identity
may be transferred while preserving legitimacy, provenance,
continuity, accountability, and governance integrity.
Governance Boundary
Begins when a governed identity changes ownership, authority,
operational control, or governance environment.
Ends when the transfer has been legitimately completed and governance
continuity has been preserved.
9. Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS)
Governed Space: Identity Continuity
Core Question
How can the governed identity remain continuous throughout its
complete identity lifecycle?
Canonical Definition
CIS defines the structural conditions under which a governed identity

preserves its continuity, legitimacy, provenance, governance
relationships, and continuous governability throughout legitimate
lifecycle change.
Governance Boundary
Begins when identity continuity must survive succession, inheritance,
merging, replacement, cloning, migration, or organizational change.
Ends when governance continuity has been successfully preserved.
10. Auditability Integrity Standard (AUDIS)
Governed Space: Identity Auditability
Core Question
Can every governance aspect of the governed identity be
independently verified?
Canonical Definition
AUDIS defines the structural conditions under which every governance
aspect of a governed identity remains independently reviewable,
evidence-supported, traceable, verifiable, and
continuously governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when governance activities require independent verification.
Ends when complete governance auditability has been
successfully demonstrated.
Core Governed Identity Spaces
Origin Integrity
Identity Integrity
Ownership Integrity
Identity Authority
Permission Integrity
Identity Responsibility
Identity Provenance
Identity Transfer
Identity Continuity
Identity Auditability
Architectural Position
OBIDENITY® governs the complete origin-bound identity
governance lifecycle.
The architecture progresses:
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
Together these identity governance spaces govern how identity

originates, becomes uniquely identifiable, acquires legitimate
ownership, receives governance authority, operates through governed
permissions, remains connected to responsibility, preserves its
historical provenance, transfers across legitimate governance
environments, maintains continuity throughout change, and remains
independently auditable throughout its complete identity lifecycle.
What OBIDENITY® Defines
OBIDENITY® defines:
where identity legitimately originates,
where identity becomes uniquely identifiable,
where ownership is established,
where governance authority is assigned,
where permissions are governed,
where responsibility is attributed,
where provenance is preserved,
where identity may be transferred,
where continuity survives legitimate change,
where governance becomes independently auditable.
OBIDENITY® provides the official identity governance language used for
identity space identification, governance classification, lifecycle
governance, and cross-domain identity interoperability across complex
operational ecosystems.
Compatible OOF® Architectures
GOA™ — Governance Architecture
ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture
AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture
AIG® — AI Governance Architecture
CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture
MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture
ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture
Canonical Principle
OBIDENITY® does not govern identity technology, authentication

platforms, identity providers, credentials, registries, or
implementation models. OBIDENITY® governs the structural conditions
under which identity remains origin-bound, uniquely identifiable,
attributable, ownable, authorized, permissioned, responsible,
historically provable, transferable, continuous, and independently
verifiable throughout its complete identity lifecycle.
Canonical Closing Statement
OBIDENITY® serves as the official identity governance reference map
for AI systems, autonomous agents, human identities, organizations,
digital assets, robotics, cross-platform environments, and future
governed identity ecosystems. By defining the primary governable
spaces of identity, OBIDENITY® provides the identity governance
architecture used to identify, classify, navigate, validate, govern,
and preserve identity throughout its complete lifecycle.

OBIDENITY®
OBIDENITY®
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture
Official Identity Governance Architecture for AI Systems, Autonomous
Agents, Digital Assets, Organizations, Human Identities, Robotics,
Cross-Platform Environments, and Future Governed Identity Ecosystems
OBIDENITY® serves as the official OOF® identity governance
architecture used for identity governance design, origin validation,
identity attribution, ownership governance, authority assignment,
permission control, responsibility attribution, provenance
preservation, transfer governance, continuity protection, and identity
auditability across digital, physical, organizational, human,
autonomous, and future intelligent environments.
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®) does not
define identity technology, authentication systems, identity
providers, registries, platforms, or implementation models. OBIDENITY®
defines the governance architecture required to ensure that identity
remains origin-bound, uniquely identifiable, attributable, ownable,
governable, transferable, continuous, and independently verifiable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
OBIDENITY® consists of 10 Core Parent Standards forming the primary
identity governance backbone of governed identity within the
OOF® ecosystem.
Additional compatible standards, bridge standards, domain-specific
identity standards, and implementation modules may extend the
architecture when new identity governance spaces are identified.

However, the standards listed below form the official core identity
governance structure of OBIDENITY®.
Canonical Definition
Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture (OBIDENITY®) is the
identity governance architecture that defines the structural
conditions under which the origin, identity, ownership, authority,
permissions, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and
auditability of an identifiable entity remain legitimate,
attributable, traceable, verifiable, and continuously governable
throughout the complete identity lifecycle.
Core Question
How can identity remain uniquely identifiable, attributable,
governable, transferable, continuous, and independently verifiable
throughout its complete lifecycle?
Governance Flow
Origin → Identity → Ownership → Authority → Permission →
Responsibility → Provenance → Transfer → Continuity → Auditability
Core Parent Standards
1. Origin Integrity Standard (OIS)
Governed Space: Origin Integrity
Core Question: Where did the governed identity originate?
2. Identity Integrity Standard (IIS)
Governed Space: Identity Integrity
Core Question: What exactly is the governed identity?
3. Ownership Integrity Standard (OWIS)
Governed Space: Ownership Integrity
Core Question: Who legitimately owns the governed identity?
4. Authority Integrity Standard (AIS)
Governed Space: Identity Authority
Core Question: Who has legitimate authority over the
governed identity?
5. Permission Integrity Standard (PIS)
Governed Space: Permission Integrity

Core Question: Who may legitimately access, use, modify, or interact
with the governed identity?
6. Responsibility Integrity Standard (RIS)
Governed Space: Identity Responsibility
Core Question: Who remains responsible for the governed identity and
its governed actions?
7. Provenance Integrity Standard (PRIS)
Governed Space: Identity Provenance
Core Question: Can the complete history of the governed identity
be proven?
8. Transfer Integrity Standard (TIS)
Governed Space: Identity Transfer
Core Question: How can the governed identity be transferred while
preserving governance integrity?
9. Continuity Integrity Standard (CIS)
Governed Space: Identity Continuity
Core Question: How can the governed identity remain continuous
throughout its complete lifecycle?
10. Auditability Integrity Standard (AUDIS)
Governed Space: Identity Auditability
Core Question: Can every governance aspect of the governed identity be
independently verified?
Compatible OOF® Architectures
OBIDENITY® interoperates with multiple OOF® architectures governing
complementary governance, accountability, cognition, memory, behavior,
operational reality, and autonomous-system spaces.
GOA™ — Governance Architecture provides the constitutional governance
layer defining how governance authority, boundaries, scope,
delegation, accountability, validation, integrity, transparency,
continuity, and interoperability are structured.
ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs operational reality,

operational validity, responsibility, authority, evidence,
coordination, and recovery across complex operational environments.
AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability
relationships, authority validation, responsibility assignment,
decision accountability, evidence accountability, continuity, and
accountability chains.
AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs the behavioral conditions
under which AI behavior remains bounded, auditable,
evidence-supported, trusted, correctable, interoperable, and safe.
CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture governs
cognition, interpretation, reasoning, cognitive reality modeling,
Human-AI cognition, collective cognition, and cognitive evolution.
MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture governs memory
integrity, agent memory, user memory, collective memory, temporal
continuity, multimodal memory, and memory evolution.
ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous
operational identity, authority, execution, constraints, risk,
coordination, escalation, accountability, compatibility,
and evolution.
OBIDENITY® serves as the foundational identity governance architecture
that establishes who or what exists, where it originated, to whom it
belongs, under whose authority it operates, what permissions apply,
who remains responsible, how its history is preserved, how it may
transfer, how continuity survives change, and how the complete

identity lifecycle can be independently verified.
Architectural Position
OBIDENITY® governs the complete origin-bound identity
governance lifecycle.
The architecture progresses through:
Origin Integrity → Identity Integrity → Ownership Integrity → Identity
Authority → Permission Integrity → Identity Responsibility → Identity
Provenance → Identity Transfer → Identity Continuity →
Identity Auditability
Together these standards govern how identity originates, becomes
identifiable, connects to ownership, receives authority, operates
through permissions, remains connected to responsibility, develops
provenance, transfers across legitimate environments, preserves
continuity through change, and remains independently auditable
throughout its complete lifecycle.
OBIDENITY® is not limited to one identity type.
It may govern:
human identity,
organizational identity,
AI identity,
autonomous-agent identity,
robotic identity,
asset identity,
document identity,
product identity,
digital-twin identity,
cross-platform identity,
inherited identity,
and future forms of governable identity.
The architecture is implementation-neutral.
A governed identity may be represented through centralized
infrastructure, distributed systems, enterprise platforms, public
registries, digital credentials, physical identifiers, cryptographic
systems, or future technologies.
The implementation may change.
The governance identity must remain continuously connected to its
origin, relationships, history, and evidence.

Strategic Position
Identity systems traditionally focus on identification,
authentication, access, or credential management.
OBIDENITY® defines a broader governance space.
It governs not only whether an entity can be recognized, but also:
where the identity originated,
whether the identity is unique,
who owns it,
who controls it,
who may use or modify it,
who remains responsible,
whether its history can be proven,
whether it can be transferred,
whether it survives succession, inheritance, cloning, merging, replacement, and technological change,
and whether every identity governance relationship can be independently audited.

complete lifecycle.

OBIDENITY™ Identity Governance Rules
OBIDENITY™ Identity Governance Rules
Rule Layer for Identity Creation, Representation, and Use
OBIDENITY™ Identity Governance Rules define the conditions under
which identity may be created, represented, transferred, and used within the OBIDENITY™ framework.
These rules establish when identity can be considered valid, trusted, and acceptable for use.
This rule layer is extensible and may evolve as new identity
use cases emerge.
Core Rules
1. AI Identity Representation Rule
An identity may be represented by AI systems only if:
the identity is bound to a verifiable origin
the representation is clearly disclosed as non-original
the linkage between identity and AI representation is traceable
the representation does not simulate identity without disclosure
2. Post-Mortem Identity Rule
The identity of a deceased individual may be created or used only under defined conditions:
if a legal or designated inheritor exists, explicit authorization is required
if no identifiable owner exists (e.g. historical figures), identity may be used as public-domain reference
representation must be clearly disclosed as simulation, reconstruction, or interpretation
interpretation must respect known characteristics and historical context
3. Identity Ownership Rule
Identity must have a clearly defined controlling authority.
ownership or control must be traceable
no entity may assume control without authorization
ownership and usage rights must be distinguishable

ownership changes must be recorded
4. Identity Transfer Rule
Identity control or usage rights may be transferred only under traceable conditions.
all transfers must be recorded
no silent or untraceable transfer is permitted
identity continuity must be preserved
responsibility must remain linked to the identity chain
Structural Principle
Identity may be used only under conditions that preserve origin, continuity, and integrity.
Closing Statement
Without rules, identity becomes imitation without accountability.

Module 1 — Identity Anchor
Module 1 — Identity Anchor
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Identity
Module: Identity Anchor
Type: Identity Module
Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 19 March 2026
Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Identity Anchor defines the structural conditions under which an identity is created
as a unique, non-replicable origin point bound to a verifiable origin event.
The Identity Anchor establishes the existence of identity and serves as the immutable
reference for its entire lifecycle.
Why This Matters
Without a defined origin, identity cannot be distinguished from duplication or imitation.
Most identity systems allow:
duplication
reassignment
overwrite
loss of origin
This creates environments where identity cannot be trusted.
Identity Anchor ensures that identity begins as a single, verifiable event that cannot be replicated or replaced.
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Create Unique Identity Anchor
Identity must be created as a unique, non-reusable anchor.
Minimum requirement:
unique identity anchor
no duplication
no reuse of identity
Step 2 — Bind to Origin Event
Identity must be linked to a verifiable origin.
Minimum requirement:
defined origin event
recorded timestamp

identifiable responsible entity
Step 3 — Ensure Non-Overwriteability
Identity Anchor must not be replaceable.
Minimum requirement:
no overwrite
no reassignment
no substitution
Step 4 — Enable Anchor Verification
The origin of identity must be verifiable.
Minimum requirement:
traceable origin record
reconstructable creation event
verifiable link to issuer
Use Case 1 — Cross-Platform Identity Ownership
Scenario
An individual or entity operates across multiple platforms, each creating separate identities.
Application
Identity Anchor establishes a single origin-bound identity independent of platforms.
Result
identity is no longer controlled by platforms
identity persists across systems
no duplication or fragmentation of identity
Use Case 2 — AI-Driven Identity Representation
Scenario
A public figure or organization uses AI agents to represent their identity in communication and interaction.
Application
Identity Anchor binds all representations to a verifiable origin identity.
Result
AI interactions remain tied to a real identity
impersonation becomes detectable
trust is preserved across digital interactions
Structural Principle
Identity begins only once. Without a verifiable beginning, identity does not exist.
Closing Statement
An identity without origin is not an identity.

Module 2 — Identity Continuity
Module 2 — Identity Continuity
Category: Governance & Enforcement

Version: 1.0

Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Identity Continuity defines the structural conditions under which an identity persists over time without loss, fragmentation, or replacement.
Continuity exists only when identity is maintained through a traceable, append-only
sequence of events that preserves its link to the original identity anchor.
Why This Matters
An identity that cannot persist over time loses its meaning.
Without identity continuity:
identity may be fragmented across systems
identity history may be lost
identity may be replaced without detection
identity may exist only as a temporary state
This creates environments where identity cannot be reliably tracked or trusted.
Identity Continuity ensures that identity is not only created, but also preserved as a continuous and traceable entity.
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Maintain Append-Only Lifecycle
Identity must evolve through an append-only event structure.
Minimum requirement:
no deletion of identity history
no overwrite of past states

continuous event recording
Step 2 — Preserve Anchor Link
All identity states must remain linked to the original Identity Anchor.
Minimum requirement:
no detachment from origin
no creation of parallel identity chains
no reassignment of identity lineage
Step 3 — Prevent Fragmentation
Identity must not split into multiple independent versions.
Minimum requirement:
single continuous identity chain
no duplicated identity branches
no hidden identity forks
Step 4 — Enable State Reconstruction
Identity must be reconstructable at any point in time.
Minimum requirement:
full event history
traceable timeline
verifiable state at any moment
Use Case 1 — Long-Term Digital Identity Persistence
Scenario
An individual uses multiple systems and platforms over time, with identities changing, merging, or disappearing.
Application
Identity Continuity ensures that identity remains consistent and traceable across all systems and time periods.
Result
identity persists beyond platforms
full identity history remains intact
no loss or fragmentation of identity over time
Use Case 2 — Identity Evolution in AI Systems
Scenario
An AI agent evolves over time through updates, training, and interaction.
Application
Identity Continuity ensures that all changes remain linked to the original identity anchor and are traceable.
Result
clear lineage of AI identity
traceable evolution of behavior and decisions
no hidden replacement or reset of identity
Structural Principle

An identity that cannot be traced through time cannot be considered the same identity.
Closing Statement
Identity does not exist only at creation. It exists only if it continues.

Step 1 — Define Control Authority
Identity must have a defined controlling authority.
Minimum requirement:
identifiable controlling entity
defined authority scope
clear ownership or control reference

All actions affecting identity must be traceable.

identifiable actor for each action

time-linked action history
Step 3 — Preserve Control Continuity
Control must remain continuous across time.

no gaps in control chain

traceable control transfer

no loss of accountability

no loss of accountability

Chain of Control ensures that all control actions and authority changes are recorded and linked to responsible actors.

traceable governance of AI identity

Even when identity has a valid origin and continuity, it can still be compromised.
Without identity integrity:
identity may be cloned or duplicated

identity attributes may be altered
unauthorized actions may go undetected
This creates systems where identity exists but cannot be trusted.
Identity Integrity ensures that identity remains authentic and resistant to manipulation.
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Prevent Identity Replication
Identity must not be duplicable.
Minimum requirement:
no creation of identical identity anchors
no reuse of identity structure
no parallel identity copies
Step 2 — Detect Unauthorized Modification

Changes to identity must be controlled and detectable.
Minimum requirement:
no silent modification
traceable identity changes
detection of unauthorized updates
Step 3 — Protect Against Impersonation
Identity must not be usable by unauthorized actors.
Minimum requirement:
verifiable control linkage
no anonymous identity usage
no identity simulation without detection
Step 4 — Maintain Structural Integrity
Identity structure must remain intact across its lifecycle.
Minimum requirement:
no hidden structural changes
no corruption of identity data
preservation of identity consistency
Use Case 1 — Protection Against Identity Cloning
Scenario
An identity is copied or recreated to impersonate a real entity.

Result
prevention of identity cloning
detection of duplicate identities
preservation of identity authenticity
Use Case 2 — Secure AI Identity Representation
Scenario
AI systems represent individuals, organizations, or agents in communication and decision-making.
Application
Identity Integrity ensures that only authorized representations are linked to the identity and that impersonation is detectable.
Result
trusted AI identity representation
prevention of unauthorized impersonation
secure interaction with identity-based systems

Integrity protects identity from becoming imitation.

Identity State defines the structural conditions under which the current status of an
identity can be determined, classified, and verified at any point in time.

An identity may exist, but without a defined state, it cannot be evaluated.
Without identity state:
identity status may be unclear
compromised identities may remain undetected
systems cannot distinguish valid from invalid identity
decisions may rely on unknown identity conditions
This creates environments where identity cannot be reliably used.
Identity State ensures that identity is always measurable and interpretable.

Step 1 — Define Identity States
The system must define observable identity states.
Minimum requirement:
valid
compromised
suspended
restored
unknown
Step 2 — Link State to Event History
Identity state must be derived from traceable events.
Minimum requirement:

state based on recorded events
no arbitrary or hidden state assignment
traceable logic for state changes
Step 3 — Enable State Verification
Identity state must be independently verifiable.
Minimum requirement:
reconstructable state from event history
observable current state
verifiable state transitions
Step 4 — Maintain State Consistency
Identity state must remain consistent with actual identity condition.
Minimum requirement:
no mismatch between state and reality
no hidden state manipulation
no undefined state changes

Scenario
A system must determine whether an identity can be trusted for interaction, transaction, or decision-making.
Application

Result

improved decision reliability

Scenario
An identity becomes compromised and requires restoration.
Application
Identity State tracks the transition from compromised to restored through verifiable events.
Result
traceable recovery process
clear state transition history
restored trust based on evidence

An identity that cannot express its state cannot be evaluated.

Identity is not only what it is. It is also the state it is in.

continuous, append-only lifecycle

physical assets as referenced identities
Institutional Position
OBIDENITY™ does not replace legal identity systems or identification documents.
It defines a structural identity layer enabling traceability, auditability, and interoperability across systems.
Structural Principle
Identity is not defined by registration. Identity is defined by origin and continuity.
