Canonical Definition
The Rights & Authorization Module (RAM™) defines who is permitted
to create, reproduce, represent, exhibit, or monetize an asset.
Authorization determines whether an action is valid,
independent of the asset form.
Why This Matters
Without clear authorization:
copies may be created without permission
representations may be misused
ownership may be violated
monetization becomes illegitimate
Authorization separates existence from permission.
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Identify the Asset
Define the asset to which rights are applied.
Step 2 — Identify the Authority
Determine the individual or entity that holds
control over the asset.
Step 3 — Define Permissions
Specify what is allowed:
create
copy
represent
exhibit
monetize
Step 4 — Assign Authorization Status
Declare whether the action is:
authorized
partially authorized
not authorized
Step 5 — Maintain Traceability
Authorization must remain linked to the asset
and its origin.
Use Case 1 — Licensed Exhibition
Scenario
A gallery receives permission to exhibit copies of an artwork.
Application

Authorization is defined under RAM™.
Result
clear exhibition rights
controlled usage
legal and structural clarity
Use Case 2 — Unauthorized Reproduction
Scenario
A copy of an artwork is created and distributed
without permission.
Application
The asset is classified as not authorized.
Result
clear identification of misuse
separation from legitimate copies
protection of original ownership
Structural Principle
Ownership defines control.
Authorization defines permission.
Closing Statement
An asset may exist without permission.
It cannot be used without it.

About the Responsibility Assignment Standard
About the Responsibility Assignment Standard
(RAS-A)
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities may be assigned, allocated,
transferred, accepted, recorded, governed, reconstructed, and
enforced while preserving legitimacy, traceability, accountability,
clarity, and operational validity throughout
the responsibility-assignment lifecycle.
RAS-A governs responsibility assignment.
The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to
determine who assigned responsibility, to whom responsibility was
assigned, what responsibility was assigned, whether the assignment
was valid, whether the assignment was accepted, and whether assigned
responsibilities remained governable throughout operational reality.
What This Standard Is
RAS-A is a parent standard of the Accountability
Governance Architecture (AGA™).
It governs:
responsibility assignment
duty allocation
task assignment governance
responsibility transfer
assignment acceptance
assignment validity
assignment traceability
responsibility ownership allocation
Human-AI responsibility assignment
agent responsibility assignment
RAS-A establishes the governance layer responsible for determining
how responsibility becomes attached to a specific actor, role,
organization, system, or agent.
What This Standard Is Not
RAS-A is not:
an authority standard
a capability standard
a control standard

an oversight standard
an evidence standard
an accountability standard
RAS-A does not determine who performed an action.
RAS-A does not determine who controlled an activity.
RAS-A determines how responsibility was assigned before those
governance questions are evaluated.
Why This Standard Exists
Many governance failures occur because organizations know that a
responsibility existed but cannot determine:
Who actually received the responsibility?
Examples include:
undocumented task assignments
responsibility gaps
overlapping responsibilities
assignment without authority
assignment without acceptance
assignment to incapable actors
hidden responsibility transfers
Human-AI responsibility ambiguity
The challenge is not identifying responsibility.
The challenge is identifying how responsibility became assigned.
RAS-A exists because responsibility assignment has become a
distinct governance space.
Core Insight
Responsibility defines the duty to act. Responsibility Assignment
defines who receives that duty.
Operational Architecture Space
RAS-A defines the operational architecture space for:
responsibility assignment governance
task allocation governance
duty assignment governance
assignment traceability
assignment validation
assignment acceptance
responsibility transfer governance
Human-AI responsibility assignment
agent responsibility assignment
operational duty governance
This space exists because responsibility cannot be fulfilled until
it is assigned.

RAS-A governs whether responsibility assignment remains valid.
General Use Case 1 — Contractor Environment
Scenario
A project involves multiple contractors, subcontractors,
supervisors, temporary workers, and operational teams working
on interconnected tasks.
Application
RAS-A determines who assigned responsibilities, how assignments were
communicated, whether assignments were accepted, and whether
assignment records remain reconstructable.
Result
Governance gains visibility into how responsibility entered
the operational environment.
General Use Case 2 — Human-AI Operational Environment
Scenario
An orchestration platform assigns tasks to AI agents while human
supervisors oversee execution and outcomes.
Application
RAS-A determines how responsibilities are allocated across humans,
AI agents, orchestration systems, and governance actors.
Result
Governance gains visibility into responsibility assignment across
intelligent operational ecosystems.
Architectural Position
Within AGA™, RAS-A serves as the second foundational standard of
the Responsibility Layer.
The architecture progresses:
Relationship → Authority → Responsibility → Responsibility
Assignment → Responsibility Continuity → Responsibility Traceability
→ Capability → Control → Oversight → Evidence → Accountability
→ Consequence
RAS-A governs how responsibility becomes assigned before governance
evaluates continuity, traceability, capability, control, oversight,
evidence, accountability, or consequences.

Strategic Importance
Many organizations can answer:
what responsibility existed
what task needed to be performed
what outcome was expected
But they cannot answer:
Who received the responsibility?
Without assignment governance:
responsibility becomes ambiguous
ownership becomes fragmented
accountability weakens
investigations become difficult
governance quality deteriorates
RAS-A exists to expose and govern these conditions.
Closing Definition
Responsibility Assignment is not the existence of responsibility.
Responsibility Assignment is the governed process through which
responsibility becomes attached to a specific actor, role,
organization, system, or agent while preserving legitimacy,
traceability, acceptance, and operational validity.
Responsibility cannot be fulfilled, traced, governed, or enforced if
responsibility was never validly assigned. Responsibility Assignment
therefore becomes a foundational condition of trustworthy
governance systems.
Related Documents
→ Responsibility Assignment Standard - (RAS-A)

AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF
Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL)
Canonical Definition System
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities may be assigned, allocated,
transferred, accepted, recorded, governed, reconstructed, and
enforced while preserving legitimacy, traceability, accountability,
clarity, and operational validity throughout
the responsibility-assignment lifecycle.
RAS-A governs responsibility assignment.
The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to

determine who assigned responsibility, to whom responsibility was
assigned, what responsibility was assigned, whether the assignment
was valid, and whether the assigned responsibility
remained governable.
Responsibility does not become operationally valid merely because
a task exists.
Responsibility becomes governable when it is properly assigned.
RAS-A governs that assignment.
A. Standard Abstract
Every governance system assigns responsibility.
Organizations assign responsibility.
Contractors assign responsibility.
Supervisors assign responsibility.
Institutions assign responsibility.
AI orchestration systems increasingly assign responsibility.
Human-AI environments require responsibility assignment governance.
Without responsibility-assignment governance:
duties become unclear
task ownership becomes fragmented
responsibility gaps emerge
responsibility conflicts increase
accountability becomes weakened
operational failures become harder to reconstruct
RAS-A exists to govern these conditions.
B. Core Principle
Responsibility assignment becomes valid only when assigned
responsibilities remain identifiable, legitimate, accepted,
traceable, reconstructable, accountable, and operationally valid
throughout the responsibility- assignment lifecycle.
C. Scope
This standard may apply to:
organizations
institutions
governments
contractor networks
subcontractor chains
temporary workforce environments
supervisory systems
operational task assignment
compliance environments
AI systems

autonomous agents
orchestrated agent systems
Human-AI operational environments
robotics ecosystems
future intelligent governance systems
RAS-A applies wherever responsibility is assigned to an actor,
system, role, organization, agent, or operational entity.
D. Why This Standard Exists
Responsibility governance requires more than
identifying responsibility.
Governance must also determine how responsibility was assigned.
Common failures include:
unclear task assignment
undocumented responsibility allocation
assignment to the wrong actor
assignment without authority
assignment without acceptance
assignment without capability
overlapping assignments
abandoned assignments
hidden responsibility transfers
The challenge is not only determining who was responsible.
The challenge is determining whether responsibility was
validly assigned.
RAS-A exists because responsibility assignment is a
distinct governance space.
E. Responsibility Assignment Integrity Logic
Responsibility assignment integrity exists only when the following
remain materially preservable:
1. Assignment Origin Integrity
The assignment remains attributable to a legitimate
assignment source.
2. Assignment Scope Integrity
The assigned responsibility remains connected to clearly defined
duties and boundaries.
3. Assignment Validity Integrity
The assignment remains legitimate, accepted, recognized,
and operationally valid.
4. Assignment Traceability Integrity
The assignment remains reconstructable throughout the

assignment lifecycle.
5. Assignment Accountability Integrity
The assignment remains connected to accountable governance
structures and consequence-bearing relationships.
F. Operational Architecture Space
RAS-A defines the operational architecture space for:
responsibility assignment governance
task allocation governance
duty assignment governance
responsibility allocation
assignment traceability
assignment validity
assignment accountability
contractor responsibility assignment
Human-AI responsibility assignment
agent responsibility assignment
operational duty governance
This space exists because responsibility must be assigned before it
can be fulfilled, traced, enforced, or connected to accountability.
RAS-A governs whether responsibility assignment remains valid.
G. Difference Between Responsibility and
Responsibility Assignment
Responsibility defines the duty to act.
Responsibility assignment defines how that duty is allocated to
a specific actor.
Responsibility may exist as an obligation.
Assignment determines who carries that obligation.
RGS governs responsibility.
RAS-A governs responsibility assignment.
Both are required.
H. Runtime Position
RAS-A operates within the Responsibility Layer of AGA™.
It follows:
Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS)
Authority Governance Standard (AGS)
Authority Delegation Standard (ADS)
Authority Validation Standard (AVS)
Authority Escalation Standard (AES)
Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS)
and supports:

Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS)
Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS)
Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS)
Chain of Control Standard (CCS)
Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A)
RAS-A governs how responsibility becomes assigned before governance
evaluates continuity, traceability, capability, control, oversight,
evidence, or accountability.
I. Responsibility Assignment Failure Rule
Responsibility assignment failure occurs when responsibility
assignments cannot be reliably identified, validated, accepted,
reconstructed, governed, enforced, or connected to
accountable governance structures.
Examples include:
undocumented assignment
unclear assignment
assignment without authority
assignment to an incapable actor
assignment without acceptance
overlapping responsibility assignment
hidden responsibility transfer
responsibility-assignment gaps
RAS-A exists to expose and govern these conditions.
J. Validity Logic
A responsibility-assignment environment is valid under RAS-A when:
assignment sources remain identifiable
assigned duties remain clearly defined
assignment legitimacy remains demonstrable
assignment acceptance remains reviewable
assignment history remains reconstructable
assignment accountability remains preservable
assigned responsibilities remain operationally valid
A responsibility-assignment environment becomes invalid when:
assignment origin is unknown
assigned duties are unclear
assignment authority cannot be demonstrated

assignment acceptance is absent or unverifiable
assignment history cannot be reconstructed
assignment accountability is lost
K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards
RAS-A derives from:
Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS)
Authority Governance Standard (AGS)
Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS)
and supports:

RGS governs responsibility.
RAS-A governs assignment of responsibility.
RCS governs whether responsibility remains preserved.
RTS governs whether responsibility can be reconstructed.
L. Foundational Principle
Responsibility cannot be enforced if responsibility was
never validly assigned.
Canonical Closing Statement
Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities may be assigned, allocated,
transferred, accepted, recorded, governed, reconstructed, and
enforced while preserving legitimacy, traceability, accountability,
clarity, and operational validity throughout
the responsibility-assignment lifecycle.
Responsibility becomes governable only when assignment is clear. If
responsibility assignment cannot be identified, validated, accepted,
or reconstructed, accountability becomes unreliable.

About the Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS)
About the Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS)
Canonical Definition
Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) defines the structural
conditions under which operational, contractual, organizational,
supervisory, delegated, collaborative, autonomous, Human-AI, and
multi-party relationships remain identifiable, classifiable,
traceable, accountable, governable, and operationally valid
throughout their lifecycle.
RAS governs relationships.
The standard establishes the conditions required to determine the
actual operational relationship between actors before authority,
responsibility, capability, control, oversight, evidence,
accountability, and consequence can be evaluated.
What This Standard Is
RAS is the foundational parent standard of the Accountability
Governance Architecture (AGA™).
It governs:
relationship identification
relationship classification
relationship boundaries
relationship continuity
relationship traceability
relationship accountability
RAS establishes the first governance layer of
accountability analysis.
Before governance can determine who possessed authority, who carried
responsibility, who exercised control, who provided oversight, or
who remains accountable, governance must first determine the
relationship structure itself.
What This Standard Is Not
RAS is not:
an authority standard
a responsibility standard
a capability standard
a control standard
an oversight standard
an evidence standard

an accountability standard
RAS does not determine who was responsible.
RAS determines how actors were connected.
The remaining governance layers are evaluated only after the
relationship structure is identified.
Why This Standard Exists
Modern operational environments increasingly operate through
complex relationship structures.
Activities are frequently performed through:
organizations
departments
contractors
subcontractors
staffing agencies
consultants
service providers
AI systems
autonomous agents
orchestrated agent systems
Human-AI operational environments
As these structures become more complex, governance failures
increasingly originate from misunderstanding the relationship
layer itself.
Organizations often attempt to determine accountability before
understanding the actual operational relationships that existed.
This creates governance blindness.
RAS exists to eliminate that problem.
Core Question
What is the actual operational relationship between the actors?
This question forms the entry point of the entire AGA™ architecture.
Core Insight
Before governance can determine who was accountable, governance must
first determine who was connected to whom and how.
Operational Architecture Space
RAS defines the operational architecture space for:
relationship governance
relationship identification
relationship classification
relationship mapping
relationship continuity
relationship traceability
relationship accountability

This space exists because every governance chain begins with
a relationship.
Without a relationship there can be no authority.
Without authority there can be no responsibility.
Without responsibility there can be no accountability.
General Use Case 1
A manufacturing organization operates through multiple contractors,
subcontractors, staffing agencies, and external service providers.
Before responsibility, oversight, or accountability can be
evaluated, governance must first identify and classify the actual
relationships between participating actors.
RAS governs this process.
General Use Case 2
An orchestrated AI environment contains humans, AI agents,
autonomous systems, external tools, and robotic execution layers.
Before governance can evaluate authority, accountability, or
consequence attribution, the relationship structure between
participating actors must first be reconstructed.
RAS governs this process.
Architectural Position
Within AGA™, RAS serves as the foundational governance layer.
The architecture begins with:
Relationship → Authority → Responsibility → Capability → Control →
Oversight → Evidence → Accountability → Consequence
RAS governs the first step of this chain.
All subsequent governance analysis depends upon the validity of
the relationship layer.
Foundational Principle
Every governance chain begins with a relationship.
Closing Definition
Relationship Accountability Standard (RAS) defines the structural

conditions under which operational, contractual, organizational,
supervisory, delegated, collaborative, autonomous, Human-AI, and
multi-party relationships remain identifiable, classifiable,
traceable, accountable, governable, and operationally valid
throughout their lifecycle.
If the relationship layer is misunderstood, every subsequent
governance conclusion may become invalid. Relationship therefore
becomes the foundational entry point of accountability governance.

About the Responsibility Continuity Standard
About the Responsibility Continuity Standard
(RCS)
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities remain preserved, connected,
governable, traceable, transferable, reconstructable, enforceable,
and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle
despite organizational, operational, contractual, technological,
supervisory, or governance changes.
RCS governs responsibility continuity.
The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to
determine whether responsibility remained continuously preserved
from assignment to outcome and whether responsibility survived
transfers, substitutions, escalations, reorganizations, automation
events, and governance transitions.
What This Standard Is
RCS is a parent standard of the Accountability
Governance Architecture (AGA™).
It governs:
responsibility continuity
responsibility preservation
responsibility succession
responsibility transfer continuity
governance handover continuity
responsibility lifecycle governance
contractor responsibility continuity
Human-AI responsibility continuity
AI responsibility continuity
continuity accountability
RCS establishes the governance layer responsible for determining
whether responsibility remains preserved throughout
operational reality.
What This Standard Is Not
RCS is not:
an authority standard
a responsibility-assignment standard
a capability standard

a control standard
an oversight standard
an evidence standard
an accountability standard
RCS does not determine who originally received responsibility.
RCS determines whether responsibility remained preserved
after assignment.
Why This Standard Exists
Many governance systems successfully assign responsibility.
Many governance systems fail to preserve responsibility.
Responsibility often becomes fragmented during:
organizational changes
management transitions
contractor handovers
subcontractor chains
temporary staffing arrangements
automation events
Human-AI operational transitions
governance restructurings
The result is often a responsibility gap.
A responsibility gap occurs when responsibility existed at one point
in time but can no longer be reliably connected to a later outcome.
The challenge is not assigning responsibility.
The challenge is preserving responsibility.
RCS exists because responsibility continuity has become a
distinct governance space.
Core Insight
Responsibility Assignment determines who receives responsibility.
Responsibility Continuity determines whether responsibility
remains preserved.
Operational Architecture Space
RCS defines the operational architecture space for:
responsibility continuity governance
responsibility preservation governance
responsibility succession governance
responsibility-transfer continuity
governance handover continuity
contractor responsibility continuity
Human-AI responsibility continuity
AI responsibility continuity

continuity traceability
responsibility lifecycle governance
This space exists because governance requires responsibility to
survive operational change.
RCS governs whether responsibility remains continuous.
General Use Case 1 — Multi-Layer Contractor Environment
Scenario
A responsibility passes through a client, contractor, subcontractor,
supervisor, and operational worker before execution occurs.
Application
RCS evaluates whether responsibility remained continuously preserved
throughout the operational chain and whether any responsibility gaps
emerged during transfers.
Result
Governance gains visibility into continuity of responsibility across
the entire operational lifecycle.
General Use Case 2 — Human-AI Operational Environment
Scenario
Responsibilities move between human supervisors, orchestration
systems, autonomous agents, and governance actors during execution
of operational activities.
Application
RCS evaluates whether responsibility remained continuously preserved
despite transitions between human and intelligent systems.
Result
Governance gains visibility into responsibility continuity across
intelligent operational ecosystems.
Architectural Position
Within AGA™, RCS serves as the third foundational standard of
the Responsibility Layer.
The architecture progresses:
Relationship → Authority → Responsibility → Responsibility
Assignment → Responsibility Continuity → Responsibility Traceability
→ Capability → Control → Oversight → Evidence → Accountability
→ Consequence

RCS governs whether responsibility remains preserved before
governance evaluates traceability, capability, control, oversight,
evidence, accountability, or consequences.
Strategic Importance
Many organizations can answer:
who received responsibility
what responsibility existed
what task was assigned
But they cannot answer:
Did responsibility remain preserved throughout the lifecycle?
Without continuity governance:
responsibility disappears
governance ownership weakens
accountability becomes fragmented
investigations become difficult
operational failures become harder to reconstruct
RCS exists to expose and govern these conditions.
Closing Definition
Responsibility Continuity is not the assignment of responsibility.
Responsibility Continuity is the governed condition through which
responsibility remains preserved, connected, governable, traceable,
transferable, reconstructable, and operationally valid despite
organizational, operational, contractual, technological,
or governance change.
Governance cannot remain trustworthy if responsibility disappears
between assignment and outcome. Responsibility Continuity therefore
becomes a foundational condition of trustworthy governance systems.
Related Documents
→ Responsibility Continuity Standard - (RCS)

Canonical Definition System
Canonical Definition
Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities remain preserved, connected,
governable, traceable, transferable, reconstructable, enforceable,
and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle
despite organizational, operational, contractual, technological,
supervisory, or governance changes.
RCS governs responsibility continuity.
The standard establishes the foundational conditions required to

determine whether responsibility remained continuously preserved
from assignment to outcome and whether responsibility survived
transitions, transfers, escalations, reorganizations, substitutions,
automation events, and governance changes.
Responsibility may be assigned.
Responsibility may be transferred.
Responsibility may be shared.
Responsibility may evolve.
RCS governs whether responsibility remains continuous.
A. Standard Abstract
Many governance failures occur because responsibility
disappears between events.
Responsibilities often pass through:
managers
supervisors
contractors
subcontractors
temporary workers
organizations
departments
AI systems
autonomous agents
Without continuity governance:
responsibility gaps emerge
ownership becomes fragmented
accountability weakens
investigations become difficult
governance reliability deteriorates
RCS exists to govern these conditions.
B. Core Principle
Responsibility remains governance-valid only when responsibility
continuity remains preservable, reconstructable, traceable, and
enforceable throughout the responsibility lifecycle.
C. Scope
This standard may apply to:
organizations
institutions
governments
contractor networks
subcontractor chains
temporary workforce environments
certification systems
operational governance systems
AI governance systems
autonomous-agent environments
Human-AI operational systems
future intelligent governance systems
RCS applies wherever responsibility must survive change.

D. Why This Standard Exists
Many systems successfully assign responsibility.
Many systems fail to preserve responsibility.
Examples include:
responsibility transferred without records
responsibility abandoned during transitions
responsibility fragmentation
responsibility gaps between organizations
contractor continuity failures
governance handover failures
Human-AI responsibility discontinuity
automation-related responsibility loss
The challenge is not assigning responsibility.
The challenge is preserving responsibility.
RCS exists because responsibility continuity is a
distinct governance space.
E. Responsibility Continuity Integrity Logic
Responsibility continuity integrity exists only when the following
remain materially preservable:
1. Continuity Origin Integrity
The continuity relationship remains attributable to
legitimate responsibility sources.
2. Continuity Scope Integrity
The preserved responsibility remains connected to clearly
defined governance boundaries.
3. Continuity Validity Integrity
Responsibility continuity remains legitimate and
operationally valid.
4. Continuity Traceability Integrity
Responsibility continuity remains reconstructable throughout
the responsibility lifecycle.
5. Continuity Accountability Integrity
Responsibility continuity remains connected to
accountable governance structures.
F. Operational Architecture Space
RCS defines the operational architecture space for:
responsibility continuity
responsibility preservation
responsibility transfers

responsibility succession
governance handovers
contractor continuity governance
Human-AI responsibility continuity
AI responsibility continuity
responsibility lifecycle governance
continuity traceability
This space exists because governance requires responsibility to
remain preserved despite operational change.
RCS governs whether responsibility remains continuous.
G. Difference Between Assignment and
Continuity
Responsibility Assignment asks:
Who received the responsibility?
Responsibility Continuity asks:
Did responsibility remain preserved afterward?
RAS-A governs assignment.
RCS governs preservation.
Both are required.
H. Runtime Position
RCS operates within the Responsibility Layer of AGA™.
It follows:
Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS)
Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A)
and supports:
Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS)
Capability Readiness Governance Standard (CRGS)
Chain of Control Standard (CCS)
Governance Oversight Standard (GOS)
Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A)
RCS governs whether responsibility survives operational reality.
I. Responsibility Continuity Failure Rule
Responsibility continuity failure occurs when responsibility cannot
be reliably preserved, reconstructed, transferred, reviewed,
governed, or connected to accountable governance structures.
Examples include:
responsibility gaps
abandoned responsibility
undocumented transfers
continuity failures
contractor responsibility discontinuity
governance handover failures

Human-AI continuity breakdowns
fragmented responsibility chains
RCS exists to expose and govern these conditions.
J. Validity Logic
A responsibility-continuity environment is valid under RCS when:
responsibility remains continuously identifiable
responsibility transitions remain visible
continuity relationships remain reconstructable
continuity accountability remains preservable
continuity governance remains reviewable
responsibility remains operationally valid
A responsibility-continuity environment becomes invalid when:
responsibility disappears
continuity relationships become unverifiable
transitions cannot be reconstructed
responsibility ownership becomes fragmented
governance continuity is lost
K. Relationship to Other OOF Standards
RCS derives from:
Responsibility Governance Standard (RGS)
Responsibility Assignment Standard (RAS-A)
and supports:
Responsibility Traceability Standard (RTS)
Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A)
Accountability Continuity Standard (ACS)
RGS governs responsibility.
RAS-A governs assignment.
RCS governs continuity.
L. Foundational Principle
Responsibility cannot remain governable if responsibility continuity
cannot be preserved.
Canonical Closing Statement
Responsibility Continuity Standard (RCS) defines the structural
conditions under which responsibilities remain preserved, connected,
governable, traceable, transferable, reconstructable, enforceable,
and operationally valid throughout the responsibility lifecycle

despite organizational, operational, contractual, technological,
supervisory, or governance changes.
Governance may assign responsibility, but trustworthy governance
requires responsibility to remain continuous. Responsibility
Continuity therefore becomes a foundational condition of
trustworthy governance systems.

Origin Declaration Standard (ODS™) · Audit in Real Time™

A. Standard Abstract
The Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) defines the structural distinction
between an original asset, its copies, and its representations
across physical, digital, and virtual environments.
The standard establishes a clear framework for identifying what a work is,
how it exists, and under what conditions it may be reproduced,
represented, exhibited, or referenced.
RCS™ does not replace ownership law, copyright law, or institutional policy.
RCS™ defines structural classification.
B. Canonical Definition
Representation & Copy Standard (RCS™) is a methodology for classifying
original assets, copies, and representations according to their origin,
form, relationship to the source, and declared mode of existence.
RCS™ distinguishes between:
what constitutes an original
what constitutes a copy
what constitutes a representation

how each form may exist without confusion of status
Origin defines what it is.
Representation defines how it exists.
C. Base
An asset may exist in more than one form,
but not in more than one origin state.
A copy is not an origin.
A representation is not the original.
A digital form does not automatically invalidate authenticity.
A physical form does not automatically guarantee originality.
Clear classification is necessary whenever value, authorship, exhibition,
insurance, licensing, or public trust depends on the declared status of a work.
D. Core Principle
A work must be classified according to its true structural state.
No copy may be presented as an original.
No representation may be treated as identical to source unless explicitly defined.
No asset may derive legitimacy from ambiguity.
Core Structural Categories
RCS™ recognizes the following core states:
Original Asset
Physical Copy
Digital Copy
Digital Original
Virtual Representation
Replica
Additional rights, authorization, and exhibition conditions may apply,
but they do not alter the underlying state of the asset.
Scope
This standard applies to:
artworks
museum objects
gallery editions
digital cultural assets
archival reproductions
virtual exhibitions
scanned or photographed works
digitally originated works
licensed reproductions
Structural Rule
Every asset must be classified according to:
origin state
form of existence
relationship to the source
declared representation status

If these elements are not clearly declared,
the asset remains structurally ambiguous.
Methodology
identify the source asset
determine whether the asset is original, copy, or representation
determine whether the form is physical, digital, or virtual
define the relationship between the asset and the source
declare the status of the asset
assign any additional rights or exhibition conditions separately
Use Context
museums and collections
galleries and edition structures
insurance and valuation contexts
virtual exhibitions
cultural archiving
licensed display systems
digital heritage systems
Positioning
Not every visible form is an original.
Not every copy is illegitimate.
Not every digital form is secondary.
Classification creates clarity.
Canonical Closing Statement
When the status of a work is unclear, trust collapses.
Representation requires classification
before value can be protected.

before they evolve into operational failures.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Define the Reality Drift Object
The organization must define which forms of reality drift require governance.
This may include:
environmental drift

operational drift
strategic drift
predictive drift
simulation drift
behavioral drift
world-model drift
autonomous-agent model drift
2. Define Reality Drift Conditions
The system must define the conditions under which reality drift
becomes operationally significant.
This includes:
divergence thresholds
measurement requirements
validation requirements
correction requirements
escalation requirements
governance-valid drift conditions
3. Define Reality Drift Detection Logic
The system must define how reality drift is identified.
This may include:
reality-model mismatches
prediction failures
environmental inconsistencies
operational deviations
evidence-model conflicts
validation anomalies
4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic
The system must define governance logic for reality-drift conditions.
Governance response may include:
model review
alignment reassessment
adaptation activation
governance intervention
escalation
model restriction
operational invalidation where required
5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions
The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of:
drift events
divergence measurements
validation activities
governance actions
corrective interventions
resulting model states
A cognition environment must not remain drift-valid if materially significant
divergence from reality cannot be detected, measured, or governed.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Environmental Monitoring System
Scenario

An autonomous monitoring environment continuously maintains models describing
changing environmental conditions and operational states.
Application
RDIM governs divergence detection, drift measurement, and governance responses
when internal models begin deviating from observed reality.
Result
The environment gains stronger situational awareness, improved adaptation capability,
and reduced exposure to unnoticed reality-model failures.
Use Case 2 — Strategic Forecasting Organization
Scenario
An organization relies on predictive models to guide investment,
planning, and operational decisions.
Application
RDIM governs reality-drift detection when forecasts increasingly diverge
from observed market and operational conditions.
Result
The organization gains stronger forecasting accountability, improved model reliability,
and reduced exposure to strategic blind spots.
Canonical Closing Statement
Reality Drift Integrity Module (RDIM) defines the structural conditions
under which divergence between internal reality models and observable reality
remains detectable, measurable, traceable, governable, and operationally valid
throughout cognition and reality-modeling processes.
Reality models cannot remain valid when divergence from reality becomes invisible.
Reality drift therefore becomes a foundational integrity condition
of governable reality modeling.

What is the actual relationship between the actors?

Who has the authority to act?

Governance Boundary

Core Question
Is the authority valid?

validity has been determined.

Has authority been delegated?

Who had the obligation to act?

Can responsibility be reconstructed?

Who actually controlled the outcome?

What do the facts prove?

EAS defines the conditions under which evidence remains valid,

14. Accountability Governance Standard (AGS-A)
Core Question
Who remains answerable?
Canonical Definition
AGS-A defines the conditions under which accountability

and enforceable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when accountability exists. Ends when accountability
ownership can be evaluated.
15. Decision Accountability Standard (DAS)
Core Question
Who made the decision?
Canonical Definition
DAS defines the conditions under which decisions remain attributable

Governance Boundary
Begins when decisions are made. Ends when decision accountability

16. Accountability Continuity Standard (ACS)
Core Question
Did accountability remain preserved?
Canonical Definition
ACS defines the conditions under which accountability remains
preserved throughout governance, operational, technological,

contractual, and organizational change.
Governance Boundary
Begins when accountability persists through time. Ends when
accountability continuity can be evaluated.
17. Accountability Chain Standard (ACS-C)
Core Question
How does accountability travel across governance structures?
Canonical Definition
ACS-C defines the conditions under which accountability
relationships remain connected, traceable, reconstructable, and
governable across multi-layer governance structures.
Governance Boundary
Begins when accountability spans multiple governance layers. Ends
when accountability-chain reconstruction becomes possible.

cognition produces decisions, conclusions, or actions.
4. Multi-Agent Cognition Integrity Standard (MCIS)
Core Question
How do multiple agents think together?
Canonical Definition
MCIS defines the conditions under which cognition emerging between
multiple autonomous agents remains synchronized, traceable,

governable, and operationally valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition is distributed across multiple agents. Ends
when collective agent cognition produces outcomes.
5. Cognitive Interpretation Integrity Standard (CIIS)
Core Question
How is meaning formed and understood?
Canonical Definition
CIIS defines the conditions under which interpretation, semantic
understanding, context formation, meaning generation, and
information understanding remain coherent, accountable,
and reality-connected.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition attempts to derive meaning. Ends when meaning
and interpretation have been formed.
6. Cognitive Reasoning Integrity Standard (CRIS)
Core Question
How does the system reason?
Canonical Definition
CRIS defines the conditions under which reasoning processes remain
logically coherent, explainable, reconstructable, accountable, and
operationally valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition performs reasoning. Ends when reasoning
produces conclusions.
7. Cognitive Reality Modeling Standard (CRMS)
Core Question
How does cognition model reality?
Canonical Definition
CRMS defines the conditions under which cognition constructs,
maintains, validates, adapts, and governs internal representations
of reality.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition creates a reality model. Ends when that
reality model influences cognition, reasoning, or
decision formation.
8. Collective Cognition Integrity Standard (CCIS)
Core Question
How do groups think together?

Canonical Definition
CCIS defines the conditions under which cognition emerging from
organizations, institutions, communities, governance systems, and
distributed collectives remains coherent, accountable,
and governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition emerges from multiple participants. Ends when
collective cognition produces shared outcomes.
9. Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS)
Core Question
How do humans and AI think together?
Canonical Definition
HAICS defines the conditions under which cognition emerging between
humans and AI systems remains synchronized, traceable,
authority-aware, trust-calibrated, accountable, and
operationally valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when human cognition and AI cognition interact. Ends when
Human-AI cognition produces decisions, actions, or outcomes.
10. Cognitive Evolution Governance Standard (CEGS)
Core Question
How may cognition evolve safely?
Canonical Definition
CEGS defines the conditions under which cognition may learn, adapt,
improve, self-modify, evolve, expand capabilities, and transform
cognitive structures while remaining accountable, traceable,
reality-connected, and governable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when cognition changes itself. Ends when cognitive evolution
has been validated and governed.
Architectural Position
CLIA® governs the complete cognition lifecycle. The
architecture progresses:
Cognition Integrity → Human Cognition → Agent Cognition → Multi-Agent Cognition → Interpretation →

Reasoning → Reality Modeling → Collective Cognition → Human-AI Cognition → Cognitive Evolution
Together these cognition spaces govern how cognition remains valid
throughout cognition formation, interpretation, reasoning, reality
modeling, collaboration, adaptation, and evolution.
What CLIA® Defines
CLIA® defines: where cognition begins, where cognition remains
valid, where interpretation occurs, where reasoning occurs, where
reality models are formed, where collective cognition emerges, where
Human-AI cognition operates, where cognition evolves, where
cognition governance applies, where cognition accountability exists.
CLIA® provides the official cognition governance language used for
cognition space identification across autonomous and
intelligent systems.
Canonical Principle
CLIA® does not govern what a system does. CLIA® governs how
cognition itself remains valid while the system thinks, interprets,
reasons, models reality, collaborates, learns, adapts, and evolves.
Canonical Closing Statement
CLIA® serves as the official OOF® cognition governance map for
autonomous and intelligent systems. By defining the primary
governable cognition spaces of intelligence, CLIA® provides a
structured cognition reference architecture used to identify,
classify, govern, validate, and understand cognition throughout the
complete cognition lifecycle.

governance map used for memory space identification, memory
governance classification, memory diagnostics, memory validation,
memory architecture analysis, and memory problem placement across AI
systems, autonomous agents, Human-AI environments, robotics,
organizations, institutions, and future intelligence ecosystems.
MGIA™ provides the primary memory governance reference architecture
used to identify where memory-related problems belong before memory
analysis, memory validation, memory governance, memory optimization,
memory preservation, or memory improvement begins. The purpose of
MGIA™ is not to manage memory. The purpose of MGIA™ is to identify
and define the governable memory spaces of intelligent systems.

Autonomous Agents

Human-AI Environments
Robotics
Cognitive Automation Systems
Intelligent Infrastructure
Organizations
Institutions
Collective Intelligence Systems

Core Architectural Principle
Every memory space answers one primary question. No memory space
duplicates the purpose of another memory space. Every memory space

begins where the previous memory space ends. Together these memory
spaces form the official memory governance map of MGIA™.
1. Memory Integrity Standard (MIS)
Core Question
Is the memory valid?
Canonical Definition
MIS defines the conditions under which memory itself remains
coherent, traceable, accountable, retrievable, reconstructable, and
operationally valid throughout the memory lifecycle.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory is formed. Ends when memory integrity can
be evaluated.
2. Agent Memory Integrity Standard (AMIS)
Core Question
How does an autonomous agent maintain valid memory?
Canonical Definition
AMIS defines the conditions under which AI agents maintain valid
memory formation, storage, retrieval, utilization, adaptation, and
memory continuity while remaining accountable and
operationally reliable.
Governance Boundary
Begins when an autonomous agent forms or uses memory. Ends when
agent memory can be evaluated for integrity.
3. User Memory Integrity Standard (UMIS)
Core Question
How does user-associated memory remain trustworthy?
Canonical Definition
UMIS defines the conditions under which user-associated memory
remains attributable, sovereign, traceable, controllable,
governable, and operationally valid throughout
Human-AI interactions.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory becomes associated with a user. Ends when user
memory integrity can be evaluated.
4. Group Memory Integrity Standard (GMIS)
Core Question
How do groups maintain shared memory?

Canonical Definition
GMIS defines the conditions under which memory shared across teams,
organizations, operational groups, and collaborative environments
remains coherent, synchronized, accountable, and
operationally valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory becomes shared across multiple participants. Ends
when group memory integrity can be evaluated.
5. Temporal Memory Integrity Standard (TMIS)
Core Question
Does memory remain valid across time?
Canonical Definition

ordered, chronologically reconstructable, historically continuous,
traceable, and operationally valid across time.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory persists beyond a single point in time. Ends when
temporal memory continuity can be evaluated.
6. Multimodal Memory Integrity Standard (MMIS)
Core Question
How do multiple memory modalities remain synchronized?
Canonical Definition
MMIS defines the conditions under which memory composed of text,
images, audio, video, sensor data, documents, spatial information,
and future modalities remains coherent, synchronized,
reconstructable, accountable, and operationally valid.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory exists across multiple modalities. Ends when
multimodal memory integrity can be evaluated.
7. Collective Memory Integrity Standard (CMIS)
Core Question
How does memory persist across collectives and generations?
Canonical Definition

CMIS defines the conditions under which memory shared across
institutions, societies, cultures, civilizations, collective
intelligence systems, and future Human-AI ecosystems remains
continuous, retrievable, accountable, and operationally valid
across generations.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory extends beyond individual or group memory
systems. Ends when collective memory continuity can be evaluated.
8. Memory Evolution Integrity Standard (MEIS)
Core Question
How may memory evolve safely?
Canonical Definition
MEIS defines the conditions under which memory may learn, adapt,
improve, refine, reorganize, optimize, and evolve while preserving
continuity, traceability, accountability, and operational validity.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory changes itself. Ends when memory evolution can be
validated and governed.
9. Memory Governance Standard (MGS)
Core Question
How should memory be governed?
Canonical Definition
MGS defines the conditions under which memory authority, memory
access, memory oversight, memory auditability, memory stewardship,
memory accountability, and memory governance remain operationally
valid throughout the memory lifecycle.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory requires governance. Ends when memory governance
effectiveness can be evaluated.
10. Skill Formation Integrity Standard (SFIS)

How does memory become capability?
Canonical Definition
SFIS defines the conditions under which knowledge, learning, memory

utilization, adaptation, experience, and operational execution
become reliable, transferable, measurable, accountable, and
operationally valid skills.
Governance Boundary
Begins when memory influences behavior or execution. Ends when skill
formation can be evaluated.

Memory Integrity → Agent Memory → User Memory → Group Memory →
Temporal Memory → Multimodal Memory → Collective Memory → Memory
Evolution → Memory Governance → Skill Formation

MGIA™ governs the complete memory lifecycle. The
architecture progresses:
Memory Integrity → Agent Memory → User Memory → Group Memory → Temporal Memory → Multimodal
Memory → Collective Memory → Memory Evolution → Memory Governance → Skill Formation
Together these memory spaces govern how memory remains valid
throughout memory formation, storage, retrieval, sharing,
preservation, evolution, governance, and capability formation.
What MGIA™ Defines
MGIA™ defines: where memory begins, where memory remains valid,
where agent memory operates, where user memory exists, where group
memory emerges, where memory persists across time, where multimodal
memory operates, where collective memory survives, where memory
evolves, where memory governance applies, where memory becomes
capability. MGIA™ provides the official memory governance language
used for memory space identification across intelligent systems.
Canonical Principle
MGIA™ does not govern what a system remembers. MGIA™ governs how

memory itself remains valid while the system remembers, learns,
adapts, collaborates, evolves, and develops capability.

MGIA™ serves as the official OOF® memory governance map for AI
systems, autonomous agents, Human-AI environments, robotics, and
future intelligence ecosystems. By defining the primary governable
memory spaces of intelligent systems, MGIA™ provides a structured
memory reference architecture used to identify, classify, govern,
validate, preserve, evolve, and understand memory throughout the
complete memory lifecycle.

chunks.text:
OOF® — Regional Methodology Infrastructure Program
Regional Infrastructure
Regional Methodology Infrastructure Program
Global Call for Regional Methodology Infrastructure
OOF establishes a controlled access pathway
for the creation of Regional Methodology Infrastructure.
This page defines the entry conditions for entities
seeking to participate in the execution layer
of the global OOF system.
OOF operates as a non-executable methodological authority
and does not perform implementation, enforcement,
or commercial activities.
Execution is performed by independent,
system-aligned regional operators under defined conditions.
A. Program Definition
The Regional Methodology Infrastructure Program defines
how methodologies are operationalized across regions.
It enables:
structured registration of methodologies as intellectual assets
controlled licensing and deployment
system-level validation and compatibility enforcement
connection between methodologies and real-world institutions and markets
The program establishes a globally governed
and regionally executed infrastructure layer.
B. Strategic Objective
The objective of this program is to build
the regional execution layer of a global methodology system.
This infrastructure enables methodologies to move
from canonical definition into real operational environments
while preserving:
canonical meaning
structural integrity
validation conditions
system governance
It is designed to connect methodologies with institutions,

markets, and regional execution capacity
without fragmenting the system.
The goal is not to create regional partners.
The goal is to build regional methodology infrastructure.
C. Regional Scope
At the time of publication,
the following regions are recognized for consideration:
European Union
United Kingdom
Switzerland
North America
South America
China
India
Middle East
Africa
Asia-Pacific
Regional Scope Clarification
The regions listed above are indicative reference zones only.
OOF does not define fixed geographical boundaries at this stage.
All regional definitions are subject to:
case-by-case evaluation
strategic system alignment
operator capability
infrastructure readiness
Detailed configurations, including territorial scope
and operational conditions, are defined individually
and may be provided upon request.
OOF reserves the right to:
redefine regional boundaries at any time
combine or subdivide regions
assign overlapping operational scopes
restrict or expand access based on system-level requirements
Regional scope does not constitute ownership.
No exclusivity is granted unless explicitly defined.
D. Call Status
Participation remains open on a rolling basis
until regional positions are fulfilled.
OOF retains full discretion to:
close or suspend participation at any time
limit the number of operators per region
delay or decline activation of any region
Submission does not guarantee evaluation, response, or selection.
OOF does not guarantee activation of all regions.

E. Role of a Regional Operator
A Regional Methodology Operator is responsible for:
operating regional methodology infrastructure
enabling methodology registration under MIP
providing licensing, validation, and implementation support
connecting methodologies to institutions and markets
localizing methodologies without altering canonical meaning
supporting third-party methodology creators
maintaining system integrity and brand protection
building long-term regional ecosystems
This role is execution-based and does not include
authority over definitions or system rules.
F. Ownership and Control Model
Each Regional Operator is structured as follows:
50% — OOF
canonical authority
system governance
global validation and integrity control
50% — Regional Operator / Investor
operational execution
regional development
partnerships
implementation
G. Authority Boundary
OOF retains exclusive authority over:
canonical definitions and meaning
system structure and governance
compatibility validation
global integrity control
Operators may not:
modify or reinterpret methodologies
create conflicting or parallel definitions
operate outside validated system scope
Violation of system integrity results in immediate loss
of operator status.
H. MIP Protection Layer
MIP protects the structural layer where:
meaning is defined
systems are structured
interpretation becomes executable
MIP provides protection beyond traditional frameworks.
It is not limited to content, mechanisms, or naming alone.

It protects methodological structure itself, including:
canonical definitions
system architecture
validation logic
cross-layer relationships
I. Eligibility Requirements
Applicants must demonstrate:
long-term operational and financial stability
understanding of methodology as an intellectual asset
ability to protect system integrity and intellectual property
capability to operate across regulatory environments
readiness to support external methodology creators
ability to translate methodologies into real-world execution
alignment with long-term ecosystem development
This is a long-term infrastructure role,
not a short-term commercial activity.
J. Selection Process
Selection is multi-stage and competitive.
Stage 1 — Initial Evaluation
Submission review and preliminary assessment.
Stage 2 — Capability and Alignment Assessment
Evaluation of strategic fit, operational readiness,
and integrity capacity.
Stage 3 — Final Selection
Final selection is based on:
regional relevance
strategic importance
execution capability
long-term alignment
OOF may select:
a single operator
multiple operators
a consortium
or no operator
K. Strategic Context
Methodologies increasingly define:
AI interpretation and decision systems
compliance and regulatory alignment
economic and value-state validation
trust and auditability
Entities operating methodology infrastructure influence
how systems interpret and execute reality.
The Regional Methodology Infrastructure Program

establishes the infrastructure layer for that function.
Canonical Closing Statement
Access to methodology infrastructure defines
access to execution.
Access to execution defines participation
in system-level reality.

ReMonet™ Standard
ReMonet™ Standard
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Global Methodology Authority
OriginID: OOF-OID-ECO-RMN-2026-01-26-0004
Category: Economic & Value Standards (ECO)
Subcategory: ReMonet™ (RMN)
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Binding
Effective Date: 26 January 2026
Compatibility:
Methodology OS™: Compatible
Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
B. Standard Abstract
This standard defines ReMonet™ as the governed transition process through which admissible economic value may be reintroduced to an asset previously classified as ZVA™.
It establishes the mandatory validation and integrity conditions required before value activation.
ReMonet™ ensures that value restoration is traceable, justified, and non- manipulative.
C. Canonical Definition
ReMonet™ is defined as the canonical transition process by which admissible economic value is formally reassigned to an asset following ZVA™ state, under governed and validated conditions.
ReMonet™ is the only permitted mechanism for transitioning from ZVA™ to Value Asset state.
D. Base
This standard is based on:
Deterministic Asset State Architecture
Non-Skippable Transition Logic
Traceable Historical Continuity
Governed Value Recognition
Integrity Restoration Requirement
Value reactivation must follow documented and validated correction.
E. Purpose & Scope
Purpose

To define the structured mechanism by which economic value may be legitimately restored to an asset after resolution of authenticity, legality, ethical, ecological, or systemic failure.
Scope
Applies to:
Assets in ZVA™ state
Digital and AI-derived systems
Economic instruments
Certified physical and virtual assets
Does not apply to speculative price increase or market-driven revaluation.
F. Applicability
ReMonet™ applies when:
identity is verified
authenticity is restored
compliance violations are resolved
ecological or ethical breaches are corrected
systemic risks are mitigated
All trigger conditions must be documented.
G. Protocol
ReMonet™ transition requires:
Verification of corrective action
Re-evaluation of authenticity and integrity
Compliance confirmation
