chunks.text:
Validation Determination Standard
Validation Determination Standard
Standard ID: VDTS
OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VDTS-2026-08-11-0008
Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Validation Determination
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 11 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) defines the governance
conditions under which the complete governed validation record is
evaluated, integrated, interpreted, bounded, and transformed into a
formal Validation Determination establishing what the executed
validation legitimately demonstrates about the Validation Object
relative to the applicable Validation Criteria, thresholds,
conditions, evidence, methodological limitations, execution
conformity, uncertainty, conflicts, and approved Validation Scope.
Canonical Definition Extension
Validation execution produces results.
Results alone do not create a legitimate validation conclusion.
A validation process may generate:
measurements,
test outputs,
statistical findings,
expert assessments,
observations,
simulations,
criterion outcomes,
contradictory findings,

unresolved uncertainty,
execution limitations,
and residual deviations.
These elements must be interpreted within the governed structure
established by VALIDOS®.
Validation Determination Standard therefore governs
the transformation:
Governed Validation Record → Validation Finding → Criterion
Determination → Integrated Validation Determination
VDTS establishes the conditions necessary to determine:
which execution results may legitimately participate in determination,
which Validation Criteria have sufficient determination basis,
whether individual criteria are satisfied,
not satisfied,
conditionally satisfied,
or not determinable,
how multiple criterion outcomes interact,
how mandatory and non-mandatory criteria differ,
how contradictory findings are treated,
how uncertainty affects determination,
how residual execution limitations propagate,
whether evidence and source conditions constrain interpretation,
whether determination must be scoped or conditional,
whether sufficient basis exists for an overall determination,
and what the governed validation record actually demonstrates.
VDTS does not create a permanent Validation State.
It does not authorize operational reliance.
It determines the validation conclusion supported by the governed
validation record.
Core Question
What does the complete governed validation record legitimately
demonstrate about the Validation Object relative to the applicable
Validation Criteria and governed validation conditions?
Purpose

The purpose of Validation Determination Standard is to prevent
validation conclusions from being reduced to:
raw test scores,
simple pass/fail labels,
majority voting,
selective evidence,
favorable averages,
ungoverned expert opinion,
arbitrary weighting,
or conclusions broader than the validation process can legitimately support.
VDTS creates the interpretive governance layer between:
Validation Execution and:
Validation State
It ensures that a validation conclusion represents what the governed
validation process actually demonstrates—not what stakeholders hoped
it would demonstrate.
Governance Objective
VDTS establishes a governed Validation Determination framework
capable of producing conclusions that are:
criterion-grounded,
evidence-aware,
source-aware,
execution-aware,
scope-bounded,
uncertainty-aware,
conflict-aware,
limitation-aware,
methodologically proportionate,
traceable,
and suitable for later Validation State assignment.
The standard seeks to ensure that:
only determination-ready execution enters conclusion formation,
criterion outcomes remain distinguishable,
critical criteria retain appropriate significance,
missing information is not converted into failure or success,
contradictory results remain visible,
uncertainty is preserved,
conditional findings remain conditional,
determination scope cannot exceed executed scope,
invalid execution portions do not silently contribute,
aggregation remains methodologically justified,

and every Validation Determination can be reconstructed from the validation record supporting it.
Operational Role
Validation Determination Standard serves as the formal conclusion
layer of the VALIDOS® validation lifecycle.
The preceding standards establish:
Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria
→ Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation
Source Reliability → Validation Execution
VDTS then asks:
What does that complete governed validation record
actually demonstrate?
Its structural progression is:
Determination-Ready Execution → Result Qualification → Criterion
Determination → Conflict & Uncertainty Integration → Cross-Criterion
Interpretation → Overall Determination → Validation
Determination Record
The resulting determination can then progress into Validation
State governance.
Governance Scope
Validation Determination Standard governs:
validation-result qualification,
determination basis,
criterion-level determination,
criterion satisfaction,
criterion non-satisfaction,
conditional satisfaction,
non-determinability,
mandatory criterion treatment,
critical criterion treatment,
cross-criterion interpretation,
determination aggregation,
determination hierarchy,
contradictory findings,
determination conflict,
uncertainty integration,
limitation integration,
residual execution impact,
evidence-condition propagation,
source-condition propagation,
determination scope,
partial determination,
conditional determination,

negative determination,
indeterminate determination,
overall Validation Determination,
determination authority where applicable,
determination traceability,
determination change,
and determination reassessment.
Validation Determination Basis
A Validation Determination should be derived from a sufficiently
governed determination basis.
This may include:
Validation Object reference,
Validation Purpose,
actual Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
Validation Criteria,
applicable thresholds,
acceptance and rejection conditions,
Validation Method Framework,
Evidence Fitness information,
Source Reliability information,
Validation Execution Record,
Execution Completeness status,
Execution Conformity status,
execution outputs,
residual deviations,
unresolved exceptions,
limitations,
conflicts,
uncertainty,
and Determination Readiness.
The determination basis defines what information may legitimately
support the validation conclusion.
Determination-Ready Execution
VDTS should consume only execution that is sufficiently ready
for determination.
This may include:
Determination Ready
or:
Determination Conditionally Ready
execution.
Where execution is:
Determination Not Ready
or:
Determination Blocked
VDTS should not manufacture a substantive validation conclusion
unsupported by the execution basis.
Execution Quality and Object Outcome Are Different
VALIDOS® maintains:
Execution Conformity ≠ Validation Success
A perfectly conformant validation may demonstrate that the

Validation Object fails.
Conversely:
Execution Invalidity ≠ Object Invalidity
Invalid execution may prevent VALIDOS® from knowing whether the
object satisfies the Validation Criteria.
VDTS therefore interprets object outcomes only from execution
capable of legitimately supporting them.
Validation Result Qualification
Not every result generated during execution should automatically
contribute to determination.
A result may be:
valid for determination,
conditionally usable,
limited in scope,
superseded,
affected by deviation,
affected by unreliable source conditions,
methodologically incomparable,
or unusable.
VDTS governs which execution results form the legitimate
determination basis.
Criterion Determination
Every applicable Validation Criterion should receive an explicit
determination where sufficient basis exists.
Possible criterion-level outcomes may include: Criterion Satisfied
The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates
satisfaction of the criterion under the applicable conditions.
Criterion Conditionally Satisfied
The criterion is satisfied only within explicit limitations,
assumptions, boundaries, operating conditions, or other
governed restrictions.
Criterion Not Satisfied
The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates that the
required criterion condition has not been satisfied.
Criterion Not Determinable
The governed validation record does not provide sufficient
legitimate basis to determine whether the criterion is satisfied or
not satisfied.

These outcomes remain distinct.
Not Determinable Is a Legitimate Outcome
VALIDOS® establishes:
Insufficient basis for determination ≠ Criterion failure
and:
Insufficient basis for determination ≠ Criterion satisfaction
Where the validation record cannot legitimately answer the criterion
question, the correct outcome is:
Criterion Not Determinable
This prevents uncertainty from being converted into false certainty.
Criterion Satisfaction
Criterion Satisfaction must remain connected to:
the exact criterion,
threshold where applicable,
acceptance conditions,
actual execution outputs,
evidence,
applicable source conditions,
scope,
object version,
and relevant limitations.
A satisfied criterion should therefore be reconstructable rather
than asserted.
Criterion Non-Satisfaction
A criterion should be classified as Not Satisfied only where the
governed validation record provides sufficient basis to
demonstrate non-satisfaction.
Absence of evidence is not automatically evidence of failure.
Therefore:
No Proof of Satisfaction ≠ Proof of Non-Satisfaction
Conditional Criterion Determination
A criterion may be satisfied only under conditions such as:
defined operating range,
limited population,
specific system version,
restricted environment,
continued mitigation,
additional monitoring,
limited time period,
or another governed boundary.
Conditional determination must preserve those conditions.
Mandatory Criteria
Some Validation Criteria may be designated mandatory.

Where a mandatory criterion is:
Not Satisfied
or in some validation contexts:
Not Determinable
the overall Validation Determination may be constrained regardless
of favorable results elsewhere.
The exact consequence must be established through the Validation
Criteria governance structure.
VDTS does not invent mandatory status retrospectively.
Critical Criteria
Certain criteria may be critical because failure has
disproportionate consequence.
A critical criterion should not be neutralized merely through
favorable performance across many less important criteria.
VALIDOS® therefore rejects blind averaging where
materiality differs.
Criterion Weighting
Some validation frameworks may legitimately assign different
significance to different criteria.
Where weighting is used, VDTS requires that weighting be:
established before outcome interpretation where reasonably possible,
justified,
traceable,
methodologically relevant,
and resistant to post-hoc manipulation.
Weighting should not be altered merely because the resulting
conclusion is inconvenient.
Aggregation Is Not Averaging
VALIDOS® establishes:
Cross-Criterion Determination ≠ Arithmetic Average
Different criteria may represent:
mandatory conditions,
critical conditions,
supporting conditions,
independent conditions,
hierarchical conditions,
conditional conditions,
or exclusionary conditions.
Aggregation must preserve their governance meaning.
Cross-Criterion Interpretation

VDTS determines how multiple criterion outcomes collectively
contribute to the overall Validation Determination.
Relevant questions may include:
Are all mandatory criteria satisfied?
Are any critical criteria not satisfied?
Are material criteria not determinable?
Do conditional outcomes restrict scope?
Do criterion conflicts remain?
Can partial validation be legitimately separated?
Does one exclusionary condition override otherwise favorable findings?
Determination Hierarchy
Complex Validation Objects may require hierarchical determination.
For example:
Module Determination → Subsystem Determination →
System Determination
or:
Criterion → Criterion Group → Validation Domain →
Overall Determination
VDTS permits hierarchical structure where the relationships remain
explicit and methodologically justified.
Partial Determination
A Validation Object may support a legitimate conclusion for part of
its Validation Scope while another part remains undetermined
or fails.
Where boundaries can be reliably separated, VDTS may permit:
Partial Positive Determination
Partial Negative Determination
Partial Conditional Determination
or: Partial Indeterminate Determination
This prevents unnecessary all-or-nothing conclusions.
Determination Scope
Every Validation Determination must remain bounded to the scope
actually supported by validation.
The determination should not extend beyond:
validated object version,
tested population,
evaluated environment,
executed scenarios,

applicable operational state,
validated jurisdiction,
or another material boundary.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Determination Scope ≤ Legitimately Executed Validation Scope
Determination and Validation Depth
The strength of a determination depends partly upon the Validation
Depth achieved.
A conclusion supported by exploratory validation should not
automatically be represented as equivalent to one supported by
high-assurance validation.
VDTS therefore preserves the relationship between determination and
achieved Validation Depth.
Contradictory Findings
Different execution results may support conflicting interpretations.
VDTS requires material contradiction to remain visible.
Contradiction may arise from:
different methods,
different environments,
different populations,
different object states,
different evidence,
different sources,
measurement variation,
or genuine object instability.
Determination Conflict
A Determination Conflict exists where legitimate validation findings
support materially incompatible criterion or overall conclusions.
Conflict may require:
additional analysis,
additional validation,
method comparison,
evidence review,
source review,
scope separation,
conditional determination,
or an indeterminate result.
Conflict should not be resolved merely by selecting the
preferred outcome.
Uncertainty Integration
Validation results may contain uncertainty arising from:
evidence,
measurement,
methodology,
source conditions,
execution,
sampling,
population variability,

object behavior,
or unresolved conflict.
VDTS integrates uncertainty into determination rather than
hiding it.
Uncertainty Does Not Automatically Block Determination
Some uncertainty is compatible with legitimate validation.
The relevant question is whether remaining uncertainty is acceptable
for the applicable Validation Criterion, Purpose, Depth, and
determination type.
VDTS therefore supports proportionate uncertainty governance.
Material Uncertainty
Where uncertainty can reasonably change the criterion or overall
conclusion, it becomes material.
Material uncertainty may require:
conditional determination,
indeterminate determination,
additional validation,
narrower scope,
or explicit limitation.
Residual Execution Limitations
Execution may be Determination Ready while carrying
residual limitations.
VDTS must preserve these limitations when interpreting results.
A limitation cannot disappear merely because execution was allowed
to proceed.
Evidence Condition Propagation
Evidence determined: Conditionally Fit
may create corresponding limitations upon Validation Determination.
The determination should not claim more than the evidence basis
can support.
Source Condition Propagation
Similarly, Source Reliability restrictions may constrain how
evidence is interpreted.
For example:
A source usable only with corroboration cannot become the sole
unrestricted basis for a determination unless that condition was
legitimately resolved.
Determination Conditions

An overall Validation Determination may be conditional.
Conditions may include:
restricted use,
specific configuration,
specific population,
defined operating range,
continued control,
continued monitoring,
limited time,
supplementary validation,
or another boundary.
These conditions become important inputs to Validation
State governance.
Overall Validation Determination
VDTS may establish overall determination classes such as:
Positive Validation Determination
The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates
satisfaction of the required Validation Criteria for the defined
scope and conditions.
Conditional Validation Determination
The governed validation record supports a positive determination
only within explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, or
reduced scope.
Negative Validation Determination
The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates
non-satisfaction of one or more criteria whose governance
significance prevents a positive determination for the
defined scope.
Indeterminate Validation Determination
The governed validation record does not provide sufficient
legitimate basis to establish either a positive or negative
overall determination.
Partial Validation Determination Different governed portions of the
Validation Object, criteria set, or Validation Scope legitimately
support different determination outcomes.
These classifications represent the validation conclusion.
They are not yet the persistent Validation State.

Positive Determination Is Not Reliance Authorization
VALIDOS® establishes:
Positive Validation Determination ≠ Authorization to Rely
A system may receive a positive determination while reliance remains
restricted because of:
time,
operational context,
regulatory authority,
risk,
changed environment,
or other governance conditions.
Reliance belongs to the tenth Parent Standard.
Negative Determination Is Not Universal Invalidity
A Negative Validation Determination applies to the Validation
Object, scope, criteria, version, and conditions actually assessed.
It should not automatically be generalized to every use or
future version.
Indeterminate Determination Is Not Failure
An Indeterminate Validation Determination means:
VALIDOS® does not possess sufficient governed basis to establish the
required conclusion.
It does not automatically mean the object is valid.
It does not automatically mean the object is invalid.
This is a legitimate methodological outcome.
Partial Determination
A Partial Validation Determination may be necessary where:
some criteria are satisfied,
some criteria fail,
some are indeterminate,
some scope areas were not executed,
or distinct components legitimately support different outcomes.
Partial determination should preserve those boundaries explicitly.
Determination Authority
Where formal determination requires an identifiable authority, VDTS
may govern:
who or what may issue the determination,
scope of determination authority,
required independence,

required competence,
and authority conditions.
VDTS does not create legal or regulatory authority where
none exists.
Human Determination
A human may perform or approve a Validation Determination.
Where material, relevant considerations may include:
competence,
assigned authority,
independence,
evidence access,
methodological understanding,
and conflict conditions.
Automated Determination
A Validation Determination may be partially or fully automated where
governance permits.
Automated determination may require:
deterministic rules,
governed aggregation logic,
explicit criterion mapping,
controlled thresholds,
system identity,
versioning,
exception handling,
and human escalation where required.
Automation must not make determination logic opaque.
AI-Assisted Determination
AI may assist in:
evidence synthesis,
conflict detection,
uncertainty identification,
criterion mapping,
traceability analysis,
or determination drafting.
However, the governing determination structure must
remain reconstructable.
AI-generated reasoning should not silently replace the approved
determination logic.
Determination Traceability
A formal Validation Determination should be traceable through:
Validation Object
↓
Validation Criteria
↓
Validation Method
↓
Evidence
↓
Sources
↓
Execution Activities
↓
Execution Outputs
↓
Criterion Determinations
↓
Overall Validation Determination
This creates the conclusion chain of VALIDOS®.
Validation Determination Record

A formal Validation Determination Record may preserve:
Determination Identifier,
Validation Object,
object version,
Validation Purpose,
actual Validation Scope,
achieved Validation Depth,
applicable Validation Criteria,
criterion-level outcomes,
mandatory criterion status,
critical criterion status,
execution basis,
evidence basis,
source conditions,
conflicts,
uncertainty,
residual limitations,
determination conditions,
overall Validation Determination,
determination authority where applicable,
effective date,
and sufficient traceability.
Determination Basis Transparency
The determination should permit a qualified reviewer to understand
why the conclusion was reached.
This does not require exposing confidential intellectual property or
unrestricted internal reasoning.
It requires sufficient methodological transparency to reconstruct
the governed basis of the conclusion.
Determination Change Governance
A Validation Determination may require reassessment when:
execution records change,
evidence changes,
Source Reliability changes,
a previously unknown deviation is discovered,
criterion interpretation is corrected,
methodological error is identified,
or another material validation fact changes.
Determination Reassessment
Possible outcomes may include:
Determination Maintained
Determination Modified
Determination Restricted
Determination Suspended
Determination Reversed
or:
Determination Withdrawn
Changes should not erase the historical determination.
Determination Correction

Where a determination error is identified, the correction
should preserve:
Original Determination → Identified Error → Corrected Determination
→ Reason
This supports methodological accountability.
Determination Suspension
A determination may require temporary suspension where material
uncertainty arises but final reassessment has not yet
been completed.
Suspension prevents continued representation of a potentially
outdated conclusion as current.
Determination Withdrawal
A determination may be withdrawn where its methodological basis is
materially destroyed.
Possible triggers include:
invalid execution,
compromised evidence,
major source failure,
critical methodological error,
wrong Validation Object,
or another fundamental defect.
Withdrawal concerns the determination.
It does not by itself establish the object's current Validation
State after reassessment.
Determination Continuity
Validation Determinations should remain historically
connected across:
corrections,
revisions,
revalidations,
system updates,
object versions,
and later Validation States.
This preserves the evolution of validation knowledge rather than
presenting only the latest conclusion.
Determination Is Not Validation State
This boundary is fundamental.
Validation Determination answers:
What does this governed validation event demonstrate?
Validation State answers:
What formal validation condition does the Validation Object
currently hold after considering the applicable determination,

validity conditions, lifecycle status, and change?
The eighth and ninth Parent Standards must therefore
remain separate.
Determination Is Not Reliance
Similarly:
Validation Determination ≠ Reliance Decision
A valid determination can exist while no party is authorized to rely
upon it operationally.
Reliance depends upon:
purpose,
risk,
authority,
time,
environment,
conditions,
intended use,
and revalidation rules.
Governance Boundary
Validation Determination Standard begins when a sufficiently
complete and conformant Validation Execution Record is ready
for determination.
It ends when the governed validation record has been interpreted
into criterion-level findings and an overall Validation
Determination with explicit scope, conditions, limitations,
conflicts, uncertainty, and traceability.
VDTS does not determine:
persistent Validation State,
Validation State expiration,
operational reliance authorization,
reliance transfer,
revalidation triggers,
or post-determination lifecycle governance.
These responsibilities belong to subsequent VALIDOS®
Parent Standards.
Minimum Governance Requirements
A conforming implementation of VDTS should establish:
1. an identifiable Validation Determination Basis,
2. determination-ready execution,
3. qualified execution results,
4. explicit criterion-level determinations,
5. treatment of mandatory and critical criteria,
6. explicit treatment of non-determinability,
7. governed aggregation or cross-criterion interpretation,

8. contradiction and conflict handling,
9. uncertainty integration,
10. propagation of material evidence, source, and execution
limitations, 11. a bounded determination scope, 12. determination
conditions and restrictions, 13. an overall Validation
Determination, 14. determination traceability, 15. and a persistent
Validation Determination Record.
Governance Outputs
VDTS may produce:
Validation Determination Basis,
Determination-Ready Result Set,
Validation Result Qualification Record,
Criterion Determination Record,
Criterion Satisfaction Map,
Criterion Non-Satisfaction Record,
Conditional Criterion Determination,
Criterion Not Determinable Record,
Mandatory Criteria Determination,
Critical Criteria Determination,
Determination Conflict Record,
Validation Uncertainty Record,
Cross-Criterion Interpretation Record,
Determination Aggregation Record,
Partial Determination Record,
Determination Scope Record,
Determination Condition Record,
Validation Determination,
Validation Determination Record,
Validation Determination Traceability Map,
Determination Reassessment Trigger,
Determination Change Record,
Determination Suspension Record,
Determination Withdrawal Record,
and Determination Continuity Reference.
Operational Applications
Validation Determination Standard may be applied across:
artificial intelligence,
machine learning,
autonomous systems,
AI-generated outputs,
software systems,
datasets,
predictions,
simulations,
scientific validation,
healthcare,
financial services,

industrial systems,
cybersecurity,
critical infrastructure,
regulatory environments,
digital identities,
operational governance,
public-sector systems,
and any governed environment requiring a formal validation conclusion.
Relationship to Other OOF Architectures
Validation Determination Standard interoperates with:
GOA™
OBIDENITY®
INTEGROS®
ORA™
AGA™
AIG®
CLIA®
MGIA™
ASGA™
RIS™
by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology through
which the complete governed validation record is transformed into a
bounded and traceable Validation Determination.
GOA™ may provide relevant determination authority and
governance conditions.
OBIDENITY® may preserve the identity and continuity of the
Validation Object and related records.
INTEGROS® may provide integrity conditions affecting evidence,
records, and determination continuity.
ORA™ may provide operational-reality context relevant
to interpretation.
AGA™ may establish accountability for determination roles
and decisions.
RIS™ may influence the strength of determination required for
high-consequence validation.
Specialized AI, cognition, memory, and autonomous-system
architectures may provide domain-specific criteria and conditions
consumed by VDTS.
VDTS does not replace those architectures.
It governs specifically what the completed validation process can
legitimately conclude.
Foundational Principle
Validation results become a legitimate determination only when the

conclusion remains bounded by what the governed validation record
can actually demonstrate.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Determination Standard establishes the formal conclusion
layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture by
transforming determination-ready execution results into
criterion-level and overall Validation Determinations. Through
governance of result qualification, criterion satisfaction,
non-satisfaction, conditionality, non-determinability, mandatory and
critical criteria, cross-criterion interpretation, conflict,
uncertainty, aggregation, scope, limitations, partial determination,
authority, traceability, reassessment, suspension, and withdrawal,
VDTS ensures that validation conclusions cannot exceed the
methodological strength, evidentiary basis, execution quality, or
operational boundaries of the validation process from which they
are derived.

chunks.text:
About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
Governing Whether Evidence Is Fit for Validation
Evidence exists everywhere.
Data exists.
Measurements exist.
Documents exist.
Observations exist.
Test results exist.
But the existence of evidence does not establish that the evidence
is fit for validation.
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) is the fifth Parent
Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture, governing
the conditions under which evidence becomes sufficiently relevant,
applicable, complete, representative, timely, precise, and
methodologically usable for a specific validation purpose.
VEFS addresses one fundamental question:
Is the available evidence actually fit for the validation question
it is expected to answer?
Why Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Exists
Validation frequently relies upon evidence.
However, evidence may be:
accurate but irrelevant,
relevant but incomplete,
extensive but unrepresentative,
precise but outdated,
technically valid but contextually inapplicable,
statistically significant but operationally insignificant,
authoritative but incapable of answering the relevant Validation Criterion,
or abundant while critical evidence remains missing.
This creates an important distinction:
Evidence Availability ≠ Evidence Fitness
VEFS exists to govern that difference.
Evidence After Method
VALIDOS® establishes a deliberate architectural progression:

Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria
→ Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness
This sequence matters.
Before determining whether evidence is fit, VALIDOS® must
already know:
what is being validated,
why it is being validated,
within which boundaries,
against which criteria,
and through which methodological approach.
Only then can the architecture meaningfully ask:
What evidence is required, and is the available evidence capable of
supporting that validation?
Evidence Must Answer a Validation Question
Evidence does not become useful merely because it concerns the same
general subject.
A validation question creates an evidentiary requirement.
The governing relationship is:
Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence →
Evidence Fitness
For example, evidence showing that an AI model performs well under
normal conditions does not necessarily answer a criterion concerning
behavior under infrastructure failure.
Likewise, evidence about one system version does not automatically
validate another version.
VEFS keeps evidence attached to the question it can
legitimately answer.
Evidence Fitness Is Contextual
There is no universal category of permanently "good evidence."
Evidence fitness depends upon its relationship to:
the Validation Object,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Method,
Validation Depth,
operational context,
temporal conditions,
and intended downstream reliance.

The same evidence may therefore be highly fit for one validation and
unusable for another.
Relevance Before Volume
Large evidence volumes can create an appearance of
validation strength.
But volume alone says little about whether the evidence addresses
the actual Validation Criteria.
One thousand irrelevant observations do not necessarily provide
stronger validation than ten highly relevant observations.
VALIDOS® therefore rejects the assumption:
More Evidence = Stronger Validation
VEFS instead asks whether additional evidence materially improves:
criterion coverage,
representativeness,
precision,
uncertainty reduction,
contextual applicability,
or evidentiary completeness.
Evidence Applicability
Relevant evidence may still be inapplicable.
Evidence generated from:
another population,
another system configuration,
another environment,
another jurisdiction,
another model version,
another operating condition,
another lifecycle stage,
or another period
cannot automatically be transferred to the current
Validation Object.
VEFS therefore governs the boundaries within which evidence can
legitimately support validation.
Evidence Completeness
Evidence completeness does not mean collecting everything that can
possibly be collected.
It means that the material evidentiary requirements created by the
Validation Criteria and Method Framework have been
sufficiently addressed.
A validation may contain thousands of evidence items and still
contain a critical Evidence Gap.

VEFS makes such gaps visible.
Evidence Representativeness
Evidence can be technically correct while systematically
representing only favorable conditions.
For example, an AI system may perform strongly across a large
dataset while:
important populations remain absent,
rare conditions remain untested,
difficult scenarios remain excluded,
edge cases remain invisible,
or deployment conditions differ materially from the evidence environment.
VEFS therefore distinguishes evidence quantity from
evidence representativeness.
Evidence Across Time
Evidence can age.
A validation based upon evidence collected before:
a model update,
system modification,
environmental change,
operational drift,
infrastructure change,
new failure discovery,
or significant contextual change
may no longer support the same validation conclusion.
VEFS therefore treats temporal applicability as a governed
evidentiary condition.
Precision and Resolution Matter
Evidence may be too aggregated to reveal what matters.
An average system-performance score may appear acceptable
while concealing:
subgroup failures,
local instability,
extreme events,
temporal degradation,
rare catastrophic behavior,
or boundary-condition failures.
VEFS asks whether evidence possesses sufficient precision and
resolution for the Validation Criterion being examined.
Contradictory Evidence Must Survive
Validation becomes methodologically weak when unfavorable evidence
disappears from the process.

VEFS therefore requires material contradictory evidence to
remain visible.
Contradiction does not automatically invalidate the
Validation Object.
It may indicate:
uncertainty,
contextual differences,
measurement differences,
operational variability,
methodological disagreement,
or a genuine unresolved problem.
The role of VEFS is not to force agreement.
Its role is to ensure that relevant evidence is not removed simply
because it complicates the conclusion.
Evidence Gaps Are Governance Information
Missing evidence is itself meaningful.
An Evidence Gap may reveal that:
a criterion cannot yet be evaluated,
an important population has not been examined,
a failure condition remains unknown,
operational evidence is unavailable,
historical records are incomplete,
or required Validation Depth has not been achieved.
VALIDOS® therefore does not automatically convert missing evidence
into either validity or invalidity.
It preserves the gap as a governed condition.
Evidence Sufficiency Depends on Purpose
Evidence sufficient for one decision may be insufficient
for another.
For example:
Research Exploration
may tolerate greater uncertainty than:
Operational Deployment
and operational deployment may require less evidence than:
High-Consequence Autonomous Authorization
where the consequences of error are materially greater.
VEFS therefore connects evidence sufficiency to the Validation
Purpose, Scope, Depth, and intended reliance.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Source Reliability

This is one of the most important architectural separations
within VALIDOS®.
Evidence Fitness asks:
Can this evidence legitimately help answer the validation question?
Source Reliability asks:
Can the source from which that evidence originates be
sufficiently trusted?
These are different governance questions.
A highly trustworthy source can provide evidence irrelevant to a
particular validation.
A highly relevant piece of evidence can originate from a source
whose reliability remains uncertain.
VALIDOS® therefore governs these spaces separately.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Truth Validation
VEFS does not determine whether every informational statement
contained within evidence represents truth.
Truth-oriented validation may exist as a specialized validation
methodology or reference capability.
VEFS performs a different architectural function.
It determines whether evidence is fit for a governed
validation role.
This keeps VALIDOS® from collapsing validation governance into truth
verification alone.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Determination
Fit evidence does not mean that the Validation Object is valid.
Evidence fitness establishes only that the evidence may legitimately
contribute to the validation process.
The later Validation Determination must evaluate what the complete
governed validation record actually demonstrates.
Therefore:
Evidence Fit ≠ Object Validated
Evidence Fitness Is Not Execution
VEFS also does not determine whether evidence was actually

collected, generated, processed, or evaluated according to the
approved methodology.
That belongs to Validation Execution governance.
This allows VALIDOS® to ask two separate questions:
Was the evidence appropriate?
and:
Was the validation process actually performed correctly using
that evidence?
Both conditions matter.
Evidence Fitness States
VEFS allows the evidence basis to be distinguished through governed
conditions such as:
Evidence Fit
Evidence Conditionally Fit
Evidence Fitness Undetermined
Evidence Insufficient
Evidence Unfit
These conditions describe the evidentiary basis.
They do not describe the Validation State of the Validation Object.
This distinction prevents an evidence assessment from prematurely
becoming a validity conclusion.
Evidence Fitness Can Change
Evidence fitness is not necessarily permanent.
A previously fit evidence basis may require reassessment when:
the Validation Object changes,
the system version changes,
Validation Criteria change,
Validation Scope expands,
Validation Depth increases,
the operating environment changes,
new contradictory evidence appears,
evidence becomes outdated,
or previously unknown limitations are discovered.
VEFS therefore treats evidence fitness as a lifecycle condition.
Position Within VALIDOS®
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard is the fifth Parent Standard of
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture.
Its architectural position is:
Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria

→ Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation
Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination
→ Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation
The first four Parent Standards establish the validation question
and methodological structure.
VEFS establishes whether the evidentiary basis is capable of
supporting that structure.
The next Parent Standard can then ask whether the sources producing
or providing that evidence are sufficiently reliable.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
VEFS operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures.
GOA™ may establish governance conditions affecting evidentiary
authority and responsibility.
OBIDENITY® may establish origin, identity, ownership, and
provenance relationships.
INTEGROS® may establish integrity conditions applicable to evidence.
ORA™ may establish whether evidence corresponds to
operational reality.
AGA™ may establish accountability for evidence creation, handling,
review, and use.
AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may generate specialized evidence
requirements for AI behavior, cognition, memory, and
autonomous operation.
RIS™ may influence required evidence depth according to risk
and consequence.
VEFS does not replace these architectures.
It determines whether relevant evidence can legitimately perform its
assigned role within validation.
Why It Matters
Without Evidence Fitness governance, validation can appear rigorous
while relying upon evidence that does not actually support

the conclusion.
An organization may possess:
large datasets,
extensive testing,
sophisticated analytics,
expert reports,
simulation results,
audit records,
and operational measurements
and still lack evidence for one critical Validation Criterion.
VEFS makes that difference visible.
It transforms the question from:
"Do we have evidence?"
into:
"Do we have the evidence required to legitimately answer this
validation question?"
That is a substantially stronger governance question.
From Evidence Collection to Evidence Governance
Traditional processes may focus heavily on collecting evidence.
VALIDOS® adds another layer:
Evidence must be governed before it can be relied upon
for validation.
This creates a structured transition:
Evidence Requirement → Evidence Identification → Evidence
Qualification → Evidence Coverage → Evidence Gap Analysis → Evidence
Fitness Determination
The result is not merely an evidence repository.
It is a governed evidentiary basis.
Foundational Principle
Evidence is not validation evidence merely because it exists; it
becomes validation evidence when it is fit for the question it is
expected to answer.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard establishes the
evidence-qualification layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance
Architecture. By distinguishing evidence availability from evidence
fitness and governing relevance, applicability, completeness,
representativeness, timeliness, precision, contradiction,

sufficiency, limitations, gaps, change, and traceability, VEFS
ensures that validation cannot derive legitimacy merely from the
existence, quantity, or apparent authority of evidence. Evidence
becomes methodologically usable within VALIDOS® only when it is
demonstrably fit for the specific validation question it is expected
to answer.

Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS)
Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Evidence Adequacy
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Evidence Adequacy
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM) defines the governance
framework for determining whether Relevant, Applicable, and
sufficiently Covered Validation Evidence possesses the necessary
completeness, representativeness, timeliness, precision, resolution,
consistency, and proportional sufficiency to support its assigned
validation role at the required Validation Depth.
It establishes the conditions under which evidentiary coverage
becomes an adequate evidentiary basis rather than merely a populated
evidence set.
Operational Role
VEADM serves as the fourth evidence-qualification gate within the
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard.

The preceding modules establish:
VERM — Does the evidence address the validation question?
VEAM — Does the evidence apply to the actual validation conditions?
VECM — Does the evidence cover the validation space that must
be evidenced?
VEADM asks:
Is the evidence within that coverage actually adequate for the
validation role it must perform?
The governed progression is:
Covered Validation Evidence → Completeness → Representativeness →
Timeliness → Precision → Resolution → Consistency → Proportional
Sufficiency → Evidence Adequacy Determination
VEADM therefore examines the qualitative and proportional adequacy
of the evidence basis after its relevance, applicability, and
coverage have been established.
Module Operational Space
VEADM governs:
evidence adequacy,
evidence completeness,
evidence representativeness,
evidence timeliness,
evidence recency,
evidence precision,
evidence resolution,
evidence granularity,
evidence consistency,
evidentiary diversity,
evidentiary concentration,
evidentiary proportionality,
evidentiary sufficiency,
adequacy thresholds,
adequacy limitations,
conditional adequacy,
adequacy uncertainty,
adequacy degradation,
adequacy change,
and adequacy traceability.
Module Function
VEADM applies after the evidence basis has been mapped against the
required validation space.
Its function is to prevent:
covered criteria being assumed adequately evidenced,
minimal evidence being treated as sufficient merely because coverage exists,

unrepresentative samples supporting broad validation conclusions,
stale evidence being used for rapidly changing Validation Objects,
low-resolution evidence concealing material differences,
imprecise measurements supporting precision-sensitive criteria,
internally inconsistent evidence being aggregated without qualification,
evidence volume substituting for evidentiary quality,
and evidence requirements being satisfied nominally while remaining substantively weak.
Coverage and Adequacy Are Different
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence Coverage asks:
Is the required validation space represented by evidence?
Evidence Adequacy asks:
Is the evidence representing that space sufficiently strong,
complete, representative, current, precise, and proportionate for
the required validation role?
A criterion may therefore possess evidence coverage while remaining
inadequately evidenced.
For example:
A safety criterion may have one relevant and applicable test result.
That creates evidence coverage.
It may still be inadequate for a high-consequence deployment
decision requiring repeated testing across multiple
operating conditions.
Evidence Completeness
Completeness examines whether the available evidence sufficiently
addresses the material components of the evidentiary requirement.
Completeness may concern:
required observations,
required measurements,
required conditions,
required populations,
required scenarios,
required documentation,
required time periods,

or other defined evidence elements.
Evidence completeness is relative to the governed requirement.
It does not mean collecting every possible piece of information.
Representativeness
Evidence must sufficiently represent the conditions to which the
validation conclusion is expected to apply.
VEADM assesses whether the evidence basis
disproportionately represents:
favorable cases,
common cases,
easy-to-measure cases,
accessible populations,
normal operating states,
or other convenient subsets.
Representativeness becomes especially important where validation
conclusions are intended to generalize across diverse or
changing conditions.
Representativeness and Coverage
Coverage and representativeness interact but remain distinct.
Evidence may technically cover several populations while
representing one population with thousands of observations and
another with only a handful.
VECM may identify that both populations possess evidence coverage.
VEADM determines whether that distribution is sufficiently
representative for the intended validation conclusion.
Evidence Timeliness
VEADM evaluates whether evidence is sufficiently current
relative to:
the Validation Object,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
operating environment,
Validation Criteria,
and intended reliance.
Evidence may become less adequate as time passes even when it
remains relevant and technically applicable.
Timeliness requirements may vary significantly between:
stable physical characteristics,

rapidly changing AI systems,
financial environments,
cybersecurity conditions,
evolving populations,
or dynamic operational systems.
Evidence Recency
Recency is one component of timeliness.
Recent evidence is not automatically better evidence.
Older evidence may remain highly adequate where the validated
condition is stable.
Conversely, evidence from several weeks earlier may already be
inadequate for a rapidly changing system.
VEADM therefore evaluates material recency, not recency for its
own sake.
Evidence Precision
Precision concerns whether evidence provides sufficient exactness
for the Validation Criterion being examined.
Where validation depends upon thresholds, small deviations
may matter.
Evidence that is too imprecise may be incapable of distinguishing:
Acceptable
from: Unacceptable
conditions.
Required precision must therefore correspond to the
validation question.
Evidence Resolution
Resolution concerns the level at which evidence can reveal
meaningful variation.
Highly aggregated evidence may conceal:
subgroup differences,
local failures,
temporal instability,
edge-case behavior,
rare events,
component-level failures,
or threshold transitions.
VEADM determines whether the evidence possesses sufficient
resolution for the relevant Validation Criterion and required
Validation Depth.
Evidence Granularity
Granularity concerns how finely evidence is divided or represented.
For example:
System-level average
may be sufficient for one criterion.

Another criterion may require:
component-level, population-level, transaction-level, or
event-level evidence.
VEADM prevents coarse evidence from supporting conclusions requiring
finer-grained visibility.
Evidence Consistency
Evidence may contain internal inconsistencies.
Consistency assessment asks whether:
repeated observations materially agree,
measurement processes produce stable outputs,
comparable conditions produce comparable evidence,
evidence records align where they should,
and material divergence is sufficiently understood.
Perfect consistency is not required.
Real operational systems may legitimately produce variation.
The objective is to distinguish explainable variability from
unresolved evidentiary inconsistency.
Evidence Diversity
Some validation questions benefit from evidentiary diversity.
Evidence may originate from different:
observations,
populations,
environments,
time periods,
scenarios,
methods,
or operational states.
Diversity can reduce dependence upon one narrow evidence condition.
However:
Evidence Diversity ≠ Source Independence
Source independence belongs to subsequent Source
Reliability governance.
VEADM governs diversity of the evidentiary basis itself.
Evidence Concentration
An evidence basis may be numerically large while concentrated around
one narrow condition.
For example:
One million observations from the same environment may provide
excellent evidence of that environment but limited adequacy for a
validation covering many environments.

VEADM therefore assesses whether concentration weakens the evidence
basis relative to the intended validation role.
Proportional Sufficiency
Evidence adequacy must be proportionate to the consequence and depth
of the validation.
A low-consequence preliminary validation may require less
evidence than:
production deployment,
regulatory approval,
medical use,
autonomous decision authority,
critical infrastructure operation,
or another high-consequence reliance context.
VEADM therefore rejects a universal evidence-volume threshold.
Sufficiency must be governed relative to the validation requirement.
Validation Depth and Adequacy
Validation Depth directly affects evidence adequacy.
For example:
Basic Validation Depth
may require evidence sufficient to establish preliminary conformity.
Enhanced Validation Depth
may require broader coverage, stronger precision, greater
representativeness, or additional evidence.
High-Assurance Validation Depth
may require extensive evidence, multiple conditions, deeper
uncertainty analysis, independent corroboration, and stronger
operational representation.
The exact depth model may be defined elsewhere within VALIDOS®.
VEADM consumes the applicable depth requirement.
Evidence Adequacy Threshold
Where useful, a Validation Criterion may establish an Evidence
Adequacy Threshold.
The threshold may define minimum acceptable conditions concerning:
evidence quantity,
sample size,
observation period,
representativeness,
precision,
resolution,

repeated testing,
or other evidentiary requirements.
Thresholds must be justified rather than selected merely to fit
available evidence.
Evidence Sufficiency
Evidence is sufficient when the governed evidence basis provides
enough legitimate support for its assigned validation role relative
to the required Validation Depth.
Sufficiency is not identical to certainty.
Evidence may be sufficient while some uncertainty remains.
The relevant question is whether remaining uncertainty is compatible
with the governed validation requirement.
Adequacy Limitations
Evidence may be adequate while carrying material limitations.
Examples include:
adequate only for one population,
adequate only for normal operation,
adequate only within a specified period,
adequate only at a defined confidence level,
or adequate only when combined with additional evidence.
Limitations must remain attached to the adequacy determination.
Conditional Adequacy
Evidence may receive Conditional Adequacy where it can support
validation only if specified conditions remain satisfied.
Conditions may include:
reduced Validation Scope,
restricted reliance,
supplementary evidence,
additional monitoring,
defined operating limits,
or future evidence collection.
Conditional adequacy must not later be represented as unrestricted
evidentiary adequacy.
Adequacy Uncertainty
Where available information is insufficient to determine whether
evidence is adequate, VEADM preserves uncertainty.
Possible causes include:

unclear evidence requirements,
insufficient sample characterization,
unknown precision,
incomplete temporal information,
unresolved inconsistency,
or uncertain representativeness.
In such cases:
Adequacy Undetermined
is methodologically preferable to unsupported confidence.
Evidence Adequacy Status
VEADM may establish:
Evidence Adequate
The evidence basis is sufficiently complete, representative, timely,
precise, resolved, consistent, and proportionate for the assigned
validation role.
Evidence Conditionally Adequate
The evidence basis is adequate only within defined conditions
or limitations.
Evidence Adequacy Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish adequacy.
Evidence Inadequate
The evidence basis does not provide sufficient support for the
assigned validation role.
These statuses describe evidence adequacy.
They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object.
Adequacy Is Role-Specific
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence adequacy is not a universal property of an evidence set.
The same evidence may be:
Adequate for preliminary assessment, Conditionally Adequate for
limited deployment,
and:
Inadequate for high-consequence reliance.
Adequacy must therefore remain attached to the validation role for
which it was assessed.
Adequacy Degradation
Evidence adequacy may degrade over time.
Degradation may result from:
object evolution,
operational drift,
changing populations,
new failure modes,
changed environments,
aging evidence,

expanded Validation Scope,
increased Validation Depth,
or newly discovered limitations.
VEADM therefore treats evidence adequacy as a potentially
dynamic condition.
Adequacy Change Governance
Material changes affecting evidence adequacy must trigger
proportionate reassessment.
Possible outcomes include:
Adequacy Maintained
Adequacy Restricted
Conditional Adequacy
Additional Evidence Required
Adequacy Withdrawn
This prevents historical adequacy determinations from surviving
material change without review.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Adequacy Requirements
Determine the evidentiary strength required by the Validation
Criteria, Purpose, Scope, Method, and Validation Depth.
2. Assess Completeness
Determine whether material evidentiary requirements are
sufficiently populated.
3. Assess Representativeness
Determine whether evidence sufficiently represents the conditions to
which the validation conclusion is expected to apply.
4. Assess Timeliness Determine whether evidence remains
sufficiently current.
5. Assess Precision and Resolution
Determine whether evidence is sufficiently exact and sufficiently
granular for the relevant Validation Criteria.
6. Assess Consistency and Diversity
Identify material inconsistencies, concentration, and whether
evidentiary diversity is sufficient where required.
7. Assess Proportional Sufficiency
Determine whether the complete evidence basis is proportionate to
the Validation Depth and intended validation role.

8. Establish Adequacy Status
Classify the evidence as:
Evidence Adequate,
Evidence Conditionally Adequate,
Evidence Adequacy Undetermined,
or Evidence Inadequate.
9. Preserve Adequacy Traceability
Maintain:
Evidence Adequacy Record,
evidence requirement references,
completeness assessment,
representativeness assessment,
timeliness assessment,
precision assessment,
resolution assessment,
consistency assessment,
diversity assessment,
concentration record,
sufficiency rationale,
Validation Depth reference,
limitations,
conditions,
adequacy status,
version,
reassessment triggers,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Evidence Adequacy Output
VEADM may produce:
Evidence Adequacy Assessment,
Evidence Completeness Record,
Evidence Representativeness Assessment,
Evidence Timeliness Assessment,
Evidence Precision Record,
Evidence Resolution Record,
Evidence Consistency Assessment,
Evidence Diversity Assessment,
Evidence Concentration Record,
Evidence Sufficiency Determination,
Conditional Adequacy Record,
Adequacy Limitation Record,
Adequacy Change Record,
and Evidence Adequacy Determination.
These outputs support the final Evidence Fitness governance stage.
Use Case 1 — Medical AI
Scenario
A diagnostic AI system has relevant and applicable evidence covering
all required patient groups.
Application
VECM establishes population coverage.
VEADM then discovers that one clinically important subgroup is
represented by only a very small number of observations,

insufficient for the required Validation Depth.
Result
The evidence possesses coverage but remains inadequately
representative for unrestricted validation of that subgroup.
Use Case 2 — Critical Infrastructure
Scenario
An autonomous control system possesses evidence covering normal,
degraded, emergency, and recovery conditions.
Application
VEADM determines that emergency-condition evidence was generated
several system versions earlier and at substantially lower
operating scale.
Result
The Evidence Coverage Map remains populated, but evidentiary
adequacy for current high-consequence operation requires
reassessment and potentially new evidence.
Architectural Position
Validation Evidence Adequacy is the fourth internal governance space
of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS).
The progression now becomes:
Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability →
Evidence Coverage → Evidence Adequacy
VERM determines whether evidence addresses the validation question.
VEAM determines whether it applies to the target conditions.
VECM determines whether the required validation space is covered.
VEADM determines whether the evidence within that coverage is
sufficiently strong and proportionate.
The final module can then determine whether the complete governed
evidence basis is ready to be recognized as fit for subsequent
VALIDOS® validation governance.
Foundational Principle
Evidence coverage shows where evidence exists; evidence adequacy

determines whether what exists is enough.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Adequacy Module establishes the governance
framework through which covered validation evidence is assessed for
substantive evidentiary strength. By governing completeness,
representativeness, timeliness, precision, resolution, granularity,
consistency, diversity, concentration, proportionality, sufficiency,
limitations, conditionality, degradation, change, and traceability,
VEADM ensures that the presence of evidence across a validation
space cannot be mistaken for an evidentiary basis strong enough to
support the validation role for which it is intended.

Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM)

AI-Readable: Yes

Governed Space
Validation Evidence Applicability
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM) defines the
governance framework for determining whether Relevant Validation
Evidence generated, observed, measured, recorded, or established
under specific conditions can legitimately be applied to the actual
Validation Object, version, configuration, population, environment,
jurisdiction, operational state, temporal condition, and Validation
Scope for which validation is being performed.
It establishes the conditions under which evidence relevance becomes
Evidence Applicability within a defined validation context.
Operational Role

VEAM serves as the second evidence-qualification gate within the
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard.
The preceding Validation Evidence Relevance Module asks:
Does this evidence meaningfully address the validation question?
VEAM asks:
Can this relevant evidence legitimately be applied to this
particular Validation Object and the conditions for which the
validation conclusion is intended?
The governed progression is:
Relevant Validation Evidence → Applicability Dimensions → Condition
Comparison → Transfer Assessment → Applicability Determination →
Applicable Validation Evidence
VEAM prevents relevant evidence from being generalized beyond the
conditions it can legitimately support.
Module Operational Space
VEAM governs:
evidence applicability,
object applicability,
version applicability,
configuration applicability,
population applicability,
environmental applicability,
jurisdictional applicability,
operational applicability,
lifecycle applicability,
temporal applicability,
scale applicability,
domain applicability,
context applicability,
evidence transfer,
applicability equivalence,
applicability divergence,
applicability boundaries,
conditional applicability,
applicability limitations,
applicability uncertainty,
applicability change,
and applicability traceability.
Module Function
VEAM applies after evidence has been determined sufficiently
relevant to one or more Validation Criteria or
evidence requirements.
Its function is to prevent:

evidence from one object being automatically applied to another,
evidence from an old system version being silently transferred to a new version,
evidence from one configuration being generalized across materially different configurations,
population-specific findings being represented as universal,
evidence from controlled environments being assumed valid in real-world environments,
jurisdiction-specific evidence being transferred without examining regulatory or contextual differences,
evidence from normal operating conditions being applied to extreme conditions,
historical evidence being treated as permanently applicable,
evidence generated at one scale being generalized to another,
and similarity being mistaken for methodological equivalence.
Relevance and Applicability Are Different
VALIDOS® establishes a strict distinction:
Evidence Relevance asks:
Does the evidence address the validation question?
Evidence Applicability asks:
Does that evidence address the validation question under conditions
sufficiently aligned with the actual validation context?
Evidence may therefore be relevant but inapplicable.
For example: A study examining the same type of AI system may be
highly relevant.
If it concerns a materially different model version, population,
deployment environment, or operating configuration, its
applicability may remain limited.
Applicability Dimensions
VEAM evaluates evidence across the dimensions capable of materially

affecting transfer into the governed validation context.
These may include:
Object
Version
Configuration
Population
Environment
Jurisdiction
Operational State
Lifecycle Stage
Time
Scale
Domain
Context
Not every validation requires every dimension.
The applicable dimensions depend upon the Validation Object and
Validation Scope.
Object Applicability
Evidence must possess a legitimate relationship to the actual
Validation Object.
Evidence generated from:
the same object,
an equivalent object,
a predecessor object,
a related object,
a representative object,
or another object class
may possess different degrees of applicability.
Object similarity alone does not establish applicability.
Material differences must be examined.
Version Applicability
Validation evidence frequently becomes version-sensitive.
A software patch, model update, dataset change, component
replacement, algorithm modification, or system redesign may alter
whether previous evidence remains applicable.
VEAM therefore asks:
Does the evidence still describe the version being validated?
Where the answer is uncertain, evidence applicability must not
be assumed.
Configuration Applicability
The same Validation Object may operate under materially
different configurations.
Evidence generated under one configuration may not support another
when differences affect the characteristic being validated.
Relevant configuration differences may include:
model parameters,
hardware,
software dependencies,
safety settings,

system permissions,
operational constraints,
infrastructure,
or integration architecture.
Applicability must remain configuration-aware.
Population Applicability
Where evidence concerns people, users, patients, customers,
operators, datasets, or other populations, VEAM evaluates whether
the represented population corresponds sufficiently to the
population within the Validation Scope.
Relevant differences may include:
age,
language,
geography,
behavior,
demographic composition,
usage pattern,
clinical characteristics,
technical capability,
or another validation-relevant characteristic.
Evidence from one population should not automatically support
conclusions about materially different populations.
Environmental Applicability
Evidence may depend upon the environment in which it was produced.
Relevant environmental dimensions may include:
physical environment,
digital environment,
network conditions,
infrastructure,
weather,
operating load,
surrounding systems,
user behavior,
security conditions,
or interaction context.
Controlled-environment evidence may remain valuable.
However, its applicability to operational reality must be
explicitly governed.
Jurisdictional Applicability
Some evidence depends upon jurisdictional conditions.
These may include:
laws,
regulatory requirements,
institutional practices,
technical standards,
healthcare systems,
financial structures,
documentation requirements,
or governance expectations.

Evidence valid within one jurisdiction may remain technically
relevant while being insufficient for validation under another
jurisdictional environment.
Operational Applicability
Evidence must correspond to the operational conditions represented
by the Validation Scope.
Evidence generated during:
Normal Operation
may not automatically apply to:
Degraded Operation
Emergency Operation
Adversarial Conditions
or:
Maximum Load
VEAM prevents one operational state from silently representing all
operational states.
Lifecycle Applicability
Validation Objects may behave differently across lifecycle stages.
Evidence from:
development,
testing,
pre-deployment,
deployment,
mature operation,
degraded operation,
maintenance,
or retirement
may have different applicability.
Lifecycle transfer requires governance where stage differences
are material.
Temporal Applicability
Evidence exists in time.
Its applicability may change because:
the Validation Object evolves,
populations change,
environments change,
dependencies change,
operating conditions drift,
external knowledge improves,
or previously unknown failure modes emerge.
VEAM therefore evaluates whether historical evidence remains
applicable to the current validation.
Scale Applicability
Evidence produced at one scale may not remain valid at another.
Examples include:
prototype → production system,
small dataset → population-scale deployment,
laboratory network → national infrastructure,
one autonomous agent → multi-agent ecosystem,

low transaction volume → high-volume financial operation.
Scale may introduce new dependencies, interactions, failure modes,
or emergent behavior.
Evidence transfer across scale therefore requires
explicit assessment.
Domain Applicability
A methodology or evidence basis may originate in one domain and be
proposed for another.
For example:
Evidence derived from industrial automation may inform
autonomous-system validation.
However, domain differences may affect:
operating assumptions,
risk conditions,
user interaction,
regulatory expectations,
or failure consequences.
VEAM governs whether cross-domain evidence transfer
remains legitimate.
Applicability Equivalence
Evidence transfer becomes stronger where the original evidence
conditions and target validation conditions can be shown to be
materially equivalent for the validation question.
Equivalence does not require every characteristic to be identical.
It requires that material differences do not invalidate the
evidentiary relationship.
VEAM therefore distinguishes:
Identical Conditions
from:
Materially Equivalent Conditions
and:
Materially Different Conditions
Applicability Divergence
An Applicability Divergence exists where the evidence-generation
conditions and target validation conditions differ in a way that may
materially affect evidentiary meaning.
Divergence does not automatically make evidence unusable.
It creates a governance requirement to determine:
whether transfer remains legitimate,

whether applicability should be conditional,
whether additional evidence is required,
or whether the evidence must be excluded from the target validation role.
Evidence Transfer
VEAM governs the transfer of evidence across conditions.
The governed relationship is:
Source Evidence Context → Material Difference Assessment → Transfer
Basis → Target Validation Context
Transfer should possess an identifiable methodological basis.
Statements such as:
"The systems are similar."
or:
"This worked before."
do not by themselves establish evidence applicability.
Transfer Conditions
Evidence transfer may depend upon conditions such as:
verified equivalence,
bounded configuration differences,
unchanged relevant components,
comparable populations,
stable operating conditions,
supplementary evidence,
independent confirmation,
or restricted Validation Scope.
Transfer conditions must remain attached to the evidence after
applicability determination.
Applicability Boundary
Every evidence item or evidence body may possess a boundary beyond
which its applicability cannot be assumed.
An Applicability Boundary may define:
versions,
configurations,
populations,
environments,
time periods,
operational states,
jurisdictions,
scale,
or other conditions.
The boundary prevents validation conclusions from silently expanding
beyond the evidence base.
Conditional Applicability
Evidence may be classified as applicable only under
explicit conditions.
Examples include:
Applicable only to software version 4.2.

Applicable only to represented patient populations.
Applicable only under nominal network conditions.
Applicable only within the validated operating range.
Applicable only when combined with current operational evidence.
Conditional applicability must remain visible throughout subsequent
VALIDOS® governance.
Applicability Uncertainty
Where evidence transfer cannot be confidently established or
rejected, VEAM preserves uncertainty.
Evidence may receive:
Applicability Undetermined
rather than being silently accepted or excluded.
This is particularly important where:
systems are novel,
evidence is scarce,
conditions are partially comparable,
or material differences are poorly understood.
Applicability Status
Relevant Validation Evidence may receive an applicability status
such as:
Applicable The evidence can legitimately support the defined
validation role under the target conditions.
Conditionally Applicable
The evidence may support the validation role only within explicit
conditions or limitations.
Applicability Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish
legitimate applicability.
Not Applicable
The evidence cannot legitimately be transferred to the target
validation context for the proposed role.
These statuses remain specific to the
evidence-to-context relationship.
Applicability Is Relationship-Specific
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence applicability is not a permanent property of evidence.
The same evidence may be:
Applicable to Object Version A,

Conditionally Applicable to Version B,
and:
Not Applicable to Version C.
Applicability must therefore remain attached to the exact conditions
for which it has been assessed.
Applicability and Evidence Gaps
When relevant evidence is found to be inapplicable, an Evidence Gap
may emerge.
This is important because evidence may appear to exist until
applicability is examined.
For example:
A system may possess extensive historical testing.
If the system has undergone a material architectural change, much of
that evidence may no longer apply.
VEAM therefore helps distinguish:
Apparent Evidence Coverage
from:
Applicable Evidence Coverage
Applicability Change Governance
Evidence applicability may change because of:
object modification,
version change,
configuration change,
population change,
environmental change,
jurisdictional change,
lifecycle progression,
operational drift,
scale expansion,
changed Validation Scope,
or new knowledge concerning material differences.
Material changes require proportionate applicability reassessment.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Evidence Origin Conditions
Identify the material conditions under which the evidence was
generated, observed, measured, or recorded.
2. Establish Target Validation Conditions
Identify the corresponding conditions of the actual Validation
Object and Validation Scope.
3. Compare Material Dimensions
Assess relevant differences across:
object,
version,
configuration,
population,
environment,
jurisdiction,

operation,
lifecycle,
time,
scale,
domain,
and context.
4. Identify Applicability Divergence
Determine whether any material difference may affect the
evidentiary relationship.
5. Establish Transfer Basis
Where evidence is transferred, document the methodological basis
supporting that transfer.
6. Establish Applicability Boundary
Define the conditions within which evidence may legitimately
support validation.
7. Establish Applicability Status
Classify the evidence as:
Applicable,
Conditionally Applicable,
Applicability Undetermined,
or Not Applicable.
8. Preserve Applicability Traceability
Maintain:
Evidence Identifier,
originating evidence conditions,
target validation conditions,
material-difference assessment,
transfer basis,
applicability dimensions,
divergence record,
applicability boundary,
conditions,
limitations,
status,
version,
reassessment triggers,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Applicability Output
VEAM may produce:
Evidence Applicability Record,
Evidence Context Profile,
Evidence-to-Target Comparison,
Applicability Divergence Record,
Evidence Transfer Assessment,
Evidence Transfer Basis,
Applicability Boundary,
Conditional Applicability Record,
Applicability Determination,
Applicability Change Record,
and Applicable Validation Evidence Set.
These outputs support subsequent Evidence Fitness governance.
Use Case 1 — Updated AI Model
Scenario
An AI model has previously undergone extensive validation.

A new version changes the model architecture and training data.
Application
The historical evidence remains relevant to the general
validation questions.
VEAM evaluates whether it remains applicable to the new
model version.
Evidence relating to unchanged external interfaces may remain
applicable, while performance and behavioral evidence affected by
the architecture and training changes may require new validation.
Result
Historical evidence is not discarded wholesale, but neither is it
automatically transferred.
Applicability is governed at the level of material change.
Use Case 2 — Healthcare Deployment
Scenario
A medical AI system was validated using evidence from hospitals in
one country and is proposed for deployment in another.
Application
VEAM assesses differences in:
patient population,
clinical workflow,
language,
healthcare infrastructure,
operating conditions,
and regulatory context.
Result
Some evidence may remain Applicable, some may become Conditionally
Applicable, and additional local evidence may be required where
material Applicability Divergence exists.
Architectural Position
Validation Evidence Applicability is the second internal governance
space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS).
The progression now becomes:
Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability
VERM establishes whether evidence addresses the validation question.
VEAM establishes whether that relevant evidence can legitimately be

applied to the actual validation conditions.
Subsequent Evidence Fitness governance can then determine whether
the applicable evidence basis provides sufficient coverage,
completeness, representativeness, timeliness, and overall fitness.
Foundational Principle
Relevant evidence cannot legitimately support a validation
conclusion beyond the conditions to which that evidence applies.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Applicability Module establishes the governance
framework through which relevant evidence is tested against the
actual conditions of validation before it may support a validation
conclusion. By governing object, version, configuration, population,
environment, jurisdiction, operation, lifecycle, temporal, scale,
domain, and contextual applicability, together with evidence
transfer, divergence, boundaries, conditionality, uncertainty,
change, and traceability, VEAM prevents validation evidence from
being silently generalized beyond the conditions it can
legitimately represent.

→ Next module: Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM)
