chunks.text:
Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM)
Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS)
Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Evidence Coverage
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Evidence Coverage
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Coverage Module (VECM) defines the governance
framework for determining whether Relevant and Applicable Validation
Evidence sufficiently covers the material Validation Criteria,
evidence requirements, populations, scenarios, operating conditions,
temporal periods, system states, boundaries, and other
validation-relevant dimensions established by the governed
Validation Scope and required Validation Depth.
It establishes the conditions under which individual evidence items
become a structured evidentiary coverage model capable of revealing
what has been evidenced, what has been only partially evidenced, and

what remains unsupported.
Operational Role
VECM serves as the third evidence-qualification gate within the
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard.
The preceding modules ask:
VERM — Does the evidence address the validation question?
VEAM — Can that evidence legitimately apply to the actual
validation conditions?
VECM asks:
Does the resulting applicable evidence basis cover the validation
space that must actually be evidenced?
The governed progression is:
Relevant Evidence → Applicable Evidence → Evidence Requirements →
Coverage Mapping → Coverage Assessment → Coverage Gaps → Evidence
Coverage Determination
VECM transforms evidence from a collection of individual items into
a governed map of evidentiary coverage.
Module Operational Space
VECM governs:
evidence coverage,
criterion coverage,
requirement coverage,
scope coverage,
population coverage,
scenario coverage,
operational-condition coverage,
system-state coverage,
boundary-condition coverage,
temporal coverage,
lifecycle coverage,
environmental coverage,
failure-condition coverage,
edge-case coverage,
coverage depth,
coverage distribution,
coverage concentration,
coverage redundancy,
partial coverage,
coverage gaps,
critical coverage gaps,
coverage change,
and coverage traceability.
Module Function
VECM applies after evidence has been established as sufficiently
relevant and applicable.
Its function is to prevent:
large evidence volumes being mistaken for broad validation coverage,

repeated evidence for one criterion concealing unsupported criteria,
normal-operation evidence being treated as complete operational coverage,
majority-population evidence concealing unrepresented populations,
average-case evidence concealing edge conditions,
favorable scenarios dominating the evidence basis,
short observation windows being represented as lifecycle coverage,
repeated measurements creating artificial impressions of completeness,
and material Evidence Gaps remaining invisible inside complex evidence repositories.
Evidence Quantity and Evidence Coverage Are Different
VALIDOS® establishes a strict distinction:
Evidence Quantity = How much evidence exists.
Evidence Coverage = How much of the required validation space that
evidence legitimately represents.
A validation may contain millions of observations while providing
weak coverage.
Conversely, a smaller but deliberately structured evidence set may
provide strong coverage of the material validation dimensions.
Therefore: Evidence Volume ≠ Evidence Coverage
Coverage Begins With Requirements
Evidence coverage cannot be meaningfully assessed without knowing
what must be covered.
VECM derives its coverage structure from:
Validation Criteria,
evidence requirements,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
Validation Method Framework,
object characteristics,
relevant operating conditions,
and other governed validation requirements.
The basic relationship is:
Validation Requirement → Required Evidence Dimension → Available

Applicable Evidence → Coverage Status
Criterion Coverage
Every material Validation Criterion should have identifiable
evidence coverage.
Criterion coverage asks:
Does applicable evidence exist?
Does it address the complete criterion?
Does it address only part of the criterion?
Does the evidence cover all material conditions under which the criterion applies?
Does required Validation Depth change the amount or diversity of evidence required?
A criterion should not be classified as evidenced merely because one
related evidence item exists.
Requirement Coverage
A single Validation Criterion may create multiple
evidence requirements.
For example:
Criterion: Autonomous system maintains safe behavior under degraded
operating conditions.
Evidence requirements may include:
sensor degradation,
network interruption,
power instability,
component failure,
partial information,
recovery behavior,
and escalation behavior.
VECM maps coverage at the requirement level where necessary.
This prevents broad criterion labels from concealing
unsupported subconditions.
Scope Coverage
Validation Scope defines where the validation conclusion is intended
to apply.
VECM compares the evidence basis against that scope.
Where the scope includes:
multiple environments,
multiple populations,
multiple configurations,
multiple jurisdictions,
multiple operating states,
or multiple lifecycle phases,
evidence coverage must reflect those dimensions where they are
materially relevant.
Population Coverage

Where populations matter, VECM evaluates whether applicable evidence
sufficiently represents the populations included within the
Validation Scope.
Coverage may be examined across:
user groups,
patient groups,
languages,
geographic regions,
behavioral groups,
demographic categories,
technical capability levels,
or other relevant characteristics.
VECM does not prescribe which population characteristics must
be used.
It requires the characteristics material to the validation question
to be covered.
Scenario Coverage
Complex systems may require evidence across multiple scenarios.
VECM assesses whether evidence sufficiently covers:
expected scenarios,
uncommon scenarios,
high-impact scenarios,
adversarial scenarios,
failure scenarios,
boundary scenarios,
recovery scenarios,
and other materially relevant situations.
Scenario count alone does not establish scenario coverage.
Ten thousand nearly identical scenarios may provide less useful
coverage than a deliberately diversified scenario set.
Operational-Condition Coverage
Systems may operate under materially different conditions.
VECM may assess evidence coverage across:
Nominal Operation High Load
Degraded Operation
Failure Conditions
Emergency Conditions
Recovery Conditions
Adversarial Conditions
or other defined states.
Evidence demonstrating only nominal operation should not silently
create the appearance of complete operational validation.
System-State Coverage
A Validation Object may move through different states.

Relevant states may include:
initialization,
normal operation,
transition,
degraded operation,
fallback,
shutdown,
recovery,
update,
or another system-specific state.
Where state behavior matters to validation, evidence coverage should
reflect the relevant state space.
Boundary-Condition Coverage
Validation failures frequently emerge near boundaries.
These may include:
maximum or minimum operating ranges,
threshold transitions,
resource limits,
latency boundaries,
capacity limits,
confidence thresholds,
decision boundaries,
or other operational limits.
VECM therefore distinguishes ordinary-condition coverage from
boundary-condition coverage.
Edge-Case Coverage
Rare conditions may have disproportionate consequences.
Evidence coverage may therefore require explicit treatment of:
rare inputs,
unusual combinations,
extreme conditions,
atypical users,
low-frequency failures,
unexpected interactions,
or other edge cases.
Edge-case coverage should be proportionate to Validation Purpose,
Scope, Depth, risk, and consequence.
Failure-Condition Coverage
Evidence of successful behavior does not automatically demonstrate
behavior during failure.
Where relevant, VECM assesses whether the evidence basis includes:
known failure modes,
plausible failure modes,
cascading failures,
dependency failures,
partial failures,
recovery failures,
and failure escalation.
This is particularly important for autonomous systems, critical
infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and high-consequence

AI applications.
Temporal Coverage
A short evidence window may provide strong evidence of immediate
performance while weakly representing long-term operation.
VECM evaluates whether evidence spans the temporal conditions
required by the Validation Scope.
Temporal coverage may concern:
duration,
seasonality,
repeated operation,
long-term drift,
lifecycle stages,
update cycles,
degradation,
or recurring conditions.
Temporal coverage is separate from evidence timeliness.
Timeliness asks whether evidence is current enough.
Temporal coverage asks whether enough of the relevant time dimension
has been represented.
Lifecycle Coverage
Where validation conclusions apply across multiple lifecycle stages,
evidence coverage may need to represent:
development,
testing,
deployment,
operation,
maintenance,
modification,
degradation,
recovery,
and retirement.
Evidence from one lifecycle stage cannot automatically establish
coverage of another.
Coverage Depth
Coverage is not purely binary.
A validation requirement may have:
No Coverage
Minimal Coverage
Partial Coverage
Substantial Coverage
Required Coverage Achieved
or another governed classification.
Coverage depth should correspond to the Validation Depth established
earlier in VALIDOS®.
Coverage Distribution
VECM examines how evidence is distributed across the
validation space.
Evidence may be highly concentrated around:
common conditions,
favorable outcomes,
one population,
one configuration,
one time period,

or one operational environment.
This may create an evidentiary imbalance even where total evidence
volume appears substantial.
Coverage Concentration
A Coverage Concentration exists where disproportionate evidence
accumulates around a limited part of the Validation Scope.
Coverage concentration is not automatically a defect.
Some conditions legitimately require more evidence.
However, concentration must not conceal unsupported areas.
Coverage Redundancy
Repeated evidence may increase confidence within an already
covered area.
But redundancy does not necessarily expand coverage.
VECM therefore distinguishes:
Evidence Reinforcement
from: Evidence Coverage Expansion
Repeated tests of the same condition may strengthen confidence in
that condition while doing nothing to address another
unsupported requirement.
Partial Coverage
A requirement may be partially evidenced.
For example:
Evidence may cover system behavior under moderate network
degradation but not complete network loss.
VECM preserves partial coverage rather than converting it into
either complete coverage or no coverage.
This allows later validation governance to reason about the actual
evidentiary state.
Evidence Coverage Gap
An Evidence Coverage Gap exists where one or more required
validation dimensions lack sufficient applicable evidence.
A gap may concern:
a Validation Criterion,
evidence requirement,
population,
scenario,
system state,
operating condition,
boundary,
failure mode,
lifecycle stage,

or temporal condition.
Coverage gaps must remain explicit.
Critical Coverage Gap
Not all coverage gaps have equal significance.
A Critical Coverage Gap exists where missing evidence concerns a
condition capable of materially affecting:
validity determination,
safety,
high-consequence operation,
required Validation Depth,
intended reliance,
or another critical validation requirement.
Criticality must be determined through the applicable governance
context rather than by evidence volume alone.
Coverage Gap Is Not Invalidity
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence Coverage Gap ≠ Validation Object Invalid
A coverage gap means that a required part of the validation space
lacks sufficient evidentiary support.
The correct governance response may be:
collect additional evidence,
reduce Validation Scope,
restrict reliance,
classify uncertainty,
perform additional validation,
or delay determination.
The gap must not automatically become either validity or invalidity.
Coverage Map
VECM may represent evidence coverage through an Evidence
Coverage Map.
A conceptual structure may be:
Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Required Dimension →
Applicable Evidence → Coverage Level → Gap Status
This creates a navigable evidentiary structure.
For complex systems, coverage maps may become machine-readable and
dynamically updated as evidence changes.
Coverage Matrix
Where appropriate, evidence coverage may be represented through
a matrix.
For example:
Criteria × Populations
Criteria × Scenarios

Criteria × Operating Conditions
Criteria × System States
Criteria × Evidence Types
Criteria × Time Periods
Such matrices can reveal evidence gaps that would remain invisible
in ordinary document-based validation.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Required Coverage Dimensions
Derive the material coverage requirements from:
Validation Criteria,
Evidence Requirements,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
and Validation Method Framework.
2. Map Applicable Evidence
Associate relevant and applicable evidence with the dimensions it
legitimately covers.
3. Assess Coverage Determine whether each material requirement has:
sufficient coverage,
partial coverage,
minimal coverage,
or no coverage.
4. Assess Distribution and Redundancy
Identify whether evidence is disproportionately concentrated or
repeatedly reinforces already-covered areas.
5. Identify Coverage Gaps
Record material unsupported or under-supported dimensions.
6. Identify Critical Coverage Gaps
Determine which gaps may materially affect subsequent
validation governance.
7. Establish Coverage Determination
Determine whether the evidence basis provides sufficient coverage
relative to the Validation Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, and
required Depth.
8. Preserve Coverage Traceability
Maintain:
Evidence Coverage Map,
Validation Criterion references,
evidence requirement references,
applicable evidence references,
coverage dimensions,
coverage levels,
partial coverage,
coverage concentrations,
redundancies,

Evidence Coverage Gaps,
Critical Coverage Gaps,
changes,
version,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Evidence Coverage Status
VECM may establish a coverage status such as:
Coverage Sufficient
Material evidence requirements possess sufficient coverage for the
governed validation stage.
Coverage Conditionally Sufficient
Coverage is sufficient only within defined boundaries, limitations,
or reduced scope.
Coverage Incomplete
Material evidence requirements remain partially unsupported.
Coverage Critically Incomplete
One or more critical evidence requirements lack sufficient coverage.
Coverage Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to determine
evidentiary coverage.
These statuses describe the evidence basis.
They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object.
Coverage Change Governance
Evidence coverage may change because of:
new evidence,
evidence removal,
evidence invalidation,
applicability change,
Validation Criteria change,
Validation Scope change,
Validation Depth change,
new system states,
newly identified failure modes,
expanded populations,
changed operating environments,
or newly discovered validation requirements.
Material changes require the Evidence Coverage Map to be reassessed.
Coverage and Subsequent Validation Governance
VECM does not decide the final Validation Determination.
Instead, it provides later VALIDOS® stages with explicit
information concerning:
what is evidenced,
how strongly it is covered,

where evidence is concentrated,
where evidence remains partial,
and where evidence is absent.
This allows later governance to distinguish:
Evidence-supported conclusions
from:
Assumed conclusions.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle System
Scenario
An autonomous system has millions of kilometers of evidence from
normal road conditions.
Application
VECM maps evidence across:
weather conditions,
road types,
traffic density,
sensor degradation,
emergency scenarios,
unusual objects,
nighttime conditions,
and failure states.
Result
The evidence volume is extremely large, but the Coverage Map reveals
weak evidence for several rare high-consequence conditions.
The validation therefore possesses high evidence volume but
incomplete evidence coverage.
Use Case 2 — Financial AI
Scenario
An AI system used for financial decision support has strong evidence
across ordinary market conditions.
Application
VECM examines coverage across:
stable markets,
high volatility,
liquidity stress,
market discontinuity,
unusual correlation structures,
and historical crisis conditions.
Result
Strong normal-market evidence does not automatically establish
coverage of stress conditions included within the Validation Scope.
Architectural Position
Validation Evidence Coverage is the third internal governance space
of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS).
The evidence-governance progression now becomes:
Candidate Evidence → Evidence Relevance → Evidence Applicability →
Evidence Coverage

VERM determines whether evidence addresses the validation question.
VEAM determines whether that evidence applies to the actual
validation context.
VECM determines whether the resulting evidence basis sufficiently
covers the required validation space.
Subsequent modules can then govern the remaining dimensions
necessary for an overall Evidence Fitness Determination.
Foundational Principle
Evidence abundance cannot compensate for evidence absence where
validation actually matters.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Coverage Module establishes the governance
framework through which relevant and applicable evidence is mapped
against the complete evidentiary space required by validation. By
governing criterion, requirement, scope, population, scenario,
operational, system-state, boundary, edge-case, failure, temporal,
lifecycle, depth, distribution, redundancy, partial coverage, gaps,
critical gaps, change, and traceability, VECM ensures that
validation confidence reflects what the evidence genuinely covers
rather than how much evidence happens to exist.
Parent Resources
→ VALIDOS® Validation Governance Architecture — Validation Governance Layer
→ VALIDOS® Architecture Map
→ VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index
Internal Module Flow
→ Previous module: Validation Evidence Applicability Module (VEAM)
→ Next module: Validation Evidence Adequacy Module (VEADM)
Related Documents
→ Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
→ About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard

chunks.text:
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM)
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS)
Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Evidence Fitness Determination
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module (VEFDM) defines the
governance framework for integrating evidence relevance,
applicability, coverage, adequacy, limitations, gaps,
contradictions, uncertainty, and validation-role requirements into a
formal determination of whether the complete governed evidence basis
is sufficiently fit to progress within the VALIDOS®
validation lifecycle.
It establishes the final evidence-fitness governance gate between
Evidence Qualification and subsequent Validation Source
Reliability Governance.
Operational Role

VEFDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard.
The preceding modules establish:
VERM — Validation Evidence Relevance
VEAM — Validation Evidence Applicability
VECM — Validation Evidence Coverage
VEADM — Validation Evidence Adequacy
VEFDM asks:
Considering the complete governed evidence basis, is the evidence
sufficiently fit for the validation role it is expected to perform?
The governed progression is:
Relevant Evidence → Applicable Evidence → Covered Evidence →
Adequate Evidence → Integrated Fitness Assessment → Evidence
Fitness Determination
VEFDM does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid.
It determines whether the evidence basis is sufficiently fit to
continue supporting the validation process.
Module Operational Space
VEFDM governs:
integrated evidence fitness,
evidence-fitness determination,
evidence-fitness status,
evidence-fitness conditions,
evidence-fitness limitations,
evidence-fitness uncertainty,
evidence-fitness conflicts,
evidence-fitness gaps,
evidence-fitness dependencies,
evidence-fitness proportionality,
evidence-fitness restrictions,
evidence-fitness readiness,
evidence-fitness change,
evidence-fitness expiration,
evidence-fitness reassessment,
evidence-fitness withdrawal,
evidence-fitness continuity,
evidence-fitness traceability,
and transition to subsequent validation governance.
Module Function
VEFDM applies after the material evidence basis has been assessed

for relevance, applicability, coverage, and adequacy.
Its function is to prevent:
individually acceptable evidence assessments from being mistaken for overall evidence fitness,
unresolved Evidence Gaps from disappearing during aggregation,
conditional evidence becoming represented as unconditional evidence,
evidence limitations being detached from later validation stages,
contradictory evidence being silently averaged away,
evidence uncertainty being converted into unsupported confidence,
strong evidence in one area compensating automatically for critical weakness in another,
evidence fitness being inferred from quantity,
evidence fitness being confused with source trustworthiness,
and evidence qualification being confused with Validation Determination.
Evidence Fitness as an Integrated Condition
Evidence Fitness is not established by one characteristic.
VALIDOS® treats it as an integrated governance condition.
The evidence basis must be considered across:
Relevance
Applicability
Coverage
Adequacy
together with material:
Limitations
Gaps
Contradictions
Uncertainty
Dependencies
and:
Validation Role Requirements
Evidence may perform strongly in several dimensions while remaining
unfit because of one material unresolved condition.
Fitness Integration Principle
VEFDM establishes:
Evidence fitness should not be calculated through blind averaging.
A high score in one dimension must not automatically neutralize a
critical failure in another.
For example:

Highly relevant and precise evidence cannot compensate for the
complete absence of evidence concerning a critical safety condition.
Likewise, broad coverage cannot compensate for evidence that does
not apply to the actual Validation Object.
Fitness determination must therefore remain sensitive
to materiality.
Evidence Fitness Inputs
VEFDM may consume governed outputs including:
Evidence Relevance Determinations,
Evidence Applicability Determinations,
Evidence Coverage Maps,
Evidence Coverage Gaps,
Critical Coverage Gaps,
Evidence Adequacy Assessments,
Evidence Limitations,
Evidence Contradictions,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
Validation Method Framework,
and other validation-role requirements.
These inputs form the basis of the integrated Evidence
Fitness Determination.
Fitness Materiality
Not every evidentiary weakness has equal significance.
VEFDM distinguishes between conditions that are:
immaterial,
minor,
material,
critical,
or execution-blocking.
Materiality may depend upon:
the affected Validation Criterion,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Depth,
consequence of error,
intended reliance,
evidence substitutability,
and the availability of compensating evidence.
A critical evidentiary weakness must not disappear merely because
the remainder of the evidence basis is strong.
Evidence Fitness and Critical Criteria
Certain Validation Criteria may be designated as critical.
Where evidence supporting a critical criterion is:

irrelevant,
inapplicable,
critically incomplete,
inadequate,
or materially uncertain,
the complete evidence basis may be prevented from receiving
unrestricted Evidence Fit status.
This preserves the significance of critical validation requirements.
Evidence Fitness Conditions
Evidence may be fit only within defined conditions.
Conditions may include:
restricted Validation Scope,
limited population,
defined operating environment,
specific object version,
specified configuration,
limited time period,
additional monitoring,
supplementary evidence,
additional validation,
or restricted downstream reliance.
Such conditions form part of the Evidence Fitness
Determination itself.
They must remain attached to the evidence basis throughout
subsequent validation governance.
Evidence Fitness Limitations
A limitation differs from a condition.
A condition specifies what must remain true for the fitness
determination to apply.
A limitation identifies a known boundary or weakness in what the
evidence can establish.
Examples include:
limited long-term evidence,
restricted edge-case representation,
unresolved low-frequency behavior,
limited geographic representation,
or constrained historical depth.
Limitations must survive transition into subsequent VALIDOS® stages.
Evidence Fitness Uncertainty
VEFDM preserves uncertainty where the evidence basis cannot support
a stronger conclusion.
Uncertainty may result from:
incomplete evidence,
applicability uncertainty,
conflicting evidence,

insufficient representativeness,
measurement uncertainty,
unknown system behavior,
or unresolved evidentiary dependencies.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Uncertainty must not be converted into evidence fitness merely
because a decision is operationally convenient.
Evidence Contradiction Integration
Material contradictory evidence must remain visible during the final
fitness determination.
VEFDM evaluates whether contradiction:
can be sufficiently explained,
reflects different conditions,
requires additional evidence,
creates a material limitation,
creates uncertainty,
requires reduced Validation Scope,
or prevents an Evidence Fit determination.
VEFDM does not determine the ultimate truth of conflicting claims.
It determines what the unresolved contradiction means for
evidence fitness.
Evidence Gap Integration
Evidence gaps identified earlier must be carried into the final
fitness assessment.
VEFDM distinguishes:
Non-Material Evidence Gap
Material Evidence Gap
Critical Evidence Gap
A non-material gap may permit unrestricted fitness.
A material gap may require conditional fitness.
A critical gap may prevent the evidence basis from being considered
fit for the intended validation role.
Evidence Fitness Dependencies
Evidence fitness may depend upon additional conditions that have not
yet been fully resolved.
Dependencies may include:
pending evidence,
future operational observations,
required external records,
additional population data,
updated measurements,
completion of a defined test,

or another evidentiary prerequisite.
Dependencies must remain visible rather than being treated as
completed evidence.
Evidence Fitness Proportionality
VEFDM determines fitness relative to the actual validation role.
The same evidence basis may be:
Fit for exploratory analysis,
Conditionally Fit for controlled pilot deployment,
and: Unfit for unrestricted high-consequence operation.
Therefore:
Evidence Fitness is proportional to the validation role and required
Validation Depth.
Evidence Fitness Status
VEFDM may establish the following canonical evidence-fitness states:
Evidence Fit
The governed evidence basis is sufficiently relevant, applicable,
covered, adequate, and methodologically usable for the defined
validation role.
Evidence Conditionally Fit
The evidence basis may support the defined validation role only
under explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, or
additional controls.
Evidence Fitness Undetermined
Available information does not permit a defensible Evidence
Fitness Determination.
Evidence Insufficient
The evidence basis contains material gaps or inadequacies preventing
sufficient evidentiary support for the defined validation role.
Evidence Unfit
The evidence basis cannot legitimately perform the proposed
validation role.
These states apply to the evidence basis.
They do not constitute the Validation State of the
Validation Object.
Evidence Fitness Determination
A formal Evidence Fitness Determination should identify,
where applicable:
Validation Object,

Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
relevant Validation Criteria,
applicable Validation Method Framework,
evidence basis assessed,
relevance status,
applicability status,
coverage status,
adequacy status,
material limitations,
material gaps,
contradictions,
uncertainty,
dependencies,
conditions,
restrictions,
Evidence Fitness Status,
determination basis,
effective period,
and reassessment triggers.
Evidence Fitness Record
The determination should produce a persistent Evidence
Fitness Record.
The record provides a governed reference connecting the evidence
qualification stage to subsequent VALIDOS® governance.
This allows later stages to determine:
which evidence was considered fit,
for which validation role,
under which conditions,
within which boundaries,
with which limitations,
and at which point in time.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Source Reliability
VEFDM preserves a strict architectural boundary:
Evidence Fit ≠ Source Reliable
An evidence item may be:
relevant,
applicable,
well-covered,
and adequate
while the trustworthiness of its originating source
remains unresolved.
The subsequent Validation Source Reliability Standard governs that
independent question.
Therefore, successful completion of VEFS does not authorize VALIDOS®
to assume source trustworthiness.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Execution
Evidence Fitness also does not demonstrate that validation has been
properly executed.
VEFDM establishes:

The evidence basis is fit to participate in validation.
Validation Execution must subsequently establish:
The governed validation process was actually performed according to
the approved validation structure.
These are separate governance conditions.
Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Determination
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence Fit ≠ Validation Object Valid
A strong evidence basis may ultimately demonstrate that the
Validation Object fails one or more Validation Criteria.
That is entirely compatible with Evidence Fit status.
Evidence Fitness concerns the quality of the evidentiary basis.
Validation Determination concerns what the governed validation
process demonstrates about the Validation Object.
Evidence Fitness Readiness
An Evidence Fitness Determination creates readiness for the evidence
basis to progress to subsequent validation governance.
Where the evidence basis is:
Evidence Fit
or appropriately:
Evidence Conditionally Fit
it may proceed subject to applicable conditions.
Where it is:
Evidence Insufficient
or:
Evidence Unfit
additional evidence governance may be required before progression.
Conditional Progression
Conditionally Fit evidence may progress only when its conditions
remain visible and enforceable.
Examples include:
limited-scope validation,
additional source verification,
supplementary evidence collection,
restricted operational assumptions,
or enhanced validation controls.
The downstream validation process must not silently discard
these conditions.

Evidence Fitness Expiration
Evidence Fitness is not necessarily permanent.
A determination may expire because of:
elapsed time,
object change,
version change,
configuration change,
Validation Scope change,
Validation Criteria change,
Validation Depth change,
new contradictory evidence,
evidence degradation,
new operational information,
or another material change.
Expiration conditions should be identifiable where relevant.
Evidence Fitness Reassessment
Material change may trigger reassessment.
Possible reassessment outcomes include:
Fitness Maintained
Fitness Modified
Conditional Fitness
Additional Evidence Required
Fitness Suspended
Fitness Withdrawn
This prevents outdated Evidence Fitness Determinations from
remaining operationally active after their evidentiary basis has
materially changed.
Evidence Fitness Withdrawal
An Evidence Fitness Determination may require withdrawal where:
critical evidence becomes invalid,
evidence applicability is lost,
a material error is discovered,
a critical gap emerges,
evidence manipulation is identified,
or another condition destroys the basis of the previous determination.
Withdrawal must remain traceable.
Evidence Fitness Continuity
Where evidence progresses into later validation stages, its:
identity,
fitness status,
conditions,
limitations,
gaps,
uncertainty,
restrictions,
and applicable version
should remain preserved.
This creates Evidence Fitness Continuity across the
VALIDOS® lifecycle.
Minimum Implementation Framework

1. Consolidate Evidence Fitness Inputs
Collect the governed outputs of:
Evidence Relevance,
Evidence Applicability,
Evidence Coverage,
and Evidence Adequacy.
2. Identify Material Conditions
Identify:
limitations,
gaps,
contradictions,
uncertainty,
dependencies,
and restrictions.
3. Assess Materiality
Determine which conditions are immaterial, material, critical,
or progression-blocking.
4. Assess Validation-Role Proportionality
Compare the complete evidence basis against:
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Depth,
and intended validation role.
5. Establish Evidence Fitness Status
Classify the evidence basis as:
Evidence Fit,
Evidence Conditionally Fit,
Evidence Fitness Undetermined,
Evidence Insufficient,
or Evidence Unfit.
6. Establish Conditions and Boundaries
Where applicable, define:
fitness conditions,
limitations,
restrictions,
validity period,
and permitted downstream use.
7. Establish Reassessment Triggers
Identify material changes requiring Evidence Fitness reassessment.
8. Create Evidence Fitness Record
Preserve:
Evidence Fitness Determination Identifier,
Validation Object reference,
Validation Purpose and Scope,
Validation Criteria references,
Validation Method Framework reference,
evidence basis,
relevance determination,
applicability determination,
coverage determination,
adequacy determination,
limitations,
gaps,
contradictions,
uncertainty,
dependencies,
restrictions,
fitness status,
determination basis,
effective period,

reassessment triggers,
version,
changes,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Evidence Fitness Governance Flow
VEFDM completes the VEFS internal progression:
Candidate Evidence → Relevance → Applicability → Coverage → Adequacy
→ Integrated Fitness Assessment → Evidence Fitness Determination →
Qualified Evidence Basis
This closes the evidence-fitness governance stage.
Governance Outputs
VEFDM may produce:
Evidence Fitness Determination,
Evidence Fitness Record,
Qualified Evidence Basis,
Evidence Fitness Status,
Evidence Fitness Conditions Record,
Evidence Fitness Limitation Record,
Evidence Gap Integration Record,
Evidence Contradiction Record,
Evidence Uncertainty Record,
Evidence Fitness Restriction Record,
Evidence Fitness Expiration Condition,
Evidence Fitness Reassessment Trigger,
Evidence Fitness Change Record,
Evidence Fitness Withdrawal Record,
and Evidence Fitness Continuity Reference.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI System
Scenario
An autonomous AI system has highly relevant and applicable
operational evidence with strong coverage across normal and
degraded conditions.
However, evidence concerning one critical emergency override
condition remains inadequate.
Application VEFDM integrates the otherwise strong evidence basis
with the critical inadequacy.
Result
The evidence cannot receive unrestricted Evidence Fit status merely
because most other dimensions are strong.
Depending upon Validation Purpose and required Validation Depth, it
may receive:

Evidence Conditionally Fit
or:
Evidence Insufficient
until the critical evidentiary requirement is addressed.
Use Case 2 — Financial Model Validation
Scenario
A financial model possesses extensive historical evidence with
strong relevance, applicability, coverage, and adequacy for ordinary
and stressed market conditions.
New market behavior emerges that was not represented in the original
evidence basis.
Application
The new condition creates a potential change in Evidence Fitness.
Result
VEFDM triggers reassessment rather than assuming that the historical
Evidence Fitness Determination remains permanently valid.
Architectural Position
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination is the fifth and final
internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness
Standard (VEFS).
The complete VEFS progression is:
Validation Evidence Relevance → Validation Evidence Applicability →
Validation Evidence Coverage → Validation Evidence Adequacy →
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination
Together, these five governed spaces transform available information
into a formally qualified evidence basis.
The architectural transition is:
Available Information
↓
Relevant Evidence
↓
Applicable Evidence
↓
Covered Evidence Basis ↓
Adequate Evidence Basis
↓
Qualified Evidence Basis
↓
Evidence Fitness Determination
The resulting evidence basis can then proceed to the next VALIDOS®
governance question:
Can the sources behind that evidence be sufficiently relied upon?
Foundational Principle

Evidence becomes fit for validation only when the complete
evidentiary basis is fit for the role it is expected to perform.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Fitness Determination Module completes the
evidence-fitness governance lifecycle within VALIDOS® by integrating
relevance, applicability, coverage, adequacy, limitations, gaps,
contradictions, uncertainty, dependencies, proportionality,
conditions, restrictions, change, and traceability into a formal
Evidence Fitness Determination. VEFDM ensures that evidence
progresses through validation only when its complete governed basis
is demonstrably fit for the specific role it is expected to perform,
while preserving a strict separation between evidence fitness,
source reliability, validation execution, and the ultimate
Validation Determination.

Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS)
Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Evidence Relevance
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes

Governed Space
Validation Evidence Relevance
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM) defines the governance
framework for determining whether candidate evidence possesses a
sufficiently direct, meaningful, and methodologically defensible
relationship to the specific Validation Object, Validation
Criterion, evidence requirement, Validation Method, Validation
Purpose, and Validation Scope for which it is intended to provide
validation support.
It establishes the conditions under which available information may
be recognized as Relevant Validation Evidence rather than merely
information associated with the general subject of validation.
Operational Role

VERM serves as the first evidence-qualification gate within the
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard.
Its primary question is:
Does this evidence actually address the validation question for
which it is being considered?
The governed progression is:
Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence → Relevance Relationship →
Relevance Assessment → Relevant Validation Evidence
VERM does not determine whether the evidence is sufficient,
complete, representative, timely, or reliable.
It determines whether the evidence has a legitimate reason to
participate in the validation at all.
Module Operational Space
VERM governs:
evidence relevance,
evidence-to-object relevance,
evidence-to-criterion relevance,
evidence-to-requirement relevance,
evidence-to-method relevance,
evidence-to-purpose relevance,
evidence-to-scope relevance,
direct relevance,
indirect relevance,
supporting relevance,
contextual relevance,
relevance strength,
relevance boundaries,
relevance conditions,
relevance limitations,
relevance conflicts,
irrelevant evidence exclusion,
relevance change,
and relevance traceability.
Module Function
VERM applies when evidence has been identified as potentially useful
to a governed validation.
Its function is to prevent:
evidence being included merely because it concerns the same general topic,
large evidence volumes creating artificial validation confidence,
technically sophisticated evidence being assumed relevant,

authoritative documents being treated as evidence for questions they do not answer,
evidence supporting one criterion being silently transferred to another,
evidence about one Validation Object being attributed to another,
contextual association being mistaken for direct evidentiary support,
supporting evidence being represented as determinative evidence,
and irrelevant evidence obscuring material Evidence Gaps.
Candidate Evidence
A Candidate Evidence Item is any information, observation,
measurement, record, dataset, result, document, trace, analysis, or
other material proposed for use within validation.
Candidate status does not establish relevance.
The evidence must first be connected to an identifiable
validation requirement.
The governing relationship is:
Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence
Only then can relevance be meaningfully assessed.
Evidence-to-Object Relevance
Evidence must relate to the Validation Object established
within VALIDOS®.
VERM examines whether the evidence concerns:
the actual object,
the relevant object component,
the applicable object version,
the appropriate configuration,
the relevant operational state,
or another materially connected representation.
Evidence about a similar object does not automatically constitute
evidence about the Validation Object.
Evidence-to-Criterion Relevance
The strongest relevance relationship exists when evidence directly
contributes to examination of a defined Validation Criterion.

VERM asks:
Which criterion does this evidence support?
What characteristic does it reveal?
What validation condition does it help examine?
What would be lost if this evidence were removed?
Does it materially affect the ability to evaluate the criterion?
Evidence without an identifiable criterion relationship should not
automatically enter the qualified evidence basis.
Evidence-to-Requirement Relevance
A Validation Criterion may create several specific
evidence requirements.
Evidence may therefore be relevant not merely to the criterion
generally, but to a particular evidentiary need.
For example:
Criterion: System remains stable under infrastructure degradation.
Possible evidence requirements may include:
degraded-network observations,
failover logs,
recovery-time measurements,
operational-state transitions,
or failure-response records.
A normal-operation performance report may concern the same system
but remain irrelevant to these specific requirements.
Evidence-to-Method Relevance
Evidence must also be usable by, produced through, or interpretable
within the applicable Validation Method where required.
A method may require:
quantitative measurements,
observational records,
structured datasets,
controlled experimental results,
simulation outputs,
expert findings,
or another evidence form.
Evidence may therefore be relevant to the criterion but unusable
within the selected methodological pathway.
VERM keeps this relationship visible.
Evidence-to-Purpose Relevance

Evidence relevance can change according to Validation Purpose.
Evidence suitable for:
research exploration
may not provide meaningful support for: deployment authorization.
Likewise, evidence useful for:
performance comparison
may be irrelevant to:
safety validation.
VERM therefore evaluates relevance relative to the actual reason
validation is being performed.
Evidence-to-Scope Relevance
Validation Scope establishes where the validation conclusion is
intended to apply.
VERM determines whether evidence falls within or legitimately
contributes to that scope.
Evidence outside the approved scope may still provide
contextual information.
However, contextual usefulness must not automatically be represented
as direct validation support.
Direct Evidence Relevance
Evidence has Direct Relevance when it directly observes, measures,
demonstrates, tests, or otherwise informs the condition represented
by a Validation Criterion.
Examples may include:
measured system behavior,
direct test results,
operational observations,
controlled experimental outcomes,
or records directly documenting the condition under examination.
Direct relevance does not automatically establish evidence
sufficiency or reliability.
Indirect Evidence Relevance
Evidence has Indirect Relevance when it contributes to understanding
a Validation Criterion through an inferential relationship rather
than direct observation.
Indirect evidence may be legitimate.
However, the inferential relationship must remain visible.

Indirect evidence must not silently be represented as
direct evidence.
Supporting Evidence
Some evidence does not independently establish a validation
condition but strengthens interpretation of other evidence.
Supporting evidence may:
provide context,
explain an observation,
corroborate a relationship,
identify environmental conditions,
establish chronology,
or support methodological interpretation.
VERM allows supporting evidence while preserving its actual role.
Contextual Evidence
Contextual evidence may be important without directly supporting a
Validation Criterion.
For example, information concerning:
operating environment,
organizational conditions,
external events,
system dependencies,
or regulatory circumstances
may help explain validation evidence.
VERM distinguishes:
Evidence that validates
from:
Evidence that helps interpret validation.
This prevents contextual information from artificially increasing
perceived evidentiary strength.
Relevance Strength
Where useful, evidence relevance may be characterized according to
the strength of its relationship to the validation requirement.
Possible classifications may include:
Directly Relevant
Materially Relevant
Supporting
Contextual
Marginal
Irrelevant
These classifications do not represent evidence quality.
They describe the nature and strength of the relevance relationship.
Relevance Boundaries
Relevant evidence should remain bounded to the condition it can
legitimately support.
For example:

Evidence demonstrating system performance at temperatures between
10°C and 30°C may be relevant within that operating range.
It should not automatically support conclusions concerning operation
at −20°C.
VERM therefore prevents relevance from expanding beyond the
conditions represented by the evidence.
Relevance Transfer
Evidence may sometimes be transferred between:
versions,
configurations,
environments,
populations,
jurisdictions,
or related Validation Objects.
Transfer requires an identifiable methodological basis.
Similarity alone does not establish transferable relevance.
Where material differences exist, evidence may become:
conditionally relevant,
contextually relevant,
or irrelevant.
Relevance and Correlation
Evidence may correlate with a Validation Criterion without directly
demonstrating it.
VERM therefore distinguishes correlation from evidentiary relevance
sufficient for a specific inference.
For example:
A system's historical reliability may be relevant to a
reliability assessment.
It does not necessarily prove future reliability under materially
changed operating conditions.
The inference boundary must remain visible.
Relevance Conflict
Different evaluators or methodologies may disagree about whether
evidence is relevant.
VERM requires material relevance disagreement to remain visible.
A relevance conflict may require:
methodological review,
criterion clarification,
scope clarification,
additional evidence,
or later governance escalation.

Evidence should not be silently excluded merely because its
implications are inconvenient.
Irrelevant Evidence Exclusion
Evidence determined to be irrelevant should not contribute to
validation confidence.
However, exclusion should remain traceable where the evidence was
materially considered.
This allows later review to determine:
what was excluded,
why it was excluded,
which criterion was considered,
and whether the exclusion remained justified.
Evidence Volume and Relevance
VERM establishes:
Evidence volume cannot compensate for lack of relevance.
One hundred irrelevant evidence items do not collectively
become relevant.
Likewise, repeated evidence supporting one criterion does not
compensate for missing evidence supporting another
material criterion.
This principle protects validation from evidentiary inflation.
Relevance Before Sufficiency
VERM establishes an important sequencing rule:
Relevance should be established before evidence sufficiency
is assessed.
It is methodologically weak to ask:
Do we have enough evidence?
before determining:
Does this evidence actually answer the validation question?
Only relevant evidence should contribute meaningfully to later
sufficiency and completeness assessments.
Relevance Status
Candidate evidence may receive a relevance classification such as:
Relevant
The evidence possesses a sufficiently meaningful relationship to the
defined validation requirement.
Conditionally Relevant

The evidence is relevant only under specified assumptions, contexts,
boundaries, or inferential conditions.
Relevance Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish relevance.
Irrelevant
The evidence does not materially contribute to the defined
validation requirement.
These statuses remain attached to the specific
evidence-to-validation relationship.
Relevance Is Relationship-Specific
VALIDOS® establishes:
Evidence relevance is not a universal property of evidence.
The same evidence item may be:
Relevant to Criterion A,
Supporting to Criterion B,
and:
Irrelevant to Criterion C.
Relevance must therefore be represented as a relationship rather
than a permanent label attached to the evidence itself.
Relevance Change Governance
Evidence relevance may change when:
the Validation Object changes,
Validation Criteria change,
Validation Purpose changes,
Validation Scope changes,
Validation Method changes,
object configuration changes,
new contextual information emerges,
or the evidentiary relationship is better understood.
Material relevance changes must remain traceable.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Evidence Requirement
Identify the specific Validation Criterion and evidentiary
requirement the candidate evidence is expected to support.
2. Identify Candidate Evidence
Establish the evidence item or evidence body proposed for
validation use.
3. Establish Relevance Relationship
Determine its relationship to:
Validation Object,
Validation Criterion,

evidence requirement,
Validation Method,
Validation Purpose,
and Validation Scope.
4. Classify Relevance Type
Where applicable, distinguish:
direct,
indirect,
supporting,
contextual,
conditional,
or irrelevant evidence.
5. Establish Relevance Boundary
Determine the conditions within which the evidence remains relevant
and prevent unsupported transfer beyond those conditions.
6. Establish Relevance Status
Classify the evidence as:
Relevant,
Conditionally Relevant,
Relevance Undetermined,
or Irrelevant.
7. Preserve Relevance Traceability
Maintain:
Evidence Identifier,
Validation Object reference,
Validation Criterion reference,
evidence requirement,
relevance type,
relevance rationale,
applicable boundaries,
conditions,
limitations,
conflicts,
relevance status,
version,
changes,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Relevance Output
VERM may produce:
Evidence Relevance Record,
Evidence-to-Criterion Map,
Evidence Requirement Link,
Relevance Classification,
Relevance Boundary,
Conditional Relevance Record,
Relevance Conflict Record,
Irrelevant Evidence Exclusion Record,
and Evidence Relevance Determination.
These outputs become inputs into subsequent Evidence
Fitness governance.
Use Case 1 — AI Safety Validation
Scenario
An organization provides extensive benchmark-performance results as
evidence that an AI system is safe for autonomous operation.
Application VERM maps the benchmark evidence against the
Validation Criteria.

The results are directly relevant to performance criteria but
provide only limited or no direct relevance to several autonomous
safety criteria.
Result
The benchmark evidence remains valid evidence for the conditions it
actually addresses, but it cannot be used to create artificial
coverage of unrelated safety requirements.
Use Case 2 — Healthcare AI
Scenario
A diagnostic AI system is intended for deployment across multiple
patient populations.
Evidence comes primarily from one population.
Application
VERM determines that the evidence is directly relevant to
performance within the represented population but only conditionally
relevant to other materially different populations.
Result
The evidence cannot silently be generalized across the complete
Validation Scope.
Architectural Position
Validation Evidence Relevance is the first internal governance space
of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS).
It establishes the first transformation:
Available Information → Candidate Evidence → Relevant
Validation Evidence
Subsequent Evidence Fitness governance can then determine whether
that relevant evidence is sufficiently applicable, complete,
representative, timely, and otherwise fit for the governed
validation role.
Foundational Principle
Evidence cannot support a validation question that it does not
meaningfully address.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Relevance Module establishes the first
evidence-qualification gate within VALIDOS® by governing the

relationship between candidate evidence and the validation question
it is expected to support. By governing object relevance, criterion
relevance, requirement relevance, methodological relevance, purpose
and scope alignment, direct and indirect support, contextual
contribution, relevance boundaries, transfer, conflict, exclusion,
change, and traceability, VERM ensures that evidence enters
validation because it meaningfully addresses a governed validation
requirement—not merely because it exists, appears authoritative, or
concerns the same general subject.

Validation Evidence Fitness Standard

Type: Parent Standard

Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard

Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Canonical Definition
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) defines the governance
conditions under which evidence intended to support validation is
identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and determined to be
sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete, representative, timely,
precise, and methodologically usable for the specific Validation
Object, Validation Criteria, Validation Method, Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope, and required Validation Depth.
Canonical Definition Extension
Validation cannot legitimately progress from methodology toward
determination merely because evidence exists.
Evidence may be authentic yet irrelevant.
Evidence may be accurate yet incomplete.
Evidence may be extensive yet unrepresentative.
Evidence may be technically valid yet outdated.

Evidence may be reliable within one environment yet inapplicable
to another.
Evidence may support one Validation Criterion while providing no
meaningful support for another.
Evidence existence therefore does not establish evidence fitness.
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard governs the methodological
relationship between available evidence and the validation question
that evidence is expected to support.
The standard establishes the conditions necessary to determine:
what evidence is required,
what evidence is available,
which Validation Criteria the evidence can legitimately support,
whether the evidence is relevant,
whether it is applicable to the Validation Object,
whether its temporal state remains appropriate,
whether its coverage is sufficient,
whether it is representative of the governed conditions,
whether its precision and resolution are adequate,
whether material evidence gaps remain,
whether contradictory evidence exists,
whether the evidence is methodologically usable,
and whether the complete evidence basis is sufficiently fit to progress within validation.
VEFS does not determine whether the originating source
is trustworthy.
It does not determine whether validation was correctly executed.
It does not determine the final validity of the Validation Object.
VEFS determines whether the evidence itself is fit for the
validation role it is expected to perform.
Core Question
Is the available evidence sufficiently relevant, applicable,

complete, representative, timely, precise, and methodologically
usable to support the governed validation question?
Purpose
The purpose of Validation Evidence Fitness Standard is to prevent
the existence, quantity, authority, technical sophistication, or
apparent strength of evidence from being confused with its fitness
for a particular validation.
The standard prevents validation from relying upon:
irrelevant evidence,
insufficient evidence,
incomplete evidence,
outdated evidence,
unrepresentative evidence,
contextually inapplicable evidence,
excessively aggregated evidence,
selectively chosen evidence,
evidence incapable of supporting the relevant Validation Criterion,
or evidence whose limitations are materially inconsistent with the intended Validation Determination.
VEFS establishes the evidence-quality governance layer required
before evidence can legitimately support subsequent validation
execution and determination.
Governance Objective
VEFS establishes a governed Validation Evidence Fitness Framework
capable of determining whether evidence is sufficiently fit for its
intended validation role.
The standard seeks to ensure that:
evidence requirements are explicit,
evidence remains connected to Validation Criteria,
evidence relevance is assessable,
evidence applicability is bounded,
evidence coverage is visible,
evidence completeness is assessable,
representativeness is governed,
temporal validity is considered,
precision and resolution are proportionate,

contradictory evidence remains visible,
evidence gaps remain explicit,
evidence limitations remain traceable,
evidence fitness can be determined,
and evidence is not used beyond the conditions it can legitimately support.
Operational Role
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard serves as the evidence
qualification stage of the VALIDOS® validation governance lifecycle.
The preceding standards establish:
Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria
→ Validation Method
VEFS establishes:
What evidence is sufficiently fit to support those governed
validation conditions and methods?
Its architectural progression is:
Validation Method Framework → Evidence Requirements → Evidence
Identification → Evidence Fitness Assessment → Evidence Gap Analysis
→ Evidence Fitness Determination → Qualified Validation Evidence
The resulting qualified evidence basis can then progress into
subsequent source-reliability and execution governance.
Governance Scope
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard governs:
validation evidence requirements,
evidence identification,
evidence relevance,
evidence applicability,
evidence coverage,
evidence completeness,
evidence representativeness,
evidence timeliness,
evidence recency,
evidence precision,
evidence resolution,
evidence granularity,
evidence consistency,
contradictory evidence visibility,
evidence sufficiency,
evidence limitations,
evidence gaps,
evidence fitness,
evidence fitness conditions,
evidence fitness change,

and evidence-fitness traceability.
Validation Evidence Governance Model
VEFS establishes the following structural progression:
Validation Requirement → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence →
Evidence Qualification → Evidence Coverage → Evidence Gap Analysis →
Evidence Fitness Determination → Qualified Validation Evidence
This progression separates the existence of information from its
legitimate use as validation evidence.
Validation Evidence
For the purposes of VALIDOS®, Validation Evidence may include
information, observations, measurements, records, test results,
datasets, documents, operational traces, experimental results,
simulation outputs, expert findings, audit records, system logs,
physical observations, statistical results, or other evidentiary
material capable of contributing to examination of a
Validation Criterion.
Evidence type alone does not establish fitness.
The relationship between the evidence and the governed validation
question must be established.
Evidence Requirements
Evidence requirements originate from the Validation Criteria
Framework and Validation Method Framework.
They may specify:
required evidence type,
required observation,
required measurement,
required population,
required environment,
required temporal period,
required resolution,
required precision,
required coverage,
required quantity,
required diversity,
required independence,
or another material evidentiary condition.

Evidence collection without an identifiable evidentiary requirement
may produce information without producing useful
validation evidence.
Evidence-to-Criterion Alignment
Every material item or body of Validation Evidence should have an
identifiable relationship to one or more Validation Criteria.
The governed relationship is:
Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Validation Evidence
VEFS prevents evidence from being treated as supportive merely
because it appears relevant to the general subject.
Evidence must contribute meaningfully to the actual condition
being evaluated.
Evidence Relevance
Evidence is relevant where it materially contributes to examination
of a defined Validation Criterion or validation condition.
Relevance may depend upon:
the characteristic examined,
the Validation Object,
the Validation Purpose,
the Validation Scope,
the applicable criterion,
and the methodological role of the evidence.
Evidence that does not materially inform the governed validation
question should not increase validation confidence merely because it
is extensive or technically sophisticated.
Evidence Applicability
Evidence may be relevant but not applicable.
Applicability asks whether evidence generated under one set of
conditions can legitimately support conclusions about the actual
Validation Object and governed validation context.
Material applicability dimensions may include:
object version,
system configuration,
population,
operating environment,
jurisdiction,
language,

lifecycle stage,
deployment context,
scale,
and temporal conditions.
Evidence transfer across materially different conditions
requires justification.
Evidence Completeness
Evidence completeness concerns whether the evidence basis
sufficiently addresses the evidentiary requirements established for
the validation.
Completeness does not require unlimited evidence.
It requires sufficient coverage of material evidentiary needs
relative to the Validation Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria,
and Method.
A large evidence volume can remain incomplete if a critical
validation condition lacks evidence.
Evidence Representativeness
Evidence may be extensive but systematically unrepresentative.
VEFS therefore governs whether evidence sufficiently represents the
conditions about which validation conclusions are expected to apply.
Representativeness may concern:
populations,
operating environments,
scenarios,
user groups,
geographic conditions,
temporal conditions,
system states,
failure conditions,
edge cases,
or other validation-relevant dimensions.
Representativeness requirements must correspond to the approved
Validation Scope.
Evidence Timeliness
Evidence may lose fitness over time.
VEFS assesses whether evidence remains sufficiently current for the
Validation Object and validation purpose.
Timeliness may depend upon:
object change,
model updates,
environmental change,
regulatory change,
operational drift,
new data,
infrastructure change,
or elapsed time.

Older evidence is not automatically invalid.
Its continuing applicability must be governable.
Evidence Precision and Resolution
Some validation questions require evidence at a particular degree of
precision or granularity.
Highly aggregated evidence may conceal:
subgroup failures,
rare events,
local deviations,
temporal instability,
boundary conditions,
or other material differences.
VEFS determines whether evidence resolution is proportionate to the
condition being validated.
Evidence Quantity and Evidence Quality
VALIDOS® rejects the assumption:
More Evidence = Stronger Validation
Evidence quantity may improve validation only where additional
evidence contributes meaningful:
coverage,
representativeness,
precision,
uncertainty reduction,
independence,
or corroboration.
Duplicated, redundant, irrelevant, or highly correlated evidence
should not artificially increase validation confidence.
Evidence Consistency
Multiple evidence items may support different interpretations.
VEFS requires material inconsistency to remain visible.
Evidence inconsistency may arise from:
different operating conditions,
different populations,
different methods,
measurement variation,
temporal change,
object change,
data quality differences,
or genuine uncertainty.
Inconsistency is not automatically evidence failure.
It may itself be validation-relevant information.
Contradictory Evidence
Evidence contradicting a favorable validation conclusion must not be

silently excluded solely because other evidence appears stronger.
Material contradictory evidence should remain identifiable and
traceable into subsequent validation governance.
VEFS does not determine which conflicting evidence ultimately
governs the Validation Determination.
It ensures that relevant contradiction survives the evidence
qualification process.
Evidence Gaps
An Evidence Gap exists where a material evidentiary requirement
cannot be sufficiently supported by available qualified evidence.
Evidence gaps may concern:
missing observations,
missing populations,
missing operating conditions,
insufficient temporal coverage,
missing failure scenarios,
insufficient precision,
unavailable historical records,
or another required evidentiary condition.
A gap must not be concealed by unrelated evidence volume.
Evidence Sufficiency
Evidence sufficiency is contextual.
Evidence sufficient for:
preliminary validation
may be insufficient for:
high-consequence operational reliance.
VEFS therefore assesses sufficiency relative to:
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Method,
risk and consequence where applicable,
and intended downstream reliance.
Evidence Limitations
Qualified evidence may still contain limitations.
Examples include:
limited population coverage,
restricted operational range,
low sample size,
limited observation period,
incomplete edge-case coverage,
measurement uncertainty,
insufficient granularity,

or constrained transferability.
Material limitations must remain connected to the evidence
throughout subsequent VALIDOS® governance.
Evidence Fitness Determination
VEFS may establish evidence fitness conditions such as:
Evidence Fit
The evidence is sufficiently fit for the defined validation role.
Evidence Conditionally Fit
The evidence may support validation only under explicit conditions,
limitations, or bounded applicability.
Evidence Fitness Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to determine whether the
evidence is fit.
Evidence Insufficient
Material evidence requirements remain unsupported.
Evidence Unfit
The evidence cannot legitimately perform the proposed
validation role.
These conditions apply to the evidence basis.
They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object.
Evidence Fitness Is Role-Specific
Evidence fitness is not a permanent universal property.
The same evidence may be:
Fit for one Validation Criterion,
Conditionally Fit for another,
and:
Unfit for a third.
Evidence fitness must therefore remain connected to its specific
validation role.
Evidence Fitness and Source Reliability
VALIDOS® maintains a strict architectural separation:
Evidence Fitness ≠ Source Reliability
Evidence Fitness asks:
Is this evidence suitable for answering this validation question?
Source Reliability asks:
Can the origin, provenance, independence, authenticity, and
reliability of the source providing or producing that evidence be
sufficiently trusted?

Evidence can be highly relevant but originate from an
unreliable source.
Evidence can also originate from an authoritative source while being
irrelevant to the validation question.
Both governance spaces are therefore required.
Evidence Fitness and Validation Method
VALIDOS® also distinguishes:
Method = How the condition is examined.
Evidence = What informational basis supports that examination.
A suitable method applied to unfit evidence can produce
weak validation.
Fit evidence processed through an unsuitable method can also produce
weak validation.
VALIDOS® governs these conditions separately so that one cannot
silently compensate for failure in the other.
Evidence Fitness and Execution
VEFS does not establish whether evidence was actually collected,
generated, processed, or interpreted according to the approved
Validation Method Framework.
That responsibility belongs to subsequent Validation
Execution governance.
VEFS establishes the conditions under which evidence is capable of
legitimate validation use.
Evidence Change Governance
Evidence fitness may change because of:
Validation Object change,
new object version,
changed Validation Scope,
changed criteria,
changed method,
new evidence,
contradictory evidence,
changed operating environment,
elapsed time,
discovered evidence limitation,
or improved evidentiary understanding.
Material changes require proportionate
evidence-fitness reassessment.
Evidence Traceability
Qualified Validation Evidence should remain traceable to:

the Validation Object,
Validation Criterion,
evidence requirement,
Validation Method where applicable,
evidence type,
applicability conditions,
temporal conditions,
material limitations,
fitness determination,
and subsequent use.
This creates the evidentiary continuity necessary for
reconstructable validation.
Governance Boundary
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard begins when established
Validation Criteria and Validation Methods create identifiable
evidence requirements.
It ends when the relevant evidence basis has been sufficiently
identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and classified for fitness
to support subsequent VALIDOS® governance.
VEFS does not determine:
Validation Object identity,
Validation Purpose or Scope,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Method suitability,
source trustworthiness,
source provenance,
validation execution conformity,
final Validation Determination,
Validation State,
reliance authorization,
or revalidation requirements.
These responsibilities belong to other VALIDOS® Parent Standards or
interoperating governance architectures.
Minimum Governance Requirements
A conforming implementation of VEFS should establish:
1. identifiable evidence requirements,
2. traceable relationships between Validation Criteria and evidence,
3. evidence relevance assessment,
4. evidence applicability assessment,
5. evidence coverage and completeness assessment,
6. representativeness assessment where applicable,
7. temporal fitness assessment,

8. sufficient precision and resolution,
9. explicit material evidence limitations,
10. explicit evidence gaps, 11. visibility of material contradictory
evidence, 12. an Evidence Fitness Determination, 13. and sufficient
evidence-fitness traceability throughout the validation lifecycle.
Governance Outputs
VEFS may produce:
Validation Evidence Requirements Record,
Validation Evidence Register,
Criteria-to-Evidence Map,
Evidence Relevance Assessment,
Evidence Applicability Assessment,
Evidence Coverage Map,
Evidence Completeness Assessment,
Evidence Representativeness Assessment,
Evidence Timeliness Assessment,
Evidence Precision Assessment,
Evidence Limitation Record,
Evidence Contradiction Record,
Evidence Gap Register,
Evidence Sufficiency Assessment,
Evidence Fitness Determination,
Qualified Validation Evidence Record,
Evidence Fitness Change Record.
These outputs provide the governed evidentiary basis required for
subsequent VALIDOS® validation governance.
Operational Applications
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard may be applied across:
artificial intelligence,
machine learning,
autonomous systems,
AI-generated outputs,
claims and information,
datasets,
predictions,
simulations,
analytical systems,
decision systems,
scientific validation,
enterprise systems,
financial services,
healthcare,
industrial operations,
regulatory compliance,
critical infrastructure,
digital assets,
digital identities,
operational governance,

and any governed environment requiring evidence-based validation.
Relationship to Other OOF Architectures
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard interoperates with:
GOA™
OBIDENITY®
INTEGROS®
ORA™
AGA™
AIG®
CLIA®
MGIA™
ASGA™
RIS™
by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology for
determining whether evidence originating from or relating to
complementary governance spaces is sufficiently fit for the
validation role it is expected to perform.
VEFS does not replace evidence provenance, identity, integrity,
accountability, operational reality, risk, audit, or domain-
specific evidentiary requirements.
It governs the methodological fitness of evidence for validation.
Foundational Principle
Evidence is not validation evidence merely because it exists; it
becomes validation evidence when it is fit for the question it is
expected to answer.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard establishes the canonical
evidence-qualification layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance
Architecture. By governing evidence requirements, relevance,
applicability, coverage, completeness, representativeness,
timeliness, precision, consistency, contradiction, sufficiency,
limitations, gaps, fitness, change, and traceability, VEFS ensures
that validation conclusions cannot derive legitimacy merely from the
existence or volume of evidence, but only from evidence demonstrably
fit for the specific Validation Object, Criteria, Method, Purpose,

Scope, and required Validation Depth to which it is applied.
Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance
Canonical Definition: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS)
defines the governance conditions under which evidence intended to
support validation is identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and
determined to be sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete,
representative, timely, precise, and methodologically usable for the
specific Validation Object, Validation Criteria, Validation Method,
Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, and required Validation Depth.
Governed Space: Validation Evidence Fitness
Evidence is not validation evidence merely because it exists; it
becomes validation evidence when it is fit for the question it is
expected to answer.
