About Validation Execution Standard
About Validation Execution Standard
Governing the Difference Between Validation Designed and
Validation Actually Performed
A validation methodology can be excellent.
The criteria can be precise.
The evidence can be fit.
The sources can be reliable.
And the validation can still fail methodologically if the required
validation process was not actually performed as governed.
Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) is the seventh Parent Standard
of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture, governing the
operational transition from an approved validation design to
demonstrable validation activity.
VEXS addresses one fundamental question:
Was the approved validation process actually performed as governed?
Why Validation Execution Standard Exists
Validation does not occur because a methodology exists.
It occurs when that methodology is applied to a specific Validation
Object under actual operational conditions.
Between:
What should happen
and:
What actually happened
there may be substantial differences.
A validation process may:
skip required steps,
examine the wrong object version,
use different evidence,
operate outside the approved scope,
substitute instruments,
change environmental conditions,
alter sequencing,
experience interruptions,
introduce manual interventions,
or fail to preserve sufficient execution records.
Without execution governance, a later validation result may appear

methodologically legitimate even though the process producing it
materially departed from the approved validation structure.
VEXS exists to make that difference governable.
Validation Design Is Not Validation Execution
VALIDOS® deliberately separates:
Validation Method
from:
Validation Execution
Validation Method asks:
How should validation be performed?
Validation Execution asks:
What was actually performed?
This distinction is fundamental.
A method is a governed design.
Execution is its operational realization.
Therefore:
Approved Method ≠ Executed Validation
From Methodology to Operational Reality
Before VEXS, VALIDOS® has established:
Validation Object
Validation Purpose & Scope
Validation Criteria
Validation Method
Validation Evidence Fitness
Validation Source Reliability
Together, these define the governed validation basis.
VEXS moves that structure into operational reality.
The lifecycle becomes: Validation Design → Execution Basis →
Execution Authorization → Execution Instance → Actual Validation
Activity → Execution Record
Only after this transition can VALIDOS® legitimately ask what the
validation demonstrated.
The Correct Object Must Be Executed Against
Validation must remain attached to the object it was designed
to examine.
If validation was approved for:
Object Version 3.2
but execution occurs against:
Object Version 3.4
the difference may be material.
Likewise, changes in:
configuration,
system state,
dependencies,
environment,
operating mode,

or object boundaries
may change what was actually validated.
VEXS therefore preserves Validation Object continuity
throughout execution.
Scope Must Survive Execution
A Validation Scope defined during planning can change during
actual execution.
Some areas may become unavailable.
Tests may be omitted.
Additional areas may be examined.
Conditions may force narrower coverage.
VEXS makes these changes explicit.
A later Validation Determination should never claim a scope broader
than the validation activity actually performed.
Criteria Must Become Activities
Validation Criteria are not operationally meaningful merely because
they appear in a validation document.
They must be connected to actual validation activities.
VEXS therefore asks:
Which criteria were actually evaluated?
Through which activities?
Using which evidence?
Under which conditions?
Were any criteria omitted?
VEXS does not yet decide whether those criteria were satisfied.
It establishes that the required evaluation actually occurred.
Planned Execution and Actual Execution
VALIDOS® creates an explicit distinction between:
Planned Execution
and:
Actual Execution
This allows the validation process to compare:
Expected Activity → Actual Activity
rather than assuming they are identical.
Where material differences exist, they become governed
Execution Deviations.
Execution Conditions Matter
Validation does not occur in abstraction.
It occurs under conditions.
These may include:
physical environment,
digital environment,

system configuration,
network conditions,
operational load,
population,
geographic context,
human involvement,
available tools,
simulation settings,
or system state.
If those conditions materially differ from those required by the
Validation Method, the difference may affect execution legitimacy.
VEXS therefore makes execution conditions part of the
validation record.
Sequence Can Matter
Some validation procedures depend upon order.
A test performed after a system has already been modified may not
establish the same thing as the same test performed
before modification.
Likewise, one validation activity may depend upon another being
completed first.
VEXS therefore governs sequence where sequence has
methodological significance.
Evidence Must Survive the Transition Into Execution
Evidence that was previously qualified by VALIDOS® should not lose
its governance conditions once execution begins.
VEXS preserves relationships to:
Evidence Fitness,
evidence version,
evidence limitations,
evidence restrictions,
Source Reliability,
source conditions,
and applicable corroboration requirements.
This prevents execution from silently substituting governed evidence
with materially different evidence.
Reliable Sources Can Still Be Used Incorrectly
Source Reliability does not guarantee correct execution.
A reliable source may be:
used outside its approved role,
used beyond its reliability boundary,
interpreted incorrectly,
substituted,
or used without required corroboration.
Therefore:

Reliable Source ≠ Correct Execution
VEXS governs how source conditions are actually respected during
validation activity.
Execution Can Be Human, Automated, or Hybrid
Modern validation may involve people, software, AI systems,
autonomous agents, instruments, or combinations of them.
VEXS is execution-model neutral.
Human Execution
A person may:
perform tests,
make observations,
interpret evidence,
operate instruments,
review outputs,
or intervene in the validation process.
Automated Execution
A system may:
execute tests,
monitor behavior,
process evidence,
run simulations,
generate measurements,
or evaluate defined conditions.
Hybrid Execution
Humans and machines may divide responsibility across the same
validation process.
VEXS governs the actual execution structure regardless of who or
what performs it.
Execution Deviations Are Governance Events
Real-world validation rarely proceeds exactly as planned.
Deviation itself does not automatically invalidate validation.
The important questions are:
What changed?
Why did it change?
Was it authorized?
What did it affect?
Was the effect material?
Were compensating controls required?
VEXS transforms deviation from an undocumented irregularity into a
governed validation event.
Not Every Deviation Has Equal Importance
VALIDOS® may distinguish:
Immaterial Deviation
Minor Deviation
Material Deviation
Critical Deviation
Execution-Invalidating Deviation
This prevents two opposite errors:
treating every deviation as catastrophic,
and:

ignoring deviations that materially undermine validation.
Authorization Does Not Erase Methodological Effect
A deviation may be formally authorized and still materially
affect validation.
Therefore: Authorized Deviation ≠ Methodologically
Harmless Deviation
Authorization establishes that the change was governed.
Its methodological consequences must still remain visible.
Substitution Must Be Visible
Real validation processes may substitute:
evidence,
sources,
instruments,
datasets,
models,
personnel,
environments,
procedures,
or controls.
Substitution may be entirely legitimate.
But equivalence should not be assumed merely because the substitute
appears similar.
VEXS requires material substitutions to remain identifiable.
Interruptions Matter
Validation may be interrupted by:
system failure,
infrastructure outage,
missing evidence,
safety conditions,
human intervention,
environmental change,
resource failure,
or unexpected system behavior.
The governance question becomes:
Can execution continue?
Must part of it be repeated?
Must it restart entirely?
Can the interruption be accepted conditionally?
VEXS provides the execution layer in which those questions can
be answered.
Failure to Validate Is Not Validation Failure
This is one of the most important distinctions in VEXS.
Suppose a required test cannot be completed because the testing
environment fails.
That does not demonstrate that the Validation Object failed
the criterion.

It demonstrates that validation could not establish the
required result.
VALIDOS® therefore establishes: Failure to Validate ≠ Validation
Failure of the Object
This prevents methodological failure from being incorrectly
transformed into an object-level conclusion.
Execution Completeness
VEXS asks whether all materially required validation activities were
actually performed.
Execution may therefore be:
Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
or:
Completeness Undetermined
Completeness concerns the validation process.
It does not indicate whether the object passed or failed.
Execution Conformity
VEXS separately asks whether actual execution sufficiently
corresponded to the approved validation basis.
Possible conditions may include:
Execution Conformant
Execution Conditionally Conformant
Execution Conformity Undetermined
Execution Non-Conformant
Execution Invalid
This creates a formal governance gate before
Validation Determination.
A Perfectly Executed Validation Can Produce a Negative Result
This distinction is essential.
A validation process may be:
complete,
perfectly conformant,
fully documented,
and methodologically strong
and demonstrate that the Validation Object fails.
That is not failed validation execution.
It is successful execution producing a negative validation finding.
Therefore:
Execution Conformant ≠ Validation Object Valid
An Apparently Valid Object Does Not Repair Invalid Execution
The opposite is equally important.

An object may in reality satisfy all required conditions.
But if the validation process used to establish that conclusion was
materially invalid, VALIDOS® should not manufacture methodological
confidence from the likely correctness of the result.
Therefore:
Probable Correctness ≠ Governed Validation
Execution Must Be Reconstructable
A strong validation process should allow a later reviewer to
reconstruct materially:
What was validated?
Which version?
Against which criteria?
Using which method?
Using which evidence and sources?
Who or what performed the activities?
Under which conditions?
In what sequence?
What deviations occurred?
What outputs were generated?
This reconstruction creates the bridge between validation activity
and auditability.
Execution Records Become Methodological Evidence
The execution process itself creates evidence.
This may include:
logs,
observations,
test outputs,
measurements,
timestamps,
system records,
operator records,
simulation outputs,
deviation records,
interruption records,
and other execution artifacts.
Together these form the Validation Execution Record.
The record establishes what the validation process can actually
demonstrate was performed.
Execution Can Be Repeated
A failed or materially deficient execution does not necessarily
end validation.
VEXS allows governance of:
Re-Execution
and where methodologically defensible:
Partial Re-Execution
This permits affected validation activities to be repeated without

automatically discarding unaffected valid execution.
Historical Execution Must Remain Visible
Repeated execution should not overwrite earlier validation history.
Where validation is repeated after:
failure,
deviation,
system change,
evidence change,
or corrective action,
the relationship between executions should remain traceable.
This creates validation execution continuity.
Determination Readiness
VEXS ultimately asks whether execution has reached a state where a
legitimate Validation Determination can begin.
This requires sufficient understanding of:
object continuity,
scope conformity,
criteria execution,
method conformity,
evidence continuity,
source conditions,
deviations,
completeness,
conformity,
and execution traceability.
Where those conditions are sufficiently established, execution
can progress.
Where they are not, VEXS can prevent premature determination.
Determination Block
A critical execution deficiency may create a Determination Block.
This means VALIDOS® does not permit methodological uncertainty about
execution to disappear merely because an organization wants a
final answer.
Possible blocking conditions include:
wrong Validation Object,
critical missing activity,
invalid method substitution,
critical scope deviation,
irrecoverable evidence discontinuity,
critical execution failure,
or insufficient execution traceability.
The validation process must first resolve the execution problem or
explicitly preserve the inability to determine.

Position Within VALIDOS®
Validation Execution Standard is the seventh Parent Standard of
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture.
Its architectural position is:
Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria
→ Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation
Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination
→ Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation
The first six Parent Standards establish the governed basis upon
which validation can operate.
VEXS establishes whether that basis was actually transformed into a
legitimate validation execution.
Only then does VALIDOS® move to the next question:
What does the governed validation record actually demonstrate about
the Validation Object?
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
VEXS operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures.
GOA™ may establish authority, delegation, and governance
responsibilities affecting validation execution.
OBIDENITY® may preserve identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and
continuity relationships.
INTEGROS® may provide integrity conditions affecting validation
activities and execution records.
ORA™ may establish complementary operational-reality conditions.
AGA™ may establish accountability for execution activities,
deviations, interventions, and decisions.
AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may provide specialized governance
conditions where AI behavior, cognition, memory, or autonomous
execution materially affects validation.

RIS™ may inform the depth, strength, and control requirements
appropriate to the consequence of validation failure.
VEXS does not duplicate these architectures.
It consumes relevant governed information and answers one
validation-specific question:
Was the validation process actually executed with sufficient
conformity, completeness, control, continuity, and traceability to
support a legitimate Validation Determination?
Why It Matters
Validation is often documented more strongly than it is executed.
Policies describe ideal processes.
Methodologies define required procedures.
Testing plans specify controlled conditions.
Standards define expectations.
But operational reality may differ.
VALIDOS® therefore refuses to infer execution from documentation.
It requires the distinction:
Designed Validation
versus:
Executed Validation
to remain visible.
From Validation Procedure to Validation Proof
Traditional validation may ask:
Was the procedure defined?
VEXS adds:
Was it actually performed?
Against the correct object?
Within the correct scope?
Under the required conditions?
Using the governed evidence?
With the required sequence?
What changed during execution?
Can we reconstruct what happened?
Is the execution sufficiently conformant to support determination?
This transforms execution from an assumed procedural step into an
independently governable validation layer.
Foundational Principle
A validation method has no operational validity until its required

validation activities are actually performed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Execution Standard establishes the operational
performance layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
by separating validation design from validation actually performed.
Through governance of execution authorization, instantiation, object
continuity, scope conformity, criteria execution, method conformity,
evidence and source continuity, conditions, participants,
sequencing, deviations, substitutions, interruptions, failures,
completeness, conformity, reconstruction, repetition, and
traceability, VEXS ensures that Validation Determination rests upon
demonstrable execution rather than methodological intention,
procedural assumption, or undocumented operational activity.

Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM)
Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS)
Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 11 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Execution Basis & Authorization
Canonical Definition
Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) defines
the governance framework for assembling, verifying, freezing,
authorizing, and preserving the complete governed basis from which a
specific Validation Execution may legitimately begin.
It establishes the conditions under which the outputs of preceding
VALIDOS® governance stages become an identifiable, versioned,
execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis.
Operational Role
VEBAM serves as the first internal governance space of the
Validation Execution Standard.
The preceding VALIDOS® Parent Standards establish:

Validation Object
Validation Purpose & Scope
Validation Criteria
Validation Method
Validation Evidence Fitness and:
Validation Source Reliability
VEBAM asks:
Are the required validation components sufficiently established,
mutually connected, current, and authorized for this specific
Validation Execution to begin?
The governed progression is:
Governed Validation Components → Execution Prerequisite Review →
Basis Assembly → Basis Consistency Check → Execution Instance
Definition → Authorization Assessment → Basis Freeze → Authorized
Validation Execution Basis
VEBAM does not perform the validation.
It establishes the governed starting condition from which validation
may be performed.
Module Operational Space
VEBAM governs:
Validation Execution Basis,
execution prerequisites,
execution readiness,
execution authorization,
execution instance identity,
Validation Object reference,
object-version reference,
Validation Purpose reference,
Validation Scope reference,
Validation Depth reference,
Validation Criteria references,
Validation Method reference,
Validation Evidence references,
Validation Source references,
Source Reliability conditions,
execution-role requirements,
resource readiness,
instrument readiness,
system readiness,
environment prerequisites,
authorization authority,
authorization scope,
authorization conditions,
basis completeness,
basis consistency,
basis versioning,
basis freeze,
basis change,
authorization change,
authorization withdrawal,

and execution-basis traceability.
Module Function
VEBAM applies immediately before operational validation
execution begins.
Its function is to prevent:
execution beginning against an undefined Validation Object,
execution using the wrong object version,
obsolete Validation Criteria being used,
unapproved methods entering execution,
Validation Scope remaining ambiguous,
insufficient Validation Depth being silently accepted,
unqualified evidence entering execution,
Source Reliability conditions being lost,
execution beginning before required prerequisites exist,
incompatible validation components being assembled,
execution roles remaining undefined,
unavailable resources being assumed available,
unauthorized validation activity being represented as governed validation,
and the validation basis changing silently after execution begins.
Validation Execution Basis
The Validation Execution Basis is the governed collection of
validation components upon which a specific execution
instance depends.
It may contain:
Validation Object reference,
object version or state,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
applicable Validation Criteria,
approved Validation Method,
qualified Validation Evidence,
Source Reliability information,
source conditions,
execution requirements,
participant requirements,
system requirements,
instrument requirements,
environmental requirements,
execution controls,
restrictions,
and authorization conditions.

The Validation Execution Basis creates the methodological starting
state for execution.
Execution Basis Is Not a Validation Plan
A Validation Execution Basis and a validation plan are related but
not identical.
A plan may describe intended activities.
The Execution Basis establishes the governed methodological
conditions that authorize those activities to begin.
VALIDOS® therefore distinguishes:
Execution Plan → What is intended to occur
from:
Validation Execution Basis → What governed validation structure
permits execution to occur
A plan cannot override the governed Validation Execution Basis.
Execution Instance Identity
Each material Validation Execution should be sufficiently
identifiable as a distinct execution instance.
An Execution Instance may be associated with:
an identifier,
Validation Object,
object version,
Validation Method version,
execution date or period,
responsible execution entity,
environment,
or another distinguishing attribute.
This allows multiple executions of the same Validation Object to
remain distinguishable.
Object Reference
VEBAM requires the Execution Basis to identify the exact Validation
Object against which execution is authorized.
The reference should remain connected to the object established
under the Validation Object Standard.
Where object identity cannot be sufficiently established, execution
should not silently proceed.
Object Version & State Reference
Where validation depends upon version, configuration, release,

state, or temporal condition, the relevant object instance must
be explicit.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Authorization to validate one object state does not automatically
authorize validation of another materially different state.
Purpose Continuity
The Validation Purpose established earlier must remain connected
to execution.
Execution activity should not silently drift toward a
different purpose.
For example:
Validation authorized to determine:
functional performance
should not silently become validation of:
regulatory compliance
unless the required governance basis for that purpose has also
been established.
Scope Continuity
The authorized Validation Scope establishes what execution may
legitimately cover.
VEBAM therefore identifies:
included scope,
excluded scope,
applicable boundaries,
temporal boundaries,
system boundaries,
population boundaries,
or other relevant limits.
This creates the baseline against which later execution deviations
can be assessed.
Validation Depth Continuity
Validation Depth affects how extensively the Validation Object must
be examined.
VEBAM ensures that the required depth remains attached to execution.
Execution should not silently substitute:
limited validation
for:
deep validation
while preserving the appearance of the original
validation objective.
Criteria Set
The applicable Validation Criteria must be sufficiently established
before execution begins.
VEBAM creates an identifiable criteria set connecting the Execution

Basis to the criteria that execution is expected to evaluate.
The criteria set may include:
mandatory criteria,
conditional criteria,
optional supporting criteria,
criterion priority,
criterion applicability,
or other governed relationships.
Criteria Version
Where Validation Criteria change over time, the applicable criteria
version must remain explicit.
This prevents a later criteria revision from being incorrectly
represented as the basis under which an earlier execution occurred.
Method Reference
The Validation Execution Basis must identify the approved
Validation Method.
Where multiple methods exist, the exact:
method,
version,
configuration,
procedure,
test protocol,
analytical process,
or other relevant methodological instance
should be sufficiently identifiable.
Method Eligibility Continuity
Where the Validation Method Standard established eligibility
conditions, those conditions must remain satisfied when
execution begins.
A method that was previously eligible may become inappropriate if:
the Validation Object changes,
the Validation Scope changes,
evidence availability changes,
environmental conditions change,
or required systems become unavailable.
VEBAM therefore checks that the methodological basis
remains current.
Validation Evidence Reference
Evidence intended for execution should remain connected to the
evidence objects qualified under Validation Evidence
Fitness governance.
The Execution Basis may identify:
required evidence,
supporting evidence,

optional evidence,
evidence versions,
evidence limitations,
evidence validity periods,
and Evidence Fitness conditions.
This prevents unqualified evidence from entering execution
without visibility.
Source Reliability Reference
Where evidence depends upon Validation Sources, VEBAM preserves the
relevant Source Reliability conditions.
These may include:
Source Reliability Status,
source-role restrictions,
required corroboration,
reliability limitations,
independence conditions,
source version,
source validity period,
or reassessment requirements.
Prerequisite Governance
Before execution begins, VEBAM determines whether material
prerequisites have been sufficiently established.
Prerequisites may include:
approved method,
qualified evidence,
reliable or conditionally reliable sources,
available instruments,
required systems,
required data,
competent participants,
required access,
environmental conditions,
authorization,
or another validation-specific requirement.
Prerequisite Status
A prerequisite may be classified as:
Satisfied
Conditionally Satisfied
Unsatisfied
or:
Undetermined
A critical Unsatisfied or Undetermined prerequisite may
prevent authorization.
Resource Readiness
Validation execution may require resources such as:
personnel,
compute,
laboratories,
testing environments,
datasets,
instruments,
infrastructure,
time,
or external services.
VEBAM determines whether required resources are sufficiently
available for the intended execution.

Resource availability does not itself establish
methodological validity.
It establishes execution readiness.
Instrument Readiness
Where instruments materially affect validation, readiness
may require:
correct instrument identity,
calibration,
required configuration,
operating range,
maintenance status,
software version,
or another applicable condition.
An instrument that exists but is not ready should not be
assumed execution-ready.
System Readiness
Validation may depend upon:
software,
testing platforms,
AI systems,
simulation environments,
data pipelines,
monitoring systems,
or infrastructure.
VEBAM may establish whether required systems are available in the
correct state and configuration.
Environment Readiness
Some Validation Methods require defined environmental conditions.
These may include:
physical conditions,
network conditions,
operational state,
simulation settings,
controlled access,
geographic conditions,
or another relevant environment.
VEBAM establishes whether the required environment is sufficiently
available before execution begins.
Participant Readiness
Where human or machine participants perform material validation
roles, VEBAM may establish:
required role,
identity,
authority,
competence requirement,
availability,
system permission,
or another prerequisite.
Participant readiness does not replace Source Capability or
accountability governance.
It ensures that required execution roles can actually be performed.
Basis Completeness

A Validation Execution Basis should contain sufficient information
for execution to begin without relying upon material
unstated assumptions.
Possible completeness conditions include:
Basis Complete
Basis Conditionally Complete
Basis Partially Complete
Basis Incomplete
Basis Completeness Undetermined
Completeness requirements should remain proportionate to
validation consequence.
Basis Consistency
A complete basis may still contain contradictions.
VEBAM therefore assesses whether its components are
materially consistent.
Examples of inconsistency include:
criteria requiring evidence not available,
method incompatible with object type,
Validation Depth inconsistent with method capability,
evidence version inconsistent with object version,
Source Reliability restriction incompatible with intended source role,
or scope broader than authorized execution capability.
Material inconsistencies must remain visible.
Basis Conflict
A Basis Conflict exists where two or more governed execution
components impose materially incompatible requirements.
A conflict may require:
correction,
escalation,
method revision,
scope revision,
evidence replacement,
source reassessment,
or another governance action.
Execution should not resolve material Basis Conflicts silently.
Execution Readiness
VEBAM may establish an Execution Readiness condition such as:
Execution Ready
All material prerequisites and basis requirements are
sufficiently established.
Execution Conditionally Ready

Execution may proceed only under explicit conditions.
Execution Readiness Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish readiness.
Execution Not Ready
Material prerequisites remain unsatisfied.
Readiness does not itself authorize execution where separate
authorization is required.
Execution Authorization
Execution Authorization establishes that a defined Validation
Execution Instance may legitimately proceed under the approved
Validation Execution Basis.
Authorization should identify, where applicable:
authorization authority,
authorized Validation Object,
authorized scope,
authorized method,
applicable conditions,
restrictions,
effective period,
and authorization status.
Authorization Authority
The entity granting authorization must possess sufficient authority
for the relevant validation context.
Authority may derive from:
governance structure,
organizational role,
contractual authority,
regulatory authority,
methodological governance,
delegated authority,
or another legitimate basis.
VEBAM does not create external legal authority.
It records and governs the authority relationship used to initiate
validation execution.
Authorization Scope
Authorization should be bounded.
It may authorize:
one Validation Object,
one object version,
one Validation Scope,
one Validation Method,
one execution environment,
one execution period,
or another defined set of conditions.
Authorization should not silently extend beyond its governed scope.
Conditional Authorization

Execution may be authorized subject to conditions.
Examples include:
specific evidence must remain available,
a source requires independent corroboration,
execution must occur within a defined environment,
a specified participant must be present,
or a particular control must remain active.
Conditional authorization remains valid only while its material
conditions remain satisfied.
Authorization Status
VEBAM may establish:
Authorized
Conditionally Authorized
Authorization Pending
Authorization Denied
Authorization Suspended
or:
Authorization Withdrawn
These statuses govern permission to execute.
They do not represent Validation State.
Basis Freeze
Immediately before execution begins, the material Validation
Execution Basis should be sufficiently frozen or version-fixed.
A Basis Freeze establishes the exact governed configuration under
which execution began.
This may include:
object version,
criteria version,
method version,
evidence set,
source conditions,
execution requirements,
and authorization conditions.
Freeze does not prohibit change.
It makes subsequent change visible.
Why Basis Freeze Matters
Without a Basis Freeze, a validation process may change its
methodological foundation during execution while later presenting
the final configuration as if it had governed the complete process.
VEBAM prevents this.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Execution history must preserve the basis that actually governed
execution at the time it occurred.
Basis Versioning

Materially different Execution Bases should remain distinguishable.
For example: Execution Basis 1.0
Execution Basis 1.1
Execution Basis 2.0
The versioning structure may vary by implementation.
The governance requirement is that material basis changes
remain reconstructable.
Basis Change
After Basis Freeze, a material change may involve:
Validation Object,
scope,
criteria,
method,
evidence,
source,
environment,
participant,
instrument,
system,
or authorization condition.
Such change becomes an execution-governance event.
Depending upon materiality, it may require:
updated authorization,
controlled deviation,
new Basis version,
execution restart,
partial re-execution,
or complete revalidation.
Authorization Change
Authorization may change because of:
scope expansion,
scope reduction,
new authority,
changed method,
object change,
source change,
environmental change,
or another material condition.
Authorization changes should remain historically traceable.
Authorization Suspension
Execution authorization may be temporarily suspended where a
material condition arises that requires review.
Examples include:
prerequisite failure,
instrument issue,
source reliability concern,
unexpected object change,
safety concern,
or governance conflict.
Suspension does not automatically terminate the validation.
It pauses authorization until the relevant condition is resolved.
Authorization Withdrawal
Authorization may be withdrawn where the basis for legitimate
execution no longer exists.

Withdrawal may require:
stopping execution,
preserving existing records,
assessing already performed activities,
and determining whether reauthorization or new execution is necessary.
Unauthorized Execution
Validation activity performed without required authorization may
still produce factual observations.
However, it should not automatically be represented as a governed
VALIDOS® Validation Execution.
VALIDOS® therefore distinguishes:
Activity Occurred
from:
Governed Validation Execution Authorized
Authorization Does Not Guarantee Valid Execution
Authorization establishes permission to begin.
It does not prove that execution will later be:
complete,
conformant,
correctly sequenced,
deviation-free,
or methodologically valid.
Therefore:
Authorized Execution ≠ Conformant Execution
Subsequent VEXS modules govern actual execution behavior.
Basis Traceability
VEBAM creates traceability between:
Validation Object → Purpose & Scope → Criteria → Method → Evidence →
Sources → Execution Requirements → Authorization → Execution
Instance This becomes the baseline against which actual execution
can later be compared.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Validation Execution Instance
Create a distinguishable reference for the intended execution.
2. Assemble Validation Execution Basis
Connect the relevant:
Validation Object,
Purpose,
Scope,
Depth,
Criteria,
Method,
Evidence,
Sources,
conditions,
and restrictions.
3. Verify Prerequisites

Determine whether required execution prerequisites are satisfied.
4. Assess Basis Completeness
Determine whether the basis contains sufficient information
for execution.
5. Assess Basis Consistency
Identify contradictions, incompatibilities, or Basis Conflicts.
6. Determine Execution Readiness
Establish whether execution is Ready, Conditionally Ready,
Undetermined, or Not Ready.
7. Establish Execution Authorization
Determine whether the defined execution instance may
legitimately begin.
8. Freeze and Version the Basis
Preserve the exact governed basis applicable at execution start.
9. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability
Maintain:
Execution Instance reference,
Validation Object reference,
object version,
Purpose,
Scope,
Depth,
Criteria set,
Method reference,
Evidence references,
Source Reliability references,
prerequisites,
readiness status,
authorization,
conditions,
restrictions,
Basis version,
Basis Freeze,
changes,
suspensions,
withdrawals,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Governance Outputs
VEBAM may produce:
Validation Execution Instance Identifier,
Validation Execution Basis,
Validation Execution Basis Record,
Execution Prerequisite Register,
Execution Prerequisite Status,
Execution Resource Readiness Record,
Instrument Readiness Record,
System Readiness Record,
Environment Readiness Record,
Participant Readiness Record,
Basis Completeness Assessment,
Basis Consistency Assessment,
Basis Conflict Record,
Execution Readiness Status,
Validation Execution Authorization,

Authorization Scope,
Authorization Condition Record,
Authorization Status,
Validation Execution Basis Version,
Basis Freeze Record,
Basis Change Record,
Authorization Change Record,
Authorization Suspension Record,
Authorization Withdrawal Record,
and Execution Basis Traceability Record.
Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation
Scenario
An organization intends to validate a new AI model release.
The validation methodology has already been approved.
Application
VEBAM establishes that:
the Validation Object is Model Version 4.2,
the approved criteria apply to Version 4.2,
the correct benchmark evidence is available,
source-reliability conditions remain current,
the required testing environment is ready,
and the approved method version is identifiable.
The complete basis is frozen as Execution Basis 1.0 and authorized.
Result
Validation begins against a reconstructable methodological baseline
rather than a loosely defined testing plan.
Use Case 2 — Industrial Equipment Validation
Scenario
A validation is scheduled for an industrial component.
The required measurement instrument exists, but its calibration
expired before execution.
Application
VEBAM identifies the calibration requirement as an unsatisfied
execution prerequisite.
Result
The validation remains:
Execution Not Ready
until the instrument condition is resolved.
The existence of the instrument is not mistaken for
instrument readiness.
Use Case 3 — Healthcare Validation
Scenario

A healthcare validation has an approved method, qualified evidence,
and competent participants.
However, one critical evidence source has become subject to a newly
identified Source Reliability restriction requiring
independent corroboration.
Application
VEBAM propagates the new source condition into the Execution Basis.
Result
Execution may become:
Conditionally Ready
and:
Conditionally Authorized
subject to the required corroboration.
The earlier source assessment is not silently treated as
permanently valid.
Architectural Position
Validation Execution Basis & Authorization is the first internal
governance space of the Validation Execution Standard (VEXS).
It establishes the transition:
Governed Validation Design → Authorized Validation Execution Basis
The next execution-governance stage can then ask:
How is that authorized basis instantiated into actual validation
activity against the Validation Object under real
execution conditions?
The VEXS internal progression therefore begins:
Execution Basis & Authorization → Execution Instantiation & Control
→ Execution Observation & Traceability → Deviation & Exception
Governance → Execution Completeness & Conformity
Foundational Principle
Validation execution should not begin until the basis governing what
may be executed is identifiable, internally coherent, sufficiently
ready, and appropriately authorized.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module establishes the

governed starting condition for operational validation within
VALIDOS® by transforming previously established Validation Object,
Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, Evidence, and Source Reliability
information into an identifiable, consistent, versioned,
execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis. Through
prerequisite governance, readiness assessment, authorization, basis
freezing, version control, change governance, and lifecycle
traceability, VEBAM ensures that validation execution begins from a
reconstructable methodological foundation rather than from
procedural assumption, incomplete preparation, or
undefined authority.
Parent Resources
→ VALIDOS® Validation Governance Architecture — Validation Governance Layer
→ VALIDOS® Architecture Map
→ VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index
Internal Module Flow
→ Next module: Validation Execution Instantiation & Control Module (VEICM)
Related Documents
→ Validation Execution Standard
→ About Validation Execution Standard

Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM)
Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS)
Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 11 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity
Canonical Definition
Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module (VECCM)
defines the governance framework for determining whether a
Validation Execution Instance has performed the materially required
validation activities with sufficient completeness, conformity,
continuity, control, reconstructability, and resolution of material
deviations to support progression into formal
Validation Determination.
It establishes the final execution-governance gate through which the
Actual Validation Execution Record is compared against the

Authorized Validation Execution Basis and classified according to
its methodological fitness for subsequent determination.
Operational Role
VECCM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the
Validation Execution Standard.
The preceding modules establish:
VEBAM — Validation Execution Basis & Authorization
VEICM — Validation Execution Instantiation & Control
VEOTM — Validation Execution Observation & Traceability
VEDEGM — Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance
VECCM asks:
Considering what was authorized, what was actually performed, what
can be reconstructed, and which deviations remain, is the complete
validation execution sufficiently complete and conformant to support
a legitimate Validation Determination?
The governed progression is:
Authorized Execution Basis → Actual Execution Record → Completeness
Assessment → Conformity Assessment → Residual Deviation Assessment →
Reconstruction Assessment → Determination Readiness → Execution
Conformity Determination
VECCM does not determine whether the Validation Object satisfies the
Validation Criteria.
It determines whether the validation execution itself is
methodologically usable for that later determination.
Module Operational Space
VECCM governs:
execution completeness,
execution conformity,
execution coverage,
required-activity completion,
criteria-execution completeness,
method-step completeness,
execution continuity,
object continuity,
scope conformity,
method conformity,

evidence-use conformity,
source-condition conformity,
configuration conformity,
control conformity,
sequence conformity,
participant-role conformity,
reconstruction sufficiency,
traceability sufficiency,
residual deviation impact,
unresolved exception impact,
execution integrity readiness,
conditional conformity,
execution invalidity,
Determination Readiness,
Determination Block,
execution completion status,
execution conformity status,
execution reassessment,
and execution-conformity traceability.
Module Function
VECCM applies when material validation execution activities have
ended, been terminated, or reached a stage where progression to
Validation Determination is being considered.
Its function is to prevent:
partially executed validation being represented as complete,
complete activity counts being mistaken for methodological conformity,
unresolved deviations disappearing at execution closure,
missing criteria being hidden by successful execution elsewhere,
scope reduction being forgotten,
wrong object versions being overlooked,
incomplete traceability being ignored,
source restrictions being lost,
execution under changed configurations being treated as equivalent,
failed or omitted activities being silently excluded,
and a final Validation Determination being issued where the execution record cannot legitimately support one.
Completeness and Conformity Are Different
VALIDOS® establishes a strict distinction:
Execution Completeness asks:

Were the materially required validation activities
actually performed?
Execution Conformity asks:
Were those activities performed with sufficient correspondence to
the Authorized Validation Execution Basis?
A validation execution may therefore be:
Complete but Non-Conformant
or:
Conformant in performed activities but Incomplete overall
For example:
Every executed test may follow the method perfectly, while one
mandatory test was never performed.
That execution is not complete.
Likewise, every required activity may have occurred, but several
were conducted against the wrong configuration.
That execution may be complete but materially non-conformant.
Execution Completeness
Execution Completeness evaluates whether all materially required
validation activities have been addressed.
This may include completeness across:
Validation Scope,
Validation Criteria,
method steps,
required evidence interactions,
required source interactions,
required operating conditions,
required scenarios,
required repetitions,
required observations,
required reviews,
and required controls.
Completeness should remain proportionate to the approved Validation
Purpose and Validation Depth.
Required Activity Completion
A required activity may be classified as:
Completed
Conditionally Completed
Partially Completed
Not Completed
Not Applicable
or:
Completion Undetermined
These classifications should remain traceable to the
execution basis.
Criteria Execution Completeness

Every material Validation Criterion requiring execution should have
sufficient execution activity associated with it.
VECCM asks:
Was the criterion actually examined?
Were all required activities performed?
Were required conditions represented?
Was execution sufficient for later criterion determination?
Are material parts of the criterion still unsupported?
This does not determine whether the criterion was satisfied.
Method-Step Completeness
Where the Validation Method requires a defined sequence or set of
steps, VECCM determines whether materially required steps
were completed.
Missing non-critical procedural detail may not always
block determination.
Missing a methodologically essential step may.
Materiality must therefore remain explicit.
Scope Completeness
Validation execution must be compared against the approved
Validation Scope.
Possible conditions include:
Scope Fully Executed
Scope Conditionally Executed
Scope Partially Executed
Scope Materially Reduced
or:
Scope Execution Undetermined
Where actual execution covers less than the authorized scope, later
Validation Determination must remain bounded accordingly.
Validation Depth Completeness
VECCM assesses whether execution achieved the required
Validation Depth.
A validation may perform all nominal activities while failing to
achieve the depth required for:
high-consequence reliance,
enhanced assurance,
regulatory use,
critical deployment,
or another governed purpose.
Therefore:

Activity Completion ≠ Required Validation Depth Achieved
Execution Conformity
Execution Conformity evaluates the degree to which Actual Validation
Execution corresponds to the Authorized Validation Execution Basis.
Conformity may include:
correct Validation Object,
correct object version,
approved scope,
approved method,
approved configuration,
required sequence,
required evidence,
governed sources,
required controls,
authorized participants,
required environment,
and applicable restrictions.
Object Conformity
VECCM verifies whether execution remained sufficiently connected to
the Validation Object authorized for validation.
Relevant questions include:
Was the correct object examined?
Was the correct version used?
Did the object materially change during execution?
Were material state changes governed?
Did outputs remain attributable to the correct object state?
A critical object mismatch may invalidate affected execution.
Scope Conformity
Execution may move outside or inside the authorized scope.
VECCM determines whether:
required scope was preserved,
unauthorized scope expansion occurred,
material scope reduction occurred,
exclusions were governed,
and actual scope can be reliably defined.
Method Conformity
VECCM evaluates whether the instantiated and performed method
remained sufficiently aligned with the approved Validation Method.
This includes consideration of:
required method steps,
parameters,
sequence,
repetition,
comparison structure,
analytical conditions,

simulation conditions,
or another method-specific requirement.
Configuration Conformity
Validation may depend materially upon:
model configuration,
system settings,
instrument settings,
environment settings,
software versions,
dataset versions,
or simulation configurations.
VECCM determines whether actual configurations remained sufficiently
aligned with those authorized.
Evidence-Use Conformity
VECCM assesses whether validation used evidence in accordance with
its approved role and Evidence Fitness conditions.
This may include:
correct evidence identity,
evidence version,
permitted role,
applicability conditions,
temporal validity,
scope limitations,
and any conditional fitness requirements.
Source-Condition Conformity
Where sources were subject to Source Reliability conditions, VECCM
determines whether execution respected those conditions.
For example:
A source approved only with independent corroboration should not be
treated as unrestricted if the required corroboration was
never performed.
Control Conformity
Required controls may include:
access controls,
logging,
environmental control,
sequence control,
oversight,
configuration locks,
safety controls,
or validation-specific controls.
VECCM determines whether required controls were sufficiently active
across the activities they were intended to govern.
Sequence Conformity
Where sequence matters methodologically, VECCM assesses whether
activities occurred in the required order.

Sequence deviation may affect only one activity or the validity of a
larger methodological chain.
Participant-Role Conformity
VECCM may assess whether material validation activities were
performed by participants or systems possessing the required
execution role.
This may include:
authorization,
role boundaries,
competence conditions,
independence requirements,
or permitted intervention rights
where those conditions formed part of the Execution Basis.
Execution Continuity
Execution Continuity concerns whether the validation process
remained sufficiently connected across its material stages.
Continuity may be affected by:
long interruptions,
object changes,
evidence replacement,
source change,
environment change,
configuration change,
participant change,
or execution restart.
A resumed execution should not automatically be treated as
continuous where material conditions changed.
Traceability Sufficiency
VECCM consumes VEOTM outputs to determine whether the execution
history is sufficiently traceable for conformity assessment.
A validation may have been performed correctly but lack sufficient
records to demonstrate that fact.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Correct Execution That Cannot Be Demonstrated ≠ Fully
Governed Execution
where demonstrability is required for the intended validation role.
Reconstruction Sufficiency
VECCM asks whether a qualified reviewer or system can
sufficiently reconstruct:
what occurred,
against which object,
using which method,
with which evidence,

from which sources,
under which conditions,
in what sequence,
with which deviations,
and with which outputs.
Reconstruction need not be perfect.
It must be sufficient for the intended Validation Determination.
Residual Deviation Assessment
VECCM consumes the complete deviation and exception record
established under VEDEGM.
It determines what residual effects remain after:
correction,
compensation,
re-execution,
escalation,
or closure.
A closed deviation may still leave a material
methodological limitation.
Resolved Does Not Mean Immaterial
VALIDOS® establishes:
Deviation Resolved ≠ Deviation Never Mattered
A resolved deviation may continue to affect:
scope,
interpretation,
confidence,
evidence use,
or later reliance.
Residual impact must remain visible.
Unresolved Deviation
A material unresolved deviation may prevent unrestricted
Execution Conformity.
Depending upon materiality, it may lead to:
Conditional Conformity,
Non-Conformity,
Determination Block,
or Execution Invalidity.
Cumulative Deviation Assessment
VECCM evaluates whether multiple minor or moderate deviations
collectively create a material conformity problem.
This prevents fragmented exception handling from missing
system-level execution degradation.
Execution Completeness Status
VECCM may establish:
Execution Complete
All materially required validation activities have been
sufficiently performed.
Execution Conditionally Complete
Execution is complete only within explicit boundaries, limitations,
or reduced scope.

Execution Partially Complete
Material validation activities remain unperformed.
Execution Incomplete
The execution cannot reasonably be treated as complete for the
intended Validation Purpose.
Execution Completeness Undetermined
Available records are insufficient to establish completeness.
Execution Conformity Status
VECCM may establish:
Execution Conformant
Actual validation execution sufficiently corresponds to the
Authorized Validation Execution Basis for the
intended determination.
Execution Conditionally Conformant
Execution may support Validation Determination only under explicit
conditions, limitations, scope restrictions, or
interpretive boundaries.
Execution Conformity Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish whether execution
was sufficiently conformant.
Execution Non-Conformant
Material execution conditions departed from the authorized basis
sufficiently to prevent unrestricted methodological reliance.
Execution Invalid
Critical execution deficiencies prevent the affected execution from
legitimately supporting the intended Validation Determination.
These states describe execution.
They do not describe the Validation Object.
Conditional Conformity
Conditional Conformity may arise where:
one validation condition remains limited,
scope was reduced,
one source required restriction,
a deviation was compensated but leaves residual uncertainty,
a subset of criteria remains usable,

or validation can support only a narrower determination than originally intended.
Conditions must remain attached to the subsequent
Validation Determination.
Partial Execution Validity
Where execution is partly valid and partly invalid, VALIDOS® should
avoid unnecessary all-or-nothing treatment where methodological
separation is possible.
VECCM may identify:
Valid Execution Portion
and:
Invalid or Unusable Execution Portion
provided the boundaries can be reliably established.
This supports precise remediation and partial re-execution.
Execution Invalidity
Execution Invalidity should be reserved for conditions that
fundamentally prevent legitimate methodological use of
affected execution.
Potential causes include:
wrong Validation Object,
critical object-version mismatch,
critical method failure,
irrecoverable sequence corruption,
critical evidence discontinuity,
critical source-condition failure,
untraceable critical activity,
severe uncontrolled deviation,
or inability to reconstruct the execution sufficiently.
Invalid Execution Does Not Mean Invalid Object
VALIDOS® establishes one of its strongest distinctions:
Execution Invalid ≠ Validation Object Invalid
Invalid execution means the validation process cannot legitimately
establish the intended conclusion.
The Validation Object may still satisfy or fail the
Validation Criteria.
VALIDOS® simply does not claim to know on the basis of
that execution.
Conformant Execution Can Demonstrate Failure
Conversely:

Execution Conformant + Criterion Failure = Legitimate Negative
Validation Finding
A validation process should not be judged by whether it produces a
positive result.
It should be judged by whether it produces a legitimate result.
Determination Readiness
VECCM creates the final execution gate into
Validation Determination.
A Validation Execution Instance may be considered Determination
Ready where sufficient basis exists to determine:
what was executed,
which criteria were examined,
which execution outputs exist,
how complete execution was,
how conformant execution was,
which deviations occurred,
what limitations remain,
and which portions of the execution may legitimately support determination.
Determination Readiness Status
Possible statuses may include: Determination Ready
Execution is sufficiently complete, conformant, reconstructable, and
governed to support Validation Determination.
Determination Conditionally Ready
Determination may proceed only within explicit conditions,
restrictions, limitations, or reduced scope.
Determination Readiness Undetermined
Available execution information is insufficient to
determine readiness.
Determination Not Ready
Material execution deficiencies must be resolved before legitimate
determination can occur.
Determination Blocked
One or more critical execution conditions prevent Validation
Determination from legitimately proceeding.
Determination Block
A Determination Block prevents the architecture from converting

deficient execution into a validity conclusion.
Potential triggers include:
critical missing validation activity,
wrong Validation Object,
critical scope failure,
execution invalidity,
unreconstructable critical activity,
unresolved critical deviation,
critical method substitution,
or another execution condition destroying the methodological basis for determination.
Determination Block Is Not Object Failure
A Determination Block means:
VALIDOS® cannot legitimately determine the object's validation
result from this execution.
It does not mean:
The object failed validation.
This preserves methodological neutrality.
Execution Completion Record
VECCM may establish a formal Validation Execution Completion
Record containing:
Execution Instance,
Validation Object reference,
actual scope,
actual Validation Depth,
executed criteria,
method execution summary,
evidence used,
sources used,
execution outputs,
deviations,
exceptions,
residual limitations,
Execution Completeness Status,
Execution Conformity Status,
reconstruction status,
Determination Readiness,
and any Determination Block.
Execution Closure
Execution may be formally closed when:
active execution has ended,
material outputs are preserved,
material deviations have status,
completeness is assessed,
conformity is assessed,
residual limitations are recorded,
and Determination Readiness has been established.
Closure does not erase the possibility of later reassessment.
Execution Reassessment

Execution completeness or conformity may require reassessment if:
new execution records emerge,
a previously unknown deviation is discovered,
a source is later found unreliable,
evidence fitness changes,
a configuration discrepancy is discovered,
a traceability error is corrected,
or another material fact changes the execution picture.
Execution Conformity Change
A prior Conformant determination may become:
Conditionally Conformant
Non-Conformant
or:
Invalid
if new material information emerges.
Likewise, an initially uncertain execution may later become
conformant after missing records or corrective execution
become available.
Historical Execution Preservation
Reassessment should not erase earlier conformity determinations.
The record should preserve: Original Determination → New Information
→ Reassessment → Revised Determination
This creates methodological continuity and auditability.
Execution Handoff to Validation Determination
VECCM closes the Validation Execution lifecycle and passes forward a
structured execution basis containing:
actual performed activities,
execution outputs,
execution limitations,
conformity conditions,
residual deviations,
scope boundaries,
completeness status,
and Determination Readiness.
The next Parent Standard can then ask:
What does this governed validation record actually demonstrate about
the Validation Object?
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Actual Execution Scope
Determine what portion of the authorized validation scope was

actually executed.
2. Assess Required Activity Completion
Determine whether materially required validation activities and
method steps were completed.
3. Assess Criteria Execution Completeness
Determine whether each applicable Validation Criterion possesses
sufficient execution activity for later determination.
4. Assess Execution Conformity
Compare Actual Validation Execution against the Authorized
Validation Execution Basis across:
object,
scope,
method,
configuration,
evidence,
sources,
sequence,
controls,
environment,
and participant roles.
5. Assess Reconstruction & Traceability
Determine whether material execution history can be
sufficiently reconstructed.
6. Integrate Deviations & Exceptions
Assess unresolved, residual, cumulative, and critical
execution deviations.
7. Establish Completeness Status Classify execution completeness.
8. Establish Conformity Status
Classify execution conformity.
9. Establish Determination Readiness
Determine whether Validation Determination may:
proceed,
proceed conditionally,
remain pending,
or be blocked.
10. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability
Maintain:
Execution Instance,
Authorized Execution Basis,
Actual Execution Scope,
executed criteria,
completed method steps,
evidence used,
sources used,
execution outputs,
traceability assessment,
reconstruction assessment,
deviations,
exceptions,
residual limitations,
Execution Completeness Status,
Execution Conformity Status,
Determination Readiness,
Determination Blocks,
reassessments,
versions,

and sufficient lifecycle continuity.
Governance Outputs
VECCM may produce:
Validation Execution Completeness Assessment,
Required Activity Completion Map,
Validation Criteria Execution Completeness Map,
Method-Step Completion Record,
Actual Validation Scope Record,
Validation Depth Execution Assessment,
Object Conformity Assessment,
Scope Conformity Assessment,
Method Conformity Assessment,
Configuration Conformity Assessment,
Evidence-Use Conformity Assessment,
Source-Condition Conformity Assessment,
Control Conformity Assessment,
Sequence Conformity Assessment,
Participant-Role Conformity Assessment,
Execution Continuity Assessment,
Traceability Sufficiency Assessment,
Reconstruction Sufficiency Assessment,
Residual Deviation Assessment,
Cumulative Deviation Assessment,
Execution Completeness Status,
Execution Conformity Status,
Valid Execution Portion Record,
Invalid Execution Portion Record,
Validation Execution Completion Record,
Determination Readiness Status,
Determination Block,
Execution Closure Record,
Execution Reassessment Record,
and Execution Conformity Change Record.
Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation
Scenario
An AI model completes 98 of 100 planned validation activities.
The two omitted tests concern a critical
autonomous-escalation criterion.
All other activities were performed correctly.
Application
VECCM does not classify the execution as complete merely because 98%
of activities were performed.
The missing activities are evaluated according to their

methodological significance.
Result
Execution may be:
Partially Complete
and:
Determination Not Ready
for the affected criterion despite otherwise strong
execution conformity.
Use Case 2 — Industrial System Validation
Scenario
All required industrial validation tests are completed, but one
section of testing was performed after an unauthorized
configuration change.
Application
VECCM distinguishes completeness from conformity.
Result
Execution may be:
Execution Complete
but: Execution Conditionally Conformant
or:
Execution Non-Conformant
for the affected section, depending upon materiality.
The relevant portion may require re-execution without discarding
unaffected activities.
Use Case 3 — Autonomous Validation Agent
Scenario
An autonomous validation agent completes every required test and
generates extensive records.
Later review discovers that several high-risk tests used an
unapproved tool outside the authorized execution configuration.
Application
VECCM integrates:
complete activity coverage,
traceability,
the tool-related deviation,
affected criteria,
and residual methodological impact.
Result
The validation cannot derive unrestricted confidence merely from
complete automation.
The affected execution portion is classified according to conformity
rather than activity count.
Architectural Position
Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity is the fifth and
final internal governance space of the Validation Execution
Standard (VEXS).
The complete VEXS progression is:

Validation Execution Basis & Authorization → Validation Execution
Instantiation & Control → Validation Execution Observation &
Traceability → Validation Execution Deviation & Exception Governance
→ Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity
Together, these five governed spaces transform an approved
validation design into a demonstrable and methodologically
classified Validation Execution Record.
The lifecycle progresses:
Authorized Validation Basis
↓
Controlled Execution Instance
↓
Observed & Reconstructable Execution
↓ Governed Deviations & Exceptions
↓
Execution Completeness & Conformity
↓
Determination Readiness
The next VALIDOS® Parent Standard can therefore address a
fundamentally different question:
What does the complete governed validation record actually
demonstrate about the Validation Object?
Foundational Principle
Validation execution becomes usable for determination only when what
was required, what was performed, and what can be demonstrated are
sufficiently aligned.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Execution Completeness & Conformity Module completes the
execution-governance lifecycle within VALIDOS® by determining
whether actual validation activity is sufficiently complete,
conformant, reconstructable, controlled, and methodologically usable
for subsequent Validation Determination. By governing
required-activity completion, criteria execution, scope and depth,
object and method conformity, evidence and source conditions,

configurations, controls, sequencing, traceability, residual
deviations, conditional conformity, execution invalidity,
Determination Readiness, Determination Blocks, reassessment, and
lifecycle continuity, VECCM ensures that VALIDOS® advances from
execution to determination only when the operational validation
record can legitimately support the conclusion it is being asked
to produce.
