chunks.text:
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage Module (VSPLM)
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage Module (VSPLM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS)
Operational Layer: Validation Source Reliability Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Source Provenance & Lineage
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage
Canonical Definition
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage Module (VSPLM) defines the
governance framework for reconstructing, representing, assessing,
and maintaining the material origin history, evidentiary pathway,
upstream dependencies, intermediary relationships, transformations,
and lineage through which Validation Evidence progresses from its
originating conditions to its use within a governed
validation process.
It establishes the conditions under which an identified and
attributed source relationship becomes a traceable Validation
Source Chain.
Operational Role

VSPLM serves as the second internal governance space of the
Validation Source Reliability Standard.
The preceding module asks:
Who or what is the source, and can the evidence be attributed to it?
VSPLM asks:
Where did the evidence originate, through which pathway did it reach
validation, what happened to it along that pathway, and upon which
upstream sources does it depend?
The governed progression is:
Identified & Attributed Source → Origin Establishment → Provenance
Reconstruction → Lineage Mapping → Intermediary Identification →
Transformation Mapping → Dependency Assessment → Traceable
Validation Source Chain
VSPLM does not determine whether the source is ultimately reliable.
It establishes the provenance and lineage structure required for
that later determination.
Module Operational Space
VSPLM governs:
validation-source provenance,
evidence origin,
source origin,
provenance depth,
provenance continuity,
source lineage,
upstream-source identification,
downstream-source relationships,
source chains,
source dependency,
shared-source dependency,
intermediary relationships,
transformation pathways,
evidence derivation,
aggregation lineage,
provenance gaps,
lineage gaps,
provenance conflicts,
lineage conflicts,
provenance uncertainty,
provenance boundaries,
provenance change,
lineage change,
and provenance traceability.
Module Function
VSPLM applies after material Validation Sources have been
sufficiently identified and evidence attribution has been
established or bounded.

Its function is to prevent:
immediate evidence providers being mistaken for original sources,
downstream reports concealing upstream evidence origins,
multiple derived sources being treated as independent origins,
shared datasets creating artificial source diversity,
intermediary transformations remaining invisible,
aggregated evidence losing its source structure,
source chains being collapsed into single-source labels,
missing provenance being interpreted as complete provenance,
derived evidence being represented as primary evidence,
historical source changes being overwritten,
and source-based confidence being assigned without understanding material upstream dependencies.
Provenance and Lineage Are Related but Distinct
VALIDOS® distinguishes:
Provenance
from:
Lineage
Provenance asks:
What material history brought this evidence from origin to
validation use?
Lineage asks:
Which upstream sources, derived sources, dependencies, and source
relationships contributed to the evidence?
Together they create a reconstructable source structure.
Evidence Origin
Evidence origin represents the earliest materially relevant point at
which the evidentiary content was:
observed,
measured,
generated,
recorded,
produced,
or otherwise established.
The first entity encountered by a validator is not necessarily the
evidence origin.
For example:
Website → Report → Research Paper → Dataset → Original Measurement
The website may be the immediate provider.

The measurement may be the relevant evidentiary origin.
Origin Precision
Not every validation requires identical origin precision.
Depending upon the Validation Purpose, Scope, Depth, consequence,
and evidentiary role, origin may need to identify:
an organization,
a specific system,
a specific instrument,
a particular dataset,
a model version,
an operational event,
a person,
a laboratory,
a repository,
or another source instance.
VSPLM requires sufficient origin precision for the reliability
question being governed.
Provenance Chain
A Validation Evidence provenance chain may conceptually include:
Origin → Generation → Recording → Processing → Transformation →
Transmission → Aggregation → Storage → Retrieval → Validation Use
Not every evidence item will contain every stage.
VSPLM identifies the material stages relevant to source reliability.
Provenance Depth
The required depth of provenance reconstruction should be
proportionate to the validation role.
Low-consequence validation may require limited provenance.
High-consequence validation may require substantially
deeper reconstruction.
Factors affecting provenance depth may include:
Validation Depth,
intended reliance,
consequence of error,
evidence criticality,
number of intermediaries,
degree of transformation,
source uncertainty,
and dependency complexity.
Provenance Continuity
Provenance continuity exists where the material evidentiary pathway
can be followed without unexplained breaks that materially affect

source reliability.
Continuity does not require every technical action to be documented.
It requires that the material source transitions remain
sufficiently reconstructable.
Provenance Gap
A Provenance Gap exists where a material portion of the evidentiary
pathway cannot be sufficiently established.
Examples include:
unknown original dataset,
missing measurement origin,
unidentified intermediary,
undocumented transformation,
unknown historical source,
missing model version,
or unavailable source records.
A Provenance Gap does not automatically make evidence unusable.
It creates a source-reliability condition that must remain visible.
Critical Provenance Gap
A Provenance Gap may become critical where the missing information
prevents meaningful assessment of:
source identity,
source capability,
independence,
transformation integrity,
evidence origin,
shared dependency,
or another material reliability condition.
Criticality must be determined relative to the validation role.
Source Lineage
Source lineage represents the relational structure connecting
evidence to the sources from which it derives.
A simple lineage may be:
Measurement Instrument → Dataset → Validation Evidence
A complex lineage may be:
Sensor Network → Local Database → Aggregation System → External Data
Provider → Analytical Model → Human Report → Validation Evidence
VSPLM makes these dependencies visible.
Upstream Source
An Upstream Source is a source upon which another source or evidence

object materially depends.
Upstream sources may include:
primary datasets,
original measurements,
external databases,
prior models,
sensor systems,
research studies,
operational records,
or other evidence origins.
Upstream dependency can materially affect downstream
Source Reliability.
Downstream Source
A Downstream Source receives, processes, transforms, interprets,
aggregates, or republishes evidentiary content derived from one or
more upstream sources.
Downstream sources may add legitimate value.
However, their existence does not create a new independent
evidentiary origin automatically.
Derived Source Lineage
Derived sources must remain connected to material upstream origins
where those origins affect validation reliability.
VALIDOS® establishes:
New Presentation ≠ New Evidentiary Origin
and:
New Analysis ≠ Independent Underlying Evidence
A derived source may contribute independent interpretation while
still depending upon non-independent underlying evidence.
Shared Source Dependency
Two or more apparently separate sources may share the same
upstream origin.
For example:
Source A → Dataset X
Source B → Dataset X
Source C → Dataset X
A superficial source count would produce three sources.
Lineage analysis reveals one shared upstream evidentiary dependency.
VSPLM therefore establishes:
Source Multiplicity ≠ Source Independence
Dependency Concentration
A validation evidence basis may appear diverse while depending
heavily upon one source.

VSPLM may identify Dependency Concentration where a significant
portion of the evidence basis ultimately depends upon:
one dataset,
one organization,
one model,
one measurement system,
one repository,
one methodology,
or another shared upstream source.
Dependency concentration does not automatically make
evidence unreliable.
It identifies a structural reliability condition.
Source Chain
A Validation Source Chain represents the sequence of materially
relevant source relationships through which evidence progresses.
Source chains may be:
Direct
Derived
Intermediated
Aggregated
Multi-Source
or:
Hybrid
The chain structure should remain sufficiently visible for
subsequent reliability assessment.
Intermediary Identification
An intermediary is an entity or system that materially handles
evidence between its upstream origin and validation use.
Intermediaries may:
transmit,
translate,
normalize,
aggregate,
filter,
classify,
summarize,
store,
reformat,
or interpret evidence.
VSPLM identifies intermediaries and their position in the
provenance chain.
Intermediary Role
Each intermediary may perform a different function.
Examples include:
Transmission Intermediary
Storage Intermediary
Transformation Intermediary
Aggregation Intermediary
Interpretation Intermediary
Publication Intermediary
Distribution Intermediary Role identification helps later governance
determine which intermediaries materially affect Source Reliability.
Transformation Pathway

Evidence may change between origin and validation use.
VSPLM maps material transformations such as:
filtering,
cleaning,
normalization,
aggregation,
translation,
anonymization,
statistical processing,
compression,
summarization,
model processing,
classification,
or interpretation.
VSPLM does not determine whether each transformation was
methodologically correct.
It establishes that the transformation occurred and where it sits
within the source chain.
Transformation Visibility
VALIDOS® establishes:
A transformed evidence object should not be represented as if it
were identical to its original source evidence.
Where transformation materially changes evidentiary representation,
the transformation must remain visible.
Aggregation Lineage
Aggregated evidence may combine multiple origins.
For example:
Dataset A + Dataset B + Dataset C → Aggregated Dataset D
VSPLM preserves the relationship between the aggregated object and
its material contributing sources.
Where source-level separation is impossible, that limitation must
remain explicit.
Lineage Branching
One evidence object may derive from multiple upstream sources.
Likewise, one upstream source may contribute to many downstream
evidence objects.
VSPLM therefore permits branching lineage structures rather than
forcing evidence into a simple linear chain.
Conceptually:
Source A + Source B → Derived Evidence C
and:
Source A → Evidence D + Evidence E This becomes particularly

important for large AI, scientific, financial, and operational
evidence ecosystems.
Circular Lineage
A source chain may sometimes contain circular dependencies.
For example:
Model A uses Dataset B
while:
Dataset B includes outputs previously generated by Model A.
Circular lineage may create hidden dependence, reinforcement,
contamination, or false corroboration.
VSPLM requires material circular relationships to remain visible.
Provenance Conflict
A Provenance Conflict exists where available records provide
materially incompatible accounts of the evidence pathway.
Examples include:
conflicting origin claims,
incompatible timestamps,
inconsistent source records,
disputed transformations,
or contradictory intermediary histories.
VSPLM preserves the conflict rather than forcing a single provenance
narrative without sufficient basis.
Lineage Conflict
A Lineage Conflict exists where the upstream dependency structure
cannot be reconciled.
For example:
one source claims an independent dataset,
while another record indicates that the dataset derives from a
shared upstream repository.
Material lineage conflicts must remain visible for later Source
Reliability Determination.
Provenance Uncertainty
Complete provenance may not always be obtainable.
Where evidence origin or pathway can only be partially
reconstructed, VSPLM may classify provenance conditions such as:
Provenance Established
Provenance Substantially Established
Provenance Partially Established
Provenance Uncertain

Provenance Unavailable These classifications describe
provenance quality.
They do not determine Source Reliability by themselves.
Lineage Uncertainty
Likewise, lineage may be:
Lineage Established
Lineage Partially Established
Lineage Uncertain
or:
Lineage Unknown
The required certainty should remain proportionate to the
validation role.
Provenance Boundary
VSPLM does not require infinite backward tracing.
Every provenance reconstruction must eventually establish a
reasonable boundary.
A Provenance Boundary may be reached when:
sufficient origin has been established,
further upstream information is immaterial,
additional reconstruction is impossible,
or the required Validation Depth has been satisfied.
The boundary should be explicit where it materially
affects reliance.
Provenance and Primary Evidence
Primary evidence may possess a shorter provenance chain.
However:
Primary Evidence ≠ Automatically Reliable Evidence
The originating instrument may be defective.
The observer may lack competence.
The source may be conflicted.
The recording mechanism may be compromised.
VSPLM establishes provenance.
Subsequent VSRS modules govern those other reliability dimensions.
Provenance and Derived Evidence
Derived evidence is not inherently inferior.
Derived evidence may provide:
stronger analysis,
useful aggregation,
improved interpretation,
cross-source comparison,
or higher operational value.
The governance requirement is that material derivation
remains visible.

Provenance and Source Independence
VSPLM provides critical input into later independence assessment.
Two sources cannot be confidently treated as independent until their
material lineage relationships are understood.
Therefore:
Apparent Independence → Lineage Assessment → Actual
Independence Assessment
This prevents duplicated upstream evidence from producing false
validation confidence.
Provenance and Corroboration
Corroboration requires more than agreement.
If three sources agree because all three reproduce the same upstream
dataset, they may represent:
Three Presentations
but:
One Evidentiary Origin
VSPLM exposes this distinction before corroboration is used within
Source Reliability governance.
Provenance Change
Provenance knowledge may change when:
new origin information emerges,
hidden intermediaries are discovered,
transformations become known,
source records are corrected,
upstream dependencies are identified,
or historical records become available.
Material changes should update the provenance structure without
erasing previous records.
Lineage Change
Lineage may change because:
a dataset is replaced,
a model changes training sources,
a provider changes upstream supplier,
a system begins using new external data,
or a source dependency is removed.
Material lineage changes may affect existing Source
Reliability Determinations.
Provenance Continuity Across VALIDOS®
Provenance information should remain connected to the
evidence throughout:

Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination
→ Validation State → Reliance
This allows later users of the validation result to reconstruct the
material evidentiary origins behind it.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Evidence Origin
Identify the earliest materially relevant evidence origin that can
reasonably be established.
2. Reconstruct Material Provenance
Map the material pathway from origin to validation use.
3. Identify Upstream and Downstream Sources
Determine the relevant source relationships and dependencies.
4. Identify Intermediaries
Record material entities or systems through which evidence passed.
5. Map Material Transformations
Identify transformations capable of affecting
evidentiary representation.
6. Assess Shared Dependencies
Determine whether apparently separate sources rely upon common
upstream origins.
7. Identify Provenance and Lineage Gaps
Record missing, uncertain, disputed, or unreconstructable portions
of the source structure.
8. Establish Provenance Boundary
Determine where provenance reconstruction can reasonably stop for
the governed validation role.
9. Preserve Provenance & Lineage Traceability
Maintain:
Validation Evidence reference,
source identity references,
evidence origin,
provenance chain,
source lineage,
upstream sources,
downstream sources,
intermediaries,
transformations,
shared dependencies,
dependency concentration,
provenance gaps,
lineage gaps,
conflicts,
uncertainty,
provenance boundary,
changes,

version,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Provenance & Lineage Outputs
VSPLM may produce:
Validation Evidence Origin Record,
Validation Source Provenance Record,
Validation Source Chain,
Source Lineage Map,
Upstream Source Register,
Downstream Source Relationship Record,
Source Dependency Map,
Shared Dependency Record,
Dependency Concentration Record,
Intermediary Map,
Evidence Transformation Pathway,
Aggregation Lineage Record,
Circular Lineage Record,
Provenance Gap Record,
Lineage Gap Record,
Provenance Conflict Record,
Lineage Conflict Record,
Provenance Boundary,
Provenance Change Record,
and Provenance & Lineage Determination.
Use Case 1 — AI Benchmark Evidence
Scenario
Five organizations publish benchmark results supporting the
performance of an AI system.
Application
VSPLM reconstructs their source lineage.
All five organizations used benchmark datasets derived from the same
original dataset.
Three also used the same evaluation framework.
Result
The validation process no longer interprets the five reports as five
completely independent evidentiary origins.
Their shared dependencies become visible for subsequent independence
and reliability assessment.
Use Case 2 — Healthcare Dataset
Scenario A healthcare AI validation relies upon a commercial dataset
supplied by a data provider.
Application
VSPLM determines that the dataset combines:
hospital records,
laboratory data,
historical public datasets,
and transformed records from another commercial provider.

Several transformation stages occurred before delivery.
Result
The commercial provider remains an identifiable source, but the
validation process now possesses a lineage map revealing the
upstream origins and transformations upon which the dataset depends.
Use Case 3 — Internet Claim
Scenario
The same factual claim appears across dozens of online sources.
Application
VSPLM traces the available source chains.
Most sources ultimately derive from one original report.
Several others cite articles that themselves cite that same report.
Result
Apparent widespread corroboration becomes correctly represented as a
highly repeated but strongly concentrated evidentiary lineage.
Architectural Position
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage is the second internal
governance space of the Validation Source Reliability
Standard (VSRS).
The progression now becomes:
Validation Evidence → Source Identity & Attribution → Source
Provenance & Lineage
VSIAM establishes:
Who or what contributed the evidence?
VSPLM establishes:
Where did that evidence originate, how did it reach validation, and
upon what upstream sources does it depend?
The next governance stage can then ask:
Are those sources actually capable and competent to perform the
evidentiary roles assigned to them?
The VSRS progression therefore continues: Identity & Attribution →
Provenance & Lineage → Capability & Competence → Independence &
Conflict → Source Reliability Determination
Foundational Principle

Source diversity cannot be established until the lineage behind the
sources is understood.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Source Provenance & Lineage Module establishes the
traceability structure through which VALIDOS® reconstructs the
material origins, pathways, dependencies, intermediaries,
transformations, and source relationships underlying Validation
Evidence. By distinguishing immediate providers from evidentiary
origins, source multiplicity from independent lineage, and
transformed evidence from its upstream foundations, VSPLM prevents
hidden dependencies and incomplete provenance from creating
artificial source confidence while establishing the traceable source
chain required for subsequent capability, independence, conflict,
corroboration, and Source Reliability governance.
Parent Resources
→ VALIDOS® Validation Governance Architecture — Validation Governance Layer
→ VALIDOS® Architecture Map
→ VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index
Internal Module Flow
→ Previous module: Validation Source Identity & Attribution Module (VSIAM)
→ Next module: Validation Source Capability & Competence Module (VSCCM)
Related Documents
→ Validation Source Reliability Standard
→ About Validation Source Reliability Standard

resources.title: Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM)
topics: Source Reliability as an Integrated Condition

chunks.text:
Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM)
Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS)
Operational Layer: Validation Source Reliability Governance Layer
Category: AI & Interpretation
Subcategory: Validation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Validation Source Reliability Determination
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 9 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Validation Source Reliability Determination
Canonical Definition
Validation Source Reliability Determination Module (VSRDM) defines
the governance framework for integrating source identity,
attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence,
independence, conflicts, incentives, dependencies, transformations,
limitations, uncertainty, corroboration, and source-role
requirements into a formal determination of whether a Validation
Source can be sufficiently relied upon for its assigned role within
a governed validation process.
It establishes the final source-reliability governance gate between

Source Qualification and subsequent Validation Execution Governance
within VALIDOS®.
Operational Role
VSRDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the
Validation Source Reliability Standard.
The preceding modules establish:
VSIAM — Validation Source Identity & Attribution
VSPLM — Validation Source Provenance & Lineage VSCCM — Validation
Source Capability & Competence
VSICM — Validation Source Independence & Conflict
VSRDM asks:
Considering the complete governed source relationship, can this
source be sufficiently relied upon for the validation role assigned
to it?
The governed progression is:
Identified Source → Traceable Source → Capable & Competent Source →
Independence & Conflict Assessment → Integrated Reliability
Assessment → Source Reliability Determination
VSRDM does not determine whether Validation Evidence is fit.
It does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid.
It determines whether the complete source relationship supporting
Validation Evidence is sufficiently reliable for its assigned
validation role.
Module Operational Space
VSRDM governs:
integrated source reliability,
source-reliability determination,
source-reliability status,
source-role reliability,
reliability materiality,
provenance reliability,
capability contribution,
competence contribution,
independence contribution,
conflict contribution,
dependency contribution,
transformation contribution,
corroboration contribution,
reliability limitations,
reliability uncertainty,

reliability conditions,
reliability restrictions,
source reliability readiness,
source reliability expiration,
source reliability reassessment,
source reliability suspension,
source reliability withdrawal,
reliability continuity,
and source-reliability traceability.
Module Function
VSRDM applies after the material source conditions have been
assessed through the preceding VSRS modules.
Its function is to prevent:
source reliability being reduced to reputation,
perfect source identity being mistaken for reliability,
strong competence overriding severe conflicts automatically,
independence being treated as sufficient without capability,
multiple source strengths being blindly averaged,
unresolved provenance gaps disappearing during final assessment,
conditional source relationships being represented as unconditional trust,
corroboration being counted without accounting for shared lineage,
source uncertainty being converted into confidence,
and qualified sources being treated as globally reliable beyond the role actually assessed.
Source Reliability as an Integrated Condition
VALIDOS® treats Source Reliability as an integrated
governance condition.
Reliability cannot be established from one characteristic alone.
VSRDM considers the complete source structure across:
Identity & Attribution
Provenance & Lineage
Capability & Competence
Independence & Conflict
together with material:
Dependencies
Transformations
Corroboration
Limitations
Uncertainty
and:
Assigned Source Role

A source may perform strongly across several dimensions while
remaining unreliable for one critical evidentiary role because of a
material weakness elsewhere.
Reliability Integration Principle
VSRDM establishes:
Source reliability should not be determined through blind averaging.
For example:
Strong competence cannot automatically neutralize an
uncontrolled conflict.
Perfect independence cannot compensate for lack of capability.
Clear source identity cannot compensate for unknown provenance where
provenance is critical.
Multiple favorable reports cannot compensate for one shared
compromised upstream source.
Reliability determination must therefore
remain materiality-sensitive.
Source Reliability Inputs
VSRDM may consume governed outputs including:
Source Identity Records,
Evidence Attribution Records,
Provenance Records,
Source Lineage Maps,
Provenance Gap Records,
Source Capability Assessments,
Source Competence Assessments,
Source Role Fitness Determinations,
Source Independence Assessments,
Conflict-of-Interest Records,
Dependency Maps,
Source Incentive Records,
Corroboration Independence Assessments,
transformation records,
limitations,
uncertainty,
Validation Purpose,
Validation Scope,
Validation Depth,
Validation Criteria,
and assigned Source Role.
These inputs form the basis of the integrated Source
Reliability Determination.
Source Role Reliability
Reliability is always assessed relative to a specific source role.
A source may therefore be:

Reliable as a measurement source
while:
Conditionally Reliable as an interpreter
and:
Unreliable as an independent assurance source
at the same time.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Source Reliability is role-specific, not universal.
Reliability Materiality
Not every source weakness has equal significance.
VSRDM may distinguish conditions that are:
immaterial,
minor,
material,
critical,
or validation-blocking.
Materiality may depend upon:
the source role,
evidence criticality,
Validation Criterion affected,
Validation Depth,
intended reliance,
consequence of error,
source substitutability,
and availability of independent corroboration.
A critical source weakness must not disappear because the overall
source profile is otherwise strong.
Critical Source Role
Certain source roles may be critical to validation.
Examples may include:
sole measurement source,
primary evidence origin,
only available expert source,
critical benchmark provider,
sole operational record system,
or independent assurance source.
Where a critical source is materially unreliable, downstream
validation may require:
replacement,
additional corroboration,
reduced scope,
restricted reliance,
or further governance action.
Provenance Reliability Contribution
Provenance and lineage affect reliability by revealing:
origin clarity,
upstream dependencies,
transformation history,
shared-source concentration,
hidden intermediaries,
or provenance gaps.
A source may be otherwise competent and independent while still

carrying substantial reliability uncertainty because its evidentiary
origin cannot be sufficiently reconstructed.
Capability & Competence Contribution
Capability and competence contribute to reliability only within the
role and boundary in which they were established.
A source should not receive reliability credit beyond:
its technical capability,
operating range,
professional competence,
domain competence,
informational access,
or demonstrated task fitness.
Independence Contribution
Independence may strengthen source reliability where the source is
expected to provide unbiased or independent evidence.
However:
Independent ≠ Automatically Reliable
Independence is one reliability dimension.
Its significance depends upon the source role.
Conflict Contribution
A conflict does not automatically produce Source Unreliable status.
VSRDM evaluates:
conflict type,
materiality,
transparency,
controls,
residual conflict,
available corroboration,
and the role of the source.
A controlled minor conflict may coexist with strong reliability.
An uncontrolled material conflict in a sole critical source may
materially constrain reliability.
Dependency Contribution
A source may depend upon:
external data,
common methods,
shared infrastructure,
upstream sources,
analytical tools,
or other systems.
VSRDM evaluates whether these dependencies materially weaken source
reliability or reduce the independence of corroboration.
Transformation Contribution

Evidence transformations may create reliability conditions.
Where a source:
aggregates,
translates,
normalizes,
filters,
summarizes,
classifies,
or analytically transforms evidence,
VSRDM considers whether the transformation pathway is sufficiently
governed for the assigned role.
Corroboration Contribution
Corroboration may strengthen source reliability confidence where
genuinely independent sources support compatible conclusions.
However:
Corroboration Strength = Agreement × Independence ×
Lineage Diversity
conceptually, not merely source count.
VSRDM therefore consumes the independence and lineage findings
established earlier rather than counting sources mechanically.
Reliability Limitation
A source may be reliable while carrying limitations.
Examples include:
reliable only within one measurement range,
reliable only for one population,
reliable only for raw data generation,
reliable only under current calibration,
reliable only within one system version,
or reliable only with independent corroboration.
Limitations remain part of the Reliability Determination.
Reliability Condition
A reliability condition specifies what must remain true for the
Source Reliability status to remain applicable.
Examples include:
continued calibration,
unchanged model version,
continued independence,
defined contractual controls,
preserved information access,
ongoing certification,
or continued availability of an independent corroborating source.

Conditions must remain visible throughout subsequent
validation governance.
Reliability Restriction
A source may be restricted to a limited validation role.
For example:
May support evidence generation but not independent assurance.
or:
May support contextual interpretation but not final
technical determination.
Role restriction allows useful sources to remain within validation
without assigning them authority or confidence beyond their
legitimate function.
Reliability Uncertainty
Where material source conditions remain unresolved, VSRDM
preserves uncertainty.
Sources may therefore receive:
Source Reliability Undetermined
rather than being forced into binary
trusted/untrusted classifications.
Uncertainty may arise from:
incomplete provenance,
uncertain source identity,
competence ambiguity,
hidden dependencies,
unresolved conflicts,
or insufficient independence evidence.
Source Reliability Status
VSRDM may establish the following canonical
source-reliability states:
Source Reliable
The source is sufficiently identifiable, traceable, capable,
competent, appropriately independent, conflict-governed, and
reliable for the defined source role.
Source Conditionally Reliable
The source may perform the assigned validation role only under
explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, corroboration
requirements, or other controls.
Source Reliability Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish a defensible
Source Reliability Determination.

Source Reliability Insufficient
Material source-reliability requirements remain unresolved or
inadequately supported.
Source Unreliable
The source cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role.
These statuses apply to the source-role relationship.
They do not represent Evidence Fitness or the Validation State of
the Validation Object.
Reliable Does Not Mean Correct
VALIDOS® establishes:
Source Reliable ≠ Every Source Output Correct
A reliable source may still make an error.
Reliability means that the source relationship is sufficiently
trustworthy for the role assigned within validation.
The actual evidentiary content must still be governed through the
wider validation process.
Unreliable Does Not Mean False
Likewise:
Source Unreliable ≠ Evidence Automatically False
Evidence from an unreliable source may occasionally be correct.
The reliability status concerns how much governed confidence the
source relationship can support.
Independent evidence may later confirm the same
underlying condition.
Source Reliability and Evidence Fitness
VSRDM preserves the separation:
Evidence Fitness → Is the evidence fit?
Source Reliability → Can the source behind it be relied upon?
A robust validation may require both.
Possible combinations include:
Evidence Fit + Source Reliable
Evidence Fit + Source Conditionally Reliable
Evidence Fit + Source Reliability Undetermined
Evidence Unfit + Source Reliable
and other combinations.
No single combination automatically produces the final

Validation Determination.
Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis
Once source reliability has been established, the evidence basis can
become a Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis.
This does not mean that evidence has become true or that the
Validation Object has passed validation.
It means that the evidentiary basis now carries both:
Evidence Fitness information
and:
Source Reliability information
necessary for subsequent validation execution.
Source Reliability Readiness
A source relationship may be sufficiently ready for subsequent
validation governance when:
source identity is established,
attribution is sufficient,
relevant provenance is available,
critical lineage dependencies are understood,
capability and competence are adequate,
independence requirements are addressed,
conflicts are governed,
limitations are explicit,
and an appropriate Source Reliability status exists.
Conditional Progression
A Conditionally Reliable source may progress only where the relevant
conditions can remain visible and enforceable.
Examples include:
independent corroboration required,
restricted source role,
specific version only,
use only within defined operating conditions,
disclosure required,
or enhanced oversight required.
These conditions must not disappear during Validation Execution.
Source Reliability Expiration
A Reliability Determination may expire or require reassessment
because of:
elapsed time,
calibration expiration,
qualification expiration,
model update,
system change,

ownership change,
organizational restructuring,
new conflict,
new upstream dependency,
provenance correction,
competence change,
or changed Validation Scope.
Expiration means the previous determination can no longer be
assumed current.
Source Reliability Reassessment
Possible reassessment outcomes include:
Reliability Maintained
Reliability Modified
Conditional Reliability
Additional Source Qualification Required
Reliability Suspended
Reliability Withdrawn
This prevents historical source trust from persisting after material
source conditions have changed.
Reliability Suspension
A source may require temporary suspension where material concerns
arise but cannot yet be fully resolved.
Examples include:
suspected compromise,
unresolved calibration issue,
disputed provenance,
newly discovered conflict,
or pending competence review.
Suspension preserves uncertainty without prematurely issuing a final
Unreliable determination.
Reliability Withdrawal
Reliability may be withdrawn where the basis of the previous
determination no longer exists.
Possible triggers include:
source manipulation,
proven provenance fraud,
critical capability failure,
uncontrolled conflict,
compromised system,
materially false attribution,
or another critical reliability failure.
Withdrawal must remain traceable.
Reliability Continuity
Source Reliability information should remain attached to the
evidence throughout:
Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State →
Reliance & Revalidation

This preserves the ability to determine which sources supported a
later validation result and what reliability conditions applied at
the time.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Consolidate Source Reliability Inputs
Collect governed outputs from:
Source Identity & Attribution,
Source Provenance & Lineage,
Source Capability & Competence,
and Source Independence & Conflict.
2. Identify Material Reliability Conditions
Identify:
limitations,
uncertainties,
dependencies,
transformations,
conflicts,
independence conditions,
corroboration requirements,
and role restrictions.
3. Assess Materiality
Determine which conditions are:
immaterial,
material,
critical,
or validation-blocking.
4. Assess Role-Specific Reliability
Evaluate the source specifically against the evidentiary role it is
expected to perform.
5. Establish Reliability Status
Classify the source as:
Source Reliable,
Source Conditionally Reliable,
Source Reliability Undetermined,
Source Reliability Insufficient,
or Source Unreliable.
6. Establish Conditions, Limitations, and Restrictions
Define the boundaries within which the Source Reliability status may
legitimately apply.
7. Establish Reassessment Triggers
Identify material events requiring future review.
8. Create Source Reliability Record
Preserve:
Validation Source reference,
source identity,
source role,
attribution status,
provenance status,
lineage structure,
capability status,
competence status,
independence status,
conflict status,
dependencies,
transformations,

corroboration information,
limitations,
uncertainty,
restrictions,
reliability status,
determination basis,
effective period,
reassessment triggers,
version,
changes,
and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Source Reliability Governance Flow
VSRDM completes the VSRS internal progression:
Source Identity & Attribution → Source Provenance & Lineage → Source
Capability & Competence → Source Independence & Conflict → Source
Reliability Determination
This transforms an evidentiary source from an assumed origin into a
formally governed reliability relationship.
Governance Outputs
VSRDM may produce:
Source Reliability Determination,
Source Reliability Record,
Source Reliability Status,
Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis,
Source Role Reliability Profile,
Source Reliability Condition Record,
Source Reliability Limitation Record,
Source Reliability Restriction Record,
Source Reliability Uncertainty Record,
Source Reliability Reassessment Trigger,
Source Reliability Expiration Condition,
Source Reliability Suspension Record,
Source Reliability Withdrawal Record,
Source Reliability Change Record,
and Source Reliability Continuity Reference.
Use Case 1 — External AI Safety Assessment
Scenario
An external consultancy performs an AI safety assessment.
The consultancy is technically competent, but the work is funded by
the AI vendor and uses several datasets supplied by that vendor.
Application
VSRDM integrates:
established source identity,
clear provenance,
strong competence,

partial informational dependence,
financial conflict,
and available independent corroboration.
Result
The consultancy may receive:
Source Conditionally Reliable
for defined assessment roles, with funding and information
dependencies preserved as explicit conditions rather than being
ignored or treated as automatic disqualification.
Use Case 2 — Industrial Measurement Source
Scenario A calibrated industrial sensor provides critical
measurements for validation.
The sensor is well identified, directly attributable, and
technically capable.
A recent maintenance event creates uncertainty about
calibration continuity.
Application
VSRDM integrates the otherwise strong reliability profile with the
unresolved calibration condition.
Result
The source may receive:
Source Reliability Undetermined
or:
Source Conditionally Reliable
until the calibration condition is resolved.
Use Case 3 — Internet Claim Verification
Scenario
Dozens of online sources repeat the same factual claim.
Application
VSRDM consumes lineage analysis showing that most sources derive
from one original report.
Several additional sources rely upon one shared secondary dataset.
Result
The apparent number of sources does not produce artificial
reliability confidence.
The actual source structure is assessed according to origin,
capability, independence, shared dependencies, and
corroboration quality.
Architectural Position
Validation Source Reliability Determination is the fifth and final

internal governance space of the Validation Source Reliability
Standard (VSRS).
The complete VSRS progression is:
Validation Source Identity & Attribution → Validation Source
Provenance & Lineage → Validation Source Capability & Competence →
Validation Source Independence & Conflict → Validation Source
Reliability Determination
Together, these five governed spaces transform source trust from an
assumption into a structured source-reliability determination.
The VALIDOS® lifecycle can now progress from:
Qualified Validation Evidence
to: Reliability-Qualified Validation Evidence
and then to the next governance question:
Was the approved validation process actually executed as governed?
Foundational Principle
A source becomes reliable for validation only when the complete
source relationship supports the role it is expected to perform.
Canonical Closing Statement
Validation Source Reliability Determination Module completes
source-reliability governance within VALIDOS® by integrating
identity, attribution, provenance, lineage, capability, competence,
independence, conflicts, incentives, dependencies, transformations,
corroboration, limitations, uncertainty, conditions, restrictions,
change, and traceability into a formal role-specific Source
Reliability Determination. VSRDM ensures that validation confidence
is never derived from source reputation, authority, popularity,
repetition, or apparent independence alone, but from a

reconstructable and governable source relationship capable of
legitimately supporting the evidentiary role upon which
validation depends.

Validation Source Reliability Standard
Standard ID: VSRS
OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VSRS-2026-08-09-0006

Category: AI & Interpretation

Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS®
· ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™

Canonical Definition
Validation Source Reliability Standard (VSRS) defines the governance
conditions under which sources providing, generating, transmitting,
recording, transforming, interpreting, or maintaining Validation
Evidence are identified, attributable, provenance-aware,
independence-assessed, integrity-aware, competence-aware,
conflict-aware, and sufficiently reliable for their assigned role
within a governed validation process.
Canonical Definition Extension
Evidence does not exist independently of origin.
It is generated, observed, recorded, measured, transmitted,
transformed, interpreted, stored, or supplied by one or
more sources.
A piece of evidence may be highly relevant, applicable,
comprehensive, and adequate while the reliability of the source
behind that evidence remains uncertain.
VALIDOS® therefore separates:

Evidence Fitness
from:
Source Reliability
Validation Source Reliability Standard governs the second question.
It establishes the conditions necessary to determine:
where Validation Evidence originated,
which source produced or supplied it,
whether the source can be sufficiently identified,
whether attribution can be established,
whether provenance is sufficiently reconstructable,
whether the source possesses the required competence or capability,
whether relevant independence exists,
whether conflicts of interest are visible,
whether the evidence passed through intermediaries,
whether material transformations occurred,
whether source integrity conditions are known,
whether corroboration is required,
whether source reliability has materially changed,
and whether the source can legitimately support the evidentiary role assigned to it.
VSRS does not determine whether evidence is relevant or adequate.
It does not determine whether the Validation Object is valid.
It determines whether the source relationship behind Validation
Evidence is sufficiently reliable for governed validation use.
Core Question
Can the source behind Validation Evidence be sufficiently
identified, traced, assessed, and relied upon for the validation
role assigned to it?
Purpose
The purpose of Validation Source Reliability Standard is to prevent
validation confidence from being derived from evidence whose source
basis is unknown, insufficiently attributable, materially

conflicted, methodologically incapable, excessively dependent,
provenance-deficient, or otherwise unreliable.
The standard prevents validation from silently treating:
anonymous origin as established origin,
publication as reliability,
institutional authority as universal competence,
repetition as independence,
multiple intermediaries as multiple independent sources,
source popularity as methodological credibility,
source confidence as evidence quality,
and source reputation as permanent reliability.
VSRS creates a governed source-reliability layer between qualified
evidence and subsequent validation execution.
Governance Objective
VSRS establishes a governed Validation Source Reliability Framework
capable of determining whether sources behind Validation Evidence
possess sufficient reliability for their assigned validation roles.
The standard seeks to ensure that:
source identity is sufficiently established,
source attribution is traceable,
provenance is reconstructable,
source roles are explicit,
material intermediaries are visible,
material transformations are traceable,
competence is proportionate to the source role,
independence is assessed where required,
conflicts of interest remain visible,
source dependencies are identifiable,
corroboration requirements can be established,
source reliability conditions remain bounded,
reliability change can be detected,
and source reliability can be formally determined.
Operational Role

Validation Source Reliability Standard serves as the
source-qualification stage of the VALIDOS® validation lifecycle.
The preceding architecture establishes:
Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria
→ Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness
VSRS then asks:
Can the sources underlying that qualified evidence basis be
sufficiently relied upon?
Its structural progression is:
Qualified Validation Evidence → Source Identification → Source
Provenance → Source Capability → Independence & Conflict Assessment
→ Source Reliability Determination → Reliability-Qualified
Evidence Basis
The resulting source-qualified evidence basis can then progress into
Validation Execution governance.
Governance Scope
Validation Source Reliability Standard governs:
validation-source identification,
source attribution,
source origin,
source provenance,
source lineage,
source roles,
source capability,
source competence,
source authority where relevant,
source independence,
source dependence,
conflicts of interest,
source incentives,
source intermediaries,
evidence transformations,
source integrity conditions,
source corroboration,
source convergence,
source reliability limitations,
source reliability uncertainty,
source reliability status,
source reliability change,
source reliability expiration,
source reliability reassessment,
and source-reliability traceability.
Validation Source
For the purposes of VALIDOS®, a Validation Source is any

identifiable entity, system, process, instrument, repository,
person, organization, model, sensor, database, document origin,
operational environment, or other origin capable of materially
contributing Validation Evidence.
A source may:
generate evidence,
observe evidence,
record evidence,
measure evidence,
transform evidence,
transmit evidence,
interpret evidence,
aggregate evidence,
preserve evidence,
or provide evidence.
Different source roles may require different reliability conditions.
Source Identity
Source reliability cannot be meaningfully governed where the
relevant source cannot be sufficiently distinguished.
Source identity may require identification of:
source entity,
source instance,
system,
instrument,
organization,
individual,
repository,
model,
dataset origin,
version,
or another relevant source representation.
The required identity precision should correspond to the validation
role and consequence.
Source Attribution
VSRS governs whether Validation Evidence can be sufficiently
attributed to the source claimed to have generated, observed,
recorded, transmitted, or supplied it.
Attribution may be:
Direct
Derived
Intermediated Aggregated
Uncertain
or:
Unattributed
Attribution status must remain visible where it materially affects
source reliability.
Source Provenance
Provenance establishes the history through which evidence reached
the validation process.
The governed progression may include:
Origin → Generation → Recording → Transformation → Transmission →

Aggregation → Storage → Retrieval → Validation Use
Not every validation requires complete reconstruction of every
technical event.
The required provenance depth must be proportionate to the
evidentiary role, Validation Depth, and consequence of reliance.
Source Lineage
Evidence may derive from multiple upstream sources.
A final report, dataset, benchmark, or analytical output may
represent a downstream source while depending upon:
primary observations,
external datasets,
prior studies,
other models,
third-party measurements,
or aggregated records.
VSRS requires material upstream dependencies to remain visible where
they affect reliability.
Primary and Derived Sources
VALIDOS® distinguishes between:
Primary Source
and:
Derived Source
A Primary Source originates the relevant observation, measurement,
record, or event representation.
A Derived Source obtains its evidentiary content through another
source or transformation.
Derived evidence is not automatically less reliable.
However, derivation creates additional lineage and transformation
conditions that may require governance.
Source Capability
A source must be capable of performing the evidentiary role assigned
to it.
Capability may concern:
measurement capability,
observation capability,
technical capability,
analytical capability,
domain capability,
operational access,
data access,
or another relevant function.
A source may be highly reputable while lacking capability for a
particular evidentiary role.
Source Competence

Where human, institutional, professional, or analytical judgment
contributes materially to Validation Evidence, competence may
require assessment.
Relevant considerations may include:
expertise,
qualification,
experience,
methodological understanding,
domain knowledge,
or demonstrated capability.
VSRS does not establish universal professional
qualification requirements.
It governs whether competence is sufficient for the role assigned
within validation.
Source Authority and Source Reliability
Authority may be relevant but is not equivalent to reliability.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Source Authority ≠ Source Reliability
An authoritative institution may be highly reliable within its
governed domain while remaining unsuitable for conclusions outside
its competence or evidentiary role.
Likewise, a non-authoritative source may provide highly reliable
primary evidence.
VSRS therefore evaluates reliability according to function rather
than title alone.
Source Independence
Some validation roles require independent evidence.
Independence may concern separation from:
the Validation Object creator,
system operator,
financial beneficiary,
decision authority,
evidence generator,
prior evaluator,
or another materially interested party.
Independence requirements should be proportionate to Validation
Purpose, Depth, and consequence.
Independence Is Not Binary
A source may possess different forms and degrees of independence.
Possible dimensions include:
organizational independence,

financial independence,
methodological independence,
operational independence,
informational independence,
analytical independence,
and decision independence.
A source should not be classified as simply "independent" without
regard to the independence dimension relevant to the
validation role.
Source Dependence
Multiple sources may appear independent while relying upon the same
upstream origin.
For example:
ten publications may all repeat information from one
original dataset.
Counting them as ten independent sources would create
false corroboration.
VSRS therefore governs source dependence and shared lineage.
Conflict of Interest
A conflict of interest does not automatically make a
source unreliable.
It creates a governance condition.
Material conflicts may include:
financial interest,
organizational interest,
reputational interest,
operational ownership,
contractual dependence,
competitive interest,
personal interest,
or another incentive capable of affecting evidentiary behavior.
Conflicts should be identified, assessed, and incorporated into the
Source Reliability Determination.
Source Incentives
Source reliability may be affected by incentives even where no
formal conflict exists.
Incentives may encourage:
selective reporting,
favorable interpretation,
omission,
exaggeration,
under-reporting,
or evidentiary framing.
VSRS therefore permits incentive analysis where material to
validation reliability.
Source Intermediaries

Evidence may pass through intermediaries before reaching validation.
Intermediaries may:
transmit,
translate,
aggregate,
reformat,
summarize,
filter,
classify,
or transform evidence.
Each material intermediary may create additional provenance and
reliability conditions.
Evidence Transformation
Transformation can change evidentiary meaning.
Examples include:
aggregation,
normalization,
translation,
compression,
filtering,
statistical processing,
model interpretation,
summarization,
anonymization,
or format conversion.
VSRS governs whether material transformations are sufficiently
identifiable and traceable.
It does not determine whether the resulting evidence is adequate;
that remains within VEFS.
Source Integrity Conditions
VSRS may consume relevant integrity information concerning whether a
source, record, system, instrument, or evidentiary pathway has
remained protected against material alteration, corruption,
substitution, or loss.
Where integrity governance is required, INTEGROS® may provide
complementary integrity conditions.
VSRS uses such information only insofar as it affects source
reliability within validation.
Source Corroboration
Some source roles may require corroboration.
Corroboration asks whether materially independent sources support
compatible evidentiary conclusions.
VSRS distinguishes genuine corroboration from repetition.
Repeated information from one upstream source does not constitute
independent corroboration.
Source Convergence

Where multiple sufficiently independent sources converge upon
compatible evidence, source reliability confidence may increase.
However, convergence must not automatically override:
shared bias,
shared methodology,
shared datasets,
shared incentives,
or common upstream dependencies.
VSRS therefore requires convergence to remain lineage-aware.
Source Reliability Limitations
A source may be reliable within defined boundaries.
For example:
reliable for raw measurement but not interpretation,
reliable for one jurisdiction but not another,
reliable for one operating environment,
reliable for one data type,
or reliable only within a defined period.
Source Reliability Determinations must preserve these boundaries.
Source Reliability Uncertainty
Where source identity, provenance, capability, independence, or
another material condition cannot be sufficiently established, VSRS
preserves uncertainty.
Possible outcomes should not be forced into a binary
trusted/untrusted classification.
Uncertainty itself is a governed source condition.
Source Reliability Status
VSRS may establish conditions such as:
Source Reliable
The source is sufficiently reliable for the defined validation role.
Source Conditionally Reliable
The source may support validation only within explicit conditions,
limitations, or restrictions.
Source Reliability Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to establish a defensible
reliability determination.
Source Reliability Insufficient

Material source-reliability requirements remain unresolved.
Source Unreliable
The source cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role.
These states apply to the source-role relationship.
They do not represent Evidence Fitness or the Validation State of
the Validation Object.
Source Reliability Is Role-Specific
VALIDOS® establishes:
A source is not universally reliable or unreliable.
The same source may be:
Reliable for direct measurement,
Conditionally Reliable for interpretation,
and:
Unreliable for conclusions outside its capability.
Reliability must therefore remain connected to the exact evidentiary
role assigned to the source.
Source Reliability and Evidence Fitness
VALIDOS® maintains the architectural separation:
Evidence Fitness asks:
Is the evidence fit for the validation question?
Source Reliability asks:
Can the source behind that evidence be sufficiently relied upon for
its assigned role?
Neither condition substitutes for the other.
Possible combinations include:
Fit Evidence + Reliable Source
Fit Evidence + Unreliable Source
Unfit Evidence + Reliable Source
Unfit Evidence + Unreliable Source
Only by governing both dimensions can VALIDOS® distinguish
evidentiary quality from source trustworthiness.
Source Reliability and Truth
A reliable source does not automatically make every statement true.
VALIDOS® establishes:
Reliable Source ≠ True Claim
Source reliability concerns the credibility of the source
relationship within validation.

Truth-oriented assessment remains a separate
methodological question.
Source Reliability and Execution
VSRS does not determine whether the approved validation methodology
was correctly executed.
A reliable source can still be used incorrectly.
An unreliable source can also be correctly processed while producing
a weak validation basis.
Execution governance therefore remains a subsequent independent
VALIDOS® responsibility.
Source Reliability Change
Source reliability may change because of:
source modification,
ownership change,
capability change,
newly discovered conflicts,
provenance discovery,
compromised systems,
altered incentives,
new upstream dependencies,
changed methodology,
or new reliability evidence.
Material change may require reassessment.
Source Reliability Expiration
A Source Reliability Determination may be time-bounded.
Expiration may be appropriate where reliability depends upon:
certification periods,
calibration,
organizational conditions,
system versions,
personnel qualifications,
current independence,
or another time-sensitive condition.
Expiration does not mean the source becomes
unreliable automatically.
It means the previous determination can no longer be assumed current
without reassessment.
Source Reliability Traceability
Source Reliability should remain traceable to:
Validation Evidence,
source identity,
source role,
provenance,
lineage,
capability,
competence where applicable,
independence,
dependencies,
conflicts,
transformations,
corroboration,

limitations,
uncertainty,
reliability status,
and subsequent validation use.
This creates reconstructable source governance across the
VALIDOS® lifecycle.
Governance Boundary
Validation Source Reliability Standard begins when qualified
Validation Evidence possesses identifiable or potentially
identifiable sources requiring reliability assessment.
It ends when the material source relationships behind the evidence
basis have been sufficiently identified, traced, assessed, bounded,
and assigned a Source Reliability status for their intended
validation roles.
VSRS does not determine:
Validation Object identity,
Validation Purpose or Scope,
Validation Criteria,
Validation Method suitability,
Evidence Relevance,
Evidence Applicability,
Evidence Coverage,
Evidence Adequacy,
Validation Execution conformity,
final Validation Determination,
Validation State,
reliance authorization,
or revalidation requirements.
These responsibilities belong to other VALIDOS® Parent Standards.
Minimum Governance Requirements
A conforming implementation of VSRS should establish:
1. identifiable validation-source relationships,
2. sufficient source attribution,
3. relevant source provenance and lineage,
4. material source roles,
5. source capability for the assigned role,
6. competence where materially required,
7. independence assessment where applicable,
8. source-dependence visibility,
9. material conflict-of-interest visibility,
10. material intermediary and transformation visibility, 11.

corroboration conditions where required, 12. source-reliability
limitations and uncertainty, 13. a Source Reliability Determination,
14. and sufficient lifecycle traceability.
Governance Outputs
VSRS may produce:
Validation Source Register,
Source Identity Record,
Source Attribution Record,
Source Provenance Record,
Source Lineage Map,
Source Role Record,
Source Capability Assessment,
Source Competence Assessment,
Source Independence Assessment,
Source Dependence Map,
Conflict-of-Interest Record,
Source Incentive Record,
Evidence Transformation Record,
Source Corroboration Assessment,
Source Reliability Limitation Record,
Source Reliability Determination,
Source Reliability Change Record,
Source Reliability Reassessment Trigger,
and Reliability-Qualified Evidence Basis.
Operational Applications
Validation Source Reliability Standard may be applied across:
artificial intelligence,
machine learning,
autonomous systems,
scientific evidence,
datasets,
benchmark results,
AI-generated information,
predictions,
simulations,
expert assessments,
sensor systems,
operational records,
enterprise analytics,
financial services,

OOF™ Value Flow Mechanism
OOF™ Value Flow Mechanism
Canonical Hierarchical Scheme (Regulator-Grade)
1. Value Flow Mechanism (VFM™)
Level: System / Governance Mechanism
Role: Primary, non-asset-specific governance logic governing how value is created, withdrawn, neutralized, and restored.
The Value Flow Mechanism defines how value moves over time within a structured system context.
It does not judge objects; it governs transitions between value states based on validated conditions.
2. Value States Layer
Level: State Logic
Value States are objective system states that may be assigned to any Value Asset.
They are not labels of worth, but results of validated evaluation under defined methodological rules.
Canonical Value States:
ORIGIN VALUE™
State of validated, origin-bound, audit-confirmed value.
DEMONET™ (De-Monetization)
State in which monetization rights are methodologically withdrawn due to validated non-compliance, integrity failure, or rule breach.
ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset)
State of confirmed zero economic value under the governing methodology.
REMONET™ (Re-Monetization)
Transitional state enabling conditional restoration of value once corrective criteria are demonstrably met.
Important: These are states , not products, sanctions, penalties, or opinions.
3. Value Asset Layer
Level: Object Layer
A Value Asset is any entity capable of carrying value within the system.
Examples include (non-exhaustive):
Physical products
Companies or projects
Data sets
AI models

Digital identities
Environmental resources
Certifications or rights
The Value Asset itself is neutral .
Only its state changes within the Value Flow Mechanism.
4. Origin Asset™ Layer
Level: Provenance Anchor
An Origin Asset™ is a Value Asset whose provenance, integrity, and origin conditions are verifiably established.
Origin Assets act as reference anchors within the Value Flow Mechanism and represent assets eligible for achieving or restoring ORIGIN VALUE™ status under validated criteria.
5. Hierarchical Flow Tree (Canonical)
VALUE FLOW MECHANISM (VFM™)
│
├─ Value States Layer
│ │
│ ├─ ORIGIN VALUE™
│ │ ↑ ↓
│ │ REMONET™ (Re-Monetization)
│ │ ↑ ↓
│ │ ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset)
│ │ ↑
│ │ DEMONET™ (De-Monetization)
│
├─ Value Asset Layer
│ ├─ Value Asset (neutral carrier)
│ └─ Origin Asset™ (provenance-anchored subset)
│
└─ Governance & Validation Rules
├─ Audit in Real Time™ (ART™)
├─ Methodological Validation
└─ State Transition Protocols
6. State Transition Logic
Level: State Logic
Value States are objective system states that may be assigned to any Value Asset.
They are not labels of worth, but results of validated evaluation under defined methodological rules.
Canonical Value States:
ORIGIN VALUE™ → DEMONET™
Triggered by validated integrity failure, non-compliance, or rule breach.
DEMONET™ → ZVA™
Confirmed removal of monetizable value under governing methodological criteria.
ZVA™ → REMONET™
Conditional eligibility phase once remediation criteria are demonstrably satisfied.

REMONET™ → ORIGIN VALUE™
Restoration of validated value following successful re-audit under defined standards.
All transitions are rule-based, auditable, and non-discretionary within the methodology.
7. Canonical Definitions (Regulator-Grade)
Value Flow Mechanism (VFM™)
A non-discretionary governance mechanism defining how value states are assigned, withdrawn, neutralized, and restored over time based on validated methodological criteria.
Value Asset
A neutral entity capable of carrying value within the system. Value Assets are not judged; only their states change.
Origin Asset™
A Value Asset with verifiable provenance and integrity, eligible for origin-based valuation and structured re-monetization.
Value States
An objective, system-validated condition reflecting the current valuation status of a Value Asset.
ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset)
A confirmed value state indicating zero economic value under the governing methodology.
DEMONET™ (De-Monetization)
A value state representing the structured withdrawal of monetization rights under defined validation rules.
REMONET™ (Re-Monetization)
A transitional value state enabling conditional restoration of value following verified remediation.
ORIGIN VALUE™
A state of validated, origin-bound, audit-confirmed value within the defined governance framework.
8. Regulatory Positioning Statement
The OOF™ Value Flow Mechanism is not a punitive system, not a market intervention, and not a discretionary rating tool.

It is a methodological governance framework designed to provide regulators, institutions, and systems with an objective, auditable, and repeatable model for managing value transitions.
OOF™ does not execute state transitions.
It defines the architectural methodology under which compliant systems may implement them within their respective legal and operational environments.
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Global Methodology Authority
VFM™ Use Case
Digital-to-Physical Value Transition
Governance
Context
Modern economic value is increasingly created in digital environments: a>
AI-generated services
cloud-based platforms
tokenized representations of physical rights
cross-border digital revenues
However, once this value enters the real economy — through taxation,
credit evaluation, asset recognition, or regulatory reporting — there is no
standardized methodology governing how that transition should be
validated.
Current systems track transactions.
They do not define structured value-state transitions.
Structural Gap
When digital value moves into physical or jurisdictional recognition,
critical questions arise:
Where did the value originate?
Under which conditions is it economically valid?
When should monetization rights be suspended?
How can value be restored after compliance failure?
There is currently no neutral governance architecture defining these
transitions across domains.
VFM™ Application
The OOF™ Value Flow Mechanism introduces:
a neutral Value Asset model

objective Value States
rule-based, non-discretionary state transitions
audit-bound validation logic
When digital economic activity enters real-world financial systems, the
framework enables:
origin-bound validation (ORIGIN VALUE™)
structured monetization withdrawal (DEMONET™)
confirmed economic neutralization (ZVA™)
controlled restoration pathways (REMONET™)
This does not replace legal or fiscal systems.
It provides a methodological structure under which value transitions may
be assessed consistently and transparently.
Relevance for Regulators
For regulatory bodies and supervisory authorities, VFM™ offers:
a structured vocabulary for cross-domain value recognition
a non-discretionary logic for economic state assignment
audit-aligned transition governance
conceptual compatibility with digital economy oversight
The framework does not intervene in markets.
It defines how value states may be methodologically interpreted across
digital and physical domains.
VFM™ Use Case
AI-Based Credit and Economic Decision Governance
Context
Financial institutions increasingly rely on automated and AI-driven systems
for:
credit approval
risk assessment
insurance pricing
capital allocation
These decisions directly impact economic value, monetization rights, and
financial stability.
However, there is no standardized governance architecture defining how
the economic state of a decision should be assigned, suspended, or
restored when model integrity changes.
Structural Gap

Current AI governance frameworks focus on:
bias mitigation
explainability
model transparency
They do not define a structured economic state logic governing the
consequences of automated decisions.
When a model fails validation:
What happens to monetization rights?
How is economic impact neutralized?
What is the structured path toward reinstatement?
There is no neutral value-state architecture governing these transitions.
VFM™ Application
Within the Value Flow Mechanism:
An AI credit model can be treated as a Value Asset.
The economic impact of its decisions may be governed by objective value states:
ORIGIN VALUE™ – validated, audit-confirmed operational integrity
DEMONET™ – temporary suspension of monetization rights following
compliance failure
ZVA™ – confirmed economic neutralization under defined methodology
REMONET™ – structured reinstatement after corrective validation
This creates a non-discretionary transition framework for managing
economic consequences of automated systems.
Relevance for Regulators
For supervisory authorities and policy frameworks, VFM™ provides:
a structured state model for economic consequence management
audit-aligned transition logic
conceptual compatibility with AI governance regimes
non-punitive, rule-based value control architecture
The framework does not replace regulatory authority.
It defines methodological governance of value transitions.
Relevance for Banks and Financial Institutions
For financial institutions, the architecture may support:

structured control of AI-driven monetization exposure
clearer internal governance of model-risk consequences
defined remediation pathways before economic reinstatement
For credit systems, this enables a governance layer where economic
consequences are state-bound rather than discretion-bound.
Long-Term Outlook
As automated systems increasingly influence economic allocation,
structured value-state governance may become necessary for maintaining
financial integrity.
The VFM™ framework defines an infrastructure model that remains
applicable across evolving AI technologies and regulatory landscapes.
OOF™ defines the architecture.
Implementation remains with compliant institutions.

Standard (VTDS)

Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™

Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
A. Standard Abstract
The Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) defines what constitutes
value and under what conditions value is considered transferred within
digital and hybrid systems.
The objective is to establish a universal, system-independent definition of
value that can be:
measured
attributed
transferred
audited
This standard does not assign value.
It defines what qualifies as value and when it becomes real.
B. Canonical Definition
Value is any unit, asset, or measurable outcome that:
can be attributed to a specific entity
can be transferred between entities
can be recorded and verified
A Value Transfer occurs only when such value moves from one entity to
another under measurable and attributable conditions.
C. Structural Base
This standard is based on:
Measurability Requirement
Attribution Principle
Transfer Condition
Auditability Requirement

Value must exist as a definable and verifiable unit.
D. Value Qualification Criteria
For something to qualify as value, it MUST meet all of the following:
1. Measurability
Value must:
have quantifiable magnitude
be expressible in units, metrics, or equivalent
2. Attribution
Value must:
be assignable to a specific entity
have a defined source and destination
3. Transferability
Value must:
be capable of moving between entities
result in a change of state, ownership, or control
4. Recordability
Value must:
be recordable within a system
be verifiable through audit or trace
If any condition is not met:
→ value does not exist within this standard
E. Non-Value Classification
The following do NOT qualify as value:
attention
views
likes
impressions
unmonetized engagement
These are:
Value Signals, not value
F. Transfer Definition (Critical)
A Value Transfer exists only when:
value moves between entities
the movement is measurable
the movement is attributable
the movement is recorded
If no transfer occurs:
→ no value event exists
G. Structural Rule
Value exists only when it can be:
measured
attributed
transferred
recorded
No implicit, assumed, or perceived value is permitted.
H. System Independence
This definition applies across:
digital platforms
financial systems
hybrid environments
AI-driven systems
Value remains structurally consistent regardless of system.
I. Methodology
Identify potential value
Verify qualification criteria
Confirm transfer capability
Confirm recordability

Classify as value or non-value
J. Threshold Logic
Value state is:
VALID VALUE → meets all criteria
NON-VALUE → fails any condition
No partial qualification is permitted.
K. Structural Principle
Value is not perceived.
Value is defined by its ability to move, be measured, and be verified.
Canonical Closing Statement
Digital systems generate signals of importance.
Only defined and transferable units constitute real value.
Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) establishes a non-negotiable
condition:
value must be measurable, attributable, transferable, and auditable.

Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS)
Value Transfer Taxation
Standard (VTTS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority

Category: Economic & Value
Subcategory: Value Transfer Governance

Version: 3.0
