DeMonet™ · ReMonet™ · Value Asset
Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
A. Standard Abstract
The Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS) defines when taxation applies
across all economic systems based strictly on actual value transfer.
This standard establishes a universal taxation condition:
taxation applies only to real value transfer
value creation alone is not taxable
non-transfer activity is excluded
taxation is triggered at the moment value becomes economically real
VTTS applies across:
digital systems
physical economies
AI-driven environments
hybrid systems
This standard does not define tax rates or jurisdictions.
It defines when taxation is structurally valid.
B. Canonical Definition
A Taxable Value Event exists only when:
valid value (VTDS)
is transferred between identifiable entities

resulting in a measurable change of economic ownership or control
Taxation applies exclusively to:
Transferred Value with Real Economic Effect
C. Structural Base
This standard is based on:
Value Qualification Principle (VTDS)
Value Event Requirement (DVIS)
Non-Signal Rule
Transfer-Based Taxation Logic
Substance Over Structure Principle
Taxation must follow value — not activity, not form, not system representation.
D. Taxation Condition
A value event is taxable only if all conditions are met:
1. Valid Value Exists
The value must be:
measurable
attributable
transferable
recordable
2. Value Transfer Occurs
value moves between entities
economic ownership or control changes
3. Transfer Has Economic Substance
The transfer must represent:
real economic effect
actual change in value availability or control
The following are not valid transfers:
internal accounting entries
artificial structuring
circular or self-referential flows
4. Transfer Is Attributable
source entity identifiable
destination entity identifiable
5. Transfer Is Recordable
trace exists within system
audit is possible
If any condition is not met:
→ NON-TAXABLE EVENT
E. Value Creation vs Transfer Rule
Value creation alone is not taxable.
Taxation applies only when:
created value is transferred
and becomes economically accessible or controlled
F. Non-Taxable Events
The following are not taxable:
views
likes
clicks
impressions
attention
behavioral signals
non-transferable engagement
unrealized value states

These are classified as:
Value Signals — not taxable events
G. Value Capture Layer™
Taxation must occur at the moment where value becomes economically real.
A Value Capture Point exists when:
value becomes accessible for use
control or ownership is transferred
value can be realized or claimed
Examples:
payment execution
smart contract settlement
asset transfer
revenue payout
withdrawal or realization
Taxation must be triggered at this exact point.
H. Economic Control Definition
Control must be interpreted as:
economic control
not merely formal or legal designation
Taxation applies when an entity gains:
ability to use value
ability to transfer value
ability to restrict access to value
I. Cross-System Condition
Taxation applies independently of system type.
No distinction is made between:
digital systems
physical systems
AI-generated environments
hybrid systems
Only relevant condition:
Value movement between entities
J. Cross-Border Condition
A Cross-Border Value Transfer exists when:
value originates in one jurisdiction
and is received or controlled in another
Taxation must be based on:
actual value movement
traceable origin and destination
measurable transfer
Non-Valid Taxation Triggers
The following are invalid:
user location
platform location
server location
interaction volume
Without value transfer:
→ no taxation applies
K. System Boundary Condition
Taxation applies only to value transfers that are:
recordable
auditable
If value exists outside recordable systems:

taxation applies only upon entry into a recordable system
or upon measurable realization
L. Value State Compatibility
1. Origin Asset™
initial value taxable only upon transfer
2. Zero Value Asset (ZVA™)
no value non-taxable
3. DeMonet™ State
value neutralized non-taxable
4. ReMonet™ State
value reintroduced taxable upon transfer
5. Value Asset
active transferable value taxable upon transfer
M. Structural Rule
Taxation applies only to:
Transferred Value with Economic Substance
Not to:
potential value
perceived value
artificial structures
non-realized states
N. Methodology
Identify interaction (DVIS)
Verify value qualification (VTDS)
Confirm value creation vs transfer
Confirm economic substance
Confirm attribution
Confirm recordability
Identify value capture point
Apply taxation condition
O. Threshold Logic
TAXABLE → valid value transfer with economic substance
NON-TAXABLE → no valid transfer
No partial taxation is permitted.
P. Structural Principle
Tax follows value.
Not system. Not time. Not activity.
Not form.
Canonical Closing Statement
Economic systems generate continuous activity.
Only value transfer with economic substance creates economic reality.
Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS) establishes a non-negotiable condition:
taxation applies only where real value moves — and at the moment it becomes economically real.

VFM™ — Value Flow Mechanism
VFM™ — Value Flow Mechanism
Defining How Value Moves Across Future Systems
Value is one of the most fundamental components of every modern
system.
Yet most infrastructures still treat value as isolated transactions,
disconnected records, or temporary accounting states.
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ approaches value differently.
VFM™ — Value Flow Mechanism defines the methodological standards
through which value:
originates
moves
transforms
remains attributable
and stays verifiable across interconnected systems
VFM™ is not merely a financial description.
It is a structural methodology for how value remains understandable
across complex operational environments.
Why VFM™ Exists
Modern systems increasingly depend on:
AI-driven operations
automated decisions
cross-border transactions
decentralized infrastructure
digital assets
machine-to-machine execution
complex redistribution structures
continuously evolving operational environments
However, the underlying logic governing value movement remains
fragmented.
Different systems:
define value differently
track value differently
validate value differently
and redistribute value under incompatible conditions
This creates:
fragmentation
inefficiency
duplication
audit difficulty
governance instability
growing trust problems across institutions and infrastructures
VFM™ exists because future systems cannot remain stable if value
continues to move without one structurally coherent methodology.
The OOF™ Position

OOF™ does not treat value merely as a number, a payment event, or
an accounting artifact.
Value is treated as a structurally traceable state operating across:
economic systems
operational systems
AI environments
governance structures
redistribution mechanisms
digital infrastructure
future autonomous ecosystems
VFM™ establishes the methodology layer that allows value to remain:
attributable
interoperable
auditable
structurally understandable across system boundaries
This is not only an economic question.
It is a system architecture question.
From Transaction Logic to Flow Logic
Traditional systems focus primarily on transactions.
VFM™ focuses on flow.
This includes:
origin state
transfer state
transformation state
redistribution state
validation state
final identifiable value state
The objective is not only to record movement.
The objective is to preserve structural meaning throughout the full
lifecycle of value.
This is the methodological difference.
Transactions describe events.
VFM™ governs the continuity of value across events.
OOF™ Develops Standards for This
OOF™ develops standards for how value:
enters a system
moves through a system
changes form inside a system
remains attributable between systems
and exits as a verifiable value state
This is why VFM™ is not a local business model or
application-specific logic.
It is a standards-based methodological architecture for value flow.
The purpose is not to describe one platform.

The purpose is to define reusable structural logic across many
platforms, industries, and environments.
Methodology Separated from the Carrier
A foundational principle of OOF™ is that methodology must remain
separated from the carrier through which it is implemented.
Under VFM™:
value logic is not bound to one application
governance logic is not restricted to one country
validation architecture is not dependent on one vendor
interoperability is not limited to one operational environment
This allows the methodology itself to become:
modular
reusable
cross-border compatible
interoperable across industries
scalable across future AI-native systems
The carrier may change.
The methodology must remain structurally stable across carriers.
That is one of the core strengths of the OOF™ approach.
Why This Matters
Modern systems are repeatedly rebuilt because value structures remain
fragmented across:
accounting systems
tax systems
operational systems
enterprise platforms
digital assets
insurance structures
redistribution models
regulatory environments
As AI systems increasingly participate in economic and operational
processes, fragmented value architectures become increasingly unstable.
Future systems require:
reusable methodology layers
canonical meaning consistency
continuous validation
interoperability
structurally traceable value flows
Without this, the same value logic must be redesigned repeatedly under
different technical, legal, and institutional conditions.
That is expensive.

That is inefficient.
And over time, that becomes structurally unsustainable.
VFM™ and Future Infrastructure
VFM™ is designed as a foundational methodology layer compatible with:
enterprise systems
AI operations
autonomous environments
redistribution models
taxation logic
insurance structures
digital assets
governance frameworks
future interoperable infrastructures
The objective is not to replace existing systems.
The objective is to create structural compatibility between them.
This is why VFM™ matters.
It does not attempt to erase complexity.
It creates a methodology through which complexity can remain
governable.
The Trust Layer
Trust in future systems cannot depend only on:
declarations
branding
institutional reputation
isolated certifications
Trust increasingly depends on whether value itself remains:
traceable
attributable
verifiable
structurally understandable across operational environments
VFM™ contributes to the Trust Layer by preserving continuity between:
origin
transformation
validation
final value state
A system becomes more trustworthy when value does not disappear into
disconnected records or incompatible local logic.
Why VFM™ Is Structurally Different
Most systems describe value after movement has already happened.
VFM™ defines the standards through which value movement remains
structurally intelligible from the beginning.
That is a much stronger position.
It means value does not need to be reconstructed only after
fragmentation.

It can remain methodologically governed throughout the process.
This is what makes VFM™ a foundational architecture rather than a
reporting tool.
Foundational Principle
Future systems will not remain stable if value can move without
structural meaning, validation, or traceable continuity.
Canonical Closing Statement
VFM™ defines the methodological standards through which value remains
structurally understandable, attributable, and interoperable across
future human, AI, economic, and operational systems.

VIM™ — Voice Identity Module
VIM™ — Voice Identity Module
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Category: AI and Interpretation
Subcategory: Content Origin Declaration
Module: Voice Identity Module (VIM™)
Type: Declaration Module
Standard: Origin Declaration Standard (ODS™)
Status: Canonical Module
Version: 1.0

Canonical Definition
The Voice Identity Module (VIM™) defines how the identity of a voice
used in digital content is declared.
The module enables clear recognition of whether a voice belongs to a real person,
an authorized identity, an imitation, or is unknown.
Declaration
Only one voice identity code may be used:
HVI — Human Voice Identity (real person)
AVI — Authorized Voice Identity (consent granted)
SVI — Sound-alike Voice Imitation
UVI — Unknown Voice Identity
Usage
Content Level (required — single code)
One voice identity code must be associated with the content where voice is present.
Examples:
HVI
AVI
SVI
UVI
Description Level (required)
The declaration must be included in the description or metadata:
Voice: HVI
OOF Compatible — ODS™ Standard
https://originopenfoundation.org
Identity Rule
Voice identity must reflect the actual source of the voice.
real person → HVI
authorized use → AVI
imitation or synthetic reproduction → SVI
unclear or undeclared → UVI
OOF Compatibility
Content using this module may include the statement:
OOF Compatible — ODS™ Standard

A reference link to the official source is required.
Use Case 1 — AI Voice Transparency
Scenario
AI-generated voices are used in content, narration, or automation.
Application
Voice is declared as AVI or SVI depending on authorization.
Result
Clear distinction between real and synthetic identity
Reduced misuse of voice likeness
Increased audience trust
Use Case 2 — Public Figure Protection
Scenario
A voice similar to a known individual is used in content.
Application
Voice identity is declared (AVI or SVI).
Result
Clear disclosure of imitation or authorization
Reduced risk of deception
Protection of identity rights
Structural Principle
Voice is identity.
Identity must be declared.
Closing Statement
A voice may sound real.
Its identity must be known.

Virtual Representation Module (VRM™)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™

Canonical Definition
A Virtual Representation is a non-physical presentation of an asset
in a digital or simulated environment that allows access, viewing,
or interaction without transferring or altering the original asset.
A virtual representation does not replace the original
and does not constitute ownership of the asset.
Why This Matters
Without clear classification of virtual representations:
digital experiences may be confused with ownership
representations may be mistaken for copies
original assets may be exposed to unnecessary risk
access and control become unclear
Virtual representation separates access from possession.
Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
Step 1 — Identify Source Asset
Define the original asset or source from which
the representation is created.
Step 2 — Confirm Non-Physical Form
Ensure the representation exists only in digital
or simulated space.
Step 3 — Define Representation Purpose
Establish that the asset is presented for viewing,
interaction, or experience — not transfer.
Step 4 — Declare Representation Status
The asset must be clearly identified

as a virtual representation.
Step 5 — Preserve Origin Link
The representation must maintain a clear relationship
to the original asset.
Use Case 1 — Virtual Museum Exhibition
Scenario
A museum creates a virtual gallery accessible worldwide.
Application
Artworks are presented as virtual representations
without moving physical originals.
Result
global access to cultural heritage
protection of original works
reduced cost and logistics
Use Case 2 — Digital Experience Platforms
Scenario
A platform offers immersive viewing of artworks or objects
in a virtual environment.
Application
Assets are classified as virtual representations.
Result
scalable access
independent exhibition models
no need for physical transfer
Structural Principle
Access does not require transfer.
Representation does not imply ownership.
Closing Statement
The original stays in place.
The experience travels.

VTTS™ — Canonical Definition Lock & Licensing Framework
Applies to: Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS™)
Status: Canonical Lock · Binding Definition Layer
Version: 1.0
Effective Date: 8 April 2026
A. Canonical Lock Principle
All core elements of VTTS™ are:
FIXED · NON-MODIFIABLE · CANONICAL
This framework establishes a permanent definition layer that:
cannot be altered
cannot be reinterpreted
cannot be partially applied
Any use of VTTS™ must:
preserve definitions exactly
maintain full structural integrity
reference OOF™ as the sole canonical authority
B. Locked Core Definitions
1. Value
Canonical Definition
Value is a measurable, attributable, transferable, and recordable
unit of economic relevance.
2. Value Transfer
Canonical Definition
A Value Transfer is the movement of valid value between entities
resulting in a change of economic ownership or control.
3. Taxable Value Event
Canonical Definition
A Taxable Value Event exists only when valid value is transferred between
identifiable entities and results in a measurable change of economic
ownership or control.
4. Value Capture Point
Canonical Definition
The Value Capture Point is the exact moment when value becomes
economically real through transfer, granting ownership or control to an
entity.
5. Economic Control
Canonical Definition
Economic Control is the ability of an entity to use, transfer, restrict, or

benefit from value, regardless of formal ownership designation.
6. Value Signal
Canonical Definition
A Value Signal is a non-transferable activity or indicator that does not
result in economic value transfer and is therefore non-taxable.
7. Non-Taxable Event
Canonical Definition
A Non-Taxable Event is any activity that does not involve the transfer of
valid value between entities.
8. Economic Substance
Canonical Definition
Economic Substance exists only when a value transfer results in real
economic effect and is not artificial, circular, or structurally simulated.
9. Recordable Transfer
Canonical Definition
A Recordable Transfer is a value transfer that can be traced, verified, and
audited within a system.
10. Cross-Border Value Transfer
Canonical Definition
A Cross-Border Value Transfer occurs when value originates in one
jurisdiction and is transferred to an entity in another jurisdiction.
11. Value Circumvention Event
Canonical Definition
A Value Circumvention Event is any structured attempt to avoid taxation
by simulating, fragmenting, delaying, masking, or rerouting value transfer
without eliminating the underlying economic effect.
12. Artificial Value Fragmentation
Canonical Definition
Artificial Value Fragmentation is the intentional division of a single value
transfer into multiple smaller transfers for the purpose of avoiding taxation
or detection.
13. Non-Declared Value Realization
Canonical Definition

A Non-Declared Value Realization occurs when value becomes economically
usable or controlled without being recorded within a taxable or auditable
system.
14. System Evasion Structure
Canonical Definition
A System Evasion Structure is any technical, legal, or procedural construct
designed to bypass, obscure, or disable the detection of value transfer.
C. Anti-Circumvention Principle
Any attempt to:
avoid value capture
simulate non-transfer
hide economic substance
fragment value artificially
shift value outside recordable systems
is automatically classified as:
STRUCTURAL VIOLATION OF VTTS™

The following actions are strictly prohibited:
modifying definitions
reinterpreting definitions
simplifying definitions
partially applying definitions
renaming core concepts without reference
creating derivative definitions with equivalent meaning

Any concept, system, or framework that:
replicates VTTS™ logic
mirrors its structure
uses equivalent definitions under different names
is considered:
FUNCTIONALLY IDENTICAL TO VTTS™
and falls under:
OOF™ canonical reference obligation

Any deviation from canonical structure results in:
LOSS OF CANONICAL VALIDITY
and classification as:
non-compliant system
unauthorized derivative

About VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
About VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
About VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms
Architecture
Governing Value Across the Complete Value Lifecycle
Value does not simply exist.
It emerges within context.
It becomes recognizable.
It enters states.
It changes.
It may develop, strengthen, mature, compound, degrade, disappear into zero, recover, or ultimately cease to remain recoverable.
Assets can retain physical existence while losing productive value.
Information can remain stored while becoming inaccessible or unusable.
Capabilities can become dormant and later recover.
Technologies can lose economic relevance while retaining strategic, historical, informational, or material value.
Entire value relationships can disappear while the underlying objects continue to exist.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture was created to provide a stable governance architecture for this complete value lifecycle.
VFM® does not define accounting systems, valuation formulas, financial markets, pricing mechanisms, payment systems, taxation, ownership structures, investment models, asset-management software, or economic policy.
VFM® governs value across its lifecycle.
Why VFM® Exists
Organizations constantly create, recognize, measure, develop, lose, recover, and abandon value.

But the existence of an asset, price, accounting entry, market, capability, technology, dataset, resource, or economic relationship does not itself answer fundamental governance questions:
Within what context does value exist?
Where did the value originate?
When did value actually emerge?
When can value legitimately be recognized?
What state is the value currently in?
Has the value changed?
Is existing value developing or degrading?
Has value merely declined, or has it reached zero?
Does zero value still retain restoration potential?
Can previously existing value legitimately be restored?
When has the same value ceased to remain recoverable?
VFM® addresses these questions by defining the governable spaces that exist throughout the complete value lifecycle.
Rather than standardizing one valuation technique or economic model, VFM® standardizes the governance conditions under which value can be contextualized, originated, emerged, recognized, state-governed, changed, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, and ultimately extinguished.
Value Before Valuation
The objective of VFM® is not to prescribe how an organization must calculate monetary value.
The objective is to define how value itself must remain governable.
Every governed value exists within a context.
Every value has an origin.
Not every potential value actually emerges.
Not every emerging value has yet been legitimately recognized.
Recognized value occupies a state.
Value states may change.
Existing value may develop.

Existing value may degrade.
Degradation may eventually reach zero.
Zero value may still retain restoration potential.
Previously existing value may become recoverable through governed restoration.
And where legitimate recoverability of the same value ends, the value lifecycle may reach extinction.
VFM® therefore treats Value Lifecycle Governance as an independent governance domain.
The Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
VFM® consists of eleven independent value governance spaces.
Each space answers one architectural question.
Each space governs one distinct part of the value lifecycle.
Each space has a defined operational purpose and governance boundary.
Together, these spaces form the complete Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
The architecture progresses through:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
These spaces are governed through eleven Parent Standards:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Value State
→ Value Change
→ Value Development
→ Value Degradation
→ Value Nullification
→ Value Restoration
→ Value Extinction
This progression represents the governance journey from establishing where and under what conditions value exists to determining whether previously existing value can still legitimately continue, recover, or has reached terminal lifecycle closure.

Value Spaces Rather Than Financial Categories
VFM® does not organize value governance around accounting categories, asset classes, currencies, markets, departments, industries, financial instruments, or valuation technologies.
Instead, it organizes governance around distinct value governance spaces.
Each space represents an independent governance responsibility that may exist regardless of the type of value being governed.
An industrial machine, dataset, patent, organizational capability, infrastructure asset, digital resource, scientific discovery, production process, technology, contractual relationship, strategic capability, or future value-bearing object may be fundamentally different.
Yet each may still require governance of:
context → origin → emergence → recognition → state → change → development / degradation → nullification → restoration / extinction.
Because these spaces are value-lifecycle based rather than technology-specific or industry-specific, VFM® can remain applicable while economic systems, technologies, assets, business models, and forms of value continue to evolve.
A Methodology Rather Than a Valuation System
VFM® is a governance methodology.
It is not a valuation formula.
It is not an accounting standard.
It is not a pricing model.
It is not an asset-management platform.
It is not an economic theory.

The architecture defines which value governance conditions must remain distinguishable, how value lifecycle spaces relate to one another, where their boundaries lie, and what must be established before a change in value can legitimately acquire a governed lifecycle meaning.
Organizations remain free to select their own:
valuation methodologies, accounting frameworks, financial models, asset-management systems, economic models, pricing mechanisms, investment methodologies, operational systems, data platforms, risk models, optimization systems, decision frameworks.
VFM® governs the methodological structure surrounding value across those implementations rather than replacing them.
This separation allows the architecture to remain stable while the mechanisms used to calculate, represent, exchange, or manage value continue to change.
From Value Context to Value Finality
Value cannot be governed as a single number.
Before value can be understood, its Value Context must be established.
Before value can be attributed to a lifecycle, its Value Origin must be distinguishable.
Before value can be recognized, it must first emerge.
Before a value state can be governed, value must be sufficiently recognized.
Before change can be understood, a prior Value State must exist.
Before development or degradation can be distinguished, Value Change must be identifiable.
Before value can be nullified, degradation or another legitimate transition toward zero must be understood.

Before zero value can be treated as terminal, its restoration potential must remain distinguishable from extinction.
Before restoration can occur, previously existing value must remain legitimately recoverable.
And before the value lifecycle can be closed, extinction must be distinguishable from degradation, dormancy, inaccessibility, nullification, failed restoration, or temporary zero.
VFM® transforms these dependencies into a structured and navigable Value Lifecycle Governance Architecture.
Value Is Not the Object
One of the most important distinctions within VFM® is:
Value ≠ Value Object
A machine can physically exist while its productive value disappears.
A building can remain standing while a particular commercial value relationship ends.
A dataset can remain stored while its informational value becomes inaccessible.
A patent can continue to exist legally while its commercial value degrades.
A technology can become economically obsolete while retaining scientific, historical, strategic, or educational value.
VFM® therefore governs value independently from the mere continued existence of the object associated with it.
This distinction allows multiple values associated with the same Value Object to follow different lifecycle paths.
Extinction of One Value ≠ Extinction of the Value Object.
And:
Extinction of One Value Dimension ≠ Extinction of All Value Dimensions.
Value Is Contextual
VFM® establishes another foundational principle:

Value does not exist independently of context.
The same object may possess different value across different relationships, purposes, environments, times, users, systems, or operational conditions.
A production machine may have:
productive value,
material value,
resale value,
replacement value,
strategic value,
historical value,
informational value,
or technological value.
These values do not necessarily emerge, develop, degrade, reach zero, recover, or become extinct at the same time.
VFM® therefore begins with Value Context rather than assuming that value is a universal property permanently embedded within an object.
This creates a methodological boundary between:
the existence of an object
and
the existence of a particular value relationship associated with that object.
Value Emergence Is Not Value Development
VFM® distinguishes the creation or appearance of value from the growth of value that already exists.
Value Emergence ≠ Value Development
Value Emergence concerns the point at which value begins to exist within a governed context.
Value Development concerns value that already exists and subsequently grows, matures, strengthens, compounds, or otherwise develops.
This distinction prevents new value from being incorrectly represented as merely an increase in an existing value.
Likewise, where a legitimately extinguished value lifecycle has already ended, genuinely new value appearing later may constitute:
New Value Emergence
rather than restoration of the extinct value.

Value State Is Not Value Change
VFM® separates what value is currently from what has happened to it.
Value State ≠ Value Change
A Value State describes the governed condition of value at a particular point or period.
Value Change describes movement relative to a previous governed value condition.
This distinction allows organizations to separate:
current condition
from
lifecycle movement.
A value may therefore remain in a positive state while degrading, remain at zero while restoration potential persists, or enter a restored state after successful recovery.
Value Degradation Is Not Value Nullification
Declining value does not automatically mean that value has disappeared.
VFM® therefore establishes:
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification
Value Degradation governs deterioration of existing value while some relevant value remains.
Value Nullification governs the transition through which the relevant governed value reaches zero.
This distinction is essential because the governance consequences of declining value and zero value are fundamentally different.
A value that has degraded may still remain positive.
A value that has been nullified has reached a governed zero-value condition.
But even then:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
DeMonet™ and the Zero-Value Boundary
VFM® introduces DeMonet™ as the governed value-nullification mechanism through which relevant existing value may transition into a zero-value condition.
The canonical transition is:

Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
DeMonet™ is a mechanism.
ZVA™ is a governed value state.
The distinction is fundamental:
DeMonet™ ≠ ZVA™
A mechanism describes how value transitions.
A state describes the resulting value condition.
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may have zero relevant value within the governed context while the underlying Value Object continues to exist.
Critically, zero does not automatically mean terminal.
A ZVA™ may retain legitimate restoration potential.
Zero Value Is Not Value Extinction
One of the central boundaries of VFM® is:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction
A value may reach zero because it is temporarily inaccessible.
A market may disappear.
A capability may become dormant.
A machine may lose productive use.
A dataset may become technologically unreadable.
A resource may become economically unusable under current conditions.
A technology may become obsolete.
None of these conditions alone proves that the same value can never legitimately return within its governed lifecycle.
VFM® therefore preserves a governance space between:
Value at Zero
and
Value Extinct.
That space is where restoration potential matters.
ReMonet™ and Value Restoration
VFM® introduces ReMonet™ as the governed value-restoration mechanism through which previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero may be acted upon so that recoverable value can re-emerge.
The canonical transition is:

Degraded / Dormant / Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State
ReMonet™ does not mean that every zero-value object should be restored.
It does not guarantee successful restoration.
And it does not create prior value where no prior value existed.
No Prior Value → No Restoration of That Value
ReMonet™ governs recovery of previously existing value.
It therefore remains distinct from Value Emergence and Value Development.
New Value ≠ Restored Value.
Existing Value Growth ≠ Restored Value.
DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ Are Not Simple
Opposites
Value lifecycles are not necessarily reversible.
The fact that a particular mechanism or event reduced value to zero does not mean that reversing the same mechanism will restore the original value.
DeMonet™ ≠ Reverse ReMonet™
Restoration may require different conditions, technologies, relationships, capabilities, information, resources, or contexts from those that existed before nullification.
VFM® therefore governs nullification and restoration as distinct lifecycle spaces rather than treating value as a number moving mechanically up and down.
The Recoverability Boundary
One of the most consequential boundaries in VFM® lies between Value Restoration and Value Extinction.
The governance question is not simply:
Is the value currently zero?
The stronger question is:
Can the same governed value still legitimately return within the defined lifecycle, context, value dimension, and restoration boundary?

A failed restoration attempt does not automatically prove extinction.
High restoration cost does not automatically prove extinction.
Current technological inability does not automatically prove extinction.
Dormancy does not automatically prove extinction.
Obsolescence does not automatically prove extinction.
Temporary impossibility does not automatically prove extinction.
VFM® therefore treats recoverability as a governed boundary rather than an assumption.
Where recoverability remains legitimate:
Value Restoration remains possible.
Where legitimate recoverability of the same value has ended:
Value Extinction becomes possible.
Value Extinction and Finality
Value Extinction represents the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to remain recoverable as the same governed value within the defined lifecycle.
This does not mean that the underlying object disappears.
It does not mean that every associated value disappears.
It does not erase historical value.
And it does not prohibit genuinely new value from emerging in the future.
Value Extinction ≠ Object Extinction.
Value Finality ≠ Historical Erasure.
Future Value Emergence ≠ Restoration of Final Value by Default.
A machine whose productive value becomes legitimately extinct may still possess material or historical value.
A dataset whose original informational value becomes irrecoverable may later support a new analytical relationship through future technology.

That later value may represent a new Value Emergence rather than reopening the extinct lifecycle.
VFM® therefore allows value lifecycles to end without declaring the Value Object permanently incapable of generating any future value.
Who May Benefit
VFM® may support:
enterprises, asset owners, infrastructure operators, industrial organizations, financial institutions, insurers, investors, public institutions, governments, technology organizations, AI systems, autonomous systems, data-intensive organizations, intellectual-property owners, research organizations, asset-management organizations, restructuring and recovery environments, strategic planning teams, risk and assurance functions,
organizations managing complex value portfolios, organizations seeking to understand how value changes across time.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures without absorbing their independent governance domains.
GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance structure, authority, boundaries, scope, delegation, accountability, continuity, and interoperability.
ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs Operational Reality and helps establish what actually exists or occurs within the operational environment from which value-relevant conditions may arise.

VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation objects, validation criteria, methods, evidence, determinations, Validation States, reliance, and revalidation.
INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across the integrity lifecycle.
OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability.
AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability, responsibility, attribution, delegation, and accountable relationships.
CLA® — Classification Architecture governs classification rather than value recognition or value state.
ADIT® — Auditability & Evidence Architecture governs auditability and evidential structures rather than the value lifecycle itself.
SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs simulation and may provide simulation-derived information relevant to future or potential value conditions without determining the VFM® Value Lifecycle.
AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs AI behavior.
ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous systems and operational autonomy.
CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture governs cognition, reasoning, interpretation, and cognitive integrity.
MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture governs memory, memory continuity, and memory integrity.

Together, these architectures allow value to interact with operational reality, identity, validation, integrity, accountability, classification, evidence, simulation, AI, autonomy, cognition, and memory without collapsing those independent governance domains into VFM®.
Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset That Reaches
Zero but May Still Recover
An industrial company operates a specialized production machine.
For years, the machine generates substantial productive value.
A technological shift causes demand for its output to decline.
Utilization falls.
Maintenance costs rise.
Its productive value degrades.
Eventually, under the current production context, its relevant productive value reaches zero.
A conventional asset process may classify the machine as obsolete, impaired, written off, or economically unusable.
VFM® asks a larger lifecycle question.
What value is actually being governed?
Within which context?
What was its origin?
When did productive value emerge?
What prior Value States existed?
How did the value change?
When did degradation begin?
Has productive value actually reached zero?
Does zero mean terminal loss?
Could a new customer, retrofit, process modification, new market, new technology, relocation, or different operational configuration restore the same productive value relationship?
If legitimate restoration potential remains, the machine may enter:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
without entering Value Extinction.

A governed ReMonet™ pathway may subsequently restore previously existing productive value.
If the relevant productive capability becomes permanently unrecoverable within the governed lifecycle, VFM® may instead support a Value Extinction determination for that specific productive value.
Yet the machine may still retain:
material value,
scrap value,
component value,
historical value,
informational value,
or other independently governed values.
VFM® therefore prevents one zero-value condition from being mistaken for the disappearance of every value associated with the asset.
Zero value can be a lifecycle state rather than the end of the value lifecycle.
Use Case 2 — Historical Data That Appears
Worthless Until Technology Changes
An organization possesses a large historical dataset created decades earlier.
The original systems required to interpret the dataset no longer exist.
Documentation is incomplete.
Formats are obsolete.
Commercial demand has disappeared.
Under the current technological and operational context, the dataset may have no usable informational value.
Its relevant value may therefore reach zero.
A conventional process may classify the dataset as worthless and permanently irrelevant.
VFM® asks whether the value is actually extinct.
If the original information remains recoverable but currently inaccessible, the dataset may remain within a zero or dormant value condition while restoration potential persists.

Years later, new decoding technologies or AI systems may reconstruct the obsolete formats.
Previously inaccessible information becomes usable again.
If the same previously existing informational value has been recovered, the transition may represent:
Zero / Inaccessible Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Informational Value
But a different situation is also possible.
Suppose the original informational meaning has been irreversibly lost and its lifecycle legitimately reaches Value Extinction.
Decades later, an AI system discovers a completely different statistical use for surviving fragments.
That new analytical relationship need not reopen the extinct informational lifecycle.
It may represent:
New Value Emergence → New Value Lifecycle
VFM® therefore distinguishes restoration of previously existing value from the emergence of genuinely new value.
The same object can carry multiple value lifecycles across time without those lifecycles being methodologically confused.
The Long-Term Vision
Value is becoming increasingly difficult to govern through conventional asset categories alone.
AI can discover value in information previously considered useless.
Autonomous systems can dynamically change how resources are utilized.
Digital assets can acquire value without conventional physical form.
Industrial systems can move between productive, dormant, obsolete, recoverable, and repurposed conditions.

Infrastructure may carry economic, operational, strategic, societal, environmental, and resilience value simultaneously.
Technological change can restore capabilities that appeared permanently lost.
New relationships can create value around objects whose earlier value lifecycles have already ended.
As systems become more interconnected, the central question will no longer be only:
What is this asset worth?
It will increasingly become:
What value exists, within which context, where did it come from, what state is it in, how is it changing, can it be developed, has it degraded, has it reached zero, can it be restored, or has its lifecycle legitimately ended?
The long-term objective of VFM® is to provide a common Value Lifecycle Governance language through which organizations, institutions, AI systems, autonomous systems, and future governance infrastructures can identify and distinguish the fundamental lifecycle conditions through which value moves.
VFM® is intended to make value governable before emergence, at recognition, during active existence, through change, during development and degradation, at the zero-value boundary, throughout restoration, and at legitimate lifecycle extinction.
Canonical Principle

Assets, technologies, markets, economic systems, organizations, information environments, and forms of value will continue to change. Value lifecycle governance must remain stable. VFM® therefore governs the methodological conditions that determine the context in which value exists, where value originates, when value emerges, when it can be recognized, what state it occupies, how it changes, how it develops or degrades, when it reaches zero, whether previously existing value can legitimately be restored, and when recoverability has ended sufficiently for the same value lifecycle to reach extinction and finality.
Canonical Closing Statement

VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture provides the governance foundation through which value can be formally contextualized, originated, emerged, recognized, state-governed, change-governed, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, and ultimately brought to governed extinction where legitimate recoverability of the same value has ended. By defining the independent governable spaces of the complete Value Lifecycle, VFM® establishes a technology-neutral and sector-neutral methodology for distinguishing the existence of value from the existence of its underlying object, value emergence from value development, value state from value change, degradation from nullification, zero value from extinction, restoration from new emergence, and terminal Value Finality from the future possibility of entirely new value. Through DeMonet™, ZVA™, ReMonet™, Value Asset™, and the wider governed lifecycle structure, VFM® provides methodological infrastructure for understanding not merely how much something may be worth, but how value itself originates, exists, moves, changes, develops, deteriorates, disappears into zero, returns where recoverability remains, and reaches legitimate closure where the same value can no longer return. VFM® therefore establishes Value Lifecycle Governance as an independent methodological domain capable of supporting enterprises, institutions, infrastructure, technology, data, AI, autonomous systems, economic environments, and future forms of value without reducing

domain capable of supporting enterprises, institutions, infrastructure, technology, data, AI, autonomous systems, economic environments, and future forms of value without reducing value governance to accounting, pricing, valuation, or the physical existence of assets.

VFM® Architecture Map
VFM® Architecture Map
VFM® Architecture Map
Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer
Official Value Lifecycle Governance Reference Map for AI Systems, Autonomous Systems, Organizations, Assets, Infrastructure, Data, Technology, Economic Systems, Public Systems, and Future Value-Based Environments
VFM® serves as the official OOF® value lifecycle governance reference map used to identify, define, classify, navigate, govern, evaluate, and understand governable value spaces across AI systems, autonomous systems, organizations, assets, infrastructure, data, technology, economic systems, public systems, and future value- based environments.
The purpose of VFM® is not to define the economic, financial, transactional, accounting, ownership, pricing, taxation, or technical implementation of a value system.
The purpose of VFM® is to identify, define, separate, and map the governable spaces through which value is established within a defined context, connected to an identifiable origin, emerges into existence, becomes recognizable, occupies a determinable state, changes, develops, degrades, reaches a zero-value condition where applicable, may be restored while recoverability remains, and ultimately reaches extinction when the same governed value ceases to remain recoverable within its lifecycle.
VFM® serves as the official value lifecycle governance reference map for:

AI Systems Autonomous Systems Autonomous Agents Organizations Industrial Systems Physical Assets Digital Assets Infrastructure Data and Information Assets Technology Intellectual Assets Organizational Capabilities Products and Services Public Systems
Economic and Financial Environments Critical Infrastructure Multi-System Environments Future Value Ecosystems
Core Architectural Principle
Every value lifecycle governance space answers one primary governance question.
No value lifecycle governance space duplicates the purpose of another value lifecycle governance space.
Every value lifecycle governance space has a defined beginning, a defined operational purpose, and a defined governance boundary.
Every value lifecycle governance space begins when the value-related governance requirement associated with that space becomes materially applicable.
Together, these value lifecycle governance spaces form the official value lifecycle governance reference map of VFM®.
Value is governed as a lifecycle, not merely as a price, asset attribute, accounting quantity, ownership condition, transaction result, or economic outcome.
Official Value Governance Flow
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction
1. Value Context Standard (VCXS)
Governed Space: Value Context
Core Question

What value is being governed, in relation to what value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference context?
Canonical Definition
Value Context Standard (VCXS) defines the governance conditions under which the value being governed is identified and bounded in relation to the relevant value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, reference framework, and contextual conditions necessary to distinguish that value from other forms, dimensions, relationships, or interpretations of value.
Governance Boundary
Begins when a value-related governance inquiry requires explicit determination of what value is actually being governed.
Ends when the governed value, relevant value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference context have been sufficiently established to determine the basis from which that value may originate.
Value Identification ≠ Asset Identity.
2. Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Governed Space: Value Origin
Core Question
From what identifiable source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other basis can the governed value originate?
Canonical Definition
Value Origin Standard (VOS) defines the governance conditions under which the source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, resource, or other basis from which governed value may originate is identified, bounded, related to the value context, and maintained as the identifiable origin basis of that value.
Governance Boundary

Begins when the governed value context has been sufficiently established and the basis from which value may arise must be identified.
Ends when the relevant value source, origin basis, origin relationship, and origin conditions have been sufficiently established to determine whether and when value actually emerges.
Value Source ≠ Existing Value.
Value Origin ≠ Value Emergence.
3. Value Emergence Standard (VES)
Governed Space: Value Emergence
Core Question
When and under what conditions does potential value become existent value?
Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Standard (VES) defines the governance conditions under which potential value arising from an identifiable origin crosses the relevant emergence conditions and threshold and becomes existent value within its governed context.
Governance Boundary
Begins when an identifiable value origin exists and there is a legitimate basis for determining whether potential value has become existent value.
Ends when value emergence has been sufficiently established or rejected to distinguish actual existing value from value that remains merely potential.
Potential Value ≠ Existing Value.
Origin Asset™ ≠ Automatically Existing Value.
4. Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
Governed Space: Value Recognition
Core Question
When can existing value be recognized as value within its defined governance context?
Canonical Definition

Value Recognition Standard (VRS) defines the governance conditions under which value that has emerged into existence may be formally recognized as value within its defined context according to an explicit recognition basis,
applicable criteria, limitations, and governed determination.
Governance Boundary
Begins when value has emerged or there is a governed basis for examining whether existing value qualifies for recognition within the relevant context.
Ends when the value has been sufficiently recognized, not recognized, or recognition has been bounded by applicable limitations so that its governed state may be determined.
Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition.
Value Recognition ≠ Classification.
Value Recognition ≠ Validation.
5. Value State Standard (VSS)
Governed Space: Value State
Core Question
What is the current governed state of value?
Canonical Definition
Value State Standard (VSS) defines the governance conditions under which existing or otherwise governable value is identified, classified, determined, and represented in its current value state independently from the mechanism, event, or transition through which that state was reached.
Governance Boundary
Begins when value exists within a sufficiently established context and its current value condition requires governed determination.
Continues throughout the value lifecycle whenever a current or resulting value state must be established.

A state determination ends when the relevant value state has been sufficiently identified and determined to support subsequent governance of material value change or lifecycle transition.
Canonical value-state concepts may include:
Value Asset™
and
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
where applicable.
Value State ≠ Value Transition.
6. Value Change Standard (VCS)
Governed Space: Value Change
Core Question
When has existing value materially changed, and what change has occurred to it?
Canonical Definition
Value Change Standard (VCS) defines the governance conditions under which a material change in existing value is identified, characterized, measured where applicable, linked to relevant causation information, and distinguished from the external event, mechanism, or system that produced the value consequence.
Governance Boundary
Begins when an existing governed value may have changed from a previously established value state.
Ends when the existence, type, direction, magnitude, and relevant causation link of the value change have been sufficiently established to determine the applicable value lifecycle consequence.
External systems may determine why an event occurred.
VFM® determines:
what happened to value as a result.
External Cause ≠ Value Consequence.
7. Value Development Standard (VDS)
Governed Space: Value Development
Core Question
How does existing value increase, strengthen, mature, compound, or otherwise develop over time?
Canonical Definition

Value Development Standard (VDS) defines the governance conditions under which existing value positively develops through growth, strengthening, maturation, compounding, or other governed forms of development while preserving the distinction between development of existing value and emergence or restoration of value.
Governance Boundary
Begins when existing value undergoes or may undergo a positive change that represents development of value already present within the governed lifecycle.
Ends when the relevant development has been sufficiently characterized and incorporated into the resulting value condition or state.
Value Emergence ≠ Value Development.
Creation of Value ≠ Growth of Existing Value.
Value Development ≠ Value Restoration.
8. Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
Governed Space: Value Degradation
Core Question
How does existing value weaken, decline, deteriorate, or become progressively impaired while value still exists?
Canonical Definition
Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) defines the governance conditions under which existing value weakens, declines, deteriorates, loses capability, or becomes progressively impaired while the relevant value continues to exist above, or otherwise prior to crossing, an applicable zero-value boundary.
Governance Boundary
Begins when existing value undergoes a negative change that materially weakens, reduces, deteriorates, or impairs the relevant value.

Ends when the degradation has been sufficiently characterized and either value remains in a degraded state or the decline reaches conditions requiring governance of potential Value Nullification.
Value Degradation → declining value remains.
Value Nullification → value reaches zero.
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification.
9. Value Nullification Standard (VNS)
Governed Space: Value Nullification
Core Question
When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition?
Canonical Definition
Value Nullification Standard (VNS) defines the governance conditions under which previously existing positive value reaches an applicable zero-value threshold, undergoes a governed nullification transition, and enters a zero-value condition without that zero-value condition being automatically interpreted as Value Extinction.
Governance Boundary
Begins when existing positive value approaches or may have reached the applicable conditions under which that value becomes zero within its governed context.
Ends when nullification has been sufficiently determined and, where applicable, the relevant value has entered a governed zero-value state.
Canonical transition:
Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
Critically:
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified.
Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction.
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
10. Value Restoration Standard (VRSS)
Governed Space: Value Restoration
Core Question

How can degraded, lost, dormant, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored?
Canonical Definition
Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) defines the governance conditions under which previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero may remain recoverable and may legitimately be restored through a governed restoration process without confusing restoration of prior value with development of existing value or emergence of genuinely new value.
Governance Boundary
Begins when previously existing value is degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, zero, or otherwise requires recovery and a legitimate restoration pathway may remain available.
Ends when restoration has been sufficiently determined and the restored value has entered an applicable resulting value state, or when restoration cannot legitimately proceed and the question of terminal recoverability must move into Value Extinction governance.
Canonical transition:
Degraded / Dormant / Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State
Value Development = existing value develops.
Value Restoration = previously impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, or zero value is recovered.
ReMonet™ ≠ New Value Emergence.
11. Value Extinction Standard (VXSS)
Governed Space: Value Extinction
Core Question
When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle?
Canonical Definition

Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) defines the governance conditions under which previously existing value crosses the terminal recoverability boundary and ceases to remain legitimately recoverable as the same governed value within its defined lifecycle, context, value dimension, and restoration boundary.
Governance Boundary
Begins when previously existing value has become sufficiently impaired, inaccessible, nullified, zero, or otherwise terminally challenged that its continuing recoverability as the same governed value must be determined.
Ends when the relevant value has either been determined to retain legitimate recoverability and therefore remains eligible for restoration governance, or has been determined to have reached Value Extinction and the applicable value lifecycle reaches governed finality.
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may retain restoration potential.
Failed Restoration ≠ Value Extinction.
Value Extinction ≠ Object Extinction.
Value Extinction ≠ Erasure of Prior Value.
Later New Value ≠ Automatic Restoration of Extinguished Value.
Core Governed Value Spaces
Value Context Value Origin Value Emergence Value Recognition Value State Value Change Value Development Value Degradation Value Nullification Value Restoration Value Extinction
Recursive Value Lifecycle
VFM® does not treat value as moving through a single irreversible linear sequence.
Once value has emerged, its lifecycle may become recursive:

Existing Value → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Resulting Value State → Further Value Change
Value may therefore develop, degrade, stabilize, change repeatedly, or move between materially different governed states without restarting its origin or emergence lifecycle.
Where value reaches zero:
Positive Value → Value Nullification → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A zero-value state does not automatically terminate the lifecycle.
Where legitimate recoverability remains:
ZVA™ / Degraded / Dormant / Lost Value → ReMonet™ → Value Restoration → Restored Value → New Value State → Continuing Value Lifecycle
Where legitimate recoverability of the same governed value ends:
Impaired / Nullified / Zero Value → Recoverability Boundary → Value Extinction → Value Finality → Governed Lifecycle Termination
Lifecycle re-entry occurs according to what has actually happened to value.
A change in the relevant beneficiary, purpose, or reference framework may require re-establishment of the Value Context.
A newly identified source or basis of value may require examination through Value Origin.
Genuinely new value arising after prior Value Extinction may enter Value Emergence as a new value lifecycle rather than being treated as restoration of extinguished value.
A material change to existing value may re-enter Value Change.
Positive development may enter Value Development.
Decline or impairment may enter Value Degradation.

A transition to zero may enter Value Nullification.
Recoverable prior value may enter Value Restoration.
Terminal loss of recoverability may enter Value Extinction.
The architecture therefore supports governed value lifecycle movement without forcing every value event through the entire architecture again.
Architectural Position
VFM® governs the complete value lifecycle.
The architecture progresses through:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
Together, these value governance spaces govern what value is being examined and within what context, where it originates, when it emerges into existence, when it becomes recognizable, what state it occupies, how it changes, how it develops or degrades, when it reaches zero, whether previously existing value remains recoverable, how that value may be restored, and when the same governed value reaches terminal extinction.
VFM® therefore provides a complete governance path from the first determination of:
What value are we actually governing?
to the terminal lifecycle determination of:
Does that same governed value still remain legitimately recoverable?
What VFM® Defines
VFM® defines:

where value lifecycle governance begins, how the governed value context is established, how value is distinguished from the identity of the underlying object, how the relevant value-bearing object is connected to the value context, how the relevant beneficiary and purpose of value are established, how the applicable reference framework is bounded, where value may originate, how a value source is distinguished from existing value, when potential value becomes existent value, how emergence is distinguished from origin, when existing value may be recognized, how recognition is distinguished from existence, classification, and validation, how the current governed value state is established, how Value Asset™ and ZVA™ concepts may operate within governed value states, when existing value has materially changed, what change occurred to value, how value consequence is separated from external causation, how existing value develops, how development is distinguished from emergence and restoration, how existing value degrades, how degradation is distinguished from nullification, when positive value reaches zero, how DeMonet™ operates as a governed value-nullification mechanism, how a zero-value condition may become a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state, why zero value does not automatically constitute extinction, when previously existing degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value remains recoverable, how ReMonet™ operates as a governed value-restoration mechanism, how restoration is

en previously existing degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value remains recoverable, how ReMonet™ operates as a governed value-restoration mechanism, how restoration is distinguished from development and new value emergence, when restoration potential remains legitimate, when recoverability of the same governed value ends, when Value Extinction is legitimately established, how extinction is distinguished from object destruction, abandonment, zero value, failed restoration, and temporary impossibility,

how Value Finality closes restoration eligibility for the same governed value lifecycle, how lifecycle history remains preserved after extinction, how genuinely new value may emerge after prior value extinction without reopening the extinguished lifecycle.
VFM® provides the official value lifecycle governance language used for value-space identification, lifecycle navigation, governance classification, value-state diagnosis, value-transition analysis, restoration governance, extinction determination, and value architecture design across complex operational environments.
Critical Architectural Distinctions
Value Identification ≠ Asset Identity
Value Context ≠ Value Origin
Value Origin ≠ Identity Origin
Value Source ≠ Existing Value
Origin Asset™ ≠ Existing Value
Value Origin ≠ Value Emergence
Potential Value ≠ Existing Value
Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition
Value Recognition ≠ Classification
Value Recognition ≠ Validation
Value State ≠ Value Transition
Value State ≠ Operational State
External Cause ≠ Value Consequence
Value Change ≠ External Event
Value Emergence ≠ Value Development
Creation of Value ≠ Growth of Existing Value
Value Development ≠ Value Restoration
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification
Declining Value ≠ Zero Value
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified
DeMonet™ ≠ Value State
Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction
ZVA™ ≠ Extinct Value
ReMonet™ ≠ Value State
ReMonet™ ≠ New Value Emergence
Failed ReMonet™ ≠ Value Extinction

Failed Restoration ≠ Terminal Non-Recoverability
Economic Non-Viability ≠ Automatic Value Extinction
Decision Not to Restore ≠ Inability to Restore
Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value
Functional Replacement ≠ Restoration of the Same Value
Value Extinction ≠ Object Extinction
Extinction of One Value Dimension ≠ Extinction of Every Value Dimension
Contextual Value Extinction ≠ Universal Value Extinction
Value Finality ≠ Historical Erasure
Later New Value ≠ Automatic Reversal of Value Extinction
Cross-Architecture Governance Boundaries
VFM® ↔ GOA™ — Governance Architecture
GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance authority, scope, delegation, accountability structures, governance continuity, and interoperability.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle.
Governance Authority ≠ Value Lifecycle.
VFM® ↔ ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture
ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs what exists and occurs in actual Operational Reality.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs the value consequence associated with relevant operational reality.
An operational event may cause value to emerge, change, develop, degrade, reach zero, become recoverable, or become extinct without VFM® assuming governance of the operational event itself.
Operational Reality ≠ Value Lifecycle.
VFM® ↔ OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture

OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, and continuity.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs value and its lifecycle.
The identity or ownership of an object does not by itself determine the existence, state, development, degradation, restoration, or extinction of value associated with that object.
Object Identity ≠ Value Identity.
Identity Origin ≠ Value Origin.
VFM® ↔ VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs whether claims, objects, methods, evidence, determinations, and intended reliance satisfy applicable validation governance requirements.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs the lifecycle condition of value.
Validation may support a determination about value without becoming the value lifecycle itself.
Validation Determination ≠ Value Determination.
VFM® ↔ INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture
INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across governed objects, structures, states, evidence, and processes.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs value lifecycle states and transitions.
Integrity State ≠ Value State.
VFM® ↔ ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture
ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, traceability, and auditability.

VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs what happened to value.
Evidence may establish the basis for a value determination without VFM® becoming an audit architecture.
Evidence of Value Change ≠ Governance of Value Change.
VFM® ↔ CLA® — Classification Architecture
CLA® — Classification Architecture governs classification structures and classification determinations.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs value recognition, states, transitions, development, degradation, restoration, and extinction.
Classification ≠ Value Recognition.
VFM® ↔ SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs how reality is represented and simulated and what simulation-derived outputs and evidence may legitimately mean.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs the actual governed lifecycle of value.
Simulation may model or project possible value states and transitions without itself establishing that those value states or transitions have occurred in Operational Reality.
Simulated Value Change ≠ Actual Value Change.
VFM® ↔ AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture
AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, and decision ownership.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs value lifecycle consequence.
Responsibility for Value Change ≠ Value Change Itself.
VFM® ↔ AIG® — AI Governance Architecture

AI systems may create, affect, optimize, degrade, restore, or destroy forms of value.
AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs the behavioral governance lifecycle of actual AI systems.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs the lifecycle consequence to value.
AI Behavior ≠ Value Lifecycle.
VFM® ↔ ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture
Autonomous systems may materially affect value.
ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs authority, autonomy, constraints, execution, coordination, escalation, and operational behavior of autonomous systems.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governs resulting value lifecycle conditions and transitions.
Autonomous Action ≠ Value Consequence.
VFM® ↔ CLIA® / MGIA™
CLIA® governs cognition and cognitive integrity.
MGIA™ governs memory.
VFM® governs value lifecycle conditions that may be associated with cognitive, informational, or memory-dependent systems without assuming governance of cognition or memory themselves.
Cognitive State ≠ Value State.
Memory State ≠ Value State.
Compatible OOF® Architectures

GOA™ — Governance Architecture ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture AIG® — AI Governance Architecture CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture CLA® — Classification Architecture ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture
Canonical Value Lifecycle
The canonical VFM® lifecycle is:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → Value Restoration where recoverability remains → Value Extinction where recoverability ends
Three transition mechanisms and concepts are particularly important to the architecture:
DeMonet™
ReMonet™
and the governed zero-value state:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
They must not be collapsed into one concept.
DeMonet™ is a value-nullification mechanism.
ZVA™ is a governed zero-value state where applicable.
ReMonet™ is a value-restoration mechanism.
Therefore:
Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™
may subsequently become:
ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value
where legitimate recoverability remains.
But where recoverability of the same governed value has legitimately ended:

ZVA™ / Terminally Impaired Value → Value Extinction → Value Finality
The distinction is fundamental:
Zero is a value state. Extinction is a lifecycle conclusion.
Canonical Principle
VFM® does not define ownership, identity, payment infrastructure, transactions, taxation, market pricing, accounting treatment, general validation, integrity, classification, auditability, accountability, governance authority, simulation, or economic systems themselves. VFM® governs the conditions under which value is identified within a defined context, connected to an identifiable origin, emerges into existence, becomes recognizable, occupies a determinable state, changes, develops, degrades, reaches zero where applicable, may be restored while legitimate recoverability remains, and reaches extinction when the same governed value ceases to remain recoverable within its defined lifecycle. External systems may determine why a value-affecting event occurred; VFM® determines what happened to value as a result.
Canonical Closing Statement

VFM® serves as the official value lifecycle governance reference map for AI systems, autonomous systems, organizations, assets, infrastructure, data, technology, economic systems, public systems, and future value- based environments. By defining the primary governable spaces of the complete value lifecycle, VFM® provides the architecture used to establish what value is being governed and within what context, identify where that value originates, determine when potential value becomes existent value, distinguish existence from recognition, establish current value state, govern material value change, separate development from degradation, determine when value reaches zero, preserve the distinction between zero value and terminal extinction, govern restoration of previously existing value through ReMonet™, and determine when legitimate recoverability of the same governed value has ended. VFM® therefore establishes value not as a static number, price, asset attribute, or economic label, but as a continuously governable lifecycle in which value can originate, emerge, exist, change, develop, degrade, reach zero, recover, enter new states, or ultimately reach finality while remaining methodologically distinct from the objects, systems, identities, transactions, evidence, and external events through which that value may be expressed or affected.
