Canonical Definition
Value Change Identification Module (VCIM) is the first Core Module of the Value Change Standard (VCS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VCIM governs the identification of a potential or confirmed material change affecting existing governed value by establishing the reference Value State, observing the subsequent value condition, detecting a relevant difference, and determining whether that difference constitutes a legitimate Value Change Candidate.
The Module establishes the first controlled transition from:
Governed Value State
to
Identified Value Change.

VCIM does not determine the final type, magnitude, or causal basis of the change.
Its foundational task is:
to determine whether something material has happened to the governed value that requires formal Value Change governance.
Architectural Position
VCIM is the first module within VCS.
It receives the governed value basis established through:
VSS — Value State Standard
and precedes:
VCTM — Value Change Type Module.
Its architectural position is:
Governed Value State → VCIM — Value Change Identification → VCTM — Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude → VCCM — Value Change Causation Link → VCRM — Value Change Record
VCIM therefore establishes whether a governable change exists before later modules determine what kind of change occurred, how significant it was, what may have caused it, and how it must be recorded.
Internal Module Flow
Governed Value State → Reference State Selection → Observed Value Condition → Difference Detection → Context Preservation → Materiality Screening → Change Candidate Identification → Change Identification Determination → Identified Value Change → VCTM — Value Change Type Module
Operational Space
VCIM governs the point at which an existing Value State is examined for evidence of material change.
Its operational space includes:

governed value identification; reference-state selection; reference-point identification; observation of subsequent value condition; difference detection; temporal comparison; contextual comparison; beneficiary-aware comparison; capability change detection; utility change detection; operational change detection; economic change detection; physical change detection; digital change detection; strategic change detection; materiality screening; change candidate creation; change identification determination;
uncertainty affecting identification; false-change prevention.
Reference State Principle
A Value Change cannot be identified meaningfully without a reference.
VCIM therefore requires identification of the governed condition against which the observed value condition is being compared.
The reference may be:
Previous Value State
Value State Record
Governed Baseline
Defined Reference Date
Reference Event
Reference Condition
Reference Capability
or another explicitly governed comparison basis.
The foundational rule is:
No Governed Reference → No Governed Value Change Identification
This prevents arbitrary claims that value has increased, decreased, deteriorated, improved, or otherwise changed without identifying what the comparison is actually against.
Observed Value Condition
VCIM distinguishes between:
Reference Value State
and
Observed Value Condition.
The Observed Value Condition represents the materially relevant condition of the governed value at the comparison point.

It may be derived from:
operational observations; system measurements; financial information; market information; physical inspection; performance data; capability assessment; utilization information; mission data; infrastructure monitoring; digital-system telemetry; contractual developments; environmental information; validated external information; other contextually appropriate evidence.
VCIM does not require one universal observation method.
The observation method must be appropriate to the value being governed.
Difference Detection
VCIM identifies whether a meaningful difference exists between:
Reference Value State
and
Observed Value Condition.
The difference may concern:
amount; capability; utility; availability; productivity; accessibility; relevance; condition; performance; scarcity; strategic importance; operational usefulness; beneficiary relationship; economic significance; physical condition; digital capability; resource requirement.
Difference detection is not yet full Value Change characterization.
It establishes that a potentially governable delta exists.
Difference ≠ Value Change
VCIM must prevent every detected variation from automatically becoming a Value Change.
A difference may arise from:
measurement noise; expected operational fluctuation; temporary observation error; seasonal variation; normal market movement; incomplete information; inconsistent measurement basis; different observation methods; different beneficiaries; changed contexts; data latency.

Therefore:
Detected Difference ≠ Identified Material Value Change
VCIM requires the difference to pass a materiality screen before it enters formal downstream Value Change governance.
Materiality Screening
VCIM performs an initial determination of whether the detected difference is sufficiently material to become a Value Change Candidate.
Materiality may depend upon:
absolute difference; relative difference; percentage change; operational consequence; capability consequence; beneficiary consequence; strategic significance; persistence; reversibility; risk consequence; resource consequence; economic consequence; mission consequence; defined organizational threshold.
The materiality basis must remain linked to the governed Value Context.
A CHF 1,000 change may be immaterial in one context and decisive in another.
Likewise, a 1% capability loss may be insignificant for one system and mission-critical for another.
Change Candidate
Where a relevant difference passes the applicable materiality screen, VCIM creates a:
Value Change Candidate.
A Value Change Candidate represents:
a sufficiently supported indication that existing governed value may have materially changed and should proceed into formal Value Change characterization.
The candidate should identify at minimum:
Governed Value
Reference State
Observed Condition
Detected Difference
Materiality Basis
Observation Point
Relevant Context
Affected Beneficiary where applicable
Identification Confidence or Uncertainty

The candidate does not yet establish full change type, magnitude, or causation.
Identification States
VCIM may assign an explicit identification state.
1. No Material Change Identified
A difference is absent or remains below the applicable materiality basis.
2. Potential Value Change
A relevant difference is observed, but additional information is required before material change can be established.
3. Material Value Change Identified
Available information sufficiently supports the conclusion that a material change to governed value has occurred.
4. Change Identification Suspended
A determination cannot currently proceed because material information is missing, contradictory, unreliable, or under review.
5. Change Identification Invalidated
A previously suspected change is shown to result from measurement error, reference mismatch, contextual mismatch, duplicated information, or another non-value-change condition.
These states prevent uncertainty from being silently converted into certainty.
Context Preservation
Value Change identification must preserve the Value Context established upstream.
A change identified for:
Beneficiary A
does not automatically establish the same change for:
Beneficiary B.
Likewise:
Value Change in Context A
does not automatically mean:
Value Change in Context B.
VCIM therefore preserves, where materially relevant:

value-bearing object; beneficiary; purpose; reference framework; operational context; temporal context; geographic context; system context; relevant conditions.
This prevents context drift during Value Change analysis.
Temporal Comparison
Value Change is frequently identified across time.
VCIM may compare:
Value at T1
with
Value Condition at T2.
But temporal sequence alone does not establish change.
The comparison basis must remain sufficiently equivalent.
For example, comparing asset productivity during:
normal production
with productivity during:
scheduled shutdown
could create an artificial Value Change if the contextual difference is ignored.
VCIM therefore requires time and context to be evaluated together.
Comparable Basis Principle
A legitimate Value Change comparison requires sufficiently comparable reference and observation bases.
The following should not be silently compared as equivalent:
Different Value Definitions
Different Beneficiaries
Different Measurement Methods
Different Units
Different Reference Frameworks
Different Operational Conditions
Different Object Configurations
unless those differences are explicitly governed.
The principle is:
Difference in Measurement Basis ≠ Difference in Value
Positive and Negative Change Candidates
VCIM may identify candidates indicating:
Potential Positive Value Change
or
Potential Negative Value Change.
However, VCIM does not perform the definitive change-type classification.
That belongs to VCTM.

VCIM only preserves the observed directional signal where it is useful for downstream governance.
Cumulative Change Detection
Material Value Change may emerge through accumulation.
Individual observations may remain below the materiality threshold while their cumulative effect becomes significant.
VCIM therefore supports:
Difference 1
Difference 2
Difference 3
Difference n
→ Cumulative Material Change Candidate
This is particularly important for:
industrial deterioration; infrastructure aging; efficiency loss; technological obsolescence; resource depletion; capability degradation; data deterioration; maintenance burden; gradual productivity improvement.
A governance system that evaluates only isolated events may systematically fail to identify slow Value Change.
Multi-Dimensional Change Identification
A value-bearing object may experience simultaneous changes across several value dimensions.
For example:
Industrial Asset
may exhibit:
Physical Condition ↓
Energy Efficiency ↓
Maintenance Requirement ↑
Production Capability ↓
while:
Market Scarcity ↑
may increase another dimension of value.
VCIM should preserve these different Value Change Candidates rather than forcing them prematurely into one net value figure.
This allows later modules to characterize each change appropriately.
Uncertainty Preservation
VCIM must preserve material uncertainty affecting identification.
Uncertainty may arise from:

incomplete observation; measurement uncertainty; conflicting evidence; uncertain reference state; uncertain beneficiary impact; insufficient temporal information; changing context; delayed information; proxy measurement; uncertain value definition.
Where uncertainty prevents legitimate determination, the result should remain:
Potential Value Change
rather than being promoted to confirmed change.
False Change Prevention
VCIM should actively distinguish real Value Change from apparent change produced by methodological inconsistency.
False change may arise through:
measurement method change
unit conversion error
reference mismatch
data correction
different valuation methodology
beneficiary substitution
context substitution
object version mismatch
duplicate observation
system migration
currency conversion effects
where those effects do not represent the governed Value Change being examined.
This is essential in automated environments where large data streams may otherwise create large numbers of false Value Change events.
Automated Change Identification
VCIM can support automated monitoring.
A machine-readable implementation may operate as:
Governed Value State
→ Continuous or Periodic Observation
→ Difference Detection
→ Materiality Screen
→ Value Change Candidate
→ Human or Automated Determination
→ Downstream Change Governance
Potential implementations include:

banking monitoring systems; asset-management platforms; digital twins; industrial IoT; blockchain analytics; infrastructure monitoring; insurance systems; AI resource governance; mission-control systems; public-asset management; automated accounting interfaces.
Automation must preserve the governed reference and context.
A system that detects numerical movement without understanding what the number represents is not yet governing Value Change.
Relationship to ZVA™
VCIM may identify a material change indicating that governed value is moving:
toward ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
or
away from ZVA™.
However, VCIM does not assign the resulting Value State.
For example:
Value State: Active Value
→ VCIM identifies material degradation
→ downstream VCS governance characterizes the change
→ VSS may subsequently determine ZVA™ where the applicable state conditions are satisfied.
Likewise:
ZVA™
may experience a material positive change that creates a candidate for a new non-zero Value State.
This preserves:
Change Identification ≠ State Determination
VCIM Boundary with VSS
VSS establishes:
What is the current governed Value State?
VCIM establishes:
Has something materially changed relative to that governed state?
Therefore:
Value State ≠ Value Change Identification
VCIM consumes the state as a reference but does not redefine the state itself.
VCIM Boundary with VCTM
VCIM determines whether a material Value Change has been identified.
VCTM determines what kind of Value Change occurred.

Therefore:
Identification ≠ Classification
VCIM must not prematurely assign the final Change Type.
VCIM Boundary with VCMM
VCIM may require a preliminary materiality screen.
VCMM performs the formal determination of Value Change magnitude.
Therefore:
Materiality Screening ≠ Change Magnitude Determination
A change can be sufficiently material to enter governance before its precise magnitude is established.
VCIM Boundary with VCCM
VCIM identifies that value changed.
VCCM governs the relationship between the Value Change and potential causal events, conditions, activities, or mechanisms.
Therefore:
Change Identification ≠ Causation
VCIM must not require complete causal knowledge before a legitimate Value Change can be identified.
VCIM Boundary with External Systems
External systems may provide observations used to identify Value Change.
Examples include:
Market System → Price Information
Banking System → Payment Information
Accounting System → Asset Information
Industrial System → Performance Information
Blockchain → Transaction or State Information
IoT System → Physical Condition Information
Mission System → Capability Information
VCIM may consume these signals.
It does not automatically govern the systems that produced them.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VCIM implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Identification
Identify the governed value being monitored.
2. Reference State
Identify the applicable governed Value State or other explicit reference.

3. Observation Basis
Define the information used to observe the subsequent value condition.
4. Comparability Check
Determine whether the reference and observed conditions are sufficiently comparable.
5. Difference Detection
Identify any materially relevant difference.
6. Context Preservation
Preserve beneficiary, purpose, reference framework, object, and relevant operational context.
7. Materiality Screening
Determine whether the difference is sufficiently significant to enter formal Value Change governance.
8. Uncertainty Assessment
Record material uncertainty affecting the identification.
9. Identification State
Assign the applicable Value Change Identification State.
10. Change Candidate Creation
Create the governed Value Change Candidate for downstream characterization where appropriate.
Governance Outputs
VCIM may produce:
Value Change Observation Record Value Change Reference Record Value Comparison Basis Value Difference Record Value Change Materiality Screen Value Change Context Record Value Change Uncertainty Record Value Change Identification State Value Change Candidate Material Value Change Identification No-Material-Change Determination Change Identification Invalidation Record
These outputs provide the governed input for:
VCTM — Value Change Type Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Early Collateral Value
Change Detection
A bank finances a production facility.
The facility's last governed Value State indicates:
high productive capability
stable operating availability

acceptable energy efficiency
and
strong collateral usefulness.
Over time, operational information begins showing:
production throughput ↓
unplanned downtime ↑
energy consumption per unit ↑
maintenance interventions ↑.
No loan payment has yet been missed.
No formal accounting impairment has necessarily been recorded.
The market price may not yet have materially moved.
VCIM compares the new operational condition with the governed reference Value State.
Instead of waiting for a financial consequence, the bank can identify:
Potential Material Value Change
and create a Value Change Candidate for downstream analysis.
VCTM can then determine the type of change.
VCMM can determine its magnitude.
VCCM can examine relevant causal links.
The practical advantage is significant:
the institution can begin governing deterioration in the underlying value before that deterioration necessarily appears as default, accounting loss, or market repricing.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Detecting Value
Created by Resource Optimization
A spacecraft has a governed computational-resource Value State.
Mission software is then optimized.
The same mission-critical computation can now be performed using:
30% less computational capacity
while preserving the required operational result.
There may be:
no transaction
no market price
no ownership change
and
no accounting recognition.
Yet the mission now possesses additional usable computational capacity.
VCIM compares:
Previous Computational Resource State
with

Observed Post-Optimization Condition.
It identifies a material difference:
more mission capability can now be produced from the same computational resource base.
VCIM therefore creates a:
Positive Value Change Candidate.
The later VCS modules can characterize and quantify the change.
This demonstrates a fundamental VFM® capability:
Value Change can be identified directly from changes in operational usefulness and capability without requiring monetary expression.
Enterprise Application
VCIM provides organizations with a systematic method for answering one deceptively simple question:
Has the value actually changed?
This question can be applied across:
banking; insurance; investment; industrial production; infrastructure; energy; blockchain; digital assets; intellectual property; AI systems; computational resources; public assets; mission systems; natural resources; organizational capability.
The Module creates a common governance mechanism through which different systems can detect material Value Change without forcing all forms of value into the same measurement model.
Foundational Principles
Value Change requires a governed reference.
Difference is not automatically Value Change.
Materiality determines whether a difference enters formal Value Change governance.
Change identification does not require complete causal knowledge.
Change identification is not change classification.
Materiality screening is not magnitude determination.

A change in measurement method must not be mistaken for a change in value.
Context-specific change must not automatically become universal change.
Beneficiary-specific change must remain beneficiary-specific.
Cumulative small differences may become a material Value Change.
Value Change may be identified without monetary expression, transaction, accounting recognition, or market repricing.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Change Identification Module establishes the entry control point of the Value Change Standard by determining whether existing governed value has materially changed relative to an explicit and sufficiently comparable reference state. Through governance of reference selection, observation, difference detection, context preservation, comparability, materiality screening, cumulative change, multi-dimensional change, uncertainty, false-change prevention, identification states, and Value Change Candidate creation, VCIM prevents ordinary variation, measurement inconsistency, contextual mismatch, or unsupported interpretation from being treated as genuine Value Change. By separating change identification from change type, magnitude, causation, resulting Value State, price movement, transaction, accounting recognition, and monetary expression, VCIM provides VFM® with the methodological gateway required to observe Value Change across physical, digital, economic, operational, strategic, financial, and future value systems. Before a system can determine what kind of change occurred or how large that change was, it must first establish that value actually changed.

Canonical Definition
Value Change Magnitude Module (VCMM) is the third Core Module of the Value Change Standard (VCS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VCMM governs the determination of the extent, scale, intensity, proportion, significance, or measurable degree of an identified and classified Value Change within its defined Value Context.
The Module establishes a controlled measurement layer through which Value Change may be expressed quantitatively, qualitatively, proportionally, comparatively, categorically, probabilistically, or through another governed measurement method appropriate to the value being assessed.

VCMM does not require all value to be expressed in monetary terms and does not assume that one measurement system can legitimately represent every form of value.
Its foundational task is:
to determine how much value has materially changed, using a measurement basis appropriate to the governed value and without confusing magnitude with cause, price, or resulting Value State.
Architectural Position
VCMM is the third module within VCS.
It follows:
VCTM — Value Change Type Module
and precedes:
VCCM — Value Change Causation Link Module.
The internal sequence is:
Governed Value State → VCIM — Value Change Identification → VCTM — Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude
→ VCCM — Value Change Causation Link → VCRM — Value Change Record
VCIM establishes:
that a material Value Change occurred.
VCTM establishes:
what kind of Value Change occurred.
VCMM establishes:
how large or significant that Value Change is.
Internal Module Flow
Identified Value Change → Governed Value Change Type → Affected Value Dimension → Reference Basis Selection → Measurement Method Selection → Baseline Establishment → Change Measurement → Uncertainty Assessment → Materiality Assessment → Magnitude Determination → Governed Value Change Magnitude → VCCM — Value Change Causation Link Module
Operational Space
VCMM governs the measurement space between:
classified Value Change
and
causal linkage of that change.
Its operational space includes:

absolute magnitude; relative magnitude; proportional magnitude; qualitative magnitude; quantitative magnitude; monetary magnitude; non-monetary magnitude; multidimensional magnitude; cumulative magnitude; incremental magnitude; comparative magnitude; threshold-based magnitude; range-based magnitude; uncertainty-bounded magnitude; materiality; measurement confidence; baseline selection; reference-period selection; normalization; magnitude aggregation; magnitude decomposition.
Magnitude Requires a Reference Basis
A statement that value changed by:
10
has little governed meaning unless the reference basis is known.
VCMM therefore requires magnitude to remain connected to an appropriate reference basis.
The reference basis may include:
previous Value State; defined baseline; initial state; expected state; target state; benchmark; comparable object; previous period; scenario baseline; operational requirement; resource baseline; replacement basis; governed index; another explicitly defined reference point.
Therefore:
Magnitude without Reference Basis ≠ Governed Value Change Magnitude
Absolute Value Change Magnitude
VCMM may express change as an absolute difference.
For a measurable value dimension:
ΔV = V₂ − V₁
where:
V₁ = governed reference value
and
V₂ = governed subsequent value.
Examples:
Production Capacity: 1,000 units/day → 1,250 units/day
Absolute Change: +250 units/day
or:
Energy Consumption: 10 MWh → 8 MWh for equivalent governed output
Absolute Change: −2 MWh.

The meaning of the change remains dependent upon the governed Value Context.
Relative Value Change Magnitude
Where appropriate, VCMM may determine relative change:
Relative Change = (V₂ − V₁) / V₁
This permits expressions such as:
+25% production capacity
−20% energy consumption
+12% availability
−8% operational capability.
Percentage movement is useful only where the underlying measurement basis legitimately supports proportional comparison.
Magnitude ≠ Direction
VCTM determines whether a change is:
positive, negative, neutral structural, mixed, or indeterminate.
VCMM determines its magnitude.
Therefore:
Direction ≠ Magnitude
A negative change can be small or catastrophic.
A positive change can be marginal or transformative.
VCMM must preserve this distinction.
Magnitude ≠ Materiality
A measurable Value Change is not necessarily materially significant.
For example:
0.01% change
may be immaterial in one context.
The same change may be critical in another if it affects:
spacecraft navigation; high-frequency financial infrastructure; structural safety; medical manufacturing; energy-grid stability; mission-critical computation.
VCMM therefore distinguishes:
Measured Magnitude
from
Governed Materiality.
Materiality must be assessed relative to the purpose, beneficiary, object, operational context, and applicable thresholds.
Qualitative Magnitude
Not every Value Change can be legitimately expressed numerically.
VCMM therefore supports qualitative magnitude states.

A governance framework may use states such as:
Negligible
Minor
Moderate
Major
Severe
Critical
Transformative
or another domain-specific classification.
The categories must have defined criteria.
Qualitative measurement must not become arbitrary merely because numerical measurement is unavailable.
Quantitative Magnitude
Where reliable measurement is possible, VCMM supports quantitative magnitude.
Possible measurement forms include:
currency; percentage; physical units; energy units; production units; time; computational resources; capacity; throughput; availability; reliability; performance; efficiency; probability; information quantity; resource consumption; another governed metric.
VCMM does not privilege monetary measurement over other legitimate measurement forms.
Monetary Magnitude
Where Value Change can legitimately be represented economically, VCMM may express magnitude in monetary terms.
Examples include:
CHF +2.4 million
EUR −600,000
USD +15 million
or another currency.
However:
Monetary Magnitude ≠ Total Value Change
where the governed value contains material non-monetary dimensions.
A monetary measure is one representation of magnitude, not a universal definition of value.
Non-Monetary Magnitude
VCMM explicitly supports non-monetary Value Change.
Examples include:
Energy Requirement: −18%
Computational Requirement: −30%
Production Capacity: +22%
System Availability: +4.5 percentage points
Mission Range: +15%
Data Utility: materially reduced

Operational Resilience: major improvement
Resource Accessibility: severe reduction.
This capability is fundamental to VFM® because value frequently changes before that change is monetized.
Multi-Dimensional Magnitude
A Value Change may affect several value dimensions simultaneously.
VCMM must therefore support:
Multi-Dimensional Magnitude Determination.
For example:
AI Infrastructure Optimization
may produce:
Compute Consumption: −25%
Energy Consumption: −18%
Latency: −12%
Operational Capacity: +30%
Infrastructure Cost: −15%
Provider Dependency: +20%.
VCMM should not automatically collapse these dimensions into one synthetic score.
Each magnitude may remain separately governed until a legitimate aggregation methodology exists.
Magnitude Aggregation
Where multiple Value Changes are aggregated, VCMM requires the aggregation basis to be explicit.
Aggregation may require:
common units; normalization; weighting; conversion; defined equivalence; temporal alignment; beneficiary alignment; contextual compatibility.
Therefore:
Multiple Magnitudes ≠ Automatically Additive Magnitudes
CHF 1 million of economic value cannot simply be added to a 20% resilience improvement or 15% energy reduction without a governed conversion basis.
Magnitude Decomposition
A large Value Change may consist of several smaller changes.
VCMM may decompose:
Total Value Change Magnitude
into:
Component A
Component B
Component C
where the measurement structure permits it.
This is especially useful for:

portfolios; industrial systems; infrastructure; organizations; complex digital systems; AI systems; supply chains; banking assets; mission systems.
Decomposition preserves visibility into where the magnitude originates before VCCM examines causation.
Incremental Value Change
VCMM may determine the magnitude of an incremental change.
Example:
Efficiency
Period 1 → +3%
Period 2 → +2%
Period 3 → +4%.
Each change can be separately governed.
This prevents cumulative outcomes from obscuring individual Value Change events.
Cumulative Value Change Magnitude
Where repeated changes accumulate, VCMM may determine cumulative magnitude across a defined period.
The cumulative basis must identify:
starting reference state; relevant changes; time interval; compounding method; aggregation method; excluded changes; measurement uncertainty.
Cumulative magnitude must not be inferred by simply adding percentages where compounding or changing baselines materially affect the result.
Comparative Magnitude
VCMM may compare Value Change across:
objects; assets; systems; periods; scenarios; organizations; technologies; portfolios; operational configurations.
Example:
System A: Energy reduction −12%
System B: Energy reduction −28%.
Comparability requires sufficiently compatible measurement bases.
Where bases differ materially, VCMM should identify the comparison as limited or non-equivalent.
Normalized Magnitude
Normalization may be required where objects differ in scale.
Examples include:

Energy per unit produced
Cost per transaction
Compute per inference
Output per employee-hour
Revenue per deployed asset
Failure rate per operating hour.
Normalization can reveal Value Change that absolute measurement alone would conceal.
VCMM requires the normalization basis to remain explicit.
Baseline Governance
Baseline selection can materially alter the apparent magnitude of Value Change.
VCMM therefore requires the baseline to be:
identifiable; relevant; temporally defined; methodologically appropriate; reproducible where applicable; resistant to opportunistic selection; documented.
Changing the baseline after observing the result can artificially enlarge or reduce apparent Value Change.
Therefore:
Baseline Manipulation = Magnitude Governance Risk
Measurement Method
The selected measurement method must correspond to the value dimension being assessed.
Possible methods include:
direct measurement; calculated measurement; comparative measurement; model-based estimation; probabilistic estimation; expert assessment; index-based measurement; proxy measurement; composite measurement; hybrid measurement.
The method must remain visible in the magnitude determination.
Measured ≠ Estimated
VCMM distinguishes between:
Measured Magnitude
and
Estimated Magnitude.
A direct operational measurement and a model-derived estimate may both be useful.
They are not methodologically identical.
Estimated magnitude should identify the estimation basis and material uncertainty.
Magnitude Range

Where a single-point estimate would create false precision, VCMM may represent magnitude as a range.
Example:
Estimated Economic Value Change: CHF +8.0M to +11.5M
or:
Expected Efficiency Improvement: +14% to +19%.
Range-based representation is preferable where uncertainty is material.
Probabilistic Magnitude
Where appropriate, magnitude may be represented probabilistically.
For example:
70% probability that the Value Change lies between +12% and +18%.
Probabilistic representation must identify the underlying method and assumptions.
Probability does not eliminate uncertainty.
It structures it.
Uncertainty-Bounded Magnitude
VCMM requires material uncertainty to remain visible.
Uncertainty may arise from:
incomplete measurement; uncertain baseline; data limitations; estimation method; model dependence; volatility; temporal instability; measurement error; conversion assumptions; aggregation assumptions.
A governed magnitude may therefore take the form:
Magnitude Estimate + Uncertainty Range + Measurement Basis.
Magnitude Confidence
Organizations may assign confidence to a magnitude determination.
Possible states may include:
Low Confidence
Moderate Confidence
High Confidence
or another governed scale.
Confidence must not substitute for the underlying magnitude.
It expresses the strength of the measurement basis.
Threshold-Based Magnitude
VCMM may define thresholds for operational classification.
Example:
< 2% → Minor
2–10% → Moderate
10–25% → Major
> 25% → Severe

These thresholds are illustrative only.
Each implementation must establish thresholds appropriate to the governed context.
VFM® does not impose one universal materiality scale across all forms of value.
Magnitude and Time
The same magnitude may have different meaning depending on how quickly it occurs.
For example:
−20% over ten years
and
−20% in one hour
represent materially different operational realities.
VCTM may classify temporal character.
VCMM may preserve the relevant time basis when measuring magnitude.
Therefore, where relevant:
Magnitude + Time Basis
should remain connected.
Rate of Value Change
Where operationally useful, VCMM may determine the rate at which value changes.
Examples:
CHF −500,000/month
Capacity +4%/quarter
Energy Efficiency +1.2%/year
Asset Utility −3%/1,000 operating hours.
Rate measurement supports monitoring and later lifecycle governance.
Magnitude Threshold Crossing
A Value Change may become operationally significant when it crosses a defined threshold.
VCMM may identify:
Threshold Not Reached
Threshold Approaching
Threshold Reached
Threshold Exceeded.
The threshold itself may originate from organizational, contractual, technical, regulatory, financial, or other governance systems.
VCMM governs its relationship to Value Change magnitude, not the external authority that created it.
Magnitude Reassessment
Magnitude may require reassessment when:

new measurements become available; baseline data changes legitimately; an estimate becomes directly measurable; uncertainty narrows; additional Value Change occurs; measurement error is discovered; the governed context materially changes.
A magnitude determination is therefore versionable.
VCMM Boundary with VCTM
VCTM determines:
what kind of Value Change occurred.
VCMM determines:
how much it changed.
Therefore:
Value Change Type ≠ Value Change Magnitude
VCMM Boundary with VCCM
VCMM determines magnitude.
VCCM establishes the governed relationship between Value Change and relevant causes.
Therefore:
Magnitude ≠ Causation
A CHF 10 million Value Change does not itself establish why the change occurred.
VCMM Boundary with VSS
VSS determines the current governed Value State.
VCMM determines the magnitude of movement between relevant value conditions.
Therefore:
Resulting State ≠ Magnitude of Change
Two objects may reach the same Value State after experiencing materially different Value Change magnitudes.
VCMM Boundary with External Valuation
Systems
VCMM may consume or produce information relevant to:
financial valuation; accounting; banking; insurance; taxation; investment; blockchain; industrial measurement; AI infrastructure; energy systems; scientific systems.
It does not replace domain-specific valuation, accounting, tax, legal, or regulatory methodologies.
VCMM governs the magnitude of Value Change within VFM®.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Value Change Input

Receive the identified and classified Value Change from VCIM and VCTM.
2. Value Dimension
Identify the exact value dimension whose magnitude is being determined.
3. Reference Basis
Establish the baseline, previous state, benchmark, target, or other governed reference basis.
4. Measurement Method
Select the appropriate quantitative, qualitative, comparative, probabilistic, monetary, non-monetary, or hybrid measurement method.
5. Measurement Unit
Define the unit, scale, classification, index, or other representation used.
6. Magnitude Determination
Determine the absolute, relative, proportional, categorical, range-based, or other appropriate magnitude.
7. Uncertainty Assessment
Identify material uncertainty affecting the determination.
8. Materiality Assessment
Determine whether the magnitude is materially significant within the governed Value Context.
9. Confidence / Qualification
Where appropriate, establish confidence or qualification attached to the magnitude.
10. Magnitude Record
Create a governed record suitable for downstream causation linkage and Value Change recording.

Use Case 1 — Banking: Detecting Material
Collateral Value Deterioration Before Price Alone
Shows It
A bank finances a large industrial production asset.
The asset remains operational and its most recent external valuation has not yet materially changed.
Operational data nevertheless shows:
Production Capacity: −14%
Energy Efficiency: −11%
Unplanned Downtime: +27%
Maintenance Requirement: +32%.
VCTM has already classified several negative operational and efficiency Value Changes.
VCMM now determines their magnitude against the governed baseline.
Instead of waiting for the changes to appear as one delayed market-price or accounting adjustment, the bank can preserve the separate magnitude of each Value Change.
This creates a governed basis for:
collateral monitoring, credit-risk review, covenant assessment, refinancing analysis, impairment investigation, and early-warning systems.

The key capability is:
material Value Change can become measurable before it becomes fully visible in market price.
Use Case 2 — AI Infrastructure: Measuring Value
Created Through Cost Reduction
An organization operates an AI platform requiring:
100 million computational units per month
and
1,000 MWh of energy
to deliver a defined operational workload.
After optimization, equivalent governed output requires:
72 million computational units
and
810 MWh of energy.
VCMM determines:
Computational Requirement Change: −28%
Energy Requirement Change: −19%.
If the organization also establishes an appropriate economic conversion basis, VCMM may separately determine:
Infrastructure Cost Change: −CHF X
and
Economic Value Change: +CHF Y.
The non-monetary and monetary magnitudes remain separately visible.
The organization can therefore determine not merely that optimization created value, but:
how much resource, operational, and economic value changed.
This supports:
AI cost governance, infrastructure planning, investment decisions, capacity allocation, ROI analysis, energy governance, and technology comparison.
Enterprise Application
VCMM provides the measurement layer required to move VFM® from:
“value changed”
to:
“value changed by this governed magnitude, against this reference basis, using this method, with these limitations and this uncertainty.”
This makes the Module directly applicable to:

banking; investment; insurance; industrial production; infrastructure; AI systems; computational infrastructure; energy; digital assets; blockchain; intellectual property; organizational capability; supply chains; public assets; mission systems; scientific systems; future value-based economic models.
VCMM is particularly valuable where organizations need to govern forms of Value Change that are real and operationally significant but not yet fully monetized.
Foundational Principles
Value Change magnitude requires a governed reference basis.
Magnitude is distinct from direction.
Magnitude is distinct from materiality.
Magnitude is distinct from causation.
Magnitude is distinct from resulting Value State.
Value Change does not need to be monetary to be measurable.
Monetary magnitude is not a universal representation of total value.
Different value dimensions should remain separately measurable where aggregation would destroy meaning.
Multiple magnitudes must not be aggregated without a governed equivalence or conversion basis.
Measured and estimated magnitudes must remain distinguishable.
Uncertainty must remain visible where measurement is uncertain.
A precise number is not automatically an accurate Value Change magnitude.
The measurement method must fit the value dimension being measured.
A Value Change becomes analytically useful when its scale can be understood without losing the context that gives that scale meaning.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Change Magnitude Module establishes the measurement layer of the Value Change Standard by determining the extent, scale, intensity, proportion, significance, or measurable degree of an identified and classified Value Change against an explicit governed reference basis. Through governance of baselines, measurement methods, units, absolute and relative change, qualitative and quantitative magnitude, monetary and non-monetary magnitude, multidimensional measurement, normalization, aggregation, decomposition, cumulative change, materiality, uncertainty, confidence, thresholds, temporal basis, and reassessment, VCMM enables VFM® to represent how much value has changed without reducing all value to market price, currency, accounting treatment, or a single universal metric. By separating magnitude from direction, causation, materiality, and resulting Value State, VCMM creates a reusable measurement layer through which operational, economic, physical, digital, strategic, computational, infrastructural, and other forms of Value Change can be compared, monitored, analyzed, and transferred into downstream governance. A Value Change should not be treated as fully characterized merely because its direction is known; its governed magnitude must establish how much changed, relative to what, by which method, and with what uncertainty.

Canonical Definition
Value Change Record Module (VCRM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Change Standard (VCS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VCRM governs the creation, structuring, preservation, linkage, versioning, and lifecycle continuity of the governed record representing a determined Value Change.
The Module consolidates the governed outputs produced through the preceding VCS modules into a coherent and reconstructable Value Change Record.
The record may preserve:
what changed,
what type of change occurred,
how materially value changed,
what causal basis is associated with the change,

when the change occurred or became determinable,
what evidence supports the determination,
what uncertainty remains,
and
what resulting Value State or subsequent lifecycle process the change may affect.
VCRM does not independently determine whether Value Change occurred, classify the change, calculate its magnitude, or establish its causal basis.
Its task is:
to preserve the governed Value Change as a persistent, traceable, context-bound, versionable, and lifecycle- usable record.
Architectural Position
VCRM is the fifth and final module within VCS.
It follows:
VCCM — Value Change Causation Link Module.
The internal sequence is:
Governed Value State → VCIM — Value Change Identification → VCTM — Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude → VCCM — Value Change Causation Link → VCRM — Value Change Record
VCRM closes the internal governance flow of VCS by transforming the preceding determinations into a persistent governed record.
Internal Module Flow
Identified Value Change → Value Change Type → Value Change Magnitude → Value Change Causation Link → Record Object Creation
→ Change Context Assembly → Temporal Anchoring → Evidence & Determination Linkage → Uncertainty & Limitation Preservation → Record Version Assignment → Lifecycle Relationship Linkage → Governed Value Change Record
Operational Space
VCRM governs the space between:
completed Value Change determination
and
persistent lifecycle representation of that change.
Its operational space includes:

Value Change record identification; record creation; record structure; change-object linkage; value-context linkage; previous-state linkage; resulting-state linkage; change-type preservation; magnitude preservation; causal-link preservation; temporal anchoring; evidence linkage; determination provenance; uncertainty preservation; limitation preservation; record versioning; correction; supersession; lifecycle continuity; record-to-record relationships; change history reconstruction; downstream governance availability.
Value Change ≠ Value Change Record
A change may occur before it is formally recorded.
Therefore:
Value Change ≠ Value Change Record.
VCRM does not create the underlying change.
It creates the governed representation through which the change can remain identifiable and usable across the value lifecycle.
This distinction is fundamental.
A record must represent reality.
It must not substitute for reality.
Value Change Record Object
Each governed Value Change should be representable as a distinct Value Change Record Object.
The record should be capable of identifying, where applicable:
Value Context
Value-Bearing Object
Prior Value State
Value Change
Value Change Type
Value Change Magnitude
Causation Link
Resulting Value State
Temporal Basis
Evidence Basis
Determination Basis
Uncertainty
Limitations
Record Version
Record Status
This creates a persistent governance object rather than an isolated analytical observation.
Record Identity

A Value Change Record should have a stable identity sufficient to distinguish it from other Value Change Records.
Identity may include:
unique record identifier; architecture reference; Parent Standard reference; module reference; governed value reference; value-bearing object reference; temporal reference; version; record status.
Record identity enables Value Change to remain referencable across systems and over time.
Value Context Linkage
Every Value Change Record must remain connected to the governed Value Context established under:
Value Context Standard (VCXS).
A statement such as:
Value decreased by 20%.
is insufficient without knowing:
which value,
of what,
for whom,
for what purpose,
and
against what reference context.
VCRM therefore preserves the contextual identity of the changed value.
Previous Value State Linkage
Where applicable, the record should identify the Value State existing before the change.
For example:
Prior State: Productive Value Asset
→ Change: Physical deterioration
→ Resulting State: Reduced productive value.
This creates a traceable relationship between:
State Before Change
and
Change Event.
Resulting Value State Linkage
Where the resulting Value State has been determined, VCRM should preserve that relationship.
The lifecycle relationship becomes:
Prior Value State → Governed Value Change → Resulting Value State.
VCRM does not independently determine the resulting state.

That determination remains governed through the appropriate Value State governance.
The record preserves the relationship.
Change Type Preservation
VCRM receives the governed Value Change Type from VCTM.
The record may preserve classifications such as:
increase; decrease; creation;
reduction; degradation; enhancement; impairment; recovery; appreciation; depreciation; conversion-related change; partial loss; complete loss; other governed change types.
The record must preserve the classification actually determined rather than silently reclassifying it downstream.
Magnitude Preservation
VCRM receives the governed Value Change Magnitude from VCMM.
Magnitude may be:
quantitative; qualitative; proportional; monetary; operational; physical; capability-based; performance-based; multi-dimensional; conditionally determined.
Where magnitude contains uncertainty, range, confidence, methodology, baseline, or reference conditions, those properties should remain connected to the record.
A stored number without its basis may lose its governed meaning.
Causation Link Preservation
VCRM receives the governed causal relationship from VCCM.
The record may preserve:
causal factor; causal basis; causal chain; contributing causes; alternative causes; causal contribution; causal-link strength; uncertainty; contested causation; unresolved causation.
VCRM must not transform:
Possible Cause
into
Established Cause
merely because the relationship has entered a formal record.
Temporal Anchoring

Value Change requires a temporal basis.
Where possible, VCRM should distinguish between:
Occurrence Time
when the underlying change occurred;
Detection Time
when the change became observable;
Determination Time
when the change was formally determined;
Recording Time
when the governed record was created.
These timestamps may differ materially.
For example:
Value deterioration occurred gradually over six months
but
was detected during a quarterly review
and
formally determined two weeks later.
Collapsing these moments into one timestamp can distort lifecycle analysis.
Point Change and Period Change
VCRM supports both:
Point-in-Time Change
and
Change Across a Period.
A payment may create a relatively discrete Value Change.
Physical deterioration, capability degradation, market decline, or operational improvement may occur progressively.
The record should therefore preserve whether the change represents:
event-based change; interval-based change; cumulative change; continuous change; progressive change; episodic change.
Evidence Linkage
A Value Change Record should remain linked to the evidence supporting its governed determinations where such evidence exists.
Evidence may include:
measurements; operational data; transaction records; market observations; technical inspection; sensor information; accounting information; contractual information; simulation outputs; valuation analysis; expert determination; external authority determination; another governed evidential basis.

VCRM does not validate the evidence itself.
It preserves the relationship between the record and the evidential basis upon which the relevant determination relies.
Determination Provenance
A governed record should preserve sufficient provenance to reconstruct how its material determinations entered the record.
This may include:
determination source; methodology; responsible process; relevant system; external determination; date; version; applicable conditions; referenced evidence; superseded determination.
The objective is not to turn VCRM into an audit architecture.
The objective is to prevent Value Change records from becoming detached from the basis that gives them meaning.
Uncertainty Preservation
Uncertainty must travel with the Value Change Record.
Examples include:
Magnitude: CHF 8–11M reduction
rather than silently storing:
Magnitude: CHF 9.5M.
Or:
Causal Link: Supported
rather than:
Cause: Established.
VCRM preserves uncertainty generated by upstream governance.
It does not erase uncertainty to make records appear simpler.
Limitation Preservation
Material limitations affecting interpretation of the Value Change should remain attached to the record.
Limitations may relate to:
incomplete evidence; partial observation; uncertain baseline; unresolved causation; model dependence; limited measurement; missing period; conditional magnitude; contested determination; scope restriction; temporal uncertainty.

A record without its material limitations may become misleading even if every stored number is technically correct.
Record Status
A Value Change Record may have a governed status.
A minimum model may include:
Draft
Active
Under Review
Contested
Corrected
Superseded
Archived
Status must remain distinguishable from the underlying Value Change itself.
Record Status ≠ Value State.
Record Versioning
Value Change records may evolve when new information becomes available.
VCRM should therefore support versioning.
For example:
Record V1
Initial magnitude:
−CHF 8M to −CHF 12M
Causal basis:
Indeterminate
Later evidence produces:
Record V2
Magnitude:
−CHF 9.4M
Causal basis:
Supported multi-causal relationship.
The new version should not silently erase the previous record.
The lifecycle should preserve:
what was known,
when it was known,
and
what changed in the determination.
Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Where a record contains an error, VCRM should support correction while preserving appropriate historical continuity.
Therefore:
Correction ≠ Deletion of Prior Governance History.
A corrected record may identify:
previous value; corrected value; correction basis; correction time; affected determination; resulting version.
This enables reconstruction of decisions made using earlier information.
Supersession
A Value Change Record may be superseded where a later governed determination replaces it.
Supersession should identify:
Superseded Record
→ Supersession Basis
→ New Record

→ Effective Relationship.
Supersession does not imply that the earlier record was necessarily erroneous.
It may simply reflect better evidence or a later determination.
Record Immutability and Controlled Evolution
VCRM does not require one universal technical implementation.
Organizations may use:
append-only records; version-controlled databases; event stores; relational systems; distributed ledgers; enterprise systems; governed data platforms; hybrid infrastructures.
The methodological requirement is that material history remain reconstructable.
Therefore:
Technical Mutability may vary.
Governance History must remain controlled.
Record Granularity
VCRM should preserve sufficient granularity to represent materially distinct Value Changes separately.
For example, an enterprise may experience:
+CHF 20M technological capability gain
and
−CHF 12M market-access deterioration
during the same period.
Recording only:
Net Value Change: +CHF 8M
may destroy materially relevant lifecycle information.
VCRM therefore supports separate change records that may later be aggregated where appropriate.
Aggregation ≠ Replacement
Multiple Value Change Records may be aggregated for:
portfolio analysis; enterprise reporting; investment assessment; asset management; banking; insurance; infrastructure management; mission management; strategic analysis.
However:
Aggregated Value Change ≠ Replacement of Constituent Change Records.
The underlying records should remain traceable where materially relevant.

Record Relationships
Value Change Records may have relationships such as:
sequential; concurrent; cumulative; causal; compensating; offsetting; dependent; cascading; reversing; recovery-related; transformation-related.
These relationships enable VFM® to represent complex value histories rather than isolated snapshots.
Value Change Chain
VCRM enables reconstruction of a Value Change Chain.
For example:
Value State A → Change Record 001: +15% → Value State B → Change Record 002: −8% → Value State C → Change Record 003: −100% → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state
The chain allows the current Value State to be understood through the sequence of governed changes that produced it.
Lifecycle Continuity
VCRM creates continuity between Value Change and subsequent VFM® governance.
A Value Change Record may become an input to:
Value State reassessment; value transition governance; value flow analysis; value loss analysis; value recovery analysis; monetization mechanisms; de-monetization mechanisms; re-monetization mechanisms; portfolio aggregation; future lifecycle standards.
This is why VCRM is not merely documentation.
It is a lifecycle interface.
Machine-Readable Record Principle
VCRM should support machine-readable representation where implementation permits.
A machine-readable Value Change Record may enable systems to identify:
Object X
Value Context Y
Previous State A
Change Type: Decrease
Magnitude: −17%
Cause Link: Supported
Resulting State B
Effective Period: T1–T2

Uncertainty: Defined
Record Version: 3
This enables automated reasoning across value histories without collapsing governance context.
Cross-System Portability
A Value Change Record should remain interpretable when transferred between systems where legitimate.
Portability requires preservation of material semantics.
A transferred record should not lose:
value context; object reference; state relationship; type; magnitude basis; causal-link state; temporal basis; uncertainty; limitations; version.
The record may change technical format.
Its governed meaning should not silently change.
VCRM Boundary with VCIM
VCIM determines:
whether Value Change occurred.
VCRM records the governed result.
Therefore:
Change Identification ≠ Change Recording.
VCRM Boundary with VCTM
VCTM determines:
what type of Value Change occurred.
VCRM preserves that determination.
Therefore:
Classification ≠ Record.
VCRM Boundary with VCMM
VCMM determines:
the magnitude of Value Change.
VCRM preserves the magnitude and its basis.
Therefore:
Magnitude Determination ≠ Magnitude Record.
VCRM Boundary with VCCM
VCCM governs:
the causal relationship associated with Value Change.
VCRM preserves that causal relationship without independently establishing it.
Therefore:
Causation Link ≠ Change Record.
VCRM Boundary with VSS
VSS governs:
the current governed Value State.
VCRM governs:
the persistent record of a Value Change.
Therefore:
Value State ≠ Value Change Record.
The two may be linked:

Prior Value State → Value Change Record → Resulting Value State.
VCRM Boundary with OBIDENITY®
VCRM may reference the identity of the value-bearing object.
It does not establish universal object identity, ownership, origin, authority, or permission.
Where those relationships require governance, OBIDENITY® remains the relevant architecture.
VCRM Boundary with INTEGROS®
VCRM requires records to preserve the information necessary for their governed meaning.
It does not replace general integrity governance.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties affecting the record, evidence, state, or supporting systems.
VCRM Boundary with ADIT®
VCRM creates and maintains the governed Value Change Record.
ADIT® may govern auditability, evidential preservation, examination, verification, or reconstruction.
Therefore:
Record Governance ≠ Audit Governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Record Object Creation
Create a uniquely identifiable Value Change Record.
2. Value Context Linkage
Link the record to the governed value and relevant value-bearing object.
3. Prior State Linkage
Identify the preceding governed Value State where applicable.
4. Change Determination Assembly
Preserve the outputs of VCIM, VCTM, VCMM, and VCCM.
5. Temporal Anchoring
Record relevant occurrence, detection, determination, and recording times or periods.
6. Evidence & Provenance Linkage
Preserve links to supporting evidence and determination provenance.
7. Uncertainty & Limitation Preservation

Attach material uncertainty, conditions, and limitations.
8. Resulting State Linkage
Link the record to the resulting governed Value State where determined.
9. Version & Status Control
Assign record version, status, correction, and supersession relationships.
10. Lifecycle Availability
Make the governed record available to authorized downstream VFM® processes without loss of material meaning.

Use Case 1 — Banking: Reconstructable
Collateral Value History
A bank monitors an industrial asset used as collateral.
During three years the asset experiences several materially different Value Changes:
Year 1: technological upgrade increases productive capability.
Year 2: major customer loss reduces operating value.
Year 3: physical deterioration reduces productive capacity.
A conventional system may preserve only periodic valuations:
CHF 30M → CHF 34M → CHF 27M → CHF 21M.
VCRM preserves the governed lifecycle behind those numbers:

Value State A → Upgrade Change Record → Value State B → Customer-Loss Change Record → Value State C → Deterioration Change Record → Current Value State D.
Each record retains its:
change type, magnitude, causal basis, evidence, temporal context, uncertainty, and version.
The bank can therefore distinguish between value deterioration caused by:
market conditions,
operational deterioration,
and
physical asset degradation.
This supports stronger:
credit monitoring, collateral governance, impairment assessment, restructuring analysis, recovery planning, and portfolio risk analysis.
The institution no longer sees only:
what the asset is worth today.
It can reconstruct:
how the asset arrived at its current governed Value State.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Preserving Mission
Value Changes Across Operations
A long-duration space mission has an initial governed mission capability and value basis.
During operations:
solar-array efficiency falls;
propellant consumption exceeds plan;
a software optimization reduces computational demand;
a scientific instrument develops a partial fault;
mission planning recovers part of the lost operational capability.
These changes do not move mission value in one direction.
Some destroy value.
Some preserve value.
Some recover value.
Some affect only one mission objective.
VCRM creates separate governed records:
Solar Degradation Record
Propellant Consumption Record
Computational Optimization Record
Instrument Degradation Record
Mission Recovery Record.

Each record remains connected to:
the relevant mission Value Context,
the prior Value State,
the magnitude of change,
the causal basis,
the applicable mission period,
the evidence supporting the determination,
and
the resulting Value State.
Mission systems can therefore reconstruct:
Initial Mission Value → Value Loss → Further Value Loss → Efficiency Gain → Capability Degradation → Value Recovery → Current Mission Value State.
This allows future mission decisions to be based not merely on the current state but on the governed history of how mission value evolved.
Enterprise Application
VCRM enables organizations to build a persistent Value Change history rather than maintaining disconnected valuations, measurements, observations, or reports.
It can support:
banking; insurance; investment; asset management; industrial production; infrastructure; energy; AI systems; computational infrastructure; blockchain and digital assets; intellectual property; supply chains; mission systems; public assets; organizational capability; technology portfolios.
Its strategic importance increases where organizations need to understand not merely:
What is the value now?
but:
How did the value get here?
A governed Value Change history can support future analysis of:
value creation,
value destruction,
value preservation,
value recovery,
causal patterns,
transition mechanisms,
and
value lifecycle performance.
Foundational Principles
Value Change is not the same as a Value Change Record.

A record represents change; it does not create the underlying change.
A Value Change Record must remain connected to its Value Context.
Current Value State should be reconstructable from materially relevant prior Value Changes where the evidence permits.
Change type, magnitude, causation, uncertainty, and limitations must not lose their governed meaning when recorded.
Occurrence time, detection time, determination time, and recording time may be different.
Correction must not require historical erasure.
Supersession must remain traceable.
Aggregation must not destroy materially relevant constituent changes.
A record version must preserve what was known at that point in the lifecycle.
Value Change history is a governed lifecycle asset, not merely administrative documentation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Change Record Module establishes the persistent record layer of the Value Change Standard by transforming identified, classified, magnitude-determined, and causally linked Value Change into a structured, traceable, context-bound, temporally anchored, evidence-linked, uncertainty-preserving, version-controlled, and lifecycle-usable governed record. Through governance of record identity, Value Context linkage, prior and resulting Value States, change type, magnitude, causation links, temporal basis, evidence, provenance, uncertainty, limitations, status, correction, supersession, record relationships, aggregation, portability, and lifecycle continuity, VCRM enables Value Change to remain reconstructable after the immediate determination has ended. By separating the reality of Value Change from its recorded representation, and by preserving the outputs of the preceding VCS modules without silently redefining them, VCRM creates the durable governance bridge between individual Value Changes and the wider VFM® value lifecycle. A governed value system should not merely know the current Value State; where materially possible, it should be able to reconstruct the governed sequence of changes through which that state emerged.
