Canonical Definition
Value Change Type Module (VCTM) is the second Core Module of the Value Change Standard (VCS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VCTM governs the structured classification of an identified Value Change according to what kind of change has occurred to the governed value.
The Module establishes a controlled classification layer through which materially different forms of Value Change can be distinguished without reducing all value movement to price, money, accounting treatment, market movement, or a single universal measurement system.
Its foundational task is:

to determine the nature and directional character of an identified Value Change before its magnitude and causal relationship are determined.
Architectural Position
VCTM is the second module within VCS.
It follows:
VCIM — Value Change Identification Module
and precedes:
VCMM — Value Change Magnitude Module.
The internal sequence is:
Governed Value State → VCIM — Value Change Identification → VCTM — Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude
→ VCCM — Value Change Causation Link → VCRM — Value Change Record
VCIM establishes:
that a material Value Change has occurred or requires governance.
VCTM establishes:
what kind of Value Change occurred.
VCMM subsequently establishes:
how large or significant that change is.
Internal Module Flow
Identified Value Change → Change Context Confirmation → Affected Value Dimension Identification → Directional Classification → Change Character Classification → Temporal Classification → Reversibility Classification → Composite Change Assessment → Value Change Type Determination → Governed Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude Module
Operational Space
VCTM governs the classification space between:
an identified material Value Change
and
its subsequent magnitude determination.
Its operational space includes:

directional change; positive change; negative change; neutral structural change; capability change; utility change; availability change; productivity change; condition change; accessibility change; scarcity change; relevance change; resilience change; strategic change; operational change; economic change; physical change; digital change; temporary change; persistent change; reversible change; irreversible change;
gradual change; sudden change; cumulative change; composite change; multi-dimensional change.
Value Change Is Multi-Dimensional
VCTM rejects the assumption that every Value Change can be represented adequately through one number.
A value-bearing object may simultaneously experience:
Operational Value ↑
Physical Condition ↓
Energy Efficiency ↑
Maintenance Burden ↑
Strategic Relevance ↑
Market Value ↓
These changes are not necessarily contradictory.
They may represent different value dimensions within the same governed context.
VCTM therefore preserves materially distinct change dimensions rather than forcing them prematurely into a single net- value classification.
Directional Classification
An identified Value Change may be classified directionally as:
1. Positive Value Change
The governed value has materially increased, improved, expanded, strengthened, become more useful, or otherwise moved positively within its defined Value Context.
2. Negative Value Change

The governed value has materially decreased, deteriorated, weakened, become less useful, or otherwise moved negatively within its defined Value Context.
3. Neutral Structural Value Change
The structure, composition, accessibility, distribution, or form of value has materially changed without sufficient basis to classify the overall movement as positive or negative.
4. Mixed Value Change
Different governed value dimensions have moved in different directions.
For example:
Productivity ↑
while
Maintenance Cost ↑.
The result should not automatically be collapsed into one directional statement.
5. Direction Indeterminate
A material Value Change has been established, but available information does not yet support a legitimate directional determination.
Positive ≠ Universally Beneficial
A positive Value Change is always contextual.
A technological development may increase value for:
Beneficiary A
while reducing value for:
Beneficiary B.
Likewise, an increase in scarcity may increase economic value while decreasing accessibility or social usefulness.
Therefore:
Positive Value Change in Context A ≠ Universal Positive Value Change
VCTM preserves the beneficiary and Value Context inherited from upstream VFM® governance.
Negative ≠ Universal Loss
A negative Value Change is equally context-dependent.
An industrial machine may lose:
market value
while gaining:
strategic value
because replacement equipment becomes unavailable.
A dataset may lose:
commercial exclusivity
while gaining:

research utility.
A building may lose:
operational usefulness
while gaining:
historical significance.
VCTM therefore requires the affected value dimension to remain explicit.
Change Character Classification
Beyond direction, VCTM may classify the character of the change.
A Value Change may be:
Capability Change
Change in what an object, system, resource, organization, or other value-bearing entity is capable of doing.
Utility Change
Change in usefulness for the governed beneficiary or purpose.
Productivity Change
Change in the amount of useful output obtainable from a governed resource basis.
Efficiency Change
Change in the relationship between useful output and consumed resources.
Availability Change
Change in whether or how much governed value can actually be accessed or used.
Condition Change
Change in physical, digital, operational, organizational, or other relevant condition affecting value.
Accessibility Change
Change in the ability of the relevant beneficiary to reach, obtain, activate, or use the value.
Scarcity Change
Change in relative availability or rarity affecting the governed value context.
Relevance Change
Change in the importance or usefulness of value relative to the governed purpose.
Resilience Change
Change in the ability of value to persist, recover, remain available, or withstand disruption.
Strategic Change
Change in longer-term importance, optionality, positioning, dependency reduction, or capability.
Economic Change

Change in economically relevant value without assuming that economic change must equal market-price movement.
Physical Change
Change arising in the physical value characteristics of an object.
Digital Change
Change in digitally represented, digitally enabled, computational, informational, or software-based value.
These types may coexist.
Monetary and Non-Monetary Change
VCTM supports:
Monetary Value Change
and
Non-Monetary Value Change.
A monetary expression may be available where appropriate.
But monetary representation is not required for Value Change classification.
Examples of non-monetary Value Change include:
increased mission capability; reduced computation requirement; increased system resilience; increased production capacity; loss of data relevance; reduced infrastructure availability; improved scientific usefulness; increased resource accessibility; loss of technological capability.
This enables VFM® to govern Value Change before or independently from monetization.
Market Price Change ≠ Value Change Type
Market price may provide an important signal.
But:
Price Movement ≠ Automatic Value Change Classification
A price can move because of:
liquidity; speculation; market sentiment; supply shock; regulatory expectations; currency movement; temporary imbalance; information asymmetry.
VCTM may classify an associated economic or market-related Value Change where the governed basis supports it.

It does not assume that every price movement proves an equivalent change in the underlying governed value.
Accounting Change ≠ Value Change Type
An accounting reclassification, impairment, depreciation entry, write-up, or other accounting event may correspond with Value Change.
But the accounting event and the governed Value Change remain distinguishable.
Therefore:
Accounting Treatment ≠ Value Change Type
Accounting systems may consume VFM® outputs or provide evidence to VFM® without becoming identical to VFM® value governance.
Temporary and Persistent Change
VCTM may classify Value Change temporally.
Temporary Value Change
The change exists for a limited period or under temporary conditions and is reasonably expected to reverse or expire.
Persistent Value Change
The change continues beyond ordinary temporary variation and materially affects the governed value over an extended period.
Persistence does not necessarily mean irreversibility.
A persistent change may later be reversed through another Value Change.
Sudden and Gradual Change
VCTM may distinguish:
Sudden Value Change
from
Gradual Value Change.
Sudden change may arise through:
failure; innovation; transaction-related event; regulatory event; discovery; damage; technological breakthrough; operational disruption.
Gradual change may arise through:
deterioration; learning; optimization; aging; resource depletion; technological obsolescence; capability accumulation; network effects.

The classification helps downstream systems understand the structure of the Value Change without assuming its cause.
Reversible and Irreversible Change
A Value Change may be classified as:
Reversible
where the relevant value condition can reasonably return toward the prior governed state,
or
Irreversible
where restoration of the prior value condition is no longer realistically possible within the governed context.
Where reversibility cannot yet be established:
Reversibility Indeterminate
should remain available.
VCTM must not manufacture certainty where the future state remains unknown.
Cumulative Change
A Value Change may emerge through accumulated smaller changes.
VCTM may classify:
Cumulative Value Change
where the governed change is materially produced through repeated or progressive changes over time.
Examples include:
Component Wear → Efficiency Loss → Maintenance Increase → Availability Reduction
or:
Repeated Optimization → Resource Reduction → Capacity Recovery → Productivity Increase.
This preserves the structural character of change before VCMM determines magnitude.
Composite Value Change
A single event or development may create several distinct Value Changes.
For example:
AI Automation Deployment
may create:
Productivity Value ↑
Computational Cost ↑
Human Labor Requirement ↓
Operational Scalability ↑
Dependency Risk ↑
VCTM may represent this as a Composite Value Change rather than forcing all consequences into one classification.

The individual value dimensions remain separately governable.
Direct and Indirect Change
VCTM may distinguish:
Direct Value Change
where the relevant value-bearing object itself materially changes,
from
Indirect Value Change
where its governed value changes because its relationship to another object, beneficiary, environment, capability, or context has materially changed.
Example:
A machine remains physically unchanged.
A new technology makes its production process obsolete.
The machine may experience:
Indirect Negative Value Change
without physical deterioration.
This distinction is important for technology, intellectual property, infrastructure, strategic assets, digital systems, and economic value.
Latent Value Change
A material Value Change may occur before its practical consequence becomes immediately visible.
VCTM may classify such a change as:
Latent Value Change
where the underlying governed value has changed but the downstream consequence has not yet fully manifested.
Examples include:
technological obsolescence before revenue decline; structural deterioration before failure; capability improvement before deployment; data degradation before decision error; resource depletion before operational shortage.
This allows VFM® to represent Value Change earlier than systems that observe only downstream consequences.
Realized and Unrealized Change
Where relevant, VCTM may distinguish:
Realized Value Change
from
Unrealized Value Change.

This classification must not automatically inherit accounting or tax definitions.
Within VFM®, the distinction concerns whether the governed change has become operationally manifested or remains present without the relevant realization event defined for that Value Context.
External accounting, legal, or tax systems may define realization differently.
VFM® does not replace those definitions.
Value Conversion ≠ Value Change
A value may change form without necessarily increasing or decreasing total governed value.
For example:
Stored Energy
→ Operational Capability
or:
Information
→ Decision Capability.
Where the relevant transformation represents a broader value-flow mechanism rather than merely a change in existing value, downstream VFM® standards may govern that transition.
VCTM should therefore avoid classifying every value transformation as positive or negative change.
Change Type Combination
VCTM permits multiple classifications where necessary.
An identified Value Change may therefore be classified as:
Positive
Capability
Operational
Persistent
Gradual
Reversible
or:
Negative
Physical
Cumulative
Persistent
Potentially Irreversible.
This creates richer machine-readable governance than a single label such as:
“value increased”
or
“value decreased.”
Classification Hierarchy
A practical VCTM classification may operate across several dimensions:
Direction → Positive · Negative · Neutral Structural · Mixed · Indeterminate

Domain Character → Operational · Economic · Physical · Digital · Strategic · Other Governed Domain
Value Character → Capability · Utility · Productivity · Efficiency · Availability · Accessibility · Scarcity · Relevance · Resilience · Other Defined Character
Temporal Character → Sudden · Gradual · Temporary · Persistent · Cumulative
Reversibility → Reversible · Irreversible · Indeterminate
Manifestation → Direct · Indirect · Latent · Realized · Unrealized
This structure can be extended where a domain requires additional classifications.
Classification Criteria
Each organization implementing VCTM should define criteria for the classifications it uses.
Classification criteria should be:
explicit; reproducible where appropriate; understandable; context-linked; beneficiary-aware; sufficiently stable; machine-readable where automated; version-controlled where changed.
The purpose is not to create one universal taxonomy for every possible form of value.
The purpose is to make Value Change classification governed rather than implicit.
Uncertainty in Classification
A Value Change may be clearly identified while its precise type remains uncertain.
VCTM therefore preserves:
Confirmed Change + Uncertain Type
where necessary.
Possible states may include:
Type Confirmed
Type Conditional
Multiple Types Applicable
Type Indeterminate
Type Under Review
This prevents uncertainty about classification from invalidating an otherwise legitimate Value Change identification.

Classification Consistency
Equivalent Value Changes within the same governed framework should be classified consistently.
Where two materially equivalent events receive different classifications, the system should be able to explain the difference through:
context; beneficiary; purpose; evidence; classification criteria; object condition; temporal basis; another governed distinction.
Classification consistency is essential if VCTM outputs are later used for analytics, automation, accounting interfaces, banking systems, taxation models, blockchain systems, or policy analysis.
VCTM Boundary with VCIM
VCIM determines:
Has a material Value Change occurred?
VCTM determines:
What kind of Value Change occurred?
Therefore:
Change Identification ≠ Change Type
VCTM receives an identified Value Change and does not independently recreate the identification process.
VCTM Boundary with VCMM
VCTM determines the type and structural character of Value Change.
VCMM determines its magnitude.
Therefore:
Change Type ≠ Change Magnitude
A Value Change may be:
Negative + Operational + Persistent
without VCTM determining whether the magnitude is:
minor, moderate, major, critical, 5%, CHF 5 million, or another measure.
VCTM Boundary with VCCM
VCTM determines what kind of Value Change occurred.
VCCM governs the relationship between the Value Change and relevant causal events, conditions, activities, or mechanisms.
Therefore:
Change Type ≠ Cause of Change
For example:
Negative Capability Change

may be classified before the system knows whether its cause was:
physical deterioration, software failure, regulatory restriction, market change, or another mechanism.
VCTM Boundary with VSS
VSS determines the governed Value State.
VCTM determines the type of movement affecting value.
Therefore:
Value State ≠ Value Change Type
A negative Value Change does not by itself determine the resulting Value State.
VCTM Boundary with External Systems
VCTM may consume information from:
Markets
Accounting
Banking
Insurance
Blockchain
Industrial Systems
AI Systems
Infrastructure Monitoring
Scientific Systems
Mission Systems
and other environments.
It classifies the resulting Value Change within VFM®.
It does not assume governance over the external mechanism.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identified Value Change
Receive the governed Value Change identified through VCIM.
2. Context Confirmation
Confirm the applicable Value Context, value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference basis.
3. Affected Value Dimension
Identify which dimension or dimensions of value materially changed.
4. Direction Classification
Determine whether the change is positive, negative, neutral structural, mixed, or directionally indeterminate.
5. Character Classification
Determine the applicable capability, utility, productivity, efficiency, availability, condition, accessibility, scarcity, relevance, resilience, strategic, economic, physical, digital, or other governed change character.

6. Temporal Classification
Determine whether the change is sudden, gradual, temporary, persistent, cumulative, or another defined temporal type.
7. Reversibility Classification
Determine whether the change is reversible, irreversible, or indeterminate.
8. Manifestation Classification
Determine whether the change is direct, indirect, latent, realized, unrealized, or another defined manifestation type where relevant.
9. Composite Assessment
Determine whether multiple Value Change types or dimensions must remain separately represented.
10. Value Change Type Determination
Create the governed classification for downstream magnitude assessment.
Governance Outputs
VCTM may produce:
Value Change Type Record Value Change Direction Classification Value Dimension Change Record Value Change Character Classification Value Change Temporal Classification Value Change Reversibility Classification Value Change Manifestation Classification Composite Value Change Record Mixed Value Change Record
Value Change Type Uncertainty Record Value Change Classification Basis Governed Value Change Type
These outputs provide the governed input for:
VCMM — Value Change Magnitude Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking: One Asset, Several
Different Value Changes
A bank has financed an industrial production facility.
Monitoring identifies material changes:
Production Capability ↓
Energy Efficiency ↓
Maintenance Requirement ↑
but at the same time:
Strategic Scarcity ↑

because comparable production facilities have become difficult to replace.
A conventional single-value model could attempt to collapse all of this immediately into one financial valuation.
VCTM preserves the structure first.
The facility may contain:
Negative Operational Value Change
Negative Efficiency Value Change
Negative Physical/Condition Value Change
and simultaneously:
Positive Strategic/Scarcity Value Change.
The change can therefore be classified as:
Mixed + Multi-Dimensional + Persistent
before VCMM determines the magnitude of each dimension.
This gives banking systems a richer basis for:
collateral monitoring, credit-risk assessment, financing decisions, restructuring, and asset lifecycle analysis.
The key advantage is:
the bank does not need to wait until several fundamentally different value changes are compressed into one market price before understanding what is happening to the asset.
Use Case 2 — AI / Computational Infrastructure:
Cost Reduction Creates Several Value Changes
An organization operates a large AI infrastructure environment.
A new orchestration method enables the same required operational output with:
25% less computation
and
18% less energy consumption
while maintaining the required service performance.
No asset has necessarily been sold.
No ownership has changed.
No market transaction is required.
VCTM can classify the resulting changes separately as:
Positive Efficiency Value Change
Positive Resource-Availability Value Change

Positive Operational Value Change
and potentially:
Positive Economic Value Change
where the reduced resource consumption produces a governed economic benefit.
At the same time, if the optimization creates increased dependence on one specialized infrastructure provider, another governed context may identify:
Negative Strategic Resilience Value Change.
The result is not simply:
“value increased.”
It is a structured map of how value changed.
This classification can subsequently support:
cost optimization, infrastructure planning, AI resource governance, investment decisions, risk assessment, and future value accounting mechanisms.
Enterprise Application
VCTM provides the classification vocabulary required for organizations to understand Value Change before they attempt to quantify, monetize, account for, tax, finance, insure, transfer, or respond to it.
It is applicable across:
banking; insurance; investment; accounting interfaces; industrial production; infrastructure; AI and computational systems; energy; blockchain; digital assets; public assets; intellectual property; science;
mission systems; organizational capability; future value-based economic systems.
Its central contribution is structural.
Without VCTM, systems may know:
that value changed.
With VCTM, they can begin to know:
how value changed.
Foundational Principles
Value Change identification must precede Value Change classification.
Value Change type must remain distinct from Value Change magnitude.

Value Change type must remain distinct from Value Change causation.
Positive and negative Value Change are context-dependent, not universal.
One value-bearing object may experience multiple Value Changes simultaneously.
Different value dimensions must not be prematurely collapsed into one net figure.
Market-price movement is not a universal definition of Value Change.
Accounting treatment is not a universal definition of Value Change.
Value Change may be monetary or non-monetary.
Value Change may be direct, indirect, latent, temporary, persistent, reversible, irreversible, sudden, gradual, cumulative, or composite.
Classification uncertainty must remain visible rather than being converted into false certainty.
The purpose of VCTM is not to impose one universal taxonomy of value, but to make the character of Value Change explicit, structured, governable, and reusable.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Change Type Module establishes the classification layer of the Value Change Standard by determining the directional, dimensional, structural, temporal, reversibility, and manifestation characteristics of an identified Value Change before magnitude and causation are determined. Through governance of positive, negative, neutral, mixed, capability, utility, productivity, efficiency, availability, condition, accessibility, scarcity, relevance, resilience, operational, economic, physical, digital, strategic, temporary, persistent, sudden, gradual, cumulative, reversible, irreversible, direct, indirect, latent, realized, unrealized, and composite Value Changes, VCTM prevents fundamentally different movements of value from being silently collapsed into a single price, monetary amount, accounting entry, or generic increase-or-decrease statement. By preserving context, beneficiary, affected value dimension, multi-dimensionality, and classification uncertainty, VCTM provides VFM® with the structured Value Change vocabulary required for downstream magnitude determination, causation linkage, recording, analytics, automation, banking, infrastructure, computational systems, and future value-governance mechanisms. Before a system can legitimately determine how much value changed, it must first establish what kind of change occurred.

Canonical Definition
Value Change Standard (VCS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the identification, characterization, magnitude determination, causation linkage, and recording of material change affecting existing governed value.
VCS establishes whether value has materially changed relative to a governed reference state, determines what kind of change occurred, establishes the magnitude and direction of that change, links the change to relevant causal events, conditions, mechanisms, or relationships where such linkage is supportable, and preserves the resulting Value Change as a governed lifecycle record.
The Standard governs:
what happened to value

rather than assuming governance over every external mechanism capable of causing the change.
A market event, technological development, payment, operational improvement, physical deterioration, regulatory event, innovation, resource depletion, infrastructure failure, environmental condition, contractual event, or other mechanism may alter value without that mechanism itself becoming governed by VFM®.
The foundational distinction is:
Cause of Change ≠ Value Change
VCS governs the change to value.
The originating mechanism may remain governed by another applicable architecture, methodology, legal framework, operational system, market system, accounting system, or domain.
Core Question
When has existing value materially changed, and what change has occurred to it?
Architectural Position
VCS occupies the sixth governed space within the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value State Standard (VSS)
which establishes:
the current governed state of value.
VCS then asks:
Has that value materially changed relative to its governed reference state, and if so, what happened to it?
The architectural sequence is:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Value State
→ Value Change
VCS therefore represents the first explicit VFM® layer in which an already established Value State is examined for material difference across time, condition, event, relationship, capability, or other relevant reference basis.
Governance Flow Position

The VFM® governance flow entering VCS is:
Governed Value State
→ Reference Value State
→ Observed Value Condition
→ Potential Difference
→ Materiality Assessment
→ Value Change Identification
→ Value Change Type
→ Value Change Magnitude
→ Value Change Causation Link
→ Value Change Record
→ Governed Value Change
The resulting Governed Value Change may subsequently inform later VFM® mechanisms governing how value moves, transforms, degrades, recovers, becomes monetized, becomes de-monetized, or otherwise progresses through its lifecycle.
Operational Space
VCS governs the methodological space between:
an established governed Value State
and
a determined material change to that value.
Its governed space includes:
reference-state identification; observed value condition; value difference detection; materiality; direction of change; type of change; magnitude of change; temporal change; event-linked change; condition-linked change; beneficiary-specific change; context-specific change; capability-related change; utilization-related change; economic change; operational change; physical value change; digital value change; strategic value change; reversible change; irreversible change; temporary change; persistent change; gradual change; sudden change; cumulative change; compound change; causal linkage; multi-causal change; uncertainty affecting change determination; change recording; change lineage.
Value Change Requires a Reference

Value cannot meaningfully be said to have changed unless the change is evaluated against a defined reference.
The reference may be:
previous Value State; previous Value State Record; defined baseline; reference date; reference event; reference condition; previous capability; previous utility; previous beneficiary relationship; previous operational state; another explicitly governed comparison point.
Therefore:
Observed Difference without Reference ≠ Governed Value Change
The Value State Record established through VSS provides a natural reference basis for VCS.
Value Difference ≠ Material Value Change
Not every measurable variation should become a governed Value Change.
Value may fluctuate within:
normal operational ranges; expected market variation; measurement uncertainty; seasonal conditions; ordinary utilization patterns; insignificant technical variation; defined tolerance bands.
VCS therefore distinguishes:
Value Variation
from
Material Value Change.
A change becomes governable under VCS when it crosses the applicable materiality basis established for the governed value context.
Materiality Principle
Materiality determines whether a difference is significant enough to enter formal Value Change governance.
Materiality may be defined through:

absolute threshold; relative threshold; percentage change; capability threshold; operational threshold; beneficiary impact; strategic significance; economic consequence; risk consequence; persistence; reversibility; regulatory significance; organizational criteria; combination of factors.
VCS does not impose one universal materiality threshold across all value.
The applicable threshold must correspond to the governed value context.
Direction of Value Change
A Value Change may move value in different directions.
A minimum distinction includes:
Positive Value Change
where governed value materially increases.
Negative Value Change
where governed value materially decreases.
Neutral Structural Change
where the structure, composition, or conditions of value materially change without an immediate net increase or decrease being determinable.
Indeterminate Direction
where material change is established but available information does not support a legitimate directional determination.
Direction must not be forced where the evidence does not support it.
Value Change Type
VCS requires material change to be characterized rather than recorded merely as:
“value changed.”
Change types may include:

increase; decrease; degradation; enhancement; impairment; recovery; activation; deactivation; conversion-related change; utilization change; capability change; scarcity change; dependency change; accessibility change; relevance change; beneficiary change; strategic change; structural change; contextual change.
Organizations may define additional domain-specific Value Change Types while preserving the canonical distinction between the change itself and the mechanism causing it.
Magnitude of Value Change
VCS governs the determination of how materially value changed.
Magnitude may be expressed through:
absolute amount; relative amount; percentage; range; ordinal class; qualitative magnitude; capability delta; utility delta; operational delta; strategic significance; multi-dimensional value delta.
A minimum qualitative model may include:
Minor
Moderate
Substantial
Critical
where the organization defines the applicable criteria.
VCS does not require every form of value to be converted into money.
This is fundamental.
Value Change ≠ Price Change
A change in value may exist even where no market price exists.
Monetary and Non-Monetary Change
VFM® must be capable of governing value before, during, and after monetary representation.
VCS therefore supports change in:
monetary value
and
non-monetary value.
Examples of non-monetary change may include:

increased productive capability; reduced mission utility; improved strategic relevance; loss of interoperability; increased computational usefulness; deterioration of infrastructure capacity; increased information utility; reduced operational availability.
A monetary consequence may later be derived from such changes through another mechanism.
But:
Value Change does not require monetary expression to exist.
Temporal Character of Change
VCS recognizes that change may occur differently across time.
A Value Change may be:
Instantaneous
Rapid
Gradual
Cumulative
Periodic
Temporary
Persistent
Recurring
Progressive
The temporal character matters because two changes of equal apparent magnitude may have very different lifecycle consequences.
Temporary vs Persistent Change
A temporary reduction in value must remain distinguishable from persistent degradation.
For example:
Industrial Machine unavailable for scheduled maintenance
may temporarily reduce operational value.
This is different from:
Industrial Machine permanently incapable of required production.
Both may affect value.
Their persistence differs.
VCS therefore requires material persistence characteristics to remain visible where relevant.
Reversible vs Irreversible Change
A Value Change may be:
Reversible
where the previous or comparable Value State can reasonably be restored.
Conditionally Reversible
where restoration depends upon defined conditions.
Irreversible

where the previous Value State cannot reasonably be restored within the governed context.
Indeterminate
where reversibility cannot yet be established.
Reversibility may become important for later value recovery and lifecycle mechanisms.
Cumulative Value Change
Some important Value Changes do not arise from one dramatic event.
They emerge through accumulation.
Examples include:
progressive wear; repeated small efficiency losses; gradual technological obsolescence; increasing maintenance burden; declining network participation; repeated data degradation; incremental capability improvement; accumulated knowledge; progressive infrastructure deterioration.
VCS therefore permits:
Multiple Individually Minor Changes
→ Cumulative Material Value Change
A governance system that evaluates only isolated events may miss the material lifecycle change created by their accumulation.
Compound Value Change
Multiple forms of Value Change may occur simultaneously.
For example, a manufacturing asset may experience:
Physical Degradation
Reduced Operational Capability
Increased Maintenance Cost
Reduced Strategic Relevance
Lower Secondary-Market Utility.
These are related but not identical dimensions of change.
VCS should preserve materially distinct change dimensions rather than collapsing them prematurely into one number.
Context-Specific Change
A value-bearing object may change in one context without changing equally in another.
Example:
A data center becomes unsuitable for:

high-performance AI training
because of power limitations.
Its value may materially decline in that context.
The same facility may remain valuable for:
conventional enterprise computing.
Therefore:
Value Change in Context A ≠ Universal Value Change
VCS preserves the Value Context established upstream.
Beneficiary-Specific Change
Value may change differently for different beneficiaries.
A technology becoming obsolete for one organization may become economically useful to another organization operating under different requirements.
Therefore:
Value Change must remain beneficiary-aware where beneficiary materially affects value.
This prevents one beneficiary's loss of value from becoming a universal conclusion about the underlying object.
Value Change and ZVA™
A Value Change may move governed value toward:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
or away from it.
Example:
Active Value
→ Negative Value Change
→ Degraded Value
→ Further Negative Value Change
→ ZVA™
But VCS itself does not determine the new Value State.
It determines the material change that occurred.
The resulting state is governed through the applicable Value State process.
This preserves the distinction:
Value Change ≠ Value State
Value Recovery
Value may increase after previous degradation or zero-value condition.
For example:
ZVA™
may later become capable of producing value because of:

technological innovation; new beneficiary; new use case; repair; regulatory change; infrastructure development; new market access; new operational capability.
VCS may govern the material positive change.
The resulting Value State remains separately determined.
This prevents zero value from becoming incorrectly permanent.
Causation Link Principle
VCS distinguishes:
Value Change Determination
from
Causal Explanation.
A material Value Change may be established even where its complete cause remains uncertain.
Where a causal relationship is sufficiently supported, VCS may link the change to:
event; activity; condition; decision; transaction; deterioration; innovation; external market development; technological change; operational intervention; regulatory development; environmental event; relationship change; multiple contributing causes.
But the Standard must not manufacture causal certainty.
Correlation ≠ Causation
Temporal sequence or statistical association alone must not automatically be treated as causal proof.
Therefore:
Event Before Change ≠ Event Caused Change
and
Correlation with Change ≠ Proven Causation
Where causation remains uncertain, VCS may preserve:
Potential Causal Link
Supported Causal Link
Multi-Causal Relationship
or
Causation Indeterminate.
Multi-Causal Value Change
Many Value Changes arise from multiple mechanisms.
Example:
A commercial building may lose value because of:
energy inefficiency
higher financing costs
tenant demand change
regulatory requirements

physical deterioration.
VCS should not force such a change into one artificial cause.
Where multiple causal relationships materially contribute, they may remain separately represented.
External Event Boundary
External mechanisms may cause value to change without becoming governed spaces of VFM®.
For example:
Interest-rate decision
→ may affect →
Financing Conditions
→ may affect →
Property Value
VFM® does not need to govern monetary policy to govern the resulting Value Change.
Likewise:
Earthquake
→ Infrastructure Damage
→ Value Change
does not make earthquake governance part of VFM®.
This boundary allows VFM® to remain broadly applicable without attempting to absorb every domain capable of affecting value.
Transaction Boundary
A payment or transaction may cause Value Change.
But:
Transaction ≠ Value Change
A transaction system governs the transfer, settlement, execution, or recording of the transaction.
VCS governs what material change occurred to the governed value as a result, where applicable.
This distinction becomes important in banking, blockchain, digital assets, taxation, and accounting.
Market Price Boundary
Market price may be an input into Value Change governance.
But:
Market Price Change ≠ Automatically Governed Value Change
A temporary market-price movement may not materially change:
productive capability; utility; strategic value; operational relevance; beneficiary-specific value.
Conversely, a major Value Change may occur before any market price reflects it.

VFM® therefore prevents market price from becoming the universal definition of value.
Accounting Boundary
Accounting systems may recognize:
impairment; depreciation; appreciation; revaluation; gain; loss.
VCS does not replace accounting rules.
It may provide a governed Value Change layer that exists independently from accounting recognition.
Therefore:
Accounting Change ≠ VFM® Value Change
although the two may legitimately interact.
Tax Boundary
VCS does not determine:
taxable gain; taxable loss; tax base; deductible impairment; depreciation allowance; realization event; tax liability.
A future tax architecture may use governed Value Change information as an input.
The boundary remains:
VFM® determines what materially happened to value.
Tax governance determines whether and how that change produces a tax consequence.
This separation is essential if VFM® is later used as part of a value-flow-based taxation architecture.
Banking and Financial-System Relevance
Traditional financial systems often observe value through:
transactions; market prices; accounting records; collateral valuations; cash flows.
VCS adds another governable layer:
Value Change itself.
This may allow institutions to identify material value deterioration or improvement before it is fully expressed through a transaction, accounting entry, default, or market repricing.
Potential applications include:

collateral monitoring; credit-risk monitoring; asset lifecycle governance; infrastructure finance; investment monitoring; recovery analysis; portfolio change detection; early-warning systems.
Blockchain and Digital Asset Relevance
Blockchain systems are highly effective at recording:
transactions
and
state changes defined by protocol.
But protocol state change does not necessarily equal Value Change.
VCS can provide a separate governance layer capable of recording:
what happened to governed value as a consequence of or alongside a blockchain event.
This allows distinction between:
Token Transfer
Ownership Change
Protocol State Change
Market Price Change
and
Governed Value Change.
AI and Automated Value Monitoring
VCS is designed to support machine-readable implementation.
Automated systems may monitor:
Reference Value State
→ New Operational Information
→ Potential Value Difference
→ Materiality Test
→ Value Change Candidate
→ Governed Value Change Determination
AI may assist with:
anomaly detection; change detection; causal candidate identification; magnitude estimation; pattern recognition; cumulative change monitoring.
Automation must not silently convert:
detected correlation
into
established causation.
Value Change Record
Every material governed Value Change should be capable of producing a reconstructable record.
A Value Change Record may include:
Change ID
Governed Value ID
Reference State
Reference Point
Observed Condition
Change Type
Direction
Magnitude

Materiality Basis
Temporal Character
Persistence
Reversibility
Beneficiary
Context
Causal Link
Causation Status
Uncertainty
Limitations
Determination Point
Record Status
This creates a machine-readable lifecycle object representing what happened to value.
Change Lineage
VCS supports reconstruction of Value Change across time.
Example:
Active Value
→ Change 001: Moderate Degradation
→ Change 002: Further Capability Loss
→ Change 003: Critical Negative Change
→ ZVA™
→ Change 004: Recovery Event
→ Recoverable Value
→ Change 005: Capability Restoration
→ Active Value
The Value State and Value Change records together create a governed lifecycle history.
Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VCS ↔ VSS
VSS determines the governed Value State.
VCS determines material change relative to a governed reference state.
Therefore:
State ≠ Change
and
Change ≠ New State Determination.
VCS ↔ ORA™
ORA™ may govern the Operational Reality in which an event, condition, capability, or outcome occurs.
VCS governs what happened to value in relation to that reality.
VCS ↔ OBIDENITY®
OBIDENITY® may govern identity, ownership, provenance, authority, or continuity of the underlying object.
VCS governs the Value Change associated with the governed value.
Ownership Change ≠ Automatically Value Change.
VCS ↔ VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may validate claims, evidence, methods, or determinations used to support a Value Change assessment.
VCS does not replace validation governance.
VCS ↔ INTEGROS®

INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of the records, evidence, processes, and states used by VCS.
VCS governs the meaning of Value Change.
VCS ↔ ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether a Value Change determination is reconstructable, supported, preserved, and traceable.
VCS does not conduct the audit.
VCS ↔ AGA™
AGA™ may govern who is responsible or accountable for actions, decisions, and determinations associated with Value Change.
VCS governs the Value Change itself.
Governance Outputs
VCS may generate:
Value Change Candidate Value Change Identification Value Change Type Value Change Direction Value Change Magnitude Value Change Materiality Determination Value Change Temporal Classification Value Change Persistence Classification Value Change Reversibility Classification Value Change Causation Link Value Change Causation Status Value Change Uncertainty Record Value Change Record Value Change Lineage Governed Value Change
These outputs establish a governed representation of what materially happened to value.
Enterprise Application
VCS allows organizations to move beyond static valuation snapshots.
Instead of observing only:
Value at T1
and later:
Value at T2
an organization can govern the difference between them:
What changed?
How much did it change?
In what direction?
Was the change material?
Was it temporary or persistent?
Was it reversible?
Which beneficiary and context were affected?
What event or condition may have caused it?
How certain is that causal relationship?

This makes VCS applicable across:
banking; insurance; accounting interfaces; investment; industrial assets; infrastructure; energy; digital assets; blockchain; intellectual property; public assets; natural resources;
AI systems; computational resources; mission systems; organizational capability.
The same architecture can therefore govern Value Change across fundamentally different value-bearing objects without requiring all value to be reduced to one universal monetary measure.
Foundational Principles
Value State is not Value Change.
Value difference is not automatically material Value Change.
Value Change requires a governed reference.
Value Change does not require monetary expression.
Price Change is not automatically Value Change.
Accounting Change is not automatically VFM® Value Change.
Transaction is not Value Change.
Ownership Change is not automatically Value Change.
Cause of Change is not Value Change.
Correlation is not causation.
Material Value Change may exist even when its complete cause remains unknown.
Multiple causes may legitimately contribute to one Value Change.
Value Change may be beneficiary-specific and context-specific.
Minor changes may accumulate into material Value Change.
Value may degrade toward ZVA™ and may later recover from ZVA™ where new conditions create legitimate value.
VFM® governs what happened to value without claiming governance over every mechanism capable of causing it.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Change Standard establishes the change-governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by determining when existing governed value has materially changed relative to an explicit reference state and by making the direction, type, magnitude, temporal character, persistence, reversibility, context, beneficiary impact, causal relationship, uncertainty, and lifecycle record of that change governable. VCS separates Value Change from Value State, price movement, transaction, ownership, accounting recognition, taxation, external events, and causal mechanisms while preserving structured interfaces through which those systems may influence or consume governed Value Change information. By supporting monetary and non- monetary value, context-specific and beneficiary-specific change, cumulative and compound change, degradation, enhancement, impairment, recovery, and movement toward or away from ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™, VCS provides a general mechanism for observing how value evolves across physical, digital, economic, operational, strategic, organizational, and future value systems. VFM® therefore does not merely identify what value is or what state it occupies; through VCS, it begins to govern what materially happens to value as reality changes.

About Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
About Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
About Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) Governed Space: Value Degradation
Canonical Definition
Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) governs how existing positive value weakens, declines, deteriorates, erodes, or becomes progressively impaired while value continues to exist.
VDGS establishes the governed space between ordinary Value Change and eventual Value Nullification.
Its central distinction is:
Value may decline without disappearing.
The Standard makes deterioration governable by identifying when degradation begins, what dimension of value is affected, how materially value has weakened, how degradation progresses over time, and what positive value remains.
Why VDGS Matters
Organizations frequently recognize value when it is created, acquired, developed, or lost.
The intermediate process of value deterioration is often much less clearly governed.
An industrial asset may gradually lose productive capability.
A technology may become increasingly obsolete.
A dataset may lose relevance.
Organizational knowledge may decay.
Infrastructure may become progressively less reliable.
A commercial capability may weaken while remaining economically useful.
None of these conditions necessarily means that value has disappeared.

VDGS creates a common governance structure for identifying and tracking this intermediate state.
It prevents:
Declining Value
from being confused with:
Zero Value.
VFM® Governance Flow
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → subsequent VFM® lifecycle spaces
VDGS occupies the eighth governed space of VFM®.
The preceding Value Development Standard (VDS) governs how existing value strengthens, matures, grows, or compounds.
VDGS governs the corresponding negative lifecycle direction:
Existing Positive Value → Value Weakening → Progressive Degradation → Reduced Positive Value
The architectural boundary is:
Value Development ≠ Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification.
What VDGS Helps Organizations Govern
VDGS provides a structured way to determine:
What value is degrading?
Which value dimension is affected?
What was the previous governed condition?
How much degradation has occurred?
How quickly is degradation progressing?
Is degradation cumulative, stable, accelerating, or intermittent?
Does positive value still remain?
Has deterioration stopped without the lost value being recovered?
This creates a governed degradation history instead of reducing the entire lifecycle to a comparison between an original value and a final value.
Value Degradation ≠ Value Change
Every degradation involves a change in value.
Not every change in value constitutes degradation.

Value may fluctuate temporarily, change composition, shift between beneficiaries, or move between different forms without entering a material deterioration pathway.
VDGS therefore asks whether the observed negative movement represents:
temporary variation
or
material Value Degradation.
This distinction prevents ordinary volatility from being incorrectly classified as structural or progressive deterioration.
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification
VDGS governs:
Positive Value → Lower Positive Value
Value Nullification governs:
Positive Value → Zero Value
This boundary is essential for VFM®.
A machine operating at 40% of its original productive capability may still possess substantial value.
A technology that has lost most of its commercial relevance may retain intellectual, strategic, technical, or reuse value.
Infrastructure approaching the end of its intended lifecycle may retain operational or residual value.
Therefore:
Severe Degradation ≠ Zero Value.
A degraded asset does not automatically become a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™.
Multidimensional Value Degradation
Value does not necessarily degrade uniformly.
One dimension may decline while another remains stable or develops.
For example:
Economic Value ↓
Operational Capability ↓
Strategic Value →
Knowledge Value ↑
VDGS therefore supports multidimensional degradation governance.

This prevents deterioration in one dimension from being incorrectly interpreted as deterioration of every form of value associated with the governed object.
It also prevents improvement in one dimension from concealing material deterioration in another.
Degradation Progression
VDGS treats degradation as a lifecycle process rather than merely a before-and-after observation.
A governed degradation pathway may appear as:
Stable Value → Initial Weakening → Observable Degradation → Material Degradation → Progressive Degradation → Severe Degradation → Residual Positive Value
Degradation may be:
linear
accelerating
decelerating
stepwise
cyclical
intermittent
cumulative
threshold-driven
or
compound.
The relevant progression depends upon the governed Value Context.
Remaining Value Principle
The defining condition of VDGS is that positive value remains.
Conceptually:
Value > 0
while the relevant value trajectory is negative.
VDGS therefore governs the space in which value is deteriorating but has not yet crossed the boundary into a governed zero-value condition.
This makes remaining value as important as lost value.
Residual Value
A degraded value-bearing object may retain value through:
remaining functionality; productive capability; alternative use; reusable components; knowledge; scarcity; strategic optionality; recoverability; conversion potential; another governed value basis.
VDGS therefore protects an important VFM® distinction:
Loss of Primary Value ≠ Loss of All Value.

Use Case 1 — Industrial Infrastructure and
Equipment
An organization operates an industrial production asset that originally delivers high productive capacity, reliability, precision, and economic utility.
Over time:
component wear increases
→ maintenance requirements rise
→ production interruptions become more frequent
→ precision deteriorates
→ energy consumption increases
→ productive capability declines.
The asset is clearly deteriorating.
But it remains operational and continues to generate positive economic value.
Without a governed degradation structure, the organization may treat each maintenance event, performance reduction, or reliability problem as an isolated operational issue.
VDGS allows these events to be interpreted as a Value Degradation trajectory.
The organization can govern:
Baseline Value Condition → Degradation Identification → Affected Value Dimensions → Degradation Magnitude → Progression → Remaining Positive Value
This provides a structured basis for understanding not merely whether the machine still works, but how its value is deteriorating through time.
The asset does not become zero-value merely because degradation is substantial.
A deteriorating asset remains a value-bearing asset until the governed value actually reaches the applicable zero-value boundary.
Use Case 2 — Technology, Knowledge, and
Digital Capability

An organization possesses a valuable technology platform, software system, dataset, proprietary methodology, knowledge base, or digital capability.
At one point it provides significant competitive and operational value.
Over time:
technology evolves
→ new alternatives emerge
→ interoperability weakens
→ knowledge becomes outdated
→ maintenance becomes more difficult
→ user adoption declines
→ operational relevance decreases.
The underlying object still exists.
It may still function.
It may still serve existing users.
It may retain intellectual, historical, strategic, technical, reuse, or migration value.
But its original value is progressively degrading.
VDGS allows the organization to separate:
existence of the asset
from
condition of its value.
It may determine that:
Operational Value ↓
Market Value ↓
Interoperability Value ↓
while:
Knowledge Value →
and potentially:
Strategic or Reuse Value ↑
This prevents a binary classification of:
valuable / worthless
and replaces it with a governed understanding of how value is actually changing across dimensions.
The result can inform modernization, migration, maintenance, reinvestment, recovery, replacement, or eventual nullification decisions without prematurely declaring the asset to have zero value.
Enterprise Value
VDGS gives organizations an explicit governance layer for detecting deterioration before value disappears.
It can support governance of:

industrial assets; infrastructure; technologies; software; data; intellectual assets; organizational capabilities; knowledge systems; networks; commercial relationships; productive systems; strategic capabilities.
Its value lies in transforming deterioration from an informal observation into a governed lifecycle condition.
Instead of asking only:
“What is this worth now?”
VDGS enables organizations to ask:
“How did its value deteriorate, in which dimensions, at what rate, through what progression, and what value still remains?”
Foundational Principle
Value does not need to disappear in order to deteriorate. Value Degradation begins when existing positive value materially weakens; Value Nullification begins only when the governed value reaches zero.

Value Degradation Condition Module (VDGCM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
Parent Standard: Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
Module: VDGCM — Value Degradation Condition Module
Operational Layer: Value Degradation Condition Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Value Degradation Condition
Origin ID: VFM-VDGS-VDGCM-008.2
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 26 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY®
AI-Readable: Yes
