Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Conditions Module (VECM) is the first Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VECM governs the identification, definition, structuring, documentation, and assessment of the conditions that must exist before potential value originating from an identified Value Origin can legitimately become existent value within a defined Value Context.
The Module establishes the governed conditions necessary for the transition:
Potential Value → Existing Value

VECM does not determine that value has emerged merely because the conditions are present.
Its purpose is to establish:
what must be true before value emergence can legitimately occur.
Architectural Position
VECM operates after the Value Origin Standard (VOS) has established the governed origin from which value may potentially emerge.
Within the Value Emergence Standard, VECM is the first module.
The internal module flow is:
Value Emergence Conditions → Value Emergence Threshold → Value Emergence Event → Value Emergence Determination
→ Value Emergence Record
VECM therefore establishes the condition basis required by the subsequent modules.
Governance Flow Position
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
VECM operates at the beginning of Value Emergence, immediately after Value Origin.
Operational Purpose
Potential value cannot legitimately be treated as existing value merely because:
an asset exists; money has been invested; a capability has been created; intellectual property exists; infrastructure has been constructed; data has been collected;
technology has been developed; resources have been allocated; an activity has occurred; a future benefit is expected.
VECM requires the conditions under which the relevant value can actually emerge to be explicitly established.
This creates a methodological separation between:

Value Source
Value Potential
and
Value Emergence Conditions
Value Emergence Condition
A Value Emergence Condition is a defined circumstance, capability, relationship, state, interaction, availability, activation, performance, accessibility, or other requirement whose existence is materially necessary for the governed potential value to become existent value.
Emergence conditions are context-dependent.
The same object may therefore require different emergence conditions for different forms of value.
For example, a dataset may possess potential value.
For informational value to emerge, relevant conditions might include:
Usability + Relevance + Accessibility + Interpretability
For operational value, additional conditions might include:
Integration + Timeliness + Applicability to an Operational Purpose
VECM does not declare these conditions universally applicable.
It governs the methodology through which the relevant conditions are established for the specific Value Context.
Necessary and Supporting Conditions
VECM may distinguish between:
Necessary Conditions — conditions without which the defined value cannot emerge.
Supporting Conditions — conditions that materially enable, strengthen, accelerate, or facilitate emergence but are not individually indispensable.
This distinction prevents every favorable circumstance from being incorrectly treated as a mandatory condition of value existence.
Single and Compound Conditions

Value emergence may depend upon one condition or a combination of conditions.
VECM therefore supports:
Single Emergence Condition
and
Compound Emergence Condition
A compound condition may take forms such as:
Condition A + Condition B + Condition C
or:
Condition A + (Condition B or Condition C)
This becomes important in complex systems where value does not emerge from one isolated factor but from interaction among multiple capabilities, resources, actors, or operational states.
Conditional Dependency
Emergence conditions may depend upon one another.
For example:
Capability Available → Capability Accessible → Capability Applied → Beneficiary Receives Material Effect
VECM requires material dependencies to remain visible where they affect whether emergence can occur.
This prevents the presence of one upstream condition from being mistaken for completion of the entire emergence basis.
Potential Value ≠ Emergence Condition
Potential value represents the possibility that value may emerge.
An emergence condition represents something that must exist or occur for that possibility to become realizable.
Therefore:
Potential Value ≠ Value Emergence Condition ≠ Existing Value
This distinction is fundamental to the Value Emergence Standard.
Conditions Must Relate to the Governed Value
VECM requires every material emergence condition to remain linked to the value identified under the Value Context Standard.
A condition cannot be treated as relevant merely because it is generally beneficial.

The governing question is whether the condition materially contributes to the emergence of the specific value being governed.
For example, increased computing capacity may be valuable in itself.
But if the governed value is a reduction in processing cost, additional computing capacity qualifies as an emergence condition only where it materially contributes to that specific value pathway.
Beneficiary Relationship
Where the Value Context identifies a beneficiary, VECM may require emergence conditions to include the circumstances necessary for the value to become capable of producing the defined benefit for that beneficiary.
This prevents a common mistake:
Capability existence ≠ beneficiary value existence.
A system may possess a capability while the intended beneficiary remains unable to receive, access, use, or realize the relevant value.
Purpose Relationship
Emergence conditions must remain connected to the purpose under which the value is being governed.
The same object may generate different value depending upon purpose.
A satellite dataset, for example, may produce:
scientific value; navigation value; commercial value; environmental-monitoring value; security value; infrastructure-planning value.
Each may require a different emergence-condition structure.
Condition States
VECM may assign condition states such as:
Undefined
The relevant emergence condition has not yet been sufficiently identified.
Defined
The condition has been identified and formally described.
Unsatisfied

The condition is defined but is not currently present or fulfilled.
Partially Satisfied
The condition exists only partially or within limited circumstances.
Satisfied
The condition has been sufficiently established for the governed emergence pathway.
Uncertain
Available information is insufficient to determine whether the condition is satisfied.
No Longer Satisfied
A previously satisfied condition has materially ceased to exist.
These states allow emergence conditions to be governed dynamically rather than treated as permanent assumptions.
Condition Change
Emergence conditions may change over time.
A condition may:
appear → strengthen → weaken → disappear → reappear
The existence of potential value therefore does not guarantee permanent readiness for emergence.
VECM requires material condition changes to remain identifiable where they affect the governed value lifecycle.
Value Emergence Conditions ≠ Value Emergence
Threshold
VECM establishes:
what conditions must exist.
The subsequent Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) establishes:
when those conditions become sufficient to cross the boundary into value existence.
Therefore:
Condition Presence ≠ Threshold Satisfaction
This distinction prevents VECM from prematurely determining that value has emerged.
Value Emergence Conditions ≠ Value Emergence
Event
Conditions establish the environment in which emergence can occur.

The Value Emergence Event Module (VEEM) governs the event, occurrence, activation, interaction, or change associated with the actual emergence transition where such an event is identifiable.
Therefore:
Conditions Enable Emergence
but
Conditions ≠ Emergence Event
Value Emergence Conditions ≠ Value
Recognition
VECM does not determine whether value is recognized by:
an organization; a market; an accounting system; a government; an investor; a regulator;
a beneficiary; another external actor.
Recognition belongs to the subsequent Value Recognition Standard (VRS).
Value may emerge before formal recognition occurs.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VECM implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Reference
Identify the value governed under the Value Context Standard.
2. Origin Reference
Identify the governed Value Origin from which the potential value arises.
3. Condition Identification
Identify circumstances materially necessary for value emergence.
4. Condition Classification
Distinguish necessary, supporting, single, compound, and dependent conditions where relevant.
5. Condition Relationship
Establish how each condition relates to the governed value, beneficiary, purpose, and context.
6. Dependency Mapping
Identify material dependencies between emergence conditions.
7. Condition State
Determine the current state of each material condition.
8. Condition Evidence
Document the basis upon which condition status is determined.
9. Condition Change

Identify material changes capable of affecting emergence readiness.
10. Threshold Transfer
Transfer the governed condition basis into the Value Emergence Threshold Module.
Governance Outputs
VECM may produce:
Value Emergence Condition Set Value Emergence Condition Definition
Necessary Condition Register Supporting Condition Register Compound Condition Structure Condition Dependency Map Value-to-Condition Relationship Record Beneficiary Condition Record Value Emergence Condition State Condition Change Record Value Emergence Condition Basis Threshold Assessment Input
These outputs provide the governed basis for the next module:
Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM).
Enterprise Application
VECM enables organizations to determine what must actually exist before expected value can become real value.
This is particularly useful where organizations routinely confuse:
investment → value
asset creation → value
technology deployment → value
capability availability → value
project completion → value
VECM inserts the missing governance layer:
Source / Investment / Capability → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Value Emergence
A bank financing new industrial infrastructure could use VECM to define the conditions under which the financed infrastructure begins creating the particular economic or operational value for which the investment was justified.

A space mission organization could use VECM to distinguish the existence of expensive technical capabilities from the conditions under which those capabilities actually produce mission value—for example, when an observation system begins delivering usable information supporting the defined mission purpose.
The same logic can be applied to AI systems, infrastructure, public investment, industrial production, digital assets, research programs, intellectual property, supply chains, healthcare systems, energy systems, and future value-bearing environments.
Foundational Principles
The existence of a value source does not establish the existence of value.
Potential value is not existing value.
Investment does not automatically create value.
Capability does not automatically create value.
Value emergence requires identifiable conditions.
Emergence conditions must relate to the specific governed value.
A condition that is generally beneficial is not automatically a Value Emergence Condition.
Condition presence does not automatically establish threshold satisfaction.
Value Emergence Conditions define what must become true before potential value can legitimately cross into existence.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Emergence Conditions Module establishes the first governed layer of value emergence by identifying, defining, structuring, relating, documenting, and assessing the conditions necessary for potential value to become capable of crossing into existent value. By separating Value Origin, Value Potential, Value Emergence Conditions, Value Emergence Threshold, Value Emergence Event, and Value Recognition, the Module prevents assets, investments, capabilities, activities, and expected benefits from being treated as proof that value already exists. VECM therefore creates the governed condition basis required to determine when potential value is genuinely ready to cross the boundary into existence.

Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Determination Module (VEDM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VEDM governs the formal determination of whether potential value has actually become existent value within the defined Value Context.
The Module receives the governed emergence conditions, emergence threshold, and emergence event established through the preceding modules and determines whether their combined basis is sufficient to establish the transition:
Potential Value → Existing Value

VEDM therefore creates the decisive methodological gate between:
a value that could exist
and
a value that has emerged.
It does not determine whether that value is legally recognized, owned, marketable, taxable, validated, correctly priced, economically beneficial to every stakeholder, or universally accepted.
It determines one narrower question:
Has the governed value actually emerged?
Architectural Position
VEDM is the fourth module within the Value Emergence Standard.
It follows:
VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module
and precedes:
VERM — Value Emergence Record Module.
The internal sequence is:
Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record
The modules perform distinct functions:
VECM establishes the conditions under which value may emerge.
VETM establishes when those conditions become sufficient for emergence.
VEEM identifies what materially occurred at the emergence boundary.
VEDM determines whether the governed basis establishes that value has actually emerged.
VERM preserves that determination as a governed lifecycle record.
Internal Value Flow

Defined Value Context → Identified Value Origin → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Determination Basis Assembly → Context Consistency Check → Threshold–Event Relationship Assessment → Value Existence Assessment → Uncertainty Assessment → Emergence Determination → Existing Value / Value Not Established / Conditional State → Emergence Record
VEDM is therefore the point where the architecture can legitimately say:
This value now exists.
Governance Flow Position
Within the complete VFM® governance flow:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
VEDM operates at the final determination stage inside Value Emergence, immediately before the result is formally recorded.
It establishes whether the lifecycle may proceed from:
Value Emergence
to:
Value Recognition.
Operational Purpose
Organizations routinely assume that value exists because something else exists.
Examples include:
Money Spent → therefore Value Created
Asset Built → therefore Value Created
Technology Deployed → therefore Value Created
Project Completed → therefore Value Created
Product Delivered → therefore Value Created
Capability Available → therefore Value Created
Revenue Generated → therefore Value Created
VEDM prevents these automatic equivalences.
Each may provide evidence relevant to value emergence.

None establishes value emergence independently unless it satisfies the governed Value Context and emergence basis.
VEDM therefore introduces an explicit Value Existence Determination rather than allowing value to be inferred from activity, expenditure, ownership, output, or institutional assertion.
Determination Basis
A Value Emergence Determination should be based upon a reconstructable relationship between:
Governed Value Context
Value Origin
Emergence Conditions
Emergence Threshold Emergence Event Material Evidence Remaining Uncertainty
The exact evidential requirement may vary according to the value being governed.
VEDM does not impose one universal formula for all value.
It requires the determination basis to be explicit.
Value Existence Test
At minimum, VEDM should establish whether:
1. the governed value remains the same value identified through the Value Context; 2. a relevant Value Origin exists; 3. required emergence conditions were materially satisfied; 4. the applicable emergence threshold was reached; 5. a qualifying emergence event occurred; 6. the event materially relates to the governed value; 7. the claimed value is distinguishable from the resources consumed to produce it; 8. material uncertainty does not make the existence claim unsupported; 9. no known contradiction defeats the determination; 10. the available basis supports an explicit emergence state.
Only then should the architecture establish:
Existing Value.
Value Existence ≠ Value Amount

VEDM determines whether value exists.
It does not necessarily determine:
how much value exists.
This distinction is essential.
A new capability may clearly create value while the exact economic magnitude of that value remains uncertain.
Therefore:
Value Existence Determination ≠ Value Quantification
and:
Unknown Value Amount ≠ No Value
A legitimate Value Emergence Determination may exist even when precise monetary valuation is impossible.
Value Existence ≠ Price
Market price may provide information concerning value.
Price does not define value existence under VFM®.
An object may:
have value without an observable market price; have a price while the governed value being assessed has not emerged;
have multiple prices across markets; temporarily have no liquid market; provide operational, strategic, scientific, social, infrastructural, or capability value without a direct market price.
Therefore:
Price ≠ Value Existence
VEDM protects the architecture from reducing value to market pricing.
Value Existence ≠ Cost
Cost establishes resource consumption.
VEDM establishes value emergence.
The two may be related, but they are not equivalent.
CHF 100 million invested
does not establish:
CHF 100 million of value created.
Equally:
CHF 1 million invested
does not prevent:
CHF 100 million of value from emerging.
This separation allows VFM® to analyze value independently from the accounting history of the resources used to create it.
Value Existence ≠ Revenue

Revenue may result from value, market position, contractual structure, scarcity, pricing power, regulation, transfer, speculation, or other mechanisms.
VEDM does not automatically treat revenue as proof that the specific governed value has emerged.
Likewise, value may emerge before revenue exists.
Therefore:
Revenue ≠ Value Emergence
and
No Revenue ≠ No Value.
Value Existence ≠ Asset Completion
A completed asset may remain only a potential value source.
Examples include:
an unused factory; unused infrastructure; dormant intellectual property; an undeployed algorithm;
an unutilized production capability; an unused satellite capability; an empty logistics facility; an installed but ineffective technology.
Asset completion may therefore precede value emergence.
VEDM requires the architecture to determine whether the defined value actually crossed into existence.
Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition
VEDM establishes whether value exists.
The subsequent Value Recognition Standard (VRS) governs whether that existing value may be recognized within a defined governance context.
This produces a critical VFM® distinction:
Value may exist before it is recognized.
Therefore:
Emergence Determination → Existing Value → Recognition Governance
not:
Recognition → Value Existence.
Recognition does not create the underlying value merely by declaring it.
Positive Emergence Determination

A Positive Emergence Determination is established where the governed basis sufficiently supports that the identified value has moved from potential to existent value.
The resulting state is:
Existing Value
This state becomes eligible to enter the Value Recognition Standard.
A positive determination should identify:
the value determined to exist; the applicable Value Context; relevant Value Origin; satisfied conditions; threshold basis; emergence event; determination time; material limitations; uncertainty; applicable context.
Negative Emergence Determination
A Negative Emergence Determination establishes that the available basis does not support the conclusion that the governed value has emerged.
This does not necessarily mean:
the value can never emerge.
It means:
Value Emergence Not Established under the current basis.
The value may remain:
Potential Value
and later undergo a new emergence pathway.
Conditional Emergence Determination
Some value may be determined to exist only under defined conditions.
For example:
Value exists for beneficiary group A under operational condition B, but has not been established outside that context.
VEDM therefore permits:
Conditional Emergence Determination.
Conditional existence must remain explicitly bounded.
It must not silently become universal value existence.
Indeterminate Emergence
Where the available basis is insufficient to support either a positive or negative determination, VEDM should permit:
Emergence Indeterminate.

This is important because methodological governance must not force certainty where certainty does not exist.
The correct outcome may be:
insufficient basis to determine whether value has emerged.
This can trigger:
further observation; additional evidence; renewed emergence event assessment; threshold reassessment; clarification of Value Context.
Emergence Determination States
VEDM may assign at least the following states:
1. Not Assessed
No formal emergence determination has yet occurred.
2. Emergence Not Established
The current basis does not establish that value has emerged.
3. Emergence Indeterminate
The available basis does not permit a sufficiently supported determination.
4. Conditionally Emerged
Value existence is established only within explicitly defined conditions.
5. Emerged
The governed basis supports that the identified value exists.
6. Determination Suspended
A previously issued determination requires reassessment because a material problem affecting its basis has arisen.
7. Determination Superseded
A later governed determination replaces the previous determination.
These states make value emergence machine-governable rather than dependent upon unstructured narrative claims.
Determination Time
VEDM should establish when the emergence determination becomes effective.
This time may differ from:

the time the Value Origin was created; the time expenditure occurred; the time an asset was completed; the time the threshold was reached; the time the emergence event began; the time evidence was reviewed; the time the determination was formally documented.
Where possible, VEDM should distinguish:
Emergence Event Time
from
Emergence Determination Time.
This supports later lifecycle reconstruction.
Retroactive Determination
Value may have emerged before the organization formally recognized or assessed that emergence.
VEDM may therefore support a retroactive determination where sufficient evidence exists.
For example:
Value Emerged at T1
but
Value Emergence Determination issued at T2.
The architecture must preserve both timestamps.
This becomes especially important for accounting, investment analysis, public policy, economic measurement, project evaluation, and future tax-governance interfaces.
Determination Scope
A Value Emergence Determination must remain connected to its defined scope.
Value may be established:
for one beneficiary but not another; in one jurisdictional or operational context but not another; for one purpose but not another; under one configuration but not another; during one period but not another; for one value dimension but not another.
VEDM therefore rejects the assumption:
Value Exists Somewhere → Value Exists Universally.
Partial Emergence
Some value structures may emerge progressively.

VEDM may therefore determine that only a defined part, dimension, capability, beneficiary relationship, or portion of the governed value has emerged.
This should not be confused with Value Development.
Partial Emergence means the original emergence process is incomplete.
Value Development means already-existing value subsequently increases, strengthens, matures, compounds, or develops.
The distinction is:
Incomplete emergence ≠ development of existing value.
Composite Value Emergence
A governed value may depend upon multiple constituent value components.
VEDM may determine:
Component A Emerged
Component B Emerged
Component C Not Established
while the composite value remains:
Not Yet Fully Emerged.
This enables VFM® to govern complex infrastructure, industrial, technological, financial, scientific, and mission systems without forcing binary simplification.
Contradictory Evidence
VEDM must account for materially contradictory evidence.
A Value Emergence Determination must not be based solely upon evidence supporting the preferred conclusion.
Contradictory evidence may:
prevent positive determination; produce an indeterminate state; narrow the determination scope; create conditional emergence; trigger reassessment of the emergence event; require additional evidence.
Preferred outcome ≠ governed determination.
Uncertainty
Uncertainty does not automatically prevent Value Emergence Determination.
VEDM distinguishes between:
uncertainty about the exact magnitude of value
and

uncertainty about whether value exists at all.
The first may permit a positive determination.
The second may require conditional or indeterminate status.
This distinction allows VFM® to operate in environments where precise valuation is impossible but value existence is nevertheless materially demonstrable.
Determination Reassessment
A Value Emergence Determination may require reassessment where:
material evidence changes; the Value Context was incorrectly defined; the emergence event was misidentified; threshold satisfaction is challenged; contradictory evidence emerges; fraud or data error is discovered; the beneficiary relationship was misunderstood; the claimed value was actually a different value; the determination was based upon an invalid dependency.
VEDM must therefore support controlled reassessment.
Emergence Determination ≠ Validation
Determination
VEDM does not replace VALIDOS®.
The distinction is:
VEDM: Has the specifically governed value emerged according to the VFM® emergence structure?
VALIDOS®: Can a defined Validation Object or claim legitimately receive a Validation Determination under the applicable validation
criteria, method, evidence, and reliance conditions?
A Value Emergence Determination may itself later become a Validation Object.
The two governance questions remain distinct.
Emergence Determination ≠ Accounting
Recognition
VEDM does not determine whether value must appear on:

a balance sheet; income statement; financial report; regulatory filing; accounting ledger.
Accounting recognition is a separate governance and regulatory question.
VFM® can provide an upstream value-lifecycle structure that accounting systems may later reference.
This distinction is strategically important:
Value may exist even where existing accounting rules do not recognize it as an accounting asset.
Emergence Determination ≠ Taxable Event
A determination that value exists does not establish that tax is due.
Taxation may depend upon:
realization; transfer; jurisdiction; legal classification; taxable event; taxpayer status; statutory rules; exemptions; timing.
Therefore:
Value Emergence ≠ Tax Liability.
A future tax-governance architecture may use VFM® value states and transitions as inputs without VFM® becoming a tax system.
Emergence Determination ≠ Ownership
VEDM determines whether value exists.
It does not determine who owns that value.
The underlying object, capability, right, or value relationship may involve separate identity, ownership, authority, provenance, or transfer governance.
Therefore:
Value Existence ≠ Value Ownership.
Determination Integrity
A Value Emergence Determination should be:
context-linked; origin-linked; threshold-linked; event-linked; evidence-aware; uncertainty-aware; scope-bounded; temporally identifiable; reconstructable; capable of reassessment.
The determination should not exist merely as an unsupported statement:
“Value was created.”

VEDM converts that assertion into a governable methodological conclusion.
Determination Logic
A minimum operational logic may be:
Value Context valid? ↓ Value Origin identified? ↓ Emergence Conditions satisfied? ↓ Emergence Threshold reached? ↓ Qualifying Emergence Event occurred? ↓ Event materially connected to governed value? ↓ Contradictory evidence assessed? ↓ Material uncertainty acceptable for determination? ↓ YES → Emerged / Conditionally Emerged NO → Emergence Not Established / Indeterminate
This logic may be implemented manually, computationally, or through AI-supported governance systems.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VEDM implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Confirmation
Confirm the exact value whose emergence is being determined.
2. Context Confirmation
Confirm the relevant Value Context, object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference framework.
3. Origin Confirmation
Confirm the governed Value Origin supporting the emergence pathway.
4. Conditions and Threshold Review
Confirm the applicable emergence conditions and threshold state.
5. Emergence Event Review
Confirm the event or composite event forming the immediate emergence basis.
6. Evidence Review
Identify the material evidence supporting and challenging emergence.
7. Uncertainty Assessment
Determine whether remaining uncertainty affects existence, magnitude, scope, or only downstream recognition.
8. Determination
Assign the appropriate Value Emergence Determination state.

9. Scope and Time Definition
Define the context and temporal boundary within which the determination applies.
10. Transfer to Record
Transfer the governed determination to VERM for preservation.
Governance Outputs
VEDM may produce:
Value Emergence Determination Value Existence Determination Value Emergence Determination State Value Emergence Basis Value Emergence Evidence Basis Value Emergence Contradiction Record Value Emergence Uncertainty Statement Conditional Emergence Statement Partial Emergence Determination Composite Value Emergence Determination Value Emergence Scope Statement Value Emergence Effective Time Value Emergence Determination Time Value Emergence Reassessment Trigger Governed Existing Value
These outputs become the governed input for:
VERM — Value Emergence Record Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking & Infrastructure Finance:
Has the Investment Actually Created Value?
A banking consortium finances a CHF 1.2 billion infrastructure project.
Construction is completed.
The asset exists physically.
The financing has been deployed.
The project appears operational.
Traditional reporting may show:
Capital Deployed → Asset Completed → Project Operational
But the financing institutions need to answer a different question:
Has the value for which the capital was deployed actually emerged?
Suppose the governed value is:
a transport capability capable of sustainably moving the required passenger volume while reducing defined network congestion.
VFM® separates:

CHF 1.2bn Expenditure → Infrastructure Asset → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Operational Emergence Event → VEDM Determination
If the infrastructure operates but does not achieve the minimum capability required by the defined Value Context, VEDM may determine:
Emergence Not Established
or:
Conditionally Emerged.
If the governed basis demonstrates that the required capability exists, VEDM may establish:
Emerged.
The bank can therefore distinguish between:
money deployed
asset completed
asset operational
and
value actually emerged.
That distinction can materially improve project finance monitoring, restructuring decisions, investment governance, portfolio analysis, public-private financing, and post-investment evaluation.
Use Case 2 — AI / Space Mission: Capability
Success vs. Actual Mission Value
A space organization develops an AI-enabled autonomous navigation system for a planetary mission.
Billions are spent on research, simulation, hardware, launch, and mission operations.
The spacecraft reaches the target.
The navigation system activates successfully.
Technically, the project has achieved major milestones.
But suppose the governed value is:
autonomous navigation capability that materially increases mission access to scientifically valuable locations unavailable under the previous control architecture.
VFM® does not infer value merely from:
R&D expenditure
launch success
system deployment
or
technical activation.

The emergence pathway may instead be:
Navigation Capability Source → Potential Mission Value → Defined Emergence Conditions → Performance Threshold → Autonomous Navigation Event → Successful Access to Previously Unreachable Scientific Target → VEDM Determination
VEDM may then establish:
Emerged
for the governed mission value.
The organization can now distinguish:
technology exists
from
technology works
from
technology created the value for which it was developed.
This makes VFM® applicable not merely to financial valuation, but to mission governance, AI investment, scientific programs, infrastructure, public spending, industrial development, and other environments where enormous resource expenditure does not itself prove value creation.
Foundational Principles
Potential value is not existing value.
Threshold satisfaction is not automatically value existence.
An emergence event is not automatically a positive emergence determination.
Value existence is not value amount.
Value is not reducible to price.
Cost is not value.
Revenue is not value.
Asset completion is not value emergence.
Capability existence is not necessarily value emergence.
Value may exist before it is recognized.
Value may exist without being owned, priced, taxed, traded, or recognized in accounting.
Uncertainty about value magnitude does not automatically mean uncertainty about value existence.

A Value Emergence Determination must remain connected to the Value Context, Value Origin, emergence conditions, threshold, event, evidence, scope, and uncertainty that support it.
VEDM establishes whether potential value has crossed into existence; it does not determine what every external system must subsequently do with that value.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Emergence Determination Module establishes the decisive existence gate within the Value Emergence Standard by determining whether the governed value has legitimately transitioned from potential value into existing value. Through explicit linkage of Value Context, Value Origin, emergence conditions, emergence thresholds, emergence events, evidence, contradictions, uncertainty, scope, and temporal position, VEDM prevents expenditure, asset completion, technical deployment, transactions, revenue, institutional assertion, or operational activity from being automatically interpreted as value creation. By separating value existence from value magnitude, price, accounting recognition, ownership, taxation, validation, and subsequent recognition, VEDM creates a distinct governable determination that can be used across banking, investment, infrastructure, industry, science, AI, public finance, mission systems, and other value-bearing environments. VEDM therefore establishes the methodological point at which VFM® may legitimately state that potential value has become existent value, while preserving the conditions and boundaries required for that value to proceed into formal Value Recognition and the subsequent value lifecycle.

Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Event Module (VEEM) is the third Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VEEM governs the identification, definition, structuring, temporal localization, contextualization, and documentation of the event, occurrence, transition, activation, realization, or materially identifiable change through which threshold- satisfied potential value moves into an emergence event capable of supporting a subsequent Value Emergence Determination.
The Module establishes the governed transition between:
Emergence-Ready Value
and

Value whose emergence has materially occurred and can now be evaluated.
VEEM does not determine conclusively that value exists.
That responsibility belongs to:
VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module.
VEEM governs what happened at the point of emergence.
VEDM governs whether what happened is sufficient to determine that value has emerged.
Architectural Position
VEEM is the third module within the Value Emergence Standard.
It follows:
VETM — Value Emergence Threshold Module
and precedes:
VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module.
The internal sequence is:
Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record
VECM establishes:
What conditions must exist?
VETM establishes:
When are those conditions sufficient?
VEEM establishes:
What materially occurred when the emergence boundary was crossed?
VEDM establishes:
Does that occurrence legitimately establish that value emerged?
VERM preserves:
What emergence was ultimately established and on what basis?
Internal Value Flow
Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Threshold Satisfaction → Threshold Crossing → Emergence-Ready Value → Emergence Event Candidate → Event Identification → Event Context → Event Temporal Position → Event-to-Value Relationship → Event State → Governed Value Emergence Event → Value Emergence Determination
This flow prevents value existence from being declared merely because a threshold was theoretically satisfied.

Something must materially occur that connects the satisfied emergence conditions to the claimed emergence of value.
Governance Flow Position
Within the complete VFM® governance flow:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
Within Value Emergence:
VECM — Value Emergence Conditions → VETM — Value Emergence Threshold → VEEM — Value Emergence Event → VEDM — Value Emergence Determination → VERM — Value Emergence Record
VEEM therefore occupies the exact transition point between:
sufficient conditions for emergence
and
formal determination that value now exists.
Operational Purpose
Value does not necessarily emerge simply because:
money was invested; an asset was created; a product was completed; infrastructure became available; a capability became technically operational; a transaction occurred; a service was launched; a resource was consumed; a project reached completion; a threshold was theoretically satisfied.
These events may be related to value.
They are not automatically Value Emergence Events.
VEEM requires the relevant occurrence to be connected to the specific governed value established through the Value Context Standard.
The Module therefore asks:
What actually happened that may mark the transition from potential value toward existing value?
Value Emergence Event

A Value Emergence Event is a materially identifiable occurrence, transition, activation, realization, interaction, outcome, state change, or other governed event through which threshold-satisfied potential value manifests in a form capable of being evaluated as existent value.
A Value Emergence Event must be connected to:
Governed Value Context
Value Origin Emergence Conditions Emergence Threshold Relevant Occurrence
The event is therefore not an isolated operational event.
It is an event interpreted specifically within the governed value lifecycle.
Operational Event ≠ Value Emergence Event
An operational event may occur without creating value.
For example:
Factory starts production.
That is an operational event.
Whether it constitutes a Value Emergence Event depends upon the governed value.
If the governed value is:
production capability, the event may be highly relevant.
If the governed value is:
reduction of customer delivery time, production startup alone may not yet establish emergence.
If the governed value is:
reduction of manufacturing cost, production startup may even occur before any relevant value has emerged.
Therefore:
Operational Event ≠ Value Emergence Event
unless the event is materially connected to the defined value context.
Transaction ≠ Value Emergence Event
A transaction may transfer money, assets, rights, obligations, or resources.
It does not automatically establish that value has emerged.
For example:
Investor pays CHF 10 million
does not establish:

CHF 10 million of value emerged.
The payment may finance a potential value source.
VEEM separates:
resource movement
from
value emergence.
This distinction is fundamental for banking, investment, public finance, accounting, infrastructure, and economic analysis.
Cost ≠ Value Emergence
Resources consumed in creating potential value must not automatically be interpreted as value created.
Therefore:
Cost Incurred ≠ Value Emerged
Capital Deployed ≠ Value Emerged
Budget Spent ≠ Value Emerged
Asset Completed ≠ Value Emerged
Technology Deployed ≠ Value Emerged
The relevant Value Emergence Event must demonstrate a material connection between the potential value and the occurrence through which that value begins to exist.
Event Identification
VEEM requires the emergence event to be identifiable.
Identification may include:
event identity; event type; event source; event time; event location or environment where relevant; participating entities; affected value object; beneficiary relationship; originating value source; applicable emergence conditions; applicable threshold; resulting observable change; event evidence; uncertainty.
The exact implementation may vary.
The governance requirement remains:
the emergence event must be reconstructable sufficiently to support downstream determination.
Event Types
Value may emerge through different types of events.
VEEM may govern:
Activation Event
A capability becomes materially usable.
Utilization Event

A previously available capability is actually used in a value-producing context.
Delivery Event
A value-bearing outcome reaches the relevant beneficiary.
Performance Event
A capability produces the defined performance associated with the governed value.
Conversion Event
A potential value source produces a materially different value-bearing result.
Interaction Event
Value emerges through interaction between multiple actors, systems, resources, or capabilities.
Availability Event
A resource or capability becomes materially available where availability itself constitutes the governed value.
Outcome Event
The defined outcome associated with the governed value occurs.
Realization Event
Previously potential value becomes materially realized.
Composite Emergence Event
Several events together establish the relevant emergence occurrence.
VFM® does not require all value to emerge through one universal event type.
Single Event vs. Composite Event
Some value may emerge through one identifiable event.
Example:
a service successfully delivered to a beneficiary.
Other value may require a sequence or combination of events.
Example:
technology activation + sustained operation + beneficiary utilization + measurable outcome.
VEEM therefore distinguishes:
Single Emergence Event
from
Composite Emergence Event.
A composite event must preserve the relationship between its constituent occurrences.
Instantaneous vs. Progressive Emergence
Value may emerge:
instantaneously
or
progressively.

An instantaneous emergence event may occur at a specific moment.
A progressive emergence event may develop across:
multiple interactions;
repeated outputs; sustained utilization; cumulative performance; continuous availability; gradual realization.
VEEM must therefore permit an emergence event to have:
Event Start
Event Progression
Event Completion
where the governed value requires it.
Temporal Localization
VEEM establishes the temporal position of the emergence event.
Where possible, the Module should distinguish:
Before Emergence Event
During Emergence Event
After Emergence Event
This enables downstream VFM® governance to identify when value entered existence and subsequently distinguish:
Value Emergence
from
Value Development
or
Value Degradation.
Without temporal localization, later value changes may be incorrectly treated as part of original value creation.
Emergence Event Boundary
VEEM must identify where the emergence event begins and where it ends.
This is especially important for progressive or composite value emergence.
The boundary may be based upon:
activation; first qualifying use; delivery; threshold crossing; outcome occurrence; sustained performance; beneficiary realization; completion of an event sequence; other context-specific conditions.
The event boundary must correspond to the governed value rather than an arbitrary project milestone.
Event-to-Value Relationship

The existence of an event does not establish that the event caused or produced the governed value.
VEEM therefore requires an explicit relationship between:
Emergence Event
and
Governed Value.
The relationship may be:
direct; enabling; contributory; composite; conditional; dependent; uncertain.
This relationship must remain visible for VEDM.
Direct Emergence
Direct emergence occurs where the event itself produces or manifests the governed value with minimal intermediate dependency.
Example:
A transportation service successfully moves the beneficiary from the defined origin to destination.
Where the governed value is:
successful transportation delivery
the completion event may have a direct relationship to value emergence.
Enabling Event
An event may enable value without itself establishing that value has emerged.
Example:
A hospital installs a new diagnostic system.
Installation creates capability.
If the governed value is:
improved diagnostic outcome
installation alone is an enabling event, not necessarily the Value Emergence Event.
This distinction prevents:
Capability Creation
from being silently transformed into:
Value Creation.
Contributory Event
Some events contribute to value emergence without independently establishing it.
Several contributory events may together form a Composite Emergence Event.
VEEM should therefore preserve:
Event A + Event B + Event C → Composite Emergence Basis
where appropriate.
Beneficiary Relationship

Where value depends upon a beneficiary, VEEM should preserve the relationship between the emergence event and that beneficiary.
A capability may exist.
An output may exist.
A product may exist.
But where the governed value depends upon beneficiary realization, value may not emerge until the relevant beneficiary relationship becomes operationally meaningful.
This does not mean all value requires a human beneficiary.
The beneficiary may be:
individual; organization; system; ecosystem; infrastructure; public institution; economy; mission; operational process; future capability.
The relevant beneficiary is inherited from the governed Value Context.
Event Materiality
Not every occurrence related to potential value should become a Value Emergence Event.
VEEM therefore requires materiality.
An event is materially relevant where it changes the governed value lifecycle sufficiently to justify progression toward Value Emergence Determination.
Materiality may depend upon:
value purpose; beneficiary; scale; duration; consequence; threshold relationship; operational significance; persistence;
context.
Event Evidence
A Value Emergence Event should have an identifiable evidential basis proportionate to its significance.
Evidence may include:
operational records; system outputs; delivery records; utilization data; performance measurements; beneficiary interaction; transaction records; physical observation; sensor data; production data; mission data; financial data; documented outcomes.

VEEM governs the event relationship.
It does not replace broader evidence governance under ADIT®, integrity governance under INTEGROS®, or validation governance under VALIDOS®.
Event Uncertainty
Not every emergence event will be perfectly observable.
VEEM therefore allows uncertainty concerning:
event timing; event completeness; event causality; event materiality; event-to-value relationship; beneficiary effect; event persistence; composite event completion.
Where material uncertainty exists, it must remain visible when the event proceeds to VEDM.
Event States
VEEM may assign governed event states including:
No Emergence Event
No materially relevant event has been identified.
Event Candidate
A potentially relevant emergence event has been identified.
Event In Progress
A progressive or composite emergence event has begun but is not complete.
Event Occurred
The governed emergence event has materially occurred.
Event Uncertain
The available basis does not support reliable characterization of the event.
Event Failed
The expected emergence event did not complete sufficiently.
Event Reversed
An event occurred but was materially reversed before emergence could be determined.
Event Superseded
A later event replaces the earlier event as the relevant emergence basis.
These states support complex and dynamic value environments.
Failed Emergence Event
A threshold may be crossed while the subsequent emergence event fails.
For example:
production capability exists
but

the first intended production process fails to produce usable output.
The lifecycle may therefore become:
Threshold Crossed → Emergence Event Attempted → Emergence Event Failed → Value Remains Potential
This is an important architectural distinction.
Emergence Readiness ≠ Successful Emergence.
Reversed Emergence Event
An emergence event may begin but reverse before a legitimate emergence determination is possible.
Example:
A digital service becomes operational but immediately fails before any material value can be realized.
VEEM allows:
Event Initiation → Event Reversal
without forcing the architecture to declare that value existed merely because activation briefly occurred.
Repeated Emergence Events
Some value may emerge repeatedly.
Examples include:
repeated service delivery; recurring energy generation; repeated transportation; recurring computation; repeated financial benefit; repeated scientific output.
VEEM must distinguish:
Initial Value Emergence
from
Repeated Value-Producing Events.
Once the governed value already exists, later events may belong to:
Value State
Value Change
or
Value Development
rather than constituting new emergence of the same value.
This prevents repeated production from being counted repeatedly as original value creation.
New Value from Existing Value
A later event may create a genuinely new value even where another value already exists.
Example:
A dataset already has operational value.

A new analytical capability later produces a new predictive value from that dataset.
The new value requires its own governed Value Context and emergence pathway.
Therefore:
Existing Value + New Capability ≠ Automatically Same Value
A new value may require:
New Value Context → New Value Origin → New Value Emergence.
Event Attribution Boundary
VEEM identifies the relationship between an event and value emergence.
It does not determine legal responsibility, ownership, entitlement, accountability, or compensation for that value.
Those questions remain outside the Module.
Therefore:
Value Emergence Event ≠ Ownership Event
Value Emergence Event ≠ Taxable Event
Value Emergence Event ≠ Payment Event
Value Emergence Event ≠ Legal Recognition Event
Value Emergence Event ≠ Accountability Determination
This separation is critical if VFM® is later combined with accounting, taxation, banking, payment, or economic governance architectures.
Internal Value Flow Control
VEEM acts as the event gate between threshold satisfaction and formal emergence determination.
The operational logic is:
No Event → Remain Emergence-Ready
Event Candidate → Assess Event
Event In Progress → Continue Observation
Event Uncertain → Hold / Clarify
Event Failed → Return to Potential / Emergence-Ready State as applicable
Event Reversed → Reassess Emergence Basis
Event Occurred → Transfer to VEDM
This makes VEEM usable as an operational governance mechanism.
Governance Outputs
VEEM may produce:

Value Emergence Event Candidate Value Emergence Event Definition Value Emergence Event Identity Value Emergence Event Type Value Emergence Event Context Value Emergence Event Timeline Value Emergence Event Boundary Value Emergence Event-to-Value Relationship Composite Emergence Event Map Value Emergence Event Materiality Assessment Value Emergence Event Evidence Basis Value Emergence Event Uncertainty Record Value Emergence Event State Failed Emergence Event Record Reversed Emergence Event Record Governed Value Emergence Event
These outputs provide the governed basis for:
VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking & Project Finance:
Investment Completion vs. Value Emergence
A bank finances a large industrial project.
The borrower completes construction.
The facility appears on the balance sheet.
Equipment is installed.
The project is officially declared operational.
These facts may demonstrate that capital has been deployed and an asset exists.
They do not automatically demonstrate that the expected value has emerged.
VFM® may establish the governed value as:
sustained productive capability capable of generating the defined economic output.
VECM identifies the conditions.
VETM establishes the emergence threshold.
VEEM then identifies the actual emergence event.
That event may require:
Operational Activation → Successful Production → Usable Output → Commercially Relevant Delivery
rather than merely:
Construction Completed.

The bank can therefore distinguish:
Capital Expenditure → Completed Asset → Potential Value → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Value Emergence Determination
This gives lenders, investors, restructuring teams, and public financing bodies a governed way to detect projects where:
money has been spent and assets exist, but the intended value has not yet emerged. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Mission Activity vs. Scientific Value Emergence
A space agency launches a scientific mission.
The spacecraft reaches its destination.
The instruments activate successfully.
From a traditional project perspective, multiple major milestones have been achieved.
But suppose the governed value is:
usable scientific knowledge concerning a defined planetary phenomenon.
Then:
Launch Success ≠ Scientific Value Emergence
Orbital Arrival ≠ Scientific Value Emergence
Instrument Activation ≠ Scientific Value Emergence
Those events create or activate the potential value source.
VEEM identifies the materially relevant emergence event.
The sequence may be:
Instrument Activation → Observation → Data Acquisition → Successful Transmission → Ground Reception → Usable Scientific Dataset Produced
Only then may the relevant occurrence proceed to VEDM for determination of whether the governed scientific value has actually emerged.
This allows mission governance to distinguish:
Mission Expenditure
from
Mission Capability
from
Mission Activity
from
Mission Value.

That distinction can support mission evaluation, portfolio prioritization, continuation decisions, cost control, scientific program assessment, and comparison of alternative mission architectures.
Foundational Principles
Threshold satisfaction is not automatically value emergence.
An operational event is not automatically a Value Emergence Event.
A transaction is not automatically a Value Emergence Event.
Cost incurred is not value emerged.
Capital deployed is not value emerged.
Asset completion is not value emerged.
Capability activation is not automatically value realization.
An emergence event must remain connected to the specific governed value context.
A Value Emergence Event may be instantaneous, progressive, composite, conditional, failed, uncertain, or reversed.
The occurrence of an event must remain distinguishable from the determination of what that event means for value existence.
VEEM governs what happened at the emergence boundary; VEDM governs whether what happened establishes that value emerged.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Emergence Event Module establishes the governed event layer through which threshold-satisfied potential value may transition toward existent value. By identifying and structuring the occurrence, activation, realization, interaction, outcome, or state change associated with value emergence, VEEM separates operational activity, transactions, expenditure, asset completion, capability creation, and technical activation from the materially relevant event through which the governed value may actually emerge. Through event identification, temporal localization, event boundaries, event-to-value relationships, materiality, beneficiary relationships, composite events, progressive emergence, uncertainty, failed events, reversals, and event-state governance, VEEM creates the evidentially identifiable transition required before Value Emergence Determination can occur. In doing so, VEEM prevents activity from being mistaken for value, cost from being mistaken for value creation, and technical completion from being mistaken for value realization, while establishing the governed bridge between emergence readiness and legitimate determination of value existence within VFM®.

Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VERM governs the formal recording, preservation, traceability, contextualization, versioning, and lifecycle transfer of a Value Emergence Determination after the emergence process has been assessed through the preceding modules.
Its purpose is to ensure that a determination that value has emerged, has not emerged, has emerged conditionally, remains indeterminate, or has been superseded does not survive merely as an isolated statement.

VERM preserves the governed relationship:
What Value → From What Origin → Under What Context → Under What Conditions → At What Threshold → Through What Event → On What Determination Basis → At What Time → With What Scope and Limitations → With What Emergence State
VERM therefore converts the result of Value Emergence governance into a persistent and reconstructable Value Emergence Record capable of entering the next stage of the VFM® lifecycle.
Architectural Position
VERM is the fifth and final module within the Value Emergence Standard.
It follows:
VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module
and completes the internal Value Emergence sequence:
Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record
The internal module roles are:
VECM establishes the conditions under which value may emerge.
VETM establishes the threshold separating potential value from existent value.
VEEM identifies the event or event structure associated with crossing that boundary.
VEDM determines whether the governed value has actually emerged.
VERM preserves that determination and its governing basis for subsequent lifecycle use.
VERM is therefore the persistence and transfer layer of Value Emergence.
Governance Flow Position
Within the complete VFM® governance flow:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation

→ Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
VERM operates at the final boundary of:
Value Emergence
immediately before:
Value Recognition.
Its architectural role is critical because the next standard must not receive merely an assertion that:
“value exists.”
It should receive a governed record explaining which value exists, why its emergence was determined, under what conditions that determination applies, and what limitations remain attached to it.
Internal Value Flow
Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Determination State → Record Assembly → Context Linkage → Origin Linkage → Conditions / Threshold / Event Linkage → Determination Basis Preservation → Scope & Limitation Preservation → Temporal Anchoring → Record Versioning → Value Emergence Record → Value Recognition Governance
This establishes a controlled lifecycle transition:
Emergence Determination → Governed Emergence Record → Recognition Candidate
Operational Purpose
Value claims frequently become detached from the conditions that originally supported them.
An organization may initially determine:
“This capability created value under these conditions.”
Months or years later, the surviving organizational statement may become simply:
“This capability has value.”
The original:
beneficiary; context; threshold; evidence; assumptions; timing; limitations; uncertainty;
configuration; determination basis
may disappear.

VERM exists to prevent this loss of methodological meaning.
The record preserves enough information to reconstruct:
what was determined
and
why that determination was legitimate at the time it was made.
Value Emergence Record
A Value Emergence Record is the governed representation of a Value Emergence Determination together with the material lifecycle information required to interpret that determination correctly.
At minimum, a record should be capable of identifying:
1. the governed value; 2. the relevant Value Context; 3. the Value Origin; 4. applicable emergence conditions; 5. applicable emergence threshold; 6. qualifying emergence event; 7. emergence determination; 8. determination state; 9. determination basis; 10. effective emergence time; 11. determination time; 12. applicable scope; 13. beneficiary where relevant; 14. material limitations; 15. material uncertainty; 16. record version; 17. subsequent changes or supersession.
The exact implementation may vary according to the value domain.
The governance requirement does not.
Record ≠ Determination
VERM maintains a strict distinction:
Value Emergence Determination ≠ Value Emergence Record
VEDM determines whether value emerged.
VERM records that determination and preserves the conditions that give it meaning.
A record must not silently change the underlying determination.
If a determination requires reassessment, that reassessment belongs in the governed determination process.
VERM then records the resulting new state.

Record ≠ Evidence
A Value Emergence Record may contain references to evidence.
It is not itself equivalent to all underlying evidence.
The record may preserve:
evidence identifiers; evidence references; evidence summaries; evidence relationships; evidence states; determination basis.
Underlying evidence may remain governed by the relevant evidence, integrity, audit, validation, operational, or external systems.
Therefore:
Record of Evidence ≠ Evidence Itself
and
Value Emergence Record ≠ Universal Evidence Repository.
Record Identity
Every material Value Emergence Record should be independently identifiable.
Record identity may include:
Record ID; governed value identifier; Value Context reference; Value Origin reference; Value Emergence Determination reference; version; status; creation time; effective time.
This enables multiple emergence records to coexist without being silently merged.
Context Preservation
VERM must preserve the Value Context under which emergence was determined.
This is necessary because the same underlying object may create different forms of value for different:
beneficiaries; purposes; environments; periods; systems; relationships; reference frameworks.
A record stating only:
“Value emerged”
is insufficient where the value cannot be understood without its context.
VERM therefore preserves:
Value Emerged → For Whom → In Relation to What → For What Purpose → Under What Reference Context
where materially applicable.
Origin Preservation

The record should preserve the relationship between the emerged value and its governed Value Origin.
This allows later lifecycle analysis to distinguish:
the value
from
the source from which that value emerged.
The distinction is essential because one Value Origin may generate multiple values, and one governed value may depend upon multiple contributing origins.
Therefore:
Origin Asset™ ≠ Emerged Value.
VERM preserves the relationship without collapsing the two.
Condition Preservation
The emergence conditions established through VECM should remain linked to the record where materially relevant.
This allows later users to determine whether the value emerged:
only under specific conditions; under a defined configuration; for a particular beneficiary; during a specific operational state; after a defined capability became available; only when multiple conditions converged.
Without this information, downstream systems may incorrectly generalize the value.
Threshold Preservation
VERM should preserve the emergence threshold that separated:
Potential Value
from:
Existing Value.
The record should make it possible to understand what threshold was crossed and why that crossing was considered sufficient.
This is particularly important where later review asks:
Why was value considered to exist at this point rather than earlier or later?
Emergence Event Preservation
Where an identifiable emergence event or composite event exists, VERM should preserve its relationship to the record.

Relevant information may include:
event identity; event type; event time; event sequence; event conditions; event relationship to threshold crossing; event relationship to the governed value.
The record does not need to reproduce the complete operational event history.
It preserves the event relationship necessary to reconstruct value emergence.
Determination Basis Preservation
VERM must preserve the basis supporting the emergence determination.
The basis may include references to:
observed outcomes; measurements; operational evidence; simulation evidence; financial evidence; scientific evidence; capability evidence; beneficiary effects; performance results; threshold evidence; contextual evidence; contradictory evidence; uncertainty.
VERM does not independently validate every source.
It preserves the basis upon which the determination was made.
Temporal Anchoring
Value emergence has more than one relevant time.
VERM should distinguish where applicable:
Value Origin Time
Emergence Condition Satisfaction Time
Threshold Crossing Time
Emergence Event Time
Value Emergence Effective Time
Emergence Determination Time
Record Creation Time
These timestamps may be identical.
They may also differ substantially.
Preserving them allows later systems to reconstruct the lifecycle without forcing one artificial timestamp onto multiple distinct events.
Retroactive Emergence Record
Where VEDM establishes retroactively that value emerged at an earlier time, VERM should preserve both:

Emergence Effective Time: T1
and
Determination / Record Time: T2.
This distinction can be important for:
investment evaluation; project assessment; public expenditure analysis; accounting interfaces; economic measurement; infrastructure governance; intellectual property; future tax-governance interfaces; historical value reconstruction.
VERM records the temporal relationship without itself determining legal or accounting consequences.
Record Scope
Every Value Emergence Record must remain bounded by the scope of the determination it represents.
Scope may include:
value type; beneficiary; object; capability; jurisdictional context; operational context; purpose; configuration; period; environment; value dimension.
A narrow determination must produce a narrow record.
VERM must not convert:
Value Emerged for Beneficiary A under Condition B
into:
Value Exists Universally.
Conditional Emergence Record
Where VEDM establishes:
Conditionally Emerged
VERM must preserve those conditions as part of the record.
The conditions are not optional annotations.
They are part of the meaning of the emergence state.
A conditional record that loses its conditions becomes methodologically misleading.
Partial Emergence Record
Where only part of a governed value structure has emerged, VERM may preserve:
emerged component; non-emerged component; component relationship; partial emergence state; remaining emergence requirements.
This enables downstream governance to distinguish:
partially emerged value

from
fully emerged value.
Composite Emergence Record
Complex value may depend upon several constituent components or emergence pathways.
VERM may therefore preserve composite structures such as:
Component A → Emerged
Component B → Emerged
Component C → Conditionally Emerged
Composite Value → Emergence Not Yet Fully Established
This is useful for infrastructure, banking, industrial systems, AI, research programs, mission systems, supply chains, public investment, and other complex value structures.
Uncertainty Preservation
Material uncertainty associated with the Value Emergence Determination must remain attached to the record.
The record should distinguish where possible between uncertainty concerning:
whether value exists; how much value exists; scope of value; beneficiary effect; duration; future persistence; causal contribution; supporting evidence.
A record should not create greater certainty than the underlying determination possessed.
Contradiction Preservation
Material contradictory information considered during the determination should not disappear from the record merely because a positive emergence determination was issued.
Where relevant, VERM may preserve:
contradiction identifier; contradiction type; effect on determination; unresolved issue; reason the determination remained supportable; reassessment trigger.
This prevents downstream users from seeing only the favorable basis.
Record Versioning
A Value Emergence Record may evolve.

VERM therefore requires controlled versioning where material changes occur.
A later version should not silently overwrite the historical record.
Possible states may include:
Active
Under Review
Amended
Superseded
Withdrawn
Archived
The applicable implementation may vary, but the lifecycle history should remain reconstructable.
Supersession
A new Value Emergence Determination may supersede an earlier determination.
VERM should preserve:
Previous Record → Superseding Record
rather than deleting the previous state.
This makes it possible to reconstruct:
what was believed; on what basis; when it changed; why it changed; which determination became authoritative afterward.
Record Correction
A factual or administrative error in a record may require correction without changing the underlying emergence determination.
VERM should distinguish:
Record Correction
from:
Determination Change.
For example, correcting an incorrect timestamp transcription does not necessarily require a new emergence determination.
Changing the conclusion from:
Emerged
to:
Emergence Not Established
does.
Record Integrity
VERM requires the record to remain sufficiently protected against uncontrolled alteration, loss of context, or ambiguous versioning.
However, VERM does not replace INTEGROS®.
The boundary is:
VERM: defines what emergence information must remain preserved and connected.
INTEGROS®: may govern the broader integrity properties of the record and supporting systems.
Record Auditability

VERM requires sufficient traceability for the emergence record to be reconstructed.
It does not own general audit governance.
ADIT® may govern:
audit observation; evidence preservation; verification; audit execution; findings; assurance.
Therefore:
Emergence Record Traceability ≠ Audit Governance.
Record ≠ Accounting Entry
A Value Emergence Record does not automatically create an accounting entry.
VFM® may determine:
Value Emerged
while accounting standards determine:
No Recognizable Accounting Asset Exists.
These outcomes are not inherently contradictory because they govern different questions.
VERM can provide a structured upstream value record that accounting systems may reference where appropriate.
Record ≠ Tax Record
A Value Emergence Record does not establish:
taxable income; taxable event; tax base; taxpayer; tax liability; jurisdiction; tax timing.
A future tax-governance architecture may consume VFM® records as inputs.
But:
Value Emergence Record ≠ Tax Assessment.
Record ≠ Ownership Record
VERM does not determine who owns the value or underlying object.
Where ownership, identity, authority, provenance, or transfer matters, the relevant governance may be supplied by OBIDENITY® or other applicable systems.
Therefore:
Emergence Record ≠ Ownership Register.
Record ≠ Validation Certificate
A Value Emergence Record records the VFM® emergence determination.
It does not automatically establish a VALIDOS® Validation State.

A Value Emergence Record or the underlying emergence claim may itself become a Validation Object.
Therefore:
Recorded Value Emergence ≠ Validated Value Claim.
Recognition Interface
VERM creates the formal interface from:
Value Emergence
to:
Value Recognition.
The next lifecycle question is no longer:
Does the value exist?
That question has already been governed through VES.
The next question becomes:
Can this existing value be recognized as value within the defined governance context?
The transfer should therefore preserve:
Governed Value Identity
Value Context Value Origin Relationship Emergence State Emergence Effective Time Determination Basis Scope Conditions Limitations
Uncertainty
This becomes the governed input to the Value Recognition Standard (VRS).
Recognition Candidate
Where emergence has been positively or conditionally established, VERM may produce a:
Value Recognition Candidate
A Value Recognition Candidate is not yet formally recognized value.
It is:
an existing value whose governed emergence basis is sufficiently recorded to enter Value Recognition governance.
This creates the lifecycle distinction:
Existing Value ≠ Recognized Value.
Machine-Readable Value History
VERM enables the value lifecycle to be represented as structured state history.
For example:
Value ID: V-2048
Origin State: Established
Potential Value State: Active
Emergence Threshold: Reached
Emergence Event: Recorded
Emergence Determination: Emerged
Effective Time: T1
Determination Time: T2

Emergence Record Version: 1.0
Next Lifecycle State: Recognition Candidate
This structure enables VFM® to become usable by:
enterprise systems;
AI governance systems; banking systems; investment platforms; public-sector systems; accounting interfaces; economic measurement systems; industrial systems; digital asset infrastructures; future value-governance platforms.

10. Lifecycle Transfer
