Use Case 1 — Banking & Investment: Persistent
Proof of Where Value Actually Emerged
A bank finances a large industrial modernization program.
The borrower installs:
new production lines; automation; robotics; AI systems; energy infrastructure; digital control systems.
The program costs CHF 800 million.
Two years later, management states that the investment “created substantial value.”
Without a governed value record, analysts may need to reconstruct the claim from fragmented:
financial reports; project documentation; operational metrics; management statements; production records; technical reports.
VFM® instead preserves the lifecycle:
Value Context → Value Origin → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination
→ Value Emergence Record
Suppose the governed value is:

additional sustainable production capability of 400,000 units annually at a defined cost and quality threshold.
VERM records:
what capability emerged, when it emerged, under which operational configuration, what threshold was crossed, what evidence supported the determination, which limitations remained, and which version of the production system generated the value.
Years later, the bank can distinguish:
Capital Invested
from
Assets Installed
from
Value Emerged
from
Value Later Recognized
from
Value Subsequently Developed or Degraded.
This gives banking and investment systems something conventional project reporting often lacks:
a reconstructable lifecycle history of value itself.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission / AI: Preserving
Value Beyond Technical Success
A space agency deploys an AI navigation capability intended to increase scientific access during a planetary mission.
The mission generates thousands of technical and scientific records.
The AI operates successfully.
But the governed value is not merely:
AI System Activated.
The governed value is:
additional scientifically relevant mission access produced by autonomous navigation capability.
The emergence pathway establishes that the capability enabled the spacecraft to reach scientifically valuable locations that could not otherwise have been accessed within the mission constraints.
VEDM determines:
Value Emerged.
VERM then preserves:
which mission value emerged
from which capability
for which mission purpose

under which conditions
at which mission phase
through which emergence event
on what evidence basis
with what remaining uncertainty
and
within what scope the determination remains legitimate.
Years later, the organization can compare this record against subsequent missions.
It can determine whether the original value:
persisted; developed; degraded; was reproduced; became obsolete; was restored; disappeared.
The technical mission archive tells the organization:
what happened.
The VFM® Value Emergence Record tells it:
what value emerged from what happened.
Foundational Principles
A Value Emergence Determination without a persistent governed record is vulnerable to loss of meaning.
A record must preserve the context that gives the emergence determination meaning.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Value Emergence Determination.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Evidence Repository.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Accounting Entry.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Tax Assessment.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Ownership Register.
Value Emergence Record ≠ Validation Certificate.
Emergence Effective Time ≠ Determination Time ≠ Record Creation Time.
A narrow emergence determination must remain narrow when recorded.
Conditional emergence must remain conditional.
Uncertainty must not disappear when value is recorded.
Historical records must not be silently overwritten by later determinations.
Existing Value ≠ Recognized Value.
The record closes Value Emergence and opens the governed path into Value Recognition.

Canonical Closing Statement
Value Emergence Record Module establishes the persistence, traceability, temporal continuity, and lifecycle- transfer layer of the Value Emergence Standard by transforming a Value Emergence Determination into a governed and reconstructable Value Emergence Record. Through preservation of the governed value, Value Context, Value Origin, emergence conditions, threshold, event, determination basis, determination state, effective time, scope, limitations, contradictions, uncertainty, version history, and supersession relationships, VERM prevents value-existence claims from becoming detached from the conditions that originally gave them meaning. By distinguishing the emergence record from evidence, accounting recognition, taxation, ownership, validation, and downstream Value Recognition, VERM preserves the architectural boundary of VFM® while enabling existing value to move through subsequent lifecycle stages without losing its origin or emergence history. VERM therefore completes the Value Emergence governance sequence and creates the persistent methodological bridge from Potential Value through established Existing Value to the next governed question: whether that existing value may legitimately become Recognized Value.

Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) is the second Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VETM governs the identification, definition, structuring, assessment, and documentation of the threshold at which sufficiently established Value Emergence Conditions become capable of supporting the transition from Potential Value to Existing Value.
The Module establishes the governed boundary separating:
conditions that may enable value
from
conditions sufficient for value to cross toward existence.

VETM does not determine that value has actually emerged.
That determination remains downstream.
Its task is:
to establish when the conditions necessary for value emergence become sufficiently satisfied for the emergence boundary to be crossed.
Architectural Position
VETM is the second module within the Value Emergence Standard.
It follows:
VECM — Value Emergence Conditions Module
and precedes:
VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module
The sequence is:
Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record
VECM establishes what must become true.
VETM establishes how much, how completely, or under what combination those conditions must become true.
VEEM then governs the identifiable event or transition through which emergence occurs.
Internal Value Flow
Defined Potential Value → Governed Emergence Conditions → Condition Satisfaction Assessment → Threshold Structure → Threshold Requirement → Threshold Comparison → Threshold State → Threshold Crossing → Emergence-Ready Value State
→ Value Emergence Event
The internal value flow establishes a controlled transition between:
Potential Value
and
Value capable of entering existence.
Governance Flow Position
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence
Within Value Emergence:
VECM — Value Emergence Conditions → VETM — Value Emergence Threshold → VEEM — Value Emergence Event
→ VEDM — Value Emergence Determination → VERM — Value Emergence Record
Then:

Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
VETM therefore governs the threshold layer inside the Value Emergence space.
Operational Purpose
Value may have:
an identifiable source; clear potential; defined beneficiaries; a legitimate purpose; favorable conditions; available capabilities; allocated resources; operational readiness;
without yet having emerged.
The missing question is:
When are the relevant conditions sufficient?
VETM prevents organizations from treating partial readiness, investment, technical completion, resource availability, market expectation, or anticipated benefit as proof that value already exists.
It creates a governed threshold between:
Possibility
and
Emergence Readiness.
Value Emergence Threshold
A Value Emergence Threshold is the defined level, combination, state, boundary, condition set, event requirement, or other governed criterion at which the established Value Emergence Conditions become sufficient to support transition toward existent value.
The threshold may be:
Quantitative
Qualitative
Binary
Composite
Conditional
Sequential
Temporal
Contextual
or a governed combination of these.
VFM® does not require one universal threshold model.
The threshold must fit the value being governed.
Threshold ≠ Condition
A condition identifies something necessary or materially relevant to value emergence.

A threshold establishes the point at which the relevant condition or combination of conditions becomes sufficient.
For example:
Condition: A capability must be operationally available.
Threshold: The capability must be available at a defined level, quality, duration, capacity, accessibility, or performance sufficient to produce the governed value.
Therefore:
Emergence Condition ≠ Emergence Threshold
and:
Condition Presence ≠ Threshold Satisfaction
Threshold ≠ Value
Crossing a threshold does not automatically mean that value exists.
The threshold establishes that the governed conditions have reached the point necessary for emergence.
The actual emergence pathway remains governed through:
Threshold Crossing → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination
Therefore:
Threshold Crossing ≠ Value Emergence Determination
This distinction protects the architecture from declaring value too early.
Threshold Structure
A Value Emergence Threshold may depend upon one requirement or several interacting requirements.
Single Threshold
One defined requirement is sufficient.
Condition A ≥ Required Level
Compound Threshold
Multiple requirements must be satisfied.
Condition A + Condition B + Condition C ≥ Emergence Requirement
Alternative Threshold
Different legitimate pathways may permit emergence.
Path A OR Path B
Sequential Threshold
Requirements must be satisfied in a defined order.
A → B → C
Contextual Threshold
The required threshold changes according to the governed context.
Temporal Threshold

A condition must remain satisfied for a defined period before emergence readiness is established.
This allows VETM to govern value emergence across very different systems without forcing them into one artificial measurement structure.
Threshold Sufficiency
VETM requires the architecture to distinguish between:
Condition Satisfaction
and
Threshold Sufficiency.
A condition may be partially or fully satisfied while the complete threshold remains unmet.
For example:
Technical Capability: Satisfied Beneficiary Access: Satisfied Operational Applicability: Partial Required Combined Threshold: Not Met
The system therefore remains within:
Potential Value
rather than progressing prematurely into value emergence.
Threshold States
VETM may assign states including:
Undefined Threshold
No sufficient emergence threshold has been established.
Defined Threshold
The threshold has been formally established.
Below Threshold
Current conditions remain insufficient.
Approaching Threshold
Conditions are materially progressing toward the defined threshold.
Threshold Satisfied
The defined threshold requirements are currently satisfied.
Threshold Crossed
The governed boundary has been crossed.
Threshold Uncertain
Available information does not support a reliable threshold assessment.
Threshold Lost
A previously satisfied threshold is no longer satisfied before emergence has been established.
These states allow emergence readiness to be governed dynamically.
Threshold Crossing

A Threshold Crossing occurs when the governed emergence conditions reach or exceed the defined emergence threshold.
The crossing must remain distinguishable from the subsequent determination that value has emerged.
The transition is:
Potential Value → Conditions Established → Threshold Satisfied → Threshold Crossed → Emergence Event / Transition → Emergence Determination → Existing Value
This creates an explicit methodological bridge between value potential and value existence.
Threshold Persistence
Some value may require only an instantaneous threshold crossing.
Other value may require persistence.
For example:
Threshold satisfied for one second
may not establish the same emergence basis as:
Threshold continuously satisfied for six months.
Where duration materially affects emergence, VETM requires that duration to become part of the threshold definition.
Therefore:
Threshold Magnitude + Threshold Duration
may jointly determine threshold sufficiency.
Threshold Reversibility
A threshold may be crossed and subsequently lost before value emergence is determined.
VETM therefore supports:
Threshold Crossing → Threshold Loss
where appropriate.
This prevents temporary conditions from being incorrectly converted into permanent value-existence claims.
Threshold Dependency
Thresholds may depend upon multiple Value Emergence Conditions established through VECM.
VETM should preserve those dependencies.
For example:
Technical Readiness

Operational Accessibility Beneficiary Usability Required Performance
→ Emergence Threshold
If one materially necessary dependency fails, the threshold may remain unsatisfied even where all other conditions are strong.
Threshold Calibration
Thresholds must be sufficiently demanding to distinguish genuine emergence readiness from mere potential.
But they must not be arbitrarily demanding.
Threshold calibration may therefore consider:
value type; value purpose; beneficiary; reference context; materiality; expected value mechanism; relevant conditions; duration; operational environment; uncertainty; consequence of premature emergence determination.
VETM governs the threshold structure.
It does not prescribe one universal numerical threshold for all value.
Threshold Evidence
A threshold assessment should have an identifiable basis.
Depending on context, this may include:
measured performance; observed capability; operational data; beneficiary access; resource availability; utilization; realized output; verified condition state; documented activation; time-based persistence; comparative evidence; governed calculation.
The evidence required should be proportional to the significance of the emergence determination.
VETM does not replace ADIT®, VALIDOS®, or INTEGROS® where their broader evidence, validation, or integrity governance is required.
Uncertainty at the Threshold
Threshold assessment may contain uncertainty.
VETM must therefore permit:
Threshold Uncertain

rather than forcing a binary conclusion.
Uncertainty may concern:
measurement; condition status; threshold definition; data; timing; beneficiary effect; causal relationship; contextual applicability.
Where uncertainty is material, it must remain visible when the threshold basis moves downstream.
Dynamic Thresholds
Some thresholds may legitimately change as the governed context changes.
For example, the emergence threshold for operational value from an energy technology may differ between:
normal demand; peak demand; emergency conditions; isolated infrastructure; highly interconnected infrastructure.
Dynamic thresholds must therefore remain tied to their applicable context.
A threshold established in one context must not silently become universal.
Threshold Change Governance
Where the threshold itself changes, VETM should preserve:
Previous Threshold → Reason for Change → New Threshold → Effective Context / Time → Effect on Current Emergence Assessment
This prevents retrospective manipulation of the threshold merely to make a preferred value claim appear to have emerged.
Emergence-Ready Value
VETM may establish an intermediate governance condition:
Emergence-Ready Value
This does not mean that value already exists.
It means:
the governed potential value has satisfied the defined threshold conditions required to proceed into the emergence event and determination stages.
This is particularly useful in complex value systems where the architecture needs to distinguish:

Potential Value
from
Threshold-Satisfied Potential Value
from
Existing Value.
Internal Value Flow Control
VETM acts as a value-flow gate.
The Module should permit progression only where the relevant threshold has been sufficiently established.
The internal logic is:
Below Threshold → Remain Potential
Threshold Uncertain → Hold / Assess
Threshold Satisfied → Eligible for Emergence Transition
Threshold Crossed → Transfer to Emergence Event
Threshold Lost → Return to Pre-Threshold State where applicable
This makes the module operational rather than merely descriptive.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VETM implementation should establish:
1. Value Reference
Identify the governed potential value.
2. Emergence Condition Input
Receive the relevant emergence conditions from VECM.
3. Threshold Definition
Define the threshold separating insufficient conditions from emergence readiness.
4. Threshold Structure
Determine whether the threshold is single, compound, alternative, sequential, contextual, temporal, or hybrid.
5. Threshold Measurement Basis
Establish how threshold satisfaction can be assessed.
6. Threshold Sufficiency Assessment
Compare current condition states against the threshold.
7. Uncertainty Assessment
Identify uncertainty affecting the threshold conclusion.
8. Threshold State Assignment
Assign the appropriate governed threshold state.
9. Threshold Crossing Record
Record a crossing where the governed threshold has been reached.
10. Downstream Transfer

Transfer the threshold basis to VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module.

Use Case 1 — Banking: Financing Capacity vs.
Actual Economic Value
A bank finances a new industrial facility.
The facility exists. Capital has been deployed. Equipment has been installed. Production capability is technically available.
None of these facts alone establishes that the financed project is already producing the economic value expected when the financing decision was made.
VECM may identify the emergence conditions:
Operational Capability + Production Readiness + Customer Demand + Deliverable Output + Beneficiary Relationship
VETM then establishes the threshold at which these conditions become sufficient for the defined value to move beyond potential.
For example, the governed threshold might require:
operational production + defined utilization + deliverable output + sustained ability to serve the intended economic purpose.
The bank can therefore distinguish:

Capital Deployed → Asset Constructed → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions Established → Threshold Crossed → Value Emergence
This creates a much stronger basis for portfolio monitoring, project finance, restructuring, investment assessment, and value-based risk analysis than simply assuming:
Asset Exists = Value Exists. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Capability vs.
Mission Value
A space agency develops an expensive observation system for a planetary mission.
The spacecraft exists.
The instruments work.
The launch succeeds.
The spacecraft reaches its target.
Yet the intended scientific or operational value may still not have emerged.
For the defined mission value, VECM may establish conditions including:
Instrument Availability + Correct Positioning + Data Acquisition + Data Integrity + Transmission Capability + Ground Reception + Scientific Usability
VETM determines when those conditions collectively become sufficient.
The threshold might require that the system not merely collect data, but produce data of sufficient quality, coverage, continuity, and usability to satisfy the defined mission-value context.
The value flow becomes:
Mission Investment → Technical Capability → Potential Mission Value → Emergence Conditions → Mission-Specific Threshold → Threshold Crossing → Emergence Event → Existing Mission Value
This allows a space organization to separate:
mission cost
from
mission capability
from
mission value.

That distinction becomes particularly powerful when comparing alternative mission architectures, evaluating cost overruns, determining whether capabilities are actually producing intended value, or deciding whether additional investment is justified.
Foundational Principles
Value potential does not become existing value merely because favorable conditions exist.
Emergence conditions define what must be true; emergence thresholds define when those conditions become sufficient.
Condition presence is not threshold satisfaction.
Threshold satisfaction is not Value Emergence Determination.
Investment completion is not a value-emergence threshold.
Technical readiness is not automatically value readiness.
A threshold must remain connected to the specific value, beneficiary, purpose, and context it governs.
A dynamic threshold must not be treated as universally fixed.
Threshold uncertainty must remain visible.
A crossed threshold may be lost before value emergence is established.
The Value Emergence Threshold is the governed boundary between potential value and value that is ready to enter the emergence transition.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Emergence Threshold Module establishes the governed boundary at which defined Value Emergence Conditions become sufficiently satisfied for potential value to proceed toward existence. Through governance of threshold structure, condition sufficiency, dependencies, measurement basis, persistence, reversibility, uncertainty, contextual variation, threshold states, threshold crossing, and threshold loss, VETM prevents investments, assets, capabilities, activities, or partially satisfied conditions from being prematurely treated as existing value. By separating Value Emergence Conditions from Value Emergence Threshold, Threshold Crossing from Value Emergence Event, and emergence readiness from Value Emergence Determination, VETM creates the controlled value-flow gate required to move from potential value toward legitimate value existence within VFM®.

Canonical Definition
Value Emergence Standard (VES) is the third Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the conditions under which potential value arising from an identified value origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context.
VES establishes the methodological transition between the existence of a potential basis capable of producing value and the point at which value can legitimately be treated as having emerged.
The Standard governs the conditions, thresholds, events, determinations, and records necessary to establish that transition.
Its fundamental distinction is:
Potential Value ≠ Existing Value

A source may possess the capability, condition, resource, relationship, knowledge, technology, asset, activity, or other basis from which value could arise without value having yet emerged.
VES therefore prevents value potential from being automatically treated as value existence.
Core Question
When and under what conditions does potential value become existent value?
Architectural Position
Value Emergence Standard occupies the third governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value Origin Standard
and precedes:
Value Recognition Standard.
The first three architectural stages establish three fundamentally different questions:
Value Context Standard → What value is being governed?
Value Origin Standard → From what basis can that value originate?
Value Emergence Standard → Has that potential value actually come into existence?
The next standard then asks:
Value Recognition Standard → Can that existing value be recognized within its defined governance context?
These stages must remain methodologically separate.
VFM® Governance Flow
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction
Governance Flow Position
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition
VES specifically governs:

Identified Value Origin → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Existing Value
This is the point in the VFM® lifecycle where value crosses the methodological boundary from:
could exist
to:
does exist.
Operational Space
VES governs the emergence of value itself.
Its operational space includes:
potential value; emergence conditions; emergence prerequisites; emergence dependencies; emergence thresholds; threshold satisfaction; emergence events; emergence timing; emergence determination; conditional emergence; partial emergence; progressive emergence; simultaneous emergence; delayed emergence; failed emergence; emergence uncertainty; emergence evidence; emergence recording; relationship between value origin and emerged value.
VES does not assume that every identified value source necessarily produces value.
Value Origin ≠ Value Emergence
The existence of a Value Origin establishes that there is an identifiable basis from which value can originate.
It does not establish that value has emerged.
For example:
A patent may contain technological potential.
A dataset may contain analytical potential.
A mineral deposit may contain extractive potential.
Unused manufacturing capacity may contain productive potential.
A scientific discovery may contain commercial or societal potential.
A new capability may contain operational potential.
An unused building may contain economic potential.

A relationship may contain strategic potential.
But the existence of these sources does not automatically establish that the relevant governed value has emerged.
VES governs the missing transition.
Value Origin → potential for value
is not equivalent to:
Value Emergence → existence of value.
Potential Value
Within VES, Potential Value represents value that may emerge from an identified Value Origin but whose existence has not yet been sufficiently established.
Potential Value may depend upon:
activation; use; transformation; combination; access; capability realization; demand; application; performance; relationship formation; technological readiness; operational deployment; knowledge application; resource conversion; fulfillment of another defined emergence condition.
Potential Value is therefore not treated as zero value.
It is also not treated as existing positive value.
This distinction is essential to the later VFM® lifecycle.
Potential Value ≠ Zero Value
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ concerns a governed zero-value state where applicable.
Potential Value concerns a condition before value has been established as existent.
Emergence Conditions
Value may emerge only where the conditions necessary for that particular form of value are sufficiently present.
VES therefore requires explicit Value Emergence Conditions.
Depending upon context, these may include:

existence of a usable capability; realization of a functional outcome; accessibility; utility; applicability; demand; operational readiness; productive use; successful transformation; scarcity; relevance; beneficiary relationship; resource availability; knowledge application; technological capability; combination with another value source; satisfaction of a defined performance condition.
VFM® does not prescribe one universal set of emergence conditions.
The emergence conditions must correspond to the specific value identified under the Value Context Standard.
Emergence Threshold
Some forms of value emerge gradually.
Others become existent only after a definable threshold has been crossed.
VES therefore establishes the concept of a Value Emergence Threshold.
The threshold represents:
the minimum governed condition at which potential value may be determined to have become existent value.
A threshold may be:
quantitative; qualitative; functional; operational; relational; temporal; capability-based; outcome-based; use-based; condition-based; composite.
For example, a technology may exist for years while remaining incapable of producing the value for which it was created.
Once a required capability, cost, reliability, performance, accessibility, or operational threshold is reached, value may emerge.
The underlying asset did not necessarily emerge at that moment.
The value did.
Emergence Event
VES distinguishes the Emergence Threshold from the Emergence Event.

The threshold defines the condition that must be satisfied.
The Emergence Event identifies the occurrence through which that condition becomes satisfied or materially observable.
An Emergence Event may include:
first successful operation; first productive use; first realized benefit; first capability activation; first successful application; completion of a transformation; establishment of a necessary relationship; crossing of a performance threshold; achievement of required accessibility; activation of a previously dormant resource; combination of previously separate value sources.
Therefore:
Emergence Condition ≠ Emergence Threshold ≠ Emergence Event.
Emergence Determination
Value existence must not depend solely upon assertion.
VES therefore requires an Emergence Determination where formal governance of value emergence is necessary.
The determination establishes whether the defined emergence conditions and applicable threshold have been sufficiently satisfied.
A determination may conclude:
Not Emerged The identified source exists, but the governed value has not yet emerged.
Emergence Pending Relevant conditions are developing, but the emergence threshold has not yet been established as satisfied.
Conditionally Emerged Value exists only under explicitly defined conditions.
Partially Emerged A divisible or multidimensional value has emerged only in part.
Emerged The governed value has crossed its applicable emergence threshold and exists within the defined Value Context.

Emergence Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to determine whether emergence has occurred.
These are governance states, not universal accounting classifications.
Emergence ≠ Recognition
A fundamental VFM® distinction is:
Value may exist before it is formally recognized.
VES therefore ends when value existence has been sufficiently established.
It does not require:
market recognition; accounting recognition; regulatory recognition; legal recognition; institutional recognition; taxation; ownership attribution; pricing; classification; validation status.
Those external systems may later interact with the value.
But they do not define the VFM® emergence boundary.
The next architectural stage — Value Recognition Standard — governs recognition within the defined value lifecycle context.
Emergence ≠ Price
Value does not need to possess a market price in order to emerge.
A new manufacturing capability may generate operational value before it is separately priced.
A scientific discovery may create knowledge value before commercial valuation exists.
A dataset may create analytical value before being monetized.
An efficiency improvement may generate cost-reduction value without being sold.
A risk-reduction capability may create value through avoided loss.
VES therefore prevents:
Price = Value Existence
from becoming an architectural assumption.
Emergence ≠ Transaction
A transaction may reveal, transfer, exchange, or influence value.

It does not necessarily create the value.
Value may emerge:
before a transaction; without a transaction; through productive activity; through knowledge; through capability; through utility; through reduced cost; through avoided loss; through improved efficiency; through a relationship; through transformation; through technological development.
Payment and transaction governance remain outside the VES boundary.
Emergence ≠ Accounting Recognition
An accounting system may recognize an asset or economic event according to its own rules.
VES governs a different question:
Has the governed value emerged?
Accounting treatment may subsequently use information produced by VFM®, but VFM® does not replace accounting standards.
This distinction enables VFM® to identify forms of value that may exist operationally before they are formally represented in conventional accounting systems.
Emergence ≠ Validation
VES does not determine that a value claim has been universally validated.
Where formal validation of evidence, claims, sources, methods, or determinations is required, VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture may govern that process.
VFM® governs the value lifecycle question:
Has value emerged?
VALIDOS® may govern:
Is the basis used to support that determination sufficiently validated for its intended reliance?
Emergence ≠ Integrity
VES does not govern the general integrity of the system, asset, evidence, or process from which value emerges.

Those questions may fall under INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture.
The architectures therefore remain distinct:
VFM® → emergence of value
INTEGROS® → integrity
Emergence Evidence
Where emergence must be formally demonstrated, the determination should be supported by sufficient information concerning:
the governed value context; the identified Value Origin; applicable emergence conditions; applicable emergence threshold; observed Emergence Event where relevant; timing; dependencies; limitations; uncertainty; basis of determination.
VES governs the relationship of this information to the value-emergence determination.
General evidence governance, auditability, validation, and integrity remain governed by their respective architectures.
Temporal Emergence
Value emergence has a temporal dimension.
VES therefore permits the emergence point to be associated with:
a specific event; a defined date; a period; a progressive interval; a condition becoming continuously satisfied; an uncertain but bounded emergence window.
This matters because different systems may subsequently rely upon the emergence point.
For example:
management systems; investment analysis; value reporting; economic analysis; taxation architectures; accounting systems;
asset governance; lifecycle analysis.
VFM® establishes the value lifecycle event.
External architectures determine their own consequences.
Progressive Emergence
Not all value appears instantaneously.
Some value may emerge progressively.

Examples include:
a developing technology; a growing network; accumulating knowledge; infrastructure becoming operational in stages; a dataset increasing in usefulness; organizational capability maturing over time.
VES therefore allows value emergence to be represented as a governed progression where binary treatment would distort reality.
Multiple Value Emergence
One Value Origin may produce multiple forms of value.
For example, a technological capability may generate:
operational value; economic value; knowledge value; strategic value; risk-reduction value; productivity value.
These forms of value must not automatically be collapsed into one undifferentiated value.
Each must remain connected to the Value Context established under the Value Context Standard.
Therefore:
One Origin ≠ One Value
and:
One Emergence Event may produce multiple distinct Value Emergence Determinations.
Failed Emergence
An identified Value Origin may never produce the anticipated value.
VES explicitly governs this possibility.
Failed emergence may occur where:
required conditions never materialize; a threshold is never reached; capability remains unusable; expected utility does not materialize;
the relevant beneficiary never receives value; technological development fails; required relationships do not form; a resource cannot be activated; the anticipated outcome does not occur.
This distinction prevents expected value from being retrospectively treated as value that necessarily existed.

Emergence Reversal Before Recognition
In some contexts, value may emerge briefly and disappear before it becomes formally recognized.
VFM® must preserve this lifecycle reality.
Such a case may produce:
Value Emergence → Existing Value → Value Change / Degradation / Nullification
even where formal Value Recognition never occurred.
Recognition therefore does not create the underlying existence of value.
It governs recognition of that existence.
Governance Outputs
VES may produce:
Potential Value Record Value Emergence Conditions Record Value Emergence Threshold Value Emergence Event Record Value Emergence Determination Value Emergence State Conditional Emergence Statement Partial Emergence Record Failed Emergence Record Value Emergence Timeline Value Emergence Dependency Record Value Emergence Limitation Record
Value Emergence Record
These outputs provide the governed input basis for the Value Recognition Standard.
Enterprise Application
Value Emergence Standard can be applied wherever organizations need to distinguish between:
something capable of creating value
and:
value that has actually come into existence.
This distinction can support:
banking; investment analysis;

enterprise valuation; innovation portfolios; intellectual property; technology development; infrastructure; manufacturing; energy; digital assets; AI systems; data assets; public investment; government programs; research; cost reduction; productivity improvement; supply chains; resource development; strategic capability.
For example, a bank may identify a portfolio of technological assets with substantial theoretical value potential.
VES provides a method for determining which of those assets have actually crossed the conditions necessary for value emergence rather than treating projected potential as existing value.
Similarly, an industrial organization may deploy an AI system intended to reduce production costs.
The software's existence does not itself establish the anticipated value.
VES can distinguish:
AI capability exists
from:
measurable cost-reduction value has emerged.
That distinction creates a stronger basis for later value recognition, state determination, development, degradation, restoration, accounting interfaces, investment analysis, and future value-based economic governance.
Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VFM® / VES governs whether potential value has become existent value.
GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance authority and governance structure.
ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs actual Operational Reality.

OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity.
CLA™ — Classification Architecture governs classification.
INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity.
ADIT® — Continuous Audit & Evidence Governance Architecture governs audit and evidence.
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation.
SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs simulation and simulation-derived meaning.
An external architecture may establish information relevant to a Value Emergence Determination.
It does not thereby acquire governance ownership of Value Emergence itself.
Foundational Principles
Potential value is not existing value.
Value origin is not value emergence.
Value emergence is not value recognition.
Value emergence is not market pricing.
Value emergence is not accounting recognition.
Value emergence is not a transaction.
Potential value is not a zero-value state.
An asset, capability, resource, relationship, or activity may exist before the relevant value emerges.
One Value Origin may produce multiple distinct forms of value.
Expected value must not be treated as existing value merely because its source exists.
Value becomes existent within VFM® only when the conditions separating potential value from existent value have been sufficiently established.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Emergence Standard establishes the third governed space of VFM® by defining the methodological transition through which potential value arising from an identified Value Origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context. Through governance of emergence conditions, emergence thresholds, emergence events, emergence determinations, temporal emergence, progressive emergence, conditional and partial emergence, failed emergence, dependencies, limitations, and emergence records, the Standard prevents potential, expectation, capability, asset existence, market anticipation, accounting treatment, or projected benefit from being automatically treated as value that already exists. By separating Value Origin from Value Emergence and Value Emergence from Value Recognition, the Standard creates a distinct and governable lifecycle boundary between the source capable of producing value and the existence of value itself. This boundary provides VFM® with the methodological foundation required to determine when value truly enters its lifecycle before recognition, state governance, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and eventual extinction can legitimately follow.

About Value Identification Standard (VIS)
About Value Identification Standard (VIS)
About Value Identification Standard (VIS)
Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Governed Space: Value Identification
Canonical Definition
Value Identification Standard (VIS) governs how potential or existing manifestations of value are identified, distinguished, bounded, contextualized, and established as governable Value Objects before their origin, existence, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be determined.
VIS establishes the first methodological control point of the VFM® value lifecycle.
Its foundational question is simple:
What exactly is the value being governed?
Why VIS Matters
Value is frequently discussed without first identifying the precise subject to which the value claim relates.
Organizations may refer to the value of an asset, capability, service, technology, relationship, right, resource, information object, infrastructure, process, opportunity, or future benefit without clearly separating:
the object or source associated with value
from
the value itself.
This creates ambiguity throughout every later stage of the value lifecycle.

Before asking where value originated, whether value exists, how much it has changed, whether it has degraded, whether it has reached zero, or whether it can be restored, the relevant value must first be identifiable as a governable object.
VIS creates that foundation.
Identification Before Valuation
VIS does not determine how much something is worth.
It does not assign a price.
It does not determine market value, accounting value, taxable value, legal value, economic value, or social value.
Its function comes earlier.
VIS establishes:
what value is being referred to, what it is associated with, where its boundaries lie, and which value manifestation is entering governance.
This distinction is fundamental:
Value Identification ≠ Value Measurement
A value cannot be meaningfully measured, classified, tracked, or governed if the subject of the value claim remains ambiguous.
The Value Object
VIS introduces the Value Object as the governable subject through which a particular manifestation of value can be identified and followed across the VFM® lifecycle.
A Value Object may relate to value associated with:
a physical asset; a digital asset; a capability; a service; a process; knowledge or information; intellectual property; infrastructure; a resource; a contractual or economic relationship; access or availability; productive capacity; technological capability; an opportunity; an operational function; another identifiable source or manifestation capable of carrying value.

The Value Object does not itself prove that value exists.
Identification establishes the object of inquiry.
Subsequent VFM® standards determine what happens to value.
Value Object ≠ Asset
Not every Value Object must be an asset.
An asset may contain, support, generate, preserve, lose, or recover multiple forms of value.
Likewise, value may arise from relationships, capabilities, conditions, access, knowledge, coordination, timing, or other phenomena that cannot be adequately described as conventional assets.
VIS therefore prevents VFM® from becoming merely an asset-governance architecture.
VFM® governs value itself.
Value Identification Before Value Origin
Value Identification precedes Value Origin for a methodological reason.
Before asking:
Where did this value originate?
the architecture must know:
Which value are we investigating?
VIS therefore creates the entry point:
Value Identification → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
Identification does not establish origin.
It establishes the governable subject for which origin can subsequently be investigated.
Multiple Values Within One Object
A single object may contain or support multiple distinct Value Objects.
For example, industrial equipment may simultaneously have:

productive value, operational value, resale value, material recovery value, technological value, strategic value, and informational value.
These values may follow different lifecycles.
One may degrade while another increases.
One may reach zero while another remains substantial.
VIS therefore requires value manifestations to be sufficiently distinguished rather than assuming that an object possesses one universal value state.
This capability becomes particularly important when VFM® is applied across complex organizations, public infrastructure, technology, finance, industrial systems, or national economic environments.
Context Matters
Value identification may depend upon context.
The same underlying object may represent different value within different:
purposes; environments; users; systems; time periods; operational conditions; economic contexts; institutional contexts; technological contexts.
VIS therefore does not treat value as automatically universal merely because the underlying object is identifiable.
It requires the relevant value context to be made explicit.
What VIS Does Not Determine
VIS does not determine:

whether the identified value actually exists; where that value originated; whether value has emerged; whether value should be recognized; the amount of value; the current Value State; whether value increased or decreased; whether value has reached zero; whether value can be restored; who owns the underlying object; whether the object is legally recognized; whether a value claim is validated; whether a transaction is taxable; whether the value is ethically desirable.
These questions belong to subsequent VFM® standards or other governance architectures.
This boundary protects VIS from becoming a general valuation, identity, ownership, accounting, taxation, or validation framework.
Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset
A factory owns a machine that is no longer used for its original production function.
A conventional assessment may simply ask:
What is the machine worth?
VIS first separates the possible Value Objects.
The machine may have lost most of its productive value while retaining:
resale value, component value, material value, replacement-part value, technological value, or strategic reserve value.
VFM® can then govern each relevant value lifecycle separately.
The machine therefore does not have to be simplistically classified as either:
valuable
or
worthless.
VIS identifies which value is actually being discussed before its lifecycle is assessed.
Use Case 2 — Digital or Technological Capability
An organization develops a software model that is no longer commercially successful.

Its immediate commercial value may have significantly degraded.
However, the same development may retain:
technical knowledge, training data relationships, reusable components, intellectual capability, research value, integration capability, or future redevelopment potential.
VIS enables these value manifestations to be distinguished before VFM® determines their respective origins, states, changes, degradation, zero-value conditions, restoration possibilities, or extinction.
This prevents the disappearance of one form of value from being incorrectly interpreted as the disappearance of all value associated with the underlying object.
Relationship to Other VFM® Standards
VIS establishes the Value Object.
The Value Origin Standard determines where the identified value originates.
The Value Emergence Standard determines whether and when value actually comes into existence.
The Value Recognition Standard governs when existing value becomes recognized within the value lifecycle.
The Value State Standard determines the current governed state of value.
Subsequent VFM® standards govern change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and extinction.
VIS therefore provides the identification layer upon which the complete VFM® lifecycle depends.
Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
VIS identifies the value being governed but does not absorb responsibilities belonging to other architectures.

OBIDENITY® may govern identity, origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity of the underlying entity.
CLA™ may govern formal classification.
VALIDOS® may govern whether relevant claims or determinations have been sufficiently validated.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity.
ADIT® may govern audit and evidence.
GOA™ may govern governance authority and structure.
VFM® remains concerned with the independent question:
What is happening to value?
Enterprise Value
VIS provides organizations with a repeatable method for identifying value before attempting to measure, manage, account for, preserve, develop, recover, tax, exchange, or govern it.
This can expose value that conventional object-level assessments may overlook.
It can also prevent fundamentally different forms of value from being combined into one ambiguous valuation.
The result is a clearer foundation for downstream value governance and for interfaces with accounting, economic, investment, taxation, asset-management, public-policy, and decision systems.
Foundational Principle
Before value can be governed, the value being governed must be identifiable.
An object may contain many forms of value.
A value may exist in many contexts.
A change in one value does not necessarily represent a change in another.
VIS therefore establishes identification before origin, emergence, state, change, or valuation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Identification Standard establishes the entry point of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by defining how potential or existing manifestations of value become identifiable, distinguishable, bounded, contextualized, and governable Value Objects. By separating the identification of value from the identification of the underlying asset, from value measurement, ownership, classification, validation, accounting, taxation, and market pricing, VIS creates the methodological foundation required to follow value independently throughout its complete lifecycle. VFM® can govern where value originates, when it emerges, how it changes, how it develops or degrades, when it reaches zero, whether it can be restored, and when it becomes extinct only after the value being governed has first been made explicit.

Canonical Definition
Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Context Standard (VCXS).
VCDM governs the structured documentation of the value context established through the preceding modules of the Value Context Standard.
The Module creates a persistent, interpretable, and reconstructable record of:
what value is being governed → what value-bearing object it relates to → who or what may benefit from that value → within which reference framework the value is understood → under which contextual conditions that meaning applies.

VCDM does not determine whether value exists, where value originated, how much value exists, whether value is legally recognized, or whether a valuation is economically correct.
Its purpose is to ensure that the meaning of the governed value context does not become detached from the conditions under which that value was identified.
Architectural Position
VCDM is the fifth and final module within the Value Context Standard.
It follows:
VIM — Value Identification Module → VOM — Value Object Module → VBM — Value Beneficiary Module → VRFM — Value Reference Framework Module
and consolidates their governed outputs into:
Value Context Record
The internal sequence is therefore:
Value Identification → Value Object → Value Beneficiary → Value Reference Framework → Value Context Documentation
Once the Value Context Record has been established, the governed value may proceed to:
Value Origin Standard (VOS).
Operational Space
VCDM governs the documentation layer between:
established Value Context
and
subsequent value lifecycle governance.
It preserves the contextual foundation necessary for later VFM® processes to determine whether they are still governing the same value under the same relevant context.
The governed documentation may include:

governed value identification; value description; value type or form where defined; value-bearing object relationship; object context; beneficiary relationship; beneficiary context; reference framework; purpose of the value context; applicable conditions; relevant boundaries; contextual assumptions; contextual dependencies; temporal context; jurisdictional context where relevant; environmental or operational context; contextual exclusions; contextual changes; documentation provenance; version state; documentation status.
Value Context Record
The principal governance object produced by VCDM is the:
Value Context Record (VCR).
The Value Context Record provides the minimum structured reference through which the governed value can be recognized consistently throughout its subsequent lifecycle.
A Value Context Record should establish, where materially relevant:
Value → What value is being governed?
Value-Bearing Object → In relation to what object, capability, activity, relationship, resource, system, right, condition, or other value-bearing basis is the value being considered?
Beneficiary → For whom or for what may the value exist?
Reference Framework → Relative to which purpose, environment, condition, comparison, objective, or reference basis is the value understood?
Context Conditions → Under which conditions does this interpretation remain applicable?
The resulting record creates a governed answer to:
What exactly do we mean when we refer to this value?
Documentation Principle

Value cannot be governed consistently if its context changes silently.
A statement such as:
“This asset has value.”
is methodologically incomplete unless the relevant value context is understood.
The same object may possess:
financial value to an investor; operational value to an organization; strategic value to a government; scientific value to a research institution; utility value to a user; recovery value to a creditor; replacement value to an insurer; informational value to an AI system; mission value to a space organization; no relevant value to another beneficiary.
VCDM therefore preserves the context that gives the value statement its meaning.
Value Record ≠ Asset Record
VCDM does not create a universal record of the underlying asset, object, person, organization, system, or resource.
It creates a record of the governed value context associated with it.
Therefore:
Object Documentation ≠ Value Context Documentation
and:
Asset Identity ≠ Value Identity
Where identity governance is required, OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture may provide the appropriate identity governance layer.
VFM® remains concerned with the value.
Context Persistence
Once value enters the wider lifecycle, its original context must remain reconstructable.
VCDM therefore preserves the relationship:
Value Lifecycle State → Value Context Record
A later observer should be able to determine:

which value was originally identified; which object it concerned; which beneficiary was relevant; which reference framework was applied; which contextual conditions existed; whether those conditions subsequently changed.
This prevents later lifecycle events from being interpreted against a context that never existed when the value was originally governed.
Context Versioning
Value context may change.
A beneficiary may change.
The relevant purpose may change.
The underlying object may change.
Operational conditions may change.
The reference framework may change.
The same physical or digital object may therefore participate in multiple legitimate value contexts.
VCDM should support explicit contextual versioning such as:
Value Context V1 → Material Context Change → Value Context V2
The previous context should not be silently overwritten where historical reconstruction remains materially important.
Context Change Record
Where a material contextual element changes, VCDM may create a:
Value Context Change Record
Material changes may include:
change of beneficiary; change of value-bearing object configuration; change of purpose; change of reference framework; change of relevant operational environment; change of material contextual assumptions; change of time horizon; change of applicable value relationship.
The existence of a contextual change does not automatically mean that the value itself has changed.
That distinction is fundamental:
Context Change ≠ Value Change

The Value Change Standard governs change in value itself.
VCDM records changes in the context through which that value is understood.
Multiple Value Contexts
One object may legitimately support multiple Value Context Records.
For example, a manufacturing robot may simultaneously possess:
Production Value for the manufacturing organization.
Resale Value for the asset owner.
Collateral Value for a financial institution.
Data Generation Value for an analytics operation.
Strategic Capability Value for the enterprise.
These should not automatically be collapsed into one undifferentiated concept of “value.”
VCDM allows each materially distinct value context to remain separately documented.
Temporal Context
Value context may be time-dependent.
A Value Context Record may therefore specify:
effective date; observation period; expected duration; relevant lifecycle phase; reference period; review condition; expiration condition where applicable.
A context established for one period must not automatically be assumed to remain unchanged indefinitely.
Context Documentation Status
VCDM may assign a documentation status such as:
Draft — context documentation is incomplete.
Established — the required contextual elements have been sufficiently documented.
Conditionally Established — the context is usable subject to explicit conditions.
Under Review — a material contextual change requires reassessment.
Superseded — a newer Value Context Record governs the current context.

Archived — the record is retained for historical reconstruction but is no longer operationally active.
These states concern the documentation record.
They do not determine whether value exists.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VCDM implementation should establish:
1. Value Reference
Record the governed value identified through the Value Identification Module.
2. Value-Bearing Object Reference
Record the relationship between the governed value and its relevant value-bearing object.
3. Beneficiary Reference
Record the beneficiary or beneficiary class relevant to the value context.
4. Reference Framework
Record the framework, purpose, objective, environment, comparison basis, or other reference condition through which the value is understood.
5. Context Conditions
Record materially relevant conditions, dependencies, assumptions, boundaries, and exclusions.
6. Temporal Context
Establish the time or lifecycle conditions relevant to the context where necessary.
7. Context Version
Assign an identifiable version or equivalent state where contextual evolution must be traceable.
8. Documentation Status
Establish whether the Value Context Record is draft, established, conditional, under review, superseded, or archived.
9. Change Traceability
Preserve material changes to the governed context.
10. Value Context Record
Consolidate the governed information into a reusable Value Context Record capable of accompanying the value into subsequent VFM® lifecycle governance.

Governance Outputs
VCDM may produce:
Value Context Record Value Context Identifier Value Context Summary Value-Bearing Object Reference Value Beneficiary Reference Value Reference Framework Record Value Context Condition Record Value Context Assumption Record Value Context Exclusion Record Value Context Version Record Value Context Change Record Value Context Documentation Status
Historical Value Context Record
These outputs provide the contextual foundation for subsequent governance under the Value Origin Standard and the wider VFM® lifecycle.
Enterprise Application
VCDM enables organizations to solve a deceptively important problem:
the word “value” is frequently used without preserving what that value actually means in context.
Without a governed Value Context Record, different departments, systems, institutions, algorithms, auditors, financial models, or decision-makers may use the same word while referring to fundamentally different value relationships.
VCDM creates a common contextual reference.
This can support:
banking and financial systems; asset management; insurance; enterprise accounting environments; public finance; infrastructure; manufacturing; supply chains; digital assets; AI systems; autonomous systems; energy systems; scientific programs; space missions; intellectual property; resource allocation; cost-reduction programs; future value-governance environments.
Use Case 1 — Banking: One Asset, Different
Value Contexts

A bank evaluates an industrial property connected to several financial relationships.
The property may simultaneously have:
market value for a potential sale,
collateral value for secured lending,
recovery value under a default scenario,
and
operational value for the company using the property.
If these contexts are not explicitly separated, systems may appear to discuss the same “asset value” while actually using different beneficiaries, purposes, conditions, time horizons, and reference frameworks.
VCDM establishes separate Value Context Records.
For example:
Property X → Collateral Value → Bank → Lending Reference Framework
and:
Property X → Operational Value → Manufacturing Company → Production Continuity Reference Framework
The underlying object may be identical.
The governed value context is not.
This gives later VFM® processes a stable basis for determining what happens to each form of value independently as conditions change.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Value as Avoided
Mission Cost
A space organization evaluates a simulation capability that can reduce the need for expensive physical testing.
The relevant value is not necessarily the purchase price of the simulation infrastructure.
A materially important value context may be:
avoided physical-test cost and avoided mission-development expenditure.
VCDM may establish:
Simulation Capability → Cost-Avoidance Value → Mission Program → Mission Development Cost Reference Framework → Defined Mission Phase and Test Conditions

Suppose the simulation capability allows the organization to identify a design failure before construction of a physical prototype.
The prevented expenditure may represent substantial value to the mission program.
VCDM does not calculate whether the claimed savings are correct.
It establishes which value is being governed and under which context the claimed value has meaning.
That governed context can then enter subsequent VFM® stages to determine:
where that value originated → whether it actually emerged → what state it entered → how it subsequently developed, changed, degraded, disappeared, or was restored.
Foundational Principles
Value without context is methodologically ambiguous.
The same object may carry multiple distinct forms of value simultaneously.
The same value-bearing object does not imply the same value.
Value for one beneficiary does not automatically constitute equivalent value for another beneficiary.
Context change is not automatically value change.
Historical value context should remain reconstructable when materially relevant.
A Value Context Record must preserve the relationship between the governed value, its value-bearing object, its beneficiary, its reference framework, and the conditions under which that value is understood.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Context Documentation Module establishes the persistent contextual record through which governed value remains identifiable, interpretable, distinguishable, and reconstructable throughout the VFM® value lifecycle. By documenting the governed value, value-bearing object, beneficiary, reference framework, contextual conditions, assumptions, exclusions, temporal context, versions, and material contextual changes, VCDM prevents value from becoming detached from the conditions that give it meaning. The Module enables multiple forms of value associated with the same object to remain methodologically distinct, preserves historical context as value moves through subsequent lifecycle states and transitions, and provides the structured Value Context Record required for downstream Value Origin governance. Before VFM® can determine where value originates, emerges, changes, develops, degrades, reaches zero, is restored, or becomes extinct, the architecture must preserve exactly which value it is governing.
