Value Context Module (VCM)
Value Context Module (VCM)
Value Context Module (VCM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS)
Module: VCM — Value Context Module
Operational Layer: Value Context Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Value Context
Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VCM-001.4
Version: 1.0
Status: Draft · Open Standard
Effective Date: 23 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY®
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Value Context Module (VCM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VCM governs the explicit identification and structuring of the context within which a bounded and differentiated Value Object is being examined for value.
The Module establishes the relevant purpose, perspective, environment, time, conditions, relationships, dependencies, use context, and other materially relevant contextual dimensions required before statements concerning the Value Object can be interpreted consistently within the value lifecycle.
VCM addresses a foundational problem:

the same Value Object may legitimately exhibit different value relevance, value states, value changes, or value trajectories under different contexts without becoming a different Value Object.
VCM does not determine whether value exists, how much value exists, whether value has emerged, what price should be assigned, whether the object is legally owned, or whether a valuation is correct.
Its task is narrower:
to establish the governed context within which subsequent statements about the Value Object and its value lifecycle are intended to apply.
Core Question
Within what context is this Value Object being examined for value, and which contextual conditions materially affect the meaning of its value lifecycle?
Architectural Position
VCM is the fourth Core Module of the Value Identification Standard.
It follows:
VOIM — Value Object Identification Module → VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module → VODM — Value Object Differentiation Module
and precedes the final identification function of VIS.
The methodological sequence is:
Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Object Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification
VOIM establishes:
What is the Value Object?
VOBM establishes:
Where does the Value Object begin and end?
VODM establishes:
What must remain distinct?
VCM establishes:
Under what context is this Value Object being examined for value?
Internal Flow Position

Identified + Bounded + Differentiated Value Object → Context Purpose Identification → Perspective Identification → Use Context Identification → Environmental Context Identification → Temporal Context Identification → Relational Context Identification → Dependency Context Identification → Condition Identification → Context Boundary Definition → Context Assumption Identification → Context Variation Assessment → Context Record → Contextualized Value Object
Operational Space
VCM governs the space between:
a structurally defined Value Object
and
a Value Object situated within an explicit value-relevant context.
This operational space includes:
value context identification; contextual purpose; contextual perspective; use context; operational context; environmental context;
temporal context; relational context; dependency context; technological context; economic context where relevant; geographic context where relevant; institutional context where relevant; condition definition; context boundaries; contextual assumptions; contextual variability; context change; multi-context relationships; context traceability; context uncertainty.
Context Principle
Value must not be interpreted as though every Value Object exists in one universal context.
A Value Object may possess materially different value relevance depending upon:

who or what uses it; where it exists; when it exists; what purpose it serves; which system it belongs to; which capabilities depend upon it; which alternatives exist; which environmental conditions apply; which relationships enable its function; which dependencies constrain it; which technological conditions exist.
Therefore:
Value Object ≠ Value Context
and:
Same Value Object + Different Context ≠ Automatically Same Value Outcome
Context Does Not Create the Value Object
VCM must preserve the distinction between:
what the Value Object is
and
the context in which it is examined.
For example, one industrial machine may be the same Value Object in:
an operating factory; an idle warehouse; a region without compatible infrastructure; a production line where it is mission-critical; a market where replacement equipment is abundant.
The machine does not necessarily become a different Value Object merely because the context changes.
Its value lifecycle, however, may be affected materially.
Context Purpose
Every governed Value Context should identify why the Value Object is being examined.
Possible purposes may include:
operational use; investment analysis; asset management; public-sector analysis; infrastructure planning; economic analysis; lifecycle management; resource allocation; strategic planning; restructuring; restoration analysis; technology transition; value-loss analysis; value-development analysis.
Purpose does not determine value.

It defines the contextual question under which value is being examined.
Perspective Identification
VCM recognizes that value may be examined from different perspectives.
These may include:
individual; organization; network; ecosystem; public institution; infrastructure system; community; economy; operational system; technological system.
A Value Object may create value for one perspective while providing little or no value for another.
VCM therefore requires perspective to remain explicit where it materially affects interpretation.
Perspective ≠ Ownership
The perspective from which value is examined does not determine ownership.
For example:
a bridge may be owned by one public authority while its value is examined from the perspective of:
commuters; logistics networks; emergency services; regional economy; infrastructure resilience.
VCM governs the perspective relevant to value analysis.
Ownership remains outside its boundary.
Use Context
VCM identifies the use context within which the Value Object is relevant.
A machine may be examined as:
active production equipment; reserve capacity; spare equipment; resale equipment; component source; training equipment; obsolete equipment; restoration candidate.
The physical object may remain identical.
Its use context may materially change the value lifecycle.
Operational Context
Operational context describes the relevant operating conditions surrounding the Value Object.
Examples include:

active operation; standby; maintenance; emergency operation; degraded operation; high-load operation; isolated operation; integrated operation.
VCM identifies the context.
It does not govern Operational Reality itself.
That remains within ORA™.
Environmental Context
Environmental conditions may materially influence value.
These may include:
physical environment; climate; infrastructure availability; energy availability; network access; resource availability; logistics conditions; surrounding system conditions.
An asset capable of producing substantial value in one environment may be unable to do so in another.
VCM makes the environmental basis explicit before downstream value governance interprets the difference.
Temporal Context
Value context must include time where time materially affects interpretation.
Relevant temporal dimensions may include:
assessment date; lifecycle period; operational phase; technology generation; market period; seasonal condition; pre-event state; post-event state; future planning horizon.
Therefore:
Value at Time T1 ≠ necessarily Value at Time T2
even where the Value Object remains unchanged.
VCM does not determine the resulting Value State.
It establishes the temporal context under which that state will later be governed.
Relational Context
Value may depend materially upon relationships.
Examples include:

supplier access; customer relationships; interoperability; contractual access; platform participation; distribution networks; collaboration; service relationships; ecosystem membership.
VCM identifies which relationships form part of the context.
Where a relationship itself constitutes a Value Object, VODM must preserve it separately.
Dependency Context
A Value Object may depend upon external capabilities for value to emerge or remain usable.
Dependencies may include:
electricity; transport; software; data; infrastructure; personnel; networks; complementary assets; regulatory access;
technical compatibility.
VCM records the dependency context where relevant.
It does not govern the external dependency itself.
Dependency ≠ Value
A Value Object's dependence upon another object does not determine its value.
Likewise, the existence of a dependency does not establish value.
VCM therefore separates:
dependency condition
from
value consequence.
The dependency may later cause value to emerge, change, degrade, reach zero, or recover.
Those consequences belong to subsequent VFM® governed spaces.
Technological Context
Technology may materially change the context in which a Value Object exists.
For example, a manufacturing machine may remain physically functional while a new production technology changes:
compatibility; usefulness; integration potential; replacement availability; productive relevance.
VCM identifies the technological context.

VFM® later governs what happens to value as a result.
Economic Context
Where materially relevant, VCM may identify economic conditions affecting the Value Object's value context.
These may include:
scarcity; abundance; availability of substitutes; demand conditions; resource constraints; access conditions; economic disruption.
VCM does not govern the economy itself.
It records economic context only where that context is necessary to understand the Value Object's value lifecycle.
Geographic Context
Location may materially influence value.
The same Value Object may have different relevance in different locations because of:
infrastructure; access; demand; scarcity; environmental conditions; logistics; compatibility; surrounding capabilities.
Therefore:
Physical Object Identity ≠ Universal Geographic Value Context
Institutional Context
Institutions may form part of the environment in which value is examined.
Examples may include:
public infrastructure systems; healthcare systems; education systems; industrial ecosystems; research environments; organizational structures.
VCM identifies the institutional context where it materially affects the Value Object.
It does not govern institutional authority or legality.
Context Boundary
Every governed Value Context should establish a Context Boundary.
The Context Boundary identifies which contextual factors are:
included
and which are:
excluded
from the current value analysis.

This prevents a Value Statement produced under one context from silently being interpreted as universal.
Context Assumptions
Some contextual conditions may be assumed rather than directly established.
Examples:
infrastructure remains available; a production line continues operating; software support continues; demand remains within a defined range; complementary assets remain accessible.
VCM requires material contextual assumptions to remain explicit.
It does not validate those assumptions.
Context Assumption ≠ Value Assumption
A contextual assumption describes the environment within which value is examined.
A value assumption directly assumes something about value itself.
The two must remain separate.
For example:
“Grid access remains available.”
is a contextual assumption.
“The facility will therefore retain high value.”
is a value conclusion or assumption.
VCM governs the first.
It does not pre-establish the second.
Multi-Context Governance
A single Value Object may be examined simultaneously across several contexts.
For example:
Electric Vehicle Battery
may be examined within:
Context A — vehicle propulsion
Context B — stationary energy storage
Context C — materials recovery
The battery may remain the same underlying Value Object while its value lifecycle differs across these contexts.
VCM therefore permits parallel contextualization.
Context Comparison
VCM enables controlled comparison between contexts.
The methodological structure may be:
Value Object X + Context A

versus
Value Object X + Context B
This makes it possible to distinguish:
change in the Value Object
from
change in the context surrounding the Value Object.
That distinction becomes critical when identifying why value changed.
Context Change
A material Context Change occurs when one or more contextual conditions change sufficiently to affect downstream value governance.
Examples include:
loss of infrastructure; new technology; disappearance of demand; new use capability; loss of compatibility; geographic relocation; dependency failure; restoration of access; new relationship; changed operational environment.
Context Change does not automatically mean Value Change.
It creates a trigger to assess whether Value Change occurred.
Context Change ≠ Value Change
This distinction is fundamental.
A context may change without materially changing value.
Likewise, value may change without a major context change.
Therefore:
Context Change → Value Reassessment Trigger
not:
Context Change = Value Change
Context and Value Emergence
Context may create conditions under which value can emerge.
For example:
an unused technology may acquire practical value when complementary infrastructure becomes available.
VCM identifies the changed context.
The Value Emergence Standard governs whether value actually emerges.
Context and Value Development
A favorable context may enable existing value to grow.
Examples include:

network expansion; complementary infrastructure; increased interoperability; improved access; new capabilities.
VCM identifies the contextual development.
The Value Development Standard governs the resulting development of value.
Context and Value Degradation
A Value Object may remain unchanged while its context deteriorates.
Examples include:
loss of compatible infrastructure; declining usefulness; disappearing ecosystem support; loss of complementary capability.
VCM governs the changed context.
The Value Degradation Standard governs the resulting value degradation where it occurs.
Context and Value Nullification
A context change may contribute to value reaching zero.
But VCM does not issue a zero-value determination.
For example:
a specialized machine may remain physically operational but become unusable because the only compatible production system disappears.
VCM identifies:
loss of compatibility context.
The Value Nullification Standard determines whether the resulting value reaches a zero-value condition.
Context and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A Value Object may be a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ in a defined context while retaining potential value under another context.
This distinction is essential.
For example:
a machine may have zero productive value in Facility A because supporting infrastructure no longer exists.
The same machine may regain productive relevance if relocated to Facility B.
Therefore, where appropriate:
Zero Value must remain context-bound.

VCM supplies the contextual basis necessary for later Value State governance.
Context and ReMonet™
A change of context may enable value restoration.
Examples include:
relocation; technological adaptation; new infrastructure; new use; restored network access; new relationships; changed demand; repurposing.
VCM identifies the contextual change.
ReMonet™ governs the value-restoration mechanism where value actually returns.
Context and Value Extinction
Value Extinction must not be inferred merely because value is absent in one context.
If a Value Object may possess recoverable value under another legitimate context, its broader value lifecycle may not yet have reached extinction.
Therefore:
Context-Specific Zero Value ≠ Automatic Value Extinction
This distinction protects VFM® from collapsing temporary contextual uselessness into terminal value loss.
Value Context ≠ Valuation Context
VCM does not establish a valuation methodology.
It may identify the context in which a valuation is being conducted, but it does not determine:
valuation method; discount rate; fair value; market value; accounting value; price; monetary amount.
Therefore:
Value Context Governance ≠ Valuation Methodology
Value ≠ Price
VCM explicitly preserves the distinction between:
value context
and
price context.
A market price may be one contextual signal relevant to a Value Object.
It does not define the complete value lifecycle governed by VFM®.
VCM Boundary with VOIM
VOIM identifies the Value Object.

VCM identifies the context in which that object is examined.
Therefore:
Object Identity ≠ Object Context
VCM Boundary with VOBM
VOBM establishes the Value Object Boundary.
VCM establishes the Value Context Boundary.
These boundaries must remain distinct.
Value Object Boundary answers:
What belongs to the object?
Value Context Boundary answers:
Which surrounding conditions belong to the present value analysis?
VCM Boundary with VODM
VODM determines whether objects, components, capabilities, relationships, or configurations must remain differentiated.
VCM then contextualizes those differentiated Value Objects.
Therefore:
Differentiation precedes contextualization.
VCM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
VCM may identify operational conditions as part of Value Context.
It does not govern those operational conditions themselves.
Therefore:
Operational Reality ≠ Value Context
VCM Boundary with GOA™
GOA™ governs governance itself, including authority, scope, delegation, accountability, and governance boundaries.
VCM governs only the contextual conditions necessary for value lifecycle interpretation.
VCM Boundary with CLA™
CLA™ may classify contextual factors.
VCM determines which contextual factors are materially relevant to the Value Object's value lifecycle.
Therefore:
Context Identification ≠ Classification Governance
VCM Boundary with VALIDOS®
VCM does not determine whether contextual claims are valid.

Where formal validation is required, VALIDOS® may govern validation of those claims.
Therefore:
Context Definition ≠ Context Validation
VCM Boundary with INTEGROS®
VCM does not determine contextual integrity.
INTEGROS® may govern whether contextual information maintains required integrity properties.
VCM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may provide evidence concerning contextual conditions and contextual changes.
VCM governs how those conditions are structured as Value Context.
Therefore:
Evidence of Context ≠ Context Governance
VCM Boundary with SIMULOS®
SIMULOS® may simulate future, hypothetical, or alternative contexts.
VCM may use a clearly identified simulated context as a value-analysis context.
It does not govern the simulation itself.
Therefore:
Simulated Context ≠ Value Context Governance
VCM Boundary with OBIDENITY®
VCM does not determine:
identity; ownership; authority; permission;
provenance; transfer.
Those may be relevant contextual inputs, but their governance remains outside VCM.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VCM implementation should establish:
1. Value Object Input
Receive the identified, bounded, and differentiated Value Object.
2. Context Purpose
Define why the Value Object is being examined.
3. Perspective
Identify the relevant perspective where material.
4. Use Context
Identify the relevant use or capability context.
5. Environmental & Operational Context
Identify materially relevant surrounding conditions.
6. Temporal Context

Define the relevant time, period, or lifecycle moment.
7. Relational & Dependency Context
Identify material relationships and dependencies.
8. Context Boundary
Define which contextual factors are included and excluded.
9. Context Assumptions
Record material contextual assumptions.
10. Context Variation
Identify alternative contexts where materially relevant.
11. Context State
Establish the current contextual basis.
12. Context Record
Create a traceable governed Value Context record.
Governance Outputs
VCM may produce:
Value Context Record Value Context Statement Value Context Boundary Value Context Purpose Record Value Perspective Record Value Use Context Record Value Environmental Context Record Value Operational Context Record Value Temporal Context Record Value Relational Context Record Value Dependency Context Record Value Context Assumption Record Value Context Variation Record Value Context Change Record Multi-Context Comparison Record Contextualized Value Object
These outputs provide the contextual basis required for the final Value Identification function and subsequent VFM® lifecycle governance.
Enterprise Application
VCM addresses one of the most important problems in real-world value analysis:
organizations frequently speak about “the value” of something without specifying the context in which that value exists.
Consider an industrial robot.
The same robot may be:

highly useful in a factory with compatible software, tooling, trained operators, energy, maintenance, and production demand;
weakly useful in a facility where only part of that supporting environment exists;
or
operationally useless in a location where the required infrastructure is absent.
The robot may not have changed.
The context has.
A conventional system may record only a financial amount.
VCM records the context necessary to understand why the value lifecycle may differ.
This becomes especially important for:
accounting; asset management; investment; taxation analysis; infrastructure; public finance; technology; AI systems; industrial equipment;
intellectual property; digital assets; energy systems; supply chains; strategic capabilities.
VCM enables later VFM® standards to distinguish:
Value Object Change
from
Value Context Change
and therefore prevents downstream value governance from attributing a value transition to the wrong cause.
Foundational Principles
Value cannot be governed consistently without governing the context in which value is being examined.
The same Value Object may exist across multiple legitimate Value Contexts.
A change in context does not automatically create a new Value Object.
A change in context does not automatically create a change in value.
Context Change is a trigger for value reassessment, not a Value Change determination.
Value Object Boundary and Value Context Boundary are different methodological controls.

Perspective does not determine ownership.
Dependency does not itself establish value.
Context does not determine price.
Context-specific zero value does not automatically establish Value Extinction.
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state may be context-dependent where recoverable value remains possible under another legitimate context.
The conditions surrounding value must remain distinguishable from value itself.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Context Module establishes the fourth methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by situating an identified, bounded, and differentiated Value Object within the explicit purpose, perspective, use, environment, operational conditions, time, relationships, dependencies, assumptions, and contextual boundaries necessary for consistent value lifecycle governance. Through governance of Value Context, VCM prevents value statements generated under one set of conditions from being silently generalized across other contexts and enables VFM® to distinguish changes in the Value Object from changes in the environment surrounding it. By separating context from object identity, object boundary, differentiation, valuation, price, validation, integrity, audit, operational reality, and value state, VCM provides the contextual foundation required to determine whether value originates, emerges, develops, degrades, reaches zero, is restored, or becomes extinct. A Value Object must therefore never be treated as though its value exists independently of context when the conditions surrounding that object materially affect the lifecycle of value.

Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM)
Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM)
Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture
Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS)
Module: VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module
Operational Layer: Value Object Boundary Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Value Object Boundary
Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VOBM-001.2
Version: 1.0
Status: Draft · Open Standard
Effective Date: 23 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY®
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM) is the second Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VOBM governs the methodological boundary of an identified Value Object by determining what belongs inside the Value Object for the relevant value lifecycle, what remains outside it, which components, relationships, capabilities, conditions, dependencies, or interfaces materially constitute the object, and where the object must be separated from its surrounding environment.

The Module transforms an identified Value Object into a bounded Value Object capable of supporting consistent downstream value governance.
VOBM does not determine whether value exists, where value originates, whether value has emerged, how much value exists, or how value changes.
Its foundational task is narrower:
to establish where the Value Object begins and ends before the value associated with that object enters the wider value lifecycle.
Core Question
Where does the identified Value Object begin and end for the value lifecycle being governed?
Architectural Position
VOBM is the second Core Module of the Value Identification Standard.
It follows:
VOIM — Value Object Identification Module
and precedes the subsequent VIS modules governing differentiation, context, and the remaining conditions necessary to establish the Value Object as a governed entry point into the value lifecycle.
VOIM establishes:
What is the Value Object?
VOBM establishes:
What belongs to that Value Object, and where does it end?
The sequence is therefore:
Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification
Internal Flow Position

Identified Value Object → Boundary Purpose Definition → Constituent Identification → Inclusion Assessment → Exclusion Assessment → Dependency Assessment → Interface Identification → Composite / Component Boundary Assessment → Temporal Boundary Assessment → Boundary Determination → Boundary State Assignment → Bounded Value Object
Operational Space
VOBM governs the space between:
an identified Value Object
and
a sufficiently bounded Value Object capable of entering further value governance.
This operational space includes:
Value Object boundary purpose; object inclusion; object exclusion; constituent identification; component boundaries; composite-object boundaries; relational boundaries; capability boundaries; process boundaries; service boundaries; digital boundaries; physical boundaries; functional boundaries; dependency boundaries; interface boundaries; contextual boundaries where necessary for object separation; temporal boundaries; configuration boundaries; boundary uncertainty; boundary change; boundary state; boundary traceability.
Why Value Boundaries Matter
Value cannot be governed consistently where the object carrying, enabling, producing, receiving, or relating to that value changes silently during analysis.
Consider an industrial facility.
One analysis may treat the Value Object as:
the land.
Another may treat it as:
land + buildings.
Another:
land + buildings + machinery.
Another:
the complete operational production capability.
Another:

the business operating from that facility.
All may appear to discuss the same asset.
They are not necessarily discussing the same Value Object.
Their boundaries differ.
VOBM exists to make that difference explicit.
Value Object Boundary
A Value Object Boundary is:
the governed methodological separation defining which elements, components, relationships, capabilities, conditions, and interfaces constitute the Value Object for the relevant value lifecycle and which remain outside it.
The boundary does not need to correspond to:
a physical perimeter; legal ownership; accounting consolidation; organizational structure; technical architecture; contractual structure; regulatory jurisdiction.
Those boundaries may provide relevant inputs.
They do not automatically determine the VFM® Value Object Boundary.
Physical Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
A physical asset may have a clear physical perimeter while the relevant Value Object extends beyond it.
For example, a factory building has a physical boundary.
But the Value Object:
Operational Production Capability
may depend upon:
machinery; energy access; workforce capability; software; process knowledge; supply access; logistics; licenses; external infrastructure.
The physical factory perimeter therefore does not automatically define the boundary of the relevant Value Object.
Conversely, the relevant Value Object may concern only one machine located inside the factory.
Therefore:
Physical Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary

Legal Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Legal ownership may identify who owns an object or right.
It does not automatically determine what constitutes the Value Object for a specific value lifecycle.
A company may legally own:
land;
machinery; patents; software; inventory; contractual rights.
But a particular Value Object may consist of only one of those elements or a governed combination of several.
Therefore:
Ownership Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Ownership remains governed outside VOBM where relevant.
Accounting Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Accounting systems may group objects according to accounting rules.
VOBM does not assume that an accounting asset corresponds exactly to a Value Object.
One accounting asset may contain multiple value-relevant objects.
Multiple accounting assets may together form one Value Object.
Some Value Objects may not be represented as conventional balance-sheet assets at all.
Examples may include:
dormant capability; network position; operational access; organizational knowledge; technological potential; unused capacity; relational capability; data-derived capability.
Therefore:
Accounting Asset Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Boundary Purpose
Every boundary determination should identify why the Value Object is being bounded.
The purpose may relate to:

value lifecycle analysis; value origin examination; value emergence; value state determination; value change analysis; value degradation; value nullification; value restoration; value extinction; comparison between Value Objects; organizational decision support; policy analysis; economic analysis; asset restructuring; other governed value purposes.
Boundary purpose prevents the same object from being bounded differently without explanation.
Constituent Identification
VOBM identifies the constituents potentially forming part of the Value Object.
Constituents may include:
physical components; digital components; information objects; capabilities; rights; processes; activities; relationships; resources; access conditions; infrastructure dependencies; contractual elements; operational elements; environmental elements; other materially relevant constituents.
Constituent identification does not automatically mean inclusion.
Each constituent must be assessed against the boundary purpose.
Inclusion Principle
An element should be included within the Value Object Boundary where its presence is materially constitutive of the object being governed.
The relevant question is:
Would removing this element materially change what the identified Value Object is?
Where the answer is yes, inclusion may be justified.
Where the element merely affects the Value Object externally, it may instead remain an external dependency or contextual condition.
This distinction is essential.
Exclusion Principle

VOBM requires explicit exclusion of elements that are adjacent, influential, related, or economically relevant but do not constitute the Value Object itself.
Examples may include:
market conditions; taxation; financing conditions; regulation; external demand; external infrastructure; customer behavior; supplier conditions; macroeconomic conditions.
These factors may strongly affect value.
That does not automatically make them part of the Value Object.
Therefore:
Influence on Value ≠ Membership in Value Object
Constituent ≠ Dependency
VOBM distinguishes:
Constituent
from
Dependency.
A constituent forms part of the Value Object.
A dependency exists outside the object but materially affects its ability to function, exist, or produce relevant value.
For example:
A data center may include servers as constituents.
Electric-grid access may remain an external dependency.
But where the Value Object is defined as:
Integrated Data-Center Operational Capability
the relevant energy infrastructure relationship may need to be represented differently.
Boundary determination therefore depends upon the precise Value Object identified by VOIM.
Dependency Boundary
External dependencies must remain identifiable even when they are excluded from the Value Object itself.
A bounded Value Object may therefore be represented as:
Internal Constituents → Object Boundary → External Dependencies
This enables later VFM® analysis to distinguish:
change to the Value Object
from

change in an external condition affecting the value of the Value Object.
Interface Boundary
Where the Value Object interacts with external systems, VOBM identifies the relevant interfaces.
Interfaces may include:
physical interfaces; digital interfaces; contractual interfaces;
resource interfaces; information interfaces; service interfaces; infrastructure interfaces; operational interfaces; market interfaces.
The interface defines where interaction occurs.
It does not automatically move the external system inside the Value Object Boundary.
Composite Value Object Boundary
A composite Value Object may contain multiple independently identifiable components.
For example:
Integrated Manufacturing Capability
may include:
Facility + Machinery + Control Software + Process Capability + Defined Operational Integration
VOBM must determine whether the governed lifecycle concerns:
each component separately
or
the integrated composite object.
This distinction is necessary because:
Value of Composite Object ≠ Sum of Isolated Component Values
A composite object may possess value that emerges only through integration.
Likewise, loss of one critical constituent may disproportionately degrade the value of the complete object.
Component Value Object Boundary
A component inside a composite Value Object may itself have an independent value lifecycle.
VOBM therefore supports nested boundaries:

Composite Value Object A → Component Value Object A.1 → Component Value Object A.2 → Component Value Object A.3
Each boundary must remain distinguishable.
This enables VFM® to govern:
component value
and
composite value
without collapsing them into one undifferentiated value object.
Relational Value Object Boundary
Some Value Objects exist primarily through relationships.
Examples may include:
distribution relationships; network participation; access arrangements; partnerships; contractual opportunities; platform relationships; supply relationships.
In such cases, VOBM must determine what constitutes the relationship-based Value Object without treating the complete identities, organizations, or assets of all participating parties as part of that Value Object.
Therefore:
Relationship Participation ≠ Full Object Inclusion
Capability Boundary
Capabilities often create difficult boundary questions.
A production capability may depend on:
equipment; people; knowledge; software; infrastructure; procedures; permissions; supply availability.
VOBM determines which of these constitute the identified capability Value Object and which remain enabling dependencies or contextual conditions.
This prevents capability value from being confused with the value of every object contributing to that capability.
Process Boundary
Where a process is the Value Object, the boundary may be defined through:

process entry; process activities; transformation stages; required resources; process exit; interfaces; dependencies.
VOBM does not govern operational execution of the process.
It establishes what process is included within the Value Object being examined.
Temporal Boundary
A Value Object Boundary may change over time.
For example:
Factory Capability — 2024
may include one production line.
After expansion:
Factory Capability — 2026
may include three lines, automation infrastructure, and a new digital control system.
VOBM therefore requires material boundary changes to remain visible.
A historical value determination must not silently inherit a later object boundary.
Configuration Boundary
Where configuration materially determines the Value Object, VOBM records the configuration associated with the boundary.
Examples include:
industrial system configuration; software stack; AI system configuration; infrastructure topology; portfolio composition; organizational composition; service bundle; production configuration.
A material configuration change may require a new or revised Value Object Boundary.
Dynamic Boundaries
Some Value Objects have boundaries that change during their lifecycle.
Examples may include:
evolving digital platforms; portfolios; supply networks; project ecosystems; integrated capabilities; data environments.
VOBM therefore permits:
Dynamic Value Object Boundaries
provided that the basis, time, conditions, and material changes remain traceable.

Dynamic does not mean undefined.
Boundary Uncertainty
Not every Value Object can initially be bounded with complete certainty.
VOBM therefore permits boundary uncertainty to be explicitly represented.
Uncertainty may concern:
component inclusion;
dependency classification; relationship extent; temporal applicability; configuration; interface definition; composite structure.
Uncertainty must not be hidden through arbitrary precision.
Where material uncertainty remains, the boundary may receive a conditional state.
Boundary States
VOBM may assign a governed boundary state.
1. Unbounded
The Value Object has been identified but its relevant boundary has not yet been established.
2. Candidate Boundary
A proposed boundary exists but requires further assessment.
3. Conditionally Bounded
The boundary is sufficiently established only under defined assumptions, contexts, configurations, or temporal conditions.
4. Bounded
The Value Object Boundary is sufficiently established for downstream value governance.
5. Boundary Under Review
A material change or unresolved issue requires reassessment.
6. Boundary Superseded
A previously governed boundary has been replaced by a newer boundary while remaining preserved for historical traceability.
Boundary states must not be confused with Value States.
Boundary State ≠ Value State
A Value Object may be:
Bounded
while its value is:
unknown, emerging, positive, developing, degrading, zero, restored, or extinct.
VOBM governs the object boundary.

Later VFM® standards govern value states and transitions.
Boundary Change
A boundary change occurs when the governed constitution of the Value Object materially changes.
Examples include:
component addition; component removal; merger; separation; integration; configuration change; relationship termination; capability expansion; capability contraction; structural reorganization.
A boundary change may affect value.
But:
Boundary Change ≠ Value Change
The boundary change is an event concerning the Value Object.
Later VFM® governance determines what happened to value as a result.
Boundary with VOIM
VOIM answers:
What is the Value Object?
VOBM answers:
Where does that Value Object begin and end?
Therefore:
Identification ≠ Boundary Determination
VOIM must provide a sufficiently identified Value Object before VOBM can establish its boundary.
Boundary with Value Differentiation &
Separation
VOBM determines what is inside and outside the Value Object.
The subsequent differentiation function determines whether multiple objects, value relationships, value types, components, or value phenomena must remain analytically separate.
Therefore:
Boundary ≠ Differentiation
An object can be correctly bounded while still containing several distinct value relationships requiring separation.
Boundary with Value Context & Condition
VOBM may use context where necessary to establish the object boundary.

The Value Context & Condition function governs the broader circumstances under which the object enters value analysis.
Therefore:
Boundary Context ≠ Value Context Governance
Boundary with Value Origin Standard
VOBM does not determine where value comes from.
It establishes the bounded object in relation to which Value Origin can subsequently be examined.
Therefore:
Object Boundary ≠ Value Origin
Boundary with Value Emergence Standard
VOBM does not determine whether value has emerged.
A perfectly bounded Value Object may still possess:
no emerged value.
Therefore:
Bounded Object ≠ Existing Value
Boundary with Value Recognition Standard
VOBM does not determine whether value is recognized.
It establishes only the object boundary required for consistent value governance.
Boundary with GOA™
GOA™ governs governance boundaries.
VOBM governs the boundary of the Value Object for the value lifecycle.
Therefore:
Governance Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality and operational boundaries.
VOBM may use operational information when defining a Value Object but does not govern Operational Reality itself.
Therefore:
Operational Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary
Boundary with OBIDENITY®
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, and continuity.
VOBM does not determine ownership boundaries or identity boundaries.
A Value Object may cross multiple ownership boundaries.

Likewise, one owner may hold multiple distinct Value Objects.
Boundary with CLA™
VOBM may identify constituents and boundary forms necessary for object separation.
Formal classification remains governed by CLA™ where required.
Boundary with VALIDOS®
VOBM does not validate the correctness of a boundary claim.
It defines the methodological boundary required by VFM®.
Where formal validation of the boundary or supporting claims is required, VALIDOS® governs that validation process.
Boundary with INTEGROS®
VOBM does not determine boundary integrity.
INTEGROS® may govern whether a defined boundary remains structurally or operationally intact where integrity governance is required.
Boundary with ADIT®
VOBM establishes the Value Object Boundary.
ADIT® may provide governed audit evidence concerning whether the recorded constituents, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, or boundary changes are supported by evidence.
Boundary Governance ≠ Audit Governance
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VOBM implementation should establish:
1. Identified Value Object
Receive the identified Value Object from VOIM.
2. Boundary Purpose
Define why the object boundary is required.
3. Constituent Candidates
Identify components, relationships, capabilities, processes, resources, or other elements potentially belonging inside the object.
4. Inclusion Assessment
Determine which constituent candidates form part of the Value Object.
5. Exclusion Assessment

Determine which adjacent or influential elements remain outside the object.
6. Dependency Assessment
Identify external dependencies without automatically incorporating them into the object.
7. Interface Identification
Define relevant interfaces between the Value Object and external systems or environments.
8. Composite / Component Assessment
Determine whether nested Value Object boundaries are required.
9. Temporal & Configuration Reference
Establish the time and configuration to which the boundary applies.
10. Boundary State
Assign the governed Value Object Boundary State.
11. Boundary Record
Document the basis, inclusions, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, uncertainty, and applicable conditions.
Governance Outputs
VOBM may produce:
Value Object Boundary Record Value Object Boundary Statement Value Object Constituent Register Value Object Inclusion Record Value Object Exclusion Record Value Object Dependency Record Value Object Interface Record Composite Value Object Boundary Record Component Value Object Boundary Record Relational Value Object Boundary Record Value Object Temporal Boundary Value Object Configuration Boundary Value Object Boundary Uncertainty Record Value Object Boundary State Value Object Boundary Change Record Bounded Value Object
These outputs provide the governed basis for the next VIS module.
Enterprise Application
VOBM enables organizations to resolve one of the most important hidden problems in value analysis:

different assessments often assign value to differently bounded objects while treating them as though they were the same object.
This can affect:
enterprise valuation; infrastructure; industrial assets; digital assets; intellectual property; data; production capacity; environmental resources; public assets; projects; services; technology platforms; dormant assets; composite systems; capabilities.
For example, two analysts may disagree about the value of a production facility.
One values:
land + building + machinery.
The other values:
the complete operational production capability, including integrated software, process capability, and operational access.
Their numerical disagreement may be secondary.
Their first disagreement is architectural:
they have not bounded the same Value Object.
VOBM makes that difference visible before downstream valuation, accounting, taxation, investment, policy, or economic analysis attempts to use the resulting value information.
Foundational Principles
A Value Object cannot be governed consistently if its boundary is undefined.
Identification establishes what the Value Object is; boundary governance establishes where it ends.
Physical boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary.
Legal ownership boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary.
Accounting asset boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary.
Influence on value does not automatically create membership in the Value Object.

A constituent is not the same as a dependency.
A composite Value Object may possess a value lifecycle distinct from the value lifecycles of its components.
A component may simultaneously be part of a composite Value Object and possess its own independently governed value lifecycle.
Dynamic boundaries must remain governed boundaries.
Boundary change is not automatically value change.
Boundary State is not Value State.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Object Boundary Module establishes the second methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by determining where an identified Value Object begins and ends for the relevant value lifecycle. Through governance of constituents, inclusions, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, composite and component structures, relational and capability boundaries, temporal applicability, configuration, uncertainty, boundary states, and boundary change, VOBM prevents value analysis from silently expanding, contracting, combining, or substituting the object whose value is being governed. By separating Value Object Boundary from physical perimeter, legal ownership, accounting treatment, governance boundary, operational boundary, classification, validation, integrity, and audit, VOBM creates a stable methodological object upon which subsequent value governance can operate. Before value origin, emergence, recognition, state, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be governed consistently, the boundaries of the object to which that value relates must first be explicit.

Canonical Definition
Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM) is the third Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VODM governs the methodological differentiation of a bounded Value Object by determining whether the object must remain governed as one Value Object or be distinguished from other objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, value-bearing configurations, or analytically separate value phenomena before the value lifecycle can be governed consistently.

The Module prevents materially different Value Objects from being collapsed into one object and prevents one Value Object from being unnecessarily fragmented into multiple objects without a governed basis.
VODM does not determine whether value exists, what value is worth, where value originates, whether value has emerged, or how value subsequently changes.
Its task is foundational:
to determine what must remain the same Value Object and what must be treated as a distinct Value Object before downstream value governance begins.
Core Question
Which Value Objects, components, relationships, capabilities, or configurations must remain distinct for their value lifecycles to be governed correctly?
Architectural Position
VODM is the third Core Module of the Value Identification Standard.
It follows:
VOIM — Value Object Identification Module
→
VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module
and precedes the subsequent VIS functions governing the context and conditions under which the identified Value Object enters the wider value lifecycle.
The methodological sequence is:
Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Object Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification
VOIM establishes:
What is the Value Object?
VOBM establishes:
Where does the Value Object begin and end?
VODM establishes:
What must remain distinct within, between, or around those bounded Value Objects?
Internal Flow Position

Bounded Value Object → Differentiation Purpose Definition → Differentiation Candidate Identification → Similarity Assessment → Material Difference Assessment → Component / Composite Assessment → Functional Differentiation → Relational Differentiation → Configuration Differentiation → Temporal Differentiation → Value-Lifecycle Independence Assessment → Differentiation Determination → Differentiation State Assignment → Differentiated Value Object Structure
Operational Space
VODM governs the space between:
a bounded Value Object
and
a differentiated Value Object structure suitable for downstream value governance.
This operational space includes:
object differentiation; object equivalence assessment; component differentiation; composite differentiation; capability differentiation; functional differentiation; relational differentiation; configuration differentiation; temporal differentiation; lifecycle differentiation; duplicate-object detection; object aggregation risk; object fragmentation risk; value-lifecycle independence; differentiation uncertainty; differentiation state; differentiation traceability; differentiation reassessment after material change.
Why Differentiation Matters
Two things may appear to be the same asset while possessing different value lifecycles.
Likewise, several things may appear separate while together constituting one meaningful Value Object.
Consider a manufacturing facility containing three production lines.
The facility may be governed as:

one integrated production capability
or the three lines may be governed as:
Value Object A — Production Line 1 Value Object B — Production Line 2 Value Object C — Production Line 3
Both approaches may be legitimate.
The correct differentiation depends upon what Value Object has been identified, how its boundary has been established, and whether the components possess materially independent value lifecycles.
Without explicit differentiation, later value analysis may silently mix:
component value; composite value; capability value; replacement value; operational value; relational value; value created through integration.
VODM makes these distinctions governable before value itself is analyzed.
Differentiation Principle
A Value Object should be differentiated where a material distinction exists that would cause its value lifecycle to be governed differently from another object or component.
A material distinction may arise through:
different constitution; different function; different capability; different relationship; different configuration; different lifecycle; different dependency structure; different temporal existence; different value-origin relationship; different value-emergence conditions; different degradation pathway; different restoration possibility; different extinction condition.
The governing question is not:
Do these objects look different?
It is:
Would treating them as the same Value Object materially distort governance of their value lifecycles?

Similarity ≠ Identity
Two Value Objects may be highly similar without being the same governed object.
Examples include:
two identical machines; two identical software licenses; two apartments in the same building; two units of inventory; two identical datasets; two equivalent production lines; two contractual rights with identical terms.
Similarity may support comparison.
It does not erase object distinction.
Therefore:
Similarity ≠ Value Object Identity
Difference ≠ Separate Value Object
Conversely, the existence of differences does not automatically require separate Value Objects.
An integrated industrial system may contain:
different machines; different software components; different operational processes; different infrastructure elements.
Those differences may remain internal to one composite Value Object where the governed object is the integrated operational capability.
Therefore:
Internal Difference ≠ Automatic Object Separation
Differentiation Candidate
A Differentiation Candidate is:
an object, component, capability, relationship, configuration, or other materially distinguishable element whose value lifecycle may require governance separately from another Value Object or from the composite object within which it exists.
Identification of a Differentiation Candidate does not automatically create a new Value Object.
It creates a requirement for differentiation assessment.
Material Difference Assessment

VODM assesses whether differences are material to the value lifecycle.
A difference may be material where it changes:
what value may originate from the object; when value may emerge; whether value may be independently recognized; the state of value; how value may change; how value may develop; how value may degrade; whether value may reach zero independently; whether value may be restored independently; whether value may become extinct independently.
This creates a powerful architectural test:
Can the relevant value lifecycle materially diverge?
If yes, separate Value Object governance may be required.
Value-Lifecycle Independence Test
VODM introduces the Value-Lifecycle Independence Test.
The test asks whether a candidate can possess a materially independent lifecycle across one or more VFM® stages.
For example:
Can it have its own:
Value Origin?
Can value emerge from it independently?
Can its value state differ from the surrounding object?
Can it develop while the surrounding object degrades?
Can it reach zero while the composite retains value?
Can it be restored independently?
Can its value become extinct while another related object continues to possess value?
The greater the lifecycle independence, the stronger the basis for differentiation.
Object Differentiation
Object differentiation separates distinct Value Objects that may otherwise be treated as one.
Example:
A company owns two physically identical warehouses.
They may share:

design; purpose; ownership; accounting category.
But they occupy different locations, have different dependencies, different operational conditions, and potentially different value lifecycles.
VODM preserves them as distinct Value Objects where required.
Component Differentiation
A component within a composite Value Object may require independent differentiation.
For example:
Aircraft
may constitute one composite Value Object.
But:
Engine A
and
Engine B
may each possess independently relevant value lifecycles.
VODM can therefore establish:
Aircraft — Composite Value Object
with nested:
Engine A — Component Value Object Engine B — Component Value Object
without dissolving the aircraft as the composite Value Object.
Composite Differentiation
Multiple components may together produce a value phenomenon that does not exist at the component level.
Consider:
Land + Building + Machinery + Software + Workforce Capability + Process Integration
Each element may possess independent value.
But their integration may create:
Operational Manufacturing Capability
with a separate value lifecycle.
VODM therefore recognizes that:
Component Value Objects
and
Composite Value Objects
may legitimately coexist.
Composite Value ≠ Component Value Sum
A composite object may possess value arising from integration.
This means:
Composite Value ≠ necessarily Σ Component Values
Integration may create:

operational capability; network effects; interoperability; coordination capability; scale effects; access; strategic capability; productive capacity.
Conversely, dysfunctional integration may reduce the value of the composite even where individual components retain substantial value.
VODM does not measure this value.
It ensures the composite and its components can be governed separately where their value lifecycles differ.
Functional Differentiation
One physical or digital object may support several functions.
Those functions may create distinct value relationships.
For example, a building may function as:
production space; storage; office space; rental property; collateral; redevelopment opportunity.
VODM determines whether these functions merely affect one Value Object or whether one or more functions constitute independently governable Value Objects or capabilities.
The distinction must be explicit.
Capability Differentiation
Capabilities may require differentiation from the physical objects that enable them.
For example:
Machine
and
Production Capability
are not automatically the same Value Object.
A machine may retain resale value even where the production capability has collapsed.
Likewise, a production capability may remain valuable after individual machines are replaced.
Therefore:
Enabling Asset ≠ Capability Value Object
where their value lifecycles are materially independent.
Relational Differentiation

Value may relate to a relationship rather than exclusively to either participating object.
Examples include:
supplier relationship; distribution relationship; customer network; platform access; partnership; licensing relationship; contractual access; interoperability relationship.
VODM may differentiate:
Party A
from
Party B
from
Relationship AB
where each represents a materially distinct Value Object or value-bearing phenomenon.
This prevents relational value from being incorrectly assigned entirely to one participant.
Configuration Differentiation
The same underlying object may possess materially different value characteristics under different configurations.
Examples include:
machine configuration; software configuration; AI model configuration; infrastructure topology; production configuration; service bundle; portfolio composition.
VODM determines whether configuration change merely modifies the same Value Object or creates a sufficiently distinct Value Object configuration requiring separate governance.
Version Differentiation
Versions may need to remain distinguishable where value-relevant characteristics materially differ.
For example:
Software Version 4.1
and
Software Version 7.0
may share identity continuity while possessing different:
capabilities; dependencies; compatibility; market relevance; operational utility; lifecycle position.
VODM may therefore preserve version-specific Value Object differentiation without redefining identity governance.

Temporal Differentiation
A Value Object may materially change across time.
The same physical object may represent different governed Value Object states or configurations at different moments.
For example:
Industrial Facility — 2024 Configuration
and
Industrial Facility — 2026 Configuration
may require differentiation where expansion, automation, restructuring, or capability changes materially alter the value lifecycle.
VODM therefore supports temporally differentiated Value Objects where required.
Value Object ≠ Legal Entity
A legal entity may contain many Value Objects.
A Value Object may also span multiple legal entities.
Therefore:
Legal Entity Boundary ≠ Value Object Differentiation Rule
VODM does not determine corporate identity, legal ownership, or legal consolidation.
Value Object ≠ Accounting Unit
Accounting systems may aggregate or separate assets according to accounting requirements.
VODM differentiates Value Objects according to the methodological requirements of value lifecycle governance.
Therefore:
Accounting Unit ≠ Value Object
and:
Accounting Separation ≠ Automatic Value Object Differentiation
Value Object ≠ Market Product
A product sold as one commercial unit may contain multiple Value Objects.
Likewise, several products may depend upon one common Value Object.
Commercial packaging therefore does not determine methodological differentiation.
Differentiation and Dependencies
Objects may share dependencies without becoming one Value Object.
For example:

two factories may depend upon the same:
energy grid; transport network; software platform; supplier; workforce pool.
Shared dependency does not erase object differentiation.
Therefore:
Shared Dependency ≠ Shared Value Object
Differentiation and Ownership
Common ownership does not merge Value Objects.
Different ownership does not automatically separate a composite Value Object.
Ownership may be relevant contextual information, but ownership governance belongs outside VODM.
Therefore:
Ownership Structure ≠ Value Object Differentiation
Differentiation and Value Origin
VODM does not determine Value Origin.
However, different value-origin relationships may indicate that differentiation is necessary.
If two components derive value through materially different origins, their value lifecycles may need to remain separately governable.
The actual governance of Value Origin belongs to the Value Origin Standard.
Differentiation and Value State
Two components of one composite object may simultaneously occupy different Value States.
For example:
Component A — positive value Component B — degraded value Component C — zero-value condition
while:
Composite Object — positive value
This is possible only if object differentiation is explicit.
VODM therefore creates the structural basis necessary for later Value State governance.
Differentiation and DeMonet™
A DeMonet™ transition may affect one differentiated Value Object without nullifying another.
For example:

a technology component may lose all admissible value while the broader system retains value through replacement, adaptation, or alternative capability.
VODM ensures that value nullification is applied to the correct Value Object.
Differentiation and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state belongs to a defined Value Object.
Without differentiation, a zero-value condition affecting one component could be incorrectly generalized to:
the entire composite object; related objects; the owner; the surrounding system.
VODM prevents this category error.
Differentiation and ReMonet™
ReMonet™ may restore value to:
one component; one capability; one relationship; one configuration; the complete composite object.
VODM provides the object structure necessary to identify exactly what is being restored.
Differentiation State
VODM may assign a governed differentiation state.
1. Undifferentiated
Potential distinctions exist but have not yet been assessed.
2. Differentiation Candidate
One or more potential independent Value Objects have been identified.
3. Conditionally Differentiated
Separate governance is required only under defined conditions, purposes, configurations, or temporal contexts.
4. Differentiated
The relevant Value Objects or components are sufficiently distinguished for downstream value governance.
5. Integrated
The assessed elements remain governed as one composite Value Object despite internal differences.
6. Differentiation Under Review

Material change or unresolved uncertainty requires reassessment.
7. Superseded Differentiation
A previous differentiation structure has been replaced while remaining preserved for historical traceability.
Differentiation State ≠ Value State
A Value Object may be:
Differentiated
while its value state remains unknown.
Likewise:
Integrated
does not mean valuable.
Differentiation states govern methodological object structure.
Value States govern the condition of value.
Over-Differentiation Risk
Excessive differentiation may fragment one meaningful Value Object into artificial pieces.
This can obscure:
integration value; network effects; system capability; relational value; composite performance; coordinated value creation.
VODM therefore requires differentiation to have a material value-lifecycle basis.
Under-Differentiation Risk
Insufficient differentiation may combine materially different Value Objects.
This can conceal:
independent value states; degradation; zero-value conditions; restoration potential; lifecycle differences; component-level extinction; independent value origins.
VODM therefore governs both:
over-differentiation
and
under-differentiation.
VODM Boundary with VOIM
VOIM identifies the Value Object.
VODM determines whether identified or bounded objects must remain methodologically distinct from other objects or components.
Therefore:
Identification ≠ Differentiation
VODM Boundary with VOBM
VOBM establishes what belongs inside or outside a Value Object Boundary.

VODM establishes whether elements inside, between, or adjacent to those boundaries require separate Value Object governance.
Therefore:
Boundary ≠ Differentiation
A component may be inside a composite boundary and simultaneously be a differentiated Value Object.
VODM Boundary with Value Context
VODM determines object separation.
The subsequent context function determines the conditions under which the differentiated object enters value analysis.
Therefore:
Object Differentiation ≠ Value Context
VODM Boundary with CLA™
VODM does not establish a universal classification system.
It distinguishes Value Objects only to the extent necessary for value lifecycle governance.
CLA™ governs formal classification structures, criteria, decisions, lifecycle, registry, and assurance.
Therefore:
Differentiation ≠ Classification
VODM Boundary with OBIDENITY®
VODM does not determine:
identity ownership; legal ownership; authority; permission; provenance; transfer rights.
OBIDENITY® governs those spaces.
A single identity may contain multiple Value Objects.
Multiple identities may participate in one relational or composite Value Object.
VODM Boundary with GOA™
GOA™ governs governance structure and governance boundaries.
VODM governs differentiation of Value Objects for value lifecycle purposes.
Therefore:
Governance Separation ≠ Value Object Differentiation
VODM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.

VODM may use operational distinctions as evidence that Value Objects differ, but it does not govern operational execution or operational-state separation.
VODM Boundary with INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® governs integrity.
VODM does not determine whether a differentiated object possesses integrity.
It determines only whether the object should remain separately governable within the value lifecycle.
VODM Boundary with VALIDOS®
VODM establishes methodological differentiation.
VALIDOS® may validate claims concerning whether a differentiation basis is sufficiently supported where formal validation is required.
Therefore:
Differentiation Determination ≠ Validation Determination
VODM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may provide evidence concerning components, configurations, relationships, historical changes, or other facts relevant to differentiation.
VODM governs what those distinctions mean for Value Object separation.
Evidence of Difference ≠ Differentiation Governance
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VODM implementation should establish:
1. Bounded Value Object Input
Receive the bounded Value Object from VOBM.
2. Differentiation Purpose
Define why differentiation is required.
3. Differentiation Candidates
Identify objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, or configurations potentially requiring separate governance.
4. Material Difference Assessment
Determine whether differences are material to the value lifecycle.
5. Value-Lifecycle Independence Test

Assess whether candidate objects may possess materially independent value origins, states, transitions, degradation, restoration, or extinction.
6. Composite / Component Assessment
Determine whether component and composite Value Objects must coexist.
7. Relational & Capability Assessment
Determine whether relationships or capabilities constitute independently governable Value Objects.
8. Configuration & Temporal Assessment
Determine whether configuration or time creates materially distinct Value Objects.
9. Differentiation Determination
Establish which objects remain integrated and which must remain distinct.
10. Differentiation State
Assign a governed differentiation state.
11. Differentiation Record
Document the basis, conditions, uncertainty, relationships, and resulting Value Object structure.
Governance Outputs
VODM may produce:
Value Object Differentiation Record Value Object Differentiation Statement Differentiation Candidate Register Material Difference Assessment Value-Lifecycle Independence Assessment Component Differentiation Record Composite Value Object Structure Capability Differentiation Record Relational Differentiation Record Configuration Differentiation Record Temporal Differentiation Record Integrated Value Object Determination Differentiation Uncertainty Record Value Object Differentiation State Differentiated Value Object Structure

These outputs provide the governed object structure required for the remaining Value Identification functions and subsequent VFM® standards.
Enterprise Application
VODM addresses a fundamental problem in valuation, accounting, taxation, investment, asset management, public finance, infrastructure, digital systems, and economic analysis:
before value can be governed, it must be clear whether analysts are talking about one Value Object or several different Value Objects.
Consider an industrial site containing:
Land + Building + Machinery + Software + Intellectual Property + Production Capability + Energy Access + Customer Relationships
A conventional analysis may treat all of these as one asset.
Another may treat each separately.
A third may recognize both individual component value and an additional integrated production capability.
VODM provides a methodology for deciding which distinctions must remain explicit.
This becomes particularly important when:
one component degrades while others remain valuable; one capability reaches zero value; one relationship disappears; a component can be sold independently; integration creates additional value; a configuration change creates a new capability; value is restored only to part of the system; one Value Object becomes extinct while another survives.
Without differentiation, later value governance may assign a value event to the wrong object.

VODM therefore establishes the methodological separation necessary before VFM® begins governing the origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and extinction of value.
Foundational Principles
Value governance requires knowing not only what the Value Object is, but what must remain distinct from it.
Similarity does not establish identity.
Difference does not automatically require separation.
Shared ownership does not create one Value Object.
Shared dependency does not create one Value Object.
A component may belong to a composite Value Object while simultaneously possessing its own value lifecycle.
A composite Value Object may possess value that does not exist independently in its components.
Value-lifecycle independence is a primary basis for Value Object differentiation.
Over-differentiation can destroy the visibility of composite value.
Under-differentiation can conceal independent value states and transitions.
Differentiation is not classification.
Differentiation State is not Value State.
A zero-value condition must attach to the correct Value Object.
Value restoration must identify exactly which Value Object is being restored.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Object Differentiation Module establishes the third methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by determining which bounded objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, configurations, and temporally distinct forms must remain separate for their value lifecycles to be governed consistently. Through governance of material difference, Value-Lifecycle Independence, component and composite structures, functional and capability distinctions, relational objects, configuration and temporal differentiation, integration, uncertainty, and differentiation states, VODM prevents materially different Value Objects from being collapsed into one analytical object while preventing one meaningful Value Object from being fragmented without methodological justification. By separating differentiation from identity, ownership, classification, validation, integrity, audit, operational reality, and value state, VODM establishes the object structure upon which subsequent VFM® governance can operate. Before value origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be attributed correctly, it must first be clear whether the value lifecycle belongs to one Value Object, one of its components, a relationship, a capability, a configuration, or the composite object created through their integration.
