Canonical Definition
Value Object Identification Module (VOIM) is the first Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VOIM governs the methodological identification of the precise Value Object whose value is to be governed through the value lifecycle.

The Module establishes whether a sufficiently identifiable object, capability, resource, activity, relationship, right, condition, information object, physical object, digital object, service, process, outcome, opportunity, or other governable subject exists to serve as the reference object to which value may relate.
VOIM separates three concepts that must not be treated as equivalent:
Underlying Object ≠ Value Object ≠ Value
An underlying object may exist without becoming relevant to a particular value lifecycle.
A Value Object is the explicitly identified subject in relation to which value is being examined.
Value itself is the governed phenomenon whose lifecycle VFM® subsequently governs.
VOIM does not determine whether the identified Value Object actually possesses value, how much value exists, where that value originated, or whether value has yet emerged.
Its foundational task is narrower:
to establish exactly what the value lifecycle is about before any determination concerning value origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction is made.
Core Question
What exactly is the Value Object whose value lifecycle is to be governed?
Architectural Position
VOIM is the first Core Module of the first Parent Standard of VFM®.
It therefore establishes the initial methodological entry point into the complete value lifecycle.
Before VFM® asks:
Where does value originate?
it must first know:

What is the object in relation to which value is being examined?
The sequence begins:
Potential Value-Relevant Subject → Value Object Candidate → Identification Basis → Value Object Determination → Governable Value Object
The identified Value Object can then proceed through the remaining modules of the Value Identification Standard before entering Value Origin Standard.
Internal Flow Position
Potential Value-Relevant Subject → Value Object Candidate Identification → Object Reference Definition → Object Type Determination → Object Distinguishability Assessment → Object Context Identification → Object Version / State Reference → Value Object Determination → Value Object Identifier → Governable Value Object → Value Object Boundary Module
Operational Space
VOIM governs the space between:
something that may be relevant to value
and
a sufficiently identified Value Object capable of entering governed value analysis.
This operational space includes:
Value Object Candidate identification; object reference; object distinguishability; object type; object form; object configuration; object version; object temporal reference; object contextual reference; composite-object identification; component-object identification; relationship-object identification; capability identification; activity identification; process identification; outcome identification; opportunity identification; Value Object determination; Value Object identifier; Value Object traceability.
Value Object Concept

For VFM®, a Value Object is:
a sufficiently identifiable and distinguishable subject in relation to which a specific value lifecycle may be governed.
A Value Object may be tangible or intangible.
It may be persistent or temporary.
It may already exist physically or digitally, or represent a sufficiently defined capability, relationship, opportunity, activity, process, or outcome.
Examples may include:
land; buildings; machinery; raw materials; infrastructure; energy capacity; software; algorithms; datasets; intellectual property; patents; licenses; contractual rights; services; skills; capabilities; processes; production capacity; organizations;
projects; relationships; access rights; information; knowledge; opportunities; environmental resources; digital assets; operational capabilities; future sufficiently defined value-bearing subjects.
The list is intentionally non-exhaustive.
VFM® must remain capable of governing value associated with forms of objects that do not yet exist today.
Underlying Object ≠ Value Object
An object does not automatically become a Value Object merely because it exists.
Consider a building.
The underlying object may be:
Building A
But different value inquiries may concern:
Building A as operational production capacity
Building A as rentable space
Building A as redevelopment potential
Building A as material recovery potential
Building A as strategic location
The physical object may be the same.

The Value Object reference may differ according to what exactly is entering the governed value lifecycle.
VOIM therefore prevents the existence of an underlying object from being mistaken for sufficient identification of the Value Object.
Value Object ≠ Value
This distinction is foundational to VFM®.
Value Object answers:
What is the subject whose value lifecycle is being examined?
Value answers a different question:
What value exists, originates, emerges, changes, develops, degrades, disappears, returns, or becomes extinct in relation to that subject?
A machine may be identifiable even where its economic use has disappeared.
A patent may remain identifiable even where its commercial value reaches zero.
A dataset may remain identifiable while its value changes across different contexts.
Therefore:
Object existence does not establish value existence.
And:
Value Object identification does not constitute Value Recognition.
Value Object Candidate
Before formal identification, a potential subject enters VOIM as a Value Object Candidate.
A Value Object Candidate is:
a subject proposed for entry into VFM® because a value lifecycle may exist in relation to it.
Candidate status does not establish:
value existence; value origin; value emergence; positive value; market value; financial value; legal value; ownership; validity; integrity; classification; price; monetary amount.
It establishes only that the subject requires examination as a possible Value Object.
Identification Basis

Every Value Object should have a sufficient Identification Basis.
Depending on the object, this may include:
name; reference number; physical description; digital identifier; location reference; technical configuration; version; temporal state; component structure; process definition; capability definition; relationship definition; contractual reference; project reference; dataset reference; asset reference; other sufficiently distinguishing characteristics.
The identification basis must be sufficient to answer:
Which exact object are we talking about?
Object Type
VOIM may classify the basic identification form of the Value Object for methodological navigation.
Examples may include:
Physical Object Digital Object Information Object Capability Resource Activity Process Service Right Relationship Opportunity Outcome Composite Object Other Governable Value Object
These are identification forms rather than universal economic classifications.
Formal classification governance remains within CLA™ — Classification Architecture where required.
Object Distinguishability Principle
A Value Object must be sufficiently distinguishable from other objects to permit its value lifecycle to be governed.
The object need not always be physically separable.
It must be methodologically distinguishable.
For example:
a production line
may be identifiable as one Value Object even though it contains hundreds of physical components.
Likewise:
production capacity

may constitute a Value Object even though the capability arises from a combination of machinery, people, processes, energy, knowledge, and infrastructure.
The requirement is not physical isolation.
The requirement is:
sufficient distinction for value governance.
Composite Value Objects
A Value Object may consist of multiple components.
Examples include:
an industrial facility; an infrastructure network; a business unit; a technology platform; a production system; a portfolio; an integrated capability.
VOIM must identify when the value inquiry concerns:
the composite object
rather than merely the sum of its individual components.
This distinction matters because:
Value of Composite Object ≠ Automatic Sum of Component Values
Interactions, dependencies, complementarities, constraints, network effects, configuration, and context may produce a different value lifecycle at the composite level.
Component Value Objects
A component of a larger object may itself become a separate Value Object where its value lifecycle requires independent governance.
Therefore:
Object A may contain:
Value Object A.1 Value Object A.2 Value Object A.3
while the complete system may simultaneously constitute:
Value Object A
Each lifecycle must remain distinguishable.
Multiple Values Associated with One Object
A single underlying object may support multiple distinct value lifecycles.
For example, a forest may carry:

timber value; carbon-related value; ecological value; recreational value; water-regulation value; strategic land value.
VOIM must therefore avoid assuming:
One Object = One Value
Instead:
One Object → Potentially Multiple Distinct Value Relationships
The subsequent modules and Parent Standards determine how those value relationships are bounded and governed.
Same Value Across Multiple Objects
Conversely, one value phenomenon may depend upon multiple underlying objects.
For example:
network value
may arise from the interaction of many participants.
production capability
may depend upon machinery, workforce, infrastructure, knowledge, and supply access.
VOIM must therefore support identification of:
Composite Value Objects
and
Relational Value Objects
where the relevant subject cannot legitimately be reduced to one isolated physical asset.
Value Object Context
Identification may require contextual information where the same object can function differently across environments.
Context may include:
intended use; operational environment; economic environment; temporal period; technological environment; organizational context; geographic context; dependency context; relationship context.
VOIM identifies relevant context necessary to distinguish the object.
It does not yet determine the value produced by that context.
Temporal Identification
A Value Object may change over time.
Therefore, identification should establish the relevant temporal reference where material.
For example:

Factory X — Configuration 2024
may not represent the same Value Object state as:
Factory X — Configuration 2026 after automation upgrade.
VOIM must preserve enough temporal distinction to prevent value analysis performed on materially different object states from being silently combined.
Version and Configuration Awareness
For digital, technological, industrial, organizational, or composite Value Objects, version and configuration may materially affect identification.
Relevant distinctions may include:
software version; model version;
machinery configuration; infrastructure configuration; organizational structure; production configuration; contractual configuration; dataset version; capability state.
VOIM does not govern configuration integrity.
It ensures only that the object being subjected to value governance is sufficiently identifiable.
Potential Value ≠ Existing Value
VOIM may identify a Value Object even where value has not yet emerged.
This is essential for the VFM® lifecycle.
A newly discovered technology may be identifiable.
A development site may be identifiable.
An unused patent may be identifiable.
An unexploited resource may be identifiable.
A future production capability may be identifiable.
None of this automatically means that value already exists.
Therefore:
Value Object Identification → does not imply → Value Emergence
This preserves the boundary with later VFM® Parent Standards.
Zero Value Does Not Eliminate the Value Object

A Value Object may remain identifiable after its relevant value reaches zero.
This is critical for the later VFM® concept:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A zero-value condition does not necessarily mean that the underlying Value Object has ceased to exist.
The object may remain identifiable while:
Value State = Zero
and may later enter:
Value Restoration
where a legitimate restoration pathway exists.
Therefore:
Object Extinction ≠ Value Nullification
and
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction
Value Object Identification State
VOIM may assign a governed identification state.
A minimum model may include:
1. Unidentified
A potentially value-relevant subject exists, but it has not been sufficiently identified.
2. Candidate
A subject has been proposed as a Value Object but requires additional identification.
3. Conditionally Identified
The subject is sufficiently identifiable only under specified contextual, temporal, configuration, or relational conditions.
4. Identified
The Value Object is sufficiently identified and distinguishable to proceed through VFM® governance.
5. Identification Suspended
A previously identified Value Object has materially changed or contains unresolved ambiguity requiring reassessment.
6. Identification Retired
The identification reference is no longer active for the governed value lifecycle but is preserved for traceability.
These states govern identification only.
They do not describe value state.
Identification State ≠ Value State
VOIM enforces:

Value Object Identification State ≠ Value State
An object may be:
Identified
while its value is:
unknown, emerging, positive, degraded, zero, restored, or extinct.
The two governance dimensions must remain separate.
VOIM Boundary with Value Object Boundary
Module
VOIM answers:
What is the Value Object?
The Value Object Boundary Module answers:
Where does that Value Object begin and end for the relevant value lifecycle?
Identification precedes boundary determination.
A subject cannot be meaningfully bounded before it is sufficiently identified.
VOIM Boundary with Value Differentiation &
Separation Module
VOIM identifies the subject.
The Value Differentiation & Separation Module determines whether multiple value phenomena, objects, components, or value relationships must remain analytically separate.
Therefore:
Identification ≠ Differentiation.
VOIM Boundary with Value Context & Condition
Module
VOIM may record context necessary to identify the object.
The Value Context & Condition Module governs the broader conditions under which the identified Value Object is being examined for value purposes.
Therefore:
Identification Context ≠ Value Context Governance.
VOIM Boundary with Value Origin Standard
VOIM identifies:
what the value lifecycle concerns.
The Value Origin Standard determines:
where the relevant value originates.
Therefore:
Value Object ≠ Value Origin
and:
Identification ≠ Origin Determination.
VOIM Boundary with Value Emergence Standard

VOIM does not determine whether value has actually come into existence.
That belongs to the Value Emergence Standard.
A Value Object may be fully identified while no value has yet emerged.
VOIM Boundary with Value Recognition Standard
VOIM does not recognize value.
It identifies the object to which a possible value lifecycle relates.
Therefore:
Object Identification ≠ Value Recognition.
VOIM Boundary with CLA™
VOIM may establish an identification type necessary to distinguish a Value Object.
It does not replace formal classification governance.
Where formal classification is required:
CLA™ — Classification Architecture governs classification.
VOIM Boundary with OBIDENITY®
VOIM does not determine:
legal identity; ownership; authority; permission; responsibility; provenance rights; transfer rights.
Where origin-bound identity governance is required, those questions remain within OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture.
A Value Object may be identified for value governance without VFM® determining who owns it.
VOIM Boundary with VALIDOS®
VOIM does not determine whether the Value Object or any claim concerning it is valid.
VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation.
Identification is a prerequisite for many validation activities but does not constitute validation.
VOIM Boundary with INTEGROS®
VOIM does not determine whether the Value Object possesses integrity.
INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity.

An object can be sufficiently identified even while its integrity remains unknown or impaired.
VOIM Boundary with ADIT®
VOIM establishes the methodological identity of the Value Object for value governance.
ADIT® — Continuous Audit & Evidence Governance Architecture may govern evidence and auditability concerning that identification and subsequent events.
Identification ≠ Audit Evidence.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VOIM implementation should establish:
1. Value Object Candidate
Identify the subject proposed for value governance.
2. Object Reference
Establish the primary reference through which the subject can be distinguished.
3. Object Form
Determine whether the subject is physical, digital, informational, relational, capability-based, process-based, composite, or another governable form.
4. Distinguishability
Determine whether the subject can be sufficiently distinguished from adjacent objects or subjects.
5. Context Reference
Record contextual information necessary for identification.
6. Temporal Reference
Establish the relevant time or lifecycle reference where material.
7. Version / Configuration
Identify the relevant version or configuration where material.
8. Composite / Component Relationship
Record whether the Value Object forms part of, contains, or depends upon other Value Objects.
9. Identification State
Assign the governed Value Object Identification State.
10. Value Object Identifier

Create or associate a stable reference enabling the Value Object to remain traceable through the VFM® lifecycle.
Governance Outputs
VOIM may produce:
Value Object Candidate Record
Value Object Identification Record Value Object Reference Value Object Type Record Value Object Context Reference Value Object Temporal Reference Value Object Version Record Value Object Configuration Reference Composite Value Object Relationship Record Component Value Object Relationship Record Value Object Identification State Value Object Identifier Governable Value Object
These outputs provide the governed input for the next module:
Value Object Boundary Module.
Enterprise Application
VOIM gives organizations a foundational capability that is often missing from conventional valuation and economic systems:
the ability to establish exactly what is being treated as the subject of value before value is measured, priced, recognized, changed, taxed, impaired, restored, or transferred.
This becomes especially important where value does not map cleanly onto a conventional asset.
An organization may use VOIM to identify value objects such as:
unused production capacity; data; algorithms; intellectual property; infrastructure capability; technological potential; resource access; contractual opportunities; network relationships; dormant assets; recovered materials; digital capabilities; environmental resources; composite operational systems.

VOIM can therefore expose a fundamental error before it propagates through later analysis:
different parties may appear to disagree about value when they are actually assigning value to different Value Objects.
By making the Value Object explicit first, VFM® creates a stable reference for the entire downstream value lifecycle.
Foundational Principles
Value cannot be governed coherently until the subject of that value is identified.
Underlying Object ≠ Value Object ≠ Value.
Object existence does not establish value existence.
Value Object identification does not establish value recognition.
One underlying object may support multiple distinct value lifecycles.
One Value Object may consist of multiple underlying objects.
A Value Object may remain identifiable when its value reaches zero.
Potential value is not existing value.
Identification state is not value state.
Ownership is not required to identify a Value Object.
Price is not required to identify a Value Object.
A governable value lifecycle requires a sufficiently identifiable subject to which that lifecycle can remain anchored.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Object Identification Module establishes the first methodological control point of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by determining exactly what subject enters the governed value lifecycle as a Value Object. Through governance of Value Object Candidates, identification basis, object reference, distinguishability, object form, contextual reference, temporal reference, version and configuration awareness, composite and component relationships, identification states, and stable Value Object identifiers, VOIM prevents value governance from beginning with an ambiguous or undefined subject. By explicitly separating the underlying object from the Value Object and the Value Object from value itself, VOIM preserves the methodological boundaries between identification, value origin, value emergence, value recognition, value state, ownership, classification, validation, integrity, and audit. VFM® can therefore begin the lifecycle of value from a precise foundational question: before asking where value comes from, how it changes, whether it reaches zero, whether it can be restored, or when it becomes extinct, first establish exactly what the value is about.

Canonical Definition
Value Identification Standard (VIS) is the first Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the methodological conditions under which a potential or existing manifestation of value can be identified, distinguished, bounded, described, and established as a governable Value Object within the value lifecycle.
VIS establishes the first governance point of VFM®.
Before value can be traced to an origin, recognized as having emerged, assigned a state, observed for change, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, or determined to have reached extinction, the subject whose value is being governed must first be identifiable.

VIS therefore establishes the governed relationship between:
Potential Value Phenomenon → Value Candidate → Value Identification → Value Object
The Standard does not determine how much something is worth.
It does not determine whether a market recognizes it, whether it is legally owned, whether it is taxable, whether it has been validated, or whether its integrity has been established.
Its task is more fundamental:
to determine what value is being referred to and whether that value can be sufficiently identified to enter a governed value lifecycle.
Core Question
What value is being governed, and how can it be sufficiently identified and bounded before its origin, existence, state, and lifecycle are determined?
Architectural Position
Value Identification is the first governed space of VFM®.
It precedes:
Value Origin Standard
and therefore establishes the object required for all subsequent value governance.
The architectural sequence begins:
Value Identification → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction
VIS asks:
What value are we talking about?
Only after that question has been sufficiently answered can the architecture ask:
Where does that value originate?
This distinction is foundational.
Identification ≠ Origin.
Something may be identified as a candidate for value governance before its actual value origin has been established.

Governance Flow Position
Potential Value Phenomenon → Value Candidate Identification → Value Object Definition → Value Boundary Determination → Value Context Identification → Value Distinction → Value Identification State → Governed Value Object → Value Origin Governance
Operational Space
VIS governs the methodological space between:
an observed, proposed, inferred, expected, claimed, or potentially relevant manifestation of value
and:
an explicitly identified Value Object capable of entering the VFM® lifecycle.
This space includes:
Value Candidate identification; Value Object identification; value-reference definition; value boundary determination; value context; value distinction; value manifestation; value subject; value relationship; value dependency awareness; value aggregation awareness; value decomposition; value identification state; identification uncertainty; identification documentation; identification reassessment.
Value Candidate
A Value Candidate is an object, capability, condition, relationship, activity, outcome, resource, right, information object, process, state, opportunity, or other phenomenon proposed for examination within the VFM® value lifecycle.
Identification as a Value Candidate does not establish that value exists.
Therefore:
Value Candidate ≠ Existing Value
The purpose of the concept is to permit governance to begin before value existence has been determined.

This prevents a circular methodological problem in which something must already be accepted as valuable before its value can be investigated.
Value Object
A Value Object is the explicitly identified and bounded subject whose value lifecycle is governed through VFM®.
A Value Object may relate to:
a physical asset; a digital asset; intellectual property; information; data; a capability; infrastructure; technology; a service; a process; an activity; an opportunity; access; capacity; a relationship; a contractual position; a productive resource; a natural resource; an economic resource; an organizational capability; a computational capability; an energy resource; a future capability;
another sufficiently identifiable value-bearing or potentially value-bearing phenomenon.
VFM® does not require the Value Object to be a legally recognized asset.
It requires the object of value governance to be methodologically identifiable.
Value Object ≠ Asset Identity
VIS must not be confused with identity governance.
A Value Object may reference an asset, entity, resource, or capability whose identity is governed elsewhere.
VIS asks:
What is the subject of value governance?
OBIDENITY® may ask:
What is the governed identity and origin-bound identity relationship of the relevant entity or asset?
These questions may interact.
They are not the same governance space.
Value Identification ≠ Value Recognition
This distinction is critical to VFM®.
Value Identification establishes:

what value or potential value is being examined.
Value Recognition establishes:
whether existing value may be recognized within the governed value lifecycle.
Something can therefore be:
identified
without yet being:
recognized as existing value.
This allows VFM® to examine dormant, uncertain, emerging, disputed, unrealized, inaccessible, latent, degraded, or potentially recoverable value without assuming the conclusion in advance.
Value Identification ≠ Valuation
VIS does not determine monetary worth.
It does not assign:
price; market value; fair value; accounting value; taxable value; liquidation value; replacement value; investment value; economic value.
Those determinations may be performed by external methodologies.
VIS establishes the object to which such determinations may later relate.
Therefore:
Identification of Value ≠ Measurement of Value.
Value Identification ≠ Value Existence
Identification does not prove that value exists.
A Value Candidate may enter VFM® and subsequently be determined not to have reached Value Emergence.
This distinction enables VFM® to govern:
potential value
without automatically declaring:
existent value.
Value Boundary
Every Value Object requires a sufficiently explicit Value Boundary.
The Value Boundary determines what is included in the Value Object being governed and what remains outside it.
A boundary may be:

physical; functional; temporal; relational; informational; operational; economic; contextual; capability-based; resource-based; outcome-based; composite.
Without a boundary, changes in value cannot be reliably attributed to the same governed Value Object.
Boundary Stability
A Value Boundary need not remain permanently unchanged.
However, material boundary change must remain visible.
Examples include:
assets being combined; assets being divided; capabilities being added; rights being removed; operational scope changing; data being incorporated; infrastructure being separated; relationships being terminated; previously separate value objects becoming interdependent.
A materially changed Value Object may require re-identification.
Value Context
Value does not necessarily exist independently of context.
VIS therefore permits the identification of a relevant Value Context.
Context may include:
intended use; user; beneficiary; operational environment; time; location; availability; scarcity; dependency; technological environment; economic environment; organizational environment; physical conditions.
VIS does not determine whether those contextual factors create value.
It preserves them so that subsequent VFM® standards can determine their relevance.
Value Distinction
VIS requires distinguishable Value Objects where different value lifecycles exist.
For example, one physical object may contain:

material value; functional value; information value; intellectual-property value; productive value; strategic value; recovery value.
These must not automatically be treated as one indivisible value phenomenon.
Where materially different value lifecycles exist, they may require separate Value Objects or explicitly defined value dimensions.
Composite Value Objects
VFM® may govern composite Value Objects.
A composite Value Object consists of multiple components whose combined configuration produces a relevant value relationship.
VIS requires the composite basis to remain identifiable.
This allows VFM® to distinguish:
component value
from:
value arising from combination.
Latent Value
A Value Candidate may contain conditions capable of producing future value even where value has not yet emerged.
VIS allows this to be identified without prematurely declaring value existence.
This creates an important pathway:
Value Candidate → Identified Potential → Value Origin → Value Emergence
Latent value is therefore not automatically an existing Value Asset.
Value Identification State
VIS establishes governed identification states.
A minimum state model may include:
1. Unidentified
A potential value phenomenon is observable or suspected but has not been sufficiently defined for governance.
2. Candidate Identified
A Value Candidate has been identified but its Value Object boundary or context remains insufficiently established.
3. Conditionally Identified

The Value Object can be identified only under explicit conditions, assumptions, boundaries, or unresolved dependencies.
4. Identified
The Value Object is sufficiently defined, bounded, distinguished, and contextualized to enter Value Origin governance.
5. Identification Suspended
A material change or unresolved inconsistency prevents continued reliance upon the current identification.
6. Re-identification Required
The Value Object has changed sufficiently that the existing identification can no longer support the subsequent lifecycle without reassessment.
These states govern identification only.
They do not establish value existence or worth.
Identification Uncertainty
VIS requires material uncertainty concerning Value Object identity or boundary to remain visible.
Uncertainty may concern:
what is included; what is excluded; whether multiple value objects exist; whether value is separable; whether a relationship is material; whether a capability exists independently; whether the relevant object has changed; whether context fundamentally changes the object being governed.
Uncertainty does not always prevent identification.
It may require conditional identification.
No Presumed Value Principle
VFM® must not assume value merely because something has been presented as valuable.
VIS therefore establishes:
Identification for Value Governance ≠ Confirmation of Value
A claimed valuable asset may be admitted as a Value Candidate.
Subsequent VFM® governance may determine that value:

has not emerged; existed previously but has degraded; has reached zero; remains recoverable; has become extinct.
This preserves methodological neutrality.
Value Granularity
Identification must occur at a granularity appropriate to the governance question.
An organization may be examined as:
one Value Object
for one purpose,
while its:
intellectual property; machinery; datasets; production capability; contracts; customer relationships; technological capabilities
may each become separate Value Objects for another purpose.
VFM® therefore does not impose one universal level of value granularity.
Temporal Identity of Value
The identity of a Value Object may persist while its value state changes.
For example:
Positive Value → Degradation → Zero Value → Restoration
may occur without the underlying Value Object ceasing to be identifiable.
This distinction is essential for ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™.
A Value Object can remain identifiable even when its admissible value reaches zero.
Therefore:
Loss of Value ≠ Loss of Value Object Identity.
Relationship to Origin Asset™
Origin Asset™ belongs primarily to the subsequent Value Origin governed space.
VIS identifies the Value Object.
Value Origin governance then determines the source, basis, capability, condition, relationship, or other origin from which its value may emerge.
Therefore:
Value Object Identification → Value Origin Determination → Origin Asset™ relationship where applicable.

VIS must not presume an Origin Asset™ before the origin relationship has been established.
Relationship to Value Asset™
A Value Object does not automatically become a Value Asset™.
Value Asset™ represents a value-bearing state where the relevant conditions have been established through subsequent VFM® governance.
Therefore:
Value Object ≠ Value Asset™
A Value Object is the governed subject.
Value Asset™ describes an applicable value-bearing state.
Relationship to ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
VIS also preserves the identity required for zero-value governance.
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ cannot be meaningfully governed unless the underlying Value Object remains identifiable.
Therefore, when value reaches zero:
Value State may change while Value Object identity persists.
This enables the later sequence:
Value Asset™ → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → ReMonet™ → restored Value State
without losing continuity of the governed Value Object.
Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VIS ↔ OBIDENITY®
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability.
VIS governs identification of the subject of value governance.
Identity Governance ≠ Value Identification.
VIS ↔ CLA™
CLA™ governs how classifications are formally established and maintained.
VIS may later consume a governed classification where useful.
It does not become a general classification architecture.
VIS ↔ VALIDOS®

VALIDOS® governs whether validation claims can legitimately be established and relied upon.
VIS does not validate value.
It identifies the Value Object to which subsequent value governance applies.
Value Identification ≠ Value Validation.
VIS ↔ INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® governs integrity.
VIS may require sufficient structural coherence to identify a Value Object but does not determine its general integrity.
VIS ↔ ADIT®
ADIT® governs audit and evidence.
VIS may generate identification records that become auditable evidence.
It does not govern auditability itself.
VIS ↔ GOA™
GOA™ governs governance authority, boundaries, scope, delegation, accountability, validation, integrity, transparency, continuity, and interoperability.
VIS governs the Value Object.
It does not establish governance authority over that object.
VIS ↔ ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
Operational conditions may help establish the context in which a Value Object exists.
VIS does not govern Operational Reality itself.
Parent Standard Modules
1. VCIM — Value Candidate Identification Module
Governs identification of a potential value phenomenon as a Value Candidate without presuming that value already exists.
Core Question: What phenomenon should enter the value lifecycle for governed examination?
2. VOIM — Value Object Identification Module
Governs establishment of the specific Value Object whose value lifecycle will be governed.
Core Question: What precisely is the subject of value governance?

3. VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module
Governs the inclusion, exclusion, extent, granularity, and boundary of the Value Object.
Core Question: Where does the governed Value Object begin and end?
4. VCXM — Value Context Module
Governs identification of the material context within which the Value Object is being examined.
Core Question: Within what context is the identified Value Object entering value governance?
5. VISM — Value Identification State Module
Governs assignment, maintenance, suspension, and reassessment of the Value Identification State.
Core Question: Has the Value Object been sufficiently identified to proceed into Value Origin governance?
Internal Module Flow
Potential Value Phenomenon → VCIM — Value Candidate Identification Module → VOIM — Value Object Identification Module → VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module → VCXM — Value Context Module → VISM — Value Identification State Module → Governed Value Object → Value Origin Standard
The internal logic is:
What may contain or represent value → what precisely is being governed → where its boundary lies → within what context it is examined → whether identification is sufficient to continue.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VIS implementation should establish:
1. Value Candidate
Identify the phenomenon proposed for value governance.
2. Value Object
Define the precise subject whose value lifecycle will be governed.
3. Value Boundary
Determine what is included and excluded.
4. Value Granularity

Determine the appropriate level at which the Value Object is governed.
5. Value Context
Identify materially relevant contextual conditions.
6. Value Distinction
Separate materially different Value Objects or value dimensions where required.
7. Dependency Awareness
Identify dependencies capable of affecting the interpretation of the Value Object.
8. Identification Uncertainty
Record unresolved uncertainty affecting identification or boundaries.
9. Identification State
Assign a governed Value Identification State.
10. Identification Record
Create a reconstructable record of the basis on which the Value Object was identified.
Governance Outputs
VIS may produce:
Value Candidate Record Value Object Record Value Object Definition Value Boundary Statement Value Inclusion Record Value Exclusion Record Value Granularity Record Value Context Record Value Distinction Record Value Dependency Record Value Identification Uncertainty Record Value Identification State Value Re-identification Trigger Governed Value Object
These outputs provide the governed input for the Value Origin Standard.
Enterprise Application
VIS enables organizations to answer a deceptively difficult question:
What exactly are we calling value?
This matters because organizations frequently aggregate fundamentally different phenomena under one financial or operational label.
A company may say:
“This asset is worth CHF 10 million.”
But that apparent single value may depend upon:

physical property; productive capacity; intellectual property; access rights; customer relationships; contractual rights; data; technology; scarcity; expected future capability.
VIS allows those value phenomena to be identified and bounded before their origins, emergence, states, changes, degradation, nullification, or restoration are governed.
The same method can be applied to:
public assets; infrastructure; corporate assets; intellectual property; digital assets; technology; data; energy resources; natural resources; productive capability; government programs; investment projects; abandoned assets; dormant assets; impaired assets; future technologies; AI-created capabilities.
This makes VIS relevant not only to conventional accounting contexts but also to value phenomena that conventional accounting systems may not yet represent effectively.
Why This Matters for Future Value Systems
A value-based accounting, economic, public-finance, or taxation methodology cannot begin reliably with:
How much is it worth?
It must first establish:
What exactly is the Value Object?
Then:
Where does its value originate?
Then:
Has value actually emerged?
Then:
What state is that value in?
Only afterward can external accounting, measurement, economic, or taxation systems determine how that governed value should be treated.
VFM® therefore creates a methodological value layer that can potentially operate beneath multiple downstream systems without becoming those systems itself.

Foundational Principles
Value cannot be governed until the subject of value governance is identifiable.
Value identification does not presume value existence.
Value identification is not valuation.
Value identification is not value recognition.
Value Object identity is distinct from asset identity.
A Value Candidate may exist before value emerges.
A Value Object may remain identifiable after its value reaches zero.
Loss of value does not necessarily mean loss of the Value Object.
Different value phenomena within one asset may require different governed Value Objects.
The boundary of the Value Object determines the boundary of the value lifecycle being governed.
Before asking how value changes, VFM® must first establish what value is being governed.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Identification Standard establishes the first governed space of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by creating the methodological conditions under which potential or existing manifestations of value can be identified, distinguished, bounded, contextualized, and established as governed Value Objects without presuming value existence, recognition, validity, price, ownership, legality, or economic treatment. Through governance of Value Candidates, Value Objects, boundaries, granularity, context, distinctions, dependencies, uncertainty, identification states, and re-identification, VIS creates the stable reference object required for the complete downstream value lifecycle. By separating value identification from asset identity, classification, validation, valuation, recognition, and value state, VIS preserves the architectural boundaries of VFM® and complementary OOF® architectures while establishing the foundation required for Value Origin governance. Before value can emerge, change, develop, degrade, reach zero, be restored, or become extinct, the value being governed must first be identifiable.

About Value Nullification Standard (VNS)
About Value Nullification Standard (VNS)
Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Governed Space: Value Nullification
Canonical Definition
Value Nullification Standard (VNS) governs the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and transitions through which previously existing positive value legitimately reaches a zero-value condition.
VNS establishes the governed boundary between value that is declining and value that has actually reached zero.
Its central distinction is fundamental:
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification.
An asset, capability, technology, right, dataset, system, service, or other Value Object may lose substantial value while still retaining positive value. VNS begins at the point where the relevant governed value crosses its defined zero-value boundary.
Why VNS Matters
Organizations frequently use terms such as obsolete, worthless, dead, expired, decommissioned, or without value without defining what has actually happened to value.
These statements may collapse very different conditions.
Value may have:
never emerged;
declined but still exist;
temporarily reached zero;
been deliberately withdrawn;
become zero in only one value dimension;
or
been permanently nullified within a defined context.

DeMonet™ governs the value mechanism through which previously existing positive value transitions into a governed zero-value condition.
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
DeMonet™ is not simply another term for depreciation, deterioration, impairment, technological obsolescence, market decline, destruction, or financial loss.
Those may be external events or mechanisms that affect value.
DeMonet™ governs:
what happens to value when the applicable positive-value boundary is legitimately crossed.
Critical Governance Distinctions
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified
There must have been positive value before there can be nullification.
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification
A value reduced from 100 to 5 remains positive if the governed zero threshold has not been reached.
Approaching Zero ≠ Zero
Severe impairment does not establish nullification by itself.
Zero Value ≠ Object Nonexistence
An object may continue to physically, digitally, legally, or informationally exist after its relevant value reaches zero.
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value
An object with zero positive value may still generate costs, liabilities, risks, or negative externalities.
Zero Value in One Context ≠ Zero Value Everywhere
A machine may have zero production value while retaining salvage, historical, evidential, or informational value.
Temporary and Permanent Nullification
VNS recognizes that zero value does not necessarily mean irreversible value loss.
A Value Object may enter:

Temporary Zero Value
where restoration remains possible,
or:
Permanent Zero Value
where the relevant value cannot reasonably be restored within the defined Value Context.
This distinction creates the direct architectural interface with:
VRSS — Value Restoration Standard.
The broader lifecycle may therefore become:
Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State
Use Case 1 — Industrial Machine Becomes
Operationally Obsolete
A manufacturing company operates a specialized production machine that has generated significant operational value for many years.
A new production technology gradually makes the machine less efficient.
Its operational value declines:
100 → 70 → 40 → 15 → 5
This is Value Degradation.
The company should not classify the machine as having zero operational value merely because a newer technology performs better.
Later, required replacement components become unavailable, the machine can no longer perform its production function, and no technically viable operating configuration remains within the defined production environment.
The applicable operational-value threshold is reached.
VNS governs the transition:
Existing Operational Value → Nullification Condition → Nullification Threshold Reached → DeMonet™ → Operational Value = 0
The machine may now legitimately enter a ZVA™ state for operational production value.
But the machine itself has not ceased to exist.
It may still possess:
salvage value;

material value;
historical value;
or
evidential value.
VNS therefore prevents the organization from converting:
“Operational production value has reached zero”
into the much broader and potentially false statement:
“The machine has no value.”
Use Case 2 — Digital Platform Capability Is
Deliberately Withdrawn
A technology company provides a digital capability that creates substantial operational value for customers.
The company later decides to discontinue the capability.
Access is progressively restricted and eventually terminated.
Before termination, the capability still creates positive value even though its remaining useful period is short.
At the termination point, however, users can no longer access or exercise the capability.
VNS can govern:
Positive Functional Value → Deliberate Value Withdrawal → Defined Nullification Condition → Threshold Reached → DeMonet™ → Zero Functional Value
This creates an important distinction.
The technology may still exist.
Its source code may still exist.
The organization may still own intellectual property.
Historical data may retain value.
But the specific governed capability available to the user has reached:
Functional Value = 0.
If the company later restores the capability, the lifecycle does not need to pretend that the zero-value period never occurred.
Instead:
Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value
can remain visible as a governed value history.
Enterprise Value

VNS gives organizations a method for answering a question that conventional asset, operational, financial, and technology systems often treat inconsistently:
When has value actually reached zero?
This can be relevant to:
industrial assets;
infrastructure; software; digital services; technologies; intellectual property; datasets; organizational capabilities; contractual rights; licenses; operational systems; AI systems; autonomous systems; products and services.
The purpose is not to declare more assets worthless.
It is to make the zero-value boundary explicit, contextual, traceable, and governable.
Foundational Principle
Value can decline without disappearing. Nullification occurs only when previously existing positive value legitimately crosses its governed zero-value boundary.

Canonical Definition
DeMonet™ Mechanism Module (VDMM) is the third Core Module of the Value Nullification Standard (VNS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VDMM governs DeMonet™, the canonical value-transition mechanism through which previously existing positive value reaches a governed zero-value condition after the applicable Value Nullification Conditions and Value Nullification Threshold have been established.
The Module governs the transition itself rather than the external event, cause, degradation process, threshold, or final determination associated with that transition.
Its foundational function is:

to make the transition from existing positive value to a zero-value condition explicit, governable, traceable, and distinguishable from value that never emerged, value that merely degraded, and value that has become permanently extinct.
Architectural Position
VDMM is the third module within VNS.
It follows:
VNTM — Value Nullification Threshold Module
and precedes:
VNDM — Value Nullification Determination Module.
VNTM establishes:
whether the applicable zero-value threshold has been reached.
VDMM establishes:
the governed mechanism through which previously existing positive value transitions into the zero-value condition.
VNDM subsequently establishes:
whether the complete governed basis supports a formal Value Nullification Determination.
The sequence is therefore:
Threshold → DeMonet™ → Determination.
Internal Module Flow
Established Value Nullification Threshold → Pre-Transition Value State Confirmation → DeMonet™ Transition Initiation → Transition Basis Identification → Affected Value Dimension Confirmation → Transition Scope Definition → Transition Characterization → Zero-Value Condition Entry → DeMonet™ Transition Record → VNDM — Value Nullification Determination Module
The internal logic is:
what positive value existed → which zero-value boundary was reached → what value is transitioning → how the transition occurs → what zero-value condition results → what must proceed to formal determination.
Operational Space
VDMM governs the space between:

established Value Nullification Threshold
and
formal Value Nullification Determination.
This operational space includes:
DeMonet™ initiation; transition identity; pre-transition value state; affected value dimension; affected Value Context; transition scope; transition basis; transition timing;
progressive transition; immediate transition; deliberate transition; externally induced transition; internally induced transition; temporary zero-value transition; potentially permanent zero-value transition; partial nullification; complete dimensional nullification; compound transition; transition evidence; transition uncertainty; transition traceability; zero-value condition entry; DeMonet™ recording.
DeMonet™
DeMonet™ is the canonical VFM® mechanism representing the governed transition of previously existing positive value into a zero-value condition.
Its canonical form is:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
The resulting zero-value condition may subsequently support classification as:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
where the applicable requirements of the architecture are satisfied.
DeMonet™ therefore represents a value transition, not an asset class and not a final lifecycle condition.
DeMonet™ Requires Prior Value
DeMonet™ can occur only where positive value previously existed.
This creates one of the most important boundaries in VNS:
Value Never Emerged ≠ DeMonet™.

If an object, capability, right, process, technology, asset, or other governed entity never acquired positive value within the relevant Value Context, there is no positive value to nullify.
Therefore:
No Prior Positive Value → No DeMonet™ Transition.
This prevents absence of value from being incorrectly represented as loss of value.
DeMonet™ ≠ Value Degradation
Value Degradation governs declining value while positive value remains.
DeMonet™ governs the transition into zero.
Therefore:
Value = 100 → 60 → 20 → 5
remains within:
Value Degradation
while:
Value > 0 → 0
creates the boundary at which:
DeMonet™
becomes applicable.
The distinction is fundamental:
Declining Value ≠ Nullified Value.
DeMonet™ ≠ Value Change
VCS governs the fact and character of material change to value.
DeMonet™ governs a specific lifecycle transition:
Positive Value → Zero-Value Condition.
Every DeMonet™ transition therefore involves a Value Change.
But:
Not Every Value Change = DeMonet™.
Value may increase, decline, fluctuate, mature, compound, transfer between states, or otherwise change without reaching zero.
DeMonet™ ≠ External Cause
The event producing the transition may originate outside VFM®.
Examples may include:
technological displacement; physical destruction; expiration; market disappearance; loss of access; regulatory prohibition; contractual termination; operational failure; strategic withdrawal; capability loss; infrastructure change; organizational decision.

VFM® does not need to govern the external event itself.
VDMM governs:
what happens to the governed value when that event causes the established zero-value boundary to be reached.
Therefore:
External Cause ≠ DeMonet™.
The external cause may trigger the transition.
DeMonet™ is the governed value-transition mechanism.
Progressive DeMonet™
A DeMonet™ transition may follow progressive degradation.
For example:
Positive Value
→ Degradation
→ Further Degradation
→ Threshold Approach
→ Threshold Reached
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition.
In this pathway, DeMonet™ does not represent the entire degradation history.
It represents the decisive transition at the zero-value boundary.
Immediate DeMonet™
DeMonet™ may also occur without a prolonged degradation pathway.
A material event may move value directly from positive to zero.
For example:
Active Access Right
→ Immediate Legal Termination
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero Functional Value within the governed context.
Therefore:
Degradation is not a prerequisite for DeMonet™.
Deliberate DeMonet™
Value may be deliberately withdrawn.
An organization may intentionally:
terminate a capability; discontinue a service; withdraw access; abandon an asset's governed use; eliminate a value-bearing function; retire a value-generating configuration.
Where the relevant positive value legitimately reaches zero, VDMM may govern the resulting transition as:
Deliberate DeMonet™.

The intentional nature of the transition does not make the value loss methodologically different from other nullification pathways.
It changes the transition basis.
Externally Induced DeMonet™
A DeMonet™ transition may result from a change outside the governed Value Object.
For example:
A technically functional system may retain its physical capability while a regulatory prohibition eliminates its legitimate operational use within a defined jurisdiction.
The object has not physically failed.
Yet:
Operationally Permitted Value > 0
may transition to:
Operationally Permitted Value = 0.
VDMM governs the value consequence.
It does not govern the regulatory decision itself.
Contextual DeMonet™
DeMonet™ is Value Context-specific.
An asset may undergo:
DeMonet™ in Context A
while retaining:
Positive Value in Context B.
For example:
A production machine may lose all production value within one manufacturing process but retain:
resale value,
salvage value,
training value,
or
component value.
Therefore:
Contextual Zero Value ≠ Universal Zero Value.
Dimensional DeMonet™
DeMonet™ may apply to a particular value dimension.
Possible dimensions include:
Economic Value
Operational Value
Functional Value
Strategic Value
Knowledge Value
Access Value
Commercial Value
Option Value
Salvage Value
A single Value Object may therefore undergo multiple distinct DeMonet™ transitions over its lifecycle.
Example:
Operational Value → DeMonet™ → 0
while:
Salvage Value > 0.

VDMM must preserve this distinction.
Partial Nullification
A complex Value Object may contain multiple value-bearing components, functions, rights, or capabilities.
DeMonet™ may affect only part of that structure.
VDMM therefore distinguishes:
Partial Value Nullification
from
Complete Dimensional Value Nullification.
Partial nullification means that a defined component of the governed value structure reaches zero while other governed value remains positive.
Temporary DeMonet™
A zero-value condition may be temporary.
For example:
A critical digital capability may become completely unavailable because of a system failure.
During the outage:
Current Functional Value = 0.
If the capability can subsequently be restored, the zero-value condition retains recovery potential.
This may create:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ later ReMonet™
→ Restored Value.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ ≠ Permanent Extinction.
Permanent-Looking Zero Value
VDMM must not classify a transition as permanently extinct merely because recovery appears unlikely.
The architecture contains a separate terminal governed space:
VXSS — Value Extinction Standard.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
Even a long-duration zero-value condition may remain recoverable.
The existence or absence of recovery potential must be governed separately.
DeMonet™ and ZVA™
DeMonet™ and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represent different architectural concepts.
DeMonet™ = Transition Mechanism

ZVA™ = Governed Zero-Value State / Asset Condition where applicable
The relationship is:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™ where applicable.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ ≠ ZVA™.
One governs movement.
The other represents the resulting governed condition.
DeMonet™ and ReMonet™
DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ form complementary but non-identical mechanisms.
DeMonet™
governs:
Positive Value → Zero-Value Condition
while:
ReMonet™
governs restoration of previously existing impaired, lost, dormant, or zero value under VRSS — Value Restoration Standard.
A lifecycle may therefore contain:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value.
This creates a governed reversible value lifecycle where recovery remains possible.
DeMonet™ and Value Extinction
DeMonet™ does not establish that recoverable value has ceased to exist permanently.
That determination belongs to:
VXSS — Value Extinction Standard.
The critical distinction is:
DeMonet™ → Value reaches zero.
Value Extinction → Value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ ≠ Extinction.
Transition Identity
Every material DeMonet™ transition should be independently identifiable.
A transition identity may connect:
Value Object; affected value dimension; Value Context; previous Value State; Nullification Condition; Nullification Threshold; transition basis; transition time; resulting zero-value condition; evidence; uncertainty; downstream determination.

This enables the transition to be reconstructed without conflating it with the object itself.
Transition Scope
VDMM requires the scope of DeMonet™ to be explicit.
The scope should identify whether the transition affects:
one value dimension
multiple value dimensions
one component
one capability
one jurisdiction
one operational context
one temporal interval
or
the entire governed value structure.
Without transition scope, a local zero-value event may be incorrectly interpreted as total value loss.
Transition Timing
Where determinable, VDMM records when DeMonet™ occurred.
Timing may be:
Exact
where the threshold crossing is identifiable at a specific point,
Bounded
where the transition occurred within a known interval,
or
Indeterminate
where evidence confirms the transition but cannot establish its precise timing.
Temporal uncertainty must remain visible.
Transition Evidence
A DeMonet™ transition must be supported by evidence sufficient to establish that previously existing positive value entered the applicable zero-value condition.
Evidence may include:
Value State records; degradation records; threshold records; operational records; technical evidence; contractual evidence; access records; expiry records;
market evidence; system records; physical evidence; authorized external determinations.
VDMM does not replace evidence validation or integrity governance.
It uses governed evidence to establish the value-transition mechanism.
Transition Uncertainty

Where evidence does not clearly establish whether the transition occurred, VDMM must preserve uncertainty.
Possible states may include:
Transition Confirmed
Transition Conditionally Established
Transition Under Review
Transition Indeterminate
Transition Not Established
The architecture must not force DeMonet™ merely because value is extremely low or because nullification is expected.
DeMonet™ Transition State
VDMM may assign a governed DeMonet™ Transition State.
A minimum state model may include:
1. Not Initiated
The applicable positive value remains above its governed Nullification Threshold.
2. Initiated
The governed basis indicates that the transition into zero value has begun or become immediately applicable.
3. In Transition
The value is undergoing a governed transition where the transition cannot legitimately be represented as instantaneous.
4. Zero-Value Entry Established
The applicable positive value has entered the zero-value condition.
5. Conditionally Established
The transition is supported only under explicitly defined conditions.
6. Indeterminate
Available evidence cannot establish whether DeMonet™ has occurred.
7. Recorded
The completed DeMonet™ transition has been formally recorded and is ready for downstream determination.
Boundary with VNTM
VNTM establishes:
where the zero-value boundary lies and whether it has been reached.
VDMM establishes:
the governed transition through that boundary.
Therefore:
Threshold ≠ Transition.
Boundary with VNDM

VDMM establishes the DeMonet™ transition basis.
VNDM determines whether the complete governed basis supports formal Value Nullification.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ Transition ≠ Value Nullification Determination.
Boundary with VDG Standard
Value Degradation governs decline while positive value remains.
VDMM governs movement into zero.
Therefore:
Decline while Value > 0 → Value Degradation
Value > 0 → 0 → DeMonet™
Boundary with VSS
VSS governs the current Value State.
VDMM governs the transition through which the prior positive Value State reaches a zero-value condition.
The resulting state may subsequently be represented within VSS.
Therefore:
Value State ≠ Value Transition Mechanism.
Boundary with VCS
VCS governs material change to value generally.
VDMM governs the specific nullifying transition:
Positive Value → Zero-Value Condition.
Therefore:
Value Change is broader than DeMonet™.
Boundary with VRSS
VRSS governs restoration.
Its canonical mechanism:
ReMonet™
operates where previously impaired, lost, dormant, or zero value is legitimately recovered.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ = movement toward zero.
ReMonet™ = recovery of previously existing value.
Boundary with VXSS
VXSS governs the terminal condition in which the relevant value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
VDMM stops at the zero-value transition.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
This boundary is essential because a ZVA™ may retain restoration potential.
Boundary with ORA™

ORA™ may establish the Operational Reality in which the causal event or condition occurred.
VDMM governs the resulting transition in value.
Therefore:
Operational Event ≠ Value Transition.
Boundary with VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may govern validation of claims, evidence, methods, or determinations associated with a DeMonet™ transition.
VDMM owns the methodological structure of the DeMonet™ mechanism itself.
Boundary with INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity of the records and evidence supporting the transition.
VDMM governs what those governed inputs establish about the movement of value into zero.
Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether the DeMonet™ transition and supporting records are observable, preserved, and reconstructable.
VDMM governs the transition itself.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Prior Positive Value Confirmation
Confirm that the affected value previously existed as positive value.
2. Threshold Input
Receive the applicable established Value Nullification Threshold from VNTM.
3. Affected Value Identification
Identify the exact value dimension, component, capability, or Value Context undergoing transition.
4. Transition Basis
Identify the governed basis supporting the DeMonet™ transition.
5. Transition Scope
Determine whether nullification is partial, dimensional, contextual, compound, or complete within the defined governed scope.
6. Transition Character

Determine whether the transition is progressive, immediate, deliberate, externally induced, temporary, or otherwise materially characterized.
7. Zero-Value Entry
Establish whether the affected value has entered the zero-value condition.
8. Transition Uncertainty
Preserve material uncertainty affecting the transition.
9. Transition State
Assign the appropriate DeMonet™ Transition State.
10. Transition Record
Create a traceable record connecting the prior positive value, threshold, transition, resulting zero-value condition, and downstream determination pathway.

VDMM may produce:
DeMonet™ Transition Record DeMonet™ Transition Identity Pre-Transition Value State Record Affected Value Dimension Record DeMonet™ Transition Basis DeMonet™ Transition Scope DeMonet™ Transition Characterization DeMonet™ Transition Timing Record DeMonet™ Transition Evidence Record DeMonet™ Transition Uncertainty Record Zero-Value Entry Record DeMonet™ Transition State Governed DeMonet™ Transition Object

Use Case 1 — Technology Loses Its Remaining
Operational Value
A company operates a specialized legacy technology that has gradually lost efficiency and compatibility.
For several years its operational value declines but remains positive because the technology still performs one critical production function.
The value therefore remains within:
Value Degradation.

A later infrastructure migration permanently removes the technical environment required for that function.
VNTM establishes that the applicable operational-value threshold has been reached.
VDMM then governs:
Existing Operational Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Operational Value = 0.
The technology may nevertheless retain:
resale value,
component value,
knowledge value,
or
historical value.
VDMM therefore records only the nullification of the relevant operational-value dimension.
The technology does not automatically become universally valueless, and its operational zero-value condition does not automatically establish Value Extinction.
Use Case 2 — Digital Capability Temporarily
Becomes Zero Value and Is Later Recoverable
A digital platform provides a specialized capability that creates continuous operational value.
A critical external dependency is terminated.
The capability becomes completely unavailable.
Its functional value within the governed operating context transitions from:
Positive Functional Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Functional Value = 0.
The underlying technology, data, configuration, and organizational capability still exist.
A replacement dependency may later restore the capability.
The resulting zero-value condition may therefore qualify as a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ while retaining restoration potential.
The subsequent lifecycle may become:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value.

If recovery eventually becomes impossible and the relevant value ceases to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle, that later condition belongs not to VDMM but to:
VXSS — Value Extinction Standard.
Enterprise Application
VDMM gives organizations a governed mechanism for identifying the precise transition at which value that genuinely existed stops being positive.
This is materially different from merely recording that an asset was written down, discontinued, abandoned, obsolete, impaired, unused, or economically unattractive.
The Module can support governance of:
physical assets; technologies; digital assets; intellectual property; licenses; contractual rights; infrastructure; organizational capabilities; products; services; data assets; AI systems; autonomous systems; operational capabilities.
Its principal enterprise value is the separation of:
value decline
from
value reaching zero
and of:
zero value
from
irrecoverable extinction.
Foundational Principles
DeMonet™ requires previously existing positive value.
Value that never emerged cannot undergo DeMonet™.
Value degradation is not DeMonet™ while positive value remains.
DeMonet™ governs transition, not external causation.
Threshold crossing and DeMonet™ are related but methodologically distinct.
DeMonet™ may be progressive or immediate.
DeMonet™ may be deliberate or externally induced.
DeMonet™ may affect one value dimension without eliminating others.
Contextual zero value is not universal zero value.

DeMonet™ does not automatically establish permanent loss.
DeMonet™ is not ZVA™.
DeMonet™ is not ReMonet™.
DeMonet™ is not Value Extinction.
A zero-value condition may retain restoration potential.
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
Canonical Closing Statement
DeMonet™ Mechanism Module establishes the canonical nullification-transition mechanism through which previously existing positive value crosses its governed zero-value boundary and enters a zero-value condition. By governing prior positive value, affected value dimensions, Value Context, transition basis, scope, timing, character, evidence, uncertainty, zero-value entry, and transition state, VDMM makes value nullification explicit and traceable without confusing degradation with zero value, external causation with value transition, or zero value with terminal extinction. DeMonet™ therefore provides VFM® with a distinct mechanism for representing the loss of existing positive value while preserving the possibility that other value dimensions remain positive and that a resulting ZVA™ may later recover through ReMonet™. The architectural boundary is fundamental: DeMonet™ establishes movement into zero value; it does not establish that recoverable value has ceased to exist.
