Canonical Definition
Zero-Value State Transition Module (VNZM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Nullification Standard (VNS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VNZM governs the formal transition of previously existing positive value, following a legitimate Value Nullification Determination, into its governed zero-value state representation.

The Module establishes when a completed nullification may be operationally recognized as a zero-value condition, what exact value dimension and scope have entered that condition, how the resulting state must be represented, and how continuity between the former positive-value state and the new zero-value state must be preserved.
Where applicable, the resulting governed object may be represented as:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
VNZM does not determine whether value has been nullified. That determination belongs to VNDM.
Its foundational function is:
to ensure that once Value Nullification has legitimately been determined, the resulting zero-value condition becomes an explicit, bounded, traceable, and lifecycle-continuous governed state rather than an ambiguous declaration that “the value is gone.”
Architectural Position
VNZM is the fifth and final module within VNS.
It follows:
VNDM — Value Nullification Determination Module.
The complete internal progression of VNS is:
Nullification Conditions
→ Nullification Threshold
→ DeMonet™ Mechanism
→ Nullification Determination
→ Zero-Value State Transition
VNZM therefore closes the Value Nullification process.
Its output creates the governed zero-value condition from which subsequent lifecycle governance can continue.
The distinction is fundamental:
Value Nullification Determination ≠ Zero-Value State Transition.
A determination establishes:
that nullification occurred.
VNZM establishes:

the governed state consequence of that determination.
Internal Module Flow
Positive Value State Record → Value Nullification Determination → Determination Scope Confirmation → Affected Value Dimension Confirmation
→ Zero-Value Condition Confirmation → Transition Eligibility Check → Previous Value State Closure → Zero-Value State Instantiation → Zero-Value Scope Assignment → Restoration Potential Preservation → Zero-Value State Record → ZVA™ Representation Where Applicable → Lifecycle Continuation
Operational Space
VNZM governs the point between:
formally determined Value Nullification
and
governed recognition of the resulting zero-value state.
Its operational space includes:
transition eligibility; determination linkage; previous-state identification; affected value identification; value-dimension identification; zero-value scope; zero-value context; transition timing; state continuity; partial zero-value states; dimensional zero-value states; temporary zero-value states; conditional zero-value states; restoration potential; zero-value state representation; ZVA™ representation; transition records; lifecycle continuity.
Transition Eligibility
A Value Object must not enter a governed zero-value state merely because:
its value has declined; its market price has fallen; it is unused; it has been written off; it is obsolete; it is temporarily inaccessible; management believes it has no value; an external classification labels it worthless.

VNZM requires an applicable governed basis from VNDM.
The minimum transition logic is:
Previously Existing Positive Value
→ Value Nullification Determination = Established
→ Zero-Value State Transition Eligible.
Without a legitimate nullification determination, VNZM must not manufacture a zero-value state.
Previous State Requirement
Every VNZM transition must identify the governed state from which the value transitioned.
This preserves lifecycle continuity.
For example:
Positive Operational Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Operational Value Nullification Determined
→ Zero Operational Value.
The zero-value state must therefore remain connected to its previous positive-value condition.
This enables later reconstruction of:
what value existed
what happened to it
when it reached zero
under what conditions
through what mechanism
and what state followed.
Zero-Value State Instantiation
VNZM creates an explicit governed zero-value state after the transition conditions have been satisfied.
The resulting state must identify, where materially applicable:
Value Object
Value Dimension
Value Context
Scope
Effective Time
Nullification Determination
Transition Basis
Restoration Potential
State Status
This prevents the statement:
“Value = 0”
from becoming detached from the conditions under which it is true.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
Where the governed object qualifies as an asset representation, VNZM may instantiate:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A ZVA™ represents:

an identifiable governed asset whose relevant previously existing positive value has reached a legitimate zero- value state while the asset remains identifiable within the governed lifecycle.
ZVA™ does not mean:
the object never had value.
It does not necessarily mean:
the object has ceased to exist.
It does not necessarily mean:
all value dimensions are zero.
And critically, it does not mean:
the value can never return.
Therefore:
ZVA™ ≠ Value Extinction.
Zero-Value State Is Governed
Zero value must be treated as a legitimate governed state rather than as the absence of governance.
This is architecturally important.
Traditional systems often govern assets while they possess value and effectively stop governing them once their value reaches zero.
VFM® preserves lifecycle continuity through zero.
Therefore:
Value Governance Does Not End at Zero.
A zero-value state may still require:
identification; ownership; responsibility; record continuity; monitoring; restoration assessment; legal treatment; operational treatment; disposition; reassessment; lifecycle decision.
Dimensional Zero-Value Transition
A Value Object may enter zero in one value dimension while retaining positive value elsewhere.
For example:
Operational Value → 0
while:
Economic Value > 0
Strategic Value > 0
Knowledge Value > 0.
VNZM must therefore permit:
Dimensional Zero-Value State Transition.
It must not convert:
Zero Value in Dimension A
into:
Zero Total Value
without a governed basis.

Partial Zero-Value Transition
A composite Value Object may contain multiple value-bearing components.
VNZM may transition only the affected component into zero value.
Example:
A software platform contains ten commercially relevant capabilities.
One capability becomes permanently unusable under the current architecture.
The governed transition may be:
Capability C7 Value → 0
while the remaining capabilities retain positive value.
Therefore:
Partial Nullification → Partial Zero-Value State
rather than:
Entire Object → Zero Value.
Contextual Zero-Value Transition
Value may become zero within one context but remain positive in another.
Examples include:
Market A = Zero Economic Value
while:
Market B = Positive Economic Value.
Or:
Configuration A = Zero Operational Value
while:
Configuration B = Positive Operational Value.
VNZM must preserve the context in the resulting state.
Therefore:
Contextual Zero ≠ Universal Zero.
Temporary Zero-Value State
VNZM permits a legitimate zero-value state to be temporary.
A temporary zero-value condition may exist where:
capability is suspended; access is unavailable; marketability temporarily disappears; a necessary dependency fails; infrastructure becomes unavailable; legal use is temporarily prohibited; functionality is temporarily impossible; external conditions remove current value.
If the applicable threshold has genuinely been reached, the state may legitimately be:
Value = 0
even where future restoration remains possible.

Conditional Zero-Value State
A zero-value state may depend upon defined conditions.
Example:
Operational Value = 0 while Critical Dependency D is unavailable.
If Dependency D returns, the state may require reassessment or restoration governance.
The zero-value state must therefore retain the conditions upon which it depends.
Zero Value ≠ Unknown Value
VNZM must never use zero as a substitute for uncertainty.
Where value cannot be determined:
Value State = Unknown / Indeterminate
not:
Value State = Zero.
This boundary is essential for analytical, accounting, AI, automated decision, and data environments where missing values are frequently encoded numerically as zero.
Therefore:
Missing Value ≠ Zero Value.
Unknown Value ≠ Zero Value.
Unmeasured Value ≠ Zero Value.
Zero Value ≠ Negligible Value
An extremely small positive value remains positive unless the applicable governed threshold establishes otherwise.
Therefore:
Negligible Value ≠ Automatically Zero Value.
VNZM accepts the zero-value state only after the applicable VNS governance process establishes that the relevant threshold has been crossed.
Zero Value ≠ Dormancy
A dormant asset may currently generate no observable value while retaining latent positive value.
Examples may include:
unused intellectual property; inactive licenses; archived datasets; dormant land rights; inactive capabilities; reserve infrastructure.
Dormancy alone does not establish zero value.
VNZM must distinguish:
No Current Activity
from:

No Current Value.
Zero Value ≠ Destruction
Physical destruction does not automatically create zero value.
A destroyed physical object may retain:
insurance value; salvage value; claim value; intellectual property value; recycling value; evidential value; replacement rights.
Likewise, a physically intact object may have zero value in a particular governed dimension.
Therefore:
Physical State ≠ Value State.
Zero Value ≠ Accounting Zero
An accounting carrying value of zero may be relevant to VNZM but does not automatically establish the governed VFM® zero-value state.
Accounting may answer:
What value is recognized under this accounting methodology?
VNZM answers:
What governed value state follows from the VFM® Value Nullification process?
These may coincide.
They need not.
Zero Value ≠ Market Price Zero
A market price of zero does not automatically establish total zero value.
A non-tradable asset may retain substantial:
operational; strategic; knowledge; option; restoration; internal-use
value.
VNZM therefore binds zero to the exact governed value dimension.
Restoration Potential Preservation
VNZM must preserve whether the zero-value state retains a plausible governed pathway to restoration.
This creates a critical lifecycle distinction between:
Zero Value with Restoration Potential
and
Value Extinction.
Restoration potential may depend upon:

repair; technological change; new market conditions; regulatory change; renewed access; new infrastructure; reconfiguration; new demand; reactivation; new use; rights restoration; capability restoration.
The presence of restoration potential does not mean restoration will occur.
It means extinction has not yet been established.
Zero-Value State Classes
VNZM may support governed zero-value state classes such as:
1. Current Zero Value
The relevant value is presently zero.
2. Temporary Zero Value
Zero value exists for a bounded or potentially reversible period.
3. Conditional Zero Value
Zero value exists while specified conditions remain true.
4. Partial Zero Value
Only a defined component or portion of value is zero.
5. Dimensional Zero Value
One value dimension is zero while others remain positive.
6. Contextual Zero Value
Value is zero within a defined jurisdiction, market, configuration, environment, or other Value Context.
7. Persistent Zero Value
The zero-value condition has persisted over a materially relevant period without yet satisfying Value Extinction conditions.
These classifications may coexist where appropriate.
Zero-Value State Record
Every governed transition should create a Zero-Value State Record.
The record may contain:

Value Object identity; prior Value State; affected value dimension; Value Context; nullification determination reference; DeMonet™ transition reference; zero-value threshold basis; effective transition time; zero-value classification; scope; conditions; restoration potential; monitoring requirement;
reassessment trigger; lifecycle status.
This provides continuity between past positive value and future lifecycle developments.
State Continuity Principle
A zero-value state must not erase its history.
The lifecycle should remain reconstructable as:
Positive Value
→ Value Change / Degradation
→ Nullification Conditions
→ Nullification Threshold
→ DeMonet™
→ Nullification Determination
→ Zero-Value State
→ Future Lifecycle Outcome.
The future outcome may include:
continued zero value
ReMonet™ restoration
or, where independently established:
Value Extinction.
Zero-Value Monitoring
Where materially relevant, a zero-value state may remain subject to monitoring.
Monitoring may identify:
restoration opportunities; changed conditions; renewed demand; technological developments; rights changes; market changes; operational reactivation; continuing deterioration; extinction conditions.
VNZM does not govern the entire monitoring architecture.
It ensures that the zero-value state can remain visible to subsequent lifecycle governance.
Reassessment Trigger
A zero-value state may require reassessment when material conditions change.
Possible triggers include:

new evidence of positive value; restoration activity; changed market conditions; changed legal conditions; new technology; object reconfiguration; dependency restoration; new operational use; changed ownership; new demand; corrected historical information.
The zero-value state should therefore remain capable of transition rather than becoming an irreversible data label.
Boundary with VNDM
VNDM determines:
whether Value Nullification has legitimately occurred.
VNZM governs:
the resulting transition into a zero-value state.
Therefore:
Determination ≠ State Transition.
Boundary with VSS
VSS governs:
the current governed Value State.
VNZM governs:
the specific transition through which a nullified value enters a zero-value state.
Once completed, the resulting state can be represented within VSS.
Therefore:
VNZM creates the transition consequence.
VSS governs the resulting current state.
Boundary with VDGS
VDGS governs declining value while positive value remains.
VNZM begins only after positive value has reached the governed zero-value condition.
Therefore:
Degradation → Positive Value Remains
Nullification Transition → Zero Value Reached.
Boundary with VRSS
VRSS governs the restoration of impaired, dormant, lost, or zero value.
A zero-value state established through VNZM may subsequently become an input into:
ReMonet™
where legitimate restoration conditions arise.
Therefore:
Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value
is a valid future lifecycle pathway.
Boundary with VXSS

VXSS governs:
Value Extinction.
VNZM governs:
Zero-Value State Transition.
The distinction is absolute:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
A ZVA™ may remain identifiable, governed, monitorable, and potentially restorable.
Value Extinction requires an independent governed determination that the relevant value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ may establish the operational reality that contributed to a zero-value condition.
VNZM governs the resulting value-state transition.
Therefore:
Operational Reality Change ≠ Zero-Value State Transition.
Boundary with VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may validate claims, evidence, methods, or determinations supporting the transition.
VNZM owns the VFM® transition into the governed zero-value state.
Boundary with INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of the information, records, and evidence supporting the state transition.
VNZM governs the meaning of that transition within the value lifecycle.
Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether the transition basis and records are observable and reconstructable.
VNZM owns the Zero-Value State Transition itself.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Nullification Determination Input
Receive the applicable governed Value Nullification Determination.
2. Previous Value State Confirmation
Identify the positive-value state preceding nullification.

Becomes Operationally Worthless but Remains
Recoverable

while preventing the unsupported conclusion:

and preserves:

affected value dimension
dependency condition
transition time
nullification basis

Enterprise Application
VNZM provides organizations with a formal method for governing assets, capabilities, rights, technologies, data, systems, products, services, infrastructure, and other Value Objects after their relevant value reaches zero.
This solves an important lifecycle problem.
Many organizational systems are optimized to track:
acquisition
creation
growth
depreciation
and
disposal
but do not maintain a rigorous distinction between:
zero current value
temporary loss of value
dormancy
recoverable zero value
and
terminal extinction of value.
VNZM creates that missing state-transition layer.
It allows organizations to preserve zero-value objects for:

restoration analysis; reactivation; repurposing; technology recovery; market recovery; rights recovery; strategic optionality; lifecycle analysis; asset governance; AI-driven value analysis.
This becomes particularly important in dynamic technological environments where something that has zero value today may acquire substantial value again after a change in technology, market structure, regulation, infrastructure, demand, or operational context.
Foundational Principles
Zero value is a governed state, not the absence of governance.
A Zero-Value State Transition requires a legitimate Value Nullification Determination.
Value Nullification Determination and Zero-Value State Transition are distinct governance acts.
Zero in one dimension does not mean zero in every dimension.
Zero in one context does not mean zero everywhere.
Partial zero value does not establish total zero value.
Temporary zero value can be a legitimate zero-value state.
Conditional zero value must retain its conditions.
Unknown value is not zero value.
Missing value is not zero value.
Dormancy is not automatically zero value.
Accounting zero is not automatically governed zero value.
Market price zero is not automatically total value zero.
Physical destruction and value nullification are not equivalent.
A ZVA™ may retain restoration potential.
A zero-value state must preserve its previous value history.
Value governance does not end when value reaches zero.
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.

Canonical Closing Statement
Zero-Value State Transition Module establishes the final transition layer of the Value Nullification Standard by converting a legitimately determined Value Nullification into an explicit, bounded, contextual, dimensional, traceable, and lifecycle-continuous zero-value state. Through governance of transition eligibility, previous-state continuity, zero-value scope, dimensional and contextual boundaries, temporary and conditional states, restoration potential, ZVA™ representation, state records, reassessment triggers, and lifecycle continuity, VNZM prevents zero value from being confused with unknown value, dormancy, accounting write-off, physical destruction, universal worthlessness, or Value Extinction. The Module ensures that value remains governable even after it reaches zero and preserves the methodological pathway through which a zero-value condition may subsequently remain zero, undergo ReMonet™ restoration, or proceed—only through a separate governed determination—toward Value Extinction. Zero is therefore not the end of value governance; it is a distinct governed state within the value lifecycle.

Canonical Definition
Value Nullification Standard (VNS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and governed transitions through which previously existing positive value reaches a legitimate zero-value condition.
VNS establishes the methodological boundary between declining value and nullified value.
The Standard governs the point at which value no longer merely weakens, deteriorates, loses utility, becomes impaired, or approaches zero, but crosses a defined value boundary through which the relevant positive value ceases to exist within its governed Value Context.

VNS is the architectural home of DeMonet™, the governed value-nullification mechanism through which existing positive value may transition toward a zero-value condition where the applicable nullification conditions and thresholds are satisfied.
The Standard also establishes the governed relationship between a determined zero-value condition and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™, while preserving the critical distinction between value that previously existed and was subsequently nullified, value that temporarily reaches zero, value that permanently reaches zero, and potential value that never emerged.
Its foundational principle is:
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified.
Core Question
When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition?
Architectural Position
VNS occupies the ninth governed space within the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value Degradation Standard (VDGS)
and precedes:
Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
The preceding VFM® lifecycle has already governed:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Value State
→ Value Change
→ Value Development
→ Value Degradation
VNS governs the next critical boundary:
when existing positive value ceases to remain positive.
The architectural transition is:
Positive Value
→ Nullification Conditions
→ Nullification Threshold
→ DeMonet™
→ Value Nullification Determination
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable

VNS therefore governs a boundary transition, not merely another degree of degradation.
VFM® Governance Flow Position
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → subsequent VFM® lifecycle spaces
Within the Value Nullification governed space:
Existing Positive Value → Nullification Condition → Nullification Threshold → DeMonet™ Mechanism → Nullification Determination → Zero-Value State Transition
The output of VNS may subsequently enter:
Value State Governance
or, where restoration becomes possible:
Value Restoration Governance.
Operational Space
VNS governs the transition between:
positive existing value
and
a governed zero-value condition.
Its operational space includes:
nullification-condition identification; zero-value boundary definition; nullification-threshold establishment; threshold crossing; deliberate value withdrawal; degradation-to-zero; functional exhaustion; contextual nullification; temporal nullification; permanent nullification; partial or dimension-specific nullification; DeMonet™ mechanism governance; nullification determination; zero-value transition; ZVA™ state relationship; nullification provenance; distinction between nullification and non-emergence; distinction between zero value and negative consequences; restoration eligibility interface.
Value Nullification Principle
Value Nullification occurs only where:

positive value previously existed
and
that value subsequently reaches a governed zero-value condition.
This creates the minimum logical sequence:
Positive Value existed at T₁
→ material value change occurred
→ the applicable zero-value boundary was reached at T₂
→ Value Nullification may be determined.
Without previously existing value, there is nothing to nullify.
Therefore:
Potential Value that never emerged cannot be nullified.
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified
This distinction is foundational to VNS.
Consider two assets.
Asset A
has potential commercial utility but never becomes operational, usable, recognized, or otherwise value-producing within the relevant Value Context.
Its potential value never emerges.
Asset B
has established operational value for ten years and subsequently becomes completely unusable within the same governed Value Context.
Asset B may undergo Value Nullification.
Asset A does not.
Therefore:
Non-Emergence
and
Nullification
represent fundamentally different value histories.
VFM® must preserve that distinction.
Degradation ≠ Nullification
Value Degradation governs declining value while positive value remains.
Value Nullification begins only where the relevant governed positive value reaches zero.
Therefore:
100 → 70 → 40 → 10
remains within Value Degradation.
The transition:
10 → 0
may enter Value Nullification.
The architectural boundary is:
Positive Value > 0
versus
Zero Value = 0

where the applicable value methodology permits quantitative expression.
Where value is qualitative rather than numerical, an equivalent governed threshold must establish when positive value ceases to exist.
Approaching Zero ≠ Zero
Severe degradation does not automatically establish nullification.
An asset may retain:
residual utility; residual knowledge; residual strategic significance; salvage value; recovery potential; operational capability; contextual usefulness; option value; informational value; another legitimate positive value dimension.
Therefore:
Near-Zero Value ≠ Zero Value.
VNS requires the zero-value condition to be determined, not presumed from severity.
Nullification Condition
A Value Nullification Condition is a governed condition under which existing positive value may legitimately become eligible for nullification determination.
Possible conditions may include:
complete loss of relevant utility; total functional failure; complete contextual irrelevance; expiry of time-dependent value; exhaustion of usable value; irreversible obsolescence within the defined context; deliberate withdrawal of a value-conferring capability; destruction of the relevant value-bearing property; complete loss of accessibility where accessibility constitutes the governed value; termination of a value-conferring relationship; another defined condition capable of eliminating the relevant positive value.
The presence of a condition does not automatically establish nullification.

The applicable threshold must also be satisfied.
Nullification Threshold
The Value Nullification Threshold establishes the boundary at which the governed value dimension ceases to remain positive.
The threshold may be:
quantitative; qualitative; functional; temporal; contextual; contractual; operational; technological; structural; capability-based.
The threshold must correspond to the defined Value Context.
A universal zero-value threshold cannot be assumed across all forms of value.
Threshold Crossing Principle
A nullification threshold must be distinguished from proximity to that threshold.
For example:
Minimum Operational Capability = 5 units
An asset operating at:
6 units
may be critically degraded.
But if the governed value remains positive above 5 units, nullification has not yet occurred.
Only when the applicable threshold is crossed or satisfied may a Value Nullification Determination become possible.
DeMonet™
DeMonet™ is the canonical VFM® mechanism governing the transition through which previously existing positive value is nullified into a governed zero-value condition.
The canonical transition is:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable
DeMonet™ is not merely another word for:
depreciation;
deterioration; financial loss; market decline; destruction; impairment; write-down; devaluation; obsolescence.
Those events or mechanisms may contribute to nullification.
DeMonet™ governs the value transition itself.

DeMonet™ ≠ Cause of Nullification
The external cause of nullification may originate outside VFM®.
Examples include:
technological change; physical destruction; market collapse; regulatory prohibition; contract expiry; loss of access; infrastructure failure; organizational decision; scientific discovery; replacement technology; environmental change; deliberate withdrawal; another external event.
VFM® does not need to own those causal systems.
Its question is:
What happened to the governed value as a result?
DeMonet™ therefore governs the value-nullification mechanism, not necessarily the external causal mechanism.
DeMonet™ ≠ Value Degradation
DeMonet™ must not be applied to every reduction in value.
If value changes:
100 → 80
or
80 → 20
positive value remains.
That remains a Value Change and potentially Value Degradation.
DeMonet™ becomes relevant when the governed transition concerns:
Positive Value → Zero Value.
This preserves the architectural separation between:
VDGS — Value Degradation
and
VNS — Value Nullification.
Deliberate Value Withdrawal
Value Nullification may occur intentionally.
An organization may deliberately withdraw or eliminate an existing value-conferring property.
Examples may include:
disabling a capability; terminating access; retiring a service; revoking a functional entitlement; withdrawing interoperability; destroying a value-bearing asset; intentionally eliminating commercial availability; permanently decommissioning an operational function.

Where such action legitimately produces a zero-value condition within the governed Value Context, VNS may govern the resulting nullification.
Therefore:
Value Nullification does not require accidental loss.
Degradation-to-Zero
One pathway into VNS is progressive degradation.
Example:
100
→ 75
→ 43
→ 18
→ 4
→ 0
The stages above zero remain governed as degradation.
The final boundary transition into zero is governed through VNS.
This creates the interface:
VDGS
→ VNS
without collapsing the two standards into one another.
Immediate Nullification
Value does not always decline progressively.
A single event may cause:
Positive Value → Zero Value
without an extended degradation phase.
Examples may include:
total destruction; immediate loss of essential functionality; instantaneous expiry; irreversible access termination; sudden contextual invalidation.
VNS therefore does not require prior progressive degradation.
It requires only that:
positive value previously existed
and
a governed zero-value condition subsequently occurred.
Temporary Zero Value
A zero-value condition may be temporary.
Example:
A production asset loses all operational value because a critical component fails.
At that moment:
Operational Value = Zero.
The asset may nevertheless remain repairable.
After restoration:
Zero Operational Value → Restored Positive Operational Value.
VNS therefore distinguishes:
Temporary Zero Value
from
Permanent Zero Value.

Temporary zero remains genuine zero within the applicable context and period.
Its potential reversibility does not mean the zero-value state never existed.
Permanent Zero Value
A zero-value condition may also be effectively permanent within the defined governance context.
Examples may include:
irreversible destruction; complete expiration of time-bound value; permanent loss of required capability; permanent contextual displacement; irrecoverable elimination of the relevant value-bearing property.
Permanent zero must nevertheless remain context-specific.
An object may have zero operational value while retaining:
historical value; informational value; material recovery value; legal relevance; evidence value; research value.
Therefore:
Permanent Zero in one Value Context ≠ Universal Absence of All Value.
Contextual Nullification
Value may be nullified in one context while remaining positive in another.
Example:
A machine may have:
Operational Production Value = 0
while retaining:
Salvage Value > 0
and
Historical Evidence Value > 0.
VNS therefore does not permit the statement:
“This object has zero value.”
unless the relevant Value Context and value dimension justify that statement.
The governed formulation is:
“The relevant value has reached zero within the defined Value Context.”
Dimension-Specific Nullification
A Value Object may contain multiple simultaneous value dimensions.
For example:
Economic Value
Operational Value
Strategic Value
Knowledge Value
Utility Value

Cultural Value
Recovery Value
One dimension may reach zero while others remain positive.
Therefore:
Nullification of Value Dimension A ≠ Nullification of the entire Value Object.
VNS must preserve dimension-specific nullification where materially relevant.
Zero-Value Condition
A Zero-Value Condition is the governed condition in which the relevant previously existing positive value no longer remains positive within its defined Value Context.
A Zero-Value Condition does not automatically establish:
destruction of the object; absence of every possible value dimension; illegality; lack of ownership; lack of market price; accounting write-off; tax treatment; invalidity; permanent irrecoverability.
It establishes one specific proposition:
the governed value represented by the determination has reached zero.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represents a governed zero-value state where applicable within VFM®.
A Value Object may enter a ZVA™ state when the applicable value dimension or governed value basis has legitimately reached zero through a recognized VFM® lifecycle pathway.
VNS provides one principal pathway:
Existing Positive Value
→ Value Nullification
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™.
But the existence of a ZVA™ designation must remain attached to its Value Context.
ZVA™ must not become an uncontrolled statement that the object possesses no conceivable value whatsoever.
Zero Value ≠ Nonexistence

An object may continue to exist after its governed value reaches zero.
Therefore:
Object Existence ≠ Value Existence.
A physical asset can remain physically present while its relevant operational value is zero.
A digital asset can continue to exist in storage while its governed utility value is zero.
A contractual right can remain documented while its time-dependent economic value has expired.
VNS governs value nullification, not object annihilation.
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value
Zero value and negative value are distinct states.
A zero-value asset may create:
disposal costs; liabilities; maintenance costs; environmental burdens; legal exposure; operational risk.
These negative consequences do not mean that zero value was incorrectly determined.
They may represent another governed value or liability dimension.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value.
VNS must not collapse positive value, zero value, cost, liability, and negative externality into one concept.
Nullification Determination
A Value Nullification Determination establishes that the applicable governed value has legitimately reached the defined zero-value condition.
A defensible determination should establish, where materially relevant:

the Value Object; the Value Context; the value dimension; evidence that positive value previously existed; the relevant prior Value State; the nullification condition; the applicable nullification threshold; whether the threshold was reached; the DeMonet™ mechanism basis; temporal point or interval of nullification; uncertainty; reversibility status where known; whether zero is temporary, persistent, or permanent; the resulting zero-value state.
The determination must remain distinguishable from the event that caused the value loss.
Nullification Time
VNS recognizes that the time of nullification may be materially important.
Relevant temporal states may include:
T₀ — Positive Value
→ T₁ — Degradation or Nullification Event
→ T₂ — Threshold Reached
→ T₃ — Nullification Determined
→ T₄ — Zero-Value State Recorded
These moments may be identical.
They may also differ.
For example, an asset may have actually lost all relevant value before an organization formally identifies or determines that the zero-value threshold was crossed.
Therefore:
Time of Nullification ≠ Time of Discovery ≠ Time of Determination.
Nullification Reversibility
VNS must preserve whether the zero-value state is potentially reversible.
A nullified value may be:
Restorable
Conditionally Restorable
Restoration Unknown
Non-Restorable within the defined context.
This classification does not itself restore value.
It establishes the interface to:
Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
VNS → VRSS Interface

VNS establishes:
the legitimate arrival at zero.
VRSS governs:
the legitimate recovery from impaired, dormant, lost, or zero value.
The interface may therefore be:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Positive Value
→ New Value State.
This creates a governed reversible lifecycle where restoration remains possible.
However:
DeMonet™ does not guarantee ReMonet™.
A value may be nullified without ever being restored.
Restoration Potential ≠ Existing Value
An object at zero value may possess restoration potential.
That potential must not be confused with currently existing positive value.
For example:
A damaged machine may have:
Current Operational Value = 0
while possessing:
high restoration potential.
Therefore:
Restoration Potential ≠ Restored Value.
This distinction prevents anticipated future recovery from erasing the legitimacy of a current ZVA™ state.
Nullification Provenance
A governed Value Nullification Determination should remain traceable to the lifecycle from which it arose.
The chain may include:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Prior Value State
→ Value Change
→ Value Degradation where applicable
→ Nullification Condition
→ Threshold
→ DeMonet™
→ Nullification Determination
→ Zero-Value State.
This allows systems to distinguish a genuinely nullified value from a value that never existed.
Nullification Record Continuity

The transition to zero must not erase the preceding positive-value history.
If an asset moves:
100 → 70 → 30 → 0
its record must not simply become:
Current Value = 0.
The lifecycle must remain capable of showing:
positive value existed
→ value changed
→ value degraded
→ the zero boundary was crossed
→ nullification occurred.
This historical continuity becomes especially important if restoration later occurs.
Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VNS ↔ VES
VES governs the emergence of value.
VNS governs the nullification of previously existing value.
Therefore:
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified.
VNS ↔ VRS
Recognition does not create nullification.
A value may cease to be recognized while still existing.
Likewise, a recognized value may subsequently be nullified.
Therefore:
Loss of Recognition ≠ Value Nullification.
VNS ↔ VSS
VSS governs the current Value State.
VNS governs the transition through which positive value reaches zero.
After nullification, VSS may identify the resulting state as:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
where applicable.
Therefore:
Transition ≠ State.
VNS ↔ VCS
VCS governs material change to existing value.
VNS governs the specific boundary transition in which existing positive value reaches zero.
Every nullification involves a value transition.
Not every Value Change is a nullification.
VNS ↔ VDS
VDS governs development of existing positive value.
VNS governs its nullification.

The two may occur at different points within the same lifecycle but must remain methodologically distinct.
VNS ↔ VDGS
VDGS governs deterioration while positive value remains.
VNS governs crossing into zero.
Therefore:
Declining Positive Value ≠ Nullified Value.
VNS ↔ VRSS
VNS governs:
Positive Value → Zero Value.
VRSS governs legitimate restoration from degraded, dormant, lost, or zero value toward restored positive value.
Therefore:
Nullification ≠ Restoration
and
Restoration Potential ≠ Existing Positive Value.
VNS ↔ ORA™
ORA™ may govern the operational reality in which events affecting value occur.
VNS governs what those events mean for the relevant value transition.
Operational Event ≠ Value Nullification Determination.
VNS ↔ VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may validate evidence, claims, determinations, methods, or other Validation Objects associated with a nullification determination.
VNS owns the value-nullification governance logic.
Validation of a determination ≠ ownership of the value-nullification space.
VNS ↔ INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties associated with value records, evidence, states, and transitions.
VNS governs whether the value has crossed the nullification boundary.
VNS ↔ ADIT®
ADIT® may audit evidence concerning the value history, threshold crossing, determination, and resulting state.
VNS governs the meaning of the value-nullification transition itself.
Governance Outputs
Implementation of VNS may produce:

Value Nullification Condition Record Value Nullification Threshold Value Nullification Threshold Status DeMonet™ Transition Record Value Nullification Determination Zero-Value Condition Record Value Nullification Time Record Value Nullification Context Record Value Dimension Nullification Record Temporary Zero-Value Determination Permanent Zero-Value Determination Nullification Reversibility Status ZVA™ State Transition Record Value Nullification Provenance Chain Value Restoration Eligibility Interface
These outputs provide the governed basis for subsequent Value State, Value Restoration, audit, validation, and broader lifecycle processes.
Enterprise Application
VNS enables organizations to answer a deceptively difficult question:
When has something actually lost its value rather than merely lost some of its value?
This distinction matters across:
physical assets; infrastructure; technology; software; intellectual property; knowledge assets; digital assets; organizational capabilities; contractual rights; licenses; data assets; operational systems; financial structures; AI systems; industrial equipment; inventory; platforms; services.
Without an explicit nullification architecture, organizations may incorrectly treat:
severe degradation as zero value,
temporary inactivity as permanent loss,
loss of recognition as loss of value,
never-realized potential as destroyed value,
or
zero value in one dimension as zero value everywhere.

VNS creates the governance structure necessary to separate these states.
Foundational Principles
Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified.
Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification.
Approaching zero is not zero.
Positive Value → Zero Value is a governed boundary transition.
DeMonet™ governs value nullification, not every decline in value.
DeMonet™ ≠ the external cause of value loss.
Nullification may be progressive or immediate.
Nullification may be deliberate or externally caused.
Temporary Zero Value ≠ Permanent Zero Value.
Zero value in one Value Context ≠ absence of all possible value.
Nullification of one value dimension ≠ nullification of the entire Value Object.
Zero Value ≠ Object Nonexistence.
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value.
Restoration potential is not currently existing positive value.
A ZVA™ state may be reversible without ceasing to be a legitimate zero-value state while it exists.
A governed zero-value state must preserve the history of the positive value from which it originated.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Nullification Standard establishes the zero-boundary governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by governing the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and transitions through which previously existing positive value legitimately reaches a zero-value condition. Through explicit separation of degradation from nullification, non-emergence from value loss, threshold proximity from threshold crossing, temporary zero from permanent zero, contextual nullification from universal absence of value, zero value from negative value, and object existence from value existence, VNS prevents materially different value states from being collapsed into a single concept of “lost value.” By establishing DeMonet™ as the governed mechanism of value nullification and defining the transition from Positive Value through a legitimate Zero-Value Condition toward ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable, VNS creates the architectural boundary at which existing positive value ceases while preserving its lifecycle provenance, Value Context, temporal history, dimensional meaning, reversibility, and potential interface with subsequent Value Restoration governance. Value may decline without disappearing, an object may remain while its relevant value reaches zero, and potential value may fail to emerge without ever being nullified; only where previously existing positive value legitimately crosses its governed zero-value boundary does Value Nullification occur.
Nahlad

About Value Origin Standard (VOS)
About Value Origin Standard (VOS)
About Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Governed Space: Value Origin
Canonical Definition
Value Origin Standard (VOS) governs how the identifiable source, basis, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other foundation from which value may emerge is identified, structured, related to the governed value context, and documented.
The Standard establishes the methodological starting point for understanding where value comes from before determining whether value has actually emerged.
Its central distinction is:
Value Source ≠ Existing Value
A resource, capability, asset, technology, relationship, right, activity, infrastructure, dataset, invention, natural resource, human capability, or other source may possess the potential to generate value while the corresponding value has not yet come into existence.
VOS makes that origin governable.
Why Value Origin Matters
Value is frequently measured, priced, exchanged, taxed, invested, depreciated, impaired, restored, or reported without a structured methodology for identifying its underlying origin.
This can create a fundamental analytical problem:
the observable value may be known while the mechanism from which that value originates remains poorly understood.

VOS establishes the value-origin layer before later VFM® standards govern emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction.
It allows an organization to ask:
What is capable of producing this value?
What is the underlying basis of that capability?
Under which conditions can that source generate value?
What relationship exists between the source and the governed value?
Has value already emerged, or does only value potential currently exist?
Value Source Before Value Emergence
VOS separates three concepts that should not be treated as equivalent:
Source of Value
Potential for Value
Existing Value
A source may exist without producing value.
A source may possess value-generating potential without that potential being realized.
Value may emerge only when the relevant conditions, relationships, capabilities, activities, or other mechanisms become effective.
This distinction creates a clear architectural boundary between:
Value Origin Standard
and the subsequent:
Value Emergence Standard.
VOS identifies where value can come from.
Value Emergence Standard determines when value actually comes into existence.
Origin Asset™
Origin Asset™ operates as a foundational value-origin concept within this governed space.

An Origin Asset™ may represent an identifiable asset, capability, resource, condition, relationship, knowledge base, technology, infrastructure, right, process, or other foundation capable of contributing to the emergence of value.
However:
Origin Asset™ ≠ Existing Value
The existence of an Origin Asset™ does not itself prove that value has emerged.
This distinction allows dormant, unused, undeveloped, inaccessible, unactivated, or unrealized value sources to remain identifiable without artificially treating their potential value as already realized value.
What VOS Governs
VOS provides the methodological structure for identifying:
the source from which governed value may originate; the basis upon which that source possesses value-generating potential; the relationship between the source and the governed value; the conditions necessary for value to originate from that source; multiple sources contributing to one form of value; one source contributing to multiple forms of value; direct and indirect value origins; dormant or unrealized value sources; changes affecting the ability of a source to generate value; documentation of the value-origin relationship.
The Standard does not determine the price of the source or the value that may eventually emerge from it.
It establishes the origin structure from which subsequent value governance can proceed.
Why This Is Different From Asset Identification

VOS does not attempt to become an identity, ownership, accounting, property, or asset-classification standard.
An underlying object may be identified through another governance architecture.
VFM® asks a different question:
What role does this object, capability, activity, relationship, or condition play in the origin of the governed value?
Therefore:
Object Identity ≠ Value Origin
Asset Ownership ≠ Value Origin
Asset Price ≠ Value Origin
Value Source ≠ Existing Value
This separation allows VFM® to examine value across physical, digital, financial, organizational, technological, environmental, intellectual, social, and future value environments without depending upon one particular asset model.
Practical Value
Value Origin Standard can help organizations move beyond observing value only after it has already become economically visible.
By identifying value sources earlier, organizations may better understand:
where value-generating capacity exists; which capabilities remain underutilized; which dependencies support existing value; which sources contribute disproportionately to value creation; where dormant value potential exists; which source conditions must be preserved; where loss of a source could later cause value degradation; where investment may activate previously unrealized value potential.

This makes Value Origin governance relevant not only to economic analysis but also to strategic planning, infrastructure, technology, public administration, banking, investment, industry, digital assets, and emerging economic systems.
Use Case 1 — Banking and Financial
Infrastructure
A financial institution possesses extensive infrastructure including transaction networks, customer relationships, data, risk models, distribution channels, specialized expertise, technology, licenses, operational capabilities, and institutional relationships.
Traditional financial reporting may assign values to some of these elements while others remain difficult to represent as direct economic value.
VOS begins with a different question:
Which identifiable sources actually generate or enable the value being governed?
The institution can map a particular form of value back to its underlying sources and distinguish between:
an asset that exists
and
a source that is actively capable of generating value.
This can expose dormant capabilities, critical value dependencies, underutilized infrastructure, and sources whose deterioration could threaten future value.
VOS therefore creates a methodological basis for understanding where economic value originates before that value is priced, exchanged, impaired, restored, or otherwise transformed.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission and Advanced
Infrastructure
A space organization develops a reusable launch system.

The program contains enormous potential sources of value:
engineering knowledge, propulsion technology, launch infrastructure, simulation capability, manufacturing processes, reusable components, mission data, intellectual capability, operational experience, and future launch capacity.
Not every source has yet produced realized economic or operational value.
VOS allows these sources to be identified without prematurely declaring their potential value to be existing value.
For example, a new reusable propulsion capability may represent a significant Value Source because it could reduce future launch costs, increase launch frequency, extend mission capability, or enable entirely new missions.
But until the relevant conditions exist and the capability produces a governed value outcome:
Value Potential ≠ Emerged Value
This distinction allows organizations to map future value-generating capacity while preserving methodological discipline between what could create value and what value actually exists.
Relationship to the VFM® Lifecycle
Value Origin Standard occupies the second governed space of VFM®, following Value Context Standard.
The sequence begins:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence
Value Context Standard establishes:
what value is being governed.
Value Origin Standard establishes:
where that value can originate.
Value Emergence Standard subsequently establishes:
when that value actually comes into existence.

This sequence prevents value potential, value source, and existing value from being collapsed into a single concept.
Foundational Principles
Value must be identified before its origin can be meaningfully governed.
A value source may exist before value emerges.
Value-generating potential is not the same as existing value.
An Origin Asset™ may exist without having produced value.
One value may originate from multiple sources.
One source may contribute to multiple forms of value.
The source of value must remain distinguishable from the systems that price, exchange, own, classify, validate, tax, or account for it.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Origin Standard establishes the origin layer of the governed value lifecycle by identifying the sources, bases, capabilities, conditions, activities, relationships, objects, and other foundations from which value may emerge. By separating Value Source, Value Potential, and Existing Value, the Standard enables value-generating capacity to be identified before value becomes economically, operationally, or institutionally visible. Value Origin Standard therefore provides the methodological foundation required to trace governed value back to its origin while preserving the fundamental principle that the existence of a value source does not itself establish the existence of value.

Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM)
Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM)
Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism
Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Module: VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module
Operational Layer: Value Origin Conditions Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Value Origin Conditions
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 23 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS).
VOCM governs the conditions that must exist, remain satisfied, become activated, or interact for an established Value Source, Value Source Basis, and Value Origin Relationship to provide a legitimate pathway toward the emergence of the governed value.
The Module establishes the conditions under which a potential value-origin relationship becomes capable of producing or enabling value.
VOCM does not determine that value has already emerged.
It establishes whether the necessary origin conditions exist for the value-origin pathway to operate.
The distinction is fundamental:
Value Source ≠ Value Source Basis ≠ Value Origin Relationship ≠ Value Origin Conditions ≠ Existing Value

Architectural Position
VOCM is the fourth module within the Value Origin Standard.
It follows:
VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module
and precedes:
VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module.
The internal sequence is:
Identified Value Source → Established Value Source Basis → Established Value Origin Relationship → Origin Condition Identification → Condition Classification → Condition Dependency Assessment → Condition State Assessment
→ Origin Readiness
→ Value Origin Conditions Record → VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module
The first three modules establish:
Where can value originate?
What about that source can contribute to value?
How is that basis related to the governed value?
VOCM asks:
What must be true for that relationship to become capable of producing or enabling value?
Operational Space
VOCM governs conditions affecting the activation and operation of a Value Origin Relationship.
These conditions may include:
availability; accessibility; capability readiness; resource availability; demand; timing; environmental conditions; operational readiness; technological compatibility; infrastructure availability; complementary capability; economic feasibility; utilization; coordination; scale; knowledge; human capability; network participation; system compatibility; temporal alignment; dependency satisfaction; threshold achievement.
The relevant conditions depend upon the governed value.
VOCM does not prescribe one universal set of conditions.

Origin Relationship ≠ Origin Condition
VORM establishes:
how a source may contribute to value.
VOCM establishes:
what must be true for that relationship to become operationally capable of contributing to value.
Example:
Solar Installation
Value Source:
solar generation system
Value Source Basis:
electricity-generation capability
Value Origin Relationship:
generation capability → production of usable electricity → potential energy value
Value Origin Conditions may include:
sufficient solar irradiation
operational equipment grid or storage connection ability to use or transfer generated electricity.
The relationship can exist while one or more required conditions are absent.
Therefore:
Existing Value Origin Relationship ≠ Satisfied Value Origin Conditions
Necessary Conditions
A Necessary Origin Condition is a condition without which the relevant Value Origin Relationship cannot operate for the governed value.
Example:
A manufacturing machine may possess productive capability.
But if production requires electrical power:
electricity availability
may be a necessary condition.
If the condition is absent:
the source remains
and
the capability remains
but the pathway toward value emergence may be inactive.
VOCM therefore prevents the existence of productive capability from being mistaken for realized value.
Enabling Conditions
An Enabling Origin Condition allows or facilitates the Value Origin Relationship without necessarily being the fundamental source of the value.

Examples may include:
infrastructure access; network connectivity; compatible software; transportation; regulatory access where relevant to operation; distribution capability;
specialized equipment; trained personnel.
VOCM governs the condition's role in the value-origin pathway.
It does not govern the external system responsible for establishing that condition.
Conditional Thresholds
Some Value Origin Relationships become materially capable of producing value only after a threshold is reached.
Examples include:
minimum production volume
minimum network participation
minimum utilization
minimum performance
minimum data availability
minimum demand
minimum energy availability
minimum reliability
VOCM may therefore establish:
Condition Variable → Required Threshold → Condition Satisfaction State
A source may be technically capable of creating value while remaining below the threshold required for meaningful value emergence.
Combined Conditions
Value origin frequently depends upon several conditions being satisfied together.
For example:
Technology Capability
Required Infrastructure Qualified Personnel Operational Demand Resource Availability
may collectively create the conditions under which a Value Origin Relationship can operate.
VOCM therefore supports:
Condition Set → Combined Origin Readiness
rather than assuming that each condition independently produces value.
Alternative Condition Paths
The same Value Origin Relationship may operate through different sets of conditions.

For example, a digital service may reach customers through:
Direct Digital Distribution
or
Partner Distribution
or
Integrated Platform Distribution.
Different condition sets may therefore activate alternative pathways toward the same governed value.
VOCM may represent:
Condition Set A → Origin Pathway
or
Condition Set B → Alternative Origin Pathway
This allows value-origin governance to remain adaptable without redefining the underlying value each time implementation changes.
Dependency Conditions
Some conditions depend upon other conditions.
Example:
A production facility may require:
raw materials
but raw-material availability may depend upon:
supplier capability → logistics availability → transport infrastructure → delivery timing.
VOCM may therefore map:
Primary Condition
→ Supporting Condition
→ Dependent Condition
→ Origin Readiness
This is particularly important in complex supply chains, financial systems, infrastructure, digital platforms, and multi-actor ecosystems.
Temporal Conditions
Value Origin Conditions may exist only during particular periods.
They may be:
Continuous
Temporary
Periodic
Seasonal
Event-Triggered
Time-Limited
Delayed
Recurring
For example:
A hydroelectric asset may possess the same physical generation capability throughout the year while water availability changes materially.
The Value Source remains.
The Value Source Basis remains.
The Value Origin Relationship remains.
But the conditions supporting actual value emergence may change over time.

External Conditions
Value origin may depend upon conditions outside the Value Source itself.
Examples include:
customer demand; network availability; weather; energy supply; access to infrastructure; complementary services; resource availability; market access; interoperability; physical environment.
VOCM may recognize these conditions without claiming governance authority over the external domain.
The principle is:
VFM® governs the condition insofar as it affects the value-origin pathway — not the external system that produces the condition.
Internal Conditions
Some conditions arise within the Value Source or Value Object.
Examples include:
operational readiness; functional capability; sufficient capacity; configuration state; resource level; availability; performance threshold.
VOCM may therefore distinguish:
Internal Origin Conditions
from
External Origin Conditions.
Both may be required for the same value-origin pathway.
Demand as a Value Origin Condition
Certain forms of value may depend materially upon demand or beneficiary need.
A capability can exist without producing the relevant value if no beneficiary needs, uses, or can access it within the defined Value Context.
For example:
A transportation service may possess:
vehicles + drivers + routes + operational capability
but passenger-service value may remain unrealized if there is no relevant demand.
VOCM therefore permits demand to function as an Origin Condition where appropriate.

It does not establish market price or economic valuation.
Access as a Value Origin Condition
Value may exist potentially while access prevents its emergence for a specific beneficiary.
Examples:
Medical capability without patient access
Digital capability without network access
Energy capability without transmission access
Knowledge without usable access
Financial infrastructure without participant access
VOCM may therefore govern:
Access Condition Satisfied / Unsatisfied
where access materially determines whether the Value Origin Relationship can operate.
Utilization Condition
Some Value Sources create value only when their capability is used.
For example:
A factory may possess unused production capacity.
The productive capability exists.
Its relationship to production value exists.
The required infrastructure may exist.
But without utilization, the corresponding production value may not emerge.
VOCM can therefore distinguish:
Available Capability
from
Activated Capability.
Complementary Capability Condition
Value may require another capability.
For example:
AI model
may possess analytical capability.
But operational value may require:
usable data + computing infrastructure + integration + decision process.
The AI model alone does not establish the complete value-origin condition set.
VOCM therefore makes complementary capability requirements explicit.
Origin Readiness
VOCM may establish a governed Value Origin Readiness State.
A minimum state model may include:
1. Undefined

The relevant Origin Conditions have not been sufficiently identified.
2. Unsatisfied
One or more necessary Origin Conditions are absent.
3. Partially Satisfied
Some required conditions exist, but the complete condition set is not established.
4. Conditionally Ready
The value-origin pathway can operate only under explicitly defined conditions.
5. Ready
The identified material Origin Conditions necessary for the governed pathway are currently satisfied.
6. Interrupted
Conditions previously supporting the pathway have materially ceased or become unavailable.
These are governance states.
They do not themselves establish Value Emergence.
Origin Readiness ≠ Value Emergence
This distinction is essential to VFM®.
A value-origin pathway may be fully ready without value having emerged yet.
For example:
A manufacturing line may be:
installed
powered
staffed
supplied
tested
ready for operation
while no product has yet been produced.
Therefore:
Origin Readiness = conditions for value emergence are present.
It does not mean:
Value has emerged.
That distinction preserves the boundary between:
Value Origin
and the subsequent:
Value Emergence
governance space.
Condition Failure
An Origin Condition may fail after previously being satisfied.
Examples:
electricity interruption; supply disruption; loss of access; infrastructure failure; disappearance of demand; unavailable personnel; incompatible system update; resource depletion.
VOCM requires material condition failure to remain identifiable.

A condition failure may:
prevent value emergence
or
interrupt the origin pathway
without necessarily destroying the Value Source itself.
Condition Restoration
A failed Origin Condition may later be restored.
Example:
Network outage
→ access condition fails → value-origin pathway interrupted → network restored → access condition satisfied again.
This does not necessarily constitute ReMonet™.
ReMonet™ belongs to later value-restoration governance where value itself has been lost, degraded, dormant, or reduced to a zero-value state as defined by the architecture.
VOCM governs restoration of the origin condition, not restoration of the value state itself.
Condition Change
Origin Conditions may change even when the source and relationship remain stable.
A condition may become:
Satisfied → Partially Satisfied
Satisfied → Unsatisfied
Unsatisfied → Satisfied
Ready → Interrupted
Conditional → Ready
VOCM therefore supports ongoing condition-state updates where Value Origin is monitored over time.
Condition Criticality
Not every Origin Condition has equal importance.
Organizations may classify conditions as:
Critical
Necessary
Enabling
Supporting
Optional
Alternative
The classification should reflect the specific governed value pathway.
A condition classified as critical should have a documented reason for that status.
Condition Dependency Map
For complex systems, VOCM may produce a Value Origin Condition Dependency Map.
Example:
Governed Value
↑
Value Origin Relationship
↑
Condition Set

↙ Energy Availability ↙ Material Availability ↙ Operational Capability ↙ Demand ↙ Distribution Access
Each condition may itself contain dependencies.
This enables organizations to see not only where value can originate, but also what the origin of that value depends upon.
Condition Evidence
Where materially relevant, a claimed Origin Condition should be supportable.
Support may include:
operational data; contractual availability; technical status; resource records; utilization data; demand indicators; system measurements; capacity information; infrastructure status; observed conditions; documented readiness.
VOCM does not own general validation or audit.
Where required:
VALIDOS® may govern validation.
ADIT® may govern audit and evidence.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity.
VOCM governs the value-origin condition being asserted.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A practical VOCM implementation should establish:
1. Value Origin Relationship Input
Receive the governed Value Origin Relationship from VORM.
2. Condition Identification
Identify the conditions materially affecting operation of the value-origin pathway.
3. Condition Classification
Determine whether each condition is necessary, enabling, supporting, critical, optional, or alternative.
4. Condition Dependency
Identify material dependencies between conditions.
5. Condition Threshold
Define relevant thresholds where the condition is not purely binary.
6. Condition State

Determine whether each condition is satisfied, partially satisfied, unsatisfied, conditional, or interrupted.
7. Temporal Applicability
Identify whether the condition is continuous, temporary, periodic, event-triggered, or time-bounded.
8. Origin Readiness
Determine the current readiness of the Value Origin pathway.
9. Condition Support
Identify the basis supporting material condition assertions where required.
10. Value Origin Conditions Record
Create the governed conditions record for downstream documentation and later Value Emergence governance.
Governance Outputs
VOCM may produce:
Value Origin Condition Record Value Origin Condition Set Necessary Origin Condition Record Enabling Origin Condition Record Critical Origin Condition Record Alternative Origin Condition Path Value Origin Condition Dependency Map Value Origin Condition Threshold Value Origin Condition State Value Origin Readiness State Value Origin Condition Failure Record Value Origin Condition Change Record Value Origin Condition Restoration Record Value Origin Conditions Assessment
These outputs provide the governed basis for:
VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module
and subsequently for the transition from:
Value Origin → Value Emergence.
Use Case 1 — Banking: AI Fraud Prevention
Value
A bank has an AI fraud-detection system.
The preceding modules establish:
Value Source: fraud-detection system
Value Source Basis: analytical and transaction-pattern detection capability

Value Origin Relationship: earlier detection of suspicious transactions may prevent or reduce financial loss.
VOCM then identifies the conditions required for that pathway to operate:
relevant transaction data available
system operational fraud patterns detectable within the available information analysis completed before irreversible settlement or loss alerts reach the appropriate decision process intervention capability exists.
This exposes an important distinction.
A bank may own an advanced AI system worth millions of francs.
The technology may function correctly.
But if alerts arrive after transactions become irreversible, one critical Origin Condition fails.
The technical asset still exists.
The analytical capability still exists.
The Value Origin Relationship still exists.
But the expected avoided-loss value may fail to emerge.
VOCM therefore allows the bank to identify exactly which conditions separate:
expensive capability
from
capability capable of originating economic value.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Reusable Launch
System
A space organization develops a reusable launch system to reduce lifecycle mission costs.
The preceding modules identify:
Value Sources: reusable vehicle, propulsion system, inspection capability, refurbishment capability, operational learning.
Value Source Bases: reuse, inspection, recovery, refurbishment, repeated operational capability.

Value Origin Relationships: reduced replacement requirements, shorter turnaround, repeated component utilization, and accumulated operational learning may contribute to lower lifecycle mission resource requirements.
VOCM then establishes the conditions necessary for those relationships to operate:
successful recovery
acceptable post-flight component condition inspection capability refurbishment within economically meaningful limits sufficient reliability across repeated use available launch demand turnaround compatible with mission schedules reuse cost below relevant replacement alternatives.
The reusable vehicle itself therefore does not automatically create cost value.
If recovery succeeds but refurbishment becomes more expensive than replacement, an important condition fails.
If refurbishment is efficient but launch frequency is too low, another condition may remain unsatisfied.
If both become favorable, the value-origin pathway may become ready.
VOCM therefore transforms:
“Reusable systems create value.”
into the governable question:
“Under which conditions does reusability actually become capable of originating value?”
Foundational Principles
A Value Origin Relationship does not automatically create value.
Value Origin Conditions determine whether the relationship is capable of operating.
Value Source existence does not establish Origin Readiness.
Capability availability does not establish capability utilization.

Necessary conditions must be distinguished from enabling and supporting conditions.
Multiple conditions may jointly determine one value-origin pathway.
External conditions may affect value origin without becoming governed external domains of VFM®.
Origin Conditions may change while the Value Source remains unchanged.
Restoration of an Origin Condition is not automatically restoration of value.
Origin Readiness is not Value Emergence.
Value should not be treated as having emerged merely because the conditions for its emergence exist.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Origin Conditions Module establishes the conditional layer of Value Origin governance by identifying, classifying, relating, and assessing the conditions required for an established Value Origin Relationship to become capable of producing or enabling the governed value. Through governance of necessary, enabling, supporting, critical, alternative, dependent, temporal, internal, external, threshold-based, and combined conditions, VOCM separates the existence of a Value Source and its capability from the operational conditions required for that capability to contribute to value. By establishing explicit Value Origin Readiness states while preserving the distinction between readiness and actual Value Emergence, VOCM prevents potential value,

available capability, operational readiness, and realized value from being treated as equivalent. The Module therefore creates the final conditional structure required before Value Origin can be documented and the architecture can proceed toward governance of the moment at which value actually comes into existence.
