Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Value Origin Standard (VOS)
2. Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism
Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS)
Operational Layer: Value Origin Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Value Origin
Origin ID: VFM-VOS-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 23 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · OBIDENITY®
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Value Origin Standard (VOS) is the second Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism and governs the identification, definition, relationship, conditions, and documentation of the origin from which governed value can emerge.
VOS establishes the methodological distinction between the source capable of producing value and value that has actually come into existence.
The Standard recognizes that value does not appear without a basis. It may originate from an object, capability, resource, activity, relationship, information, knowledge, right, condition, process, infrastructure, system, opportunity, natural resource, human capability, technological capability, or another identifiable source.

VOS does not determine whether value has already emerged, how much value exists, what its current state is, how it changes, or whether it will ultimately be realized.
Its purpose is foundational:
to establish where the governed value can originate and the basis connecting that potential value to its source.
Core Question
From what identifiable source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other basis can the governed value originate?
Architectural Position
VOS occupies the second governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value Context Standard (VCXS)
and precedes:
Value Emergence Standard (VES).
The preceding standard establishes:
What value is being governed?
VOS then establishes:
Where can that value come from?
The next standard determines:
Has value actually emerged?
The sequence is therefore:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence
This distinction prevents a potential source of value from being treated automatically as existing value.
Governance Flow Position
Governed Value Context → Value Source Identification → Value Source Basis → Value Origin Relationship → Value Origin Conditions → Value Origin Documentation → Governed Value Origin → Value Emergence
Operational Space
VOS governs the space between:
identified value context
and
actual emergence of value.
Its governed space includes:
value source identification; value-source differentiation;

source basis; source capability; origin relationships; origin dependencies; origin conditions; latent value potential; multiple-source value origin; composite value origin; conditional value origin; temporal origin; origin continuity; origin change; origin documentation.
The Standard asks whether a sufficiently identifiable basis exists from which the governed value can arise.
It does not presume that value already exists.
Value Source Principle
A Value Source is an identifiable basis from which a defined form of value may potentially emerge.
A Value Source may include:
physical assets; natural resources; intellectual property; knowledge; data; infrastructure; technology; human capability; organizational capability; production capability; relationships; networks; contractual rights; access rights; operational capacity; energy resources; financial resources; land; biological resources; algorithms; software; inventions; scientific discoveries; market access; time; location; information; combinations of multiple sources.
A source becomes relevant to VOS only in relation to the governed value context established by VCXS.
Value Source ≠ Value
The central distinction of VOS is:
Value Source ≠ Existing Value
An object, capability, resource, or relationship may possess the capacity to generate value without that value having yet emerged.
For example:
A mineral deposit may exist without economically recoverable value having emerged.

A patent may exist without generating licensing value.
A manufacturing machine may exist without producing operational value.
A dataset may exist without creating informational or economic value.
A technology may exist without creating cost-saving value.
A scientific discovery may exist before commercial or operational value emerges.
VOS therefore prevents potential from being silently treated as realized value.
Origin Asset™
Origin Asset™ has its natural architectural home within Value Origin governance.
An Origin Asset™ represents an identifiable asset, capability, resource, relationship, condition, or other governed basis capable of functioning as an origin from which value may emerge.
The concept does not itself establish:
existing value; monetary value; ownership; legality; validation; market recognition; accounting recognition; taxable value; asset identity; value realization.
Its function within VFM® is narrower:
Origin Asset™ identifies a potential value-origin basis.
Therefore:
Origin Asset™ ≠ Value Asset™
An Origin Asset™ may become associated with a Value Asset™ only after the relevant value has legitimately emerged and entered an applicable value state.
Source Basis
Identifying a source is insufficient unless the basis through which that source may produce value is understood.
VOS therefore distinguishes:
Value Source
from
Value Source Basis.
For example:
Factory → source.
Capability to manufacture a required product → source basis.
Dataset → source.

Capability to reduce decision uncertainty → source basis.
Satellite → source.
Capability to generate Earth-observation information → source basis.
Patent → source.
Exclusive technological capability capable of enabling commercial exploitation → source basis.
The source identifies where value may originate.
The basis explains why that source is capable of producing the governed value.
Value Origin Relationship
Value may originate through a relationship rather than through an isolated object.
VOS therefore governs the relationship between:
Value Source → Governed Value
The relationship may be:
direct; indirect; enabling; dependent; conditional; composite; sequential; network-based; temporal; reciprocal.
A source should not be attributed as the origin of value merely because it is associated with the value-bearing object.
There must be a methodologically intelligible relationship between the source and the value capable of emerging from it.
Multiple Value Sources
One form of value may originate from multiple sources.
For example:
AI service value
may originate from a combination of:
model capability + data + computing infrastructure + software + human expertise + distribution network.
No single source may independently explain the value.
VOS therefore supports:
Composite Value Origin
where multiple sources jointly establish the basis from which value may emerge.
One Source, Multiple Values
The reverse is also possible.
One source may generate several distinct forms of value.

A satellite may generate:
scientific value commercial data value strategic value navigation value security value environmental monitoring value
These values must remain distinguishable according to the Value Context established under VCXS.
Therefore:
One Value Source ≠ One Value
Latent Value Origin
Some sources contain a value-generating capability that has not yet produced actual value.
VOS recognizes this as:
Latent Value Origin
Examples may include:
unused intellectual property; undeveloped land; unexploited mineral resources; dormant datasets; unused production capacity; uncommercialized scientific discoveries; unused spectrum; inactive infrastructure; unused technological capabilities.
Latent origin is not equivalent to zero value.
Nor is it equivalent to positive value.
It identifies a potential value-origin condition prior to value emergence.
Value Origin Conditions
A Value Source may require particular conditions before value can emerge.
These conditions may include:
access; demand; technological capability; infrastructure; complementary resources; operational readiness; environmental conditions; human capability; network participation;
timing; scarcity; usability; interoperability; availability; deployment; combination with another source.
The existence of a source therefore does not imply that the conditions necessary for value emergence are present.
Conditional Value Origin
Where value can originate only under specified conditions, VOS recognizes:

Conditional Value Origin
For example:
A renewable-energy installation may become a source of grid value only where grid connection exists.
A dataset may become a source of analytical value only where sufficient processing capability exists.
A manufacturing capability may become a source of commercial value only where demand exists.
A technology may become a source of cost-saving value only when integrated into an operational process.
The source exists.
Its ability to produce the governed value remains conditional.
Origin Dependency
Some value origins depend upon other origins.
For example:
Software Service Value
may depend upon:
Software → Compute Infrastructure → Energy → Network Access
VOS may therefore document Origin Dependencies where the ability of one source to produce value depends materially upon another source.
This enables later lifecycle governance to distinguish between:
loss of value
and
loss of a condition enabling the source to produce value.
Value Origin Change
A Value Source may change over time.
Its capability may:
increase; decrease; become inaccessible;
become obsolete; combine with another source; split into multiple sources; become substituted; disappear.
VOS therefore permits a governed Value Origin to be versioned or reassessed where material source conditions change.
However:
Value Origin Change ≠ Value Change
A change in the source may eventually cause a change in value, but VFM® must preserve these as distinct lifecycle events.

Origin Extinction ≠ Value Extinction
A source may disappear while previously generated value continues to exist.
Likewise, a source may continue to exist after the value associated with it has disappeared.
Therefore:
Value Source Extinction ≠ Value Extinction
This distinction becomes important later in the VFM® lifecycle.
Parent Standard Modules
1. VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module
Governs identification and differentiation of the source, capability, resource, activity, relationship, condition, object, or other basis from which the governed value may originate.
It establishes the identifiable Value Source.
2. VSBM — Value Source Basis Module
Governs the basis explaining how and why the identified Value Source is capable of producing the governed value.
It distinguishes simple association from an intelligible value-origin basis.
3. VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module
Governs the relationship connecting the Value Source to the governed value.
It supports direct, indirect, composite, enabling, conditional, sequential, and multi-source origin relationships.
4. VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module
Governs the conditions, dependencies, circumstances, thresholds, capabilities, or environmental states required for the identified source to function as an origin of the governed value.
5. VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module
Governs the structured documentation, traceability, versioning, dependencies, conditions, and reconstruction of the governed Value Origin.

Internal Module Flow
Governed Value Context → VSOIM — Value Source Identification → VSBM — Value Source Basis → VORM — Value Origin Relationship → VOCM — Value Origin Conditions → VODM — Value Origin Documentation → Governed Value Origin → Value Emergence Standard
The logic is:
Where could the value originate? → Why can this source produce it? → How is the source connected to the value? → Under what conditions can that relationship operate? → How is the complete origin basis preserved?
Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VOS governs value origin, not general identity, validation, integrity, audit, authority, classification, or operational execution.
OBIDENITY® may establish the identity, origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, or continuity of an underlying entity.
VALIDOS® may determine whether a claim concerning a Value Source or origin relationship is sufficiently validated.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity of the source, records, conditions, or supporting information.
ADIT® may govern audit and evidence concerning how the origin determination was established.
GOA™ may govern authority and responsibility for the process.
VFM® retains the narrower question:
From where can this governed value originate?
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VOS implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Context
Identify the value context inherited from VCXS.
2. Value Source
Identify the source or sources from which the value may originate.
3. Source Basis

Define why the source is capable of producing the governed value.
4. Origin Relationship
Define how the source relates to the value.
5. Origin Conditions
Identify conditions required for the value-origin relationship to operate.
6. Dependencies
Identify material dependencies affecting the source's ability to produce value.
7. Multi-Source Structure
Where necessary, identify composite or interacting sources.
8. Temporal Basis
Identify material timing or lifecycle conditions affecting origin.
9. Origin Status
Establish whether the origin is active, latent, conditional, changed, unavailable, or otherwise appropriately governed.
10. Value Origin Record
Document the complete governed origin basis for transfer into Value Emergence governance.
Governance Outputs
VOS may produce:
Value Source Record Value Source Identifier Value Source Basis Record Value Origin Relationship Record Composite Value Origin Map Value Origin Dependency Record Value Origin Condition Record Latent Value Origin Record Conditional Value Origin Record Value Origin Change Record Value Origin Status Value Origin Record
These outputs establish the basis required by the next lifecycle stage:
Value Emergence Standard (VES).
Enterprise Application
VOS allows an organization to distinguish between:
what exists
and
what actually creates the possibility of value.

This is particularly useful in banking, investment, public finance, industrial systems, intellectual property, digital assets, AI, infrastructure, energy, natural resources, scientific research, and technology portfolios.
Instead of beginning with an assumed monetary value, an organization can trace the governed value backward to the source or combination of sources capable of producing it.
This creates a stronger methodological basis for later determining whether value has actually emerged, what state it occupies, and how it subsequently changes.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Identifying the Real
Source of Credit Value
A financial institution evaluates a manufacturing company seeking financing.
Traditional analysis may begin with assets, financial statements, collateral, and expected cash flows.
VOS permits a different question:
From what sources does the company's ability to generate the relevant value actually originate?
The analysis may identify:
manufacturing equipment + skilled workforce + production knowledge + customer relationships + intellectual property + supply-chain access
as a composite Value Origin.
This distinction matters because the physical equipment alone may not explain the value-generating capability.
If critical customer relationships disappear or specialized production knowledge is lost, the underlying Value Origin may weaken even though the accounting assets remain physically present.

VOS therefore provides a structured method for understanding the origin architecture behind value-generating capability before later VFM® stages govern actual value emergence and change.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Locating the
Source of Cost-Avoidance Value
A space organization introduces a high-fidelity simulation capability intended to reduce expensive physical testing.
The governed value context established under VCXS is:
Cost-Avoidance Value → Mission Program → Mission Development Reference Framework.
VOS then identifies where that value can originate.
The source may not simply be:
simulation software.
The actual Value Origin may be composite:
simulation model + computing infrastructure + validated engineering knowledge + scenario capability + mission data + engineering expertise.
The source basis is the capability to detect design problems before expensive physical construction or testing occurs.
The value has not necessarily emerged yet.
VOS establishes only the governed origin from which that cost-avoidance value can emerge.
When the simulation subsequently identifies a design defect and prevents a CHF 20 million physical-test failure, the architectural question moves from:
Value Origin
to:
Value Emergence.
This clean separation allows VFM® to trace the value lifecycle from its source rather than recognizing value only after financial consequences appear.
Foundational Principles
Value must not be assumed merely because a potential source of value exists.

Value Source ≠ Existing Value.
Origin Asset™ ≠ Value Asset™.
One source may originate multiple forms of value.
One form of value may originate from multiple sources.
Value origin may be latent, active, conditional, composite, dependent, or changing.
The source of value and the conditions enabling value emergence must remain distinguishable.
A change in Value Origin does not automatically constitute a change in value.
The disappearance of a Value Source does not automatically constitute Value Extinction.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Origin Standard establishes the governed origin layer of the VFM® value lifecycle by identifying the sources, capabilities, resources, activities, relationships, objects, conditions, and composite structures from which a defined form of value may emerge. Through governance of Value Sources, source bases, origin relationships, enabling conditions, dependencies, latent origins, conditional origins, multi-source structures, temporal changes, and origin documentation, VOS prevents potential value from being confused with existing value and establishes the methodological distinction between the capability to produce value and the actual emergence of value. By positioning Origin Asset™ as a value-origin concept rather than an automatic declaration of value, VOS provides the traceable foundation required for the next lifecycle question: not merely where value could come from, but whether value has actually come into existence.
Nahlad

About Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
About Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
About Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Recognition Standard (VRS) Governed Space: Value Recognition
Canonical Definition
Value Recognition Standard (VRS) governs when existing value may be formally recognized as value within a defined governance context and establishes the criteria, basis, determination, limitations, and traceability required for that recognition.
VRS creates a governed separation between two fundamentally different conditions:
Value exists.
and
Value is recognized.
Recognition does not create value merely by declaration, and failure to recognize value does not prove that value does not exist.
Why VRS Matters
Many systems recognize only the forms of value they are designed to see.
An accounting system may recognize one form of value. A bank may recognize another. A company may recognize operational or strategic value that does not appear on its balance sheet. A government may recognize public or infrastructural value that has no direct market price. A technological system may reveal previously unrecognized value in data, capacity, energy, knowledge, or resources.
Without an explicit recognition layer, these different recognition systems can easily be confused with the existence of value itself.
VRS prevents that confusion.
It asks:

What existing value is being recognized?
Within what context?
According to what criteria?
On what basis?
With what limitations?
For how long does that recognition remain applicable?
Governance Flow
Within the complete VFM® lifecycle:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
VRS governs the fourth governed space:
Existing Value → Recognition Criteria → Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination → Recognition Limitations → Recognition Record → Recognized Value → Value State Governance
This position is important because recognition can occur only after the architecture has established what value is being governed, where it originates, and whether that value has actually emerged.
What VRS Helps Organizations Govern
VRS provides a structured method for distinguishing:
Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition
Recognition ≠ Value Creation
Non-Recognition ≠ Zero Value
Recognition Status ≠ Value State
Recognition Change ≠ Value Change
Market Price ≠ Value Recognition
Accounting Recognition ≠ VFM® Value Recognition
Recognized Value ≠ Taxable Value
The result is a recognition layer that can coexist with financial, accounting, market, regulatory, operational, technological, or institutional systems without allowing any one of those systems to become the universal definition of whether value exists.
Contextual Recognition

Recognition under VRS is explicitly contextual.
The same value may simultaneously be:
recognized operationally,
unrecognized financially,
recognized strategically,
conditionally recognized institutionally,
or
recognized for one beneficiary but not another.
These outcomes are not necessarily contradictory.
They may reflect different recognition contexts, purposes, criteria, and beneficiaries.
VRS therefore preserves the relationship:
Value + Context + Recognition Basis + Recognition Determination + Limitations
rather than reducing value recognition to a universal yes/no declaration.
Recognition Does Not Control Value Existence
One of the strongest protections created by VRS is that the recognizing system does not automatically gain authority over the existence of value.
A bank failing to recognize a particular form of value does not prove that the value does not exist.
An accounting framework not representing a form of operational value does not automatically eliminate that value.
A market assigning no price does not automatically establish a zero-value state.
An institution withdrawing recognition does not automatically extinguish the underlying value.
These questions belong to different stages of the VFM® lifecycle.
Recognition governs the relationship to existing value — not the existence of value itself.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Recognizing Value
Beyond Conventional Asset Representation

A bank evaluates a company whose conventional financial statements show physical assets, cash flows, liabilities, and recognized intangible assets.
However, the company also possesses substantial capabilities that may materially affect its future performance:
proprietary datasets, specialized operational knowledge, AI capability, infrastructure access, technological capacity, established networks, or other resources that may not be represented in the same way within conventional financial reporting.
VRS does not tell the bank what those resources are worth.
Nor does it replace accounting standards, valuation methodology, credit methodology, or financial regulation.
Instead, VRS provides a governance layer for asking:
Does value associated with this resource already exist?
If so:
Does the bank recognize that value for this specific analytical purpose?
What criteria support recognition?
What evidence or basis supports it?
What limitations apply?
The bank might therefore establish:
Existing Value → Recognized for Strategic Assessment
while simultaneously maintaining:
Not Recognized as Accounting Asset
and:
Not Yet Recognized for Collateral Purposes.
Instead of forcing one recognition system to represent every form of value, VRS allows several recognition relationships to coexist transparently.
This creates a potentially powerful foundation for more sophisticated banking, investment, credit, enterprise-value, and risk-analysis systems.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Recognizing Value

Created by Avoided Cost and Preserved
Capability
A space organization develops a new mission-planning system that reduces unnecessary fuel consumption, simulation workload, mission preparation time, hardware testing, or operational risk.
Traditional project accounting can record many of the costs involved.
But the organization may also need to understand another question:
What value has been created by resources that no longer need to be consumed?
Suppose improved mission planning avoids:
500 hours of engineering work,
thousands of simulation executions,
unnecessary hardware testing,
or
additional mission fuel requirements.
The underlying benefit may already exist because the organization has materially avoided resource consumption.
VRS provides the recognition layer for determining whether that existing benefit is recognized as value within the relevant mission, operational, strategic, or resource-efficiency context.
The recognition can remain explicitly bounded:
Recognized Operational Value
without automatically becoming:
Accounting Asset
Market Value
or
Taxable Value.
Subsequent VFM® standards can then govern the state, development, degradation, nullification, or restoration of that value.
This allows organizations to govern value that conventional systems may not have been designed to represent directly.
Enterprise Value

VRS gives organizations a common methodological layer for recognizing different forms of existing value without collapsing them into price, accounting treatment, taxation, ownership, or market acceptance.
This can be particularly useful across banking, investment, public finance, industrial systems, infrastructure, technology, AI, energy, science, digital assets, intellectual property, resource optimization, and government decision-making.
The deeper advantage is interoperability.
Different systems may disagree about whether they recognize a value while still referring to the same governed value object and lifecycle.
That makes recognition differences visible, comparable, traceable, and eventually machine-readable.
Foundational Principle
Value does not begin to exist because a system recognizes it, and it does not cease to exist merely because a system fails to recognize it.

Canonical Definition
Value Recognition Basis Module (VRBM) is the second Core Module of the Value Recognition Standard (VRS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VRBM governs the identifiable basis upon which an existing value may be considered for formal recognition against the recognition criteria established by VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria Module.
The Module establishes what information, observation, relationship, condition, capability, effect, measurement, evidence, or other support forms the basis for determining whether applicable recognition criteria are satisfied.
Its purpose is not to create value, establish value existence, define recognition criteria, or issue the final recognition determination.
Its function is narrower:

to establish the governed basis upon which recognition can be assessed.
This creates the methodological relationship:
Recognition Criteria → Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination
Architectural Position
VRBM operates within the fourth governed space of the VFM® lifecycle:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
Within the Value Recognition Standard, VRBM follows the establishment of recognition criteria and precedes the actual recognition determination.
Internal Module Flow
Existing Value → VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria → VRBM — Value Recognition Basis → VRDM — Value Recognition Determination → VRLM — Value Recognition Limitation → VRRM — Value Recognition Record → Recognized Value
The internal logic is:
What must be satisfied → What supports that assessment → What recognition determination follows → What limitations apply → How recognition is recorded
VRBM therefore provides the methodological bridge between recognition rules and recognition decisions.
Operational Space
VRBM governs the basis used to support, challenge, condition, or prevent recognition of existing value within a defined context.
A recognition basis may derive from:

observable effects; measurable outcomes; demonstrated capability; operational contribution; beneficiary benefit; resource availability; resource preservation; cost avoidance; efficiency improvement; productive capacity; strategic capability; technological capability; economic contribution; functional utility; realized benefit; documented relationships; comparative performance; temporal persistence; accessibility; usability; reproducible outcomes; governed evidence; other contextually relevant support.
The relevant basis depends upon the recognition context and the criteria established by VRCM.
VRBM does not prescribe one universal form of proof for all value.
Recognition Basis Principle
A recognition determination should not rest solely upon an unsupported assertion that something is valuable.
The basis for recognition must be identifiable.
The governing relationship is:
Existing Value + Recognition Criteria + Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination
The recognition basis answers:
What supports the conclusion that this existing value satisfies, fails to satisfy, or conditionally satisfies the applicable recognition criteria?
Basis Must Relate to Criteria
VRBM requires a traceable relationship between:
Recognition Criterion
and
Recognition Basis.
A large amount of information is not necessarily a relevant recognition basis.
The basis must address the criterion actually being assessed.
For example, if the criterion concerns:
measurable reduction in resource consumption,

relevant basis may include:
before-and-after resource consumption; controlled operational measurements; comparative execution results; documented avoided consumption; attributable efficiency effects.
Information concerning unrelated market popularity would not automatically satisfy that criterion.
Therefore:
Available Information ≠ Applicable Recognition Basis
Recognition Basis ≠ Recognition Criteria
VRCM determines what must be demonstrated.
VRBM determines what supports the assessment of whether it has been demonstrated.
For example:
Criterion: The capability must materially reduce operating cost.
Basis: Operational records demonstrate a recurring 18% reduction in the governed cost category after deployment.
These are methodologically distinct.
If criteria and basis are collapsed into one layer, organizations can silently change the recognition rule according to whatever information happens to be available.
VRBM prevents this.
Recognition Basis ≠ Recognition Determination
A strong recognition basis does not itself issue recognition.
The basis is evaluated by the subsequent VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module.
Therefore:
Recognition Basis → Input to Determination
not:
Recognition Basis = Recognition
This distinction enables the same underlying basis to be examined consistently by different authorized systems, processes, or decision mechanisms.
Recognition Basis ≠ Value Existence
Value existence precedes recognition governance.

VRBM therefore does not determine whether the underlying value exists.
That architectural question belongs to the Value Emergence Standard (VES).
VRBM asks only what basis supports recognition of that existing value within the specified context.
Therefore:
Insufficient Recognition Basis ≠ No Value
An existing value may remain unrecognized because the basis required by a particular recognition system is unavailable, incomplete, inaccessible, or insufficiently established.
Recognition Basis ≠ Value Measurement
Recognition basis may include quantitative measurements.
But the existence of measurement does not mean VRBM governs value magnitude.
For example:
500 engineering hours avoided
may form part of a recognition basis.
Determining the full magnitude, economic significance, financial valuation, or market price associated with that effect may require another methodology or governance system.
Therefore:
Measured Effect ≠ Complete Value Measurement
Recognition Basis Types
A governed recognition system may distinguish several forms of basis.
1. Observational Basis
Recognition is supported by directly observable conditions, effects, states, or outcomes.
2. Measurement Basis
Recognition is supported by measurable changes, quantities, performance, resource effects, or other quantified relationships.
3. Operational Basis
Recognition is supported by demonstrated contribution to actual operations.
4. Capability Basis

Recognition is supported by an existing capability capable of producing a defined benefit.
5. Beneficiary Basis
Recognition is supported by an identifiable benefit to the relevant beneficiary.
6. Comparative Basis
Recognition is supported by comparison between alternatives, states, periods, systems, or configurations.
7. Evidential Basis
Recognition is supported by governed evidence produced through another applicable governance or evidential process.
8. Composite Basis
Recognition depends upon multiple basis types considered together.
These categories are not required to be exhaustive.
They provide a structured vocabulary for distinguishing how recognition is supported.
Direct and Indirect Recognition Basis
VRBM distinguishes:
Direct Recognition Basis
from
Indirect Recognition Basis.
A direct basis has a relatively immediate relationship to the recognition criterion.
Example:
Criterion: reduction of electricity consumption.
Direct Basis: verified electricity consumption decreased by 20% under comparable operating conditions.
An indirect basis supports recognition through an intermediate relationship.
Example:
new control capability → reduced machine idle time → reduced electricity consumption → operational benefit.
Indirect basis is not automatically weaker.
However, the relationship between the basis and the recognition criterion must remain explicit.
Internal and External Recognition Basis
Recognition basis may originate internally or externally.
Internal Basis may include:

operational records; internal measurements; production data; capability records; cost records; resource records; performance data; internal simulations; internal assessments.
External Basis may include:
market information; external measurements; independent assessments; public data; customer outcomes; external evidence; scientific observations; regulatory information; third-party analysis.
VRBM does not assume that external information is inherently superior to internal information.
The relevant question is whether the basis legitimately supports the recognition criterion within the defined context.
Actual and Prospective Basis
Recognition may concern value whose effects are already observable or value associated with a capability whose future benefit remains contextually relevant.
VRBM therefore distinguishes:
Actual Basis
from
Prospective Basis.
Actual basis derives from effects that have already occurred or are currently observable.
Prospective basis derives from a governed relationship between an existing capability and a future value-relevant effect.
Prospective basis must not be silently represented as realized benefit.
Therefore:
Expected Benefit ≠ Realized Benefit
Both may support recognition in appropriate contexts, but they must remain distinguishable.
Attribution Principle
Where recognition is based upon an observed benefit or effect, VRBM should establish whether the effect can reasonably be related to the governed value.
For example:
operating cost decreased

does not automatically establish:
the governed capability created the reduction.
Other factors may have contributed.
VRBM therefore requires the recognition basis to preserve material attribution conditions where relevant.
This may include:
causal relationship; contributory relationship; comparative relationship; temporal relationship; dependency relationship; beneficiary relationship.
VRBM does not need to establish universal causality.
It requires the claimed relationship supporting recognition to be explicit.
Counterfactual Basis
Some forms of value are most visible through what did not occur.
Examples include:
cost avoided; downtime prevented; energy not consumed; failure prevented; material waste avoided; capacity preserved; risk exposure reduced; engineering work eliminated; infrastructure expansion avoided.
These forms of benefit may require a counterfactual basis:
Observed or Expected State
compared with
Relevant Alternative State
VRBM permits counterfactual recognition basis where the comparison is sufficiently defined for the relevant recognition context.
This is particularly important because value does not always appear as a new asset, payment, or revenue stream.
Sometimes value appears as:
resources that no longer need to be consumed.
Basis Quality
VRBM does not reduce basis quality to a single universal score.
However, the recognition basis should be sufficiently characterized to determine whether it is suitable for the recognition context.

Relevant characteristics may include:
relevance; completeness; traceability; specificity; temporal relevance; representativeness; reproducibility; attribution strength; uncertainty; consistency; independence; accessibility; comparability.
The required quality depends upon the significance and purpose of recognition.
Basis Sufficiency
VRBM may determine whether the available basis is sufficiently established to proceed to recognition determination.
Possible basis states may include:
Established Basis
The basis required for assessment is sufficiently available and applicable.
Conditional Basis
The basis supports assessment only under explicitly defined conditions.
Partial Basis
Some required support exists, but material elements remain incomplete.
Conflicting Basis
Material supporting and opposing information coexist and require explicit treatment.
Insufficient Basis
The available basis does not sufficiently support a recognition assessment.
Unavailable Basis
The required basis cannot presently be established or accessed.
These states describe the recognition basis.
They do not determine the final recognition outcome.
Conflicting Recognition Basis
Recognition governance must preserve materially conflicting information.
For example:
operational records may indicate that a capability reduces cost,
while another dataset indicates that maintenance requirements eliminate much of the benefit.
VRBM should not discard one basis merely because it produces an inconvenient result.

Instead, the conflict should remain visible for VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module.
Therefore:
Recognition Basis Governance includes supporting, limiting, and contradictory basis.
Temporal Basis
A recognition basis may weaken or become obsolete over time.
Examples include:
technology changes; operational conditions change; beneficiary needs change; market structure changes; resource scarcity changes; capability deteriorates; new information becomes available; the underlying value changes; recognition criteria change.
VRBM therefore requires material temporal applicability to remain identifiable.
A basis valid in one period should not automatically be treated as permanently applicable.
Multiple Recognition Contexts
The same existing value may have different recognition bases in different contexts.
For example, an AI optimization capability may have:
Operational Recognition Basis: measured reduction in process time.
Energy Recognition Basis: measured reduction in electricity consumption.
Strategic Recognition Basis: demonstrated capability unavailable to competitors.
Financial Recognition Basis: documented recurring cost reduction.
Collateral Recognition Basis: insufficient basis.
These different outcomes do not alter the existence of the underlying value.
They describe different relationships between the value and different recognition systems.
Basis Traceability
A governed recognition basis should remain traceable to its source.

Where relevant, the record should identify:
Value Reference → Recognition Context → Recognition Criterion → Basis Object → Basis Source → Basis Relationship → Basis Conditions → Basis Limitations → Basis State
This makes recognition reconstructable rather than dependent upon undocumented judgment.
Machine-Readable Recognition Basis
VRBM provides a structure suitable for machine-readable value recognition.
A machine-readable implementation may represent:
Value ID → Recognition Context ID → Criterion ID → Basis ID → Basis Type → Source → Observed / Prospective Status → Attribution Relationship → Temporal Applicability → Uncertainty → Basis State → VRDM Determination
This can allow AI, banking, enterprise, public-sector, infrastructure, and other systems to distinguish between:
a value claim
and
the basis supporting recognition of that value claim.
Boundary with VRCM
VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria Module establishes the criteria that must be satisfied.
VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module establishes the basis used to assess those criteria.
Therefore:
Criteria = What must be demonstrated
Basis = What supports whether it has been demonstrated
Boundary with VRDM
VRBM does not issue the recognition determination.
VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module evaluates the applicable criteria against the governed recognition basis and determines the recognition outcome.
Therefore:
Criteria + Basis → Determination
Boundary with VALIDOS®

VRBM does not replace general validation governance.
Where a recognition process requires formally validated evidence, VALIDOS® may govern whether that evidence is sufficiently validated for its intended reliance.
VRBM governs a different question:
What basis is being used for value recognition?
VALIDOS® governs:
Can a validation claim legitimately be established and relied upon?
The same evidence may participate in both systems while the governance questions remain distinct.
Boundary with ADIT®
VRBM may use audit evidence or auditable records as recognition basis.
It does not govern audit execution or general evidence governance.
ADIT® may establish what occurred and preserve evidence concerning it.
VRBM determines how that information functions as a basis for value recognition.
Boundary with INTEGROS®
VRBM does not govern general integrity.
Where the integrity of a recognition-basis object is material, INTEGROS® may govern its integrity properties.
VRBM governs the role of that object within value recognition.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VRBM implementation should establish:
1. Value Reference
Identify the existing value being considered for recognition.
2. Recognition Context
Identify the context within which recognition is being assessed.
3. Applicable Recognition Criteria
Receive the applicable criteria established through VRCM.
4. Basis Identification

Identify the information, observation, capability, relationship, effect, measurement, evidence, or other support relevant to those criteria.
5. Basis Source
Identify where the recognition basis originates.
6. Criterion-to-Basis Relationship
Establish which basis supports, challenges, limits, or conditions each criterion.
7. Attribution Relationship
Identify material relationships between the governed value and observed or expected benefit where relevant.
8. Basis Conditions and Limitations
Preserve material assumptions, conditions, uncertainty, temporal limits, and exclusions.
9. Basis State
Determine whether the recognition basis is established, conditional, partial, conflicting, insufficient, or unavailable.
10. Recognition Basis Record
Preserve the governed basis for downstream recognition determination.
Governance Outputs
VRBM may produce:
Value Recognition Basis Record Recognition Basis Object Recognition Basis Source Record Criterion-to-Basis Mapping Recognition Basis Type Classification Direct / Indirect Basis Record Actual / Prospective Basis Record Attribution Relationship Record Counterfactual Basis Record Recognition Basis Condition Record Recognition Basis Limitation Record Recognition Basis Conflict Record Recognition Basis State Recognition Basis Traceability Chain
These outputs provide the governed input for VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Recognition of
Operational and Strategic Value

A bank assesses a company that has developed a proprietary automation platform.
The company claims that the platform represents substantial value.
The claim itself is not a sufficient recognition basis.
VRCM may already have established criteria such as:
material operational contribution; recurring economic benefit;
demonstrated capability; continued usability; beneficiary relevance.
VRBM then establishes the basis against those criteria.
The governed basis might include:
production time reduced by 27% → operational measurement basis
external software expenditure reduced by CHF 1.8 million annually → cost-avoidance basis
system deployed across 14 production locations → capability and operational basis
three years of recurring performance improvement → temporal persistence basis
continued dependence of critical workflows upon the platform → operational relevance basis
The bank can now distinguish:
“Management claims this technology is valuable.”
from:
“A defined recognition basis exists showing how this capability produces material value within the specified enterprise context.”
VRBM does not determine collateral eligibility, accounting recognition, market valuation, or credit treatment.
It provides a governed basis that those downstream systems may use according to their own rules.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Value Through
Avoided Resource Consumption
A space organization introduces a new mission-planning and simulation capability.

The organization believes the capability creates value because it reduces mission preparation cost and resource consumption.
VRCM establishes recognition criteria such as:
measurable resource reduction; preserved mission capability; avoided engineering workload; reduced simulation consumption; reduced physical testing; reduced fuel requirement.
VRBM establishes the recognition basis.
For example:
8,000 engineering hours avoided → labor-resource basis
35% fewer high-performance simulation executions required → computational-resource basis
two physical prototype test campaigns eliminated → avoided-testing basis
projected mission fuel requirement reduced within the governed mission configuration → mission-resource basis
The recognition basis can also preserve the relevant counterfactual:
mission preparation with the capability
versus
mission preparation without the capability.
The organization can therefore establish a governed basis for recognizing value created through non-consumption of resources.
This is important because no new physical asset necessarily appears.
The value may exist precisely because something costly no longer has to happen.
Enterprise Application
VRBM gives organizations a governed answer to a fundamental question:
What is the basis for saying that this existing value should be recognized?

This is applicable across banking, investment, enterprise management, public finance, infrastructure, AI, energy, manufacturing, science, digital systems, intellectual assets, resource optimization, government programs, and mission- critical operations.
It allows recognition systems to move from:
asserted value
toward:
basis-supported recognition.
More importantly, it allows different recognition systems to use different legitimate bases without redefining value itself.
The same value may have a strong operational basis, a partial financial basis, an insufficient collateral basis, and a strong strategic basis simultaneously.
VFM® can preserve all of those relationships without forcing them into one universal recognition outcome.
Foundational Principles
Recognition requires an identifiable basis.
Recognition basis does not create value.
Recognition basis is not recognition criteria.
Recognition basis is not recognition determination.
Insufficient recognition basis does not prove absence of value.
Available information is not automatically applicable recognition basis.
Recognition basis must remain connected to the criterion it is intended to support.
Expected benefit must remain distinguishable from realized benefit.
Supporting and contradictory recognition basis must both remain visible.
Value may be recognized through what is created, preserved, enabled, improved, or no longer needs to be consumed.

A value claim becomes governable when the basis supporting its recognition can be identified, related to explicit criteria, and reconstructed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Recognition Basis Module establishes the governed support layer of the Value Recognition Standard by defining the identifiable basis upon which existing value may be assessed against explicit recognition criteria. Through governance of basis identity, source, type, criterion relationship, attribution, direct and indirect support, actual and prospective effects, counterfactual comparison, conflicting information, temporal applicability, limitations, basis states, and traceability, VRBM prevents value recognition from resting solely upon unsupported assertion, institutional convention, or undocumented judgment. By separating recognition criteria from recognition basis and recognition basis from final recognition determination, VRBM creates a reconstructable methodological chain from existing value to recognition decision while preserving the foundational VFM® principle that insufficient recognition basis within one context does not establish that the underlying value does not exist.

Canonical Definition
Value Recognition Criteria Module (VRCM) is the first Core Module of the Value Recognition Standard (VRS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VRCM governs the explicit criteria under which already existing value may become eligible for formal recognition within a defined value governance context.
The Module establishes what conditions must be satisfied before an existing value can proceed toward a governed recognition determination.
Its purpose is not to determine whether value exists.
Value existence has already been established through the preceding Value Emergence Standard (VES).
VRCM asks the next question:

What must be true for that existing value to become eligible for recognition within this specific context?
This creates a controlled methodological boundary between:
Existing Value → Recognition Eligibility
Architectural Position
VRCM operates within the fourth governed space of the VFM® lifecycle:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
Within Value Recognition, VRCM is the entry module.
It receives an established existing value from the preceding lifecycle stage and establishes the recognition criteria against which that value can subsequently be assessed.
Internal Module Flow
Existing Value → VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria → VRBM — Value Recognition Basis → VRDM — Value Recognition Determination → VRLM — Value Recognition Limitation → VRRM — Value Recognition Record → Recognized Value
VRCM therefore governs the rules of recognition before recognition is decided.
Operational Space
VRCM governs the identification, definition, structuring, applicability, and documentation of criteria used to determine whether existing value is eligible for recognition.
Recognition criteria may concern:

relevance; materiality; beneficiary relationship; purpose relationship; contextual applicability; usability; accessibility; capability contribution; operational contribution; economic contribution; strategic contribution; resource contribution; temporal relevance; measurable effect; attributable benefit; cost avoidance; efficiency contribution; capability preservation; future utility where the context permits it.
The criteria used depend upon the value context established under the Value Context Standard (VCXS).
VRCM does not impose one universal definition of valuable.
It governs how the recognition criteria must be made explicit.
Recognition Criteria Principle
Value recognition must not occur through an undefined intuition that something is “valuable.”
A recognition system must be capable of identifying the criteria under which recognition is possible.
The methodological relationship is:
Existing Value + Defined Recognition Context + Applicable Recognition Criteria → Recognition Eligibility
Without explicit criteria, recognition becomes difficult to compare, reproduce, challenge, govern, or automate.
Context-Specific Recognition
Recognition criteria are context-dependent.
A capability may satisfy recognition criteria for one purpose while failing them for another.
For example, a proprietary dataset may have:
high operational relevance
but
no current collateral recognition.
A technological capability may have:
strategic value recognition
without

current accounting recognition.
A reduction in energy consumption may satisfy:
operational efficiency recognition criteria
without automatically satisfying:
financial asset recognition criteria.
These are not contradictions.
They are different recognition contexts.
VRCM makes those contexts explicit.
Recognition Criteria ≠ Value Existence
VRCM enforces a critical architectural distinction:
Failure to satisfy recognition criteria does not establish that value does not exist.
It establishes only that the value does not currently satisfy the defined criteria for recognition within the specified context.
Therefore:
Existing Value + Criteria Not Satisfied → Unrecognized Existing Value
not:
Criteria Not Satisfied → No Value
This distinction protects the VFM® lifecycle from allowing external recognition systems to redefine value existence.
Recognition Criteria ≠ Value Measurement
Recognition criteria establish whether value may qualify for recognition.
They do not necessarily quantify how much value exists.
For example:
Does this capability materially reduce operational resource consumption?
may be a recognition criterion.
Determining the magnitude of that value is a different governance question.
Therefore:
Recognition Eligibility ≠ Value Magnitude
Recognition Criteria ≠ Market Price
Market price may be relevant to a particular recognition context.
It is not a universal recognition criterion.
Value may exist and be recognized even where:

no market exists; no transaction has occurred; no price has been established; the value is internally consumed; the value consists of avoided cost; the value represents preserved capability; the value benefits a public system rather than a buyer; the value cannot presently be exchanged.
VFM® therefore does not reduce recognition to monetization.
Recognition Criteria Structure
A governed recognition criterion should identify, where relevant:
Criterion Identity → What criterion is being applied?
Recognition Context → Within what context does it apply?
Value Relationship → What characteristic or effect of the existing value does it examine?
Beneficiary Relationship → For whom or what is the value relevant?
Threshold or Condition → What must be demonstrated?
Applicability → To which value objects or situations does the criterion apply?
Temporal Condition → For what period does the criterion remain relevant?
Exclusions → What does the criterion explicitly not establish?
This creates recognition criteria that can be interpreted independently of the person or system that originally created them.
Recognition Eligibility
VRCM may establish recognition eligibility states such as:
Eligible
The existing value satisfies the applicable criteria sufficiently to proceed toward recognition determination.
Conditionally Eligible
The criteria are satisfied only under explicitly defined conditions.
Insufficiently Established

The available basis does not yet establish whether the criteria are satisfied.
Not Eligible in Context
The existing value does not satisfy the applicable recognition criteria within the defined context.
These are recognition-governance states.
They are not statements about whether the underlying value exists.
Multiple Recognition Contexts
The same existing value may be assessed simultaneously against multiple recognition criteria frameworks.
For example:
Operational Recognition Criteria → Eligible
Strategic Recognition Criteria → Eligible
Financial Recognition Criteria → Conditionally Eligible
Collateral Recognition Criteria → Not Eligible
This enables VFM® to represent value without forcing all institutions and systems to adopt one universal recognition model.
The value remains one governed value.
Its recognition relationships may be multiple.
Criteria Stability and Change
Recognition criteria may change over time.
Changes may result from:
organizational priorities; technology;
operational conditions; available capabilities; resource scarcity; market conditions; institutional requirements; new knowledge; beneficiary needs; environmental conditions.
VRCM requires material criteria changes to remain distinguishable from changes in the underlying value.
Therefore:
Recognition Criteria Change ≠ Value Change
A value may remain unchanged while its eligibility for recognition changes.
Machine-Readable Recognition

Explicit recognition criteria create an important foundation for machine-readable value governance.
A machine-readable implementation may represent:
Value ID → Recognition Context ID → Criterion Set → Criterion Conditions → Eligibility State
→ Recognition Basis
→ Recognition Determination
This can allow different systems to determine not merely whether something has been labelled valuable, but why it is eligible for recognition within a particular context.
Boundary with Value Emergence
The Value Emergence Standard (VES) determines when potential value becomes existent value.
VRCM begins only after value existence has been established.
Therefore:
VES: Does the value exist?
VRCM: What criteria must that existing value satisfy to become eligible for recognition here?
Emergence ≠ Recognition Eligibility
Boundary with Value Recognition Basis
VRCM establishes the criteria that must be satisfied.
VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module governs the basis used to demonstrate or support satisfaction of those criteria.
Therefore:
Criteria → What must be demonstrated
Basis → What supports the assessment
This separation prevents criteria from being silently rewritten according to whatever information happens to be available.
Boundary with Value Recognition Determination
VRCM does not issue the final recognition determination.
It establishes the criteria against which that determination will later be made.
VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module governs the actual determination.

Therefore:
Criteria ≠ Determination
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VRCM implementation should establish:
1. Existing Value Reference
Identify the existing value entering recognition governance.
2. Recognition Context
Define the context within which recognition is being considered.
3. Recognition Purpose
Identify why recognition is required.
4. Applicable Criteria
Define the criteria that must be satisfied.
5. Criterion Meaning
Specify what each criterion actually tests.
6. Applicability Conditions
Define where each criterion applies.
7. Thresholds or Conditions
Establish any relevant threshold, condition, or qualifying requirement.
8. Exclusions
Identify what satisfying the criterion does not establish.
9. Eligibility Assessment
Determine whether the value is eligible to proceed through the recognition process.
10. Criteria Record
Preserve the applicable criteria and eligibility state for downstream recognition governance.
Governance Outputs
VRCM may produce:
Value Recognition Criteria Set Recognition Context Record Recognition Purpose Statement Recognition Criterion Record Recognition Applicability Record Recognition Threshold Record Recognition Exclusion Record Recognition Eligibility Assessment Recognition Eligibility State Value Recognition Criteria Record
These outputs provide the governed input for VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking and Enterprise Capability

A bank evaluates a technology company containing significant operational capabilities, proprietary datasets, specialized systems, intellectual resources, and internal infrastructure.
Some of these resources may generate existing value even though conventional accounting or collateral systems do not recognize them in the same manner.
VRCM allows the bank to establish explicit criteria for a particular analytical context.
For strategic enterprise assessment, the criteria might examine whether a capability:
materially contributes to revenue generation; reduces operating cost; creates defensible capability; can continue producing benefit; contributes materially to future operations.
A capability may satisfy those criteria and become:
Eligible for Strategic Value Recognition
without automatically becoming:
Recognized Accounting Asset
or:
Eligible Collateral.
The bank can therefore govern multiple forms of recognition without confusing them with one another.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission Resource
Optimization
A space organization introduces a mission-planning capability that reduces fuel requirements, simulation workload, engineering time, hardware testing, or mission risk.
The organization wants to determine whether these effects should be recognized as value within its mission-efficiency framework.
VRCM can define criteria such as:

measurable resource reduction; preserved mission capability; avoided operational expenditure; increased mission capacity; reduced engineering workload; improved resource utilization.
If the existing benefit satisfies the criteria, it may proceed as:
Eligible Mission-Efficiency Value
for formal recognition.
This does not determine its market price, accounting treatment, or tax consequence.
It establishes that the existing value meets the defined criteria for recognition within the mission context.
Enterprise Application
VRCM enables organizations to replace implicit value recognition with explicit recognition logic.
This can support banking, investment, government, infrastructure, industrial operations, AI systems, energy systems, scientific programs, public administration, digital ecosystems, and resource optimization.
Its deeper importance is methodological.
Two organizations may disagree about whether they recognize the same value.
With VRCM, that disagreement can be decomposed into:
different contexts → different criteria → different eligibility outcomes
rather than being reduced to an undefined disagreement over whether something “has value.”
That makes value recognition more transparent, comparable, auditable, interoperable, and machine-readable.
Foundational Principles
Value recognition requires explicit criteria.
Recognition criteria do not create value.
Failure to satisfy recognition criteria does not prove absence of value.

Recognition criteria are context-specific, not universally absolute.
Recognition eligibility is not value magnitude.
Market price is not a universal recognition criterion.
Different recognition contexts may legitimately produce different recognition outcomes for the same existing value.
A change in recognition criteria does not necessarily represent a change in value.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Recognition Criteria Module establishes the first governed control point within the Value Recognition Standard by defining the explicit criteria under which already existing value may become eligible for recognition within a specified context. By separating value existence from recognition eligibility, recognition criteria from recognition basis, and recognition eligibility from final recognition determination, VRCM prevents institutional, financial, market, technological, or organizational recognition systems from silently becoming definitions of
value itself. It enables recognition decisions to become explicit, contextual, comparable, traceable, interoperable, and machine-readable while preserving the foundational VFM® distinction that value may exist independently of whether any particular system chooses or is able to recognize it.
