Canonical Definition
ReMonet™ Mechanism Module (VRMM) is the third Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
VRMM governs ReMonet™, the mechanism through which previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is acted upon in order to recover previously existing value.
The Module establishes how restoration is initiated, what restoration mechanism acts upon the affected value, how that mechanism operates, what value relationship it is intended to recover, what resources and interventions participate in the mechanism, and how the restoration process remains traceable from its governed starting condition to its resulting restoration candidate.
VRMM does not determine merely whether favorable conditions for restoration exist.

It governs the actual mechanism of restoration.
Its foundational function is:
to govern the mechanism through which previously existing but impaired value is intentionally or operationally moved toward recoverable value again.
ReMonet™
ReMonet™ is the canonical VFM® mechanism for restoration of previously existing value.
ReMonet™ may operate upon value that is:
Degraded
Impaired
Dormant
Lost
Inaccessible
or:
Zero.
ReMonet™ is therefore deliberately broader than recovery from absolute zero.
Its canonical meaning is:
a governed value-restoration mechanism through which previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero is acted upon so that recoverable value may re-emerge.
This establishes the critical distinction:
Value Development = existing value grows.
ReMonet™ = previously impaired value is recovered.
Architectural Position
VRMM is the third module within VRSS.
It follows:
VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module
VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module
and precedes:
VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module
VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module
VRSM establishes:
what previously existing value is proposed for restoration.
VRCM establishes:
whether the conditions necessary for restoration exist.
VRMM establishes:
how the restoration mechanism acts upon that value.
VRDM subsequently determines:
whether restoration actually occurred and what value was restored.
Internal Flow

Governed Restoration Scope → Satisfied Restoration Conditions → Restoration Mechanism Identification → ReMonet™ Initiation
→ Restoration Intervention → Mechanism Execution → Value Recovery Observation → Restoration Candidate → Mechanism Record → VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module
Operational Space
VRMM governs the space between:
restoration readiness
and
a value condition capable of being evaluated as potentially restored.
Its operational space includes:
restoration mechanism identification; ReMonet™ initiation; mechanism purpose; restoration intervention; mechanism inputs; mechanism resources; mechanism dependencies; restoration actions; mechanism sequence; mechanism execution; mechanism modification; mechanism interruption; mechanism failure; mechanism completion; restoration observation; restoration candidate generation; mechanism traceability; restoration mechanism record.
Mechanism Principle
ReMonet™ is not the favorable condition that makes restoration possible.
It is the mechanism acting upon the affected value under those conditions.
Therefore:
Restoration Condition ≠ ReMonet™ Mechanism.
A market may reopen.
A regulation may change.
New technology may become available.
Financing may become available.
Demand may return.
These events can create restoration conditions.
They do not automatically constitute ReMonet™.
ReMonet™ begins when a mechanism actually acts upon the affected value in a manner directed toward recovery.
Mechanism Identification

Every governed ReMonet™ process should identify the mechanism through which restoration is expected to occur.
A restoration mechanism may involve:
repair; rehabilitation; reactivation; reconfiguration; reconstruction; recovery; reprocessing; modernization; reaccess; reintegration; repurposing; remediation; rights restoration; capability recovery; market re-entry; operational restart; technological adaptation; data recovery; another defined restoration mechanism.
The mechanism must remain linked to the restoration scope established through VRSM.
Mechanism ≠ Outcome
The existence or execution of a ReMonet™ mechanism does not prove that value has been restored.
Therefore:
ReMonet™ Executed ≠ Value Restored.
A repair may fail to recover functional value.
A software modernization may fail to recover operational value.
A data recovery process may retrieve information that no longer carries useful value.
A market re-entry strategy may fail commercially.
The mechanism creates a Restoration Candidate.
VRDM determines whether restored value actually exists.
Restoration Intervention
A Restoration Intervention is an action or structured set of actions performed through the ReMonet™ mechanism to recover the scoped value.
An intervention may be:
Physical
Digital
Technical
Operational
Economic
Organizational
Legal
Informational
Market-based
or:
Hybrid.
The intervention type does not define whether restoration has succeeded.
It identifies how the recovery mechanism operates.

Single-Mechanism Restoration
Some value may be restored through one dominant mechanism.
Example:
Damaged Equipment → Repair → Recovered Function
The repair may constitute the primary ReMonet™ mechanism.
However, the resulting recovered function still requires determination through VRDM.
Multi-Mechanism Restoration
Complex value may require several mechanisms.
For example:
Dormant Industrial Facility
may require:
Equipment Rehabilitation → Software Modernization → Workforce Reconstitution → Operational Restart → Market Reintegration
These mechanisms may collectively constitute a governed ReMonet™ process.
VRMM must preserve their relationships rather than treating restoration as one undefined action.
Sequential ReMonet™
Restoration mechanisms may depend upon a sequence.
For example:
Data Access Recovery → Data Reconstruction → Format Migration
→ System Reintegration → Operational Reuse
If sequence materially affects restoration, VRMM should preserve that order.
Parallel ReMonet™
Some mechanisms may operate simultaneously.
For example:
Physical Rehabilitation
and
Digital System Modernization
may occur in parallel before an industrial asset can return to productive use.
VRMM therefore supports both sequential and parallel restoration structures.
Partial ReMonet™
ReMonet™ does not require complete recovery.
A mechanism may restore only part of previously existing value.
Therefore:
Partial Recovery May Constitute Legitimate ReMonet™.
For example:

A degraded production system once provided productive value of 100.
Its value declines to 20.
A restoration mechanism recovers the system to 65.
The movement:
20 → 65
may represent restored value.
The fact that historical value of 100 has not been fully recovered does not invalidate the restoration mechanism.
ReMonet™ from ZVA™
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may enter ReMonet™ where:
the relevant value is currently zero
but:
recoverable value remains within the governed lifecycle.
The mechanism may then act upon the Value Object to recover previously existing value.
Therefore:
ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Potentially Restored Value
does not imply:
ZVA™ = Value Extinction.
This distinction is fundamental.
ReMonet™ from Degraded Value
ReMonet™ may begin before value reaches zero.
For example:
100 → 40
through degradation.
A restoration mechanism may subsequently move the value:
40 → 75.
The recovered portion may constitute restored value.
Therefore:
ReMonet™ does not require prior Value Nullification.
ReMonet™ from Dormant Value
Value may remain latent or dormant rather than destroyed.
Examples include:
unused intellectual property; inaccessible historical data; idle production capacity; inactive infrastructure; dormant licenses; abandoned technologies; unused organizational capability.
Reactivation may constitute ReMonet™ where the mechanism restores previously existing value.
ReMonet™ from Inaccessible Value
Value may continue to exist conceptually while becoming inaccessible.

Examples include:
inaccessible data; locked digital assets; unavailable rights; inaccessible infrastructure; isolated systems; unavailable knowledge repositories.
A mechanism restoring access may produce restored value where access is materially required for the value to become usable again.
Restoration by Repurposing
A Value Object may recover previously existing value through a different use.
This requires careful classification.
If the new use recovers a relevant value relationship that previously existed, the process may contain ReMonet™.
If the new use creates an entirely new value relationship that never previously existed, the process may represent Value Emergence.
Therefore:
Repurposing ≠ Automatically ReMonet™.
The classification depends upon what value is actually being recovered.
Restoration Through External Change
Sometimes relatively little changes within the Value Object itself.
External conditions may change so that previously dormant or zero value becomes recoverable.
For example:
A mineral asset may have zero economic value because extraction is uneconomic.
A new processing technology may change the economics.
The technology itself is an external condition.
The mechanism through which the asset is brought back into economically productive use may constitute ReMonet™.
VRMM governs the value-restoration mechanism.
It does not govern the external technological system as a whole.
Restoration Inputs
A ReMonet™ mechanism may require inputs such as:

capital; technology; labor; information; energy; materials; infrastructure; permissions; rights; access; data; expertise; organizational capacity; time.
VRMM identifies materially relevant mechanism inputs where necessary for understanding how restoration occurred.
Restoration Resource Principle
The amount of resources consumed by restoration does not determine the amount of value restored.
Therefore:
Restoration Cost ≠ Restored Value.
An organization may spend CHF 10 million attempting to restore an asset and recover only CHF 2 million of value.
Another asset may require a minor intervention and recover substantial value.
The mechanism record must not confuse resource expenditure with value outcome.
Mechanism Causation Link
VRMM should establish a traceable relationship between:
Restoration Intervention
and
Observed Value Recovery Candidate.
This does not require VRMM to determine universal causality.
It requires enough mechanism linkage to show why the observed change is being considered a restoration candidate rather than an unrelated value event.
Mechanism Attribution
Where multiple mechanisms contribute to recovery, VRMM should preserve their contributions where materially distinguishable.
For example:
Repair
Market Recovery
Software Upgrade
New Access Rights
may jointly contribute to the resulting value condition.
The Module should avoid assigning all restored value to one intervention where the recovery basis is materially multi- mechanistic.

ReMonet™ ≠ Value Development
This boundary is critical.
Suppose value historically existed at 100.
It degrades to 40.
After intervention, value reaches 130.
The process may contain:
40 → 100 = restoration of previously existing value
and:
100 → 130 = development or newly emerging value
depending upon the governed value basis.
Therefore:
Recovery Beyond Prior Value Requires Classification.
ReMonet™ must not automatically absorb all positive value created after restoration begins.
ReMonet™ ≠ Value Emergence
Where value never previously existed, its appearance is not restoration.
Therefore:
No Prior Value → No ReMonet™ of That Value.
A restoration project may simultaneously produce new value.
That new value must remain distinguishable from restored value.
ReMonet™ ≠ Value Change
Value Change governs the fact and character of material change to value.
VRMM governs a specific restoration mechanism acting upon previously impaired value.
Therefore:
Every ReMonet™ may produce Value Change.
But:
Every Value Change is not ReMonet™.
ReMonet™ ≠ Value State
A Value State describes the governed condition of value.
ReMonet™ describes the mechanism through which restoration is attempted.
Therefore:
State ≠ Mechanism.
A ZVA™ is a Value State.
ReMonet™ is a restoration mechanism.
Restored Value is a resulting value condition subject to determination and state assignment.
ReMonet™ ≠ DeMonet™

The two mechanisms operate in opposite lifecycle directions but must not be treated as simple mathematical inverses.
DeMonet™ governs the mechanism through which existing positive value reaches a zero-value condition.
ReMonet™ governs the mechanism through which previously impaired value is acted upon toward recovery.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ ≠ Reverse ReMonet™
and:
ReMonet™ ≠ Reverse DeMonet™.
The mechanisms may involve completely different causes, interventions, conditions, and value relationships.
Mechanism Initiation
A ReMonet™ mechanism should have an identifiable initiation point.
The initiation point establishes when the governed restoration process begins.
This may be:
repair commencement; reactivation authorization; data recovery initiation; system migration start; rights reinstatement; rehabilitation commencement; market re-entry; operational restart process; another defined event.
The initiation point helps distinguish the restoration mechanism from preceding restoration conditions.
Mechanism Modification
A ReMonet™ mechanism may change during execution.
Changes may include:
intervention method; technology; resources; sequence; scope; dependencies; restoration target; execution strategy.
Material modifications should remain traceable because they may affect downstream restoration determination.
Mechanism Interruption
A restoration mechanism may be interrupted.
Interruption may result from:

missing resources; failed conditions; technical failure; regulatory change; market change; safety issue; loss of access; strategic decision; another material event.
Interruption does not automatically establish mechanism failure.
The mechanism may remain suspended and later resume.
Mechanism Failure
A ReMonet™ mechanism may fail.
Failure means the restoration intervention did not produce a restoration candidate capable of supporting the intended restoration determination.
Failure should remain recorded.
A failed ReMonet™ attempt is still a governed lifecycle event.
Repeated ReMonet™
A Value Object may undergo multiple restoration attempts.
For example:
Attempt 1 → Failed
Attempt 2 → Partial Recovery
Attempt 3 → Additional Recovery
Each material restoration attempt should remain distinguishable.
This prevents later value analysis from collapsing multiple interventions into one artificial restoration event.
Mechanism Completion
Completion of the restoration mechanism means the defined intervention has reached its governed endpoint.
It does not mean restored value has been established.
Therefore:
Mechanism Completion ≠ Restoration Determination.
The resulting condition proceeds to VRDM.
Restoration Candidate
The principal output of VRMM is a:
Restoration Candidate.
A Restoration Candidate is:
a value condition produced or materially affected through a governed ReMonet™ mechanism and presented for determination as potentially restored value.

This preserves the methodological sequence:
Mechanism first.
Determination second.
Boundary with VRSM
VRSM determines:
what value is being restored.
VRMM determines:
how restoration acts upon that value.
Therefore:
Restoration Scope ≠ ReMonet™ Mechanism.
Boundary with VRCM
VRCM determines:
whether the conditions necessary for restoration exist.
VRMM determines:
what mechanism acts under those conditions to recover value.
Therefore:
Restoration Readiness ≠ Restoration Mechanism.
Boundary with VRDM
VRMM produces the Restoration Candidate.
VRDM determines:
whether value was actually restored and to what governed extent.
Therefore:
ReMonet™ ≠ Restoration Determination.
Boundary with VRTRM
VRMM governs the restoration mechanism.
VRTRM governs the formal movement of determined restored value into its resulting Value State.
Therefore:
Mechanism ≠ Transition.
Boundary with Value Degradation
Value Degradation governs progressive decline while value remains.
ReMonet™ may act upon degraded value to recover previously existing value.
Therefore:
Degradation → ReMonet™ may occur before zero value is reached.
Boundary with Value Nullification
Value Nullification governs the transition through which positive value reaches zero.
ReMonet™ may subsequently act upon the resulting ZVA™ where restoration potential remains.
Therefore:
Value Nullification does not automatically prevent future ReMonet™.
Boundary with Value Extinction
ReMonet™ requires recoverable prior value.

Once the relevant value has reached legitimate Value Extinction, restoration of that same value within the governed lifecycle is no longer available.
Therefore:
ZVA™ may enter ReMonet™.
Extinguished Value may not.
If value later appears after extinction, it requires classification as a new value event rather than automatic restoration.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Receive Governed Restoration Scope
Identify the previously existing value governed through VRSM.
2. Confirm Restoration Conditions
Confirm the relevant readiness basis established through VRCM.
3. Identify ReMonet™ Mechanism
Define the mechanism through which restoration will be attempted.
4. Identify Restoration Inputs
Record materially relevant resources, capabilities, technologies, rights, or other inputs.
5. Initiate Mechanism
Establish the governed starting point of the restoration intervention.
6. Execute Restoration Intervention
Apply the defined mechanism to the scoped value.
7. Record Material Mechanism Events
Preserve material modifications, interruptions, failures, dependencies, and interventions.
8. Observe Recovery Candidate
Identify the resulting value condition potentially attributable to the restoration mechanism.
9. Establish Mechanism Traceability
Connect the resulting candidate to the governed restoration mechanism and relevant intervention basis.
10. Transfer Restoration Candidate
Transfer the candidate to VRDM for formal restoration determination.
Governance Outputs
VRMM may produce:

ReMonet™ Mechanism Record Restoration Mechanism Identification Restoration Intervention Record Restoration Input Record Restoration Resource Record Restoration Mechanism Dependency Record ReMonet™ Initiation Record Mechanism Modification Record Mechanism Interruption Record Mechanism Failure Record Mechanism Completion Record Restoration Mechanism Traceability Record Restoration Candidate ReMonet™ Record
These outputs provide the governed input for:
VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module.
Use Case 1 — ReMonet™ of a ZVA™ Industrial
Asset
A production facility previously generated substantial productive value.
Technological obsolescence and loss of market demand eventually reduce its relevant productive value to zero.
The facility becomes a:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
within the defined productive-value context.
Years later, new market demand and new manufacturing technology create the conditions under which the facility may again become useful.
Those changes establish restoration conditions under VRCM.
They do not themselves restore the facility's value.
A ReMonet™ mechanism is then initiated.
The mechanism includes:
equipment rehabilitation → control-system modernization → production-line reconfiguration → operational restart
The facility begins producing again.
VRMM records the intervention, resources, mechanism sequence, modifications, and resulting recovery candidate.
The facility is not yet automatically classified as restored.

The resulting productive-value condition proceeds to VRDM, where the amount and legitimacy of restored value are determined.
This distinction prevents:
investment in restoration
from being confused with:
successful restoration of value.
Use Case 2 — ReMonet™ of Dormant Intellectual
Property
A company owns an industrial technology patent portfolio that previously generated licensing and strategic value.
Market conditions change and the technology becomes commercially dormant.
The intellectual property continues to exist, but its active economic value falls dramatically.
Years later, a new technological application makes part of the original patent portfolio relevant again.
The new market opportunity is a restoration condition.
It is not itself ReMonet™.
The company initiates a ReMonet™ mechanism through:
technical reassessment → portfolio reconfiguration → new application mapping → licensing redevelopment → commercial reactivation
Some patents regain licensing value.
Others remain commercially inactive.
Still others support entirely new applications that did not exist previously.
VRMM preserves these distinctions.
The recovered licensing capability may become a Restoration Candidate.
Value generated by entirely new uses may require separate classification as Value Emergence or Value Development rather than being automatically absorbed into ReMonet™.
This allows the organization to distinguish:
value recovered
from
value newly created.
Enterprise Application

VRMM gives organizations a governed method for identifying how previously impaired value is actually being recovered.
It can be applied to:
distressed assets; industrial rehabilitation; infrastructure recovery; dormant intellectual property; legacy software; historical data; abandoned projects; impaired investments; unused productive capacity; digital assets; inactive rights; organizational capabilities; obsolete technologies; system reactivation; asset repurposing.
The Module makes it possible to distinguish:
favorable restoration conditions
from
the mechanism that actually acts upon value
and from:
the eventual determination that value has been restored.
This creates a traceable methodological bridge between restoration readiness and restored value.
Foundational Principles
ReMonet™ governs restoration of previously existing value.
ReMonet™ may operate upon degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value.
ReMonet™ does not require prior Value Nullification.
A ZVA™ may retain restoration potential and therefore may enter ReMonet™.
Value Extinction terminates restoration of the same value within the governed lifecycle.
Restoration conditions are not the restoration mechanism.
Execution of a restoration mechanism does not prove restoration success.
Restoration cost is not restored value.
Partial restoration may constitute legitimate ReMonet™.
ReMonet™ must remain distinguishable from Value Development and Value Emergence.

DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are not simple inverse mechanisms.
A completed ReMonet™ mechanism produces a Restoration Candidate, not an automatic declaration of restored value.
Canonical Closing Statement
ReMonet™ Mechanism Module establishes the mechanism layer of Value Restoration by governing how previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is acted upon toward recovery. Through identification of restoration mechanisms, interventions, inputs, resources, dependencies, initiation, execution, modification, interruption, failure, completion, partial recovery, multi-mechanism restoration, mechanism traceability, and Restoration Candidates, VRMM separates the conditions that make restoration possible from the
mechanism that actually attempts to recover value and from the later determination that restoration has succeeded. By defining ReMonet™ broadly enough to operate before or after Value Nullification while preserving the boundaries between restored value, Value Development, Value Emergence, ZVA™, and Value Extinction, VRMM establishes a reusable mechanism for governing value recovery across physical, digital, economic, operational, technological, informational, organizational, and future value systems. ReMonet™ does not declare that value has returned; it governs the mechanism through which previously existing value is given a legitimate pathway to return.

Canonical Definition
Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) is the first Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
VRSM governs the identification and bounding of the exact previously existing value proposed for restoration.
The Module establishes what value existed, what part of that value became degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero, what portion remains relevant for recovery, and what exact value dimension, object, context, and boundary the restoration process is permitted to address.
VRSM prevents restoration from being treated as an undefined claim that an object has simply “become valuable again.”
Its foundational function is:

to establish exactly what previously existing value is being proposed for restoration before restoration conditions or mechanisms are considered.
Architectural Position
VRSM is the first module within VRSS.
It precedes:
VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module
VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module
VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module
VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module
VRSM establishes the governed restoration scope.
The subsequent modules determine whether restoration conditions exist, how restoration occurs, whether value was actually restored, and how the resulting value enters a new governed Value State.
Internal Flow
Previously Existing Value → Prior Value State Identification → Impaired / Lost Value Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Dimension Boundary → Value Context Boundary → Restoration Target Definition → Restoration Exclusions → Governed Restoration Scope → VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module
Operational Space
VRSM governs the space between:
recognition that previously existing value has been impaired or lost
and
a formally bounded value-restoration scope.
Its operational space includes:

prior value identification; prior Value State; Value Object identification; affected value component; affected value dimension; degradation or loss boundary; dormant-value scope; zero-value scope; restoration context; temporal boundary; restoration target; restoration exclusions; partial restoration scope; dimensional restoration scope; contextual restoration scope; restoration dependencies; restoration-scope record.
Prior Value Requirement
Restoration requires a relationship to previously existing value.
VRSM therefore begins by establishing:
What value existed before the impairment, degradation, dormancy, loss, inaccessibility, or zero-value condition occurred?
Without an identifiable prior value basis, the process may represent:
Value Emergence
rather than:
Value Restoration.
Therefore:
No Identifiable Prior Value → No Established Restoration Scope.
This does not mean new value cannot emerge.
It means that newly emerging value must not be mislabeled as restored value.
Prior Value State Identification
Where available, VRSM should establish the prior governed Value State against which restoration is being considered.
The prior state may identify:
Value Object; value type; value dimension; value magnitude; value context; temporal state; operational condition; dependencies; limitations; supporting basis.
The historical value state does not automatically become the restoration target.
It provides the reference point from which the restoration relationship can be understood.

Value Object Boundary
VRSM must identify the Value Object to which the restoration claim applies.
The object may be:
a physical asset; infrastructure; technology; software; data; intellectual property; capability; process; organizational resource; digital asset; right; license; product; service; system; operational capability; another governable Value Object.
Restoration of one object must not automatically be attributed to a larger system containing that object.
Restored Component ≠ Restored System.
Affected Value Identification
VRSM identifies the value that became impaired.
The affected value may have become:
Degraded
Impaired
Dormant
Lost
Inaccessible
or:
Zero.
More than one condition may coexist.
For example, an industrial facility may retain physical value while its productive economic value becomes zero.
VRSM therefore scopes the affected value, not merely the physical or digital object carrying that value.
Value Dimension Boundary
Value is frequently multidimensional.
A Value Object may simultaneously possess:
economic value; operational value;
strategic value; functional value; informational value; technological value; market value; productive value; utility value; option value; another governed value dimension.
VRSM requires the restoration scope to specify which dimension is being restored.
Therefore:
Restoration of One Value Dimension ≠ Restoration of the Entire Value Object.
Partial Restoration Scope

The restoration target does not need to represent complete recovery.
VRSM may establish a scope for:
Partial Restoration.
Example:
A production asset previously operated at full productive capability.
After deterioration, only 30% of that capability remains.
The restoration project may legitimately target recovery to 70%.
VRSM therefore records:
Prior Capability: 100%
Current Capability: 30%
Restoration Scope: recovery toward 70%
The remaining 30% difference is outside the current restoration scope.
Context Boundary
Value may exist only within a particular context.
VRSM therefore identifies the context within which restoration is being proposed.
Context may include:
jurisdiction; market; organization; operational environment; technological environment; regulatory environment; geographic region; customer segment; infrastructure configuration; temporal period; use condition.
An asset may regain value in one context while remaining valueless in another.
Therefore:
Contextual Restoration ≠ Universal Restoration.
Temporal Boundary
Restoration scope may also be time-bound.
VRSM may distinguish between:
temporary restoration
and:
persistent restoration.
For example, a dormant energy asset may regain economic value during a temporary supply shortage.
Its value may subsequently decline again when market conditions normalize.
The restoration scope must therefore preserve the relevant temporal context.
Restoration Target

VRSM establishes the value condition toward which restoration is directed.
A Restoration Target may represent:
previous value magnitude; partial previous value; previous functionality; previous utility; previous productive capability; previous accessibility; previous economic condition; previous operational state; an explicitly defined equivalent value condition.
The target must be measurable or otherwise determinable through an appropriate governed basis.
Restoration Target ≠ Guaranteed Restoration Outcome.
It defines what recovery is being attempted.
Historical State ≠ Mandatory Restoration Target
VRSM does not require restoration to reproduce the exact historical state.
A Value Object may be restored through:
new technology; new operating conditions; different infrastructure; changed market conditions; modified configuration; new access mechanisms.
The restored value may therefore be equivalent in relevant function or value without recreating the original historical configuration.
Restoration Exclusions
A strong restoration scope must identify not only what is included but also what is excluded.
Exclusions may include:
value dimensions not being restored; unrelated Value Objects; newly emerging value; future speculative value; unsupported historical value claims; value belonging to another context; value outside the restoration period; improvements beyond the restoration target.
Explicit exclusions prevent scope expansion after the restoration process begins.

Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Potential
VRSM may identify a value as potentially recoverable.
This does not establish that restoration is possible or justified.
Therefore:
Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Eligibility.
Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Conditions.
Restoration Scope ≠ Restored Value.
VRCM subsequently determines the conditions under which the scoped value may legitimately be restored.
Restoration Scope ≠ Value Development Scope
VRSM must prevent ordinary growth from being classified as restoration.
Suppose an asset currently possesses positive value of 70 and historically possessed value of 100.
An intervention increases its value to 120.
The movement may contain two different value processes:
70 → 100 = potentially restored value
100 → 120 = potentially developed or newly emerged value
The exact classification depends upon the governed value basis.
VRSM provides the scope boundary needed to separate them.
Restoration Scope and ZVA™
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may enter VRSM where previously existing value has reached a governed zero-value state while restoration potential remains.
VRSM must identify:
which previous value reached zero
and:
which value is now proposed for restoration.
The existence of the underlying object alone does not establish restoration scope.
The relevant value relationship must remain identifiable.
Scope Revision
Restoration scope may require revision where new information establishes that:

prior value was incorrectly identified; the affected value dimension differs; additional impairment exists; restoration dependencies changed; the object boundary changed; the restoration target changed; contextual conditions changed; previously assumed value never existed; part of the expected restored value is actually new Value Emergence.
Scope revision must remain documented rather than silently changing the restoration basis.
Boundary with VRCM
VRSM determines:
what value is proposed for restoration.
VRCM determines:
under what conditions that value may legitimately be restored.
Therefore:
Scope ≠ Conditions.
Boundary with VRMM
VRSM establishes the restoration target and boundary.
VRMM governs the ReMonet™ mechanism through which restoration occurs.
Therefore:
Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Mechanism.
Boundary with VRDM
VRSM defines what restoration is attempting to recover.
VRDM determines whether the scoped value was actually restored.
Therefore:
Restoration Target ≠ Restoration Determination.
Boundary with VRTRM
VRSM establishes the initial restoration boundary.
VRTRM governs the formal transition of legitimately restored value into its resulting Value State.
Therefore:
Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Transition.
Boundary with Value Development
Value Development governs strengthening, maturation, growth, or compounding of existing positive value.
VRSM governs the scope of recovery of previously impaired value.
Therefore:

Existing Value Growth ≠ Previously Lost Value Recovery.
Boundary with Value Emergence
Where no relevant prior value existed, restoration cannot be established merely because new value later appears.
Therefore:
New Value ≠ Restored Value.
VRSM protects this distinction by requiring a traceable prior-value basis.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify the Value Object
Define the object carrying the value proposed for restoration.
2. Establish Prior Value
Identify the relevant previously existing value.
3. Establish Prior Value State
Determine the historical state or reference basis where available.
4. Identify Impaired Value
Determine what value became degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, impaired, or zero.
5. Define Value Dimension
Specify the exact value dimension or dimensions within scope.
6. Define Context
Establish the market, jurisdiction, operational environment, technology environment, or other relevant context.
7. Define Restoration Target
Specify the value condition restoration is intended to recover.
8. Establish Exclusions
Identify what value, dimensions, objects, contexts, or improvements remain outside scope.
9. Establish Temporal Boundary
Define the relevant restoration period where materially applicable.
10. Record Governed Restoration Scope
Create a persistent record of the approved restoration boundary before downstream restoration governance proceeds.

VRSM may produce:

Value Restoration Scope Record Prior Value Identification Record Prior Value State Reference Affected Value Record Value Dimension Scope Value Object Boundary Record Restoration Context Record Restoration Target Statement Restoration Exclusion Record Temporal Restoration Boundary Partial Restoration Scope ZVA™ Restoration Scope Record Governed Restoration Scope
These outputs provide the governed input for:
VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module.
Use Case 1 — Restoring a Zero-Value Industrial
Asset
A specialized production line previously generated substantial productive and economic value.
A technological shift makes its original production function commercially obsolete.
The machinery remains physically intact, but its relevant productive value reaches zero and the asset enters a ZVA™ state.
Several years later, a new manufacturing process can reuse approximately 70% of the existing equipment.
Before deciding whether ReMonet™ can occur, VRSM establishes exactly what is being proposed for restoration.
It separates:
physical asset existence
from:
previous productive value
and defines:
Value Object: existing production line Prior Value: productive manufacturing capability Current Condition: zero productive value in the original context Restoration Dimension: productive and operational value Restoration Target: recovery of reusable productive capability Excluded: entirely new capabilities created by newly installed technology

This prevents the organization from treating every future improvement to the facility as restored value.
VRSM establishes which portion represents recovery of previously existing value and which portion must be governed separately as new value.
Use Case 2 — Recovering Dormant Value from
Historical Data
An organization holds twenty years of industrial operating data.
The dataset previously supported engineering and operational decisions, but changes in systems and analytical methods gradually make much of it inaccessible and practically unusable.
Its informational potential remains, but its active operational value becomes dormant.
A new AI-based analytical capability later makes the historical dataset usable again.
VRSM does not immediately classify the resulting opportunity as restored value.
It first defines the restoration scope:
Value Object: historical industrial dataset Prior Value: operational and informational utility Impaired Condition: practical inaccessibility and analytical dormancy Restoration Dimension: recoverable informational utility Restoration Context: defined industrial analytics environment Restoration Target: recovery of usable historical information Excluded: new predictive capabilities created solely by the AI system
This separation is critical.
The historical information that becomes usable again may constitute:
Restored Value.
Predictive capabilities that never previously existed may constitute:
New Value Emergence.

VRSM establishes the boundary before the two forms of value become mixed.
Enterprise Application
VRSM enables organizations to define exactly what they are attempting to recover before investing resources into restoration.
This can be applied to:
distressed industrial assets; infrastructure rehabilitation; legacy software; historical data; dormant intellectual property;
abandoned projects; impaired investments; unused licenses; obsolete technologies; organizational capabilities; digital assets; inactive production capacity.
The Module prevents organizations from combining restoration, development, new value creation, and speculative future value into one undefined recovery claim.
It creates a precise starting point for determining:
what value existed, what was lost, what remains recoverable, and what exactly is being proposed for restoration.
Foundational Principles
Restoration requires an identifiable relationship to previously existing value.
No identifiable prior value means no established restoration scope.
Restoration of one value dimension does not establish restoration of the entire Value Object.
Restoration of one component does not establish restoration of the whole system.
Contextual restoration is not universal restoration.
A Restoration Target is not a Restoration Determination.
Restoration Scope is not Restoration Potential.
Restoration Scope is not ReMonet™.
New Value Emergence must remain distinguishable from recovery of previously existing value.

The value proposed for restoration must be bounded before the mechanism intended to restore it is governed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value Restoration Scope Module establishes the first control point of Value Restoration by identifying and bounding the precise previously existing value proposed for recovery. Through governance of prior value, prior Value State, Value Object boundaries, affected value, value dimensions, restoration context, temporal scope, restoration targets, exclusions, partial restoration, and the distinction between restored and newly emerging value, VRSM prevents restoration from becoming an undefined claim that value has simply returned. By establishing exactly what value is being recovered before restoration conditions, ReMonet™, restoration determination, or transition are considered, VRSM creates the governed foundation upon which the entire Value Restoration process depends.

Canonical Definition
Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
VRTRM governs the formal transition through which value that has been determined as legitimately restored is transferred from its prior degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition into a new governed Value State.
The Module establishes the transition boundary between:
Restoration Determination
and
Resulting Value State.
VRTRM does not determine whether restoration occurred. That determination belongs to VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module.
Its function is:

to ensure that determined restored value enters the value lifecycle through an explicit, traceable, bounded, and governable transition rather than appearing as an unexplained new Value State.
Architectural Position
VRTRM is the fifth and final module within VRSS.
It follows:
VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module.
The preceding modules establish:
restoration scope
→ restoration conditions
→ ReMonet™ mechanism
→ restoration determination.
VRTRM then governs:
the formal transition of determined restored value into its resulting Value State.
Internal Flow
Value Restoration Determination → Pre-Transition Value State Identification → Restored Value Identification → Transition Basis Confirmation → Transition Boundary Definition → Resulting Value Condition Identification → Transition Execution → Resulting Value State Entry
→ Transition Record
Operational Space
VRTRM governs the space between:
value determined as restored
and
value formally recognized in its resulting governed state.
Its operational space includes:
restoration determination receipt; pre-transition Value State; restored-value identity; transition eligibility; transition basis; transition conditions; transition boundaries; partial restoration transitions; conditional restoration transitions; temporary restoration transitions; zero-to-positive transitions; degraded-to-improved transitions;

dormant-to-active transitions; inaccessible-to-accessible transitions; restored-value separation; resulting Value State entry; transition timestamp; transition provenance; transition record; downstream Value State governance.
Restoration Determination ≠ Restoration
Transition
VRTRM establishes a fundamental distinction:
Determination ≠ Transition.
VRDM may determine that value has been restored.
That determination does not itself update the governed lifecycle state.
VRTRM controls the formal movement from the previous condition into the resulting Value State.
This prevents a restoration assessment from silently rewriting the lifecycle record.
Transition Eligibility Principle
A restoration transition should occur only where a valid restoration determination exists.
The transition basis should establish, where materially relevant:
what value was restored; what prior value condition existed; what restoration determination was issued; what extent of value was restored; whether restoration is partial; whether restoration is conditional; whether restoration is temporary; what limitations remain; what resulting Value State is appropriate.
Therefore:
Restoration Attempt ≠ Transition Eligibility.
Pre-Transition Value State
VRTRM requires the value condition immediately preceding transition to remain identifiable.
The pre-transition state may represent:
Degraded Value
Dormant Value
Impaired Value
Inaccessible Value
Lost Value
or
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
where applicable.

This creates continuity between the historical value condition and the restored state.
Resulting Value State
Every completed restoration transition must produce or enter a defined resulting Value State.
The resulting state may represent:
partially restored value; conditionally restored value; temporarily restored value; substantially restored value; fully restored value; another governed positive-value condition.
The resulting Value State itself is governed under:
Value State Standard (VSS).
VRTRM governs the transition into that state.
It does not replace VSS.
Zero-to-Positive Transition
One of the most important transitions governed by VRTRM is:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → Positive Value State
where legitimate restoration has occurred.
This transition demonstrates why:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
A zero-value condition may preserve restoration potential.
Where ReMonet™ successfully restores recoverable value and VRDM determines that restoration occurred, VRTRM formally governs the return from zero to positive value.
Degraded-to-Restored Transition
Value does not need to reach zero before restoration occurs.
Example:
Prior Value = 100
Degraded Value = 35
Restored Value = 75
VRTRM governs:
35 → 75
as the formal restoration transition.
The remaining difference:
75 → 100
does not invalidate the transition.
The resulting Value State simply reflects partial restoration.
Dormant-to-Active Transition
Value may continue to exist while becoming dormant.
Examples may include:

unused intellectual property; inaccessible data; inactive productive capacity; temporarily unusable infrastructure; dormant rights; inactive organizational capability.
Where the value becomes usable again through a governed restoration process, VRTRM may govern:
Dormant Value → Active Restored Value.
Partial Restoration Transition
Where VRDM determines only partial restoration, VRTRM must preserve that limitation.
A partially restored value must not transition into a state implying complete recovery.
Therefore:
Partial Restoration Determination → Partial Restored Value State.
The transition must carry forward the unresolved value deficit where materially relevant.
Conditional Restoration Transition
Where restored value depends upon defined conditions, those conditions must survive the transition.
For example:
Conditionally Restored Value
may depend upon:
restricted operating conditions; continued maintenance; external infrastructure; temporary authorization; specific environmental conditions; continuing data access; limited technical configurations.
VRTRM must prevent:
Conditional Restoration
from becoming:
Unconditional Value State
merely through transition.
Temporary Restoration Transition
Restoration may be explicitly temporary.
VRTRM must therefore preserve:
temporal limitation; review date; expiry condition; triggering event; expected degradation; required reassessment;
where applicable.
A temporary restoration transition may establish:

Zero / Degraded Value → Temporarily Restored Value.
If the temporary basis later expires, a new governed value event must be recognized.
Transition Boundary
The restoration transition must have a defined boundary.
The boundary identifies where:
the prior value condition ends
and
the restored Value State begins.
Depending upon the value context, this boundary may be established through:
timestamp; threshold achievement; operational activation; restoration acceptance; verified capability recovery; access restoration; legal effectiveness; technical commissioning; functional recovery; another governed transition event.
Transition Threshold
Where a threshold is required, VRTRM may use a defined transition threshold.
The threshold should represent the minimum condition necessary for the restoration determination to become operationally reflected in the Value State.
A transition threshold must not be invented merely for administrative convenience.
It must correspond to the governed restoration basis.
Transition Execution
Transition execution is the formal act through which the value lifecycle record recognizes the restoration outcome.
Execution may include:
state update; asset record update; lifecycle record update; value classification update; operational status update; registry update; system-of-record update; activation of restored-value status; another governed state-recognition mechanism.
VRTRM does not prescribe one technical implementation.

It governs the methodological requirements of the transition.
Transition Continuity
A restoration transition must preserve lifecycle continuity.
The lifecycle should remain capable of showing:
Previous Value State
→ Restoration Process
→ Restoration Determination
→ Restoration Transition
→ Resulting Value State.
The restored state must therefore not erase the fact that degradation, dormancy, nullification, or another impairment previously occurred.
Historical State Preservation
Restoration does not rewrite history.
Where value was previously:
degraded
dormant
impaired
or
zero
that historical condition remains part of the governed lifecycle.
VRTRM therefore requires:
New State ≠ Erasure of Prior State.
Restored Value Identity
VRTRM must preserve the relationship between restored value and the value that previously existed.
This is essential because restoration is fundamentally different from new Value Emergence.
The transition record should therefore preserve sufficient identity continuity to establish:
what value returned.
Where identity continuity cannot be established, the resulting value may require treatment as newly emerged value rather than restored value.
Restoration Transition ≠ Value Emergence
VRTRM governs return of previously existing value.
It does not govern the first legitimate appearance of new value.
Therefore:
Previously Existing Value → Recovery → Restoration Transition
is distinct from:
No Prior Value → Value Emergence.

Restoration Transition ≠ Value Development
A restoration transition may place an asset into a positive Value State from which further development occurs.
Example:
Degraded Value = 30
→ Restored Value = 80
→ Developed Value = 120
VRTRM governs:
30 → 80.
Value Development governs:
80 → 120.
This boundary prevents growth following restoration from being retroactively classified as restoration.
Restoration Transition ≠ Value Change
Governance
Every restoration transition represents a change in value.
But VRTRM governs a specific lifecycle transition:
recovery of previously impaired value into a resulting Value State.
The broader fact and character of value change remain governed through the Value Change Standard (VCS).
Restoration Transition ≠ Nullification Reversal
A restoration transition from zero value does not invalidate the previous nullification.
If value legitimately reached zero, that historical state remains valid.
The lifecycle may therefore contain:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Positive Value.
The restoration does not mean the nullification never occurred.
Restoration Transition ≠ Extinction Reversal
VRTRM cannot reverse a legitimate Value Extinction determination within the same governed value lifecycle.
Where value has reached:
Value Extinction
the relevant value is no longer considered recoverable within that lifecycle.
Therefore:
Value Extinction → ReMonet™ → Restoration

is not a legitimate restoration pathway within the same governed lifecycle.
If value later appears, it requires assessment as a new value event.
Transition Failure
A valid restoration determination does not guarantee that the corresponding transition will be successfully executed.
Transition failure may occur because of:
missing state authority; unresolved identity; conflicting lifecycle records; incomplete transition conditions; technical record failure; contradictory determination; unavailable system-of-record; unresolved boundary conditions.
VRTRM must therefore distinguish:
Restoration Determined
from
Restoration Transition Completed.
Pending Transition
Where restoration has been determined but the state transition has not yet legitimately occurred, the Module may establish:
Pending Restoration Transition.
This prevents premature state recognition while preserving the valid restoration determination.
Transition Rejection
A proposed transition may be rejected where:
no valid restoration determination exists; the determination applies to another Value Object; transition conditions are unmet; the proposed resulting state exceeds the restoration determination; the restoration basis has materially changed; required lifecycle continuity cannot be established; extinction has already been legitimately determined.
A rejected transition does not automatically invalidate the restoration process.
It means the proposed lifecycle transition cannot currently be governed as legitimate.

Transition Record
Every material restoration transition should create a reconstructable record.
The record may contain:
Value Object identity; prior Value State; restoration determination reference; restored-value identity; restoration extent; transition conditions; transition boundary; transition threshold where applicable; transition time; resulting Value State; remaining limitations; uncertainty; transition authority where externally governed; transition status; relevant provenance.
Transition States
VRTRM may recognize minimum transition states such as:
1. Not Eligible
No sufficient governed basis exists for restoration transition.
2. Pending
A restoration determination exists, but transition requirements remain incomplete.
3. Conditional Transition
Transition is legitimate only under explicitly defined conditions.
4. Temporary Transition
Transition establishes a temporally bounded restored Value State.
5. Completed
The determined restored value has formally entered its resulting Value State.
6. Rejected
The proposed transition does not satisfy the governed transition requirements.
These are transition states, not Value States.
VRTRM Boundary with VRDM
VRDM determines:
whether value has been restored.
VRTRM determines:
whether and how that determined restoration enters the governed value lifecycle as a state transition.
Therefore:
Restoration Determination ≠ Restoration Transition.
VRTRM Boundary with VSS
VRTRM governs:
movement into the resulting Value State.
VSS governs:

what the resulting current Value State is.
Therefore:
Transition Governance ≠ State Governance.
VRTRM Boundary with VDS
VRTRM governs restoration.
VDS governs subsequent development of existing value.
A restored asset may immediately become subject to Value Development after its restoration transition, but the two lifecycle events must remain distinguishable.
VRTRM Boundary with VNS
VNS governs transition of existing positive value into a zero-value condition.
VRTRM may govern a later legitimate restoration from ZVA™ where recoverability remains.
Therefore:
Nullification and Restoration are distinct lifecycle transitions, not cancellation operations.
VRTRM Boundary with VXSS
VXSS governs terminal Value Extinction.
VRTRM cannot be used to bypass a legitimate extinction determination.
This maintains the architectural distinction:
Zero Value may remain recoverable.
Extinguished Value does not remain recoverable within the governed lifecycle.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Receive Restoration Determination
Receive the governed restoration determination from VRDM.
2. Identify Pre-Transition State
Establish the Value State or value condition immediately preceding restoration transition.
3. Confirm Restored Value
Identify the value determined as restored and its relationship to previously existing value.
4. Confirm Transition Eligibility
Verify that the restoration determination and transition conditions support formal state movement.
5. Define Transition Boundary

Establish when or under what governed condition the restoration transition occurs.
6. Preserve Conditions
Carry forward partial, conditional, temporary, uncertain, or otherwise material limitations.
7. Execute Transition
Formally recognize the movement from the previous condition into the resulting Value State.
8. Establish Resulting State Entry
Transfer the restored value into Value State governance under VSS.
9. Preserve Lifecycle Continuity
Maintain the relationship between prior state, restoration process, determination, transition, and resulting state.
10. Create Transition Record
Create a reconstructable record of the completed, pending, conditional, temporary, rejected, or otherwise governed transition.
Governance Outputs
VRTRM may produce:
Restoration Transition Eligibility Record Pre-Transition Value State Record Restored Value Identity Record Restoration Transition Basis Restoration Transition Boundary Restoration Transition Condition Record Partial Restoration Transition Record Conditional Restoration Transition Record Temporary Restoration Transition Record Pending Restoration Transition Record Restoration Transition Rejection Record Restoration Transition Completion Record Resulting Value State Entry Value Restoration Transition Record
Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset Returned from
Zero Value
A production asset has lost all economically usable productive value and has legitimately entered:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™.

The physical asset still exists and retains recoverability.
A ReMonet™ program replaces obsolete controls, repairs critical components, restores certification requirements, and returns the equipment to productive operation.
VRDM determines that meaningful productive value has legitimately returned.
VRTRM then governs the formal lifecycle transition:
ZVA™
→ Restoration Determination
→ Restoration Transition
→ Positive Value State.
The transition record preserves the previous zero-value condition rather than deleting it.
The lifecycle can therefore show that the asset:
possessed value
→ lost value
→ reached zero
→ retained restoration potential
→ was restored
→ returned to positive value.
This creates a governable value history rather than a sequence of disconnected valuations.
Use Case 2 — Dormant Intellectual Property
Reactivated
A company owns intellectual property that historically generated substantial value but has remained commercially dormant for years.
The underlying rights continue to exist, but the asset no longer generates meaningful operational or commercial value.
A new technological environment creates an opportunity to reactivate the intellectual property.
Following a governed ReMonet™ process, the organization establishes new licensing capability and VRDM determines that part of the previously dormant economic value has legitimately been restored.
VRTRM does not classify the asset simply as:
valuable again.
It governs the transition:
Dormant Value

→ Partially Restored Value
and preserves:
the previous dormant condition
the restoration determination
the transition basis
the remaining limitations
the resulting Value State.
If the intellectual property subsequently generates additional value beyond the restored historical value relationship, that additional increase can enter Value Development rather than being indefinitely attributed to restoration.
Enterprise Application
VRTRM provides organizations with the lifecycle control required to convert a restoration determination into a formally recognized Value State.
It can be applied across:
industrial asset recovery; infrastructure rehabilitation; distressed assets; dormant intellectual property; digital asset recovery; legacy-system restoration; data recovery; productive-capacity restoration; operational restart; impaired investments;
rights restoration; capability recovery; asset reactivation; technological rehabilitation.
The Module prevents restored value from appearing in organizational records without a governed relationship to:
where the value came from
what happened to it
how restoration was determined
and
when the restored state legitimately began.
Foundational Principles
Restoration Determination is not Restoration Transition.
Restoration Transition is not Value State governance.
A restoration attempt does not create transition eligibility.
A restored Value State must remain connected to the value condition from which it emerged.

Partial restoration must not transition into a state implying full restoration.
Conditional restoration must remain conditional after transition.
Temporary restoration must remain temporally bounded.
Restoration does not erase prior degradation or nullification.
Zero Value may transition back to positive value where restoration potential remains.
Value Extinction cannot be reversed through restoration within the same governed lifecycle.
Restored value must remain distinguishable from newly emerged value.
Value created beyond restoration must remain distinguishable from Value Development.
Every material restoration transition should preserve lifecycle continuity.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Restoration Transition Module establishes the final transition layer of the Value Restoration Standard by governing how value formally moves from a degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition into a resulting governed Value State after restoration has been legitimately determined. Through transition eligibility, pre-transition state identification, restored-value identity, transition boundaries, partial, conditional and temporary transitions, zero-to-positive recovery, lifecycle continuity, historical-state preservation, transition execution, resulting-state entry, failure, rejection, and transition records, VRTRM ensures that restored value does not simply reappear within the lifecycle without a governed explanation of how and when that change occurred. By separating Restoration Determination from Restoration Transition and Restoration Transition from Value State governance, the Module preserves the architectural boundaries between VRSS, VSS, VDS, VNS, and VXSS. VRTRM therefore completes the restoration pathway by ensuring that recovered value enters its new governed state without erasing the history, conditions, limitations, or value relationships that make that restoration legitimate.
