Canonical Definition
Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) is the tenth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately re-emerge as governed value.
VRSS establishes the methodological structure through which a prior Value State is identified, the recoverable value scope is bounded, restoration conditions are established, the ReMonet™ mechanism is governed, restoration is determined, and the resulting transition into a restored Value State is formally recorded.

The Standard distinguishes restoration of previously existing value from creation of new value and development of value that already remains positively present.
Its foundational rule is:
Value Restoration requires a governed relationship between previously existing value, its impairment or loss, the mechanism enabling recovery, and the value that subsequently re-emerges.
Core Question
How can degraded, lost, dormant, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored?
Architectural Position
VRSS occupies the tenth governed space within VFM®.
It follows:
Value Nullification Standard (VNS)
and precedes:
Value Extinction Standard (VXSS).
However, restoration is not restricted to value that has passed through complete nullification.
VRSS may receive value from multiple lifecycle conditions:
Degraded Value
Impaired Value
Dormant Value
Lost Value
Inaccessible Value
Zero Value
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
where a legitimate restoration pathway remains available.
This creates an essential architectural distinction:
Value Development = existing positive value develops.
Value Restoration = previously impaired, lost, dormant, degraded, or zero value is recovered.
Governance Flow Position
Prior Value State → Value Impairment / Degradation / Dormancy / Loss / Zero State → Restoration Scope → Restoration Conditions → ReMonet™ Mechanism → Restoration Determination → Restoration Transition → Restored Value
→ New Value State
For a zero-value pathway:

Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value
→ New Value State
VRSS therefore creates a governed recovery pathway inside the value lifecycle.
Operational Space
VRSS governs the space between:
a previously existing value that has become materially impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, degraded, or zero
and
the legitimate re-establishment of that value as a governed positive Value State.
Its operational space includes:
identification of previously existing value; restoration scope; restoration eligibility; recoverability; restoration conditions; restoration dependencies; restoration mechanisms; ReMonet™; partial restoration; dimensional restoration; contextual restoration; temporary restoration; restoration magnitude; restoration determination; restoration transition; restored-state identification; restoration provenance; restoration records; lifecycle continuity.
Restoration Requires Prior Value
VRSS governs restoration only where a legitimate relationship to previously existing value can be established.
Therefore:
Value That Never Existed ≠ Restored Value.
Where value emerges for the first time, the applicable governance belongs to Value Emergence.
Where positive existing value increases, the applicable governance belongs to Value Development.
Where impaired or lost previous value is recovered, VRSS applies.
The distinction is:
No Prior Value → Value Emergence
Existing Positive Value → Value Development

Previously Existing but Impaired/Lost/Zero Value → Value Restoration
Restoration Scope
Before restoration is governed, the exact Restoration Scope must be established.
The scope should identify, where materially applicable:
Value Object; previous Value State; affected value dimension; Value Context; value component; impairment or loss condition; restoration target; temporal scope; restoration boundary; dependencies; exclusions.
This prevents an improvement in one dimension from being represented as restoration of the entire value object.
Restoration Eligibility
Not every impaired or zero-value object is necessarily restorable.
VRSS therefore requires a governed distinction between:
Restoration Possible
Restoration Conditional
Restoration Currently Unsupported
and, where VXSS independently establishes it:
Value Extinct.
Restoration eligibility may depend upon:
continued object existence; retained identity; retained rights; technical recoverability; economic feasibility; legal permissibility; operational accessibility; restoration capability; availability of dependencies; recoverable information; recoverable functionality; recoverable demand; recoverable utility.
Eligibility does not establish successful restoration.
It establishes whether a legitimate restoration pathway remains available.
Restoration Conditions
VRSS requires the conditions necessary for restoration to be explicitly identified.
These may include:

repair; reactivation; reconfiguration; reconstruction; technological improvement;
infrastructure recovery; dependency restoration; rights restoration; market recovery; regulatory change; data recovery; capability recovery; demand recovery; access recovery; ownership clarification; environmental change; operational reintegration.
Restoration conditions establish what must become true before previously impaired value can legitimately re-emerge.
ReMonet™
VRSS is the architectural home of:
ReMonet™
ReMonet™ is the governed mechanism through which previously existing value that became degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero is restored into a positive governed Value State.
The canonical mechanism is:
Previously Existing Value
→ Value Impairment / Loss / Dormancy / Zero
→ Restoration Conditions
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value
→ New Value State
ReMonet™ must remain broad enough to govern restoration before and after complete nullification.
Therefore:
ReMonet™ ≠ Restoration from Zero Only.
ReMonet™ from Degraded Value
Value does not need to reach zero before restoration becomes possible.
Example:
An industrial asset loses 60% of its operational value because of deterioration.
Repair restores most of the lost capability.
The transition may be:
100 Value
→ Degradation
→ 40 Value
→ ReMonet™
→ 85 Value.
This is restoration because previously existing impaired value has been recovered.
It is not ordinary Value Development.
ReMonet™ from Zero Value

Where value has been nullified, VRSS creates the governed recovery pathway from the zero-value condition.
Canonical transition:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ Zero-Value Condition
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Positive Value
→ New Value State
This establishes one of VFM®'s central lifecycle relationships:
DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are directionally opposite value-transition mechanisms, but they are not automatic reversals of one another.
A prior DeMonet™ event does not guarantee future ReMonet™ eligibility.
Restoration ≠ Reversal
Restoration does not require the Value Object to return to its exact historical state.
A restored object may:
regain only part of its former value; regain value through a different mechanism; operate in a new context; serve a different function; acquire a different value composition; regain one value dimension but not another.
Therefore:
Restoration ≠ Exact Historical Reversal.
The legitimate question is whether previously impaired or lost value has been recovered—not whether history has been perfectly reconstructed.
Partial Restoration
VRSS supports restoration of only part of previously lost value.
Example:
Prior Value = 100
→ Degraded Value = 20
→ Restored Value = 65.
The object has experienced legitimate restoration even though its former value has not been fully recovered.
VRSS must therefore distinguish:
Partial Restoration
from:
Full Restoration.
Full Restoration

Full restoration occurs where the relevant previously existing value has been restored to the defined restoration target.
The restoration target may correspond to:
previous value level; previous capability; previous utility; previous economic condition; previous operational condition; another explicitly governed equivalent state.
Full restoration must not automatically imply that every historical property of the object has been restored.
Dimensional Restoration
Value may be restored in one dimension without being restored in another.
For example:
Operational Value: restored
while:
Market Value: remains zero.
Or:
Economic Value: restored
while:
Strategic Value: remains impaired.
VRSS therefore requires restoration determinations to identify the exact value dimension affected.
Restoration in Dimension A ≠ Restoration in All Dimensions.
Contextual Restoration
Value may be restored only within a particular context.
For example:
A technology that became commercially unusable in one jurisdiction may become valuable again after regulatory change.
The restoration may therefore be:
Jurisdiction-Specific
rather than universal.
Similarly:
Market A → Restored Value
while:
Market B → Zero Value.
Context must remain attached to the restoration determination.
Restoration Magnitude
VRSS must preserve the magnitude of restoration where materially relevant.
Restoration magnitude may be expressed through:

absolute restored value; relative restored value; percentage recovery; restored capability; restored utility; restored economic value; restored operational value; restored strategic value; another governed measure.
The architecture does not require one universal valuation method.
It requires the restoration claim to remain tied to a defined basis.
Restoration Determination
Restoration activity alone does not establish restored value.
VRSS distinguishes:
Restoration Attempt
from:
Restoration Determination.
A repair may fail.
A reactivation may not restore utility.
A regulatory change may not restore demand.
A technological upgrade may not restore the affected value dimension.
Therefore:
Restoration Action ≠ Restored Value.
A governed determination must establish whether value actually re-emerged.
Restoration Determination States
A restoration determination may result in:
1. Restoration Not Established
Restoration activity occurred, but recovery of the relevant value has not been established.
2. Partial Restoration
A defined portion of previously impaired or lost value has returned.
3. Conditional Restoration
Value has returned only while specified conditions remain satisfied.
4. Contextual Restoration
Value has returned within a defined context.
5. Full Restoration
The governed restoration target has been satisfied.
6. Restoration Indeterminate
Available information is insufficient to determine whether restoration occurred.

These states prevent binary treatment of complex restoration processes.
Restoration Transition
Once restoration is legitimately determined, VRSS governs the transition into the resulting positive Value State.
The transition is:
Impaired / Dormant / Lost / Zero Value
→ ReMonet™
→ Restoration Determination
→ Restored Positive Value
→ New Value State.
The resulting state then becomes governable under:
Value State Standard (VSS).
New Value State
Restored value must enter a new governed Value State.
The new state should identify, where materially relevant:
Value Object; restored value dimension; restoration magnitude;
Value Context; restoration conditions; effective time; dependencies; remaining impairment; restoration limitations; previous state; ReMonet™ basis.
The new Value State must not erase the restoration history.
Restoration Provenance
Every material restoration should remain traceable to:
Previous Positive Value
→ Impairment / Loss / Dormancy / Nullification
→ Restoration Scope
→ Restoration Conditions
→ ReMonet™ Mechanism
→ Restoration Determination
→ Restoration Transition
→ New Value State.
This enables later analysis of how value was lost and how it returned.
Restored Value May Differ from Historical Value
VRSS recognizes that recovered value may not have the same composition as the original value.
An obsolete industrial building may lose manufacturing value but later recover substantial value after conversion into a data center.

An old dataset may lose immediate commercial value but regain value after new AI capabilities make previously inaccessible information usable.
A dormant patent may regain value after technological change.
In each case, VRSS must distinguish between:
restoration of previously impaired value
and:
emergence of genuinely new value.
Both may occur simultaneously.
Mixed Restoration and Emergence
A single event may produce both restored value and newly emerged value.
Example:
A legacy factory is modernized.
The modernization restores:
previous production capability
while simultaneously creating:
new automation capability that never existed before.
The resulting value should therefore be decomposed:
Restored Value → VRSS
Newly Emerged Value → Value Emergence governance.
This prevents all post-recovery improvement from being mislabeled as restoration.
Restoration and Development May Coexist
After restoration, the recovered value may continue to grow.
Example:
Zero Value
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value = 30
→ Value Development
→ Value = 60.
The first transition belongs to VRSS.
The subsequent growth belongs to VDS.
Therefore:
Restoration Ends Where Development of the Restored Positive Value Begins.
Restoration Potential ≠ Restored Value
A ZVA™ may possess substantial restoration potential.
That potential does not mean value has already been restored.
Therefore:
Restoration Potential ≠ Restoration Determination.

This distinction is essential for dormant technologies, distressed assets, abandoned infrastructure, intellectual property, data, rights, and recoverable capabilities.
Restoration Cost ≠ Restored Value
The resources spent on restoration do not determine the amount of value restored.
An organization may spend:
CHF 10 million
and restore:
CHF 2 million of value.
Or spend:
CHF 1 million
and restore:
CHF 20 million of value.
VRSS therefore distinguishes:
Restoration Input
from:
Restored Value Outcome.
Restoration Activity ≠ Value Creation
Repair, investment, modernization, restructuring, data recovery, technological intervention, or regulatory action may enable restoration.
These activities are not themselves proof that value has returned.
The value consequence must be independently determined.
Restoration Failure
VRSS explicitly recognizes failed restoration.
A restoration process may:
fail completely; restore less value than expected; restore value temporarily; restore one dimension while damaging another; restore functionality without restoring economic value; create new value without restoring the old value; reveal that the value is no longer recoverable.
Failed restoration must remain visible in the lifecycle record.
Repeated Restoration
A Value Object may undergo multiple restoration cycles.
For example:
Positive Value
→ Degradation
→ ReMonet™
→ Restoration
→ New Degradation
→ ReMonet™
→ Restoration.
VRSS therefore supports recursive restoration across the lifecycle.

Each restoration event must retain its own basis and record.
Restoration and Value Extinction
VRSS creates the strongest boundary with VXSS.
A zero-value state may still possess restoration potential.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
VRSS remains available while recoverable value continues to exist within the governed lifecycle.
Once VXSS legitimately determines that the relevant value has become extinct:
ReMonet™ cannot simply be assumed to remain available for that same extinct value.
If value later appears after genuine extinction, governance must determine whether this represents:
new Value Emergence
rather than restoration of the extinct value.
Boundary with VDS
VDS governs:
development of existing positive value.
VRSS governs:
recovery of previously impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, degraded, or zero value.
Therefore:
Growth ≠ Restoration.
Boundary with VDGS
VDGS governs:
decline while positive value remains.
VRSS may begin where intervention reverses or recovers the value lost through degradation.
Therefore:
Degradation → Value Loss
may subsequently become:
ReMonet™ → Value Restoration.
Boundary with VNS
VNS governs the transition of positive value into zero value.
VRSS may govern a subsequent recovery from that zero-value condition.
Therefore:
DeMonet™ → Zero
and
ReMonet™ → Restored Value
are distinct lifecycle mechanisms.
Boundary with VSS
VSS determines the current governed state of value.
VRSS governs the restoration transition.
After restoration:

VRSS → New Value State → VSS.
Boundary with VCS
VCS governs the fact and character of material change to value.
VRSS governs the specific class of change in which previously impaired or lost value is restored.
Therefore:
Every restoration is a Value Change.
But:
Not every Value Change is a Value Restoration.
Boundary with VXSS
VXSS governs the terminal condition in which the relevant value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
VRSS governs value while restoration remains legitimately possible.
Therefore:
Restoration Potential → VRSS remains relevant.
Value Extinction Determined → VRSS no longer governs restoration of that same extinct value.
Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ may govern changes in Operational Reality that enable or prevent restoration.
VRSS governs the value consequence:
whether previously impaired value actually returned.
Boundary with VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may validate evidence, methods, claims, or determinations supporting restoration.
VRSS owns the governed meaning of Value Restoration within VFM®.
Boundary with INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of restoration records, evidence, objects, and supporting information.
VRSS governs the restoration lifecycle itself.
Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit restoration actions, records, determinations, evidence, and transitions.
VRSS defines what constitutes governed Value Restoration.
Parent Standard Modules
1. VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module

Governs identification and bounding of the exact previously existing value proposed for restoration.
It establishes:
what value is being restored, from what prior condition, in which value dimension, and within what context.
2. VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module
Governs the conditions that must exist before legitimate restoration can occur.
It establishes restoration eligibility, dependencies, constraints, prerequisites, and recoverability conditions.
3. VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module
Governs the mechanism through which previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is recovered.
It is the canonical module-level home of:
ReMonet™.
4. VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module
Governs the determination of whether restoration actually occurred and, where applicable, its scope, magnitude, conditions, and completeness.
It separates:
Restoration Activity
from:
Restored Value.
5. VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module
Governs the formal transition from the impaired, dormant, lost, degraded, or zero-value condition into the resulting restored positive Value State.
It preserves lifecycle continuity between:
Previous Value → Loss/Impairment → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State.
Internal Module Flow

Previously Existing Value Basis → VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module → VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module → VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module → VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module → VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module → Restored Value
→ New Value State
The internal logic is:
What value can be restored
→ under what conditions
→ through what restoration mechanism
→ whether restoration actually occurred
→ how restored value enters its new governed state.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Prior Value Identification
Establish that the relevant value previously existed.
2. Restoration Scope
Identify the exact object, dimension, component, context, and prior Value State proposed for restoration.
3. Current Condition
Identify the current degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition.
4. Restoration Eligibility
Determine whether a legitimate restoration pathway remains available.
5. Restoration Conditions
Establish the conditions and dependencies necessary for recovery.
6. ReMonet™ Mechanism
Identify and govern the mechanism through which recovery is attempted.
7. Restoration Evidence
Establish the evidence required to determine whether value actually returned.
8. Restoration Determination
Determine whether restoration is absent, partial, conditional, contextual, full, or indeterminate.
9. Restoration Transition
Govern the transition into the resulting positive Value State.
10. Lifecycle Record

Preserve the complete restoration pathway and resulting state for future governance.
Governance Outputs
VRSS may produce:
Value Restoration Scope Record Prior Value State Record Restoration Eligibility Determination Value Restoration Conditions Record Restoration Dependency Record ReMonet™ Mechanism Record Restoration Attempt Record Restoration Evidence Record Value Restoration Determination Restoration Magnitude Record Restoration Limitation Record Restoration Transition Record Restored Value Record New Value State Record Restoration Provenance Chain
Enterprise Application
VRSS enables organizations to govern something conventional asset systems often treat inconsistently:
the return of value after material impairment or complete loss.
Organizations may use VRSS across:
distressed assets; industrial equipment; infrastructure; intellectual property; data; digital assets; software; AI capabilities; organizational capabilities; technologies; licenses; rights; brands; products; supply-chain capabilities; dormant projects; abandoned assets; recovered resources.
The Standard enables organizations to distinguish whether an intervention:
restored old value
developed existing value
created new value
or merely:
spent resources without restoring value.

This distinction becomes especially important in restructuring, technological recovery, asset reuse, digital transformation, distressed investment, infrastructure rehabilitation, data recovery, IP reactivation, and AI-enabled rediscovery of previously unusable assets.
Foundational Principles
Value restoration requires previously existing value.
Value restoration does not require value to have reached zero first.
ReMonet™ governs restoration from degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value conditions.
Restoration potential is not restored value.
Restoration activity is not restoration determination.
Restoration cost is not restored value.
Partial restoration is legitimate restoration.
Restoration in one dimension does not establish restoration in every dimension.
Restoration in one context does not establish universal restoration.
Restoration does not require exact historical reversal.
Restored value may coexist with newly emerged value.
Restored value may subsequently enter Value Development.
DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are distinct governed value-transition mechanisms.
Zero Value does not prevent restoration.
Value Extinction does.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Restoration Standard establishes the governed recovery layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by defining how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately re-emerge as governed positive value. Through governance of restoration scope, eligibility, conditions, dependencies, ReMonet™, restoration evidence, determination, magnitude, partial and dimensional recovery, contextual restoration, transition, provenance, and the resulting new Value State, VRSS distinguishes genuine recovery from ordinary growth, new Value Emergence, restoration attempts, expenditure, and unsupported claims that value has returned. By allowing restoration both before and after complete Value Nullification, VRSS establishes ReMonet™ as the general governed mechanism of value recovery while preserving the critical boundary that Zero Value remains potentially recoverable whereas Value Extinction represents the terminal loss of recoverability. VRSS therefore ensures that value which disappears from active use, deteriorates, becomes dormant, loses accessibility, or reaches zero does not simply vanish from governance, but remains methodologically traceable through any legitimate pathway by which it may return.

Value State
Canonical Definition
Value State Standard (VSS) governs the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value.
VSS establishes the methodological layer through which an organization can determine not merely whether value exists, but what condition that value currently occupies within a defined context and reference point.
The Standard creates a critical distinction:
Value ≠ Value State
and:
Value State ≠ Value Change
A value can continue to exist while moving through materially different states over time.
Why VSS Matters
Organizations frequently know that an asset, capability, resource, technology, relationship, or other value-bearing object exists, but lack a structured method for determining what state its value is actually in now.
Traditional systems may show that an object:
exists on an asset register; has an accounting value; remains legally owned; has a market price; remains physically available.
None of these facts necessarily establishes its current governed value state.
A machine may still exist but provide zero operational value.

A technology may currently have little commercial value while carrying substantial strategic value.
A capability may temporarily have zero value in one context while remaining highly valuable in another.
VSS makes these distinctions explicit and governable.
Governance Flow
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change
Within VSS:
Governed Value Recognition Record → Value State Identification → Value State Classification → Value State Determination → Value State Transition Readiness → Value State Record → Governed Current Value State
The resulting state becomes the baseline for downstream Value Change Governance.
What VSS Helps Organizations Govern
VSS provides a structured method for answering:
What value is currently present?
What state does that value occupy?
Under what context is that state valid?
At what reference point was the state determined?
What conditions or limitations apply?
Is the state stable or approaching a possible transition?
What evidence supports the current state?
When must the state be reviewed?
This creates a persistent value-state layer rather than treating value as a static number.
Value Asset™
VSS provides the natural governance location for the canonical concept:
Value Asset™

A Value Asset™ represents a governed value-bearing condition in which an identified object, capability, relationship, resource, right, process, system, or other governed basis carries recognized value within a defined VFM® context.
Importantly:
Value Asset™ ≠ Accounting Asset
Value Asset™ ≠ Legal Property
Value Asset™ ≠ Marketable Asset
An organization may therefore identify forms of operational, technological, strategic, informational, infrastructural, or other value that conventional asset classifications do not adequately represent.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
VSS also provides the governance location for:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
ZVA™ represents a governed state in which an identifiable value-bearing object or basis continues to exist while its value within the defined context has reached zero.
This creates several important distinctions:
Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value
Zero Value ≠ Permanent Extinction
Zero Value in Context A ≠ Zero Value in Context B
A ZVA™ may therefore remain identifiable, monitorable, transferable, recoverable, or capable of future value restoration.
Current State Before Change
VSS establishes an essential requirement for the wider VFM® lifecycle:
You cannot govern what changed in value unless you first know what state the value was in.
A value-state record creates that reference baseline.
For example:
State at T₁: Value Asset™ — Active → material event → State at T₂: Value Asset™ — Degraded

VFM® can then govern the difference between the two states through the subsequent Value Change Standard (VCS).
Without VSS, value change can become an assertion without a governed baseline.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Dynamic Collateral and
Enterprise Value State
A bank evaluates a corporate borrower whose balance sheet contains industrial equipment, intellectual property, production capabilities, software, contracts, inventories, and other value-bearing objects.
Conventional financial records may establish accounting values and legal ownership.
But the bank may need a different question answered:
What state is the underlying value actually in today?
A production machine may remain on the balance sheet while being technologically obsolete.
A patent may carry little current revenue but substantial strategic value.
A manufacturing capability may be temporarily inactive but readily recoverable.
Another asset may still physically exist while providing zero value within the operating model for which it was acquired.
VSS allows these conditions to be represented as governed value states rather than forcing every object into a single static valuation view.
The bank can therefore preserve:
Object → Value Context → Recognized Value → Current Value State → State Conditions → Transition Readiness
This does not replace accounting, credit analysis, collateral valuation, or banking regulation.

It provides an additional value-state governance layer through which changing economic and operational conditions can be represented more explicitly.
The bank no longer sees only what the borrower owns. It can govern what state the underlying value is actually in.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Capability Value
Across Mission Phases
A space mission contains thousands of systems, capabilities, resources, technologies, data assets, components, and operational options.
Their value is not constant throughout the mission.
A propulsion capability may carry extremely high value during one mission phase and little operational value after the relevant maneuver is complete.
A backup system may remain dormant for months while carrying substantial contingency value.
A component that has exhausted its original function may enter a ZVA™ state for that mission purpose while remaining valuable for another scientific, technical, recovery, or diagnostic purpose.
VSS allows mission planners to represent:
Mission Phase → Capability → Value Context
→ Current Value State → Dependencies
→ Transition Readiness
This creates a dynamic map of mission value.
The organization can identify capabilities whose value is:
active
conditional
dormant
constrained
degraded
zero
or otherwise classified according to the mission's governed value-state taxonomy.
This can support better resource allocation, redundancy decisions, mission planning, capability preservation, and cost reduction.
Instead of asking only:

“Does this capability still exist?”
mission governance can ask:
“Does this capability still create value for the mission, in what state, and under what conditions?”
Enterprise Value
VSS enables organizations to build a dynamic value-state layer across assets, capabilities, technologies, infrastructure, resources, relationships, digital systems, projects, and other value-bearing objects.
It can reveal situations where:
physical existence ≠ operational value
accounting recognition ≠ current value state
market price ≠ strategic value state
zero current value ≠ permanent value extinction
one object ≠ one universal value state
This makes VSS particularly relevant to banking, investment, industry, public finance, infrastructure, technology portfolios, AI systems, resource management, mission systems, and other environments where value continuously changes.
Foundational Principle
A governed value lifecycle must know the current state of value before it can legitimately determine how that value has changed.

Canonical Definition
Value State Classification Module (VSCM) is the second Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VSCM governs the systematic classification of an identified Value State Candidate into a defined value-state class according to the governed value context, reference point, observed condition, applicable classification criteria, and material limitations.

The Module establishes a common methodological structure through which materially different value conditions can be distinguished without prematurely issuing the final Value State Determination.
Its purpose is to transform:
Identified Value Condition → Governed Value-State Class
while preserving the distinction:
Classification ≠ Determination
VSCM does not determine whether the classified state is formally established.
That function belongs to:
VSDM — Value State Determination Module.
Architectural Position
VSCM is the second module within VSS.
It follows:
VSIM — Value State Identification Module
and precedes:
VSDM — Value State Determination Module.
VSIM establishes:
what current value condition is being examined.
VSCM establishes:
what kind of value state that condition represents.
VSDM subsequently establishes:
whether that state can be formally determined as the governed current Value State.
The sequence is:
Identification → Classification → Determination
Internal Module Flow
Value State Candidate → Value Context Confirmation → Classification Basis Selection → Classification Criteria Application → State Characteristic Assessment → Contextual State Separation → State Class Assignment → Classification Limitation Identification → Classification Record → VSDM — Value State Determination Module
Operational Space
VSCM governs the space between:
an identified current value condition
and
a formally determined current Value State.
Its operational space includes:

value-state taxonomy; classification basis; classification criteria; value-state characteristics; state differentiation; context-specific classification; active value; conditional value; dormant value; constrained value; degraded value; zero value;
negative-value conditions where applicable; recoverable value; state ambiguity; multi-context classification; classification uncertainty; classification limitations; classification traceability.
The classification structure may be adapted to the governed environment while preserving the canonical distinctions established by VFM®.
Classification Basis
Every classification must remain linked to the value context established upstream.
A classification should therefore identify, where applicable:
Governed Value
Value-Bearing Object
Beneficiary
Value Context
Reference Framework
Reference Point
Observed Condition
Classification Criteria
Classification Result
Without these relationships, a value-state label can become detached from the conditions that give it meaning.
Value-State Taxonomy
VSCM permits organizations to establish a governed taxonomy appropriate to their value environment.
A minimum taxonomy may distinguish states such as:
Active Value
Value currently contributes materially within the governed context.
Conditional Value
Value exists, but its realization or usefulness depends upon defined conditions.
Dormant Value
Value exists but is not currently being exercised, utilized, or realized.
Constrained Value

Value exists but material restrictions limit its present realization or use.
Degraded Value
Value remains present but has materially declined relative to the applicable reference condition.
Recoverable Value
Value is not presently realized at its expected level but may be restored through identifiable conditions or actions.
Zero Value
The governed value within the defined context is classified as having reached a zero-value condition.
Where the applicable requirements are subsequently satisfied through VSDM, this classification may support determination of:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
Other Governed State
Organizations may define additional value-state classes where materially necessary.
The taxonomy must remain explicit and interpretable.
Value Asset™ Classification
VSCM provides the classification layer through which a governed value condition may be classified as belonging to a value-bearing state capable of supporting downstream determination as a:
Value Asset™
This classification does not depend solely upon:
accounting recognition; legal ownership; marketability; physical existence; purchase price; book value.
Instead, classification remains connected to the governed VFM® value context.
A capability with no conventional accounting asset entry may therefore still qualify for a value-bearing classification where recognized value exists within the governed context.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Classification
VSCM provides the classification pathway for a potential:

ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A zero-value classification means that the governed value has reached zero within the specific defined context and reference point.
It does not automatically mean that:
the underlying object has ceased to exist.
It does not automatically mean that:
the object has zero value in every context.
It does not automatically mean that:
the state is permanent.
It does not automatically mean that:
the object should be disposed of.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence
Zero Value ≠ Universal Worthlessness
Zero Value ≠ Disposal Requirement
Zero Value ≠ Permanent State
This distinction is fundamental to VFM®.
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value
VSCM must preserve a further distinction:
Zero Value
and
Negative Value
are not necessarily the same state.
An object may create no positive value within a context while imposing:
maintenance cost; storage cost; energy consumption; regulatory burden; operational burden; risk; disposal cost; capital lock-up; infrastructure burden.
Where an organization chooses to govern negative-value conditions, they must remain distinguishable from the canonical zero-value condition.
This prevents:
no value
from being confused with:
value destruction or burden.
Dormant Value ≠ Zero Value
A dormant capability may not currently generate observable operational output.
That does not establish zero value.
For example:
Emergency Backup System
may remain unused for years while carrying substantial contingency value.
Likewise:
Unused Patent

may carry strategic or defensive value despite generating no current licensing income.
Therefore:
Non-Use ≠ Zero Value
and:
No Current Revenue ≠ Zero Value
VSCM requires the relevant value context to decide which classification is appropriate.
Constrained Value ≠ Degraded Value
A value may remain fundamentally intact while its realization is externally constrained.
For example:
a production capability may remain technically functional but unavailable because of:
regulatory restriction; missing input; temporary infrastructure failure; contractual limitation; market access restriction.
This may support:
Constrained Value
rather than:
Degraded Value.
By contrast, degradation concerns deterioration in the value condition itself relative to the governed reference.
This distinction can be operationally significant because the restoration pathway may be completely different.
Conditional Value
Conditional value exists where the value-bearing condition depends materially upon identifiable circumstances.
Examples may include:
Technology valuable only if regulatory approval occurs
Mineral resource valuable only if extraction becomes economically viable
Digital capability valuable only within a compatible ecosystem
Contractual right valuable only upon occurrence of a defined event
VSCM preserves those conditions as part of the classification.
A conditional state must not be represented downstream as unconditional value.
Recoverable Value

Recoverable value is particularly important where current underperformance does not imply permanent value loss.
A machine may currently be unusable but repairable.
A customer relationship may be inactive but recoverable.
A technological capability may become relevant after system reconfiguration.
A data asset may be unusable until missing metadata or permissions are restored.
Classification as recoverable value enables organizations to distinguish:
value that has disappeared
from
value whose realization is temporarily interrupted.
Multi-Context Classification
The same value-bearing object may occupy multiple value-state classes simultaneously across different governed contexts.
For example:
Legacy Industrial Machine
may be:
Zero Value — Current Production Context
while simultaneously:
Active Value — Spare Parts Context
and:
Conditional Value — Resale Context
and:
Strategic Value — Emergency Capacity Context
VSCM therefore prohibits universalizing a context-specific classification without a governed basis.
The canonical rule is:
One Object ≠ One Universal Value State
Multi-Beneficiary Classification
Value state may also differ according to beneficiary.
An asset may have:
low value to Organization A
while having:
high value to Organization B.
A technology abandoned by one enterprise may be strategically valuable to another.
A dataset may have limited internal value but substantial research value to a different beneficiary.

Where beneficiary materially affects value state, VSCM preserves that distinction.
Classification Granularity
Classification must occur at a level appropriate to the governed value.
For example:
Factory
may remain a Value Asset™ overall.
Yet:
Production Line 4
may contain degraded value.
Within that line:
Machine 12
may be a potential ZVA™.
Within that machine:
Control Unit
may remain independently recoverable or transferable.
VSCM prevents higher-level value from automatically masking lower-level zero or degraded value.
It equally prevents one lower-level failure from automatically determining the value state of the entire system.
Classification Criteria
Organizations implementing VSCM should establish explicit criteria for each state class.
Criteria may consider:
current value contribution; operational usability; beneficiary relevance; realization conditions; utilization; functional capability; recoverability; strategic relevance; economic relevance; technological relevance; constraints; dependency availability; deterioration; substitution; temporal relevance; cost burden; value realization potential.
Classification criteria must be appropriate to the governed value context.
VFM® does not impose one universal economic formula across every form of value.
Classification Evidence
Classification should be supported by a sufficient basis appropriate to the governed context.
This may include:

operational information; financial information; market information; utilization records; technical assessments; system telemetry; production records; contractual information; strategic assessments; capability records; resource data; external valuation information; governed observations.
VSCM does not own these evidence systems.
It governs their use in supporting value-state classification.
Classification Uncertainty
Where available information supports more than one plausible classification, uncertainty must remain visible.
For example:
Dormant Value?
or:
Zero Value?
may remain unresolved where future usability, strategic relevance, or recoverability is unclear.
VSCM must not force artificial certainty merely because a classification system requires a field to be populated.
Possible treatment may include:
Provisional Classification
Conditional Classification
Multiple Candidate Classes
Unresolved Classification
until sufficient basis exists for downstream determination.
Classification Conflict
Different organizational functions may classify the same value differently.
For example:
Finance: low-value asset
Operations: critical backup capability
Engineering: technologically obsolete
Strategy: essential transition asset
VSCM does not automatically select one organizational view.
It separates the underlying value contexts and determines whether the apparent conflict represents:
different classifications of the same governed value
or

different governed values attached to the same object.
This distinction can eliminate false organizational disagreement.
Classification ≠ Valuation
VSCM does not require every state to have a monetary amount.
Classification may exist independently from monetary valuation.
Therefore:
Value State Class ≠ Price
Value State Class ≠ Market Value
Value State Class ≠ Book Value
Value State Class ≠ Tax Value
A monetary valuation may become relevant through another methodology or system.
VSCM governs the state class of value, not the universal financial amount assigned to it.
Classification ≠ Accounting Treatment
An accounting system may classify an item according to applicable accounting standards.
VSCM does not replace those classifications.
An accounting asset may occupy a zero-value operational state.
A non-capitalized capability may occupy an active strategic-value state.
VFM® therefore creates a value-governance layer capable of operating alongside accounting rather than attempting to become accounting itself.
Classification ≠ Legal Status
VSCM does not determine:
ownership; legal title; regulatory status; tax treatment; contractual enforceability; intellectual-property rights.
Those characteristics may affect value classification where relevant.
They do not become governed by VSCM merely because they influence value.
Classification Stability
A classification should remain valid only while the conditions supporting it remain materially unchanged.

Potential review triggers may include:
operational change; technological change; market change; regulatory change; beneficiary change; context change; restoration; deterioration; new dependency; lost dependency; new evidence; material cost change.
VSCM identifies the classification.
Later modules govern determination, transition readiness, and state recording.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VSCM implementation should establish:
1. Value State Candidate
Receive the identified Value State Candidate from VSIM.
2. Context Confirmation
Confirm the governed value, object, beneficiary, context, and reference point.
3. Classification Taxonomy
Define the state classes available within the governed environment.
4. Classification Criteria
Define the conditions required for each applicable state class.
5. Candidate Assessment
Compare the identified condition against applicable classification criteria.
6. Context Separation
Separate materially different value contexts or beneficiaries where necessary.
7. Classification Assignment
Assign the most appropriate state class or provisional classification.
8. Uncertainty and Limitation
Preserve material uncertainty, competing classifications, and classification limitations.
9. Classification Basis
Record the information and reasoning supporting the classification.
10. Downstream Transfer
Transfer the classified Value State Candidate to VSDM for formal Value State Determination.

VSDM — Value State Determination Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Separating Real
Collateral Value States Before Risk Decisions
A bank finances an industrial enterprise whose collateral pool contains hundreds of machines, technologies, production systems, licenses, inventories, and other value-bearing objects.
A conventional register may show:
Asset exists → Ownership confirmed → Recorded amount available
But these objects may occupy fundamentally different value states.
VSCM can classify them individually:
Machine A → Active Value → currently essential to profitable production.
Machine B → Dormant Value → currently unused but immediately deployable as backup capacity.
Machine C → Constrained Value → functional but unavailable because a critical input is temporarily unavailable.
Machine D → Degraded Value → operational but technologically deteriorated relative to current production requirements.

Machine E → Potential ZVA™ → physically present but carrying zero identified value within the governed production context.
Patent F → Conditional Value → no current revenue but potentially valuable if a planned product receives market authorization.
Instead of treating the collateral base as one homogeneous stock of assets, the bank gains a classified map of the actual states through which underlying value exists.
This can support more precise:
collateral review; credit monitoring; restructuring analysis; recovery planning; portfolio surveillance; early-warning systems.
Most importantly, VSCM can expose a hidden risk:
the legal and accounting asset base may remain relatively stable while the operational value-state composition underneath it is deteriorating.
That divergence may become visible before conventional asset disappearance occurs.
Use Case 2 — Blockchain and Digital Assets:
Separating Token Existence From Actual Value
State
A blockchain ecosystem may contain millions of tokens, digital rights, protocol assets, liquidity positions, smart-contract relationships, digital credentials, or tokenized claims.
The technical existence of these objects is easy to establish.
Their current value state is much harder.
A token may still exist on-chain while:
its underlying service has disappeared.
Another token may have no active market but retain redemption rights.

A digital asset may be temporarily unusable because a bridge, oracle, protocol dependency, or access mechanism is unavailable.
Another may have no present utility but retain strategic governance rights.
A tokenized real-world claim may remain technically transferable while the underlying economic relationship has materially deteriorated.
VSCM can classify these states separately:
Active Value
Conditional Value
Dormant Value
Constrained Value
Degraded Value
Recoverable Value
Potential ZVA™
rather than allowing:
Token Exists
to become equivalent to:
Token Has Current Value.
The classification can remain attached to:
Digital Object → Value Context → Beneficiary → Reference Point → Current Condition → Value-State Class
This creates a powerful governance distinction for digital economies:
technical persistence is not value persistence.
A blockchain may preserve an object's existence indefinitely.
VFM® can separately govern whether the value associated with that object remains active, dormant, constrained, degraded, recoverable, conditional, or zero within the defined context.
Foundational Principles
Identified condition must be classified before the governed state can be formally determined.
Classification is not determination.
Value-state classification is context-specific, not universally transferable.
One object may carry multiple value states across different contexts.
One object may carry different value states for different beneficiaries.

Non-use is not automatically zero value.
Dormant value is not zero value.
Constrained value is not necessarily degraded value.
Zero value is not negative value.
Zero value is not non-existence.
Zero value in one context does not establish zero value in every context.
A Value State is not a price.
A Value State is not an accounting classification.
Technical existence does not establish current value.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value State Classification Module establishes the classification layer of the Value State Standard by transforming an identified Value State Candidate into an explicit, context-bound, criteria-based Value-State Class before formal determination occurs. Through governance of classification taxonomy, state criteria, active, conditional, dormant, constrained, degraded, recoverable and zero-value conditions, multi-context and multi-beneficiary distinctions, granularity, uncertainty, classification conflicts, and the separation of value state from price, accounting treatment, legal status, physical existence, and technical persistence, VSCM creates a common methodological language for distinguishing materially different conditions of value. By preserving the distinctions between dormant and zero value, constrained and degraded value, zero and negative value, and contextual and universal value claims, VSCM provides the classified basis required for VSDM to determine what governed state value actually occupies.

Canonical Definition
Value State Determination Module (VSDM) is the third Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VSDM governs the formal determination of the current governed Value State by evaluating whether a classified Value State Candidate is sufficiently supported, contextually bounded, temporally applicable, and methodologically coherent to become the authoritative state representation of the governed value at the defined reference point.
The Module transforms:
Classified Value State Candidate → Governed Value State Determination

VSDM establishes the point at which a classification ceases to be merely a candidate interpretation and becomes the governed current state used by downstream VFM® processes.
Its foundational distinction is:
Classification ≠ Determination
A value condition may be identified.
It may be classified.
But it must not become the authoritative governed Value State until the basis for that determination is established.
Architectural Position
VSDM is the third module within VSS.
It follows:
VSIM — Value State Identification Module
→ VSCM — Value State Classification Module
and precedes:
VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module.
The internal logic is:
Identify the current condition → Classify the condition → Determine the governed Value State → Assess readiness for subsequent state transition
VSDM therefore represents the formal determination gate within Value State governance.
Internal Module Flow
Classified Value State Candidate → Determination Context Confirmation → Classification Basis Review → Supporting Basis Assessment → Contradiction Review → Uncertainty Review → Temporal Applicability Review → Determination Threshold Assessment → Value State Determination → Determination Status Assignment → VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module
Operational Space
VSDM governs the methodological space between:
a classified value condition
and
an authoritative governed Value State.
Its operational space includes:

determination object; determination context; classification basis review; supporting basis; determination criteria;
determination thresholds; contextual applicability; temporal applicability; contradictory information; uncertainty; determination confidence where used; determination limitations; provisional determination; conditional determination; confirmed determination; indeterminate state; determination suspension; determination withdrawal; determination traceability.
Determination Object
Every VSDM process must identify exactly what is being determined.
The determination object should preserve, where applicable:
Governed Value
Value-Bearing Object
Beneficiary
Value Context
Reference Framework
Reference Point
Observed Condition
Value-State Classification
This prevents a state determination from becoming detached from the value relationship that gives it meaning.
Determination Basis
A Value State Determination must have an identifiable basis.
The basis may include:
VSIM identification records; VSCM classification records; operational information; technical condition; financial information; utilization information; capability information; market information; contractual information; dependency status; resource information; system telemetry; governed observations; relevant external assessments; other context-appropriate information.
VSDM does not require every value type to use the same evidence structure.

It requires the basis to be sufficient for the determination being made.
Determination Threshold
Organizations implementing VSDM should establish the threshold required before a classified candidate becomes a governed Value State.
The threshold may depend upon:
importance of the value; consequence of incorrect determination; operational significance; financial significance; strategic significance; reversibility; uncertainty; available information; decision context.
A low-consequence internal resource may require a relatively simple determination basis.
A value state affecting:
major financing; public infrastructure; critical industrial capacity; investment; mission capability; systemic financial exposure; strategic assets
may require substantially stronger support.
VSDM therefore permits proportional determination governance.
Determination Status
A VSDM implementation may use explicit determination statuses.
1. Indeterminate
Available information does not support a sufficiently grounded determination.
2. Provisional
A state can be determined temporarily, but material uncertainty or missing information remains.
3. Conditional
The determination remains valid only while explicitly defined conditions remain satisfied.
4. Determined
The applicable determination threshold has been satisfied and the classified state becomes the governed current Value State.
5. Suspended
A previously determined state can no longer be relied upon pending reassessment.
6. Withdrawn

The previous determination has ceased to represent the governed current state.
These statuses prevent a binary system from forcing:
determined
or
not determined
where reality is more complex.
Value Asset™ Determination
Where the classified value condition satisfies the applicable determination requirements, VSDM may establish a governed state corresponding to:
Value Asset™
A Value Asset™ represents value that exists and occupies a positively governed value state within the applicable context.
The determination remains tied to:
what value
for whom
in what context
at what reference point
under what conditions
has been determined.
The existence of a Value Asset™ under VFM® does not automatically establish:
legal ownership; accounting recognition; market price; tax treatment; regulatory classification; transferability.
Those questions remain governed by their appropriate systems.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Determination
VSDM provides the formal determination gate for:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A value-bearing object must not become a governed ZVA™ merely because it is:
unused; old; unprofitable; written down; technologically outdated;
temporarily inaccessible; non-revenue-producing; operationally inactive.
The determination must establish that the governed value has reached a zero-value state within the defined context and reference point.
The canonical logic is:

Value-Bearing Object Exists → Relevant Value Context Identified → Current Condition Identified → Zero-Value Classification Candidate → Determination Basis Assessed → Zero-Value State Determined → ZVA™
Therefore:
ZVA™ ≠ Object Non-Existence
and:
ZVA™ ≠ Universal Worthlessness
Zero-State Determination Protection
Because a zero-value determination may trigger significant downstream consequences, VSDM must protect against false zero states.
A zero determination should examine whether relevant value remains through:
another current use; backup function; strategic capability; recoverability; transferability; component value; knowledge value; data value; contingency value; alternative beneficiary; alternative context; future defined use where relevant to the governed context.
This does not mean every hypothetical future possibility prevents a zero-value determination.
It means material existing value must not be ignored merely because the primary use has disappeared.
Unknown ≠ Zero
VSDM preserves one of the most important VSS rules:
Insufficient Information ≠ Zero Value
If the organization cannot establish whether value exists, the appropriate state may be:
Indeterminate
rather than:
ZVA™
This prevents missing information from becoming a mechanism for manufacturing zero-value determinations.
Dormant ≠ Zero
A dormant asset may currently generate no operational output.
Yet its governed value may remain intact.
Examples include:

emergency infrastructure; reserve production capacity; backup computing systems; strategic inventories; unused intellectual property; contingency equipment; inactive but recoverable capabilities.
VSDM must therefore distinguish:
no current utilization
from
no current value.
Recoverable ≠ Zero
A capability that has temporarily lost its ability to generate value may remain recoverable.
For example:
Machine unavailable because one replaceable component failed
is fundamentally different from:
Machine incapable of producing value within the governed context and with no materially relevant recovery pathway.
The first may support a:
Recoverable Value State
rather than a ZVA™ determination.
Negative Value Determination
Where the applicable VFM® implementation governs negative-value states, VSDM must distinguish:
Zero Value
from
Negative Value.
A value-bearing object may impose more burden than the value it produces through:
maintenance; energy; storage; compliance; capital lock-up; operational complexity; environmental burden;
risk exposure; disposal obligation.
That condition must not be hidden inside a zero-value classification where the distinction is materially relevant.
Multi-Context Determination
The same object may receive multiple valid Value State Determinations simultaneously.
For example:
Legacy Data Center
may be determined as:
Degraded Value — Primary Computing Context
Active Value — Backup Capacity Context
Conditional Value — Resale Context

Strategic Value — Business Continuity Context
The determinations are not contradictory where they govern different value relationships.
Therefore:
One Object ≠ One Universal Value State
Multi-Beneficiary Determination
Value may also differ by beneficiary.
A manufacturing tool may have zero production value to one company while carrying active production value to another.
An abandoned technology may have low value to its developer while carrying significant research value to a university.
VSDM must preserve the beneficiary relationship where it materially affects the determination.
Temporal Determination
Every Value State Determination exists relative to a reference point.
A determined state is therefore not automatically permanent.
The same governed value may move through:
Active Value
→ Degraded Value
→ Zero Value
→ Recoverable Value
→ Active Value
as circumstances change.
VSDM determines the current state.
It does not freeze value into that state indefinitely.
State Determination ≠ State Transition
VSDM determines:
what state value currently occupies.
It does not govern:
the mechanism by which value moved into that state.
That distinction is fundamental.
The fact that a machine is currently in a degraded-value state does not require VSDM to govern the technical event that damaged the machine.

Likewise, determining that a digital asset has reached zero value does not require VSDM to govern the external market, legal, technological, or operational event responsible for the change.
Those external mechanisms remain outside the VSDM governed space.
Determination Contradiction
Material contradictory information must be addressed before a final determination where it could alter the result.
For example:
Operations: capability is obsolete.
Engineering: capability remains technically deployable.
Finance: asset is fully depreciated.
Strategy: capability remains essential during transition.
VSDM should first determine whether these statements concern:
the same governed value
or
different value contexts.
Only genuine contradictions within the same governed value relationship require reconciliation at the determination level.
Determination Uncertainty
Uncertainty must remain visible where it materially affects the state determination.
VSDM may preserve uncertainty relating to:
future usability; current capability; dependency availability; market relevance; recoverability; strategic importance; technological condition; beneficiary relevance; data completeness; reference-point accuracy.
A determination may remain provisional or conditional where uncertainty does not justify a fully determined state.
Determination Expiry
A Value State Determination may require expiry or review where the value environment changes rapidly.
An implementation may define:
Review Date
Validity Period

Material Change Trigger
Reassessment Trigger
Examples include:
new market conditions; new technology; restoration; deterioration; regulatory change; beneficiary change; operational reconfiguration; dependency restoration; dependency failure; new evidence.
A determination that no longer represents the governed reality must not remain authoritative merely because it exists in a record.
Determination Authority
Organizations should identify who or what may issue a Value State Determination.
Depending upon context, this may involve:
authorized personnel; defined governance function; automated rules; AI-supported assessment; committee decision; system-generated determination; hybrid human-machine process.
VSDM governs the determination structure.
Where authority, responsibility, accountability, or delegation itself requires governance, the appropriate governance architecture remains responsible for those questions.
Automated Value State Determination
VSDM can operate in automated environments.
A system may continuously receive:
Operational Data
→ Current Condition
→ State Classification
→ Determination Assessment
→ Current Governed Value State
This enables value-state governance to move beyond periodic static reporting.
However, automated determination must preserve:
criteria; reference context; input basis; uncertainty; determination logic; determination timestamp; applicable limitations; state history.
Automation must not turn a contextual Value State into an unexplained label.

Determination Traceability
A governed Value State should be traceable backward through the VSS process.
The minimum chain is:
Governed Value State
→ Determination Basis
→ State Classification
→ State Candidate
→ Observed Condition
→ Reference Point
→ Value Context
→ Governed Value
This creates reconstructability of the state without requiring VFM® to take ownership of the external systems that generated the underlying information.
Determination ≠ Valuation
VSDM does not determine monetary value.
It may determine:
Active Value
Dormant Value
Degraded Value
Zero Value
or another governed state.
It does not automatically determine:
CHF 4.7 million
or another monetary amount.
Therefore:
Value State Determination ≠ Monetary Valuation
A valuation methodology may use the determined state as an input.
Determination ≠ Accounting Recognition
A VSDM determination does not replace accounting standards.
An asset may remain recognized in financial accounts while VSDM determines that its operational value has reached zero within a particular context.
Conversely, an organizational capability may have no separately recognized accounting asset while carrying an active strategic Value State.
This is precisely why the two governance spaces must remain separate.
Determination ≠ Tax Treatment
A governed Value State does not itself establish tax liability, deductibility, taxable value, depreciation treatment, or tax recognition.

However, a future tax architecture may consume VFM® Value State Determinations as governed inputs where legislation or policy chooses to recognize value-state information.
The boundary remains:
VFM® determines the governed Value State.
The tax system determines the legal tax consequence.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VSDM implementation should establish:
1. Classified Candidate Input
Receive the classified Value State Candidate from VSCM.
2. Determination Context
Confirm governed value, object, beneficiary, context, and reference point.
3. Determination Criteria
Define what must be established before the classified state may become authoritative.
4. Supporting Basis Review
Review the information supporting the classified state.
5. Contradiction Review
Identify material conflicting information capable of changing the determination.
6. Uncertainty Review
Identify material uncertainty affecting determination legitimacy.
7. Determination Threshold Assessment
Determine whether the required threshold has been satisfied.
8. Value State Determination
Issue the applicable Value State or preserve an indeterminate, provisional, conditional, suspended, or withdrawn status.
9. Determination Conditions
Record material limitations, validity periods, conditions, or review triggers.
10. Determination Record
Create the governed determination basis for transfer to VSTM.
Governance Outputs
VSDM may produce:

Value State Determination Value State Determination Status Value State Determination Basis Value State Determination Criteria Record Value State Determination Threshold Record Value State Determination Uncertainty Record Value State Contradiction Record Value State Applicability Statement Value State Validity Period Value State Review Trigger Value Asset™ Determination ZVA™ Determination Value State Determination Record
These outputs provide the governed basis for:
VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module.
Use Case 1 — Public Finance and Infrastructure:
Determining Which Assets Still Carry
Operational Value
A government or public infrastructure operator may control thousands of:
buildings; roads; facilities; machines; IT systems; land parcels; equipment; licenses; infrastructure components.
Traditional asset registers can establish that these objects exist and may assign accounting amounts to them.
But they do not necessarily establish the current operational state of the value attached to each object.
VSDM allows the organization to formally determine, within defined contexts:
Active Value
Dormant Value
Constrained Value
Degraded Value
Recoverable Value
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
Consider an unused public building.
Its non-use does not automatically establish zero value.
The building may retain:
Emergency Capacity Value
Alternative Public-Service Value
Rental Value
Redevelopment Value
or
Strategic Land Value.
VSDM prevents a simplistic:
unused → zero value
determination.

But where the relevant value contexts have been examined and the applicable determination threshold establishes that a specific governed value has genuinely reached zero, the organization can create an explicit ZVA™ determination.
Across a large public asset base, this creates the possibility of identifying where resources remain tied to value-bearing objects whose governed value state no longer justifies their continued treatment as productive capacity.
The result can support better:
asset management, capital allocation, maintenance prioritization, infrastructure renewal, reuse analysis, and public spending discipline.
Use Case 2 — AI and Data-Center Infrastructure:
Determining When Computing Capacity Stops
Creating Useful Value
An organization operates a large AI infrastructure environment containing:
GPUs; servers; storage; models; software licenses; datasets; networking capacity; specialized accelerators;
legacy computing systems.
Physical and accounting existence alone does not reveal whether each resource continues to create useful value.
A GPU cluster may remain technically operational while its energy cost, performance profile, software compatibility, workload suitability, or infrastructure requirements make it unsuitable for the governed workload.
Another older cluster may appear obsolete for frontier-model training but remain highly valuable for inference, testing, simulation, or lower-complexity workloads.
VSDM can determine separate states by context:

Cluster A → Active Value — Frontier Training
Cluster B → Zero Value — Frontier Training but → Active Value — Batch Inference
Cluster C → Recoverable Value — Current Workload
Cluster D → Negative Value Candidate — Legacy Infrastructure Context
This prevents organizations from making the expensive mistake of equating:
technological age
with
zero value.
It also prevents the opposite mistake:
physical availability
with
continued productive value.
At infrastructure scale, VSDM can provide a governed state layer showing where computing, energy, capital, cooling, maintenance, and physical space remain attached to resources that no longer create sufficient value within their intended context.
That state information can subsequently support VFM® value-change and transition governance and other architectures concerned with resource allocation, efficiency, investment, or operational optimization.
Foundational Principles
Classification is not determination.
A Value State becomes authoritative only through an explicit determination basis.
Value State Determination must remain bound to value context, beneficiary, and reference point.
Unknown value is not zero value.
Dormant value is not zero value.
Recoverable value is not zero value.
Zero value is not negative value.
Zero value does not mean non-existence.
Zero value in one context does not establish zero value in every context.
One object may legitimately carry multiple Value State Determinations.

A Value State Determination is not monetary valuation.
A Value State Determination is not accounting recognition.
A Value State Determination is not tax treatment.
The current Value State must remain revisable when the reality supporting it materially changes.
Canonical Closing Statement
Value State Determination Module establishes the formal determination gate of the Value State Standard by transforming a classified Value State Candidate into an explicit, context-bound, reference-point-specific, supportable, uncertainty-aware, and reviewable governed Value State. Through governance of determination criteria, supporting basis, thresholds, contradictions, uncertainty, applicability, determination status, temporal validity, authority, traceability, Value Asset™ determination, and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ determination, VSDM prevents classifications, accounting records, physical existence, non-use, technological age, missing information, or assumptions of worthlessness from becoming authoritative statements about the current state of value without a governed basis. By separating Value State Determination from monetary valuation, accounting recognition, tax treatment, external causation, and state transition, VSDM establishes the authoritative current- state layer required before VFM® can determine whether value is ready to move into another governed state.
