Canonical Definition
Value State Identification Module (VSIM) is the first Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VSIM governs the identification of the specific current value condition that must be examined as a Value State Candidate before that condition can be classified, formally determined, assessed for transition readiness, and recorded.
The Module establishes the reference relationship between:
Governed Value → Value Context → Reference Point → Observed Value Condition
→ Value State Candidate

Its purpose is to ensure that value-state governance begins with an explicitly identified condition rather than an assumed, inherited, outdated, or context-free statement about value.
VSIM does not determine the final value state.
It establishes what current value condition is being submitted to state governance.
Architectural Position
VSIM is the first module within VSS.
It receives the governed value basis established through the preceding VFM® lifecycle and creates the state candidate required for subsequent classification.
It precedes:
VSCM — Value State Classification Module
The internal sequence begins:
Governed Recognized Value → VSIM — Value State Identification → VSCM — Value State Classification
The distinction is essential:
Identifying the condition to be governed ≠ determining the final state.
Internal Module Flow
Governed Recognized Value → Value Reference Confirmation → Value Context Confirmation → Reference Point Definition → Current Condition Observation → Condition Boundary Identification → Condition Relevance Assessment → Value State Candidate Identification → Identification Record → VSCM — Value State Classification Module
Operational Space
VSIM governs the point at which an existing governed value becomes the subject of a current-state examination.
Its operational space includes:

value reference confirmation; governed value linkage; value-context linkage; current-condition identification; reference-point identification; temporal reference; operational reference; relevant condition identification; state-candidate creation; state-candidate boundary; context separation; condition observability; uncertainty identification; stale-state detection; conflicting-condition identification; identification traceability.
VSIM answers neither:
“What category does this state belong to?”
nor:
“What is the formally determined state?”
Those questions belong downstream.
Value Reference Confirmation
State identification must begin with a defined governed value.
The Module must therefore establish which value is being examined.
This may be value associated with:
an asset; a capability; a resource;
a technology; a relationship; a right; a process; a system; infrastructure; intellectual property; information; a digital object; an organizational capability; another value-bearing basis.
VSIM does not redefine the value.
It links the state-identification process to the value already established within the VFM® lifecycle.
Value Context Confirmation
The same object may carry different values under different contexts.
Therefore, VSIM must preserve the value context before identifying the state candidate.
For example:
Industrial Robot
may carry:
Production Value
Resale Value
Spare-Part Value
Strategic Capability Value
Training Value

These are not automatically the same governed value.
Consequently, the statement:
“The robot has zero value.”
is insufficient for governed state identification.
VSIM requires the more precise structure:
Value Object: Industrial Robot Value Context: Production Capability Reference Point: Current Production Configuration Observed Condition: Cannot perform required production function
Only then can the relevant Value State Candidate proceed downstream.
Reference Point Definition
A current value condition must be anchored to a defined reference point.
The reference point may be:
current time; reporting date; accounting period;
mission phase; production configuration; system version; project phase; contractual state; market condition; operating environment; infrastructure configuration; technological generation; another governed reference condition.
Without this reference point, the identified state may already be obsolete when it enters downstream governance.
Current Condition Observation
VSIM identifies the observable or otherwise supportable condition of the governed value at the applicable reference point.
The condition may concern:
availability; usability; functionality; demand; utilization; strategic relevance; operational relevance; technological relevance; accessibility; compatibility; recoverability; constraint; inactivity; deterioration; absence of current value; another context-relevant condition.

VSIM does not yet translate the condition into a formal state classification.
It preserves the condition before classification.
Condition ≠ State
A central VSIM distinction is:
Observed Condition ≠ Governed Value State
For example:
“Machine is not currently used.”
is a condition.
It does not automatically mean:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
The machine may remain strategically necessary, readily deployable, valuable as backup capacity, transferable, or useful within another value context.
Likewise:
“Patent generates no current licensing revenue.”
does not automatically establish zero strategic value.
VSIM therefore prevents premature state assignment.
Value State Candidate
A Value State Candidate is the identified current value condition submitted for subsequent classification and determination.
A candidate should preserve, where applicable:
Governed Value Reference
Value Object Reference
Value Context
Beneficiary Context
Reference Point
Observed Condition
Relevant Dependencies
Material Constraints
Available Supporting Basis
Uncertainty
Identification Timestamp
The candidate is not yet the authoritative current value state.
Context Separation Principle
Where the same value-bearing object participates in multiple value contexts, VSIM should identify separate state candidates where materially necessary.
For example:
Technology Platform
may produce:
Commercial Value State Candidate
and separately:
Strategic Technology Value State Candidate
and separately:

Operational Capability Value State Candidate
This prevents one condition from incorrectly propagating across all value contexts.
Current State Identification ≠ Historical State
Historical information may help identify the present condition.
It must not replace it.
A previous record showing:
High Operational Value
does not establish that the same state exists today.
VSIM therefore distinguishes:
Historical Condition
from:
Current Condition Candidate.
This is particularly important in automated systems where old records may otherwise continue to be treated as current truth.
Current State Identification ≠ Predicted State
Forecasts may indicate that a value condition is likely to change.
VSIM does not convert that forecast into a current-state candidate unless the relevant condition actually exists at the applicable reference point.
Therefore:
Expected Future Condition ≠ Current Value Condition
and:
Predicted State ≠ Identified Current State.
Conflicting Conditions
Value-state identification may encounter conflicting information.
For example:
Financial Record: asset remains productive
while:
Operational Record: production capability has been unavailable for six months.
VSIM must preserve the conflict rather than silently selecting the more convenient source.
A conflicting state candidate may proceed with explicit uncertainty or require additional information before classification.
Unknown Condition ≠ Zero Value

Where the current condition cannot be established sufficiently, VSIM must permit an unresolved identification state.
Therefore:
Unknown ≠ Zero
Missing Data ≠ Zero
Unobserved ≠ Zero
Uncertain ≠ ZVA™
This prevents absent information from becoming an artificial zero-value determination.
Stale State Detection
VSIM should identify situations where a previously recorded state may no longer represent the current condition.
Potential stale-state indicators include:
expired reference period; material operational change; technology replacement; market change; contract termination; capability degradation; infrastructure change; new evidence; changed value context; changed beneficiary; restoration event; material external event.
The purpose is not to determine that the old state is wrong.
It is to determine that current-state identification must be performed again.
Multi-Level Identification
State candidates may exist at different organizational levels.
For example:
Component
→ Machine
→ Production Line
→ Factory
→ Enterprise Capability
VSIM must prevent a condition observed at one level from automatically becoming the state of another level.
A failed component does not automatically mean the production line has zero value.
Likewise, a profitable enterprise does not mean every underlying capability is value-producing.
Identification Granularity
VSIM should identify value conditions at the level necessary for meaningful downstream governance.
Excessive aggregation may hide:

dormant value; degraded value; zero-value assets; recoverable capabilities; critical dependencies; unused capacity; value concentration.
Excessive fragmentation may create unnecessary governance complexity.
The identification level should therefore correspond to the intended value-governance purpose.
Identification Basis
A Value State Candidate may be identified using relevant information such as:
operational records; financial information; utilization data; technical condition; system telemetry; market information; contractual information; production data; capability assessments; resource availability; infrastructure status; expert observations; external valuations; governed digital records.
VSIM does not take ownership of those information systems.
It governs how they are connected to the identification of the current value condition.
Identification Uncertainty
VSIM must preserve material uncertainty affecting the identified condition.
Uncertainty may concern:
incomplete information; conflicting information; timing; object configuration; operational availability; market relevance; dependency status; technological condition; context applicability.
A state candidate may remain usable with uncertainty attached.
The uncertainty must not disappear merely because the candidate moves downstream.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VSIM implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Reference
Identify the governed value whose current condition is being examined.

2. Value Object Reference
Identify the value-bearing object, capability, resource, relationship, system, or other basis associated with the value.
3. Value Context Confirmation
Confirm the context within which the current value condition is being identified.
4. Reference Point Definition
Establish the temporal, operational, technological, contractual, mission, or other applicable reference point.
5. Current Condition Identification
Identify the materially relevant present condition of the governed value.
6. Condition Boundary
Determine the level and scope to which the identified condition applies.
7. Supporting Basis
Link the condition to available supporting information.
8. Uncertainty Identification
Record material uncertainty or conflicting information.
9. State Candidate Creation
Create an explicit Value State Candidate without prematurely determining its classification.
10. Identification Record
Preserve the candidate and its governing context for transfer to VSCM.
Governance Outputs
VSIM may produce:
Value State Candidate Value Reference Record Value Context Link Value Object Reference Value State Reference Point Current Value Condition Record Condition Boundary Record Supporting Basis Record State Identification Uncertainty Record Conflicting Condition Record Stale State Indicator Value State Identification Record
These outputs provide the governed input for:
VSCM — Value State Classification Module.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Identifying Hidden Value-

State Risk Before Credit Exposure
A bank has financed an industrial company with a large asset base.
The borrower's financial records still contain machinery, production infrastructure, intellectual property, inventories, software systems, and other assets with substantial recorded values.
A conventional portfolio view may therefore indicate that significant value remains available.
VSIM introduces a different examination.
For each materially relevant value-bearing basis, the bank can establish:
Governed Value → Credit-Relevant Value Context → Current Reference Point → Observed Current Condition
→ Value State Candidate
A production machine may still exist physically and remain on the borrower's balance sheet while no longer being compatible with the company's current production process.
Another machine may be idle but immediately deployable.
A patent may produce no revenue but remain strategically important.
A production line may be operational but dependent upon a supplier whose critical component is no longer available.
VSIM prevents all four conditions from being treated simply as:
“assets with value.”
It identifies the materially different current conditions before classification and formal state determination occur.
This can give the bank an earlier governance signal that the economic condition of the underlying value base may be diverging from its static recorded representation.

VSIM does not replace collateral valuation, accounting, credit models, or regulatory capital requirements.
It creates the identification layer required to ask a more fundamental question:
What is actually happening to the value underlying the exposure now?
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Finding Value That
Can Be Removed Without Losing Mission
Capability
A space mission operates under severe constraints on:
mass; energy; computing capacity; storage; communication bandwidth; maintenance capacity; crew time; redundancy; mission cost.
As the mission evolves, systems and capabilities that were valuable during one phase may no longer create material value during another.
VSIM can continuously identify current value conditions across mission capabilities.
For example:
Capability A
may remain essential.
Capability B
may be dormant but critical as emergency redundancy.
Capability C
may no longer contribute to the current or future mission configuration.
Capability D
may have lost its original function but remain useful for diagnostics or scientific observation.
Without explicit value-state identification, all four capabilities may continue consuming mission resources merely because they still exist.
VSIM establishes:
Mission Value Context → Mission Phase → Capability Reference → Current Condition → Dependency Check
→ Value State Candidate

The downstream VSS modules can then determine whether a capability remains a Value Asset™, occupies another defined state, or may qualify as ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ within the relevant mission context.
This creates a practical path toward identifying where resources can potentially be removed, reassigned, deactivated, or preserved without confusing physical existence with mission value.
In resource-constrained environments, that distinction can translate directly into lower operating burden and better allocation of scarce mission resources.
Foundational Principles
A value state must be identified before it can be classified.
Observed condition is not automatically governed state.
Value state identification must remain connected to the governed value context.
A historical state is not automatically the current state.
A predicted state is not the current state.
Unknown condition is not zero value.
Physical existence does not establish current value condition.
One value-bearing object may require multiple state candidates across different value contexts.
State identification must occur at the level at which the relevant value condition actually exists.
The first requirement of current-state governance is to identify what condition is actually being governed now.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value State Identification Module establishes the entry point into Value State governance by identifying the precise current condition of governed value that must be examined before classification, determination, transition-readiness assessment, and state recording can occur. Through explicit linkage of governed value, value-bearing object, value context, reference point, observed condition, scope, supporting basis, uncertainty, stale-state indicators, and multi-context distinctions, VSIM prevents historical records, predictions, accounting classifications, physical existence, missing information, or premature zero-value assumptions from being mistaken for the current governed state of value. By creating an explicit Value State Candidate, VSIM provides
the methodological foundation upon which the remaining Value State Standard modules can determine what state value actually occupies.

Canonical Definition
Value State Record Module (VSRM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VSRM governs the creation, structuring, preservation, linkage, updating, and lifecycle continuity of the governed Value State Record representing the current determined state of value and the material basis upon which that state was established.
The Module transforms:
Determined Value State + Transition Readiness
→ Governed Value State Record

VSRM ensures that the result of Value State governance does not remain an isolated determination, temporary analytical conclusion, undocumented classification, or context-free label.
It establishes a persistent and reconstructable representation of:
what value state was determined
for what governed value
in what context
for which beneficiary
at what reference point
on what basis
with what limitations
with what transition-readiness status.
Its foundational distinction is:
Value State ≠ Value State Record
The state describes the governed condition of value.
The record preserves the governed representation of that condition.
Architectural Position
VSRM is the fifth and final module within VSS.
It follows:
VSIM — Value State Identification Module
→ VSCM — Value State Classification Module
→ VSDM — Value State Determination Module
→ VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module
and completes the internal VSS sequence through:
VSRM — Value State Record Module
The internal logic is:
Identify State
→ Classify State
→ Determine State
→ Assess Transition Readiness
→ Record State
VSRM therefore creates the governed output through which the current Value State can remain available to subsequent VFM® processes.
VFM® Governance Flow Position
VSRM completes the fifth governed space within the VFM® governance flow:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Value State
→ Value Change

The VSRM output forms the reference basis against which subsequent material Value Change can be identified.
The architectural bridge is:
Governed Value State Record
→ Observed New Condition
→ Potential Difference
→ Value Change Governance
This is essential because change cannot be meaningfully established without a governed reference state against which the new condition can be compared.
Internal Module Flow
Value State Identification
→ Value State Classification
→ Value State Determination
→ Transition Readiness Assessment
→ Record Object Creation
→ Context Linkage

→ Reference Point Assignment
→ Limitation & Uncertainty Preservation

→ Record Status Assignment
→ Governed Value State Record
→ VCS — Value Change Standard
Operational Space
VSRM governs the methodological space between:
a completed Value State determination
and
a persistent governed representation capable of supporting subsequent value governance.
Its operational space includes:
Value State record identity; governed-value linkage; value-bearing object linkage; beneficiary linkage; context linkage; reference framework linkage; determined state; determination status; determination basis; temporal reference point; applicability; uncertainty; limitations; transition readiness; transition conditions; record version; record status; supersession; historical continuity; state lineage; downstream VFM® availability.
Value State Record Object

Every VSRM process should create an identifiable Value State Record Object.
The Record Object should establish, where applicable:
Record ID
Governed Value ID

Record Status
This creates a machine-readable and human-interpretable representation of the governed Value State.
Record Context Principle
A Value State Record must not detach the state from the context that gives it meaning.
A record containing only:
Asset X — Zero Value
is methodologically insufficient where the actual determination was:
Asset X — Zero Value for Beneficiary B within Operational Context C at Reference Point T.
The difference is fundamental.
Without context preservation, a valid narrow determination may later be interpreted as a universal statement about the object.
VSRM therefore requires:
State + Context + Reference Point
to remain linked.
Record Identity
Every material Value State Record should be uniquely identifiable.
Record identity allows organizations to distinguish:
current records; historical records; superseded records; corrected records; parallel context-specific records; beneficiary-specific records; provisional records; conditional records.
Record identity is not the same as identity of the underlying asset or object.

Therefore:
Value State Record Identity ≠ Asset Identity
OBIDENITY® or another applicable identity architecture may govern the underlying object identity.
VSRM governs the identity of the Value State Record itself.
Reference Point
Every Value State Record must preserve the temporal or event-based point to which the determination applies.
This may be:
timestamp; date; reporting period; transaction point; operational event; assessment point; lifecycle milestone; defined condition.
Without a reference point, the organization may later confuse:
what was true then
with
what is true now.
This becomes particularly important where value changes rapidly.
State Record ≠ Permanent Truth
A Value State Record represents the governed determination applicable at its reference point.
It does not establish permanent value reality.
A record may legitimately state:
Active Value — 25 August 2026
while a later record states:
Degraded Value — 14 October 2026
and another later record states:
ZVA™ — 9 January 2027.
These records do not invalidate one another where each accurately represents its applicable governed reference state.
Together they create:
Value State History.
Current Record and Historical Record
VSRM distinguishes between:
Current Value State Record
and
Historical Value State Record.

When a new Value State is legitimately determined, the previous record should normally remain preserved as historical state information rather than being overwritten as though the earlier determination never existed.
The logic is:
Current Record
→ Material Change
→ New Determination
→ New Current Record
while:
Previous Current Record
→ Historical Record
This creates state continuity.
Record Versioning
A Value State Record may require versioning where:
information is corrected; uncertainty is updated; limitations change; supporting information changes; determination status changes; transition readiness changes; contextual information is refined.
Versioning must distinguish:
Record Revision
from
Value State Change.
Correcting a spelling error does not mean value changed.
Adding missing documentation does not necessarily mean value changed.
Updating transition readiness may not mean the underlying Value State changed.
Therefore:
Record Change ≠ Value Change
Record Supersession
Where a new governed Value State replaces the previous current state, VSRM should preserve the supersession relationship.
Example:
VSR-000145 / Active Value
→ superseded by →
VSR-000186 / Degraded Value
→ superseded by →
VSR-000241 / ZVA™
The chain creates a reconstructable value-state lifecycle.
The previous record should not disappear merely because it is no longer current.
Parallel Value State Records
One value-bearing object may legitimately have multiple simultaneous Value State Records.
For example:

Industrial Facility
may have:
Active Value — Production Context
Strategic Value — Emergency Capacity Context
Degraded Value — Energy Efficiency Context
Conditional Value — Redevelopment Context
These records are not necessarily contradictory.
They represent distinct governed value relationships.
VSRM must therefore support:
One Object → Multiple Context-Bound Value State Records
Beneficiary-Specific Records
The same value-bearing object may carry different Value States for different beneficiaries.
For example:
Legacy Industrial Equipment
may represent:
ZVA™ — Company A / Current Production Context
while simultaneously representing:
Active Value — Company B / Secondary Production Context.
VSRM must preserve these beneficiary distinctions.
Otherwise, a zero-value determination for one beneficiary could incorrectly erase value existing for another.
Value Asset™ Record
Where VSDM determines a governed state corresponding to:
Value Asset™
VSRM preserves that determination as an explicit Value State Record.
The record should preserve:
why the governed value qualifies as existing positive value
and
the context within which that determination applies.
A Value Asset™ Record does not automatically establish:
legal title; accounting asset recognition; market price; tax status; regulatory classification; transfer rights.
It records the VFM® Value State.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Record
Where a governed value has legitimately reached:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™

VSRM creates a persistent record of that zero-value determination.
The record must preserve:
what value reached zero
for which beneficiary
within which context
at what reference point
on what determination basis
subject to what limitations
with what recovery or transition conditions where applicable.
This prevents:
ZVA™
from becoming an unexplained universal label attached permanently to an object.
A later state may legitimately move away from ZVA™ where new value emerges, is recognized, and a new state is determined.
Unknown-State Record
Where VSDM determines that available information is insufficient to establish the current Value State, VSRM may preserve:
Indeterminate Value State
rather than forcing a positive or zero-value record.
This protects the architecture from converting:
missing information
into
false value certainty.
Conditional-State Record
A conditional determination must preserve its conditions.
Example:
Conditional Value
may depend upon:
License Renewal
Critical Supplier Availability
Network Access
Regulatory Approval
Energy Availability
Restoration Completion
If those conditions disappear from the record, downstream systems may incorrectly treat conditional value as unconditional value.
VSRM therefore treats conditions as part of the governed record.
Uncertainty Preservation
Material uncertainty affecting the Value State must remain connected to the record.
Relevant uncertainty may concern:

capability; utilization; recoverability; beneficiary relevance; market relevance; technical condition; dependency availability; strategic significance; temporal applicability; data completeness.
VSRM does not eliminate uncertainty.
It ensures that downstream use cannot silently forget it.
Limitation Preservation
A Value State determination may contain explicit limitations.
For example:
ZVA™ applies only to the current manufacturing context and does not assess component resale value.
That limitation must remain part of the record.
Without it, a valid context-specific state can become an invalid universal conclusion.
Therefore:
State Record without Material Limitations = Incomplete Governance Record
where those limitations affect legitimate interpretation.
Transition Readiness Record
VSRM preserves the transition-readiness result produced through VSTM.
The record may therefore contain:
Current Value State: Active Value
Transition Readiness: Transition-Sensitive
or:
Current Value State: ZVA™
Transition Readiness: Recovery-Ready
This creates a richer state representation than a static value label.
It allows downstream systems to know both:
where value is now
and
whether that state is becoming unstable or ready to change.
State Lineage
VSRM enables the construction of a Value State Lineage.
Example:
Potential Value
→ Value Emergence
→ Recognized Value
→ Active Value
→ Degraded Value
→ ZVA™
→ Recoverable Value
→ Active Value

The record lineage does not itself govern all these transitions.
It preserves the sequence of governed states and their relationships as they pass through VFM®.
This creates the informational foundation required to reconstruct the value lifecycle.
Record Continuity
Value governance becomes substantially stronger when state records remain continuous across time.
A continuous record can answer:
What was the value state before the event?
What changed?
When did it change?
What state followed?
Was the previous state already transition-sensitive?
Was zero value temporary or persistent?
Was value later recovered?
This is essential for downstream Value Change governance.
Record Integrity Boundary
VSRM defines what must be represented within the Value State Record.
It does not replace general information-integrity governance.
Where record integrity, tamper resistance, provenance assurance, authenticity, or broader integrity controls are required, the relevant integrity architecture may govern those properties.
The boundary is:
VSRM governs what the Value State Record must represent.
INTEGROS® may govern whether that record remains trustworthy and intact.
Auditability Boundary
VSRM creates a reconstructable Value State Record.
It does not itself conduct an audit.
ADIT® may subsequently examine:

whether the record existed; whether supporting information is preserved; whether changes are traceable; whether determinations can be reconstructed; whether state history was altered; whether records correspond to observed evidence.
Therefore:
Value State Recording ≠ Audit
Accounting Boundary
A Value State Record is not an accounting ledger entry.
The same physical or digital object may have:
accounting carrying value
and
VFM® governed Value State
simultaneously.
These may differ legitimately because they answer different questions.
VSRM must not redefine accounting treatment.
However, accounting systems may consume VFM® state information where an organization or future methodology chooses to use it as a governed analytical input.
Tax Boundary
A Value State Record does not itself create:
taxable income; tax liability; deductible loss; depreciation; taxable asset value; tax recognition.
A future tax architecture could use VFM® Value State Records as governed inputs into a separate tax determination mechanism.
The architectural separation remains:
VFM® records the governed state of value.
The tax architecture determines the tax consequence.
Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Compatibility
VSRM can be implemented using conventional databases, enterprise systems, distributed ledgers, blockchain systems, digital asset infrastructures, or future record technologies.
A blockchain may preserve:

record timestamp; record identity; state version; supersession; provenance reference; state-transition reference.
But:
Blockchain Record ≠ Governed Value State
The technology may preserve the record.
VFM® defines the methodological meaning of what the record represents.
This distinction allows VSRM to remain technology-neutral.

Machine readability must not remove contextual meaning.

Use Case 2 — Blockchain and Digital Assets:
Recording Value State Without Confusing

A digital infrastructure may contain millions of tokens, digital rights, licenses, data assets, computational resources, digital objects, or blockchain-linked assets.

Foundational Principles
Value State is not Value State Record.
A Value State Record must preserve the context that gives the state meaning.
A Value State Record represents a governed reference point, not permanent truth.
Historical states must not disappear merely because a new current state exists.
Record revision is not automatically Value Change.
One object may carry multiple legitimate context-specific Value State Records.
One object may carry different Value States for different beneficiaries.

ZVA™ in one context does not establish universal zero value.
Unknown value must remain distinguishable from zero value.
Conditional value must preserve its conditions.
Material uncertainty and limitations must travel with the Value State Record.
Transition readiness should remain visible alongside the current Value State.
Blockchain may preserve a Value State Record; it does not determine the Value State.
Accounting value, market price, ownership, tax treatment, and VFM® Value State remain distinct concepts.
A governed history of value requires states to remain reconstructable across time.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value State Record Module completes the Value State Standard by transforming identified, classified, determined, and transition-readiness-assessed value conditions into persistent, context-bound, beneficiary- aware, reference-point-specific, uncertainty-preserving, limitation-aware, versioned, and historically reconstructable Value State Records. Through governance of record identity, state representation, context linkage, determination basis, temporal applicability, conditions, uncertainty, transition readiness, versioning, supersession, parallel states, historical continuity, Value Asset™ records, and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ records, VSRM prevents current value conditions from becoming detached from the circumstances that give them meaning or from overwriting the value history that preceded them. By separating Value State recording from object identity, accounting, taxation, blockchain technology, audit, integrity, and Value Change itself, VSRM creates the persistent reference layer required for VFM® to compare what value was with what value subsequently becomes. A value lifecycle becomes governable only when its states can remain identifiable, contextualized, connected, and reconstructable across time.

Canonical Definition
Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VSTM governs whether a determined current Value State has reached the conditions under which a potential transition away from that state must become governable, observable, or ready for downstream value-change governance.
The Module establishes the methodological bridge between:
Current Governed Value State
and
Potential Value State Transition

without determining that a value change has already occurred.
Its foundational distinction is:
Transition Readiness ≠ Value Change
VSTM answers:
Is the current Value State sufficiently exposed to, approaching, or meeting defined transition conditions that downstream change governance should become active?
The actual identification and governance of material value change belongs to:
Value Change Standard (VCS).
Architectural Position
VSTM is the fourth module within VSS.
It follows:
VSIM — Value State Identification Module
→ VSCM — Value State Classification Module
→ VSDM — Value State Determination Module
and precedes:
VSRM — Value State Record Module.
The internal logic is:
Identify State
→ Classify State
→ Determine State
→ Assess Transition Readiness
→ Record State
VSTM therefore prevents a determined Value State from being treated as static when material conditions indicate that the value may be approaching another state.
VFM® Governance Flow Position
VSTM occupies an important transition point in the broader VFM® governance flow:
Value Context
→ Value Origin
→ Value Emergence
→ Value Recognition
→ Value State
→ Value Change
VSTM operates at the end of the active Value State assessment and creates the readiness interface toward Value Change.
The architectural relationship is:
Current Value State
→ Transition Readiness
→ Potential Material Change
→ Value Change Governance
VSTM does not move value between states.

It determines whether the conditions for monitoring or examining such movement have become materially relevant.

→ Dependency Assessment
→ Transition Constraint Assessment
→ Transition Readiness Assessment
→ Readiness State Assignment
→ Transition Readiness Record
→ VSRM — Value State Record Module
Where a material change is subsequently observed:
Transition Signal
→ VCS — Value Change Standard
Operational Space
VSTM governs the space between:
a determined current Value State
and
a potentially emerging change to that state.
Its operational space includes:
transition sensitivity; transition conditions;
transition indicators; transition signals; transition thresholds; threshold proximity; value-state instability; state persistence; transition dependencies; transition constraints; transition blockers; transition enablers; recovery conditions; degradation conditions; zero-value approach; reactivation conditions; readiness classification; transition uncertainty; transition monitoring requirements; downstream change-governance triggers.
Transition Readiness Principle
A Value State may remain formally unchanged while conditions around it materially evolve.
For example:
Active Value
may remain the determined state while operational performance is deteriorating.
Dormant Value

may remain the determined state while reactivation conditions are approaching.
Degraded Value
may remain the determined state while recovery becomes increasingly feasible.
Conditional Value
may remain the determined state while its defining condition approaches satisfaction.
Zero Value
may remain the determined state while a new use case creates a credible pathway toward renewed value.
VSTM governs this intermediate space.
It allows VFM® to distinguish:
Current State
from
Readiness to Leave Current State.
Transition Condition
A Transition Condition is a defined condition whose satisfaction, deterioration, restoration, appearance, disappearance, or material alteration may make movement from the current Value State possible or relevant.
Transition conditions may concern:
utilization; capability;
demand; technological relevance; operational performance; cost; resource availability; dependency availability; regulatory conditions; market access; beneficiary needs; infrastructure availability; system compatibility; recoverability; deterioration; restoration; strategic relevance; environmental conditions; contractual conditions.
VSTM does not govern these external systems themselves.
It governs their relevance to Value State transition readiness.
Transition Signal
A Transition Signal is an observable indication that one or more relevant transition conditions may be changing.
Signals may include:

declining utilization; increasing failure frequency; rising maintenance burden; disappearing demand; increasing operational cost; technological displacement; restored infrastructure; renewed customer demand; new compatibility; regulatory approval; dependency restoration; new beneficiary; new use case; resource scarcity; capability recovery; measurable deterioration.
A signal does not prove that value has changed.
Therefore:
Transition Signal ≠ Value Change
Transition Threshold
Organizations may establish thresholds indicating when a Value State requires closer transition governance.
Examples may include:
Utilization below defined level
Operating cost above defined level
Capability below defined requirement
Recovery probability above defined level
Dependency restored
Critical technology support withdrawn
Strategic demand activated
A threshold may be:
quantitative; qualitative; event-based; condition-based; composite.
Crossing a transition-readiness threshold does not automatically establish a new Value State.
It establishes that transition governance has become materially relevant.
Threshold Proximity
VSTM should not operate only after a threshold has already been crossed.
Where useful, it may govern proximity to a transition threshold.
A state may therefore be:
Stable
while far from any relevant transition threshold.
It may become:
Transition-Sensitive
as conditions begin moving materially toward a threshold.
It may become:
Transition-Ready

when defined readiness conditions are satisfied.
This gives VFM® the ability to identify value movement before a formal state change is determined.
Transition Readiness States
A minimum VSTM implementation may use the following states:
1. Stable
No material transition condition currently indicates credible movement from the determined Value State.
2. Transition-Sensitive
Material indicators exist that could affect the persistence of the current Value State.
3. Approaching Transition
One or more relevant transition conditions are materially approaching a defined threshold.
4. Transition-Ready
Defined conditions exist under which transition from the current Value State has become materially actionable or governable.
5. Transition-Constrained
A potential transition exists but one or more material constraints currently prevent or materially limit it.
6. Transition-Indeterminate
Available information is insufficient to establish transition readiness.
These are governance states.
They do not themselves establish that value has changed.
Transition Readiness ≠ Prediction
VSTM does not predict with certainty what the next Value State will be.
It may identify:
credible transition pathways
without asserting:
future transition outcome.
For example:
Degraded Value
may have potential pathways toward:
Recoverable Value
or
Zero Value.
VSTM may establish that both pathways are materially possible.
It does not need to predict which will occur.
Therefore:

Transition Readiness ≠ Transition Prediction
Where formal prediction governance is required, that belongs to the appropriate prediction architecture.
Transition Readiness ≠ Transition Execution
A system may be ready for value transition without anyone deciding to execute an intervention.
For example:
a dormant production line may be ready for reactivation.
VSTM can establish:
Reactivation-Ready
without deciding:
Reactivate Production Line.
Likewise, an obsolete system may be ready for retirement without VSTM authorizing disposal.
Therefore:
Readiness ≠ Decision
and:
Readiness ≠ Execution
Value Degradation Pathway
VSTM can identify when a currently positive Value State approaches degradation.
Example:
Active Value
→ declining capability
→ increasing maintenance
→ decreasing utilization
→ reduced beneficiary relevance
→ Transition-Sensitive
→ Approaching Transition
If a material value change subsequently occurs, the matter proceeds into VCS.
This enables organizations to observe value deterioration before it becomes invisible inside static asset records.
Zero-Value Approach
One of the strongest applications of VSTM is governance of the pathway toward:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
A Value Asset™ may remain in a positive Value State while moving progressively toward zero value.
VSTM can identify:
Active Value
→ Degradation Signals
→ Transition-Sensitive
→ Approaching Zero-Value Threshold
→ Transition-Ready
without prematurely determining:
ZVA™

The zero-value state itself must still be established through the applicable state and change governance.
This prevents both:
premature zero-value classification
and
late recognition of value collapse.
Recovery Pathway
Transition governance is equally important in the opposite direction.
A zero-value, dormant, constrained, or degraded object may develop new value potential.
Examples include:
new technology; new beneficiary; restored dependency; new market; regulatory change; infrastructure restoration; new use case; component reuse; new strategic requirement.
VSTM can identify:
Current Low/Zero Value State
→ Recovery Signal
→ Recovery Conditions
→ Transition Readiness
without automatically determining that value has already re-emerged.
This provides an important foundation for future VFM® concepts concerning ReMonet™ and value restoration.
State Persistence
Not every changing external condition requires a Value State transition.
VSTM therefore considers whether the current state remains sufficiently persistent despite changing conditions.
For example:
a temporary market decline may not materially alter the strategic value of a capability.
A short operational outage may not change an Active Value state.
A temporary cost increase may not establish degradation.
The Module therefore protects VFM® from excessive state volatility.
Transition Dependencies
Some transitions depend upon external conditions.
A dormant asset may become active only if:
energy supply returns
or:

regulatory approval is granted
or:
a critical component becomes available.
VSTM records those dependencies as part of transition readiness.
The transition may therefore be classified as:
Transition-Constrained
until the dependency is satisfied.
Transition Constraints
Material constraints may prevent an otherwise credible value transition.
These may include:
technical constraints; resource constraints; legal constraints; contractual constraints; infrastructure constraints; capability constraints; market constraints; timing constraints; dependency constraints.
VSTM does not resolve those constraints.
It makes their effect on transition readiness explicit.
Multiple Transition Pathways
A current Value State may have several potential next states.
For example:
Dormant Value
may transition toward:
Active Value
if demand returns,
toward:
Degraded Value
if deterioration continues,
or toward:
Zero Value
if the capability loses all relevant value within the governed context.
VSTM may preserve multiple credible transition pathways simultaneously.
Therefore:
One Current State ≠ One Inevitable Next State
Context-Specific Transition Readiness
The same value-bearing object may have different transition readiness across different contexts.
For example:
Industrial Robot
may be:
Stable — Current Production Context
while:
Transition-Ready — Resale Context
and:
Transition-Sensitive — Technology Relevance Context.
VSTM therefore preserves the context established upstream.

Transition readiness must not be universalized across unrelated value contexts.
Beneficiary-Specific Transition Readiness
A transition may also be beneficiary-specific.
A technology may be approaching zero value for one organization while simultaneously becoming increasingly valuable to another.
VSTM can preserve both relationships.
This is particularly important for:
secondary markets; asset transfer; technology reuse; industrial restructuring; intellectual property; data; infrastructure; circular economy models.
Transition Uncertainty
Where readiness cannot be established confidently, uncertainty must remain visible.
Sources may include:
incomplete data; uncertain demand; unknown recoverability; unclear dependency status; unstable technology conditions; ambiguous beneficiary relevance; uncertain regulatory outcome; incomplete cost information.
VSTM should not convert uncertainty into artificial readiness.
The appropriate state may remain:
Transition-Indeterminate
until sufficient information becomes available.
Transition Monitoring
A determined Value State may require monitoring where transition sensitivity is material.
Monitoring may focus on:
threshold variables; critical dependencies; deterioration indicators; recovery indicators; utilization; operational output; cost burden; beneficiary demand; market relevance; technology relevance; regulatory conditions.
VSTM governs what transition-relevant signals should remain observable.

It does not become a general monitoring architecture.
Interface with Value Change Standard
VSTM provides an explicit methodological bridge to:
6. Value Change Standard (VCS)
VSTM determines:
whether conditions indicate readiness or sensitivity for potential movement from the current Value State.
VCS determines:
whether existing value has materially changed and what change has occurred.
Therefore:
VSTM: Potential movement becomes governable.
VCS: Material value change becomes identifiable.
The architectural boundary is:
Readiness ≠ Change
Interface with Value Emergence
A transition from zero or non-realized value toward positive value may eventually interact with Value Emergence Standard (VES) where genuinely new value emerges.
VSTM does not determine value emergence.
It may identify conditions indicating that a current state is approaching a transition requiring reassessment through the appropriate VFM® governed space.
This preserves the distinction:
State Transition Readiness ≠ Value Emergence
Interface with Value Recognition
A changed or newly emerged value may require recognition under:
Value Recognition Standard (VRS).
VSTM does not recognize value.
It identifies transition readiness within an already governed Value State.
Interface with External Events
External events may influence transition readiness.
Examples include:

market shocks; innovation; regulation; physical damage; infrastructure failure; technological substitution; contractual change; payment; environmental event.
VFM® does not need to govern the external event itself.
VSTM governs:
what that event means for readiness of the governed value to leave its current state.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VSTM implementation should establish:
1. Current Value State
Receive the determined current Value State from VSDM.
2. Transition Sensitivity
Identify conditions capable of materially affecting persistence of that state.
3. Transition Conditions
Define conditions relevant to movement from the current state.
4. Transition Signals
Identify observable signals associated with those conditions.
5. Transition Thresholds
Establish thresholds where appropriate.
6. Dependency Assessment
Identify dependencies enabling or constraining transition.
7. Readiness Assessment
Determine whether the current state is stable, sensitive, approaching transition, transition-ready, constrained, or indeterminate.
8. Potential Pathways
Identify materially credible next-state pathways without treating them as predictions.
9. Monitoring Requirement
Identify transition-relevant conditions requiring continued observation.
10. Downstream Trigger
Where material change is subsequently identified, transfer the matter into Value Change governance.
Governance Outputs
VSTM may produce:

Value State Transition Readiness Assessment Transition Condition Record Transition Signal Record Transition Threshold Record Threshold Proximity Assessment Transition Dependency Record Transition Constraint Record Transition Readiness State Potential Transition Pathway Record Zero-Value Approach Signal Recovery Readiness Signal Transition Monitoring Requirement Value Change Governance Trigger
These outputs preserve the bridge between current Value State governance and downstream Value Change governance.
Use Case 1 — Banking: Detecting Collateral
Value Deterioration Before the Asset Reaches
Zero
A bank finances an industrial company whose loan is secured by production equipment.
The equipment remains:
operational
and therefore retains a determined:
Active Value State.
Traditional collateral monitoring may continue to treat the machinery as performing collateral until a major impairment, default, valuation event, or operational failure becomes visible.
VSTM introduces an earlier governance layer.
The bank may observe:
utilization decline
→ maintenance cost increase
→ technology obsolescence
→ loss of spare-part support
→ declining secondary-market demand
→ reduced productive relevance.
None of these signals alone necessarily establishes a new Value State.
Together, however, they may move the asset from:
Stable
to:
Transition-Sensitive
and eventually:
Approaching Transition.

The bank can therefore identify that the governed value supporting its collateral is approaching a materially different state before the underlying machine disappears, defaults, or becomes formally worthless.
This creates a potential early-warning layer between:
asset existence
and
value deterioration.
For banking, credit, insurance, restructuring, and collateral governance, that distinction can be materially significant.
Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Determining When
Mission Assets Become Ready for a Different
Value State
A space mission contains satellites, scientific instruments, computing systems, communication infrastructure, energy systems, spare capacity, data resources, and mission capabilities.
A scientific instrument may currently occupy:
Active Value
because it is producing mission-relevant data.
Over time:
sensor degradation increases
→ energy consumption rises
→ measurement precision declines
→ mission priorities change
→ new instruments become available.
The instrument may still carry active value.
VSTM therefore does not prematurely classify it as degraded or zero.
Instead, it determines whether the current state has become:
Transition-Sensitive
or:
Approaching Transition.
At the same time, an apparently obsolete instrument may gain a new use:
secondary observation
backup capability
calibration support
experimental reuse
or
new scientific purpose.
VSTM can therefore identify both:
declining value pathways
and
renewed value pathways.

This is important in environments such as space missions where physical replacement may be impossible and extracting additional value from existing resources can materially reduce mission cost and extend mission capability.
The result is a governed answer not merely to:
What is this asset worth now?
but to:
Is its current Value State stable, deteriorating, recoverable, or approaching a materially different state?
Foundational Principles
Current Value State does not imply permanent Value State.
Transition readiness is not Value Change.
Transition signal is not Value Change.
Threshold proximity is not threshold crossing.
Transition readiness is not prediction.
Transition readiness is not authorization.
Transition readiness is not execution.
One current Value State may have multiple credible transition pathways.
Value deterioration may become governable before zero value occurs.
Value recovery may become governable before positive value re-emerges.
A Value Asset™ may approach ZVA™ without yet becoming ZVA™.
A ZVA™ may develop transition readiness toward renewed value without yet possessing renewed value.
VFM® must govern not only what state value occupies, but when that state is becoming materially unstable.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value State Transition Readiness Module establishes the transition-readiness layer of the Value State Standard by determining whether a governed current Value State remains stable or has become sensitive, constrained, indeterminate, approaching transition, or ready for potential movement into another value condition. Through governance of transition conditions, signals, thresholds, threshold proximity, dependencies, constraints, uncertainty, state persistence, degradation pathways, zero-value approach, recovery pathways, monitoring requirements, and potential next-state pathways, VSTM makes value-state instability governable before a material value change is formally established. By separating transition readiness from prediction, authorization, execution, value emergence, value recognition, and actual Value Change, VSTM preserves the boundary between the current governed state and downstream change governance while creating the early-warning and recovery interface required for dynamic value governance.

Canonical Definition
Value State Standard (VSS) is the fifth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value.
VSS establishes a structured governance layer through which value that has emerged and entered the governed value lifecycle can be represented according to its current condition without confusing that condition with its origin, recognition, previous condition, future condition, or the mechanism through which change occurred.
The Standard establishes the methodological distinction between:
the existence of value
and
the current state in which that value exists.
Its governing principle is:
Value State ≠ Value Transition.
VSS determines where value currently stands.

It does not determine the mechanism through which value arrived there or the mechanism through which it may subsequently move to another state.
Core Question
What is the current governed state of value?
Architectural Position
VSS occupies the fifth governed space within the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
and precedes:
Value Change Standard (VCS).
The VFM® governance flow at this point is:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction
The architectural transition is therefore:
What value is being governed? → Where can that value originate? → Has value actually emerged? → Can that existing value be recognized within the defined context? → What is its current governed state?
VSS establishes the baseline state against which subsequent value change can be governed.
Governance Flow Position
Governed Value Recognition Record → Value State Identification → Value State Classification → Value State Determination → Value State Transition Readiness → Value State Record → Governed Current Value State → Value Change Governance
This creates a critical lifecycle control:
Recognized Value → Governed Current Value State
Once that state exists, subsequent VFM® standards can determine whether the value has materially changed.
Operational Space

VSS governs the operational space in which existing value is assigned an explicit and current governed state.
This includes:
value-state identification; value-state classification; state criteria; state determination; state applicability; state conditions; state boundaries; state uncertainty; state temporal applicability; zero-value state; positive-value state; conditional value state; state review; state transition readiness; state versioning; state history; current-state representation; machine-readable value-state records.
The purpose is to prevent value from being treated merely as:
present
or
absent
when its actual governed condition may be materially more complex.
Value State Principle
A value can exist while occupying different states.
For example, a capability may have:
Potential Value
before emergence.
After emergence and recognition it may become:
Recognized Existing Value
and later occupy states representing materially different conditions within the value lifecycle.
The state is therefore not the value itself.
It is a governed representation of the value's current condition.
Thus:
Value ≠ Value State
and:
Value Identity ≠ Value State
The same governed value may persist while its state changes repeatedly.
State Independence Principle
VSS requires the current value state to be determinable independently from the historical pathway that produced it.
Two values may arrive at the same current state through completely different mechanisms.
For example:

Value A: innovation → development → current state X
Value B: degradation → restoration → current state X
Their histories differ.
Their current governed state may nevertheless be equivalent.
VSS therefore governs:
Current Condition
rather than:
Historical Mechanism.
The historical pathway remains relevant to other VFM® lifecycle spaces but must not prevent consistent state representation.
Value State ≠ Value Recognition
Recognition and state answer different governance questions.
Value Recognition asks:
Can existing value be recognized as value within this defined governance context?
Value State asks:
What is the current governed condition of that value?
A recognition determination may therefore remain valid while the underlying value subsequently changes state.
Recognition must not be repeatedly mistaken for the current value condition.
Value State ≠ Value Change
VSS establishes the state.
VCS establishes whether that state or its underlying value condition has materially changed.
Therefore:
State(t₁) ≠ Change(t₁→t₂)
A state is a condition at a governed reference point.
A change is a relationship between conditions across reference points.
This distinction enables VFM® to represent value dynamically without collapsing state and movement into the same concept.
Value State ≠ Value Transition
A value may be in a particular state without currently transitioning.

Likewise, evidence may indicate that a transition is becoming possible or imminent without establishing that the transition has occurred.
VSS therefore preserves:
Current State
separately from:
Transition Readiness
and:
Completed Transition.
Transition readiness is a state-governance signal.
Actual value change belongs downstream.
State Reference Point
Every meaningful value-state determination requires a reference point.
The reference point may be:
a date; a reporting period; an operational configuration; a transaction stage; a technological stage; a project phase; an accounting period; a mission phase; a contractual condition; a system version; another governed temporal or operational reference.
Without a reference point, the statement:
“The value is in State X.”
may become detached from the conditions under which it was true.
VSS therefore treats state as reference-bound.
State Classification
VSS permits value states to be classified according to the governance context in which value is being represented.
VFM® does not require every sector, asset type, organization, or value system to use one rigid universal state taxonomy.
Instead, state classifications must be:
explicitly defined; mutually interpretable where required; connected to the governed value; contextually appropriate; sufficiently distinguishable; consistently applied; machine-readable where implementation requires.

This allows VFM® to govern value across financial, industrial, technological, public, digital, environmental, scientific, infrastructure, and other contexts without forcing unlike value systems into an artificial common scale.
Canonical Value-State Concepts
VFM® may establish canonical value-state concepts where they represent recurring value conditions across multiple domains.
Two foundational concepts are:
Value Asset™
and
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™.
These concepts must remain governed states or value-state constructs within the VFM® lifecycle and must not silently acquire meanings belonging to accounting, property, taxation, securities law, valuation, or another external system.
Value Asset™
Value Asset™ represents a governed value-bearing condition in which an identified object, capability, relationship, resource, right, process, system, or other governed basis carries recognized value within a defined VFM® context.
The concept is broader than conventional accounting recognition.
Therefore:
Value Asset™ ≠ Accounting Asset
Value Asset™ ≠ Legal Property
Value Asset™ ≠ Marketable Asset
Value Asset™ ≠ Taxable Asset
A Value Asset™ may have significant operational, strategic, technological, social, informational, infrastructure, or other value even where an external accounting or legal framework does not classify it as an asset.
External systems remain responsible for their own classifications.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™

ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represents a governed zero-value state where an identified value-bearing object or basis remains governable but its value within the defined VFM® context is determined to be zero.
The concept establishes an important distinction:
Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence
An object can continue to exist while the governed value associated with it is zero.
Likewise:
Zero Value ≠ Extinction
A zero-value state does not automatically establish that value can never return.
And:
Zero Value ≠ Worthless in Every Context
An object may occupy a zero-value state under one value context while carrying value under another.
ZVA™ therefore creates a governed representation of zero value without forcing the lifecycle immediately into extinction.
Zero as a Governed State
Zero is not merely the absence of a number.
Within VFM®, zero may represent a materially meaningful lifecycle condition.
For example, an industrial capability may temporarily have no operational value because the production system it serves has been suspended.
A technological asset may have zero value within a current architecture but regain value after compatibility is restored.
A digital resource may have zero current utility while retaining recoverable future value.
A mission capability may have zero value for one mission configuration while remaining valuable for another.
VSS makes those distinctions governable.
Zero Value ≠ Negative Value

Where a governance context supports negative-value conditions, VSS must distinguish them from zero.
Zero Value
means the governed value state is zero within the defined context.
Negative Value
may indicate that the governed object, condition, activity, or relationship creates a net adverse value effect under the applicable value model.
These states are not interchangeable.
A zero-value object may create neither value nor material value loss.
A negative-value condition may actively destroy, consume, offset, or impose value.
The applicable methodology must define the distinction.
State Granularity
A value-state system may operate at different levels of granularity.
For example:
High-Level State
may indicate whether value is:
Positive / Zero / Negative / Indeterminate
while a more detailed state model may distinguish:
Active / Conditional / Constrained / Dormant / Degraded / Zero / Recoverable / Other Defined State.
VSS does not require unnecessary complexity.
The state taxonomy should be sufficiently granular to support the decisions and downstream governance for which it is intended.
Conditional Value State
A value state may depend upon defined conditions.
For example:
Value Asset™ — Conditional
may indicate that the governed value remains present only while:

a capability remains available; a contract remains active; a technology remains compatible; an infrastructure dependency remains available; a regulatory condition remains satisfied; a resource remains accessible; a particular operational configuration remains active.
The condition must remain attached to the state determination.
Indeterminate Value State
VSS must permit an indeterminate state where available information does not support a legitimate current-state determination.
This prevents governance systems from forcing false certainty.
Unknown ≠ Zero
and:
Indeterminate ≠ No Value
An inability to determine the current value state must not automatically convert into a zero-value determination.
State Determination Principle
A Value State Determination should identify:
Value Reference → Governance Context → State Reference Point → Applicable State Criteria → Available State Basis → Current State Determination → Conditions → Limitations → Uncertainty → Review Conditions
The determination must be sufficiently explicit to distinguish:
what state was determined
from:
why that determination was made.
State Evidence
VSS may use information produced elsewhere to support state determination.
Such information may include:

operational results; market information; technical condition; capability availability; utilization; performance; demand; contractual status; financial information; resource availability; technological compatibility; external valuations; governed recognition records; other relevant evidence.
VSS governs how that information supports a Value State Determination.
It does not take ownership of the external systems that generated the information.
Temporal State Principle
Value state is inherently temporal.
A value may be:
State A at T₁
and:
State B at T₂.
The current state must therefore be distinguishable from:
previous state; projected state; target state; possible state; historical state.
This is especially important for AI and automated systems, which may otherwise confuse an old value record with the current value condition.
Current State ≠ Future State
VSS does not predict what value will become.
A state determination may identify transition readiness, but it does not establish the future state.
Therefore:
Transition Readiness ≠ Predicted Transition
and:
Predicted State ≠ Current State.
Prediction governance remains outside VSS.
Transition Readiness
VSS includes transition readiness because a current state may contain conditions indicating that state reassessment or downstream change governance is required.
Transition-readiness indicators may include:

threshold proximity; material dependency change; deterioration signal; capability activation; value recovery condition; market threshold; contractual trigger; technological transition; resource exhaustion; restoration condition; material uncertainty change.
Transition readiness does not itself establish a value change.
It establishes that the current state may no longer remain stable or sufficient as the sole representation of value.
State Review Trigger
A state review may be triggered when:
material new evidence appears; a value-change signal is detected; recognition conditions change; the value object changes materially; a dependency changes; a state condition fails; a defined threshold is crossed; the reference period expires; the governance context changes; uncertainty becomes material; an external event potentially affects value.
The trigger initiates review.
It does not predetermine the new state.
State Persistence
A value state remains the governed current state until:
a new state is legitimately determined; the existing determination expires; the state is suspended; the applicable governance context ceases; or another defined lifecycle condition invalidates its applicability.
This prevents uncontrolled state changes based merely on unverified signals.
State History
VSS requires historical states to remain distinguishable where lifecycle traceability is required.
A value lifecycle may therefore show:
State A — Active → State B — Constrained

→ State C — ZVA™ → State D — Restored Value Asset™
The state history provides a governed record of where value has been.
The mechanisms responsible for those movements remain governed through the relevant downstream standards.
Multi-Context State
The same underlying object may legitimately occupy different value states in different contexts.
For example:
Industrial Machine
may be:
ZVA™ within Production Line A
while remaining:
Value Asset™ within Spare-Part Recovery Context B.
Likewise, intellectual property may have:
high strategic value
and simultaneously:
zero current licensing value.
VSS therefore prohibits silent collapse of multiple value contexts into one universal state.
Aggregation Principle
Value states may be aggregated for portfolio, enterprise, infrastructure, governmental, or analytical purposes.
However:
State Aggregation ≠ State Homogenization
An enterprise containing:
high-value assets; conditional-value assets; zero-value assets; degraded-value assets; indeterminate-value objects
must not be represented as though every underlying value object occupies the same state merely because a portfolio- level metric exists.
Granular states should remain traceable where material.
State Transfer Principle
A value-state record may move between systems.
For example:
Operational System → Enterprise System
→ Banking Analysis → Investment Analysis → Government Analysis

The technical transfer of a state record does not force the receiving institution to adopt the same value-state determination.
Therefore:
State Record Transfer ≠ Institutional State Adoption
The receiving system may apply its own governance context and criteria.
Boundary with Value Recognition Standard
VRS establishes whether existing value may be recognized within the defined context.
VSS establishes its current governed state.
Therefore:
Recognition → State
but:
Recognition ≠ State.
A recognition record may serve as an input to state governance without dictating every future state determination.
Boundary with Value Change Standard
VSS establishes the current value state.
VCS governs whether existing value has materially changed and what change occurred.
The boundary is:
VSS: What is the current governed state?
VCS: Has that value materially changed, and what changed?
Therefore:
State ≠ Change.
Boundary with Value Development and Value
Degradation
VSS may identify that value currently occupies a developed, constrained, degraded, zero, or other defined state where the applicable state taxonomy supports such classifications.
It does not govern the mechanism or lifecycle pathway of development or degradation.
Those processes belong to their respective downstream governed spaces.
Boundary with Value Nullification
A ZVA™ determination identifies a governed zero-value state.
It does not automatically determine that a formal Value Nullification event or process has occurred.

This distinction is essential:
Zero-Value State ≠ Nullification Mechanism
VSS answers:
What is the value state now?
Value Nullification governance answers:
Through what governed lifecycle condition did value become nullified?
Boundary with Value Restoration
A ZVA™ may later regain value.
VSS may record the resulting new state once legitimately determined.
The restoration mechanism itself belongs to Value Restoration Governance.
Therefore:
Restored State ≠ Restoration Process.
Boundary with External Valuation Systems
VSS does not determine:
market price; fair value; accounting value; tax value; collateral value; insurance value; legal ownership; regulatory classification.
Those systems may provide inputs into a Value State Determination where appropriate.
VFM® preserves the methodological distinction between:
governed value state
and:
external institutional valuation or classification.
Machine-Readable Value State
A machine-readable VSS implementation may represent:
Value ID → Context ID → Value Object Reference → Recognition Record Reference → State Taxonomy ID → Current State → State Reference Point → State Conditions → State Limitations
→ State Uncertainty → Transition Readiness → Review Triggers → State Version → Previous State Reference → Current State Record Status
This enables AI and digital systems to distinguish between:
what value exists
and:
what state that value currently occupies.
Governance Outputs
Implementation of VSS may produce:

Value State Identification Record Value State Classification Value State Determination Value State Basis Record Value State Condition Record Value State Limitation Record Value State Uncertainty Record Value State Reference Point Value State Transition Readiness Record Value State Review Trigger Value State History ZVA™ State Record Value Asset™ State Record Governed Current Value State Machine-Readable Value State Record
These outputs create the baseline required for downstream Value Change Governance.
Enterprise Application
VSS enables organizations to maintain an explicit map of what state their governed value currently occupies rather than relying only upon static asset lists, accounting classifications, market valuations, or isolated management judgments.
The Standard can be applied to:
enterprises; banking; investment; public finance; industrial assets; technology portfolios; intellectual property; infrastructure; energy systems; supply chains; digital assets; AI capabilities; organizational capabilities; scientific programs; space missions; resource systems; public-sector assets.
This makes it possible to identify value that conventional systems may fail to represent clearly.

An organization may discover, for example, that an object still exists on its asset register while occupying a ZVA™ state operationally, or that a capability not recognized as a conventional accounting asset nevertheless constitutes a material Value Asset™ within the organization's operational context.
VSS therefore creates a structured bridge between value existence and dynamic value lifecycle governance.
Foundational Principles
Value is not the same thing as its current state.
Value recognition is not value state.
Value state is reference-bound and context-bound.
Current state is not historical state.
Current state is not predicted state.
Value State ≠ Value Change.
Value State ≠ Value Transition.
Transition readiness does not establish that transition occurred.
Unknown value state is not zero value.
Zero value is not non-existence.
Zero value is not automatically extinction.
Zero value is not automatically negative value.
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may remain capable of future restoration.
Value Asset™ does not automatically mean accounting, legal, taxable, collateral, or market-recognized asset.
The same object may legitimately occupy different value states under different value contexts.
A governed value lifecycle requires an explicit current state before material change can be meaningfully determined.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value State Standard establishes the current-condition governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by providing a structured method for identifying, classifying, determining, recording, reviewing, and representing the current governed state of value. Through explicit separation of value identity, recognition, state, change, transition, nullification, restoration, external valuation, and institutional classification, VSS enables value to remain governable as its condition evolves across time and context. By introducing persistent state representation, contextual and temporal reference points, state conditions, uncertainty, transition readiness, historical traceability, multi-context state governance, machine-readable state records, and canonical concepts including Value Asset™ and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™, the Standard establishes the baseline from which subsequent changes in value can be detected and governed without confusing the state of value with the mechanisms that produced it. A governed value lifecycle can determine what changed only when it can first determine what state the value was in.
