Canonical Definition
Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) is the fifth and final Core Module of the Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VXRM governs the creation, structuring, preservation, linkage, and lifecycle positioning of the authoritative governance record produced when previously existing value has legitimately reached Value Extinction and, where applicable, Value Finality.
Its purpose is to ensure that terminal value outcomes do not disappear into undocumented organizational decisions, accounting actions, asset disposal processes, system changes, or historical ambiguity.
VXRM establishes a persistent methodological record of:

what governed value became extinct; which Value Object or relationship carried that value; which Value Context applied; which value dimension was affected; what extinction boundary applied; what extinction determination was reached; whether Value Finality was established; what residual values remained; what lifecycle pathways were closed; what lifecycle history preceded extinction; and what distinction must be preserved between the extinguished value and any future new value.
The Module therefore ensures:
Value Extinction becomes a governed lifecycle fact rather than an undocumented terminal assumption.
Architectural Position
VXRM is the final Core Module of VXSS and the terminal recording point of the VFM® Value Lifecycle.
The VXSS module sequence is:
VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module → VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module → VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module → VXFM — Value Finality Module → VXRM — Value Extinction Record Module
VXFM establishes:
Value Finality.
VXRM preserves:
the governed record of how that terminal lifecycle state was reached and what exactly it means.
Therefore:
Value Finality ≠ Value Extinction Record.
Internal Flow

Value Extinction Determination → Value Finality Status where applicable → Governed Value Identification → Extinction Scope Capture → Extinction Basis Capture → Lifecycle History Linkage → Residual Value Separation Capture → Finality Boundary Capture → Terminal Status Capture → Record Integrity Requirements → Value Extinction Record Creation → Record Preservation → Terminal VFM® Lifecycle Record
Operational Space
VXRM governs the recording space associated with terminal Value Lifecycle outcomes.
Its operational space includes:
extinction record creation; terminal value identification; lifecycle linkage; Value Context linkage; Value Object linkage; value-dimension identification; extinction-scope recording; extinction-basis recording; threshold-reference recording; extinction-determination recording; finality-status recording; residual-value recording; restoration-pathway closure recording; lifecycle chronology; terminal-state provenance; record status; record correction; record supersession; future Value Emergence separation;
cross-system referenceability.
Operational Scope
VXRM does not determine whether value is extinct.
It does not determine whether the extinction threshold was reached.
It does not establish Value Finality.
It records the governed results produced through the preceding VXSS lifecycle.
Therefore:
Record Creation ≠ Extinction Determination.
Record Creation ≠ Value Finality.
VXRM preserves governance outcomes; it does not manufacture them.

Value Extinction Record Principle
A Value Extinction Record is the structured governance representation of the terminal lifecycle outcome of a defined governed value.
The record should make it possible to determine:
What value existed?
What happened to it?
Which lifecycle boundary was crossed?
What exactly became extinct?
Was extinction partial, dimensional, contextual, or complete within the defined scope?
Was Value Finality established?
What remained outside the extinction boundary?
What lifecycle history supports the terminal status?
The record therefore preserves the meaning of extinction beyond the moment when the determination occurred.
Extinction Record ≠ Value Object Record
VXRM records the extinction of governed value.
It does not automatically become the master record of the underlying Value Object.
An object may continue to exist after one of its values becomes extinct.
Therefore:
Value Object Record ≠ Value Extinction Record.
The two may be linked, but they remain methodologically distinct.
Extinction Record ≠ Deletion Record
Value Extinction does not require deletion of the object, data, evidence, or lifecycle history.
Likewise, the Value Extinction Record is not a deletion instruction.
Therefore:
Value Extinction Record ≠ Data Deletion Record.
Record retention and data deletion may be governed by separate legal, operational, security, privacy, or information- governance requirements.
Record Identity

Each governed Value Extinction Record should possess a distinguishable record identity sufficient to prevent confusion between:
different Value Objects; different values associated with the same object; different value dimensions; different Value Contexts; different lifecycle instances; repeated extinction assessments; corrected determinations; superseded records; future newly emerged value.
Record identity must preserve the distinction between:
the object
and
the value whose lifecycle ended.
Governed Value Identification
VXRM should identify the value to which the extinction record applies.
The identification should be sufficiently precise to distinguish:
Extinguished Value A
from:
Remaining Value B
and:
Future New Value C.
This prevents terminal records from being interpreted as universal statements about all possible value associated with the underlying object.
Value Object Linkage
Where the extinguished value is associated with a Value Object, the record should maintain a governed reference to that object.
However:
Object Linkage ≠ Value Identity.
The same Value Object may support multiple values and multiple value lifecycles.
The extinction of one does not automatically terminate the others.
Value Context Capture
Because value is contextual, VXRM should preserve the Value Context within which extinction was determined.
This may include relevant:

operational context; economic context; technological context; temporal context; organizational context; relational context; jurisdictional context; strategic context;
where those dimensions materially define the governed value.
Therefore:
Extinction Without Context May Become Semantically Ambiguous.
Value Dimension Capture
Where extinction applies only to a particular value dimension, that dimension must remain explicit.
Examples may include:
productive value; operational value; informational value; strategic value; economic value; functional value; temporal value; relational value.
The record must prevent:
Dimensional Extinction
from being interpreted as:
Universal Value Extinction.
Extinction Scope Capture
VXRM should preserve the exact scope of the extinction determination.
The scope may be:
total within the governed value lifecycle; partial; dimensional; contextual; relational; temporal; capability-specific.
Therefore:
Extinction Record Scope must not exceed Extinction Determination Scope.
Extinction Basis Capture
The record should preserve the governed basis on which extinction was determined.
This may include references to:
extinction conditions; threshold satisfaction; recoverability findings; restoration limitations; relevant Value States; prior ReMonet™ attempts where applicable; material dependencies; relevant external determinations; final extinction determination.
VXRM does not independently validate these inputs.

It preserves their relationship to the terminal lifecycle conclusion.
Threshold Reference
Where an extinction threshold was used, VXRM should preserve sufficient reference to establish:
which threshold applied; which governed value it applied to; which context applied; when the threshold was considered satisfied; which determination relied upon it.
This creates continuity between:
Threshold
and
Terminal Lifecycle Outcome.
Determination Capture
The Value Extinction Record should preserve the actual extinction determination.
The record should distinguish among outcomes such as:
extinction not established; extinction indeterminate; partial extinction; dimensional extinction; contextual extinction; Value Extinction established.
Only a legitimately established terminal outcome should be represented as final extinction.
Finality Status Capture
Where VXFM has established Value Finality, VXRM should preserve that status separately from the extinction determination.
This maintains the distinction:
Value Extinct
from:
Value Final.
The record should therefore be capable of representing an extinction determination before finality where the architecture requires an intermediate governance state.
Finality Boundary Capture
Where Value Finality applies, VXRM should preserve its exact boundary.
This may include:
value identity; lifecycle identity; value dimension; Value Context; affected relationship; effective point; excluded residual values; same-value restoration closure.

This ensures that Finality remains bounded rather than becoming an uncontrolled universal conclusion.
Residual Value Record
VXRM must preserve material residual value where it exists.
For example:
Productive Value → Extinct and Final
may coexist with:
Material Value → Active
Historical Value → Active
Informational Value → Active
The terminal record should therefore distinguish:
what ended
from:
what remained.
Residual Value ≠ Exception to Extinction
The presence of another surviving value does not invalidate extinction of the governed value.
A machine may permanently lose its original production value while retaining scrap value.
Therefore:
Residual Value ≠ Persistence of the Extinguished Value.
Lifecycle History Linkage
VXRM should maintain sufficient linkage to the preceding VFM® lifecycle so that terminal status is not isolated from its methodological history.
The lifecycle may include:
Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → ZVA™ where applicable → Value Restoration where applicable → Value Extinction → Value Finality → Value Extinction Record
Not every lifecycle must pass through every optional branch.
The record should preserve the actual governed pathway.
Lifecycle Record ≠ Lifecycle Reconstruction
VXRM should not invent missing historical states merely to produce a complete-looking record.

Where lifecycle information is unavailable, the record should preserve that limitation.
Therefore:
Unknown Lifecycle History ≠ Assumed Lifecycle History.
Chronology Integrity
VXRM should preserve the temporal ordering of relevant lifecycle events.
Important distinctions may include:
degradation date; zero-value date; restoration attempt date; extinction-threshold date; extinction-determination date; finality effective date; record creation date; correction date.
These dates must not be collapsed into a single terminal timestamp where doing so would distort lifecycle reality.
Record Creation Time ≠ Extinction Time
The record may be created after the value actually became extinct.
Therefore:
Record Creation Date ≠ Value Extinction Effective Date by Default.
Both should remain separately identifiable where known.
Terminal Status
VXRM should establish a record status indicating the governance position of the terminal record.
Possible statuses may include:
1. Draft Extinction Record
Terminal information is being assembled.
2. Pending Extinction Record
Required terminal governance inputs remain incomplete.
3. Active Extinction Record
A governed extinction determination has been recorded.
4. Final Extinction Record
Value Finality has been established and terminal lifecycle recording is complete.
5. Record Under Review
Material information challenges the existing record.
6. Corrected Extinction Record
The record has been formally corrected while preserving prior history.

7. Superseded Extinction Record
A later governed record replaces the current authoritative representation without erasing the earlier record.
These are VFM® governance statuses rather than accounting, legal, archival, or regulatory classifications.
Record Finality ≠ Immutability
A final record should be stable.
However, stability does not mean that factual or governance errors must remain permanently uncorrectable.
Therefore:
Record Finality ≠ Absolute Immutability.
A governed correction pathway should remain available where legitimate evidence demonstrates that the record is inaccurate.
Correction Principle
Where a Value Extinction Record is incorrect, VXRM should permit controlled correction.
A correction should preserve:
the original record; the corrected information; the reason for correction; the relationship between versions; the effective status of the correction.
The architecture should avoid silent replacement of terminal lifecycle history.
Therefore:
Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Supersession Principle
Where a new authoritative record supersedes an earlier record, the relationship should remain visible.
The earlier record should not silently disappear.
This enables reconstruction of:
what was previously believed
versus:
what is currently governed as authoritative.
New Evidence After Finality
New evidence may emerge after a terminal record has been created.
VXRM should distinguish two fundamentally different situations:
Situation A — Prior Determination Was Wrong

Evidence demonstrates that the value was not legitimately extinct.
The appropriate pathway is:
Review → Correction → Lifecycle Repositioning
Situation B — Genuine New Value Appears
The original value was legitimately extinct, but new circumstances create a different value.
The appropriate pathway is:
New Value Emergence → New Value Lifecycle
Therefore:
New Evidence ≠ Automatic Restoration.
Future Value Separation
The extinction record should provide sufficient semantic separation to prevent future new value from being confused with the extinguished value.
This is particularly important where the same Value Object later acquires:
new technological use; new economic relevance; new cultural significance; new strategic importance; new informational value; new relational value.
The future value may share the same object.
It does not necessarily share the same Value Lifecycle.
Record Continuity
VXRM should preserve continuity between the terminal record and the lifecycle that produced it.
Continuity may include references to:
value identity; Value Object; Value Context; prior Value States; relevant Value Changes; DeMonet™ where applicable; ZVA™ where applicable; ReMonet™ where applicable; extinction conditions; extinction threshold; extinction determination; finality status.
The purpose is not to duplicate every prior record.
The purpose is to make the terminal outcome traceable to its governed lifecycle.
Record Integrity

VXRM requires that the Value Extinction Record remain sufficiently reliable for its governance purpose.
This includes preservation of:
completeness appropriate to scope; internal consistency; lifecycle linkage; version relationships; correction history; finality status; record identity.
However, broader integrity governance belongs to INTEGROS®.
Therefore:
VXRM defines what the Value Extinction Record must represent.
INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of that representation.
Auditability Boundary
VXRM establishes the terminal value record.
It does not replace independent auditability or evidence governance.
Where auditability is required:
ADIT® may govern the evidence and audit trail supporting the record.
Therefore:
Value Extinction Record ≠ Independent Audit Evidence.
Validation Boundary
VXRM may reference validated inputs.
It does not independently validate the truth of every external claim used in the extinction process.
Where formal validation is required:
VALIDOS® governs the validation process.
Therefore:
Recorded Claim ≠ Validated Claim by Default.
Identity Boundary
VXRM may link the terminal record to a Value Object.
The authoritative identity, provenance, ownership, or origin of that object may be governed through OBIDENITY®.
Therefore:
Value Extinction Record ≠ Object Identity Governance.
Record Retention Boundary
VXRM establishes the methodological requirement to preserve terminal lifecycle meaning.
It does not prescribe universal legal retention periods.

Retention duration may depend on:
law; regulation; contractual obligations; industry requirements; organizational policy; evidence requirements; operational needs.
Therefore:
Methodological Preservation Requirement ≠ Universal Retention Period.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VXRM implementation should establish:
1. Record Identity
Assign a distinguishable identity to the Value Extinction Record.
2. Governed Value Identification
Identify the specific value whose lifecycle reached extinction.
3. Value Object Linkage
Link the record to the relevant Value Object or relationship where applicable.
4. Value Context Capture
Preserve the context within which extinction was determined.
5. Extinction Scope
Record whether extinction is total, partial, dimensional, contextual, temporal, or otherwise bounded.
6. Extinction Basis
Reference the governed basis supporting the extinction determination.
7. Extinction Determination
Capture the authoritative determination produced by VXDM.
8. Finality Status
Capture the Value Finality status produced by VXFM where applicable.
9. Residual Value Separation
Record material values remaining outside the extinction boundary.
10. Lifecycle Linkage
Maintain traceability to relevant preceding VFM® lifecycle stages.
11. Chronology
Preserve material lifecycle and terminal timestamps separately.
12. Record Status
Assign the appropriate terminal record status.
13. Correction Governance

Provide a controlled pathway for review, correction, and supersession.
14. Future Value Separation
Prevent future new Value Emergence from being misrepresented as restoration of legitimately extinguished value.
15. Preservation
Maintain the terminal record for the period and governance purpose required by applicable systems.

Enterprise Application
VXRM provides organizations with a structured terminal record for values that have legitimately completed the VFM® lifecycle.
This is particularly useful where organizations manage:
industrial assets; infrastructure; technology portfolios; legacy systems; digital assets; data; intellectual property; product portfolios; research programs; organizational capabilities; strategic resources; long-lived operational assets.
Without a governed terminal record, organizations may lose the distinction between:
value that is currently zero
and

value that has actually become extinct.
They may also lose the distinction between:
an extinguished value
and
new value that later emerges from the same object.
VXRM preserves these distinctions across time.
Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset Extinction Record
A production machine has permanently lost its original specialized productive value.
The preceding VXSS modules establish:
Extinction Conditions Satisfied → Extinction Threshold Reached → Productive Value Extinct → Productive Value Final
However, the physical machine remains.
It retains:
Material Value
and potentially:
Historical Value.
VXRM creates a terminal record specifying:
Governed Value: Original Specialized Productive Value Extinction Scope: Productive Value Dimension Finality: Established ReMonet™ Pathway: Closed for Original Productive Value Residual Value: Material Value retained Object Status: Object continues to exist
Years later, the machine becomes historically significant.
That new historical value can enter a new or continuing applicable Value Lifecycle without rewriting the extinction record of the original productive value.
Use Case 2 — Extinction Record for
Irrecoverable Digital Information
An organization possesses fragments of a legacy dataset.
The original contextual structure required to interpret the information has been irreversibly lost.
Following governed assessment:
Original Informational Value → Extinct
and:
Original Informational Value → Final.
VXRM records:

Value Object: Surviving Data Fragments Governed Value: Original Contextual Informational Value Extinction Scope: Original Informational Relationship Extinction Basis: Irrecoverable loss of required contextual structure Finality: Established Residual Value: Raw data fragments remain Lifecycle Status: Closed for Original Informational Value
Several years later, a new analytical technology discovers a different use for the fragments.
The original extinction record remains valid.
The newly created analytical usefulness is governed as:
New Value Emergence
rather than:
restoration of the original extinguished informational value.
Foundational Principles
Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Extinction Determination.
Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Finality.
Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Object Record.
Value Extinction Record ≠ Data Deletion Record.
Value Extinction Record ≠ Independent Audit Evidence.
Recorded Claim ≠ Validated Claim by Default.

Supersession ≠ Silent Replacement.

Canonical Closing Statement
Value Extinction Record Module establishes the terminal recording layer of the Value Extinction Standard by preserving the governed identity, context, scope, basis, determination, finality, chronology, residual value, and lifecycle history of value that has legitimately reached extinction. VXRM ensures that terminal value outcomes remain distinguishable from object destruction, accounting write-offs, data deletion, temporary zero value, dormancy, failed restoration, and future new Value Emergence. Through explicit record identity, lifecycle linkage, bounded extinction scope, residual-value separation, correction governance, supersession continuity, and terminal-state preservation, the Module converts Value Extinction from a transient organizational conclusion into a persistent and interpretable governance record. The VFM® Value Lifecycle therefore ends not by erasing value history, but by preserving exactly what value existed, how its governed lifecycle ended, what remained, and where any future value must begin anew.

Canonical Definition
Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) is the second Core Module of the Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture.
VXTM governs the definition, application, testing, and documentation of the threshold separating value that remains legitimately recoverable from value whose recoverability has become sufficiently exhausted, unavailable, or terminated to justify formal Value Extinction determination.

The Module receives qualified extinction conditions from VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module and evaluates whether those conditions collectively reach the governed boundary beyond which restoration of the same relevant value can no longer be treated as a legitimate continuation pathway within the defined value lifecycle.
Its operational purpose is:
to establish whether the governed boundary between recoverable value loss and potential terminal non- recoverability has been reached before any formal Value Extinction determination is made.
Architectural Position
VXTM occupies the critical boundary between:
Extinction Conditions
and
Extinction Determination.
Its architectural position is:
VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module → VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module
→ VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module
VXCM establishes which conditions are materially relevant.
VXTM establishes whether those conditions reach the required terminal boundary.
VXDM subsequently determines whether the relevant value is legitimately extinct.
Therefore:
Condition ≠ Threshold.
Threshold ≠ Determination.
Internal Flow

Governed Extinction Conditions → Relevant Value Boundary Confirmation → Recoverability Criteria Definition → Restoration Boundary Definition → Threshold Criteria Definition → Threshold Evidence Association → Alternative Recovery Pathway Test → Residual Recoverability Test → Threshold Satisfaction Assessment → Threshold Status → Governed Extinction Threshold Result → VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module
Operational Space
VXTM governs the space between:
material conditions threatening recoverability
and
formal determination that the relevant value has become extinct.
Its operational space includes:
recoverability criteria; restoration boundaries; extinction-threshold criteria; threshold evidence; threshold dependencies; threshold satisfaction; residual recoverability; alternative recovery pathways; partial threshold satisfaction; dimensional thresholds; contextual thresholds; temporal thresholds; compound thresholds; uncertainty; threshold reassessment; threshold status.
VXTM does not itself declare Value Extinction.
It establishes whether the required boundary for such a determination has been reached.
The Extinction Threshold
The Value Extinction Threshold is the governed boundary separating:
value that remains recoverable within its defined lifecycle
from
value for which legitimate recoverability has been sufficiently exhausted to permit formal extinction determination.
The threshold must be connected to:

the specific governed value; the relevant Value Object; the relevant value dimension; the relevant Value Context; the defined lifecycle; the restoration boundary; the available recovery pathways; the applicable recoverability criteria.
An extinction threshold cannot be meaningfully governed in abstraction from the value to which it applies.
Threshold ≠ Zero
The extinction threshold is not automatically reached when value reaches zero.
A value may enter:
ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™
while retaining significant restoration potential.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Extinction Threshold.
The zero-value condition describes the present Value State.
The extinction threshold addresses whether the pathway for recovery of that same value has reached its terminal boundary.
Threshold ≠ Nullification
DeMonet™ may move positive value into a zero-value condition.
That transition does not establish that the value is unrecoverable.
The architecture therefore preserves:
Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ → Recoverability Remains → ReMonet™ remains possible
and separately:
ZVA™
→ Extinction Conditions
→ Extinction Threshold Reached
→ Extinction Determination
Therefore:
Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction Threshold.
Recoverability Criteria
Before an extinction threshold can be applied, the meaning of recoverability must be sufficiently defined.
Recoverability criteria may include, where relevant:

technical recoverability; functional recoverability; informational recoverability; operational recoverability; relational recoverability; contextual recoverability; temporal recoverability; legal or rights-dependent recoverability; economic recoverability; structural recoverability.
Not every criterion must apply to every value.
The applicable criteria must derive from the nature of the governed value and its defined restoration boundary.
Recoverability Is Value-Specific
A Value Object may contain multiple forms or dimensions of value.
The extinction threshold must therefore apply to the relevant value rather than automatically to the entire object.
For example, a production machine may permanently lose:
productive value
while retaining:
material value
component value
historical value
or
informational value.
Therefore:
Threshold Reached for One Value Dimension ≠ Threshold Reached for Every Value Dimension.
Restoration Boundary
VXTM requires a defined restoration boundary.
The restoration boundary identifies the legitimate space within which recovery of the same value may still be treated as Value Restoration rather than creation of a different value.
This distinction is essential.
Without it, almost any future value associated with an object could incorrectly be interpreted as restoration of the original value.
The restoration boundary may include:

identity of the prior value; value dimension; value relationship; relevant context; functional continuity; temporal continuity; permissible transformation; restoration mechanism; required dependencies; acceptable discontinuities.
Same Value Test
VXTM must distinguish recovery of the same relevant value from creation of another value.
For example:
A destroyed industrial machine is replaced by a new machine.
Production capability returns.
But the new machine's productive value may represent:
New Value Emergence
rather than:
restoration of the extinguished productive value of the original machine.
Therefore:
Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value.
The extinction threshold concerns recoverability of:
the same governed value
not whether some substitute value can eventually perform a similar function.
Alternative Recovery Pathway Test
Before the extinction threshold is treated as satisfied, materially credible alternative restoration pathways should be considered.
Potential pathways may include:
repair; reconstruction; remanufacturing; technological conversion; data recovery; reconstruction from secondary sources; reactivation; rights recovery; contextual transfer; dependency replacement; controlled substitution where continuity of the same value remains legitimate.
The existence of one failed pathway does not establish threshold satisfaction.
Failed Recovery Pathway ≠ Exhausted Recoverability.
Residual Recoverability
Recoverability does not need to be complete to remain material.

A value may retain:
partial recoverability; conditional recoverability; dimensional recoverability; contextual recoverability; delayed recoverability; uncertain but credible recoverability.
Where such recoverability remains legitimately material:
the extinction threshold may not yet be satisfied.
Restoration Potential ≠ Restoration Certainty
A value does not need to be easily recoverable to remain below the extinction threshold.
The architecture distinguishes:
Restoration Potential
from
Restoration Certainty.
A difficult, expensive, technically complex, or uncertain restoration pathway may still represent legitimate recoverability.
Therefore:
Low Probability of Restoration ≠ Automatic Extinction Threshold.
Economic Threshold Principle
Current restoration cost may exceed current economic value.
That fact may influence organizational decisions.
But it does not universally establish Value Extinction.
For example:
Restoration Cost > Current Economic Return
may justify:
Do Not Restore
without establishing:
Cannot Be Restored as the Same Value.
Therefore:
Economic Non-Viability ≠ Universal Non-Recoverability.
Where economic recoverability is itself the governed value dimension, however, economic criteria may legitimately form part of the extinction threshold.
Technical Possibility ≠ Unlimited Recoverability
The opposite error must also be avoided.

The mere theoretical possibility that some future technology might recover value does not require VFM® to preserve the lifecycle indefinitely.
VXTM operates within a governed restoration boundary.
Recoverability should therefore be evaluated against:
established capabilities; reasonably identifiable pathways; materially credible dependencies; applicable governance criteria; known constraints; defined lifecycle assumptions.
Therefore:
Theoretical Future Possibility ≠ Established Restoration Pathway.
Threshold Criteria
A Value Extinction Threshold may require one or more criteria to be satisfied.
Examples may include:
essential value basis irreversibly lost; required value relationship permanently terminated; critical information irrecoverably unavailable; required capability no longer reconstructable; all legitimate restoration pathways exhausted; necessary dependencies permanently unavailable; restoration would create fundamentally new value rather than recover the prior value; contextual conditions permanently eliminate the relevant value relationship; temporal boundary permanently passed; required continuity irreversibly broken.
The applicable threshold must remain specific to the governed value.
Single-Criterion Threshold
Certain value relationships may depend upon one indispensable condition.
If that condition is irreversibly lost, a single criterion may be sufficient to satisfy the extinction threshold.
For example:

A unique cryptographic key may be indispensable to a particular access value.
If the key is irretrievably lost and no legitimate recovery or reconstruction pathway exists, the loss of that single dependency may be sufficient to reach the threshold for that specific access value.
Compound Threshold
Many extinction cases require multiple criteria.
A Compound Extinction Threshold exists where several conditions collectively establish terminal non-recoverability.
For example:
Critical Component Loss
Source Documentation Loss
Control-System Incompatibility
No Reconstruction Capability
No Alternative Restoration Pathway
may collectively satisfy the threshold even where no single condition would independently be terminal.
Necessary and Sufficient Criteria
VXTM may distinguish:
Necessary Criteria
from
Sufficient Criteria.
A necessary criterion must be present before the threshold can be reached.
A sufficient criterion, where legitimately defined, may independently establish threshold satisfaction.
Compound thresholds may require:
Criterion A + Criterion B + Criterion C
before terminal-boundary satisfaction occurs.
This structure prevents arbitrary threshold interpretation.
Threshold Materiality
Threshold criteria must be materially connected to recoverability.
A condition should not contribute to threshold satisfaction merely because it is negative, inconvenient, costly, or undesirable.
The relevant question remains:

Does this criterion materially affect whether the same governed value can legitimately be recovered?
Threshold Satisfaction States
VXTM may recognize:
1. Threshold Not Reached
Material recoverability remains.
2. Threshold Approaching
Extinction conditions are materially reducing recoverability, but the terminal boundary has not been reached.
3. Threshold Conditionally Reached
The threshold is satisfied only under defined contextual, temporal, or dependency conditions.
4. Threshold Partially Reached
The threshold is satisfied for one value dimension or portion of the governed value but not others.
5. Threshold Reached
Applicable extinction-threshold criteria have been satisfied sufficiently to permit formal Value Extinction determination.
6. Threshold Indeterminate
Available information is insufficient to establish whether the threshold has been reached.
These states preserve uncertainty and prevent binary conclusions where evidence does not support them.
Threshold Reached ≠ Value Extinct
This is the central governance boundary of VXTM.
Reaching the threshold means:
the case is eligible for formal Value Extinction determination.
It does not mean:
Value Extinction has already been formally determined.
Therefore:
Threshold Reached ≠ Extinction Determined.
The formal determination belongs to:
VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module.
Partial Threshold Satisfaction
A Value Object may cross the extinction threshold for only part of its value.
For example:

An industrial system may permanently lose its original production capability while retaining valuable materials and technical documentation.
VXTM may therefore establish:
Productive Value → Threshold Reached
while:
Material Value → Threshold Not Reached
and:
Informational Value → Recoverability Retained.
Contextual Threshold
The threshold may be reached within one context without being reached universally.
A technology may become permanently unusable under one regulatory, technical, or operational environment while remaining usable elsewhere.
Therefore:
Contextual Threshold Reached ≠ Universal Value Extinction.
The context must remain explicit.
Temporal Threshold
Certain value depends upon a time-bound opportunity.
Where the relevant temporal boundary passes irreversibly, the associated value may become unrecoverable.
However, VXTM must distinguish:
loss of a specific historical opportunity
from
loss of every future value associated with the underlying object.
The expired opportunity may cross its extinction threshold while other value persists.
Threshold Uncertainty
Where material uncertainty remains concerning:
alternative restoration pathways; condition reversibility; missing evidence; technological recoverability; dependency reconstruction; continuity of the same value;
VXTM should preserve that uncertainty.
A threshold should not be declared reached merely because recovery has not yet been demonstrated.

Absence of Demonstrated Recovery ≠ Demonstration of Non-Recoverability.
Threshold Reassessment
Material new information may justify reassessment before formal extinction determination.
Examples include:
discovery of backup data; identification of an alternative repair pathway; recovery of missing documentation; discovery of a previously unknown dependency; new evidence that a condition is reversible; discovery that the relevant value dimension was incorrectly defined.
VXTM therefore permits threshold reassessment while the lifecycle remains open.
Boundary with VXCM
VXCM asks:
What conditions materially threaten recoverability?
VXTM asks:
Have those conditions reached the governed terminal boundary?
Therefore:
Extinction Conditions ≠ Extinction Threshold.
Boundary with VRSS
VRSS governs the pathway through which previously existing value may be restored.
VXTM governs whether legitimate restoration potential has become sufficiently exhausted to permit extinction determination.
The architecture therefore creates a decisive branch:
Recoverability Retained → VRSS — Value Restoration Standard
Recoverability Terminally Exhausted → VXSS — Value Extinction Pathway
Boundary with VNS
VNS governs the transition to zero value.
VXTM governs whether recoverability of that zero value has reached its terminal boundary.
Therefore:
ZVA™ may remain below the extinction threshold.
Boundary with VXDM
VXTM determines threshold status.
VXDM determines extinction status.
Therefore:

Threshold Assessment ≠ Extinction Determination.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum VXTM implementation should establish:
1. Governed Value Boundary
Confirm the exact value, dimension, context, and lifecycle under assessment.
2. Extinction Condition Input
Receive qualified Extinction Conditions from VXCM.
3. Recoverability Criteria
Define what constitutes legitimate recovery of the same value.
4. Restoration Boundary
Define the boundary separating restoration from replacement, substitution, or New Value Emergence.
5. Threshold Criteria
Define necessary, sufficient, compound, contextual, dimensional, or temporal threshold criteria.
6. Alternative Pathway Test
Assess materially credible restoration pathways.
7. Residual Recoverability Test
Determine whether partial, conditional, contextual, or other material recoverability remains.
8. Threshold Satisfaction Assessment
Evaluate the governed conditions against the applicable threshold.
9. Threshold Status
Assign the appropriate threshold state.
10. Determination Transfer
Transfer the governed threshold result to VXDM for formal Value Extinction determination.
Governance Outputs
VXTM may produce:

Value Recoverability Criteria Record Value Restoration Boundary Value Extinction Threshold Definition Threshold Criteria Record Alternative Recovery Pathway Assessment Residual Recoverability Assessment Compound Threshold Assessment Dimensional Threshold Record Contextual Threshold Record Temporal Threshold Record Threshold Uncertainty Record Threshold Satisfaction Assessment Value Extinction Threshold Status Governed Extinction Threshold Result
Enterprise Application
VXTM provides organizations with a governed boundary for deciding when impaired, dormant, inaccessible, zero-value, or failed-restoration assets should move from recovery governance into formal extinction consideration.
This is especially relevant to:
industrial asset portfolios; legacy infrastructure; distressed investments; intellectual property portfolios; abandoned technologies; obsolete platforms; digital assets; historical data; discontinued products; stranded assets; long-term research programs; organizational capabilities.
Without such a threshold, organizations may make two opposite errors:
Premature Extinction — abandoning recoverable value.
or
Artificial Recoverability — indefinitely treating terminally lost value as recoverable.
VXTM creates the governance boundary between those two states.
Use Case 1 — Specialized Industrial Asset
A specialized industrial machine has reached ZVA™ after severe degradation.

The manufacturer no longer exists, essential components are unavailable, original control software has been lost, and two restoration attempts have failed.
VXCM has already established material Extinction Conditions.
VXTM now tests:
ZVA™ → Recoverability Criteria → Restoration Boundary → Component Reconstruction Possibility → Software Reconstruction Possibility → Alternative Modernization Pathway → Residual Productive Value Recoverability → Threshold Assessment
If a legitimate modernization pathway can restore the same productive value relationship, the threshold remains unreached.
If every legitimate pathway has been exhausted and any replacement would constitute New Value rather than restoration of the machine's prior productive value:
Productive Value Extinction Threshold → Reached
The machine may still retain material or historical value.
Use Case 2 — Irretrievably Lost Digital Access
Value
A digital asset depends upon a unique cryptographic credential.
The credential has been permanently lost.
No backup exists.
No recovery key exists.
No reconstruction pathway exists.
The underlying system remains operational, but the specific access relationship represented by the credential cannot be recreated as the same governed access value.
VXTM evaluates:
Credential Loss → Recoverability Criteria → Alternative Recovery Pathways → Dependency Reconstruction Test → Same Value Test → Residual Recoverability Test → Threshold Satisfaction

If a replacement credential would establish a fundamentally new access relationship rather than restore the prior one:
Original Access Value Extinction Threshold → Reached
This permits the case to proceed to formal extinction determination without incorrectly declaring every other value associated with the digital asset extinct.
Foundational Principles
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction Threshold.
Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction Threshold.
Extinction Condition ≠ Extinction Threshold.
Extinction Threshold ≠ Extinction Determination.
Threshold Reached ≠ Value Extinct.
Failed ReMonet™ ≠ Extinction Threshold Reached.
Failed Recovery Pathway ≠ Exhausted Recoverability.
Low Restoration Probability ≠ Automatic Extinction.
Economic Non-Viability ≠ Universal Non-Recoverability.
Theoretical Future Possibility ≠ Established Restoration Pathway.
Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value.
Residual Recoverability must be tested before terminal threshold satisfaction.
Thresholds apply to specific value dimensions, contexts, relationships, and lifecycles.
A threshold may be reached for one value dimension while other value persists.
Absence of demonstrated recovery is not proof of non-recoverability.
The extinction threshold exists to determine when formal extinction determination becomes legitimate—not to make that determination itself.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Extinction Threshold Module establishes the governed boundary between recoverable value loss and potential terminal non-recoverability within VFM®. Through explicit recoverability criteria, restoration boundaries, threshold criteria, alternative recovery pathway testing, residual recoverability assessment, dimensional and contextual boundaries, uncertainty preservation, and formal threshold status, VXTM prevents zero value, failed restoration, obsolescence, economic non-viability, or severe impairment from being automatically interpreted as Value Extinction. The Module determines when the governed basis for formal extinction determination has been reached while preserving the architectural distinction between Value Nullification, Value Restoration, and Value Extinction. Value crosses the extinction threshold not merely because recovery is difficult or absent today, but because the legitimate pathway for recovery of that same governed value has reached its defined terminal boundary.

Canonical Definition
Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
VXSS establishes the methodological boundary between zero value and extinguished value by determining when a value condition has moved beyond degradation, dormancy, impairment, loss, nullification, or recoverable zero value into a state in which restoration of the relevant value is no longer legitimately available within the same governed lifecycle.
The Standard does not define every physical, economic, technological, legal, organizational, market, environmental, or operational event capable of causing extinction.
Its task is narrower:

to determine when the value consequence of those events has crossed the governed boundary from recoverable value into terminal value finality.
Core Question
When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle?
Architectural Position
VXSS occupies the eleventh and final governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle.
It follows:
Value Restoration Standard (VRSS).
The preceding standards govern value as it:
emerges
→ is identified
→ is attributed
→ enters a governed state
→ changes
→ develops
→ degrades
→ reaches zero where applicable
→ may be restored where recoverability remains.
VXSS governs the final question:
When is restoration no longer a legitimate continuation of the same value lifecycle?
This makes Value Extinction the terminal lifecycle boundary of VFM®.
Governance Flow Position
Existing Value → Value Development / Value Change → Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable → Restoration Potential Assessment → Value Extinction Conditions → Value Extinction Threshold → Value Extinction Determination → Value Finality → Value Extinction Record
The critical architectural boundary is:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
Operational Space
VXSS governs the space between:
value that remains recoverable
and
value that has ceased to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
Its operational space includes:

extinction-condition identification; recoverability assessment; restoration-potential exhaustion; extinction-threshold definition; threshold satisfaction; irreversible value loss; lifecycle termination; value identity discontinuity; terminal impairment; terminal obsolescence; terminal loss of utility; terminal loss of capability; terminal loss of relevance; terminal loss of rights where value-dependent; terminal loss of recoverable economic function; extinction determination; value finality; terminal-state recording; distinction between extinction and temporary zero value; distinction between extinction and dormancy; distinction between extinction and degradation; distinction between extinction and new Value Emergence.
Operational Scope
VXSS may apply to value associated with:
physical assets; industrial assets; infrastructure; digital assets; data; intellectual property; technologies; products; services; productive capabilities; operational capabilities; contractual or economic rights; organizational capabilities; financial or economic assets; information; knowledge structures; platforms; systems; market relationships; other governable Value Objects.
Value Extinction does not require destruction of the underlying object.
An object may continue to exist while a particular value associated with it becomes extinct.
Value Object ≠ Value
VXSS preserves a fundamental distinction:
Object Existence ≠ Value Existence.

A machine may physically remain after its productive value becomes extinct.
A dataset may remain stored after its relevant informational value becomes extinct.
A technology may remain technically functional after its commercial value becomes extinct.
An intellectual property right may remain legally registered after a particular economic value becomes extinct.
The continued existence of the object therefore does not prove continued recoverability of the governed value.
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction
This is the foundational distinction of VXSS.
A value may reach:
zero
without becoming extinct.
A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may retain:
restoration potential; dormant utility; technological recoverability; economic recoverability; informational recoverability; functional recoverability; strategic recoverability; rights-based recoverability; future relevance.
Therefore:
Zero Value may be a state.
Value Extinction is a terminal lifecycle determination.
ZVA™ and Extinction
A ZVA™ may remain within the active governed lifecycle because ReMonet™ may still restore previously existing value.
The lifecycle may therefore legitimately contain:
Positive Value
→ DeMonet™
→ ZVA™
→ ReMonet™
→ Restored Value.
VXSS applies when that restoration pathway is no longer legitimately available for the relevant value within the same governed lifecycle.
Therefore:
ZVA™ ≠ Extinguished Value.
Value Extinction Principle

Value Extinction occurs only when sufficient governed conditions establish that the relevant previously existing value no longer remains recoverable within the governed lifecycle.
The determination must relate to a defined value.
It must not be inferred merely because:
current value is zero; an asset is unused; an asset is obsolete; a market temporarily disappeared; restoration is expensive; restoration has not yet been attempted; one restoration attempt failed; current technology cannot restore the value; an organization no longer wants the asset; a business model has temporarily failed.
Extinction requires a stronger governed basis.
Recoverability Principle
Recoverability is the central boundary variable of VXSS.
The relevant question is not merely:
Does the value exist now?
It is:
Does the previously existing value remain legitimately recoverable within the governed lifecycle?
Recoverability may depend upon:
physical possibility; technical possibility; informational continuity; legal continuity; identity continuity; economic viability where materially relevant; functional continuity; restoration mechanism availability; remaining asset capability; preservation of the underlying value basis; temporal conditions; contextual conditions.
Recoverability ≠ Immediate Restorability
A value does not need to be immediately restorable in order to remain recoverable.
Restoration may require:

new technology; capital; time; infrastructure; regulatory change; reconstruction; market recovery; technical intervention; data reconstruction; new operational capability.
Therefore:
Not Currently Restorable ≠ Extinct.
VXSS must avoid premature extinction determinations based solely on current limitations.
Restoration Cost ≠ Extinction
A value may be economically irrational to restore while still technically recoverable.
Conversely, unlimited expenditure does not guarantee that extinct value can be restored.
VXSS therefore separates:
Restoration Economics
from
Value Existence.
High restoration cost may influence organizational decisions.
It does not automatically establish Value Extinction.
Failed Restoration ≠ Extinction
A failed ReMonet™ process does not automatically prove extinction.
Failure may result from:
incorrect restoration method; insufficient resources; incomplete intervention; technical execution failure; incorrect assumptions; missing capabilities; premature intervention; temporary external conditions.
VXSS requires the failure of a particular restoration attempt to remain distinct from the broader determination that the relevant value itself is no longer recoverable.
Therefore:
Failed ReMonet™ ≠ Value Extinction.
Extinction Conditions
VXSS requires explicit conditions capable of supporting an extinction determination.
Depending upon the governed value, conditions may include:

destruction of the underlying value basis; irreversible loss of required information; irreversible loss of identity continuity; permanent loss of necessary rights; irreversible functional destruction; permanent technological incompatibility; irreversible disappearance of the relevant utility; loss of the conditions necessary for restoration; permanent elimination of the relevant economic relationship; irreversible environmental change;
terminal structural deterioration; exhaustion of all legitimate restoration pathways; another defined terminal condition.
No single universal condition applies to every value class.
Extinction Threshold
Value Extinction requires a threshold separating:
recoverable impairment
from
terminal value loss.
The threshold may be:
physical; functional; informational; technological; legal; economic; operational; temporal; contextual; composite.
The threshold must correspond to the governed value relationship.
VXSS does not require one universal numerical extinction threshold.
Threshold Crossing ≠ Automatic Determination
Even where an extinction threshold appears to have been crossed, the lifecycle should not automatically terminate without a governed determination.
The threshold provides the basis for evaluation.
The extinction determination establishes the terminal state.
Therefore:
Threshold Crossing ≠ Extinction Determination.
Extinction Determination
A Value Extinction Determination establishes that:

the relevant previously existing value no longer remains recoverable within the governed lifecycle.
The determination should identify:
the Value Object; the relevant value; prior Value State; applicable extinction conditions; extinction threshold; recoverability basis; restoration pathways considered; material uncertainty;
determination basis; effective extinction point; finality consequences.
Extinction Uncertainty
Value Extinction should not be declared where material uncertainty prevents a legitimate terminal determination.
Where recoverability cannot currently be established or excluded, the appropriate state may remain:
Indeterminate
rather than:
Extinct.
This is especially important for:
emerging technologies; inaccessible data; future reconstruction capability; uncertain rights; unresolved ownership; rapidly changing markets; evolving scientific capability.
VXSS must not transform uncertainty into finality.
Temporary Impossibility ≠ Extinction
A value may temporarily be impossible to restore because of:
unavailable technology; regulatory restriction; inaccessible infrastructure; temporary market conditions; missing resources; geopolitical conditions; temporary legal barriers.
If the underlying value remains recoverable when those conditions change, extinction has not necessarily occurred.
Dormancy ≠ Extinction
Dormant value may remain recoverable even where it has not produced active utility for a long period.
Examples include:

dormant intellectual property; archived data; inactive infrastructure; unused productive capacity; inactive rights; temporarily irrelevant technology.
Time alone does not establish extinction.
Obsolescence ≠ Automatic Extinction
Obsolescence may contribute to Value Degradation or Value Nullification.
It does not automatically establish extinction.
An obsolete technology may:
regain historical value; gain collector value; become strategically relevant; be repurposed; be modernized; regain functionality; support another value relationship.
VXSS therefore requires the specific governed value to be evaluated rather than treating the label obsolete as a terminal determination.
Extinction of One Value ≠ Extinction of All Value
A single Value Object may support multiple value relationships.
For example, an industrial machine may lose:
productive manufacturing value
while retaining:
scrap value
historical value
training value
or
component value.
VXSS may therefore determine extinction of one governed value without declaring the entire object valueless.
This distinction prevents Value Extinction from becoming an object-destruction classification.
Value Identity Continuity
Restoration requires continuity between:
the value that previously existed
and
the value claimed to have returned.
Where that continuity is permanently lost, restoration may no longer be a legitimate description.
This creates an important extinction boundary.

If a later value appears but represents a materially different value relationship, it may constitute:
new Value Emergence
rather than restoration of the extinguished value.
Extinction ≠ New Emergence Prohibition
Value Extinction terminates a particular governed value lifecycle.
It does not mean the Value Object can never possess value again.
A new value may later emerge through:
new technology; new use; new market; new rights; new information; new functionality; new context; new demand; new strategic relevance.
Where the later value does not represent recovery of the extinguished value, it should enter governance as:
new Value Emergence.
Therefore:
Value Extinction ≠ Permanent Prohibition of Future Value.
Value Finality
Once Value Extinction has been legitimately determined, VXSS establishes Value Finality for the relevant value lifecycle.
Value Finality means that the extinguished value is no longer treated as:
degraded value; dormant value; zero value awaiting restoration; a ReMonet™ candidate; pending restored value.
The lifecycle has reached its terminal condition.
Finality ≠ Erasure
Value Finality does not erase the previous value lifecycle.
The governed record should preserve:
Value Emergence
→ Value States
→ Value Changes
→ Value Development
→ Value Degradation
→ Value Nullification where applicable
→ Restoration history where applicable
→ Value Extinction
→ Value Finality.
Extinction ends the lifecycle.
It does not delete it.
Finality Reopening

A legitimate extinction determination should not be casually reversed.
Where new evidence later demonstrates that the extinction determination itself was incorrect, the organization may require:
Determination Review
rather than treating the value as having been restored.
This distinction is important.
If the value was never actually extinct, correcting the record is:
Extinction Determination Correction
not
ReMonet™.
Value Extinction States
VXSS may recognize minimum governance states such as:
1. Extinction Not Established
Available evidence does not establish that the value has ceased to be recoverable.
2. Extinction Indeterminate
Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether recoverability remains.
3. Extinction Threshold Approaching
Material conditions indicate proximity to a defined extinction threshold, but terminal loss has not yet been established.
4. Extinction Threshold Reached
The defined threshold has been reached, requiring formal extinction determination.
5. Value Extinct
The relevant value has been determined to no longer exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
6. Value Final
The extinction determination has entered final lifecycle status and the value is no longer eligible for restoration governance within that lifecycle.
These are governance states and should be adapted to the relevant implementation context.
VXSS Boundary with Value Degradation
Standard
VDGS governs declining value while value continues to exist.

VXSS governs the terminal condition where recoverable value no longer exists.
Therefore:
Declining Value ≠ Extinguished Value.
VXSS Boundary with Value Nullification
Standard
VNS governs the transition from positive value into a zero-value condition.
VXSS governs whether recoverability itself has ended.
Therefore:
Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction.
A ZVA™ may remain recoverable.
An extinguished value does not.
VXSS Boundary with Value Restoration Standard
VRSS governs recovery of previously impaired, degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value where restoration remains legitimate.
VXSS establishes the boundary beyond which restoration no longer represents continuation of the same value lifecycle.
Therefore:
Recoverable Value → VRSS
Non-Recoverable Value → VXSS
VXSS Boundary with Value State Standard
VSS determines the current governed state of value.
VXSS determines terminal lifecycle extinction and finality.
A zero Value State under VSS must not automatically be interpreted as Value Extinction.
VXSS Boundary with Value Change Standard
Value Change governs what materially happened to value.
Value Extinction governs whether the consequence has become terminal.
A material change may contribute to extinction without itself constituting an extinction determination.
VXSS Boundary with Value Emergence
Once a value has legitimately reached Value Finality, later value cannot automatically be classified as restoration.

The architecture must first determine whether the later value represents:
correction of an incorrect extinction determination
or
new Value Emergence.
This protects the semantic integrity of the lifecycle.
Foundational Principles
Zero Value is not Value Extinction.
ZVA™ may retain restoration potential.
Value Extinction requires loss of recoverability, not merely absence of current value.
Object existence does not prove value existence.
Object destruction is not required for Value Extinction.
Not currently restorable does not mean extinct.
Restoration cost does not determine whether value exists.
Failed restoration does not automatically establish extinction.
Dormancy is not extinction.
Obsolescence is not automatically extinction.
Extinction of one value does not extinguish every value associated with the same object.
Threshold crossing is not itself an Extinction Determination.
Uncertainty must not be converted into finality.
Value Finality ends a governed value lifecycle; it does not erase its history.
An extinguished value cannot legitimately enter ReMonet™ within the same governed lifecycle.
Future value may emerge after extinction, but new Value Emergence must remain distinct from restoration of extinguished value.
Canonical Closing Statement

Value Extinction Standard establishes the terminal governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by determining when previously existing value ceases to remain recoverable within its governed lifecycle. Through governance of extinction conditions, recoverability, restoration potential, extinction thresholds, terminal uncertainty, extinction determination, Value Finality, value identity continuity, historical preservation, and terminal lifecycle records, VXSS establishes the critical distinction between zero value and extinguished value. The Standard prevents temporary impairment, dormancy, obsolescence, failed restoration, high restoration cost, or a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ from being prematurely interpreted as terminal value loss while also providing a formal point at which a value that can no longer legitimately be recovered ceases to remain within restoration governance. By preserving the distinction between Value Extinction, Value Nullification, Value Restoration, and future Value Emergence, VXSS closes the governed value lifecycle without preventing new value from later emerging from the same underlying object. Value Extinction therefore represents not the
moment when value merely reaches zero, but the moment when the governed lifecycle can no longer legitimately support the proposition that the same value can return.

Input Transparency Principle
Source Disclosure Requirement

Responsibility Declaration Logic
Non-Substitution of Regulatory Authority

Why Organizations Need Meaning Governance™
Why Organizations Need Meaning Governance™
The Hidden Risk Layer Beneath Every System
Organizations govern:
people
processes
information
systems
quality
risk
compliance
security
Yet one critical layer often remains largely unmanaged:
Meaning
Every decision depends on meaning.
Every instruction depends on meaning.
Every procedure depends on meaning.
Every regulation depends on meaning.
Every AI system depends on meaning.
Every operational action depends on meaning.
When meaning is assumed rather than governed, organizations introduce
idden risk layer that often remains invisible until failure occurs.
Most Failures Do Not Begin With Catastrophic Errors
Most failures begin with small misunderstandings.
A person receives an instruction.
A manager explains a task.
A contractor interprets a requirement.
An employee follows a procedure.
An AI system processes documentation.
Everyone believes they understand the same thing.
Later, the same conversation often produces familiar statements:
"I thought it meant this."
"That is not what I meant."
"You should have known."
"Everybody knows that."
"That is obvious."
"I understood it differently."
"Nobody explained that."
"The requirement was unclear."
At that point the failure has already occurred.
The disagreement is not about execution.
The disagreement is about meaning.
Meaning Failure Creates Operational Failure
A task may be executed correctly and still produce the wrong result.
Why?

Because the underlying meaning was incomplete, ambiguous, assumed, or never validated.
This can result in:
operational errors
project delays
quality failures
contractual disputes
compliance violations
safety incidents
insurance disputes
regulatory findings
AI decision failures
The larger the system, the greater the consequences.
Why This Matters for Organizations
Organizations often assume shared understanding.
In reality:
departments develop local interpretations
terminology evolves over time
procedures accumulate inconsistencies
documentation diverges
contractors introduce alternative meanings
acquired companies bring different terminology
Over time, the organization begins operating with multiple versions of the
e meaning.
This increases:
coordination costs
governance complexity
operational risk
decision inconsistency
Meaning Governance™ reduces these risks by making critical meanings
ible, traceable, validated, and governable.
Why This Matters for Governments
Government systems depend on interpretation.
Policies depend on interpretation.
Regulations depend on interpretation.
Legal obligations depend on interpretation.
Public administration depends on interpretation.
When different institutions interpret critical concepts differently:
implementation becomes inconsistent
enforcement becomes fragmented
coordination becomes difficult
public trust decreases
Meaning Governance™ creates a foundation for more consistent
interpretation across administrative environments.

Why This Matters for Emergency Management
Emergency environments operate under time pressure.
There is often no opportunity for lengthy clarification.
Words such as:
emergency
escalation
containment
evacuation
critical
severe
immediate
must produce consistent action.
A misunderstanding during an emergency may have consequences far
ond normal operational environments.
Meaning Governance™ helps ensure that critical operational language
duces predictable and coordinated responses.
Why This Matters for Critical Infrastructure
Critical infrastructure depends on coordinated action.
Examples include:
electricity networks
water systems
transportation systems
telecommunications networks
healthcare infrastructure
operational control centers
Failures often occur at the boundaries between systems, organizations,
ponsibilities, and interpretations.
When critical meanings are not aligned:
response slows
coordination weakens
risk increases
Meaning Governance™ helps create common operational understanding
re reliability matters most.
Why This Matters for Healthcare
Healthcare environments process enormous volumes of information and decisions.
Misunderstood terminology may affect:
diagnosis
treatment
escalation
responsibility
patient safety
operational coordination
The challenge is not information availability.
The challenge is ensuring that critical meanings remain clear and
consistent across teams, systems, and institutions.
Why This Matters for Insurance

Insurance systems depend on definitions.
Coverage depends on definitions.
Risk depends on definitions.
Liability depends on definitions.
Claims depend on definitions.
A single disputed meaning may trigger:
delayed claims
contractual disputes
legal proceedings
financial losses
As risk environments become increasingly complex, insurers require stronger
governance of the meanings that drive policy interpretation and
risk evaluation.
Why This Matters for Regulators
Regulators seek consistency.
Regulation becomes difficult when identical language produces different
operational interpretations.
Meaning Governance™ provides mechanisms for:
semantic traceability
validation
ownership
version control
governance accountability
As AI systems become more widespread, regulators will increasingly
require evidence that critical meanings are governed rather than assumed.
Why This Matters for AI
AI systems do not understand meaning by default.
AI predicts.
AI associates patterns.
AI infers context.
AI fills gaps.
Humans often compensate for ambiguity.
AI systems amplify ambiguity.
A poorly governed meaning may propagate through:
AI agents
autonomous workflows
decision-support systems
orchestration environments
multi-agent ecosystems
at machine speed.
What appears to be a small semantic inconsistency may become a
large-scale operational failure.
The AI era increases the value of Meaning Governance™ because
ambiguity becomes increasingly expensive.

Why This Matters for Robotics and Autonomous Systems
Robotics and autonomous systems operate in physical environments.
Physical environments do not tolerate semantic confusion.
A misunderstanding may result in:
incorrect execution
unsafe behavior
damaged assets
interrupted operations
human safety risks
As autonomy increases, validation of meaning becomes as important as
validation of software.
The Financial Reality
Many organizations invest heavily in:
cybersecurity
compliance
quality management
risk management
process optimization
Few invest in governing meaning.
Yet meaning sits underneath all of them.
A misunderstood meaning may trigger:
project overruns
operational failures
compliance penalties
litigation
insurance disputes
AI failures
reputational damage
The financial consequences of semantic failure often appear elsewhere in
the organization, making the root cause difficult to identify.
The Emerging Governance Layer
For decades organizations focused on governing:
information
systems
processes
The next governance layer is meaning.
As organizations become increasingly interconnected, regulated,
automated, and AI-enabled, the pressure to validate, govern, register, and
maintain critical meanings will continue to grow.
Meaning Governance™ is not a replacement for existing governance systems.
It is a foundational layer beneath them.
OOF Position
OOF® believes that many future operational, regulatory, AI, safety, and

interoperability challenges will ultimately be traced back to meaning.
Not because people lack intelligence.
Not because systems lack information.
But because critical meanings were never explicitly governed.
Governance of Meaning™ exists to address this challenge before
ambiguity becomes failure.
Canonical Closing Statement
Most organizations believe they suffer from information problems.
Many actually suffer from meaning problems. As systems become
larger, faster, more autonomous, and more interconnected, the ability
to govern meaning may become one of the most important
infrastructure capabilities of the AI era.

Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ Standard (WPPI™)
Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ Standard (WPPI™)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
OriginID: OOF-OID-ENV-PMI-WPPI-2026-02-25-0013
Category: Environmental Integrity Standards (ENV)
Subcategory: Process & Material Integrity
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 25 February 2026
Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English
A. Standard Abstract
The Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ (WPPI™) Standard establishes a structured methodology for
evaluating plastic exposure across the full operational lifecycle of a product or material system.
Unlike product-only plastic claims, WPPI™ evaluates plastic interaction across the entire production chain including
raw materials, production systems, equipment contact, auxiliary materials, packaging, storage, and logistics.
The standard introduces transparent classification tiers that allow organizations to declare the level of plastic exposure control
within their operational processes.
WPPI™ is designed for cross-industry application including manufacturing, food production, agriculture, pharmaceuticals,
textiles, industrial materials, and supply chain systems.
B. Canonical Definition
Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ (WPPI™) is a structured process and material integrity standard defining conditions for

transparent disclosure and structural control of plastic exposure across all operational layers involved in the creation,
handling, storage, and distribution of a product.
Plastic integrity under WPPI™ is defined as the measurable minimization, documentation, and management of both intentional plastic use
and non-intentional plastic contamination throughout the production lifecycle.
C. Scope
WPPI™ applies to operational systems including:
manufacturing processes
food and beverage production
agricultural and herbal processing
pharmaceutical production
textile and fiber systems
industrial component manufacturing
packaging production
raw material processing
B2B supply chains
Evaluation may include:
raw material inputs
production equipment contact
auxiliary materials
packaging systems
storage environments
transport and distribution systems
D. Plastic Integrity Classification Model
WPPI™ introduces three process-based classification tiers.
Tier 1 — Process Plastic Controlled (PPC)
At least 95% plastic-free across the documented production process.
Plastic components may be used where technically unavoidable, provided they are transparently disclosed.
Tier 2 — Process Plastic Minimal (PPM)
At least 98% plastic-free across the documented production process.
No intentional plastic components in the primary product structure.
Trace contamination must be documented.
Tier 3 — Whole Process Plastic-Free (WPPF)
At least 99.5% plastic-free across the documented production process.

No intentional plastic components permitted.
Only analytically negligible contamination may exist.
E. Intentional vs Non-Intentional Plastic Exposure
WPPI™ distinguishes between two structural exposure categories.
Intentional Plastic Use
Examples include:
structural plastic components
plastic packaging
polymer coatings or liners
polymer processing aids
synthetic composite materials
Non-Intentional Plastic Contamination
Examples include:
microplastic transfer
equipment abrasion
transport contamination
environmental particulate exposure
auxiliary system cross-contact
Integrity classification depends on declared presence and documented control.
F. Process Integrity Layers
WPPI™ evaluates six operational integrity layers:
Raw Material Integrity Layer
Production Integrity Layer
Equipment Contact Layer
Auxiliary Materials Layer
Packaging Integrity Layer
Logistics & Storage Layer
Integrity classification depends on transparency across all relevant layers.
G. Fail-State Conditions
A WPPI™ classification becomes invalid if:
intentional plastic exceeds the declared threshold
undisclosed plastic components are identified
process boundaries are not clearly defined
process documentation is incomplete
declared exposure controls cannot be demonstrated
H. Implementation Modes
WPPI™ may be applied under three operational models:
Self-Declaration Transparency
Structured Implementation
Third-Party Laboratory-Supported Verification
The standard itself does not require certification.

It establishes a structural framework for transparent process disclosure.
I. Compatibility
WPPI™ operates within the Environmental Integrity Standards architecture
and may function alongside:
Origin Eco™ Standard
Soil Integrity™ Standard
Water Integrity™ Standard
Carbon Integrity™ Standard
Air Integrity™ Standard
WPPI™ introduces a Process & Material Integrity layer complementing environmental transparency standards.
Canonical Closing Statement
Plastic integrity is not defined by the final product alone.
It is defined by transparency across the entire production process.
Related Documents
