→ About WPPI™ Standard

ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset) Standard
ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset) Standard
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Global Methodology Authority
OriginID: OOF-OID-ECO-ZVA-2026-01-20-0001
Category: Economic & Value Standards (ECO)
Subcategory: Zero Value Asset (ZVA)
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Binding
Effective Date: 26 January 2026
Compatibility:
Methodology OS™: Compatible
Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
B. Standard Abstract
This standard defines ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset) as a formally recognized asset state in which an asset exists but carries zero admissible economic value.
It establishes the structural, ethical, ecological, legal, and authenticity conditions under which value nullification occurs.
The standard defines Zero Value as a stable and governed state within a deterministic asset lifecycle.
C. Canonical Definition
A ZVA™ (Zero Value Asset) is defined as an asset that formally exists, retains identity and history, but is assigned zero admissible economic value within a governed system.
ZVA™ represents a state, not a number, loss, debt, negative valuation, or accounting write-off.
D. Base
This standard is based on:
The Canonical Definition System™
Asset State Determinism
Traceable Identity and Origin Integrity
Non-Skippable State Transitions
Value as a governed condition rather than a subjective assignment
ZVA™ operates within a sequential asset state architecture.
E. Purpose & Scope

Purpose
To establish a deterministic global classification for assets that must be excluded from economic participation due to failure of authenticity, legality, ethical compliance, ecological integrity, or systemic safety.
Scope
This standard applies to:
Physical assets
Digital assets
Virtual assets
Hybrid systems
AI-generated outputs
Economic instruments
This standard does not define pricing models, valuation methods, or market mechanisms.
F. Applicability
This standard applies when an asset:
cannot establish verified identity
fails authenticity validation
violates ecological or ethical conditions
breaches legal or regulatory compliance
poses systemic economic risk
cannot be safely licensed or responsibly integrated
Applicability is determined through governed evaluation layers.
G. Protocol
ZVA™ classification follows multi-layer evaluation:
Identity & Verification Layer
Failure of origin traceability or authenticity verification results in ZVA™ assignment.
Ecological & Ethical Evaluation Layer
Assets causing ecological harm or ethical violations qualify for ZVA™ status.
Authenticity & Integrity Layer
Assets containing falsified, manipulated, contradictory, or unverifiable data qualify for ZVA™ status.
Legality & Compliance Layer
Assets illegal to produce, trade, or operate qualify for ZVA™ status.
Economic Function Layer
Assets that cannot be validated, licensed, safely used, or integrated into the real economy may be classified as ZVA™.

All classifications must be recorded and remain traceable.
H. Classification & States
Canonical Asset State Sequence
Origin Asset™
DeMonet™
ZVA™
ReMonet™
Value Asset™
ZVA™ is a stable asset state within this sequence.
Transition Rule
ZVA™ cannot transition directly to Value Asset™.
ReMonet™ is the only permitted transition mechanism.
Skipping states, rewriting history, or direct value injection constitutes systemic manipulation within governed systems.
I. Licensing & Usage
Reference use of this standard is permitted without license.
Implementation of ZVA™ classification mechanisms in operational or commercial systems requires an OOF™ license.
Derivative frameworks replicating the governed zero-value asset state logic require explicit authorization under MIP™ protection.
J. Compatibility & Dependencies
This standard is compatible with:
Methodology OS™
DeMonet™ Standard
ReMonet™ Standard
Canonical Meaning Framework
MTVF™ (Truth Layer)
CAP™ (Chain of Authenticity Protocol)
ZVA™ operates as a foundational classification within the Economic & Value Standards domain.
K. Non-Compliance Consequences
Assets processed in contradiction to this standard:
are classified as non-admissible
cannot enter value-based systems
cannot participate in governed economic processes
Improper value assignment without ReMonet™ transition is invalid within canonical systems.
Canonical Closing Statement
ZVA™ is not failure.
It is a controlled suspension of economic value within a governed lifecycle.

Canonical Footer

Designation: Global Methodology Authority
Issued by: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property
All rights reserved.

Canonical Definition
The Event Amendment Module (EADM) governs how a continuing Tax-Relevant Event may receive materially relevant additions, refinements, or modifications without treating every legitimate lifecycle update as a Correction or New Event Formation.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Continuity State
↓
Event Amendment Governance
↓
Governed Event Amendment State
EADM governs amendments that update the governed Event while preserving legitimate Event Continuity.
Its foundational distinction is:
Amendment ≠ Correction.
And:

Amendment ≠ New Event by default.
Operational Role
After ECOM establishes that the same Event may legitimately continue, new information may need to be incorporated into the governed Event state.
That information may not correct an error.
It may simply add, refine, or extend what is known.
EADM answers:
How can new materially relevant information be incorporated into the continuing Event without erasing prior state, misclassifying the change as a correction, or creating a new Event unnecessarily?
EADM prevents: silent Event modification; uncontrolled data enrichment; loss of prior Event state; amendment/correction confusion; over-expansion of Event scope; amendment without continuity basis; amendment without materiality assessment; and amendment that improperly overrides upstream governance.

EADM governs: Amendment Trigger identification; Amendment eligibility; Amendment scope; Amendment materiality; amendment content; prior-state preservation; current-state update; amendment qualification; Event component refinement; supporting-information addition; Event Context amendment; Participation amendment; Timing amendment reference; Location amendment reference; Value Association amendment reference; Relationship amendment reference; Determination-impact reference; amendment conflict; amendment ambiguity; amendment withdrawal; amendment replacement; amendment continuity; and amendment handoff.
Operational Scope
EADM may govern amendments within: physical transactions; digital services; commercial transactions; financial activity; platform Events; AI-agent Events; machine-to-machine Events; autonomous systems; distributed environments; digital assets; smart contracts; industrial systems; cross-border activity; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies.
The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Amendment Object
The Amendment Object is the materially relevant new or refined information proposed for incorporation into an existing continuing Event.
The Amendment Object may modify the governed Event state without asserting that the prior state was wrong.
New Information ≠ Prior Error by default.
Amendment Trigger

An Amendment Trigger may arise from: newly available information; newly identified participant involvement; additional supporting records; refined Event Context; new Location information; expanded Timing information; updated Value Association; new relationship information; later operational development; improved machine-generated information; new cross-system representation; or previously unavailable governed reference.
Not every new data point requires formal amendment.
Amendment Eligibility
An amendment is eligible where: Event Continuity remains valid or sufficiently qualified; the new information belongs to the same governed Event; the change is not primarily the correction of known error; the amendment does not illegitimately redefine Event Formation or Boundary; and the information is materially relevant to Event governance or downstream reliance.
Available Information ≠ Eligible Amendment by default.
Amendment vs Correction
The principal distinction is:
Amendment adds or refines legitimate Event information.
Correction replaces or rectifies information that was materially wrong or improperly represented.
For example:
A newly identified supporting participant may require Amendment.
A participant that was incorrectly identified may require Correction.
Additional Information ≠ Correction by default.
Amendment vs New Event
An amendment remains within the same Event only while Continuity remains legitimate.

Where the proposed change materially alters Event Formation, Event Boundary, or the underlying occurrence, the change may no longer qualify as an Amendment.
It may require upstream reassessment or New Event Formation.
Amendment Scope
EADM shall define which governed part of the Event is being amended.
Possible scopes include: Context; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; supporting references; Determination-related qualification; lifecycle metadata.
Scope should remain explicit.
Amending One Event Component ≠ Reopening the Entire Event by default.
Amendment Materiality
Amendments should be governed according to materiality.
A material amendment may affect: interpretation of Event state; downstream tax evaluation; Continuity; Determination; Event Relationships; Value Association; traceability; jurisdiction readiness.
A non-material amendment may only improve metadata or operational clarity.
Non-Material Amendment
Examples may include: additional internal reference; technical documentation enrichment; supplementary supporting information; non-substantive descriptive clarification.
Such amendments should not create unnecessary lifecycle complexity.
Material Amendment
A Material Amendment changes information sufficiently to affect governed understanding or downstream reliance while still preserving legitimate Event Continuity.
Material amendments should remain traceable and clearly distinguishable from prior Event state.
Prior-State Preservation

Every materially relevant Amendment shall preserve access to the prior governed Event state.
The canonical pattern is:
Prior Event State
↓
Amendment
↓
Amended Event State
not:
Prior Event State
↓
Silent Replacement Current Effective State
Once validly integrated, the amended state may become the current effective Event state.
The prior state remains historically reconstructable.
Current Amended State ≠ Only Event State That Ever Existed.
Amendment Addition
An amendment may add information that was previously unknown.
Examples include: additional Event participant; newly identified operational Location; additional Event relationship; supplementary Value reference; new supporting Record.
Addition does not automatically imply the earlier Event state was defective.
Amendment Refinement
An amendment may improve precision.
Examples include: more precise Location; better Timing granularity; richer Participant Role information; refined Context; more specific Value reference.
Refinement may preserve both Event identity and earlier historical state.
Amendment Extension
An amendment may extend governed information where the Event is still active or continuing.
This is common in long-running digital or machine Events.
Extension must not be used to absorb a substantively separate occurrence.
Extension ≠ Unlimited Event Expansion.
Event Context Amendment
TRECS owns Event Context.

EADM may incorporate an amended Context result where new context becomes legitimately relevant during Event lifecycle.
EADM does not redefine Context independently.
Timing Amendment
Additional Timing information may become available.
Where the prior Timing was not wrong but incomplete, Amendment may be appropriate.
If the prior Timing was materially incorrect, ECRTM may instead be required.
TRETS remains authoritative.
Location Amendment
A new operational Location may legitimately be added without correcting an earlier Location.
For example, a distributed Event may later involve another valid operational node.
Additional Location ≠ Location Correction by default.
TRELS remains authoritative over Location.
Participation Amendment
A continuing Event may acquire additional participants or participant roles.
EADM may govern the lifecycle incorporation of those results after TREPS governance.
New Participant ≠ New Event by default.
Where participant change materially alters Event Formation, ECOM continuity reassessment may be required.
Value Association Amendment
An additional governed Value Association may be incorporated where the Event remains the same Event.
TRVAS owns the Value Association result.
VFM® owns the Value lifecycle itself.
Event Relationship Amendment
A new Event Relationship may become known after the initial Event Record was established.
TRERLS governs the relationship.
EADM governs the lifecycle incorporation of the resulting relationship information.

Supporting Reference Amendment
New supporting records may be added to the Event without redefining the Event.
Examples include: later invoice; additional settlement record; supporting technical log; contract reference; machine-state record.
New Supporting Record ≠ New Event.
Determination Impact
An Amendment may affect the basis on which TREDS previously determined the Event as tax-relevant.
Where material, EADM should trigger or reference TREDS reconsideration.
EADM does not independently modify Determination.
Amendment Impact ≠ Determination Authority.
Amendment Qualification
An Amendment may be incorporated with qualification where: supporting information remains incomplete; the amendment scope remains bounded; downstream reliance should be limited; one upstream governance result remains unresolved.
Qualification shall remain visible.
Amendment Ambiguity
Amendment Ambiguity exists where it is unclear: whether new information belongs to the same Event; whether it is amendment or correction; whether the change is material; whether upstream reassessment is required.
The amendment shall remain unresolved until sufficient governance exists.
Amendment Conflict
Conflict exists where materially authoritative governance information supports incompatible amendment outcomes.

Examples include: one source supports adding a Participant; another establishes that the actor did not participate; one system extends Event Timing; another authoritative result establishes Event completion earlier.
Conflict shall remain explicit.
Amendment Rejection
A proposed Amendment may be rejected where: the information does not belong to the Event; continuity is invalid; the amendment attempts to overwrite a Correction; it would materially redefine Event Formation or Boundary; governance basis is insufficient; or the amendment would import downstream tax conclusions into canonical Event governance.
Amendment Withdrawal
A proposed Amendment may be withdrawn before becoming effective.
Withdrawal should preserve relevant governance history where material.
Withdrawn Amendment ≠ Never-Proposed Amendment.
Amendment Replacement
A proposed Amendment may be replaced by a more complete or authoritative Amendment before final integration.
Replacement should not silently erase earlier materially relevant lifecycle state.
Amendment Sequence
An Event may undergo multiple amendments:
Original State
↓
Amendment A
↓
Amendment B
↓
Amendment C
Each materially relevant Amendment should remain reconstructable.
Multiple amendments do not automatically create multiple Events.
Amendment Continuity
Where an Amendment materially changes the Event enough to call Continuity into question, EADM shall return the case to ECOM.
Valid Prior Continuity ≠ Permanent Continuity Guarantee.

Cross-System Amendment
An amendment may originate in a different system from the one holding the canonical Event Record.
The amendment should be associated with the same governed Event identity.
Different systems do not create different amendment realities by default.
Cross-Organization Amendment
Different organizations may contribute legitimate Event updates.
EADM shall preserve the distinction between: amendment source; amendment authority; canonical Event state.
External Contribution ≠ Automatic Canonical Amendment.
Cross-Border Amendment
New cross-border information may amend the Event.
For example: new operational Location; new Participant; new Value Association; new Event Relationship.
The amendment itself remains jurisdiction-neutral.
Cross-Border Amendment ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination.
Machine-Generated Amendment
Autonomous systems may propose amendments automatically.
Examples include: additional machine participant; refined sensor-derived Timing; new supporting transaction reference; newly correlated Value information.
Automated generation does not eliminate governance requirements.
Machine-Generated Update ≠ Governed Amendment by default.
Amendment Frequency
High-frequency systems may generate many candidate amendments.
Formal lifecycle governance should apply only where changes are materially relevant.
More Updates ≠ More Amendments by default.
Amendment and Historical Reconstruction

Amendments should preserve sufficient information to reconstruct: prior Event state; amendment trigger; amendment scope; amendment basis; amended state; current effective state.
ERTM remains authoritative for Record Traceability.
Amendment and Record Governance
TREGS owns Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, and interoperability.
EADM governs the Event lifecycle effect of amendment.
The Event Record may then need to be updated through TREGS-compatible mechanisms.
Event Amendment ≠ Record Mutation by default.
Amendment and Tax Law
A jurisdiction may react to an Amendment by: reassessing tax; requiring new filing; changing Tax Base; changing legal treatment.
Those are downstream outcomes.
Event Amendment ≠ Tax Reassessment Decision.

Ready for Correction Governance Governance Requirements

EADM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Continuity State exists; the proposed change belongs to the continuing Event; Amendment remains distinct from Correction; Amendment remains distinct from New Event Formation; amendment scope is explicit where material; amendment materiality is assessed; materially relevant prior Event state remains reconstructable; current amended state remains distinguishable from prior state; additional information is not automatically treated as prior error; amendment does not independently redefine upstream TREGA™ results; Context, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, and Relationship amendments use authoritative upstream governance where required; Determination impact is referred to TREDS where material; qualified amendments remain explicit; ambiguity and conflict remain visible; rejected or withdrawn material amendments remain reconstructable where necessary; amendments do not silently absorb substantively separate occurrences; continuity is reassessed where amendment materiality challenges same-Event identity; machine-generated changes are not automatically accepted; high-frequency update volume does not determine amendment count; downstream tax conclusions remain outside amendment governance; and the resulting Event state is suitable for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance.
Governance Logic
IF no valid Governed Event Continuity State exists, THEN EADM shall not establish a canonical Event Amendment.

IF new information does not belong to the same governed Event, THEN it shall not be integrated as an Amendment.
IF the change primarily rectifies materially incorrect information, THEN the change shall be referred to ECRTM rather than treated as Amendment.
IF the change adds or refines materially relevant information while Event Continuity remains valid, THEN Amendment Governance may proceed.
IF amendment scope materially changes Event Formation or Boundary, THEN continuity shall be reassessed before integration.
IF a material Amendment affects Event Determination, THEN TREDS reconsideration shall be triggered or referenced.
IF Amendment information is materially ambiguous or conflicted, THEN it shall remain qualified or unresolved rather than silently integrated.
IF the proposed Amendment contains downstream legal tax conclusions, THEN those conclusions shall remain outside canonical Event Amendment.
IF a proposed Amendment is withdrawn or rejected, THEN it shall not become the current effective Event state.
IF the Amendment is validly governed and integrated, THEN the amended Event state may become the current effective state while the prior state remains historically reconstructable.

Enterprise Application
EADM provides the controlled update layer that allows a governed Event to absorb legitimate new information without destabilizing Event identity.
The operational pattern is:
Governed Event Continuity State
→ New Information
→ Amendment Eligibility
→ Amendment Scope & Materiality
→ Amendment Integration
→ Governed Event Amendment State
Where the proposed change is actually an error correction:
Amendment Candidate
↓
ECRTM — Event Correction Governance
Where the proposed change threatens continuity:
Amendment Candidate
↓
ECOM — Continuity Reassessment

This prevents ordinary lifecycle updates from becoming either uncontrolled Record edits or unnecessary New Event Formation. Use Case 1 — New Participant Added to a Continuing Digital Service Event
A cross-border digital service Event has already been governed and remains active.
After the original Record was created, another platform is identified as having materially participated in execution.
The original Event was not wrong when first governed; the additional participation information simply was not previously available.
TREPS establishes the new Participation result.
EADM governs its lifecycle incorporation:
Existing Event State
↓
New Participation Information
↓
Amendment Eligible
↓
Amended Event State
The Event remains continuous.
The prior Event state remains historically reconstructable.
No Correction or New Event Formation is required solely because another legitimate participant became known. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Event Receives Additional Value Association
An autonomous machine Event has already been governed.
Later, a newly completed operational stage creates an additional Value Association that belongs to the same continuing Event.
TRVAS governs the Value Association.
ECOM confirms Event Continuity.
EADM integrates the additional Value Association into the current Event state.
The lifecycle becomes:
Prior Event State
↓
Additional Governed Value Association
↓
Material Amendment
↓
Amended Current Event State

If the new Value relationship had instead represented a substantively separate occurrence, ECOM would require continuity reassessment rather than allowing EADM to expand the original Event indefinitely.
Canonical Boundary
EADM owns the governance of Event Amendment eligibility, Amendment Triggers, Amendment scope, Amendment type, Amendment materiality, incorporation of legitimate new or refined information, prior-state preservation, current amended state, amendment qualification, ambiguity, conflict, withdrawal, replacement, continuity reassessment triggers, and establishment of the Governed Event Amendment State.
EADM does not determine whether the Event remains continuous; ECOM owns Event Continuity.
It does not govern correction of materially wrong information; ECRTM owns Event Correction.
It does not govern Event Supersession or Closure.
It does not independently redefine Event Context, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, or Event Determination.
It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, reassessment obligations, filing requirements, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
Its governance begins with a valid:
Governed Event Continuity State
and a proposed or required Event Amendment.
Its governance ends with:
Governed Event Amendment State
or with referral to:
ECOM for Continuity Reassessment
or:

ECRTM where Correction Governance is required.

↓

↓
ECRTM — Event Correction Governance
Where continuity becomes materially uncertain:
EADM
↓

Canonical Closing Statement
EADM allows a governed Event to learn more about itself without pretending that every new fact corrects an error or creates a new Event.
Amendment preserves legitimate Event evolution while keeping prior state, continuity, and upstream governance boundaries intact.
Amendment ≠ Correction.
Amendment ≠ New Event by default.
New Information ≠ Prior Error.

Canonical Definition
The Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM) governs how elements provisionally associated with or contained within a Governed Event Boundary Scope are evaluated and, where materially justified, excluded from the governed Event Boundary because they represent surrounding activity, dependencies, contextual conditions, technical artifacts, supporting infrastructure, independent operational structures, or other non-member elements.
EBEM establishes the negative side of Event Boundary governance:

what must not remain inside the event merely because it is related, connected, proximate, technically linked, or operationally supportive.
Its specific task is:
to establish a governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure that removes materially unjustified scope elements while preserving their relevant external relationships, traceability, and downstream governance significance.
EBEM governs what must remain outside the event.
It does not yet determine whether excluded or adjacent structures constitute separate governed events or how multiple events must be separated from one another. ------------------------------
Operational Role
EBSCM establishes:
what provisionally belongs within the Event Boundary Scope.
EBEM asks:
which of those provisionally associated elements must not remain inside the governed Event Boundary?
This distinction is essential.
Positive scope governance identifies a sufficiently coherent candidate extent.
Exclusion governance then tests that scope for elements that are materially relevant but do not legitimately belong to the event itself.
Therefore:
Scope Membership Candidate ≠ Final Boundary Membership.
And:
Operational Relevance ≠ Event Membership.
EBEM protects the boundary from uncontrolled expansion through related, dependent, supporting, contextual, or technically adjacent activity. ------------------------------ Internal Flow
Governed Event Boundary Scope

↓
Exclusion Basis Assessment
↓
Membership Reassessment
↓

External Relevance Preservation
↓

EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module ------------------------------ Operational Space
EBEM operates within the governance space where potentially included elements must be tested for legitimate exclusion from the Event Boundary.
Its Operational Space includes: Exclusion Candidate identification exclusion basis assessment surrounding-activity exclusion dependency exclusion context-only exclusion technical-artifact exclusion duplicate-representation exclusion supporting-infrastructure exclusion non-member participant activity exclusion non-member machine activity exclusion external value-related activity exclusion external process-stage exclusion external relationship preservation exclusion ambiguity exclusion conflict exclusion uncertainty exclusion qualification exclusion traceability
EBEM governs boundary exclusion.
It does not own Event Separation between distinct governed event candidates. ------------------------------ Operational Scope
EBEM may govern exclusions involving: commercial activity financial activity digital services platform operations distributed systems autonomous systems AI agents robotic operations machine-to-machine interactions payments logistics production infrastructure digital assets service execution enterprise workflows hybrid physical-digital activity future machine economies

The module remains actor-neutral, technology-neutral, organization-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral.
An element may be excluded regardless of whether it was created by a human, enterprise, machine, autonomous system, API, robot, platform, or distributed infrastructure. ------------------------------ Exclusion Principle
A valid Event Boundary must not absorb every element that helps explain, enable, evidence, support, or relate to the event.
Many operational structures can be relevant without being members of the event.
Therefore:
Relevant ≠ Included.
And more specifically:
Related Activity ≠ Event Membership.
EBEM exists to make this distinction explicit. ------------------------------ Exclusion Candidate
An Exclusion Candidate is an element currently associated with the Governed Event Boundary Scope whose continued inclusion requires reassessment.
Possible Exclusion Candidates may include: background activity contextual information supporting infrastructure prior dependencies later dependencies technical copies duplicate representations monitoring records authentication events administrative records accounting representations platform-management operations unrelated machine actions shared resource operations surrounding contractual structures
Candidate status does not establish exclusion.
Therefore:
Exclusion Candidate ≠ Excluded Element. ------------------------------ Exclusion Basis

An element should be excluded only where a governed basis demonstrates that it does not legitimately form part of the event's structural extent.
Possible exclusion bases may include: the element is merely contextual the element is a dependency rather than event membership the element is technical representation only the element duplicates another governed representation the element is background infrastructure the element belongs to a surrounding process the element is operationally related but structurally independent the element supports several unrelated events the element belongs to another formation candidate inclusion would materially distort the event inclusion would cause uncontrolled event expansion
Exclusion must remain reasoned and traceable.
Exclusion Convenience ≠ Exclusion Legitimacy. ------------------------------ Dependency Exclusion
Formation Dependencies are a major source of Event Boundary over-expansion.
A formed event may depend on prior authorization, infrastructure, delegated authority, an account relationship, a platform relationship, or a prior operational state.
Those dependencies may remain relevant.
They do not automatically belong inside the Event Boundary.
Therefore:
Qualified Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership.
EBEM may explicitly exclude such dependencies while preserving their association with the event.
This maintains the distinction established earlier by EFDM. ------------------------------ Context Exclusion

TRECS may establish extensive context around the occurrence.
That context can remain important throughout the TREGA™ lifecycle.
But contextual relevance does not mean boundary inclusion.
Examples may include: market conditions organizational environment infrastructure state prior contractual framework system configuration broader business process surrounding supply-chain activity
Therefore:
Context Relevance ≠ Event Membership.
EBEM may exclude context-only elements while preserving their contextual references. ------------------------------ Technical Artifact Exclusion
Operational systems frequently produce records that appear closely attached to the event but represent only technical implementation.
Examples include: API retries synchronization messages database replication telemetry logging system-status messages internal reconciliation records cache operations monitoring records duplicated ledger views
Such elements may be useful for evidence, auditability, or technical reconstruction.
They do not automatically belong to the governed event.
Therefore:
Technical Trace ≠ Event Membership. ------------------------------ Shared Infrastructure Exclusion
An event may rely on infrastructure used by many unrelated activities.
Examples include: cloud infrastructure payment networks energy grids identity services shared production lines network infrastructure distributed ledgers warehouse systems
Use of the same infrastructure does not make that infrastructure part of each event.

Therefore:
Shared Infrastructure ≠ Shared Event Membership.
EBEM must prevent infrastructure dependency from becoming unlimited event scope. ------------------------------ Shared Participant Activity
The same participant may perform multiple activities around one event.
Not all of those activities must belong inside the Event Boundary.
For example, a provider may: authenticate a customer perform the service issue an invoice provide unrelated support process a later complaint
The shared participant does not collapse these activities into one event.
Therefore:
Same Participant ≠ Same Event Membership.
Participation itself is later governed by TREPS. ------------------------------ Temporal Proximity
Activity occurring shortly before or after an event may appear to belong within it.
Temporal closeness may provide useful information.
It does not independently determine Event Boundary membership.
Therefore:
Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Membership.
Event Timing is governed later by TRETS.
EBEM must not convert time proximity into automatic inclusion or exclusion. ------------------------------ Spatial and Digital Proximity
Activities may occur: at the same physical location within the same data center within the same platform inside the same digital environment through the same API ecosystem
This proximity may be operationally relevant.
It does not establish Event Membership.
Therefore:
Shared Location ≠ Shared Event Boundary.
And:
Shared Digital Environment ≠ Shared Event Membership.

Event Location belongs later to TRELS. ------------------------------ Contractual Relationship
A contract may govern numerous operational events over time.
Conversely, one event may involve several contractual structures.
Therefore:
Same Contract ≠ Same Event Boundary.
EBEM must prevent contractual packaging from automatically becoming event membership logic. ------------------------------ Accounting Relationship
Accounting systems may group several activities under: one ledger entry one invoice one settlement one accounting period one cost center one journal reference
Such grouping may be useful for financial reporting.
It does not automatically govern Event Membership.
Therefore:
Accounting Grouping ≠ Event Boundary Membership. ------------------------------ Commercial Relationship
Long-running commercial relationships may generate many events.
A customer, provider, marketplace, or supplier relationship can continue for years.
The existence of that relationship does not make the whole relationship one event.
Therefore:
Commercial Relationship ≠ Event Membership.
EBEM excludes relationship-level structures where they do not legitimately belong inside the event. ------------------------------ Excluded ≠ Irrelevant
Exclusion is not equivalent to deletion, rejection, or irrelevance.
An excluded element may remain important for: context dependencies evidence event relationships validation auditability accountability later legal analysis tax analysis operational reconstruction

Therefore:
Excluded from Event Boundary ≠ Removed from Governance.
This is a foundational EBEM principle. ------------------------------ External Relationship Preservation
When an element is excluded, EBEM should preserve relevant association with the event.
Possible external associations may include: dependency reference contextual reference supporting-system reference prior-event reference subsequent-event reference evidential reference participant reference infrastructure reference
This prevents exclusion from destroying operational understanding. ------------------------------ Exclusion and Event Separation
Some Exclusion Candidates may appear to represent independent event structures.
EBEM must not decide whether they constitute separate events.
That belongs to:
EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module.
EBEM may identify:
Potential Independent Structure
or
Separation Review Required
but must not complete the separation itself.
Therefore:
Boundary Exclusion ≠ Event Separation. ------------------------------ Exclusion Ambiguity
In some cases, it may remain unclear whether an element belongs within or outside the Event Boundary.
Possible exclusion states include:
Exclusion Candidate
Excluded
Retained in Scope
Exclusion Qualified
Exclusion Conflict
Exclusion Unresolved
EBEM must preserve uncertainty where the governance basis remains insufficient.
Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Exclusion.
Likewise:

Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Inclusion. ------------------------------ Exclusion Conflict
Different systems may support different membership conclusions.
For example:
the ERP may treat a payment settlement as part of the commercial transaction.
The marketplace may treat it as a separate financial operation.
The payment system may represent it independently.

Canonical Definition
The Event Boundary Identification Module (EBIM) governs how the potential structural perimeter of a sufficiently formed event is identified before its detailed scope, exclusions, separation conditions, or subsequent boundary revisions are established.
EBIM receives a Governed Formed Event from the Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) and identifies the materially relevant structural limits that may define where the event begins, where it ends, and where surrounding operational activity may require distinction.
Its specific task is:

to establish an evidence-linked Candidate Event Boundary that can legitimately proceed into Event Boundary Scope governance without treating technical, commercial, organizational, platform, or machine structures as authoritative Event Boundaries by default.
EBIM identifies the candidate boundary.
It does not finalize the complete Event Boundary. ------------------------------

EBIM establishes where the potential structural perimeter of that formed event appears to lie.
This distinction is fundamental.
A formed event may contain a coherent internal structure while its precise perimeter relative to surrounding activity remains unresolved.
Therefore:
Formed Event ≠ Bounded Event.
And:
Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Final Event Boundary.
EBIM provides the first governed transition from Event Formation into Event Boundary governance. ------------------------------ Internal Flow

Its Operational Space includes: identification of potential Event Boundary signals identification of candidate boundary elements recognition of possible beginning and ending limits identification of structural perimeter indicators assessment of potential boundary anchors detection of competing boundary representations detection of incomplete boundary information detection of ambiguous boundary conditions identification of technical structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries identification of commercial structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries identification of machine or autonomous execution structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries traceability of the basis used to identify the Candidate Event Boundary
EBIM governs boundary identification, not complete boundary adjudication. ------------------------------ Operational Scope
EBIM applies to formed events arising from: commercial transactions financial operations contractual activity digital services platform activity distributed systems autonomous agents AI systems robotic operations machine-to-machine activity infrastructure operations digital assets value-affecting processes mixed physical-digital activity future machine economies
The module is actor-neutral and technology-neutral.

The same governance logic applies whether the underlying activity was performed by humans, organizations, software, autonomous systems, machines, or combinations of them. ------------------------------ Boundary Signals
A Candidate Event Boundary may be indicated by multiple forms of operational information.
Potential Boundary Signals may include: initiation or termination of a materially coherent activity transition between materially distinct operational structures completion of a defined operational objective change in the governed formation structure emergence of an independent operational result separation between coordinated but distinguishable activities discontinuity in operational execution transition between materially different participant structures transition between materially different value-affecting structures separation between independently reconstructable operational occurrences
No individual signal automatically establishes the Event Boundary.

EBIM identifies the elements that may contribute to the structural perimeter of the event.

Candidate Boundary Elements must remain traceable to the underlying Governed Formed Event and supporting operational information.
Candidate Boundary Element ≠ Confirmed Boundary Element.
Confirmation of what belongs within the Event Boundary is handled through subsequent Boundary Scope governance. ------------------------------ Boundary Anchors
Operational systems frequently contain apparent boundary anchors.
These may include: order IDs invoice numbers payment IDs settlement records shipment numbers contract identifiers workflow instances API sessions database transactions machine jobs robotic tasks autonomous objectives blockchain transactions accounting entries

Boundary Candidate Insufficient

EBIM must therefore support boundary identification without requiring a single transaction record or discrete technical execution.

Likewise, one autonomous objective may generate multiple materially distinguishable events.

Machine Action ≠ Event Boundary by Default.

The governed boundary must follow operational structure rather than machine execution granularity. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements
EBIM requires that:
1.

EBIM follows the following governance logic:
If a Governed Formed Event exists, its potential structural perimeter must be identifiable before detailed Boundary Scope can be governed.
If sufficient Boundary Signals exist:
→ establish a Candidate Event Boundary.
If several legitimate Candidate Boundaries exist:
→ preserve the alternatives for subsequent governance.
If Boundary Signals conflict:

→ classify the boundary identification as ambiguous or unresolved.
If technical or commercial structures are the only available basis:
→ retain them as provisional boundary evidence rather than automatically accepting them as the governed boundary.
If the available information cannot support meaningful boundary identification:
→ the event must not be represented as boundary-ready. ------------------------------

This is particularly important where governed event information must later be consumed by multiple tax systems or jurisdictions. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Across Multiple Operational Structures
A customer places one marketplace order containing products from three merchants.
The platform creates one order ID.
The merchants generate three invoices.
Two logistics providers create four shipments.
The payment provider performs two settlements.
One item is subsequently refunded.
Each system presents a different apparent boundary.
EBIM does not automatically accept the order ID, invoice, shipment, settlement, or refund record as the Event Boundary.
Instead, it identifies the materially relevant Boundary Signals and constructs one or more Candidate Event Boundaries for subsequent scope governance.
This prevents the platform's technical architecture from deciding the governed structure of the event.

The order identifier is boundary evidence — not boundary authority. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Continuous Autonomous Cloud Infrastructure
An autonomous AI infrastructure platform continuously allocates compute, storage, networking, model execution, and settlement resources across multiple data centers.
Millions of technical actions occur every day.
There is no single transaction record representing the complete operational activity.
Treating every machine action as an Event Boundary would produce artificial fragmentation.
Treating the entire continuous platform operation as one permanent event would produce artificial aggregation.
EBIM identifies materially meaningful Boundary Signals within the continuous operational structure and establishes Candidate Event Boundaries capable of progressing into Boundary Scope governance.
Continuous machine execution does not eliminate the need for governed Event Boundaries. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary

Canonical Definition
The Event Boundary Revision Module (EBRM) governs how an established or developing Event Boundary is reconsidered, revised, confirmed, or preserved when new information, corrected information, structural change, resolved uncertainty, separation results, conflicting representations, or other materially relevant boundary evidence affects the legitimacy of the existing boundary structure.
EBRM establishes the governance conditions under which Event Boundary revision may occur while preserving traceability between the previous boundary state and the revised boundary state.
Its specific task is:

to ensure that an Event Boundary can change when materially justified without allowing revision to become uncontrolled reconstruction, retrospective convenience, historical erasure, or downstream tax-driven redefinition of the event.
EBRM is the final Core Module of the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard.
It converts the boundary structures established through EBIM, EBSCM, EBEM, and EBSM into a sufficiently governed and revision-controlled Event Boundary capable of proceeding into Event Timing governance. ------------------------------
Operational Role
The preceding TREBS modules establish:
EBIM — where a candidate Event Boundary may exist.
EBSCM — what belongs within its provisional scope.
EBEM — what must remain outside that scope.
EBSM — whether materially distinct event structures must be separated.
EBRM asks:
Does the resulting Event Boundary remain legitimate in light of the complete governed boundary structure, and how must any justified change to that boundary be controlled and preserved?
EBRM therefore governs the transition:
Developing Event Boundary
↓
Revision-Controlled Event Boundary
↓
Governed Bounded Event
Its narrow task is:
to govern material revision, confirmation, preservation, and traceability of the Event Boundary before the event proceeds into subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. ------------------------------ Internal Flow

TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------ Operational Space
EBRM operates within Event Boundary Revision.
Its Operational Space includes: Boundary Revision readiness revision trigger identification revision materiality affected boundary identification inclusion revision exclusion revision separation revision boundary expansion boundary contraction boundary restructuring boundary preservation boundary confirmation revision conflict revision uncertainty revision traceability previous-boundary preservation revised-boundary linkage boundary version continuity downstream boundary impact signalling final Event Boundary readiness
EBRM owns controlled revision of the Event Boundary.
It does not reopen the entire event lifecycle by default. ------------------------------ Operational Scope
EBRM may govern boundary revision across: commercial transactions digital transactions financial operations logistics manufacturing marketplaces platform activity subscriptions digital services banking distributed systems autonomous systems AI-agent activity machine-to-machine operations robotic operations digital assets infrastructure operations hybrid physical-digital events future machine economies

The revision logic remains technology-neutral, actor-neutral, organization-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision Principle
An Event Boundary must not be treated as permanently immutable merely because it was previously established.
Operational reality may later become clearer.
New information may reveal that: relevant activity was omitted, external activity was incorrectly included, one event was incorrectly aggregated, one event was incorrectly fragmented, an assumed separation was unsupported, an unresolved boundary condition has become resolvable, a source representation was incorrect, or a material structural change occurred.
A governed architecture must therefore support revision.
However:
Revisability ≠ Arbitrary Mutability.
Boundary revision requires a governed basis. ------------------------------ Revision Readiness
Before revision begins, EBRM must establish whether sufficient reason exists to reopen the current Event Boundary.
A boundary may be:
Revision Not Indicated
Revision Candidate
Revision Required
Revision Unresolved
Revision readiness prevents every new technical record or minor informational difference from reopening an otherwise legitimate Event Boundary.
Therefore:
New Information ≠ Revision Requirement by Default. ------------------------------ Revision Trigger
A Revision Trigger is a materially relevant condition that creates a legitimate basis for reconsidering an existing Event Boundary.

Potential triggers may include: newly discovered operational information corrected source information previously unavailable evidence resolved boundary uncertainty resolved boundary conflict incorrect inclusion incorrect exclusion incorrect separation newly established event distinctness newly established event unity structural transformation system reconciliation material inconsistency downstream discovery of a boundary defect autonomous-system correction machine-generated correction prior governance error
A trigger initiates reconsideration.
It does not predetermine the result.
Therefore:
Revision Trigger ≠ Boundary Change. ------------------------------ Revision Materiality
Not every difference justifies revision.
EBRM must determine whether the identified issue is materially capable of affecting the governed Event Boundary.
A difference may be:
Non-Material
Potentially Material
Material
Materiality Unresolved
Non-material differences may be recorded without changing the Event Boundary.
Material differences require governed reconsideration.
This prevents unnecessary boundary instability. ------------------------------ Affected Boundary Elements
Where revision is justified, EBRM must identify which part of the Event Boundary is affected.

Affected elements may include: included activity excluded activity separation structure overlapping structure nested structure composite structure distributed structure machine-generated structure autonomous structure boundary qualification unresolved boundary condition
Revision should remain proportionate to the affected boundary element.
Therefore:
Local Boundary Defect ≠ Full Event Reconstruction by Default. ------------------------------ Boundary Preservation
EBRM must explicitly allow the existing Event Boundary to remain unchanged where reconsideration does not establish a material reason for revision.
Possible outcome:
Boundary Reviewed — Existing Boundary Preserved
This is important because revision governance is not a mechanism for producing change.
It is a mechanism for governing whether change is legitimate.
Therefore:
Boundary Review ≠ Boundary Revision. ------------------------------ Boundary Expansion
A boundary may require expansion when materially relevant activity was incorrectly excluded or previously unavailable information establishes legitimate inclusion.
Boundary expansion must identify: what is being added, why it is being added, the prior state, the revised state, supporting basis, downstream implications.
However:
Additional Related Activity ≠ Automatic Boundary Expansion.
The activity must satisfy the governed boundary basis. ------------------------------ Boundary Contraction

A boundary may require contraction where activity previously included is later established as outside the legitimate structural extent of the event.
Boundary contraction must preserve the historical fact that the activity was previously included.
Therefore:
Boundary Contraction ≠ Historical Deletion.
The previous boundary state remains reconstructable. ------------------------------ Boundary Restructuring
Some revisions cannot be represented merely as expansion or contraction.
New information may establish that: one boundary should become multiple boundaries, multiple boundaries should be consolidated, overlapping structures require reorganization, nested structures were incorrectly represented, separation logic must be reconsidered.
Such cases may require Boundary Restructuring.
Where restructuring creates materially distinct event structures, EBRM must preserve linkage to the EBSM separation basis.
EBRM must not independently absorb EBSM's separation function. ------------------------------ Revision of Inclusion
Where previous inclusion becomes materially questionable, EBRM may reopen the relevant inclusion result established through EBSCM.
The revision record must identify: previous inclusion state, reason for reconsideration, new information, revised state, resulting boundary effect.
EBRM governs the revision.
It does not replace EBSCM's underlying scope methodology. ------------------------------ Revision of Exclusion

Where previous exclusion becomes materially questionable, EBRM may reopen the relevant exclusion result established through EBEM.
The revision must preserve: previous exclusion basis, revision trigger, revised determination, resulting Event Boundary impact.
Therefore:
Previously Excluded ≠ Permanently Excluded.
But equally:
New Association ≠ Automatic Inclusion. ------------------------------ Revision of Separation
Where later information materially challenges an existing separation structure, EBRM may trigger reconsideration of the EBSM result.
Possible outcomes include: separation preserved, separation modified, separation removed, additional separation required, separation remains unresolved.
EBRM governs revision control.
EBSM remains the owner of separation logic. ------------------------------ Boundary Version Continuity
Every material Event Boundary revision must preserve continuity between boundary states.
A conceptual version sequence may be represented as:
Boundary State B1
↓
Revision Trigger
↓
Boundary Review
↓
Boundary State B2
↓
Subsequent Revision
↓
Boundary State B3
Each state must remain distinguishable and traceable.
Therefore:
Current Boundary ≠ Only Boundary State That Matters. ------------------------------ Historical Preservation
Revision must never silently overwrite prior governed reality.

The architecture must preserve: previous Event Boundary previous governance basis revision trigger changed elements unchanged elements revision rationale revised Event Boundary time of governance revision linkage between states
This supports later reconstruction of what the system knew and how the Event Boundary evolved.
Therefore:
Event Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure. ------------------------------ Correction ≠ Revision
A purely technical correction may not materially change the Event Boundary.
For example: spelling correction identifier formatting correction duplicate metadata removal non-material system-field correction
Such corrections should not automatically create a new material boundary version.
Therefore:
Technical Correction ≠ Material Boundary Revision by Default.
Materiality governs whether EBRM revision logic is required. ------------------------------ New Event ≠ Boundary Revision
Not every later development should modify an existing Event Boundary.
New operational activity may represent a new event rather than an extension of the existing event.
Therefore:
New Activity ≠ Existing Boundary Expansion by Default.
Where the later activity represents a materially new occurrence, it may require new TREGA™ Event Recognition and Event Formation rather than revision of the previous boundary.
EBRM must prevent revision from becoming unlimited event absorption. ------------------------------ Material Transformation

In exceptional cases, new information may establish that the event has transformed so materially that revision of the existing boundary would no longer preserve event identity coherently.
Such a condition may require escalation back into appropriate TREGA™ lifecycle governance.
Therefore:
Material Event Transformation may require New Event Formation.
EBRM must not force continuity where operational continuity no longer exists. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Event Timing
The time at which a boundary is revised is not necessarily the operational time of the event.
Likewise, discovering an omitted component later does not mean that component occurred at the time of revision.
Therefore:
Boundary Revision Time ≠ Event Time.
Final Event Timing belongs to:
TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Tax Rules
Tax law may change after an Event Boundary has already been governed.
A jurisdiction may later classify or tax the event differently.
This does not automatically justify reconstructing the Event Boundary.
Therefore:
Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Boundary Change by Default.
TREGA™ must preserve operational event representation independently of downstream tax-rule evolution. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Tax Outcome
A tax authority, tax engine, or compliance system may identify that a different Event Boundary would produce a different tax result.

That fact alone does not authorize TREGA™ to revise operational reality.
Therefore:
Different Tax Outcome ≠ Boundary Revision Basis by Default.
Revision must remain grounded in governed event structure. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Jurisdiction
A jurisdiction may legally aggregate or divide operational events differently for taxation.
Such legal treatment does not automatically alter TREGA's governed Event Boundary.
Therefore:
Jurisdictional Aggregation ≠ Operational Event Aggregation.
Jurisdictional Separation ≠ Operational Event Separation.
The same governed event layer may support multiple jurisdictional evaluations. ------------------------------ Autonomous Boundary Revision
Autonomous systems may discover inconsistencies or new information without direct human intervention.
Examples include: reconciliation agents machine monitoring distributed ledgers automated settlement systems AI anomaly detection autonomous logistics systems
An autonomous system may generate a Revision Trigger.
It must not silently rewrite the Event Boundary.
Therefore:
Autonomous Detection ≠ Autonomous Authority to Rewrite Governed Event History.
The same governed revision requirements apply regardless of whether the trigger originates from a human, organization, machine, or autonomous agent. ------------------------------ Revision Conflict
Different sources may propose incompatible boundary revisions.

For example: one system indicates expansion, another indicates contraction, one participant disputes separation, an autonomous system detects conflicting structure, later records contradict earlier operational representations.
EBRM must preserve the conflict.
It must not select a revision merely because one source has technical priority.
Possible state:
Boundary Revision Conflict
The boundary may remain qualified or unresolved until sufficient governance basis exists. ------------------------------ Revision Uncertainty
A Revision Trigger may be legitimate while the correct revised boundary remains uncertain.
EBRM must distinguish:
Reason to Reconsider
from
Sufficient Basis to Change
Therefore:
Revision Readiness ≠ Revision Determination.
Where uncertainty remains material, EBRM preserves:
Boundary Revision Unresolved
rather than creating artificial certainty. ------------------------------ Boundary Confirmation
Once revision analysis is complete, EBRM must establish whether the resulting Event Boundary is sufficiently governed to proceed.
Boundary Confirmation may result from: preservation of the existing boundary, legitimate expansion, legitimate contraction, legitimate restructuring, resolution of separation, qualified acceptance of non-material uncertainty.
The confirmation does not establish taxability.

It establishes only that the structural Event Boundary is sufficiently governed for subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. ------------------------------ Governed Bounded Event
The principal final output of EBRM and TREBS is:
Governed Bounded Event
A Governed Bounded Event is an event whose structural extent has been sufficiently: identified, scoped, excluded, separated where necessary, revised where materially justified, preserved where revision was not justified, traceably maintained, and confirmed for progression.
It does not yet establish final Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or legal taxability.
Therefore:
Governed Bounded Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements
EBRM requires that:
1.
revision begins from a governed Event Boundary structure. 2.
a legitimate Revision Trigger is identified before material revision occurs. 3.
Revision Trigger and revision outcome remain distinct. 4.
revision materiality is evaluated. 5.
non-material differences do not automatically reopen the Event Boundary. 6.
affected boundary elements are explicitly identified. 7.
revision remains proportionate to the affected boundary condition. 8.
preservation of the existing boundary remains a legitimate outcome. 9.
expansion requires a governed inclusion basis. 10.
contraction preserves historical inclusion state. 11.

restructuring preserves linkage to prior boundary states. 12.
inclusion revision remains traceable to EBSCM. 13.
exclusion revision remains traceable to EBEM. 14.
separation revision remains traceable to EBSM. 15.
previous Event Boundary states remain reconstructable. 16.
material revisions maintain Boundary Version Continuity. 17.
technical corrections do not automatically become material revisions. 18.
new activity is not automatically absorbed into an existing Event Boundary. 19.
material transformation may require new Event Formation rather than boundary revision. 20.
revision time remains distinct from Event Timing. 21.
tax-rule change does not automatically alter Event Boundary. 22.
tax outcome does not determine revision legitimacy. 23.
jurisdictional aggregation or separation does not redefine operational Event Boundary. 24.
autonomous systems may identify revision triggers but may not silently rewrite governed history. 25.
revision conflict and uncertainty remain explicit. 26.
confirmed Event Boundary is sufficiently governed before transfer to TRETS.
------------------------------ Governance Logic
EBRM applies the following logic:
Has a legitimate Boundary Revision Trigger been identified?
If no:
→ preserve the existing Event Boundary.
If yes:
→ assess materiality.
Is the identified difference materially relevant to the Event Boundary?
If no:
→ record the information and preserve the boundary.
If yes:
→ identify affected boundary elements.

Does the new governance basis support a boundary change?
If no:
→ preserve the existing boundary and record the review.
If yes:
→ determine whether expansion, contraction, restructuring, or reconsideration of prior scope, exclusion, or separation is required.
Would the proposed change destroy coherent continuity with the existing event?
If yes:
→ evaluate whether the condition requires new Event Formation rather than Event Boundary revision.
If no:
→ construct the revised boundary.
Can the previous and revised states remain reconstructable and traceably linked?
If no:
→ Boundary Revision Unresolved.
If yes:
→ preserve Boundary Version Continuity.
Is the resulting Event Boundary sufficiently governed for subsequent lifecycle processing?
If yes:
→ confirm Governed Bounded Event.
If no:
→ preserve qualified, conflicting, or unresolved state. ------------------------------
Minimum Implementation Framework
A conforming implementation of EBRM must be capable of:
1.
receiving the Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure from EBSM 2.
determining Boundary Revision readiness 3.
identifying Revision Triggers 4.
evaluating revision materiality 5.
identifying affected boundary elements 6.
distinguishing material revision from technical correction 7.
governing boundary preservation 8.
governing boundary expansion 9.
governing boundary contraction 10.
governing boundary restructuring 11.
reconnecting revision to relevant EBSCM, EBEM, or EBSM governance where necessary 12.

preserving previous Event Boundary states 13.
establishing Boundary Version Continuity 14.
maintaining revision traceability 15.
identifying Revision Conflict 16.
representing Revision Uncertainty 17.
preventing tax-driven boundary rewriting 18.
preventing jurisdictional rules from silently redefining operational Event Boundary 19.
preventing autonomous systems from silently overwriting governed event history 20.
distinguishing boundary revision from new Event Formation 21.
confirming the resulting Event Boundary 22.
producing a Governed Bounded Event 23.
transferring the Governed Bounded Event to TRETS
------------------------------
Governance Outputs
EBRM may produce: Boundary Revision Readiness Record Boundary Revision Trigger Record Revision Materiality State Affected Boundary Element Record Boundary Preservation Decision Boundary Expansion Record Boundary Contraction Record Boundary Restructuring Record Boundary Revision Conflict Boundary Revision Uncertainty Boundary Version Record Previous-to-Revised Boundary Linkage Boundary Revision Traceability Record Boundary Confirmation Record New Event Formation Referral Governed Bounded Event
Its principal output is:
Governed Bounded Event
This proceeds to:
TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions
Revisability ≠ Arbitrary Mutability
New Information ≠ Revision Requirement by Default
Revision Trigger ≠ Boundary Change

Local Boundary Defect ≠ Full Event Reconstruction by Default
Boundary Review ≠ Boundary Revision
Additional Related Activity ≠ Automatic Boundary Expansion
Boundary Contraction ≠ Historical Deletion
Previously Excluded ≠ Permanently Excluded
New Association ≠ Automatic Inclusion
Current Boundary ≠ Only Boundary State That Matters
Event Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure
Technical Correction ≠ Material Boundary Revision by Default
New Activity ≠ Existing Boundary Expansion by Default
Boundary Revision Time ≠ Event Time
Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Boundary Change by Default
Different Tax Outcome ≠ Boundary Revision Basis by Default
Jurisdictional Aggregation ≠ Operational Event Aggregation
Jurisdictional Separation ≠ Operational Event Separation
Autonomous Detection ≠ Autonomous Authority to Rewrite Governed Event History
Revision Readiness ≠ Revision Determination
Governed Bounded Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event ------------------------------ Enterprise Application
Enterprise event records evolve.
Initial representations are frequently incomplete because information arrives asynchronously from: commerce systems payment systems logistics platforms banks suppliers customers autonomous systems distributed infrastructure reconciliation processes
Without controlled revision governance, organizations commonly face two bad options:
freeze an incorrect historical event representation
or
silently overwrite the original representation whenever new information appears.

EBRM provides a third model:
governed event evolution with preserved historical continuity.
A boundary may legitimately change while every material state remains reconstructable.
This enables ERP systems, digital platforms, tax infrastructure, AI systems, auditors, regulators, and downstream jurisdictional engines to understand not only the current Event Boundary, but also how and why that boundary became legitimate. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Marketplace Event Changes After Partial Refund and Fulfilment Reconciliation
A marketplace initially records one customer order containing products from several sellers.
TREBS establishes several governed Event Boundaries based on the operational structures available at the time.
Weeks later, reconciliation reveals that: one shipment never occurred, one product was fulfilled by a different seller, one settlement was incorrectly associated with the original fulfilment, and a partial refund relates only to one previously bounded event.
The platform cannot simply overwrite the original Event Boundaries.
EBRM identifies the new reconciliation information as potential Revision Triggers.
It evaluates materiality and determines which Event Boundaries are affected.
One boundary is preserved.
Another is contracted.
A third requires reconsideration of its separation structure.
Every previous boundary state remains linked to the revised state.

The resulting Governed Bounded Events can then proceed through Event Timing and later TREGA™ governance.
The tax engines of different jurisdictions may subsequently interpret the events differently, but those tax interpretations do not rewrite the underlying operational boundary history. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Network Discovers That Previously Unified Machine Activity Contained a Distinct Event
An autonomous manufacturing network coordinates robots, procurement agents, inventory systems, production equipment, and settlement services.
Initial operational information indicates that thousands of machine actions belong to one governed production event.
After reconciliation, an autonomous monitoring system discovers that part of the resource consumption and machine execution was independently initiated by another production objective.
The new information creates a legitimate Revision Trigger.
EBSM separation logic is reconsidered through the governed revision process.
The previously unified boundary is restructured into two materially distinct event structures.
EBRM preserves: the original Event Boundary, the new information, the revision trigger, the separation reconsideration, the revised Event Boundaries, and the linkage between all boundary states.
The autonomous monitoring system therefore contributes new information without gaining uncontrolled authority to rewrite historical event reality.

Machine-discovered reality can change a governed Event Boundary — but only through governed, traceable revision. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary
EBRM governs the readiness, triggering, materiality, reconsideration, preservation, expansion, contraction, restructuring, version continuity, conflict, uncertainty, traceability, and confirmation of Event Boundary revisions. It does not perform original Event Boundary Identification, original Event Boundary Scope determination, original Event Boundary Exclusion, original Event Boundary Separation, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationship determination, final Event Determination, legal taxability determination, Tax Jurisdiction determination, taxpayer determination, tax-base calculation, tax-rate application, exemptions, deductions, tax liability, reporting obligations, payment, collection, or enforcement.
EBRM begins with the:
Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure
and ends with the:
Governed Bounded Event ------------------------------ Module Handoff
EBSM — Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure
↓
EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Governance
↓
Governed Bounded Event
↓
TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------
Canonical Closing Statement
The Event Boundary Revision Module ensures that a governed Event Boundary can respond to better information without losing methodological control over its history.

It allows legitimate correction of the governed structural extent of an event while preserving previous boundary states, revision reasons, material changes, unresolved conditions, and continuity between representations.
It prevents both rigid preservation of a materially incorrect boundary and uncontrolled rewriting of operational reality.
An Event Boundary may change when reality justifies the change — but governed history must never disappear merely because the current representation has changed.

OOF™ Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM)
Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™

AI-Readable: Yes
