Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM) governs how a Candidate Event Boundary is translated into a defined Event Boundary Scope by determining which materially relevant structures, components, relationships, operational states, and supporting elements fall within the governed perimeter under examination.
EBSCM establishes the positive scope of the Event Boundary: what is provisionally governed as belonging within the event perimeter for subsequent Boundary Exclusion and Boundary Separation governance.
Its specific task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Event Boundary Scope without treating technical grouping, commercial packaging, organizational structure, shared identifiers, or jurisdiction-specific tax treatment as authoritative scope criteria.
EBSCM governs what falls within the candidate event perimeter.
It does not yet determine formal exclusions, separation into distinct event structures, or later Boundary Revision. ------------------------------
Operational Role
EBIM identifies where the potential Event Boundary appears to lie.
EBSCM determines what the identified boundary is intended to contain.
This creates the transition:
Candidate Event Boundary
↓
Governed Event Boundary Scope
A Candidate Event Boundary may appear structurally plausible while still leaving uncertainty about which surrounding elements properly belong within its scope.
Therefore:
Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary Scope.
And:
Structural Proximity ≠ Scope Membership by Default.
EBSCM converts boundary identification into an explicit positive scope that can be tested by the subsequent Boundary Exclusion and Boundary Separation modules. ------------------------------ Internal Flow
Candidate Event Boundary
↓
Scope Candidate Identification
↓
Scope Relevance Assessment
↓
Scope Membership Assessment
↓
Scope Coherence Assessment
↓
Scope Ambiguity / Conflict Handling
↓
Governed Event Boundary Scope
↓

EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------ Operational Space
EBSCM operates within the governance space where the content of an identified Candidate Event Boundary must be explicitly defined.
Its Operational Space includes: identification of Candidate Scope Elements assessment of material relevance to the Event Boundary assessment of provisional scope membership structural coherence of included elements treatment of shared operational structures treatment of supporting activities treatment of composite event structures treatment of distributed event structures treatment of machine-generated and autonomous structures treatment of overlapping Candidate Scope Elements detection of over-inclusive scope detection of under-inclusive scope representation of scope ambiguity representation of scope conflict preservation of scope traceability
EBSCM owns the positive definition of Event Boundary Scope.
It does not own formal exclusion decisions or separation of distinct event structures. ------------------------------ Operational Scope

EBSCM applies wherever a Candidate Event Boundary must be converted into an explicit governed scope across: physical operations commercial transactions financial activity digital services platform operations distributed systems autonomous agents AI systems robotic operations machine-to-machine activity infrastructure operations digital assets value-affecting activity composite physical-digital events cross-organizational activity future machine economies
The module remains actor-neutral, technology-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral.
Scope membership must follow the governed operational structure of the event rather than the architecture of the system recording it. ------------------------------ Candidate Scope Elements
A Candidate Event Boundary may contain many structures that appear potentially relevant.
These become Candidate Scope Elements.
They may include: qualified Event Formation Components materially connected operational actions materially connected states materially connected transitions supporting operational structures distributed execution elements machine-generated activity autonomous execution structures value-affecting operational elements operational interfaces structurally connected records or representations
Candidate Scope Elements must be assessed before being treated as part of the governed scope.
Candidate Scope Element ≠ Scope Member. ------------------------------ Scope Membership

EBSCM determines whether a Candidate Scope Element has sufficient structural relevance to be provisionally included within the Event Boundary Scope.
Scope membership may be supported where an element: forms part of the governed event structure materially contributes to the operational coherence of that structure represents a materially relevant state or transition within the candidate perimeter is necessary to represent the event without material structural distortion belongs to a distributed but coherent execution structure cannot be removed from the represented scope without materially changing what the formed event represents
Scope membership must not be established merely because an element: shares an identifier appears in the same database belongs to the same workflow occurs under the same contract belongs to the same customer order was executed by the same machine or agent belongs to the same organization occurs close in time occurs close in physical or digital space is processed under the same accounting structure
Therefore:
Association ≠ Scope Membership. ------------------------------ Positive Scope Governance
EBSCM establishes the positive representation of what belongs within the Event Boundary Scope.
This is distinct from exclusion governance.
The module asks:
What is sufficiently justified to remain within the governed scope at this stage?
It does not yet ask:
What must formally be excluded from that scope?

That distinction preserves the separation between EBSCM and the subsequent Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM).
Therefore:
Scope Definition ≠ Exclusion Determination.
An element may remain provisionally within scope while requiring later exclusion analysis. ------------------------------ Scope Coherence
The Event Boundary Scope must remain structurally coherent.
A scope is not coherent merely because all included elements are individually relevant.
The combined scope must represent a meaningful operational event structure.
EBSCM therefore evaluates whether included elements collectively produce: sufficient structural unity meaningful operational coherence proportionate representation continuity with the Governed Formed Event consistency with the Candidate Event Boundary sufficient differentiation from surrounding activity
A scope that combines unrelated structures may be over-inclusive.
A scope that omits materially necessary structures may be under-inclusive.
Relevant Elements ≠ Coherent Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Over-Inclusive Scope
Over-inclusion occurs where the Event Boundary Scope absorbs surrounding activity beyond what is materially necessary to represent the formed event.
Potential causes include: shared commercial identifiers shared contracts common workflows common organizational ownership continuous technical execution broad autonomous objectives shared infrastructure platform-level aggregation common accounting treatment

EBSCM must detect potential over-inclusion before the scope progresses further.
Shared Operational Environment ≠ Shared Event Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Under-Inclusive Scope
Under-inclusion occurs where materially necessary structures are omitted from the Event Boundary Scope.
This may happen where systems artificially fragment operational reality into: separate technical records separate platform operations separate machine instructions separate database transactions separate payment steps separate system instances
Technical fragmentation must not produce artificial event fragmentation.
Technical Separation ≠ Scope Separation by Default. ------------------------------ Composite and Distributed Scope
A governed Event Boundary Scope may legitimately span: multiple systems multiple organizations multiple technical processes multiple machines multiple autonomous agents physical and digital environments distributed infrastructure multiple operational stages
Distributed execution does not automatically require distributed Event Boundaries.
Likewise, operational distribution does not justify unlimited scope expansion.
EBSCM must preserve the materially coherent scope without allowing technical distribution to determine the event structure.
Distributed Execution ≠ Distributed Event Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Autonomous and Machine Scope
Autonomous systems may create particularly difficult scope conditions.

One autonomous objective may generate: thousands of API calls multiple model executions resource allocations robotic actions financial operations external service interactions settlement operations
EBSCM must determine which of those structures materially belong within the Event Boundary Scope.
Neither extreme is acceptable by default:
One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Unlimited Event Scope.
One Machine Action ≠ One Independent Event Scope.
The scope must follow material operational coherence. ------------------------------ Scope Ambiguity and Conflict
The appropriate Event Boundary Scope may remain uncertain.
Potential states include:
Scope Candidate
Scope Established
Scope Ambiguous
Scope Conflict
Scope Insufficient
Scope Unresolved
Ambiguity may arise where different systems, evidence sources, or operational representations support competing scope structures.
EBSCM must preserve that ambiguity rather than silently selecting the most convenient system representation.
System Preference ≠ Governed Scope Resolution. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements
EBSCM requires that:
1.
Scope governance begins from a Candidate Event Boundary established through EBIM. 2.
Candidate Scope Elements are explicitly identified. 3.
Scope membership is based on material operational relevance and structural coherence. 4.
Shared identifiers do not automatically establish common scope. 5.
Shared contracts do not automatically establish common scope. 6.

Common workflows do not automatically establish common scope. 7.
Common organizational ownership does not automatically establish common scope. 8.
Technical fragmentation does not automatically create separate scopes. 9.
Distributed execution does not automatically create separate scopes. 10.
Autonomous objectives do not automatically create unlimited Event Scope. 11.
Machine actions do not automatically create independent Event Scope. 12.
Over-inclusive and under-inclusive scope conditions are detectable. 13.
Scope ambiguity and conflict remain visible. 14.
Scope decisions remain traceable to their operational basis. 15.
Scope governance remains independent of jurisdiction-specific tax treatment. 16.
Formal exclusions remain governed by EBEM. 17.
Separation between distinct event structures remains governed by EBSM.
------------------------------ Governance Logic
EBSCM applies the following logic:
If a Candidate Event Boundary exists, the materially relevant structures potentially belonging within that perimeter must be assessed before the boundary can progress toward exclusion and separation governance.
If an element is materially necessary to represent the event coherently:
→ retain it within the Governed Event Boundary Scope.
If its membership remains uncertain:
→ preserve it as an unresolved Scope Candidate.
If inclusion would materially over-expand the event:
→ flag potential over-inclusion for further governance.
If omission would materially distort the event:

→ flag potential under-inclusion.
If competing scope structures remain legitimate:
→ preserve the competing representations.
EBSCM must not force scope certainty where operational reality does not support it. ------------------------------
Minimum Implementation Framework
A conforming implementation of EBSCM must be capable of:
1.
receiving the Candidate Event Boundary from EBIM 2.
identifying Candidate Scope Elements 3.
assessing material scope relevance 4.
assessing provisional scope membership 5.
distinguishing association from scope membership 6.
evaluating structural coherence 7.
detecting potential over-inclusion 8.
detecting potential under-inclusion 9.
supporting composite and distributed scope structures 10.
supporting autonomous and machine-generated structures 11.
representing scope ambiguity and conflict 12.
maintaining traceability of scope decisions 13.
assigning a governed scope state 14.
producing a Governed Event Boundary Scope 15.
transferring that scope to EBEM 16.
preventing Event Boundary Scope governance from becoming Event Exclusion, Event Separation, Tax Jurisdiction, or taxability determination
------------------------------
Governance Outputs
EBSCM may produce: Governed Event Boundary Scope Candidate Scope Element Set Scope Membership Record Scope Coherence Record Scope Ambiguity Indicator Scope Conflict Indicator Potential Over-Inclusion Indicator Potential Under-Inclusion Indicator Distributed Scope Representation Scope Traceability Record

Its principal governed output is:
Governed Event Boundary Scope
This output proceeds to:
EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions
Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary Scope
Candidate Scope Element ≠ Scope Member
Association ≠ Scope Membership
Operational Relevance ≠ Scope Membership by Default
Relevant Elements ≠ Coherent Scope by Default
Scope Definition ≠ Exclusion Determination
Shared Identifier ≠ Shared Event Scope
Shared Contract ≠ Shared Event Scope
Shared Workflow ≠ Shared Event Scope
Shared Organization ≠ Shared Event Scope
Technical Separation ≠ Scope Separation by Default
Distributed Execution ≠ Distributed Event Scope by Default
One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Unlimited Event Scope
One Machine Action ≠ One Independent Event Scope
System Preference ≠ Governed Scope Resolution
Event Boundary Scope ≠ Event Boundary Exclusion
Event Boundary Scope ≠ Event Separation
Event Boundary Scope ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Event Boundary Scope ≠ Taxability Determination ------------------------------ Enterprise Application
Modern enterprise activity is rarely represented consistently across systems.
One economically coherent activity may appear as multiple objects across:
CRM
↓
Commerce Platform
↓
ERP
↓
Payment Infrastructure
↓
Logistics
↓
Accounting
↓
Tax Systems
Each system may define its own internal scope.
EBSCM prevents those internal scopes from automatically becoming the governed Event Boundary Scope.

Instead, the module establishes a neutral operational scope capable of being consumed by downstream governance and, eventually, multiple jurisdiction-specific taxation systems.
This reduces dependence on system-specific interpretations of what constitutes the event. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Global SaaS Service Across Multiple Technical Systems
A multinational SaaS provider receives one enterprise subscription agreement.
Provisioning occurs across several cloud regions.
Authentication is handled by another system.
Usage is continuously measured.
Billing is monthly.
Payments may be split across several corporate entities.
Support services operate separately.
A contract-centric model may place the entire relationship inside one enormous event scope.
A technical model may fragment the same relationship into millions of infrastructure operations.
EBSCM evaluates which operational structures materially belong within the Candidate Event Boundary and establishes a coherent Event Boundary Scope without allowing either contractual aggregation or technical fragmentation to dictate the result.
The governed scope follows operational coherence — not the architecture of the systems recording it. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Network Across Multiple Machines
An autonomous manufacturing system receives a production objective.

The objective triggers material allocation, robotic handling, machining, welding, inspection, internal transport, packaging, inventory updates, and automated settlement actions.
Thousands of machine operations are generated.
Some operations directly contribute to the formed event.
Others are shared infrastructure activities supporting many unrelated production cycles.
EBSCM determines which structures provisionally belong within the Event Boundary Scope and which merely surround or support it.
The module prevents both unlimited expansion into the entire factory environment and artificial fragmentation into thousands of machine-defined scopes.
Operational participation in the same infrastructure does not automatically create common Event Scope. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary
EBSCM governs the identification, assessment, positive inclusion, structural coherence, ambiguity, conflict, and traceability of the materially relevant structures provisionally contained within a Candidate Event Boundary. It does not perform formal Event Boundary exclusions, separate distinct event structures, revise previously established boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ Module Handoff
EBIM — Candidate Event Boundary
↓
EBSCM — Governed Event Boundary Scope
↓

EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------
Canonical Closing Statement
The Event Boundary Scope Module establishes what a Candidate Event Boundary is intended to contain.
It prevents shared identifiers, contracts, workflows, organizations, platforms, machines, autonomous objectives, and technical system structures from becoming automatic rules of Event Scope.
EBSCM produces a coherent and traceable positive scope while preserving uncertainty where operational reality remains unresolved.
EBSCM determines what provisionally belongs within the event perimeter — before subsequent governance determines what must be excluded or separated.

Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Boundary Separation Module (EBSM) governs how materially distinct event structures that are adjacent, overlapping, interconnected, technically combined, operationally continuous, commercially grouped, or otherwise at risk of being represented as one event are identified and separated into distinguishable governed Event Boundary structures.

EBSM establishes whether activity surrounding or intersecting a developing Event Boundary represents: part of the same governed event, structurally external activity, a materially distinct event candidate, multiple event candidates requiring separation, or an unresolved separation condition.
Its specific task is:
to prevent materially distinct events from being incorrectly collapsed into one Event Boundary while also preventing one coherent event from being artificially fragmented into multiple event structures.
EBSM governs event separation at the boundary level.
It does not determine the later semantic, economic, causal, contractual, tax, or other governed relationships among separated events. ------------------------------
Operational Role
EBIM identifies where the Event Boundary may exist.
EBSCM establishes what provisionally belongs within its scope.
EBEM determines what should remain outside that scope.
EBSM asks:
Does the resulting boundary structure still contain, overlap with, or become conflated with materially distinct event structures that must be separated?
The governing problem is two-sided:
Over-Aggregation Risk
and
Over-Fragmentation Risk
Over-aggregation combines materially distinct events into one governed event.
Over-fragmentation divides one coherent event into artificial event units.
Therefore:
Operational Connection ≠ Same Event.
And:
Technical Separation ≠ Separate Event.
EBSM must govern both errors. ------------------------------ Internal Flow

Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure
↓
Separation Candidate Identification
↓
Distinctness Assessment
↓
Overlap / Conflation Assessment
↓
Over-Aggregation / Over-Fragmentation Assessment
↓
Separation Structure Determination
↓
Separation Conflict / Uncertainty Handling
↓
Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure

EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Module ------------------------------ Operational Space

Modern enterprise systems rarely agree on what constitutes one event.
A single operational reality may appear as:
1 order in Commerce
3 shipments in Logistics
2 settlements in Payments
1 invoice in ERP
14 technical transactions in Infrastructure
hundreds of API operations in Platform Systems
Without governed separation logic, organizations may either collapse materially different events into one record or treat every technical operation as an independent event.
EBSM creates a system-independent event separation layer.

It allows downstream systems to consume event structures grounded in governed operational reality rather than database architecture, application boundaries, commercial packaging, or tax-specific assumptions. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Produces Multiple Operationally Distinct Outcomes
A marketplace receives one customer order containing goods from three independent sellers.
The platform assigns: one customer order ID, three seller fulfilments, three shipments, two payment settlements, one later refund.
The commerce system represents the activity as one order.
The logistics system represents three delivery structures.
The payment system represents multiple financial operations.
The existence of one order ID cannot decide whether one or several governed events exist.
EBSM evaluates the operational structures independently of those system representations.
Where materially distinct event structures are established, it separates their Event Boundaries while preserving the common order reference.
The result avoids both:
one oversized event created by the commercial order ID
and
dozens of artificial events created by technical system records.
The downstream tax system can subsequently evaluate the separated governed events under applicable law without TREGA™ deciding their tax treatment. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Cloud Agent Executes One Objective Through Multiple Independent Operations

An autonomous AI agent receives a high-level objective:
Acquire and deploy computational resources required to complete a complex workload.
The agent independently: purchases compute capacity, reserves storage, acquires specialized model access, initiates network resources, executes workloads across multiple providers, releases unused capacity, performs settlement operations.
Thousands of API calls occur.
One interpretation would treat the entire autonomous objective as one event.
Another would treat every API operation as a separate event.
Both may distort operational reality.
EBSM evaluates whether materially independent event structures exist within the autonomous activity.
It may distinguish independently coherent resource acquisitions and executions while preserving technical sub-operations as components or supporting activity rather than artificial independent events.
Autonomous complexity is therefore converted into governable event structure without allowing machine granularity to dictate event granularity. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary

The Event Boundary Separation Module prevents operational reality from being distorted by either excessive aggregation or excessive fragmentation.

Canonical Definition
Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the preservation, linkage, traceability, and reconstructability of Event Context across contextual states, material changes, corrections, system transitions, and subsequent stages of the TREGA™ lifecycle.
ECCM establishes how the contextual representation surrounding an occurrence remains governably connected to its preceding and succeeding contextual states without requiring those states to remain unchanged.
Its task is specific:

to preserve the continuity and reconstructability of governed Event Context across change without freezing context, erasing historical states, or treating every contextual modification as a new event or new contextual identity.
Operational Role
Context may evolve after its initial establishment.
ECIM identifies contextual elements.
ECSM determines their legitimate scope.
ECRM establishes their material relationships.
ECCHM governs material changes.
ECCM ensures that these states do not become disconnected fragments.
Its operational question is:
Can the governed contextual history surrounding an occurrence still be reconstructed and understood after the context has changed?
ECCM therefore provides the continuity layer through which TRECS can preserve: original contextual states; subsequent contextual states; contextual revisions; contextual corrections; contextual supersessions; relationships between contextual states; historical applicability; continuity across system transitions; continuity across organizational change; continuity across long-running event governance.

This output preserves the contextual chain required for subsequent TREGA™ governance and later reconstruction.

Operational Space
ECCM governs the space between:
separate governed contextual states
and
a continuous, traceable, and reconstructable contextual history associated with the same occurrence or developing event-governance process.
Its operational space includes: contextual state linkage; historical contextual preservation; continuity references; contextual version relationships; correction continuity; supersession continuity; contextual lineage; temporal contextual traceability; continuity across system migration; continuity across organizational change; continuity across distributed environments; continuity uncertainty; contextual reconstruction.
ECCM governs continuity of Event Context.
It does not govern the complete lifecycle of the Tax-Relevant Event itself.
Operational Scope
ECCM applies where more than one contextual state, representation, version, correction, or materially relevant contextual configuration exists.
The module ensures that later context can remain connected to earlier context without collapsing the two into one representation.
A continuity relationship may be required where: contextual information is updated; material context changes; an earlier contextual representation is corrected; context is superseded; systems are migrated; organizations restructure; platforms change; contextual information is reconstructed later; historical occurrences are reviewed; multiple systems retain different portions of contextual history.

ECCM must preserve sufficient continuity to determine which contextual state applied, when it applied, and how it relates to other governed contextual states.
Continuity Principle
Continuity does not require immutability.
A context can change while remaining part of the same governed contextual history.
Therefore:
Context Continuity ≠ Context Permanence.
The purpose of ECCM is not to prevent change.
Its purpose is to ensure that change does not destroy the ability to understand the contextual chain.
Continuity Across Change
Where ECCHM establishes a material Context Change, ECCM preserves the relationship between:
Previous Context State
↓
Context Change
↓
Subsequent Context State
This allows downstream systems to distinguish evolution from replacement.
A new contextual state should not automatically become disconnected from the state from which it developed.
At the same time, continuity must not be artificially maintained where the contextual relationship has genuinely ended.
Historical Context Preservation
Historical contextual states may remain materially important long after they cease to represent current conditions.
ECCM preserves the ability to answer:
What context surrounded the occurrence at the relevant time?
This is essential where tax-relevant activity is: reported later; audited later; disputed later; reconstructed from archived systems; re-evaluated after legal changes; examined by another jurisdiction; transferred between enterprise systems.
Therefore:

Historical Context ≠ Obsolete Context.
A contextual state can cease to be current while remaining essential governance information.
Continuity Across Correction
A corrected contextual record should remain connected to the representation it corrected.
ECCM preserves:
Original Representation
↓
Correction
↓
Corrected Representation
where traceability is materially required.
This enables later governance to distinguish what was originally known from what was subsequently established.
Therefore:
Correction Continuity ≠ Preservation of Error as Current Truth.
The earlier representation may remain historically visible without remaining operationally authoritative.
Continuity Across Supersession
Where one contextual state supersedes another, ECCM establishes the continuity relationship between them.
Supersession must not silently destroy the previous contextual state.
The architecture should be capable of representing:
Context State A
↓
Superseded By
↓
Context State B
while preserving the period or governance purpose for which Context State A remained applicable.
Therefore:
Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion.

Enterprise and public-sector systems change.
ERP platforms are replaced.
Databases are migrated.
Cloud providers change.
Platform identifiers are regenerated.
Legacy systems are retired.
Data structures evolve.
ECCM requires that a technical migration does not automatically break the governed contextual chain.
Therefore:

System Continuity ≠ Context Continuity.
The technical system may change completely while the governed contextual history remains continuous.
Conversely, technical persistence of the same database record does not by itself prove contextual continuity.

Companies merge.

Legal entities are reorganized.
Operational responsibilities change.

ECCM preserves contextual continuity where the surrounding governed context remains legitimately related across those changes.

Context Reconstruction

A governed system should be capable, where sufficient information exists, of reconstructing:

the changes affecting it,
the corrections applied to it,
the states that superseded it,
and

This capability becomes particularly important when the same governed occurrence is evaluated years later or by several downstream jurisdictions.
Governance Requirements

ECCM requires that: materially distinct contextual states remain distinguishable; continuity relationships are explicitly governable; historical context remains reconstructable where required; corrections remain linked to the states they correct; superseded states are not silently deleted; system migration does not automatically break contextual continuity; organizational succession does not automatically prove contextual continuity; continuity uncertainty remains explicit; continuity breaks can be represented; contextual history remains separable from current contextual state; continuity does not itself establish Event Continuity; continuity does not determine legal tax consequences.
Governance Logic
ECCM applies four principal questions:
Which contextual state is being continued?
What relationship connects the previous and subsequent contextual states?
Has continuity remained sufficiently established across change, correction, migration, or supersession?
Can the relevant contextual history still be reconstructed without rewriting previous states?

ECCM does not prescribe a blockchain, ledger, event-sourcing architecture, database, knowledge graph, ERP platform, AI model, archival technology, or tax infrastructure.

Enterprise Application

ECCM addresses a structural problem in long-lived taxation and enterprise information environments:
operational systems change faster than the lifecycle of the records that governments, organizations, auditors, and tax systems may later need to evaluate.
An event recorded today may be reviewed years later after:
ERP replacement
↓
cloud migration
↓
corporate restructuring
↓
platform migration
↓
identifier changes
↓
archive transfer
↓
tax-system modernization.
Without contextual continuity governance, each migration may progressively disconnect the record from the reality in which it originally existed.
ECCM provides a technology-neutral mechanism for maintaining the governed contextual chain independently of the systems that happen to store individual parts of that chain.
This allows downstream tax infrastructure to consume historical context without requiring historical technology to remain operational forever. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Tax Audit Years After Enterprise Systems Have Been Replaced
A multinational enterprise completes millions of transactions across ERP, payment, logistics, and digital commerce systems.
Over the following six years, the company replaces its ERP, migrates cloud infrastructure, restructures several business units, changes internal identifiers, and archives portions of the original operational data.
A tax authority later examines a historical cross-border transaction.

The current systems contain the transaction, but the organizational and operational context surrounding the original activity has materially changed.
Without governed continuity, the historical record may be interpreted using relationships, identifiers, system structures, or organizational conditions that did not exist when the occurrence took place.
ECCM preserves the chain between the original Event Context, subsequent contextual changes, corrections, system migrations, and current representations.
The historical occurrence can therefore be reconstructed against its historically applicable context rather than being silently reinterpreted through the enterprise environment that exists years later. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Economy Without Stable Technical Infrastructure
An autonomous commercial agent operates continuously for several years, purchasing services, allocating computing resources, interacting with marketplaces, coordinating machines, and initiating machine-to-machine transactions.
During that period its underlying models are replaced, APIs change, infrastructure migrates, platform accounts are transferred, identifiers evolve, and operational components are distributed across new providers.
The economic activity continues even though much of the technical infrastructure that originally generated its records no longer exists.

ECCM preserves governed contextual continuity across these transitions without assuming that identical technology, identifiers, or infrastructure must remain in place.
Where continuity cannot legitimately be established, the module records the break rather than manufacturing an artificial chain.
This addresses a fundamental problem of future machine economies:
economic activity may remain continuous even when the technical systems producing it are repeatedly replaced.
Canonical Boundary
ECCM governs continuity of Event Context across contextual states. It does not govern continuity of the Tax-Relevant Event itself, continuity of legal tax obligations, identity continuity, value continuity, or jurisdictional tax treatment.

Canonical Closing Statement

Event Context Continuity Module establishes the continuity and reconstructability layer of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by preserving the governed relationships among historical, current, corrected, changed, and superseded contextual states surrounding an occurrence. Through governance of contextual state linkage, historical preservation, correction continuity, supersession, continuity status, continuity breaks, distributed reconstruction, organizational transition, and system migration, ECCM prevents evolving technologies, changing enterprise structures, disappearing platforms, modified identifiers, later corrections, or current operational conditions from severing or silently rewriting the contextual history required to understand earlier activity. The Module preserves the distinction between continuity and permanence, similarity and continuity, Context Continuity and Event Continuity, and contextual history and current state. ECCM therefore ensures that Event Context can evolve across systems, organizations, technologies, and time while remaining sufficiently traceable and reconstructable for subsequent TREGA™ governance without allowing contextual continuity itself to determine event identity, legal taxability, tax jurisdiction, or tax consequence.

chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Context Change Module (ECCHM)
Event Context Change Module (ECCHM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS)
Module: ECCHM — Event Context Change Module
Operational Layer: Event Context Change Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Context Change
Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECCHM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 29 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Context Change Module (ECCHM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the identification, qualification, assessment, and representation of material changes affecting the governed context surrounding an occurrence throughout tax-relevant event governance.
ECCHM establishes whether previously governed contextual conditions remain valid, have changed, require revision, or have been superseded, while preserving the historical contextual state against which the occurrence was originally understood.
Its task is specific:

to govern material change in Event Context without automatically converting contextual change into a new event, rewriting historical context, or determining a new legal tax consequence.
Operational Role
Context is not necessarily static.
Between occurrence, recognition, event formation, determination, recording, and later review, relevant contextual conditions may change.
An organization may restructure.
A platform relationship may change.
A machine may move between operational environments.
A service may migrate between infrastructures.
A business process may be modified.
A digital asset may enter another operating environment.
Previously unavailable contextual information may become known.
ECCHM determines whether such changes materially affect the governed Event Context.
The governing question is:
Has the context materially changed, and if so, what part of the governed contextual representation must change with it?
Internal Flow
Governed Context State
↓
Context Change Detection
↓
Change Relevance Assessment
↓
Change Materiality Assessment
↓
Context Impact Determination
↓
Context Revision / Preservation / Supersession
↓
Governed Context Change Result
The principal output is:
Governed Context Change Result Operational Space
ECCHM governs the space between:
an established Event Context
and
a materially changed contextual condition requiring governed treatment.

A governed occurrence must remain interpretable against the context legitimately associated with it at the relevant time.
Later reality may differ.
That later reality does not automatically replace historical reality.
Therefore:
Current Context ≠ Historical Context.
Change Detection
ECCHM requires mechanisms capable of identifying materially relevant changes affecting previously governed context.
A change may originate from: new operational information; organizational restructuring; participant environment changes; platform migration; system migration; infrastructure relocation; process modification; new contextual relationships; terminated contextual relationships; corrected source information; previously unavailable evidence; autonomous-system reconfiguration; material changes in surrounding value conditions.
Detection alone does not establish materiality.
Change Materiality
A detected change becomes materially relevant where it can reasonably affect the interpretation or subsequent governance of the occurrence.
ECCHM therefore distinguishes:
Detected Change
from
Material Context Change.
A software version update may be operationally visible but irrelevant to Event Context.
A change in the economic role of a platform may materially alter contextual interpretation.
A cloud migration may be irrelevant in one case but material in another.
Materiality depends upon the relationship between the change and the governed occurrence. Context Change ≠ New Event

One of the most important ECCHM boundaries is:
Context Change ≠ New Event by Default.
A contextual change does not automatically mean that a new Tax-Relevant Event exists.
For example: an organization changes its internal structure; a platform changes infrastructure provider; a service migrates to another system; a machine changes operating location; additional contextual evidence becomes available.
These changes may require contextual revision without creating a new governed event.
Whether a materially transformed reality requires new Event Recognition or Event Formation belongs to later TREGA™ governance.
Context Change Impact
A material contextual change may affect:
Context Elements — an existing contextual element changes.
Context Scope — previously included or excluded elements require reconsideration.
Context Relationships — relationships among contextual elements change.
Context Interpretation — the same occurrence requires a revised contextual understanding.
Context Status — the previous contextual state becomes superseded.
ECCHM must identify which layer has been affected rather than treating every change as a complete reconstruction of context.
Context Correction
Not every difference between two contextual states represents a real-world change.
Sometimes the underlying reality did not change.
The earlier contextual representation was simply wrong or incomplete.
ECCHM therefore distinguishes:
Context Change — surrounding reality changed.
from

Context Correction — representation of surrounding reality was corrected.
This distinction is critical for historical reconstruction. Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
When an earlier contextual representation is corrected, the previous governed representation should not simply disappear where traceability is materially required.
The architecture should be capable of distinguishing:
what was previously represented,
what was later corrected,
and
why the correction occurred.
Therefore:
Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. New Information ≠ New Reality
A later-discovered fact may describe a condition that already existed when the occurrence happened.
Its discovery is new.
The underlying reality may not be.
ECCHM must therefore distinguish:
New Contextual Information
from
New Contextual Condition.
This prevents the date on which information becomes available from being confused with the date on which the underlying contextual reality changed.
Context Supersession
Where a contextual state is materially replaced by a later governed state, ECCHM may establish contextual supersession.
Supersession means that a newer contextual representation becomes applicable for the relevant subsequent governance purpose.
It does not mean the previous state never existed.
Therefore:
Superseded Context ≠ Deleted Context.
Temporal Integrity of Context
ECCHM must preserve the ability to answer:
What context was applicable when the occurrence happened?
and separately:

What context became applicable later?
This distinction is essential where tax-relevant events are reconstructed months or years after operational activity occurred.
A current system state must not automatically be projected backward onto historical occurrences.
Change Uncertainty
A suspected contextual change may not always be sufficiently established.
ECCHM should permit states such as:
Change Not Established
Change Detected
Change Under Assessment
Material Change Established
Context Corrected
Context Superseded
where appropriate to the implementation.
Uncertainty should remain governed rather than converted into an assumed change.
Governance Requirements
ECCHM requires that: contextual change be distinguishable from ordinary system activity; detected change be evaluated for materiality; change be associated with the contextual element or relationship affected; current context remain distinguishable from historical context; real-world change be distinguishable from information correction; newly discovered information not automatically become a newly occurring condition; scope-impacting changes be capable of returning to appropriate TRECS governance; relationship changes be capable of updating the governed relationship structure; superseded context remain historically traceable where required; Context Change not automatically create a new Tax-Relevant Event; contextual change not determine legal tax consequences.
Governance Logic
ECCHM applies four principal questions:

What changed?
Did reality change, or did our representation of reality change?
Is the change materially relevant to Event Context?
What part of the governed contextual representation must now be revised, preserved, or superseded?
The governing transformation is:
Existing Governed Context
→ Detected Difference
→ Qualified Material Change
→ Governed Context Change Result
A change that is not materially relevant should not destabilize the governed context.
A material change should not silently overwrite it.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ECCHM implementation must be capable of:
1. referencing an established governed Context State; 2. detecting potentially relevant contextual changes; 3. distinguishing change from correction where reasonably possible; 4. assessing contextual change materiality; 5. identifying affected contextual elements, scope, or relationships; 6. recording the effective contextual change where materially relevant; 7. preserving prior contextual states where traceability requires it; 8. representing uncertainty where change cannot yet be established; 9. producing a Governed Context Change Result; 10. transferring continuity requirements to ECCM.
No particular change-detection technology, database, ledger, ERP platform, AI model, event-stream architecture, or tax system is required.
Governance Outputs
ECCHM may produce:
Governed Context Change Result — the qualified representation of a material contextual change.

Context Change Record — identification of what changed.
Change Materiality Result — determination of whether the change materially affects Event Context.
Affected Context Reference — identification of affected contextual elements, scope, or relationships.
Context Correction Record — where the representation rather than underlying reality was corrected.
Context Supersession Reference — identification of a previous contextual state replaced for subsequent governance purposes.
Change Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved contextual change conditions.
Historical Context Reference — linkage preserving the previous governed contextual state.
Critical Distinctions
Context Change ≠ New Event.
A changed environment does not automatically create another Tax-Relevant Event.
Context Change ≠ Context Correction.
Reality changing is different from correcting how reality was represented.
New Information ≠ New Reality.
Later discovery does not establish that the underlying condition began when it was discovered.
Current Context ≠ Historical Context.
Current conditions must not automatically redefine the environment surrounding a historical occurrence.
Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Correction should preserve material governance history.
Context Supersession ≠ Context Deletion.
A superseded contextual state may remain essential for reconstruction and auditability.
Context Change ≠ Tax Consequence Change.

A material contextual change does not itself determine that taxation treatment has changed.
Context Change ≠ Context Continuity.
ECCHM determines and governs change.
ECCM governs continuity across contextual states and changes.
Enterprise Application
ECCHM becomes particularly important where tax-relevant activity is reconstructed from systems that continuously evolve.
A modern enterprise may change:
ERP systems
↓
corporate structures
↓
cloud providers
↓
payment providers
↓
platform configurations
↓
logistics systems
↓
autonomous workflows
while the underlying tax-relevant records remain subject to later reporting, audit, dispute, or regulatory review.
Without governed Context Change, a system may reconstruct an old occurrence using today's configuration.
That can produce a representation of reality that never existed when the occurrence happened.
ECCHM enables organizations and downstream public-sector systems to distinguish:
historical context
from
later contextual change
and from
later correction of historical information. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Historical Cross-Border Transaction After Corporate Restructuring
A multinational digital business completes large volumes of cross-border transactions.
Two years later, the group restructures its entities, migrates customer contracts, changes payment providers, modifies platform responsibilities, and relocates parts of its infrastructure.
A later tax review reconstructs transactions from current enterprise systems.

Without governed Context Change, the current organizational and platform structure may be incorrectly projected backward, making historical transactions appear to have occurred within relationships that did not exist at the time.
ECCHM separates the historical Event Context from later organizational, platform, and infrastructure changes.
Where newly discovered information corrects the historical representation, it records the correction without pretending that the underlying historical reality changed at the date of discovery.
The result preserves a fundamental requirement for reliable taxation infrastructure:
a historical event must be evaluated against its historical context, not automatically against the organization that exists today. Use Case 2 — Autonomous System Changes During Continuous Machine Commerce
An autonomous procurement system continuously purchases computing capacity, digital services, machine components, and operational resources from multiple providers.
During operation, the system is reconfigured, authority pathways change, infrastructure is relocated, supplier relationships are modified, and parts of the autonomous workflow are transferred to another platform.
Millions of machine records continue to be generated throughout the transition.
A conventional transaction system may have difficulty determining which contextual configuration applied to which activity.
ECCHM identifies material contextual changes and separates them from ordinary technical updates.

It preserves the contextual states necessary to determine which operational environment surrounded an occurrence at the relevant time without declaring that every system reconfiguration created a new Tax-Relevant Event.
This provides a governed method for handling a future problem of autonomous economies:
the systems generating economic activity may change faster than the taxation systems evaluating that activity.
Canonical Boundary
ECCHM governs material change to Event Context. It does not govern continuity of the contextual identity across the complete lifecycle, determine whether contextual transformation creates a new Tax-Relevant Event, or determine the tax consequence of the change.
The TRECS internal progression remains:
ECIM — What contextual elements may matter?
→ ECSM — Which contextual elements belong within the relevant Context Scope?
→ ECRM — How are those contextual elements materially related?
→ ECCHM — What has materially changed in that governed context?
→ ECCM — How is contextual continuity preserved across those changes?
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Context Change Module establishes the contextual change governance capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by determining when the economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or relational conditions surrounding an occurrence have materially changed and how those changes must be represented without rewriting the contextual reality that previously existed. Through governance of change detection, materiality, affected context, correction, supersession, uncertainty, historical preservation, and temporal contextual integrity, ECCHM prevents current system states, later organizational structures, newly discovered information, technical migrations, or autonomous-system reconfigurations from silently redefining the context of historical activity. The Module preserves the critical distinctions between Context Change and Context Correction, new information and new reality, current context and historical context, contextual supersession and deletion, and contextual change and new Event Formation. ECCHM therefore allows Event Context to evolve while ensuring that the governed representation of what surrounded an occurrence remains reconstructable according to the reality that existed when that context was relevant.
Model 5

Jasné. Module 5 — ECCM uzatvára TRECS. Jeho úloha je zásadná: po identifikácii, scope, vzťahoch a zmenách musí zabezpečiť, že kontext zostáva rekonštruovateľný ako ten istý governed contextual chain, aj keď sa jeho jednotlivé stavy menia.

OOF™ Event Context Identification Module (ECIM)
Event Context Identification Module (ECIM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS)
Module: ECIM — Event Context Identification Module
Operational Layer: Event Context Identification Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Context Identification
Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECIM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 29 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Context Identification Module (ECIM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the identification of materially relevant contextual elements surrounding an observed occurrence entering the TREGA™ lifecycle.
ECIM establishes which economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other contextual conditions are potentially relevant to understanding the occurrence before Context Scope, contextual relationships, contextual change, and contextual continuity are governed.
Its task is specific:

to identify the contextual elements that may be necessary to understand an occurrence without determining what ultimately belongs within the governed Context Scope or whether a Tax-Relevant Event exists.
Operational Role
ECIM is the entry module of TRECS.
An observed occurrence may arrive from an ERP system, transaction platform, financial infrastructure, industrial process, autonomous system, digital service, machine network, API, marketplace, or another operational environment.
The occurrence alone may not contain enough information to establish its meaning.
ECIM identifies the surrounding contextual elements that should become candidates for further context governance.
These may include: economic environment; operational process; organizational setting; transaction structure; digital environment; technological system; platform environment; infrastructure; autonomous-system conditions; machine-execution environment; value-related conditions; relevant process or activity; distributed operational environment; potentially relevant cross-border circumstances.
ECIM identifies context.
It does not yet decide the complete governed extent of that context.
Internal Flow
Observed Occurrence
↓
Context Signal Detection
↓
Context Element Identification
↓
Relevance Screening
↓
Context Element Qualification
↓
Identified Context Set
The governed output is:
Identified Context Set
This output provides the contextual candidates required by the next TRECS governance stages.

Governance Requirements
ECIM requires that contextual identification: begins from an identifiable occurrence; distinguishes the occurrence from its surrounding context; identifies materially plausible contextual elements; permits multiple context types where required; does not assume that one technical record represents one economic event; preserves uncertainty where contextual meaning remains unresolved; distinguishes identified context from confirmed Event Recognition; avoids treating tax rules as the primary constructor of operational context; permits machine-generated and autonomous contexts; preserves references to upstream governed information where available; produces an identifiable contextual result suitable for subsequent governance.
Identification must remain proportionate.
ECIM should not collect unrelated surrounding information merely because that information is technically available.
Governance Logic
ECIM applies a simple methodological question:
What surrounding conditions may materially affect how this occurrence should be understood within subsequent tax-relevant event governance?

A contextual element may be identified where it has a plausible material relationship to: the operational meaning of the occurrence; its economic environment; its transaction structure; the process in which it occurred; its organizational environment; its digital or technological environment; autonomous or machine execution; relevant value conditions; subsequent Event Recognition or Event Formation.
ECIM does not require that every identified element ultimately remain within the governed context.
Identification precedes scope determination.
Therefore:
Potential Context Relevance
↓
Identification
does not mean:
Potential Context Relevance
↓
Final Context Inclusion.
That later determination belongs to ECSM — Event Context Scope Module.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum implementation of ECIM must be capable of:
1. receiving or referencing an observed occurrence; 2. identifying available surrounding contextual signals; 3. distinguishing contextual information from the occurrence itself; 4. identifying one or more potentially relevant context types; 5. recording the basis for material contextual relevance where necessary; 6. representing uncertainty or missing context; 7. preserving references to upstream governed sources where available; 8. producing an Identified Context Set for subsequent TRECS processing.

The implementation may operate through human governance, structured workflows, enterprise systems, rule-based systems, automated processes, AI-assisted systems, or combinations of these approaches.
ECIM does not prescribe a particular database, ontology, AI model, ERP platform, tax engine, or technical implementation.
Governance Outputs
ECIM may produce:
Identified Context Set — the governed collection of contextual elements identified around the occurrence.
Context Type References — identification of relevant economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, autonomous, value-related, or other context types.
Context Element References — references to individual contextual elements requiring subsequent governance.
Context Relevance Basis — the governed reason an element has been identified as potentially material.
Context Uncertainty Indicator — identification of missing, ambiguous, or unresolved contextual information.
Upstream Governance References — references to relevant governed results supplied by other systems or OOF® architectures where available.
These outputs provide input to ECSM — Event Context Scope Module and other subsequent TRECS modules.
Critical Distinctions
Occurrence ≠ Context.
The occurrence is the observed action, condition, transaction, signal, or operation.
Context describes the environment necessary to understand it.
Context Identification ≠ Context Scope.
ECIM identifies potentially relevant contextual elements.

ECSM subsequently determines the governed extent of context.
Identified Context ≠ Tax-Relevant Event.
Identification of relevant context does not establish that a Tax-Relevant Event exists.
Context Relevance ≠ Taxability.
A contextual element may be important for downstream taxation analysis without itself establishing any legal tax consequence.
Cross-Border Context ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Identifying several geographic or operational environments does not determine taxation rights.
Actor Context ≠ Taxpayer Determination.
Identifying a person, organization, machine, platform, or autonomous agent within context does not establish taxpayer status.
Enterprise Application
ECIM can operate as the first contextual identification layer between heterogeneous enterprise systems and the broader TREGA™ event lifecycle.
Potential environments include:
ERP
↓
ECIM
Commerce Platform
↓
ECIM
Banking Infrastructure
↓
ECIM
Industrial System
↓
ECIM
Digital Platform
↓
ECIM
AI Agent
↓
ECIM
Machine Network
↓
ECIM
Distributed Infrastructure
↓
ECIM
The module allows these environments to provide different technical records while applying a common methodological question:
What contextual information must be identified before this occurrence can be interpreted coherently?

This is particularly useful where one economic activity produces multiple technical records or where machine-generated activity crosses organizational, technological, or geographic boundaries. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Autonomous Digital Purchase
An autonomous agent purchases a digital service through a platform using an automated payment infrastructure.
The transaction produces records from the agent, platform, API, payment system, and service provider.
ECIM identifies the potentially relevant agent environment, platform context, service context, payment context, operational relationships, and distributed infrastructure surrounding the occurrence.
It does not determine whether these elements constitute one event or several events, which jurisdiction may tax the activity, or whether tax is legally due.
Its output is an Identified Context Set ready for Context Scope governance. Use Case 2 — Automated Industrial Movement
An automated manufacturing system transfers a component between production, internal storage, and logistics systems.
Several systems record the movement differently.
ECIM identifies the relevant production process, internal organizational environment, inventory context, logistics environment, system relationships, and associated operational circumstances.
The module does not assume that every system record represents a separate economic event.

It identifies the contextual elements required before subsequent TREGA™ governance determines how the occurrence should be interpreted.
Canonical Closing Statement
Event Context Identification Module establishes the entry-level contextual identification capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by determining which economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, and other surrounding conditions may be materially relevant to understanding an observed occurrence. Through governed identification of context signals, context types, contextual elements, relevance bases, uncertainty, and upstream governance references, ECIM prevents isolated records from entering the TREGA™ lifecycle without their potentially material surrounding reality while preserving the boundaries between Context Identification, Context Scope, Event Recognition, and legal taxation determination. ECIM therefore does not determine what the final event is or what tax consequence follows; it establishes the contextual elements from which those later governance processes can legitimately begin.
