chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM)
Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS)
Module: EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module
Operational Layer: Event Formation Assembly Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Formation Assembly
Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFAM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 30 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM) governs how qualified Event Formation Components are structurally organized, related, grouped, ordered, and assembled into a coherent Event Formation Candidate.
EFAM determines whether qualified components can legitimately operate together as one structurally meaningful formation, whether alternative assembly structures must remain visible, and whether the available component set supports coherent progression through TREFS.
Its task is specific:

to assemble qualified Event Formation Components into a governed event structure without determining final Event Boundary, Formation Dependencies, Event Formation Root, Formation Integrity, or legal tax consequences.
Operational Role
EFCM establishes:
which elements qualify as Event Formation Components.
EFAM then determines:
how those qualified components fit together structurally.
This distinction is necessary because a valid component set does not automatically produce a valid event structure.
Several legitimate components may: belong to one coherent formation; belong to different formation candidates; represent parallel parts of one activity; represent sequential stages; represent alternative structural interpretations; require further differentiation before assembly.
Therefore:
Qualified Components ≠ Coherent Event Structure by Default.
EFAM creates the governed structural arrangement required before Formation Dependencies and the Event Formation Root can be established.
Internal Flow
Governed Event Formation Component Set
↓
Assembly Relationship Identification
↓
Structural Grouping
↓
Assembly Pattern Determination
↓
Assembly Coherence Assessment
↓
Alternative / Conflicting Assembly Handling
↓
Governed Event Formation Assembly
The principal output is:
Governed Event Formation Assembly
This output proceeds to:
EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module Operational Space
EFAM governs the space between:
a governed set of qualified Event Formation Components
and

a coherent structural assembly capable of supporting further Event Formation governance.
Its operational space includes: component relationship identification; structural grouping; ordering where materially relevant; parallel assembly; sequential assembly; composite assembly; distributed assembly; autonomous assembly; machine-generated assembly; assembly coherence; assembly ambiguity; assembly conflict; alternative formation structures; over-aggregation risk; over-fragmentation risk; assembly traceability.
EFAM governs how qualified components are structurally brought together.
It does not determine whether every surrounding dependency belongs to the event.
Operational Scope
EFAM may assemble formation components originating from: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; fulfilment; logistics; service delivery; platform activity; digital services; enterprise systems; banking infrastructure; software systems; APIs; autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; machine-to-machine exchanges; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital activity.
The assembly may involve: human actions; organizational actions; digital actions; machine actions; autonomous actions; distributed actions.
EFAM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral.
Assembly Relationship
Qualified components require a legitimate structural basis for being assembled together.

Possible assembly relationships may include: sequential; parallel; conditional; composite; coordinated; distributed; hierarchical; mutually supporting.
These relationships describe structural formation.
They do not yet establish the broader relationship between separate governed events.
Therefore:
Assembly Relationship ≠ Event Relationship Governance.
Relationships among governed events are later governed by TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard.
Structural Grouping
EFAM may group components where their combined structure materially represents one formation candidate.
Grouping should be based on governed structural relevance.
Components should not be grouped solely because they: share an identifier; appear in the same ERP workflow; involve the same participant; occur close together in time; are processed by the same platform; share a payment reference; belong to the same database record.
Therefore:
Technical Grouping ≠ Event Assembly. Shared Identifier ≠ One Assembly by Default
A shared identifier can support assembly analysis.
It cannot determine assembly by itself.
One order identifier may include: several deliveries; several settlements; several service executions; several reversals; several materially distinct operational actions.
Conversely, one event formation may span several identifiers across different systems.
Therefore:
Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Assembly by Default.
Assembly Coherence

A governed assembly should represent a structurally understandable event candidate.
Assembly coherence may consider whether: components materially relate to the same formation; their arrangement is structurally consistent; no material contradiction prevents assembly; the assembly does not depend only on technical proximity; the structure does not artificially collapse distinct activity; the structure does not unnecessarily fragment one coherent activity.
EFAM must protect against both over-aggregation and over-fragmentation.
Over-Aggregation Risk
Over-aggregation occurs when distinct activity is incorrectly combined into one Event Formation Assembly.
For example:
a marketplace may place:
Order + Refund + Later Replacement Order
under one customer reference.
That does not establish that all three belong to one formation.
Therefore:
Common Process ≠ One Assembly by Default.
Over-Fragmentation Risk
Over-fragmentation occurs when one coherent event structure is divided merely because several technical systems or operational records are involved.
For example:
Authorization
↓
Activation
↓
Delivery
↓
Settlement
may be represented across four systems.
The existence of four system records does not itself justify four formation assemblies.
Therefore:
Multiple Systems ≠ Multiple Assemblies by Default.
Sequential Assembly
Some Event Formation Components may form a meaningful sequence.
For example:
Commitment
↓
Execution
↓
Fulfilment
The sequence may support structural understanding.

However:
Assembly Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination.
EFAM may represent structural order without determining the legally or operationally definitive Event Time.
Event Timing belongs to TRETS.
Parallel Assembly
Some components may occur in parallel while contributing to the same event formation.
For example:
an autonomous platform may simultaneously allocate: computing capacity; energy; storage; network resources.
Parallel execution does not automatically imply separate events.
EFAM determines whether these components can legitimately participate in one formation candidate.
Composite Assembly
A composite assembly may contain several materially different components that collectively form one coherent structure.
For example:
Service Activation + Resource Allocation + Delivery Confirmation
may participate in one formation candidate.
But:
Composite Assembly ≠ Final Event Boundary.
TREBS later determines the final extent of the event.
Distributed Assembly
An event structure may need to be assembled from components held across several systems.
For example:
Marketplace Component
→ Payment Component
→ Service Provider Component
→ Enterprise Component
EFAM permits distributed assembly where sufficient governed linkage exists.
Therefore:
Distributed Components ≠ Separate Assemblies by Default.
Machine and Autonomous Assembly
Autonomous systems may generate complex chains of qualified components.

EFAM must assemble those components according to structural reality rather than machine-process topology.
For example, one autonomous objective may produce:
Negotiation
↓
Reservation
↓
Allocation
↓
Consumption
↓
Settlement
Some elements may form one structure.
Others may later become separate formations.
Therefore:
One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Assembly by Default.
And:
Many Machine Actions ≠ Many Assemblies by Default.
Assembly Ambiguity
The same qualified component set may support more than one plausible assembly.
For example:
three related service actions may represent: one composite formation; two connected formations; three independent formations.
Where the available information does not justify one structure, EFAM must preserve assembly ambiguity.
Possible states may include:
Assembly Candidate
Assembly Established
Assembly Ambiguous
Assembly Conflict
Assembly Unresolved Alternative Assembly Structures
EFAM may preserve several alternative assembly candidates where each has material support.
The system should not select one simply because it is operationally convenient.
Alternative assemblies may later be clarified through: additional dependency analysis; root analysis; integrity assessment; new evidence; later boundary governance.
Therefore:
Preferred System Structure ≠ Governed Assembly by Default.
Assembly Conflict
An Assembly Conflict exists where qualified components support materially incompatible formation structures.
For example:

one system indicates one composite event;
another indicates two materially separate operational outcomes.
EFAM should preserve the conflict rather than silently resolving it through system precedence.
Assembly Traceability
A Governed Event Formation Assembly should remain traceable to: the component set received from EFCM; the structural relationship basis; grouping decisions; exclusions from a particular assembly; alternative assembly structures; unresolved ambiguity; material assembly revisions.
This permits later modules to understand how the formation structure was constructed.
Governance Requirements
EFAM requires that: only governed Event Formation Components enter assembly; structural relationships are identified before grouping; assembly is not determined by technical records alone; shared identifiers do not automatically create one assembly; multiple systems do not automatically create multiple assemblies; over-aggregation risk is controlled; over-fragmentation risk is controlled; distributed components may be assembled where justified; autonomous and machine-generated structures remain actor-neutral; assembly ambiguity remains visible; conflicting structures are preserved where unresolved; assembly decisions remain traceable; EFAM does not determine final Event Boundary; EFAM does not determine Formation Dependencies; EFAM does not determine Event Formation Root; EFAM does not determine legal taxability.
Governance Logic
EFAM applies a focused structural logic:

How do the qualified Event Formation Components materially relate to one another?
Which components can legitimately be grouped within the same formation structure?
Does the proposed assembly avoid both artificial aggregation and artificial fragmentation?
Are alternative or conflicting assembly structures materially plausible?
What Governed Event Formation Assembly can legitimately proceed into dependency governance?
The transformation is:
Governed Component Set
→ Structural Relationships
→ Grouping
→ Assembly
→ Coherence Assessment
→ Governed Event Formation Assembly
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EFAM implementation must be capable of:
1. receiving the Governed Event Formation Component Set from EFCM; 2. identifying material structural relationships among qualified components; 3. grouping components on a governed basis; 4. representing sequential, parallel, composite, or distributed assembly where relevant; 5. preventing technical identifiers from automatically defining assembly; 6. detecting over-aggregation risk; 7. detecting over-fragmentation risk; 8. preserving alternative assembly candidates where materially justified; 9. representing Assembly Ambiguity or Assembly Conflict; 10. preserving assembly traceability; 11. producing a Governed Event Formation Assembly; 12. transferring that assembly to EFDM for Formation Dependency governance; 13. preventing assembly from determining Event Boundary or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.

EFAM does not prescribe a specific graph model, workflow engine, ERP structure, event-stream format, database schema, AI model, tax engine, or transaction architecture.
Governance Outputs
EFAM may produce:
Governed Event Formation Assembly — the principal Module output.
Assembly Relationship Structure — governed representation of how components relate structurally.
Component Grouping Result — the governed grouping used in formation.
Composite Assembly Candidate — a multi-component formation structure.
Alternative Assembly Candidate — a materially plausible alternative structure.
Assembly Ambiguity Indicator — unresolved uncertainty concerning assembly.
Assembly Conflict Record — materially incompatible assembly structures.
Over-Aggregation Indicator — risk that distinct activity has been combined.
Over-Fragmentation Indicator — risk that one coherent activity has been unnecessarily divided.
Assembly Traceability Record — the basis through which the assembly was established.
Critical Distinctions
Qualified Components ≠ Coherent Event Structure by Default.
Component qualification does not determine assembly.
Technical Grouping ≠ Event Assembly.
System structure does not establish governed event structure.
Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Assembly by Default.
Technical identifiers are supporting signals, not structural proof.
Multiple Systems ≠ Multiple Assemblies by Default.
Distributed representation does not establish event multiplicity.

Common Process ≠ One Assembly by Default.
One operational workflow may contain several event formations.
Assembly Relationship ≠ Event Relationship Governance.
TRERLS later governs relationships among formed events.
Assembly Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination.
TRETS owns Event Timing.
Composite Assembly ≠ Final Event Boundary.
TREBS owns final event extent.
One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Assembly by Default.
Autonomous purpose does not establish event granularity.
Assembly Conflict ≠ Assembly Failure.
Conflicting structures may remain governed and unresolved.
Preferred System Structure ≠ Governed Assembly by Default.
Operational convenience does not establish methodological legitimacy.
Event Assembly ≠ Taxability Determination.
EFAM does not determine tax law.
Enterprise Application
EFAM addresses a common problem in complex systems:
different systems group the same operational reality differently.
A marketplace may group activity by order.
A bank may group by settlement.
An ERP may group by invoice.
A logistics system may group by shipment.
An autonomous platform may group by machine objective.
Each grouping may be valid internally.
None automatically defines the governed Event Formation Assembly.
EFAM creates a neutral structural layer capable of assembling qualified components according to event formation logic rather than the data model of any single system. Use CasesUse Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Contains Three Deliveries, Two Settlements, and a Partial Refund

A global marketplace uses one order identifier for a customer purchase.
The order results in: three separate deliveries; two payment settlements; one partial refund; multiple ERP records; several provider fulfilment actions.
EFCM has already qualified the relevant formation components.
If EFAM simply groups everything under the order identifier, the architecture may create one oversized formation that hides materially distinct activity.
If every delivery and settlement is separated automatically, the architecture may create unnecessary fragmentation.
EFAM evaluates the structural relationships among the qualified components and creates one or more legitimate Assembly Candidates while preserving ambiguity where required.
The key principle is:
the commercial identifier must not decide the event structure. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Cloud Marketplace Executes One Objective Across Hundreds of Parallel Resource Operations
An AI agent purchases computing capacity for a complex workload.
The workload is distributed across multiple providers and creates hundreds of qualified operational components involving: compute allocation; storage allocation; network reservation; execution; release; settlement.
The underlying autonomous objective is one workload, but the operational components may support several event structures.

EFAM determines whether particular components form coherent composite assemblies, whether separate provider operations require distinct assembly candidates, and whether any structure remains ambiguous.
It prevents both extremes:
one autonomous objective becoming one artificial mega-event
and
every machine-level resource allocation becoming a separate event formation.
Canonical Boundary
EFAM governs the structural relationship, grouping, arrangement, ambiguity, conflict, and coherent assembly of qualified Event Formation Components into a Governed Event Formation Assembly. It does not identify the original components, determine Formation Dependencies, establish the Event Formation Root, assess complete Formation Integrity, determine the final Event Boundary, govern relationships among completed events, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The handoff is:
EFCM — Governed Event Formation Component Set
→ EFAM — Governed Event Formation Assembly
→ EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Formation Assembly Module establishes the structural assembly layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining how qualified formation components can legitimately operate together as a coherent Event Formation Assembly. By separating governed structural relationships from technical grouping, shared identifiers, system workflows, platform representations, machine topology, and operational convenience, EFAM prevents both artificial aggregation and artificial fragmentation of recognized economic activity. The Module preserves alternative and conflicting formation structures where necessary and produces a traceable assembly ready for Formation Dependency governance without prematurely determining Event Boundary, Event Timing, relationships among completed events, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.

topics: EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module Operational Space

chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Formation Component Module (EFCM)
Event Formation Component Module (EFCM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS)
Module: EFCM — Event Formation Component Module
Operational Layer: Event Formation Component Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Formation Components
Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFCM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 30 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Formation Component Module (EFCM) governs how materially relevant elements of a Governed Recognized Occurrence are identified, differentiated, qualified, and prepared as legitimate components for subsequent Event Formation.
EFCM determines which observable or governed elements may participate in the formation of the event structure and which elements should remain outside the formation-component set because they represent technical noise, duplicate representation, background activity, contextual information, or non-forming dependencies.
Its task is specific:

to establish the governed set of materially relevant Event Formation Components without assembling those components into the final event structure or determining the Event Boundary.
Operational Role
TREFS begins after TRERS has established that an occurrence legitimately warrants Event Formation.
But a recognized occurrence may still contain many different elements: operational actions; transaction stages; technical records; system messages; machine operations; value-affecting actions; supporting activities; duplicated representations; contextual information; dependencies.
EFCM separates the elements that may legitimately participate in Event Formation from those that should not automatically become formation components.
It therefore creates the first structural input to TREFS.
The distinction is fundamental:
Recognized Information ≠ Formation Component by Default.
Internal Flow
Governed Recognized Occurrence
↓
Candidate Formation Element Identification
↓
Element Differentiation
↓
Formation Relevance Assessment
↓
Component Qualification / Exclusion
↓
Duplicate and Technical-Noise Screening
↓
Governed Event Formation Component Set
The principal output is:
Governed Event Formation Component Set
This output proceeds to:
EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module Operational Space
EFCM governs the space between:
a recognized occurrence containing potentially relevant structural elements
and
a governed set of qualified Event Formation Components ready for assembly.

Its operational space includes: candidate component identification; component differentiation; structural relevance; formation materiality; component qualification; component exclusion; duplicate component risk; technical-record filtering; machine-operation filtering; distributed component identification; autonomous activity component identification; component uncertainty; component traceability.
EFCM governs what may become part of Event Formation.
It does not govern how those components are assembled.
Operational Scope
EFCM may identify formation components originating from: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; fulfilment; delivery; service execution; platform activity; digital services; software systems; APIs; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machine-to-machine activity; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital processes.
A formation component may represent a human, organizational, digital, machine-generated, or autonomous operational element.
EFCM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral.
Candidate Formation Elements
A recognized occurrence may contain more observable information than Event Formation requires.

Candidate elements may include: initiating actions; operational state changes; transfer actions; fulfilment actions; service executions; resource consumption; resource provision; machine instructions with material operational significance; settlement actions; digital activations; delivery actions; materially relevant autonomous actions.
Candidate status means only that the element requires formation assessment.
Therefore:
Candidate Element ≠ Qualified Formation Component.
Formation Relevance
An element should become a formation component only where it materially contributes to the structure of the event being formed.
Formation relevance may arise where the element helps establish: what operational action occurred; what materially changed; what was executed; what was transferred; what was delivered; what service was performed; what operational stage is structurally necessary; what activity materially contributes to event formation.
An element should not become a formation component merely because it exists in the technical record. Technical Record ≠ Formation Component
Modern systems may produce many records for the same underlying activity.
Examples include: synchronization records; API retries; database replication; monitoring messages; internal status updates; duplicate ledger representations; audit logs; telemetry.
These records may be useful evidence or context.
They do not automatically become Event Formation Components.
Therefore:

Technical Record ≠ Formation Component by Default.
This distinction prevents system architecture from defining event architecture. Component ≠ Independent Event
A qualified formation component may be materially important without independently constituting a separate event.
For example:
Authorization
Service Activation
Delivery
Settlement
may each contribute to a broader event formation.
Whether any of these should later become separate events is not determined by EFCM.
Therefore:
Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default.
Component Materiality
EFCM should apply a materiality principle.
A component is materially relevant where removing it would materially weaken, distort, or misrepresent the structural understanding of the event formation.
Materiality should not be confused with legal tax materiality.
Therefore:
Formation Materiality ≠ Tax Materiality.
EFCM asks whether the element matters to event structure.
It does not determine whether the element affects tax liability.
Duplicate Component Risk
One operational action may appear several times across systems.
For example:
Payment Gateway Record
→ Bank Record
→ ERP Record
→ Reporting Database
These may represent one underlying operational element.
EFCM must avoid treating each representation as a separate formation component merely because each exists independently in a system.
Therefore:
Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Formation Components.
At the same time:
Shared Identifier ≠ Same Component by Default.

Distinct actions may legitimately share identifiers.
Distributed Formation Components
A legitimate component may be visible only through distributed information.
For example:
one system may record authorization;
another execution;
another confirmation.
EFCM may use governed distributed information to establish a component where no single system contains a complete representation.
Therefore:
Distributed Evidence ≠ Multiple Components by Default.
Machine-Generated Components
Machine environments create a particular risk of structural over-fragmentation.
An automated process may generate thousands of instructions while only a few materially contribute to Event Formation.
EFCM must distinguish:
technical execution
from
structurally relevant operational action.
Therefore:
Machine Instruction ≠ Formation Component by Default.
Only machine activity materially contributing to the event structure should enter the component set.
Autonomous Components
Autonomous agents may create legitimate Event Formation Components without direct human initiation.
For example, an AI agent may: commit to a service; initiate a transfer; allocate a resource; activate a contractually governed service; trigger settlement; release an asset.
EFCM may qualify those actions where structurally relevant.
It does not determine legal personhood, responsibility, taxpayer status, authority, or liability of the autonomous actor.
Component Uncertainty

Where it is unclear whether an element materially belongs in Event Formation, EFCM should preserve the uncertainty.
Possible states may include:
Component Candidate
Component Qualified
Component Excluded
Component Unresolved
A component should not be included solely because the system requires a binary decision.
Component Traceability
A qualified component should remain traceable to the basis on which it entered Event Formation.
Where materially required, traceability may preserve: source reference; recognized occurrence reference; component type; qualification basis; materiality basis; duplicate-resolution basis; uncertainty state; exclusion reason where relevant.
This allows EFAM and later TREGA™ stages to understand why the element entered the formation structure.
Governance Requirements

EFCM requires that: components originate from a Governed Recognized Occurrence; technical records do not automatically become components; candidate elements are differentiated before qualification; structural relevance is established; formation materiality is considered; duplicate representations are controlled; distributed information may support component identification; machine activity is filtered for structural relevance; autonomous activity may qualify without human initiation; component uncertainty remains visible; component qualification remains traceable; component status does not determine independent event status; component inclusion does not determine the final Event Boundary; component qualification does not determine taxability.
Governance Logic
EFCM applies a simple structural logic:
What materially relevant elements are present within the Governed Recognized Occurrence?
Which of those elements contribute to Event Formation rather than merely represent technical, contextual, duplicate, or background information?
Which elements can be qualified as legitimate Event Formation Components?
Which elements must be excluded or remain unresolved?
The transformation is:
Recognized Occurrence
→ Candidate Elements
→ Formation Relevance
→ Qualification / Exclusion
→ Governed Event Formation Component Set
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EFCM implementation must be capable of:

1. receiving the Governed Recognized Occurrence from TRERS; 2. identifying candidate formation elements; 3. distinguishing operational elements from technical representations; 4. assessing structural formation relevance; 5. applying formation materiality; 6. identifying and controlling duplicate component representations; 7. qualifying legitimate Event Formation Components; 8. excluding non-forming technical or background elements; 9. representing unresolved component status where necessary; 10. preserving source and qualification traceability; 11. producing a Governed Event Formation Component Set; 12. transferring that set to EFAM for Event Formation Assembly; 13. preventing component qualification from becoming Event Boundary or tax determination.
EFCM does not prescribe a specific ERP schema, transaction model, data format, AI model, rules engine, database, event-stream implementation, or tax platform.
Governance Outputs
EFCM may produce:
Governed Event Formation Component Set — the principal output of the Module.
Qualified Formation Component — an element accepted for subsequent assembly.
Excluded Formation Element — an element determined not to participate in Event Formation.
Unresolved Formation Component Candidate — an element whose formation relevance remains unresolved.
Component Qualification Record — the basis for inclusion or exclusion.
Duplicate Component Indicator — indication that several records may represent one underlying component.

Component Traceability Reference — linkage between the component and its governed basis.
Critical Distinctions
Recognized Information ≠ Formation Component by Default.
Recognition does not automatically establish event structure.
Candidate Element ≠ Qualified Formation Component.
Identification precedes qualification.
Technical Record ≠ Formation Component by Default.
System observability does not define structural relevance.
Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default.
Event multiplicity is not determined by component count.
Formation Materiality ≠ Tax Materiality.
Structural relevance is not tax-law significance.
Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Formation Components.
Duplicate representation must not create artificial structure.
Shared Identifier ≠ Same Component by Default.
Technical linking is not proof of structural identity.
Machine Instruction ≠ Formation Component by Default.
Technical granularity must not become event granularity.
Component Qualification ≠ Event Assembly.
EFAM owns assembly.
Component Inclusion ≠ Event Boundary.
TREBS later determines final event extent.
Component Qualification ≠ Taxability Determination.
EFCM does not apply tax law.
Enterprise Application
EFCM addresses a common structural problem in enterprise and public-sector systems:
the data available for an event is usually much larger than the event structure itself.
A modern platform may expose:
Order Record
↓
API Records
↓
Payment Records
↓
ERP Records
↓
Fulfilment Records
↓

Analytics Records
↓
Tax Interface Records
Without EFCM, every technically available record may be carried forward as if it contributes equally to formation.
This produces oversized, duplicated, and unstable event structures.
EFCM creates the first structural filter inside TREFS.
It identifies the operational elements that genuinely matter to Event Formation and separates them from technical representation. Use CasesUse Case 1 — One Global Transaction Produces Twenty Records Across Six Systems
A multinational digital platform processes one service transaction.
The activity produces: an order record; three API messages; a payment authorization; a payment confirmation; two ERP postings; a service activation; a usage record; an invoice; reporting copies; replicated warehouse records; tax-interface records.
TRERS has already recognized the underlying occurrence.
Without EFCM, all records could be forwarded into Event Formation and treated as structural elements.
EFCM identifies which records represent materially relevant operational elements and which are duplicates, technical copies, or supporting records.
The resulting component set may contain only:
Order Commitment
Service Activation
Service Delivery
Settlement
while preserving traceability to the broader evidence base.
This prevents the event structure from being defined by system record volume. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Factory Generates 50,000 Machine Actions Around One Commercial Production Cycle

An autonomous factory executes a customer production order.
Robots, sensors, production software, inventory systems, autonomous transport, and energy-management systems generate more than 50,000 technical actions.
TRERS recognizes the economically relevant production occurrence.
EFCM then determines which actions materially contribute to Event Formation.
Machine telemetry, synchronization signals, internal retries, and control-loop instructions remain outside the formation component set.
Material production completion, resource transformation, transfer to finished inventory, and delivery release may qualify as formation components.
The key result is:
machine execution volume no longer determines event structure.
Canonical Boundary
EFCM governs the identification, differentiation, qualification, exclusion, uncertainty, and traceability of materially relevant Event Formation Components within a Governed Recognized Occurrence. It does not assemble those components into the event structure, determine formation dependencies, establish the Event Formation Root, assess complete Formation Integrity, determine the final Event Boundary, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The handoff is:
Governed Recognized Occurrence
→ EFCM — Governed Event Formation Component Set
→ EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Formation Component Module establishes the first structural layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining which materially relevant elements of a Governed Recognized Occurrence may legitimately participate in the formation of the event. By separating operationally meaningful components from technical records, duplicate representations, machine noise, background activity, and unresolved elements, EFCM prevents system granularity from becoming event granularity and ensures that subsequent Event Formation begins from a governed component set rather than an uncontrolled collection of data. EFCM therefore establishes what may enter Event Formation while preserving the boundaries between component qualification, Event Assembly, Event Boundary, and jurisdiction-specific tax determination.

resources.title: OOF™ Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM)
topics: EFRM — Event Formation Root Module Operational Space

chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM)
Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS)
Module: EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module
Operational Layer: Event Formation Dependency Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Formation Dependencies
Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFDM-003
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 30 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM) governs how material dependencies supporting, enabling, conditioning, constraining, or otherwise affecting a Governed Event Formation Assembly are identified, differentiated, qualified, related, and preserved without automatically incorporating those dependencies into the formed event itself.
EFDM determines which external or surrounding conditions, actions, structures, systems, permissions, resources, prior activities, or operational states are materially necessary to understand how the event formation became possible or structurally coherent.
Its task is specific:

to establish the governed dependency structure supporting Event Formation without treating dependency as automatic Event Membership, legal causality, Event Root, or final Event Boundary.
Operational Role
EFCM establishes:
which elements qualify as Event Formation Components.
EFAM establishes:
how those components are assembled into a coherent formation structure.
EFDM then determines:
what that formation materially depends upon.
This distinction is necessary because an event may depend on surrounding activity that does not belong inside the event itself.
For example:
a payment may depend on an existing account.
A digital service may depend on prior authentication.
An autonomous transaction may depend on delegated authority.
A production event may depend on infrastructure availability.
A machine-to-machine exchange may depend on a previously established protocol or resource allocation.
Those conditions may be essential to understanding Event Formation.
They do not automatically become Event Formation Components.
Therefore:
Formation Dependency ≠ Formation Component.
And more importantly:
Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership.
Internal Flow
Governed Event Formation Assembly
↓
Dependency Candidate Identification
↓
Dependency Relevance Assessment
↓
Dependency Type Differentiation
↓
Dependency Qualification / Exclusion
↓
Dependency Relationship Establishment
↓
Dependency Conflict / Uncertainty Handling
↓
Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure
The principal output is:

Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure
This output proceeds to:
EFRM — Event Formation Root Module Operational Space
EFDM governs the space between:
a Governed Event Formation Assembly
and
a formation structure whose material dependencies are sufficiently identified and governed for Event Formation Root analysis.
Its operational space includes: dependency candidate identification; dependency relevance; enabling dependencies; conditional dependencies; structural dependencies; resource dependencies; system dependencies; authorization-related dependencies; prior-activity dependencies; infrastructure dependencies; distributed dependencies; machine dependencies; autonomous-system dependencies; dependency qualification; dependency exclusion; dependency relationships; dependency chains; dependency uncertainty; dependency conflict; dependency traceability.
EFDM governs what the Event Formation materially depends upon.
It does not determine the operational root of the event or whether a dependency ultimately belongs inside the final Event Boundary.
Operational Scope

EFDM may govern dependencies associated with: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; supply chains; fulfilment; logistics; service delivery; digital platforms; marketplaces; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; APIs; software services; digital assets; infrastructure; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machine-to-machine exchanges; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital environments.
Dependencies may originate from human, organizational, contractual, digital, infrastructural, machine-generated, or autonomous environments.
EFDM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral.
Formation Dependency Principle
An event does not exist in isolation.
Its formation may rely on surrounding conditions or prior activity.
But dependency must remain distinct from structural membership.
For example:
Account Creation
↓
Payment
The payment may depend on the account.
That does not mean account creation becomes part of every later payment event.
Similarly:
Delegated Authority
↓
Autonomous Purchase
The purchase may depend on valid delegation.
That does not automatically make the delegation itself part of the purchase event.
Therefore:
Necessary for Formation ≠ Part of the Event by Default.
Dependency Candidate
A Dependency Candidate is an element that may materially support, enable, condition, constrain, or explain the Event Formation Assembly.

Possible candidates may include: prior authorization; existing contractual state; account status; infrastructure availability; prior resource allocation; system permission; operational prerequisite; platform access; prior transfer; machine configuration; delegated authority; external service availability; prerequisite production state.
Candidate status does not establish a dependency.
Therefore:
Dependency Candidate ≠ Qualified Formation Dependency.
Dependency Relevance
A dependency should be qualified only where it materially affects the formation or structural understanding of the event.
A dependency may be relevant because the event: could not have occurred without it; could not have formed in the observed manner without it; requires it to explain a material structural relationship; relies on it for execution; relies on it for access or authorization; relies on a prior operational state; relies on external infrastructure or resources.
Minor background conditions should not automatically become governed dependencies.
Otherwise, dependency chains could expand indefinitely. Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency
Every event ultimately depends on countless background conditions.
A digital payment depends on electricity.
Electricity depends on infrastructure.
Infrastructure depends on other systems.
Those facts do not mean every background condition must enter Event Formation governance.
EFDM therefore requires material dependency relevance.

Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency by Default.
Only dependencies materially necessary to understand the formation should be governed within EFDM.
Enabling Dependency
An Enabling Dependency makes the formation operationally possible.
Examples may include: activated service access; available payment infrastructure; valid system access; available production capability; machine availability; resource allocation.
The enabling condition supports formation.
It does not automatically belong to the event.
Conditional Dependency
A Conditional Dependency exists where Event Formation depends upon a particular condition being satisfied.
For example:
Approval
↓
Release
Authorization
↓
Execution
Inventory Availability
↓
Fulfilment
The condition may be structurally relevant even where it represents a separate operational occurrence.
Therefore:
Conditional Dependency ≠ Event Component by Default.
Prior-Activity Dependency
A current formation may depend on earlier activity.
For example:
a refund may depend on a previous purchase.
A subscription renewal may depend on an existing subscription.
A machine settlement may depend on earlier resource consumption.
A later delivery may depend on a prior production action.
EFDM may preserve that dependency.
It does not automatically merge the earlier activity into the current event.
Therefore:
Prior Event Dependency ≠ Same Event.
Dependency Chain
Some formations rely on several dependencies.
For example:
Delegation
↓
Agent Authorization
↓

Resource Reservation
↓
Service Execution
EFDM may represent a dependency chain where materially necessary.
However, dependency chains must remain proportionate.
The existence of a chain does not require every historical prerequisite to become part of the governed formation.
Therefore:
Dependency Chain ≠ Event Expansion. Dependency ≠ Legal Causality
EFDM governs structural and operational dependency.
It does not determine legal causation.
For example, establishing that one operational condition enabled another action does not establish: legal responsibility; contractual causation; tax liability; damages; fault; legal attribution.
Therefore:
Formation Dependency ≠ Legal Causality.
Where accountability or liability must be determined, other governance or legal systems own those questions. Dependency ≠ Authority
An autonomous action may depend on delegated authority.
EFDM may record that the formation relies upon an authority-related condition.
It does not determine whether the authority was legally valid or who owns that authority relationship.
Therefore:
Authority Dependency ≠ Authority Governance.
Where available, EFDM may consume governed authority information from OBIDENITY®, ASGA™, or other relevant architecture. Dependency ≠ Identity
An event may depend on an existing account, actor relationship, device, organization, or autonomous agent.
That does not make identity itself part of Event Formation Dependency governance.
Therefore:
Identity Reference ≠ Identity Governance.

EFDM may consume identity references.
It does not establish identity origin, ownership, continuity, or provenance.
Distributed Dependencies
A formation may depend on several systems or organizations.
For example:
Marketplace
↓
Identity Service
↓
Payment Network
↓
Cloud Infrastructure
↓
Service Provider
No single system may contain the complete dependency representation.
EFDM must permit distributed dependencies to be represented where materially relevant.
Therefore:
Distributed Dependency ≠ Multiple Events by Default.
Machine Dependencies
Machine-generated events may depend on: software state; resource availability; sensor state; machine permission; automated authorization; infrastructure capacity; prior machine execution.
EFDM must distinguish dependencies that materially affect formation from ordinary machine operating conditions.
Therefore:
Machine Prerequisite ≠ Formation Dependency by Default.
Autonomous Dependencies
Autonomous systems may rely on complex chains of permissions, delegated objectives, resource conditions, or other agents.
EFDM may govern these dependencies where they materially affect Event Formation.
However:
Autonomous Dependency ≠ Autonomous Responsibility.
The existence of a dependency does not determine who is accountable for the resulting event.
Dependency Conflict
Different systems may provide incompatible representations of the dependencies supporting the same formation.
For example:
a platform may state that authorization preceded execution;

another system may indicate that execution occurred before final authorization.
EFDM must preserve material dependency conflict rather than silently selecting one representation.
Possible states may include:
Dependency Candidate
Dependency Qualified
Dependency Excluded
Dependency Conflict
Dependency Unresolved Dependency Uncertainty
Where a material dependency cannot be sufficiently established, EFDM must preserve uncertainty.
The system should not invent a dependency merely because one would make the event structure easier to explain.
Therefore:
Expected Dependency ≠ Established Dependency.
Dependency Traceability
A qualified Formation Dependency should remain traceable to its governed basis.
Where materially required, traceability may preserve: dependency reference; dependency type; related formation or component; qualification basis; source reference; dependency relationship; uncertainty; conflict; revision history.
This allows subsequent modules to distinguish the event structure from the conditions upon which that structure depends.
Dependency Independence from Event Boundary
EFDM identifies dependencies before TREBS establishes the final Event Boundary.
This means a qualified dependency may later: remain outside the Event Boundary; contribute to Boundary analysis; relate the event to another event; become relevant to Event Relationships; require separate governance.
Therefore:
Qualified Dependency ≠ Boundary Inclusion.
TREBS later determines final event extent.

Governance Requirements
EFDM requires that: dependencies are assessed against a Governed Event Formation Assembly; dependency candidates are distinguished from qualified dependencies; dependency relevance is materially established; background conditions do not automatically become dependencies; dependencies remain distinct from Event Formation Components; dependencies remain distinct from Event Membership; prior activity is not automatically merged into the current event; dependency chains remain proportionate; structural dependency remains distinct from legal causality; identity and authority dependencies do not absorb identity or authority governance; distributed dependencies may be represented; machine prerequisites are filtered for material relevance; dependency conflicts remain visible; unresolved dependencies remain explicitly unresolved; dependency decisions remain traceable; dependency qualification does not determine Event Boundary; dependency qualification does not determine legal taxability.
Governance Logic
EFDM applies a focused dependency logic:
What surrounding condition, action, structure, system, resource, or prior activity materially supports this Event Formation Assembly?
Is the relationship sufficiently material to qualify as a Formation Dependency?
Is the dependency part of the formation structure, or merely a condition upon which that structure relies?
Are dependency relationships conflicting or unresolved?

What dependency structure must remain visible before Event Formation Root analysis begins?
The transformation is:
Governed Event Formation Assembly
→ Dependency Candidates
→ Dependency Relevance
→ Qualification / Exclusion
→ Dependency Relationships
→ Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EFDM implementation must be capable of:
1. receiving the Governed Event Formation Assembly from EFAM; 2. identifying candidate Formation Dependencies; 3. assessing material dependency relevance; 4. distinguishing dependencies from Event Formation Components; 5. distinguishing dependencies from ordinary background conditions; 6. qualifying or excluding dependency candidates; 7. representing enabling, conditional, prior-activity, infrastructural, distributed, machine, or autonomous dependencies where relevant; 8. representing material dependency chains without uncontrolled expansion; 9. identifying Dependency Conflict or Dependency Uncertainty; 10. preserving dependency traceability; 11. preventing dependency from automatically becoming Event Membership; 12. producing a Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure; 13. transferring the governed formation and dependency structure to EFRM for Event Formation Root governance; 14. preventing dependency analysis from becoming Event Boundary, legal causality, responsibility, or jurisdiction-specific tax determination.

EFDM does not prescribe a specific dependency graph, ERP model, workflow system, database schema, AI model, transaction architecture, tax engine, identity system, or legal causality model.
Governance Outputs
EFDM may produce:
Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure — the principal Module output.
Qualified Formation Dependency — a materially established dependency supporting Event Formation.
Excluded Dependency Candidate — a candidate determined not to require dependency governance.
Unresolved Formation Dependency — a materially relevant dependency whose status remains unresolved.
Dependency Relationship Record — the governed relationship between a dependency and the formation.
Dependency Chain Reference — representation of materially relevant connected dependencies.
Dependency Conflict Indicator — indication of materially incompatible dependency representations.
Dependency Qualification Record — the basis for dependency qualification or exclusion.
Dependency Traceability Reference — linkage between the dependency and its governed basis.
Critical Distinctions
Formation Dependency ≠ Formation Component.
A dependency may support formation without becoming a component.
Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership.
Dependency does not determine final inclusion.
Necessary for Formation ≠ Part of the Event by Default.
Operational necessity and structural membership are different questions.
Dependency Candidate ≠ Qualified Formation Dependency.
Identification precedes qualification.

Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency by Default.
Dependency governance must remain materially bounded.
Conditional Dependency ≠ Event Component by Default.
A condition may remain external to the formed event.
Prior Event Dependency ≠ Same Event.
Dependency does not merge separate activity.
Dependency Chain ≠ Event Expansion.
Historical prerequisites must not create unlimited event structures.
Formation Dependency ≠ Legal Causality.
EFDM does not determine legal consequence.
Authority Dependency ≠ Authority Governance.
Authority remains governed by the architecture owning that space.
Identity Reference ≠ Identity Governance.
EFDM may reference identity without governing identity.
Machine Prerequisite ≠ Formation Dependency by Default.
Ordinary machine operation does not automatically become governed dependency.
Autonomous Dependency ≠ Autonomous Responsibility.
Dependency does not determine accountability.
Expected Dependency ≠ Established Dependency.
Structural assumptions require governed support.
Qualified Dependency ≠ Boundary Inclusion.
TREBS owns final Event Boundary.
Formation Dependency ≠ Taxability Determination.
EFDM does not determine tax law.
Enterprise Application
EFDM addresses a major structural problem in complex enterprise and digital systems:
systems frequently confuse what an event depends on with what the event actually is.
A payment may depend on an account.
A delivery may depend on a warehouse release.
A digital service may depend on authentication.

An autonomous transaction may depend on delegated authority.
A production action may depend on resource allocation.
If every prerequisite is absorbed into the event, the event can expand indefinitely.
If dependencies are ignored entirely, the event loses the structural conditions necessary to understand how it formed.
EFDM creates the governed middle layer:
the dependency remains visible without automatically becoming part of the event. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Global Digital Service Depends on Multiple Prior Activities Across Different Companies
A customer purchases a cloud-based enterprise service through a global marketplace.
The Event Formation Assembly includes: service commitment; activation; service execution; settlement.
However, the formation also relies on: prior customer account creation; platform authentication; an existing provider agreement; payment authorization infrastructure; previously allocated cloud capacity.
Without EFDM, a system may either ignore these dependencies completely or absorb them all into one oversized event.
EFDM determines which dependencies materially support the formation and preserves their relationship without automatically treating them as Event Formation Components.
The customer account does not become part of every service event.
The provider agreement does not become part of every execution.
The cloud infrastructure does not become the event merely because execution depends on it.

The result is a governed dependency structure that explains how the formation became possible without redefining what the formation is. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Network Creates a Deep Chain of Machine Dependencies
An AI-controlled manufacturing network autonomously accepts a production requirement and coordinates: production capacity; energy allocation; robotic equipment; material availability; autonomous transport; machine authorization; digital settlement.
The resulting Event Formation Assembly depends on several prior machine and infrastructure states.
If every dependency is recursively absorbed, the event could expand from one production formation into the entire factory, energy grid, software stack, and historical authorization chain.
If dependencies are ignored, critical structural relationships disappear.
EFDM identifies only the dependencies materially necessary to understand the formation.
It may preserve:
Production Formation
→ depends on Material Availability
→ depends on Production Capacity Allocation
→ depends on Authorized Machine Execution
without converting every underlying technical prerequisite into an Event Formation Component.
The key result is:
dependency remains governable without allowing the event to expand indefinitely through the systems that made it possible.
Canonical Boundary

EFDM governs the identification, differentiation, qualification, relationship, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability of material dependencies supporting a Governed Event Formation Assembly. It does not identify original Event Formation Components, assemble those components, establish the Event Formation Root, determine complete Formation Integrity, determine final Event Boundary, establish legal causality, govern identity or authority, determine accountability, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The handoff is:
EFAM — Governed Event Formation Assembly
→ EFDM — Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure
→ EFRM — Event Formation Root Module
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Formation Dependency Module establishes the dependency governance layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining what conditions, actions, structures, resources, systems, or prior activities materially support a Governed Event Formation Assembly without automatically incorporating those dependencies into the event itself. By separating dependency from Formation Components, Event Membership, identity, authority, legal causality, responsibility, and final Event Boundary, EFDM preserves the operational conditions necessary to understand how an event formation became possible while preventing unlimited structural expansion through every prerequisite on which the event ultimately relies. The Module therefore produces a bounded, traceable Event Formation Dependency Structure ready for Event Formation Root governance without allowing dependency analysis to redefine the event or determine jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
