OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS)
Module: ELCM — Event Location Correlation Module
Operational Layer: Event Location Correlation Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Location Correlation
Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELCM-005
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Location Correlation Module (ELCM) governs how the physical, digital, distributed, temporal, and supporting spatial representations of a Tax-Relevant Event are correlated into a coherent, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral final location representation of the governed event.
ELCM operates after the relevant Event Location signals have been identified through ELIM, Physical Event Location has been governed through ELPM, Digital Event Location has been governed through ELDM, and Distributed Event Location has been governed through ELDSM.

Its canonical task is:
to correlate the legitimate spatial representations of the governed event into a coherent Governed Event Location without collapsing distinct physical, digital, distributed, or temporally changing locations into an artificial single point and without converting operational location correlation into Tax Jurisdiction determination.
ELCM completes the spatial governance of the Tax-Relevant Event.
The principal transition is:
Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location + Governed Event Distributed Location + Governed Event Timing
↓
Governed Event Location Correlation
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
The resulting event is sufficiently governed in operational time and operational space to proceed to:
TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Operational Role
An event may contain several legitimate spatial representations.
It may possess: one or more physical locations; one or more digital locations; distributed locations; changing locations; simultaneous locations; sequential locations; machine locations; autonomous-system locations; infrastructure locations; and location signals with different levels of precision, confidence, and evidential strength.
These locations may describe different spatial dimensions of the same event.

Without correlation, downstream systems may incorrectly: select one location and discard others; treat different spatial dimensions as contradictions; confuse infrastructure location with Event Location; confuse participant location with Event Location; interpret distributed execution as multiple events; infer Tax Jurisdiction directly from operational geography; or convert uncertain spatial evidence into false geographic certainty.
ELCM establishes the final governance layer that determines how already-governed location components relate to the same Tax-Relevant Event.
Location Correlation ≠ Location Simplification.
Its purpose is not to make complex spatial reality appear simple.
Its purpose is to make complex spatial reality governable.
Internal Flow
Within TRELS, ELCM occupies the fifth and final operational position:
ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented?
↓
ELCM — How are the legitimate event locations correlated into a coherent governed spatial representation?
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
ELCM receives:
Governed Event Physical Location
Governed Event Digital Location
Governed Event Distributed Location
together with relevant governed temporal information from TRETS.
It produces: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event

This output completes TRELS and becomes the governed input to TREPS.
Operational Space
ELCM governs the final correlation of Event Location information.
Its operational space includes: physical-digital location correlation; distributed-location correlation; temporal-spatial correlation; multi-location correlation; location-role correlation; location-type differentiation; location consistency; location coexistence; location hierarchy; location equivalence; location divergence; location conflict; location uncertainty; location precision; location confidence; location transitions; simultaneous location; sequential location; hybrid location; dynamic location; machine and autonomous location correlation; spatial evidence correlation; location correction; location continuity; location traceability; final Event Location representation; and readiness for Event Participation governance.
Operational Scope
ELCM shall support final spatial correlation for events involving: physical commerce; digital commerce; cross-border transactions; cloud services; digital platforms; financial infrastructure; payment systems; distributed computing; AI systems; AI agents; autonomous systems; robotics; machine-to-machine activity; IoT systems; telecommunications; industrial automation; logistics; supply chains; manufacturing; digital assets; distributed ledgers; infrastructure networks; hybrid physical-digital services; and future decentralized or machine-mediated economic environments.

1. Location Correlation Readiness
ELCM shall determine whether sufficient governed spatial information exists to begin final location correlation.
Correlation readiness may include: Governed Event Physical Location; Governed Event Digital Location; Governed Event Distributed Location; relevant Event Timing; Event Boundary; spatial evidence; spatial precision; uncertainty states; conflict states; and traceability references.
Not every event requires every location type.
Therefore:
Missing Location Type ≠ Correlation Failure by Default.
A purely physical event may legitimately possess no Digital Event Location.
A purely digital event may possess no meaningful Physical Event Location.
A distributed event may require several spatial components.
ELCM shall correlate only spatial dimensions legitimately belonging to the event. 2. Location Component Identification
ELCM shall identify the governed spatial components requiring correlation.
Each component shall remain distinguishable by type and operational role.
Possible components include: physical; digital; distributed; hybrid; sequential; simultaneous; dynamic; machine; autonomous; infrastructural; or qualified spatial representations.
Correlation ≠ Erasure of Spatial Type.
Physical and digital locations shall not lose their governance meaning merely because they are incorporated into a final Event Location representation. 3. Physical-Digital Correlation

Where both physical and digital locations materially belong to the event, ELCM shall establish their operational relationship.
For example:
Physical Machine Location ↔ Edge Environment ↔ Cloud Execution Environment
or:
Physical Service Delivery Location ↔ Digital Platform Environment
The resulting representation may legitimately contain both dimensions.
Physical Location ≠ Digital Location.
Physical-Digital Correlation ≠ Requirement to Select One. 4. Distributed Location Correlation
Where ELDSM establishes a Governed Event Distributed Location, ELCM shall correlate its constitutive spatial components into the final Event Location representation.
ELCM shall preserve: distributed structure; component roles; temporal association; supported precision; uncertainty; conflict; and traceability.
Distributed Location Correlation ≠ Geographic Consolidation by Default.
A distributed event shall remain distributed where that is the legitimate operational representation. 5. Temporal-Spatial Correlation
Event Location may change throughout the governed Event Timing.
ELCM shall support correlation such as:
T1
↓
Location A
T2
↓
Location B
T3
↓
Location B + Digital Environment C
T4
↓
Distributed Locations D/E/F
Temporal-spatial correlation shall preserve the relationship between when and where without changing ownership boundaries.
TRETS owns Event Timing.
TRELS owns Event Location.

ELCM correlates governed spatial representation with the temporal structure necessary to represent location correctly.
Temporal-Spatial Correlation ≠ Event Relationship Determination. 6. Sequential Location Correlation
Where an event moves through several locations sequentially, ELCM shall preserve that sequence.
For example:
Location A
↓
Location B
↓
Location C
ELCM shall not automatically select the first, last, longest, or commercially preferred location as the definitive Event Location.
First Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default.
Final Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default.
Longest-Duration Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default. 7. Simultaneous Location Correlation
An event may legitimately occur across several locations simultaneously.
ELCM shall represent simultaneous spatial states without treating them as contradictory.
Different Concurrent Locations ≠ Location Conflict by Default.
Simultaneous distributed activity can be a legitimate property of one bounded event. 8. Dynamic Location Correlation
Events involving mobile machines, vehicles, devices, autonomous systems, migrating workloads, or changing infrastructure may possess dynamic spatial states.
ELCM shall preserve materially relevant changes without forcing every movement into a separate event.
Dynamic Location ≠ Unstable Governance.
Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 9. Location Role Correlation
Different locations may perform different operational roles.

ELCM may classify location roles such as: constitutive; execution; physical performance; digital execution; coordination; processing; transitional; supporting; infrastructure; storage; observation; recording; or other justified operational roles.
Role classification shall prevent unlike locations from being treated as equivalent merely because all are associated with the event.
Location Association ≠ Location Equivalence. 10. Constitutive and Supporting Location Correlation
ELCM shall preserve the distinction between locations constituting the event and locations merely supporting it.
A supporting data center, payment processor, logging environment, corporate office, or routing node may be spatially relevant without constituting Event Location.
Supporting Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location.
A supporting location shall not be elevated to constitutive status merely because it is easier to identify. 11. Location Hierarchy
Spatial information may exist at several levels:
Coordinates
↓
Facility
↓
City
↓
Region
↓
Country
or:
Execution Instance
↓
Availability Zone
↓
Cloud Region
↓
Distributed Cloud Environment
ELCM shall preserve legitimate hierarchical relationships where relevant.
However:
Higher Geographic Level ≠ More Authoritative Location.
Country-Level Classification ≠ Complete Event Location by Default.
The final representation shall preserve the precision justified by operational evidence. 12. Location Equivalence

Different location records may refer to the same operational place.
For example: coordinates and facility address; facility identifier and industrial site; cloud-region code and named cloud region; machine identifier and known machine installation location.
ELCM may establish operational equivalence where supported.
Different Location Representations ≠ Different Locations by Default.
Equivalence shall be evidence-based and traceable. 13. Location Divergence
Two legitimate locations may differ because they describe different spatial dimensions of the same event.
For example:
Physical execution: Switzerland
Digital execution: Germany
This is not necessarily a conflict.
Location Divergence ≠ Location Conflict by Default.
ELCM shall preserve legitimate divergence where operational reality supports it. 14. Location Conflict
Location Conflict exists where two or more location claims purport to describe the same spatial property of the event but cannot be reconciled under available evidence.
Examples may include: incompatible physical-location evidence; conflicting device-location records; contradictory infrastructure-location records; inconsistent geolocation sources; or incompatible event-location claims.
ELCM shall distinguish conflict from legitimate multi-location reality.
Multiple Locations ≠ Conflict by Default.
Contradictory Claims About the Same Location Property = Potential Location Conflict. 15. Conflict Isolation

A conflict affecting one spatial component shall not automatically invalidate the entire Event Location representation.
For example: Physical Location may be established; Digital Location may be established; one cloud-region component may remain conflicted.
ELCM shall isolate the unresolved component.
Partial Spatial Conflict ≠ Total Spatial Invalidity. 16. Location Uncertainty
ELCM shall preserve uncertainty where available evidence does not support exact spatial determination.
Possible representations include: exact; bounded; approximate; regional; multi-region; distributed; inferred; qualified; partially known; conflicted; or unresolved.
Location Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Manufacture Geographic Certainty.
Where the event can only legitimately be situated at regional level, ELCM shall not create artificial city-level or facility-level precision. 17. Location Precision
ELCM shall maintain the highest spatial precision legitimately supported by evidence and operational relevance.
However:
Technical Location Precision ≠ Governance Accuracy.
Exact GPS coordinates can be irrelevant or misleading.
A broad cloud region may be the most legitimate representation of a digital component.
Precision shall therefore be governed, not merely inherited from source systems. 18. Location Confidence
ELCM may associate confidence with spatial components where useful.
Confidence shall reflect governance quality of the location representation, not the convenience of the source.

A highly precise but weakly supported signal may legitimately receive lower confidence than a broader but strongly evidenced location.
Precision ≠ Confidence.
Confidence ≠ Legal Certainty. 19. Spatial Evidence Correlation
ELCM shall preserve the evidence supporting each material spatial conclusion.
Evidence may include: operational system records; machine records; infrastructure records; device data; network information; physical records; transaction data; platform records; cloud metadata; logistics records; or other governed evidence sources.
ADIT® governs evidence and auditability.
ELCM governs how legitimate spatial evidence supports Event Location correlation. 20. Infrastructure Location Correlation
Infrastructure locations may support an event without defining it.
ELCM shall distinguish:
Infrastructure Location
from:
Event Location
Examples include: server facilities; cloud regions; network nodes; storage facilities; payment infrastructure; data centers; telecommunications infrastructure; or replicated systems.
Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 21. Server Location Correlation
A server may process part of an event.
That does not automatically make server geography the definitive location of the event.
Server Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Where server execution is materially constitutive, it may form one component of Digital or Distributed Event Location.
It shall not automatically displace other legitimate locations. 22. IP Location Correlation

IP-based geolocation may provide useful spatial evidence.
However:
IP Address Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
IP Geolocation ≠ Participant Residence.
IP Geolocation ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
ELCM may use IP-derived information only at the level of confidence and precision justified by the evidence. 23. Device Location Correlation
Device location may contribute to Event Location where the device materially participates in the event.
However:
Device Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
A device may be remote from: service execution; value creation; physical performance; participant residence; organizational location; or other event components.
ELCM shall preserve these distinctions. 24. Participant Location Correlation
Event participants may have locations relevant to downstream analysis.
However, Participant Location is not automatically Event Location.
TREPS governs Event Participation.
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity.
Therefore:
Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Participant Residence ≠ Event Location.
Event Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence.
ELCM shall not determine participant identity, residence, taxpayer status, or legal presence. 25. Corporate Location Correlation
Corporate headquarters, registered offices, operational offices, subsidiaries, branches, or management locations may be associated with an event.
Their existence does not automatically establish Event Location.
Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location by Default.

Registered Office ≠ Event Location by Default.
Corporate Presence ≠ Event Location by Default.
Legal consequences associated with corporate presence remain outside TREGA™. 26. Autonomous-System Location Correlation
Autonomous systems may operate across: physical machines; edge infrastructure; cloud services; external APIs; distributed databases; other autonomous agents; and digital platforms.
ELCM shall correlate materially constitutive spatial components without attempting to create a fictional legal residence for the autonomous system.
Autonomous System Location ≠ Legal Residence.
Autonomous Execution Geography ≠ Tax Residence. 27. AI Agent Location Correlation
AI-agent activity may have no meaningful single physical location.
The agent may operate through a distributed orchestration environment while invoking models, tools, services, databases, and physical systems in different places.
ELCM shall permit:
Distributed Agent Operational Location
where that representation best reflects the event.
AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location.
AI Agent Location ≠ Developer Location.
AI Agent Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. 28. Machine-to-Machine Location Correlation
Machine-to-machine events may involve several physical machines and multiple digital environments.
ELCM shall correlate these spatial components without requiring human geography to define the event.
For example:
Machine A — Physical Location A
Machine B — Physical Location B
Edge Controller — Digital Environment C

Cloud Orchestrator — Digital Environment D
may jointly form the governed spatial representation.
Machine Event Geography ≠ Human Participant Geography. 29. Platform Location Correlation
A digital platform may operate globally while an individual event uses only a limited subset of its infrastructure.
ELCM shall correlate event-specific locations rather than the entire geographic footprint of the platform.
Platform Presence ≠ Event Presence.
Global Platform Infrastructure ≠ Global Event Location. 30. Distributed Ledger Location Correlation
Distributed ledger infrastructure may contain nodes across many jurisdictions.
ELCM shall not treat every node maintaining, validating, observing, or replicating ledger state as a constitutive location of every event.
Ledger Distribution ≠ Event Distribution by Default.
Only operationally material spatial components shall enter the final Event Location representation. 31. Location Correlation and Event Boundary
ELCM shall remain within the Event Boundary established under TREBS.
It shall not expand the event merely because additional spatial information exists.
Spatial Association ≠ Event Inclusion by Default.
A location outside the governed Event Boundary shall not become part of Event Location merely through technical, commercial, or organizational association. 32. Location Correlation and Event Timing
TRETS provides the temporal structure necessary to determine when particular spatial states belong to the event.

ELCM may correlate those spatial states with time.
It shall not redefine Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, or Event Temporal Order.
Location Correlation ≠ Timing Governance.
TRETS governs when.
TRELS governs where. 33. Location Correlation and Event Participation
The next Parent Standard, TREPS, determines who or what participated in the event and in what governed role.
ELCM shall therefore preserve spatial information without prematurely converting location into participation.
Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Event Participation ≠ Taxpayer Determination. 34. Location Correlation and Value Association
TRVAS subsequently governs which governed value result belongs to the event.
ELCM shall not infer value ownership, value origin, value state, value movement, value recognition, or value allocation from location alone.
Value at a Location ≠ Event Value Association by Default.
VFM® governs what happened to value.
TREGA™ later governs which governed value result belongs to the event. 35. Location Correlation and Event Relationships
Spatial proximity or shared location may indicate that events warrant further relationship analysis.
It does not establish the relationship.
Same Location ≠ Same Event.
Same Location ≠ Event Relationship by Default.
Spatial Proximity ≠ Causation.
TRERLS governs Event Relationships. 36. Location Correlation and Event Determination
ELCM prepares spatially governed information for later TREGA stages.

It does not determine whether the event is legally taxable.
Governed Event Location ≠ Taxability Determination.
Spatial Completeness ≠ Legal Taxability.
TREDS governs Tax-Relevant Event Determination.
Jurisdiction-specific systems subsequently govern legal tax consequences. 37. Event Location Correction
Final Event Location correlation may require correction as evidence improves or errors are identified.
ELCM shall preserve: previous spatial state; corrected spatial state; correction reason; supporting evidence; timestamp; governance authority; and traceability.
Event Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. 38. Event Location Continuity
ELCM shall preserve continuity of spatial representation across material location changes.
A governed event may move from:
Location State 1
↓
Location State 2
↓
Location State 3
without losing its Event Identity.
Location Continuity ≠ Spatial Immutability.
The location representation may change while the same bounded event continues. 39. Final Event Location Representation
ELCM shall construct the final operational location representation appropriate to the event.
Possible representations include:
Single Physical Location
Single Digital Location
Physical + Digital Location
Sequential Multi-Location
Simultaneous Multi-Location
Distributed Physical Location
Distributed Digital Location
Hybrid Distributed Location
Dynamic Location
Qualified Location
Partially Resolved Location
No Legitimate Single Primary Location

The final representation shall reflect operational reality rather than downstream schema convenience. 40. Single-Location Reduction Control
ELCM shall prevent unjustified reduction of a complex event into a single location.
A downstream system may require a country code or one location field.
Such technical requirements shall not redefine the governed event.
Single Database Location Field ≠ Single Event Location Reality.
Where necessary, downstream mappings may derive jurisdiction-specific representations from the governed event layer while the canonical TREGA™ record preserves the richer operational reality. 41. Location Correlation and Tax Jurisdiction
ELCM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational Event Location and legal Tax Jurisdiction.
ELCM does not determine: Tax Jurisdiction; tax nexus; residence; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; legal situs; customs origin; taxable presence; taxing rights; profit allocation; revenue allocation; tax-base allocation; transfer-pricing treatment; Legal Tax Point; Tax Period; Tax Liability; or jurisdiction-specific reporting obligations.
The foundational distinction is: Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Related distinctions include:
Operational Location ≠ Legal Tax Situs.
Digital Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply.
Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus.
Data Center Location ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default.
Participant Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence.

Distributed Location ≠ Distributed Taxing Rights.
Location Correlation ≠ Jurisdiction Determination. 42. Jurisdiction-Ready Spatial Representation
The output of ELCM shall be capable of supporting multiple downstream jurisdictional evaluations without being rewritten for each jurisdiction.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Event
↓
One Governed Temporal-Spatial Reality
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
Jurisdiction A may evaluate the physical component.
Jurisdiction B may apply digital-service rules.
Jurisdiction C may apply participant, source, nexus, residence, or place-of-supply rules.
These legal evaluations may differ.
The underlying governed event should not.
Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. 43. Governance States
ELCM may assign states including:
Correlation Ready Required governed spatial inputs are sufficiently available.
Correlation Under Governance Spatial components are being correlated.
Correlation Established Material spatial components are coherently correlated.
Correlation Single-Location One location legitimately represents the event.
Correlation Multi-Location Several locations legitimately represent the event.
Correlation Distributed Distributed representation is required.
Correlation Hybrid Physical and digital spatial dimensions jointly represent the event.
Correlation Dynamic The event's legitimate spatial state changes materially over time.

Correlation Partial A legitimate spatial representation exists but some components remain unresolved.
Correlation Qualified The representation requires explicit qualification.
Correlation Conflicted Material spatial evidence remains conflicting.
Correlation Unresolved Available evidence cannot support a legitimate final correlation.
Spatially Situated The event has achieved sufficient location governance to proceed to Event Participation governance. 44. Governance Requirements

ELCM implementations shall: consume governed spatial outputs from ELIM, ELPM, ELDM, and ELDSM as applicable; consume relevant governed Event Timing from TRETS; identify spatial components requiring correlation; preserve location types; preserve physical-digital distinctions; preserve distributed spatial structure; support temporal-spatial correlation; support sequential location; support simultaneous location; support dynamic location; distinguish constitutive from supporting locations; distinguish divergence from conflict; support location hierarchy; support location equivalence; preserve spatial precision; preserve uncertainty; preserve confidence; isolate conflicts; preserve evidence references; preserve correction history; preserve location continuity; preserve Event Boundary; prevent artificial single-location reduction; prevent participant location from becoming Event Location by default; prevent infrastructure location from becoming Event Location by default; prevent Event Location from becoming Tax Jurisdiction; maintain jurisdiction neutrality; produce a traceable final Event Location representation; and produce a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event suitable for TREPS.
45. Governance Logic
ELCM follows the canonical logic:
Governed Physical Location + Governed Digital Location + Governed Distributed Location + Governed Event Timing
↓
identify legitimate spatial components
↓

correlate physical, digital, distributed, sequential, simultaneous, hybrid, and dynamic spatial states
↓
distinguish coexistence, equivalence, divergence, and conflict
↓
preserve precision, uncertainty, confidence, continuity, correction, and traceability
↓
establish final Governed Event Location
↓
produce Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event.
The governing rule is:
Preserve spatial reality first. Permit legal interpretation later. 46. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ELCM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference Reference to the bounded Tax-Relevant Event.
Location Correlation Identifier Unique identifier for the final location-correlation record.
Physical Location Reference Governed ELPM output where applicable.
Digital Location Reference Governed ELDM output where applicable.
Distributed Location Reference Governed ELDSM output where applicable.
Temporal Reference Relevant governed TRETS information.
Location Components Material spatial components belonging to the event.
Location Type Physical, digital, distributed, hybrid, dynamic, or other legitimate type.
Location Role Operational role of each spatial component.
Constitutive State Whether the location materially constitutes the event.
Temporal Association Relevant time or interval associated with each location.
Location Relationship Operational spatial relationship among components.
Location Equivalence State Whether different records describe the same operational place.

Location Divergence State Whether legitimate spatial dimensions differ.
Location Conflict State Whether incompatible claims remain.
Location Precision Supported geographic or digital precision.
Location Uncertainty Known spatial uncertainty.
Location Confidence Governance confidence where applicable.
Primary Location State Primary, non-primary, no-primary, or unresolved where relevant.
Evidence References Evidence supporting correlation.
Correction History Material corrections.
Traceability Reference Governance history.
Jurisdiction-Neutrality State Confirmation that no jurisdiction-specific tax conclusion has been embedded.
Governance State Current ELCM state.
Handoff State Readiness for TREPS. 47. Governance Outputs
ELCM may produce: Location Correlation Readiness Record; Spatial Component Register; Physical-Digital Correlation Record; Distributed Location Correlation Record; Temporal-Spatial Correlation Record; Sequential Location Record; Simultaneous Location Record; Dynamic Location Record; Location Role Record; Constitutive Location Record; Supporting Location Record; Location Hierarchy Record; Location Equivalence Record; Location Divergence Record; Location Conflict Record; Location Uncertainty Record; Location Precision Record; Location Confidence Record; Spatial Evidence Correlation Record; Location Correction Record; Location Continuity Record; Final Event Location Representation; Jurisdiction-Neutrality Record; and the principal TRELS output:

Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
This output becomes the governed input to: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard48. Critical Distinctions
Location Correlation ≠ Location Simplification
Missing Location Type ≠ Correlation Failure
Correlation ≠ Erasure of Spatial Type
Physical Location ≠ Digital Location
Physical-Digital Correlation ≠ Requirement to Select One
Distributed Location Correlation ≠ Geographic Consolidation
Temporal-Spatial Correlation ≠ Event Relationship Determination
First Location ≠ Primary Event Location
Final Location ≠ Primary Event Location
Longest-Duration Location ≠ Primary Event Location
Different Concurrent Locations ≠ Location Conflict
Dynamic Location ≠ Unstable Governance
Location Change ≠ New Event
Location Association ≠ Location Equivalence
Supporting Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location
Higher Geographic Level ≠ More Authoritative Location
Country-Level Classification ≠ Complete Event Location
Different Location Representations ≠ Different Locations
Location Divergence ≠ Location Conflict
Multiple Locations ≠ Conflict
Partial Spatial Conflict ≠ Total Spatial Invalidity
Location Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Manufacture Geographic Certainty
Technical Location Precision ≠ Governance Accuracy
Precision ≠ Confidence
Confidence ≠ Legal Certainty
Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location
Server Location ≠ Event Location
IP Address Location ≠ Event Location
IP Geolocation ≠ Participant Residence
Device Location ≠ Event Location

Participant Location ≠ Event Location
Participant Residence ≠ Event Location
Event Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence
Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location
Registered Office ≠ Event Location
Autonomous System Location ≠ Legal Residence
AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location
AI Agent Location ≠ Developer Location
Machine Event Geography ≠ Human Participant Geography
Platform Presence ≠ Event Presence
Global Platform Infrastructure ≠ Global Event Location
Ledger Distribution ≠ Event Distribution
Spatial Association ≠ Event Inclusion
Location Correlation ≠ Timing Governance
Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation
Value at a Location ≠ Event Value Association
Same Location ≠ Same Event
Spatial Proximity ≠ Causation
Governed Event Location ≠ Taxability Determination
Spatial Completeness ≠ Legal Taxability
Event Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Location Continuity ≠ Spatial Immutability
Single Database Location Field ≠ Single Event Location Reality
Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Operational Location ≠ Legal Tax Situs
Digital Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply
Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus
Data Center Location ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default
Distributed Location ≠ Distributed Taxing Rights
Location Correlation ≠ Jurisdiction Determination
Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined 49. Enterprise Application
ELCM provides the final spatial-governance layer between complex operational reality and jurisdiction-specific taxation infrastructure.

A generalized enterprise implementation may operate as:
ERP + Commerce + Banking + Digital Platform + Cloud Infrastructure + AI Agents + Autonomous Machines + Operational Systems
↓
TREGA™ Event Layer
↓
TRETS Governed Event Timing
↓
TRELS Governed Event Location
↓
ELCM Location Correlation
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
↓
TREPS Event Participation
↓
Subsequent TREGA Governance
↓
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines
This allows organizations to maintain one governed operational representation of the event while multiple jurisdictions independently evaluate its legal tax implications.
The operational record therefore does not need to be reconstructed differently for every tax regime.
One governed event reality can support multiple legitimate legal interpretations without allowing those interpretations to rewrite the event itself. 50. Use Case 1 — Global Cloud and AI Service Event
A corporate customer initiates a complex AI service from Switzerland.
The service is orchestrated through a European cloud region.
Model inference is executed through several computational environments.
A specialist external API processes part of the workload in another region.
Data is retrieved from distributed infrastructure.
An autonomous agent coordinates the workflow.
The final digital output is delivered to a business system operating from Switzerland.
ELPM may identify relevant physical components.
ELDM establishes materially relevant digital environments.

ELDSM determines that the event possesses a legitimate distributed digital structure.
ELCM correlates these spatial components with the governed Event Timing.
It does not force the event into: customer location; cloud-provider headquarters; one server location; billing address; model-provider country; or one arbitrary country code.
The result is a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event preserving the actual operational geography.
Different jurisdictions may subsequently evaluate place of supply, nexus, source, residence, or other tax rules independently.
ELCM preserves one governed operational reality even where several tax systems may later interpret that reality differently. 51. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine-to-Machine Economic Event
An autonomous industrial machine in Country A detects that a component is required.
An AI agent operating through distributed infrastructure identifies a supplier.
A machine in Country B manufactures the component.
Payment authorization occurs through infrastructure in Country C.
An autonomous logistics system transports the component.
Final installation occurs at an industrial site in Country A.
The event contains physical, digital, machine, autonomous, distributed, and changing spatial components.
Selecting the buyer machine, seller machine, payment infrastructure, AI execution environment, logistics location, or corporate headquarters as the sole Event Location would materially distort the event.

ELCM correlates the legitimate spatial components and their temporal associations into one governed representation.
The resulting event can subsequently be evaluated by the relevant jurisdiction-specific tax systems.
ELCM itself does not decide: which jurisdiction taxes the event; whether a permanent establishment exists; where legal place of supply lies; which participant is a taxpayer; how tax base is allocated; or whether tax is legally due.
The machine economy may be spatially distributed while the governed event remains methodologically coherent. 52. Canonical Boundary
ELCM owns the final correlation of governed Event Location information within TRELS, including physical-digital correlation, distributed-location correlation, temporal-spatial correlation, sequential and simultaneous location, dynamic location, location roles, constitutive/supporting distinctions, location hierarchy, equivalence, divergence, conflict, uncertainty, precision, confidence, evidence correlation, correction, continuity, final Event Location representation, and construction of the Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event.
ELCM does not own Event Location Signal Identification, which belongs to ELIM.
It does not own Physical Event Location, which belongs to ELPM.
It does not own Digital Event Location, which belongs to ELDM.
It does not own Distributed Event Location, which belongs to ELDSM.
It does not own Event Timing, which belongs to TRETS.

It does not own Event Participation, which belongs to TREPS.
It does not own origin-bound identity, which belongs to OBIDENITY®.
It does not own Value Lifecycle governance, which belongs to VFM®.
It does not own semantic Event Relationships, which belong to TRERLS.
It does not own Tax-Relevant Event Determination, which belongs to TREDS.
It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, legal situs, customs origin, taxable presence, taxing rights, profit allocation, revenue allocation, tax-base allocation, transfer-pricing treatment, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The complete TRELS internal handoff is:
ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location
↓
ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location
↓
ELDSM — Governed Event Distributed Location
↓
ELCM — Governed Event Location Correlation
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
↓
TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Canonical Closing Statement
ELCM completes the spatial governance of the Tax-Relevant Event by correlating its legitimate physical, digital, distributed, dynamic, and temporally associated locations into one coherent representation without erasing the complexity of operational reality.

A governed event does not require one location. It requires a spatial representation that truthfully reflects where the event occurred.
ELCM determines how the locations of the event fit together — not which jurisdiction acquires the legal right to tax it.
TRELS governs where the event occurred as governed operational reality — not where tax law decides that the event is taxable.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

Canonical Definition
The Event Digital Location Module (ELDM) governs how materially relevant digital spatial signals associated with a Tax-Relevant Event are identified, differentiated, evaluated, qualified, and assembled into a governed representation of where the event digitally occurs, is executed, is instantiated, is processed, or materially manifests within digital operational environments.
ELDM operates on the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM and alongside the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM.
Its canonical task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Digital Location without allowing IP addresses, server positions, cloud regions, user-device locations, platform registrations, network routes, corporate addresses, or jurisdiction-specific legal rules to become the digital location of the event merely because they contain geographic information.
The principal transition is:
Governed Event Location Signal Set + Governed Event Physical Location
↓
Governed Event Digital Location
ELDM governs digital Event Location.
It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, digital tax nexus, legal place of supply, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
Operational Role
Digital events frequently have no single obvious geographic position.
A transaction may be initiated from a device in one country, authenticated by infrastructure in another, processed across several cloud regions, executed through a platform operated from another jurisdiction, recorded in distributed databases, and consumed by a user located elsewhere.
An AI agent may initiate and complete an economic operation without a human being physically present at the location where computational execution occurs.
A machine may act physically in one country while its decision logic, orchestration, data processing, and supporting services operate across globally distributed digital infrastructure.

Traditional information systems frequently represent such events through whichever geographic field is easiest to obtain: IP address; billing country; user profile country; server region; platform registration; device location; merchant address; or infrastructure location.
ELDM prevents these signals from being treated as authoritative by default.
Its purpose is to govern the digital spatial reality of the event.
Internal Flow
Within TRELS, ELDM occupies the third operational position:
ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented?
↓
ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation?
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
ELDM receives:
Governed Event Location Signal Set + Governed Event Physical Location
and produces:
Governed Event Digital Location
for subsequent distributed-location governance.
Operational Space
ELDM governs the digital spatial representation of the Tax-Relevant Event.

Its operational space includes: digital execution environments; platform environments; application environments; cloud environments; cloud regions; cloud availability zones; edge environments; network environments; API environments; digital service environments; virtualized infrastructure; distributed computing environments; digital transaction environments; machine-to-machine environments; AI-agent environments; autonomous-system environments; device-associated digital locations; server-associated locations; infrastructure-associated locations; network-associated locations; digital endpoint locations; digital resource locations; logical locations; digital-location transitions; digital-location precision; digital-location uncertainty; digital-location conflict; digital-location continuity; and digital-location traceability.
ELDM governs digital location only to the extent required to represent the operational digital reality of the event.
Operational Scope
ELDM shall support digital-location governance for: e-commerce; digital marketplaces; cloud services; SaaS; digital content; streaming; financial technology; digital payments; banking systems; API transactions; telecommunications; online platforms; distributed applications; AI services; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine transactions; robotics; IoT; edge computing; digital assets; virtualized infrastructure; hybrid physical-digital systems; and future machine economies.

ELDM shall support both digitally centralized and digitally distributed events. 1. Digital Location Candidate Identification
ELDM shall identify digital-location candidates from the Governed Event Location Signal Set.
Candidates may include: server location; cloud region; availability zone; edge node; network endpoint; API endpoint; device location; IP-derived location; application environment; platform environment; execution environment; processing environment; storage environment; digital resource location; logical service location; or other materially relevant digital spatial references.
A candidate shall not become Governed Event Digital Location merely because it is technically observable.
Digital Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Digital Location. 2. Constitutive Digital Location
ELDM shall determine whether a digital environment materially participates in the constitution of the governed event.
A Constitutive Digital Location is a digital environment in which activity forming part of the event itself is executed, instantiated, processed, or materially realized.
This distinction prevents infrastructure merely supporting the event from being mistaken for the digital location of the event.
Supporting Digital Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Digital Location by Default. 3. Digital Execution Location
Where an event involves computational execution, ELDM shall govern the digital environment in which material event execution occurs.

Execution may occur through: application servers; cloud workloads; edge systems; platform services; distributed applications; AI inference systems; autonomous agents; smart-contract environments; machine controllers; or other computational environments.
Digital execution shall be governed according to its role in the event rather than the geographic location of infrastructure alone.
Infrastructure Geography ≠ Digital Event Location by Default. 4. Server Location
A server may participate in the event, support the event, store event data, authenticate participants, or merely route information.
ELDM shall determine the operational significance of the server before its location is attributed to the event.
Server Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
A server physically located in a country does not, by itself, establish that the digital event operationally occurred in that country.
Nor does it establish taxation authority. 5. Cloud Region Location
Cloud platforms frequently distribute workloads across regions, availability zones, and dynamic infrastructure.
A cloud region may be materially relevant where event execution is deliberately or operationally bound to that region.
However:
Cloud Region ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
Cloud Region ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Infrastructure allocation decisions made by a cloud provider shall not automatically redefine the operational spatial identity of the event. 6. Availability Zone and Infrastructure Instance Location

Cloud workloads may migrate between availability zones, physical hosts, containers, virtual machines, or other infrastructure components.
ELDM shall distinguish the operational digital environment from transient infrastructure implementation.
Infrastructure Instance Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
The movement of a workload between infrastructure instances shall not automatically constitute a change in the governed digital location of the event. 7. Edge Computing Location
Edge systems may perform material event processing near devices, machines, users, infrastructure, or physical operations.
Where edge execution forms a constitutive part of the event, ELDM may govern the edge environment as a relevant Digital Event Location.
However:
Edge Node Location ≠ Complete Event Digital Location by Default.
An edge node may represent one component of a broader distributed digital event. 8. User Device Location
A user's device may provide relevant spatial information.
However, the device may be: mobile; remotely controlled; connected through VPN; using roaming services; operating through proxies; shared; automated; or physically separated from the event's principal digital execution.
Therefore:
User Device Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
The operational role of the device shall be established before its location is attributed to the event. 9. IP Address Location
IP addresses may provide evidence about network connectivity.

They shall not be treated as definitive Event Location.
IP geolocation may be affected by: VPNs; proxies; corporate networks; carrier routing; mobile networks; cloud gateways; content-delivery networks; network address translation; satellite connectivity; privacy services; and inaccurate geolocation databases.
Therefore:
IP Address ≠ Event Location.
IP Geolocation ≠ Governed Digital Location by Default.
IP-derived information may remain a governed signal with explicit confidence and provenance. 10. Network Route Location
Digital communications may traverse infrastructure across many countries.
Network routing can change dynamically without changing the governed event itself.
Therefore:
Network Transit Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
Packet Route ≠ Event Location.
Transit infrastructure may be recorded where operationally material but shall not automatically become part of the constitutive Digital Event Location. 11. API Location
An event may be initiated, mediated, executed, or completed through APIs.
An API may possess: logical endpoint; domain; gateway; service region; execution region; provider infrastructure; and downstream service dependencies.
ELDM shall determine which of these are materially relevant to the event.
API Endpoint ≠ Geographic Event Location by Default.
API Provider Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. 12. Platform Location
Digital marketplaces and platforms may operate across many jurisdictions simultaneously.

A platform may have: legal headquarters; regional offices; infrastructure regions; user markets; seller markets; payment entities; data centers; operational subsidiaries; and globally distributed services.
ELDM shall not reduce these structures to a single platform location unless operational evidence supports such representation for the governed event.
Platform Headquarters ≠ Event Digital Location.
Platform Registration Country ≠ Event Digital Location. 13. Digital Service Location
Digital services may be provided through distributed infrastructure without a clear physical point of delivery.
ELDM shall govern the operational digital environment through which the event is materially performed.
This representation may be: centralized; multi-region; distributed; logical; hybrid; or qualified as unresolved.
Digital Service Delivery ≠ Single Geographic Location by Default. 14. Data Storage Location
Event-related data may be stored separately from where the event is executed.
Data may also be replicated across multiple regions.
Therefore:
Data Storage Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
Database Location ≠ Event Execution Location by Default.
Storage location may remain a relevant digital spatial signal but requires independent operational qualification. 15. Processing Location
Data processing may constitute part of the event or merely support it.
ELDM shall determine whether processing activity belongs to the governed Event Boundary.

Where processing is constitutive, its digital environment may form part of the Governed Event Digital Location.
Where processing is ancillary:
Processing Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default. 16. Digital Resource Location
Digital assets, records, files, models, tokens, software components, or other digital resources may be associated with an event.
Their technical storage or registration position shall not automatically establish the location of the event.
Digital Resource Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default.
The resource's operational role must first be established. 17. Logical Digital Location
Some digital environments are better represented through logical rather than physical geography.
Examples include: platform tenancy; virtual network; distributed ledger environment; application namespace; service domain; computational cluster; autonomous-agent environment; or governed digital operational space.
ELDM shall support logical location where geographic representation would distort operational reality.
Digital Location ≠ Geographic Coordinate by Default. 18. AI Agent Location
AI agents may operate across distributed computational environments and interact with platforms, APIs, machines, digital assets, and other agents.
An AI agent may possess no stable physical location.

ELDM shall therefore distinguish: agent execution environment; orchestration environment; model execution environment; tool environment; external service environment; and physical infrastructure.
AI Agent Location ≠ Server Location by Default.
AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location.
AI Agent Location ≠ User Location.
Agent identity, authority, and responsibility remain outside ELDM. 19. Autonomous-System Digital Location
Autonomous systems may continuously migrate workloads, invoke external services, distribute processing, and coordinate with other systems.
ELDM shall preserve the actual digital execution structure without artificially assigning the event to the corporate or physical location of a supervising human.
Autonomous Execution ≠ Human Supervisor Location.
Autonomous System Location ≠ Operator Residence. 20. Machine-to-Machine Event Location
Machine-to-machine events may involve: physical machines; embedded controllers; edge systems; cloud services; APIs; payment systems; AI agents; and distributed infrastructure.
ELDM governs the digital dimension of such events independently from the physical location governed by ELPM.
A machine-to-machine event may legitimately possess both:
Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location
without requiring those locations to coincide. 21. Digital Location Transition
The digital location of an event may change during its lifecycle.
Workloads may migrate.
Agents may invoke services in different environments.

Processing may move between edge and cloud systems.
Transactions may pass through sequential digital execution stages.
ELDM shall preserve materially relevant transitions where they form part of the bounded event.
Digital Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 22. Digital Location and Event Timing
Digital location may vary over the duration of an event.
ELDM shall support temporal association where required.
For example:
Time T1
↓
Edge Environment A
Time T2
↓
Cloud Environment B
Time T3
↓
Platform Environment C
TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing.
ELDM governs only the spatial association. 23. Digital Location Precision
Digital spatial representation shall use only the precision supported by evidence and operational relevance.
Possible representations may include: specific execution instance; service; cluster; availability zone; cloud region; platform environment; logical environment; distributed environment; or qualified unknown digital location.
Technical Infrastructure Precision ≠ Governed Event Location Precision.
Greater technical detail does not automatically produce better governance. 24. Digital Location Uncertainty
Digital environments may obscure or dynamically change infrastructure location.
ELDM shall preserve uncertainty where the digital spatial reality cannot legitimately be reduced further.

Permissible states may include: exact; logical; regional; multi-region; distributed; dynamic; approximate; qualified; conflicted; partially established; or unresolved.
Unknown Infrastructure Geography ≠ Unknown Digital Event Location by Default.
A logical or distributed location may still be governed even where exact physical infrastructure geography is unavailable. 25. Digital Location Conflict
ELDM shall govern conflicts among digital-location signals.
Examples include: IP geolocation indicating one country; cloud execution indicating another; device location indicating another; platform profile indicating another; network routing indicating another; and user billing information indicating another.
Such differences do not necessarily represent evidence conflict.
They may represent different legitimate spatial dimensions.
Different Digital Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict by Default.
Conflict exists only where signals make incompatible claims about the same governed spatial dimension. 26. Digital Location Continuity
ELDM shall preserve continuity of Digital Event Location across changes in infrastructure where the event itself remains continuous.
Container migration, load balancing, failover, scaling, routing changes, or infrastructure replacement shall not automatically create a new event or new digital location identity.
Infrastructure Change ≠ Event Change by Default.
Failover ≠ New Event by Default. 27. Physical and Digital Location Separation

ELDM shall preserve the distinction established with ELPM.
A physical event may be digitally coordinated elsewhere.
A digital event may trigger physical execution elsewhere.
A machine may operate physically in one country while its digital control environment spans several others.
Therefore:
Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location.
Neither dimension automatically overrides the other.
Their relationship is governed later within TRELS. 28. Digital Location and Participant Location
Participant location shall not automatically establish Digital Event Location.
A participant may connect remotely to an event executed elsewhere.
A customer may travel.
A seller may operate through a platform.
An AI agent may act on behalf of an organization.
A machine may transact without contemporaneous human participation.
Therefore:
Participant Location ≠ Digital Event Location by Default.
TREPS governs participation.
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, and authority where applicable. 29. Digital Location and Corporate Location
Corporate headquarters, incorporation country, registered office, business establishment, billing entity, and contractual entity may be relevant downstream.
They do not automatically establish Digital Event Location.
Corporate Location ≠ Digital Event Location.
Company Registration ≠ Digital Execution Location.
Contracting Entity Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. 30. Digital Location and Tax Jurisdiction

ELDM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational digital location and jurisdiction-specific taxation.
Governed Event Digital Location may become an input to downstream tax analysis.
It does not itself determine: Tax Jurisdiction; digital tax nexus; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; tax residence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; place of effective management; customer location under tax law; supplier establishment; marketplace tax responsibility; legal situs; or any other jurisdiction-specific taxation criterion.
Digital Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus.
Cloud Region ≠ Permanent Establishment.
IP Geolocation ≠ Legal Place of Supply.
Digital Execution Location ≠ Tax Residence.
These determinations belong to jurisdiction-specific tax systems. 31. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness
ELDM shall preserve digital operational reality independently from jurisdiction-specific interpretation.
Canonical logic:
One Governed Digital Event Reality
↓
Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations
The same governed digital event may legitimately be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions.
TREGA™ therefore establishes the event representation once.
Jurisdictions subsequently apply their own legal rules. 32. Governance States
ELDM may assign states including:
Digital Location Ready Relevant digital spatial signals are available.
Digital Location Under Governance Candidate environments are being evaluated.

Digital Location Established A sufficient digital spatial representation has been established.
Digital Location Logical The event is legitimately represented through a logical digital environment.
Digital Location Multi-Region Material execution spans multiple regions.
Digital Location Dynamic Material digital location changes during the event.
Digital Location Distributed The digital event cannot legitimately be reduced to one execution location.
Digital Location Qualified The location is established subject to explicit qualification.
Digital Location Conflicted Material evidence concerning the same digital dimension conflicts.
Digital Location Unresolved Available evidence is insufficient for legitimate determination. 33. Governance Requirements

ELDM implementations shall: consume the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM; preserve the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM; identify materially relevant digital-location candidates; distinguish constitutive digital environments from supporting infrastructure; differentiate execution, processing, storage, routing, platform, device, and resource locations; support logical digital location; support cloud, edge, API, platform, AI-agent, autonomous-system, and machine-to-machine environments; support centralized, dynamic, multi-region, and distributed digital events; preserve digital-location transitions where materially relevant; preserve supported precision; preserve uncertainty and conflict; prevent infrastructure convenience from becoming location authority; maintain physical/digital separation; prevent jurisdiction-specific rules from redefining operational digital reality; maintain traceability; and produce a Governed Event Digital Location suitable for subsequent TRELS processing.
34. Governance Logic
ELDM follows the canonical logic:
Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
identify digital-location candidates
↓
determine their operational roles
↓
distinguish constitutive execution from supporting infrastructure
↓
evaluate logical, platform, cloud, edge, device, network, and distributed dimensions
↓
govern precision, uncertainty, continuity, and conflict
↓
establish Governed Event Digital Location.

Digital infrastructure shall describe operational reality.
It shall not silently determine legal geography. 35. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ELDM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference Reference to the event under digital-location governance.
Digital Location Identifier Unique reference for each governed digital location.
Digital Location Type Execution environment, platform, cloud region, edge environment, API environment, logical environment, network environment, device-associated environment, or other legitimate type.
Operational Role Constitutive, supporting, contextual, transitional, or other governed role.
Digital Environment Reference Relevant service, platform, cluster, region, logical environment, or infrastructure reference.
Physical Infrastructure Association Physical infrastructure relationship where known and materially relevant.
Temporal Association Relationship to governed Event Timing.
Execution State Whether material event execution occurs within the environment.
Distribution State Centralized, multi-region, dynamic, or distributed.
Precision State Supported digital-location precision.
Uncertainty State Known uncertainty.
Conflict State Known evidence conflict.
Evidence Reference Supporting operational evidence.
Traceability Reference Governance history enabling reconstruction.
Governance State Current ELDM determination state.
Handoff State Readiness for distributed-location governance. 36. Governance Outputs

ELDM may produce: Digital Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Digital Location Record; Digital Execution Location Record; Cloud Environment Record; Edge Environment Record; API Location Record; Platform Location Record; Device Location Association; Network Location Association; Logical Digital Location Record; AI Agent Execution Location Record; Machine-to-Machine Digital Location Record; Digital Location Transition Record; Digital Location Precision Record; Digital Location Uncertainty Record; Digital Location Conflict Record; Digital Location Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Event Digital Location
This output becomes an input to ELDSM. 37. Critical Distinctions
Digital Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Digital Location
Digital Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Digital Location
Supporting Digital Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Digital Location
Infrastructure Geography ≠ Digital Event Location
Server Location ≠ Event Digital Location
Cloud Region ≠ Event Digital Location
Infrastructure Instance Location ≠ Event Location
Edge Node Location ≠ Complete Event Digital Location
User Device Location ≠ Event Digital Location
IP Address ≠ Event Location
IP Geolocation ≠ Governed Digital Location
Network Transit Location ≠ Event Digital Location
Packet Route ≠ Event Location
API Endpoint ≠ Geographic Event Location
API Provider Location ≠ Event Digital Location
Platform Headquarters ≠ Event Digital Location

Platform Registration Country ≠ Event Digital Location
Data Storage Location ≠ Event Digital Location
Database Location ≠ Event Execution Location
Digital Resource Location ≠ Event Digital Location
AI Agent Location ≠ Server Location
AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location
AI Agent Location ≠ User Location
Autonomous Execution ≠ Human Supervisor Location
Participant Location ≠ Digital Event Location
Corporate Location ≠ Digital Event Location
Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location
Digital Location Change ≠ New Event
Infrastructure Change ≠ Event Change
Digital Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus
Cloud Region ≠ Permanent Establishment
IP Geolocation ≠ Legal Place of Supply
Digital Execution Location ≠ Tax Residence
Operational Digital Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 38. Enterprise Application
ELDM can operate as the digital spatial-governance layer between modern computational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure.
A generalized implementation pattern is:
Digital Platform / Cloud Service / API / AI Agent / Autonomous System / Machine Network
↓
ELIM
↓
ELPM
↓
ELDM
↓
Governed Event Digital Location
↓
ELDSM
↓
ELCM
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
↓
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines
This allows tax infrastructure to consume a governed representation of digital reality without forcing the event itself to adopt the assumptions of one tax regime. 39. Use Case 1 — Global AI Agent Transaction

An autonomous AI procurement agent operating for an enterprise identifies a supplier, negotiates through APIs, obtains authorization, initiates a digital purchase, and coordinates fulfillment.
The agent's orchestration service operates through a European cloud region.
Model inference may occur in another region.
The supplier platform operates globally.
Payment authorization passes through infrastructure in additional countries.
The purchasing organization is headquartered elsewhere.
The human who configured the agent is not involved when the transaction occurs.
ELDM distinguishes the digital environments materially constituting the event from infrastructure that merely supports, routes, stores, or observes it.
It does not select the company's headquarters, server country, user location, IP geolocation, or cloud region as the legal location of the transaction.
The result is a governed digital spatial representation capable of being consumed by multiple jurisdictional tax systems.
Autonomous digital execution requires governed location before legal jurisdiction can legitimately interpret that location. 40. Use Case 2 — Multi-Region Digital Service
A customer accesses a digital service through a mobile device while traveling.
The account was created in another country.
The billing address belongs to another jurisdiction.
The service platform dynamically routes the session through edge infrastructure.
Application processing occurs across two cloud regions.

Data is replicated globally.
Payment is handled by a separate provider.
A conventional system may derive location from the IP address, billing country, server region, or customer profile depending on which field is available.
ELDM instead governs each signal according to its operational role.
It establishes the digital spatial structure of the event without allowing any single technical or administrative signal to become authoritative by default.
The digital event is governed as it actually operates before any jurisdiction determines what that operational reality means under tax law. 41. Canonical Boundary
ELDM owns the governance of the digital spatial manifestation of the Tax-Relevant Event, including constitutive digital environments, digital execution locations, cloud and edge environments, API environments, platform environments, device-associated locations, network-associated locations, logical digital locations, AI-agent execution environments, autonomous-system digital environments, machine-to-machine digital locations, digital-location transitions, digital-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability.
ELDM does not own final Distributed Event Location or final Event Location Correlation.
It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Physical Event Location, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance.

It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, digital tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, customer location under tax law, supplier establishment, marketplace tax responsibility, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The canonical handoff is:
ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location
↓
ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location
↓
ELDSM — Event Distributed Location Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ELDM establishes where the governed event materially exists and operates within digital environments without allowing servers, IP addresses, cloud regions, devices, platforms, network routes, or corporate locations to become authoritative merely because they can be geographically identified.
Digital infrastructure can reveal where parts of an event operate. It cannot, by itself, determine where the event legally belongs.
ELDM governs where the event occurs digitally — not which jurisdiction may tax the digital activity.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
