Canonical Definition
The Event Distributed Location Module (ELDSM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event is spatially represented when its materially constitutive activity occurs across multiple physical, digital, hybrid, machine, autonomous, or infrastructural locations and cannot legitimately be reduced to one operational location without distorting the reality of the event.
ELDSM operates on the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM and the Governed Event Digital Location established by ELDM.
Its canonical task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Distributed Location where multiple locations materially constitute the same governed event, without forcing that event into an artificial single-location representation or converting distributed operational reality into jurisdiction-specific tax allocation.
The principal transition is:
Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location
↓
Governed Event Distributed Location
ELDSM governs spatial distribution of the event.
It does not determine how taxation rights, tax bases, revenues, profits, obligations, or liabilities are allocated among jurisdictions.
Operational Role
Modern economic activity increasingly occurs across distributed operational environments.
A single governed event may involve: physical activity in several places; digital execution across several cloud regions; edge and central infrastructure; machines operating at different sites; autonomous agents invoking services across multiple systems; platform activity spanning several operational environments; distributed ledger infrastructure; cross-border logistics; remote control and physical execution; or simultaneous physical and digital activity.
Traditional systems often attempt to reduce such events to one location.
They may select: customer country; seller country; server country; billing address; headquarters; IP location; transaction-processing location; device location; or another convenient geographic proxy.

Such reduction may simplify downstream processing while materially misrepresenting the event.
ELDSM exists to prevent that distortion.
Where the event is genuinely distributed, its governed location may also be distributed.
Distributed Operational Reality ≠ Governance Failure.
A legitimate governance result does not require artificial spatial simplicity.
Internal Flow
Within TRELS, ELDSM occupies the fourth operational position:
ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented?
↓
ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation?
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
ELDSM receives:
Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location
and produces:
Governed Event Distributed Location
for final location correlation by ELCM.
Operational Space
ELDSM governs distributed spatial representation of Tax-Relevant Events.

Its operational space includes: multi-location events; cross-border operational events; distributed physical events; distributed digital events; hybrid physical-digital events; multi-site operations; multi-region digital execution; edge-cloud distribution; machine-to-machine distribution; autonomous-system distribution; AI-agent distributed execution; distributed infrastructure; distributed platform operations; multi-node events; distributed transaction execution; distributed service delivery; distributed production; distributed logistics; distributed financial operations; location transitions; simultaneous multi-location activity; sequential multi-location activity; location contribution; location dependency; distributed-location continuity; distributed-location precision; distributed-location uncertainty; distributed-location conflict; and distributed-location traceability.
Operational Scope
ELDSM shall support distributed-location governance for: international commerce; digital marketplaces; cloud computing; distributed applications; AI services; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine economies; robotics; industrial automation; IoT networks; telecommunications; banking; financial infrastructure; payment networks; logistics; manufacturing; supply chains; digital assets; distributed ledgers; remote services; cross-border professional services; platform economies; infrastructure operations; and future decentralized or machine-mediated economic systems.

1. Distributed Location Candidate Identification
ELDSM shall identify whether the governed physical and digital locations indicate that materially constitutive parts of the same event occur across more than one location.
A Distributed Location Candidate exists where multiple locations may legitimately belong to the same governed event.
However:
Multiple Location Signals ≠ Distributed Event by Default.
The locations must materially relate to the bounded event itself. 2. Constitutive Location Assessment
ELDSM shall distinguish locations constituting the event from locations that merely support, observe, record, route, finance, administer, or provide infrastructure to it.
A location may be relevant without being constitutive.
Therefore:
Relevant Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default.
Only locations with a materially justified operational relationship to the event shall form the Governed Event Distributed Location. 3. Distributed Event Determination
ELDSM shall determine whether the event is legitimately represented as distributed.
A distributed representation is appropriate where: no single location sufficiently represents the event; multiple locations contain constitutive activity; the event exists through coordinated activity across locations; physical and digital components materially interact across locations; execution migrates between locations; or simultaneous distributed execution forms part of the event.
Multiple Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default.

The Event Boundary remains governed by TREBS.
ELDSM shall not fragment one bounded event merely because its spatial reality is complex. 4. Physical Distribution
An event may contain constitutive physical activity across multiple locations.
Examples include: goods moving through multiple operational stages; coordinated manufacturing across facilities; infrastructure operations across sites; distributed energy systems; multi-site industrial processes; logistics networks; or machines performing coordinated operations in different locations.
ELDSM shall preserve those locations where they materially form part of the same event.
Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. 5. Digital Distribution
Digital events may execute across multiple computational environments.
Relevant locations may include: cloud regions; edge nodes; execution clusters; platform environments; API services; autonomous-agent environments; distributed databases; or networked machine systems.
Where these environments materially constitute the event:
Distributed Digital Execution ≠ Single Digital Location by Default.
ELDSM shall preserve the distributed structure rather than selecting one infrastructure component as the authoritative location. 6. Hybrid Physical-Digital Distribution
Many modern events combine physical and digital activity.
For example:
Physical Machine
↓
Edge Controller
↓
Cloud AI Service
↓
External API
↓
Machine Execution

The event may therefore possess both physical and digital spatial dimensions.
ELDSM shall permit a hybrid distributed representation.
Physical Location + Digital Location ≠ Requirement to Select One Dominant Location.
Both may legitimately belong to the governed event. 7. Simultaneous Distribution
Constitutive activity may occur in several locations at the same time.
ELDSM shall support simultaneous multi-location representation.
Examples include: distributed computing; synchronized industrial systems; multi-node autonomous operations; replicated digital execution; coordinated machine networks; or concurrent platform processes.
Simultaneous Multi-Location Activity ≠ Spatial Conflict.
Several locations can legitimately describe one event simultaneously. 8. Sequential Distribution
An event may move through locations over time.
For example:
Location A
↓
Location B
↓
Location C
ELDSM shall preserve this spatial progression where all stages remain within the same governed Event Boundary.
Location Transition ≠ New Event by Default.
TRETS governs the temporal structure.
ELDSM governs the spatial progression. 9. Dynamic Location
Some events possess locations that change dynamically.
Examples include: mobile machines; vehicles; aircraft; vessels; mobile devices; migrating cloud workloads; autonomous robots; mobile edge systems; or dynamic digital services.
ELDSM shall support dynamic location without requiring every location change to create a new event.

Changing Location ≠ Changing Event Identity by Default. 10. Location Contribution
Not every constitutive location contributes equally to the event.
ELDSM may represent the operational contribution of locations where supported by evidence.
Possible states may include: primary constitutive; secondary constitutive; supporting constitutive; transitional; simultaneous; sequential; conditional; or indeterminate.
However:
Operational Location Contribution ≠ Tax Allocation Weight.
A location's operational significance shall not automatically become a percentage of taxation rights, profit allocation, or tax base. 11. Primary Location
Some distributed events may possess an operationally dominant location.
ELDSM may identify such a location where evidence supports it.
However:
Primary Operational Location ≠ Exclusive Event Location.
Primary Operational Location ≠ Primary Tax Jurisdiction.
Dominance shall not erase other constitutive locations. 12. No Primary Location
A distributed event may legitimately have no single primary location.
This is a valid governance outcome.
No Single Primary Location ≠ Unresolved Event Location.
Where operational reality is genuinely distributed, the correct representation may be:
Governed Distributed Location — No Single Dominant Location
rather than an artificial geographic assignment. 13. Distributed Cloud Execution
Cloud services may distribute event execution dynamically across multiple regions.

ELDSM shall distinguish: deliberate multi-region execution; dynamic workload migration; redundancy; replication; failover; storage distribution; and constitutive processing.
Only materially constitutive locations shall form the distributed event representation.
Cloud Replication ≠ Distributed Event Execution by Default.
Redundant Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default. 14. Edge-Cloud Distribution
An event may begin at an edge device, undergo local processing, invoke cloud services, and return a result to physical infrastructure.
ELDSM shall preserve this structure where the components form one bounded event.
Edge Location ≠ Complete Event Location.
Cloud Location ≠ Complete Event Location.
The legitimate governed representation may be their operationally justified combination. 15. AI Agent Distributed Location
AI agents may operate through: orchestration environments; model providers; external tools; APIs; databases; payment systems; digital platforms; physical machines; and other agents.
The agent's activity may therefore have no stable single digital location.
ELDSM shall govern the distributed operational environments materially constituting the event.
AI Agent Distributed Execution ≠ Agent Legal Residence.
AI Agent Execution Geography ≠ Owner Tax Residence.
AI Agent Infrastructure Distribution ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Allocation. 16. Autonomous-System Distribution

Autonomous systems may coordinate decisions and actions across multiple physical and digital locations without contemporaneous human control.
ELDSM shall preserve this spatial reality independently from the location of: system owner; operator; developer; supervising organization; manufacturer; or human beneficiary.
Autonomous Event Location ≠ Human Controller Location by Default. 17. Machine-to-Machine Distribution
Machine-to-machine events may involve machines physically located in different places while their communications and decision processes operate through distributed digital infrastructure.
ELDSM shall support representation such as:
Machine A Physical Location + Machine B Physical Location + Edge Environment + Cloud Execution Environment
↓
Governed Event Distributed Location
without prematurely assigning the event to one jurisdiction. 18. Platform Distribution
Platforms may coordinate events across: buyers; sellers; service providers; infrastructure; payment systems; logistics providers; and digital services.
ELDSM shall govern only locations materially constituting the bounded event.
Platform Global Presence ≠ Event Distributed Location by Default.
A platform's worldwide infrastructure shall not automatically become the spatial footprint of every event processed through it. 19. Distributed Ledger Environments
Events involving distributed ledgers may be technically replicated across many nodes.

Node distribution alone shall not establish the distributed location of the event.
Ledger Node Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution by Default.
ELDSM shall determine whether specific distributed components materially constitute the governed event rather than merely maintaining replicated infrastructure. 20. Network Distribution
Network traffic may traverse numerous jurisdictions.
Transit does not automatically constitute event distribution.
Network Path ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default.
Routing infrastructure shall be included only where its operational role materially forms part of the event. 21. Data Distribution
Event-related data may be stored or replicated globally.
Such distribution shall not automatically create distributed Event Location.
Distributed Data Storage ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default.
Storage becomes spatially constitutive only where its role forms part of the governed event itself. 22. Distributed Service Delivery
Services may be delivered through multiple locations.
For example, a digital service may involve: customer interaction in one place; computational execution elsewhere; specialized processing elsewhere; and physical fulfillment elsewhere.
ELDSM shall preserve materially constitutive locations without forcing them into one geographic point.
Distributed Service Delivery ≠ Single Place of Supply by Default.
Legal place-of-supply determination remains outside TREGA™. 23. Distributed Production

Production may occur across several facilities or machine environments while remaining part of one governed event.
ELDSM shall preserve the spatial structure established by operational evidence.
It shall not infer: origin law; customs origin; tax situs; permanent establishment; transfer-pricing allocation; or taxation rights.
Operational Production Location ≠ Legal Origin Determination. 24. Distributed Logistics
Logistics events may involve movement through many locations.
ELDSM shall distinguish spatial progression belonging to one event from separate events formed under TREFS and bounded under TREBS.
Route Complexity ≠ Event Multiplicity by Default.
A multi-location journey can remain one governed event where its Event Boundary supports that representation. 25. Cross-Border Distribution
A Tax-Relevant Event may operationally cross national borders.
ELDSM shall record such distribution where materially relevant.
However:
Cross-Border Event ≠ Multi-Jurisdiction Tax Liability by Default.
Operational border crossing may become an input to jurisdiction-specific tax or customs analysis.
It is not itself a legal conclusion. 26. Distribution and Event Boundary
ELDSM shall not redefine the Event Boundary merely because the event spans multiple locations.
TREBS remains authoritative for Event Boundary.
Spatial Distribution ≠ Boundary Expansion by Default.

A location belongs to the distributed representation only where the activity at that location is already legitimately associated with the bounded event. 27. Distribution and Event Timing
Distributed locations may correspond to different points or intervals in Event Timing.
ELDSM shall support temporal-spatial association such as:
T1
↓
Physical Location A
T2
↓
Digital Environment B
T3
↓
Physical Location C + Cloud Environment D
T4
↓
Distributed Execution E/F/G
TRETS owns Event Timing.
ELDSM owns distributed spatial representation. 28. Distribution and Participation
Participants may operate from locations different from the locations constituting the event.
Therefore:
Participant Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution by Default.
TREPS governs Event Participation.
ELDSM shall not infer taxpayer status, participant legal residence, identity, authority, or responsibility from spatial distribution. 29. Distribution and Value
Value may originate, move, change state, develop, degrade, or be recognized across different locations.
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
ELDSM may associate governed spatial information with an event involving value.
It shall not determine value ownership or value lifecycle state.
Distributed Value Activity ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default. 30. Distribution and Event Relationships
Multiple events may occur in different locations and remain related.
Conversely, one event may occur across multiple locations.
These are distinct governance questions.

Multiple Locations Within One Event ≠ Multiple Related Events.
Multiple Related Events ≠ One Distributed Event.
TRERLS governs Event Relationships.
ELDSM governs spatial distribution within the bounded event. 31. Distribution Precision
ELDSM shall represent distributed locations only at precision supported by evidence and operational relevance.
Possible levels may include: exact point; facility; city; region; country; cloud region; logical digital environment; multi-region environment; network zone; distributed physical network; distributed digital environment; or qualified unknown location.
More Location Data ≠ Greater Governance Precision by Default. 32. Distribution Uncertainty
Some constitutive locations may be known while others remain uncertain.
ELDSM shall permit partial spatial governance.
For example:
Location A — Established
Location B — Established
Location C — Regional Only
Digital Environment D — Distributed / Exact Infrastructure Unknown
The event may still possess a legitimate Governed Event Distributed Location.
Partial Location Uncertainty ≠ Total Location Failure. 33. Distribution Conflict
Conflicting evidence concerning one spatial component shall not invalidate correctly established components.
ELDSM shall isolate the conflict.
One Conflicted Location ≠ Entire Distributed Location Invalid.
Likewise:
Multiple Different Locations ≠ Conflict by Default.
Different locations may all legitimately constitute the event. 34. Distribution Continuity

Distributed spatial representation shall preserve continuity as locations enter, leave, migrate, fail, recover, or change during the event.
A constitutive location may cease participation while the event continues elsewhere.
Location Departure ≠ Event Completion.
Location Addition ≠ New Event by Default.
Infrastructure Failover ≠ Event Replacement by Default. 35. Distributed Location Traceability
Every constitutive location shall remain traceable to: source evidence; operational role; Event Boundary; relevant Event Timing; location type; confidence; uncertainty; conflicts; corrections; and governance decisions.
A downstream system shall be able to reconstruct why a location was included in or excluded from the distributed representation. 36. Distributed Location Correction
Distributed Event Location may require correction when evidence changes.
Corrections shall preserve governance history.
Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
A corrected location record shall preserve the previous state, reason for correction, supporting evidence, and resulting state where required. 37. Distributed Location and Tax Jurisdiction
ELDSM shall maintain a strict separation between distributed operational reality and legal jurisdiction allocation.

It shall not determine: Tax Jurisdiction; tax nexus; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; place of supply; source jurisdiction; residence; legal situs; customs origin; taxable presence; taxing rights; tax-base allocation; profit allocation; revenue allocation; transfer-pricing outcome; or jurisdiction-specific tax liability.
Distributed Event Location ≠ Distributed Tax Liability.
Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Tax Jurisdictions by Default.
Operational Location Contribution ≠ Taxing Rights Allocation.
Cross-Border Distribution ≠ Legal Nexus Determination.
Distributed Digital Infrastructure ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default. 38. Jurisdiction-Neutral Representation
ELDSM shall preserve the event independently from the legal rules of any single jurisdiction.
The canonical logic is:
One Distributed Operational Event
↓
One Governed Distributed Event Representation
↓
Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations
Jurisdiction A may legally interpret the event differently from Jurisdiction B.
Jurisdiction C may apply another nexus, source, place-of-supply, residence, or allocation rule.
TREGA™ shall not alter the underlying governed event to satisfy any one of them. 39. Governance States
ELDSM may assign states including:
Distribution Ready Sufficient physical and digital location inputs exist.
Distribution Under Governance Potential constitutive locations are being assessed.

Distribution Not Required A distributed representation is not operationally justified.
Distribution Established Multiple constitutive locations are sufficiently governed.
Distribution Sequential The event progresses through multiple locations.
Distribution Simultaneous Constitutive activity occurs in multiple locations concurrently.
Distribution Hybrid Physical and digital locations jointly constitute the event.
Distribution Dynamic Constitutive locations materially change during the event.
Distribution Partial Some spatial components are established while others remain unresolved.
Distribution Qualified The representation is subject to explicit qualifications.
Distribution Conflicted Material evidence concerning one or more spatial components conflicts.
Distribution Unresolved Available evidence cannot support a legitimate distributed representation. 40. Governance Requirements

ELDSM implementations shall: consume Governed Event Physical Location from ELPM; consume Governed Event Digital Location from ELDM; determine whether distributed spatial representation is operationally justified; distinguish multiple location signals from genuine event distribution; identify constitutive locations; distinguish constitutive from supporting locations; support physical distribution; support digital distribution; support hybrid physical-digital distribution; support simultaneous distribution; support sequential distribution; support dynamic location; support AI-agent, autonomous-system, and machine-to-machine distribution; preserve Event Boundary; preserve temporal-spatial association; preserve supported precision; preserve uncertainty; isolate location conflicts; preserve continuity; preserve corrections; maintain traceability; prevent artificial single-location reduction; prevent operational distribution from becoming legal jurisdiction allocation; and produce a Governed Event Distributed Location suitable for ELCM.
41. Governance Logic
ELDSM follows the canonical logic:
Governed Physical Location + Governed Digital Location
↓
identify potential spatial distribution
↓
determine which locations materially constitute the same bounded event
↓
classify physical, digital, hybrid, simultaneous, sequential, and dynamic distribution
↓
preserve temporal association, precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability
↓

establish Governed Event Distributed Location.
Where one location legitimately represents the event, ELDSM shall not manufacture complexity.
Where several locations legitimately constitute the event, ELDSM shall not manufacture simplicity. 42. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ELDSM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference Reference to the bounded event.
Distributed Location Identifier Unique identifier for the governed distributed-location structure.
Constitutive Location References Locations forming the distributed event representation.
Location Type Physical, digital, or hybrid.
Distribution Type Sequential, simultaneous, dynamic, hybrid, or other legitimate form.
Operational Role Role of each location in the event.
Contribution State Operational significance where legitimately established.
Temporal Association Relevant governed Event Timing for each spatial component.
Primary Location State Primary, non-primary, no-primary, or unresolved.
Distribution Precision Supported spatial precision.
Distribution Uncertainty Known uncertainty.
Distribution Conflict Known evidence conflict.
Evidence References Evidence supporting inclusion or exclusion.
Continuity State Location continuity through the event.
Correction History Material spatial corrections.
Traceability Reference Governance history.
Governance State Current ELDSM state.
Handoff State Readiness for Event Location Correlation. 43. Governance Outputs

ELDSM may produce: Distributed Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Location Register; Physical Distribution Record; Digital Distribution Record; Hybrid Distribution Record; Sequential Location Record; Simultaneous Location Record; Dynamic Location Record; Location Contribution Record; Primary Location Assessment; No-Primary-Location Determination; Temporal-Spatial Association Record; Distribution Precision Record; Distribution Uncertainty Record; Distribution Conflict Record; Distribution Continuity Record; Distribution Correction Record; Distribution Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Event Distributed Location
This output becomes an input to ELCM. 44. Critical Distinctions
Multiple Location Signals ≠ Distributed Event
Relevant Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location
Multiple Locations ≠ Multiple Events
Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events
Distributed Digital Execution ≠ Single Digital Location
Physical Location + Digital Location ≠ Requirement to Select One Dominant Location
Simultaneous Multi-Location Activity ≠ Spatial Conflict
Location Transition ≠ New Event
Changing Location ≠ Changing Event Identity
Operational Location Contribution ≠ Tax Allocation Weight
Primary Operational Location ≠ Exclusive Event Location
Primary Operational Location ≠ Primary Tax Jurisdiction
No Single Primary Location ≠ Unresolved Event Location
Cloud Replication ≠ Distributed Event Execution
Redundant Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Event Location

Edge Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Cloud Location ≠ Complete Event Location
AI Agent Distributed Execution ≠ Agent Legal Residence
AI Agent Execution Geography ≠ Owner Tax Residence
Autonomous Event Location ≠ Human Controller Location
Platform Global Presence ≠ Event Distributed Location
Ledger Node Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution
Network Path ≠ Distributed Event Location
Distributed Data Storage ≠ Distributed Event Location
Distributed Service Delivery ≠ Single Place of Supply
Operational Production Location ≠ Legal Origin Determination
Route Complexity ≠ Event Multiplicity
Cross-Border Event ≠ Multi-Jurisdiction Tax Liability
Spatial Distribution ≠ Boundary Expansion
Participant Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution
Multiple Locations Within One Event ≠ Multiple Related Events
Multiple Related Events ≠ One Distributed Event
Partial Location Uncertainty ≠ Total Location Failure
One Conflicted Location ≠ Entire Distributed Location Invalid
Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Distributed Event Location ≠ Distributed Tax Liability
Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Tax Jurisdictions
Operational Location Contribution ≠ Taxing Rights Allocation
Cross-Border Distribution ≠ Legal Nexus Determination
Distributed Digital Infrastructure ≠ Permanent Establishment 45. Enterprise Application
ELDSM can operate as the distributed spatial-governance layer between modern operational systems and downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation infrastructure.

A generalized implementation pattern is:
Physical Operations + Digital Platforms + Cloud Infrastructure + Edge Systems + AI Agents + Autonomous Machines
↓
ELIM
↓
ELPM
↓
ELDM
↓
ELDSM
↓
Governed Event Distributed Location
↓
ELCM
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
↓
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines
This allows the same governed event to remain operationally coherent even when several jurisdictions later evaluate it differently. 46. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Cross-Border Manufacturing Network
A multinational industrial network uses autonomous production systems across several facilities.
A machine in one country identifies a production requirement.
An AI orchestration service running through distributed cloud infrastructure generates a production plan.
A specialized component is manufactured at a second facility.
An autonomous logistics system transfers the component to a third facility.
Final machine processing occurs there.
Digital coordination continues across edge systems, cloud services, APIs, and machine controllers throughout the process.
If TREBS establishes that the relevant activity forms one bounded Tax-Relevant Event, ELDSM does not force that event into the country containing the first machine, the AI server, corporate headquarters, or final facility.
It governs the materially constitutive spatial structure of the event.
The output may legitimately contain multiple physical and digital locations.

It does not decide which country possesses taxation rights.
The event may be operationally distributed before any jurisdiction decides how that distribution matters under law. 47. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Global Digital Service
An AI agent autonomously acquires and coordinates a digital service.
The agent executes through one cloud environment.
Model inference occurs through an external provider in another region.
Data processing occurs across several regions.
A specialized API is invoked through another provider.
Payment infrastructure operates elsewhere.
The service is delivered to a machine-controlled system in another country.
No single technical location adequately represents the event.
Selecting the server location, customer device, corporate headquarters, billing country, or one cloud region would erase material parts of the operational reality.
ELDSM establishes a Governed Event Distributed Location containing only those physical and digital environments that materially constitute the event.
Downstream jurisdictions may then independently apply their own nexus, place-of-supply, source, residence, or other tax rules.
Distributed digital reality is governed once; legal jurisdictional interpretation may occur many times. 48. Canonical Boundary

ELDSM owns the governance of distributed spatial representation within the bounded Tax-Relevant Event, including physical distribution, digital distribution, hybrid distribution, simultaneous distribution, sequential distribution, dynamic location, constitutive-location assessment, operational location contribution, primary/no-primary location states, temporal-spatial association, distributed-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, correction, and traceability.
ELDSM does not own Event Location Signal Identification, which belongs to ELIM.
It does not own Physical Event Location, which belongs to ELPM.
It does not own Digital Event Location, which belongs to ELDM.
It does not own final Event Location Correlation, which belongs to ELCM.
It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance.
It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, legal situs, customs origin, taxable presence, taxing rights, tax-base allocation, revenue allocation, profit allocation, transfer-pricing outcome, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The canonical handoff is:

ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location
↓
ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location
↓
ELDSM — Governed Event Distributed Location
↓
ELCM — Event Location Correlation
Canonical Closing Statement
ELDSM preserves the spatial reality of events that genuinely exist across multiple physical, digital, machine, autonomous, or infrastructural locations without forcing operational complexity into an artificial single-location model.
A distributed event does not become geographically simple merely because a downstream system requires one country field.
ELDSM governs where the event is distributed — not how taxation rights are distributed among jurisdictions.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

OOF™ The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial
The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS)
Module: ELIM — Event Location Identification Module
Operational Layer: Event Location Identification Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Location Identification
Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELIM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial information potentially associated with a Governed Temporally Situated Event is discovered, identified, contextualized, differentiated, correlated, and qualified before any specific physical, digital, distributed, or composite Event Location is established.
ELIM creates the governed spatial-input layer required for subsequent Event Location governance.
Its canonical task is:

to establish a coherent and traceable Governed Event Location Signal Set representing the materially relevant spatial signals associated with the governed event without prematurely determining Physical Event Location, Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, place of supply, source jurisdiction, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
ELIM therefore answers:
What location information legitimately belongs to the event?
It does not yet answer:
What is the final governed location of the event?
And it never answers:
Which jurisdiction has authority to tax the event?
Operational Role
A modern event may generate numerous location-bearing signals.
These may originate from physical facilities, devices, users, machines, networks, servers, cloud regions, delivery points, payment infrastructure, operational systems, autonomous agents, transaction records, digital platforms, sensors, logistics systems, or other sources.
The existence of such information does not automatically establish Event Location.
ELIM determines which spatial signals are materially associated with the bounded event and creates the governed location evidence structure that subsequent TRELS modules can evaluate.
Its operational transition is:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
↓
Governed Event Location Signal Set

The module prevents downstream systems from selecting the easiest, earliest, most commercially convenient, or legally advantageous location signal and treating it as operational truth.
Internal Flow
Within TRELS, ELIM occupies the first operational position:
ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented?
↓
ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation?
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
ELIM therefore establishes the spatial signal foundation.
It does not perform the downstream determinations owned by ELPM, ELDM, ELDSM, or ELCM.
Operational Space
ELIM governs the identification layer between an event that has already been bounded and temporally situated and the subsequent determination of its operational spatial characteristics.

Its operational space includes: physical location signals; digital location signals; infrastructure location signals; device-derived location signals; machine-generated location signals; platform-recorded location signals; network-derived location signals; transaction-associated location signals; service-execution location signals; delivery and fulfillment location signals; participant-associated spatial signals where materially relevant to the event; distributed-system location signals; autonomous-system location signals; spatial metadata; location-source relationships; location-signal relevance; location-signal precision; location-signal uncertainty; location-signal ambiguity; conflicting location signals; spatial traceability.
The module governs these signals as potential descriptors of operational reality.
It does not assume that any one signal represents the Event Location.
Operational Scope
ELIM shall support the identification and governance of spatial signals associated with physical, digital, hybrid, distributed, transactional, service-based, machine-generated, autonomous, and value-affecting events.

The module shall be capable of distinguishing between: where an actor is located; where an object is located; where infrastructure is located; where a device is located; where a system records an event; where computation occurs; where a service executes; where goods move; where goods are delivered; where instructions originate; where an autonomous action executes; where payment processing occurs; where records are stored; and where the governed event itself may operationally occur.
These locations may coincide.
They must not be assumed to coincide. 1. Spatial Signal Discovery
ELIM shall identify available spatial signals materially associated with the Governed Temporally Situated Event.
A spatial signal may include a coordinate, address, facility identifier, device position, infrastructure region, network-derived location, system location attribute, delivery point, service execution environment, machine location, or another spatial descriptor.
Signal discovery shall not itself establish Event Location.
Available Location Data ≠ Governed Event Location.
The purpose of discovery is to identify the spatial evidence environment surrounding the event. 2. Spatial Signal Identification
Each materially relevant spatial signal shall be identifiable as a distinct governed object within the location-identification process.

Where feasible, the signal shall retain information concerning: source; type; spatial representation; associated event component; temporal relevance; precision; acquisition method; confidence or qualification state; transformation history; and traceability reference.
Spatial signals shall not be collapsed merely because they appear to reference the same geographic area.
Two signals may describe different operational dimensions of the same event. 3. Spatial Signal Source Governance
ELIM shall distinguish the source of location information from the operational meaning of that information.
Potential sources include: human-provided information; organizational records; sensors; mobile devices; machines; autonomous systems; platform records; logistics systems; payment systems; network infrastructure; cloud infrastructure; geolocation services; digital identity systems; transaction systems; or external evidence sources.
A source may provide useful spatial information without possessing authority to define Event Location.
Location Source ≠ Event-Location Authority by Default. 4. Physical and Digital Signal Differentiation
ELIM shall preserve the distinction between physical and digital spatial signals.
Physical signals may describe facilities, devices, machines, persons, goods, infrastructure, delivery destinations, or other physically situated components.

Digital signals may describe logical infrastructure, service execution environments, cloud regions, network endpoints, platform environments, or other digitally represented operational spaces.
The presence of a digital signal shall not automatically establish physical location.
The presence of a physical signal shall not automatically establish the location of a digital operation.
Digital Location Signal ≠ Physical Event Location.
Physical Location Signal ≠ Digital Event Location.
Final governance of these dimensions belongs to subsequent TRELS modules. 5. Participant-Associated Location Signals
Participants may produce location information materially relevant to an event.
Examples include customer location, provider location, employee location, machine operator location, autonomous-agent infrastructure location, organization address, or recipient location.
ELIM may identify these signals where they materially describe the event environment.
It shall not infer that Participant Location is automatically Event Location.
Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Participant identity and participation governance remain outside ELIM. 6. Infrastructure Location Signals
Digital and machine-mediated events may rely upon infrastructure distributed across multiple places.

ELIM may identify locations associated with: servers; data centers; cloud regions; edge infrastructure; telecommunications infrastructure; payment infrastructure; machine controllers; industrial facilities; storage infrastructure; or computational environments.
Infrastructure location may be operationally relevant.
It shall not automatically define the location of the event.
Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 7. Device and Machine Location Signals
Devices, robots, industrial machines, vehicles, sensors, autonomous systems, and connected equipment may generate precise spatial information.
ELIM shall distinguish the location of the device or machine from the spatial meaning of the event.
A machine may participate in an event without its physical location being sufficient to represent the complete event.
Similarly, a mobile device may generate geolocation data without proving that the relevant economic or operational event occurred at that exact position.
Device Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 8. Network-Derived Location Signals
IP addresses, network endpoints, routing information, telecommunications records, and similar technical signals may provide spatial indicators.
ELIM may identify these signals where materially relevant.
Network-derived location shall be qualified according to its evidential characteristics and operational meaning.
IP Location ≠ Event Location by Default.

Technical geolocation may contribute to Event Location governance without becoming operational truth merely because it is machine-readable. 9. Transaction and Payment Location Signals
Transaction systems may associate events with merchant locations, terminal locations, bank locations, payment-processor locations, account addresses, settlement locations, or other spatial attributes.
ELIM shall distinguish such signals from the location of the underlying governed event.
Payment Processing Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Settlement Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Financial infrastructure may describe part of the event environment without defining where the event itself occurred. 10. Delivery and Fulfillment Location Signals
Events involving physical goods may contain origin, dispatch, transit, warehouse, transfer, delivery, collection, and destination locations.
ELIM shall identify materially relevant signals without assuming that any one logistics point constitutes the Event Location.
The meaning of each location depends upon the bounded event under governance.
Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. 11. Service Execution Location Signals
A service may involve several operational locations.
The customer, service provider, personnel, platform, infrastructure, data processing, and actual service execution may all be spatially separated.
ELIM shall identify the relevant signals while preserving their distinct operational meanings.

For digital services, a server or cloud region shall not automatically become the service's governed Event Location.
For human-delivered services, corporate registration address shall not automatically become the operational location of service performance. 12. Distributed Location Signal Sets
An event may legitimately contain materially relevant spatial signals from several locations.
ELIM shall not treat multiplicity as an error requiring artificial reduction.
Multiple Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict by Default.
Several signals may accurately describe different spatial dimensions of one governed event.
Determining whether the event is genuinely distributed belongs downstream within TRELS. 13. Spatial Signal Correlation
ELIM shall establish relevant associations between identified spatial signals and the bounded event.
Correlation may consider: event component; activity; object; infrastructure; participant role; machine action; transaction stage; service stage; temporal position; or other legitimate event relationships.
Correlation shall preserve distinctions among signals.
Spatial Correlation ≠ Spatial Equivalence.
Two signals associated with the same event need not describe the same location function. 14. Spatial Relevance Assessment
Not every location appearing in surrounding systems materially describes the governed event.

ELIM shall support differentiation among: materially relevant location signals; contextual location signals; supporting location signals; technically generated but operationally weak signals; administratively associated signals; redundant signals; and unrelated spatial information.
The purpose is not to eliminate complexity but to prevent irrelevant location data from acquiring false governance significance. 15. Location Precision
Spatial signals may exist at different levels of precision.
Examples include: exact coordinates; facility; building; site; municipality; region; country; infrastructure zone; cloud region; network region; or unknown / qualified spatial range.
ELIM shall preserve the precision legitimately supported by the underlying information.
Recorded Spatial Precision ≠ Proven Spatial Accuracy.
A coordinate with many decimal places is not automatically more operationally reliable than a qualified facility-level location. 16. Spatial Ambiguity
Where available information supports more than one legitimate spatial interpretation, ELIM shall preserve that ambiguity.
Systems shall not manufacture false precision solely because downstream data structures require a single location field.
A governed result may legitimately indicate: approximate location; bounded location; multiple candidate locations; distributed spatial signals; conflicting location information; or unresolved location.

Required Location Field ≠ Permission to Invent Location Certainty. 17. Conflicting Location Signals
Conflicting signals shall be identifiable and traceable.
Conflict may arise because: systems use different location sources; devices report inconsistent positions; network-derived location differs from physical location; participant information is outdated; infrastructure is distributed; timestamps correspond to different operational stages; records were transformed; or systems apply different location conventions.
ELIM shall not resolve such conflict by arbitrary source preference.
System Preference ≠ Governed Spatial Resolution. 18. Machine and Autonomous Event Environments
Autonomous systems may generate large volumes of location-bearing information.
An autonomous economic event may involve: an AI agent operating through one infrastructure environment; a robot acting in another location; a cloud service executing elsewhere; a payment system in another region; and a recipient in another location.
ELIM shall identify the materially relevant spatial signals without equating infrastructure topology with Event Location.
Machine Location Data Volume ≠ Event Spatial Granularity.
One Machine Location ≠ One Event Location. 19. Location Normalization
Spatial data may require normalization for interoperability.
Normalization may include standardized coordinates, address structures, facility identifiers, region identifiers, or other spatial representations.

The original location information shall remain traceable where material.
Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence.
Normalization shall improve interoperability without rewriting the spatial evidence history of the event. 20. Location Signal Correction
Where a spatial signal is later shown to be incorrect, incomplete, or improperly associated, correction shall remain traceable.
Correction shall not silently erase the previous state where historical reconstruction is required.
Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Correction of a signal also does not automatically change the Event Boundary or create a new event. 21. Governance Requirements
ELIM implementations shall: identify materially relevant spatial signals; preserve signal-source traceability; distinguish signal type from Event Location; distinguish physical, digital, infrastructure, participant, device, machine, transaction, and other location dimensions; preserve legitimate spatial multiplicity; identify ambiguity and conflict; maintain appropriate spatial precision; avoid false geographic certainty; preserve original spatial evidence where normalization occurs; support distributed and autonomous environments; prevent downstream legal assumptions from redefining operational spatial information; and produce a governed location signal set suitable for subsequent TRELS processing.

No individual spatial signal shall become authoritative Event Location solely because it is technically available, commercially convenient, administratively preferred, or required by a downstream tax system. 22. Governance Logic
ELIM follows the canonical logic:
Location information exists
↓
identify its source
↓
determine its relationship to the governed event
↓
classify its spatial function
↓
assess material relevance
↓
preserve precision
↓
identify ambiguity or conflict
↓
correlate legitimate signals
↓
establish Governed Event Location Signal Set.
The module deliberately stops before final Event Location determination. 23. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ELIM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference Reference to the event received from TRETS.
Spatial Signal Identifier Unique reference for each materially relevant spatial signal.
Spatial Signal Type Physical, digital, infrastructure, device, machine, participant-associated, network-derived, transactional, logistics, service-execution, or other legitimate category.
Spatial Signal Source System, device, actor, infrastructure, record, or evidence source producing the signal.
Spatial Representation The location information itself at the legitimately supported precision.
Event Association Relationship between the signal and the governed event.
Operational Function The spatial role represented by the signal.

Temporal Association Relevant relationship between the location signal and governed Event Timing where necessary.
Precision State Level of spatial precision legitimately supported.
Relevance State Material, contextual, supporting, weak, redundant, excluded, or unresolved.
Ambiguity State Known ambiguity associated with the signal.
Conflict State Known conflict with other spatial signals.
Traceability Reference Evidence or governance reference supporting reconstruction.
Governance State Current state of the signal within ELIM.
Handoff State Readiness for downstream Physical, Digital, Distributed, and Correlation governance. 24. Governance Outputs
ELIM may produce: Spatial Signal Register; Spatial Source Map; Spatial Relevance Assessment; Physical Signal Set; Digital Signal Set; Infrastructure Signal Set; Machine / Autonomous Spatial Signal Set; Spatial Precision Record; Spatial Ambiguity Record; Spatial Conflict Record; Spatial Correlation Map; Spatial Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Event Location Signal Set
This output becomes the spatial governance input for ELPM. 25. Critical Distinctions
Location Data ≠ Event Location
Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Location
Location Source ≠ Event-Location Authority
Participant Location ≠ Event Location
Organization Address ≠ Event Location
Device Location ≠ Event Location
Machine Location ≠ Event Location
Server Location ≠ Event Location
Cloud Region ≠ Event Location
IP Location ≠ Event Location

Payment Processing Location ≠ Event Location
Settlement Location ≠ Event Location
Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Digital Location Signal ≠ Physical Event Location
Physical Location Signal ≠ Digital Event Location
Multiple Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict
Spatial Correlation ≠ Spatial Equivalence
Recorded Precision ≠ Proven Accuracy
Required Location Field ≠ Governed Location Certainty
Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence
Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Operational Spatial Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 26. Enterprise Application
ELIM can operate as the spatial-input governance layer between operational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure.
A generalized implementation pattern is:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Digital Platform / Logistics / Cloud / AI Agent / Machine System
↓
Spatial Signal Discovery
↓
ELIM
↓
Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
TRELS Location Modules
↓
Governed Event Location
↓
TREGA™ Event Layer
↓
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines
This allows organizations to preserve one governed operational representation of spatial reality while enabling multiple downstream legal systems to interpret that reality independently. 27. Use Case 1 — Distributed Digital Marketplace
A customer initiates a digital purchase from a mobile device in Country A.
The platform operator is established in Country B.
Authentication infrastructure operates in Country C.

The application executes through cloud regions in Countries D and E.
Payment authorization is processed through Country F.
The customer's account contains an address in Country G.
The platform therefore contains several technically valid location signals.
A conventional implementation may select the customer's IP address, billing address, merchant address, or server region and immediately treat it as transaction location.
ELIM instead identifies each materially relevant spatial signal, records its source and operational function, preserves its precision, and establishes its relationship to the governed event.
It does not decide which location is the final Event Location.
It does not decide which country may tax the transaction.
The output is a Governed Event Location Signal Set that subsequent TRELS modules can evaluate.
Complex spatial reality must be governed before it is compressed into a legal jurisdictional conclusion. 28. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Event
An AI-controlled production network receives a manufacturing requirement.
Planning occurs through cloud infrastructure in one country.
A robotic production cell operates in another.
Components arrive from a separate facility.
Machine coordination uses edge infrastructure in another region.
Quality verification occurs through remote computational infrastructure.
The finished component is transferred to an autonomous logistics system serving another country.

Thousands of machine, sensor, infrastructure, network, and logistics records contain location information.
ELIM identifies which spatial signals materially belong to the governed event and distinguishes machine location, infrastructure location, computational location, logistics location, and other relevant spatial dimensions.
It does not allow the physical position of the AI infrastructure, the robot, or a server to become Event Location automatically.
The location of the machine performing an action is evidence about the event — not automatically the complete spatial identity of the event. 29. Canonical Boundary
ELIM owns the identification, contextualization, differentiation, relevance assessment, correlation, precision qualification, ambiguity recognition, conflict recognition, normalization traceability, and governance of spatial signals materially associated with the Tax-Relevant Event.
ELIM does not determine final Physical Event Location, Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, or final Event Location Correlation.
It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance.

It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, tax residence, permanent establishment, place of supply, source jurisdiction, customs jurisdiction, taxpayer status, legal taxability, Tax Liability, Tax Period, Legal Tax Point, tax rate, tax calculation, filing obligation, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The canonical handoff is:
TRETS — Governed Temporally Situated Event
↓
ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM — Event Physical Location Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ELIM establishes which spatial signals legitimately describe the governed event before any individual address, device, machine, server, infrastructure region, or participant location is permitted to define where that event occurred.
ELIM identifies the locations that may describe the event — it does not yet decide the final Event Location, and it never decides the Tax Jurisdiction.
