Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS)
Module: ELPM — Event Physical Location Module
Operational Layer: Event Physical Location Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Physical Location
Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELPM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Physical Location Module (ELPM) governs how materially relevant physical spatial signals associated with a Tax-Relevant Event are evaluated, differentiated, qualified, and assembled into a governed representation of where the event physically occurred, was performed, manifested, or materially interacted with operational reality.
ELPM operates on the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM and determines the physical spatial characteristics legitimately attributable to the event.
Its canonical task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Physical Location without allowing participant addresses, device coordinates, infrastructure positions, contractual locations, administrative records, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine the physical location of the governed event.
The principal transition is:
Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
Governed Event Physical Location
ELPM determines physical Event Location.
It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction.
Operational Role
Physical events frequently involve more than one location.
Goods may be produced in one facility, inspected in another, transferred through several logistics nodes, and delivered elsewhere.
A service may involve a provider, customer, equipment, and operational object situated in different places.
An autonomous machine may act physically in one country while being controlled through infrastructure located elsewhere.
A transaction may contain addresses belonging to participants, payment systems, warehouses, corporate entities, and delivery destinations without any one of those addresses fully representing where the governed event physically occurred.
ELPM establishes which physical locations materially constitute, host, contain, support, or otherwise describe the physical manifestation of the event.
Its purpose is not to find a convenient geographic field.
Its purpose is to govern physical spatial reality.
Internal Flow

Within TRELS, ELPM occupies the second operational position:
ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event?
↓
ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented?
↓
ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation?
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
ELPM receives:
Governed Event Location Signal Set
and produces:
Governed Event Physical Location
for subsequent integration with digital and distributed location governance.
Operational Space
ELPM governs the physical spatial representation of the Tax-Relevant Event.
Its operational space includes: physical event sites; facilities; buildings; production locations; service-performance locations; machine operating locations; equipment locations; goods locations; object locations; transfer locations; delivery locations; collection locations; storage locations; logistics locations; physical interaction points; mobile-event locations; multi-site events; physically distributed events; physical-location precision; physical-location uncertainty; physical-location conflict; physical-location transitions; physical-location traceability; and physical spatial continuity.
ELPM governs physical location only to the extent required to represent the operational spatial reality of the event.
Operational Scope

ELPM shall support physical-location governance for: manufacturing; logistics; transportation; construction; physical services; retail; warehousing; infrastructure operations; energy systems; healthcare operations; automated facilities; robotics; autonomous vehicles; IoT environments; machine-to-machine operations; hybrid physical-digital events; and other events possessing a material physical spatial dimension.
The module shall support both stationary and mobile events.
It shall also support events whose physical manifestation spans more than one location. 1. Physical Location Candidate Identification
ELPM shall identify physical-location candidates from the Governed Event Location Signal Set produced by ELIM.
Candidates may include: coordinates; addresses; facilities; operational sites; warehouses; factories; stores; terminals; construction sites; machines; vehicles; delivery points; collection points; physical infrastructure; or other materially relevant spatial references.
A physical-location candidate shall not become Governed Event Physical Location merely because it is available.
Physical Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Physical Location. 2. Constitutive Physical Location
ELPM shall determine whether a physical location materially participates in the constitution of the event.
A constitutive physical location is one at which activity forming part of the governed event actually occurs or materially manifests.

This distinction prevents surrounding locations from being mistaken for the physical location of the event.
For example, the registered office of a company may be associated with the event while no constitutive event activity occurs there.
Associated Physical Location ≠ Constitutive Physical Location. 3. Physical Performance Location
Where an event involves physical performance, ELPM shall govern the location at which that performance occurs.
Examples may include: manufacturing; assembly; repair; installation; inspection; construction; physical service delivery; machine operation; loading; unloading; or other material activity.
The physical performance location shall be established from operational evidence rather than administrative convention.
Registered Address ≠ Physical Performance Location by Default. 4. Object Location
Where a physical object materially participates in the event, ELPM may govern the object's location as a relevant spatial dimension.
Objects may include: goods; machinery; equipment; components; vehicles; infrastructure assets; physical documents; commodities; or other tangible objects.
Object Location shall not automatically become complete Event Location.
Object Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default.
Its significance depends upon the governed Event Boundary and the object's operational role. 5. Goods Location
Events involving goods may include several legitimate physical locations.

Goods may be: produced; stored; transferred; transported; inspected; modified; delivered; returned; or destroyed
at different places.
ELPM shall preserve these distinctions where they materially describe the event.
Location of Goods at One Stage ≠ Location of the Entire Event by Default. 6. Machine and Equipment Location
Where machines, robots, industrial equipment, autonomous vehicles, or other physical systems participate in the event, their physical position may form a material component of Event Location.
ELPM shall determine the operational significance of that position.
A machine's physical location may represent: the place of execution; one component location; a supporting location; a mobile location; or merely the position of equipment associated with a larger event.
Machine Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default.
The location of computational infrastructure controlling the machine is governed separately as appropriate. 7. Human Physical Presence
Human presence may be materially relevant to the physical event.
ELPM may govern the physical location of persons where their presence forms part of the event's operational spatial reality.
However:
Human Presence Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
A customer may be physically located in one place while a service is performed elsewhere.
An operator may control machinery remotely.
An employee's location may differ from the location of the operational object.

Participant role governance remains with TREPS. 8. Facility Location
Facilities may provide strong physical anchors for an event.
Examples include factories, warehouses, offices, hospitals, stores, laboratories, terminals, data facilities, construction sites, and energy installations.
ELPM shall distinguish between: facility where constitutive event activity occurs; facility supporting the event; facility merely associated with a participant; facility appearing only in administrative records; and facility unrelated to the bounded event.
Facility Association ≠ Event Location by Default. 9. Delivery and Collection Location
Delivery or collection may form a constitutive part of some events.
Where so bounded, ELPM shall govern the relevant physical location.
However:
Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default.
Collection Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default.
The significance of delivery or collection depends upon the event under governance rather than downstream legal preference. 10. Mobile Event Location
Some events move through physical space.
Examples include: transportation; logistics; autonomous vehicle operations; maritime operations; aviation; mobile services; infrastructure inspection; robotics; and moving industrial processes.
ELPM shall not force such events into a single static coordinate where the operational reality is spatially mobile.

A mobile event may require: origin location; destination location; route; relevant intermediate locations; spatial intervals; or a governed spatial trajectory.
Mobile Event ≠ Single Static Location by Default. 11. Multi-Site Physical Events
One governed event may legitimately span several physical sites.
ELPM shall preserve multi-site physical reality where supported by the Event Boundary.
Examples include distributed manufacturing, coordinated construction, multi-facility processing, supply-chain operations, and infrastructure events.
Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default.
Conversely:
One Commercial Transaction ≠ One Physical Location by Default.
Whether multiple activities belong to one event is governed upstream through Event Formation and Event Boundary. 12. Physical Location Transition
Where the physical position of the event or a constitutive event object changes over time, ELPM shall preserve materially relevant location transitions.
This may require correlation with the governed Event Timing established under TRETS.
The representation may include:
Location A
↓
Location B
↓
Location C
without implying that each transition constitutes a new event.
Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 13. Physical Location and Event Timing
Physical location may change throughout the duration of an event.
ELPM shall therefore support temporal association of location where necessary.

A location record may specify that a physical location applies: at Event Start; during a defined interval; during a particular event phase; at Event Completion; or across the full governed duration.
ELPM does not redefine Event Timing.
TRETS remains authoritative for temporal governance. 14. Physical Location Precision
Physical Event Location shall be represented only at the precision legitimately supported by evidence.
Possible representations include: exact coordinate; machine position; room; building; facility; site; municipality; region; corridor; route; bounded geographic area; or qualified unknown location.
Technical Coordinate Precision ≠ Operational Location Certainty.
An exact GPS coordinate with uncertain provenance may be less governance-reliable than a verified facility-level location. 15. Physical Location Uncertainty
Where physical location cannot be established with full certainty, ELPM shall preserve the uncertainty.
Permissible states may include: exact; bounded; approximate; multi-candidate; mobile; distributed; conflicted; partially established; or unresolved.
Downstream requirements for a single country or address shall not override operational uncertainty.
Required Geographic Field ≠ Permission for False Location Certainty. 16. Conflicting Physical Locations
ELPM shall govern conflicts among physical-location signals.

Conflicts may arise from: inconsistent sensor data; inaccurate addresses; stale records; mobile devices; machine movement; participant movement; delayed system updates; incorrect geocoding; inconsistent facility identifiers; or conflicting operational records.
Resolution shall be evidence-based and traceable.
Administrative Preference ≠ Governed Physical Location. 17. Physical Location Continuity
Where an event persists across time, ELPM shall support continuity of its physical spatial representation.
Continuity may be: stationary; mobile; sequential; multi-site; interrupted; or distributed.
Physical continuity shall be evaluated against the existing Event Boundary.
A spatial transition alone shall not automatically split the event. 18. Physical and Digital Separation
ELPM shall preserve a strict distinction between physical and digital location.
A physical operation may depend upon digital infrastructure elsewhere.
A digital transaction may interact with physical goods or devices.
Neither dimension shall automatically redefine the other.
Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location.
Digital location governance belongs to ELDM. 19. Physical Location and Participant Location
A participant may be physically situated somewhere relevant to the event without that location representing the physical event itself.

Examples include: remote employee; remote machine operator; customer placing an order while traveling; corporate headquarters; beneficial owner; platform administrator; or service recipient.
ELPM shall not derive Event Physical Location solely from Participant Location.
Participant Location ≠ Physical Event Location by Default. 20. Physical Location and Organizational Address
Registered office, headquarters, billing address, correspondence address, branch address, or contractual address may provide useful contextual information.
They do not automatically establish where the event physically occurred.
Legal Address ≠ Operational Physical Location.
Billing Address ≠ Physical Event Location.
Corporate Residence ≠ Physical Event Location. 21. Physical Location and Tax Jurisdiction
ELPM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational physical location and jurisdiction-specific taxation.
Physical Event Location may become an input to downstream jurisdictional analysis.
It does not itself establish: tax jurisdiction; tax nexus; permanent establishment; tax residence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; place of performance under tax law; customs jurisdiction; legal situs; or taxing authority.
Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
A physical event may occur in one or several places while different legal systems legitimately apply different tax rules to that same governed spatial reality. 22. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness

ELPM shall preserve operational spatial reality in a form capable of supporting multiple downstream jurisdictional evaluations.
Canonical logic:
One Governed Physical Reality
↓
Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations
The physical event representation shall therefore remain independent from any single jurisdiction's legal interpretation.
This enables TREGA™ to maintain a stable governed event layer while tax rules change across countries and over time. 23. Governance States
ELPM may assign states including:
Physical Location Ready Relevant physical signals are available for governance.
Physical Location Under Governance Candidate locations are being evaluated.
Physical Location Established A sufficient physical representation has been established.
Physical Location Multi-Site The event legitimately spans multiple physical sites.
Physical Location Mobile The event materially moves through physical space.
Physical Location Qualified The location is established subject to explicit qualification.
Physical Location Conflicted Material physical-location evidence conflicts.
Physical Location Unresolved Available evidence is insufficient for legitimate determination.
These states shall remain traceable. 24. Governance Requirements

ELPM implementations shall: consume the Governed Event Location Signal Set produced by ELIM; identify materially relevant physical-location candidates; distinguish constitutive from contextual physical locations; govern physical performance location where relevant; preserve object, goods, machine, facility, participant-associated, and logistics location distinctions; support stationary, mobile, multi-site, and physically distributed events; preserve temporal association where location changes during the event; maintain evidence-supported spatial precision; preserve uncertainty and conflict; avoid artificial single-location reduction; maintain physical/digital separation; prevent legal or tax classifications from redefining operational physical reality; preserve traceability; and produce a Governed Event Physical Location suitable for subsequent TRELS processing.
25. Governance Logic
ELPM follows the canonical logic:
Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
identify physical-location candidates
↓
determine their operational roles
↓
distinguish constitutive from contextual locations
↓
assess physical performance and manifestation
↓
evaluate mobility and multi-site structure
↓
govern precision, uncertainty, and conflict
↓
establish Governed Event Physical Location.
No downstream legal tax rule may substitute for this operational determination. 26. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ELPM implementation should support:

Governed Event Reference Reference to the event under location governance.
Physical Location Identifier Unique reference for each governed physical location.
Physical Location Type Facility, coordinate, site, route, machine location, object location, delivery point, mobile position, or other legitimate type.
Operational Role Constitutive, supporting, contextual, transitional, or other governed role.
Spatial Representation Physical location at the legitimately supported precision.
Temporal Association Relevant relationship to Event Timing.
Physical Object Association Object, goods, machine, infrastructure, or other physical component where relevant.
Mobility State Stationary, mobile, transitional, or mixed.
Multi-Site State Whether the event materially spans multiple sites.
Precision State Supported spatial precision.
Uncertainty State Known uncertainty.
Conflict State Known evidence conflict.
Evidence Reference Supporting operational evidence.
Traceability Reference Governance history enabling reconstruction.
Governance State Current ELPM determination state.
Handoff State Readiness for subsequent digital and distributed location governance. 27. Governance Outputs

ELPM may produce: Physical Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Physical Location Map; Physical Performance Location Record; Object Location Record; Goods Location Record; Machine Location Record; Facility Location Record; Mobile Event Location Map; Multi-Site Event Map; Physical Location Transition Record; Physical Location Precision Record; Physical Location Uncertainty Record; Physical Location Conflict Record; Physical Location Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Event Physical Location
This output becomes an input to subsequent TRELS modules. 28. Critical Distinctions
Physical Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Physical Location
Physical Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Physical Location
Associated Physical Location ≠ Constitutive Physical Location
Registered Address ≠ Physical Performance Location
Object Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Goods Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Machine Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Human Presence Location ≠ Event Location
Facility Association ≠ Event Location
Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Collection Location ≠ Complete Event Location
Mobile Event ≠ Single Static Location
Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events
Location Change ≠ New Event
Technical Coordinate Precision ≠ Operational Location Certainty
Administrative Preference ≠ Governed Physical Location
Participant Location ≠ Physical Event Location
Legal Address ≠ Operational Physical Location
Billing Address ≠ Physical Event Location

Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location
Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Nexus
Physical Event Location ≠ Permanent Establishment
Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Residence
Physical Event Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply
Physical Event Location ≠ Source Jurisdiction
Operational Physical Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 29. Enterprise Application
ELPM can operate as the physical spatial-governance layer between operational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure.
A generalized implementation pattern is:
ERP / Manufacturing / Logistics / Commerce / IoT / Robotics / Infrastructure System
↓
ELIM Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM
↓
Governed Event Physical Location
↓
Remaining TRELS Modules
↓
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
↓
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines
This allows operational systems to preserve physical reality independently from the legal rules later applied to that reality. 30. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Manufacturing and Logistics Event
A component is manufactured at Facility A in Country A.
It is transferred to Facility B in Country B for specialized processing.
Quality verification occurs at Facility C.
The component is then transported through several logistics nodes before delivery to a customer in Country D.

Operational systems contain the manufacturer's registered address, production coordinates, warehouse addresses, transport locations, customs facilities, customer address, and delivery location.
A conventional system may select one of these locations because a downstream tax field requires a country.
ELPM instead determines which physical locations materially constitute the bounded event.
It preserves the event's multi-site physical structure where required and distinguishes production, processing, inspection, transit, and delivery locations.
It does not determine which country has taxation authority.
A cross-border event may possess one governed physical reality and still support several legitimate jurisdictional interpretations. 31. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Mobile Industrial Operation
An autonomous industrial vehicle receives instructions through cloud infrastructure and performs inspection and repair operations across a large energy facility.
The vehicle moves through multiple physical zones.
Its onboard systems record coordinates continuously.
Remote AI infrastructure analyzes sensor information from another country.
Human supervisors may monitor the operation from additional locations.
ELPM governs the physical spatial reality of the event by identifying where the autonomous vehicle materially performs the bounded operation, preserving relevant movement, operational zones, and spatial transitions.

It does not treat the cloud infrastructure location, supervisor location, company headquarters, or every individual GPS coordinate as the complete Event Physical Location.
Where the operation is genuinely mobile, ELPM preserves that mobility.
A moving event must be governed as a moving event rather than forced into a static location merely because downstream systems expect one address. 32. Canonical Boundary
ELPM owns the governance of the physical spatial manifestation of the Tax-Relevant Event, including constitutive physical locations, physical performance locations, object and goods locations, machine and equipment locations, facility locations, relevant physical presence, mobile locations, multi-site structures, physical-location transitions, physical-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability.
ELPM does not own final Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, or final cross-dimensional Event Location Correlation.
It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance.

It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, tax residence, permanent establishment, place of supply, source jurisdiction, legal situs, customs jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, filing obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
The canonical handoff is:
ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set
↓
ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location
↓
ELDM — Event Digital Location Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ELPM establishes where the governed event materially manifests in physical reality without allowing addresses, facilities, devices, machines, logistics points, or administrative conventions to become authoritative merely because they contain geographic information.
ELPM governs where the event physically occurred — not which jurisdiction may tax what occurred there.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Module: EPAM — Event Actor Association Module
Operational Layer: Event Actor Association Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Actor Association
Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPAM-003
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Actor Association Module (EPAM) governs how identified Participant Candidates and their governed operational roles are materially associated with a specific Tax-Relevant Event.
EPAM determines whether the available actor, role, event, temporal, spatial, and operational information is sufficient to establish that an actor materially participates in the governed event.
Its principal transition is: Governed Participant Candidate + Governed Participation Role
↓
Governed Actor–Event Association
EPAM does not identify the actor.
EPIM owns Participant Identification.

EPAM does not establish the actor's operational role.
EPRM owns Participation Role governance.
EPAM establishes the governed relationship between the actor and the specific event.
The foundational distinction is: Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default
An actor becomes a Governed Event Participant only when its association with the event is sufficiently supported and materially relevant.
Operational Role
Modern event records may contain many identifiable actors and many technically plausible relationships.
An actor may appear because it: owns infrastructure; appears in a contract; operates a platform; holds an account; processes information; provides connectivity; owns a machine; receives a notification; appears in a payment record; is geographically nearby; or belongs to the same corporate structure as another actor.
None of these conditions alone necessarily establishes material participation.
EPAM exists to determine whether the relationship between an identified actor, its governed operational role, and the specific event is sufficient to establish Event Participation.
Internal Module Flow
TREPS operates through:
EPIM — Participant Identification
→ EPRM — Participation Role
→ EPAM — Actor Association
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event
EPAM receives:
Governed Participant Candidate Set
and:
Governed Participant Role Set

and establishes: Governed Actor–Event Association SetOperational Transition
The canonical EPAM transition is:
Governed Participant Candidate + Governed Participation Role + Governed Event
→ Actor–Event Association Governance
→ Governed Actor–Event Association
Where multiple actors are involved:
Governed Event
↓
Multiple Governed Actor–Event Associations
The existence of multiple associations does not create multiple events by default.
Operational Space
EPAM governs: actor-event linkage; association materiality; association basis; direct participation; indirect participation; supporting association; multi-actor association; role-event alignment; temporal association; spatial association; operational association; association strength; association uncertainty; association conflict; association change; and association traceability.
EPAM governs whether an actor's relationship to the event constitutes material Event Participation.
Operational Scope
EPAM may operate across: commercial transactions; services; manufacturing; logistics; banking; digital platforms; marketplaces; infrastructure operations; AI-mediated events; autonomous transactions; machine-to-machine operations; robotic systems; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital events; and other governable operational events.
The association logic remains jurisdiction-neutral and technology-neutral.
Association Basis
A Governed Actor–Event Association requires an operationally justified basis.

Association may be supported by information showing that an actor materially: initiated; executed; provided; received; transferred; processed; authorized; coordinated; facilitated; controlled; operated; delivered; consumed; or otherwise performed a governed operational role within the event.
The existence of actor information alone is insufficient.
Actor Record Presence ≠ Actor–Event Association.
Material Association
EPAM shall distinguish materially relevant participation from incidental or background association.
An actor may be connected to an event without materially participating in it.
Therefore:
Event Connection ≠ Material Event Participation.
A material association exists only where the actor's governed operational relationship is sufficiently relevant to the event being governed.
Materiality shall be determined according to operational reality rather than downstream tax convenience.
Direct and Indirect Association
Participation may occur through direct or indirect operational relationships.
A direct association may exist where an actor directly performs a material function within the event.
An indirect association may exist where an actor materially contributes through an intermediate operational structure.
EPAM shall preserve this distinction where it materially improves the event representation.
However:
Indirect Association ≠ Non-Participation by Default.
Likewise:
Direct Technical Connection ≠ Material Participation by Default.

The operational function and event relationship remain decisive.
Supporting Association
Some actors or systems may support an event without becoming material Event Participants.
Examples may include generic infrastructure, background communications, passive hosting, administrative systems, or other supporting resources.
EPAM shall permit supporting association to remain distinguishable from material participation.
Supporting Association ≠ Governed Event Participation by Default.
This prevents every technical dependency from becoming a participant. Role–Event Alignment
A Governed Participation Role must relate materially to the specific event before it can support Event Participation.
An actor may perform the same general role across many activities without participating in every event occurring within that environment.
Therefore:
Governed Role ≠ Event Participation by Default.
EPAM establishes whether the governed role is actually exercised in relation to the specific event.
Temporal Association
Actor participation shall be compatible with the governed temporal structure of the event.
An actor appearing in records before or after an event does not automatically establish participation during that event.
EPAM may use TRETS-governed temporal information to evaluate association.
However:
Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Participation by Default.
EPAM does not redefine Event Timing.
TRETS remains authoritative for the event's temporal structure.
Spatial Association

An actor may be physically or digitally located at, near, or within an Event Location without materially participating.
Likewise, an actor may participate remotely.
Therefore:
Spatial Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Remote Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default.
EPAM may consume TRELS-governed location information when evaluating Actor–Event Association but shall not redefine Event Location.
Transactional Association
An actor may appear within a transaction record without being materially involved in the underlying governed event.
Likewise, an actor may materially participate even where a conventional transaction record does not explicitly name it.
Therefore:
Transaction Record Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Transaction Record Absence ≠ Non-Participation by Default.
EPAM governs operational association rather than database visibility alone.
Contractual Association
Contracts may provide important evidence of actor relationships.
They do not automatically establish what operationally occurred.
Therefore:
Contractual Party ≠ Event Participant by Default.
Conversely:
Non-Contractual Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default.
EPAM preserves the distinction between contractual representation and operational participation.
Ownership Association
Ownership may connect an actor to assets, machines, infrastructure, organizations, or systems involved in an event.
Ownership alone does not establish participation.
Therefore:
Owner ≠ Event Participant by Default.

Ownership governance remains outside EPAM.
Where necessary, governed ownership information may be consumed from OBIDENITY®.
Organizational Association
Corporate groups may contain parent companies, subsidiaries, branches, operating entities, service companies, and other related organizations.
EPAM shall not transfer participation automatically across organizational relationships.
Corporate Relationship ≠ Shared Event Participation.
Parent Company Participation ≠ Subsidiary Participation by Default.
Subsidiary Participation ≠ Parent Company Participation by Default.
Each Actor–Event Association requires its own sufficient operational basis.
Platform Association
A digital platform may host, facilitate, coordinate, execute, intermediate, or merely technically support an event.
EPAM shall determine whether the platform's governed operational role creates a material Actor–Event Association in the specific event.
Platform Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Platform participation shall be based on operational function rather than platform category alone.
Machine and Autonomous Association
Machines, AI agents, robots, and autonomous systems may possess material Actor–Event Associations independently from humans or organizations connected to them.
EPAM may establish such associations where operational evidence supports them.
However, specialized governance of machine and autonomous participation belongs to:
EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module

EPAM therefore establishes the association while EPMAM governs the specific characteristics of non-human participation.
Machine Association ≠ Owner Association.
AI Agent Association ≠ Developer Association.
Multiple Actor Associations
One governed event may legitimately contain multiple Actor–Event Associations.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Event
→ Actor A Association
→ Actor B Association
→ Actor C Association
→ Actor N Association
These associations may differ in role, materiality, timing, location, directness, and operational significance.
Multiple Actor Associations ≠ Equal Participation.
Association Strength
Actor–Event Associations may possess different levels of operational support.
EPAM shall permit association strength or confidence to be qualified where required.
An association may be:
Established
Qualified
Partial
Ambiguous
Conflicted
Unresolved
Qualification shall reflect available operational support rather than desired downstream legal outcomes.
Association Uncertainty
Where available evidence does not sufficiently establish or reject participation, uncertainty shall remain visible.
Association Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Participation.
Likewise:
Association Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Exclude Participation Arbitrarily.
The event representation shall preserve uncertainty where legitimate resolution is not available.
Association Conflict
Different sources may provide incompatible representations of an actor's relationship to the event.

EPAM shall preserve material conflicts until sufficient governance supports resolution.
Association Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Participant Selection.
Original materially relevant representations shall remain traceable.
Association Change
An actor's relationship to an event may evolve.
A supporting actor may become materially active.
A direct participant may cease involvement.
An intermediary may assume execution.
A machine may replace a human process.
EPAM shall preserve materially relevant association changes.
However:
Association Change ≠ New Event by Default.
Participation Continuity is governed subsequently by EPCM.
Association and Identity
EPAM does not determine who an actor fundamentally is.
EPIM provides the Participant Candidate reference, while OBIDENITY® may provide deeper governed identity structures.
EPAM governs the relationship:
Actor ↔ Specific Governed Event
Therefore:
Actor–Event Association ≠ Identity Governance.
Association and Participation Role
EPRM determines the operational role.
EPAM determines whether that role materially connects the actor to the specific event.
The distinction is:
EPRM: What operational function may the actor perform?
EPAM: Does that governed function materially associate this actor with this event?
Therefore:
Participation Role ≠ Actor–Event Association.
Association and Accountability
Material participation does not automatically establish responsibility or accountability.
Therefore:

Governed Actor–Event Association ≠ Accountability.
Governed Event Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default.
AGA™ remains authoritative for accountability governance where applicable.
Association and Liability
Actor–Event Association does not establish liability.
An actor may materially participate without being legally liable for the event or its consequences.
Therefore:
Event Participation ≠ Liability.
HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability where applicable.
Association and Value
Material participation does not determine which value belongs to an actor or which value result belongs to the event.
Therefore:
Actor–Event Association ≠ Value Association.
Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default.
TRVAS subsequently governs Value Association.
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle itself.
Association and Tax Status
EPAM shall not transform Event Participation into a jurisdiction-specific legal classification.
A Governed Event Participant is not automatically: a taxpayer; taxable person; supplier; customer; employer; employee; principal; legal agent; marketplace facilitator; withholding party; permanent establishment; beneficial owner; liable party; or reporting party.
Therefore: Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer
A jurisdiction may subsequently interpret the participation according to its own law.
EPAM preserves the operational participation reality on which such interpretation can operate.
Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness

The same Actor–Event Association may support different legal conclusions across jurisdictions.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Actor–Event Association
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
EPAM shall therefore avoid embedding one jurisdiction's legal assumptions into the governed participation structure.
Governance States
EPAM may represent:
Association Ready
Association Under Governance
Association Established
Association Qualified
Association Supporting
Association Partial
Association Ambiguous
Association Conflicted
Association Unresolved
Governed Event Participant Established
These states govern Actor–Event Association only.
They do not determine legal or tax status.
Governance Requirements

EPAM implementations shall ensure that: associations refer to governed Participant Candidates; relevant Participation Roles are preserved; association with the specific event is operationally justified; material participation is distinguished from incidental connection; direct and indirect associations can be differentiated where relevant; supporting relationships do not automatically become material participation; role existence does not automatically establish Event Participation; temporal proximity does not automatically establish participation; spatial presence does not automatically establish participation; transaction-record presence does not automatically establish participation; contractual status does not automatically establish participation; ownership does not automatically establish participation; corporate relationships do not automatically transfer participation; machine and autonomous actors can possess independent associations; multiple actor associations can coexist; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; material association changes remain traceable; identity governance remains separate; accountability and liability remain separate; Value Association remains separate; and legal tax status remains downstream.
Governance Logic
IF a Governed Participant Candidate and a Governed Participation Role exist, THEN their relationship to the specific governed event may be evaluated.

IF the actor's governed role is materially exercised in relation to the event, THEN a Governed Actor–Event Association may be established.
IF the relationship is merely incidental, technical, administrative, or insufficiently material, THEN it shall not automatically establish Event Participation.
IF participation evidence is uncertain, THEN the association shall remain qualified or unresolved.
IF materially conflicting representations exist, THEN the conflict shall remain visible until legitimately resolved.
IF the Actor–Event Association is sufficiently governed, THEN the actor may be represented as a Governed Event Participant.
EPAM SHALL NOT convert Event Participation into taxpayer status, accountability, liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EPAM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference
The specific governed event to which association is evaluated.
Participant Candidate Reference
The EPIM-governed actor.
Participation Role Reference
The EPRM-governed operational role.
Association Identifier
The stable reference for the Actor–Event Association.
Association Type
The operational nature of the association.
Association Basis
The basis supporting material association.
Association Materiality
Whether the relationship is materially relevant to Event Participation.
Association Directness
Whether the relationship is direct, indirect, supporting, or otherwise qualified.
Temporal Association

The relationship between participation and governed Event Timing.
Spatial Association
The relationship between participation and governed Event Location where relevant.
Association Confidence
The qualified confidence attached to the association.
Association Ambiguity State
Whether participation remains materially ambiguous.
Association Conflict State
Whether material association conflicts exist.
Association Change State
Whether the Actor–Event relationship materially changes.
Evidence / Traceability Reference
The information required to reconstruct the association result.
Governance State
The current EPAM state.
Handoff State
Whether the association is sufficiently governed for subsequent TREPS processing.
Governance Outputs
EPAM may produce: Governed Actor–Event Association; Governed Event Participant; Association Type; Association Materiality State; Direct Association Representation; Indirect Association Representation; Supporting Association Representation; Temporal Association Record; Spatial Association Record; Association Confidence State; Association Ambiguity State; Association Conflict State; Association Change Record; Association Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Actor–Event Association Set
This output represents actors whose relationships to the specific event have been sufficiently governed.
Critical Distinctions
Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default
Actor Record Presence ≠ Actor–Event Association

Event Connection ≠ Material Event Participation
Indirect Association ≠ Non-Participation by Default
Direct Technical Connection ≠ Material Participation by Default
Supporting Association ≠ Governed Event Participation by Default
Governed Role ≠ Event Participation by Default
Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Participation by Default
Spatial Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default
Remote Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default
Transaction Record Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default
Transaction Record Absence ≠ Non-Participation by Default
Contractual Party ≠ Event Participant by Default
Non-Contractual Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default
Owner ≠ Event Participant by Default
Corporate Relationship ≠ Shared Event Participation
Platform Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default
Machine Association ≠ Owner Association
AI Agent Association ≠ Developer Association
Multiple Actor Associations ≠ Equal Participation
Actor–Event Association ≠ Identity Governance
Participation Role ≠ Actor–Event Association
Governed Actor–Event Association ≠ Accountability
Event Participation ≠ Liability
Actor–Event Association ≠ Value Association
Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default
Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer Enterprise Application
EPAM establishes the material connection between governed actors and the specific event:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set

→ EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event
This prevents downstream tax and compliance systems from treating every actor appearing in operational data as an Event Participant. Use Case 1 — Global Digital Commerce Event
A digital purchase contains records relating to a customer, merchant, marketplace, payment processor, cloud provider, analytics provider, logistics company, and several technical services.
EPIM identifies the relevant Participant Candidates and EPRM establishes their possible operational roles.
EPAM then determines which of those actors possess a materially relevant relationship to the specific governed event.
A cloud provider appearing in infrastructure records or an analytics service receiving technical data does not automatically become a Governed Event Participant.
The resulting Actor–Event Association structure provides downstream tax systems with a governed representation of actual operational participation rather than an unfiltered list of technically connected entities. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Procurement Event
An AI agent detects a production requirement, evaluates suppliers, initiates procurement, and communicates with an autonomous logistics system.
A manufacturing robot later receives and uses the component.

The AI developer, robot manufacturer, equipment owner, cloud provider, operating company, supplier, and monitoring systems may all appear in available records.
EPAM determines which governed roles materially associate which actors with the specific event.
Ownership, development, technical hosting, or monitoring alone does not automatically establish Event Participation.
The resulting associations can proceed to specialized machine and autonomous participation governance without prematurely determining responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, or another legal consequence.
Canonical Boundary
EPAM owns the governance of the material relationship between governed Participant Candidates, their governed operational roles, and a specific Tax-Relevant Event, including association basis, materiality, directness, supporting association, temporal and spatial relevance, uncertainty, conflict, change, and traceability.
EPAM does not own Participant Identification, Participation Role definition, complete identity governance, specialized Machine & Autonomous Actor governance, Participation Continuity, Event Timing, Event Location, Value Association, Event Relationships, accountability, responsibility, liability, ownership, authority, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.

Its governance ends when the Actor–Event relationship is sufficiently established for subsequent TREPS governance.
Canonical Handoff
EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set
→ EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set
→ EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
EPAM establishes whether an identified actor and its governed operational role materially belong to the specific event — not what legal consequence follows from that participation.
Being connected to an event is not the same as participating in it. Being a participant is not the same as being legally responsible or taxable.
Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer.

chunks.text:
OOF™ The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how
The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Module: EPCM — Event Participation Continuity Module
Operational Layer: Event Participation Continuity Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Participation Continuity
Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPCM-005
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how participation in a Tax-Relevant Event is preserved, updated, qualified, and traced when participants, roles, associations, machine or autonomous actors, or participation states change during the lifecycle of the same governed event.
EPCM determines whether changes in participation represent continuity within the same event or indicate a material transformation that must be referred back to the appropriate upstream TREGA™ governance layer.
Its principal task is: Governed Participation Structure
↓

Governed Participation Continuity
EPCM does not identify participants.
EPIM owns Participant Identification.
EPCM does not determine Participation Roles.
EPRM owns Participation Role governance.
EPCM does not establish the original Actor–Event Association.
EPAM owns Actor–Event Association.
EPCM does not establish specialized machine or autonomous participation.
EPMAM owns that governance.
EPCM governs what happens after participation has already been established and subsequently changes.
The foundational distinction is: Participation Change ≠ New Event by DefaultOperational Role
Participation in real-world and digital events is not always static.
A participant may: enter the event; leave the event; pause participation; resume participation; change role; be replaced; act through another system; transfer execution; become inactive; re-enter later; move from human to machine execution; or participate only during one stage of the event.
Without continuity governance, systems may incorrectly: create duplicate participants; erase historical participation; merge distinct actors; treat every role change as a new event; lose the sequence of participation; or rewrite prior participation states.
EPCM preserves participation as a governed lifecycle structure.
Internal Module Flow
TREPS operates through:
EPIM — Participant Identification
→ EPRM — Participation Role
→ EPAM — Actor Association
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity

→ Governed Participatory Event
EPCM is the final Core Module within TREPS.
It receives the governed participation structures produced by the preceding modules and establishes whether participation remains coherent across change.
Operational Transition
The canonical EPCM transition is:
Governed Participant References + Governed Participation Roles + Governed Actor–Event Associations + Governed Machine / Autonomous Participation
→ Participation Continuity Governance
→ Governed Participation Continuity Structure
→ Governed Participatory EventOperational Space
EPCM governs: participant entry; participant exit; participation pause; participation resumption; role change; participant replacement; actor substitution; participation transfer; sequential participation; overlapping participation; participation interruption; participation reactivation; participation-state change; participation-history preservation; machine/human participation transitions; continuity uncertainty; continuity conflict; and continuity traceability.
EPCM governs these mechanisms only within the already governed event boundary.
Operational Scope
EPCM may operate across: commercial events; digital transactions; manufacturing; logistics; banking; marketplaces; platform operations; distributed services; AI-agent workflows; autonomous systems; robotic operations; machine-to-machine events; multi-stage processes; cross-border operations; and other events in which participation changes while the event continues.

Participation Continuity
Participation Continuity means that changes in the participant structure remain linked to the same governed event where the event itself has not materially transformed into a different event.
The continuity question is therefore:
Does the participation change represent evolution within the same event, or does it require upstream event re-evaluation?
EPCM governs the participation side of this question.
It does not independently redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary.
Participant Entry
A participant may become materially involved after the event has already begun.
EPCM shall support legitimate participant entry without forcing the creation of a new event.
Therefore:
Participant Entry ≠ New Event by Default.
The new participant must still satisfy the relevant TREPS governance requirements.
Participant Exit
A participant may cease material involvement before the event ends.
EPCM shall preserve both: the fact that the actor participated; and the point at which participation ended where materially relevant.
Therefore:
Participant Exit ≠ Historical Non-Participation.
Past governed participation shall not be erased merely because an actor later exits.
Participation Pause and Resumption
Participation may temporarily stop and later resume.
EPCM shall distinguish temporary interruption from permanent exit where operational reality supports that distinction.
Participation Pause ≠ Participant Exit by Default.
Likewise:

Participation Resumption ≠ New Participant by Default.
Role Change
A participant may change operational role while remaining part of the same event.
EPCM shall preserve the transition between governed roles.
For example:
Initiator
↓
Coordinator
Processor
↓
Transfer Actor
Human Operator
↓
Supervisor
Autonomous Agent
↓
Escalated Human Control
Such change shall remain traceable.
Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default.
Role Change ≠ New Event by Default.
EPRM remains authoritative for the actual role definitions.
EPCM governs continuity across the change.
Participant Replacement
One actor may replace another during an event.
Replacement does not mean the actors are the same actor.
Therefore:
Participant Replacement ≠ Actor Identity Continuity.
EPCM shall preserve: outgoing participant; incoming participant; transition relationship; participation interval where relevant; and historical traceability.
Actor Substitution
An operational process may substitute one actor for another.
Examples may include: employee replacement; service-provider replacement; machine replacement; agent handoff; system failover; or autonomous actor substitution.
EPCM shall not overwrite the original participant merely because another actor assumes the same role.
Same Role ≠ Same Participant.
Participation Transfer
An actor may transfer an operational function to another actor.

Where this occurs within the same governed event, EPCM shall preserve the transfer relationship without automatically treating the entire event as newly formed.
Participation Transfer ≠ Event Transfer.
Authority or legal delegation related to that transfer remains outside EPCM.
Sequential Participation
Actors may participate one after another.
EPCM shall support sequence where materially relevant.
For example:
Actor A
↓
Actor B
↓
Actor C
may all legitimately belong to the same governed event.
Therefore:
Sequential Participants ≠ Sequential Events by Default.
Event Relationships remain governed by TRERLS where separate events exist.
Overlapping Participation
Two or more participants may be active during overlapping periods.
EPCM shall preserve overlap without forcing artificial exclusivity.
Overlapping Participation ≠ Shared Identity.
Overlapping Participation ≠ Equal Role.
Participation Interruption
Operational disruptions may temporarily alter participation.
A network outage may remove one system.
A machine may fail.
A human may intervene.
A backup provider may take over.
EPCM shall preserve the participation history through such interruptions where the event remains the same governed event.
Human-to-Machine Transition
An event may begin with human execution and later continue through automated or autonomous systems.
EPCM shall preserve the transition rather than rewriting the entire event under one actor type.
Example:
Human Operator
↓
Automated System
↓
Autonomous Agent

may remain one participation-continuity structure.
Human-to-Machine Transition ≠ New Event by Default.
Machine-to-Human Transition
The opposite may also occur.
An autonomous system may escalate control to a human.
EPCM shall preserve both participation states.
Machine-to-Human Escalation ≠ Erasure of Prior Machine Participation.
This is particularly important for auditability and later legal analysis.
Machine Replacement
A machine may be replaced by another machine during the event.
Where the event itself continues, EPCM shall preserve both machine participants and their participation periods or transitions.
Replacement Machine ≠ Original Machine.
Machine Replacement ≠ New Event by Default.
Autonomous Actor Replacement
One AI agent or autonomous system may transfer activity to another.
EPCM shall preserve actor continuity without assuming that two autonomous instances represent the same governed actor.
EPIM and EPMAM remain authoritative for actor identity and non-human participation classification.
Participation State
Participation may occupy different operational states.
EPCM may represent states such as:
Active
Inactive
Paused
Resumed
Transferred
Replaced
Exited
Completed
Qualified
Unresolved
These states describe participation continuity only.
Historical Preservation
A current participation state shall not overwrite materially relevant historical states.
The canonical rule is: Current Participation State ≠ Complete Participation History

EPCM shall preserve reconstructability of prior participation states where materially relevant.
Correction Versus Historical Erasure
An earlier participation record may later be found incorrect.
A legitimate correction may amend the governed participation history.
However:
Participation Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
The original state and correction should remain traceable where governance requires reconstruction.
Continuity and Actor Identity
Participation continuity does not prove identity continuity.
The same role may pass between different actors.
The same actor may appear through changing references.
Therefore:
Participation Continuity ≠ Actor Identity Continuity.
EPIM and OBIDENITY® remain authoritative for actor identification and deeper identity governance.
Continuity and Event Boundary
EPCM operates inside the existing governed Event Boundary.
If a participation change appears to fundamentally alter what constitutes the event, EPCM shall not independently redefine that event.
Instead, the issue must be referred to the relevant upstream TREGA™ layer.
Therefore:
Participation Change ≠ Permission to Redefine Event Boundary.
TREBS remains authoritative for Event Boundary.
Continuity and Event Formation
Some changes may be so material that they indicate the formation of another event.
EPCM shall support escalation where this possibility exists.
However:
Material Participation Change ≠ New Event Automatically.

TREFS and TREBS determine whether a new event actually exists.
Continuity and Timing
Participation continuity may use governed Event Timing to establish entry, exit, sequence, overlap, pause, or resumption.
EPCM does not redefine Event Timing.
Therefore:
Participation Interval ≠ Event Timing Governance.
TRETS remains authoritative for the temporal structure of the event.
Continuity and Location
A participant may change location while participation continues.
Likewise, the event itself may move across operational locations.
EPCM shall not treat participant movement as automatic participation discontinuity.
Participant Location Change ≠ Participation Break by Default.
TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location.
Continuity and Role
EPCM consumes roles governed under EPRM.
It does not redefine role meaning.
Its responsibility is to preserve how those roles change over time.
Therefore:
Role Governance ≠ Role Continuity Governance. Continuity and Machine / Autonomous Participation
EPCM consumes non-human participation structures from EPMAM.
It governs how they persist or change across the event.
Examples may include: autonomous execution becoming supervised; one agent replacing another; machine failover; human escalation; autonomous delegation; or return from human intervention to autonomous execution.
EPCM preserves continuity while EPMAM remains authoritative for machine/autonomous participation characteristics.
Continuity and Value

Participation changes do not automatically determine changes in value ownership, value entitlement, benefit, cost, revenue, or Tax Base.
Therefore:
Participation Continuity ≠ Value Continuity.
TRVAS governs Value Association.
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
Continuity and Accountability
A participant entering, leaving, or changing role does not automatically determine accountability.
Therefore:
Participation Continuity ≠ Accountability Continuity.
AGA™ governs accountability where applicable.
Continuity and Liability
Historical participation may become relevant to later liability analysis.
EPCM preserves the facts necessary for such analysis but does not determine liability.
Therefore:
Participation History ≠ Liability Determination.
HALIA™ governs harm and liability lifecycle where applicable.
Continuity and Tax Status
A participant may change role or involvement while a jurisdiction later assigns different legal significance to different parts of that participation.
EPCM does not determine such tax consequences.
Therefore:
Participation State Change ≠ Tax Status Change by Default.
Participant Exit ≠ End of Tax Obligation by Default.
Participant Entry ≠ Creation of Tax Liability by Default.
These are jurisdiction-specific determinations.
Continuity Uncertainty
It may be unclear whether participation genuinely continued, ceased, resumed, transferred, or was replaced.
EPCM shall preserve uncertainty where available information cannot legitimately resolve the state.

Continuity Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Invent Continuous Participation.
Continuity Conflict
Different records may present conflicting participation histories.
One source may indicate continuous activity.
Another may indicate termination and later re-entry.
EPCM shall preserve materially relevant conflict until sufficiently resolved.
Continuity Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Convenient Timeline.
Continuity Traceability
A governed participation structure shall remain reconstructable across change.
The record should permit determination of: who participated; when participation began; what role was held; when role changed; whether participation paused; whether participation resumed; whether another actor replaced the participant; whether machine/human control changed; when participation ended; what uncertainty existed; and what corrections were later made.
This traceability supports downstream governance without converting participation history into legal conclusions.
Governance States
EPCM may represent continuity states including:
Continuity Ready
Continuity Under Governance
Continuous Participation
Interrupted Participation
Paused Participation
Resumed Participation
Transferred Participation
Replaced Participation
Participation Exited
Participation Completed
Continuity Qualified
Continuity Conflicted
Continuity Unresolved
Participation Continuity Established Governance Requirements

EPCM implementations shall ensure that: participation changes remain linked to the governed event; participant entry can be represented; participant exit does not erase historical participation; pause and resumption can be distinguished; role changes remain traceable; participant replacement does not merge identities; actor substitution preserves outgoing and incoming actors; participation transfer can be represented; sequential participants can belong to one event where legitimate; overlapping participation can be represented; human-to-machine transitions can be preserved; machine-to-human transitions can be preserved; machine and autonomous replacement can be represented; historical participation states remain reconstructable; corrections do not erase prior governance history; participant-location changes do not automatically break continuity; participation changes do not automatically redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; Value Association remains separate; accountability and liability remain separate; and tax status remains downstream.
Governance Logic
IF a Governed Event Participant already exists and its participation changes, THEN EPCM shall determine whether the change can remain within the same governed participation lifecycle.
IF a participant enters or exits while the governed event remains the same, THEN participation history shall be updated without automatic event reformation.

IF a participant changes role, THEN the role transition shall remain traceable without automatically creating a new participant.
IF one actor replaces another, THEN both actors shall remain separately attributable.
IF human and machine execution transition during the event, THEN both participation states shall remain preserved where materially relevant.
IF participation change may indicate a fundamentally different event, THEN EPCM shall escalate the issue to the relevant upstream TREGA™ governance layer rather than redefining the event independently.
IF continuity remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the uncertainty or conflict shall remain visible.
IF participation continuity is sufficiently governed, THEN TREPS may produce a Governed Participatory Event.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EPCM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference
The event whose participation continuity is being governed.
Participant Reference
The governed participant whose continuity is being evaluated.
Participation Continuity Identifier
The stable reference for the continuity record.
Prior Participation State
The immediately preceding governed participation state.
Current Participation State
The current governed participation state.
Role Reference
The governed role applicable to the participation state.
State Effective Point
The governed temporal reference associated with the state change.
Entry State
Whether the actor enters participation.
Exit State

Whether the actor exits participation.
Pause / Resume State
Whether participation temporarily stops or resumes.
Replacement Reference
The outgoing or incoming actor where replacement occurs.
Transfer Reference
The relationship representing transfer of participation.
Human / Machine Transition State
Whether execution transitions between human and non-human actors.
Continuity Confidence
The qualified confidence attached to the continuity representation.
Ambiguity State
Whether continuity remains materially ambiguous.
Conflict State
Whether materially conflicting histories exist.
Correction Reference
Any governed correction affecting participation history.
Traceability Reference
The information required to reconstruct participation continuity.
Governance State
The current EPCM state.
Handoff State
Whether TREPS participation governance is complete.
Governance Outputs
EPCM may produce: Governed Participation Continuity Record; Participant Entry Record; Participant Exit Record; Participation Pause Record; Participation Resumption Record; Participation Role Transition Record; Participant Replacement Record; Participation Transfer Record; Sequential Participation Structure; Overlapping Participation Structure; Human–Machine Transition Record; Machine–Human Transition Record; Participation History; Participation Continuity Confidence State; Participation Continuity Ambiguity State; Participation Continuity Conflict State; Participation Correction Record; and the principal output:

Governed Participation Continuity Structure
When combined with the preceding TREPS outputs, this enables the Parent Standard to produce: Governed Participatory EventCritical Distinctions
Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default
Participant Entry ≠ New Event by Default
Participant Exit ≠ Historical Non-Participation
Participation Pause ≠ Participant Exit by Default
Participation Resumption ≠ New Participant by Default
Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default
Role Change ≠ New Event by Default
Participant Replacement ≠ Actor Identity Continuity
Same Role ≠ Same Participant
Participation Transfer ≠ Event Transfer
Sequential Participants ≠ Sequential Events by Default
Overlapping Participation ≠ Shared Identity
Human-to-Machine Transition ≠ New Event by Default
Machine-to-Human Escalation ≠ Erasure of Prior Machine Participation
Machine Replacement ≠ New Event by Default
Current Participation State ≠ Complete Participation History
Participation Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Participation Continuity ≠ Actor Identity Continuity
Participation Change ≠ Permission to Redefine Event Boundary
Material Participation Change ≠ New Event Automatically
Participation Interval ≠ Event Timing Governance
Participant Location Change ≠ Participation Break by Default
Role Governance ≠ Role Continuity Governance
Participation Continuity ≠ Value Continuity
Participation History ≠ Liability Determination
Participation State Change ≠ Tax Status Change by Default

Participant Exit ≠ End of Tax Obligation by Default
Participant Entry ≠ Creation of Tax Liability by Default Enterprise Application
EPCM completes the TREPS participation-governance chain:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set
→ EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set
→ EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set
→ EPCM — Governed Participation Continuity Structure
→ Governed Participatory Event
→ TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard
This allows downstream systems to consume a stable participation history rather than only a snapshot of who appears to participate at one moment. Use Case 1 — Multi-Stage Cross-Border Service Event
A service begins with one operating entity and one specialist.
During execution, the specialist is replaced, another organization performs a later stage, and a digital platform takes over part of the coordination.
The customer remains the same, while participation roles change over time.
EPCM preserves the original participant, replacement actor, role transitions, entry and exit points, and overlapping periods without automatically creating a new event for every participation change.

The resulting Governed Participatory Event allows downstream tax systems to evaluate the complete participation history rather than a misleading final-state participant list. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Operation with Human Escalation
An autonomous machine begins an industrial operation under normal autonomous control.
An AI agent coordinates the process until an anomaly is detected.
A human operator temporarily takes control, performs corrective action, and then returns execution to the autonomous system.
EPCM preserves the sequence:
Autonomous Machine Participation
↓
AI-Agent Coordination
↓
Human Intervention
↓
Return to Autonomous Execution
without erasing the original non-human participation or treating every control transition as a separate event.
The complete governed participation history can later support jurisdiction-specific evaluation, accountability analysis, audit, or liability governance without EPCM itself determining any of those legal conclusions.
Canonical Boundary
EPCM owns the governance of continuity, change, entry, exit, pause, resumption, role transition, replacement, substitution, transfer, sequence, overlap, human-machine transition, history preservation, correction, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability of already-governed Event Participation.

EPCM does not own Participant Identification, Participation Role definition, original Actor–Event Association, specialized Machine & Autonomous Actor qualification, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, identity, ownership, authority, Value Association, Event Relationships, accountability, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, filing, reporting, collection, payment, or enforcement.
Its governance ends when participation throughout the event is sufficiently coherent, historically reconstructable, and ready to become part of the final TREPS output.
Canonical Handoff
EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set
→ EPCM — Governed Participation Continuity Structure
→ TREPS — Governed Participatory Event
→ TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard
Canonical Closing Statement
EPCM preserves who or what participated as participation changes over time without allowing every entry, exit, role change, replacement, or human-machine transition to redefine the event itself.
Participation may change while the governed event remains continuous.
Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default.
