OOF™ The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors
The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Module: EPIM — Event Participant Identification Module
Operational Layer: Event Participant Identification Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Participant Identification
Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPIM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors potentially relevant to a Tax-Relevant Event are identified, distinguished, referenced, and maintained as stable Participant Candidates for subsequent participation governance.
EPIM establishes whether available actor information is sufficient to distinguish one actor from another within the context of the governed event.
Its purpose is not to determine whether an identified actor materially participated in the event.

Its purpose is to establish which actor is under participation governance.
The principal distinction is: Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant
An actor may be identifiable without materially participating in the event.
Participation role, actor-event association, machine and autonomous participation, and participation continuity are governed by subsequent TREPS modules.
Operational Role
Modern operational events may contain references to many actors.
These may include humans, organizations, platforms, software systems, machines, AI agents, autonomous systems, infrastructure providers, intermediaries, accounts, devices, or other operational entities.
The same actor may also appear differently across multiple systems.
A company name may vary.
A person may appear through different account identifiers.
A machine may be represented through a device ID, asset record, serial number, or system identifier.
An AI agent may operate through multiple sessions or technical instances.
A platform may appear through several legal, commercial, or technical references.
EPIM establishes sufficient actor differentiation so that subsequent TREPS governance does not confuse different actors or incorrectly treat multiple references to the same actor as multiple participants.
Internal Module Flow
TREPS is operationalized through the following internal flow:
EPIM — Participant Identification
→ EPRM — Participation Role
→ EPAM — Actor Association
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance

→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event
EPIM is the first module.
It establishes the actor reference upon which subsequent participation governance can operate.
Operational Transition
EPIM receives actor-related information associated with the:
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
and produces: Governed Participant Candidate Set
The canonical transition is:
Actor Information Associated with the Governed Event
↓
EPIM
↓
Governed Participant Candidate Set
A Participant Candidate is an actor sufficiently identified for participation governance.
It is not yet a confirmed Governed Event Participant.
Operational Space
EPIM governs participant-identification operations including: actor discovery; actor differentiation; actor reference establishment; duplicate actor detection; ambiguous actor handling; conflicting actor identification; human actor references; organizational actor references; digital actor references; machine actor references; autonomous actor references; cross-system actor references; identification confidence; identification traceability; and participant-candidate formation.
EPIM governs these mechanisms only to the extent necessary to establish stable actor references for TREPS.
It does not replace comprehensive identity governance.
Operational Scope

EPIM may operate across events involving: individuals; companies; institutions; marketplaces; platforms; software services; accounts; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machines; devices; infrastructure systems; machine-to-machine environments; and other distinguishable operational actors.
EPIM remains neutral to whether an actor is human, organizational, digital, or autonomous.
Actor Identification
EPIM shall establish whether an actor can be sufficiently distinguished from other actors relevant to participation governance.
Identification may rely on one or more available references.
These may include, where appropriate: governed identity references; organizational identifiers; account identifiers; platform identifiers; system identifiers; machine identifiers; device identifiers; transaction-associated actor references; operational records; external governed references; or combinations of relevant identification information.
No single identifier type is universally authoritative.
Identifier Availability ≠ Actor Identification Sufficiency.
Identification must be adequate for the operational purpose of TREPS.
Participant Candidate
Where an actor is sufficiently distinguishable for subsequent participation governance, EPIM may establish that actor as a: Participant Candidate
Participant Candidate means:
an identified actor whose possible participation in the governed event requires subsequent TREPS governance.
This state deliberately precedes confirmed Event Participation.

Therefore:
Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant
EPRM and EPAM subsequently determine the relevant participation structure.
Actor Reference Stability
A governed participant candidate requires a sufficiently stable reference.
The reference must allow subsequent TREPS modules to determine that they are operating on the same actor.
A stable reference does not require every underlying source system to use the same identifier.
Instead, EPIM shall preserve sufficient linkage to distinguish:
Same Actor / Multiple References
from:
Different Actors / Similar References
This prevents fragmented source data from unnecessarily fragmenting the participation structure.
Multiple References to the Same Actor
One actor may appear through multiple records.
For example:
Company Name + Platform Account + Merchant ID + Payment Account
may represent the same underlying organization.
Likewise:
Machine Serial Number + Asset ID + Device ID + Network Identifier
may refer to the same machine.
EPIM shall permit multiple references to be associated with one Participant Candidate where sufficient governance supports that association.
However:
Multiple Actor References ≠ Multiple Actors by Default.
Similar References to Different Actors
The opposite problem must also be governed.
Different actors may share: similar names; shared addresses; shared infrastructure; group-level identifiers; platform accounts; devices; corporate branding; or organizational relationships.

EPIM shall not merge actors merely because available records appear similar.
Reference Similarity ≠ Actor Equivalence.
Human Actor Identification
Where the potential participant is human, EPIM shall establish only the degree of identification required for participation governance.
EPIM shall not unnecessarily reconstruct or govern the person's complete identity.
Where authoritative identity governance is required, governed identity information may be consumed from OBIDENITY® or another legitimate identity source.
Participant Identification ≠ Complete Human Identity Governance.
Organizational Actor Identification
Organizations may appear under: legal names; trading names; subsidiaries; branches; business units; platform accounts; group structures; or technical system references.
EPIM shall distinguish the actor actually under participation governance from related organizations where available evidence permits.
Corporate Relationship ≠ Actor Equivalence.
A parent company, subsidiary, branch, platform operator, and merchant shall not automatically be treated as the same actor.
Digital Actor Identification
Digital environments may contain actors represented primarily through technical references.
EPIM shall permit digital actors to be identified where they can be sufficiently distinguished for participation governance.
A technical identifier may support identification without establishing participation.
Therefore:
Digital Identifier ≠ Event Participation.

Machine and Autonomous Actor Identification
Machines, robots, AI agents, and autonomous systems may require identification independently from their owners, developers, operators, or supervising organizations.
EPIM shall support such actors as distinct Participant Candidates where operational reality requires it.
Therefore:
Machine Identity Reference ≠ Owner Identity.
AI Agent Reference ≠ Developer Identity.
Autonomous System Reference ≠ Human Operator Identity.
Whether these actors materially participate is governed subsequently within TREPS.
Identification Source Governance
Actor identification may originate from multiple sources.
EPIM shall preserve the distinction between the actor and the source describing the actor.
Identification Source ≠ Identified Actor.
A source may be incomplete, outdated, ambiguous, conflicting, or technically generated.
EPIM shall therefore preserve sufficient source traceability to support later review.
Identification Confidence
Not every actor can be identified with equal certainty.
EPIM shall allow identification confidence to be qualified where required.
Possible conditions may include:
Established
Qualified
Ambiguous
Conflicted
Unresolved
An actor shall not be assigned artificial certainty merely because downstream systems require a participant field.
Required Participant Field ≠ Permission to Invent Actor Certainty.
Ambiguous Actor Identification

Where available information may correspond to more than one actor, EPIM shall preserve that ambiguity until sufficient information supports differentiation.
Ambiguity shall not be resolved through convenience alone.
Actor Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Actor Selection.
Conflicting Actor Identification
Different sources may provide materially incompatible identification information.
EPIM shall preserve material conflicts and prevent silent replacement of one actor reference by another.
Where conflict cannot legitimately be resolved, the Participant Candidate may remain qualified or unresolved.
Identification Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Identity Selection.
Duplicate Identification
EPIM shall reduce the risk that the same actor becomes represented as several independent Participant Candidates merely because different systems use different identifiers.
Duplicate resolution shall remain traceable.
The objective is:
One Governed Actor Reference where evidence supports one actor.
However, consolidation shall not occur where actor equivalence remains materially uncertain.
Identification Change
Actor information may change while the governed event remains the same.
Examples include changes to: names; account identifiers; system references; organizational labels; machine identifiers; or platform representations.
EPIM shall preserve materially relevant identification changes without automatically creating a new actor.
Identification Change ≠ New Actor by Default.

Historical references required for traceability shall remain reconstructable.
Cross-System Identification
The same actor may appear across ERP, commerce, banking, logistics, platform, machine, or autonomous-system records.
EPIM shall support governed linkage across these systems where sufficient evidence establishes that the references concern the same actor.
Cross-system linkage must remain traceable.
Cross-System Match ≠ Actor Equivalence Without Sufficient Support.
Relationship to OBIDENITY®
EPIM does not own comprehensive identity governance.
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity structures including identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability where applicable.
EPIM consumes only the actor-identification information necessary for Event Participation governance.
The boundary is:
OBIDENITY® governs who the actor is as a governed identity.
EPIM governs whether that actor can be sufficiently distinguished as a Participant Candidate within the TREPS process.
Therefore:
Actor Identity ≠ Participant Identification
and:
Participant Identification ≠ Event Participation Relationship to Event Location
An actor may be identified through location-associated records.
Location alone does not establish actor identity or participation.
Therefore:
Location Reference ≠ Actor Identification by Default.
Actor Location ≠ Event Participation.
TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location.
Relationship to Participation Role

EPIM does not determine what operational role an identified actor performs.
That belongs to:
EPRM — Event Participation Role Module
Therefore:
Participant Identification ≠ Participation Role.
EPIM answers:
Which actor is under participation governance?
EPRM answers:
What operational participation role does that actor perform? Relationship to Actor–Event Association
EPIM does not establish that a Participant Candidate materially participates in the governed event.
That relationship is governed subsequently through EPAM.
Therefore:
Identified Actor ≠ Actor–Event Association
and:
Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant.
This separation prevents the existence of an actor in a record from becoming automatic proof of participation.
Governance States
EPIM may assign identification states including:
Actor Reference Detected
Identification Under Governance
Actor Distinguished
Actor Qualified
Actor Ambiguous
Actor Conflicted
Actor Unresolved
Participant Candidate Established
These states describe identification governance only.
They do not establish Event Participation.
Governance Requirements

EPIM implementations shall ensure that: actor references relevant to participation governance can be identified; materially different actors remain distinguishable; multiple references to the same actor can be governed; similar references are not automatically merged; human, organizational, digital, machine, and autonomous actors can be represented; identification sources remain traceable; identification uncertainty remains visible; material identification conflicts remain visible; duplicate actor representations can be governed; identification changes remain traceable; cross-system references can be linked where sufficiently supported; complete identity governance is not duplicated; participation roles are not prematurely assigned; actor-event participation is not prematurely established; and taxpayer or other legal status is not inferred from identification.
Governance Logic
IF actor-related information is materially relevant to participation governance, THEN EPIM shall evaluate whether the actor can be sufficiently distinguished.
IF sufficient identification exists, THEN a stable Participant Candidate reference may be established.
IF multiple references sufficiently correspond to the same actor, THEN they may be governed under one Participant Candidate while preserving source traceability.
IF actor equivalence remains uncertain, THEN separate or qualified references shall be preserved.
IF identification is ambiguous or conflicted, THEN uncertainty shall remain visible.

IF a Participant Candidate is established, THEN the actor may proceed to subsequent TREPS governance.
EPIM SHALL NOT treat identification alone as proof of Event Participation.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EPIM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference
The event within which participant identification is being performed.
Participant Candidate Identifier
The stable reference created for the identified actor.
Actor Type
The governed actor category relevant to participation processing.
Source Actor Reference
The original actor reference supplied by a source system or governed source.
Identification Source
The source from which identification information originates.
Reference Linkage
The relationship between multiple references believed to concern the same actor.
Differentiation State
Whether the actor is sufficiently distinguishable from other actors.
Duplicate State
Whether multiple references may represent the same actor.
Identification Confidence
The qualified confidence attached to the identification.
Ambiguity State
Whether actor identity remains materially ambiguous.
Conflict State
Whether identification sources materially conflict.
Traceability Reference
The information required to reconstruct the identification decision.
Governance State
The current EPIM identification state.
Handoff State
Whether the Participant Candidate is sufficiently governed to proceed to EPRM.
Governance Outputs

EPIM may produce: Governed Actor Reference; Participant Candidate Identifier; Actor Type Representation; Actor Reference Linkage; Duplicate Actor Resolution; Identification Confidence State; Actor Ambiguity State; Actor Conflict State; Identification Traceability Record; Participant Candidate Governance State; and the principal output:
Governed Participant Candidate Set
The output represents actors sufficiently identified for subsequent participation governance.
It does not represent confirmed Event Participants.
Critical Distinctions
Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant
Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant
Participant Identification ≠ Event Participation
Actor Identity ≠ Participant Identification
Participant Identification ≠ Complete Identity Governance
Identifier Availability ≠ Actor Identification Sufficiency
Multiple Actor References ≠ Multiple Actors by Default
Reference Similarity ≠ Actor Equivalence
Corporate Relationship ≠ Actor Equivalence
Digital Identifier ≠ Event Participation
Machine Identity Reference ≠ Owner Identity
AI Agent Reference ≠ Developer Identity
Autonomous System Reference ≠ Human Operator Identity
Identification Source ≠ Identified Actor
Required Participant Field ≠ Permission to Invent Actor Certainty
Actor Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Actor Selection
Identification Change ≠ New Actor by Default
Participant Identification ≠ Participation Role
Identified Actor ≠ Actor–Event Association

Participant Identification ≠ Taxpayer Identification Enterprise Application
EPIM can operate between operational systems and the remaining TREPS participation-governance process:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ Actor-Related Event Information
→ EPIM
→ Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Participation Role Governance
→ Remaining TREPS Modules
→ Governed Participatory Event
This provides downstream systems with stable actor references without prematurely assigning participation, legal identity, or tax status. Use Case 1 — Multi-Platform Commercial Event
A commercial event contains a merchant name, marketplace seller ID, payment-account reference, logistics customer number, and corporate identifier.
Several references may describe the same organization, while another similarly named company belongs to the same corporate group.
EPIM governs the references, distinguishes the relevant actors, prevents unsupported merging, and establishes a stable Participant Candidate for subsequent participation governance.
It does not yet determine whether the merchant, marketplace, payment provider, or logistics provider materially participated in the event or what legal tax status any actor possesses. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Event
An autonomous production event contains references to an industrial robot, machine controller, AI optimization agent, equipment owner, software provider, operating company, and remote monitoring system.

EPIM distinguishes the machine and autonomous actors from the organizations and humans associated with them and establishes stable Participant Candidates where sufficient identification exists.
It does not assume that the machine owner is the machine participant, that the AI developer is the AI participant, or that every identifiable actor materially participated in the event.
Those questions proceed through subsequent TREPS governance.
Canonical Boundary
EPIM owns the identification, differentiation, stable referencing, duplicate governance, ambiguity governance, conflict preservation, cross-system linkage, and identification traceability required to establish Participant Candidates for TREPS.
EPIM does not own complete identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, or provenance governance.
It does not determine Participation Role, final Actor–Event Association, machine/autonomous participation status, Participation Continuity, Event Location, Value Association, accountability, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, legal taxability, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Its governance ends when actors are sufficiently identified and represented as Participant Candidates for subsequent TREPS processing.
Canonical Handoff
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event + Actor Information
→ EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Event Participation Role Governance

Canonical Closing Statement
EPIM establishes which actor is sufficiently identifiable to enter participation governance without treating identification itself as proof of participation.
Knowing who an actor is does not establish whether or how that actor participated in the event.
Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant.

OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Module: EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module
Operational Layer: Machine & Autonomous Event Participation Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Machine & Autonomous Event Participation
Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPMAM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module (EPMAM) governs how machines, software agents, AI agents, robots, autonomous systems, machine-to-machine actors, and other non-human operational actors are represented as participants in a Tax-Relevant Event once their Actor–Event Association has been sufficiently established.

EPMAM governs the specific conditions under which non-human participation can be represented independently from the identities, ownership, authority, supervision, development, operation, or legal status of humans and organizations associated with the machine or autonomous actor.
Its principal task is: Governed Actor–Event Association
↓
Governed Machine / Autonomous Participation
EPMAM does not establish general Actor–Event Association.
EPAM owns that governance.
EPMAM governs the additional participation characteristics that arise when the actor itself is machine-based, software-based, autonomous, or capable of materially acting without contemporaneous human execution.
The foundational distinction is: Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner
and: Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by DefaultOperational Role
Traditional event models often assume that economically relevant action is performed directly by a human or organization.
That assumption is increasingly insufficient.
A machine may: detect a requirement; select an action; initiate a workflow; place an order; receive a service; transfer information; operate equipment; allocate resources; trigger payment; negotiate with another system; coordinate another machine; or execute economically relevant activity.
An AI agent may perform similar functions without a human selecting each individual action.
EPMAM ensures that operational reality can represent these actors directly where they materially participate.

It prevents non-human participation from being automatically rewritten as human participation merely because legal responsibility must eventually attach somewhere.
Internal Module Flow
TREPS operates through:
EPIM — Participant Identification
→ EPRM — Participation Role
→ EPAM — Actor Association
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event
EPMAM receives machine or autonomous Actor–Event Associations already established through EPAM.
It qualifies those associations for the specific characteristics of non-human participation.
Operational Transition
The canonical EPMAM transition is:
Governed Machine / Autonomous Actor–Event Association
→ Machine & Autonomous Participation Governance
→ Governed Machine / Autonomous Event Participation
Where human and non-human actors participate together, EPMAM preserves their distinct participation structures.
Operational Space
EPMAM governs: machine participation; AI-agent participation; software-agent participation; robotic participation; autonomous-system participation; machine-to-machine participation; autonomous action state; execution independence; human-supervision relationship; ownership separation; operator separation; developer separation; delegated machine action; system-mediated participation; multi-agent participation; autonomous coordination; machine-participation uncertainty; and non-human participation traceability.

It does not determine legal personality or legal capacity.
Operational Scope
EPMAM may operate across: autonomous procurement; robotic manufacturing; machine-to-machine commerce; automated logistics; AI-agent transactions; autonomous financial operations; smart infrastructure; distributed industrial systems; automated marketplaces; IoT ecosystems; software-agent workflows; autonomous service delivery; and future machine economies.
The module remains neutral to the technology used.
Machine Actor
A Machine Actor is a non-human operational actor capable of performing a materially relevant function within the governed event.
Its existence as equipment or infrastructure does not automatically make it a participant.
Therefore:
Machine Presence ≠ Machine Participation by Default.
The machine must possess a governed Actor–Event Association and materially perform a participation role.
Autonomous Actor
An Autonomous Actor is an operational actor capable of selecting, initiating, adapting, coordinating, or executing materially relevant activity with a degree of operational independence.
Autonomy may exist at different levels.
EPMAM does not require complete independence from human design, configuration, ownership, or supervision.
However:
Human Supervision ≠ Human Execution by Default.
A supervised autonomous system may still be the actor that operationally performs the governed function.
Automation Versus Autonomy

EPMAM shall distinguish where materially relevant between automated execution and autonomous action.
Automation may execute predetermined logic.
Autonomy may include decision selection, adaptation, goal-directed behavior, or independent operational choice.
The distinction shall reflect actual system behavior rather than marketing terminology.
Automated System ≠ Autonomous System by Default.
Likewise:
AI Label ≠ Autonomous Participation by Default.
Actor Versus Tool
A machine or software system may function merely as a tool used by another participant.
In other cases, it may itself perform a materially distinct operational role.
EPMAM shall preserve this distinction.
Tool Use ≠ Independent Machine Participation by Default.
A calculator, passive database, or static software component does not become an independent participant merely because it contributes technically to an event.
Execution Actor
Where a machine or autonomous system directly executes a materially relevant event function, EPMAM may represent that system as an Execution Actor.
However:
Execution Actor ≠ Legal Responsible Party.
The fact that a system executed an action does not determine who legally authorized, owns, controls, benefits from, or bears responsibility for that action.
Decision Actor
An AI agent or autonomous system may materially select among alternatives.
Where such decision activity forms part of the governed event, EPMAM may preserve the system's operational decision role.
However:

Operational Decision Actor ≠ Legal Decision-Maker.
Questions of authority, permission, accountability, and legal responsibility remain separate.
Machine Ownership Separation
The owner of a machine may be relevant to downstream governance.
Ownership does not determine who operationally participated in the event.
Therefore:
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner
Machine Ownership ≠ Machine Participation
OBIDENITY® governs ownership where applicable.
EPMAM consumes ownership information only where it is relevant to representing the participation structure.
Operator Separation
A machine may be operated directly by a person or organization.
It may also act with substantial operational independence.
EPMAM shall not automatically collapse machine participation into operator participation.
Therefore:
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Operator by Default.
Likewise, the operator's existence does not remove the machine's own materially relevant role from the event representation.
Developer Separation
Software developers, AI-model developers, system integrators, and equipment manufacturers may be identifiable and operationally relevant in some contexts.
Their development relationship does not automatically establish Event Participation.
Therefore:
AI Agent Participant ≠ AI Developer
Autonomous System Participant ≠ System Developer
Machine Participant ≠ Manufacturer by Default
Development provenance and operational participation are separate governance questions.

Controller and Supervisor Separation
A supervising or controlling actor may coexist with a machine participant.
EPMAM shall permit both to remain distinct where operational reality supports both associations.
Therefore:
Supervisory Relationship ≠ Participation Equivalence.
Control Capability ≠ Execution by Default.
The system that acts and the actor with control authority may be different participants.
Delegated Machine Action
A human or organization may delegate operational authority to a machine or software agent.
EPMAM may represent the machine as the executing participant while preserving the existence of delegation where relevant.
However:
Delegation ≠ Identity Transfer.
Delegated Execution ≠ Delegator Execution by Default.
Authority and delegation governance remain outside EPMAM.
Machine-to-Machine Participation
A governed event may contain no contemporaneous human action.
For example:
Machine A
↓
Service Request
↓
Machine B
↓
Resource Transfer
or:
AI Agent A
↓
Autonomous Marketplace
↓
AI Agent B
EPMAM shall support such participation structures without forcing a human actor into the event record merely to satisfy a traditional transaction model.
Machine-to-Machine Event ≠ Human-to-Human Event by Default.
Multi-Agent Participation
Multiple autonomous systems may participate in the same event.
They may: collaborate; compete; negotiate; delegate; coordinate; sequence actions; exchange information; or perform complementary functions.

EPMAM shall support distinct non-human Actor–Event Associations without merging them into a generic “system” participant.
Multiple Autonomous Actors ≠ One Autonomous Participant by Default.
Agent Instance Versus Persistent Actor
An autonomous actor may operate through multiple sessions, runtime instances, devices, or execution environments.
EPMAM shall distinguish the technical instance from the governed actor where necessary.
Therefore:
Agent Instance ≠ Autonomous Actor by Default.
Likewise:
New Runtime Instance ≠ New Participant by Default.
Actor continuity across instances may require governed references from EPIM and continuity governance from EPCM.
Model Versus Agent
A model may support an AI agent without itself constituting the operational participant.
EPMAM shall distinguish where relevant between: model; agent; application; orchestration layer; execution environment; and autonomous actor.
Therefore:
AI Model ≠ AI Agent by Default.
Model Invocation ≠ Independent Event Participation by Default.
Infrastructure Versus Actor
Cloud infrastructure, compute resources, networks, databases, and communication layers may enable autonomous action without becoming Event Participants.
Therefore:
Infrastructure Execution ≠ Infrastructure Participation by Default.
The operational role and material Actor–Event Association remain decisive.
Autonomy State
EPMAM may preserve the degree or state of autonomy relevant to the event.

The purpose is not to create a universal technical autonomy scale.
The purpose is to record whether the actor's participation was, for example: directly controlled; automated; delegated; semi-autonomous; autonomous; or otherwise qualified where materially relevant.
Autonomy State ≠ Legal Capacity.
Human Intervention
Human intervention may occur before, during, or after autonomous participation.
EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant intervention without automatically treating the human as the executing participant.
Possible intervention may include: configuration; approval; supervision; override; correction; escalation; or post-event review.
Therefore:
Human Intervention ≠ Human Participation in Every Operational Step. Override
An autonomous actor may operate subject to human or system override.
The existence of override capability does not prove that the override was exercised.
Therefore:
Override Capability ≠ Override Execution.
Likewise, override capability does not eliminate autonomous participation.
Autonomous Coordination
One autonomous actor may instruct, trigger, coordinate, or delegate to another.
EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant distinctions among the actors involved.
However:
Autonomous Coordination ≠ Actor Identity Merger.
Each governed actor remains separately attributable where operationally justified.
Machine Participation and Event Location
A machine's physical or digital location may be relevant to participation.

It does not automatically determine Event Location.
Therefore:
Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Execution Node Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location.
Machine Participation and Timing
Machine activity may generate highly granular timestamps.
These do not redefine Event Timing.
Therefore:
Machine Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default.
TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing.
Machine Participation and Identity
EPMAM does not establish comprehensive machine or autonomous identity.
EPIM establishes the governed Participant Candidate.
OBIDENITY® may govern deeper identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance.
Therefore:
Machine Identity ≠ Machine Participation.
Autonomous Identity ≠ Autonomous Participation.
EPMAM governs the participation characteristics of already associated machine or autonomous actors.
Machine Participation and Authority
A machine may operationally execute an action without having legally valid authority to do so.
Therefore:
Machine Participation ≠ Authority.
Autonomous Execution ≠ Legal Authorization.
Authority and permission remain separate governance spaces.
Machine Participation and Accountability
Non-human participation does not itself determine accountability.
Therefore:
Machine Participant ≠ Accountable Party by Default.
Autonomous Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default.
AGA™ governs accountability where applicable.
Machine Participation and Liability

A machine or AI agent may participate operationally without possessing legal liability.
Likewise, its participation does not automatically assign liability to the owner, developer, operator, or supervisor.
Therefore:
Machine Participation ≠ Legal Liability.
Autonomous Participation ≠ Owner Liability by Default.
HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability where applicable.
Machine Participation and Value
A machine may create, consume, transfer, transform, or interact with value.
Its participation does not by itself determine value ownership or entitlement.
Therefore:
Machine Participation ≠ Value Ownership.
Autonomous Participation ≠ Value Entitlement.
TRVAS governs Value Association.
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
Machine Participation and Tax Status
EPMAM does not determine whether a machine or autonomous actor can legally possess taxpayer status or another tax-law status in any jurisdiction.
Nor does it automatically transfer such status to an associated human or organization.
Therefore: Machine Participant ≠ Taxpayer
and: Autonomous Participant ≠ Taxpayer
Jurisdictions may later determine how non-human operational participation is legally attributed.
EPMAM preserves the governed operational facts required for that analysis.
Participation Uncertainty
It may be unclear whether a system acted independently, merely executed instructions, or functioned only as technical infrastructure.
EPMAM shall preserve such uncertainty.

Autonomy Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Human or Machine Participation.
Where the participation mode cannot be sufficiently established, qualification shall remain visible.
Participation Conflict
Different systems may describe the same actor differently.
One record may identify autonomous execution while another describes manual control.
EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant conflicts until they can be legitimately resolved.
Machine Participation Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Attribution.
Governance States
EPMAM may represent states including:
Machine Participation Ready
Machine Participation Under Governance
Machine Participation Established
Autonomous Participation Established
Machine-to-Machine Participation
Multi-Agent Participation
Human-Supervised Autonomous Participation
Delegated Machine Participation
Participation Qualified
Participation Ambiguous
Participation Conflicted
Participation Unresolved
These states describe operational machine/autonomous participation only.
They do not establish legal status.
Governance Requirements

EPMAM implementations shall ensure that: machine and autonomous actors can be represented independently; non-human actors are linked to governed Actor–Event Associations; tools are distinguished from independent participants; automated execution can be distinguished from autonomy where materially relevant; machine execution is not automatically attributed to the owner; autonomous action is not automatically attributed to the developer; operator, controller, supervisor, owner, and machine can remain distinct actors; delegated execution can be represented; machine-to-machine events can be governed without artificial human insertion; multi-agent participation can be represented; technical instances are not automatically treated as separate actors; AI models are distinguished from autonomous agents where relevant; infrastructure does not automatically become a participant; autonomy state can be qualified; human intervention and override can be preserved; machine location does not determine Event Location; machine timestamps do not redefine Event Timing; identity, authority, accountability, liability, and value governance remain separate; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; and machine participation does not determine taxpayer status or another legal tax conclusion.
Governance Logic

IF EPAM establishes an Actor–Event Association for a machine, software agent, AI agent, robot, autonomous system, or other non-human actor, THEN EPMAM shall evaluate the specific participation characteristics of that actor.
IF the actor materially performs an operational function, THEN non-human participation may be represented independently from associated humans or organizations.
IF the actor merely serves as a passive tool or infrastructure component, THEN independent machine participation shall not be established by default.
IF autonomous execution occurs under supervision, THEN the autonomous actor and supervisor may remain distinct participants where operational reality supports both.
IF machine-to-machine participation occurs, THEN human participation shall not be invented solely to fit a traditional transaction model.
IF autonomy or machine participation remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the state shall remain qualified.
EPMAM SHALL NOT determine legal personality, taxpayer status, authority, accountability, responsibility, or liability.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EPMAM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference
The governed event within which machine or autonomous participation occurs.
Actor–Event Association Reference
The EPAM-governed association being qualified.
Machine / Autonomous Actor Reference
The governed non-human participant reference.
Actor Type

The relevant machine, AI-agent, robot, autonomous-system, software-agent, or other non-human actor type.
Participation Mode
The operational participation mode relevant to the event.
Automation / Autonomy State
The qualified execution state where materially relevant.
Operational Independence State
The degree to which the actor materially executes or selects activity independently.
Human Supervision Reference
Relevant human or organizational supervision where applicable.
Operator Reference
The operator relationship where applicable.
Owner Reference
The ownership relationship where relevant and governed elsewhere.
Developer / Provider Reference
The technical provider relationship where materially relevant.
Delegation State
Whether operational action is performed through governed delegation.
Machine-to-Machine State
Whether another non-human actor is directly involved.
Multi-Agent State
Whether multiple autonomous actors participate.
Human Intervention State
Whether materially relevant human intervention occurred.
Override State
Whether override capability or actual override is materially relevant.
Participation Confidence
The qualified confidence attached to machine/autonomous participation.
Ambiguity State
Whether participation mode remains ambiguous.
Conflict State
Whether materially conflicting representations exist.
Traceability Reference
The evidence and information required to reconstruct the participation result.
Governance State
The current EPMAM state.
Handoff State

Whether the non-human participation structure is sufficiently governed for EPCM.
Governance Outputs
EPMAM may produce: Governed Machine Event Participation; Governed Autonomous Event Participation; Governed AI-Agent Participation; Governed Robotic Participation; Governed Machine-to-Machine Participation; Governed Multi-Agent Participation; Automation / Autonomy State; Operational Independence State; Human Supervision Association; Delegated Machine Participation State; Human Intervention State; Override State; Machine Participation Confidence State; Machine Participation Ambiguity State; Machine Participation Conflict State; Machine Participation Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set
This output proceeds to Participation Continuity governance under EPCM.
Critical Distinctions
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner
Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by Default
Machine Presence ≠ Machine Participation by Default
Human Supervision ≠ Human Execution by Default
Automated System ≠ Autonomous System by Default
AI Label ≠ Autonomous Participation by Default
Tool Use ≠ Independent Machine Participation by Default
Execution Actor ≠ Legal Responsible Party
Operational Decision Actor ≠ Legal Decision-Maker
Machine Ownership ≠ Machine Participation
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Operator by Default
AI Agent Participant ≠ AI Developer
Autonomous System Participant ≠ System Developer
Machine Participant ≠ Manufacturer by Default

Control Capability ≠ Execution by Default
Delegated Execution ≠ Delegator Execution by Default
Machine-to-Machine Event ≠ Human-to-Human Event by Default
Multiple Autonomous Actors ≠ One Autonomous Participant by Default
Agent Instance ≠ Autonomous Actor by Default
New Runtime Instance ≠ New Participant by Default
AI Model ≠ AI Agent by Default
Infrastructure Execution ≠ Infrastructure Participation by Default
Autonomy State ≠ Legal Capacity
Override Capability ≠ Override Execution
Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default
Machine Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default
Machine Participation ≠ Authority
Machine Participant ≠ Accountable Party by Default
Machine Participation ≠ Legal Liability
Machine Participation ≠ Value Ownership
Machine Participant ≠ Taxpayer Enterprise Application
EPMAM provides the specialized governance layer required when operational participants are no longer exclusively human or organizational:
ERP / Platform / AI Agent / Autonomous System / Robotics / Machine Network
→ EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set
→ EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set
→ EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event

This enables downstream systems to preserve what machines and autonomous actors actually did without prematurely converting their participation into human identity, ownership, responsibility, or taxpayer status. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Procurement Agent
An industrial AI agent detects that a production line requires a replacement component.
It evaluates available suppliers, selects an offer within delegated operational limits, submits the order, and communicates with an automated payment and logistics system.
The operating company, AI developer, cloud provider, machine owner, supplier, payment system, and AI agent may all appear in the operational record.
EPAM has already established the relevant Actor–Event Associations.
EPMAM distinguishes the AI agent's own operational execution from the roles of its developer, owner, supervisor, and infrastructure providers.
The agent can therefore remain represented as the actor that selected and initiated the procurement activity without EPMAM determining whether the agent has legal capacity or whether another actor becomes the taxpayer, responsible party, or liable party under law. Use Case 2 — Machine-to-Machine Industrial Service
A connected production machine detects abnormal vibration and autonomously requests diagnostic analysis from another machine-based service.
The diagnostic system analyzes telemetry, identifies a likely component failure, triggers a maintenance robot, and initiates a replacement workflow.

No human selects the individual sequence of actions while the governed event is occurring.
EPMAM preserves the distinct participation of the production machine, diagnostic system, autonomous maintenance system, and other materially involved non-human actors.
It does not artificially replace those actors with their owners, manufacturers, software developers, or remote supervisors.
The resulting governed machine-participation structure can proceed to Participation Continuity and later jurisdiction-specific evaluation without altering the operational reality.
Canonical Boundary
EPMAM owns the specialized governance of machine, AI-agent, software-agent, robotic, autonomous-system, machine-to-machine, and other non-human participation after Actor–Event Association has been established.
It governs automation/autonomy distinctions, operational independence, tool-versus-actor differentiation, owner/operator/developer/supervisor separation, delegation, human intervention, override, multi-agent structures, machine-to-machine participation, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability where materially relevant.

EPMAM does not own Participant Identification, general Participation Role governance, general Actor–Event Association, Participation Continuity, complete machine identity, ownership, authority, permission, Event Timing, Event Location, Value Association, accountability, responsibility, liability, legal personality, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, or any other jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Its governance ends when machine and autonomous participation are sufficiently represented for participation-continuity governance.
Canonical Handoff
EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set
→ EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set
→ EPCM — Event Participation Continuity Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
EPMAM preserves the operational reality that machines and autonomous systems can materially participate in events without automatically becoming their owners, developers, operators, supervisors, or legal representatives.
Who or what performs the action and who the law later holds responsible for that action are separate governance questions.
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner.
Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by Default.

chunks.text:
OOF™ The Event Participation Role Module (EPRM) governs how operational
The Event Participation Role Module (EPRM) governs how operational
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
Module: EPRM — Event Participation Role Module
Operational Layer: Event Participation Role Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Participation Role
Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPRM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Participation Role Module (EPRM) governs how operational participation roles associated with Participant Candidates are identified, differentiated, qualified, and represented within a Tax-Relevant Event before final Actor–Event Association is established.
EPRM determines the operational function through which an identified Participant Candidate may participate in the governed event.
Its principal task is: Governed Participant Candidate
↓
Governed Participation Role

EPRM does not determine whether the actor is legally a seller, buyer, taxpayer, taxable person, employer, employee, principal, agent, permanent establishment, beneficial owner, withholding party, liable party, or another jurisdiction-specific legal actor.
The foundational distinction is: Operational Participation Role ≠ Legal Tax RoleOperational Role
EPIM establishes which actor is under participation governance.
EPRM establishes what operational function that actor performs in relation to the event.
Modern events may involve multiple actors whose functions cannot be accurately represented through simple labels such as buyer and seller.
An actor may initiate an activity, provide a service, operate infrastructure, authorize an action, transfer an object, execute a process, receive an output, coordinate another actor, or perform several operational functions within the same event.
EPRM provides a governed representation of those operational roles before legal interpretation begins.
Internal Module Flow
TREPS operates through:
EPIM — Participant Identification
→ EPRM — Participation Role
→ EPAM — Actor Association
→ EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
→ EPCM — Participation Continuity
→ Governed Participatory Event
EPRM receives the Governed Participant Candidate Set from EPIM.
It produces governed participation-role information for subsequent Actor–Event Association governance.
Operational Transition
The canonical EPRM transition is:
Governed Participant Candidate Set

→ Participation Role Governance
→ Governed Participant Role Set
The output describes the operational roles potentially performed by identified Participant Candidates.
It does not yet establish final governed participation in the event.
Operational Space
EPRM governs: participation-role identification; role differentiation; role qualification; multi-role participation; shared roles; sequential roles; simultaneous roles; supporting versus material operational roles; role ambiguity; role conflict; role changes; role traceability; human roles; organizational roles; digital roles; machine roles; and autonomous operational roles.
EPRM governs the operational function of the actor.
It does not govern the actor's complete identity or jurisdiction-specific legal classification.
Operational Scope
EPRM may govern roles across: commercial transactions; manufacturing; logistics; financial operations; digital services; platforms; marketplaces; infrastructure operations; machine-to-machine activity; autonomous procurement; AI-mediated transactions; robotic operations; hybrid physical-digital events; and other governable economic or operational events.
Role governance shall remain neutral to technology, industry, and jurisdiction.
Operational Participation Role
An Operational Participation Role describes the materially relevant function through which a Participant Candidate acts in relation to the governed event.

Depending on operational reality, such functions may include: initiation; provision; reception; execution; authorization; coordination; facilitation; transfer; delivery; processing; operation; control; intermediation; consumption; or another materially distinguishable operational function.
These are operational representations.
They shall not automatically be interpreted as legally defined roles.
Operational Function ≠ Legal Classification.
Role Evidence
A participation role shall be supported by information sufficient to justify its operational representation.
Relevant information may originate from: transaction records; operational logs; workflow records; contractual information; system activity; platform records; machine telemetry; communication records; authorization records; transfer records; execution records; or other governed sources.
A label supplied by one system does not automatically establish the governed role.
Source Role Label ≠ Governed Participation Role by Default.
Declared Role Versus Observed Role
An actor may be described under one role while operational evidence indicates another function.
For example, a system may label an actor as a “provider,” while the actor merely supplies infrastructure.
EPRM shall preserve the distinction between declared and operationally supported roles.
Declared Role ≠ Observed Operational Role.
Where the distinction is materially relevant, both representations shall remain traceable.
Material Role Versus Incidental Involvement

Not every function associated with an event constitutes a materially relevant participation role.
Technical, administrative, passive, incidental, or background involvement may exist without becoming a material role in the governed event.
Therefore:
Operational Involvement ≠ Material Participation Role by Default.
EPRM shall support differentiation between materially relevant roles and merely incidental involvement.
Final Actor–Event Association remains governed by EPAM.
Multiple Roles
One Participant Candidate may perform more than one materially relevant operational role.
Therefore:
One Participant Candidate
↓
Multiple Operational Roles
where operational reality supports such representation.
EPRM shall not force one actor into a single role merely because a downstream data model expects one role field.
One Actor ≠ One Role by Default.
Shared Roles
Multiple Participant Candidates may perform the same or overlapping operational function.
Therefore:
One Operational Role
↓
Multiple Participant Candidates
may be legitimate.
A shared role shall not automatically collapse several actors into one participant.
Shared Role ≠ Shared Identity.
Role Granularity
Participation roles shall be represented at a level of detail sufficient to preserve materially relevant operational differences.
Excessive generalization may hide meaningful differences.
Excessive fragmentation may create artificial distinctions that do not improve governance.

The role structure shall therefore reflect the actual operational function relevant to the governed event.
More Detailed Role ≠ More Accurate Role by Default.
Role Hierarchy
Where operational reality requires it, roles may exist at different levels.
A broad function may contain narrower operational functions.
For example:
Service Provision
↓
Processing
↓
Execution
or:
Logistics
↓
Transport
↓
Delivery
Role hierarchy may support representation but shall not automatically create separate participants or separate events.
Role Hierarchy ≠ Event Hierarchy.
Role Sequence
Roles may occur sequentially.
One actor may initiate an event and another may subsequently execute, transfer, process, or receive an operational result.
EPRM shall preserve materially relevant role sequencing where necessary for participation governance.
However:
Role Sequence ≠ Event Sequence by Default.
Event Relationships remain governed by TRERLS.
Simultaneous Roles
Several actors may perform materially relevant roles at the same time.
Likewise, one actor may perform multiple simultaneous functions.
EPRM shall permit these structures without forcing artificial sequencing.
Simultaneous Roles ≠ Role Equivalence.
Role Change
An actor's operational role may change during the same governed event.
A Participant Candidate may move from initiation to supervision, from processing to transfer, or from passive availability to active execution.
EPRM shall preserve materially relevant role changes.

Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default.
Role Change ≠ New Event by Default.
Participation continuity is subsequently governed by EPCM.
Human and Organizational Roles
Human and organizational actors may perform different operational functions even when they are connected through employment, ownership, delegation, or corporate relationships.
EPRM shall not automatically transfer one actor's operational role to another related actor.
Organizational Relationship ≠ Shared Participation Role by Default.
Employment Relationship ≠ Operational Role Equivalence.
Identity, authority, and accountability remain separate governance spaces.
Digital Platform Roles
Digital platforms may perform materially different functions across different events.
A platform may provide infrastructure in one event, actively intermediate another, execute a process in another, or perform multiple operational functions.
EPRM shall govern the role according to the specific event rather than the generic category of the platform.
Platform Type ≠ Event Participation Role by Default.
Machine and Autonomous Roles
Machines, AI agents, robots, and autonomous systems may perform operational functions independently of the roles performed by their owners, developers, operators, or supervising organizations.
EPRM shall allow such functions to be represented without automatically attributing them to another actor.
Machine Function ≠ Owner Function.
AI Agent Function ≠ Developer Function.

Autonomous Execution Role ≠ Human Supervision Role.
Special governance of machine and autonomous participation is subsequently provided by EPMAM.
Infrastructure Roles
Infrastructure may support an event without materially participating in it.
A server, network, cloud environment, payment rail, warehouse, communication system, or other infrastructure component may enable an event while remaining merely supporting infrastructure.
Therefore:
Infrastructure Support ≠ Material Participation Role by Default.
EPRM shall prevent technical presence from automatically becoming operational participation.
Role and Event Location
The location of an actor does not determine its operational participation role.
Likewise, the location at which a role is performed does not redefine Event Location.
Participant Location ≠ Participation Role.
Role Performance Location ≠ Event Location Governance.
TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location.
Role and Identity
A governed identity may support role attribution, but identity does not itself determine operational role.
Actor Identity ≠ Participation Role.
OBIDENITY® remains authoritative for identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance where applicable.
EPRM governs only the operational role relevant to participation in the event.
Role and Authority
An actor may perform an operational function without possessing legal authority for that function.

Conversely, an actor may possess authority without directly performing the operation.
Therefore:
Operational Role ≠ Authority.
Questions of authority and permission remain outside EPRM.
Role and Accountability
Performing an operational role does not automatically establish accountability, responsibility, fault, or liability.
Therefore:
Participation Role ≠ Accountability.
Participation Role ≠ Responsibility.
Participation Role ≠ Liability.
These conclusions require separate governance.
Role and Value
An operational role does not automatically determine value ownership, entitlement, benefit, consideration, revenue, cost, or tax base.
Therefore:
Participation Role ≠ Value Association.
Operational Role ≠ Value Entitlement.
TRVAS governs Value Association after TREPS.
VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
Role and Tax Classification
Jurisdictions may subsequently interpret operational participation roles under legal categories.
The same governed operational role may produce different legal classifications under different tax systems.
Therefore:
One Governed Operational Role
↓
Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Interpretations
EPRM preserves the operational role independently from those interpretations.
It does not determine: taxpayer; supplier under tax law; taxable person; marketplace facilitator; withholding agent; employer; employee; principal; legal agent; permanent establishment; importer; exporter; beneficial owner; or another jurisdiction-specific legal status.
Role Uncertainty

Where available information supports more than one plausible operational role, EPRM shall preserve uncertainty.
Role Uncertainty ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Role Selection.
A role shall not be chosen merely because it produces a preferred downstream legal or tax result.
Role Conflict
Different sources may assign incompatible roles to the same Participant Candidate.
EPRM shall preserve material conflict until sufficient governance supports resolution.
Role Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Legal Classification.
Original source representations shall remain traceable where materially relevant.
Role Confidence
Operational role representation may carry different levels of confidence.
EPRM shall permit roles to remain qualified where evidence does not support full certainty.
A downstream system requirement for a role field shall not override this requirement.
Required Role Field ≠ Permission to Manufacture Role Certainty.
Role Traceability
A governed role shall remain reconstructable.
The governance structure should permit determination of: which Participant Candidate the role concerns; which operational function was represented; which information supported the role; whether the role was declared, observed, derived, or otherwise established; whether uncertainty or conflict existed; whether the role changed; and what governance state applied.
Role traceability supports subsequent Actor–Event Association without replacing it.
Governance States
EPRM may represent states including:

Role Ready
Role Under Governance
Role Qualified
Role Established
Multi-Role
Shared Role
Role Changed
Role Ambiguous
Role Conflicted
Role Unresolved
These states describe participation-role governance only.
They do not establish final Event Participation.
Governance Requirements
EPRM implementations shall ensure that: roles are associated with governed Participant Candidates; operational functions are distinguished from legal classifications; source role labels are not automatically authoritative; declared and observed roles can be differentiated; material roles can be distinguished from incidental involvement; one actor may hold multiple roles; multiple actors may share a role; role granularity remains operationally justified; sequential and simultaneous roles can be represented; material role changes remain traceable; human, organizational, digital, machine, and autonomous roles can be represented; infrastructure support does not automatically become participation; role uncertainty remains visible; role conflicts remain visible; role evidence remains traceable; roles do not determine identity, authority, accountability, liability, or value entitlement; roles do not determine taxpayer status; and final Actor–Event Association remains downstream.
Governance Logic
IF a Governed Participant Candidate exists, THEN operational functions potentially relevant to Event Participation may be evaluated.

IF an operational function is sufficiently supported, THEN a Governed Participation Role may be established.
IF one Participant Candidate performs multiple materially distinct functions, THEN multiple roles may be preserved.
IF multiple Participant Candidates perform the same function, THEN shared role representation may be preserved without merging actors.
IF role evidence is uncertain or conflicting, THEN the role shall remain appropriately qualified.
IF the operational role is sufficiently governed, THEN it may proceed to Actor–Event Association governance.
EPRM SHALL NOT convert an operational participation role into a jurisdiction-specific legal or tax role.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum EPRM implementation should support:
Governed Event Reference
The governed event within which role governance occurs.
Participant Candidate Reference
The EPIM-governed actor to whom the role relates.
Participation Role Identifier
The stable reference for the governed role.
Operational Role Type
The operational function represented.
Role Source
The source supporting the role representation.
Role Basis
The operational basis upon which the role is attributed.
Role Materiality State
Whether the function is materially relevant to participation governance.
Role Multiplicity State
Whether the Participant Candidate performs multiple roles.
Shared Role State
Whether the same role is performed by multiple Participant Candidates.
Role Sequence State

Where materially relevant, the role's position relative to other operational roles.
Role Change State
Whether the role materially changes during the event.
Role Confidence
The qualified confidence attached to the role.
Role Ambiguity State
Whether multiple plausible role interpretations remain.
Role Conflict State
Whether material source conflicts exist.
Traceability Reference
The information required to reconstruct the role governance result.
Governance State
The current EPRM state.
Handoff State
Whether the role is sufficiently governed for EPAM.
Governance Outputs
EPRM may produce: Governed Participation Role; Participant Role Reference; Operational Role Type; Multi-Role Structure; Shared Role Structure; Role Sequence Representation; Role Change Record; Role Materiality State; Role Confidence State; Role Ambiguity State; Role Conflict State; Role Traceability Record; and the principal output:
Governed Participant Role Set
This output provides the operational role structure required by EPAM.
It does not establish final Actor–Event Association.
Critical Distinctions
Operational Participation Role ≠ Legal Tax Role
Participant Identification ≠ Participation Role
Participant Candidate ≠ Participation Role
Operational Function ≠ Legal Classification
Source Role Label ≠ Governed Participation Role by Default
Declared Role ≠ Observed Operational Role
Operational Involvement ≠ Material Participation Role by Default
One Actor ≠ One Role by Default
Shared Role ≠ Shared Identity

More Detailed Role ≠ More Accurate Role by Default
Role Hierarchy ≠ Event Hierarchy
Role Sequence ≠ Event Sequence by Default
Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default
Role Change ≠ New Event by Default
Platform Type ≠ Event Participation Role by Default
Machine Function ≠ Owner Function
AI Agent Function ≠ Developer Function
Infrastructure Support ≠ Material Participation Role by Default
Actor Identity ≠ Participation Role
Operational Role ≠ Authority
Participation Role ≠ Accountability
Participation Role ≠ Liability
Participation Role ≠ Value Association
Operational Role ≠ Value Entitlement
Role Uncertainty ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Role Selection
Required Role Field ≠ Permission to Manufacture Role Certainty Enterprise Application
EPRM provides the role-governance layer between actor identification and final Actor–Event Association:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set
→ EPAM — Actor–Event Association
→ Remaining TREPS Modules
→ Governed Participatory Event
This enables downstream systems to understand what actors operationally did without embedding jurisdiction-specific legal classifications into the event record. Use Case 1 — Digital Marketplace Participation Roles
A marketplace transaction involves a customer, merchant, platform, payment provider, and logistics provider.
EPIM has already established the relevant Participant Candidates.

EPRM determines their operational functions based on the governed event: one actor initiates acquisition, another provides goods, another facilitates interaction, another processes payment, and another performs delivery.
The marketplace is not automatically classified as the legal supplier merely because it facilitates the transaction, and the payment provider is not automatically treated as a taxable intermediary merely because it processes payment.
EPRM preserves the operational roles for subsequent Actor–Event Association and jurisdiction-specific evaluation. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Production and Procurement
An AI agent detects a production requirement, evaluates suppliers, selects an option, initiates procurement, and instructs an autonomous machine system.
A robot later receives and uses the supplied component while organizational systems supervise the broader process.
EPRM governs the distinct operational functions performed by the AI agent, machine system, robot, supplier organization, and supervising organization without automatically transferring machine or autonomous functions to owners, developers, or humans.
The resulting role structure preserves what each actor operationally did while leaving authority, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, and other legal conclusions to their appropriate governance and jurisdictional layers.
Canonical Boundary

EPRM owns the identification, differentiation, qualification, representation, multiplicity, sequencing, change, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability of operational participation roles associated with governed Participant Candidates.
EPRM does not own Participant Identification, complete actor identity, final Actor–Event Association, specialized Machine & Autonomous Actor governance, Participation Continuity, Event Timing, Event Location, Value Association, Event Relationships, authority, permission, accountability, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Its governance ends when operational participation roles are sufficiently governed for Actor–Event Association.
Canonical Handoff
EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set
→ EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set
→ EPAM — Event Actor Association Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
EPRM establishes what operational function an identified actor performs without converting that function into a jurisdiction-specific legal or tax role.
What an actor does in the event and what the law later calls that actor are separate governance questions.
Operational Participation Role ≠ Legal Tax Role.
