OOF™ The Event Record Identification Module (ERIDM) governs how a Determined
The Event Record Identification Module (ERIDM) governs how a Determined
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard
Module: ERIDM — Event Record Identification Module
Operational Layer: Event Record Identification Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Record Identification
Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Identity
Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERIDM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 3 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Record Identification Module (ERIDM) governs how a Determined Tax-Relevant Event receives a stable, distinguishable, persistent, and traceable Event Record identity through which its canonical governed representation can be referenced across systems, organizations, transformations, and downstream environments.
ERIDM establishes the authoritative association between the Record being created and the Determined Tax-Relevant Event that the Record represents.
Its principal transition is:

Determined Tax-Relevant Event
↓
Event Record Identification Governance
↓
Governed Event Record Identity
ERIDM does not identify the Event itself.
The Event has already been identified, formed, bounded, governed, and determined through preceding TREGA™ layers.
ERIDM identifies its governed Record representation.
Its foundational distinction is:
Record Identity ≠ Event Identity.
Operational Role
After TREDS establishes a Determined Tax-Relevant Event, TREGS requires a stable Record through which that Event can persist as governed information.
Before Record structure, linkage, traceability, or interoperability can be governed, the Record itself must be identifiable.
ERIDM answers:
Which governed Record represents this Determined Tax-Relevant Event?
The module prevents: anonymous Event Records; unstable Record identifiers; accidental duplicate Record creation; confusion between Event identity and Record identity; confusion between canonical and technical representations; identifier reuse; cross-system Record identity fragmentation; and loss of Event-to-Record association.
Internal Module Flow
TREGS operates through:
ERIDM — Event Record Identification
↓
ERSTM — Event Record Structure
↓
ERLKM — Event Record Linkage
↓
ERTM — Event Record Traceability
↓
ERINM — Event Record Interoperability
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
ERIDM is the first operational module.
Its output is:
Governed Event Record Identity
which becomes the identification foundation for ERSTM.

Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Determined Tax-Relevant Event
↓
Record Candidate
↓
Record Identity Establishment
↓
Event-to-Record Association
↓
Identity State
↓
Governed Event Record Identity
The module establishes identity before the Record receives its complete governed structure.
Operational Space
ERIDM governs: Record candidate identification; Record identity establishment; Record identifier assignment; Record identifier uniqueness; Record identifier persistence; Record identifier stability; Record identifier scope; Event-to-Record association; canonical Record reference; technical identifier distinction; duplicate Record identity detection; identifier collision governance; identifier reassignment restrictions; identity continuity; identity state; and identification handoff.
Operational Scope
ERIDM may identify governed Event Records originating from or represented across: commerce systems; ERP environments; accounting systems; banking infrastructure; payment networks; digital marketplaces; logistics systems; digital platforms; APIs; blockchain environments; smart contracts; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine environments; distributed systems; industrial infrastructure; and future machine economies.
The identification logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Record Candidate
A Record Candidate is a proposed canonical representation of a Determined Tax-Relevant Event entering TREGS Record Governance.

A Record Candidate shall reference a valid upstream TREDS Determination.
A technical object does not become a governed Record merely because it exists in a system.
Technical Object ≠ Governed Record Candidate by default.
Identification Eligibility
A Record Candidate becomes eligible for ERIDM governance where: a valid Determined Tax-Relevant Event exists; the candidate is intended to represent that Event; the Event-to-Record association can be established; and no known identity conflict prevents reliable identification.
Record Eligibility ≠ Record Identification Completion.
Record Identity Establishment
ERIDM establishes the governed identity of the Event Record.
The Record identity shall allow the Record to remain distinguishable throughout its operational existence.
The identity should remain usable despite: storage migration; schema transformation; API exchange; organizational transfer; technical replication; or downstream consumption.
Record Identifier
A Governed Event Record Identity shall possess a stable identifier or equivalent canonical reference mechanism.
The identifier shall distinguish the governed Record from other Record identities within the relevant governance environment.
A Record identifier may be implemented through different technical mechanisms.
ERIDM governs its methodological function rather than prescribing a specific technology.
Identifier Uniqueness
A governed Record identifier shall be sufficiently unique within its defined identification scope.

Two materially distinct Governed Event Records shall not intentionally share the same canonical Record identifier.
Shared Identifier ≠ Shared Record Identity by default.
Identifier Scope
Uniqueness shall be evaluated within an explicit scope.
Possible scopes may include: system; organization; network; platform; federation; or globally coordinated governance infrastructure.
The scope shall be sufficient for the intended Record interoperability.
Identifier Stability
A Record identifier should remain stable while the same governed Record identity continues.
Technical changes should not create new canonical Record identities unnecessarily.
Therefore:
System Migration ≠ New Record Identity.
Schema Change ≠ New Record Identity.
Storage Location Change ≠ New Record Identity.
Identifier Persistence
Record identity should persist for as long as the governed Record must remain reconstructable.
Persistence is particularly important where the Record becomes: inactive; superseded; corrected; archived; or replaced in downstream systems.
A non-current Record may still require persistent identity for historical reconstruction.
Identifier Immutability Boundary
Stable identity does not require every technical identifier to be immutable.
Systems may replace internal keys or migrate technical infrastructure.
ERIDM requires preservation of canonical identity continuity.
Technical Identifier Change ≠ Canonical Record Identity Change by default.
Event-to-Record Association

Every Governed Event Record Identity shall be associated with the Determined Tax-Relevant Event it represents.
The association establishes:
Governed Event Reference ↔ Governed Record Identity
This association prevents the Record from becoming detached from the Event Reality established upstream.
Association Cardinality
ERIDM shall not assume that every technical representation creates a new canonical Record.
One governed Event may have: one canonical governed Record; multiple technical representations; multiple system-specific identifiers; multiple downstream copies.
These technical representations may reference the same canonical Record identity.
One Event
↓
Multiple Technical Representations ≠ Multiple Canonical Records by default.
Record Identity and Event Identity
Event identity and Record identity shall remain distinct.
The Event represents governed economic or operational reality.
The Record represents that Event as governed information.
Therefore:
Event Identifier ≠ Record Identifier.
A system may associate both, but shall not collapse their methodological functions.
Record Identity and Technical Identity
A system may create: database primary keys; transaction IDs; document IDs; message IDs; invoice numbers; ledger hashes; API request IDs; internal object IDs.
These identifiers may contribute to Record identification.
They do not automatically become the canonical Governed Event Record Identity.
Technical Identifier ≠ Governed Record Identifier by default.

Canonical Record Reference
ERIDM establishes a canonical reference through which other TREGS modules and downstream systems can identify the same governed Record.
The reference enables a common answer to:
Which governed Event Record are we discussing?
without requiring every system to use the same internal identifier.
Local and Canonical Identifiers
A Record may possess both:
Canonical Record Identifier
and:
Local Technical Identifier(s)
Local identifiers may change between systems.
The canonical identity shall remain associable across those representations.
This supports:
Canonical Record Identity
↓
System A Identifier / System B Identifier / System C Identifier
without creating multiple Event realities.
Identifier Mapping
Where multiple systems maintain different local identifiers, mappings may associate them with the canonical Record identity.
ERIDM governs the identification meaning of that mapping.
Detailed cross-system interoperability belongs to ERINM.
Identifier Mapping ≠ Full Record Interoperability.
Record Identity Duplication
Duplicate identity occurs where multiple canonical Record identities are unintentionally established for the same intended governed Record.
ERIDM shall support detection and governance of potential duplication.
Potential indicators include: same Event reference; same Determination reference; overlapping Record creation; duplicate ingestion; system retry; replicated processing; or migration error.
Duplicate Record Candidate

Where multiple Record Candidates appear to represent the same Determined Tax-Relevant Event, ERIDM shall not automatically establish multiple canonical Record identities.
The candidates should be evaluated for whether they represent: the same canonical Record; legitimate separate governed Records; technical copies; or identity conflict.
Duplicate Candidate ≠ Duplicate Governed Record by default.
Identifier Collision
Identifier Collision occurs where the same identifier appears to refer to materially different Record identities.
A collision shall be governed explicitly.
The system shall not resolve a collision merely by assuming the records are identical.
Identifier Equality ≠ Record Identity Equality.
Identity Conflict
Record Identity Conflict exists where available identification information supports incompatible Record identity conclusions.
Possible states include: Same Record; Different Records; Duplicate Candidate; Collision; Ambiguous; Unresolved.
An unresolved material identity conflict should prevent unqualified Record identification.
Record Identity Ambiguity
Ambiguity exists where the Record cannot yet be reliably distinguished from one or more candidate Records.
Ambiguity may require: additional Event association; Determination reference; technical-source reconciliation; or escalation.
Ambiguous Record Identity ≠ Permission to Select an Arbitrary Identifier.
Identifier Reuse

A canonical Record identifier should not be reassigned to an unrelated governed Record after the original Record becomes inactive, superseded, or closed.
Historical identity must remain reconstructable.
Inactive Identifier ≠ Available Identifier for Reuse by default.
Record Identity Continuity
The same governed Record should preserve identity continuity through technical change.
Continuity may span:
Creation
↓
Active Use
↓
Transformation
↓
Migration
↓
Supersession Reference
↓
Historical Preservation
ERIDM establishes the identity foundation.
TRECLS later governs broader Event lifecycle continuity.
Record Identity and Correction
A correction to Record content does not automatically create a new Record identity.
Whether identity remains continuous depends on whether the same governed Record continues to represent the same Event.
Record Correction ≠ New Record Identity by default.
Record structure correction itself belongs to the appropriate TREGS/TRECLS governance layer.
Record Identity and Supersession
A superseding Record may require a distinct Record identity while retaining explicit association with the superseded Record.
ERIDM governs the distinguishability of those Record identities.
TRECLS governs broader lifecycle supersession.
Superseding Record ≠ Same Record Identity by default.
Record Identity and Event Correction
Where the underlying Event changes materially through upstream governance, ERIDM shall not independently decide whether the Event remains the same Event.

That determination belongs to the authoritative Event-governance layer.
ERIDM consumes the resulting Event identity state.
Record Identity and Merge
Where several Events are merged under TRERLS, existing Record identities shall not automatically collapse into one identity.
A resulting governed Event may require an appropriate canonical Record identity while prior Record identities remain traceable.
Event Merge ≠ Automatic Record Identifier Merge.
Record Identity and Split
Where one Event is split into multiple governed Events, the original Record identity shall not automatically be copied to every resulting Record.
Event Split ≠ Record Identity Replication.
Record Identity and Determination Reconsideration
A reconsidered Determination does not automatically require a new Record identity.
If the same governed Record continues to represent the same Event, identity continuity may remain.
If Event identity or canonical representation materially changes, further governance may be required.
Determination Reconsideration ≠ New Record Identity by default.
Cross-System Identity
Different systems may refer to the same governed Record using different local identifiers.
ERIDM supports association of those identifiers with one canonical Record identity.
Different System Identifier ≠ Different Governed Record.
Cross-Organization Identity
Organizations may maintain independent internal identifiers for the same exchanged governed Record.

Canonical identity enables those representations to remain associated without requiring identical internal infrastructure.
Different Organizational Identifier ≠ Different Event Reality.
Cross-Border Record Identity
A Record may be consumed in several jurisdictions.
Each jurisdiction may assign its own: case number; tax reference; filing identifier; assessment identifier; reporting reference.
Those identifiers remain downstream jurisdiction-specific references.
They do not replace the canonical TREGA™ Record identity.
Tax Authority Identifier ≠ Canonical Event Record Identifier.
Multi-Jurisdiction Identity Continuity
The same governed Record may support:
Canonical Record ID
↓
Jurisdiction A Evaluation
Canonical Record ID
↓
Jurisdiction B Evaluation
Canonical Record ID
↓
Jurisdiction C Evaluation
This allows different legal evaluations to remain associated with the same underlying governed Event Record.
Invoice Identifier Boundary
An invoice number may be referenced by a Governed Event Record.
It does not automatically identify the governed Event Record itself.
Invoice Number ≠ Governed Event Record Identifier by default.
Payment Identifier Boundary
A payment transaction identifier may identify a payment record.
It does not automatically identify the Tax-Relevant Event Record.
Payment ID ≠ Event Record ID by default.
Blockchain Identifier Boundary
A transaction hash may uniquely identify a blockchain transaction.
It does not automatically identify the governed Event Record.

Blockchain Transaction Hash ≠ Governed Event Record Identifier by default.
Smart-Contract Identifier Boundary
A contract address or execution identifier may contribute to Record identification but does not replace canonical Event Record identity.
Smart-Contract Execution ID ≠ Governed Event Record ID by default.
AI-Agent Record Identity
AI agents may autonomously create technical records.
ERIDM requires stable governed Record identification independently of whether a human or machine created the representation.
Agent-Generated Identifier ≠ Governed Record Identity by default.
Machine-Scale Identification
Machine environments may create millions of technical identifiers.
ERIDM prevents identifier volume from becoming governed Record volume.
Canonical Record identities should correspond to governed Record objects rather than raw technical activity.
Technical Identifier Count ≠ Governed Record Count.
Record Identity Authority
ERIDM requires an identifiable governance basis for establishing canonical Record identity.
The specific technical or organizational authority may vary by implementation.
The authority shall be capable of establishing identity without contradicting upstream Event governance.
Record identity authority does not confer tax authority.
Record Identification Authority ≠ Tax Authority.
Identity Trace Reference
The Record identity should retain sufficient references to reconstruct:
Determined Event
↓
Record Candidate
↓
Canonical Record Identity

Detailed Record traceability is subsequently governed by ERTM.
ERIDM establishes the minimum identification lineage necessary for identity governance.
Identification Confidence
Where automated matching or probabilistic identity resolution is used, confidence may support the identification process.
Confidence shall not substitute for governed identity.
High Match Confidence ≠ Established Record Identity by default.
Identity Escalation
Material ambiguity, duplication, or collision may require escalation.
Escalation should occur where an unqualified Record identity cannot be responsibly established.
Possible escalation states include: Manual Review Required; Cross-System Reconciliation Required; Event Reference Review Required; Duplicate Resolution Required; Identity Conflict Resolution Required.
Proportional Identification Governance
Identification governance should be proportional to Record complexity and downstream reliance.
A simple single-system Event may require limited identification infrastructure.
A distributed cross-border Event spanning multiple platforms may require stronger canonical identity controls.
Greater Identifier Complexity ≠ Stronger Identification by default.
Governance States
ERIDM may represent:
Identification Not Initiated
Record Candidate Identified
Identification Eligibility Under Review
Identification Eligible
Canonical Identifier Pending
Canonical Identifier Established
Event Association Pending
Event Association Established

Duplicate Candidate Detected
Identifier Collision Detected
Identity Ambiguous
Identity Conflicted
Escalation Required
Identity Continuity Established
Governed Event Record Identity Established
Ready for Record Structure Governance Governance Requirements

ERIDM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Determined Tax-Relevant Event exists before canonical Record identification; the Record Candidate can be associated with the Event it represents; Record identity remains distinct from Event identity; canonical Record identity remains distinguishable from local technical identifiers; identifiers are sufficiently unique within their declared scope; identifier scope is explicit where material; canonical identity can remain stable across technical transformations; technical identifier change does not automatically create new canonical identity; Record identity remains persistent where historical reconstruction is required; multiple technical representations do not automatically create multiple canonical Records; duplicate Record Candidates can be detected; identifier collisions are governed explicitly; ambiguous identity does not result in arbitrary identification; identifiers are not silently reused for unrelated Records; Record corrections do not automatically create new identities; Event Merge does not automatically merge Record identities; Event Split does not automatically replicate Record identity; Determination reconsideration does not automatically create new Record identity; local system identifiers may map to canonical identity; jurisdiction-specific tax identifiers remain downstream references; machine-generated identifiers do not automatically become governed Record identities; probabilistic confidence does not replace

cific tax identifiers remain downstream references; machine-generated identifiers do not automatically become governed Record identities; probabilistic confidence does not replace governed identification; unresolved material identity conflicts can be escalated; and the resulting Governed Event Record Identity is suitable for ERSTM.

Governance Logic
IF no valid Determined Tax-Relevant Event exists, THEN ERIDM shall not establish a canonical Governed Event Record Identity.
IF a Record Candidate cannot be reliably associated with a Determined Tax-Relevant Event, THEN canonical identification shall remain incomplete.
IF a technical identifier exists but no canonical Record identity has been governed, THEN the technical identifier shall not automatically become the Governed Event Record Identifier.
IF several technical representations refer to the same intended governed Record, THEN ERIDM shall preserve one canonical identity unless distinct governed Record identities are materially justified.
IF two Record Candidates appear to represent the same Event and same intended canonical Record, THEN duplicate resolution shall occur before independent canonical identities are established.
IF the same identifier refers to materially different Record identities, THEN Identifier Collision shall be established and resolved before unqualified identification.
IF the same Record moves between systems while its canonical governance identity remains unchanged, THEN canonical Record identity shall persist.
IF a local technical identifier changes, THEN canonical Record identity shall remain unchanged unless a materially new governed Record has been established.

IF an Event Merge or Split changes the underlying governed Event structure, THEN ERIDM shall consume the authoritative Event result rather than infer new Record identity independently.
IF identity remains materially ambiguous or conflicted, THEN escalation shall occur rather than arbitrary identifier assignment.
IF Record identity and Event association are sufficiently established, THEN ERIDM shall produce the Governed Event Record Identity and hand it to ERSTM.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERIDM implementation should support:
Record Identification Governance ID A stable reference for the ERIDM governance process.
Determined Event Reference The TREDS-governed Event represented by the Record.
Final Determination Reference The applicable TREDS Determination state.
Record Candidate Reference The proposed governed Record representation.
Canonical Record Identifier The stable governed identifier established for the Record.
Identifier Type The technical or methodological form of the canonical identifier.
Identifier Scope The environment within which uniqueness is governed.
Identifier Authority Reference The process or authority responsible for canonical identifier establishment.
Identifier Creation State Pending, Established, Rejected, Ambiguous, or Conflicted.
Event-to-Record Association The governed association between Event and Record identity.
Event Association State Pending, Established, Ambiguous, Conflicted, or Invalid.

Local Identifier Reference(s) Any system-specific identifiers associated with the canonical Record.
Identifier Mapping Reference Mappings between canonical and local identifiers where applicable.
Duplicate Candidate State Whether potential duplicate Record identity exists.
Duplicate Candidate Reference References to potentially duplicate Record Candidates.
Identifier Collision State Whether identifier collision has been detected.
Collision Reference The competing Record identities involved.
Identity Ambiguity State Whether Record identity remains ambiguous.
Identity Conflict State Whether materially incompatible identity conclusions exist.
Prior Record Identity Reference Any previous canonical Record identity relevant to continuity.
Superseding Record Identity Reference Any later Record identity that supersedes the current Record where applicable.
Identity Continuity State Whether canonical identity continuity remains established.
Identification Confidence Reference Supporting confidence information where automated identity matching is used.
Escalation State Whether identity governance requires escalation.
Identification Trace Reference Minimum lineage from Determined Event to canonical Record identity.
Governance State The current ERIDM governance state.
Handoff State Whether the identified Record is ready for ERSTM.
Governance Outputs

ERIDM may produce: Record Candidate Identification; Identification Eligibility State; Canonical Record Identifier; Identifier Scope; Identifier Authority Reference; Event-to-Record Association; Local Identifier References; Identifier Mapping Reference; Duplicate Candidate State; Identifier Collision State; Identity Ambiguity State; Identity Conflict State; Identity Continuity State; Identification Escalation; Identification Trace Reference; and the principal output: Governed Event Record Identity.
Critical Distinctions
Record Identity ≠ Event Identity.
Technical Object ≠ Governed Record Candidate by default.
Record Eligibility ≠ Record Identification Completion.
Shared Identifier ≠ Shared Record Identity by default.
System Migration ≠ New Record Identity.
Schema Change ≠ New Record Identity.
Storage Location Change ≠ New Record Identity.
Technical Identifier Change ≠ Canonical Record Identity Change by default.
Event Identifier ≠ Record Identifier.
Technical Identifier ≠ Governed Record Identifier by default.
Identifier Mapping ≠ Full Record Interoperability.
Duplicate Candidate ≠ Duplicate Governed Record by default.
Identifier Equality ≠ Record Identity Equality.
Ambiguous Record Identity ≠ Permission to Select an Arbitrary Identifier.
Inactive Identifier ≠ Available Identifier for Reuse by default.
Record Correction ≠ New Record Identity by default.
Superseding Record ≠ Same Record Identity by default.
Event Merge ≠ Automatic Record Identifier Merge.

Event Split ≠ Record Identity Replication.
Determination Reconsideration ≠ New Record Identity by default.
Different System Identifier ≠ Different Governed Record.
Different Organizational Identifier ≠ Different Event Reality.
Tax Authority Identifier ≠ Canonical Event Record Identifier.
Invoice Number ≠ Governed Event Record Identifier by default.
Payment ID ≠ Event Record ID by default.
Blockchain Transaction Hash ≠ Governed Event Record Identifier by default.
Smart-Contract Execution ID ≠ Governed Event Record ID by default.
Agent-Generated Identifier ≠ Governed Record Identity by default.
Technical Identifier Count ≠ Governed Record Count.
Record Identification Authority ≠ Tax Authority.
High Match Confidence ≠ Established Record Identity by default.
Greater Identifier Complexity ≠ Stronger Identification by default.
Enterprise Application
ERIDM provides the identity anchor for Event Record Governance.
A canonical enterprise pattern is:
Determined Tax-Relevant Event
→ ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
→ ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure
→ ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage
→ ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability
→ ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability
→ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
This enables different systems to reference the same governed Record without forcing them to use identical technical identifiers. Use Case 1 — One Marketplace Event Across Multiple Systems

A marketplace Event has completed TREDS and exists as a Determined Tax-Relevant Event.
The marketplace platform assigns transaction identifier A, the ERP assigns object identifier B, the payment infrastructure uses transaction reference C, and a downstream tax system creates processing reference D.
ERIDM establishes one canonical Governed Event Record Identity associated with the Determined Event and maps the relevant local identifiers to that Record identity.
The four technical identifiers therefore remain distinguishable technical references rather than four separate governed Event Records.
Different Technical Identifiers
↓
One Canonical Governed Record Identity. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Producing Duplicate Record Candidates
An autonomous platform completes one governed service Event.
Because of distributed processing and retry logic, three infrastructure nodes independently create Record Candidates for the same Determined Tax-Relevant Event.
Each candidate receives a different local system identifier.
ERIDM detects that all three candidates reference the same Determined Event and the same intended canonical Record.
Instead of establishing three canonical Event Record identities, the module identifies the candidates as duplicate technical representations and establishes one Governed Event Record Identity.
The technical records remain traceable without multiplying the canonical Event Record.
Canonical Boundary

ERIDM owns the governance of Record candidate identification, identification eligibility, canonical Record identity establishment, identifier assignment, uniqueness, scope, stability, persistence, Event-to-Record association, distinction between canonical and technical identifiers, duplicate identity detection, identifier collision, identity ambiguity, identity continuity, identifier mapping at identification level, and establishment of the Governed Event Record Identity.
ERIDM does not identify or determine the underlying Event.
It does not govern the full structural contents of the Record; ERSTM owns Record Structure.
It does not govern broader Record Linkage; ERLKM owns that space.
It does not govern complete Record Traceability; ERTM owns that space.
It does not govern cross-system semantic interoperability; ERINM owns that space.
It does not govern Event lifecycle amendment, correction, supersession, or closure; TRECLS owns those lifecycle functions.
It does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, exemption, deduction, filing obligation, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
Its governance begins when a valid Determined Tax-Relevant Event requires a canonical Record identity.
Its governance ends when the Governed Event Record Identity and its association with the underlying Event are sufficiently established for Record Structure Governance.
Canonical Handoff

TREDS — Determined Tax-Relevant Event
↓
ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
↓
ERSTM — Event Record Structure Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERIDM establishes the identity anchor through which a Determined Tax-Relevant Event can persist as one governed Record across changing systems, identifiers, organizations, and technical representations.
The Record must be identifiable without being mistaken for the Event it represents.
Record Identity ≠ Event Identity.
Different Technical Identifiers ≠ Different Governed Records.

OOF™ The Event Record Interoperability Module (ERINM) governs how a traceable
The Event Record Interoperability Module (ERINM) governs how a traceable
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard
Module: ERINM — Event Record Interoperability Module
Operational Layer: Event Record Interoperability Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Record Interoperability
Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Interoperability State
Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERINM-005
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 3 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Record Interoperability Module (ERINM) governs how a traceable Tax-Relevant Event Record is exchanged, translated, mapped, transformed, consumed, and reused across systems, organizations, technical environments, and jurisdiction-specific downstream infrastructures without losing its canonical Event meaning, Record identity, governance state, qualifications, materially relevant traceability, or jurisdiction-neutral character.
Its principal transition is:

Governed Event Record Traceability State
↓
Event Record Interoperability Governance
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
ERINM is the final Core Module of TREGS.
It establishes whether the Event Record can remain governably equivalent across different technical and organizational environments.
Its foundational distinction is:
Data Exchange ≠ Interoperability.
Operational Role
A Record may be correctly identified, structurally governed, linked, and traceable but still fail when transferred to another system.
A receiving system may: rename fields; change schemas; transform data types; omit qualifications; collapse state distinctions; lose Event references; reinterpret Value; alter timing semantics; discard trace references; or inject jurisdiction-specific assumptions.
ERINM governs against this semantic degradation.
It answers:
Can another system receive and use this Event Record while preserving what the governed Event actually means?
Internal Module Flow
TREGS operates through:
ERIDM — Event Record Identification
↓
ERSTM — Event Record Structure
↓
ERLKM — Event Record Linkage
↓
ERTM — Event Record Traceability
↓
ERINM — Event Record Interoperability
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
ERINM receives:
Governed Event Record Traceability State
and produces:
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
as the final TREGS output.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Governed Event Record Traceability State
↓
Interoperability Requirement Identification
↓
Semantic Mapping
↓

Structural Transformation
↓
Governance Preservation Assessment
↓
Interoperability State
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Operational Space
ERINM governs: interoperability scope; source and target environment identification; semantic preservation; structural mapping; field mapping; state mapping; identifier preservation; Event-reference preservation; Determination preservation; qualification preservation; uncertainty preservation; linkage preservation; traceability preservation; transformation governance; loss detection; semantic conflict; compatibility; interoperability qualification; cross-system exchange; cross-organization exchange; cross-border reuse; machine interoperability; API interoperability; schema evolution; version compatibility; and final TREGS handoff.
Operational Scope
ERINM may govern interoperability among: ERP systems; accounting systems; banking systems; payment networks; marketplaces; commerce platforms; tax engines; reporting systems; data warehouses; APIs; distributed platforms; blockchain systems; smart-contract environments; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine infrastructure; industrial systems; public-sector systems; and future digital economies.
The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Interoperability Object
The interoperability object is the governed meaning of the Event Record as it moves between environments.
ERINM does not require identical technology.

It requires preservation of materially relevant governance semantics.
Interoperability Object ≠ Technical File Format.
Source Environment
The Source Environment is the technical or organizational environment from which the governed Record is transferred or exposed.
The source may use its own: schema; identifier; field names; data types; storage architecture; API design.
These technical properties do not define the canonical Event meaning.
Target Environment
The Target Environment is the system or organization receiving or consuming the Record.
The target may use a materially different technical representation.
ERINM determines whether canonical meaning can survive that difference.
Semantic Preservation
Semantic Preservation exists where the receiving environment can interpret materially relevant Record elements consistently with their governed meaning.
This includes preservation of distinctions such as: Event vs Record; Participant vs Taxpayer; Event Location vs Tax Jurisdiction; Event Time vs Legal Tax Point; Value Association vs Tax Base; Determination vs Taxability; qualification vs unqualified conclusion.
Same Data Value ≠ Same Semantic Meaning by default.
Semantic Equivalence
Two Record representations may be semantically equivalent even where their: schemas differ; field names differ; encoding differs; system architecture differs.
Equivalence depends on preserved governance meaning.
Technical Difference ≠ Semantic Difference by default.
Semantic Drift

Semantic Drift occurs where the Record's meaning changes during exchange or transformation.
Examples include: Event Location converted into Tax Jurisdiction; Participant converted into Taxpayer; Event Timing converted into legal tax point; Value Association converted into taxable amount; Conditional Determination represented as final legal Taxability; qualification removed; uncertainty discarded.
Semantic Drift shall prevent unqualified interoperability.
Structural Mapping
ERINM may map one Record structure into another technical schema.
Mapping shall preserve canonical structural meaning established by ERSTM.
Schema Mapping ≠ Semantic Permission to Redefine Fields.
Field Mapping
Field Mapping governs correspondence between source and target representations.
A mapped field should retain its governed concept even where its name or format changes.
For example:
Source: EventLocation
↓
Target: OperationalLocation
may remain compatible.
But:
Source: EventLocation
↓
Target: TaxJurisdiction
would represent semantic transformation and require separate downstream governance.
State Mapping
Governance states shall remain distinguishable across systems.
A target system should not collapse materially distinct states such as: Determination State; Record State; uncertainty state; lifecycle state.
State Mapping ≠ State Collapse.
Identifier Preservation
The canonical Record identity should remain preserved or reliably mapped across systems.
Local identifiers may change.

The canonical association shall not be lost.
Local ID Change ≠ Record Identity Change.
Event Reference Preservation
The target representation shall preserve the association between the Record and the underlying Determined Tax-Relevant Event.
A target Record detached from its Event reference may lose canonical TREGS meaning.
Determination Preservation
The applicable TREDS Determination state shall remain interpretable after exchange.
The target system shall not transform:
Tax-Relevant Event Determination
↓
Legal Taxability Conclusion
without downstream jurisdictional governance.
Qualification Preservation
Material qualifications shall survive interoperability.
Interoperability Transformation ≠ Permission to Remove Qualification.
Uncertainty Preservation
Material uncertainty references shall remain preserved where required for responsible downstream reliance.
A receiving system shall not create artificial certainty by discarding uncertainty.
Linkage Preservation
Material ERLKM links shall remain identifiable or reconstructable after transfer where necessary.
Interoperability does not require identical technical link mechanisms.
It requires preservation of link semantics.
Traceability Preservation
The Record's materially relevant ERTM traceability shall survive system exchange.
A receiving system need not physically copy every trace object if it can preserve reliable governed references.
Trace Reference Preservation ≠ Full Historical Data Replication.
Transformation Governance

Transformation occurs where a Record changes: schema; format; encoding; data type; API representation; storage model; semantic model.
Each material transformation should preserve the canonical Record meaning.
Loss Detection
ERINM shall detect where transformation causes material information loss.
Loss may involve: identity; Event reference; Determination state; qualification; uncertainty; links; traceability; state semantics.
Successful Transmission ≠ Lossless Governance Transfer.
Material Loss
A transformation is materially lossy where omitted or altered information could change downstream interpretation of the Event Record.
Material loss shall result in: qualification; remediation; rejection; or restricted use.
Non-Material Loss
Technical detail may be omitted where it does not materially affect governed meaning or downstream use.
Information Loss ≠ Governance Loss by default.
Interoperability Compatibility
Compatibility may be: Full; Conditional; Partial; Qualified; Incompatible; Unresolved.
Compatibility should be assessed against governed meaning rather than technical connectivity alone.
Full Interoperability
Full Interoperability exists where materially relevant canonical meaning can be preserved without unresolved governance loss.
Conditional Interoperability
Conditional Interoperability exists where exchange is valid only under explicit limitations.

For example: one qualification cannot be represented directly; one uncertainty state requires external reference; one linkage type requires custom mapping.
The condition shall remain visible.
Partial Interoperability
Partial Interoperability exists where only part of the governed Record can be exchanged without semantic distortion.
A partial exchange shall not be represented as full canonical equivalence. Incompatibility
A target system is incompatible where it cannot preserve materially necessary governed meaning.
Technical connectivity does not override this conclusion.
Connected Systems ≠ Interoperable Systems.
Interoperability Conflict
Conflict exists where source and target systems assign materially incompatible meanings to the same concept.
Example:
Source: Participant = actor materially involved in Event
Target: Participant = legally liable taxpayer
The concepts shall not be treated as equivalent.
Cross-System Interoperability
ERINM supports the movement of one governed Record across multiple technical systems.
A canonical pattern is:
Marketplace
↓
ERP
↓
Accounting
↓
Tax Engine
while preserving one governed Record meaning.
Cross-Organization Interoperability
Different organizations may receive and use the same governed Record while maintaining separate technical environments.
Interoperability should preserve the shared methodological meaning without requiring identical internal systems.
Cross-Border Interoperability

A Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record may enter several jurisdictional environments.
The source Record remains jurisdiction-neutral.
Downstream jurisdictions may add their own legal layers.
Cross-Border Interoperability ≠ Tax Harmonization.
Jurisdiction-Neutral Core
The canonical TREGS Record shall remain distinguishable from jurisdiction-specific extensions.
The target tax environment may add: nexus; taxpayer determination; tax point; Tax Base; Tax Rate; legal classification; exemption; filing state.
These are downstream outputs.
They shall not alter the canonical TREGA™ Record semantics.
Multi-Jurisdiction Reuse
ERINM supports:
One Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Tax Engines
This allows the same governed Event Reality to be consumed repeatedly without being rebuilt independently.
Jurisdictional Result Separation
Different tax engines may produce different conclusions.
ERINM preserves their association with the same Event Record while keeping those conclusions distinct.
Different Tax Outcomes ≠ Different Governed Event Records by default.
API Interoperability
APIs may transport governed Event Records.
ERINM requires API mappings to preserve material semantics.
A technically valid API response may still be governance-incompatible.
API Success ≠ Interoperability Success.
Message-Based Interoperability
Event streams, queues, or messaging systems may exchange partial representations.

ERINM shall ensure that message fragmentation does not destroy canonical meaning.
Batch Interoperability
Bulk files may contain multiple Event Records.
Batch packaging shall not collapse Record identities or Event boundaries.
One File ≠ One Event.
Graph Interoperability
Graph-based systems may represent Events and Records through nodes and edges.
ERINM governs preservation of canonical meaning regardless of graph representation.
Blockchain Interoperability
Blockchain systems may consume or emit Record representations.
On-chain immutability does not establish semantic compatibility with off-chain Event governance.
On-Chain Compatibility ≠ Governance Interoperability by default.
AI-Agent Interoperability
AI agents may consume, transform, and generate governed Event Records.
Agent inference shall not redefine canonical field meaning without explicit governance.
AI Interpretation ≠ Canonical Semantic Authority.
Autonomous-System Interoperability
Autonomous platforms may exchange Event Records without human intervention.
ERINM requires governed meaning to remain stable even in machine-to-machine exchange.
Machine-to-Machine Interoperability
M2M environments may operate at massive scale.
Interoperability shall be based on canonical governance semantics rather than the ability of machines to parse each other's messages.
Machine Readability ≠ Governance Interoperability.
Schema Evolution
Systems may evolve schemas over time.

ERINM shall support continued interpretation of canonical concepts across schema versions.
Version Compatibility
A newer Record representation may remain interoperable with an older environment where canonical semantics can still be preserved.
Compatibility shall not be assumed merely because version numbers are close.
Version Compatibility ≠ Semantic Compatibility by default.
Backward Interoperability
Where older systems consume newer Records, transformation may reduce available detail.
Material governance meaning shall still be preserved or the exchange qualified.
Forward Interoperability
Future systems should be able to interpret prior canonical Record semantics where materially required for continuity. Extensibility
Extensions may add sector-specific or jurisdiction-specific information.
Extensions shall remain distinguishable from the canonical TREGA™ core.
Extension Compatibility ≠ Canonical Modification.
Interoperability Qualification
Where full semantic preservation is impossible but use remains legitimate, the Record may carry an interoperability qualification.
Possible qualifications include: Missing Non-Critical Field; External Reference Required; Limited State Mapping; Partial Traceability Transfer; Conditional Link Preservation; Jurisdiction-Specific Extension Present.
Interoperability Failure
Interoperability fails where transformation or exchange would materially distort the governed Event Record.

Failure should result in: rejection; remediation; alternate mapping; manual review; or restricted use.
Interoperability Reassessment
Interoperability may require reassessment when: source schema changes; target schema changes; canonical structure evolves; new governance states appear; new system behavior changes semantic interpretation; downstream requirements materially change.
Interoperability Continuity
Interoperability should remain maintainable across infrastructure evolution.
System Upgrade ≠ Permission for Semantic Drift.
Record Portability
A governed Event Record should remain portable where its canonical identity and meaning can be preserved.
Portability is one practical outcome of interoperability.
Portability ≠ Mere Export Capability.
Semantic Compression Boundary
A target system may summarize a Record.
The summary shall not be treated as canonical equivalent if material governance meaning was omitted.
Interoperability and Record Identity
ERIDM establishes Record identity.
ERINM preserves or maps that identity across environments.
Identity Mapping ≠ Identity Re-establishment.
Interoperability and Structure
ERSTM establishes canonical Record Structure.
ERINM maps that meaning into target structures.
Schema Translation ≠ Record Restructuring Authority.
Interoperability and Linkage
ERLKM governs material links.
ERINM preserves their meaning across environments.
Link Translation ≠ Link Governance.
Interoperability and Traceability

ERTM establishes reconstructable lineage.
ERINM preserves sufficient access to that lineage after exchange.
Traceability Transfer ≠ Traceability Creation.
Interoperability and Validation
ERINM may assess interoperability compatibility.
It does not perform general validation governance.
VALIDOS™ remains authoritative.
Interoperability Assessment ≠ Validation Certification.
Interoperability and Integrity
ERINM protects semantic preservation during exchange.
Broader integrity governance belongs to INTEGROS®.
Semantic Preservation ≠ General Integrity Governance.
Interoperability and Tax Law
ERINM does not harmonize tax law or determine legal tax consequences.
It ensures that tax systems receive the same governed Event Reality before they apply their own rules.
Interoperability ≠ Tax Harmonization.
Governance States
ERINM may represent:
Interoperability Governance Not Initiated
Source Environment Identified
Target Environment Identified
Mapping Requirements Identified
Semantic Mapping Under Review
Structural Mapping Established
Identity Preservation Established
Event Reference Preservation Established
Determination Preservation Established
Qualification Preservation Established
Traceability Preservation Established
Material Loss Detected
Semantic Conflict Detected
Compatibility Partial
Compatibility Conditional
Compatibility Full
Interoperability Qualified
Interoperability Failed
Interoperability Reassessment Required
Governed Event Record Interoperability State Established
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Established Governance Requirements

ERINM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Record Traceability State exists; source and target environments are identifiable; canonical Record identity remains preserved or reliably mapped; underlying Event reference remains preserved; canonical Record semantics remain distinguishable from technical schema; Determination state remains correctly interpretable; qualifications remain visible; material uncertainty remains preserved; material links retain their governed meaning; sufficient traceability remains accessible; schema transformation does not silently redefine canonical concepts; technical data transfer is not treated as semantic interoperability by default; materially lossy transformations are detected; compatibility states remain explicit; partial interoperability is not represented as full equivalence; incompatible semantics are not silently mapped; jurisdiction-specific extensions remain separate from canonical Record meaning; different jurisdictional outcomes do not create different Event Records by default; APIs, messages, files, graphs, blockchains, and AI systems remain subject to the same semantic preservation requirements; machine readability is not treated as sufficient interoperability; schema and version changes trigger reassessment where material; extensions do not redefine the canonical TREGA™ core; interoperability remains distinct from validation, integrity, tax harmonization, identity establishment, linkage, and traceability; and th

o not redefine the canonical TREGA™ core; interoperability remains distinct from validation, integrity, tax harmonization, identity establishment, linkage, and traceability; and the resulting Record is suitable for TREGS completion and TRECLS handoff.

Governance Logic
IF no valid Governed Event Record Traceability State exists, THEN ERINM shall not establish complete TREGS Interoperability.
IF source and target systems use different schemas but preserve canonical meaning, THEN interoperability may remain valid.
IF a field mapping changes a canonical concept into a materially different legal or operational concept, THEN the mapping shall not be treated as semantically equivalent.
IF Record identity can be reliably mapped across systems, THEN different local identifiers shall not prevent interoperability.
IF material qualification or uncertainty cannot be preserved, THEN interoperability shall remain conditional, partial, or failed depending on materiality.
IF a transformation removes materially necessary traceability, THEN the resulting Record shall not qualify as fully interoperable.
IF a jurisdiction-specific tax system adds legal conclusions, THEN those conclusions shall remain downstream extensions rather than canonical TREGA™ fields.
IF technical transmission succeeds but semantic preservation fails, THEN interoperability shall be considered failed or qualified.
IF only non-material information is lost, THEN interoperability may remain valid with appropriate governance state.
IF the Record preserves canonical identity, Event reference, Determination, materially relevant state, linkage, traceability, and semantic meaning across the intended environment, THEN ERINM shall establish the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record.

Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERINM implementation should support:
Interoperability Governance ID A stable identifier for the ERINM governance process.
Canonical Record Identifier The ERIDM-established Record identity.
Traceability State Reference The applicable ERTM output.
Source Environment ID The environment from which the Record originates.
Target Environment ID The environment receiving or consuming the Record.
Source Schema Reference The applicable source representation.
Target Schema Reference The applicable target representation.
Mapping Profile ID The governed mapping used between environments.
Canonical Concept Reference The governed TREGA™ concept being transferred.
Source Field / Component Reference Its source representation.
Target Field / Component Reference Its target representation.
Semantic Equivalence State Equivalent, Qualified, Partial, Conflicted, or Incompatible.
Identifier Preservation State Whether canonical Record identity remains preserved.
Event Reference Preservation State Whether underlying Event association remains preserved.
Determination Preservation State Whether TREDS state remains correctly represented.
Qualification Preservation State Whether material qualifications remain available.
Uncertainty Preservation State Whether material uncertainty remains represented.
Linkage Preservation State Whether materially relevant links remain interpretable.
Traceability Preservation State Whether sufficient reconstruction remains possible.

Transformation Type Schema, Format, Encoding, API, Storage, Semantic, or other transformation.
Material Loss State None, Non-Material, Material, Critical, or Unresolved.
Semantic Drift State Whether canonical meaning changed during transformation.
Compatibility State Full, Conditional, Partial, Incompatible, or Unresolved.
Interoperability Qualification Any restrictions on downstream use.
Jurisdiction-Specific Extension State Whether downstream legal-tax extensions are present.
Version Compatibility State The compatibility status between source and target versions.
Reassessment State Whether interoperability reassessment is required.
Governance State The current ERINM governance state.
TREGS Completion State Whether all required TREGS module outputs are sufficiently governed.
Handoff State Whether the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record is ready for TRECLS.
Governance Outputs

ERINM may produce: Source Environment State; Target Environment State; Mapping Profile; Semantic Equivalence State; Structural Mapping State; Identifier Preservation State; Event Reference Preservation State; Determination Preservation State; Qualification Preservation State; Uncertainty Preservation State; Linkage Preservation State; Traceability Preservation State; Material Loss State; Semantic Drift State; Compatibility State; Interoperability Qualification; Version Compatibility State; Cross-System Interoperability State; Cross-Organization Interoperability State; Cross-Border Interoperability State; Multi-Jurisdiction Reuse State; TREGS Completion State; and the principal output: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record.
Critical Distinctions
Data Exchange ≠ Interoperability.
Interoperability Object ≠ Technical File Format.
Same Data Value ≠ Same Semantic Meaning by default.
Technical Difference ≠ Semantic Difference by default.
Schema Mapping ≠ Semantic Permission to Redefine Fields.
State Mapping ≠ State Collapse.
Local ID Change ≠ Record Identity Change.
Interoperability Transformation ≠ Permission to Remove Qualification.
Trace Reference Preservation ≠ Full Historical Data Replication.
Successful Transmission ≠ Lossless Governance Transfer.
Information Loss ≠ Governance Loss by default.
Connected Systems ≠ Interoperable Systems.
Cross-Border Interoperability ≠ Tax Harmonization.
Different Tax Outcomes ≠ Different Governed Event Records by default.

API Success ≠ Interoperability Success.
One File ≠ One Event.
On-Chain Compatibility ≠ Governance Interoperability by default.
AI Interpretation ≠ Canonical Semantic Authority.
Machine Readability ≠ Governance Interoperability.
Version Compatibility ≠ Semantic Compatibility by default.
Extension Compatibility ≠ Canonical Modification.
System Upgrade ≠ Permission for Semantic Drift.
Portability ≠ Mere Export Capability.
Identity Mapping ≠ Identity Re-establishment.
Schema Translation ≠ Record Restructuring Authority.
Link Translation ≠ Link Governance.
Traceability Transfer ≠ Traceability Creation.
Interoperability Assessment ≠ Validation Certification.
Semantic Preservation ≠ General Integrity Governance.
Interoperability ≠ Tax Harmonization.
Enterprise Application
ERINM provides the final TREGS capability required to turn a governed Event Record into reusable tax-infrastructure input.
The canonical enterprise path is:
ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
→ ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure
→ ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage State
→ ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State
→ ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability State
→ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
The resulting Record can then support:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Digital Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ TREGA™ Governed Event Record Layer
→ Jurisdiction A Tax Engine
→ Jurisdiction B Tax Engine
→ Jurisdiction C Tax Engine

without requiring each downstream system to reconstruct the Event independently. Use Case 1 — One Global Commerce Event Across Three Jurisdictional Tax Engines
A global digital platform produces one Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record.
The Record must be consumed by three national tax engines using different schemas.
Jurisdiction A expects one JSON model.
Jurisdiction B uses a legacy structured format.
Jurisdiction C uses an API-based tax service.
ERINM maps the same canonical Record into all three environments while preserving: Record identity; underlying Event reference; Determination state; Event Timing; Event Location; Participation; Value Association; material qualifications; and traceability.
Each jurisdiction subsequently reaches its own legal tax result.
The Record itself remains unchanged in canonical meaning.
One Governed Event Record
↓
Three Technical Representations
↓
Three Independent Jurisdictional Evaluations. Use Case 2 — AI-Agent Marketplace Migrating Between ERP Platforms
An autonomous marketplace uses AI agents to negotiate and execute services.
Its governed Event Records are originally stored in ERP System A.
The organization migrates to ERP System B, which uses different: data models; field names; identifier formats; state architecture.
ERINM establishes governed mappings between the systems.
The migration preserves: canonical Record identity; Event associations; Determination states; qualifications; Record links; and historical traceability.

Local technical identifiers change.
The governed Record does not.
System Migration changes the representation — not the governed Event meaning.
Canonical Boundary
ERINM owns the governance of Event Record semantic interoperability, source-target mapping, structural and field mapping, state mapping, canonical identity preservation, Event-reference preservation, Determination/qualification/uncertainty preservation, link and traceability preservation, transformation governance, material-loss detection, semantic-drift governance, compatibility, interoperability qualification, cross-system exchange, cross-organization exchange, cross-border reuse, version compatibility, and establishment of the final Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record.
ERINM does not establish Record identity; ERIDM owns identification.
It does not define the canonical Record Structure; ERSTM owns structure.
It does not establish material Record links; ERLKM owns linkage.
It does not create Record lineage; ERTM owns traceability.
It does not validate the Event or Record generally; VALIDOS™ owns validation.
It does not own general integrity governance; INTEGROS® remains authoritative.
It does not harmonize jurisdiction-specific taxation and does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing obligation, collection, or enforcement.
Its governance begins when a valid Governed Event Record Traceability State exists.

Its governance ends when the Event Record can preserve its canonical governed meaning across the intended system and organizational environments and the final Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record is established.
Canonical Handoff
ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State
↓
ERINM — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
↓
TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERINM ensures that a Tax-Relevant Event Record can move without changing what the Event means.
Different systems may store, encode, transmit, and process the Record differently, but technical diversity must never become semantic fragmentation.
Data Exchange ≠ Interoperability.
Different Technical Representations ≠ Different Governed Event Realities.
One governed Event can remain one governed Record across many systems, organizations, and jurisdictional evaluations.
