OOF™ The Event Relationship Dependency Module (ERLDM) governs how dependency
The Event Relationship Dependency Module (ERLDM) governs how dependency
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard
Module: ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency Module
Operational Layer: Event Relationship Dependency Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Relationship Dependency
Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-ERLDM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Relationship Dependency Module (ERLDM) governs how dependency among already-identified Event Relationship Candidates is established, distinguished, directed, qualified, and represented within TRERLS.
ERLDM determines whether one governed event depends materially on another event, whether the dependency is directional or mutual, whether it is conditional, partial, structural, operational, or value-related, and whether the dependency is sufficiently established for further Event Relationship governance.
Its principal transition is:

Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set
↓
Event Dependency Governance
↓
Governed Event Dependency Structure
ERLDM does not determine event sequence, grouping, merge, split, Event Identity, Event Boundary, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
The foundational distinction is:
Event Dependency ≠ Event Identity.
Operational Role
Events can be strongly related without being the same event.
A payment may depend on an earlier purchase.
A refund may depend on an earlier settlement.
A machine execution may depend on a prior instruction.
A settlement may depend on several earlier transactions.
A later service event may depend on the completion of an earlier operational event.
ERLDM provides the governance required to represent those dependency structures without collapsing dependent events into one event.
It also prevents the opposite error: assuming that two events are independent merely because they were recorded separately.
Internal Module Flow
TRERLS operates through:
ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification
↓
ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency
↓
ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence
↓
ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping
↓
ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split
↓
Governed Event Relationship Structure
ERLDM receives Relationship Candidates from ERLIM.
Its output is passed to ERLSM for sequence governance.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set + Dependency Indicators
↓
Dependency Governance
↓

Governed Event Dependency Structure
ERLDM determines the dependency relationship among candidate events without yet deciding their final sequence or group structure.
Operational Space
ERLDM governs: dependency existence; dependency direction; unidirectional dependency; mutual dependency; conditional dependency; partial dependency; structural dependency; operational dependency; value-related dependency; execution dependency; fulfillment dependency; settlement dependency; reversal dependency; dependency strength; dependency qualification; dependency uncertainty; dependency conflict; dependency reconsideration; dependency continuity; and dependency-specific traceability.
Operational Scope
ERLDM may govern dependencies across: commerce; payments; banking; ERP systems; accounting; supply chains; logistics; marketplaces; digital platforms; blockchain; smart contracts; digital assets; energy systems; industrial systems; AI agents; autonomous machines; distributed systems; machine-to-machine environments; cross-border operations; and other governed economic infrastructures.
The dependency structure is technology-neutral.
Dependency Object
A Dependency Object is a governed representation of a dependency between two or more Tax-Relevant Events.
It identifies: the involved events; the direction of dependency; the basis of dependency; the dependency condition where applicable; the degree or extent of dependency; the current governance state; and relevant uncertainty or conflict.

Dependency Object ≠ Event Identity.
Dependency Establishment
A dependency exists where one event materially relies on another event for its occurrence, execution, completion, continuation, settlement, reversal, or another governed function.
Dependency shall be established on governed information rather than assumption.
Relationship Candidate ≠ Dependency by default.
Unidirectional Dependency
A dependency may operate in one direction.
The canonical form is:
Event B depends on Event A
This does not automatically imply:
Event A depends on Event B
Therefore:
A
↓
B ≠ B
↓
A.
Direction must remain explicit.
Mutual Dependency
Two events may depend on each other.
For example, two coordinated autonomous processes may each require the other to complete a broader operation.
ERLDM may establish mutual dependency where supported.
However:
Mutual Dependency ≠ Single Event by default.
The events may remain independently formed and bounded.
Conditional Dependency
An event may depend on another event only if a governed condition is satisfied.
Examples include: payment after delivery; refund after return; release after approval; machine execution after authorization; settlement after threshold completion.
ERLDM may represent the condition.
It does not govern authority or permission itself.
Conditional Dependency ≠ Authority Governance.
Partial Dependency
An event may depend only partially on another event.

For example, a settlement may include several transactions but only part of its value may depend on a specific earlier event.
ERLDM shall support partial dependency.
Partial Dependency ≠ Full Event Dependency.
Structural Dependency
Events may be structurally dependent within a broader operational process.
One event may create a condition, state, or reference required for another event to exist or proceed.
Structural Dependency ≠ Same Event Structure.
Structural dependence does not eliminate Event Independence.
Operational Dependency
An event may depend on another event for operational execution.
Examples include: fulfillment depending on order acceptance; machine execution depending on resource allocation; shipment depending on production completion; settlement depending on payment processing.
ERLDM may govern that relationship.
Operational Dependency ≠ Legal Dependency.
Value-Related Dependency
One event may depend on the value result of another event.
For example: refund depends on earlier payment value; settlement depends on accumulated transaction value; rebate depends on earlier purchase volume; machine billing depends on measured resource consumption.
ERLDM governs the dependency relationship.
TRVAS remains authoritative for the underlying Value Association.
Value Dependency ≠ Value Ownership.
Execution Dependency
A later event may require completion or execution of an earlier event.
ERLDM may represent:
Execution of Event B depends on Event A

This does not determine chronological sequence in full.
ERLSM remains authoritative for sequence.
Fulfillment Dependency
A fulfillment event may depend on an earlier commercial or operational event.
The dependency may be strong even if fulfillment occurs much later.
Time Distance ≠ No Dependency.
Settlement Dependency
Settlement events frequently depend on earlier payment, transaction, or value-related events.
One settlement may depend on: one event; several events; an Event Group; or a larger Event Network.
Settlement Dependency ≠ Event Merge.
Refund Dependency
A refund event may depend on an earlier purchase, payment, or settlement event.
ERLDM may govern that dependency without determining tax adjustment.
Refund Dependency ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination.
Reversal Dependency
A reversal event usually depends on an earlier event that is being reversed or offset.
ERLDM may establish that dependency.
It does not determine whether the reversal is complete or partial unless that dependency extent is materially governed.
Reversal Dependency ≠ Original Event Erasure.
Replacement Dependency
A replacement event may depend on an earlier failed or superseded event.
ERLDM may preserve the dependency relationship.
Replacement Dependency ≠ Event Identity.
Continuation Dependency
A continuation event may depend on an earlier event for context, state, or operational progression.
ERLDM may represent that dependency.
Continuation Dependency ≠ Same Event Continuity by default.

TRECLS remains authoritative for continuity of one event. Parent–Child Dependency
Some event structures may exhibit hierarchical dependency.
A child event may depend on a parent event without being absorbed into it.
Parent–Child Dependency ≠ Event Ownership.
and:
Child Dependency ≠ Same Event.
One-to-One Dependency
One event may depend on one other event.
The form is:
A
↓
B
where B depends on A.
One-to-Many Dependency
One event may create dependency for several later events.
Example:
Event A
↓
Event B, Event C, Event D
This may occur in commerce, machine systems, or digital platforms.
One Source Event ≠ One Dependent Event.
Many-to-One Dependency
One event may depend on several earlier events.
Example:
Event A + Event B + Event C
↓
Event D
This is common in settlements, aggregation processes, machine operations, and composite services.
Many Dependencies ≠ Event Merge by default.
Many-to-Many Dependency
Complex systems may produce networks where several events depend on several others.
ERLDM shall support such structures without forcing simplification into one-to-one relationships.
Direct Dependency
A direct dependency exists where one event materially depends on another without an intermediate governed event being required to express the relationship.
Direct Dependency ≠ Stronger Legal Consequence by default.
Indirect Dependency
An event may depend on another through one or more intermediate events.
Example:
A
↓
B
↓
C
Event C may indirectly depend on Event A.

ERLDM may represent indirect dependency where materially relevant.
Indirect Dependency ≠ Irrelevant Dependency.
Immediate Dependency
A dependency may be immediate in the operational chain.
This does not necessarily mean the events occur close in time.
Immediate Dependency ≠ Temporal Immediacy.
Deferred Dependency
A later event may depend on an event that occurred much earlier.
For example, an annual rebate event may depend on purchases throughout the year.
ERLDM shall support deferred dependency.
Dependency Condition
Where dependency is conditional, the condition shall be represented separately from the event itself.
Examples may include: completion threshold; participant action; system state; resource availability; prior payment; approval; return; failure; or another governed condition.
Dependency Condition ≠ Event Identity.
Dependency Trigger
A specific occurrence may activate a dependency.
ERLDM may preserve the trigger reference where relevant.
However:
Dependency Trigger ≠ New Event by default.
If the trigger itself qualifies as an event, upstream TREGA™ governance applies.
Dependency Strength
Dependencies may be qualified by strength.
Possible forms may include: essential; material; supporting; partial; qualified; weak; ambiguous; conflicted.
Strength should reflect governed operational reality.
Strong Dependency ≠ Event Merger.
Essential Dependency
An event may be unable to occur or retain its governed meaning without another event.

This may be classified as essential dependency.
Even then:
Essential Dependency ≠ Same Event.
Supporting Dependency
An event may rely on another event without that dependency being existential.
ERLDM may preserve supporting dependency where materially relevant.
Dependency Extent
Dependency may apply to: the whole event; part of the event; one Value Association; one participant relationship; one operational component; one execution phase.
Dependency of Part ≠ Dependency of Whole by default.
Dependency Qualification
Dependency may require qualification.
Examples include: direct; indirect; partial; conditional; deferred; provisional; uncertain.
Qualification shall remain explicit.
Qualified Dependency ≠ Defective Dependency.
Dependency Uncertainty
Available information may indicate that dependency exists without establishing its exact form.
ERLDM shall preserve uncertainty.
Dependency Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Independence.
Dependency Conflict
Different systems may describe dependency differently.
For example: ERP says Event B depends on Event A; payment system says Event B depends on Event C; marketplace data suggests both A and C.
ERLDM shall preserve the conflict.
Dependency Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Dependency Selection.
Dependency Reconsideration
New information may justify reconsidering an earlier Dependency determination.
ERLDM shall support reconsideration while preserving prior history.
Dependency Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure.

Dependency Stability
Once dependency is established, it should remain stable unless materially relevant information changes.
Technical migrations or identifier changes should not alter dependency by themselves.
System Change ≠ Dependency Change by default.
Dependency and Sequence
Dependency and sequence are related but distinct.
An event may depend on another event without necessarily following it in a simple linear time sequence.
Likewise, one event may follow another without depending on it.
Therefore:
Dependency ≠ Sequence.
ERLSM governs sequence.
Dependency and Causation
Dependency may suggest causal relevance.
However:
Dependency ≠ Causation by default.
ERLDM does not establish full causal responsibility.
Dependency and Event Formation
ERLDM does not form new events.
Dependency Discovery ≠ New Event Formation.
TREFS remains authoritative.
Dependency and Event Boundary
Strong dependency does not remove Event Boundary.
Dependency ≠ Shared Event Boundary.
TREBS remains authoritative.
Dependency and Participation
A shared participant may contribute to dependency, but shared participation does not establish dependency by itself.
Shared Participant ≠ Dependency.
TREPS remains authoritative.
Dependency and Value Association
Value relationships may support dependency.
However:
Shared Value ≠ Dependency by default.
TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association.
Dependency and Grouping
Several dependent events may later form an Event Group or Event Network.

ERLDM does not establish that grouping.
Dependency Structure ≠ Event Group.
ERLGM governs grouping. Dependency and Merge / Split
Strong dependency may reveal potential formation or boundary issues.
It does not authorize merge or split.
Dependency ≠ Merge Criterion by itself.
Dependency ≠ Split Criterion by itself.
ERLMM, together with upstream TREFS and TREBS governance, remains authoritative.
Dependency and Taxation
Dependency may later be legally relevant for tax analysis.
However:
Governed Event Dependency ≠ Tax Dependency Determination.
ERLDM does not determine: taxable supply chains; tax aggregation; taxable series; Tax Base; tax jurisdiction; Tax Liability; related-party rules; withholding; deductibility; or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence.
Cross-Border Dependency
Events in different jurisdictions may be dependent.
For example: order in one country; production in another; settlement in another; delivery elsewhere.
ERLDM preserves the dependency structure.
It does not determine taxing rights.
Cross-Border Dependency ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Blockchain Dependency
Blockchain activity may include dependencies among: smart-contract calls; bridge transactions; settlement transactions; token transfers; protocol states; off-chain events.
Technical execution dependency may be relevant.
However:
Blockchain Execution Dependency ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Dependency by default.
The governed Event structure remains decisive.
AI-Agent Dependency

Autonomous agents may create complex dependency graphs.
One agent may request activity.
Another may execute it.
A machine may provide resources.
A separate agent may settle value.
ERLDM shall support these relationships.
Agent Coordination ≠ Same Event.
Machine Dependency
Machine-generated events may depend on: prior instructions; system states; resource allocations; sensor conditions; other machine events.
ERLDM may represent these dependencies without requiring human involvement.
Machine Dependency ≠ Ungoverned Dependency.
Dependency Traceability
Dependency decisions shall remain reconstructable.
Traceability may include: candidate relationship; dependency indicators; direction; conditions; qualification; extent; confidence; ambiguity; conflict; correction; and reconsideration.
Dependency Traceability ≠ Event Record Governance.
TREGS remains authoritative for the complete Event Record.
Governance States
ERLDM may represent:
Dependency Governance Ready
Dependency Under Governance
No Material Dependency Established
Direct Dependency
Indirect Dependency
Unidirectional Dependency
Mutual Dependency
Conditional Dependency
Partial Dependency
Structural Dependency
Operational Dependency
Value-Related Dependency
Execution Dependency
Settlement Dependency
Dependency Qualified
Dependency Ambiguous
Dependency Conflicted
Dependency Unresolved
Governed Event Dependency Established Governance Requirements

ERLDM implementations shall ensure that: dependency is governed only after Event Relationship candidacy is established; dependency remains distinct from Event Identity; dependency direction is explicit; unidirectional and mutual dependency can be represented; conditional dependency can be represented; partial dependency can be represented; structural and operational dependency remain distinguishable; value-related dependency does not replace TRVAS governance; one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many dependencies can be represented; direct and indirect dependencies remain distinguishable; dependency strength and extent can be qualified; dependency uncertainty remains visible; dependency conflict remains visible; dependency reconsideration remains traceable; system changes do not automatically change dependency; dependency remains distinct from sequence; dependency does not establish causation by default; Event Formation remains under TREFS; Event Boundary remains under TREBS; Event Participation remains under TREPS; Value Association remains under TRVAS; grouping remains under ERLGM; merge and split remain under ERLMM; and jurisdiction-specific tax interpretation remains downstream.
Governance Logic
IF ERLIM establishes a valid Relationship Candidate, THEN ERLDM shall evaluate whether a material dependency exists among the involved events.
IF Event B materially relies on Event A, THEN a dependency may be established with explicit direction.

IF dependency operates in both directions, THEN mutual dependency may be represented without merging the events.
IF dependency exists only under a condition, THEN the condition shall remain explicit.
IF dependency applies only to part of an event, THEN partial dependency shall be preserved rather than generalized to the entire event.
IF multiple events contribute to one dependent event, THEN many-to-one dependency may be represented without merging the source events.
IF one event creates dependencies for several events, THEN one-to-many dependency may be represented without creating one combined event.
IF dependency is uncertain or conflicted, THEN the applicable governance state shall remain visible.
IF dependency information suggests a potential Event Formation or Boundary problem, THEN the issue shall be referred to the appropriate upstream governance layer rather than resolved inside ERLDM.
IF the dependency structure is sufficiently governed, THEN it shall proceed to ERLSM for Event Relationship Sequence governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERLDM implementation should support:
Relationship Candidate Reference The ERLIM candidate under dependency governance.
Primary Event Reference The first governed event involved.
Dependent Event Reference The event potentially dependent on another event.
Dependency Identifier A stable identifier for the dependency relationship.
Dependency Direction The directional structure of dependency.

Dependency Type Direct, indirect, conditional, partial, structural, operational, value-related, or other governed type.
Dependency Basis The governed information supporting dependency.
Dependency Condition Any condition required for the dependency to operate.
Dependency Trigger Reference Where a trigger contributes materially to dependency.
Dependency Extent Whole-event or partial-event dependency.
Dependency Cardinality One-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many.
Dependency Strength The qualified strength of dependency.
Dependency Confidence Confidence in the dependency determination.
Ambiguity State Whether material uncertainty remains.
Conflict State Whether materially conflicting dependency information exists.
Prior Dependency Reference Where dependency has been reconsidered or corrected.
Correction / Reconsideration Reference The relevant governance history.
Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the dependency decision.
Governance State The current ERLDM state.
Handoff State Whether the dependency structure is ready for ERLSM.
Governance Outputs

ERLDM may produce: Governed Event Dependency; Unidirectional Dependency; Mutual Dependency; Conditional Dependency; Partial Dependency; Structural Dependency; Operational Dependency; Value-Related Dependency; Execution Dependency; Fulfillment Dependency; Settlement Dependency; Refund Dependency; Reversal Dependency; Replacement Dependency; Continuation Dependency; Parent–Child Dependency; One-to-One Dependency; One-to-Many Dependency; Many-to-One Dependency; Many-to-Many Dependency; Dependency Direction Record; Dependency Condition Record; Dependency Extent Record; Dependency Strength State; Dependency Confidence State; Dependency Ambiguity State; Dependency Conflict State; Dependency Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Dependency Structure.
Critical Distinctions
Event Dependency ≠ Event Identity.
Relationship Candidate ≠ Dependency by default.
A
↓
B ≠ B
↓
A.
Mutual Dependency ≠ Single Event by default.
Conditional Dependency ≠ Authority Governance.
Partial Dependency ≠ Full Event Dependency.
Structural Dependency ≠ Same Event Structure.
Operational Dependency ≠ Legal Dependency.
Value Dependency ≠ Value Ownership.
Settlement Dependency ≠ Event Merge.
Refund Dependency ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination.
Reversal Dependency ≠ Original Event Erasure.
Continuation Dependency ≠ Same Event Continuity by default.
Parent–Child Dependency ≠ Event Ownership.
One Source Event ≠ One Dependent Event.
Many Dependencies ≠ Event Merge by default.

Indirect Dependency ≠ Irrelevant Dependency.
Immediate Dependency ≠ Temporal Immediacy.
Dependency Condition ≠ Event Identity.
Strong Dependency ≠ Event Merger.
Essential Dependency ≠ Same Event.
Dependency of Part ≠ Dependency of Whole by default.
Qualified Dependency ≠ Defective Dependency.
Dependency Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Independence.
Dependency Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Dependency Selection.
System Change ≠ Dependency Change by default.
Dependency ≠ Sequence.
Dependency ≠ Causation by default.
Dependency Discovery ≠ New Event Formation.
Dependency ≠ Shared Event Boundary.
Shared Participant ≠ Dependency.
Shared Value ≠ Dependency by default.
Dependency Structure ≠ Event Group.
Dependency ≠ Merge Criterion by itself.
Governed Event Dependency ≠ Tax Dependency Determination.
Cross-Border Dependency ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Blockchain Execution Dependency ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Dependency by default.
Agent Coordination ≠ Same Event.
Dependency Traceability ≠ Event Record Governance.
Enterprise Application
ERLDM provides a governed dependency layer for systems in which one event relies materially on another event but must remain independently identifiable.
A typical path is:
ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set
→ ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure
→ ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence
→ ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping
→ ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance
→ Governed Event Relationship Structure

This enables enterprises, platforms, banks, autonomous systems, and tax infrastructure to distinguish between events that merely occur near each other and events that are operationally dependent. Use Case 1 — Settlement Dependent on Multiple Commercial Events
A payment platform creates one merchant settlement covering hundreds of earlier sales events.
The settlement event cannot be understood independently from those earlier events, but the sales remain separate governed events.
ERLDM establishes a many-to-one dependency structure between the sales and the settlement.
The dependency can remain explicit without merging the sales into one event or treating the settlement as identical to any one purchase.
The resulting dependency structure can then move to ERLSM for sequence governance and later to grouping where appropriate. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Resource Execution Dependency
An AI agent requests additional computational capacity.
A resource-allocation event occurs only after the request is accepted.
A machine-execution event then depends on that allocation.
Digital settlement depends on measured resource consumption.
ERLDM governs the dependencies among these independently formed events:
Request
↓
Allocation
↓
Execution
↓
Settlement
It does not determine their final sequence, grouping, tax treatment, or whether some technical operations belong to the same event.
The result is a governed dependency structure suitable for subsequent TRERLS processing.
Canonical Boundary

ERLDM owns the establishment, direction, qualification, extent, cardinality, conditionality, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, continuity, and dependency-specific traceability of dependencies among Event Relationship Candidates admitted by ERLIM.
ERLDM does not identify initial Relationship Candidates, govern Event Sequence, create Event Groups or Event Networks, merge or split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, accountability, liability, tax aggregation, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Its governance ends when material Event Dependencies are sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Sequence governance under ERLSM.
Canonical Handoff
ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set
↓
ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure
↓
ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERLDM governs how events rely on one another without allowing dependency to erase their independent Event Identity.
An event may depend completely on another event and still remain a distinct governed event.
Event Dependency ≠ Event Identity.
Dependency ≠ Sequence.

chunks.text:
OOF™ The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how
The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard
Module: ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping Module
Operational Layer: Event Relationship Grouping Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Relationship Grouping
Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-ERLGM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how already-related, dependency-qualified, and sequence-governed Tax-Relevant Events are organized into coherent multi-event structures without destroying their individual Event Identity.
ERLGM establishes when related events may legitimately be represented as an Event Group, Event Chain, Event Network, parent–child structure, component structure, parallel structure, or other governed multi-event configuration.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Sequence Structure
↓
Event Grouping Governance
↓

Governed Event Group Structure
ERLGM does not merge events into one Event Identity, split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, or determine tax aggregation.
The foundational distinction is:
Event Group ≠ Single Event.
Operational Role
Complex economic activity rarely produces isolated Event Relationships.
A marketplace transaction may involve purchase, payment, delivery, settlement, commission, refund, and reversal events.
A machine economy may generate resource requests, allocations, executions, measurements, settlements, and later corrective events.
A supply chain may contain dozens of related events distributed across multiple organizations and countries.
ERLGM provides the governance layer that allows these events to be represented together as coherent structures while preserving the independence of each governed event.
Grouping therefore solves a different problem from Event Formation or Event Merge.
Grouping organizes events. It does not redefine what the events are.
Internal Module Flow
TRERLS operates through:
ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification
↓
ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency
↓
ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence
↓
ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping
↓
ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split
↓
Governed Event Relationship Structure
ERLGM receives the Governed Event Sequence Structure from ERLSM.
Its output is passed to ERLMM.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:

Governed Event Sequence Structure + Governed Relationship Information
↓
Grouping Governance
↓
Governed Event Group Structure
ERLGM uses already-governed: Event Relationships; dependencies; sequences; participants; contexts; Value Associations; and other relevant governed information.
It does not recreate those upstream determinations.
Operational Space
ERLGM governs: Event Group identification; Event Group qualification; Event Group membership; Event Group boundary; group entry; group exit; group membership change; group identifier; group purpose; group basis; Event Chain formation; Event Network formation; parent–child grouping; component grouping; parallel-event grouping; branching structures; converging structures; cross-system grouping; cross-organization grouping; cross-border grouping; multi-jurisdiction-ready grouping; machine-generated grouping; autonomous-system grouping; group uncertainty; group conflict; group reconsideration; group continuity; and grouping-specific traceability.
Operational Scope
ERLGM may govern event structures across: commerce; marketplaces; banking; payment systems; ERP; accounting; logistics; supply chains; digital platforms; blockchain ecosystems; smart-contract systems; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial environments; energy infrastructure; distributed systems; machine-to-machine activity; cross-border operations; and future machine economies.
Event Group

An Event Group is a governed representation of several distinct Tax-Relevant Events that possess sufficient material relationship to be represented together for downstream governance.
The events remain independently identifiable.
Therefore:
Event Group ≠ Single Event.
An Event Group is a relationship structure, not a replacement Event Identity.
Group Membership
Each event included in an Event Group shall retain its own governed Event Reference.
Membership indicates that the event belongs to the governed multi-event structure.
It does not transfer the identity of the event to the group.
Group Membership ≠ Event Identity Transfer.
Group Membership Basis
Membership shall be supported by materially relevant relationship information.
Possible bases may include: dependency; sequence; shared economic activity; shared operational process; shared settlement structure; shared contractual arrangement; shared Value Relationship; parent–child structure; component structure; reversal relationship; or another governed basis.
Shared Attribute Alone ≠ Group Membership by default.
Group Purpose
An Event Group shall have a governable purpose.
Examples may include representing: one broader commercial activity; a settlement structure; a fulfillment structure; a supply-chain segment; a refund and reversal structure; an autonomous workflow; a machine-service process; or a distributed Event Network.
The group purpose shall describe why the events are represented together.
Group Identifier

A group may receive a stable identifier.
However:
Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier.
The group identifier references the multi-event structure.
Each event retains its own Event Identifier.
Group Boundary
An Event Group requires a defined membership boundary.
The boundary determines which events belong to the group and which do not.
This is not the same as TREBS Event Boundary governance.
Event Group Boundary ≠ Event Boundary.
TREBS governs the boundary of an individual event.
ERLGM governs the membership boundary of a multi-event structure.
Group Entry
An event may enter a group when sufficient governed relationship information supports membership.
Entry shall remain traceable.
Group Entry ≠ New Event Formation.
Group Exit
An event may be removed from a group where later governance establishes that membership was incorrect or no longer valid.
Removal from the group does not erase the event.
Group Exit ≠ Event Deletion.
Group Membership Change
Group membership may evolve when: new events occur; new relationships are discovered; prior relationships are corrected; an event is superseded; a reversal occurs; new evidence becomes available.
Membership changes shall remain historically reconstructable.
Group Membership Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default.
Event Chain
An Event Chain is a governed multi-event structure in which events form a materially relevant progression.
Example:
Event A
↓
Event B
↓
Event C
↓
Event D
The chain may incorporate dependency and sequence.

However:
Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default.
Several independently governed events may form one chain.
Linear Event Chain
A simple Event Chain may contain one primary progression path.
Example:
Order
↓
Payment
↓
Delivery
↓
Settlement
Each event remains distinct.
Branching Event Chain
A chain may branch.
Example:
Order
↓
Payment
and:
Order
↓
Fulfillment
Those branches may later converge.
ERLGM may preserve the branching structure.
Converging Event Chain
Multiple event paths may converge into a later event.
Example:
Sale A + Sale B + Sale C
↓
Settlement
This does not merge the source events.
Chain Convergence ≠ Event Merge.
Event Network
An Event Network is a multi-event relationship structure containing more complex connections than a simple chain.
A network may contain: several branches; multiple convergence points; parallel paths; direct and indirect dependencies; reversals; replacement relationships; multiple participants; multiple value flows.
Event Network ≠ Single Event.
Network Node
Each governed event may function as a node within an Event Network.
Node status does not alter Event Identity.
Network Node ≠ Sub-Event by default.
Network Edge
A governed Event Relationship may function as an edge connecting events.
The edge may represent: dependency; sequence; reversal; continuation; settlement linkage; or another governed relationship.
Relationship Edge ≠ Event. Parent–Child Group Structure
Some events may be represented hierarchically.

A Parent Event may be related to several Child Events.
However:
Parent Event ≠ Owner of Child Event.
and:
Child Event ≠ Component of Parent Event by default.
The relationship structure must remain explicit.
Component Event Structure
Several distinct events may constitute components within a broader Event Group.
Component grouping does not mean they should be merged into one event.
Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default.
Parallel Event Group
Several events may proceed in parallel while belonging to the same broader activity.
ERLGM may represent that structure.
Parallel Events ≠ Same Event.
Shared Participant Grouping
Events may share one or more participants.
This may support grouping.
However:
Same Participant ≠ Same Event Group by default.
Shared participation must be materially relevant to the group purpose.
Shared Value Grouping
Events may share or reference the same governed value.
This may support grouping.
However:
Shared Value Reference ≠ Event Group by default.
TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association.
Shared Context Grouping
Events may occur within the same governed context.
This may support grouping.
However:
Shared Context ≠ Event Group by default.
TRECS remains authoritative for Event Context.
Shared Contract Grouping
Several events may arise under the same contract.
This may support grouping but does not automatically require it.
One Contract ≠ One Event Group by default.

A contract may govern thousands of unrelated or only loosely related events.
Shared Invoice Grouping
Events appearing on one invoice may be grouped where relationship governance supports it.
However:
One Invoice ≠ One Event Group by default.
Shared Payment Grouping
A single payment may reference several events.
This may create a legitimate group structure.
However:
One Payment ≠ One Event Group by default.
The payment relationship must remain governed.
Settlement Grouping
Settlement processes frequently bring many earlier events together.
ERLGM may establish a settlement-related Event Group where appropriate.
The underlying events remain independent.
Settlement Group ≠ Merged Event.
Refund and Reversal Grouping
An original event, refund event, and reversal event may belong to one governed group.
Grouping preserves their relationship without erasing historical Event Identity.
Refund Grouping ≠ Original Event Cancellation.
Reversal Grouping ≠ Historical Erasure.
One Economic Activity and Event Grouping
One economic activity may justify representing several events together.
However:
One Economic Activity ≠ One Event.
ERLGM provides a way to represent common economic structure without forcing Event Identity collapse.
Multiple Technical Operations
Multiple technical operations may relate to one event, several events, or a broader Event Group.
The number of technical records does not determine the number of group members.
More Technical Operations ≠ Larger Event Group by default.

Cross-System Grouping
Events belonging to one relationship structure may reside in different systems.
ERLGM shall support grouping across: ERP; payment systems; banking; marketplaces; logistics; blockchain; autonomous systems; and other operational infrastructure.
System Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary.
Cross-Organization Grouping
One Event Group may span several organizations.
For example:
Marketplace
↓
Merchant
↓
Bank
↓
Logistics Provider
ERLGM may represent the broader relationship while preserving each organization's event references.
Organization Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary by default.
Cross-Border Grouping
Related events may belong to one Event Group even when they occur in several countries.
This does not determine tax jurisdiction.
Cross-Border Event Group ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness
A Governed Event Group may later be evaluated differently by different jurisdictions.
The underlying group structure remains jurisdiction-neutral.
The canonical principle is:
One Governed Event Group
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
ERLGM does not determine how a jurisdiction legally aggregates the events.
Blockchain Event Grouping
Blockchain systems may generate multiple on-chain operations associated with a broader governed activity.
ERLGM may group independently governed Tax-Relevant Events where relationship governance supports it.
However:
One Smart Contract ≠ One Event Group by default.
One Wallet ≠ One Event Group by default.

One Block ≠ One Event Group.
Technical ledger architecture does not determine economic grouping.
AI-Agent Event Grouping
One autonomous agent may coordinate numerous events.
Those events may form one group, several groups, or remain independent.
Therefore:
One Agent Workflow ≠ One Event Group by default.
Grouping depends on governed Event Relationships.
Multi-Agent Event Networks
Several agents may create distributed Event Networks.
ERLGM may represent the resulting multi-event structure across agents without assigning identity, authority, or accountability.
Those domains remain under their respective architectures.
Machine-to-Machine Grouping
Machine-generated events may be grouped where they belong to a common governed operational or economic structure.
Machine Correlation ≠ Event Group by default.
Technical coordination alone is insufficient.
Group Cardinality
An Event Group may contain any number of governed events necessary to represent the materially relevant relationship structure.
Cardinality shall not determine Event Identity.
Group Size ≠ Economic Importance.
Nested Group Structures
Where necessary, an Event Group may participate in a broader grouping structure.
For example:
Local Fulfillment Group
↓
Regional Settlement Group
↓
Global Commercial Event Network
Nested grouping shall preserve the identity of underlying events.
Nested Group ≠ Event Merge.
Overlapping Groups

An event may legitimately belong to more than one relationship group where the groups represent different governed purposes.
For example, one payment event may belong to: a customer purchase group; and a merchant settlement group.
ERLGM may support such overlap where explicit.
Multiple Group Membership ≠ Multiple Event Identity.
Group Independence
Two Event Groups may remain independent even where some attributes are similar.
Similar Groups ≠ Same Group.
Group Identity requires governed relationship basis, not superficial similarity.
Group Qualification
A group may be qualified according to its structure or purpose.
Examples include: commercial; payment; settlement; fulfillment; reversal; autonomous workflow; machine-service; distributed; cross-border; multi-system.
Qualification provides structure but does not determine tax treatment.
Group Confidence
Group membership may carry a governance confidence state where uncertainty remains.
Possible states may include:
Confirmed · Qualified · Limited · Ambiguous · Conflicted · Unresolved
Confidence shall not substitute for evidence or validation.
Group Ambiguity
Available information may establish that events belong to a broader relationship structure without identifying the exact membership boundary.
ERLGM shall preserve that uncertainty.
Group Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Convenient Membership Selection.
Group Conflict
Different systems may represent group structure differently.

For example: ERP groups A, B, C; payment system groups B, C, D; marketplace records indicate A, B, C, D.
ERLGM shall preserve the conflict until sufficient governance resolves it.
Group Conflict ≠ Permission for Selective Aggregation.
Group Reconsideration
New information may justify group reconsideration.
Events may be: added; removed; reclassified; moved to another group; linked across groups.
Previous group states shall remain traceable.
Group Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure.
Group Stability
A governed Event Group should remain stable unless materially relevant information changes.
System migration, database consolidation, or platform replacement shall not automatically alter group structure.
System Change ≠ Event Group Change by default.
Grouping and Event Identity
Grouping does not redefine the events.
Each member remains independently governed.
Grouped Events ≠ Same Event.
Grouping and Event Formation
ERLGM does not form events.
Grouping Discovery ≠ New Event Formation.
TREFS remains authoritative.
Grouping and Event Boundary
ERLGM does not redefine individual Event Boundaries.
Group Boundary ≠ Individual Event Boundary.
TREBS remains authoritative.
Grouping and Dependency
Dependency may contribute to group structure.
ERLGM does not redetermine dependency.
Group Membership ≠ Dependency by default.
ERLDM remains authoritative.
Grouping and Sequence
Sequence may contribute to Event Chain or Event Network structure.
ERLGM does not redetermine sequence.

Group Membership ≠ Sequence Relationship by default.
ERLSM remains authoritative.
Grouping and Merge
Grouping is not merge.
This is a critical distinction.
Event Group ≠ Merged Event.
Grouping preserves separate Event Identities.
Merge governance may determine that two or more event representations should instead constitute one event, but that belongs to ERLMM together with upstream Event Formation and Boundary authority.
Grouping and Split
A complex Event Group does not automatically mean an underlying event should be split.
Group Complexity ≠ Event Split Criterion.
ERLMM remains authoritative.
Grouping and Tax Aggregation
A tax jurisdiction may later decide to aggregate several related events for legal purposes.
That decision does not alter the underlying TREGA™ Event Group.
Therefore:
Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination.
Grouping and Taxpayer Determination
A group may contain events involving several participants.
Group membership does not establish taxpayer status.
Event Group Participant Set ≠ Taxpayer Set.
Grouping and Tax Jurisdiction
A cross-border Event Group may span several jurisdictions.
ERLGM does not determine which country has taxing rights.
Event Group Geography ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination.
Grouping and Tax Base
Values associated with events within a group shall not automatically be aggregated into one taxable amount.
Grouped Value ≠ Tax Base.
TRVAS governs Value Association; jurisdiction-specific tax systems determine legal Tax Base.

Governance States
ERLGM may represent:
Grouping Governance Ready
Grouping Under Governance
Group Candidate
Group Membership Qualified
Event Group Established
Linear Event Chain
Branching Event Chain
Converging Event Chain
Parallel Event Structure
Parent–Child Event Structure
Component Event Structure
Event Network
Nested Event Group
Overlapping Group Membership
Cross-System Event Group
Cross-Organization Event Group
Cross-Border Event Group
Autonomous Event Group
Group Ambiguous
Group Conflicted
Group Under Reconsideration
Group Superseded
Governed Event Group Structure Established Governance Requirements

ERLGM implementations shall ensure that: grouping operates only on already-governed Event Relationships; each group member retains independent Event Identity; group membership has an explicit governance basis; Event Group purpose is identifiable; Event Group identifiers remain distinct from Event Identifiers; group membership boundaries can be represented; group entry and exit remain traceable; group membership change remains historically reconstructable; Event Chains can be represented; Event Networks can be represented; branching and converging structures can be represented; parent–child and component structures can be represented; overlapping group membership can be supported where justified; nested group structures can be represented where materially necessary; shared context, participants, value, contracts, invoices, or payments do not automatically establish group membership; cross-system grouping can be represented; cross-organization grouping can be represented; cross-border grouping does not determine tax jurisdiction; blockchain and autonomous-system groups remain independent of technical architecture; ambiguity remains visible; conflict remains visible; reconsideration remains traceable; Event Formation remains under TREFS; Event Boundary remains under TREBS; dependency remains under ERLDM; sequence remains under ERLSM; Merge & Split remains under ERLMM; and tax aggregation remains jurisdiction-specific.
Governance Logic

IF several governed related events possess a materially coherent common relationship structure, THEN ERLGM may establish an Event Group.
IF events belong to the same group, THEN their independent Event Identities shall remain preserved.
IF one event progresses into several related branches, THEN a branching Event Chain or Event Network may be represented.
IF several event paths converge into one later event, THEN convergence may be represented without merging the source events.
IF an event belongs legitimately to more than one group for different governed purposes, THEN overlapping membership may be represented explicitly.
IF group membership becomes ambiguous or conflicted, THEN the applicable governance state shall remain visible.
IF new materially relevant information changes group membership, THEN the group may be reconsidered while preserving prior history.
IF group structure suggests that existing Event Identity or Event Boundary may be incorrect, THEN the issue shall proceed to ERLMM and, where necessary, upstream TREFS or TREBS rather than being silently resolved through grouping.
IF the group structure is sufficiently governed, THEN it shall proceed to ERLMM for Merge & Split governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERLGM implementation should support:
Sequence Structure Reference The ERLSM output entering grouping governance.
Event Group Identifier A stable identifier for the governed multi-event structure.

Group Purpose The governed reason the events are represented together.
Group Basis The materially relevant Relationship information supporting grouping.
Group Type Event Group, Event Chain, Event Network, parent–child structure, component structure, parallel structure, or another governed form.
Group Member Event References The individual governed events included in the structure.
Group Membership State The governance state of each event's membership.
Group Entry Reference Where and why an event entered the group.
Group Exit Reference Where and why an event was removed.
Group Membership Boundary The governed membership boundary of the group.
Parent Event Reference Where a parent–child structure exists.
Child Event References Where child relationships exist.
Component Event References Where component structure is governed.
Event Chain Reference Where a linear or branching chain exists.
Event Network Reference Where a broader network exists.
Branch References Where group structure branches.
Convergence References Where event paths converge.
Nested Group Reference Where the group belongs to a broader grouping structure.
Overlapping Group Reference Where an event belongs to another legitimate group.
Group Qualification The applicable structural or operational qualification.
Group Confidence The qualified confidence in the grouping decision.
Ambiguity State Whether group membership or structure remains uncertain.

Conflict State Whether materially conflicting grouping information exists.
Prior Group State Reference The preceding group state where reconsideration has occurred.
Correction / Reconsideration Reference The relevant change history.
Grouping Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the grouping decision.
Governance State The current ERLGM governance state.
Handoff State Whether the group structure is ready for ERLMM.
Governance Outputs
ERLGM may produce: Governed Event Group; Event Group Identifier; Event Group Membership Record; Event Group Boundary Record; Event Chain; Linear Event Chain; Branching Event Chain; Converging Event Chain; Event Network; Parent–Child Event Structure; Component Event Structure; Parallel Event Structure; Nested Event Group; Overlapping Event Group Membership; Cross-System Event Group; Cross-Organization Event Group; Cross-Border Event Group; Autonomous Event Group; Group Qualification State; Group Confidence State; Group Ambiguity State; Group Conflict State; Group Reconsideration Record; Group Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Group Structure.
Critical Distinctions
Event Group ≠ Single Event.
Grouping Organizes Events ≠ Redefining Events.
Group Membership ≠ Event Identity Transfer.
Shared Attribute Alone ≠ Group Membership by default.
Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier.
Event Group Boundary ≠ Event Boundary.
Group Entry ≠ New Event Formation.
Group Exit ≠ Event Deletion.

Group Membership Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default.
Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default.
Chain Convergence ≠ Event Merge.
Event Network ≠ Single Event.
Network Node ≠ Sub-Event by default.
Relationship Edge ≠ Event.
Parent Event ≠ Owner of Child Event.
Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default.
Parallel Events ≠ Same Event.
Same Participant ≠ Same Event Group by default.
Shared Value Reference ≠ Event Group by default.
Shared Context ≠ Event Group by default.
One Contract ≠ One Event Group by default.
One Invoice ≠ One Event Group by default.
One Payment ≠ One Event Group by default.
Settlement Group ≠ Merged Event.
Refund Grouping ≠ Original Event Cancellation.
One Economic Activity ≠ One Event.
More Technical Operations ≠ Larger Event Group by default.
System Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary.
Cross-Border Event Group ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
One Smart Contract ≠ One Event Group by default.
One Agent Workflow ≠ One Event Group by default.
Machine Correlation ≠ Event Group by default.
Nested Group ≠ Event Merge.
Multiple Group Membership ≠ Multiple Event Identity.
Group Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Convenient Membership Selection.
Group Conflict ≠ Permission for Selective Aggregation.
Group Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure.
System Change ≠ Event Group Change by default.
Grouped Events ≠ Same Event.
Grouping Discovery ≠ New Event Formation.
Group Boundary ≠ Individual Event Boundary.
Group Membership ≠ Dependency by default.

Group Membership ≠ Sequence Relationship by default.
Event Group ≠ Merged Event.
Group Complexity ≠ Event Split Criterion.
Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination.
Event Group Participant Set ≠ Taxpayer Set.
Event Group Geography ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination.
Grouped Value ≠ Tax Base.
Enterprise Application
ERLGM provides the organizational layer required to represent large multi-event structures without destroying the identity of their component events.
A typical path is:
ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set
→ ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure
→ ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure
→ ERLGM — Governed Event Group Structure
→ ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split Governance
→ Governed Event Relationship Structure
This makes it possible for enterprises, platforms, banks, distributed systems, and autonomous infrastructures to represent broad economic activities as coherent multi-event structures without prematurely treating those structures as one event. Use Case 1 — Marketplace Purchase, Settlement, and Refund Network
A marketplace processes hundreds of customer purchases.
Each purchase may generate payment, fulfillment, delivery, platform-fee, settlement, refund, and reversal events.
Several sales are later combined into one merchant settlement while individual refunds remain linked to particular purchases.
ERLGM can establish purchase-related Event Groups while also representing broader settlement Event Groups.

One settlement event may therefore legitimately participate in a settlement structure involving several purchase groups.
The underlying purchases remain independently governed.
This creates a coherent Event Network without collapsing hundreds of events into a single “transaction.” Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Service Network
An industrial AI system coordinates multiple machines to provide a continuously delivered service.
Resource-request events, machine allocations, execution events, energy-consumption events, measurement events, digital settlements, and later corrections occur across several systems.
ERLGM groups the events into appropriate service, execution, and settlement structures while preserving individual Event Identities.
Events may participate in overlapping structures where operational reality requires it.
The resulting Governed Event Group Structure provides ERLMM with the organized relationship context required to determine whether any Event Formation or Boundary representation requires Merge or Split governance.
Canonical Boundary

ERLGM owns the formation and governance of multi-event relationship structures, including Event Groups, Event Chains, Event Networks, group membership, membership boundaries, parent–child structures, component structures, parallel structures, nested groups, overlapping groups, cross-system groups, cross-organization groups, cross-border groups, qualification, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and grouping-specific traceability.
ERLGM does not create new events, redefine individual Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, establish Event Participation or Value Association, redetermine dependency or sequence, merge or split Event Identities, determine taxpayer status, aggregate taxable value, determine tax jurisdiction, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence.
Its governance ends when the multi-event structure is sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Merge & Split governance under ERLMM.
Canonical Handoff
ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure
↓
ERLGM — Governed Event Group Structure
↓
ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERLGM organizes related events into coherent structures without allowing the convenience of grouping to erase the identity of the events themselves.
A group can explain how many events belong together without claiming that those events are one event.
Event Group ≠ Single Event.
Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination.
