OOF™ The Event Relationship Sequence Module (ERLSM) governs how
The Event Relationship Sequence Module (ERLSM) governs how
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard
Module: ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence Module
Operational Layer: Event Relationship Sequence Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Relationship Sequence
Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-ERLSM-003
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Relationship Sequence Module (ERLSM) governs how already-identified and dependency-qualified Tax-Relevant Events are ordered, sequenced, positioned, and related across temporal and operational progression.
ERLSM determines whether events occur before, after, concurrently with, conditionally following, or otherwise in a governed sequence relative to one another.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Dependency Structure
↓
Event Sequence Governance
↓
Governed Event Sequence Structure

ERLSM does not determine Event Timing itself, Event Dependency, Event Grouping, Event Merge, Event Split, causation, Event Identity, or tax consequence.
The foundational distinction is:
Event Sequence ≠ Event Identity.
Operational Role
Dependency alone does not fully explain how events unfold.
Two events may be dependent without occurring immediately one after another.
Several events may occur in parallel.
A later event may depend on an earlier event but be separated from it by several intermediate events.
One Event Network may contain multiple valid sequences.
ERLSM provides the governance needed to represent how governed events progress relative to each other without converting chronology into causation or Event Identity.
Internal Module Flow
TRERLS operates through:
ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification
↓
ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency
↓
ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence
↓
ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping
↓
ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split
↓
Governed Event Relationship Structure
ERLSM receives the Governed Event Dependency Structure from ERLDM.
Its output is passed to ERLGM.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Governed Event Dependency Structure + Governed Event Timing Information
↓
Sequence Governance
↓
Governed Event Sequence Structure
ERLSM uses already-governed timing information from TRETS.
It does not redefine Event Timing.
Operational Space

ERLSM governs: sequence existence; sequence direction; predecessor relationships; successor relationships; concurrent sequence; parallel progression; conditional sequence; immediate sequence; deferred sequence; multi-stage sequence; branching sequence; converging sequence; interrupted sequence; resumed sequence; cyclic technical patterns where relevant; sequence qualification; sequence uncertainty; sequence conflict; sequence reconsideration; and sequence-specific traceability.
Operational Scope
ERLSM may govern sequence structures across: commerce; banking; payments; ERP; accounting; logistics; marketplaces; supply chains; blockchain systems; smart contracts; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous machines; industrial processes; energy systems; distributed digital infrastructure; cross-border operations; and machine-to-machine environments.
Sequence Object
A Sequence Object is a governed representation of the relative order between two or more governed events.
It may identify: predecessor event; successor event; concurrent event; sequence branch; convergence point; sequence condition; interruption; resumption; or other materially relevant order structure.
Sequence Object ≠ Event Timing Record.
TRETS owns Event Timing.
ERLSM owns the relationship among those governed times.
Sequence Establishment
A sequence may be established where governed information supports a meaningful order between events.

The sequence may arise from: Event Timing; operational workflow; dependency structure; settlement progression; machine execution; contractual process; system state transition; or another materially relevant basis.
Earlier Event ≠ Sequence Relationship by default.
Chronological order alone does not always establish a materially relevant Event Relationship.
Predecessor Relationship
An event may act as a predecessor to another event.
The canonical structure is:
Event A
↓
Event B
where Event A precedes Event B within the governed relationship.
However:
Predecessor ≠ Cause by default.
Successor Relationship
An event may follow one or more predecessor events.
A successor relationship describes governed progression.
It does not automatically mean the successor depends on every earlier event.
Successor ≠ Dependent Event by default.
ERLDM remains authoritative for dependency.
Immediate Sequence
Two events may occur directly next to one another in the governed process.
For example:
Authorization
↓
Settlement
This may be represented as immediate sequence.
However:
Immediate Sequence ≠ Same Event.
Deferred Sequence
Events may be separated by significant time while still forming a governed sequence.
For example:
Purchase
↓
Annual Rebate
Time distance does not invalidate sequence where a material structural relationship exists.
Time Distance ≠ Sequence Absence.
Concurrent Events
Two or more events may occur at the same or overlapping time.
ERLSM shall support concurrent sequence states.

Concurrent Events ≠ Same Event.
Concurrency does not remove separate Event Identities.
Parallel Progression
Several event paths may proceed simultaneously.
Example:
Purchase
↓
Payment
and simultaneously:
Purchase
↓
Fulfillment
The two branches may later converge.
ERLSM shall support parallel progression.
Parallel Sequence ≠ Event Group by default.
Grouping remains under ERLGM.
Branching Sequence
One event may lead into several sequence branches.
The structure may be:
A
↓
B
A
↓
C
A
↓
D
This does not require the resulting events to be merged.
Sequence Branching ≠ Event Fragmentation.
Converging Sequence
Several sequences may converge into one later event.
Example:
A
↓
D
B
↓
D
C
↓
D
This is common in settlement, aggregation, production, and autonomous systems.
Sequence Convergence ≠ Event Merge.
Multi-Stage Sequence
Complex activity may contain multiple governed sequence stages.
Example:
Order
↓
Authorization
↓
Fulfillment
↓
Delivery
↓
Settlement
↓
Refund
Each event may remain distinct.
ERLSM preserves the progression.
Conditional Sequence
An event may follow another only when a condition is satisfied.
Example:
Return Accepted
↓
Refund Event
ERLSM may preserve that sequence condition.
It does not govern authority or permission.
Conditional Sequence ≠ Permission Governance.
Sequence and Dependency
Sequence and dependency must remain separate.
An event may follow another without depending on it.
An event may depend on another while several unrelated events occur between them.

Therefore:
Sequence ≠ Dependency.
Sequence and Event Timing
TRETS establishes Event Timing.
ERLSM does not determine: Event Start; Event Completion; Event Duration; legal tax point; tax period.
It consumes governed timing information to establish relative Event Sequence.
Event Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination.
Temporal Sequence
A temporal sequence represents order based on governed time.
The form may be:
Event A before Event B
or:
Event A concurrent with Event B
Temporal sequence is one form of Event Sequence.
Operational Sequence
Operational order may differ from simple timestamp order.
For example, a system may technically record settlement before another system finalizes a related fulfillment record.
ERLSM may preserve operational sequence separately from raw system timestamps.
System Timestamp Order ≠ Operational Sequence by default.
Sequence and Causation
Sequence is not proof of causation.
Before ≠ Because Of.
and:
Event Sequence ≠ Causation.
ERLSM does not determine legal, economic, or scientific causation.
Sequence Direction
Sequence shall preserve direction where material.
A
↓
B
is distinct from:
B
↓
A
Reversal of sequence may materially change event interpretation.
Sequence Cardinality
ERLSM shall support: one-to-one; one-to-many; many-to-one; many-to-many
sequence structures.
One-to-Many Sequence
One event may precede several events.
Example:
Order
↓
Payment
Order
↓
Fulfillment
Order
↓
Logistics
This does not mean the later events are one event.

Many-to-One Sequence
Several earlier events may precede one later event.
Example:
Multiple Sales
↓
Settlement
ERLSM may represent the sequence without merging the source events.
Many-to-Many Sequence
Complex systems may contain several interacting sequence paths.
ERLSM shall support those structures without forcing artificial linearization.
Interrupted Sequence
A process may stop after one event and resume later.
ERLSM may preserve:
A
↓
interruption
↓
B
where the interruption is materially relevant.
Interrupted Sequence ≠ Broken Event Relationship by default.
Resumed Sequence
A later event may resume a previously interrupted Event Relationship path.
Resumption does not imply continuity of the same event.
Sequence Resumption ≠ Same Event Continuity.
TRECLS remains authoritative for Event Lifecycle continuity.
Reversal Sequence
A later reversal event may follow an earlier event or sequence.
ERLSM may preserve:
Original Event
↓
Reversal Event
The sequence does not erase the original event.
Reversal Sequence ≠ Historical Erasure.
Refund Sequence
A refund may occur after one or more earlier events.
ERLSM governs the sequence relationship.
It does not determine tax adjustment.
Refund Sequence ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination.
Replacement Sequence
A replacement event may follow a failed, rejected, cancelled, or superseded event.
ERLSM may represent the sequence.
Replacement Sequence ≠ Original Event Invalidity by default.
Correction Sequence

A corrective event may follow an earlier event.
The corrected relationship shall remain historically reconstructable.
Correction Sequence ≠ Earlier Event Erasure.
Sequence Across Systems
Related events may be recorded in systems using different clocks, time zones, timestamps, or processing rules.
ERLSM shall rely on governed Event Timing rather than blindly trusting raw technical timestamps.
System Timestamp ≠ Governed Sequence by default.
Sequence Across Organizations
Different organizations may record related events independently.
One system may show:
A
↓
B
while another reflects:
B recorded before A
ERLSM shall distinguish record order from governed Event Sequence.
Record Order ≠ Event Sequence by default.
Cross-Border Sequence
Events may occur across multiple jurisdictions and time zones.
ERLSM preserves their governed sequence without determining tax jurisdiction or tax period.
Cross-Border Sequence ≠ Tax Period Determination.
Blockchain Sequence
Blockchain systems provide deterministic ledger ordering within particular technical contexts.
However:
Blockchain Order ≠ Complete Economic Event Sequence by default.
Off-chain events may occur before, during, or after on-chain activity.
ERLSM may integrate both governed forms.
Smart-Contract Sequence
One smart contract may trigger a series of technical actions.
Those technical execution steps may inform sequence.
They do not automatically define the sequence of Tax-Relevant Events.

Smart-Contract Execution Order ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Sequence by default.
AI-Agent Sequence
AI agents may coordinate numerous actions concurrently.
For example:
Request
↓
Resource Search
↓
Allocation
while another branch performs:
Request
↓
Pricing
↓
Settlement Preparation
ERLSM shall support branching, parallel, and converging agent sequences.
Agent Action Order ≠ Event Identity.
Machine Sequence
Machine systems may execute events based on: sensor states; instructions; resource availability; control logic; completion signals.
ERLSM may represent these sequences without assuming human participation.
Sequence Qualification
A sequence may be: direct; indirect; immediate; deferred; parallel; conditional; partial; qualified; ambiguous; conflicted.
Qualification shall remain visible.
Qualified Sequence ≠ Invalid Sequence.
Sequence Uncertainty
Available information may establish that events are related but not establish their exact order.
ERLSM shall preserve uncertainty.
Unknown Order ≠ Unrelated Events.
Sequence Conflict
Different systems may report incompatible ordering.
ERLSM shall preserve the conflict until resolved.
Sequence Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Convenient Order.
Sequence Reconsideration
New governed timing or operational information may require sequence reconsideration.
Prior sequence representations shall remain traceable.
Sequence Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure.
Sequence Stability

Once governed sequence is established, technical migration or storage changes shall not alter it without materially relevant information.
System Change ≠ Sequence Change by default.
Sequence and Grouping
ERLSM may produce sequence structures that later support Event Groups, Event Chains, or Event Networks.
It does not itself create those structures.
Sequence Structure ≠ Event Group.
ERLGM remains authoritative. Sequence and Merge / Split
Sequence complexity does not by itself justify event merge or split.
Sequential Proximity ≠ Merge Criterion.
Sequence Divergence ≠ Split Criterion by itself.
ERLMM remains authoritative together with upstream TREFS and TREBS.
Sequence and Taxation
ERLSM does not determine: legal tax point; tax period; realization moment; accrual date; recognition date; tax aggregation; tax jurisdiction; Tax Base; Tax Liability; or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence.
Therefore:
Governed Event Sequence ≠ Tax Timing Determination.
Governance States
ERLSM may represent:
Sequence Governance Ready
Sequence Under Governance
Predecessor Established
Successor Established
Immediate Sequence
Deferred Sequence
Concurrent Sequence
Parallel Sequence
Branching Sequence
Converging Sequence
Conditional Sequence
Interrupted Sequence
Resumed Sequence
Reversal Sequence
Replacement Sequence
Correction Sequence
Sequence Qualified
Sequence Ambiguous
Sequence Conflicted
Sequence Unresolved
Governed Event Sequence Established Governance Requirements

ERLSM implementations shall ensure that: sequence governance operates on governed Event Relationships; Event Timing remains under TRETS; predecessor and successor relationships can be represented; immediate and deferred sequence remain distinguishable; concurrent events can be represented; parallel progression can be represented; branching and convergence can be represented; conditional sequence can be represented; interrupted and resumed sequence can be represented; sequence remains distinct from dependency; sequence remains distinct from causation; operational sequence can be distinguished from raw timestamp order; one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many sequence structures can be represented; cross-system sequence can remain reconstructable; cross-organization sequence can remain reconstructable; cross-border sequence does not become Tax Period determination; blockchain ordering is not automatically treated as complete economic sequence; autonomous and machine-generated sequence can be governed; sequence uncertainty remains visible; sequence conflict remains visible; sequence reconsideration remains traceable; system changes do not automatically alter sequence; grouping remains under ERLGM; Merge & Split remains under ERLMM; and jurisdiction-specific tax timing remains downstream.
Governance Logic
IF ERLDM establishes a materially relevant Event Dependency Structure, THEN ERLSM shall evaluate the relative Event Sequence where required.

IF Event A materially precedes Event B within the governed relationship, THEN a predecessor–successor relationship may be established.
IF events occur concurrently, THEN concurrency shall be preserved rather than forcing artificial linear order.
IF one event precedes multiple events, THEN branching sequence may be represented.
IF multiple earlier events converge into one later event, THEN converging sequence may be represented without merging the earlier events.
IF sequence depends on a condition, THEN the conditional state shall remain explicit.
IF system timestamps conflict with governed operational information, THEN raw timestamp order shall not automatically determine sequence.
IF sequence remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the applicable governance state shall remain visible.
IF sequence information suggests Event Formation or Boundary problems, THEN those issues shall be referred upstream rather than resolved inside ERLSM.
IF the Event Sequence Structure is sufficiently governed, THEN it shall proceed to ERLGM for Event Relationship Grouping governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERLSM implementation should support:
Dependency Structure Reference The ERLDM output entering sequence governance.
Sequence Identifier A stable identifier for the governed sequence relationship.
Primary Event Reference The event whose sequence relationship is being governed.
Related Event Reference The event positioned relative to the primary event.

Predecessor Event Reference Where a governed predecessor exists.
Successor Event Reference Where a governed successor exists.
Sequence Direction The governed directional order.
Sequence Type Immediate, deferred, concurrent, parallel, conditional, branching, converging, interrupted, resumed, or other governed sequence type.
Sequence Basis The governed information supporting sequence.
Event Timing References The relevant TRETS outputs used in sequence governance.
Operational Sequence Reference Where operational order differs from simple timestamp ordering.
Sequence Condition Any governed condition controlling progression.
Branch Reference Where the event belongs to a branching sequence.
Convergence Reference Where multiple sequence paths converge.
Sequence Cardinality One-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many.
Sequence Extent The part of the relationship to which sequence applies.
Sequence Confidence The qualified confidence in the sequence determination.
Ambiguity State Whether exact ordering remains uncertain.
Conflict State Whether materially conflicting ordering information exists.
Prior Sequence Reference Where a prior governed sequence has been reconsidered.
Correction / Reconsideration Reference The relevant change history.
Sequence Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the sequence decision.
Governance State The current ERLSM governance state.
Handoff State Whether the sequence structure is ready for ERLGM.
Governance Outputs

ERLSM may produce: Governed Event Sequence; Predecessor Relationship; Successor Relationship; Immediate Sequence; Deferred Sequence; Concurrent Sequence; Parallel Sequence; Branching Sequence; Converging Sequence; Conditional Sequence; Interrupted Sequence; Resumed Sequence; Reversal Sequence; Refund Sequence; Replacement Sequence; Correction Sequence; Sequence Direction Record; Sequence Cardinality Record; Sequence Confidence State; Sequence Ambiguity State; Sequence Conflict State; Sequence Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Sequence Structure.
Critical Distinctions
Event Sequence ≠ Event Identity.
Sequence Object ≠ Event Timing Record.
Earlier Event ≠ Sequence Relationship by default.
Predecessor ≠ Cause by default.
Successor ≠ Dependent Event by default.
Immediate Sequence ≠ Same Event.
Time Distance ≠ Sequence Absence.
Concurrent Events ≠ Same Event.
Parallel Sequence ≠ Event Group by default.
Sequence Branching ≠ Event Fragmentation.
Sequence Convergence ≠ Event Merge.
Conditional Sequence ≠ Permission Governance.
Sequence ≠ Dependency.
Event Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination.
System Timestamp Order ≠ Operational Sequence by default.
Before ≠ Because Of.
Event Sequence ≠ Causation.
Interrupted Sequence ≠ Broken Event Relationship by default.
Sequence Resumption ≠ Same Event Continuity.
Reversal Sequence ≠ Historical Erasure.
Refund Sequence ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination.
Replacement Sequence ≠ Original Event Invalidity by default.

Correction Sequence ≠ Earlier Event Erasure.
System Timestamp ≠ Governed Sequence by default.
Record Order ≠ Event Sequence by default.
Cross-Border Sequence ≠ Tax Period Determination.
Blockchain Order ≠ Complete Economic Event Sequence by default.
Smart-Contract Execution Order ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Sequence by default.
Agent Action Order ≠ Event Identity.
Qualified Sequence ≠ Invalid Sequence.
Unknown Order ≠ Unrelated Events.
Sequence Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Convenient Order.
System Change ≠ Sequence Change by default.
Sequence Structure ≠ Event Group.
Sequential Proximity ≠ Merge Criterion.
Governed Event Sequence ≠ Tax Timing Determination.
Enterprise Application
ERLSM provides the sequencing layer needed to reconstruct how related events progress across fragmented systems.
A typical path is:
ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set
→ ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure
→ ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure
→ ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping
→ ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance
→ Governed Event Relationship Structure
This allows systems to preserve operational progression without confusing timestamps, dependencies, or technical processing order with legal tax timing. Use Case 1 — Cross-System Commerce Sequence
A global commerce transaction generates an order event, payment authorization, fulfillment event, shipment event, settlement event, and later refund event.

Different systems record these events at different times and in different technical orders.
ERLSM uses governed Event Timing and operational relationships to establish the actual Event Sequence while preserving concurrency, delays, and later reversal activity.
It does not determine the legal tax point or tax period.
The resulting Governed Event Sequence Structure can then proceed to ERLGM for grouping. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Parallel Event Sequence
An AI agent initiates a resource request.
One branch performs machine allocation and execution.
Another branch performs pricing and settlement preparation.
The branches later converge when consumption data is finalized and settlement occurs.
ERLSM represents the parallel, branching, and converging sequence without collapsing the autonomous workflow into one event or forcing a false linear order.
The sequence remains jurisdiction-neutral and suitable for subsequent Event Grouping governance.
Canonical Boundary
ERLSM owns the governance of relative order, predecessor–successor relationships, concurrency, parallel progression, branching, convergence, conditional sequence, interruption, resumption, sequence qualification, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and sequence-specific traceability among governed related events.

ERLSM does not determine Event Timing itself, establish dependency, create Event Groups, determine Event Networks, merge or split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, determine participation, Value Association, causation, accountability, liability, legal tax point, tax period, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Its governance ends when the relevant Event Sequence is sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Grouping governance under ERLGM.
Canonical Handoff
ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure
↓
ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure
↓
ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERLSM governs how related events progress without allowing chronology to become Event Identity, dependency, causation, or legal tax timing.
The fact that one event happens before another explains order. It does not, by itself, explain why the event happened or what tax law should do with it.
Event Sequence ≠ Event Identity.
Event Sequence ≠ Tax Timing Determination.

OOF™ Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM)
Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS)
Module: ERRM — Event Recognition Rule Module
Operational Layer: Event Recognition Rule Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Recognition Rules
Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-ERRM-003
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 29 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs the criteria, logic, conditions, rule structures, decision pathways, exceptions, and traceable recognition mechanisms used to determine whether a relevance-screened occurrence should be formally recognized for continued progression through the TREGA™ event-governance lifecycle.

ERRM receives an occurrence that has passed or remained eligible after Event Relevance Screening and establishes the governed recognition logic through which the occurrence can be advanced, withheld, rejected, conditionally recognized, or referred for further recognition governance.
Its task is specific:
to govern how recognition decisions are made without converting recognition logic into jurisdiction-specific tax law, taxability rules, or legal tax determinations.
Operational Role
ORIM determines whether a distinguishable occurrence exists.
ERSM determines whether that occurrence has sufficient potential relevance to remain within tax-event governance.
ERRM answers the next question:
What governed rules determine whether this relevance-screened occurrence should be formally recognized?
The distinction is critical.
Potential relevance alone should not automatically create recognition.
At the same time, recognition should not depend on undocumented, inconsistent, or opaque logic.
ERRM therefore establishes the rule-governance layer between:
potential relevance
and
formal Event Recognition.
Internal Flow
Relevance-Screened Occurrence
↓
Applicable Recognition Rule Identification
↓
Recognition Condition Evaluation
↓
Rule Interaction / Priority Resolution
↓
Exception and Uncertainty Handling
↓
Recognition Rule Result
↓
Recognition Decision Candidate
The principal output is:
Governed Recognition Rule Result

This output proceeds to ERCM — Event Recognition Confidence Module for assessment of the strength and reliability of the recognition basis.
Operational Space
ERRM governs the space between:
an occurrence that has sufficient potential relevance
and
a governed rule-based basis for formal recognition.
Its operational space includes: recognition rule identification; recognition criteria; recognition conditions; recognition thresholds where appropriate; rule applicability; rule precedence; rule combinations; exception handling; conflict resolution; deterministic recognition logic; probabilistic recognition logic; AI-assisted recognition logic; hybrid recognition logic; manual recognition logic; rule versioning; rule traceability; recognition-rule change; recognition-rule uncertainty; rule-based rejection; rule-based conditional recognition.
ERRM governs the mechanism by which recognition logic is applied.
It does not determine whether those rules represent legal tax obligations.
Operational Scope
ERRM may support recognition methods implemented through: deterministic rules; decision trees; policy logic; threshold logic; pattern-based rules; statistical criteria; AI-assisted classification; machine-learning outputs; human review rules; hybrid human-machine processes; rule engines; workflow systems; enterprise event processors; public-sector tax infrastructure.
The implementation technology may vary.
The governance requirement remains the same:

the basis for recognition must remain explicit, traceable, bounded, and separable from jurisdiction-specific tax determination.
Recognition Rule Principle
ERRM establishes a foundational distinction:
Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule.
A Recognition Rule determines whether an occurrence should continue through TREGA™ event governance.
A Tax Rule determines legal consequences under a jurisdiction.
A Recognition Rule may ask:
Does this occurrence satisfy sufficient conditions to be formally recognized for Event Formation?
A Tax Rule may later ask:
Does this governed event create a taxable obligation under applicable law?
These are different questions and must remain architecturally separated.
Rule Applicability
Not every Recognition Rule applies to every occurrence.
Rule applicability may depend on governed characteristics such as: occurrence type; operational environment; economic characteristics; transaction characteristics; machine or autonomous execution; value-related attributes; distributed-system characteristics; available context; evidence availability; relevance domain.
ERRM must establish which Recognition Rules are applicable before those rules are evaluated.
Therefore:
Rule Availability ≠ Rule Applicability.
Recognition Conditions
A Recognition Rule may contain one or more conditions that must be evaluated.

Conditions may examine whether: the occurrence is sufficiently distinguishable; the occurrence passed relevance screening; required contextual elements exist; material relationships are available; duplicate occurrence risk is sufficiently controlled; minimum evidence conditions are satisfied; unresolved contradictions remain within acceptable limits; required governance references exist.
These conditions remain methodological recognition conditions.
They are not statutory taxation conditions.
Recognition Thresholds
Some implementations may use thresholds.
For example, a threshold may determine whether: sufficient information exists; a probabilistic model has adequate support; duplicate risk is below an acceptable governance level; contextual coverage is sufficient; rule confidence is adequate for automatic progression.
ERRM allows such thresholds where appropriate.
However:
Recognition Threshold ≠ Statutory Threshold.
A governance threshold should not be confused with a monetary tax threshold, filing threshold, exemption threshold, or other legal threshold.
Rule Interaction
Several Recognition Rules may apply to the same occurrence.
ERRM must govern their interaction.
Rules may be: complementary; cumulative; alternative; conditional; hierarchical; mutually exclusive; conflicting.
The existence of several applicable rules must not automatically create several recognition decisions.
ERRM requires a governed method for resolving rule interaction.
Rule Priority

Where multiple rules conflict, precedence must not be arbitrary.
Rule priority may be established through: architecture-defined precedence; implementation policy; rule specificity; evidence quality; system authority; approved governance hierarchy.
ERRM must preserve the reason why one rule prevailed over another where the decision is materially significant.
Therefore:
Rule Priority ≠ Hidden System Preference.
Rule Conflict
Recognition rules may produce contradictory results.
For example:
one rule may support recognition;
another may reject;
a probabilistic model may indicate uncertainty;
a human-review rule may require escalation.
ERRM must represent the conflict rather than suppress it.
Possible outcomes may include:
Recognition Rule Conflict
Conditional Recognition
Recognition Withheld
Escalation Required
Rule conflict is a governance state, not a system failure.
Deterministic Recognition Rules
A deterministic rule produces a defined outcome where its conditions are satisfied.
Example logic may take the form:
If Condition A + Condition B + Condition C are established
↓
Recognition Rule Satisfied.
Deterministic logic can improve consistency.
But deterministic logic does not guarantee correctness if its inputs, scope, or assumptions are wrong.
Therefore:
Deterministic Rule ≠ Correct Recognition by Default.
Probabilistic Recognition Rules
Some occurrence types may require probabilistic assessment.

Examples may include: pattern recognition; transaction clustering; machine-generated activity classification; distributed occurrence association; anomaly-driven recognition.
ERRM permits probabilistic methods where governed.
However:
Model Probability ≠ Recognition Truth.
A probability score must remain distinct from the final recognition outcome.
Its use must be subject to governed confidence, uncertainty, and escalation mechanisms.
AI-Assisted Recognition
AI systems may assist in determining whether an occurrence satisfies Recognition Rules.
They may: classify occurrences; detect patterns; identify duplicates; assess rule applicability; surface missing information; detect contradictions; recommend recognition outcomes.
But AI output cannot become an ungoverned substitute for Recognition Rules.
Therefore:
AI Recommendation ≠ Governed Recognition Decision.
Where AI participates, ERRM requires the applicable rule basis to remain sufficiently interpretable and governable for the implementation context.
Human Recognition
Manual review may also form part of recognition governance.
Human reviewers may resolve: unusual activity; incomplete evidence; rule conflicts; novel machine-generated occurrences; exceptional economic arrangements.
But manual involvement does not remove the need for governance.
Therefore:
Human Decision ≠ Governed Decision by Default.
The decision basis must remain traceable where materially required.
Hybrid Recognition
Many operational systems will combine:

Automated Rules + AI Analysis + Human Escalation
ERRM supports hybrid recognition where the division of responsibilities remains explicit.
For example:
Rule Engine
↓
AI-Assisted Assessment
↓
Confidence Evaluation
↓
Human Escalation
The architecture remains technology-neutral.
Recognition Rule Versioning
Recognition Rules may evolve.
Operational systems change.
New activity types emerge.
AI and machine economies create new patterns.
Governance methodologies improve.
ERRM therefore requires that materially relevant rule changes remain distinguishable.
A historical occurrence should not silently be represented as if a Recognition Rule created years later had been applied originally.
Therefore:
Current Recognition Rule ≠ Historical Recognition Rule. Rule Change ≠ Occurrence Change
A Recognition Rule may change while the underlying occurrence remains identical.
This is especially important where organizations reprocess historical data.
A newly revised Recognition Rule may lead to a different governance result.
But:
Rule Change ≠ Change in Operational Reality.
The historical occurrence must remain separable from the recognition logic later applied to it.
Recognition Rule Independence from Tax-Law Change
Jurisdiction-specific tax laws may change frequently.
TREGA™ Recognition Rules should not need to be reconstructed solely because a tax rate, exemption, legal test, or filing obligation changes downstream.

Where a legal change alters what occurrences need to reach tax systems, implementation-level recognition rules may be updated.
But the architecture itself preserves the separation:
Tax-Law Change ≠ Recognition Rule Change by Default.
Rule Transparency
A Recognition Rule should be sufficiently explainable to establish: what rule applied; why it applied; what conditions were evaluated; what result it produced; what exceptions or conflicts occurred; what version was used.
Transparency does not require disclosure of every implementation detail to every actor.
It requires enough governance traceability to reconstruct materially important recognition decisions.
Rule Traceability
Where materially required, ERRM should preserve:
Occurrence Reference
↓
Applied Rule
↓
Rule Version
↓
Evaluated Conditions
↓
Rule Result
This creates a traceable bridge between potential event relevance and formal recognition.
Recognition Exceptions
Some occurrences may fall outside ordinary rule logic.
Exceptions may arise where: a novel economic model appears; autonomous agents create unfamiliar activity; existing rules do not cover a new platform structure; available information is incomplete; a transaction structure is materially unusual.
ERRM must allow exceptions to be governed rather than forcing them into inappropriate rule categories.
Possible handling includes:
Exception Review
Conditional Recognition
Recognition Withheld
Escalation Recognition Rule Failure

A Recognition Rule may fail because: required inputs are unavailable; conditions cannot be evaluated; the rule conflicts with another rule; the rule is technically unavailable; the occurrence falls outside the rule's valid scope.
Such failure should not automatically become rejection.
Therefore:
Rule Failure ≠ Occurrence Rejection.
The appropriate result may instead be unresolved recognition or escalation.
Rule Coverage
A governance system should understand whether the relevant occurrence is covered by available Recognition Rules.
Possible states may include:
Rule Coverage Established
Partial Rule Coverage
Rule Coverage Gap
Rule Applicability Unresolved
A coverage gap is important in new economic environments.
It may reveal that the methodology does not yet adequately govern a type of occurrence.
Governance Requirements

ERRM requires that: Recognition Rules remain distinct from Tax Rules; rule applicability is established; rule conditions are explicit; rule outputs are governable; rule conflicts can be represented; rule precedence is governed; thresholds remain distinguishable from legal thresholds; deterministic outputs are not treated as truth by default; probabilistic outputs remain distinguishable from recognition outcomes; AI-assisted recommendations remain governed; manual decisions remain traceable where materially required; rule versions are distinguishable; historical recognition remains reconstructable; rule failure does not automatically become occurrence rejection; exceptions can be governed; rule coverage gaps remain visible; recognition logic does not establish legal taxability.
Governance Logic
ERRM applies five principal questions:
Which Recognition Rule or Rules legitimately apply to this occurrence?
What recognition conditions must be evaluated?
What happens if several rules interact or conflict?
What governed result does the applicable rule logic produce?
Is the resulting rule basis suitable for confidence assessment or must it remain unresolved?
The transformation is:
Relevant Occurrence
→ Applicable Recognition Rules
→ Condition Evaluation
→ Rule Resolution
→ Governed Recognition Rule Result
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERRM implementation must be capable of:

1. receiving a relevance-screened occurrence from ERSM; 2. identifying applicable Recognition Rules; 3. evaluating Recognition Conditions; 4. representing rule applicability; 5. resolving or representing multiple-rule interactions; 6. preserving rule conflicts; 7. distinguishing governance thresholds from statutory thresholds; 8. recording rule versions where materially required; 9. representing exceptions and rule failures; 10. producing a Governed Recognition Rule Result for ERCM; 11. preserving enough traceability to reconstruct the recognition logic; 12. preventing Recognition Rules from becoming jurisdiction-specific Tax Determinations.
ERRM does not prescribe a specific rules engine, programming language, machine-learning model, AI system, tax platform, or workflow technology.
Governance Outputs
ERRM may produce:
Governed Recognition Rule Result — the result produced by applicable recognition logic.
Applicable Recognition Rule Set — the rules determined to apply to the occurrence.
Recognition Condition Result — the outcome of individual or combined rule conditions.
Recognition Rule Conflict Record — representation of contradictory rule outcomes.
Recognition Exception Record — representation of an occurrence requiring exception handling.
Recognition Rule Version Reference — identification of the rule version used.
Rule Coverage Status — whether adequate recognition-rule coverage exists.

Rule Failure Indicator — representation of a recognition rule that could not be legitimately executed.
Recognition Decision Candidate — the rule-supported candidate result transferred to confidence assessment.
Critical Distinctions
Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule.
Recognition governs architecture progression. Tax law governs legal consequence.
Rule Availability ≠ Rule Applicability.
A rule existing in the system does not mean it applies to the occurrence.
Recognition Threshold ≠ Statutory Threshold.
Governance thresholds must not become legal tax thresholds.
Deterministic Rule ≠ Correct Recognition by Default.
Predictability of logic is not proof of validity.
Model Probability ≠ Recognition Truth.
A probability score is an input, not a legal or governance fact.
AI Recommendation ≠ Governed Recognition Decision.
AI assistance remains subject to rule governance.
Human Decision ≠ Governed Decision by Default.
Human review also requires a legitimate basis.
Rule Priority ≠ Hidden System Preference.
Precedence must remain governed.
Rule Conflict ≠ Recognition Failure.
Conflict may legitimately require additional governance.
Rule Failure ≠ Occurrence Rejection.
Failure of logic execution does not prove non-relevance.
Current Recognition Rule ≠ Historical Recognition Rule.
Rule evolution must not rewrite past governance.
Rule Change ≠ Occurrence Change.
Methodology may evolve while operational reality remains the same.
Recognition Rule Result ≠ Recognition Confidence.

ERRM determines what the rule logic says. ERCM determines how strong the basis for relying on that result is.
Recognition Rule Result ≠ Taxability Determination.
No recognition rule establishes that tax is legally due.
Enterprise Application
ERRM addresses a major governance weakness in large transaction-processing environments:
recognition logic often exists, but is fragmented across systems, undocumented, embedded in code, mixed with tax logic, or changed without preserving historical meaning.
A multinational enterprise may process the same activity through:
Commerce Rules
↓
Payment Rules
↓
ERP Logic
↓
Tax Engine Filters
↓
Reporting Rules
while an autonomous platform may add:
AI Classification
↓
Machine Rules
↓
Dynamic Policies
↓
Human Exception Review.
Without ERRM, different systems can decide independently what counts as an event candidate.
The result may be inconsistent recognition across systems, duplication, missing events, non-reconstructable historical logic, and premature legal assumptions.
ERRM creates a governed recognition-rule layer that can sit before jurisdiction-specific Tax Engines. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Historical Tax Review After Recognition Logic Has Changed Repeatedly
A multinational digital platform processes hundreds of millions of transactions each year.
Over six years, it changes: payment infrastructure; transaction classification logic; ERP workflows; event filters; AI models; tax engines; internal recognition thresholds.

A tax authority later asks why a particular historical transaction entered one reporting pathway while another apparently similar transaction did not.
The current recognition logic cannot answer the question because the rules have changed several times.
ERRM preserves the applicable Recognition Rule, rule version, conditions, exceptions, and resulting rule outcome associated with the historical occurrence.
The organization can reconstruct:
what recognition logic existed when the decision was made
without pretending that today's rules governed yesterday's activity.
This preserves a critical institutional distinction:
historical economic reality and historical recognition methodology must remain independently reconstructable. Use Case 2 — AI Recognition System Changes Behavior Across a Machine-to-Machine Marketplace
A machine-to-machine marketplace processes continuous exchanges of computing capacity, energy, digital services, data access, and autonomous resource reservations.
An AI model assists in identifying which occurrences should enter full Event Formation.
As the marketplace evolves, the model is retrained and begins treating certain resource reservations differently.
Two operationally similar machine interactions processed six months apart now produce different recognition recommendations.

Without governed Recognition Rules, the organization may be unable to explain whether the difference resulted from: changed economic activity; changed model behavior; changed thresholds; changed policy; changed evidence; or genuine methodological improvement.
ERRM separates the underlying occurrence from the recognition logic applied to it.
AI output becomes one governed input within a traceable Recognition Rule structure rather than the invisible definition of what constitutes a Tax-Relevant Event candidate.
This allows machine-scale recognition to evolve without surrendering methodological control to the model producing the recommendation.
Canonical Boundary
ERRM governs the criteria, rules, conditions, logic, interactions, exceptions, and traceable mechanisms through which a relevance-screened occurrence receives a governed recognition-rule result. It does not determine the confidence that should be placed in that result, resolve unresolved recognition through escalation, form the Tax-Relevant Event, or determine legal taxability.
The TRERS internal progression remains:
ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur?
→ ERSM — Does it possess sufficient potential relevance?
→ ERRM — What governed Recognition Rules apply and what result do they produce?
→ ERCM — How strong and reliable is the recognition basis?
→ EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation?
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Recognition Rule Module establishes the rule-governance layer of Tax-Relevant Event Recognition by ensuring that progression from relevance-screened occurrence to formal recognition is governed through explicit, applicable, traceable, and bounded recognition logic rather than through undocumented system behavior, hidden AI outputs, arbitrary thresholds, or jurisdiction-specific tax conclusions. Through governance of rule applicability, conditions, thresholds, rule interaction, precedence, conflict, deterministic and probabilistic logic, AI-assisted and human decisions, exceptions, rule failure, versioning, coverage, and traceability, ERRM enables recognition methodology to evolve without rewriting the operational reality to which that methodology is applied. The Module preserves the distinctions between Recognition Rules and Tax Rules, governance thresholds and statutory thresholds, model probability and recognition truth, rule change and occurrence change, and rule result and Recognition Confidence. ERRM therefore establishes not whether tax is legally due and not yet how confidently an occurrence should be recognized, but the governed methodological basis upon which that recognition decision can legitimately be assessed.

Canonical Definition
Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs whether a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence possesses enough plausible economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other tax-event relevance to justify continued progression through the TREGA™ recognition process.
ERSM receives a Recognized Occurrence from ORIM and determines whether that occurrence should remain within the candidate population for potential Tax-Relevant Event Formation.
Its task is specific:

to screen recognized occurrences for legitimate potential relevance to tax-event governance without determining legal taxability, tax jurisdiction, tax liability, or the final structure of the Tax-Relevant Event.
Operational Role
ORIM answers:
Did a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence occur?
ERSM asks the next question:
Does that occurrence have enough potential relevance to justify further tax-relevant event governance?
This distinction prevents TREGA™ from processing every recognized occurrence through the complete event lifecycle.
Many genuine occurrences may have no material relationship to taxation analysis.
For example: a machine performs routine internal diagnostics; a software service updates a configuration; a warehouse sensor records temperature; an employee opens an internal application; an autonomous system performs non-economic optimization; a platform generates technical housekeeping operations.
These may be real occurrences.
They do not automatically require Tax-Relevant Event Formation.
ERSM acts as the relevance gateway.
Internal Flow
Recognized Occurrence
↓
Potential Relevance Signal Identification
↓
Relevance Domain Screening
↓
Material Relevance Assessment
↓
Relevance Sufficiency Determination
↓
Relevant / Non-Relevant / Unresolved Screening Result
The principal output is:
Event Relevance Screening Result
Where relevance is sufficiently established, the occurrence proceeds toward governed Recognition Rules.
Operational Space

ERSM governs the space between:
a recognized occurrence
and
an occurrence sufficiently relevant to remain within the TRERS recognition process.
Its operational space includes: relevance-signal identification; economic relevance; transactional relevance; operational relevance; digital economic relevance; autonomous-system relevance; value-related relevance; transfer relevance; exchange relevance; service relevance; resource relevance; distributed activity relevance; machine-generated economic relevance; relevance materiality; relevance uncertainty; non-relevance determination.
ERSM governs potential relevance to event governance.
It does not govern legal relevance under any particular tax code.
Operational Scope
ERSM may identify plausible relevance where an occurrence is materially associated with activity such as: provision of goods; provision of services; payments; transfers; exchanges; production; consumption; resource allocation; asset movement; value creation; value change; value transfer; value extinguishment; ownership-related activity; commercial execution; financial activity; digital-service activity; platform-mediated activity; autonomous purchasing; machine-to-machine exchange; distributed economic activity; other activity capable of requiring downstream taxation evaluation.
This list is not itself a legal tax rule.
It defines a broad governance screening space.
Potential Relevance Principle
ERSM deliberately operates on potential relevance, not legal taxability.

This is essential.
A transaction may later be exempt.
A transfer may later fall outside a particular tax.
A service may not create nexus.
A value movement may be legally neutral.
A machine-generated action may have no independent tax consequence.
Those questions belong downstream.
ERSM asks only:
Is there a sufficient governance basis to keep this occurrence within the tax-event analysis lifecycle?
Therefore:
Potential Tax Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability.
Relevance Signal
A relevance signal is any governed characteristic indicating that the occurrence may materially matter to downstream taxation analysis.
Possible signals include: exchange of value; transfer of an asset or resource; provision or receipt of a service; economic benefit; economic sacrifice; commercial commitment; payment; settlement; ownership-related change; operational production; consumption; resource allocation; cross-border economic activity; platform-mediated exchange; autonomous commercial action; machine-to-machine economic execution.
A single relevance signal may be sufficient in some contexts.
In others, several signals may need to be considered together. Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger
ERSM must preserve a strict distinction:
Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger.
A payment may indicate relevance.
It does not prove tax liability.
A transfer may indicate relevance.
It does not prove a taxable disposition.
A service activation may indicate relevance.
It does not establish a jurisdictional tax point.

Recognition infrastructure must not smuggle legal tax conclusions into the relevance-screening stage.
Economic Relevance
ERSM may identify economic relevance where the occurrence materially affects, represents, enables, transfers, consumes, generates, allocates, or relates to economic value or resources.
However:
Economic Relevance ≠ Taxability.
Economic meaning is a reason for further governance, not a legal conclusion.
Operational Relevance
An occurrence may be operationally significant without appearing immediately as a conventional transaction.
For example: production completion; delivery; automated resource consumption; asset deployment; machine execution; platform fulfilment.
Such activity may require downstream event governance even where no payment occurs at the same moment.
Therefore:
Payment ≠ Required Condition for Relevance.
Transactional Relevance
A transaction record may provide a strong relevance signal.
But ERSM must not assume that:
Transaction Record = Tax-Relevant Event.
A transaction record may represent: initiation; authorization; partial execution; reversal; synchronization; settlement; internal technical posting.
Its actual event structure belongs to later governance.
Value-Related Relevance
Where governed value information is available, ERSM may consume it as a relevance signal.

For example, a governed representation may indicate: Value Emergence; Value Change; Value Development; Value Degradation; Value Nullification; Value Restoration; Value Extinction.
But TREGA™ does not recreate Value Governance.
Therefore:
VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ governs whether the governed value result is relevant to event construction.
Cross-Border Relevance
An occurrence spanning multiple locations, organizations, platforms, or infrastructures may justify continued governance because different taxation systems may later require evaluation.
However:
Cross-Border Relevance ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
ERSM does not decide which jurisdiction has taxation rights.
It preserves the occurrence for later jurisdiction-specific evaluation where appropriate.
Machine and Autonomous Relevance
Autonomous systems create a major relevance-screening challenge.
An AI agent may: reserve capacity; compare prices; negotiate; acquire digital resources; release reservations; initiate payment; terminate services; transfer machine resources.
Some actions may have economic significance.
Others may be purely technical.
ERSM distinguishes plausible tax-event relevance from ordinary machine activity.
Therefore:
Autonomous Activity ≠ Economic Relevance by Default.
and:
Economic Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability.
Relevance Materiality
ERSM should prevent insignificant technical or operational activity from advancing unnecessarily through the architecture.

Material relevance may depend upon whether an occurrence could reasonably affect: economic interpretation; transaction interpretation; value association; participant relationships; resource transfer; service provision; downstream Event Formation; later jurisdictional taxation evaluation.
Materiality at this stage remains governance materiality.
It is not a statutory threshold.
Therefore:
Governance Materiality ≠ Legal Tax Materiality.
Relevance Sufficiency
An occurrence becomes relevance-sufficient when enough governed information exists to justify continued recognition processing.
This does not require every downstream fact to be known.
ERSM may legitimately advance an occurrence while uncertainty remains regarding: Event Boundary; Event Timing; Event Location; participants; value; jurisdiction; tax treatment.
Those questions belong later in TREGA™. Non-Relevance
ERSM must permit a recognized occurrence to exit the recognition pathway where no sufficient potential relevance exists.
Examples may include: purely technical system housekeeping; duplicated internal processing; non-economic diagnostic activity; irrelevant sensor activity; routine state synchronization; machine operations with no material relationship to economic activity.
A non-relevant result means:
the recognized occurrence does not currently justify further TREGA™ recognition processing.
It does not mean:
the occurrence has been legally determined non-taxable.
Relevance Uncertainty

Some occurrences cannot be confidently screened.
For example: an autonomous agent action may have unclear economic purpose; a platform transfer may lack sufficient business context; a machine resource movement may or may not be internal; a digital-asset movement may have ambiguous operational meaning.
ERSM must preserve an unresolved condition rather than forcing a binary result.
Possible outcomes may include:
Relevant
Not Relevant
Relevance Unresolved
Further Context Required
This allows uncertainty to remain visible and governable.
False Positive and False Negative Risk
Relevance screening must control two opposing risks.
False Positive
An occurrence proceeds through expensive governance even though it has no plausible tax-event relevance.
False Negative
A potentially important occurrence is filtered out prematurely.
Both matter.
In machine-scale economies, false positives can create massive processing volumes.
In fragmented or novel economic environments, false negatives can remove activity that should have proceeded to Event Formation.
ERSM therefore seeks proportionate relevance screening, not maximum exclusion.
Governance Requirements

ERSM requires that: screening begins from a Recognized Occurrence; relevance remains distinct from occurrence existence; economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, and value-related signals may be evaluated; relevance criteria remain jurisdiction-neutral at the architecture layer; potential relevance remain distinct from legal taxability; legal tax rules do not become mandatory upstream recognition rules; non-relevance can be governed explicitly; uncertainty can remain unresolved; machine-generated activity is not assumed economically relevant; lack of payment does not automatically eliminate relevance; cross-border characteristics do not determine Tax Jurisdiction; relevance decisions remain traceable where materially required.
Governance Logic
ERSM applies four principal questions:
What characteristics of this occurrence may make it relevant to downstream tax-event governance?
Are those characteristics materially meaningful rather than purely technical?
Is the relevance basis sufficient to justify continued TREGA™ processing?
If relevance cannot yet be established, should the occurrence be preserved as unresolved rather than rejected?
The transformation is:
Recognized Occurrence
→ Potential Relevance Signals
→ Material Relevance Assessment
→ Event Relevance Screening Result
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERSM implementation must be capable of:

1. receiving a Recognized Occurrence from ORIM; 2. identifying potential relevance signals; 3. evaluating one or more relevant governance domains; 4. distinguishing technical significance from potential economic or tax-event relevance; 5. assessing governance materiality; 6. determining relevance sufficiency; 7. representing non-relevance; 8. preserving unresolved relevance; 9. recording the screening basis where materially required; 10. transferring relevance-positive occurrences to ERRM.
ERSM does not prescribe jurisdiction-specific tax logic, statutory classifications, legal thresholds, AI models, rules engines, ERP platforms, or tax software.
Governance Outputs
ERSM may produce:
Event Relevance Screening Result — the governed outcome of relevance screening.
Relevant Occurrence — an occurrence sufficiently relevant to continue through TRERS.
Non-Relevant Occurrence Result — a recognized occurrence that does not currently justify further event-recognition governance.
Relevance Signal Set — the materially relevant characteristics supporting screening.
Relevance Domain References — economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, value-related, or other relevant domains.
Relevance Materiality Result — the governed assessment of whether identified relevance is sufficient.
Relevance Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved conditions affecting the screening outcome.

Further Context Requirement — identification of material contextual information required before screening can be completed.
Critical Distinctions
Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Relevance Screening.
ORIM establishes that something sufficiently distinguishable occurred.
ERSM determines whether that occurrence plausibly matters to downstream tax-event governance.
Occurrence ≠ Relevant Occurrence.
Not every genuine occurrence requires TREGA™ progression.
Potential Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability.
Relevance keeps an occurrence in governance. It does not create tax liability.
Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger.
Operational or economic characteristics cannot replace legal tax analysis.
Economic Relevance ≠ Tax Liability.
Economic significance does not establish a legal obligation.
Payment ≠ Required Condition for Relevance.
Economically meaningful activity may exist before or without payment.
Transaction Record ≠ Tax-Relevant Event.
A record remains a representation, not a final event determination.
Governance Materiality ≠ Statutory Materiality.
ERSM does not establish legal thresholds.
Cross-Border Relevance ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Several jurisdictions may later evaluate the same occurrence.
Non-Relevant ≠ Legally Non-Taxable.
ERSM's negative result is methodological, not legal.
Enterprise Application
ERSM provides an important scaling mechanism for enterprises and tax infrastructures processing very high volumes of operational data.

Without relevance screening, every recognized occurrence could proceed through:
Formation
↓
Boundary
↓
Timing
↓
Location
↓
Participation
↓
Value Association
↓
Relationships
↓
Determination
even where most occurrences have no plausible need for taxation analysis.
In a machine-intensive environment this becomes operationally unrealistic.
ERSM creates a governed filtering layer between occurrence recognition and full event construction.
This allows high-volume platforms, banks, industrial systems, autonomous systems, and digital infrastructures to focus deeper TREGA™ governance on occurrences with a legitimate relevance basis while preserving unresolved cases that should not yet be discarded. A global cloud provider operates millions of servers and automated services across many regions.
Its systems generate enormous volumes of recognizable occurrences:
resource allocation,
container creation,
internal network routing,
temporary storage allocation,
service activation,
resource release,
customer consumption,
billing events,
machine balancing,
and technical maintenance.
If every recognizable occurrence proceeds into full tax-event formation, the governance system becomes dominated by infrastructure activity rather than economically meaningful operations.
ERSM screens these occurrences.

Internal load balancing and technical maintenance may be recognized as genuine occurrences but screened as non-relevant to further tax-event governance.
Customer resource consumption, service provision, billable allocation, or economically meaningful transfers may remain relevant and proceed.
ERSM therefore separates:
what genuinely happens inside a digital economy
from
what legitimately requires deeper tax-event governance. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Marketplace Where Machines Trade Resources Continuously
An automated marketplace allows autonomous agents and machines to purchase computing capacity, energy, data access, transport capacity, and digital services from one another.
Millions of machine interactions occur every hour.
Some are quotations.
Some are rejected offers.
Some reserve capacity temporarily.
Some change resource availability.
Some create actual exchanges.
Some trigger settlements.
Some are merely technical negotiation messages.
A conventional system may either treat all interactions as transactions or apply rigid rules that discard novel forms of machine commerce.
ERSM evaluates recognized occurrences for plausible economic, transactional, resource, and value-related relevance before deeper Event Formation begins.
It does not determine whether a reservation, resource transfer, machine exchange, or settlement is legally taxable.

Instead it ensures that potentially meaningful machine-economic activity survives the recognition gateway while technical negotiation noise does not automatically flood the downstream tax architecture.
This establishes a crucial capability for future tax infrastructure:
the system can scale with machine economies without equating computational activity with taxable economic activity.
Canonical Boundary
ERSM governs whether a Recognized Occurrence possesses sufficient potential relevance to remain within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition. It does not determine the rules by which formal recognition is made, the confidence of that recognition, whether escalation is required, how the event is formed, or whether any jurisdiction legally taxes it.
The TRERS internal progression remains:
ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur?
→ ERSM — Does the occurrence have sufficient potential relevance to tax-event governance?
→ ERRM — What governed Recognition Rules determine progression?
→ ERCM — How strong is the recognition basis?
→ EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation?
Canonical Closing Statement

Event Relevance Screening Module establishes the relevance-gating capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard by determining which sufficiently distinguishable occurrences possess enough plausible economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other material relevance to justify continued progression through TREGA™ recognition governance. Through governance of relevance signals, relevance domains, materiality, sufficiency, non-relevance, uncertainty, cross-border characteristics, machine activity, and false-positive and false-negative screening risk, ERSM prevents every genuine technical or operational occurrence from automatically entering full Tax-Relevant Event Formation while preserving potentially meaningful activity that should not be discarded merely because its eventual legal treatment remains unknown. The Module preserves the boundaries between occurrence existence and relevance, governance materiality and statutory materiality, relevance signals and taxable triggers, potential tax relevance and legal taxability, and cross-border significance and Tax Jurisdiction. ERSM therefore establishes not whether an occurrence is taxable, but whether it matters enough for TREGA™ to continue asking what governed Tax-Relevant Event, if any, should ultimately be formed from it.
