OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard
Module: ERSTM — Event Record Structure Module
Operational Layer: Event Record Structure Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Record Structure
Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Structure
Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERSTM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 3 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) governs how an identified Tax-Relevant Event Record is structured so that the materially relevant meaning of the Determined Tax-Relevant Event can be represented in a sufficiently complete, coherent, bounded, and machine-readable form.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Record Identity
↓
Event Record Structure Governance
↓
Governed Event Record Structure

ERSTM determines what structural elements a governed Record must contain or reference in order to preserve the Event meaning established by preceding TREGA™ governance layers.
It does not recreate those upstream governance results.
Its foundational distinction is:
Record Structure ≠ Event Structure.
Operational Role
ERIDM establishes which governed Record represents the Event.
ERSTM determines how that Record must be structurally represented.
Its core function is to ensure that the Record does not become: too sparse to preserve Event meaning; too fragmented to be reconstructable; overloaded with unnecessary data; detached from its Determination state; structurally inconsistent; or dependent on one proprietary technical schema.
The module answers:
What structure must the governed Event Record possess so that the Determined Tax-Relevant Event remains meaningfully represented?
Internal Module Flow
TREGS operates through:
ERIDM — Event Record Identification
↓
ERSTM — Event Record Structure
↓
ERLKM — Event Record Linkage
↓
ERTM — Event Record Traceability
↓
ERINM — Event Record Interoperability
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
ERSTM receives:
Governed Event Record Identity
and produces:
Governed Event Record Structure
for ERLKM.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Governed Event Record Identity
↓
Structural Requirement Identification
↓
Component Structuring
↓
Sufficiency Assessment
↓
Structural State
↓
Governed Event Record Structure Operational Space

ERSTM governs: Record component identification; structural requirement definition; mandatory and conditional components; Record composition; field grouping; governed references; representational sufficiency; structural completeness; structural coherence; structural consistency; structural modularity; representation boundaries; qualification representation; uncertainty representation; Determination-state representation; relationship-reference capacity; lifecycle-reference capacity; structural extensibility; and structure handoff.
Operational Scope
ERSTM may govern Event Record structures used across: ERP systems; commerce systems; banking infrastructure; accounting platforms; marketplaces; tax platforms; payment systems; distributed systems; blockchain environments; smart contracts; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial systems; machine-to-machine infrastructure; cross-border platforms; and future machine economies.
The structural logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Structural Object
The structural object is the identified Governed Event Record whose canonical representation must be defined.
ERSTM structures the Record.
It does not redefine the underlying Event.
Structural Object ≠ Underlying Event.
Structural Requirement Identification
ERSTM shall identify which information categories are materially necessary for the Record to perform its TREGS function.
Requirements may include direct values or governed references.

The module should avoid indiscriminate data replication.
More Fields ≠ Better Record Structure by default.
Mandatory Components
Every governed Event Record should contain or reference, where applicable: Canonical Record Identifier; underlying Event Reference; Determination Reference; current Record State; governance-state references necessary to preserve meaning; relevant qualification state; relevant uncertainty state; and structural governance status.
These form the minimum structural foundation.
Conditional Components
Some components are required only where materially relevant.
Examples include: Location representation; Participation representation; Value Association; Event Relationship references; Merge/Split references; reconsideration references; cross-system references; or jurisdiction-neutral processing metadata.
Conditional Component ≠ Optional Irrelevance.
A component may be conditionally required where its absence would materially distort the Event.
Reference Versus Replication
ERSTM shall distinguish between: information that should be represented directly; and information that may be referenced from another governed source.
The standard does not require all upstream TREGA™ data to be copied into the Record.
Governed Reference ≠ Missing Information.
Structural Completeness
A Record is structurally complete when all materially required components are either: represented directly; or reliably referenced.

Structural completeness is determined by governance sufficiency, not by maximum field population.
Structural Completeness ≠ Every Field Populated.
Structural Sufficiency
Structural Sufficiency exists where the Record structure is sufficient to preserve the meaning and downstream usability of the governed Event.
A Record may be structurally sufficient even where non-material detail is absent.
Structural Coherence
Record components shall not materially contradict each other.
For example, a Record should not simultaneously represent: incompatible Determination states; contradictory Event references; incompatible Record states; or mutually exclusive qualification states
without explicitly governing that conflict.
Data Presence ≠ Structural Coherence.
Structural Consistency
The Record should apply the same structural meaning consistently across equivalent representations.
Consistency includes: field semantics; state semantics; identifier usage; component relationships; and reference logic.
Record Composition
The Record may be composed of: core components; conditional components; embedded substructures; external references; state objects; and governed metadata.
ERSTM governs their canonical function, not their physical storage implementation.
Core Record Component
A Core Record Component is structurally necessary for the Record to remain identifiable and interpretable.
Core components should not be removable without materially affecting the Record's governance function.

Supporting Record Component
Supporting components provide additional governed context without defining the Record identity itself.
They may include: technical references; implementation metadata; supporting source references; processing metadata; or non-material extensions.
Structural Modularity
ERSTM may permit modular Record structures where different Event classes require different component sets.
Modularity shall preserve a common canonical core.
Modular Structure ≠ Fragmented Governance.
Event Reference Structure
The Record shall structurally preserve the association with the Determined Tax-Relevant Event.
The Event Reference should be distinguishable from: Record ID; transaction ID; document ID; external tax ID.
Event Reference ≠ Record Identifier.
Determination Reference Structure
The Record shall contain or reference the applicable TREDS Determination state.
This may include: final Decision state; qualification; uncertainty; reconsideration result.
ERSTM represents the Determination state structurally.
It does not govern that Determination.
Qualification Structure
Where TREDS produces a qualification, ERSTM shall preserve a structural location for that qualification.
The Record shall not collapse:
Conditional Determination
↓
Unqualified Record
through omission.
Structural Omission ≠ Qualification Removal.
Uncertainty Structure
Where material uncertainty remains, the Record should preserve an explicit structural representation or reference.

The uncertainty shall not disappear merely because the Record is finalized.
Record Finalization ≠ Uncertainty Elimination.
Participation Representation
Where Participation is materially relevant to downstream interpretation, the Record should contain or reference the governed Participation result.
ERSTM does not determine participant identity or taxpayer status.
Timing Representation
The Record may structurally preserve: Event Start; Event Completion; Event Duration; Temporal Order; or relevant Event Time references.
These remain operational Event times.
Record Time Field ≠ Legal Tax Point.
Location Representation
The Record may preserve governed physical, digital, or distributed Location results.
This does not establish Tax Jurisdiction.
Location Component ≠ Jurisdiction Component.
Value Representation
The Record may preserve the governed Value Association established by TRVAS.
ERSTM does not calculate: Tax Base; taxable amount; valuation under tax law.
Value Representation ≠ Tax Base Representation.
Relationship Representation Capacity
The Record structure should support references to Event Relationships governed by TRERLS.
ERSTM provides the structural capacity.
ERLKM later governs actual Record linkage.
Relationship Capacity ≠ Relationship Linkage.
Merge and Split Representation
Where Events have been merged or split, the Record structure should support the resulting governance references.
ERSTM does not govern the Merge or Split decision.
Reconsideration Representation

Where EDREM has changed the effective Determination state, the Record structure should support representation of: current state; prior state reference; reconsideration reference; supersession relationship where relevant.
Detailed traceability belongs to ERTM.
Record State Representation
The structure shall support clear representation of Record state.
Possible Record states may include: Draft; Structurally Incomplete; Structurally Sufficient; Qualified; Active; Superseded; Archived; Ready for Lifecycle Governance.
These states shall remain distinguishable from Event Determination states.
Record State ≠ Determination State.
State Separation
Different governance dimensions shall not be collapsed into one generic status field where that would create ambiguity.
For example: Record State; Determination State; Uncertainty State; Lifecycle State
should remain conceptually distinguishable.
One Status Field ≠ Complete Governance State by default.
Structural Boundaries
The Record should have a clear structural boundary defining which components belong to the canonical governed Record and which are external references.
This prevents uncontrolled technical metadata from becoming part of the canonical Event representation.
Structural Extensibility
The Record should support extensions without destabilizing its canonical meaning.
Extensions may support: sector-specific needs; implementation-specific fields; jurisdiction-specific downstream references; future technologies.

Extensions shall not redefine the canonical TREGA™ Event.
Extension ≠ Canonical Redefinition.
Jurisdiction-Specific Extension Boundary
A jurisdiction may append: tax classification; tax codes; filing references; tax base; rate; exemption; legal treatment.
These fields remain downstream extensions.
They should not become part of the canonical jurisdiction-neutral TREGS Record structure by default.
Schema Independence
ERSTM does not require one universal technical schema.
The governed structure may be implemented through: relational databases; JSON; XML; graph structures; event streams; distributed ledgers; object stores; semantic models; or future data systems.
Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema.
Schema Mapping Boundary
Mapping the canonical structure into specific system schemas may be necessary.
ERSTM defines the structural meaning.
ERINM governs broader interoperability.
Data-Type Flexibility
Different technical implementations may represent the same governed concept using different data types.
ERSTM requires semantic preservation rather than identical physical encoding.
Record Granularity
The Record structure shall correspond to the governed Event granularity.
It shall not fragment or aggregate Events merely because a system prefers a particular storage model.
Storage Granularity ≠ Event Granularity.
Nested Records
Some complex Events may require nested structural representations.

Nested structures may be used where they preserve: Event hierarchy; components; relationship references; or conditional data.
Nested technical structures do not automatically create separate governed Events.
Distributed Record Structure
A governed Event Record may be physically distributed across multiple systems.
ERSTM permits distributed representation where: canonical identity remains stable; required structural components remain reconstructable; and governance meaning remains coherent.
Distributed Storage ≠ Distributed Record Identity.
Record Compression
Systems may compress or abstract data.
Compression shall not remove materially necessary governance meaning.
Compact Representation ≠ Incomplete Representation.
Structural Versioning
Record structure may evolve over time.
Versioning shall preserve: semantic continuity; interpretability; canonical identity association; and historical reconstruction.
Schema Version Change ≠ New Governed Event.
Backward Compatibility
Where structure versions change, older Record representations should remain interpretable where material to historical continuity.
ERSTM does not require indefinite technical compatibility, but it does require governance interpretability.
Forward Extensibility
Future components may be added where new system types or governance requirements emerge.
Extensions should not invalidate the canonical core.
Structural Validation Boundary
ERSTM may assess structural sufficiency and coherence.

It does not perform general validation governance.
VALIDOS™ remains authoritative for validation.
Structural Sufficiency ≠ Validation.
Structural Integrity Boundary
ERSTM requires internally coherent representation.
Broader integrity governance belongs to INTEGROS®.
Structural Coherence ≠ General Integrity Certification.
Traceability Boundary
ERSTM provides fields or references necessary for later traceability.
ERTM governs the actual Record Traceability space.
Traceability Capacity ≠ Traceability Governance.
Linkage Boundary
ERSTM provides structural slots for links.
ERLKM governs the creation and governance of those links.
Link Field ≠ Governed Linkage.
Interoperability Boundary
ERSTM establishes canonical structural meaning.
ERINM governs preservation of that meaning across systems and organizations.
Canonical Structure ≠ Interoperability Completion.
Governance States
ERSTM may represent:
Structure Governance Not Initiated
Structural Requirements Identified
Core Components Defined
Conditional Components Identified
Structure Under Construction
Structure Incomplete
Structure Ambiguous
Structure Conflicted
Structure Coherent
Structure Sufficient
Structure Qualified
Structure Ready for Linkage Governance
Governed Event Record Structure Established Governance Requirements

ERSTM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Record Identity exists; Record Structure remains distinct from Event Structure; structurally required components are identified; mandatory and conditional components remain distinguishable; material components are represented or reliably referenced; Record completeness does not require indiscriminate data replication; Event Reference remains structurally distinguishable from Record Identifier; Determination state is structurally preserved; qualifications are not removed through omission; material uncertainty remains representable; Participation, Timing, Location, Value, and Relationship information is represented only where materially required; tax-law conclusions remain downstream extensions; Record State remains distinct from Determination State; state dimensions are not collapsed where this creates ambiguity; canonical structure remains technology-neutral; schema differences do not automatically create governance differences; structure can support extension without redefining the canonical Event; record granularity follows governed Event granularity; distributed representation remains reconstructable; structural versioning preserves semantic continuity; structural sufficiency remains distinct from validation; structural coherence remains distinct from general integrity governance; linkage, traceability, and interoperability remain delegated to their respective modules; and the resulting Governed Event Record S

ains distinct from general integrity governance; linkage, traceability, and interoperability remain delegated to their respective modules; and the resulting Governed Event Record Structure is suitable for ERLKM.

Governance Logic
IF no valid Governed Event Record Identity exists, THEN ERSTM shall not establish a canonical Record Structure.
IF a materially necessary component is neither represented nor reliably referenced, THEN the Record Structure shall remain incomplete.
IF a component is not materially required, THEN its absence shall not automatically make the Record incomplete.
IF upstream governance information can be reliably referenced, THEN ERSTM shall not require unnecessary duplication.
IF structural components materially contradict each other, THEN the structure shall not be considered coherent until the conflict is governed.
IF a Determination qualification exists, THEN the Record Structure shall preserve that qualification explicitly or by reliable reference.
IF material uncertainty exists, THEN the Record Structure shall provide a governed representation or reference for it.
IF a jurisdiction-specific tax field is added, THEN it shall remain distinguishable from the canonical jurisdiction-neutral Record structure.
IF system schema changes while the governed Event meaning remains stable, THEN Record Structure continuity may remain intact.
IF the structure preserves the materially necessary Event meaning and supports downstream linkage, traceability, and interoperability, THEN ERSTM shall establish the Governed Event Record Structure.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERSTM implementation should support:

Record Structure Governance ID A stable identifier for the ERSTM governance process.
Canonical Record Identifier The ERIDM-established Record identity.
Determined Event Reference The underlying governed Event.
Structural Version The active canonical Record structure version.
Core Component Set The structurally mandatory Record components.
Conditional Component Set Components required only under specified governance conditions.
Event Reference Component The canonical reference to the underlying Event.
Determination Reference Component The applicable TREDS Determination state.
Record State Component The current TREGS Record state.
Qualification Component Any material Determination qualification.
Uncertainty Component Any material governed uncertainty or reference.
Timing Representation Relevant Event Timing reference where required.
Location Representation Relevant Event Location reference where required.
Participation Representation Relevant governed Participation reference where required.
Value Association Representation Relevant TRVAS output where required.
Relationship Representation Capacity Structural capability to support ERLKM linkage.
Reconsideration Reference Relevant EDREM state where applicable.
Prior Structure Version Reference The previous structural version where applicable.
Extension Reference Any implementation or sector-specific extensions.
Jurisdiction-Specific Extension State Whether downstream jurisdictional fields are attached separately.

Structural Completeness State Incomplete, Partial, Complete, or Qualified.
Structural Coherence State Coherent, Ambiguous, Conflicted, or Unresolved.
Structural Sufficiency State Insufficient, Conditionally Sufficient, or Sufficient.
Governance State The current ERSTM governance state.
Handoff State Whether the Record is ready for ERLKM.
Governance Outputs
ERSTM may produce: Structural Requirement Set; Core Component Set; Conditional Component Set; Event Reference Structure; Determination Representation; Qualification Representation; Uncertainty Representation; Record State Representation; Value Representation; Participation Representation; Timing Representation; Location Representation; Relationship Representation Capacity; Structural Completeness State; Structural Coherence State; Structural Sufficiency State; Structural Version Reference; Extension State; and the principal output: Governed Event Record Structure.
Critical Distinctions
Record Structure ≠ Event Structure.
Structural Object ≠ Underlying Event.
More Fields ≠ Better Record Structure by default.
Conditional Component ≠ Optional Irrelevance.
Governed Reference ≠ Missing Information.
Structural Completeness ≠ Every Field Populated.
Data Presence ≠ Structural Coherence.
Modular Structure ≠ Fragmented Governance.
Event Reference ≠ Record Identifier.
Structural Omission ≠ Qualification Removal.
Record Finalization ≠ Uncertainty Elimination.
Record Time Field ≠ Legal Tax Point.

Location Component ≠ Jurisdiction Component.
Value Representation ≠ Tax Base Representation.
Relationship Capacity ≠ Relationship Linkage.
Record State ≠ Determination State.
One Status Field ≠ Complete Governance State by default.
Extension ≠ Canonical Redefinition.
Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema.
Storage Granularity ≠ Event Granularity.
Distributed Storage ≠ Distributed Record Identity.
Compact Representation ≠ Incomplete Representation.
Schema Version Change ≠ New Governed Event.
Structural Sufficiency ≠ Validation.
Structural Coherence ≠ General Integrity Certification.
Traceability Capacity ≠ Traceability Governance.
Link Field ≠ Governed Linkage.
Canonical Structure ≠ Interoperability Completion.
Enterprise Application
ERSTM provides the structural layer that converts an identified Record into a governed representation capable of being linked, traced, exchanged, and later maintained.
The canonical enterprise path is:
ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
→ ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure
→ ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage
→ ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability
→ ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability
→ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
This allows organizations to use different technologies while preserving one canonical Event meaning. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Marketplace Record with Conditional Location Data
A marketplace Event has completed TREDS and ERIDM has established the canonical Record identity.

The Event contains fully governed: Formation; Participation; Value Association; and Determination.
Its distributed digital Location remains qualified.
ERSTM creates the governed Record structure with: Record Identifier; Event Reference; Determination Reference; Participation reference; Value Association reference; Location qualification; and current Record State.
The Record does not duplicate all TREGA™ data and does not remove the Location qualification.
It remains structurally sufficient for downstream Record Linkage and later jurisdiction-specific evaluation. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine Event Across Heterogeneous Systems
An autonomous industrial Event is represented across an ERP platform, machine-control system, payment infrastructure, and AI-agent environment.
Each system uses a different schema.
ERIDM has already established one canonical Record identity.
ERSTM defines the canonical structural meaning required across those representations, including: Event Reference; Determination state; relevant Participation; Value Association; material machine context; and Record State.
Each system may implement the structure differently.
The underlying governed meaning remains consistent.
Different Schemas
↓
One Governed Record Structure.
Canonical Boundary

ERSTM owns the governance of Record structural requirements, mandatory and conditional components, Record composition, material representation, structural completeness, sufficiency, coherence, consistency, modularity, Event and Determination representation, qualification and uncertainty representation, state separation, structural extensibility, schema independence, structural versioning, and establishment of the Governed Event Record Structure.
ERSTM does not establish canonical Record identity; ERIDM owns that function.
It does not govern actual Record links; ERLKM owns linkage.
It does not govern complete Record lineage; ERTM owns traceability.
It does not govern cross-system semantic exchange; ERINM owns interoperability.
It does not recreate upstream TREGA™ Event governance and does not determine legal tax consequences.
Its governance begins when a valid Governed Event Record Identity exists.
Its governance ends when a sufficiently coherent and complete Governed Event Record Structure is established for Record Linkage Governance.
Canonical Handoff
ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
↓
ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure
↓
ERLKM — Event Record Linkage Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERSTM ensures that a governed Event Record contains enough structure to preserve what the Event means without forcing every system to store the Event in the same way.

The structure must be complete enough to govern the Record, but never so rigid that the technical schema becomes the Event itself.
Record Structure ≠ Event Structure.
Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema.

OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard
Module: ERTM — Event Record Traceability Module
Operational Layer: Event Record Traceability Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Record Traceability
Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Traceability State
Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERTM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 3 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) governs how a linked Tax-Relevant Event Record remains reconstructable across its materially relevant governance lineage, source references, state transitions, corrections, reconsiderations, transformations, and downstream representations.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Record Linkage State
↓
Event Record Traceability Governance
↓
Governed Event Record Traceability State

ERTM establishes whether the Record's governed history can be reconstructed sufficiently to determine: what Record is being examined; which Event it represents; which Determination applies; which material governance states contributed to it; what changed; why a materially relevant change occurred; and which Record state is currently effective.
Its foundational distinction is:
Traceability ≠ Audit.
Operational Role
A Record may be correctly identified, structurally complete, and richly linked while still being difficult to reconstruct over time.
ERTM addresses this problem.
It answers:
Can the governed Record and its materially relevant history be reconstructed from its present state back through the governance states and transitions that produced it?
ERTM prevents: orphaned Record states; undocumented Record transformation; loss of prior material states; broken Determination lineage; invisible correction; silent supersession; unexplained Record changes; and historical state collapse.
Internal Module Flow
TREGS operates through:
ERIDM — Event Record Identification
↓
ERSTM — Event Record Structure
↓
ERLKM — Event Record Linkage
↓
ERTM — Event Record Traceability
↓
ERINM — Event Record Interoperability
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
ERTM receives:
Governed Event Record Linkage State
and produces:
Governed Event Record Traceability State
for ERINM.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Governed Event Record Linkage State
↓
Trace Scope Identification
↓

Lineage Construction
↓
State Transition Reconstruction
↓
Traceability Sufficiency Assessment
↓
Governed Event Record Traceability State Operational Space
ERTM governs: trace scope; Record lineage; Event-to-Record lineage; Determination lineage; governance-state lineage; source-reference lineage; state-transition traceability; qualification traceability; uncertainty traceability; reconsideration traceability; correction traceability; supersession traceability; transformation traceability; version lineage; cross-system trace references; trace continuity; trace gaps; trace ambiguity; trace conflict; reconstruction sufficiency; and traceability handoff.
Operational Scope
ERTM may govern Record Traceability across: ERP systems; digital commerce; financial systems; tax infrastructure; payment systems; marketplaces; distributed systems; blockchain environments; smart contracts; AI systems; autonomous systems; industrial environments; machine-to-machine infrastructure; cross-border systems; and future machine economies.
The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Traceability Object
The traceability object is the governed lineage through which the Event Record and its materially relevant states can be reconstructed.
Traceability is not merely the presence of links.
It is the governed ability to reconstruct meaningful sequence and state history.
Link Network ≠ Traceability by itself.
Trace Scope
ERTM shall define the materially required scope of reconstruction.

Trace scope may include: Record identity; underlying Event; TREDS Determination; material upstream governance states; Record structure state; Record linkage state; material qualifications; uncertainty; reconsideration; corrections; supersession; transformations; current effective Record state.
Traceability should remain proportional.
Maximum Historical Data ≠ Optimal Traceability.
Canonical Trace Path
The canonical TREGS trace path is:
Determined Tax-Relevant Event
↓
Governed Record Identity
↓
Governed Record Structure
↓
Governed Record Linkage
↓
Governed Record Traceability State
Where deeper reconstruction is required, the Record may reference upstream TREGA™ governance.
Event-to-Record Lineage
ERTM shall preserve sufficient lineage to establish how the Event became represented by the Record.
The reconstructable path should answer:
Which Determined Event does this Record represent, and how can that association be verified through governed references?
Determination Lineage
The Record shall remain traceable to the applicable TREDS Determination state.
Where the Determination was reconsidered, traceability should distinguish: prior Determination; reconsideration trigger; reconsideration outcome; current effective Determination.
Current Determination ≠ Only Relevant Determination History.
Governance-State Lineage
Where material to interpretation, ERTM may preserve lineage to earlier TREGA™ governance outputs.

This can include: Context; Recognition; Formation; Boundary; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; Determination.
ERTM does not reopen these governance processes.
State Transition Traceability
Material transitions in Record state should be reconstructable.
Possible transitions include:
Draft
↓
Structurally Sufficient
Structurally Sufficient
↓
Linked
Linked
↓
Traceable
Active
↓
Corrected
Active
↓
Superseded
Qualified
↓
Unqualified after valid resolution
Each material transition should preserve sufficient basis.
Transition Basis
A materially relevant state transition should possess a traceable reason or governance reference.
Examples include: upstream correction; new supporting information; Determination reconsideration; Record correction; superseding representation; Merge/Split outcome; identity resolution; link correction.
State Change ≠ Self-Explanatory Change.
Prior-State Preservation
Where a material Record state changes, ERTM shall preserve sufficient reference to the prior state.
Current State ≠ Historical Replacement.
Historical Reconstruction
ERTM should support reconstruction of materially relevant historical Record states without requiring historical states to remain operationally active.
The objective is to answer:
What did the governed Record state mean at that time?
Effective-State Traceability
ERTM shall distinguish: historical Record state; superseded Record state; current effective Record state.

Historical State ≠ Current Effective State.
Qualification Traceability
Where a qualification appears, changes, or is removed through legitimate governance, ERTM should preserve: prior qualification; reason for change; resulting qualification state.
Qualification Removal ≠ Qualification Never Existed.
Uncertainty Traceability
Where material uncertainty affects Record use, ERTM should preserve the transition from:
Uncertainty Identified
↓
Uncertainty Governed
↓
Uncertainty Resolved / Reduced / Persisting
ERTM does not govern the uncertainty itself.
EDUM remains authoritative for determination uncertainty.
Reconsideration Traceability
Where EDREM reopens a Determination, ERTM shall support reconstruction of:
Prior Determination
↓
Reconsideration Trigger
↓
Reconsideration Process Reference
↓
New Effective Determination
Reconsideration ≠ Historical Reset.
Correction Traceability
A Record correction should preserve enough information to determine: what was corrected; why; when; what prior state existed; what current state became effective.
Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Representational Correction
Where only Record representation changes, traceability should preserve that representational correction without falsely implying a new Event.
Record Correction ≠ New Event by default.
Event-Level Correction Boundary
If the underlying Event Reality changes, ERTM records the resulting governance transition.
It does not decide the Event correction.

That function belongs to the authoritative TREGA™ governance layer or TRECLS where applicable.
Supersession Traceability
Where one Record supersedes another, ERTM should preserve: superseded Record reference; successor Record reference; supersession basis; effective transition state; relevant continuity references.
Supersession ≠ Deletion.
Version Traceability
Technical or structural versions may change while canonical Record identity remains continuous.
ERTM should distinguish:
Version Change
↓
Same Canonical Record
from:
New Governed Record Identity
where applicable.
Version History ≠ Event History by default.
Transformation Traceability
A Record may be transformed between: schemas; platforms; storage environments; organizations; formats; APIs.
ERTM should preserve enough lineage to determine whether the transformed Record remains the same canonical governed Record.
Format Transformation ≠ Governance Break by default.
Cross-System Traceability
Where the same Record appears across multiple systems, ERTM may preserve:
Canonical Record
↓
System A Representation
↓
System B Representation
↓
System C Representation
This helps reconstruct how the Record moved through infrastructure.
Cross-Organization Traceability
Where organizations exchange the Record, traceability may preserve materially relevant handoff references without making TREGS responsible for contractual or legal accountability.
Record Handoff Trace ≠ Accountability Assignment.
Cross-Border Traceability

A Governed Event Record may enter several jurisdictional tax environments.
ERTM may preserve downstream references such as: evaluation ID; filing reference; assessment reference; processing reference.
These remain downstream tax objects.
Tax Evaluation Trace ≠ Tax Determination Governance.
Traceability and Jurisdictional Divergence
Different jurisdictions may reach different tax conclusions from the same governed Event Record.
ERTM should preserve the association of those downstream outcomes with the same Record without merging them into one canonical tax result.
Source Reference Traceability
ERTM may preserve references to source records or source systems where materially required for reconstruction.
It does not own broader evidence governance.
Source Reference ≠ Evidence Validation.
Technical Log Boundary
System logs may contribute trace information.
They do not automatically constitute governed traceability.
Logging ≠ Traceability.
Blockchain Boundary
An immutable blockchain ledger may provide strong technical chronology.
It does not automatically establish complete Event Record Traceability.
Immutability ≠ Complete Traceability.
Timestamp Boundary
Timestamp presence alone does not make a Record traceable.
Traceability requires meaningful state and transition reconstruction.
Timestamp ≠ Traceability.
Audit Trail Boundary
A technical audit trail may support ERTM.
ERTM itself does not become a complete audit function.

ADIT® remains authoritative for evidence and auditability governance.
Audit Trail ≠ Governance Audit.
Traceability Depth
Traceability depth should reflect: Event complexity; downstream reliance; materiality; system distribution; change frequency; multi-jurisdiction use; uncertainty; correction history.
A simple Event may require shallow traceability.
A distributed autonomous Event may require deep lineage.
Traceability Granularity
Traceability may apply at: Record level; component level; state level; link level; transition level.
Granularity should be sufficient to reconstruct materially relevant changes.
Traceability Continuity
Traceability should survive: system migration; schema change; technical identifier change; Record correction; Record supersession; organizational handoff; infrastructure replacement.
Infrastructure Change ≠ Traceability Loss by default.
Trace Gap
A Trace Gap exists where a materially necessary part of Record history cannot be reconstructed.
Possible causes include: missing prior state; broken link; unknown transformation; deleted technical source; identifier loss; incomplete migration; unresolved lineage.
Trace Gap Materiality
Not every missing historical detail is material.
ERTM shall evaluate whether the gap affects: Record interpretation; Determination reliance; lifecycle continuity; downstream use; reconstruction.
Missing Data ≠ Material Trace Gap by default.
Trace Ambiguity

Trace ambiguity exists where multiple plausible histories exist and one cannot be sufficiently established.
Ambiguity should remain explicit.
Plausible History ≠ Established Trace.
Trace Conflict
Trace conflict exists where material sources support incompatible Record histories.
Conflict may involve: inconsistent state sequence; incompatible Determination references; contradictory correction histories; competing supersession paths.
ERTM should not silently select one history without governance basis.
Trace Reconstruction Sufficiency
A Record is sufficiently traceable where materially relevant lineage can be reconstructed with sufficient confidence and governance clarity for its intended downstream use.
Complete reproduction of every technical interaction is not required.
Machine-Generated Traceability
Autonomous systems may produce massive logs and event streams.
ERTM governs the meaningful lineage of the Record rather than preserving every machine action indiscriminately.
Machine Log Volume ≠ Traceability Quality.
AI-Generated Record Changes
Where AI or agents modify Record representations, ERTM should preserve materially relevant change lineage.
The use of automated systems does not reduce traceability requirements.
Automated Change ≠ Untraceable Change.
Traceability Authority
ERTM requires an identifiable governance basis for accepting the Record lineage as sufficiently reconstructable.
Traceability authority does not establish legal truth or tax authority.

Traceability Acceptance ≠ Legal Determination.
Traceability and Record Identity
ERIDM establishes identity.
ERTM reconstructs identity continuity over time.
Identity Continuity Trace ≠ Identity Establishment.
Traceability and Record Structure
ERSTM establishes structure.
ERTM reconstructs materially relevant structural state changes.
Structure History ≠ Structure Governance.
Traceability and Linkage
ERLKM establishes links.
ERTM uses materially relevant links to reconstruct lineage.
Linkage ≠ Traceability.
Traceability and Interoperability
ERTM establishes reconstructable lineage.
ERINM governs whether Record meaning survives system exchange.
Traceability ≠ Interoperability.
Traceability and Lifecycle
TRECLS governs broader Event lifecycle amendment, correction, supersession, and closure.
ERTM supports reconstruction of Record-level history but does not own the entire Event lifecycle.
Record Traceability ≠ Event Lifecycle Governance.
Governance States
ERTM may represent:
Traceability Governance Not Initiated
Trace Scope Defined
Lineage Under Construction
Event Lineage Established
Determination Lineage Established
State Transition Lineage Established
Trace Gap Detected
Trace Gap Material
Trace Ambiguous
Trace Conflicted
Trace Qualified
Trace Continuity Established
Historical Reconstruction Sufficient
Current Effective State Reconstructable
Traceability Sufficient
Governed Event Record Traceability State Established
Ready for Interoperability Governance Governance Requirements

ERTM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists; materially required trace scope is defined; Record identity lineage remains reconstructable; Event-to-Record association remains traceable; Determination lineage remains reconstructable; materially relevant governance-state references are preservable; material state transitions remain traceable; transition basis is recorded or referenced where necessary; prior material states are not silently erased; current effective state remains distinguishable from historical state; qualification history remains reconstructable where material; uncertainty history remains traceable where relevant; reconsideration does not erase prior Determination history; corrections preserve materially relevant prior states; supersession preserves predecessor/successor lineage; technical version history remains distinguishable from Event history; transformations remain traceable where they could affect meaning; cross-system representations can be associated where material; technical logs are not treated as sufficient traceability by default; immutable records are not treated as complete traceability by default; trace gaps are assessed for materiality; ambiguity and conflict remain visible; machine-generated changes remain traceable; Record Traceability remains distinct from Audit, Linkage, Interoperability, and Event Lifecycle Governance; and the resulting Traceability State is suitable for ERINM.
Governance Logic

IF no valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists, THEN ERTM shall not establish complete Record Traceability.
IF a materially relevant Record state changed, THEN sufficient transition basis shall be preserved or referenced.
IF a prior Record state materially affects interpretation of the current Record, THEN that state shall remain reconstructable.
IF a Determination was reconsidered, THEN prior and current effective Determination states shall remain distinguishable.
IF a Record was corrected, THEN the correction shall not silently erase materially relevant prior representation.
IF a Record was superseded, THEN predecessor and successor lineage shall remain reconstructable.
IF technical transformation occurs while canonical Record identity remains continuous, THEN transformation lineage should preserve that continuity.
IF a trace gap exists but does not materially affect reconstruction, THEN the Record may remain traceable with appropriate qualification.
IF a material trace gap, ambiguity, or conflict prevents reliable reconstruction, THEN Traceability shall remain qualified or insufficient.
IF materially relevant Record lineage can be reconstructed sufficiently, THEN ERTM shall establish the Governed Event Record Traceability State and hand it to ERINM.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ERTM implementation should support:
Traceability Governance ID A stable identifier for the ERTM governance process.

Canonical Record Identifier The ERIDM-established Record identity.
Record Structure Reference The ERSTM-governed structure.
Record Linkage Reference The ERLKM-governed Linkage State.
Underlying Event Reference The Determined Tax-Relevant Event represented by the Record.
Determination Reference The applicable TREDS Determination.
Prior Determination Reference Any materially relevant prior Determination.
Reconsideration Reference Any relevant EDREM process or outcome.
Trace Scope The required depth and granularity of reconstruction.
Trace Entry Identifier A stable identifier for materially relevant trace entries.
Trace Entry Type Identity, Structure, Linkage, Determination, Qualification, Uncertainty, Correction, Supersession, Transformation, Handoff, or other governed type.
Prior State Reference The previous materially relevant Record state.
Current State Reference The resulting Record state.
Transition Type The nature of the state transition.
Transition Basis Reference Why the transition occurred.
Transition Time Reference The applicable time reference where material.
Qualification Trace Reference Any relevant qualification history.
Uncertainty Trace Reference Any relevant uncertainty history.
Correction Trace Reference Any Record correction lineage.
Supersession Trace Reference Any predecessor/successor lineage.
Transformation Trace Reference Any schema, platform, or system transformation.
Cross-System Trace Reference Representations across technical environments.

Cross-Organization Trace Reference Relevant organizational handoffs.
Jurisdictional Evaluation Reference Any downstream jurisdiction-specific evaluation reference where appropriate.
Trace Gap State None, Non-Material, Material, Critical, or Unresolved.
Trace Ambiguity State Whether multiple plausible histories remain.
Trace Conflict State Whether incompatible histories exist.
Historical Reconstruction State Incomplete, Partial, Qualified, or Sufficient.
Current Effective State Reference The presently effective governed Record state.
Trace Continuity State Whether materially relevant lineage remains continuous.
Governance State The current ERTM governance state.
Handoff State Whether the Record is ready for ERINM.
Governance Outputs
ERTM may produce: Trace Scope; Event-to-Record Lineage; Determination Lineage; Governance-State Lineage; Record State Transition History; Qualification Trace; Uncertainty Trace; Reconsideration Trace; Correction Trace; Supersession Trace; Transformation Trace; Version Lineage; Cross-System Trace; Cross-Organization Trace; Trace Gap State; Trace Ambiguity State; Trace Conflict State; Historical Reconstruction State; Current Effective State Reference; Trace Continuity State; and the principal output: Governed Event Record Traceability State.
Critical Distinctions
Traceability ≠ Audit.
Link Network ≠ Traceability by itself.
Maximum Historical Data ≠ Optimal Traceability.
Current Determination ≠ Only Relevant Determination History.

State Change ≠ Self-Explanatory Change.
Current State ≠ Historical Replacement.
Historical State ≠ Current Effective State.
Qualification Removal ≠ Qualification Never Existed.
Reconsideration ≠ Historical Reset.
Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Record Correction ≠ New Event by default.
Supersession ≠ Deletion.
Version History ≠ Event History by default.
Format Transformation ≠ Governance Break by default.
Record Handoff Trace ≠ Accountability Assignment.
Tax Evaluation Trace ≠ Tax Determination Governance.
Source Reference ≠ Evidence Validation.
Logging ≠ Traceability.
Immutability ≠ Complete Traceability.
Timestamp ≠ Traceability.
Audit Trail ≠ Governance Audit.
Infrastructure Change ≠ Traceability Loss by default.
Missing Data ≠ Material Trace Gap by default.
Plausible History ≠ Established Trace.
Machine Log Volume ≠ Traceability Quality.
Automated Change ≠ Untraceable Change.
Traceability Acceptance ≠ Legal Determination.
Identity Continuity Trace ≠ Identity Establishment.
Structure History ≠ Structure Governance.
Linkage ≠ Traceability.
Traceability ≠ Interoperability.
Record Traceability ≠ Event Lifecycle Governance.
Enterprise Application
ERTM provides the reconstructability layer required before a governed Event Record can be safely exchanged across systems and organizations.
The canonical enterprise path is:
ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity
→ ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure
→ ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage State

→ ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State
→ ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability
→ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
This allows organizations to determine not only what the current Record says, but how that governed Record reached its present state. Use Case 1 — Record Reconsidered After New Participation Information
A cross-border digital Event has already produced a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record.
Later, new governed Participation information causes TREDS to reconsider the original Determination.
EDREM produces a new effective Determination.
ERTM preserves: original Determination; reconsideration reference; prior Record state; resulting Determination; updated Record state; and the transition basis.
A downstream tax engine can consume the current state without losing the history of how that state was reached. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Migrated Across Three Technical Systems
An autonomous platform creates one governed Event Record.
Over several years, the Record is migrated from:
System A
↓
System B
↓
System C
The technical schema, local identifiers, and storage model change.
The canonical Record identity remains continuous.
ERTM preserves the relevant transformation lineage and allows the Record to be reconstructed across all three environments.
The system can therefore demonstrate that the current Record is the continued governed representation of the original Determined Event rather than an unrelated new Event.
Canonical Boundary

ERTM owns the governance of Record lineage, Event-to-Record lineage, Determination lineage, governance-state lineage, materially relevant state transitions, prior-state preservation, historical reconstruction, qualification/uncertainty/reconsideration/correction/supersession traceability, transformation lineage, version lineage, trace gaps, ambiguity, conflict, trace continuity, reconstruction sufficiency, and establishment of the Governed Event Record Traceability State.
ERTM does not establish Record identity; ERIDM owns identification.
It does not define Record Structure; ERSTM owns structure.
It does not establish material Record links; ERLKM owns linkage.
It does not govern semantic preservation across systems; ERINM owns interoperability.
It does not perform general evidence or audit governance; ADIT® remains authoritative.
It does not govern the substantive Event lifecycle; TRECLS owns lifecycle and continuity governance.
It does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, filing obligation, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
Its governance begins when a valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists.
Its governance ends when the materially relevant history and present state of the Record are sufficiently reconstructable and the Governed Event Record Traceability State is ready for Interoperability Governance.
Canonical Handoff

ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage State
↓
ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State
↓
ERINM — Event Record Interoperability Governance
Canonical Closing Statement
ERTM ensures that a governed Event Record can change without losing the history required to understand what it was, what changed, why it changed, and which state is now effective.
Traceability preserves governed continuity through change without turning historical data into an audit conclusion.
Traceability ≠ Audit.
Current State ≠ Historical
Replacement.

chunks.text:
OOF™ The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed
The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard
Module: ESPM — Event Supersession Module
Operational Layer: Event Supersession Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Supersession
Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Supersession State
Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-ESPM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 3 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language
Canonical Definition
The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed Tax-Relevant Event state or Event Record representation is replaced as the current effective state by a later governed state while preserving historical continuity, predecessor-successor relationships, prior-state reconstructability, and the distinction between Event Supersession and New Event Formation.
Its principal transition is:
Governed Event Correction State / Current Governed Event State
↓
Event Supersession Governance
↓

Governed Event Supersession State
ESPM establishes which governed state is currently effective without deleting the state that preceded it.
Its foundational distinction is:
Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion.
Operational Role
A Tax-Relevant Event may accumulate multiple governed states over time.
A later state may need to become authoritative for current lifecycle use because of: Amendment; Correction; reconsideration; Record replacement; Merge/Split consequences; schema or representation change; improved governance state; or another legitimate lifecycle transition.
ESPM answers:
Which governed Event state now replaces the prior effective state, what exactly was superseded, why, and what historical relationship must remain preserved?
Its purpose is to prevent: competing current states; silent replacement; historical erasure; ambiguous predecessor-successor chains; accidental creation of new Events; and confusion between Record replacement and Event replacement.
Internal Module Flow
TRECLS operates through:
ECOM — Event Continuity
↓
EADM — Event Amendment
↓
ECRTM — Event Correction
↓
ESPM — Event Supersession
↓
ECLM — Event Closure
↓
Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event
ESPM receives the applicable current governed Event state and produces:
Governed Event Supersession State
for Closure Governance.
Operational Transition
The canonical transition is:
Current Governed Event State
↓
Supersession Trigger
↓
Predecessor Identification
↓
Successor Identification
↓
Supersession Basis
↓

Effective-State Transition
↓
Governed Event Supersession State Operational Space
ESPM governs: Supersession Trigger identification; predecessor-state identification; successor-state identification; supersession eligibility; supersession scope; supersession basis; Event-state supersession; Record-state supersession; effective-state transition; predecessor-successor relationship; supersession materiality; partial supersession; full supersession; supersession qualification; supersession ambiguity; supersession conflict; supersession chain; supersession reversal; supersession withdrawal; continuity impact; upstream reassessment; historical-state preservation; and supersession handoff.
Operational Scope
ESPM may govern supersession in: physical Events; digital transactions; commercial Events; financial Events; platform activity; AI-agent Events; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine Events; distributed systems; digital assets; industrial activity; cross-border Events; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies.
The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral.
Supersession Object
The Supersession Object is the prior governed Event state or governed Event Record representation that is proposed to be replaced as the current effective state.
The object being superseded may be: Event state; lifecycle state; corrected state; amended state; Record representation; Determination-linked state; qualified state.
Superseded State ≠ Deleted State.

Supersession Trigger
A Supersession Trigger may arise from: validated Amendment; established Correction; revised Determination; successor Record creation; schema migration; representation replacement; Merge/Split result; continuity decision; governance reconciliation; reopening; or other lifecycle transition.
Not every change requires formal Supersession.
Supersession Eligibility
A state is eligible for Supersession where: a valid predecessor state exists; a valid successor state exists or is being established; the successor legitimately replaces the predecessor for current use; the predecessor remains reconstructable; continuity remains valid or appropriately governed; and the transition does not improperly conceal New Event Formation.
Predecessor State
The Predecessor State is the governed state that was current or materially effective before Supersession.
It must remain identifiable.
A system should be able to answer: what the predecessor was; when it was effective; why it ceased to be current; and what replaced it.
Successor State
The Successor State is the governed state that becomes current after valid Supersession.
It may result from: Amendment; Correction; reconsideration; Record replacement; or other lifecycle governance.
Successor State ≠ New Event by default.
Effective-State Transition
Supersession governs the transition:
Prior Effective State
↓
Supersession
↓
New Effective State
The transition shall preserve both lifecycle meaning and historical reconstructability.

Event-State Supersession
Event-State Supersession occurs where a later governed state of the same Event replaces an earlier state as current.
Examples include: corrected Location state; revised Participation state; amended Value Association; reconsidered Determination-linked lifecycle state.
The Event may remain the same Event.
Record-State Supersession
A Record representation may be superseded while the Event remains unchanged.
Examples include: schema replacement; canonical Record version replacement; corrected Record structure; migrated Record representation.
Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default.
TREGS remains authoritative over Record Governance.
Event Supersession vs New Event Formation
Supersession must not be used to hide a genuinely new Event.
If the successor represents a materially different operational occurrence, Continuity must be reassessed.
Supersession ≠ Permission to Replace One Event with Another Under the Same Identity.
Full Supersession
Full Supersession occurs where the prior governed state is no longer current in its entirety.
The prior state remains historical.
Partial Supersession
Partial Supersession occurs where only part of the prior state is replaced.
The remaining unaffected components may continue as current.
Partial Supersession ≠ Full State Replacement.
Supersession Scope
The supersession scope should identify exactly what is being replaced.

Possible scopes include: full Event state; one Event component; one lifecycle state; one Record representation; one Determination-linked state; one downstream representation reference.
Supersession Basis
A valid Supersession should possess an identifiable basis.
Examples include: Correction result; Amendment result; TREDS reconsideration result; Record Governance outcome; upstream governance revision; Merge/Split consequence; continuity decision.
The basis should remain reconstructable.
Supersession Effective Time
Where materially relevant, the system should distinguish: predecessor effective period; successor establishment time; supersession decision time; successor effective time.
These governance timestamps do not establish legal tax timing.
Current Effective State
After valid Supersession, the successor becomes the current effective state.
The predecessor remains historical.
Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State.
Historical Preservation
ESPM shall preserve materially relevant predecessor states.
The canonical principle is:
Supersession Replaces Current Effect — Not Historical Existence.
Supersession Chain
An Event may undergo multiple Supersessions:
State A
↓
State B
↓
State C
↓
State D
The chain should remain reconstructable.
The system should identify: immediate predecessor; immediate successor; current state; historical supersession path.
Broken Supersession Chain

A Broken Supersession Chain exists where one or more predecessor-successor relationships cannot be reconstructed.
A materially broken chain may prevent reliable lifecycle closure or jurisdiction readiness.
Supersession Conflict
Conflict exists where multiple successor states claim to supersede the same predecessor without clear governance priority.
Examples include: two corrected states; competing jurisdiction-neutral Record versions; incompatible upstream governance results.
Conflict shall remain explicit.
Supersession Ambiguity
Ambiguity exists where it is unclear: whether Supersession occurred; which state was superseded; which successor is current; whether replacement is partial or full; whether continuity remains valid.
Supersession Qualification
A Supersession may be qualified where: some predecessor information remains partially current; successor state remains incomplete; one upstream governance issue is unresolved; downstream use requires limitation.
Qualification shall remain visible.
Supersession Reversal
A Supersession may later be reversed where the successor is invalidated and a prior state becomes current again or another successor is established.
Reversal shall not erase the intermediate state.
A valid pattern may be:
State A
↓
State B
↓
Reversal
↓
State A Reinstated
or:
State A
↓
State B
↓
State C State Reinstatement
A prior state may be reinstated where governance establishes it as current again.

Reinstatement does not mean the intervening lifecycle history never occurred.
Reinstatement ≠ Historical Reset.
Supersession Withdrawal
A proposed Supersession may be withdrawn before becoming effective.
Materially relevant withdrawal history should remain reconstructable.
Supersession Replacement
A pending Supersession may itself be replaced by a superior successor decision.
The latest valid governance result should remain clearly distinguishable.
Supersession and Amendment
An Amendment may create a new current Event state.
ESPM may then govern its replacement relationship to the prior state.
Amendment ≠ Supersession by default.
Supersession and Correction
A Correction may create a corrected successor state.
ESPM may establish that corrected state as the current effective state.
Correction ≠ Supersession by default.
The mechanisms remain distinct.
Supersession and Continuity
Supersession assumes that Event Continuity remains valid unless explicitly broken.
Where successor state materially challenges Event identity, ECOM must reassess Continuity.
Valid Successor State ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity.
Supersession and Closure
Before an Event is closed, ECLM should be able to identify which state is currently effective.
ESPM provides that effective-state clarity.
A Superseded state should not be mistaken for the state being closed.
Supersession and Reopening
A reopened Event may create a successor to the previously Closed state.

The prior Closure remains historically reconstructable.
Supersession and Event Relationships
TRERLS owns Merge and Split.
ESPM governs whether valid Merge/Split results supersede prior lifecycle states or require predecessor-successor relationships.
Merge Supersession
A Merge may cause prior Event states to cease being current in favor of a merged successor Event.
Where that successor is a new Event, Formation remains upstream.
Merge Supersession ≠ Merge Formation.
Split Supersession
A Split may supersede one prior Event state with multiple successor Event states.
Event identity implications require ECOM and TREFS where appropriate.
Cross-System Supersession
Different systems may hold different versions of one Event Record.
ESPM helps establish which canonical state is current.
Most Recent Technical Record ≠ Current Governed State by default.
Cross-Organization Supersession
Organizations may independently produce successor candidates.
Canonical Supersession requires governed authority and basis.
Later External Record ≠ Canonical Successor by default.
Cross-Border Supersession
Different jurisdictions may maintain different tax assessments based on different Event Record versions.
Those legal states do not determine canonical TREGA™ Supersession.
Jurisdictional Tax Replacement ≠ Event Supersession.
Machine-Generated Supersession
Autonomous systems may continuously emit newer state representations.

A later timestamp or version number does not automatically make a state the governed successor.
Newest Machine State ≠ Canonical Successor by default.
High-Frequency Supersession
In high-volume systems, frequent technical state replacement should not generate unnecessary canonical Supersession events.
Formal Supersession is required only where current governed Event meaning materially changes.
Version Supersession
A newer technical Record version may supersede an older version.
Version Supersession remains distinct from Event Supersession.
Record Version Change ≠ Event State Change by default.
Semantic Supersession
Where a successor materially changes the canonical meaning of the Event state, the change should be governed substantively rather than treated as simple version replacement.
Supersession and Traceability
Material Supersession shall remain traceable through predecessor-successor relationships.
ERTM owns Record Traceability.
ESPM owns lifecycle supersession meaning.
Supersession and Interoperability
The current effective state should propagate across systems without semantic drift.
ERINM owns Interoperability.
ESPM identifies which governed state should be treated as current.
Supersession and Tax Law
A successor Event state may produce a new downstream tax outcome.
ESPM does not determine: reassessment; amended filing; tax adjustment; refund; additional Tax Liability.
These remain jurisdiction-specific.
Event Supersession ≠ Tax Assessment Supersession.

Governance States
ESPM may represent:
Supersession Governance Not Initiated
Supersession Trigger Identified
Predecessor State Identified
Successor Candidate Identified
Supersession Eligibility Under Review
Supersession Eligible
Supersession Scope Defined
Partial Supersession
Full Supersession
Supersession Under Governance
Supersession Qualified
Supersession Ambiguous
Supersession Conflicted
Continuity Reassessment Required
Upstream Review Required
Supersession Rejected
Supersession Withdrawn
Successor State Established
Predecessor State Preserved
Current Effective State Established
Governed Event Supersession State Established
Ready for Closure Governance Governance Requirements

ESPM implementations shall ensure that: a valid current governed Event state exists; predecessor state is identifiable; successor state is identifiable or governably proposed; Supersession remains distinct from Amendment and Correction; Record Supersession remains distinct from Event Supersession; Supersession does not conceal New Event Formation; supersession scope is explicit; partial and full Supersession remain distinguishable; predecessor state remains reconstructable; successor state becomes current only through valid governance; supersession basis is identifiable; predecessor-successor relationship remains traceable; current effective state is unambiguous where possible; Supersession Conflict remains explicit; Supersession Ambiguity remains explicit; qualified Supersession remains distinguishable from complete Supersession; reversal and reinstatement preserve lifecycle history; Merge/Split ownership remains with TRERLS; Continuity is reassessed where Event identity is materially challenged; technical recency is not treated as canonical authority; downstream tax replacement remains outside ESPM; and the resulting state is suitable for Event Closure Governance.
Governance Logic
IF no valid predecessor state exists, THEN ESPM shall not establish canonical Supersession.
IF no valid successor state exists, THEN Supersession shall remain pending or unresolved.

IF a successor merely adds information without replacing the current state, THEN EADM may remain the relevant mechanism.
IF the successor primarily corrects error, THEN ECRTM shall establish the corrected state before ESPM establishes Supersession where needed.
IF the replacement affects only technical Record representation, THEN Event Supersession shall not be assumed.
IF successor and predecessor represent the same Event and continuity remains valid, THEN Supersession may proceed.
IF successor state materially represents a different occurrence, THEN ECOM Continuity reassessment and potentially TREFS New Event Formation shall be required.
IF multiple successor candidates conflict, THEN no single current state shall be silently selected without governance basis.
IF the Supersession is partial, THEN unaffected predecessor components may remain current.
IF a valid successor is established, THEN the predecessor shall cease to be current but remain historically reconstructable.
IF a later valid governance result reverses Supersession, THEN the reversal shall preserve the supersession history.
IF the current effective state is clear, historically reconstructable, and continuity remains governed, THEN ESPM shall establish the Governed Event Supersession State.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ESPM implementation should support:
Supersession Governance ID Stable identifier for the ESPM governance process.
Canonical Event Reference The Event under Supersession Governance.

Current Governed Event State Reference The state existing before Supersession.
Supersession Trigger Type Amendment, Correction, Reconsideration, Record Replacement, Merge/Split, Reopening, Technical Migration, or other governed trigger.
Predecessor State Reference The state proposed to be superseded.
Successor State Reference The proposed or established successor.
Supersession Scope Full Event State, Partial Event State, Record State, Lifecycle State, or other governed scope.
Supersession Type Full, Partial, Record-Level, Event-Level, Qualified, Reversal, Reinstatement.
Supersession Basis Reference The governance result supporting replacement.
Supersession Materiality State Non-Material, Material, Critical, Unresolved.
Supersession Eligibility State Eligible, Qualified, Ineligible, Unresolved.
Predecessor Effective State The prior effective status.
Successor Effective State The new effective status.
Supersession Effective Time Reference Where materially relevant.
Predecessor Preservation State Whether prior state remains reconstructable.
Predecessor-Successor Link Reference The governed relationship between states.
Supersession Qualification Any limitation attached to replacement.
Supersession Ambiguity State Whether the replacement remains uncertain.
Supersession Conflict State Whether competing successors exist.
Continuity Reassessment State Whether ECOM reassessment is required.
Upstream Review Reference Any referral to another TREGA™ Parent Standard.

Supersession Withdrawal State Whether proposed Supersession was withdrawn.
Supersession Reversal Reference Any later reversal.
Reinstatement Reference Any prior state restored as current.
Historical Supersession Chain Reference The sequence of materially relevant predecessor-successor states.
Current Effective State Reference The state current after Supersession.
Governance State The current ESPM governance state.
Supersession Outcome Superseded, Partial, Qualified, Rejected, Withdrawn, Reversed, or Unresolved.
Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for ECLM Closure Governance.
Governance Outputs
ESPM may produce: Supersession Trigger State; Predecessor State; Successor State; Supersession Scope; Supersession Type; Supersession Basis; Supersession Materiality State; Supersession Eligibility State; Partial Supersession State; Full Supersession State; Predecessor-Successor Relationship; Predecessor Preservation State; Current Effective State; Supersession Qualification; Supersession Ambiguity State; Supersession Conflict State; Continuity Reassessment State; Supersession Reversal State; Reinstatement State; Historical Supersession Chain; and the principal output: Governed Event Supersession State.
Critical Distinctions
Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion.
Superseded State ≠ Deleted State.
Successor State ≠ New Event by default.
Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default.
Supersession ≠ Permission to Replace One Event with Another Under the Same Identity.

Partial Supersession ≠ Full State Replacement.
Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State.
Supersession Replaces Current Effect — Not Historical Existence.
Reinstatement ≠ Historical Reset.
Amendment ≠ Supersession by default.
Correction ≠ Supersession by default.
Valid Successor State ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity.
Merge Supersession ≠ Merge Formation.
Most Recent Technical Record ≠ Current Governed State by default.
Later External Record ≠ Canonical Successor by default.
Jurisdictional Tax Replacement ≠ Event Supersession.
Newest Machine State ≠ Canonical Successor by default.
Record Version Change ≠ Event State Change by default.
Event Supersession ≠ Tax Assessment Supersession.
Enterprise Application
ESPM gives organizations a controlled way to determine which Event state is current when several valid historical states exist.
The operational pattern is:
Prior Governed Event State
→ Amendment / Correction / Reconsideration / Replacement
→ Successor Candidate
→ Supersession Governance
→ Current Effective State
→ Historical Predecessor Preserved
→ Governed Event Supersession State
This enables downstream systems to consume one clear current Event state without losing the Event’s lifecycle history. Use Case 1 — Corrected Event State Replaces Prior State Across Multiple Tax Systems
A cross-border Event has been consumed by several downstream systems.
Later, ECRTM establishes a valid corrected Location and Participation state.

ESPM identifies: the prior effective Event state; the corrected successor state; the correction basis; the predecessor-successor relationship.
The corrected state becomes current.
The earlier state remains reconstructable as superseded.
Downstream jurisdictions may reassess their own tax outcomes independently.
TREGA™ maintains one Event lifecycle.
One current state replaces another without rewriting Event history. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Generates New Record Version After System Migration
An autonomous platform migrates its canonical Event Records into a new infrastructure.
A new Record version is created with different schema, local identifiers, and storage architecture.
The underlying Event remains unchanged.
TREGS establishes valid Record Governance and interoperability.
ESPM determines that the new Record representation supersedes the prior technical representation for current use while the Event itself remains continuous.
The result is:
Prior Record Representation
↓
Successor Record Representation
↓
Record Supersession
↓
Same Governed Event
The technical successor does not become a new Tax-Relevant Event.
Canonical Boundary

ESPM owns the governance of Event and Record Supersession state, predecessor identification, successor identification, Supersession eligibility, scope, basis, full and Partial Supersession, current effective-state transition, predecessor-successor relationships, historical preservation, Supersession qualification, ambiguity, conflict, reversal, reinstatement, withdrawal, Supersession chains, Continuity-reassessment triggers, and establishment of the Governed Event Supersession State.
ESPM does not own Event Continuity; ECOM does.
It does not own Amendment; EADM does.
It does not own Correction; ECRTM does.
It does not own Closure; ECLM does.
It does not independently govern Merge or Split; TRERLS does.
It does not create New Events; TREFS governs Event Formation.
It does not determine Event Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, or interoperability; TREGS governs those spaces.
It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, tax nexus, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Base, Tax Rate, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing, reassessment, payment, collection, or enforcement.
Its governance begins when a valid predecessor state and a legitimate successor candidate exist.
Its governance ends with:
Governed Event Supersession State
and a clearly identifiable:
Current Effective Event State
ready for Event Closure Governance.
Canonical Handoff
ECRTM / Current Governed Event State
↓
ESPM — Governed Event Supersession State
↓

ECLM — Event Closure Governance
Where Event identity becomes materially uncertain:
ESPM
↓
ECOM — Continuity Reassessment
Where a materially different occurrence is identified:
ESPM
↓
ECOM
↓
TREFS — New Event Formation Review
Canonical Closing Statement
ESPM establishes which governed Event state is current without allowing the state it replaces to disappear from history.
Supersession gives lifecycle governance a clear present while preserving a reconstructable past.
Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion.
Successor State ≠ New Event by default.
Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State.

IF materially constitutive event activity remains incomplete,
IF confirmation occurs after operational completion,
