chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Completion Module (ETCM)
Event Completion Module (ETCM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Module: ETCM — Event Completion Module
Operational Layer: Event Completion Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Completion
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETCM-003
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Completion Module (ETCM) governs how the operational completion of a Governed Bounded Event is determined after its Governed Event Start has been established, by identifying, evaluating, qualifying, and establishing the temporal condition at which the governed event has sufficiently completed as the event under examination.
ETCM distinguishes operational Event Completion from later settlement, confirmation, invoicing, reconciliation, reporting, warranty, monitoring, archival activity, accounting closure, contractual closure, legal finality, and jurisdiction-specific taxation points that may occur after the event has operationally completed.

Its specific task is:
to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Completion without allowing technical workflow closure, administrative processing, commercial settlement, accounting recognition, contractual conventions, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine when the governed event itself operationally completes.
ETCM governs when the bounded event has completed as an operational event.
It does not determine when that event is legally completed, recognized, reportable, taxable, or settled under a jurisdiction-specific framework. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role
ETSM establishes when the Governed Bounded Event begins.
ETCM determines when that same governed event has sufficiently completed.
The transition governed by ETCM is:
Governed Event Start
↓
Governed Event Completion
The module must distinguish completion of the governed event from activities that merely follow it.
An event may operationally complete before: payment settlement, invoice issuance, system confirmation, reconciliation, accounting posting, reporting, administrative closure, contractual closure, legal acceptance, tax recognition.
Likewise, the last available timestamp in a technical workflow may represent downstream processing rather than Event Completion.
Latest Timestamp ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow
The TRETS Internal Module Flow is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓

ETSM — Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETCM governs:
Governed Event Start
↓
Completion Candidate Identification
↓
Completion Condition Assessment
↓
Constitutive Activity Completion Assessment
↓
Post-Event Activity Differentiation
↓
Completion Qualification
↓
Completion Ambiguity / Conflict Handling
↓
Governed Event Completion
↓
ETDM
ETCM may consume relevant temporal signals identified by ETIM but does not recreate the temporal signal inventory.
It establishes the legitimate operational completion of the same event whose start was governed by ETSM. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space
ETCM governs the operational space in which the completion of the bounded event must be distinguished from surrounding or subsequent temporal activity.
This space includes: completion candidates, completion signals, completion conditions, final constitutive activity, operational fulfillment, physical completion, digital completion, transactional completion, service completion, transfer completion, machine execution completion, autonomous operation completion, distributed completion, phased completion, conditional completion, partial completion, failed completion, interrupted completion, post-event activity, delayed confirmation, delayed settlement, completion ambiguity, completion conflict, completion precision, completion traceability.

The continued existence of related processes after operational completion does not automatically extend the Event Completion point. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope
ETCM governs:
1. identification of candidate Event Completion signals; 2. assessment of candidate completion conditions; 3. determination of final constitutive event activity; 4. distinction between Event Completion and post-event activity; 5. assessment of physical, digital, transactional, service, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous completion; 6. treatment of partial completion; 7. treatment of interrupted or failed event execution; 8. treatment of conditional completion; 9. treatment of phased or distributed completion; 10. detection of completion ambiguity; 11. detection of conflicting completion representations; 12. establishment of supported completion precision; 13. preservation of completion uncertainty; 14. maintenance of traceability to relevant temporal signals; 15. production of Governed Event Completion for ETDM.
ETCM does not calculate Event Duration, determine final Temporal Order, establish Event Location, determine legal taxability, or establish a Legal Tax Point. ------------------------------ 5. Event Completion Candidate Identification
ETCM identifies temporal signals or conditions that could plausibly establish Event Completion.

Potential candidates may include: final material operational action, completion of physical transformation, completion of transfer, final delivery, service fulfillment, digital execution completion, final constitutive machine action, autonomous objective execution completion, completion of required event components, final governed state transition, operational release of the completed result.
A candidate is not automatically authoritative.
Completion Candidate ≠ Governed Event Completion. ------------------------------ 6. Constitutive Event Completion
A legitimate Event Completion should represent the point or condition at which the materially constitutive activity belonging to the governed event has sufficiently concluded.
ETCM therefore asks:
When did the governed event finish occurring as the event under examination?
This differs from asking:
When did all activity associated with the event stop?
Supporting, administrative, technical, financial, monitoring, or reporting processes may continue after the event itself has completed.
End of Constitutive Activity ≠ End of All Related Activity. ------------------------------ 7. Post-Event Activity Differentiation
Events commonly generate activity after operational completion.
Examples include: confirmation messages, invoice generation, payment settlement, reconciliation, bookkeeping, reporting, quality review, monitoring, warranty processing, customer feedback, data synchronization, audit logging, archival activity.

Such activities may remain materially related to the event while occurring outside its operational completion.
ETCM must prevent downstream activity from silently extending the governed event.
Post-Event Relevance ≠ Event Continuation. ------------------------------ 8. Completion vs. Confirmation
A system may confirm an event after the event has already operationally completed.
Examples include: delivery confirmation after physical delivery, transaction confirmation after execution, machine completion signal after physical operation, cloud-service acknowledgement after processing, settlement confirmation after transfer execution.
Confirmation can provide evidence of completion without necessarily constituting completion itself.
Completion Confirmation ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 9. Completion vs. Settlement
Financial and commercial settlement frequently occurs after the underlying operational event.
A service may be delivered today and paid later.
Goods may be transferred before final settlement.
A digital transaction may execute before financial reconciliation.
ETCM preserves these distinctions.
Settlement Time ≠ Event Completion by Default.
Settlement may constitute Event Completion only where settlement itself belongs to the governed event structure established by TREBS. ------------------------------ 10. Completion vs. Administrative Closure

Administrative systems often maintain workflow states such as: completed, closed, archived, reconciled, posted, approved, finalized.
These labels do not automatically define operational Event Completion.
A workflow may remain technically open after the event has completed, or may be administratively closed before all constitutive activity has finished.
Workflow Closure ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 11. Physical Event Completion
Physical events may complete when the material physical activity constituting the event has concluded.
Examples include: completion of manufacturing transformation, physical delivery, unloading completion, construction-stage completion, transfer of a physical object, completion of machine operation.
Later inspection, documentation, invoicing, or payment does not automatically extend Event Completion.
Physical Process End ≠ Administrative Process End. ------------------------------ 12. Digital Event Completion
Digital events may complete through conditions such as: processing completion, digital delivery, successful execution, completed data transfer, completed deployment, access provision, final governed state transition.
Digital systems frequently generate additional logs and synchronization events afterward.
ETCM must distinguish these downstream technical traces from the completion of the governed digital event.

Last System Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 13. Transactional Event Completion
Transactional processes may contain multiple possible completion points.
For example:
Execution
↓
Confirmation
↓
Clearing
↓
Settlement
↓
Reconciliation
↓
Accounting Posting
ETCM does not impose a universal completion point.
It determines completion according to the Governed Bounded Event.
If the event represents execution, later settlement may remain downstream.
If the governed event legitimately includes settlement, completion may occur later.
Transaction Completion Depends on Governed Event Structure — Not System Convention Alone. ------------------------------ 14. Service Event Completion
Service events may complete: at delivery, at fulfillment of a defined operational objective, after a period of continuous performance, after completion of required service components, upon legitimate operational termination.
A contract end date or billing date does not automatically determine service completion.
For continuing services, ETCM must avoid manufacturing a completion point where the governed event remains operationally active.
Billing Boundary ≠ Service Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 15. Machine and Autonomous Event Completion
Autonomous and machine-mediated events may produce large numbers of internal operations before the governed event completes.

A machine may: execute, verify, adjust, communicate, self-check, release resources, generate logs.
An autonomous agent may continue monitoring or reporting after its primary governed operation has completed.
ETCM determines which operational condition represents completion of the governed event rather than simply selecting the final machine-generated timestamp.
Last Machine Action ≠ Event Completion by Default.
Autonomous Reporting ≠ Autonomous Event Continuation by Default. ------------------------------ 16. Distributed Event Completion
Distributed events may complete across multiple systems, participants, machines, or locations.
Different components may finish at different times.
ETCM must determine whether: one component establishes completion, all required components must complete, a defined completion threshold must be satisfied, a bounded completion interval is required, completion remains unresolved.
The methodology must reflect the governed event structure rather than impose artificial simultaneity.
Distributed Completion ≠ Single-System Closure. ------------------------------ 17. Phased Event Completion
Some events complete through multiple operational phases.
Where the event remains one coherent Governed Bounded Event, completion occurs only when the required constitutive phases have sufficiently concluded.
However, ETCM must not absorb Event Boundary governance by deciding that phases are actually separate events.

If evidence indicates a potential boundary problem, the issue should be routed to appropriate boundary governance rather than silently resolved inside ETCM.
Event Phase ≠ Separate Event by Default. ------------------------------ 18. Partial Completion
An event may begin and progress without reaching complete fulfillment.
Examples include: partial delivery, partially completed manufacturing, interrupted data transfer, partially executed service, incomplete autonomous operation.
ETCM must distinguish partial progress from legitimate Event Completion.
Possible representations may include:
Completion Pending
Partial Completion
Completion Qualified
Completion Failed
Completion Unresolved
Partial Performance ≠ Full Event Completion. ------------------------------ 19. Failed or Interrupted Events
An event that does not reach its intended operational outcome may still constitute a governed event.
Failure does not automatically erase the event.
ETCM must determine whether: the event completed unsuccessfully, the event terminated before completion, the event remains suspended, the event was aborted, the completion state is unresolved.
The module must not equate successful outcome with event existence.
Event Failure ≠ Event Non-Existence.
Likewise:
Termination ≠ Successful Completion. ------------------------------ 20. Conditional Completion
Some events complete only when defined operational conditions are satisfied.

For example: required delivery elements are fulfilled, required data reaches the destination, specified transformation finishes, required machine state is achieved, required service result is delivered.
A timestamp may record when the condition was detected, but the underlying condition governs operational completion.
Completion Timestamp ≠ Completion Condition by Default. ------------------------------ 21. Completion Ambiguity
Completion ambiguity exists when more than one plausible completion representation remains and available information does not sufficiently establish which one represents operational completion.
Possible causes include: asynchronous systems, incomplete logs, delayed observations, unclear completion criteria, conflicting operational records, distributed execution, uncertain final activity.
ETCM must preserve ambiguity rather than fabricate certainty.
Required Completion Field ≠ Completion Certainty. ------------------------------ 22. Completion Conflict
Completion conflict exists when materially relevant information supports incompatible completion determinations.
Examples include: machine logs show completion before ERP closure; physical delivery records conflict with platform records; autonomous-system logs disagree across nodes; service records show performance continuing after administrative closure.
ETCM must identify and preserve such conflict until sufficient governance can resolve it.

Preferred System Timestamp ≠ Authoritative Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 23. Event Completion Precision
Governed Event Completion may be represented as: exact timestamp, second, minute, hour, date, bounded interval, approximate period, condition-relative completion.
The selected precision must not exceed the temporal support available.
Recorded Precision ≠ Evidential Precision.
Where only a bounded interval can legitimately be established, ETCM should preserve the interval. ------------------------------ 24. Event Completion States
ETCM may represent Event Completion through states such as:
Completion Candidate A signal or condition may represent operational completion.
Completion Qualified The candidate is sufficiently supported.
Completion Established Operational completion is sufficiently established.
Completion Approximate Completion is established without exact temporal precision.
Partial Completion Only part of the required event structure has completed.
Completion Pending The governed event remains active.
Completion Interrupted Execution has stopped without normal completion.
Completion Failed The event reached a governed unsuccessful termination condition.
Completion Ambiguous Multiple plausible completion representations remain.
Completion Conflicted Materially incompatible completion evidence exists.
Completion Insufficient Available information cannot support reliable determination.
Completion Unresolved Further governance is required.

Completion Established ≠ Legal Completion Established. ------------------------------ 25. Governance Requirements
A conforming ETCM implementation should:
1. consume the Governed Event Start from ETSM; 2. maintain reference to relevant ETIM temporal signals; 3. identify plausible Event Completion candidates; 4. assess candidates against the Governed Bounded Event; 5. identify final constitutive event activity or completion condition; 6. distinguish Event Completion from post-event activity; 7. distinguish completion from confirmation; 8. distinguish completion from settlement; 9. distinguish completion from administrative closure; 10. support physical, digital, transactional, service, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous events; 11. support partial, failed, interrupted, conditional, and approximate completion; 12. preserve ambiguity and conflict; 13. avoid artificial temporal precision; 14. maintain completion traceability; 15. avoid jurisdiction-specific taxation assumptions; 16. produce a Governed Event Completion suitable for ETDM.
------------------------------ 26. Governance Logic
The minimum ETCM governance logic is:
IF one or more temporal signals plausibly represent completion,
THEN they must be evaluated as Completion Candidates.
IF materially constitutive event activity remains incomplete,
THEN normal Event Completion must not be established.
IF later activity is merely administrative, financial, technical, reporting, monitoring, or archival,

THEN that activity must not automatically extend Event Completion.
IF confirmation occurs after operational completion,
THEN confirmation may support completion without redefining it.
IF settlement occurs after operational completion,
THEN settlement must remain distinct unless settlement belongs to the Governed Bounded Event itself.
IF an event terminates unsuccessfully,
THEN its termination state must be represented without treating the event as nonexistent.
IF completion is distributed,
THEN the completion representation must reflect the required distributed event structure.
IF multiple completion candidates materially conflict,
THEN the conflict must remain explicit.
IF exact completion cannot be legitimately established,
THEN supported approximation or interval representation should be used.
IF jurisdiction-specific law assigns another legal point,
THEN that determination must remain outside ETCM. ------------------------------ 27. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ETCM implementation should support:
1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event.
2. Governed Event Start Reference Reference to ETSM output.
3. Temporal Signal Reference Reference to relevant ETIM signals.
4. Completion Candidate Identifier Unique reference for each candidate completion condition.
5. Completion Candidate Type Physical, digital, transactional, service, machine, autonomous, distributed, conditional, or other.

6. Completion Condition The operational condition potentially establishing completion.
7. Constitutive Completion Assessment Whether required event activity has sufficiently concluded.
8. Post-Event Activity Indicator Whether later related activity remains outside Event Completion.
9. Completion Type Normal, partial, interrupted, failed, conditional, approximate, or unresolved.
10. Completion Precision Supported temporal precision.
11. Completion Traceability Reference Links to relevant temporal and operational records.
12. Ambiguity / Conflict State Representation of unresolved completion issues.
13. Completion Governance State Candidate, qualified, established, approximate, partial, pending, interrupted, failed, ambiguous, conflicted, insufficient, or unresolved.
14. Governed Event Completion The established operational completion representation.
15. Handoff State Readiness for ETDM. ------------------------------ 28. Governance Outputs

ETCM may produce: Governed Event Completion Event Completion Candidate Set Completion Condition Record Constitutive Completion Assessment Post-Event Activity Record Completion Qualification Record Partial Completion Indicator Completion Pending Indicator Interrupted Completion Record Failed Completion Record Completion Precision Record Completion Ambiguity Indicator Completion Conflict Indicator Completion Insufficiency Indicator Distributed Completion Representation Machine / Autonomous Completion Representation Event Completion Traceability Record Event Duration Governance Readiness State
The principal output is:
Governed Event Completion
This output proceeds to:
ETDM — Event Duration Module ------------------------------ 29. Critical Distinctions
Completion Candidate ≠ Governed Event Completion
Latest Timestamp ≠ Event Completion by Default
End of Constitutive Activity ≠ End of All Related Activity
Post-Event Relevance ≠ Event Continuation
Completion Confirmation ≠ Event Completion by Default
Settlement Time ≠ Event Completion by Default
Workflow Closure ≠ Event Completion by Default
Physical Process End ≠ Administrative Process End
Last System Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Completion by Default
Billing Boundary ≠ Service Completion by Default
Last Machine Action ≠ Event Completion by Default
Autonomous Reporting ≠ Autonomous Event Continuation by Default
Distributed Completion ≠ Single-System Closure
Event Phase ≠ Separate Event by Default

Partial Performance ≠ Full Event Completion
Event Failure ≠ Event Non-Existence
Termination ≠ Successful Completion
Completion Timestamp ≠ Completion Condition by Default
Recorded Precision ≠ Evidential Precision
Event Completion ≠ Event Duration
Event Completion ≠ Final Temporal Order
Event Completion ≠ Accounting Closure
Event Completion ≠ Contractual Closure
Operational Event Completion ≠ Legal Tax Point
Event Completion ≠ Tax Period Determination
Event Completion ≠ Tax Liability Determination ------------------------------ 30. Enterprise Application
ETCM can support Event Completion governance across: ERP systems, banking infrastructure, payment systems, digital marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, logistics networks, SaaS environments, manufacturing systems, industrial automation, robotics, autonomous agents, IoT infrastructure, machine-to-machine systems, distributed computing, digital-asset infrastructure, cross-border commerce, automated accounting infrastructure, tax technology platforms.
ETCM enables these systems to maintain a governed operational completion representation independently of how downstream systems subsequently interpret settlement, accounting recognition, legal completion, reporting obligations, or taxation. ------------------------------ 31. Real-System Use Case 1 — Marketplace Delivery, Confirmation, and Settlement Occur at Different Times
A marketplace transaction generates the following timeline:
10:03 — Order accepted
10:08 — Payment authorized

13:42 — Seller dispatches goods
Next day 11:16 — Goods physically delivered
11:31 — Carrier system uploads delivery confirmation
12:05 — Marketplace marks order “completed”
Following day — Merchant settlement occurs
Three days later — Accounting reconciliation closes
Multiple systems therefore contain different plausible “completion” timestamps.
ETCM does not automatically accept the marketplace's completed status, carrier confirmation, payment settlement, or accounting closure.
It evaluates the Governed Bounded Event and determines when its constitutive operational activity actually completed.
If the bounded event concerns fulfillment and delivery, physical delivery may establish the Governed Event Completion even though platform confirmation, settlement, and reconciliation occur later.
Those later activities remain traceably associated without silently extending the event.
The resulting completion record can subsequently be consumed by taxation systems without TREGA™ deciding which jurisdiction-specific legal tax point applies.
The event can operationally finish before the systems surrounding it finish processing it. ------------------------------ 32. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Event Continues After Human Systems Think It Is Finished
An autonomous manufacturing system begins material transformation at 08:04.
Primary machining finishes at 08:47.
The production management system automatically marks the job “complete” at 08:48.

However, the governed manufacturing operation requires an autonomous finishing stage.
A robotic finishing unit continues processing until 08:55.
Machine verification occurs at 08:56.
Quality telemetry is uploaded until 08:59.
Administrative production records are closed at 09:12.
An accounting entry is generated later.
ETCM determines whether the 08:48 system status legitimately represents completion of the Governed Bounded Event.
Because required constitutive manufacturing activity continues until the finishing stage concludes, the administrative “complete” flag cannot independently establish Event Completion.
At the same time, telemetry upload and administrative closure after operational completion do not automatically extend the event.
ETCM therefore establishes the supported operational completion condition while preserving all later signals as associated temporal information.
A system may declare an event finished before operational reality has actually finished — or continue processing it long after operational reality has ended. ------------------------------ 33. Canonical Boundary
ETCM governs the identification, assessment, qualification, establishment, precision, ambiguity, conflict, partial completion, interruption, failure, and traceability of the operational completion of the Governed Bounded Event after its Governed Event Start has been established.

It does not redefine the Governed Event Start, calculate Event Duration, determine final Event Temporal Order, redefine Event Boundary, determine Event Location, govern Event Participation, determine Event-to-Value Association, establish Event Relationships, perform Event Determination, determine Legal Tax Point, establish Tax Period, determine Tax Jurisdiction, identify the taxpayer, determine legal taxability, calculate tax, or establish jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
ETCM receives:
ETSM — Governed Event Start
ETCM produces:
Governed Event Completion
The output is handed to:
ETDM — Event Duration Module
The canonical handoff is:
ETSM — Governed Event Start
↓
ETCM — Governed Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration Module ------------------------------ 34. Canonical Closing Statement
ETCM establishes when the governed event has finished occurring in operational reality without allowing the administrative, financial, technical, or legal processes surrounding that event to redefine its operational end.
ETCM determines when the event completes — not when a system closes it, a payment settles, or a jurisdiction decides that a legal tax point has occurred.

resources.title: OOF™ Event Duration Module (ETDM)
topics: IF Governed Event Start and Governed Event Completion are established,

chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Duration Module (ETDM)
Event Duration Module (ETDM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Module: ETDM — Event Duration Module
Operational Layer: Event Duration Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Duration
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETDM-004
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Duration Module (ETDM) governs how the temporal extent of a Tax-Relevant Event is established from its governed temporal structure, including its Governed Event Start, Governed Event Completion, intermediate temporal conditions, interruptions, suspensions, phases, distributed execution, and supported temporal precision.
ETDM determines how long the governed event persisted as operational reality without converting that duration into a jurisdiction-specific tax period, accounting period, reporting period, contractual period, billing period, or legal duration.
Its specific task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified representation of the temporal extent occupied by the governed event between its legitimate operational start and completion.
ETDM governs how long the event existed or persisted as the governed event .
It does not determine the period in which a jurisdiction recognizes, reports, assesses, or taxes that event. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role
ETSM establishes the Governed Event Start.
ETCM establishes the Governed Event Completion.
ETDM governs the temporal extent between and across those governed temporal conditions.
The primary transition is:
Governed Event Start + Governed Event Completion
↓
Governed Event Duration
Duration may appear mathematically simple, but governed duration cannot always be reduced to:
Completion Timestamp − Start Timestamp
Events may contain: pauses, suspensions, inactive intervals, phased execution, asynchronous components, distributed operations, partial completion, uncertain temporal boundaries, approximate timestamps, open-ended activity, machine execution cycles, autonomous continuation.
ETDM therefore governs the meaning and representation of duration rather than merely calculating elapsed clock time.
Elapsed Clock Time ≠ Governed Event Duration by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow
The TRETS Internal Module Flow is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓
ETSM — Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration

↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETDM governs:
Governed Event Start + Governed Event Completion
↓
Temporal Extent Construction
↓
Active / Inactive Interval Assessment
↓
Interruption / Suspension Assessment
↓
Phase and Distributed Duration Assessment
↓
Duration Precision & Uncertainty Governance
↓
Governed Event Duration
↓
ETOM
ETDM consumes the governed temporal results established by preceding TRETS modules.
It does not reopen Event Start or Event Completion merely to produce a preferred duration.
Where a material inconsistency is discovered, ETDM must preserve the issue and route it to the relevant prior temporal governance process. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space
ETDM governs the space in which the temporal extent of the event must be represented.
This includes: total event span, active duration, inactive duration, interrupted duration, suspended duration, continuous duration, discontinuous duration, phased duration, distributed duration, overlapping execution intervals, machine execution duration, autonomous-system duration, approximate duration, bounded duration, open duration, duration uncertainty, duration conflict, duration precision, duration traceability.
The governed duration must remain anchored to the event's operational reality. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope
ETDM governs:

1. construction of Event Duration from governed temporal inputs; 2. establishment of total temporal extent; 3. differentiation between total span and active duration; 4. identification of inactive intervals; 5. governance of interruptions; 6. governance of suspensions; 7. representation of continuous and discontinuous events; 8. representation of phased events; 9. representation of distributed events; 10. treatment of overlapping temporal components; 11. machine and autonomous-system duration; 12. treatment of incomplete or open events; 13. duration precision; 14. duration uncertainty; 15. duration conflicts; 16. duration correction; 17. duration traceability; 18. readiness for Event Temporal Order governance.
ETDM does not determine jurisdiction-specific tax periods, reporting periods, accounting periods, contractual durations, billing periods, or statutory time periods. ------------------------------ 5. Temporal Extent Construction
The baseline temporal extent of an event is established from its Governed Event Start and Governed Event Completion.
Conceptually:
Governed Event Start
↓
Temporal Extent
↓
Governed Event Completion
Where both endpoints are sufficiently established, ETDM may derive an overall event span.
However, this span does not automatically represent the event's active operational duration.
For example:
08:00 Start
↓
12:00 Suspension
↓
14:00 Resumption
↓
18:00 Completion
The overall temporal span is ten hours.

The event may have only eight hours of active execution.
Whether suspension belongs inside the governed duration representation depends on what the duration is intended to represent operationally.
ETDM must preserve this distinction.
Total Temporal Span ≠ Active Event Duration by Default. ------------------------------ 6. Continuous Event Duration
A continuous event proceeds without materially relevant interruption between its Governed Event Start and Governed Event Completion.
For such events:
Start
↓
Continuous Activity
↓
Completion
the temporal span may legitimately represent the event duration.
Examples may include: continuous machine operation, uninterrupted data transfer, physical transport, continuous service execution, single-stage transformation.
Even here, system latency, logging delays, confirmation delays, or downstream processing must not artificially extend the duration.
Continuous Event Duration ≠ System Processing Window by Default. ------------------------------ 7. Discontinuous Event Duration
Some governed events legitimately persist across interruptions or inactive intervals.
Their structure may be:
Start
↓
Activity
↓
Pause
↓
Activity
↓
Suspension
↓
Activity
↓
Completion
ETDM must distinguish: overall temporal span, active execution duration, inactive duration, suspension duration, interruption duration.
The event may remain the same Governed Bounded Event despite discontinuity.

ETDM does not split it into multiple events merely because execution was interrupted.
Temporal Discontinuity ≠ New Event by Default.
Event separation remains governed by TREBS. ------------------------------ 8. Active Duration
Active Duration represents the time during which constitutive operational activity belonging to the event is actively occurring.
It may differ substantially from the total temporal span.
Examples include: machine processing time, active service performance, autonomous execution time, physical transformation time, active transfer time.
Active Duration must be derived from operationally meaningful activity rather than system uptime or record availability.
System Activity ≠ Event Activity by Default. ------------------------------ 9. Inactive Duration
Inactive Duration represents temporal intervals within the broader event span during which constitutive event activity is not actively occurring but the same event may remain operationally open.
Examples include: waiting periods, temporary pauses, resource unavailability, queued continuation, scheduled interruption, external dependency waiting.
Inactive time should not automatically be removed from every duration representation.
ETDM must preserve whether the governed output represents:
Total Event Duration
or:
Active Event Duration
or both.
Inactive Time ≠ Event Absence by Default. ------------------------------ 10. Event Interruption

An interruption temporarily stops event activity without necessarily ending the governed event.
ETDM must determine: interruption start, interruption end, interruption duration, whether the event remains continuous as one governed event, whether the interruption affects active duration, whether the interruption introduces uncertainty.
An interruption must not automatically create a new Event Start or Event Completion.
Interruption ≠ Completion.
Resumption ≠ New Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 11. Event Suspension
Suspension is a governed state in which continuation is intentionally or operationally deferred while the event remains capable of resumption.
Suspension may arise from: human intervention, system control, external dependency, resource constraints, safety procedures, autonomous decision logic, operational authorization.
ETDM may represent suspended time separately from active time.
It does not determine whether a legal framework treats suspension differently.
Operational Suspension ≠ Legal Suspension. ------------------------------ 12. Phased Duration
An event may contain multiple constitutive phases:
Phase A
↓
Phase B
↓
Phase C
↓
Completion
ETDM may represent: phase duration, transition intervals, aggregate active duration, total event span.
Where phases overlap, simple addition may produce an incorrect result.
For example:
Phase A = 3 hours
Phase B = 2 hours
with one hour of overlap.

The event does not necessarily have five hours of elapsed duration.
ETDM must preserve the temporal relationship among phases.
Sum of Phase Durations ≠ Event Duration by Default. ------------------------------ 13. Overlapping Duration
Multiple components of the same event may execute simultaneously.
This is common in: distributed computing, manufacturing, logistics, autonomous systems, digital services, multi-party operations.
ETDM must avoid double-counting overlapping intervals where the objective is to establish elapsed event duration.
At the same time, component-level active duration may legitimately exceed overall elapsed duration when multiple components operate concurrently.
Therefore:
Aggregate Component Time ≠ Elapsed Event Duration. ------------------------------ 14. Distributed Event Duration
A distributed event may span: multiple machines, multiple systems, multiple locations, multiple participants, multiple technical environments.
Different components may begin and complete at different times.
ETDM must construct duration from the governed event as a whole rather than selecting one system's local execution window.
Possible representations include: global event span, component durations, active distributed duration, overlapping execution, asynchronous intervals, completion lag.
Distributed Event Duration ≠ Duration of One Component. ------------------------------ 15. Machine Event Duration
Machine-generated events may produce extremely precise temporal records.

A machine may report:
08:00:00.000001
↓
08:00:02.983746
Technical precision does not automatically establish that the governed event legitimately has microsecond-level temporal precision.
Machine clocks may contain: synchronization differences, clock drift, buffering, delayed logging, asynchronous recording, system-specific temporal semantics.
ETDM must therefore distinguish computational precision from governed temporal precision.
Machine Precision ≠ Governed Duration Precision. ------------------------------ 16. Autonomous Event Duration
Autonomous systems may independently initiate, pause, modify, resume, and complete operations.
An autonomous event may therefore include:
Initiation
↓
Execution
↓
Self-Pause
↓
Replanning
↓
Resumption
↓
Completion
↓
Monitoring
ETDM determines the governed temporal extent of the event without assuming that all autonomous-system activity belongs inside the event duration.
Post-completion monitoring may remain outside the governed event.
Likewise, internal computational cycles may not constitute separate duration components unless operationally relevant.
Autonomous System Runtime ≠ Governed Event Duration by Default. ------------------------------ 17. Open Event Duration
An event may have a Governed Event Start while no legitimate Event Completion has yet been established.
In such cases, ETDM must not fabricate final duration.
The event may be represented as:
Open Duration
Duration Pending
Duration To-Date
Completion Unresolved

A duration-to-date representation must clearly indicate that it is not final.
Elapsed Time To Date ≠ Final Event Duration. ------------------------------ 18. Partial and Interrupted Completion
Where ETCM establishes partial, interrupted, or failed completion, ETDM must preserve the corresponding temporal condition.
A failed event may still have a legitimate duration.
An interrupted event may have: active duration, interruption duration, total span, termination point.
Failure does not invalidate the temporal history of the event.
Failed Event ≠ Zero Duration. ------------------------------ 19. Duration Precision
ETDM must represent duration only at the precision legitimately supported by governed temporal inputs.
Possible representations include: exact duration, rounded duration, approximate duration, minimum duration, maximum duration, bounded duration range, unresolved duration.
If Event Start is known only within a one-hour interval and Event Completion only within another interval, an artificially exact duration must not be generated.
Precise Calculation from Imprecise Inputs ≠ Precise Governed Duration. ------------------------------ 20. Duration Uncertainty
Duration uncertainty may arise from: uncertain Event Start, uncertain Event Completion, missing intermediate signals, disputed interruption periods, clock synchronization problems, distributed systems, approximate observations, incomplete records.

ETDM must propagate relevant temporal uncertainty rather than hide it through mathematical calculation.
A numerically exact result derived from uncertain inputs remains uncertain.
Mathematical Exactness ≠ Governance Certainty. ------------------------------ 21. Duration Conflict
Duration conflict exists when materially relevant records produce incompatible duration representations.
For example: machine logs show 47 minutes; ERP records show 55 minutes; operator records show approximately one hour; autonomous-system logs omit a suspension interval.
ETDM must identify the source of the conflict and preserve it where it cannot be legitimately resolved.
Preferred Data Source ≠ Automatically Correct Duration. ------------------------------ 22. Duration Correction
New information may justify correction of a previously established duration.
Corrections must preserve: prior duration representation, reason for correction, affected temporal inputs, revised duration, correction authority, traceability.
Correction must not silently overwrite governed history.
Duration Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
If the correction originates from an incorrect Event Start or Event Completion, the relevant issue should be routed to ETSM or ETCM rather than being concealed through ETDM calculation. ------------------------------ 23. Event Duration States
ETDM may represent duration through governance states including:
Duration Ready Required temporal inputs are available.

Duration Under Governance Temporal extent is being constructed.
Duration Established A sufficiently governed duration exists.
Duration Approximate Duration is established with limited precision.
Duration Bounded Duration can be represented only as a supported range.
Duration Open The event has not reached Governed Event Completion.
Duration Partial Only part of the temporal extent can be governed.
Duration Conflicted Materially incompatible duration representations exist.
Duration Uncertain Relevant uncertainty remains.
Duration Insufficient Available information cannot support a legitimate duration.
Duration Corrected A prior duration has been revised through governed correction.
Governed Event Duration ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Period. ------------------------------ 24. Tax Period Separation
One of ETDM's most important boundaries is the separation between operational Event Duration and jurisdiction-specific Tax Period.
An event may: begin in one tax period and complete in another; last seconds but be recognized legally later; continue across multiple reporting periods; be operationally completed before legal recognition; have different tax-period treatment across jurisdictions.
ETDM does not resolve these questions.
It provides governed temporal reality for downstream systems.
Event Duration ≠ Tax Period Determination. ------------------------------ 25. Reporting and Accounting Period Separation

Operational duration must also remain distinct from: accounting period, reporting period, billing cycle, fiscal period, contractual period, settlement window.
These periods may consume or interpret TREGA temporal outputs but must not redefine the operational duration governed by ETDM.
Accounting Period ≠ Event Duration.
Reporting Period ≠ Event Duration.
Billing Period ≠ Event Duration. ------------------------------ 26. Governance Requirements
A conforming ETDM implementation should:
1. consume Governed Event Start from ETSM; 2. consume Governed Event Completion or corresponding completion state from ETCM; 3. construct the event's temporal extent; 4. distinguish total span from active duration where materially relevant; 5. identify inactive intervals; 6. identify interruptions and suspensions; 7. support continuous and discontinuous events; 8. support phased events; 9. support overlapping temporal components; 10. support distributed events; 11. support machine-generated and autonomous events; 12. support open and incomplete events; 13. preserve supported temporal precision; 14. propagate uncertainty; 15. identify duration conflicts; 16. preserve correction history; 17. maintain traceability to governed temporal inputs; 18. prevent jurisdiction-specific Tax Period logic from entering ETDM; 19. produce a Governed Event Duration suitable for ETOM.
------------------------------ 27. Governance Logic
The minimum ETDM governance logic is:

IF Governed Event Start and Governed Event Completion are established,
THEN the event's temporal extent may be constructed.
IF the event contains materially relevant inactive periods,
THEN total span and active duration should be distinguished where necessary.
IF the event is interrupted but remains the same Governed Bounded Event,
THEN interruption must not automatically create a new event.
IF event phases overlap,
THEN phase durations must not be mechanically summed as elapsed Event Duration.
IF distributed components execute asynchronously,
THEN duration must be governed from the event structure rather than a single component clock.
IF Event Completion remains unresolved,
THEN final Event Duration must remain open or pending.
IF temporal inputs are approximate,
THEN the resulting duration must preserve corresponding uncertainty.
IF machine timestamps provide greater precision than operational evidence supports,
THEN governed duration precision must be reduced accordingly.
IF materially conflicting duration representations remain,
THEN conflict must remain explicit.
IF new evidence changes Event Start or Event Completion,
THEN the affected upstream temporal governance must be reconsidered.
IF a jurisdiction assigns a Tax Period,
THEN that determination remains outside ETDM. ------------------------------ 28. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ETDM implementation should support:
1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event.

2. Governed Event Start Reference Reference to ETSM output.
3. Governed Event Completion Reference Reference to ETCM output or completion state.
4. Total Temporal Span Overall governed span between temporal endpoints.
5. Active Duration Supported period of constitutive event activity.
6. Inactive Duration Supported period of inactivity within the event span.
7. Interruption Record Governed interruption intervals.
8. Suspension Record Governed suspension intervals.
9. Phase Duration Record Temporal representation of relevant event phases.
10. Overlap Record Representation of concurrent event components.
11. Distributed Duration Record Temporal representation across distributed components.
12. Duration Precision Supported level of temporal precision.
13. Duration Uncertainty State Known uncertainty affecting duration.
14. Duration Conflict State Known incompatible duration representations.
15. Duration Correction History Governed revisions to duration.
16. Duration Governance State Established, approximate, bounded, open, partial, conflicted, uncertain, insufficient, or corrected.
17. Governed Event Duration Principal ETDM output.
18. Handoff State Readiness for ETOM. ------------------------------ 29. Governance Outputs

ETDM may produce: Governed Event Duration Total Event Span Active Event Duration Inactive Duration Record Event Interruption Record Event Suspension Record Phase Duration Structure Overlapping Duration Structure Distributed Duration Structure Machine Event Duration Record Autonomous Event Duration Record Open Duration Indicator Partial Duration Indicator Duration Precision Record Duration Uncertainty Indicator Duration Conflict Indicator Duration Correction Record Duration Traceability Record Event Temporal Order Governance Readiness State
The principal output is:
Governed Event Duration
This output proceeds to:
ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module ------------------------------ 30. Critical Distinctions
Elapsed Clock Time ≠ Governed Event Duration by Default
Total Temporal Span ≠ Active Event Duration by Default
Continuous Event Duration ≠ System Processing Window by Default
Temporal Discontinuity ≠ New Event by Default
System Activity ≠ Event Activity by Default
Inactive Time ≠ Event Absence by Default
Interruption ≠ Completion
Resumption ≠ New Event Start by Default
Operational Suspension ≠ Legal Suspension
Sum of Phase Durations ≠ Event Duration by Default
Aggregate Component Time ≠ Elapsed Event Duration
Distributed Event Duration ≠ Duration of One Component
Machine Precision ≠ Governed Duration Precision
Autonomous System Runtime ≠ Governed Event Duration by Default
Elapsed Time To Date ≠ Final Event Duration
Failed Event ≠ Zero Duration

Precise Calculation from Imprecise Inputs ≠ Precise Governed Duration
Mathematical Exactness ≠ Governance Certainty
Duration Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Event Duration ≠ Event Temporal Order
Event Duration ≠ Tax Period Determination
Event Duration ≠ Accounting Period
Event Duration ≠ Reporting Period
Event Duration ≠ Billing Period
Governed Event Duration ≠ Legal Tax Duration ------------------------------ 31. Enterprise Application
ETDM can support duration governance across: ERP systems, financial infrastructure, payment platforms, digital marketplaces, e-commerce systems, manufacturing environments, logistics networks, service platforms, SaaS infrastructure, industrial automation, robotics, autonomous agents, AI-operated systems, machine-to-machine environments, IoT systems, distributed computing, digital assets, cross-border transactions, accounting infrastructure, tax technology systems.
ETDM provides these systems with a common operational representation of how long an event persisted before downstream legal, accounting, reporting, or taxation frameworks interpret that temporal reality. ------------------------------ 32. Real-System Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Logistics Event with Suspension and Multiple Operational Clocks
A governed logistics event begins when a shipment enters the operational transport process at:
Monday 08:00
Transport proceeds until:
Monday 16:00
The shipment is then held because an external infrastructure dependency prevents continuation.

Transport resumes:
Tuesday 06:00
Physical delivery completes:
Tuesday 12:00
The carrier's administrative system closes the shipment at:
Tuesday 15:30
Financial settlement occurs on Wednesday.
Several duration representations are therefore possible.
A simple calculation from Monday 08:00 to Tuesday 15:30 would incorrectly include post-event administrative processing.
A calculation from Monday 08:00 to Tuesday 12:00 establishes the overall operational span but includes the suspension period.
Active transport duration may represent a different operational measure.
ETDM preserves these distinctions through governed representations of:
Total Event Span
Active Duration
Suspension Duration
and:
Governed Event Duration
The downstream tax infrastructure may later determine which tax period, reporting period, jurisdictional rule, or legal tax point applies.
ETDM does not make that decision.
Operational duration describes how the event persisted in reality; it does not decide how a jurisdiction places that event into tax law. ------------------------------ 33. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Distributed AI Operation Across Multiple Machines
An autonomous industrial AI initiates a governed optimization event at:
14:00:00
Machine A begins execution immediately.
Machine B begins at:
14:00:08
Machine C begins at:
14:00:15
Machine A completes its component at:
14:03:40
Machine B temporarily pauses for 35 seconds and completes at:
14:04:12
Machine C completes at:
14:04:05

The autonomous orchestration layer completes the governed operational objective at:
14:04:20
Diagnostic monitoring continues until:
14:07:00
System logs remain active for another ten minutes.
Adding the runtime of Machines A, B, and C would significantly overstate the elapsed duration because their operations overlap.
Using the final diagnostic timestamp would also extend the event beyond its constitutive operational activity.
ETDM constructs the governed duration from the temporal structure of the bounded autonomous event.
It can preserve: overall event span, component execution durations, overlapping intervals, pause duration, distributed execution, autonomous completion.
The resulting Governed Event Duration can then enter downstream Event Temporal Order governance without treating system runtime or aggregated machine execution time as the event's temporal extent.
In autonomous and distributed systems, more machine time does not necessarily mean more event time. ------------------------------ 34. Canonical Boundary
ETDM governs the construction, representation, qualification, precision, uncertainty, conflict, correction, and traceability of the temporal duration of the Governed Bounded Event using the temporal conditions established through TRETS.

It owns: Total Event Span, Active Duration, Inactive Duration, interruption duration, suspension duration, phased duration, overlapping duration, distributed duration, machine and autonomous duration representation, open duration, approximate duration, bounded duration, duration uncertainty, duration conflict, duration correction, duration traceability.
ETDM does not own Event Time Identification, independently redefine Event Start, independently redefine Event Completion, determine final Event Temporal Order, redefine Event Boundary, determine Event Location, determine Event Participation, govern Value Association, establish Event Relationships, perform final Event Determination, determine Legal Tax Point, determine Tax Period, determine Tax Jurisdiction, determine Taxpayer status, calculate tax liability, or establish jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
ETDM receives:
ETSM — Governed Event Start
and:
ETCM — Governed Event Completion
ETDM produces:
Governed Event Duration
The output is handed to:
ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module
The canonical handoff is:
ETSM — Governed Event Start + ETCM — Governed Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Governed Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module ------------------------------ 35. Canonical Closing Statement

ETDM establishes how long the governed event persisted in operational reality while preserving the difference between elapsed time, active time, interrupted time, distributed execution, and downstream legal or administrative periods.
ETDM governs the duration of the event — not the tax period into which a jurisdiction may later place it.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
