chunks.text:
OOF™ Event Time Identification Module (ETIM)
Event Time Identification Module (ETIM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Module: ETIM — Event Time Identification Module
Operational Layer: Event Time Identification Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Time Identification
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETIM-001
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Time Identification Module (ETIM) governs how temporally relevant signals associated with a Governed Bounded Event are identified, distinguished, contextualized, and prepared as a traceable temporal evidence structure from which subsequent Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, and Event Temporal Order governance can proceed.

ETIM identifies operationally relevant temporal signals originating from human activity, transactions, physical operations, digital systems, distributed infrastructure, autonomous systems, machines, records, observations, communications, and other governed sources without assuming that any individual timestamp automatically represents the authoritative time of the event.
Its specific task is:
to establish a coherent and traceable Governed Event Time Signal Set representing the materially relevant temporal signals associated with the bounded event without prematurely determining Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
ETIM governs the identification of temporal signals relevant to the event.
It does not yet determine the event's complete temporal structure. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role
TREBS produces a Governed Bounded Event whose structural perimeter has been sufficiently established.
TRETS must now determine how that bounded event exists in operational time.
The first requirement is not to choose a date.
The first requirement is to identify the temporal signals capable of legitimately informing that determination.
ETIM performs this function.

It examines the bounded event and identifies the timestamps, temporal observations, sequence indicators, state transitions, physical occurrences, digital records, machine signals, and other temporal references materially associated with it.
The transition governed by ETIM is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
Governed Event Time Signal Set
ETIM therefore creates the temporal input structure required by the remaining TRETS modules.
Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow
The TRETS Internal Module Flow is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓
ETSM — Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETIM governs the first operational transition:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
Temporal Signal Discovery
↓
Temporal Signal Identification
↓
Temporal Signal Contextualization
↓
Temporal Signal Relevance Assessment
↓
Temporal Signal Correlation
↓
Temporal Ambiguity / Conflict Detection
↓
Governed Event Time Signal Set
↓
ETSM
ETIM does not determine which identified signal constitutes Event Start.
That determination belongs to ETSM — Event Start Module. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space
ETIM governs the operational space in which temporal signals associated with the bounded event must be discovered and structured before temporal determinations are made.

This space includes: operational timestamps, transaction timestamps, physical occurrence times, observation times, system-generated timestamps, machine timestamps, autonomous-system timestamps, communication timestamps, authorization times, execution times, confirmation times, recording times, transmission times, receipt times, settlement-related temporal signals, state-transition times, distributed-system timestamps, synchronized and unsynchronized clocks, approximate temporal signals, temporal intervals, incomplete temporal records, conflicting timestamps, duplicated temporal signals, derived temporal references, sequence indicators, temporal uncertainty, temporal source traceability.
ETIM does not treat these signals as equivalent.
Their existence establishes potential temporal relevance, not authoritative event timing. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope
ETIM governs:

1. identification of temporal signals materially associated with the bounded event; 2. identification of the source producing or recording each temporal signal; 3. distinction between operational occurrence time and system-recording time; 4. distinction between observed, generated, transmitted, received, recorded, and derived temporal signals; 5. contextualization of temporal signals within the bounded event; 6. assessment of whether a temporal signal is materially relevant to subsequent timing governance; 7. correlation of multiple signals referring to the same or related event activity; 8. detection of conflicting or inconsistent temporal signals; 9. detection of missing or insufficient temporal information; 10. representation of temporal uncertainty; 11. preservation of temporal provenance and traceability; 12. preparation of the Governed Event Time Signal Set for Event Start governance.
ETIM does not determine Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, final Temporal Order, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, or tax consequences. ------------------------------ 5. Temporal Signal Identification
A governed event may produce many temporal records.
Only some may be materially relevant to its operational temporal representation.
ETIM identifies candidate temporal signals by examining the governed event's actual operational structure rather than relying on one preferred system of record.
Potential temporal signals may originate from:

Human Activity action initiation, approval, acceptance, physical performance, acknowledgement.
Transactional Systems order creation, authorization, transaction execution, confirmation, settlement.
Physical Systems sensor activation, production initiation, movement, delivery, inspection, physical completion.
Digital Systems request creation, API execution, processing, database commit, digital delivery, service activation.
Autonomous Systems autonomous decision, agent instruction, machine activation, automated execution, autonomous confirmation.
Records and Communications document creation, message transmission, receipt, ledger entry, accounting entry.
The presence of a timestamp in any of these systems does not establish its authority over the event.
Recorded Time ≠ Operational Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ 6. Temporal Signal Source Governance
Every material temporal signal should remain associated with the source from which it originated.
ETIM therefore distinguishes between the time represented by a signal and the mechanism that produced or recorded it.
A temporal source may include: human observation, sensor, machine controller, application, API, transaction platform, distributed ledger, accounting system, payment infrastructure, logistics system, autonomous agent, external service, trusted time service, documentary record.
The source relationship must remain traceable because different systems may record different temporal aspects of the same event.

Source Timestamp ≠ Source Authority Over Event Time.
A system may accurately report when it recorded something without establishing when the governed event itself occurred. ------------------------------ 7. Occurrence Time vs. Recording Time
One of ETIM's critical functions is distinguishing operational occurrence from later recording.
For example:
Operational action: 10:02:14 System transmission: 10:02:16 Database recording: 10:02:18 Accounting posting: 11:45:00 Settlement record: following day
All may be valid timestamps.
They do not describe the same temporal fact.
ETIM preserves these distinctions instead of collapsing them into one generic date field.
Occurrence Time ≠ Recording Time.
Recording Time ≠ Accounting Time.
Accounting Time ≠ Settlement Time.
Settlement Time ≠ Legal Tax Point. ------------------------------ 8. Temporal Signal Relevance
A temporal signal becomes relevant to ETIM when it materially contributes to understanding the operational temporal structure of the bounded event.
Relevance may depend on whether the signal: represents an actual event activity, records a material state transition, confirms occurrence of an event component, establishes a meaningful temporal constraint, contributes to reconstruction of event sequence, helps distinguish event activity from surrounding activity, supports subsequent Event Start or Event Completion governance.
A technically valid timestamp may nevertheless be operationally immaterial.

For example, a database backup time may relate to records describing an event without being relevant to when the event occurred.
Technical Timestamp ≠ Material Temporal Signal by Default. ------------------------------ 9. Multiple Temporal Signals
Modern events frequently contain multiple legitimate temporal signals.
ETIM must preserve this multiplicity rather than forcing premature selection of a single timestamp.
A commercial event may contain:
Order Created
↓
Order Accepted
↓
Payment Authorized
↓
Service Activated
↓
Delivery Completed
↓
Payment Settled
A machine-generated event may contain:
Signal Detected
↓
Autonomous Decision
↓
Command Issued
↓
Machine Activated
↓
Operation Executed
↓
Result Confirmed
Each temporal signal may be operationally relevant.
ETIM identifies and structures these signals.
Later TRETS modules determine their role in the governed temporal representation.
Multiple Temporal Signals ≠ Temporal Conflict by Default. ------------------------------ 10. Temporal Signal Correlation
Different systems may record the same operational occurrence differently.
ETIM therefore supports correlation between temporal signals that appear to describe the same or closely related operational activity.
Correlation may consider: common event identifiers, operational relationships, sequence consistency, source relationships, transaction references, machine execution references, physical observations, bounded-event components, state transitions.

Correlation must not erase source differences.
Two timestamps may refer to the same operational occurrence while preserving separate provenance.
Temporal Correlation ≠ Temporal Equivalence. ------------------------------ 11. Distributed Event Timing
A bounded event may operate across multiple systems, networks, devices, organizations, or geographical environments.
Temporal signals may therefore originate from clocks that are: synchronized, partially synchronized, independently maintained, delayed, offset, intermittently connected, subject to network latency.
ETIM must preserve the relevant temporal signals together with their source context and known temporal limitations.
A distributed event must not be forced into artificial temporal precision that available evidence cannot support.
Distributed Execution ≠ Single-System Time Authority. ------------------------------ 12. Machine and Autonomous Temporal Signals
Machine and autonomous environments may generate extremely high volumes of timestamps.
ETIM does not assume that every machine action represents a material temporal signal for the governed event.
A robot may generate thousands of control-cycle timestamps while performing one materially relevant operation.
An AI agent may perform dozens of API calls while executing one governed activity.
A distributed autonomous process may produce multiple confirmation times across independent systems.

ETIM identifies the temporal signals materially relevant to the governed event while preserving necessary underlying traceability.
Machine Timestamp Volume ≠ Event Temporal Granularity.
One Machine Timestamp ≠ One Event Time. ------------------------------ 13. Temporal Ambiguity
Not every event contains sufficient temporal information for precise temporal identification.
Possible conditions include: missing timestamps, contradictory timestamps, approximate times, incomplete records, clock synchronization uncertainty, delayed recording, unknown source reliability, conflicting human observations, inconsistent system logs.
ETIM must preserve such uncertainty explicitly.
It must not manufacture precision merely because downstream systems require a date or timestamp.
Required Data Field ≠ Legitimate Temporal Certainty. ------------------------------ 14. Temporal Conflict
Temporal conflict exists when two or more materially relevant temporal signals cannot be reconciled within the available governed representation.
For example:
System A indicates execution at 14:02.
System B indicates the same operation completed at 13:58.
A physical sensor indicates activation at 14:01.
The conflict must remain visible until sufficient governance resolves or contextualizes it.
ETIM may identify and structure the conflict.
It does not arbitrarily choose the timestamp preferred by a particular operational, accounting, commercial, or taxation system.

System Preference ≠ Governed Temporal Resolution. ------------------------------ 15. Temporal Precision Governance
Temporal information may exist at different levels of precision.
Examples include: year, month, date, hour, minute, second, millisecond, bounded interval, approximate period, sequence-only representation.
ETIM preserves the precision legitimately supported by the underlying temporal information.
It must not increase apparent precision beyond what the available governed signals justify.
Recorded Precision ≠ Proven Temporal Accuracy. ------------------------------ 16. Temporal Signal States
ETIM may classify identified temporal signals into governance states such as:
Identified A temporal signal has been detected and associated with the bounded event.
Contextualized The operational meaning and source of the signal are sufficiently understood.
Relevant The signal materially contributes to subsequent Event Timing governance.
Correlated The signal has a governed relationship with one or more other temporal signals.
Ambiguous The signal's temporal meaning remains insufficiently clear.
Conflicting The signal materially conflicts with another relevant temporal representation.
Insufficient Available information does not support adequate temporal use.
Unresolved The signal requires subsequent governance or additional information before reliable temporal use.
These states preserve uncertainty rather than hiding it. ------------------------------ 17. Governance Requirements

A conforming ETIM implementation should:
1. identify materially relevant temporal signals associated with the Governed Bounded Event; 2. preserve the source of each material signal; 3. distinguish occurrence, observation, transmission, recording, posting, settlement, and derived times where relevant; 4. assess temporal relevance rather than accepting timestamps indiscriminately; 5. preserve multiple legitimate temporal signals; 6. correlate related signals without erasing provenance; 7. detect temporal ambiguity and conflict; 8. preserve legitimate uncertainty; 9. avoid artificial temporal precision; 10. support physical, digital, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous events; 11. maintain sufficient traceability for reconstruction; 12. prevent legal tax assumptions from controlling operational temporal identification; 13. produce a Governed Event Time Signal Set suitable for ETSM.
------------------------------ 18. Governance Logic
The minimum ETIM governance logic is:
IF a Governed Bounded Event contains or can be associated with temporal information,
THEN materially relevant temporal signals must be identified and associated with their sources.
IF multiple signals describe different temporal aspects of the event,
THEN they must remain distinguishable.
IF multiple signals appear to represent the same occurrence,
THEN they may be correlated without automatically being treated as temporally identical.
IF temporal signals conflict,

THEN the conflict must remain explicit until sufficiently resolved or contextualized.
IF available information supports only approximate timing,
THEN ETIM must preserve approximate timing rather than manufacture exactness.
IF a timestamp exists only because a technical system recorded the event,
THEN that timestamp must not automatically become authoritative Event Time.
IF a jurisdiction-specific tax rule prefers a particular date,
THEN that preference must not redefine the operational temporal signals governed by ETIM. ------------------------------ 19. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ETIM implementation should support:
1. Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event received from TREBS.
2. Temporal Signal Identifier Unique reference for each materially relevant temporal signal.
3. Temporal Value Timestamp, date, interval, approximate period, or sequence indicator.
4. Temporal Signal Type Occurrence, observation, execution, confirmation, recording, transmission, receipt, settlement, or other relevant type.
5. Temporal Source System, person, machine, sensor, platform, document, or other source.
6. Source Context Operational context in which the temporal signal was created or observed.
7. Precision Level Supported temporal precision.
8. Relevance State Whether the signal is materially relevant to subsequent Event Timing governance.
9. Correlation Reference Relationship to other temporal signals where applicable.

10. Ambiguity / Conflict Indicator Explicit representation of temporal uncertainty or contradiction.
11. Traceability Reference Link to the supporting operational record or governed source.
12. Handoff State Readiness of the temporal signal set for ETSM. ------------------------------ 20. Governance Outputs
ETIM may produce: Governed Event Time Signal Set Temporal Signal Inventory Temporal Source Map Temporal Signal Type Record Temporal Relevance Record Temporal Correlation Record Temporal Precision Record Temporal Ambiguity Indicator Temporal Conflict Indicator Temporal Insufficiency Indicator Distributed Timing Representation Machine / Autonomous Timing Representation Temporal Traceability Record Event Start Governance Readiness State
The principal output is:
Governed Event Time Signal Set
This output becomes the governed input to:
ETSM — Event Start Module ------------------------------ 21. Critical Distinctions
Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time
Temporal Signal ≠ Event Start
Temporal Signal ≠ Event Completion
Recorded Time ≠ Operational Event Time by Default
Occurrence Time ≠ Recording Time
Recording Time ≠ Accounting Time
Accounting Time ≠ Settlement Time
Multiple Temporal Signals ≠ Temporal Conflict by Default
Temporal Correlation ≠ Temporal Equivalence
Technical Timestamp ≠ Material Temporal Signal by Default
Machine Timestamp Volume ≠ Event Temporal Granularity
One Machine Timestamp ≠ One Event Time
Distributed Execution ≠ Single-System Time Authority

Required Data Field ≠ Legitimate Temporal Certainty
Recorded Precision ≠ Proven Temporal Accuracy
System Preference ≠ Governed Temporal Resolution
Event Time Identification ≠ Event Start Determination
Event Time Identification ≠ Event Completion Determination
Event Time Identification ≠ Event Duration Determination
Event Time Identification ≠ Legal Tax Point
Event Time Identification ≠ Tax Period Determination
Operational Temporal Signal ≠ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Time ------------------------------ 22. Enterprise Application
ETIM can operate as a temporal governance layer across: ERP systems, accounting platforms, payment infrastructure, banking systems, digital marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, logistics systems, manufacturing environments, IoT infrastructure, cloud platforms, distributed systems, digital-asset infrastructure, autonomous agents, robotic systems, machine-to-machine environments, cross-border transaction infrastructure.
A system implementing ETIM does not need to replace existing timestamps.
Instead, ETIM provides a governed methodology for determining what those timestamps represent, how they relate to the bounded event, and whether they are materially relevant to subsequent Event Timing governance. ------------------------------ 23. Real-System Use Case 1 — Global Marketplace Transaction with Conflicting System Times
A customer submits an order to a global digital marketplace at 23:58:42.
The marketplace application records the order at 23:58:44.

Payment authorization occurs at 23:59:51.
The merchant system receives the transaction at 00:00:08.
The merchant accepts it at 00:04:17.
An accounting system creates its record at 00:07:30.
The payment provider settles the transaction the following day.
Several valid timestamps therefore exist around a calendar-day boundary.
A conventional system may simply choose the order date, invoice date, payment date, or accounting date according to whichever database controls the process.
ETIM instead identifies each materially relevant temporal signal, records its source and operational meaning, distinguishes occurrence from recording and settlement, preserves the cross-midnight temporal structure, and identifies any uncertainty or conflict.
The result is a Governed Event Time Signal Set.
ETIM does not decide which timestamp constitutes Event Start or which date constitutes the Legal Tax Point.
Those determinations belong to subsequent governance.
The existence of a timestamp does not grant that timestamp authority over the event. ------------------------------ 24. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Production Event
An autonomous production system receives a manufacturing objective.
An AI scheduler allocates resources at 08:01:12.
A robotic material system begins movement at 08:01:48.
A machine controller initiates production at 08:03:04.
Multiple robots execute thousands of control operations during production.
Inspection systems continuously record sensor measurements.

The manufactured component completes processing at 08:47:19.
Automated quality verification occurs at 08:49:03.
Inventory state changes at 08:50:11.
The autonomous settlement system records resource consumption later.
The environment contains thousands of technically valid timestamps.
ETIM does not treat each machine timestamp as a separate authoritative representation of Event Time.
It identifies which temporal signals materially describe the bounded event, preserves their source and operational context, distinguishes machine-control noise from event-relevant temporal information, and constructs a traceable Governed Event Time Signal Set.
ETSM may subsequently determine which governed temporal condition establishes Event Start.
Machine-generated precision must not be confused with governed temporal meaning. ------------------------------ 25. Canonical Boundary
ETIM governs the identification, contextualization, relevance assessment, correlation, precision, ambiguity, conflict, source association, and traceability of materially relevant temporal signals associated with a Governed Bounded Event.
It does not determine Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, final Event Temporal Order, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, tax liability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
ETIM receives:
TREBS — Governed Bounded Event
ETIM produces:

Governed Event Time Signal Set
The output is handed to:
ETSM — Event Start Module
The canonical handoff is:
TREBS — Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Governed Event Time Signal Set
↓
ETSM — Event Start Module ------------------------------ 26. Canonical Closing Statement
ETIM establishes the governed temporal evidence structure of the event before any individual timestamp is permitted to define when that event begins, ends, or becomes legally significant.
ETIM identifies the times that may describe the event — it does not yet decide which of those times defines its start.

OOF™ Event Temporal Order Module (ETOM)
Event Temporal Order Module (ETOM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Module: ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module
Operational Layer: Event Temporal Order Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Temporal Order
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETOM-005
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Temporal Order Module (ETOM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event is positioned within a relevant temporal sequence after its Event Time, Event Start, Event Completion, and Event Duration have been sufficiently governed.
ETOM establishes whether the governed event occurred before, after, during, concurrently with, overlapping, or within another relevant temporal condition or event, while preserving uncertainty, partial ordering, distributed timing, and supported temporal precision.
Its specific task is:

to establish the governed temporal position of the event relative to relevant events and temporal references without converting temporal sequence into causation, legal priority, tax-period assignment, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
ETOM transforms the completed temporal governance structure of TRETS into a:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
This becomes the canonical TRETS output for downstream Event Location governance. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role
ETIM identifies temporal information legitimately associated with the event.
ETSM establishes its operational start.
ETCM establishes its operational completion.
ETDM establishes its governed duration.
ETOM establishes where that temporally governed event stands relative to other relevant temporal objects.
The principal transition is:
Governed Event Time + Governed Event Start + Governed Event Completion + Governed Event Duration
↓
Governed Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
Temporal order answers questions such as: Did Event A occur before Event B? Did Event B begin while Event A remained active? Did two events occur concurrently? Did their temporal spans overlap? Can only a partial ordering be established? Does available evidence support sequence but not exact timestamps? Are distributed components temporally synchronized? Does uncertainty prevent definitive ordering?
ETOM governs these temporal relationships.
It does not determine why one event followed another.

Temporal Order ≠ Causal Relationship. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow
The TRETS Internal Module Flow is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓
ETSM — Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETOM governs:
Governed Temporal Inputs
↓
Relevant Temporal Reference Identification
↓
Temporal Comparison
↓
Sequence Assessment
↓
Concurrency / Overlap Assessment
↓
Partial-Order Assessment
↓
Temporal Conflict & Uncertainty Governance
↓
Temporal Order Establishment
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
The resulting event proceeds to:
TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space
ETOM governs the operational space in which the temporal position of a Tax-Relevant Event must be established relative to relevant temporal references.
This includes: event-before-event ordering, event-after-event ordering, simultaneous events, concurrent events, overlapping events, nested temporal structures, partially ordered events, distributed event ordering, machine event ordering, autonomous event ordering, sequence uncertainty, sequence conflict, temporal equivalence, temporal precedence, temporal succession, temporal traceability, temporal-order correction.
ETOM does not own semantic Event Relationships governed later by TRERLS.
Its concern is specifically:

when events stand relative to one another. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope
ETOM governs:
1. identification of relevant temporal references; 2. comparison of governed event timing structures; 3. establishment of temporal precedence; 4. establishment of temporal succession; 5. identification of simultaneous temporal positions; 6. governance of concurrency; 7. governance of temporal overlap; 8. representation of nested temporal spans; 9. representation of partial temporal ordering; 10. ordering of distributed events; 11. ordering of machine-generated events; 12. ordering of autonomous-system events; 13. handling of timestamp collisions; 14. temporal-order precision; 15. temporal-order uncertainty; 16. temporal-order conflict; 17. temporal-order correction; 18. temporal-order traceability; 19. construction of the Governed Temporally Situated Event; 20. readiness for TRELS.
ETOM does not determine causation, dependency, semantic Event Relationships, legal priority, tax jurisdiction, tax period, taxability, or tax consequence. ------------------------------ 5. Relevant Temporal Reference Identification
An event cannot be meaningfully ordered against every event in a system.
ETOM must first identify the temporal references relevant to the governed purpose.

Possible temporal references include: another Governed Event, a governed operational milestone, a machine operation, an autonomous action, a transaction event, a physical event, a digital event, a system state transition, an external temporal reference, a governed temporal boundary.
Relevance must be operationally justified.
Available Event ≠ Relevant Temporal Reference by Default. ------------------------------ 6. Temporal Comparison
Once relevant temporal references are identified, ETOM compares their governed temporal structures.
The comparison may use: Governed Event Time, Governed Event Start, Governed Event Completion, Governed Event Duration, supported temporal precision, uncertainty states, temporal intervals.
Temporal comparison must use governed temporal outputs rather than arbitrarily selected raw timestamps.
Timestamp Comparison ≠ Governed Temporal Comparison by Default. ------------------------------ 7. Temporal Precedence
Temporal precedence exists where sufficient governed temporal information establishes that one event occurred before another relevant event or temporal condition.
Conceptually:
Event A
↓
Event B
may establish:
Event A Temporally Precedes Event B
This statement concerns sequence only.
It does not establish: causation, dependency, responsibility, authorization, economic relationship, legal priority, tax consequence.
Temporal Precedence ≠ Causation. ------------------------------ 8. Temporal Succession

Temporal succession establishes that an event follows another event or temporal reference.
For example:
Event A completes
↓
Event B begins
may support:
Event B Temporally Succeeds Event A
However, temporal succession alone does not establish that Event A produced, triggered, authorized, or required Event B.
Temporal Succession ≠ Dependency.
Semantic relationships between events remain governed by:
TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard ------------------------------ 9. Simultaneous Events
Two events may have temporal representations indicating the same temporal position.
However, apparent timestamp equality does not automatically establish true simultaneity.
For example:
Event A: 10:14:23
Event B: 10:14:23
may reflect only one-second recording precision.
The events may actually have occurred hundreds of milliseconds apart.
ETOM must therefore distinguish:
Same Recorded Timestamp
from:
Governed Temporal Simultaneity
Timestamp Equality ≠ Event Simultaneity by Default. ------------------------------ 10. Concurrent Events
Events are concurrent where their governed temporal execution exists during at least part of the same relevant temporal interval while remaining distinct governed events.
For example:
Event A: 10:00–10:20
Event B: 10:05–10:15
Event B occurs during the active temporal span of Event A.
This establishes concurrency.
It does not establish that the events are part of the same economic activity or that one caused the other.

Temporal Concurrency ≠ Event Unity. ------------------------------ 11. Temporal Overlap
Two events overlap where their governed temporal spans intersect.
For example:
Event A: 08:00–11:00
Event B: 10:30–12:00
produces an overlap from:
10:30–11:00
ETOM may preserve: overlap existence, overlap start, overlap completion, overlap duration, overlap precision, overlap uncertainty.
Overlap is a temporal property.
Temporal Overlap ≠ Operational Dependency. ------------------------------ 12. Nested Temporal Structures
One governed event may occur entirely within the temporal span of another event.
For example:
Event A: 08:00–18:00
Event B: 11:00–12:30
Temporal structure:
Event A Start
↓
Event B Start
↓
Event B Completion
↓
Event A Completion
ETOM may represent Event B as temporally nested within Event A.
This does not automatically make Event B a component, child, sub-event, or dependent event of Event A.
Those are separate governance questions.
Temporal Containment ≠ Structural Containment. ------------------------------ 13. Partial Temporal Ordering
Complex systems frequently contain sufficient information to establish some ordering relationships without supporting a complete timeline.
For example:
A occurred before B
and:
C occurred after A
but available information cannot determine whether:
B occurred before C
or:
C occurred before B
ETOM must support:
Partial Temporal Order
rather than fabricate a complete sequence.
A legitimate partial ordering is preferable to false precision.

Incomplete Order ≠ Invalid Temporal Governance. ------------------------------ 14. Temporal Equivalence
Where available governed information cannot distinguish the temporal ordering of two events at the supported precision, ETOM may represent them as temporally equivalent within that precision.
For example:
Event A: approximately 14:00
Event B: approximately 14:00
If no legitimate finer-grained evidence exists, ETOM must not invent an order.
Insufficient Ordering Precision ≠ Permission to Infer Sequence. ------------------------------ 15. Distributed Event Ordering
Distributed systems may produce events across: multiple servers, multiple machines, multiple geographic locations, multiple networks, multiple time zones, asynchronous infrastructure.
Local clocks may not be perfectly synchronized.
Event A may appear earlier than Event B in raw timestamps while system latency or clock drift indicates that the true order is uncertain.
ETOM must distinguish:
Recorded Distributed Order
from:
Governed Distributed Temporal Order
Where deterministic ordering cannot be supported, ETOM should preserve partial or uncertain ordering.
Distributed Timestamp Order ≠ Governed Event Order by Default. ------------------------------ 16. Machine Event Ordering
Machine environments can generate millions of temporal signals.
Sequence numbers, log timestamps, processing timestamps, telemetry timestamps, database commits, message queues, and execution clocks may represent different temporal semantics.

ETOM must not assume that the order in one technical log represents the operational order of governed events.
It must use the governed timing structure established through TRETS.
Log Order ≠ Event Order by Default. ------------------------------ 17. Autonomous Event Ordering
Autonomous systems may initiate and execute multiple events without direct human sequencing.
For example:
Agent Decision A
Machine Action B
External Response C
Agent Replanning D
may occur across overlapping computational and physical timelines.
ETOM governs their temporal positions without determining whether: A caused B, C justified D, the agent possessed authority, a participant bears responsibility.
Those questions belong to other governance spaces.
Autonomous Sequence ≠ Autonomous Authority. ------------------------------ 18. Event Order Across Time Zones
Events may be recorded in different local time zones.
For example:
09:00 Zurich
and:
16:00 Singapore
cannot be ordered merely by comparing displayed local clock values.
ETOM must preserve: original local timestamp, time zone, offset, normalized comparison time where legitimate, normalization method, supported precision.
Normalization may support comparison.
It must not erase the original temporal representation.
Normalized Time ≠ Original Recorded Time. ------------------------------ 19. Clock Synchronization
Distributed environments may use clocks with different synchronization states.

Potential issues include: clock drift, delayed synchronization, incorrect device time, network latency, timestamp buffering, offline operation, asynchronous transmission.
ETOM must preserve the effect of these conditions on temporal ordering.
Clock Precision ≠ Clock Accuracy.
Clock Synchronization ≠ Event Synchronization. ------------------------------ 20. Timestamp Collision
A timestamp collision occurs when multiple events receive the same timestamp despite being distinct and potentially sequential events.
This may occur because of: limited timestamp precision, batch processing, synchronized recording, system architecture, database constraints.
ETOM must not arbitrarily order events solely because a database returns them in a particular sequence.
Database Record Order ≠ Governed Temporal Order. ------------------------------ 21. Temporal Order Precision
Temporal ordering can only be established at the precision supported by governed temporal information.
Possible precision levels may include: date, hour, minute, second, millisecond, microsecond, bounded interval, approximate temporal range.
If two events occur within the same supported temporal interval, their exact internal ordering may remain unresolved.
Technical Precision ≠ Operational Temporal Precision. ------------------------------ 22. Temporal Order Uncertainty
Temporal-order uncertainty exists where the available governed information does not support a definitive sequence.
ETOM may represent:
Order Established

Order Probable
Order Partial
Order Equivalent at Supported Precision
Order Conflicted
Order Unresolved
Uncertainty must remain explicit.
Temporal Uncertainty ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Ordering. ------------------------------ 23. Temporal Order Conflict
Conflict exists where credible temporal sources support incompatible orderings.
For example:
System A indicates:
Event X
↓
Event Y
while System B indicates:
Event Y
↓
Event X
ETOM must evaluate the governed temporal structures and preserve unresolved conflict where legitimate resolution is unavailable.
The system must not select whichever sequence produces a preferred downstream outcome.
Preferred Outcome ≠ Valid Basis for Temporal Ordering. ------------------------------ 24. Temporal Order Correction
New evidence may justify correction of an established temporal order.
Correction must preserve: prior order, revised order, affected events, supporting temporal information, reason for correction, correction authority, version continuity, traceability.
Where correction reveals that Event Start, Completion, Duration, or Time Identification was incorrect, the issue must be routed to the relevant TRETS module.
Temporal Order Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. ------------------------------ 25. Temporal Order and Causation
ETOM establishes sequence.
It does not establish causation.
The observation:
Event A occurred before Event B
does not establish:
Event A caused Event B.
Similarly:
Event B occurred while Event A was active

does not establish:
Event B is part of Event A.
Temporal evidence may later contribute to relationship, investigation, attribution, or accountability analysis.
ETOM itself does not make those determinations.
Before ≠ Because Of. ------------------------------ 26. Temporal Order and Event Relationships
TRERLS later governs Event Relationships, including relevant dependencies, sequences, groupings, merges, and splits at the architecture relationship layer.
ETOM supplies governed temporal structure that such analysis may consume.
ETOM owns:
Temporal Sequence
TRERLS owns:
Governed Event Relationship
Therefore:
Temporal Sequence ≠ Event Relationship by Default. ------------------------------ 27. Temporal Order and Legal Priority
Legal systems may assign significance to event order.
Examples may include: priority, recognition, filing sequence, settlement precedence, contractual effects, statutory timing.
ETOM does not determine those legal consequences.
It establishes governed operational temporal order for downstream interpretation.
Operational Temporal Priority ≠ Legal Priority. ------------------------------ 28. Temporal Order and Tax Determination
Tax systems may interpret event sequence when determining: tax point, tax period, recognition timing, reporting obligation, jurisdictional treatment, transaction treatment.
ETOM does not perform those determinations.
Its output remains jurisdiction-neutral.
Temporal Order ≠ Legal Tax Point.
Temporal Order ≠ Tax Period Determination.

Temporal Order ≠ Taxability Determination. ------------------------------ 29. Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETOM completes the TRETS temporal governance layer.
A Tax-Relevant Event becomes a:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
when its temporal representation is sufficiently governed across: Event Time Identification, Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, Event Temporal Order.
The resulting structure should preserve:
Event Temporal Identity Which temporal signals belong to the event.
Governed Event Start When the event operationally began.
Governed Event Completion When the event operationally completed.
Governed Event Duration How long the event persisted.
Governed Event Temporal Order Where the event stands relative to relevant temporal references.
Temporal Precision How precisely its temporal position is supported.
Temporal Uncertainty What remains uncertain.
Temporal Conflict What remains materially disputed.
Temporal Traceability How the temporal representation can be reconstructed.
The Governed Temporally Situated Event is the canonical output of TRETS. ------------------------------ 30. Temporal Governance States
ETOM may represent temporal-order governance through states including:
Order Ready Required governed temporal inputs exist.
Order Under Governance Relevant temporal comparisons are being evaluated.
Order Established A sufficiently governed sequence exists.
Order Partial Only part of the relevant sequence can be established.

Order Concurrent Events are governed as temporally concurrent.
Order Overlapping Relevant event spans overlap.
Order Equivalent Ordering cannot be differentiated at supported precision.
Order Qualified Order exists subject to material qualification.
Order Conflicted Credible temporal representations conflict.
Order Unresolved No legitimate definitive order can be established.
Order Corrected Previously governed order has been revised.
Temporally Situated TRETS temporal governance is sufficiently complete for downstream Event Location governance. ------------------------------ 31. Governance Requirements
A conforming ETOM implementation should:

1. consume governed temporal outputs from ETIM, ETSM, ETCM, and ETDM; 2. identify relevant temporal references; 3. compare governed temporal structures rather than arbitrary timestamps; 4. establish precedence where supported; 5. establish succession where supported; 6. identify simultaneity only at legitimate precision; 7. identify concurrency; 8. identify temporal overlap; 9. support nested temporal structures; 10. support partial ordering; 11. support distributed-system ordering; 12. support machine-generated event ordering; 13. support autonomous-system event ordering; 14. preserve original time-zone representations; 15. support legitimate temporal normalization; 16. account for clock synchronization limitations; 17. govern timestamp collisions; 18. preserve temporal-order precision; 19. preserve uncertainty; 20. preserve conflict; 21. preserve correction history; 22. maintain traceability; 23. prevent sequence from being treated as causation; 24. prevent temporal order from becoming legal priority; 25. prevent temporal order from becoming Tax Period or Legal Tax Point determination; 26. produce a Governed Temporally Situated Event suitable for TRELS.
------------------------------ 32. Governance Logic
The minimum ETOM governance logic is:
IF relevant events possess sufficiently governed temporal structures,
THEN their temporal positions may be compared.
IF Event A completes before Event B begins,
THEN temporal precedence may be established.
IF Event B follows Event A,

THEN succession may be established without inferring dependency.
IF governed temporal spans intersect,
THEN temporal overlap may be established.
IF distinct events remain active during the same temporal interval,
THEN concurrency may be established.
IF one event occurs entirely inside another event's temporal span,
THEN temporal containment may be represented without inferring structural containment.
IF only some ordering relationships can be supported,
THEN ETOM must preserve a partial order.
IF timestamps are equal only because of limited precision,
THEN simultaneity must not be assumed.
IF distributed clocks conflict,
THEN raw timestamp order must not automatically determine governed order.
IF sequence remains uncertain,
THEN uncertainty must remain explicit.
IF credible temporal evidence conflicts,
THEN conflict must not be resolved according to preferred downstream outcome.
IF temporal order changes because upstream temporal governance changes,
THEN ETOM must preserve correction history and reconstruct the order.
IF temporal sequence is established,
THEN causation must remain a separate governance question.
IF a jurisdiction assigns legal significance to sequence,
THEN that determination remains outside ETOM. ------------------------------ 33. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ETOM implementation should support:
1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the event under temporal-order governance.

2. Temporal Governance Structure Relevant outputs from ETIM, ETSM, ETCM, and ETDM.
3. Temporal Reference Set Relevant events or temporal conditions used for comparison.
4. Temporal Comparison Record Governed comparison between temporal structures.
5. Precedence State Whether the event precedes another reference.
6. Succession State Whether the event succeeds another reference.
7. Simultaneity State Whether simultaneity is legitimately supported.
8. Concurrency State Whether events coexist temporally.
9. Overlap State Whether event spans overlap.
10. Temporal Containment State Whether one temporal span lies within another.
11. Partial Order Structure Supported ordering where complete sequence cannot be established.
12. Distributed Order Record Ordering across distributed systems.
13. Machine Order Record Ordering derived from machine-generated temporal structures.
14. Autonomous Order Record Ordering involving autonomous-system events.
15. Temporal Precision Record Precision at which ordering is supported.
16. Temporal Uncertainty State Known uncertainty affecting order.
17. Temporal Conflict State Known incompatible order representations.
18. Temporal Correction History Governed revisions to order.
19. Temporal Traceability Record Reconstructable basis for the order.
20. Governed Event Temporal Order Principal ETOM module result.
21. Governed Temporally Situated Event Canonical TRETS output.

22. TRELS Handoff State Readiness for Event Location governance. ------------------------------ 34. Governance Outputs
ETOM may produce: Relevant Temporal Reference Set Temporal Comparison Record Temporal Precedence Record Temporal Succession Record Temporal Simultaneity State Temporal Concurrency Record Temporal Overlap Record Temporal Containment Record Partial Temporal Order Structure Distributed Temporal Order Record Machine Temporal Order Record Autonomous Temporal Order Record Temporal Precision Record Temporal Uncertainty Indicator Temporal Conflict Indicator Temporal Correction Record Temporal Traceability Record Governed Event Temporal Order TRELS Readiness State
The principal TRETS output is:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
This output proceeds to:
TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------ 35. Critical Distinctions
Temporal Order ≠ Causal Relationship
Available Event ≠ Relevant Temporal Reference by Default
Timestamp Comparison ≠ Governed Temporal Comparison by Default
Temporal Precedence ≠ Causation
Temporal Succession ≠ Dependency
Timestamp Equality ≠ Event Simultaneity by Default
Temporal Concurrency ≠ Event Unity
Temporal Overlap ≠ Operational Dependency
Temporal Containment ≠ Structural Containment
Incomplete Order ≠ Invalid Temporal Governance
Insufficient Ordering Precision ≠ Permission to Infer Sequence
Distributed Timestamp Order ≠ Governed Event Order by Default
Log Order ≠ Event Order by Default

Autonomous Sequence ≠ Autonomous Authority
Normalized Time ≠ Original Recorded Time
Clock Precision ≠ Clock Accuracy
Clock Synchronization ≠ Event Synchronization
Database Record Order ≠ Governed Temporal Order
Technical Precision ≠ Operational Temporal Precision
Temporal Uncertainty ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Ordering
Preferred Outcome ≠ Valid Basis for Temporal Ordering
Temporal Order Correction ≠ Historical Erasure
Before ≠ Because Of
Temporal Sequence ≠ Event Relationship by Default
Operational Temporal Priority ≠ Legal Priority
Temporal Order ≠ Legal Tax Point
Temporal Order ≠ Tax Period Determination
Temporal Order ≠ Taxability Determination
Governed Temporally Situated Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event ------------------------------ 36. Enterprise Application
ETOM can support temporal-order governance across: ERP systems, commerce platforms, financial infrastructure, payment systems, banking infrastructure, digital marketplaces, logistics networks, supply chains, manufacturing systems, industrial automation, robotics, AI agents, autonomous systems, machine-to-machine environments, IoT networks, distributed computing, cloud infrastructure, digital asset systems, cross-border operations, accounting systems, tax technology infrastructure.

ETOM provides a common governed temporal ordering layer for environments in which operational events may occur rapidly, concurrently, asynchronously, or across multiple systems and jurisdictions. ------------------------------ 37. Real-System Use Case 1 — Global Marketplace with Concurrent Commercial Events
A global marketplace records a sequence involving: customer order submission, payment authorization, seller acceptance, inventory reservation, invoice generation, shipment release, payment settlement.
The systems operate across different countries and time zones.
The order is recorded at:
10:00:02
Payment authorization begins at:
10:00:03
Inventory reservation begins at:
10:00:03
Seller acceptance is recorded at:
10:00:05
Payment authorization completes at:
10:00:06
Inventory reservation completes at:
10:00:07
Invoice generation occurs at:
10:00:08
A simple database listing may present these records sequentially.
ETOM establishes that payment authorization and inventory reservation were partially concurrent rather than mechanically treating one as preceding the other.
It also preserves that seller acceptance occurred during both operational processes.
ETOM does not infer that payment authorization caused seller acceptance or that invoice generation represents the legal tax point.
It produces a governed temporal sequence that downstream relationship and jurisdictional tax systems may interpret independently.

The order in which systems record commercial activity must not silently become the legal meaning of that activity. ------------------------------ 38. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Network with Unsynchronized Machine Clocks
An autonomous industrial network contains three machines and an AI orchestration agent.
Machine A records an operational event at:
14:22:10.480
Machine B records a response at:
14:22:10.320
The orchestration agent records its instruction at:
14:22:10.410
Raw timestamps appear to indicate:
Machine B Response
↓
Agent Instruction
↓
Machine A Event
However, governance data shows: Machine A clock is synchronized; the orchestration agent clock is 40 milliseconds behind; Machine B clock is approximately 240 milliseconds behind; network transmission introduces variable latency.
The raw timestamp sequence therefore cannot legitimately establish operational order.
ETOM normalizes and qualifies the available temporal information while preserving the original timestamps and synchronization uncertainty.
Where evidence supports only:
Machine A Event
↓
Agent Processing
↓
Machine B Response
within bounded temporal ranges, ETOM records that governed sequence.
Where exact micro-ordering remains unsupported, it remains unresolved.
ETOM does not infer responsibility, causation, authority, or liability from the sequence.

The resulting structure can be consumed by downstream governance architectures without corrupting operational reality through misleading timestamp precision.
In distributed autonomous systems, the earliest timestamp is not necessarily the earliest event. ------------------------------ 39. Canonical Boundary
ETOM governs the temporal ordering of the Tax-Relevant Event relative to relevant governed temporal references after Event Time Identification, Event Start, Event Completion, and Event Duration have been established through TRETS.
It owns: temporal comparison, temporal precedence, temporal succession, simultaneity, concurrency, overlap, temporal containment, partial ordering, distributed ordering, machine ordering, autonomous ordering, temporal-order precision, temporal-order uncertainty, temporal-order conflict, temporal-order correction, temporal-order traceability, construction of the Governed Temporally Situated Event.
ETOM does not own Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, semantic Event Relationships, causation, dependency, attribution, responsibility, accountability, legal priority, Tax Jurisdiction, Taxpayer determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, tax liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
ETOM receives:
ETDM — Governed Event Duration
together with the governed temporal structure produced by:
ETIM
↓
ETSM
↓
ETCM
↓
ETDM

ETOM produces:
Governed Event Temporal Order
and completes the Parent Standard output:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
The canonical handoff is:
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓
ETSM — Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
↓
TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------ 40. Canonical Closing Statement
ETOM completes the temporal governance of the Tax-Relevant Event by establishing where the event stands in operational time relative to relevant events and temporal references while preserving uncertainty, concurrency, distributed timing, and the boundary between sequence and meaning.
Temporal order can establish what came before, after, during, or alongside an event. It cannot, by itself, establish why it happened, what caused it, or what legal consequence follows.
TRETS governs when the event occurred as governed operational reality — not when tax law decides that the event becomes taxable.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
