OOF™ Event Start Module (ETSM)
Event Start Module (ETSM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Module: ETSM — Event Start Module
Operational Layer: Event Start Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Event Start
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETSM-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Event Start Module (ETSM) governs how the operational beginning of a Governed Bounded Event is determined from the Governed Event Time Signal Set by identifying, evaluating, qualifying, and establishing the temporal condition at which the governed event legitimately begins as the event under examination.
ETSM distinguishes the operational beginning of the governed event from earlier preparatory activity, system initialization, authorization, scheduling, communication, recording, technical activation, contractual milestones, accounting recognition, and jurisdiction-specific legal or taxation points that may occur before, at, or after the event begins.
Its specific task is:

to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Start without allowing technical timestamps, administrative conventions, contractual dates, accounting treatment, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine the operational beginning of the governed event.
ETSM governs when the bounded event begins as an operational event.
It does not determine when that event is legally recognized for taxation. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role
ETIM identifies and structures the materially relevant temporal signals associated with the Governed Bounded Event.
ETSM determines which temporal condition legitimately establishes the beginning of that event.
The transition governed by ETSM is:
Governed Event Time Signal Set
↓
Governed Event Start
This requires more than selecting the earliest available timestamp.
The earliest recorded activity may represent: preparation, authorization, scheduling, system initialization, resource reservation, communication, preliminary machine activity, data creation, contractual formation, administrative processing.
None necessarily establishes that the governed event itself has begun.
ETSM therefore determines the operational threshold separating activity preceding the event from activity constituting the event.
Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow
The TRETS Internal Module Flow is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
ETIM — Event Time Identification
↓
ETSM — Event Start
↓

ETCM — Event Completion
↓
ETDM — Event Duration
↓
ETOM — Event Temporal Order
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
ETSM governs:
Governed Event Time Signal Set
↓
Start Candidate Identification
↓
Start Condition Assessment
↓
Pre-Event Activity Differentiation
↓
Start Qualification
↓
Start Ambiguity / Conflict Handling
↓
Governed Event Start
↓
ETCM
ETSM receives temporal evidence from ETIM.
It does not recreate the temporal signal inventory.
It determines which governed temporal condition establishes Event Start. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space
ETSM governs the operational space in which the beginning of the bounded event must be distinguished from surrounding temporal activity.
This space includes: candidate start signals, candidate start conditions, operational initiation, first constitutive event activity, preparatory activity, authorization activity, scheduling, resource allocation, system initialization, machine activation, autonomous-system initiation, transaction initiation, service activation, physical commencement, digital commencement, distributed commencement, conditional commencement, phased commencement, approximate start conditions, conflicting start signals, start uncertainty, start traceability.
The presence of earlier activity does not automatically extend the governed event backward to that activity. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope
ETSM governs:

1. identification of candidate Event Start signals; 2. assessment of candidate start conditions; 3. distinction between pre-event activity and constitutive event activity; 4. determination of the operational commencement threshold; 5. evaluation of physical, digital, transactional, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous starts; 6. treatment of multiple possible start signals; 7. treatment of phased or distributed commencement; 8. detection of start ambiguity; 9. detection of conflicting start representations; 10. preservation of start uncertainty where necessary; 11. establishment of Event Start precision; 12. maintenance of traceability to ETIM temporal signals; 13. production of the Governed Event Start for ETCM.
ETSM does not determine Event Completion, Event Duration, final Event Temporal Order, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ 5. Event Start Candidate Identification
ETSM begins by identifying temporal signals that could plausibly establish Event Start.
Candidate signals may include: first material operational action, physical commencement, transaction execution, service activation, transfer initiation, machine execution, autonomous execution, first constitutive state transition, digital process commencement, first material performance, first governed event component entering execution.
Candidate identification does not establish Event Start.

Each candidate must be evaluated against the governed structure of the bounded event.
Start Candidate ≠ Governed Event Start. ------------------------------ 6. Constitutive Event Activity
A legitimate Event Start should correspond to a temporal condition at which the governed event begins to exist operationally as the event defined by its governed structure.
ETSM therefore distinguishes constitutive activity from activity merely associated with the event.
Constitutive activity materially participates in the event's operational realization.
Associated activity may support, prepare, authorize, document, or anticipate the event without itself constituting commencement.
The relevant question is not:
What happened first?
The relevant question is:
When did the governed event begin to occur as the event under examination?
First Related Activity ≠ First Constitutive Event Activity. ------------------------------ 7. Pre-Event Activity Differentiation
Many operational processes contain substantial activity before the governed event begins.
Examples include: quotation, negotiation, scheduling, reservation, planning, approval, authorization, resource allocation, software initialization, machine warm-up, preliminary data exchange, contract preparation, risk screening.
ETSM must prevent such activity from automatically extending Event Start backward.
However, activity that appears preparatory in one event model may be constitutive in another.

The determination must therefore remain tied to the Governed Bounded Event received from TREBS.
Event Association ≠ Event Commencement. ------------------------------ 8. Authorization vs. Execution
Authorization frequently occurs before operational execution.
A payment may be authorized before settlement.
A machine may receive authorization before physical operation.
An autonomous agent may receive permission before executing an action.
A service may be approved before activation.
ETSM preserves this distinction.
Authorization may constitute Event Start only where the governed event itself is legitimately defined around the authorization activity.
Otherwise:
Authorization Time ≠ Event Start by Default.
Likewise:
Permission ≠ Execution. ------------------------------ 9. System Activation vs. Event Start
Technical systems often activate before the governed event begins.
Examples include: application session creation, API authentication, device wake-up, machine initialization, database transaction creation, cloud resource provisioning, workflow initialization.
Such timestamps may be operationally relevant without constituting Event Start.
ETSM must prevent technical architecture from redefining event reality.
System Activation ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 10. Transactional Event Start
Transactional environments may contain several plausible commencement signals.
For example:
Order Creation
↓
Order Submission
↓
Merchant Acceptance
↓

Payment Authorization
↓
Execution
↓
Confirmation
The correct operational start depends on the structure of the Governed Bounded Event.
ETSM does not impose a universal rule that every transaction begins with order creation, acceptance, payment, or settlement.
Instead, it determines the start condition from the governed event itself.
Transaction Record Creation ≠ Transaction Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 11. Physical Event Start
Physical events may begin through observable operational activity.
Examples include: movement, production commencement, loading, construction activity, physical transfer, machine execution, delivery commencement, resource transformation.
Where physical commencement is relevant, ETSM must associate the start determination with sufficient supporting temporal signals.
Physical events may nevertheless contain preparatory physical activity that does not belong to the governed event.
Physical Activity ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 12. Digital Event Start
Digital events may begin without a physical action.
Potential start conditions include: execution of a digital service, transfer initiation, access activation, processing commencement, digital delivery, deployment, state transition, autonomous instruction execution.
ETSM evaluates when the governed digital event actually begins rather than automatically using the first timestamp generated by the technical system.

First Digital Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 13. Distributed Event Start
A governed event may begin across multiple systems or locations.
There may therefore be no single perfectly synchronized timestamp representing commencement.
ETSM may need to establish: one sufficiently supported start timestamp, a bounded start interval, a start condition represented across multiple correlated signals, an approximate operational start, a distributed commencement state.
The methodology must preserve the temporal precision actually supported by the evidence.
Distributed Commencement ≠ Artificial Single-Time Precision. ------------------------------ 14. Machine and Autonomous Event Start
Autonomous systems introduce additional complexity because planning, decision, authorization, communication, and execution may occur without direct human intervention.
A sequence may be:
Objective Received
↓
Autonomous Analysis
↓
Decision
↓
Resource Reservation
↓
Command
↓
Machine Execution
The first autonomous computation does not necessarily constitute Event Start.
Nor does the first machine-generated timestamp.
ETSM identifies the point at which the governed autonomous or machine-mediated event begins operationally.
Autonomous Decision ≠ Event Start by Default.
Machine Command ≠ Machine Execution. ------------------------------ 15. Conditional Event Start
Some events begin only when specified operational conditions become true.

A process may be initialized earlier but remain inactive until: acceptance occurs, resources become available, required input arrives, physical execution begins, threshold conditions are reached, service activation occurs.
ETSM may therefore represent Event Start through a governed condition rather than merely selecting a pre-existing timestamp field.
Process Creation ≠ Operational Commencement. ------------------------------ 16. Phased Event Start
Some bounded events begin through several tightly connected actions rather than one instantaneous transition.
Where operational reality does not support a single precise start moment, ETSM may represent commencement as a governed temporal interval or composite start condition.
This should occur only when supported by the event structure and temporal evidence.
ETSM must not manufacture precision where operational reality is genuinely gradual.
Temporal Precision Requirement ≠ Operational Reality. ------------------------------ 17. Start Ambiguity
Start ambiguity exists where available governed information supports more than one plausible Event Start and available evidence does not sufficiently justify selection.
ETSM should preserve such ambiguity explicitly.
Possible causes include: incomplete logs, contradictory records, uncertain event formation, asynchronous systems, delayed recording, approximate physical observations, insufficient machine telemetry, competing operational interpretations.

An unresolved start should not be silently converted into an exact timestamp.
Required Start Field ≠ Governed Start Certainty. ------------------------------ 18. Start Conflict
Start conflict exists when materially relevant temporal evidence supports incompatible commencement representations.
ETSM must identify and preserve the conflict until sufficient governance can establish a legitimate resolution.
Resolution should be based on operational event structure and evidence rather than system hierarchy alone.
A preferred ERP timestamp does not automatically override contradictory physical or digital evidence.
System Authority ≠ Event-Time Authority by Default. ------------------------------ 19. Event Start Precision
Event Start may legitimately be represented at different precision levels.
Examples include: exact timestamp, second, minute, hour, date, bounded interval, approximate period, sequence-relative start.
The selected precision must not exceed what the governed temporal evidence supports.
Timestamp Precision ≠ Temporal Certainty. ------------------------------ 20. Event Start States
ETSM may represent Event Start governance through states such as:
Start Candidate A temporal signal or condition may represent Event Start.
Start Qualified The candidate is sufficiently supported as constitutive commencement.
Start Established A legitimate operational Event Start has been established.
Start Approximate Commencement is sufficiently known but not precisely timestamped.

Start Ambiguous Multiple plausible commencement representations remain.
Start Conflicted Material evidence supports incompatible start determinations.
Start Insufficient Available information is inadequate for reliable determination.
Start Unresolved Further governance or evidence is required.
Start Established ≠ Legal Tax Point Established. ------------------------------ 21. Governance Requirements
A conforming ETSM implementation should:
1. consume the Governed Event Time Signal Set from ETIM; 2. identify plausible Event Start candidates; 3. evaluate start candidates against the Governed Bounded Event; 4. distinguish preparatory activity from constitutive event activity; 5. distinguish authorization from execution where relevant; 6. distinguish technical activation from operational commencement; 7. support physical, digital, distributed, transactional, machine-generated, and autonomous events; 8. preserve ambiguity and conflict; 9. prevent artificial temporal precision; 10. maintain traceability to supporting temporal signals; 11. avoid jurisdiction-specific tax assumptions; 12. avoid treating accounting, contractual, technical, or administrative dates as authoritative by default; 13. establish a Governed Event Start suitable for Event Completion governance.
------------------------------ 22. Governance Logic
The minimum ETSM governance logic is:
IF one or more temporal signals plausibly represent commencement,
THEN they must be evaluated as Event Start candidates.

IF a signal represents only preparatory or supporting activity,
THEN it must not establish Event Start unless that activity is constitutive of the Governed Bounded Event.
IF authorization precedes execution,
THEN authorization must not automatically establish Event Start.
IF system initialization precedes operational commencement,
THEN initialization must remain distinct from Event Start.
IF multiple start candidates are compatible,
THEN they may support one governed commencement representation.
IF multiple start candidates materially conflict,
THEN the conflict must remain explicit until sufficiently resolved.
IF precise commencement cannot be legitimately established,
THEN an approximate time or bounded interval must be preserved where appropriate.
IF a jurisdiction-specific tax rule uses a different legal date,
THEN that legal date must not retroactively redefine the operational Event Start governed by ETSM. ------------------------------ 23. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ETSM implementation should support:
1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event.
2. Temporal Signal Set Reference Reference to ETIM output.
3. Start Candidate Identifier Unique reference for each candidate commencement signal or condition.
4. Start Candidate Type Physical, digital, transactional, machine, autonomous, conditional, distributed, or other.
5. Start Condition Operational condition represented by the candidate.

6. Constitutive Activity Assessment Whether the candidate represents actual commencement of the governed event.
7. Pre-Event Activity Indicator Whether preceding activity remains outside Event Start.
8. Start Precision Supported temporal precision.
9. Start Evidence / Traceability Reference Links to supporting temporal signals and operational records.
10. Ambiguity / Conflict State Explicit representation of unresolved start issues.
11. Start Governance State Candidate, qualified, established, approximate, ambiguous, conflicted, insufficient, or unresolved.
12. Governed Event Start The established operational commencement representation.
13. Handoff State Readiness for ETCM. ------------------------------ 24. Governance Outputs
ETSM may produce: Governed Event Start Event Start Candidate Set Start Condition Record Constitutive Activity Assessment Pre-Event Activity Record Start Qualification Record Start Precision Record Start Ambiguity Indicator Start Conflict Indicator Start Insufficiency Indicator Distributed Start Representation Machine / Autonomous Start Representation Event Start Traceability Record Event Completion Governance Readiness State
The principal output is:
Governed Event Start
This output proceeds to:
ETCM — Event Completion Module ------------------------------ 25. Critical Distinctions
Temporal Signal ≠ Event Start
Start Candidate ≠ Governed Event Start
Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default
First Related Activity ≠ First Constitutive Event Activity

Event Association ≠ Event Commencement
Preparation ≠ Event Start
Authorization Time ≠ Event Start by Default
Permission ≠ Execution
System Activation ≠ Event Start by Default
Transaction Record Creation ≠ Transaction Event Start by Default
Physical Activity ≠ Event Start by Default
First Digital Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Start by Default
Autonomous Decision ≠ Event Start by Default
Machine Command ≠ Machine Execution
Process Creation ≠ Operational Commencement
Distributed Commencement ≠ Artificial Single-Time Precision
Timestamp Precision ≠ Temporal Certainty
Required Start Field ≠ Governed Start Certainty
System Authority ≠ Event-Time Authority by Default
Event Start ≠ Event Completion
Event Start ≠ Event Duration
Event Start ≠ Final Temporal Order
Operational Event Start ≠ Legal Tax Point
Event Start ≠ Tax Period Determination
Event Start ≠ Tax Liability Determination ------------------------------ 26. Enterprise Application
ETSM can support operational event governance across: ERP systems, banking infrastructure, payment systems, digital marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, SaaS environments, logistics networks, manufacturing systems, IoT infrastructure, autonomous agents, robotics, machine-to-machine systems, distributed computing environments, digital-asset infrastructure, cross-border transaction platforms, automated accounting and tax infrastructure.

ETSM enables these systems to preserve one governed operational Event Start independently of how downstream accounting, regulatory, contractual, or jurisdiction-specific taxation systems subsequently interpret the event. ------------------------------ 27. Real-System Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Service
A business customer requests a cloud service at 23:56.
The platform records the order at 23:57.
Payment authorization occurs at 23:59.
The provider accepts the request at 00:01.
Cloud resources are provisioned at 00:03.
The service becomes operationally available at 00:04.
The invoice is generated at 00:06.
Payment settles the following day.
Several systems could independently claim that their timestamp represents the beginning of the transaction.
ETSM does not automatically choose the earliest timestamp, invoice date, payment authorization, or settlement date.
It evaluates the Governed Bounded Event and the temporal signals produced by ETIM to determine which condition represents the actual commencement of the event under governance.
Where the governed event concerns operational delivery of the digital service, service activation may provide the constitutive commencement condition even though multiple related activities occurred earlier.
The resulting Governed Event Start remains distinct from any jurisdiction-specific rule determining when a taxable supply legally occurs.

Operational commencement must be established from the event itself — not inherited from whichever downstream system needs a date. ------------------------------ 28. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Operation
An AI production controller receives an objective at 07:52.
It begins planning at 07:53.
Resources are reserved at 07:56.
Production authorization is issued at 08:00.
A robotic handling system moves raw material at 08:02.
The production machine begins material transformation at 08:04.
Quality sensors and supporting robots subsequently perform thousands of machine operations.
A naive implementation could define Event Start using the objective receipt, AI planning, authorization, first robotic movement, or first machine-control timestamp.
ETSM evaluates which activity constitutes commencement of the Governed Bounded Event.
If the bounded event represents the manufacturing transformation itself, preliminary AI planning and resource allocation remain pre-event activities, while commencement of material transformation may establish the legitimate operational start.
ETSM records that determination without asserting when any jurisdiction considers the resulting activity legally taxable.
Autonomous preparation can precede the event without becoming the event. ------------------------------ 29. Canonical Boundary

ETSM governs the identification, assessment, qualification, establishment, precision, ambiguity, conflict, and traceability of the operational commencement of a Governed Bounded Event using the Governed Event Time Signal Set produced by ETIM.
It does not determine Event Completion, Event Duration, final Event Temporal Order, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, tax liability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
ETSM receives:
ETIM — Governed Event Time Signal Set
ETSM produces:
Governed Event Start
The output is handed to:
ETCM — Event Completion Module
The canonical handoff is:
ETIM — Governed Event Time Signal Set
↓
ETSM — Governed Event Start
↓
ETCM — Event Completion Module ------------------------------ 30. Canonical Closing Statement
ETSM establishes when the governed event begins in operational reality before accounting systems, legal frameworks, or taxation regimes determine what that beginning means for their own purposes.
ETSM determines when the event begins — not when a jurisdiction decides that tax begins.

chunks.text:
OOF™ Governance Architecture Implementation
Governance Architecture Implementation
Implementing OOF® Architectures Across AI, Software and Enterprise Systems
OOF® governance architectures can be translated from methodological structures into operational capabilities that integrate with existing AI, software, data, and enterprise environments.
Organizations do not need to replace their existing systems.
OOF® architectures can operate as a methodological governance layer that structures how operational data is identified, evaluated, validated, connected, and transformed into governed outputs.
Enterprise Systems / AI / Operational Data
↓
OOF® Governance Architecture Layer
↓
Selected Governance Architectures
↓
Governance Standards & Modules
↓
Governed Analysis
↓
Operational Output
From Architecture to Operational Capability
An OOF® architecture defines a distinct governable space.
For implementation, relevant architectures can be selected and composed according to the operational problem being addressed.
This allows organizations to implement specific governance capabilities without requiring every OOF® architecture to be deployed.
Operational Problem
↓
Required Governance Capabilities
↓
Relevant OOF® Architectures
↓
Software Integration
↓
Governed Operational Output
The architecture provides the methodological structure.
The organization's existing systems provide operational data.
AI and software can perform analysis within that governed structure.

Six Architecture Implementation Use Cases
The following examples illustrate how the same OOF® methodological infrastructure can support distinct economic and organizational decisions without reducing value to a single financial number.
1. Insurance → Insurable Value Reality
An insurer may need to understand whether the value presented by an organization corresponds to its actual operational capability, evidence, dependencies, and current value state.
A governance implementation could combine relevant OOF® architectures to examine:
Declared Organizational Value
↓
Value Origin & Identity
↓
Operational Reality
↓
Current Value State
↓
Evidence
↓
Critical Dependencies
↓
Value Degradation Exposure
↓
Restoration Capacity
↓
Validation
↓
Insurable Value Reality
The resulting output can provide a structured view of:
Declared Value
Operationally Supported Value
Active Value
Value at Risk
Critical Dependencies
Evidence State
Restoration Capacity
Validation State
This does not replace actuarial valuation, underwriting judgment, or regulated insurance processes.
It provides an additional methodological governance layer for understanding the operational reality supporting the value being assessed.
2. Investor → Investment Value Reality
Financial statements and management presentations can describe what an organization reports.
Investors may additionally need to understand what the organization can actually sustain operationally.
OOF® architectures can structure that assessment across:

Reported Enterprise Value
↓
Value Origin
↓
Operational Capability
↓
Actual Performance
↓
Evidence
↓
Dependencies
↓
Value Sustainability
↓
Degradation Exposure
↓
Scenario Simulation
↓
Investment Value Reality
The assessment can distinguish between:
Reported Performance
Operational Performance
Evidence-Supported Capability
Dependency-Concentrated Value
Sustainable Value
Value at Risk
Potential Value Degradation
Restoration Potential
Alternative operational conditions can then be evaluated through governed simulation.
Examples may include:
Loss of a Critical Customer
Production Capacity Reduction
Supply-Chain Disruption
Loss of Critical Infrastructure
Automation Investment
AI Deployment
Rapid Expansion
Operational Recovery
The objective is not to replace conventional financial valuation.
The objective is to provide a structured methodology for determining what operational reality exists beneath the reported value and performance of an organization.
3. Bank → Lending Value & Continuity
A bank evaluating a company may need to understand more than historical financial statements, collateral values, and projected cash flows. It may also need a structured view of whether the operational capabilities supporting repayment can continue under changing conditions.
Borrower Profile
↓
Value-Producing Capabilities
↓
Operational Performance
↓
Critical Dependencies
↓
Continuity Capacity
↓
Degradation Exposure
↓
Evidence & Validation
↓
Lending Value & Continuity

The governed output can support a structured view of operationally supported value, dependency concentration, continuity exposure, evidence strength, recovery capacity, and material conditions that could affect the organization's ability to sustain performance.
This capability complements conventional credit analysis rather than replacing regulated lending decisions or financial risk models.
4. M&A → Acquisition Value Reality
An acquisition target may contain value that is visible in financial reporting but dependent on capabilities, people, customers, infrastructure, intellectual assets, relationships, or operational conditions that may change after ownership transfers.
Reported Acquisition Value
↓
Value Origin & Identity
↓
Operationally Supported Value
↓
Critical Dependencies
↓
Transferability
↓
Post-Acquisition Continuity
↓
Scenario Simulation
↓
Acquisition Value Reality
This can help distinguish value that is owned, transferable and sustainable from value that depends heavily on specific employees, customers, suppliers, infrastructure, permissions, relationships, or operating conditions.
The objective is to provide an additional methodological layer for due diligence and post-acquisition value continuity analysis.
5. Management → Enterprise Value Intelligence
Management may need to understand where value actually exists across the organization, what produces it, what sustains it, what is degrading, and where future value could emerge.
Organization
↓

Value Objects & Capabilities
↓
Value Origin
↓
Operational Contribution
↓
Current Value State
↓
Dependencies & Degradation Signals
↓
Development / Restoration Potential
↓
Enterprise Value Intelligence
This creates a governed view across physical assets, digital assets, organizational capabilities, processes, relationships, knowledge, infrastructure, and other identifiable sources of enterprise value.
Management can use this layer to understand not merely how much the organization reports, but where operational value is produced, how it changes, and what threatens or strengthens it.
6. Organization → Workforce Value Intelligence
Employees are not interchangeable cost units. Different roles and individuals can contribute different forms of operational value through capability, knowledge, productivity, quality, continuity, problem solving, relationships, specialization, and organizational dependency.
OOF® architectures can support a governed assessment of role and workforce contribution without reducing a person to a monetary score.
Role & Responsibility
↓
Capability & Competence
↓
Operational Contribution
↓
Performance Evidence
↓
Knowledge & Dependency
↓
Cost of Capability
↓
Replacement / Transition Exposure
↓
Continuity Impact
↓
Workforce Value Intelligence

The resulting view could identify dimensions such as operational contribution, capability scarcity, knowledge concentration, replacement difficulty, transition time, continuity impact, development potential, and the organizational cost of losing or replacing a capability.
For example, replacing an experienced specialist may involve recruitment cost, onboarding time, training, certification, temporary productivity loss, knowledge transfer, quality exposure, and operational disruption. These effects can be evaluated as separate governed dimensions rather than collapsed into an unsupported estimate of a person's monetary value.
The purpose is not to assign a financial price to a human being or automate employment decisions. It is to help organizations understand the operational value, dependencies, continuity requirements, and development potential associated with their workforce capabilities.
Integration Model
OOF® architectures are designed to complement existing technology environments.
ERP / Financial Systems / Operational Systems / Data Platforms / AI
↓
OOF® Governance Layer
↓
Architecture Composition
↓
Governed Analysis
↓
Customer Application / Dashboard / Decision System
This creates a pathway from governance architecture to practical software capability without requiring the underlying enterprise infrastructure to be replaced.
One Infrastructure — Multiple Applications
The same methodological infrastructure can support different operational objectives.

Insurance Insurable Value Reality
Investment Investment Value Reality
Banking Lending Value & Continuity
M&A Acquisition Value Reality
Enterprise Management Enterprise Value Intelligence
Workforce & Organization Workforce Value Intelligence
AI Systems Governed Decision & Operational Reality Analysis
The application changes.
The underlying principle remains:
Identify the relevant governance space, apply the appropriate architecture, evaluate the operational reality, and produce a governed output.
Architecture on Demand
Where an existing OOF® architecture can address the required governance problem, it can provide the methodological foundation for implementation.
Where the operational environment requires a different governance configuration, Architecture on Demand can determine the appropriate architecture composition for the required capability.
Governance Architecture Implementation connects methodological architecture with operational use — enabling OOF® architectures to move from reference structures toward practical governance capabilities across AI, software, and enterprise systems.

Type: Core Module

Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-ORIM-001

Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs the identification and establishment of a distinguishable occurrence from the signals, records, messages, state changes, transactions, instructions, observations, or other representations through which real-world, digital, operational, or machine activity becomes observable.
ORIM determines whether available observations provide a sufficient basis to establish that an occurrence exists as a distinct governance object for subsequent recognition processing.
Its task is specific:

to distinguish a governable occurrence from the technical signals and records through which it is observed without determining whether that occurrence is tax-relevant, how it should be formed into an event, or whether any tax is legally due.
Operational Role
Modern systems rarely present economic reality as clean, pre-defined events.
They produce records.
A payment system produces authorization and settlement messages.
An ERP creates transaction entries.
A marketplace creates orders and status changes.
An API produces requests and responses.
A robot generates commands and execution records.
A sensor generates observations.
An autonomous agent may create hundreds of machine interactions while pursuing one operational objective.
Before TREGA™ can ask whether any of this activity may be relevant to taxation analysis, it requires a more basic determination:
What occurrence can legitimately be distinguished from these observations?
ORIM performs this first recognition function.
Internal Flow
Governed Context + Observable Signals / Records
↓
Observation Qualification
↓
Occurrence Candidate Identification
↓
Signal Association / Differentiation
↓
Duplicate and Noise Screening
↓
Occurrence Distinguishability Assessment
↓
Recognized Occurrence
The principal output is:
Recognized Occurrence
This output proceeds to ERSM — Event Relevance Screening Module.
Operational Space
ORIM governs the space between:
observable operational or digital representations
and

a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence capable of entering further TRERS governance.
Its operational space includes: observation qualification; signal interpretation; record association; occurrence candidate identification; occurrence differentiation; duplicate signal screening; technical-noise separation; repeated observation handling; distributed observation association; machine-generated occurrence identification; occurrence distinguishability; occurrence uncertainty.
ORIM governs whether a distinguishable occurrence can be established.
It does not govern whether the occurrence has sufficient potential tax relevance.
Operational Scope
ORIM may process observations originating from: transactions; payments; orders; invoices; ERP records; banking systems; logistics systems; production systems; digital platforms; marketplaces; APIs; software services; digital assets; sensors; machines; robots; autonomous agents; AI systems; machine-to-machine systems; distributed infrastructure; automated workflows; hybrid physical-digital systems.
Multiple observations may support one occurrence.
One observation may also contain evidence relevant to more than one occurrence.
ORIM must therefore avoid assuming a fixed relationship between record count and occurrence count. Signal ≠ Occurrence
This is the foundational distinction of ORIM.
A signal indicates that a system observed, recorded, transmitted, or represented something.

An occurrence represents something sufficiently distinguishable as having happened.
For example:
Payment Authorization Message ≠ New Economic Occurrence by Default.
API Retry ≠ New Occurrence by Default.
Database Replication ≠ New Occurrence by Default.
Sensor Update ≠ New Occurrence by Default.
ERP Synchronization ≠ New Occurrence by Default.
ORIM prevents the technical architecture producing the data from automatically defining the governance architecture of reality. Record ≠ Reality
Operational systems represent reality according to their own technical purposes.
A warehouse system may represent a movement.
A payment system may represent a settlement.
A marketplace may represent an order.
An accounting system may represent a posting.
These records can describe different aspects of the same underlying activity.
Therefore:
Record ≠ Occurrence by Default.
ORIM must be capable of looking across available representations rather than assuming that each database object is an independent governance object.
Occurrence Candidate Identification
ORIM may initially establish one or more Occurrence Candidates from available observations.
A candidate may be created where the observations provide a plausible basis for believing that a distinguishable action, transition, condition, exchange, execution, transfer, or other occurrence took place.
Candidate identification does not yet mean that occurrence recognition is complete.

Where distinguishability remains unresolved, the candidate must remain qualified accordingly.
Observation Association
Several signals may relate to the same occurrence.
For example:
Order Creation
Payment Authorization
Payment Confirmation
ERP Posting
Invoice Generation
may all relate to one broader commercial activity.
ORIM may associate observations where a legitimate governance basis exists.
Possible association indicators may include: shared references; temporal relationships; operational relationships; system relationships; process relationships; participant references; contextual relationships; upstream governed context.
But no single indicator should automatically establish occurrence identity. Shared Identifier ≠ Same Occurrence
Two records containing the same transaction number, account, customer, device, session, asset, or system identifier may still represent distinct occurrences.
Conversely, records with different identifiers may describe the same underlying occurrence.
Therefore:
Identifier Equality ≠ Occurrence Identity.
Technical identifiers may support recognition.
They must not replace governance reasoning.
Duplicate Observation
One occurrence may be recorded repeatedly.
Duplicates may arise through: system synchronization; retries; replicated databases; mirrored infrastructure; multiple reporting systems; platform integrations; archival processes; redundant sensors; distributed ledgers; downstream accounting systems.

ORIM must prevent duplicated representations from automatically generating duplicated occurrences.
Therefore:
Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Occurrence.
Technical Noise
Some observations do not represent materially distinguishable real-world or economic occurrences.
Examples may include: health-check signals; heartbeat messages; failed API retries; synchronization traffic; caching operations; internal logging; monitoring events; non-material state refreshes; technical acknowledgements.
ORIM may classify such observations as non-occurrence technical activity where sufficient governance basis exists.
This prevents technical system complexity from artificially expanding the number of occurrences entering TREGA™.
Distributed Occurrence
A distinguishable occurrence may be visible only through several systems.
For example:
Marketplace Record
↓
Payment Record
↓
Service Activation Record
↓
Provider Record
No individual record may establish the complete occurrence.
ORIM must permit distributed observations to contribute to one occurrence-recognition process.
Therefore:
Distributed Observation ≠ Distributed Occurrence by Default.
The number of systems observing activity does not determine the number of occurrences.
Machine-Generated Occurrence
ORIM is actor-neutral.
An occurrence may arise from: human action; organizational process; software execution; AI agent activity; autonomous-system operation; robot action; machine-to-machine interaction.
However:

Machine Execution ≠ Distinct Occurrence by Default.
A machine may perform thousands of technical operations in executing one higher-level action.
ORIM determines which activity can legitimately be distinguished as an occurrence before any assessment of potential tax relevance begins.
Occurrence Distinguishability
A Recognized Occurrence should be sufficiently distinguishable from surrounding activity.
Distinguishability may depend upon: observable change; operational separation; contextual separation; identifiable execution; transaction separation; process transition; value-related change; sufficient evidential support; reliable association of observations.
The required degree of distinguishability should remain proportionate to the governance purpose.
ORIM does not require absolute knowledge of every aspect of the occurrence.
Occurrence Uncertainty
Some observations may indicate that something happened without allowing the occurrence to be sufficiently distinguished.
ORIM must preserve this uncertainty.
Possible conditions may include:
Occurrence Candidate
Occurrence Unresolved
Occurrence Recognized
Observation Rejected as Noise
Potential Duplicate
This prevents incomplete information from becoming false occurrence certainty.
Governance Requirements

ORIM requires that: occurrence recognition begins from observable information and governed context; signals remain distinguishable from occurrences; technical records do not automatically define occurrence identity; multiple observations may support one occurrence; one observation may require further decomposition where justified; duplicate observations are considered; technical noise can be excluded; distributed observations can be associated where legitimately supported; machine-generated activity is treated actor-neutrally; occurrence uncertainty remains explicit; recognized occurrences remain traceable to supporting observations where materially required; occurrence recognition does not determine tax relevance or legal taxability.
Governance Logic
ORIM applies four principal questions:
What has actually been observed?
Do the observations indicate that a distinguishable occurrence exists?
Do multiple observations represent the same occurrence, separate occurrences, or an unresolved relationship?
Is the occurrence sufficiently distinguishable to proceed to relevance screening?
The transformation is:
Signals / Records
→ Qualified Observations
→ Occurrence Candidate
→ Recognized Occurrence
Only after this transformation should the next module ask whether the occurrence has potential relevance to tax-event governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum ORIM implementation must be capable of:

1. receiving governed contextual information and observable records or signals; 2. qualifying observations; 3. identifying occurrence candidates; 4. associating potentially related observations; 5. distinguishing duplicate representations; 6. identifying technical noise where sufficiently established; 7. assessing occurrence distinguishability; 8. preserving unresolved occurrence conditions; 9. producing a Recognized Occurrence; 10. transferring the recognized occurrence to ERSM for relevance screening.
ORIM does not prescribe a particular database, event-stream system, ERP, AI model, knowledge graph, ledger, sensor architecture, or tax platform.
Governance Outputs
ORIM may produce:
Recognized Occurrence — a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence eligible for further TRERS governance.
Occurrence Reference — a governed reference enabling subsequent processing.
Supporting Observation Set — the records, signals, or observations associated with the recognized occurrence.
Occurrence Association Result — the governed relationship between multiple observations and the occurrence.
Duplicate Observation Indicator — identification of potentially duplicated representations.
Technical Noise Classification — observations excluded from occurrence recognition where sufficiently justified.
Occurrence Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved conditions affecting occurrence distinguishability.
Occurrence Recognition Basis — the governance basis supporting recognition.
Critical Distinctions

Signal ≠ Occurrence.
A technical observation does not automatically establish something independently happened.
Record ≠ Reality.
The representation produced by a system is not identical to the reality it represents.
Record ≠ Occurrence by Default.
A database entry is not automatically a governance object.
Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Occurrences.
One activity may produce many technical representations.
Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Occurrence.
Replication of information does not replicate reality.
Shared Identifier ≠ Same Occurrence.
Technical identifiers support governance but do not determine occurrence identity.
Machine Execution ≠ Distinct Occurrence by Default.
Technical execution granularity must not automatically become economic-event granularity.
Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Relevance Screening.
ORIM establishes that a distinguishable occurrence exists.
ERSM determines whether it has sufficient potential relevance to proceed further.
Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Formation.
Recognition does not construct the governed Tax-Relevant Event.
Occurrence Recognition ≠ Taxability Determination.
Nothing in ORIM establishes that tax is legally due.
Enterprise Application
ORIM addresses a major structural problem in modern enterprise and public-sector data environments:
the number of records generated by systems is increasingly disconnected from the number of meaningful occurrences in the underlying economy.
A single commercial activity may appear across:
Commerce Platform
↓

Payment Gateway
↓
Bank
↓
ERP
↓
Warehouse
↓
Logistics
↓
Accounting
while an autonomous workflow may generate thousands of additional machine-level records.
Without occurrence recognition governance, downstream systems may either:
over-fragment reality by treating every record as a separate occurrence,
or
over-aggregate reality by assuming records sharing an identifier represent one occurrence.
ORIM establishes a common governance layer capable of distinguishing occurrences independently of the technical systems that record them. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Duplicate Transaction Explosion Across Government and Enterprise Systems
A cross-border seller completes one commercial activity.
The marketplace creates an order record.
The payment provider creates authorization and settlement records.
The bank creates transaction records.
The ERP creates sales and accounting records.
The logistics provider creates shipment and delivery records.
Several systems subsequently replicate these records into reporting and compliance environments.
A downstream tax-data platform may receive dozens of records associated with the same underlying activity.
Without ORIM, each technical representation risks becoming an independent event candidate, producing duplicate analysis, inconsistent reporting, and artificial transaction volumes.
ORIM associates the relevant observations and determines which distinguishable occurrences can legitimately be established.

It does not yet determine which occurrences are tax-relevant.
It prevents the architecture of the IT systems from becoming the architecture of economic reality. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Agent Producing Thousands of Operations for One Commercial Objective
An autonomous procurement agent receives an objective to acquire computing capacity at an acceptable price.
It queries hundreds of providers, invokes APIs, performs availability checks, compares offers, requests quotations, retries failed connections, reserves temporary capacity, releases unsuitable reservations, selects a provider, executes a purchase, and initiates payment.
Thousands of machine records may be generated.
A system that treats every technically observable action as an independent occurrence could create thousands of potential tax-event candidates from one autonomous commercial process.
ORIM distinguishes technical signals, retries, observations, and machine execution from sufficiently distinguishable occurrences.
The resulting Recognized Occurrence or Occurrences can then proceed to ERSM for tax-relevance screening.
This establishes a critical governance capability for machine economies:
machine execution can scale almost without limit, but governed occurrence recognition must remain tied to distinguishishable reality rather than computational activity volume.
Canonical Boundary

ORIM governs whether a distinguishable occurrence can be established from observable activity. It does not determine whether that occurrence has sufficient potential tax relevance, how it becomes a formed Tax-Relevant Event, or whether any legal tax consequence exists.
The TRERS internal progression begins:
ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur?
→ ERSM — Does that occurrence have sufficient potential relevance to tax-event governance?
→ ERRM — What governed recognition rules apply?
→ ERCM — How strong is the recognition basis?
→ EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation?
This preserves the critical sequence:
Observable Signal
↓
Recognized Occurrence
↓
Relevance Screening
↓
Governed Recognition
Canonical Closing Statement

Occurrence Recognition Module establishes the occurrence-identification layer of the Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard by transforming observable signals, records, messages, state changes, machine operations, and distributed system representations into sufficiently distinguishable occurrences capable of entering further TREGA™ governance. Through governance of observation qualification, occurrence candidate identification, signal association, duplicate detection, technical-noise separation, distributed observation, machine-generated activity, distinguishability, and uncertainty, ORIM prevents database entries, API calls, replicated records, system retries, sensor messages, or autonomous execution steps from automatically becoming independent representations of economic reality. The Module preserves the distinctions between Signal and Occurrence, Record and Reality, technical representation and occurrence identity, Occurrence Recognition and Event Relevance Screening, and occurrence existence and legal taxability. ORIM therefore establishes not whether an occurrence is tax-relevant, but whether something sufficiently distinguishable has happened for TREGA™ to legitimately ask that question.

Reality Abstraction
Canonical Definition
Reality Abstraction Module (RAM) defines the governance conditions under which Reality Elements selected as materially relevant to a simulation are simplified, generalized, aggregated, decomposed, parameterized, discretized, approximated, or otherwise transformed into representations suitable for simulation while preserving the characteristics necessary to answer the governed simulation inquiry.

RAM establishes the governance boundary between selected reality and its simulation-level representation, ensuring that reduction of real-world complexity remains explicit, justified, traceable, and bounded by Simulation Purpose & Scope.
Operational Role
RSM establishes:
What parts of reality matter to the simulation?
RAM asks the next question:
At what level of abstraction may those selected parts of reality be represented without removing characteristics material to the simulation inquiry?
The governed progression is:
Reality Selection Basis → Reality Element → Material Characteristics → Abstraction Requirement → Abstraction Decision → Abstraction Limitation → Abstracted Reality Representation → Representation Fidelity
RAM does not determine the required fidelity or resolution of the completed representation.
It governs how real-world complexity may legitimately be reduced before those subsequent representation properties are established.
Module Operational Space

RAM governs: abstraction objectives, abstraction levels, abstraction boundaries, material characteristic preservation, simplification, generalization, aggregation, decomposition, parameterization, discretization, approximation, behavioral abstraction, structural abstraction, environmental abstraction, temporal abstraction, spatial abstraction, interaction abstraction, dependency abstraction, state abstraction, process abstraction, actor abstraction, abstraction assumptions, abstraction justification, abstraction limitations, abstraction uncertainty, abstraction sensitivity, abstraction consistency, abstraction completeness, abstraction traceability, abstraction change, and Abstraction Basis governance.
Module Function
Reality contains more complexity than most simulations can or should reproduce.
A governed simulation therefore requires abstraction.
Abstraction itself is not a defect.
Uncontrolled abstraction is.
RAM exists to prevent: arbitrary simplification, convenience-driven abstraction, abstraction based solely on computational limitations, removal of materially relevant characteristics, excessive aggregation, hidden assumptions, loss of important dependencies, elimination of relevant failure behavior, unrealistic behavioral simplification, abstraction inconsistent with Simulation Purpose, inconsistent abstraction across related simulation components, and representation of an abstracted model as if it preserved characteristics that were intentionally removed.

Reality Abstraction Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Reality may be simplified only to the extent that the simplification does not remove characteristics materially necessary to the governed simulation inquiry.
The objective is not:
maximum realism.
The objective is:
sufficient representation of material reality for the intended simulation purpose.
Abstraction Is a Governed Transformation
Reality Abstraction transforms:
Selected Reality
into:
Abstracted Reality Representation
This transformation should remain reconstructable.
For every material abstraction, it should be possible to understand:
What existed in Relevant Reality?
What was selected?
What characteristics were retained?
What characteristics were simplified or removed?
Why was that abstraction considered acceptable?
What limitations does the abstraction create?
Abstraction Object
An Abstraction Object is the Reality Element, relationship, behavior, process, environment, condition, or other selected reality component undergoing abstraction.
An Abstraction Object may include: a physical entity, a human actor, an autonomous actor, a process, an environment, a dependency, an interaction, a failure mechanism, a temporal process, a spatial relationship, or another selected Reality Element.
Material Characteristic
A Material Characteristic is a property of a selected Reality Element whose removal, distortion, aggregation, or simplification could materially affect the simulation inquiry.

Material Characteristics may include: physical properties, behavior, state transitions, response characteristics, dependencies, constraints, timing, geometry, variability, uncertainty, interaction patterns, failure behavior, or environmental sensitivity.
RAM requires these characteristics to be identified before significant abstraction occurs.
Abstraction Requirement
An Abstraction Requirement defines what characteristics must remain represented after abstraction.
It connects:
Reality Selection
to:
Representation Design
and prevents important characteristics from disappearing silently during model simplification.
Abstraction Level
An Abstraction Level describes the degree to which a Reality Element is represented with reduced complexity.
Conceptually, representation may range from:
Detailed Representation
through:
Reduced Representation
Aggregated Representation
Parameterized Representation
to:
Highly Abstract Representation
These are methodological descriptions rather than universal technical classes.
SIMULOS® does not prescribe one abstraction scale for all simulation domains.
Abstraction Must Be Purpose-Relative
There is no universally correct abstraction level.
A representation that is sufficient for one simulation may be inadequate for another.
For example, a pedestrian may be represented as:
a moving point
for one traffic-flow simulation,
but may require:
orientation, reaction time, visibility, movement variability, decision behavior, and interaction characteristics

for an autonomous-vehicle safety simulation.
The correct abstraction depends upon what the simulation must legitimately examine. Simplification
Simplification removes unnecessary complexity while retaining characteristics required by the simulation inquiry.
A simplification should be distinguishable from an omission.
RSM determines whether the Reality Element belongs in the representation.
RAM determines which characteristics of that selected element may be simplified. Generalization
Generalization represents multiple detailed real-world characteristics through a broader representation.
Generalization may be appropriate where detailed differences are not material to the simulation inquiry.
Where differences could materially affect outcomes, generalization requires stronger justification or should not be used. Aggregation
Aggregation combines multiple Reality Elements, states, behaviors, events, or properties into a collective representation.
Aggregation may reduce computational and structural complexity.
However, it may also hide: local variation, minority behavior, extreme conditions, nonlinear interactions, individual failures, dependency structure, or rare but consequential states.
RAM therefore requires material aggregation effects to remain visible. Decomposition
Abstraction does not always mean combining reality.
A Reality Element may need to be decomposed into smaller representational components where its internal structure materially affects simulation behavior.

RAM governs whether such decomposition is necessary to preserve the characteristics relevant to the inquiry. Parameterization
Parameterization represents complex real-world behavior or characteristics through governed parameters.
Parameterization should preserve: parameter meaning, applicable conditions, source basis, assumptions, ranges, and known limitations
where these materially affect representation. Discretization
Continuous real-world phenomena may be represented through discrete: time steps, spatial cells, states, categories, events, or value ranges.
RAM governs the methodological decision to discretize.
The specific granularity required is subsequently governed through Representation Resolution. Approximation
Approximation may be necessary where exact representation is impossible, unnecessary, or computationally disproportionate.
An approximation should remain bounded by: the simulation inquiry, material characteristics, expected behavior, known error, applicable conditions, and downstream interpretation.
Behavioral Abstraction
Real-world actors may exhibit highly complex behavior.
RAM may govern abstraction of: human behavior, autonomous behavior, organizational behavior, agent behavior, biological behavior, or system response.
Behavioral abstraction must not silently eliminate behavior that is material to the simulation inquiry.
Human Abstraction

Humans may be represented as: deterministic actors, probabilistic actors, behavioral classes, population distributions, decision rules, or more complex cognitive representations.
RAM governs whether the selected abstraction is appropriate to the simulation inquiry.
It does not govern human cognition itself.
Where cognition requires independent governance, CLIA® provides the relevant complementary architecture.
Autonomous Actor Abstraction
Autonomous actors may require abstraction of: perception, reasoning, decision behavior, permissions, constraints, coordination, escalation, adaptation, or response.
RAM governs only how these characteristics are represented inside the simulation.
Governance of the autonomous system itself remains within ASGA™ and other applicable architectures.
Structural Abstraction
Complex systems may be structurally simplified.
Structural abstraction may combine or omit internal components while preserving externally relevant behavior.
RAM should determine whether internal structures that are removed could materially affect: failure propagation, dependencies, performance, interaction, safety, or simulation outcomes.
Environmental Abstraction
Simulation environments may abstract: terrain, infrastructure, atmosphere, weather, lighting, electromagnetic conditions, population, traffic, resources, physical obstacles, or other environmental characteristics.
Environmental abstraction should remain appropriate to the scenarios the simulation must support.

Temporal Abstraction
Reality may operate across different timescales.
RAM governs whether temporal processes may be: compressed, aggregated, approximated, event-driven, discretized, or otherwise simplified.
Temporal abstraction should not remove material: latency, accumulation, sequence, delay, degradation, adaptation, feedback, or timing dependencies.
Spatial Abstraction
Spatial reality may be simplified through: reduced geometry, zones, cells, coordinates, topological relationships, representative distances, or other spatial models.
The abstraction must preserve spatial characteristics material to the simulation inquiry.
Interaction Abstraction
Two Reality Elements may be represented accurately individually while their interaction is represented inadequately.
RAM therefore governs abstraction of: coupling, communication, influence, collision, transfer, feedback, synchronization, coordination, and dependency.
Dependency Abstraction
Dependencies may be simplified only where their material effect remains sufficiently represented.
A hidden dependency removed through abstraction can create a simulation that behaves correctly internally while failing to represent real-world system behavior.
Failure Abstraction
Failure behavior often differs from nominal behavior.

Where failure is material to Simulation Purpose, RAM should determine whether the abstraction preserves: failure initiation, failure propagation, degraded states, recovery behavior, cascading effects, and relevant interaction with other elements.
Abstraction Assumption
Every material abstraction may create assumptions.
An Abstraction Assumption states what is presumed to remain sufficiently true despite reduction of real-world complexity.
Example:
Individual variation is assumed not to materially affect the aggregate outcome within the defined scenario range.
Such assumptions should remain explicit and traceable.
Abstraction Justification
A material abstraction should have a governed reason.
Possible reasons may include: characteristic immateriality, known equivalence, validated simplification, bounded approximation, computational necessity, data limitation, scenario limitation, or established domain methodology.
Computational necessity alone does not prove methodological acceptability.
Computational Constraint Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A computational limitation may explain an abstraction, but it does not by itself justify that abstraction.
Where computational limits force removal of material characteristics, the resulting limitation must remain visible.
Abstraction Limitation
An Abstraction Limitation identifies where the abstracted representation no longer sufficiently reflects some characteristic of Relevant Reality.

Limitations may constrain: scenarios, operating conditions, interpretation, output applicability, comparison, extrapolation, or operational reliance.
Abstraction Uncertainty
Abstraction may introduce uncertainty because multiple real-world states become represented through one simplified model.
Where material, this uncertainty should remain explicit.
It should not disappear merely because the abstraction itself is deterministic.
Abstraction Sensitivity
Where the acceptability of an abstraction is uncertain, its effect may require sensitivity examination.
The key governance question is:
Would a materially different abstraction plausibly change the simulation outcome or interpretation?
Where yes, the abstraction should receive additional scrutiny.
Abstraction Consistency
Related Reality Elements should not use incompatible abstraction assumptions without explicit justification.
For example, one subsystem should not assume:
instantaneous communication
while another relies upon:
material communication latency
unless the relationship is governed.
Cross-Element Abstraction
Abstraction decisions should therefore be evaluated not only independently but also collectively.
The combined abstraction structure may create effects not visible when each element is reviewed separately.
Abstraction Completeness
Abstraction Completeness asks whether every materially selected Reality Element has received sufficient abstraction treatment to proceed into representation governance.

This does not mean every element must be simplified.
Some may remain detailed.
The requirement is that the abstraction status is known.
Abstraction Status
A selected Reality Element may receive an abstraction status such as:
Detailed Representation Required
Reduced Representation Approved
Aggregated Representation Approved
Parameterized Representation Approved
Approximation Approved
Conditional Abstraction
Abstraction Constraint
or:
Abstraction Undetermined Conditional Abstraction
An abstraction may be acceptable only within defined: scenarios, ranges, environments, time periods, operating modes, populations, or system states.
These conditions should propagate forward into subsequent representation governance.
Abstraction Constraint
An Abstraction Constraint exists where required real-world complexity cannot currently be represented at an acceptable abstraction level.
This should not be silently converted into an approved simplification.
Abstraction Traceability
A governed abstraction should support the chain:
Simulation Purpose → Reality Selection → Reality Element → Material Characteristic → Abstraction Requirement → Abstraction Decision → Abstracted Representation → Limitation
This provides a reconstructable explanation of how reality became simulation representation.
Abstraction Change

Abstraction may require reassessment where: Simulation Purpose changes, Simulation Scope changes, Reality Selection changes, new interactions are identified, new failure modes emerge, representation capability changes, new evidence becomes available, scenario requirements expand, or simulation outputs demonstrate sensitivity to abstraction.
Abstraction Change Propagation
Material abstraction changes may affect:
Fidelity → Resolution → Representation Limitations → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Outputs → Reality Correlation
Abstraction is therefore an upstream simulation-governance dependency.
Abstraction Basis
The principal governed output of RAM is the Abstraction Basis.
It should establish: Abstraction Objects, material characteristics, abstraction requirements, selected abstraction levels, simplifications, aggregations, decompositions, parameterizations, approximations, abstraction assumptions, abstraction limitations, abstraction uncertainty, abstraction constraints, applicable conditions, and traceability to Reality Selection.
Relationship to Reality Selection
RSM determines:
What reality enters the simulation?
RAM determines:
How may the complexity of that selected reality be reduced?
The distinction protects SIMULOS® from treating omission and abstraction as the same methodological act.
Relationship to Representation Fidelity
RAM does not establish whether the resulting representation achieves the required fidelity.

That is governed by:
RFM — Representation Fidelity Module
RAM provides the abstraction basis against which fidelity can subsequently be evaluated.
Relationship to Representation Resolution
RAM may determine that a phenomenon can be discretized or aggregated.
It does not determine the exact resolution at which representation must operate.
That belongs to:
RRM — Representation Resolution Module Relationship to Representation Limitation
RAM identifies limitations created specifically by abstraction.
RLM — Representation Limitation Module subsequently consolidates and governs the broader limitations of the simulation's Reality Representation.
Cross-Architecture Boundary
RAM does not determine what Operational Reality is.
That remains governed by ORA™.
RAM does not validate whether a simulation may support an external validation claim.
That remains within VALIDOS®.
RAM does not govern general integrity.
That remains within INTEGROS®.
RAM governs one specific transformation:
the controlled reduction of selected reality into simulation-suitable representation.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Reality Selection Basis
Identify the selected Reality Elements and their connection to Simulation Purpose & Scope. 2. Identify Material Characteristics
Determine which properties, behaviors, states, interactions, dependencies, temporal effects, spatial effects, and failure characteristics must survive abstraction. 3. Establish Abstraction Requirements

Define what must remain represented after complexity reduction. 4. Select the Abstraction Approach
Determine whether the element requires detailed, simplified, generalized, aggregated, decomposed, parameterized, discretized, or approximated representation. 5. Evaluate Material Loss
Determine what real-world characteristics are removed, compressed, merged, or approximated. 6. Assess Abstraction Acceptability
Determine whether the resulting representation remains sufficient for the governed simulation inquiry. 7. Record Assumptions, Conditions, and Limitations
Preserve the boundaries under which the abstraction remains legitimate. 8. Assess Cross-Element Consistency
Determine whether abstraction decisions remain compatible across interacting Reality Elements. 9. Establish the Abstraction Basis
Create the governed representation basis required for fidelity governance. 10. Preserve Traceability and Reassessment
Maintain:
Reality Selection → Material Characteristics → Abstraction → Limitation → Representation
and reassess after material change.
Governance Outputs

RAM may produce: Abstraction Object Register, Material Characteristic Record, Abstraction Requirement, Abstraction Level Record, Simplification Record, Generalization Record, Aggregation Record, Decomposition Record, Parameterization Record, Discretization Record, Approximation Record, Behavioral Abstraction Record, Structural Abstraction Record, Environmental Abstraction Record, Temporal Abstraction Record, Spatial Abstraction Record, Interaction Abstraction Record, Dependency Abstraction Record, Failure Abstraction Record, Abstraction Assumption Register, Abstraction Justification Record, Abstraction Limitation Record, Abstraction Uncertainty Record, Abstraction Sensitivity Record, Abstraction Consistency Assessment, Conditional Abstraction Record, Abstraction Constraint Record, Abstraction Completeness Assessment, Abstraction Change Record, Abstraction Traceability Map, and Abstraction Basis.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous-driving simulation has already selected pedestrians as materially relevant Reality Elements.
Representing every biological and cognitive characteristic of every pedestrian would be unnecessary. Application
RAM determines which characteristics must remain represented, such as: position, movement, direction, speed, reaction variability, visibility, road-crossing behavior, and relevant interaction with the vehicle.

Other characteristics may legitimately remain abstracted where they cannot materially affect the simulation inquiry. Result
The simulation receives a governed pedestrian abstraction that preserves characteristics necessary for the intended safety scenarios without attempting to reproduce the complete human being. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Thermal Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft thermal simulation includes the spacecraft structure, solar exposure, internal heat generation, radiation, and relevant environmental conditions. Application
RAM determines whether individual structural components require detailed representation or whether some may be represented through aggregated thermal masses and parameterized heat-transfer relationships.
Where local thermal behavior could materially affect critical components, excessive aggregation is prohibited or recorded as a material limitation. Result
The abstraction remains aligned with the thermal inquiry rather than with computational convenience alone. Use Case 3 — Industrial Digital Twin
Scenario
A digital twin represents a complex industrial production system containing thousands of individual operational components. Application
RAM allows non-material components to be aggregated while preserving individually significant: bottlenecks, dependencies, failure paths, resource constraints, timing relationships, and critical interactions.
Result

The digital twin remains computationally manageable without silently eliminating operational relationships material to the simulation objective.
Architectural Position
Reality Abstraction is the second internal governance space of the Reality Representation Standard (RRS).
The complete RRS progression is:
Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Representation Limitation
RSM establishes:
What parts of reality matter?
RAM establishes:
How may their complexity be reduced?
RFM establishes:
How faithfully must the resulting representation reproduce the material characteristics required by the simulation?
This sequence prevents three fundamentally different questions from being collapsed into one modeling decision.
Foundational Principle
Abstraction is legitimate only when reducing the complexity of reality does not silently remove the characteristics that make that reality material to the simulation inquiry.
Canonical Closing Statement

Reality Abstraction Module establishes the governed transformation through which selected reality becomes simulation-suitable representation without allowing simplification, aggregation, parameterization, discretization, approximation, or computational constraint to silently remove characteristics material to the simulation inquiry. By governing abstraction requirements, material-characteristic preservation, abstraction levels, assumptions, limitations, uncertainty, cross-element consistency, change propagation, and traceability, RAM ensures that simulation complexity may be reduced where justified while preserving a transparent and reconstructable relationship between the reality selected for simulation and the representation subsequently evaluated for fidelity, resolution, and limitation.
