OOF™ Simulation Assumption Basis Module (SABM)
Simulation Assumption Basis Module (SABM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Basis
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Assumption Basis
Canonical Definition
Simulation Assumption Basis Module (SABM) defines the governance framework for establishing, documenting, qualifying, and maintaining the basis upon which an identified Simulation Assumption is introduced, accepted, retained, modified, or rejected within a simulation.

It establishes the methodological mechanism through which a Simulation Assumption is connected to the rationale, observations, knowledge, evidence references, models, prior experience, expert judgment, theoretical foundations, engineering constraints, or other grounds that explain why the assumption is being used.
SABM does not determine whether an assumption is universally true.
It governs whether the assumption has a sufficiently explicit and traceable Simulation Assumption Basis for its defined role inside the simulation.
Operational Role
SABM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The preceding SAIM — Simulation Assumption Identification Module establishes:
Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant to the simulation?
SABM asks:
On what basis is each identified Simulation Assumption being used, and is that basis sufficiently explicit, relevant, bounded, and traceable for its role within the simulation?
The governed progression is:
Identified Simulation Assumption → Basis Discovery → Basis Attribution → Basis Classification → Basis Relevance → Basis Sufficiency → Basis Limitation → Assumption-Basis Record
The resulting governed basis supports subsequent examination of:
Assumption Dependency → Assumption Uncertainty → Assumption Limitation
Module Operational Space

SABM governs: assumption basis identification, assumption rationale, basis attribution, basis origin, basis classification, empirical basis, theoretical basis, historical basis, observational basis, engineering basis, expert-judgment basis, model-derived basis, inherited basis, precedent-based basis, constraint-derived basis, mixed basis, basis relevance, basis applicability, basis sufficiency, basis currency, basis specificity, basis strength representation, unsupported assumptions, weakly supported assumptions, conditionally supported assumptions, conflicting assumption bases, basis limitations, basis change, basis-to-assumption traceability, and maintenance of the Simulation Assumption Basis Record.
Module Function
SAIM makes assumptions visible.
SABM makes the reason for using them visible.
A simulation may explicitly document an assumption while providing no explanation for why that assumption was selected.
For example:
Battery performance is assumed to remain constant throughout the simulated mission.
The statement identifies an assumption.
It does not establish: why constant performance was selected, which operating conditions support it, whether historical observations support it, whether it derives from engineering specifications, whether it is merely a modeling convenience, or whether contrary information exists.
SABM prevents the presence of an assumption statement from being mistaken for the existence of an assumption basis.
Simulation Assumption Basis

A Simulation Assumption Basis is the governed rationale or supporting foundation explaining why a Simulation Assumption is introduced or retained for a defined simulation context.
The basis may contain one or several supporting elements.
Conceptually:
Simulation Assumption
↓
Why is this premise being used?
↓
Simulation Assumption Basis Basis Does Not Equal Truth
SIMULOS® establishes:
A documented basis explains why an assumption is used; it does not automatically establish that the assumption is true.
An assumption may possess a rational basis while still containing substantial uncertainty.
This distinction preserves the boundary between SABM and later assumption governance.
Basis Types
A Simulation Assumption may derive from different basis types.
Empirical Basis
Derived from observations, measurements, experiments, operational records, or other empirical information.
Theoretical Basis
Derived from an accepted or proposed theoretical model, scientific principle, mathematical relationship, or conceptual framework.
Historical Basis
Derived from historical behavior, prior events, previous simulations, or longitudinal observations.
Engineering Basis
Derived from technical specifications, design properties, engineering constraints, tolerances, or established engineering reasoning.
Expert-Judgment Basis
Derived materially from the judgment of one or more qualified persons.
Model-Derived Basis

Derived from another model, simulation, analytical system, or computational representation.
Inherited Basis
Transferred from a prior simulation, external component, reused simulation asset, or existing model.
Precedent-Based Basis
Derived from previous accepted practice, comparable cases, or established operational precedent.
Constraint-Derived Basis
Introduced because available resources, data, model capabilities, computation, time, or simulation design make a more complete representation impractical.
Mixed Basis
Derived from several materially relevant basis types.
Basis Attribution
Each material assumption should be attributable to the basis supporting it.
The minimum relationship is:
Assumption → Basis
Where several basis elements exist:
Assumption → Basis Element A + Basis Element B + Basis Element C
Where several assumptions depend upon one basis:
Basis → Assumption A + Assumption B + Assumption C
This allows later changes in the basis to propagate to affected assumptions.
Basis Origin
Where available, SABM identifies where the basis originated.
Possible origins include: measurement systems, operational records, scientific literature, engineering documentation, subject-matter experts, external models, prior simulations, organizational experience, technical standards, vendor information, environmental observations, AI-generated analysis, or internal simulation design decisions.
Origin identification improves traceability without automatically establishing reliability.

Basis Relevance
A basis must be relevant to the specific assumption it supports.
For example:
historical performance under normal temperature conditions may provide some basis for an assumption about normal-temperature operation.
It may provide little basis for the same assumption under extreme heat.
SABM therefore asks:
Does the identified basis actually address the condition represented by the assumption?
Basis Applicability
A basis may be valid only within a bounded context.
Relevant applicability dimensions may include: object version, model version, population, environment, operating range, geography, temporal period, scenario, configuration, system state, physical conditions, or behavioral context.
A basis should not silently expand beyond the context from which it was derived.
Basis Sufficiency
SABM evaluates whether the identified basis is sufficiently developed to justify using the assumption for its intended simulation role.
Basis sufficiency is contextual.
An assumption used for exploratory simulation may legitimately operate on a weaker basis than an assumption controlling a high-consequence simulation conclusion.
SABM therefore evaluates sufficiency relative to:
Simulation Purpose + Simulation Scope + Assumption Materiality + Consequence Basis Strength Representation
Where useful, a Simulation Assumption Basis may be represented as:
Strongly Established Basis
Sufficient Basis
Conditional Basis
Limited Basis
Weak Basis
Unsupported
or:
Basis Undetermined

These states describe the governance condition of the assumption basis.
They do not constitute universal validation of the assumption itself.
Unsupported Assumption
An Unsupported Simulation Assumption is an identified assumption for which no sufficiently identifiable basis has been established.
Unsupported does not automatically mean false.
It means:
the simulation depends upon a premise whose supporting basis has not been sufficiently established.
This condition must remain visible.
Weakly Supported Assumption
A Weakly Supported Simulation Assumption possesses an identifiable basis, but that basis may be: indirect, incomplete, outdated, contextually weak, narrow, dependent upon judgment, poorly traceable, or insufficient relative to the consequence of the assumption.
Weak support should not be represented as strong support merely because the simulation requires the assumption to proceed.
Conditionally Supported Assumption
An assumption may have sufficient basis only while specified conditions remain true.
For example:
Sensor degradation remains negligible during the simulated mission
may be supported only where:
temperature remains within the qualified operating range.
The assumption basis should therefore preserve the relevant condition.
Basis Currency
A basis may lose relevance over time.

Examples include: outdated operational records, obsolete engineering specifications, changed environments, changed system versions, updated scientific knowledge, changed populations, or superseded models.
SABM therefore preserves the temporal relationship between the basis and the simulation.
Inherited Basis Governance
An assumption inherited from another simulation may arrive with an inherited basis.
SABM does not automatically accept that basis.
It asks whether the inherited basis remains applicable to: the current Simulation Object, current purpose, current scope, current representation, current model, current environment, and current simulation conditions.
Expert-Judgment Basis
Expert judgment may constitute a legitimate Simulation Assumption Basis.
Where material, SABM should make visible: the domain of expertise, the question addressed, the context of the judgment, material conditions, known limitations, and whether materially different expert judgments exist.
The existence of expertise should not transform judgment into empirical fact.
Model-Derived Basis
A simulation assumption may be supported by another model.
This creates a methodological chain:
External Model → Derived Basis → Simulation Assumption → Current Simulation
Where the external model changes materially, assumptions dependent upon that model may require reassessment.
Constraint-Derived Assumptions
Some assumptions exist because the simulation cannot practically represent everything.
For example:

a computationally expensive physical interaction may be simplified into a stable approximation.
The basis may therefore be:
Simulation Constraint + Acceptable Approximation Rationale
SABM requires this rationale to remain visible rather than presenting the approximation as established reality.
Convenience Is Not Sufficient Basis by Itself
SIMULOS® establishes:
An assumption should not be represented as methodologically supported merely because it makes the simulation easier to construct or execute.
Modeling convenience may explain why an assumption exists.
It does not automatically establish that the assumption is appropriate.
Authority Is Not Sufficient Basis by Itself
An assumption should not receive unlimited methodological strength solely because it originates from: a senior person, a recognized institution, a regulator, a vendor, a previous project, an established model, or a widely used practice.
Authority may contribute to the basis.
The assumption remains bounded by the relevance and applicability of that basis.
Repeated Use Is Not Validation
SIMULOS® establishes:
Repeated use of an assumption does not transform the assumption into an established fact.
An assumption used across many simulation generations may still require reassessment when: the object changes, reality changes, the environment changes, new evidence emerges, or the intended simulation use changes.
Conflicting Assumption Basis
Different basis elements may support materially different assumptions.

For example:
historical observations may suggest one behavioral range,
while:
recent operational measurements suggest another.
SABM requires material conflict to remain visible.
A conflict should not be silently resolved by selecting the basis that produces the preferred simulation outcome.
Basis Conflict Record
Where material conflict exists, SABM may preserve:
Assumption
Basis A
Basis B
Nature of Conflict
Materiality
Current Treatment
and:
Required Reassessment Basis Limitation
Every assumption basis may contain limitations.
Examples include: narrow sample, incomplete observations, environmental mismatch, outdated information, uncertain extrapolation, limited expertise, model dependency, incomplete traceability, or reliance upon indirect evidence.
SABM identifies these basis limitations.
The broader consequences of the assumption itself are governed subsequently by SALM — Simulation Assumption Limitation Module.
Basis-to-Assumption Traceability
SABM should preserve:
Basis Origin
↓
Basis Element
↓
Applicable Context
↓
Simulation Assumption
↓
Affected Simulation Element
This allows later reviewers to reconstruct why the assumption entered the simulation.
Basis Change
A basis may materially change.
Examples include: new measurements, new scientific findings, revised engineering specifications, changed expert judgment, corrected historical data, new operational experience, or replacement of an external model.

Material basis change should trigger reassessment of affected assumptions.
Basis Change Propagation
The governance relationship is:
Basis Change → Affected Assumption → Affected Simulation Element → Reassessment Need
SABM identifies the propagation path.
It does not itself govern the complete resimulation lifecycle.
Basis Expiration
Some assumption bases may have an explicit or implicit useful period.
Where a basis is time-sensitive, its continued use should be reassessed when: the defined period expires, the underlying reality materially changes, or the Simulation Object materially changes.
Basis Rejection
A previously accepted assumption basis may become unsuitable.
Possible causes include: contradiction by stronger information, invalid source, changed context, model replacement, discovered methodological defect, or loss of applicability.
Basis rejection should not erase historical use.
The prior basis should remain traceable to simulations that relied upon it.
Assumption Basis Record
For every material Simulation Assumption, SABM may establish a Simulation Assumption Basis Record containing: Assumption ID, Basis ID, Basis Statement, Basis Type, Basis Origin, Applicable Context, Supporting References, Basis Relevance, Basis Sufficiency, Basis Currency, Basis Conditions, Basis Limitations, Basis Conflicts, Basis Status, and traceability references.
Assumption Basis Status
A basis may carry a status such as:
Identified
Under Assessment
Sufficient
Conditional
Limited
Weak

Unsupported
Conflicted
Superseded
Rejected
or:
Undetermined Basis Sufficiency Gap
A Simulation Assumption Basis Gap exists where: no basis is identifiable, the basis does not address the assumption, the basis is materially outdated, applicability cannot be established, material conflict remains unresolved, or the basis is insufficient relative to the role of the assumption.
The gap must remain visible to downstream simulation governance.
No Basis Laundering Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A weak, indirect, inherited, conditional, or disputed basis must not become represented as strong merely because it passes through a simulation model.
The simulation does not strengthen the basis simply by consuming it.
No Circular Basis Principle
An assumption should not be represented as supported where its basis ultimately depends upon the same assumption.
For example:
Assumption A is accepted because Model X predicts it.
But:
Model X predicts it because Model X itself assumes A.
This creates circular support.
SABM requires material circularity to remain visible.
No Output-as-Basis Circularity
Simulation output should not automatically become the basis proving the assumption that generated that output.
Conceptually:
Assumption → Simulation → Output
cannot, without independent justification, become:
Output → Proof of Assumption
This distinction is essential to simulation governance.
Assumption Basis Sufficiency Assessment

At the completion of SABM, each material assumption should be capable of receiving a basis assessment such as:
Basis Sufficient
Basis Conditionally Sufficient
Basis Limited
Basis Insufficient
Basis Conflicted
or:
Basis Undetermined
This assessment becomes an input to subsequent assumption governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Bind the Basis Inquiry to the Assumption
Identify the exact Simulation Assumption and simulation context being assessed. 2. Identify the Supporting Basis
Determine why the assumption is being used and identify the material basis elements. 3. Classify and Attribute the Basis
Establish basis type, origin, and relationship to the assumption. 4. Assess Relevance and Applicability
Determine whether the basis actually supports the assumption within the applicable simulation context. 5. Assess Sufficiency
Evaluate whether the basis is sufficiently developed relative to the assumption's materiality, simulation purpose, scope, and consequence. 6. Identify Conditions, Conflicts, and Limitations
Preserve material qualifications rather than converting them into unconditional support. 7. Establish Basis Status
Record whether the basis is sufficient, conditional, limited, insufficient, conflicted, or undetermined. 8. Preserve Basis-to-Assumption Traceability
Maintain the relationship:
Basis → Assumption → Affected Simulation Element 9. Govern Basis Change

Identify material changes capable of requiring assumption reassessment. 10. Transfer the Governed Basis Forward
Provide the qualified Simulation Assumption Basis to dependency, uncertainty, and limitation governance.
Governance Outputs
SABM may produce: Simulation Assumption Basis Record, Assumption Basis Identifier, Assumption Basis Classification, Assumption Basis Origin Record, Empirical Basis Record, Theoretical Basis Record, Historical Basis Record, Engineering Basis Record, Expert-Judgment Basis Record, Model-Derived Basis Record, Inherited Basis Record, Constraint-Derived Basis Record, Assumption Basis Relevance Assessment, Assumption Basis Applicability Assessment, Assumption Basis Sufficiency Assessment, Assumption Basis Currency Assessment, Assumption Basis Condition Record, Assumption Basis Limitation Record, Assumption Basis Conflict Record, Assumption Basis Gap Record, Assumption Basis Change Record, Assumption Basis Status, Assumption Basis Traceability Map, and Governed Simulation Assumption Basis Set.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Simulation
Scenario
A warehouse robot simulation assumes:
Human workers will maintain a minimum reaction distance under normal operating conditions.
The assumption is material because collision-avoidance performance depends upon it. Application
SABM identifies the basis as a combination of: historical facility observations, worker-movement measurements, and an existing behavioral model.

The records show that the measurements were collected during normal operation and do not cover emergency evacuation conditions. Result
The assumption receives:
Basis Conditionally Sufficient — Normal Operating Conditions
The simulation cannot legitimately treat the same basis as supporting emergency-condition behavior without additional grounds. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft simulation assumes:
A communication subsystem will remain available for at least 99% of the simulated mission window. Application
SABM identifies: engineering specifications, historical subsystem performance, environmental qualification data, and mission-design constraints
as the assumption basis.
However, the historical observations do not include the full radiation environment expected during the proposed mission. Result
The basis remains explicit and traceable but is classified:
Limited Basis — Radiation Environment Coverage Incomplete
The limitation can then propagate into subsequent assumption uncertainty and limitation governance.
Architectural Position
Simulation Assumption Basis is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The complete SAS progression is:
Simulation Assumption Identification → Simulation Assumption Basis → Simulation Assumption Dependency → Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation
SAIM establishes:
Which assumptions exist?
SABM establishes:

Why is each assumption being used and what supports it?
SADM establishes:
What depends upon each assumption and how do assumptions interact?
SAUM establishes:
How uncertain is each assumption and how must that uncertainty remain visible?
SALM establishes:
Where does each assumption cease to apply and what limitations follow?
Together, these modules prevent assumptions from functioning as invisible or unsupported premises within simulation design, execution, output interpretation, and downstream reliance.
Foundational Principle
A simulation assumption becomes methodologically supportable only when the basis for using that assumption is explicit, relevant to the simulation context, sufficiently bounded, and traceable to the assumption it supports.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Assumption Basis Module establishes the supporting-basis layer of assumption governance within SIMULOS® by governing why identified Simulation Assumptions are introduced, retained, modified, or rejected within a simulation. Through basis identification, classification, attribution, relevance, applicability, sufficiency, currency, conditions, conflict, limitation, change governance, anti-circularity controls, and complete basis-to-assumption traceability, SABM prevents modeling convenience, inherited practice, authority, repetition, or simulation output from being mistaken for sufficient methodological support and ensures that every material assumption carries a visible and bounded basis into subsequent dependency, uncertainty, and limitation governance.

OOF™ Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM)
Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Applicability Context
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 16 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Applicability Context
Canonical Definition
Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) defines the governance conditions under which the operational, environmental, temporal, spatial, population, configuration, capability, behavioral, dependency, scenario, and decision contexts to which a simulation inquiry is intended to apply are explicitly identified, bounded, documented, and maintained throughout the simulation lifecycle.
SACM establishes the contextual envelope within which the simulation is intended to produce meaningful simulation outputs.

It prevents a simulation designed for one context from being interpreted as if it represented every context in which the Simulation Object may exist.
Operational Role
SACM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The preceding modules establish:
SPM — Why is the simulation being performed?
SSCM — What exactly must the simulation cover?
SEXM — What remains outside the governed Simulation Scope?
SACM asks:
Within which contexts is the governed simulation inquiry intended to apply?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Applicability Dimensions → Applicability Conditions → Applicability Boundary → Applicability Context
SACM therefore transforms a bounded Simulation Scope into an explicitly contextualized simulation inquiry.
Module Operational Space

SACM governs: Simulation Applicability Context, applicability dimensions, applicability conditions, applicability boundaries, operational applicability, environmental applicability, spatial applicability, temporal applicability, population applicability, configuration applicability, capability applicability, behavioral applicability, interaction applicability, autonomy applicability, scenario applicability, dependency applicability, decision-context applicability, consequence-context applicability, organizational applicability, infrastructure applicability, applicability assumptions, applicability dependencies, applicability combinations, applicability restrictions, applicability uncertainty, conditional applicability, partial applicability, applicability conflicts, applicability change, applicability expansion, applicability narrowing, applicability traceability, and Applicability Context status.
Module Function
A simulation may be properly scoped and correctly executed while still being misused because its results are applied outside the context for which the simulation was designed.
SACM exists to prevent:
Simulation Performed in Context A → Results Produced → Context Forgotten → Results Applied to Context B
without a governed basis.
Its function is to preserve the relationship:
Simulation Purpose + Scope + Exclusions → Intended Context → Simulation Design → Simulation Outputs → Context-Bounded Interpretation

SACM does not determine whether the simulation is ultimately valid for operational reliance.
It establishes the context the simulation is designed to address.
Simulation Applicability Context
A Simulation Applicability Context is the defined combination of conditions within which the simulation inquiry is intended to represent, examine, or explore the Simulation Object.
The context may include:
Where
When
Under Which Conditions
For Which Population
For Which Configuration
At Which Capability State
Under Which Behaviors
Within Which Dependencies
For Which Scenario Class
and:
For Which Intended Decision Context Applicability Context Is Multidimensional
Simulation applicability should not normally be represented as a single universal label.
A simulation may simultaneously be:
Applicable — Environment A
Applicable — Configuration 3.2
Applicable — Population X
Applicable — Normal Operation
Not Intended — Emergency Operation
Not Intended — Configuration 4.0
The resulting applicability envelope is multidimensional. Applicability Context ≠ Simulation Scope
Simulation Scope and Simulation Applicability Context are related but distinct.
Simulation Scope asks:
What must the simulation examine?
Simulation Applicability Context asks:
Under which contextual conditions is that inquiry intended to apply?
For example:
Scope: Autonomous emergency braking performance.
Applicability Context: Passenger vehicles operating on paved European roads at defined speeds and environmental conditions.

The first defines the inquiry.
The second defines its intended contextual envelope. Applicability Context ≠ Simulation Exclusion
An exclusion identifies what remains outside the governed Simulation Scope.
An applicability boundary identifies where the simulation inquiry is intended to apply.
These may interact without becoming identical.
For example:
Snow explicitly excluded
may create:
Applicability restricted to non-snow conditions.
SEXM governs the exclusion.
SACM governs the resulting applicability context. Applicability Context ≠ Operational Reality
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SACM does not determine what conditions currently exist in the real world.
It governs:
the contextual conditions for which the simulation is designed.
The relationship may later be examined as:
Simulation Applicability Context ↔ Actual Operational Reality
but the two spaces remain architecturally distinct.
Operational Applicability
Operational applicability identifies the operating conditions addressed by the simulation.
Examples may include: normal operation, degraded operation, emergency operation, maintenance state, startup, shutdown, autonomous operation, supervised operation, remote operation, or defined mission phases.
A simulation intended for nominal operation should not silently acquire emergency-operation applicability.
Environmental Applicability
Environmental applicability establishes which environmental conditions form part of the intended simulation context.

Examples may include: temperature range, weather, visibility, radiation, terrain, atmospheric conditions, electromagnetic environment, network conditions, traffic density, industrial environment, or other environmental factors.
Spatial Applicability
Spatial applicability defines the physical, geographic, virtual, or logical spaces for which the simulation inquiry is intended.
Examples include:
specific facility
defined road network
airspace class
orbital region
geographic region
digital network environment
or:
virtual operational domain Temporal Applicability
Temporal applicability identifies time-related contextual boundaries.
It may govern: simulation period, operational duration, mission phase, lifecycle stage, seasonal conditions, time horizon, system age, or another temporally bounded condition.
A simulation of short-duration system behavior must not automatically imply long-duration applicability.
Population Applicability
Where humans, users, organizations, agents, vehicles, devices, or other populations are relevant, SACM identifies which population characteristics belong to the intended context.
Examples:
Adult Population
Pediatric Population
Trained Operators
General Public
Vehicle Class A
Robot Type B
Population applicability prevents results generated for one defined population from being automatically generalized to another.
Configuration Applicability

A simulation may apply only to a particular: hardware configuration, software version, model version, component combination, system architecture, parameter set, or deployment configuration.
SACM preserves this contextual binding.
Capability Applicability
Simulation applicability may depend upon the capability state of the Simulation Object.
For example:
AI advisory capability
may be represented while:
autonomous tool execution
is outside the intended applicability context.
A material capability change may therefore invalidate or narrow the applicability of the existing simulation inquiry.
Behavioral Applicability
A simulation may address only defined behavioral modes.
Examples include:
Nominal Behavior
Cooperative Behavior
Adversarial Behavior
Human-Supervised Behavior
Autonomous Behavior
Failure Behavior
Behavioral applicability should remain explicit wherever behavioral differences materially affect the simulation inquiry.
Interaction Applicability
Where multiple actors or systems interact, applicability may depend upon defined interaction structures.
Examples: human–AI interaction, robot–human interaction, vehicle–vehicle interaction, multi-agent coordination, infrastructure–system interaction, or cross-system communication.
Representation of the actors alone does not establish applicability to every possible interaction among them.
Autonomy Applicability
For autonomous systems, the degree of autonomy may materially define applicability.
A simulation performed under:

Human-in-the-Loop
conditions cannot automatically support applicability to:
Fully Autonomous Operation.
SACM preserves the applicable autonomy context.
Scenario Applicability
A simulation may apply to a defined scenario class.
Examples include:
Nominal Scenarios
Edge Cases
Emergency Scenarios
Adversarial Scenarios
Rare Events
High-Density Operations
Failure & Recovery Scenarios
The applicability record should distinguish the scenario classes actually intended by the simulation inquiry.
Dependency Applicability
Simulation meaning may depend upon external conditions or systems.
Examples include: network availability, sensor infrastructure, positioning services, human supervision, external data, power availability, third-party services, or supporting infrastructure.
Applicability may therefore be conditional upon those dependencies remaining present.
Infrastructure Applicability
Where simulation outcomes depend upon infrastructure characteristics, the applicable infrastructure context should be identified.
For example:
Warehouse Infrastructure Type A
may differ materially from:
Open Industrial Yard
even when the same autonomous robot is simulated.
Decision-Context Applicability
A simulation may be designed to inform a specific class of decisions.
Examples include: design selection, engineering analysis, safety investigation, mission planning, operational planning, capacity planning, training, policy exploration, validation evidence generation, or research.

A simulation designed for exploratory research should not automatically be treated as suitable for high-consequence operational authorization.
SACM identifies the intended decision context.
It does not itself authorize reliance.
Consequence Context
The consequence of using simulation outputs may affect how narrowly applicability should be established.
A simulation informing:
early concept exploration
may operate under a different applicability requirement than one intended to support:
safety-critical deployment decisions.
SACM preserves the intended consequence context so downstream governance can apply the appropriate requirements.
Applicability Conditions
A Simulation Applicability Condition is a condition that must hold for the intended contextual relationship between the simulation and its governed inquiry to remain applicable.
Examples:
Software Version = 4.2
Temperature = −10°C to +40°C
Human Supervisor Present
Maximum Payload ≤ 500 kg
Network Latency ≤ Defined Threshold
Applicability conditions should be explicit where their violation materially changes simulation meaning.
Conditional Applicability
A simulation may be applicable only while specific conditions remain true.
This may be represented as:
Conditionally Applicable
The condition should remain traceable to the relevant applicability dimension.
Partial Applicability
A simulation may apply to only part of the intended operational context.
For example:
Applicable — Normal Operation

Partially Applicable — Degraded Operation
Not Intended — Emergency Operation
Partial applicability should remain visible rather than being collapsed into a universal applicability statement.
Applicability Boundary
The Simulation Applicability Boundary separates:
Context Addressed by the Simulation Inquiry
from:
Context Not Addressed by the Simulation Inquiry
This boundary may be: operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population-based, configuration-based, capability-based, behavioral, scenario-based, dependency-based, or multidimensional.
Applicability Envelope
Multiple applicability dimensions may be combined into a Simulation Applicability Envelope.
Conceptually:
Environment × Time × Population × Configuration × Capability × Behavior × Scenario × Dependencies
defines the contextual space in which the simulation inquiry is intended to operate.
The envelope is conceptual and need not be numerical.
Applicability Combination
Individual applicability conditions may interact.
For example:
Rain
may be individually included.
Night
may be individually included.
But:
Night + Heavy Rain
may not have been included as a combined simulation context.
SACM therefore distinguishes:
Individual Context Applicability
from:
Combined Context Applicability
where interaction effects are material.
No Applicability by Component Rule
The fact that individual conditions were represented separately does not automatically establish applicability to every combination of those conditions.

Applicability Assumption
An applicability context may depend upon assumptions.
For example:
Communication infrastructure assumed continuously available.
The applicability record should preserve the dependency on that assumption.
The assumption itself is governed by the appropriate downstream SIMULOS® assumption governance.
Applicability Dependency
An applicability context may depend upon another condition remaining valid.
Conceptually:
Applicability Context → Required Dependency → Dependency State
Where the dependency materially changes, applicability may require reassessment.
Applicability Restriction
A Simulation Applicability Restriction explicitly prevents interpretation outside a defined contextual boundary.
Examples:
Not applicable to outdoor operation
Not applicable above defined velocity
Not applicable to pediatric population
Not applicable to fully autonomous operation
Restrictions should remain visible in downstream simulation interpretation.
Applicability Uncertainty
Sometimes it may be unclear whether a simulation remains applicable to a context.
Such uncertainty should not be converted automatically into positive applicability.
Possible status:
Applicability Undetermined
until sufficient governance information exists.
Applicability Conflict
An applicability conflict exists where different parts of the governed simulation record imply incompatible applicability boundaries.
For example:
Simulation Scope: Global operation.

Environmental Applicability: Temperate climates only.
The conflict should be resolved or explicitly preserved before broad simulation claims are made. Applicability–Purpose Alignment
The applicability context must remain capable of supporting the Simulation Purpose.
If the purpose requires:
global autonomous navigation safety
but applicability is limited to:
daytime operation on one mapped campus,
the mismatch is material.
SACM should expose that mismatch rather than allowing the narrow simulation context to satisfy the broader purpose implicitly. Applicability–Scope Alignment
Applicability must remain consistent with the governed Simulation Scope.
A scope describing multiple environments cannot be treated as satisfied where the applicability context covers only one environment unless the difference is explicitly governed. Applicability–Exclusion Alignment
Material exclusions should be reflected in applicability where appropriate.
Conceptually:
Material Exclusion → Applicability Consequence
For example:
Emergency Operation Excluded
should prevent the applicability context from silently including emergency operation.
No Universal Applicability Rule
No simulation should be treated as universally applicable merely because its applicability boundary was not documented.
Undefined applicability is not universal applicability.
No Context Transfer Rule

A simulation designed for Context A must not automatically acquire applicability to Context B merely because the Simulation Object is the same.
No Context Generalization Rule
Simulation outputs must not be generalized beyond the governed applicability context without an additional basis.
No Configuration Transfer Rule
Results associated with one materially relevant configuration must not automatically transfer to another materially different configuration.
No Population Transfer Rule
Results associated with one population must not automatically be generalized to another materially different population.
No Environment Transfer Rule
Results associated with one environment must not automatically be treated as applicable to another materially different environment.
No Autonomy Transfer Rule
Simulation under one autonomy condition must not automatically establish applicability under a materially different autonomy condition.
No Scenario Inflation Rule
Simulation of selected scenarios must not be represented as applicability to all possible scenarios.
Applicability Change
Applicability may change when the simulation inquiry, Simulation Object, assumptions, model, environment, scenario structure, or operational context changes.
SACM therefore treats applicability as a governed contextual state rather than permanent metadata.
Applicability Expansion

An applicability context may expand when new simulation work sufficiently addresses additional: environments, populations, configurations, scenarios, capabilities, behaviors, or dependencies.
Expansion should have a traceable basis.
Applicability Narrowing
New information may demonstrate that the simulation applies to less than originally expected.
Narrowing is a legitimate governance outcome.
For example:
Originally Intended: Urban Roads
may become:
Supported Simulation Context: Urban Roads Below 60 km/h
after limitations are identified.
SACM permits the applicability context to become narrower without treating this as methodological failure.
Applicability Change Trigger
Material changes that may require applicability reassessment include: Simulation Object version change, configuration change, new capability, new autonomy level, new environment, new population, new scenario class, changed dependency, changed purpose, changed scope, or changed exclusions.
Applicability Status
Possible statuses may include:
Applicable Context Established
Conditionally Applicable
Partially Applicable
Applicability Restricted
Applicability Under Review
Applicability Conflicted
or:
Applicability Undetermined Applicability Context Record

A governed simulation may maintain a Simulation Applicability Context Record identifying: Simulation Object, Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, material exclusions, applicable operational conditions, applicable environments, spatial boundaries, temporal boundaries, applicable populations, configurations, capability states, behavioral modes, autonomy conditions, scenario classes, dependencies, decision context, consequence context, applicability conditions, restrictions, uncertainties, status, and change history.
Applicability Traceability
Material applicability conditions should remain traceable through the simulation lifecycle.
A downstream reviewer should be capable of determining:
For which context was this simulation actually designed?
and:
Does the current interpretation remain inside that context?
Failure Conditions

SACM governance failure may exist where: applicability context is undefined, a bounded simulation is represented as universally applicable, applicability conflicts with Simulation Purpose, applicability conflicts with Simulation Scope, material exclusions are not reflected in applicability, results are transferred between materially different environments without basis, population differences are ignored, configuration changes are ignored, autonomy changes are ignored, scenario applicability is inflated, dependencies affecting applicability remain undocumented, combined-context effects are ignored, applicability uncertainty is represented as established applicability, applicability expansion occurs without supporting simulation work, applicability restrictions disappear from downstream interpretation, or simulation outputs are represented outside the context for which the simulation was designed.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Applicability Dimensions
Determine the operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population, configuration, capability, behavioral, autonomy, scenario, dependency, and decision dimensions material to the simulation inquiry. 2. Establish Applicability Conditions
Define the contextual conditions under which the simulation is intended to apply. 3. Define the Applicability Boundary

Distinguish applicable, conditionally applicable, partially applicable, restricted, and undetermined contexts. 4. Align Applicability With Purpose, Scope, and Exclusions
Verify that the applicability context does not exceed the governed Simulation Purpose, Scope, or material exclusions. 5. Preserve Applicability Traceability
Maintain the Simulation Applicability Context Record and propagate material contextual boundaries into downstream simulation design, outputs, interpretation, and lifecycle reassessment.
Governance Outputs

SACM may produce: Simulation Applicability Context, Simulation Applicability Context Record, Applicability Dimension Map, Operational Applicability Record, Environmental Applicability Record, Spatial Applicability Record, Temporal Applicability Record, Population Applicability Record, Configuration Applicability Record, Capability Applicability Record, Behavioral Applicability Record, Interaction Applicability Record, Autonomy Applicability Record, Scenario Applicability Record, Dependency Applicability Record, Infrastructure Applicability Record, Decision-Context Applicability Record, Consequence-Context Applicability Record, Applicability Condition Record, Conditional Applicability Record, Partial Applicability Record, Applicability Restriction Record, Applicability Uncertainty Record, Applicability Dependency Map, Combined Context Applicability Record, Simulation Applicability Envelope, Applicability–Purpose Alignment Record, Applicability–Scope Alignment Record, Applicability–Exclusion Alignment Record, Applicability Conflict Record, Applicability Change Record, Applicability Expansion Record, Applicability Narrowing Record, Simulation Applicability Status, and Simulation Applicability Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous-driving simulation evaluates collision avoidance.
The Simulation Scope covers urban driving.
The simulation environment represents:
daylight,
dry and wet roads,
speeds up to 60 km/h,
and:

defined European road configurations.
Snow, severe fog, and speeds above 60 km/h are outside the governed inquiry. Application
SACM establishes the Simulation Applicability Context as:
Urban European Road Environment
Daylight Operation
Dry / Wet Surface Conditions
≤ 60 km/h
The simulation is not assigned applicability to severe fog, snow, higher speeds, or materially different road environments. Result
The simulation outputs retain a clear contextual boundary.
The fact that collision avoidance performed successfully within the governed context cannot be used to imply equivalent simulation coverage across all driving environments. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Autonomous Navigation Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft navigation system is simulated for autonomous orbital insertion.
The simulation represents:
defined spacecraft configuration,
specified orbital conditions,
nominal communication availability,
and:
a bounded propulsion-performance range.
A later spacecraft configuration introduces a modified propulsion system. Application
SACM binds the original Simulation Applicability Context to the original configuration and propulsion conditions.
The new propulsion configuration creates an Applicability Change Trigger.
The previous simulation is not automatically considered applicable to the modified spacecraft. Result
The simulation lifecycle preserves the distinction between:
same mission purpose
and:
different applicability context.

Additional simulation work can determine whether applicability may legitimately expand to the new configuration.
Architectural Position
Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The internal progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Simulation Depth & Precision
SPM establishes why the simulation exists.
SSCM establishes what it must cover.
SEXM establishes what remains outside the governed inquiry.
SACM establishes the contextual envelope within which that inquiry is intended to apply.
SDPM subsequently establishes how deeply and precisely the simulation must examine that governed inquiry.
SACM does not govern actual Operational Reality under ORA™, general validation applicability under VALIDOS®, integrity under INTEGROS®, or the quality and fidelity with which reality is represented under the subsequent Reality Representation Standard (RRS).
It governs specifically:
the contextual applicability boundary of the simulation inquiry.
Foundational Principle
A simulation can legitimately represent only the contextual space for which its inquiry was designed; applicability must therefore remain explicitly bounded wherever changes in environment, time, population, configuration, capability, behavior, scenario, or dependency could materially change the meaning of its results.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) establishes the contextual boundary of governed simulation by defining the operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population, configuration, capability, behavioral, autonomy, scenario, dependency, and decision conditions within which a simulation inquiry is intended to apply. Through applicability dimensions, contextual conditions, applicability envelopes, restrictions, dependency mapping, alignment with purpose, scope, and exclusions, anti-generalization rules, change governance, and lifecycle traceability, SACM prevents simulation outputs produced within one bounded context from silently acquiring meaning across materially different contexts. By preserving where, when, for whom, under which configuration, and under which conditions a simulation is intended to apply, SACM ensures that contextual boundaries remain part of the simulation itself rather than becoming invisible after results are produced.
