chunks.text:
OOF™ Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM)
Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Dependency
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Assumption Dependency
Canonical Definition
Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM) defines the governance framework for identifying, structuring, mapping, classifying, propagating, and maintaining the dependencies through which Simulation Assumptions influence other assumptions, model elements, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, outputs, and downstream simulation conclusions.
It establishes the methodological mechanism through which an identified and sufficiently based Simulation Assumption is connected to everything within the simulation that materially depends upon it.

SADM does not determine whether an assumption is universally true, quantify its complete uncertainty, or determine the ultimate validity of simulation outputs.
It governs where an assumption matters, what depends upon it, how dependencies interact, and how changes or failures in an assumption must remain traceable through the simulation.
Operational Role
SADM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The preceding modules establish:
SAIM — Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant?
SABM — On what basis is each assumption being used?
SADM asks:
What depends upon each Simulation Assumption, which assumptions depend upon one another, and how can those dependencies remain visible throughout the simulation lifecycle?
The governed progression is:
Governed Simulation Assumption → Dependency Discovery → Dependency Classification → Dependency Mapping → Dependency Materiality → Dependency Interaction → Dependency Propagation → Dependency Change → Dependency Record
The resulting dependency structure becomes an input to subsequent:
Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation
Module Operational Space

SADM governs: assumption dependency identification, assumption-to-assumption dependency, assumption-to-model dependency, assumption-to-parameter dependency, assumption-to-environment dependency, assumption-to-input dependency, assumption-to-scenario dependency, assumption-to-execution dependency, assumption-to-output dependency, assumption-to-conclusion dependency, direct dependencies, indirect dependencies, upstream dependencies, downstream dependencies, conditional dependencies, shared dependencies, chained dependencies, circular dependencies, hidden dependencies, compound dependencies, dependency concentration, dependency criticality, dependency materiality, dependency interaction, dependency propagation, dependency change, dependency failure propagation, dependency reassessment, and complete assumption-dependency traceability.
Module Function
A Simulation Assumption may appear to be a single statement while influencing a substantial part of the simulation.
For example:
Atmospheric density is assumed to remain within Range X.
That assumption may influence:
Aerodynamic Model → Vehicle Dynamics → Energy Consumption → Trajectory → Mission Outcome
If the assumption changes, every materially dependent element may also change.
SADM prevents assumptions from being governed as isolated statements when their consequences are structurally distributed throughout the simulation.
Its function is therefore to transform:
Assumption
into:

Assumption + Dependency Structure + Affected Simulation Elements + Propagation Path Simulation Assumption Dependency
A Simulation Assumption Dependency exists where the state, configuration, behavior, interpretation, execution, or output of one simulation element materially depends upon a Simulation Assumption.
Conceptually:
Simulation Assumption
↓
Dependent Element
↓
Affected Simulation Behavior
A dependency may be explicit or implicit.
SADM requires material dependencies to become governable regardless of how they originated.
Dependency Object
A Simulation Assumption may affect: another assumption, a model component, a simulation environment, a parameter, an input, a transformation, a scenario, an execution condition, an interaction, an output, an interpretation, or a simulation conclusion.
Each materially affected element may become a Dependency Object for purposes of assumption governance.
Direct Dependency
A Direct Dependency exists where an element immediately relies upon an assumption.
Example:
Assumption A → Parameter P
If Parameter P is directly assigned from Assumption A, the dependency is direct.
Indirect Dependency
An Indirect Dependency exists where the influence of an assumption passes through one or more intermediate elements.
Example:
Assumption A → Parameter P → Model M → Output O
Output O may therefore depend materially upon Assumption A even though the output does not reference the assumption directly.

SADM requires material indirect dependencies to remain discoverable.
Upstream Dependency
An assumption may itself depend upon another assumption or governed simulation condition.
Example:
Assumption B depends upon Assumption A.
Assumption A is therefore upstream of Assumption B.
Changes in upstream assumptions may require reassessment of downstream assumptions.
Downstream Dependency
Every materially affected element following an assumption in the dependency chain is downstream of that assumption.
A single assumption may have many downstream dependencies.
SADM preserves these relationships so that assumption change can be propagated rather than treated locally.
Assumption-to-Assumption Dependency
Simulation Assumptions may depend upon one another.
For example:
Assumption A: Road friction remains above threshold X.
Assumption B: Vehicle braking distance remains below threshold Y.
If B relies upon A, the relationship should be explicit.
The simulation should not represent B as independently established where its operation materially depends upon A.
Assumption-to-Model Dependency
A model component may depend upon one or several assumptions.
Example:
Human Response Model
may depend upon assumptions concerning: reaction time, attention, movement speed, compliance, environmental visibility, or behavioral variability.
SADM maps these relationships.
Assumption-to-Parameter Dependency
Parameters frequently encode assumptions.

A fixed parameter may appear to be a technical value while actually representing an assumption about reality.
SADM therefore asks:
Does this parameter derive from an assumption, and would the parameter require reassessment if that assumption changed?
Where yes, the dependency should remain explicit.
Assumption-to-Environment Dependency
A simulation environment may rely upon assumptions concerning: temperature, gravity, terrain, traffic, radiation, network conditions, human presence, resource availability, or other environmental states.
SADM maps the relationship between those assumptions and the affected environmental representation.
Assumption-to-Input Dependency
An input may depend upon assumptions used during: selection, transformation, interpolation, extrapolation, normalization, generation, estimation, or preprocessing.
The input should not be treated as assumption-independent where such dependence materially exists.
Assumption-to-Scenario Dependency
Scenarios may exist only because certain assumptions hold.
For example:
Emergency evacuation completes within five minutes
may be a scenario condition dependent upon assumptions about: population mobility, route availability, communication, human response, and environmental conditions.
SADM makes those dependencies visible.
Assumption-to-Execution Dependency
Simulation execution itself may depend upon assumptions.

Examples include assumptions about: convergence, timing, resource availability, computational behavior, event ordering, system stability, or execution constraints.
Where execution behavior materially depends upon an assumption, the dependency belongs within the governed map.
Assumption-to-Output Dependency
A simulation output may materially depend upon one or many assumptions.
SADM establishes the traceability relationship:
Assumption → Simulation Path → Output
This relationship is critical because a simulation output may appear precise even when it depends heavily upon assumptions.
Assumption-to-Conclusion Dependency
A simulation conclusion may depend upon outputs that themselves depend upon assumptions.
The complete chain may therefore become:
Assumption → Model Element → Execution → Output → Simulation Conclusion
SADM preserves this dependency path.
It does not determine whether the conclusion may legitimately support external reliance; that remains outside the module boundary.
Conditional Dependency
A dependency may exist only under specified conditions.
Example:
Assumption A affects Output O only when Temperature > T.
SADM should preserve the triggering condition rather than treating the dependency as universally active.
Shared Dependency
Multiple simulation elements may depend upon the same assumption.
Conceptually:
Assumption A
↙ ↓ ↘
Element 1 · Element 2 · Element 3

Shared dependencies can create concentration risk because one assumption may influence many apparently independent outputs.
Dependency Concentration
Dependency Concentration exists where a large or critical portion of the simulation depends upon one assumption or a small set of assumptions.
This condition should remain visible.
A simulation containing hundreds of parameters may still depend materially upon only a few foundational assumptions.
SADM prevents structural complexity from hiding assumption concentration.
Compound Dependency
A simulation element may depend simultaneously upon multiple assumptions.
For example:
Output O = dependent upon A + B + C
Where the assumptions interact materially, the dependency should be represented as compound rather than as three unrelated relationships.
Dependency Chain
A Simulation Assumption Dependency Chain represents the sequence through which assumption influence propagates.
Example:
Assumption A
↓
Parameter B
↓
Model Component C
↓
Scenario D
↓
Output E
↓
Conclusion F
SADM requires material chains to remain reconstructable.
Dependency Depth
Dependency Depth describes how far an assumption's influence extends through the simulation structure.
A shallow dependency may affect one parameter.
A deep dependency may propagate through multiple model components, scenarios, outputs, and conclusions.
Depth may therefore be relevant when determining assumption materiality.
Dependency Breadth

Dependency Breadth describes how many materially distinct simulation elements depend upon an assumption.
An assumption may have:
Low Breadth
or:
High Breadth
depending upon how widely its influence is distributed.
Dependency Materiality
Not every dependency requires equal governance attention.
SADM may evaluate materiality according to factors such as: effect on model behavior, effect on scenario behavior, effect on outputs, effect on conclusions, dependency breadth, dependency depth, sensitivity, reversibility, and consequence of dependency failure.
The objective is not to eliminate minor dependencies.
The objective is to ensure that material dependencies cannot remain invisible.
Critical Assumption Dependency
A Critical Assumption Dependency exists where failure, invalidation, or material change of an assumption may substantially alter: simulation behavior, a critical scenario, a key output, a major conclusion, or the intended use of the simulation.
Critical dependencies should receive explicit identification.
Dependency Interaction
Dependencies may interact.
For example:
Assumption A alone may have limited influence.
Assumption B alone may have limited influence.
But:
A + B
may materially change the simulation outcome.
SADM therefore recognizes that dependency governance cannot always be reduced to isolated one-to-one relationships.
Dependency Amplification
A small change in an assumption may produce a disproportionately large downstream effect.

This creates Dependency Amplification.
Example:
Small change in friction assumption
↓
Large change in stopping-distance output
Where amplification is material, the dependency should be identifiable for subsequent uncertainty governance.
Dependency Dampening
The opposite may also occur.
A substantial assumption change may produce little downstream effect because other model mechanisms dampen the influence.
SADM may preserve this relationship where relevant.
Hidden Dependency
A Hidden Simulation Assumption Dependency exists where a material relationship influences the simulation but is not represented within the governed dependency structure.
Hidden dependencies may arise through: inherited models, reused code, default parameters, embedded constants, external libraries, external datasets, model coupling, undocumented transformations, or inherited assumptions.
SADM requires material hidden dependencies, once discovered, to be brought into governance.
Inherited Dependency
A reused model or simulation component may carry dependency relationships from an earlier simulation.
These dependencies should not automatically be assumed applicable.
SADM asks whether they remain relevant to the current: Simulation Object, purpose, scope, reality representation, assumptions, model, environment, and scenario context.
Circular Dependency
A Circular Assumption Dependency exists where assumptions or simulation elements depend recursively upon one another.
Example:

Assumption A → Model B → Derived Condition C → Assumption A
Circularity is not automatically prohibited.
Some dynamic systems legitimately contain feedback loops.
However, material circular dependencies must be visible so they are not mistaken for independent support. Dependency vs. Basis
SADM maintains a strict distinction:
SABM asks: Why is this assumption being used?
SADM asks: What depends upon this assumption?
The basis is upstream justification.
The dependency structure is downstream influence.
The two should not be conflated. Dependency vs. Uncertainty
SADM identifies the pathways through which an assumption matters.
SAUM — Simulation Assumption Uncertainty Module subsequently governs uncertainty associated with assumptions and its relevance.
SADM therefore identifies:
Where uncertainty may propagate
without replacing uncertainty governance itself. Dependency vs. Limitation
SADM identifies affected simulation elements.
SALM — Simulation Assumption Limitation Module governs where assumptions cease to remain applicable and how those limitations must remain visible.
This preserves clean module boundaries.
Dependency Propagation
Where an assumption changes materially, SADM identifies the downstream path requiring reassessment.
Conceptually:
Assumption Change
↓
Direct Dependencies
↓
Indirect Dependencies
↓
Affected Outputs
↓
Affected Conclusions
This is Simulation Assumption Dependency Propagation.
Dependency Change Trigger

Dependency reassessment may be triggered by: assumption modification, assumption removal, assumption replacement, basis change, model change, environment change, parameter change, scenario change, new dependency discovery, or changed simulation purpose or scope.
Assumption Removal
Removing an assumption does not necessarily remove its effects.
A parameter, model component, or scenario may continue to encode the old assumption.
SADM therefore requires the affected dependency path to be examined when an assumption is removed.
Assumption Replacement
Where:
Assumption A
is replaced by:
Assumption B
the simulation should not merely update the assumption register.
Material dependencies should be reassessed against the replacement assumption.
Dependency Failure Propagation
Where an assumption becomes unsupported, materially changed, or otherwise unsuitable for its simulation role, dependent elements may require reassessment.
SADM establishes:
Assumption Failure ≠ Local Failure Only
The impact may propagate throughout the simulation.
No Dependency Isolation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material assumption must not be treated as isolated when simulation elements, outputs, or conclusions materially depend upon it.
No Hidden Propagation Principle
A change to an assumption should not be considered fully governed while material downstream consequences remain unidentified.
No False Independence Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Two simulation outputs must not be represented as assumption-independent merely because they are produced by different model components when both materially depend upon the same underlying assumption.
This is particularly important when multiple outputs appear to provide independent confirmation.
No Dependency Laundering Principle
An assumption dependency does not disappear merely because the assumption passes through: a parameter, another model, a scenario, an external component, or multiple computational transformations.
The dependency remains methodologically relevant while material influence persists.
Dependency Traceability
SADM should preserve the relationship:
Assumption
↓
Direct Dependency
↓
Intermediate Dependency
↓
Affected Simulation Element
↓
Affected Output
↓
Affected Conclusion
where applicable.
This creates the Simulation Assumption Dependency Traceability Chain.
Dependency Map
A Simulation Assumption Dependency Map may represent: assumptions, dependency objects, direct relationships, indirect relationships, conditional relationships, shared dependencies, critical dependencies, dependency chains, and affected outputs.
The map may be implemented graphically, computationally, or structurally.
SIMULOS® governs the required methodological relationships rather than prescribing the implementation technology.
Dependency Matrix
Where useful, assumptions and affected elements may be represented through a dependency matrix.

Conceptually: Assumption Model Parameter Scenario Output Conclusion A1 ✓ ✓ — ✓ ✓ A2 — ✓ ✓ ✓ — A3 ✓ — ✓ ✓ ✓
The matrix does not replace the underlying dependency records.
It provides a compact representation of them.
Dependency Status
A dependency may be classified as:
Identified
Confirmed
Conditional
Indirect
Critical
Under Assessment
Changed
Inactive
Superseded
or:
Undetermined Dependency Gap
A Simulation Assumption Dependency Gap exists where a material dependency: is unknown, cannot be traced, is incompletely mapped, has ambiguous direction, has uncertain affected elements, or cannot be connected to relevant outputs or conclusions.
Dependency gaps should remain visible.
Dependency Reassessment
When a material assumption or dependency changes, affected relationships should be reassessed.
The reassessment asks:
Does the dependency still exist?
Has its strength or materiality changed?
Have new dependencies appeared?
Have prior dependencies disappeared?
Which downstream elements require renewed examination?
Dependency Continuity
SADM preserves dependency history across simulation changes.
Where assumptions or model configurations change, prior dependency maps should remain traceable to the simulation versions in which they applied.
This supports reconstruction of historical simulation results.
Simulation Version Binding
Dependency structures should be bound to the relevant simulation configuration or version.

A dependency map from Simulation Version 1 should not automatically be treated as valid for Simulation Version 2 where assumptions, models, parameters, or environments materially changed.
Dependency Record
For each material dependency, SADM may establish a Simulation Assumption Dependency Record containing: Dependency ID, Assumption ID, Dependency Object ID, Dependency Type, Dependency Direction, Direct / Indirect Status, Applicable Conditions, Dependency Chain, Dependency Breadth, Dependency Depth, Materiality, Criticality, Interaction References, Propagation Path, Change Status, affected outputs, affected conclusions, simulation version, and traceability references.
Dependency Set
All material assumption dependencies may form a:
Governed Simulation Assumption Dependency Set
This provides a structured basis for subsequent uncertainty and limitation governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Bind the Dependency Inquiry
Identify the Simulation Assumption and simulation configuration being examined. 2. Identify Direct Dependencies
Determine which assumptions, parameters, models, scenarios, environments, execution conditions, or outputs immediately depend upon the assumption. 3. Trace Indirect Dependencies
Follow material dependency chains through intermediate simulation elements. 4. Classify Dependency Relationships
Distinguish direct, indirect, conditional, shared, compound, inherited, circular, and other relevant dependency forms. 5. Assess Materiality and Criticality

Determine which dependencies can materially influence simulation behavior, outputs, or conclusions. 6. Identify Dependency Interactions
Determine whether multiple assumptions or dependency paths interact, amplify, dampen, or concentrate influence. 7. Establish Propagation Paths
Map how assumption change or failure may affect downstream simulation elements. 8. Record Dependency Gaps
Preserve unknown, incomplete, or unresolved material dependency relationships. 9. Bind Dependencies to Simulation Version
Ensure the dependency structure remains associated with the simulation configuration to which it applies. 10. Preserve Dependency Traceability
Maintain the reconstructable relationship:
Assumption → Dependency → Simulation Element → Output → Conclusion
Governance Outputs

SADM may produce: Simulation Assumption Dependency Identifier, Simulation Assumption Dependency Record, Direct Dependency Record, Indirect Dependency Record, Conditional Dependency Record, Shared Dependency Record, Compound Dependency Record, Circular Dependency Record, Inherited Dependency Record, Critical Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Assumption Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Model Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Parameter Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Scenario Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Execution Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Output Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Conclusion Dependency Record, Dependency Materiality Assessment, Dependency Criticality Assessment, Dependency Interaction Record, Dependency Concentration Record, Dependency Amplification Record, Dependency Propagation Path, Dependency Change Record, Dependency Reassessment Record, Dependency Gap Record, Simulation Assumption Dependency Map, Simulation Assumption Dependency Matrix, Simulation Assumption Dependency Traceability Chain, and Governed Simulation Assumption Dependency Set.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario
A vehicle simulation assumes:
Road friction remains above coefficient X.
The assumption is explicitly identified and has a documented engineering basis. Application
SADM maps the dependency chain:
Road-Friction Assumption
↓
Tire-Road Interaction Model
↓
Braking Model
↓
Stopping Distance
↓
Collision-Avoidance Scenario
↓
Safety-Relevant Simulation Output

The same assumption also affects steering stability. Result
The assumption is classified as having:
High Dependency Breadth + Critical Downstream Dependency
A change to the friction assumption therefore requires reassessment of more than the braking model alone. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation
Scenario
A mission simulation assumes:
Solar-array degradation remains within the modeled annual range. Application
SADM identifies dependencies across:
Energy Generation → Battery State → Communications Availability → Thermal Control → Mission Operations
The dependency is conditional upon the simulated radiation environment. Result
The assumption is recorded as a:
Conditional Critical Dependency
If the radiation environment changes materially, the dependency chain becomes subject to reassessment before affected mission outputs are treated as unchanged.
Architectural Position
Simulation Assumption Dependency is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The complete SAS progression is:
Simulation Assumption Identification → Simulation Assumption Basis → Simulation Assumption Dependency → Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation
SAIM establishes:
Which assumptions exist?
SABM establishes:
Why is each assumption being used?
SADM establishes:
What depends upon each assumption?
SAUM establishes:
What uncertainty exists around the assumptions and how must it remain visible?
SALM establishes:

Where do the assumptions cease to remain applicable and what limitations follow?
Together, these modules ensure that Simulation Assumptions remain identifiable, supported, structurally connected to their consequences, uncertainty-aware, and bounded throughout the simulation lifecycle.
Foundational Principle
A Simulation Assumption cannot be fully governed unless the material simulation elements, outputs, and conclusions that depend upon it can be identified and traced.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Assumption Dependency Module establishes the dependency-governance layer of the Simulation Assumption Standard by identifying and preserving the pathways through which Simulation Assumptions influence other assumptions, parameters, models, environments, scenarios, execution conditions, outputs, and simulation conclusions. Through direct and indirect dependency mapping, shared and compound dependency governance, materiality and criticality assessment, interaction analysis, dependency propagation, change reassessment, version binding, gap visibility, and complete assumption-to-consequence traceability, SADM prevents material assumptions from functioning as isolated or hidden premises and ensures that changes to an assumption can be systematically propagated to every materially affected part of the simulation.
Modul 4

OOF™ Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM)
Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Identification
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Assumption Identification
Canonical Definition
Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM) defines the governance framework for identifying, distinguishing, classifying, documenting, and maintaining the assumptions upon which a simulation materially depends.
It establishes the methodological mechanism through which explicit and implicit premises are converted into identifiable Simulation Assumptions before those premises become embedded invisibly within simulation models, environments, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, or interpretation of simulation outputs.

Operational Role
SAIM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The preceding Reality Representation Standard (RRS) establishes which aspects of reality are represented within the simulation and at what abstraction, fidelity, resolution, and limitation.
SAIM begins where that governed representation requires additional premises in order to become operationally usable within a simulation.
SAIM asks:
What is being assumed in order for this simulation to operate, and which of those assumptions are material enough to require explicit governance?
The governed progression begins:
Governed Reality Representation → Assumption Discovery → Assumption Identification → Assumption Classification → Materiality Assessment → Assumption Registration → Governed Simulation Assumption Set
The resulting Simulation Assumption Set becomes the basis for subsequent governance of:
Assumption Basis → Assumption Dependency → Assumption Uncertainty → Assumption Limitation
Module Operational Space

SAIM governs: assumption discovery, explicit assumption identification, implicit assumption identification, embedded assumption identification, inherited assumption identification, model assumption identification, environment assumption identification, parameter assumption identification, behavioral assumption identification, temporal assumption identification, scenario assumption identification, operational-condition assumptions, external-dependency assumptions, assumption classification, assumption materiality, assumption ownership reference, assumption-to-simulation binding, assumption identifiers, assumption status, assumption documentation, assumption traceability, assumption duplication, assumption interaction visibility, assumption change detection, and maintenance of the governed Simulation Assumption Set.
Module Function
SAIM applies after the relevant reality representation has been sufficiently established.
Its primary function is to prevent assumptions from becoming invisible components of the simulation.
A simulation may contain sophisticated models, extensive data, realistic environments, and technically correct execution while still depending upon premises that were never formally identified.
SAIM therefore establishes a controlled distinction between:
what is represented,
what is known,
what is supplied as input,
and:
what must be assumed.
Simulation Assumption

A Simulation Assumption is a premise accepted for the purpose of constructing, configuring, executing, or interpreting a simulation where the relevant condition is not established as a complete governed fact within the simulation basis.
An assumption may concern: reality, system behavior, human behavior, environmental conditions, physical conditions, relationships, dependencies, timing, availability, future states, operating conditions, boundary behavior, parameter behavior, failure behavior, or another condition required by the simulation.
Assumption Identification Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A premise that materially influences simulation behavior should not remain methodologically invisible merely because it is embedded inside a model, configuration, parameter, scenario, or technical implementation.
Identification makes the assumption governable.
It does not establish that the assumption is correct.
Explicit Assumptions
An Explicit Simulation Assumption is intentionally declared as an assumption.
For example:
Average human response time is assumed to remain within the defined operating range.
Because the premise is explicit, it can be examined, challenged, changed, tested, or bounded.
Implicit Assumptions
An Implicit Simulation Assumption exists where the simulation depends upon a premise that has not been formally declared.

Implicit assumptions may arise through: default values, model architecture, omitted variables, simplified relationships, expected behavior, inherited engineering practice, software defaults, scenario construction, or interpretation conventions.
SAIM seeks to convert materially relevant implicit assumptions into explicit governed assumptions.
Embedded Assumptions
Some assumptions are embedded directly inside simulation components.
For example, a model may mathematically encode that:
a relationship remains linear within a particular operating range.
Even where no human explicitly labels this as an assumption, the simulation depends upon it.
SAIM therefore treats materially consequential embedded premises as governance-relevant assumptions.
Inherited Assumptions
A simulation may inherit assumptions from: previous simulations, external models, datasets, engineering models, scientific literature, digital twins, third-party components, vendor models, standard operating models, or reused simulation environments.
Inherited assumptions should not automatically receive governance acceptance merely because the originating component was previously used.
Their role in the current simulation must remain identifiable.
Assumption Versus Fact
SAIM requires a clear methodological distinction between:
Established Condition
and:
Assumed Condition

An assumption must not be silently converted into a fact merely because: it has been used repeatedly, it appears plausible, it originates from an authoritative source, it is embedded in software, it reflects common practice, or previous simulation results were consistent with it.
Assumption Versus Input
Not every simulation input is an assumption.
For example:
Measured temperature = 22°C
may be a governed simulation input.
But:
temperature will remain approximately 22°C throughout the simulated period
may be an assumption.
SAIM preserves this distinction because inputs and assumptions create different governance questions.
Assumption Versus Representation Limitation
A representation limitation identifies something that the simulation does not fully represent.
An assumption identifies a premise accepted so that the simulation can nevertheless proceed.
These may be connected but should remain distinguishable.
For example:
Wind turbulence is represented at reduced resolution
may be a Representation Limitation.
Reduced-resolution turbulence remains sufficient for the simulated flight condition
may be a Simulation Assumption.
Assumption Discovery
Assumption discovery should examine the simulation from multiple directions.
Relevant questions include:
What must be true for this simulation model to behave as intended?
What conditions are being treated as stable?
Which variables have been simplified or held constant?
Which relationships are presumed rather than directly established?

Which external dependencies are expected to behave in a particular way?
Which future conditions are presumed?
Which model defaults contain substantive premises?
Which omitted elements require compensating assumptions?
Assumption Sources
Assumptions may originate from: simulation designers, engineers, scientists, domain experts, model developers, operators, datasets, external models, technical specifications, historical experience, organizational practice, prior simulations, automated model-generation systems, AI systems, or inherited technical components.
SAIM identifies the assumption and its origin where available.
The strength of the supporting basis is governed subsequently by SABM — Simulation Assumption Basis Module.
Assumption Classification
Identified assumptions may be classified according to their role.
Possible classes include:
Reality Assumption
A premise concerning the represented reality.
Model Assumption
A premise required by the simulation model.
Environment Assumption
A premise concerning the simulated environment.
Behavioral Assumption
A premise concerning expected behavior of humans, systems, agents, or other actors.
Parameter Assumption
A premise concerning a parameter or parameter range.
Temporal Assumption
A premise concerning time, sequence, duration, or persistence.
Dependency Assumption
A premise concerning an external or internal dependency.
Scenario Assumption
A premise specific to a particular simulation scenario.
Boundary Assumption

A premise concerning behavior at or beyond a simulation boundary.
Other classifications may be established where required by the simulation domain.
Assumption Materiality
Not every assumption requires the same governance attention.
SAIM distinguishes assumptions according to whether they can materially influence: model behavior, scenario behavior, execution, outputs, output interpretation, operational conclusions, downstream validation, or reliance.
A Material Simulation Assumption is an assumption whose change or failure could materially alter a relevant simulation behavior, output, conclusion, or subsequent decision basis.
Critical Simulation Assumption
A Critical Simulation Assumption is a material assumption whose failure could fundamentally alter: a principal simulation outcome, a high-consequence conclusion, safety-relevant behavior, operational feasibility, or the legitimacy of downstream reliance.
Critical classification does not itself determine whether the assumption is acceptable.
It determines that the assumption requires stronger visibility and downstream governance.
Assumption Materiality Test
A practical materiality test asks:
If this assumption were materially wrong, could the simulation behave differently in a way relevant to its purpose?
If yes, the assumption should normally enter the governed Simulation Assumption Set.
Assumption-to-Simulation Binding
Every material assumption should be connected to the simulation context in which it applies.

The binding may identify:
Simulation Object
Simulation Version
Applicable Model
Applicable Environment
Applicable Scenario
Applicable Parameter
Applicable Execution Condition
or:
Applicable Output Domain
This prevents an assumption from being interpreted as universally applicable when it belongs only to a bounded simulation context.
Assumption Identifier
A governed assumption should receive a sufficiently stable identifier where traceability requires one.
Conceptually:
SA-001 — Network Availability Assumption
SA-002 — Human Response-Time Assumption
SA-003 — Environmental Stability Assumption
The identifier allows downstream simulation artifacts to reference the exact assumption upon which they depend.
Assumption Status
An identified assumption may carry a current governance status such as:
Identified
Under Review
Accepted for Simulation Use
Conditional
Challenged
Superseded
Withdrawn
or:
Unresolved
The status does not substitute for validation.
It communicates the assumption's current role within the simulation governance process.
Assumption Duplication
The same underlying assumption may appear in several parts of a simulation.
SAIM should distinguish between:
multiple references to one assumption
and:
multiple materially different assumptions expressed similarly.
This prevents artificial multiplication of assumption records while preserving real differences.
Assumption Interaction Visibility

Identification should also expose where multiple assumptions may jointly influence the same simulation component or outcome.
Detailed dependency governance belongs to SADM — Simulation Assumption Dependency Module.
SAIM establishes the visibility required for that later analysis.
Assumption Change
An assumption may change because: new evidence appears, operational reality changes, model design changes, simulation scope changes, parameters change, external dependencies change, or the assumption is challenged.
Material changes should preserve continuity between the previous and successor assumption states.
No Hidden Assumption Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material assumption must not remain hidden merely because exposing it would weaken confidence in the simulation.
Simulation governance requires methodological visibility, not presentation convenience.
No Assumption Inflation Principle
An assumption should not gradually become represented as:
known, demonstrated, verified, validated, or factual
without a separate governed basis supporting that transition.
No Assumption Laundering Principle
A premise should not escape assumption governance by being embedded into: a parameter, a model constant, a default configuration, a reused component, a scenario, or a third-party simulation asset.
Its methodological role determines whether it is an assumption.
Assumption Register

SAIM may establish a Simulation Assumption Register containing material assumptions associated with the simulation.
The register may include: Assumption ID, Assumption Statement, Assumption Class, Simulation Object, applicable model or environment, applicable scenario, origin, materiality, criticality, current status, affected simulation elements, and traceability references.
The register provides the structured basis for subsequent SAS modules.
Assumption Set Completeness
SAIM does not require the impossible claim that every conceivable assumption has been discovered.
Instead, it asks whether materially relevant assumptions have been identified with sufficient rigor for the simulation purpose and scope.
Possible states may include:
Assumption Set Sufficiently Identified
Assumption Set Conditionally Identified
Material Assumption Gap Detected
or:
Assumption Identification Undetermined Assumption Gap
A Simulation Assumption Gap exists where a materially relevant premise appears necessary to the simulation but has not been sufficiently identified or governed.
An assumption gap may require: further model examination, expert review, scenario analysis, technical inspection, documentation review, or simulation redesign.
Assumption Identification Traceability
SAIM should preserve:
Simulation Requirement / Representation
↓
Assumption Need
↓
Identified Assumption
↓
Assumption Classification
↓
Materiality
↓
Affected Simulation Element
↓
Assumption Record

This creates a traceable bridge between reality representation and assumption governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Assumption Identification Context
Bind assumption discovery to the relevant: Simulation Object, Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, Reality Representation, and simulation version.
2. Discover Explicit and Implicit Assumptions
Examine: model premises, environmental conditions, parameters, behaviors, scenarios, dependencies, defaults, inherited components, and omitted or simplified reality elements.
3. Convert Material Premises Into Explicit Assumptions
Document materially relevant assumptions as governed Simulation Assumptions. 4. Classify and Bind the Assumptions
Establish: assumption class, simulation context, affected elements, origin, and applicable boundaries.
5. Assess Materiality
Determine which assumptions can materially influence simulation behavior, outputs, interpretation, or downstream reliance. 6. Identify Critical Assumptions
Flag assumptions whose failure could fundamentally affect significant or high-consequence simulation outcomes. 7. Establish the Simulation Assumption Register
Assign identifiers and preserve the governed assumption set. 8. Assess Assumption Identification Sufficiency
Determine whether material assumption gaps remain. 9. Preserve Traceability
Maintain the relationship:
Representation → Assumption → Simulation Element → Assumption Record 10. Transfer the Governed Assumption Set

Provide identified assumptions to subsequent governance of:
Basis → Dependency → Uncertainty → Limitation
Governance Outputs
SAIM may produce: Simulation Assumption Identification Record, Simulation Assumption Register, Explicit Assumption Record, Implicit Assumption Record, Embedded Assumption Record, Inherited Assumption Record, Simulation Assumption Classification, Assumption Materiality Assessment, Critical Simulation Assumption Record, Assumption-to-Simulation Binding Record, Assumption Origin Record, Assumption Status Record, Assumption Interaction Reference, Assumption Change Record, Simulation Assumption Gap Record, Assumption Identification Sufficiency Assessment, Simulation Assumption Traceability Map, and Governed Simulation Assumption Set.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle simulation models urban operation.
The simulation explicitly defines road geometry and traffic signals but implicitly assumes that surrounding human drivers generally remain within modeled behavioral ranges. Application
SAIM identifies:
Human Driver Behavioral Range
as a material Behavioral Assumption.
The assumption is bound to the relevant traffic scenarios and identified as potentially critical where collision-avoidance behavior depends upon it. Result
The premise can no longer remain hidden inside the traffic model.

It enters the Simulation Assumption Register and proceeds to basis, dependency, uncertainty, and limitation governance. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft mission simulation depends upon expected communication availability during several mission phases.
Communication availability is represented through predefined environmental and infrastructure conditions. Application
SAIM identifies:
Expected Communication Availability
as a material Dependency Assumption.
The assumption is bound to the relevant mission phases and to simulation outputs that depend upon command availability. Result
The simulation can explicitly distinguish outcomes that remain robust from outcomes materially dependent upon the communication assumption.
Architectural Position
Simulation Assumption Identification is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The complete SAS progression is:
Simulation Assumption Identification → Simulation Assumption Basis → Simulation Assumption Dependency → Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation
SAIM establishes:
Which assumptions exist and which are material?
SABM then establishes:
What basis supports each assumption?
SADM establishes:
What depends upon each assumption and how do assumptions depend upon one another?
SAUM establishes:
How uncertain is the assumption and how must that uncertainty remain represented?
SALM establishes:

Where does the assumption cease to apply and what limitations follow from it?
Together, these modules transform simulation assumptions from hidden premises into explicit, bounded, traceable governance objects.
Foundational Principle
A simulation assumption becomes governable only when the premise upon which the simulation materially depends is made explicit, distinguishable, bounded, and traceable to the simulation elements it can influence.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Assumption Identification Module establishes the entry point of assumption governance within SIMULOS® by identifying explicit, implicit, embedded, inherited, and materially consequential premises upon which simulation models, environments, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, and outputs depend. Through assumption discovery, classification, materiality assessment, criticality identification, simulation binding, registration, gap detection, and traceability, SAIM prevents materially relevant premises from remaining invisible inside simulation design and creates the governed Simulation Assumption Set required for subsequent governance of assumption basis, dependency, uncertainty, and limitation.

OOF™ Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM)
Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Limitations
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Assumption Limitations
Canonical Definition
Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM) defines the governance framework for identifying, defining, bounding, classifying, propagating, disclosing, reassessing, and preserving the limitations created by Simulation Assumptions throughout the simulation lifecycle.

It establishes the methodological conditions under which every material Simulation Assumption remains connected to the boundaries within which it may legitimately operate, the conditions under which it may cease to remain applicable, the simulation elements and outputs affected by those limitations, and the consequences those limitations create for interpretation and downstream use.
SALM does not determine whether a Simulation Assumption is universally valid.
It governs where an assumption stops being safely or legitimately applicable inside the simulation and what consequences follow when that boundary is approached, crossed, changed, or remains unknown.
Operational Role
SALM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The preceding modules establish:
SAIM — Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant?
SABM — On what basis is each assumption being used?
SADM — What depends upon each assumption?
SAUM — What remains uncertain about each assumption and where may that uncertainty propagate?
SALM asks:
Within which conditions may the assumption legitimately operate, where does its applicability end, and what limitations does it impose upon the simulation?
The governed progression is:
Governed Simulation Assumption → Limitation Identification → Applicability Boundary → Limiting Condition → Dependency Connection → Limitation Propagation → Consequence Assessment → Disclosure → Reassessment → Limitation Record

SALM closes the internal governance lifecycle of the Simulation Assumption Standard.
Module Operational Space
SALM governs: assumption limitation identification, assumption applicability boundaries, limiting conditions, applicability conditions, environmental limitations, temporal limitations, spatial limitations, population limitations, behavioral limitations, operational limitations, parameter limitations, model-context limitations, scenario limitations, evidence-related limitations, uncertainty-derived limitations, dependency-derived limitations, conditional applicability, partial applicability, non-applicability, limitation thresholds, limitation proximity, limitation breach, limitation propagation, limitation interaction, compound limitations, limitation materiality, limitation consequences, output limitations, interpretation limitations, limitation disclosure, limitation reassessment, limitation change, limitation version binding, historical limitation preservation, limitation gaps, and complete assumption-limitation traceability.
Module Function
Simulation Assumptions allow a simulation to operate where complete representation of reality is impossible, unnecessary, unavailable, or methodologically inappropriate.
But every assumption creates a boundary.
An assumption may be reasonable:
within one environment
but not another.
It may apply:
within one parameter range
but fail outside it.
It may represent:
one population
but not another.
It may remain useful:

during one period
but become obsolete after material change.
SALM prevents these boundaries from disappearing once an assumption has been incorporated into a model.
It transforms:
Simulation Assumption
into:
Simulation Assumption + Applicability Boundary + Limiting Conditions + Affected Dependencies + Consequences Simulation Assumption Limitation
A Simulation Assumption Limitation is a governed condition that restricts where, when, how, or to what extent a Simulation Assumption may legitimately represent the condition for which it is used.
A limitation may constrain: applicability, parameter range, environment, population, time, scenario, operating state, interpretation, simulation output, or downstream conclusions.
Assumption Applicability Boundary
Every material assumption should have an identifiable applicability boundary where reasonably possible.
The boundary answers:
Under which conditions is this assumption intended to apply?
and:
Under which conditions should it no longer be treated as applicable?
Conceptually:
Applicable Conditions → Boundary → Non-Applicable Conditions Applicability Context
Assumption applicability should be understood relative to:
Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Model + Environment + Scenario
The same assumption may therefore be legitimate in one simulation context and inappropriate in another.
Limiting Condition

A Limiting Condition is a condition that narrows or terminates the legitimate applicability of an assumption.
Examples may include: temperature above a defined range, velocity outside tested conditions, different population characteristics, changed environmental behavior, altered system configuration, different operating mode, unavailable supporting evidence, changed temporal context, or newly discovered dependency.
Conditional Applicability
Some assumptions remain legitimate only while specified conditions remain true.
Conceptually:
Assumption Applicable IF Conditions A + B + C remain satisfied
If a material condition changes, the assumption should enter reassessment.
Partial Applicability
An assumption may remain applicable to only part of the Simulation Object, scenario set, operating envelope, or population.
SALM requires that partial applicability remain visible rather than being represented as universal applicability. Non-Applicability
A Simulation Assumption becomes non-applicable when the conditions required for its legitimate use are no longer satisfied.
Non-applicability should not automatically be interpreted as failure of the entire simulation.
It establishes that the affected simulation pathway can no longer legitimately rely upon that assumption without reassessment, replacement, or explicit restriction.
Environmental Limitation
An assumption may apply only within specified environmental conditions.

Examples include: temperature, humidity, radiation, terrain, atmospheric conditions, lighting, network conditions, infrastructure availability, or another environmental state.
Temporal Limitation
An assumption may be valid only for a defined period or temporal context.
Examples include: market behavior derived from a historical period, component degradation assumptions, demographic conditions, seasonal behavior, or technology-performance assumptions.
A materially changing temporal context may therefore create a limitation.
Spatial Limitation
An assumption may apply only within defined geographic, physical, or spatial conditions.
An assumption derived from one region should not automatically be treated as applicable globally.
Population Limitation
An assumption based upon one population may not legitimately represent another.
Population limitations may concern: age, behavior, operating experience, physical characteristics, user group, system class, or another materially relevant population property.
Behavioral Limitation
Human, organizational, AI, autonomous-system, or environmental behavior may be represented through assumptions.
Where behavior changes beyond the assumed range, the assumption may cease to provide an adequate representation.
Operational Limitation
An assumption may apply only within a defined operating envelope.
For example:
Normal Operation
may not legitimately represent:
Emergency Operation
or:
Failure-State Operation.
Parameter Limitation

An assumption may depend upon parameter ranges.
Example:
Linear Response Assumption
may apply between:
Parameter X = 0–100
but not beyond that range.
SALM preserves this boundary explicitly.
Scenario Limitation
Some assumptions apply only to particular scenarios.
A scenario-specific assumption should not silently propagate into unrelated scenarios merely because it already exists in the simulation environment.
Evidence-Related Limitation
SABM may establish that an assumption depends upon limited evidence.
SALM governs the resulting applicability restriction where that evidence cannot legitimately support broader use.
Conceptually:
Limited Basis → Limited Applicability Uncertainty-Derived Limitation
SAUM may establish uncertainty that materially constrains assumption use.
Where uncertainty becomes sufficiently significant, it may create: narrower applicability, stronger conditions, restricted interpretation, scenario restrictions, or a requirement for reassessment.
SAUM governs the uncertainty.
SALM governs the limitation that follows from it.
Dependency-Derived Limitation
SADM identifies what depends upon an assumption.
SALM determines where assumption limitations affect those dependencies.
Conceptually:
Assumption Limitation
↓
Dependency Path
↓
Affected Simulation Element
↓
Affected Scenario
↓
Affected Output / Conclusion Limitation Propagation
A limitation attached to an assumption may propagate through the simulation.
Example:

Battery Temperature Assumption Limited to −10°C to +45°C
↓
Battery Performance Model
↓
Power Availability
↓
Vehicle Range
↓
Mission Feasibility
A mission simulated outside the applicable temperature range cannot legitimately inherit the same assumption without reassessment.
No Limitation Disappearance Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A limitation attached to a material Simulation Assumption does not disappear when that assumption is embedded inside a model, scenario, computation, or simulation output.
The limitation must remain traceable wherever it materially constrains downstream interpretation.
Limitation Materiality
Not every limitation has equal significance.
Materiality may depend upon: affected assumption, dependency depth, dependency breadth, scenario significance, output sensitivity, consequence, intended simulation purpose, and Simulation Depth.
The governing question is:
Could crossing or ignoring this limitation materially change the simulation behavior, output, or legitimate interpretation?
Limitation Threshold
Where appropriate, SALM may establish a threshold at which a limitation becomes operationally significant.
Conceptually:
Within Boundary → Applicable
Near Boundary → Conditional / Monitor
Beyond Boundary → Reassessment / Non-Applicable
The exact states depend upon the simulation context.
Boundary Proximity
A simulation operating very close to an assumption boundary may require different treatment from one operating comfortably inside it.

SALM may therefore distinguish:
Inside Boundary
Boundary Proximity
Boundary Reached
Boundary Exceeded
This prevents binary treatment of limitations where proximity itself is materially relevant.
Limitation Breach
A Simulation Assumption Limitation Breach occurs when simulation conditions exceed an established applicability boundary.
A breach should trigger evaluation of: affected assumption, affected dependencies, affected scenarios, affected outputs, and required reassessment.
SALM does not automatically determine that the entire simulation is invalid.
It identifies the affected governance condition.
Limitation Interaction
Multiple assumption limitations may interact.
An individual assumption may remain within its own boundary while the combination of several limiting conditions creates a materially different simulation context.
Material interactions should therefore remain visible.
Compound Limitation
A Compound Limitation exists where multiple assumption limitations jointly constrain a simulation more strongly than each limitation considered independently.
This may be particularly important in: coupled systems, multi-agent simulations, environmental simulations, complex engineering simulations, and high-dimensional scenario spaces.
Limitation Concentration
A simulation may depend heavily upon a small number of assumptions with narrow applicability.

SALM may identify such concentration as a governance signal because small changes in context may cause large portions of the simulation to leave their supported assumption boundaries.
Output Limitation
An assumption limitation may constrain the meaning of simulation outputs.
For example:
Output applies only under Environment A
must not silently become:
Output applies universally.
SALM therefore preserves the relationship:
Assumption Boundary → Output Boundary
where materially applicable.
Interpretation Limitation
Simulation results may be technically produced outside an assumption's legitimate boundary.
Computational executability does not establish interpretive legitimacy.
SIMULOS® therefore establishes:
A simulation can produce an output under conditions where the assumptions supporting that output no longer justify its interpretation.
No Computational Legitimacy Principle
The ability of a simulation to execute does not prove that its assumptions remain applicable.
Execution capability and assumption applicability are separate governance conditions.
No Scope Inflation Principle
An assumption established for a bounded context must not be silently generalized beyond that context.
Conceptually:
Assumption Scope ≤ Governed Applicability Basis
Broader application requires an additional governed basis.
No Hidden Limitation Principle

A material assumption limitation must not be omitted merely because disclosure weakens the apparent usefulness, precision, coverage, or confidence of the simulation.
Limitation Disclosure
Material limitations should remain visible to downstream simulation governance.
Disclosure may include: limitation description, applicability boundary, limiting condition, affected assumption, affected dependencies, affected scenarios, affected outputs, materiality, boundary status, and required reassessment conditions.
Limitation Gap
A Simulation Assumption Limitation Gap exists where: applicability boundaries are unknown, material limiting conditions are unidentified, dependency effects are unclear, downstream consequences cannot be determined, or the assumption is being used outside its documented context without sufficient governance basis.
The gap should remain visible.
Unknown Boundary Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
An unknown applicability boundary must not be represented as unlimited applicability.
Where the boundary cannot be established, the correct governance state may be:
Applicability Boundary Undetermined
rather than:
Universally Applicable.
Limitation Change
Assumption limitations may change when: the Simulation Object changes, the assumption changes, new evidence becomes available, uncertainty changes, dependencies change, model structure changes, simulation environment changes, scenarios change, operational conditions change, or new limiting conditions are discovered.

Limitation Reassessment
Material changes should trigger reassessment of affected assumption limitations.
The reassessment asks:
Does the existing applicability boundary still represent the conditions under which this assumption may legitimately operate?
Boundary Expansion
New evidence may support broader assumption applicability.
Conceptually:
Previous Boundary → New Basis → Expanded Boundary
Expansion should be governed rather than presumed.
Boundary Restriction
New evidence may demonstrate that an assumption has narrower applicability than previously believed.
Conceptually:
Previous Boundary → New Evidence → Restricted Boundary
Affected simulation outputs produced under the previous broader boundary may require reassessment.
Boundary Withdrawal
Where an assumption can no longer be supported within its previous context, its applicability boundary may be withdrawn.
The assumption may require: replacement, redesign, scenario restriction, or removal.
Version Binding
Material assumption limitations should remain bound to the relevant: Simulation Object version, assumption version, model version, simulation environment version, scenario version, and simulation configuration
where these distinctions affect applicability.
Historical Limitation Preservation
Later expansion or restriction of an assumption boundary should not erase the limitation state that applied when earlier simulations were executed.

Historical preservation supports: reconstruction, comparison, audit, incident analysis, and lifecycle governance.

Was the assumption under reassessment?

Simulation Assumption Uncertainty
Canonical Definition
Simulation Assumption Uncertainty Module (SAUM) defines the governance framework for identifying, characterizing, bounding, classifying, propagating, reassessing, and preserving uncertainty associated with Simulation Assumptions throughout the simulation lifecycle.

It establishes the methodological conditions under which uncertainty attached to an assumption remains explicitly connected to the assumption, the simulation context in which that assumption operates, the dependencies through which its influence propagates, and the simulation outputs and conclusions that may be materially affected by it.
SAUM does not attempt to eliminate uncertainty.
It governs what is uncertain about a Simulation Assumption, why that uncertainty exists, how significant it may be within the simulation, where its influence may propagate, and how that uncertainty must remain visible rather than being converted into false certainty.
Operational Role
SAUM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS).
The preceding modules establish:
SAIM — Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant?
SABM — On what basis is each assumption being used?
SADM — What depends upon each assumption?
SAUM asks:
What uncertainty exists around each Simulation Assumption, how should that uncertainty be represented, and where can it materially influence the simulation?
The governed progression is:
Governed Simulation Assumption → Uncertainty Identification → Uncertainty Source → Uncertainty Characterization → Uncertainty Bound → Dependency Connection → Uncertainty Propagation → Materiality → Reassessment → Uncertainty Record
The resulting uncertainty structure becomes an input to:
SALM — Simulation Assumption Limitation Module

Module Operational Space
SAUM governs: assumption uncertainty identification, uncertainty source identification, uncertainty characterization, uncertainty classification, quantitative uncertainty, qualitative uncertainty, bounded uncertainty, unbounded uncertainty, known uncertainty, partially known uncertainty, unresolved uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, variability-related uncertainty, uncertainty ranges, uncertainty distributions where applicable, uncertainty confidence, uncertainty sensitivity, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty dependency, uncertainty interaction, uncertainty accumulation, uncertainty amplification, uncertainty dampening, uncertainty propagation, compound uncertainty, correlated uncertainty, uncertainty concentration, uncertainty thresholds, uncertainty change, uncertainty reassessment, uncertainty disclosure, and complete assumption-uncertainty traceability.
Module Function
Simulation Assumptions are often necessary precisely because complete knowledge is unavailable.
An assumption may represent: an estimated future condition, an incompletely observed physical property, an uncertain human behavior, an environmental condition, an engineering approximation, an unknown operational response, an incomplete dataset condition, or another state that cannot be represented with complete certainty.
The existence of an assumption therefore does not imply that its uncertainty has been sufficiently governed.
SAUM transforms:
Assumption
into:

Assumption + Uncertainty + Uncertainty Basis + Bound + Dependency Context + Propagation Consequence
The purpose is to prevent uncertainty from disappearing merely because an uncertain condition has been expressed as a fixed simulation assumption.
Simulation Assumption Uncertainty
Simulation Assumption Uncertainty is the governed lack of complete certainty concerning the truth, value, range, stability, applicability, behavior, or future state represented by a Simulation Assumption.
The relevant uncertainty must be understood relative to:
Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Assumption + Simulation Context
An assumption may therefore carry different uncertainty significance in different simulations.
Uncertainty Identification
Every material Simulation Assumption should be examined for uncertainty.
The inquiry asks:
What about this assumption is not known with sufficient certainty?
The answer may concern: the assumed value, expected range, probability, stability, timing, frequency, applicability, underlying evidence, environmental conditions, behavioral response, or another materially relevant property.
Uncertainty Source
SAUM distinguishes the assumption from the source of its uncertainty.

Uncertainty may arise because: measurements are incomplete, evidence is limited, future conditions are unknown, observed populations are incomplete, physical variability exists, behavior varies, environmental states change, models simplify reality, historical information is sparse, expert judgment differs, dependencies are incompletely understood, or relevant knowledge does not yet exist.
Material uncertainty should remain attributable to its identifiable source where possible.
Known Uncertainty
A Known Uncertainty exists where the existence and relevant nature of uncertainty are recognized.
Example:
Wind speed is expected to vary between defined operational bounds.
The exact future wind speed is unknown, but the uncertainty itself is understood sufficiently to be represented.
Partially Known Uncertainty
A Partially Known Uncertainty exists where some properties of the uncertainty are understood while others remain unresolved.
For example:
a likely range may be known while the probability distribution remains uncertain.
The unresolved portion must remain visible.
Unresolved Uncertainty
An Unresolved Uncertainty exists where material uncertainty is known to exist but cannot yet be sufficiently characterized or bounded.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Unknown magnitude does not justify zero uncertainty.
Where uncertainty cannot be sufficiently quantified, it should remain explicitly represented as unresolved.
Quantitative Uncertainty

Where justified, uncertainty may be represented quantitatively through: ranges, intervals, distributions, probabilities, tolerances, confidence bounds, sensitivity values, or another applicable quantitative representation.
The representation should not imply greater precision than the underlying uncertainty basis supports.
Qualitative Uncertainty
Not all uncertainty can legitimately be reduced to numbers.
Qualitative uncertainty may be represented through governed classifications such as:
Low
Moderate
High
Critical
or another defined classification scheme.
The classification basis should remain explicit.
No False Quantification Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Uncertainty must not be assigned numerical precision merely to make the simulation appear more rigorous.
Where the basis supports only qualitative characterization, quantitative representation should not manufacture unsupported certainty.
Bounded Uncertainty
A Bounded Uncertainty exists where an assumption can reasonably be constrained within defined limits.
Example:
Temperature Assumption: 18–25°C
The bound should identify: lower limit, upper limit, basis, applicable context, and conditions under which the bound remains meaningful.
Unbounded Uncertainty
Some uncertainty cannot be sufficiently bounded.
Where a material assumption contains unbounded uncertainty, SAUM requires that condition to remain visible.

Unbounded uncertainty may materially constrain: simulation interpretation, scenario confidence, output confidence, or the legitimate strength of conclusions.
SAUM identifies the condition without making the external validation determination.
Uncertainty Range
An Assumption Uncertainty Range defines the governed interval within which the relevant assumed condition is reasonably expected to vary.
A range should not automatically be interpreted as:
all values equally likely
unless that interpretation is independently justified.
Uncertainty Distribution
Where sufficient basis exists, uncertainty may be represented through a probability distribution.
The distribution itself may depend upon assumptions.
SAUM therefore requires the basis of the distribution to remain distinguishable from the uncertainty being represented.
Uncertainty Confidence
A simulation may possess uncertainty not only about an assumed value, but about the uncertainty estimate itself.
Example:
Assumed Range: 10–15
may itself have:
Low Confidence
if based upon limited observations.
SAUM permits this second-order uncertainty to remain visible rather than treating the range as absolute.
Epistemic Uncertainty
Epistemic Uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge.
It may potentially be reduced through: better evidence, additional measurement, improved observation, further research, or stronger understanding.

Examples include uncertainty concerning: material properties, system behavior, causal relationships, or poorly observed conditions.
Variability-Related Uncertainty
Some uncertainty arises because reality itself varies.
Examples include: weather, human behavior, traffic, biological response, market behavior, manufacturing variability, or environmental fluctuation.
This uncertainty may persist even where extensive information exists.
SAUM preserves the distinction where it materially affects simulation governance.
Uncertainty Materiality
Not every uncertainty requires the same governance depth.
Materiality may depend upon: uncertainty magnitude, affected assumption, dependency breadth, dependency depth, affected model components, sensitivity, output consequence, scenario consequence, and intended simulation use.
The governing question is:
Could this uncertainty materially change simulation behavior, outputs, or conclusions?
Uncertainty Sensitivity
An assumption may contain substantial uncertainty while the simulation remains relatively insensitive to it.
Another assumption may contain only small uncertainty while simulation outputs are highly sensitive to small changes.
SAUM therefore separates:
Uncertainty Magnitude
from:
Simulation Sensitivity
Conceptually:
Small Uncertainty + High Sensitivity
may be more material than:
Large Uncertainty + Low Sensitivity Uncertainty Dependency
SADM establishes what depends upon an assumption.

SAUM uses that dependency structure to determine where assumption uncertainty may matter.
Conceptually:
Assumption
↓

↓
Dependency Path
↓
Affected Simulation Element
↓

Simulation Assumption Uncertainty Propagation occurs where uncertainty attached to an assumption influences downstream simulation elements.
Example:

↓

↓
