chunks.text:
OOF™ Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions
Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS)
Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Correlation Uncertainty
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 19 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Correlation Uncertainty
Canonical Definition
Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions under which uncertainty affecting the relationship between simulation and Operational Reality is identified, attributed where supportable, classified, bounded, propagated, documented, communicated, and preserved throughout Simulation-to-Reality Correlation.
SCUM governs uncertainty concerning:

how confidently a simulation can be said to correspond to reality within a defined object, condition, scenario, environment, time, comparison basis, and correlation scope.
Its purpose is not to eliminate uncertainty.
Its purpose is to prevent uncertainty from disappearing when simulation results are compared with reality, aligned against observations, or subsequently used as evidence.
Operational Role
SCUM is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
The preceding modules establish:
SRCM — What simulation and reality observations may legitimately be compared?
SCCM — According to which criteria should correspondence be assessed?
SDMM — Where and how materially do simulation and reality differ?
SRAM — Which deviations require alignment, and how should that alignment occur?
SCUM asks:
How certain are we about the resulting Simulation-to-Reality Correlation, what remains unknown, and where does that uncertainty limit interpretation or downstream reliance?
The complete internal progression is:
Simulation-Reality Comparison
↓
Correlation Criteria
↓
Simulation-Reality Deviation
↓
Reality Alignment
↓
Correlation Uncertainty
Module Operational Space

SCUM governs: correlation uncertainty identification, uncertainty source identification, uncertainty classification, uncertainty attribution, uncertainty magnitude, uncertainty bounds, measurement uncertainty, observational uncertainty, representation uncertainty, model uncertainty, assumption-related uncertainty, environmental uncertainty, input uncertainty contribution, scenario uncertainty contribution, execution uncertainty contribution, temporal uncertainty, spatial uncertainty, behavioral uncertainty, interaction uncertainty, reality-reference uncertainty, comparison uncertainty, correlation-criteria uncertainty, deviation uncertainty, alignment uncertainty, residual uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, aleatory uncertainty, unknown uncertainty, uncertainty dependency, uncertainty interaction, uncertainty propagation, uncertainty accumulation, uncertainty reduction, irreducible uncertainty, condition-specific uncertainty, uncertainty thresholds, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty disclosure, uncertainty traceability, uncertainty status, and downstream uncertainty transfer.
Module Function
SCUM prevents a correlation statement such as:
“The simulation matches reality.”
from being treated as complete unless the uncertainty surrounding that statement is also visible.
A governed correlation statement should instead be capable of expressing:
what corresponds,
under which conditions,
against which reality basis,
with what observed deviations,
with what remaining uncertainty,

and:
where that uncertainty becomes material.
Correlation Is Not Certainty
SIMULOS® establishes:
Observed correlation does not eliminate uncertainty about the simulation-reality relationship.
Strong correspondence may coexist with uncertainty concerning: unobserved conditions, rare events, measurement limitations, model structure, environmental variability, future conditions, human behavior, autonomous behavior, interaction effects, or incomplete Operational Reality knowledge.
Correlation Uncertainty Object
Material Correlation Uncertainty should be capable of becoming a governed object.
Conceptually:
Correlation Uncertainty ID
↓
Affected Correlation Relationship
↓
Uncertainty Source
↓
Uncertainty Type
↓
Affected Condition / Scenario
↓
Magnitude / Bound where supportable
↓
Dependencies
↓
Materiality
↓
Reducibility
↓
Downstream Consequence
↓
Uncertainty Status Uncertainty Source
SCUM should identify the origin of uncertainty where evidence permits.
Potential sources include: incomplete Operational Reality observations, measurement error, sensor limitations, sparse data, uncertain Reality Representation, uncertain assumptions, model simplification, unknown environmental conditions, input variability, scenario incompleteness, stochastic behavior, execution variability, incomplete comparison, uncertain correlation criteria, deviation measurement limitations, alignment effects, or unknown causes.
Unknown Source Must Remain Unknown
SIMULOS® establishes:

Uncertainty must not be assigned a cause merely because governance requires a classification.
Where its source cannot be sufficiently established:
Uncertainty Source Undetermined
is a legitimate governed state.
Epistemic Uncertainty
Epistemic Uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge.
Examples include: insufficient observations, incomplete model knowledge, uncertain parameter values, poorly understood interactions, limited environmental knowledge, and incomplete causal understanding.
Epistemic uncertainty may potentially be reduced through additional:
evidence, measurement, modeling, experimentation, or observation.
Aleatory Uncertainty
Aleatory Uncertainty arises from inherent variability or stochastic behavior in the represented reality.
It may not be eliminable simply by obtaining more information.
SCUM distinguishes:
uncertainty caused by what we do not know
from:
uncertainty caused by reality itself being variable.
Unknown Uncertainty
Some uncertainty cannot yet be meaningfully classified as epistemic or aleatory.
SCUM preserves:
Unknown / Unclassified Correlation Uncertainty
rather than forcing artificial certainty about the nature of uncertainty itself.
Reality-Reference Uncertainty
Operational Reality is not always perfectly observable.
Reality observations may themselves contain: measurement uncertainty, sampling limitations, missing states, incomplete telemetry, human reporting error, sensor limitations, temporal gaps, or inaccessible conditions.
Therefore:

Reality Observation ≠ Perfect Reality Knowledge.
Simulation Uncertainty and Reality Uncertainty Must Remain Distinguishable
A simulation-reality difference may arise from:
Simulation Uncertainty
Reality Observation Uncertainty
or:
Both.
SCUM should preserve this distinction where possible.
Comparison Uncertainty
Even where both simulation and reality observations are individually strong, uncertainty may exist in whether they are sufficiently comparable.
Possible causes include: different environmental conditions, different timing, different configurations, different measurement resolution, different object states, or incomplete contextual equivalence.
Criteria Uncertainty
Correlation Criteria may themselves contain uncertainty.
For example, an organization may not know whether:
±2%
or:
±5%
represents a materially sufficient correspondence boundary for a particular operational purpose.
SCUM preserves uncertainty in the criterion rather than hiding it inside the correlation result.
Deviation Uncertainty
An observed deviation may have uncertainty around: magnitude, direction, frequency, localization, cause, propagation, or materiality.
Therefore:
Deviation Record
and:
Deviation Uncertainty
should remain distinguishable.
Alignment Uncertainty
A Reality Alignment action may improve observed correlation while creating uncertainty about: generalization, unobserved scenarios, model interactions, new parameter regions, or unintended downstream effects.

Alignment therefore does not automatically reduce total uncertainty.
Residual Correlation Uncertainty
After comparison, deviation assessment, and alignment, uncertainty may remain.
This becomes:
Residual Correlation Uncertainty.
Residual uncertainty should be explicitly preserved rather than implicitly converted into confidence.
Uncertainty Magnitude
Where evidence permits, uncertainty may be expressed quantitatively through: confidence intervals, probability distributions, error ranges, tolerance intervals, sensitivity ranges, variance, credible intervals, or other appropriate methods.
Where numerical quantification is not supportable, structured qualitative classification may be used.
No False Precision Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Correlation uncertainty must not be expressed more precisely than the available evidence permits.
A numerical percentage can create misleading authority where the underlying evidence cannot support that precision.
Qualitative Uncertainty Classification
Where quantitative measurement is inappropriate, implementation may use classifications such as:
Low
Moderate
High
Critical
or:
Undetermined.
These classifications must remain bounded to the applicable correlation context.
Uncertainty Bounds
Where possible, SCUM should establish the range within which the correlation relationship is reasonably supported.
For example:
Strong Correlation — Nominal Conditions
Moderate Uncertainty — High Temperature
High Uncertainty — Extreme Combined Conditions

Unknown — Unobserved Failure Configuration
This is more informative than a single global confidence score.
Condition-Specific Uncertainty
Correlation uncertainty may vary significantly across conditions.
Therefore:
Correlation Confidence is a surface, not necessarily a single number.
A simulation may be highly correlated with reality in one operational region and poorly understood in another.
Scenario-Specific Uncertainty
Each materially relevant scenario may possess a different uncertainty profile.
This is particularly important for: edge cases, stress conditions, rare events, novel environments, and combinations never directly observed in Operational Reality.
Temporal Uncertainty
A simulation may correspond well with current reality while uncertainty increases over time because: the environment changes, system behavior evolves, components degrade, software changes, populations change, or Operational Reality drifts.
SCUM therefore allows correlation uncertainty to be time-dependent.
Spatial Uncertainty
Correlation may be strong in observed geographic or physical regions while remaining uncertain elsewhere.
This matters for: autonomous vehicles, robotics, climate simulation, aerospace, infrastructure, and geographically distributed systems.
Behavioral Uncertainty
Behavioral uncertainty concerns uncertainty about whether simulated actors or systems behave sufficiently like their real counterparts.

This can be particularly material for: humans, AI agents, autonomous systems, multi-agent systems, adaptive systems, and adversarial environments.
Interaction Uncertainty
Even where individual components are well represented, their interactions may remain uncertain.
SCUM therefore governs uncertainty arising from:
component × component
human × system
agent × agent
system × environment
and other interaction relationships.
Uncertainty Dependency
Uncertainties may depend upon one another.
For example:
Environmental Uncertainty
↓
Sensor Uncertainty
↓
Perception Uncertainty
↓
Behavioral Uncertainty
↓
Trajectory Correlation Uncertainty
SCUM should preserve material dependencies where identifiable.
Uncertainty Interaction
Multiple individually modest uncertainties may interact to produce a materially larger uncertainty.
For example:
Sensor Noise Weather Variability Timing Uncertainty
may create:
High Autonomous Behavior Correlation Uncertainty.
Uncertainty Propagation
Correlation uncertainty may propagate downstream through the simulation lifecycle and into later governance architectures.
Conceptually:
Correlation Uncertainty
↓
Simulation Output Interpretation
↓
Validation Evidence
↓
Validation Determination
↓
Operational Reliance
SCUM therefore requires material uncertainty to remain transferable rather than disappearing at the SIMULOS® boundary.
No Uncertainty Laundering Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Uncertainty identified within Simulation-to-Reality Correlation must not disappear merely because the simulation output enters another governance process.
If VALIDOS® uses the simulation as validation evidence, the relevant uncertainty must travel with it.
Uncertainty Accumulation
Where multiple uncertain relationships contribute to one correlation conclusion, SCUM should determine whether uncertainty accumulates materially.
A simulation should not claim high overall certainty merely because each individual uncertainty appears small when assessed separately.
Uncertainty Reduction
Where uncertainty is reducible, SCUM may identify actions such as: additional Operational Reality observations, additional measurements, broader scenario execution, targeted experiments, higher-fidelity representation, model refinement, parameter reassessment, additional comparison, or repeated execution.
Reducible vs Irreducible Uncertainty
SCUM distinguishes:
Reducible Uncertainty
from:
Currently Irreducible Uncertainty.
This matters because governance responses differ.
Reducible uncertainty may create an evidence or simulation improvement requirement.
Irreducible uncertainty may instead require:
bounded interpretation, explicit conditions, or restricted reliance.
Uncertainty Reduction Has a Cost
Reducing uncertainty may require: computation, testing, physical experiments, additional missions, new sensors, more data, time, or operational exposure.

SIMULOS® does not require uncertainty to be reduced indefinitely.
The appropriate reduction depth depends upon the simulation purpose and downstream consequence.
Material Uncertainty
Uncertainty becomes material when it can materially affect: interpretation, correlation classification, simulation output meaning, validation, safety assessment, operational decision-making, autonomous-system behavior, mission planning, or reliance.
Uncertainty Threshold
Where appropriate, implementations may establish thresholds beyond which:
additional evidence,
additional simulation,
alignment,
validation restriction,
or:
reliance limitation
is required.
SIMULOS® does not prescribe one universal uncertainty threshold.
Correlation Confidence
An implementation may derive a bounded Correlation Confidence representation from the governed uncertainty basis.
However:
Correlation Confidence must never conceal the conditions, scope, or unresolved uncertainty upon which it depends. Correlation Confidence ≠ Probability of Reality
A confidence representation must not imply that the simulation itself has become reality or that all future real-world behavior has been probabilistically captured.
Correlation Uncertainty Status
Possible implementation states may include:
Sufficiently Bounded
Conditionally Bounded
Material Uncertainty Present
High Uncertainty
Critical Uncertainty
or:
Uncertainty Undetermined.
Correlation Uncertainty Record
A governed record may include:
Correlation Uncertainty ID

Simulation Object / Version
Reality Reference
Comparison Basis
Affected Scenario / Condition
Uncertainty Source
Uncertainty Type
Magnitude / Range
Dependencies
Propagation Path
Materiality
Reducibility
Reduction Requirement
Residual Uncertainty
Downstream Limitation
Status
Evidence Basis
Timestamp / Version Context Uncertainty Across Versions
SCUM should support comparison of uncertainty across simulation versions.
For example:
Simulation v1 → High uncertainty in thermal extremes
Simulation v2 → Moderate uncertainty
Simulation v3 → Low uncertainty within tested range / Unknown beyond tested range
This creates a more meaningful improvement record than simply declaring newer versions “more accurate.” Uncertainty Trend
Repeated simulation-reality correlation may reveal:
Decreasing Uncertainty
Stable Uncertainty
Increasing Uncertainty
Migrating Uncertainty
or:
Newly Emergent Uncertainty.
These trends may indicate where simulation governance should re-enter upstream spaces.
Correlation Coverage and Uncertainty
High correlation inside a narrow observed region does not establish low uncertainty outside that region.
Therefore:
Observed Correlation Coverage must remain distinguishable from Unobserved Correlation Uncertainty.
Unknown Regions
Where no sufficient Operational Reality basis exists, SCUM should permit explicit classification such as:
Correlation Unknown — Insufficient Reality Observation.

This is especially important where simulation exists precisely because direct real-world testing is difficult or impossible.
Novel Conditions
A simulation may be used to explore conditions that have never occurred or cannot safely be reproduced.
SCUM does not prohibit this.
Instead, it requires the distinction between:
Empirically Correlated Region
and:
Simulation-Only / Uncorrelated Region.
Extrapolation Uncertainty
Where simulation extends beyond observed reality, SCUM should identify:
Extrapolation Uncertainty.
The farther the simulation moves beyond the governed correlation basis, the more carefully its correspondence claims should be bounded.
No Correlation Transfer by Similarity
SIMULOS® establishes:
Correlation established for one condition, environment, configuration, or system version must not automatically transfer to another merely because the two appear similar.
Transfer requires a governed basis.
Cross-Version Reality Correlation
A new system or simulation version may inherit some correlation evidence from a previous version only where the relevant relationship remains materially comparable.
Otherwise new correlation assessment is required.
Correlation Uncertainty and Decision Consequence
The same uncertainty level may be acceptable for:
early design exploration
but unacceptable for:
safety-critical deployment authorization.
SCUM therefore preserves downstream consequence context without itself making the final reliance decision.
Uncertainty Communication

Material uncertainty should be communicated in a form usable by: engineers, decision-makers, validators, auditors, regulators, autonomous systems, and downstream AI systems.
The communication should preserve both:
what is known
and:
what remains uncertain.
Machine-Readable Uncertainty
For AI-readable implementations, uncertainty should be capable of being represented structurally.
Conceptually:
Correlation Scope
Correlation Status
Uncertainty Type
Uncertainty Bound
Applicable Conditions
Excluded Conditions
Known Deviations
Unknown Regions
Downstream Restrictions
This allows downstream systems to consume uncertainty rather than merely consuming a correlation score.
Relationship to SRCM
SRCM determines whether simulation and reality observations are sufficiently comparable.
SCUM preserves uncertainty remaining in that comparison basis.
Relationship to SCCM
SCCM establishes the criteria for judging correspondence.
SCUM governs uncertainty affecting the interpretation and application of those criteria.
Relationship to SDMM
SDMM governs observed Simulation-Reality Deviations.
SCUM governs uncertainty concerning those deviations and the broader correlation relationship.
Therefore:
Deviation ≠ Uncertainty.
A deviation is an observed difference.
Uncertainty concerns how confidently that difference and the resulting correlation relationship are understood.
Relationship to SRAM
SRAM governs Reality Alignment.
SCUM determines what uncertainty remains before, during, and after alignment.

Therefore:
Alignment may reduce deviation without eliminating uncertainty.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.
SCUM does not assign certainty to Operational Reality itself.
It governs how uncertainty in the available reality basis affects the simulation-to-reality relationship.
Relationship to VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® may use simulation and Simulation-to-Reality Correlation as part of a Validation Evidence basis.
SCUM ensures that material correlation uncertainty remains attached to that evidence.
Therefore:
VALIDOS® must not receive simulation correlation as stronger evidence than SIMULOS® has actually established.
Relationship to INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of: observations, measurements, datasets, records, and uncertainty artifacts.
SCUM governs the simulation-specific uncertainty relationship.
Relationship to SOGS
SOGS governs what simulation outputs are and what may legitimately be inferred from them.
SCUM provides a correlation-uncertainty basis that may materially constrain those inferences where outputs are interpreted as representations of reality.
Relationship to Operational Reliance
SCUM does not itself authorize operational reliance.
It provides the uncertainty basis required by downstream governance to determine whether reliance is legitimate.
Therefore:
Correlation Uncertainty → Reliance Input
not:
Correlation Uncertainty → Reliance Authorization.
Autonomous Systems Application

An autonomous system may show excellent simulation-reality correlation across millions of nominal simulation events.
However, limited real-world observations may exist for: rare pedestrian behavior, unusual weather combinations, degraded sensors, adversarial interactions, infrastructure failures, multi-agent conflicts, or emergency recovery.
SCUM prevents nominal correlation from being generalized automatically into low uncertainty across the entire autonomous operating domain.
A machine-readable Correlation Uncertainty Map can identify where the system's simulation evidence is strong and where real-world correspondence remains uncertain.
Space and Mission Simulation Application
Space agencies frequently rely on simulation precisely where direct reality evidence is sparse.
A spacecraft or planetary-landing simulation may possess strong correlation evidence for: subsystem tests, terrestrial hardware testing, known orbital conditions, previous mission telemetry, and observed environmental parameters.
But uncertainty may remain high for: never-observed surface interactions, extreme radiation combinations, long-duration degradation, unknown atmospheric behavior, rare subsystem combinations, autonomous recovery, or first-of-kind mission conditions.
SCUM allows those regions to remain explicitly:
Simulation-Supported but Reality-Correlation Uncertain
rather than silently inheriting the confidence of well-tested regions.

This can reveal exactly where additional testing, observation, instrumentation, scenario coverage, or conservative mission constraints provide the greatest value.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Correlation Basis
Identify the simulation, Operational Reality reference, comparison basis, criteria, deviations, and alignment state. 2. Identify Material Uncertainty
Determine where the correlation relationship remains uncertain. 3. Identify the Uncertainty Source
Attribute uncertainty where evidence permits.
Otherwise record:
Source Undetermined. 4. Classify the Uncertainty
Determine whether uncertainty is: epistemic, aleatory, mixed, or unknown.
5. Localize the Uncertainty
Identify the affected: condition, scenario, component, environment, behavior, interaction, time, or output.
6. Bound or Quantify Where Supportable
Use numerical or qualitative bounds appropriate to the evidence. 7. Map Dependencies and Interaction
Determine whether uncertainties depend upon or amplify one another. 8. Assess Propagation
Identify where uncertainty can affect downstream interpretation or governance. 9. Determine Materiality
Assess whether the uncertainty materially affects the intended simulation purpose or downstream use. 10. Determine Reducibility
Identify whether additional evidence or simulation activity can materially reduce the uncertainty. 11. Preserve Residual Uncertainty

Record what remains unresolved after available reduction or alignment actions. 12. Establish Correlation Uncertainty Status
Assign a bounded status appropriate to the applicable correlation scope. 13. Transfer Material Uncertainty Downstream
Ensure that simulation outputs, validation processes, audits, or reliance decisions receive the relevant uncertainty information. 14. Preserve Traceability
Maintain the relationship:
Reality Basis → Comparison → Criteria → Deviation → Alignment → Uncertainty → Downstream Use.
Governance Outputs

SCUM may produce: Correlation Uncertainty ID, Correlation Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Source Record, Uncertainty Classification, Epistemic Uncertainty Record, Aleatory Uncertainty Record, Unknown Uncertainty Record, Reality-Reference Uncertainty Record, Comparison Uncertainty Record, Criteria Uncertainty Record, Deviation Uncertainty Record, Alignment Uncertainty Record, Residual Correlation Uncertainty Record, Quantitative Uncertainty Bound, Qualitative Uncertainty Classification, Condition-Specific Uncertainty Map, Scenario-Specific Uncertainty Map, Temporal Uncertainty Record, Spatial Uncertainty Record, Behavioral Uncertainty Record, Interaction Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Dependency Map, Uncertainty Propagation Map, Uncertainty Accumulation Assessment, Uncertainty Reduction Requirement, Reducibility Assessment, Extrapolation Uncertainty Record, Unknown Correlation Region Record, Correlation Uncertainty Status, Correlation Confidence Record, Downstream Uncertainty Transfer Record, and Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Uncertainty Basis.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Beyond Tested Conditions
An autonomous driving simulation demonstrates strong correlation with Operational Reality across extensive urban driving tests.
However, only limited real-world evidence exists for:
heavy snow + partially blocked sensors + unusual pedestrian movement + low visibility.
SCUM prevents the strong nominal correlation from automatically extending into this region.

The system records:
Nominal Urban Conditions → Correlation Uncertainty Low
Heavy Snow → Correlation Uncertainty Moderate
Heavy Snow + Sensor Degradation + Rare Pedestrian Interaction → Correlation Uncertainty High
This uncertainty can then travel with the simulation evidence into validation and operational decision-making. Use Case 2 — First-of-Kind Space Mission
A space agency uses simulation to assess an autonomous landing sequence for a destination where direct Operational Reality observations are necessarily limited.
The simulation correlates strongly with: terrestrial hardware testing, propulsion tests, sensor testing, and comparable prior mission data.
However, the exact combination of:
surface properties + environmental conditions + autonomous response + landing dynamics
has never been directly observed.
SCUM prevents correlation from known regions from being silently transferred into the unknown mission region.
The resulting correlation basis may state:
Subsystem Correlation — Strong
Known Environmental Range — Sufficiently Bounded
Exact Landing Environment — Material Epistemic Uncertainty
Combined First-of-Kind Landing Interaction — Correlation Unknown / Simulation-Supported
This gives engineers and decision-makers a governed map of where additional evidence can reduce uncertainty and where uncertainty must instead remain an explicit mission constraint.
Architectural Position
SCUM is the fifth and final module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).

The complete SRCS progression is:
SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison
↓
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria
↓
SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation
↓
SRAM — Reality Alignment
↓
SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty
Together, these five modules answer:
What can be compared?
↓
According to what criteria?
↓
Where does simulation differ from reality?
↓
What should be aligned?
↓
How certain are we about the resulting relationship?
This closes the governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation space without converting correlation into validation or simulation into reality.
Foundational Principle
Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence, and correlation confidence must never exceed the reality evidence, comparison basis, observed conditions, and unresolved uncertainty that actually support it.
Canonical Closing Statement

Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) completes the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard by governing what remains uncertain after simulation and Operational Reality have been compared, deviations identified, and justified alignment performed. By distinguishing simulation uncertainty from reality-reference uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty from aleatory variability, observed correlation from unobserved regions, deviation from uncertainty, alignment from certainty, and empirical correspondence from extrapolation, SCUM prevents strong correlation in known conditions from becoming an unsupported claim about reality as a whole. Through uncertainty identification, classification, bounding, dependency mapping, propagation, reduction, residual-uncertainty preservation, machine-readable disclosure, and downstream transfer, SCUM ensures that every Simulation-to-Reality Correlation remains only as certain, broad, and operationally meaningful as the evidence actually permits.

OOF™ Scenario Variation Module (SCVM)
Scenario Variation Module (SCVM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Scenario Governance Layer
Category: AI & Simulation
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Variation
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Scenario Variation
Canonical Definition
Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) defines the governance framework for deliberately varying materially relevant conditions within and across identified Simulation Scenarios so that simulation behavior can be examined beyond a single nominal, expected, convenient, or fixed configuration.
SCVM governs how variation dimensions, ranges, levels, combinations, dependencies, sequences, distributions, and controlled differences are established, bounded, documented, executed as scenario configurations, and preserved for comparison.

Its purpose is to ensure that a Simulation Scenario is not treated as one static point where the governed simulation inquiry requires examination across a materially relevant range of possible conditions.
Operational Role
SCVM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS).
The preceding module:
SCIM — Scenario Identification Module
establishes:
Which materially relevant conditions should become identifiable Simulation Scenarios?
SCVM asks:
Across which materially relevant variations of those scenarios must the simulation operate to understand how changing conditions affect behavior and outcomes?
The progression is:
Governed Scenario Register
↓
Variation Requirement Identification
↓
Variation Dimension
↓
Variation Range
↓
Variation Level / Distribution
↓
Controlled Scenario Variation
↓
Multi-Dimensional Variation
↓
Variation Dependency & Interaction
↓
Variation Configuration Set
↓
Edge-Case Governance
SCVM therefore converts identified scenarios into a structured variation space.
Module Operational Space

SCVM governs: variation requirements, variation dimensions, variation variables, variation ranges, variation levels, continuous variation, discrete variation, categorical variation, stochastic variation, temporal variation, environmental variation, input variation, parameter variation, behavioral variation, configuration variation, dependency variation, interaction variation, sequential variation, single-factor variation, multi-factor variation, correlated variation, conditional variation, distribution-based variation, controlled comparison, reference configurations, variation boundaries, variation exclusions, variation sufficiency, variation gaps, variation traceability, variation versioning, and Variation Configuration Sets.
Variation Requirement
A Variation Requirement identifies a materially relevant dimension along which a Simulation Scenario should change.
It answers:
What can vary here in a way capable of materially changing simulation behavior or interpretation?
A Variation Requirement may arise from: Simulation Purpose, Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, Input Uncertainty, system operating ranges, environmental ranges, actor behavior, system configuration, timing, dependencies, resource availability, known sensitivities, or scenario-specific conditions.
Variation Dimension
A Variation Dimension is a governed characteristic across which scenario conditions may change.
Examples include:
Speed
Temperature
Power Availability
Communication Latency

Sensor Confidence
System Load
Actor Density
Human Response Time
Resource Availability
Environmental State
Autonomy Level
Failure Timing
or another simulation-specific dimension.
Variation Variable
A Variation Dimension may contain one or more variables.
For example:
Communication Condition
may contain: latency, bandwidth, packet loss, interruption duration, and connection stability.
SCVM keeps the broader condition distinct from the technical variables used to represent it.
Variation Range
A Variation Range defines the governed interval or set across which a variable may change.
Conceptually:
Minimum Relevant Condition → Expected Range → Maximum Relevant Condition
The range should derive from the Simulation Purpose and governed representation of the condition rather than arbitrary technical convenience.
Range Boundary
Every material Variation Range should establish where the intended variation begins and ends.
Where the simulation cannot represent the complete relevant range, the limitation should remain visible.
The result may be:
Required Range: X–Z
Simulation-Capable Range: X–Y
Variation Gap: Y–Z
rather than silently treating X–Y as complete coverage.
Variation Level
A continuous range does not necessarily require simulation of every possible value.
SCVM allows governed selection of representative Variation Levels.
For example:
Low
Nominal
Elevated
High
may represent one governed sampling structure.
Another inquiry may require substantially finer resolution.

The appropriate level depends on the simulation question.
Variation Resolution
Variation Resolution describes how densely a relevant range is examined.
Too little resolution may hide material behavior changes.
Excessive resolution may consume resources without materially improving understanding.
SCVM therefore asks:
At what variation resolution can materially relevant changes in behavior be detected for this Simulation Purpose?
Continuous Variation
A condition may vary continuously.
Examples include: velocity, temperature, pressure, distance, load, latency, signal strength, or resource availability.
SCVM governs how continuous ranges are bounded and sampled.
Discrete Variation
Some conditions exist as discrete states.
For example:
Mode A / Mode B / Mode C
or:
Primary System / Backup System / Emergency System
These states should not be artificially treated as continuous numerical variation where the underlying system behavior is categorical.
Categorical Variation
A scenario may vary across categories such as: environment type, actor type, vehicle class, terrain class, mission phase, population group, operational mode, or system configuration.
Material categories should remain explicitly identifiable.
Stochastic Variation
Some simulation conditions contain randomness or probabilistic behavior.
SCVM allows governed stochastic variation where appropriate.

This may include: random arrival, behavioral variability, component variation, environmental noise, uncertain timing, or probabilistic failure.
Stochastic variation should remain connected to its: distribution basis, range, assumptions, sampling method, and applicable Scenario Identity.
Distribution-Based Variation
Where a variable is represented by a distribution, the simulation should not automatically examine only its mean or most likely value.
SCVM may require examination across materially relevant portions of that distribution.
This may include:
central conditions
tails
asymmetry
multiple modes
or:
low-probability regions
where those regions materially affect the simulation inquiry.
No Mean-Only Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A representative average does not establish adequate variation where materially different behavior can occur away from the average.
Input Variation
Inputs governed under SIDS may vary within scenarios.
SCVM governs how those permitted inputs are configured into deliberate scenario variation.
Therefore:
SIDS → What inputs may enter
SCVM → How materially relevant input conditions should vary across scenarios Parameter Variation
Simulation parameters may materially influence behavior.
SCVM may establish: parameter ranges, parameter levels, parameter combinations, and parameter dependencies
for scenario examination.
Parameter governance remains connected to SMES.
SCVM governs their deliberate use as scenario variation.
Environmental Variation

Simulation environments may require deliberate variation across conditions such as: weather, temperature, lighting, radiation, terrain, pressure, gravity, traffic density, network state, or another relevant environmental condition.
SCVM does not govern the environment itself.
It governs variation of environment conditions within Scenario Design.
Behavioral Variation
Where humans, AI systems, autonomous agents, organizations, or other actors participate in a simulation, their behavior may require variation.
Behavioral variation may include: reaction time, cooperation, non-cooperation, uncertainty, unexpected action, decision strategy, communication behavior, or response to system behavior.
Temporal Variation
The same event may produce materially different behavior depending upon when it occurs.
SCVM therefore recognizes:
event timing
as a potential variation dimension.
For example:
Communication Failure Before Handover
may differ materially from:
Communication Failure During Handover
or:
Communication Failure After Handover.
Sequence Variation
Where event order matters, scenario variation may require multiple sequences.
Conceptually:
A → B → C
may not be equivalent to:
B → A → C.
SCVM governs sequence variation where ordering materially changes the simulation.
Duration Variation
A condition may become material only after a certain duration.
Examples include: communication outage, resource depletion, thermal exposure, degraded sensing, delayed intervention, or sustained load.

SCVM therefore allows duration itself to become a governed variation dimension.
Rate-of-Change Variation
Not only the final value but the speed at which a condition changes may matter.
For example:
slow temperature increase
may produce different behavior from:
rapid temperature increase
even if both reach the same final value.
SCVM may therefore govern rate of change where material.
Single-Factor Variation
Single-Factor Variation changes one material condition while maintaining other relevant conditions sufficiently stable.
Conceptually:
Reference Scenario
↓
Change Variable X
↓
Observe Difference
This can help determine sensitivity to a particular variable.
Controlled Comparison
Where a simulation seeks to understand the effect of one variation, other materially relevant conditions should remain sufficiently controlled or their differences explicitly documented.
SCVM establishes:
A comparison is meaningful only to the extent that the conditions producing the difference are known.
Multi-Factor Variation
Real systems rarely experience one changing condition at a time.
SCVM therefore supports Multi-Factor Variation.
For example:
Low Power + High Communication Latency + Reduced Sensor Confidence
may represent a materially different condition from each factor independently.
Variation Interaction
Two variation dimensions may interact.
A change in Variable A may have little effect alone.
A change in Variable B may have little effect alone.
But:
A + B

may create materially different behavior.
SCVM therefore treats interaction as a governance question rather than assuming additive effects.
Correlated Variation
Some variables are not independent.
For example:
Severe Weather
may simultaneously affect: visibility, sensor performance, communication quality, energy consumption, and human behavior.
SCVM should preserve these relationships where independent random variation would create unrealistic scenario configurations.
No False Independence Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Scenario variables must not be treated as independent where material real-world dependencies make their variation structurally connected.
Conditional Variation
Some variation becomes applicable only when another condition exists.
For example:
Emergency Battery Duration
may become relevant only after:
Primary Power Loss.
SCVM allows:
Condition A → Activate Variation Dimension B
where appropriate.
Dependency Variation
Dependencies themselves may vary.
A simulation may examine: dependency available, dependency degraded, dependency intermittent, dependency delayed, dependency unavailable, or dependency recovered.
This is especially important in interconnected systems.
Configuration Variation
Different system configurations may require separate scenario variations.
Examples include: software versions, hardware configurations, sensor packages, autonomy settings, control modes, or infrastructure configurations.

Materially different configurations should remain traceable to the scenario variation in which they are used.
Variation Combination
Variation dimensions may be combined into a Variation Configuration.
Conceptually:
Scenario Identity Input Condition Environment Parameter State Behavioral Condition Timing
=
Variation Configuration Variation Configuration Identity
Every materially distinct Variation Configuration should be sufficiently identifiable.
It may include: Scenario ID, Variation Configuration ID, variable values, categorical states, applicable ranges, dependency conditions, sequence, timing, environment configuration, parameter configuration, input configuration, and version.
Variation Configuration Set
A Variation Configuration Set is the governed collection of variation configurations selected for a Scenario or Scenario Family.
It represents the condition space that subsequent simulation activities may execute.
Combinatorial Explosion
Complex simulations may contain hundreds or thousands of possible variation dimensions.
Their combinations may become effectively unlimited.
SCVM therefore does not require:
every variable × every value × every other variable
to be simulated.
Instead it requires governed selection of combinations capable of materially improving examination of the Simulation Purpose.
Variation Prioritization

Where exhaustive variation is impractical, prioritization may consider: materiality, uncertainty, sensitivity, consequence, dependency, interaction potential, boundary proximity, historical behavior, operational relevance, novelty, and downstream reliance.
Variation Sufficiency
Variation Sufficiency asks:
Has the scenario been varied sufficiently to expose materially different behavior that could reasonably occur within the governed simulation inquiry?
This is not a universal numerical threshold.
It is a governed sufficiency determination relative to: Simulation Purpose, Scenario Requirement, represented reality, uncertainty, consequence, and available simulation capability.
Variation Gap
A Variation Gap exists where a materially relevant range, category, dependency, interaction, sequence, or configuration has not been sufficiently represented.
A gap may result from: unavailable data, model limitations, computational constraints, unknown distributions, insufficient scenario resolution, excluded conditions, or undiscovered dependencies.
No Capability-Erasure Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation limitation does not eliminate the variation requirement that exposed the limitation.
Where required variation cannot be simulated, the gap should remain explicit.
Variation Exclusion

A potential variation may be excluded where it is: outside Simulation Scope, materially impossible, irrelevant to the Scenario Requirement, redundant, or sufficiently represented by another governed configuration.
Material exclusions should be documented where omission could affect interpretation.
No Convenience-Range Principle
A Variation Range should not be narrowed solely because: available data cover only part of it, the model performs poorly outside a comfortable region, computation becomes expensive, results become unstable, or unfavorable behavior appears.
These may justify a limitation.
They do not justify hiding the limitation.
Variation Traceability
SCVM should preserve relationships such as:
Scenario Requirement
↓
Scenario ID
↓
Variation Requirement
↓
Variation Dimension
↓
Variation Range
↓
Variation Configuration
↓
Simulation Execution
This allows a simulation result to be traced back to the exact variation conditions under which it occurred.
Variation Versioning
Variation definitions may change.
Material changes to: ranges, distributions, categories, parameter values, dependencies, or configuration logic
should remain version-distinguishable.
Variation Change Trigger
Reassessment may be required where: new operational evidence appears, system configuration changes, environmental understanding changes, new dependencies are discovered, assumptions change, input distributions change, or previous simulations expose new sensitivities.
Adaptive Variation Expansion

Simulation execution may reveal that a particular region of the variation space produces unusual behavior.
SCVM may support:
Initial Variation → Observed Sensitivity → Increased Variation Resolution → Additional Configurations
This allows simulation resources to be concentrated where new information is being discovered.
No Static Sampling Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A predefined variation plan should not prevent expansion when simulation behavior reveals a materially important region that was not sufficiently examined.
Variation and Uncertainty
Variation and uncertainty are related but not identical.
Uncertainty asks:
What do we not know sufficiently?
Variation asks:
Across which different conditions should the simulation deliberately operate?
Uncertainty may create a Variation Requirement.
But not every variation represents uncertainty.
Some variation represents known operational diversity.
Variation and Edge Cases
SCVM governs the structured variation of scenarios.
The following module:
SECM — Scenario Edge-Case Module
examines conditions near unusual, sparse, boundary, extreme, or otherwise materially atypical regions of that variation space.
Therefore:
SCVM maps the variation space.
SECM interrogates its difficult edges.
Variation and Stress Conditions
SCVM establishes ordinary and materially relevant variation.
SSCM — Scenario Stress-Condition Module subsequently governs deliberate stress beyond ordinary scenario conditions where required.

Variation should therefore not be inflated to absorb the separate governance purpose of stress testing.
Variation and Coverage
Variation configurations become inputs to:
SCCM — Scenario Coverage Module.
Coverage asks whether the selected variations collectively examine the materially relevant Scenario Space.
SCVM does not make the final Scenario Coverage determination.
Space and Mission Systems
Space systems demonstrate why controlled variation matters.
A mission simulation may examine a spacecraft under: different communication delays, changing power availability, navigation uncertainty, thermal conditions, radiation environments, timing deviations, subsystem degradation, and mission-phase configurations.
The important question is not simply whether each variable was simulated.
It may be whether materially relevant combinations and timing relationships were examined.
For example:
Reduced Power + Communication Delay + Navigation Uncertainty during Autonomous Recovery
may expose behavior not visible in isolated variation.
SCVM provides the structure for governing those combinations without prescribing which combinations every mission must simulate.
Autonomous Systems
Autonomous-system behavior can depend strongly on simultaneous variation in: perception quality, environmental complexity, actor behavior, communication, resource availability, autonomy state, decision timing, and system confidence.

A system that performs well when these dimensions are varied individually may behave differently when several change together.
SCVM therefore provides a structured way to move from:
“We tested many conditions.”
to:
“We can show which dimensions changed, across what ranges, in which combinations, and why those variations were selected.” AI and Multi-Agent Systems
Multi-agent environments can create especially large variation spaces because each agent may introduce: behavior variation, objective variation, timing variation, communication variation, strategy variation, and interaction variation.
SCVM does not require exhaustive enumeration.
It requires that material variation and excluded variation remain visible and governable.
Industrial Simulation
An industrial system may perform correctly at:
normal load + normal temperature + full sensor availability
while becoming unstable under:
high load + elevated temperature + partial sensor degradation.
SCVM makes the difference between these configurations explicit and traceable.
Existing Simulation Program Diagnostic
SCVM can be applied to an existing simulation program.
An organization can ask:
Which variables do our scenarios actually vary?
Across what ranges?
Why were those ranges selected?
Which dimensions are held constant?
Which variables are correlated?
Which combinations have never been examined?
Are we testing distributions or only averages?
Where are our Variation Gaps?

This can reveal that a simulation program has high execution volume but low variation diversity.
Module Boundary
SCVM begins when SCIM has established sufficiently identifiable Simulation Scenarios and Scenario Requirements.
SCVM ends when materially relevant variation dimensions, ranges, levels, dependencies, interactions, combinations, and configurations have been sufficiently governed to form a Variation Configuration Set suitable for Edge-Case, Stress-Condition, and Coverage governance.
SCVM does not govern: general Simulation Input governance, general model parameter governance, complete edge-case identification, stress-condition design, final Scenario Coverage, Simulation Execution, or simulation-output interpretation.
It governs specifically:
how identified scenarios are deliberately varied across materially relevant conditions.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Variation Requirements
Determine which conditions within each Scenario can materially vary. 2. Define Variation Dimensions
Identify: variables, categories, states, timing, sequences, environmental conditions, behavioral conditions, and dependencies.
3. Establish Variation Ranges
Define materially relevant: minimums, maximums, categories, distributions, and applicability boundaries.
4. Establish Variation Structure
Determine whether variation is: continuous, discrete, categorical, stochastic, temporal, sequential, single-factor, multi-factor, correlated, or conditional.

5. Construct Variation Configurations
Create governed combinations suitable for simulation. 6. Assess Variation Sufficiency
Determine whether materially relevant ranges and relationships are sufficiently represented. 7. Record Variation Gaps and Exclusions
Preserve conditions that remain unexamined or cannot currently be represented. 8. Establish Variation Configuration Set
Produce the governed variation basis for downstream Scenario Design.
Governance Outputs

SCVM may produce: Variation Requirement, Variation Dimension Register, Variation Variable Record, Variation Range, Variation Boundary, Variation Level, Variation Resolution Record, Continuous Variation Record, Discrete Variation Record, Categorical Variation Record, Stochastic Variation Record, Distribution Basis, Input Variation Record, Parameter Variation Record, Environmental Variation Record, Behavioral Variation Record, Temporal Variation Record, Sequence Variation Record, Duration Variation Record, Rate-of-Change Variation Record, Single-Factor Variation Record, Multi-Factor Variation Record, Correlated Variation Record, Conditional Variation Record, Dependency Variation Record, Configuration Variation Record, Variation Interaction Map, Variation Configuration, Variation Configuration Identifier, Variation Configuration Set, Variation Prioritization Record, Variation Sufficiency Assessment, Variation Gap, Variation Exclusion Record, Variation Traceability Map, Variation Version Record, and Governed Scenario Variation Basis.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving
Scenario
An autonomous-driving simulation contains a pedestrian-crossing scenario.
Testing initially varies only vehicle speed.
SCVM identifies additional materially relevant Variation Dimensions: visibility, pedestrian speed, pedestrian direction, occlusion, road surface, sensor confidence, reaction timing, surrounding traffic, and pedestrian behavior.
Application

The program first examines controlled single-factor variation.
It then identifies materially relevant interactions, including:
Low Visibility + Partial Occlusion + Reduced Sensor Confidence + Late Pedestrian Entry
rather than treating each variable as independent. Result
One static pedestrian scenario becomes a governed variation space.
The program can identify which combinations were examined and which remain Variation Gaps. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Autonomous Recovery
Scenario
A spacecraft simulation includes autonomous recovery after loss of nominal navigation.
The existing program tests the recovery under one standard communication and power configuration.
SCVM identifies material variation in: navigation uncertainty, communication delay, communication interruption duration, available power, thermal condition, recovery initiation timing, and subsystem availability.
Application
The variables are not treated as universally independent.
Reduced power affects which subsystems remain available.
Communication condition affects ground-intervention opportunity.
Recovery timing interacts with mission phase.
SCVM establishes governed Variation Configurations reflecting those relationships. Result
The organization can distinguish:
Recovery Was Simulated
from the stronger and more useful statement:
Recovery was examined across these defined operating ranges, dependencies, timing conditions, and materially relevant combinations. Use Case 3 — Industrial Autonomous Robot
Scenario

An autonomous industrial robot operates safely during simulations with normal production load.
The facility wants to understand performance under changing operational conditions. Application
SCVM establishes variation across: production density, human proximity, sensor confidence, payload, floor conditions, communication latency, actuator performance, and human reaction timing.
Simulation results reveal unusual behavior only when:
High Production Density + Reduced Sensor Confidence + Increased Payload
occur together. Result
The variation program exposes a system behavior that would not have appeared through isolated one-variable testing.
The finding can then generate new Edge-Case or Stress-Condition requirements without altering the purpose of SCVM itself.
Architectural Position
Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS).
The complete SSS progression is:
Scenario Identification
↓
Scenario Variation
↓
Scenario Edge Cases
↓
Scenario Stress Conditions
↓
Scenario Coverage
SCIM establishes which scenarios matter.
SCVM establishes how those scenarios must vary.
SECM determines which difficult edges and atypical conditions require deliberate examination.
SSCM governs material stress conditions.
SCCM determines whether the resulting Scenario Space is sufficiently covered.
Foundational Principle

A scenario examined at only one convenient configuration cannot demonstrate behavior across a condition space that materially varies.
Canonical Closing Statement
Scenario Variation Module transforms identified Simulation Scenarios from static test conditions into governed variation spaces by defining which dimensions may materially change, across what ranges, distributions, states, sequences, dependencies, and combinations those changes must be examined, and how resulting configurations remain identifiable and traceable. Through controlled single-factor variation, multi-factor interaction, correlated conditions, temporal and sequence variation, variation sufficiency, explicit gaps, exclusions, adaptive expansion, and complete configuration traceability, SCVM ensures that simulation programs do not mistake testing one representative condition—or many repetitions of similar conditions—for systematic examination of the materially relevant variation space surrounding the Simulation Object.

Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
