Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation-Reality Deviation
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 19 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation-Reality Deviation
Canonical Definition
Simulation-Reality Deviation Module (SDMM) defines the governance conditions under which material differences between simulated behavior, conditions, states, events, relationships, trajectories, and outputs and their corresponding Operational Reality observations are identified, measured, localized, classified, contextualized, traced, and documented.
SDMM establishes the governed deviation layer between:
Simulation-Reality Comparison
and:
Reality Alignment.
Its purpose is not to require simulation and reality to be identical.

Its purpose is to determine:
where they differ, by how much, under which conditions, whether the deviation is systematic or conditional, and which part of the simulation-to-reality relationship is affected.
Operational Role
SDMM is the third internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
The progression is:
SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison Module
→ establishes comparable simulation and reality observations.
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module
→ establishes the criteria against which correspondence is assessed.
SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module
→ identifies and structures material differences revealed by that comparison.
SRAM — Reality Alignment Module
→ governs how the simulation-reality relationship is reassessed or aligned in response to identified differences.
SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module
→ governs uncertainty remaining in the correlation relationship.
SDMM therefore asks:
Where does the simulation depart from reality, how material is that departure, and what does the deviation actually affect?
Module Operational Space

SDMM governs: simulation-reality deviation identification, deviation measurement, deviation localization, deviation classification, deviation magnitude, deviation direction, deviation persistence, deviation frequency, deviation distribution, temporal deviation, spatial deviation, behavioral deviation, state deviation, event deviation, trajectory deviation, response deviation, interaction deviation, environmental deviation, output deviation, threshold deviation, systematic deviation, conditional deviation, intermittent deviation, localized deviation, cumulative deviation, correlated deviation, deviation clustering, deviation dependency, deviation propagation, deviation attribution, unresolved deviation, deviation materiality, deviation documentation, and deviation traceability.
Module Function
SDMM prevents a simulation from being described as simply:
“close to reality”
or:
“different from reality”
without identifying the structure of that difference.
A useful simulation-reality assessment must be capable of distinguishing, where relevant:
what matched,
what deviated,
where the deviation occurred,
under which conditions it occurred,
how large it was,
whether it repeated,
and:
what downstream interpretation may be affected.
Deviation Object
Every material deviation should be capable of being represented as a governable object.
Conceptually:
Deviation ID
↓
Simulation Observation
↓
Reality Observation
↓
Correlation Criterion
↓
Observed Difference
↓
Deviation Classification
↓

Materiality
↓
Affected Simulation Element
↓
Known / Suspected Basis
↓
Uncertainty
↓
Governance Status
This prevents significant deviations from disappearing inside aggregate correlation metrics.
Deviation Identification
A Simulation-Reality Deviation exists when a materially comparable simulated and real-world observation differs according to an applicable correlation criterion.
The difference may concern: magnitude, direction, timing, sequence, frequency, duration, state, response, interaction, distribution, threshold crossing, failure mode, recovery behavior, or another materially relevant property.
Deviation ≠ Failure
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation-Reality Deviation is not automatically a simulation failure.
A deviation may arise because: the simulation is simplified, reality contains unmodeled variables, measurements are imperfect, the Operational Reality state changed, boundary conditions differ, assumptions apply only conditionally, stochastic behavior exists, the comparison basis is incomplete, or the simulation genuinely misrepresents reality.
SDMM preserves the deviation before determining its consequence.
Deviation Magnitude
Where measurable, deviation magnitude should establish the size of the observed difference.

Magnitude may be expressed through: absolute difference, relative difference, percentage difference, distributional distance, timing offset, positional error, trajectory error, frequency difference, state mismatch, categorical difference, or another appropriate measure.
SIMULOS® does not prescribe one universal deviation metric.
Deviation Direction
Where relevant, SDMM should distinguish whether the simulation:
Overestimates Reality
Underestimates Reality
Leads Reality
Lags Reality
Diverges Bidirectionally
or exhibits another defined directional relationship.
Direction may be operationally more important than aggregate error magnitude.
Deviation Localization
A deviation should be localized as precisely as the available evidence permits.
Localization may identify: Simulation Object component, subsystem, agent, environment region, scenario, parameter range, operating condition, time interval, state transition, interaction, input region, or output dimension.
Global ≠ Local Correlation
A simulation may correlate strongly with reality overall while failing badly in a specific operational region.
Therefore:
Strong aggregate correlation must not erase material localized deviation.
Temporal Deviation
Temporal deviation exists where simulated behavior differs from reality in: initiation time, response latency, event ordering, duration, synchronization, recovery time, transition speed, or temporal pattern.
A simulation may predict the correct event but at the wrong time.

That difference may be material.
Spatial Deviation
Spatial deviation concerns differences in: position, trajectory, distribution, physical location, movement, coverage, geometry, or spatial interaction.
This may be especially important in: robotics, autonomous vehicles, aerospace, orbital systems, manufacturing, logistics, and physical infrastructure simulation.
Behavioral Deviation
Behavioral deviation exists where the simulated system responds differently from the corresponding real system under materially comparable conditions.
Examples include: different action selection, different recovery behavior, different escalation behavior, different human response, different agent coordination, or different autonomous decision pathways.
Environmental Deviation
A simulation may reproduce the target system accurately while inadequately reproducing its environment.
SDMM therefore distinguishes:
System Deviation
from:
Environment Deviation.
Environmental deviation may concern: weather, terrain, friction, radiation, communication conditions, traffic, human behavior, physical noise, infrastructure state, or another environmental variable.
Interaction Deviation
Complex systems may behave correctly in isolation but diverge when interacting with: humans, other agents, infrastructure, external systems, physical environments, or unexpected events.
SDMM therefore governs deviations in interaction dynamics separately where material.
Trajectory Deviation

For systems whose behavior evolves over time, a small initial deviation may produce substantial downstream divergence.
Conceptually:
Initial Difference
↓
State Divergence
↓
Behavioral Divergence
↓
Trajectory Divergence
↓
Material Outcome Difference
SDMM should preserve this progression where observable.
Systematic Deviation
A Systematic Deviation repeatedly occurs in the same direction or under comparable conditions.
Examples:
simulation consistently underestimates braking distance
or:
simulation consistently overestimates communication reliability.
Systematic deviations may indicate a persistent representational or model relationship requiring further governance.
Conditional Deviation
A simulation may correlate well with reality under normal conditions but diverge under a specific condition.
For example:
Normal Temperature → Strong Correlation
Extreme Temperature → Material Deviation
The correct conclusion is not necessarily:
Simulation Poor
but potentially:
Correlation is conditionally bounded.
Intermittent Deviation
Some deviations occur irregularly.
This may arise from: stochastic processes, rare interactions, timing, emergent behavior, nondeterministic systems, or incomplete observation.
Intermittent deviations should not automatically be discarded as noise where their consequences may be material.
Deviation Frequency
Where relevant, SDMM may govern:
how often the deviation occurs.

A small deviation occurring continuously may be more important than a larger deviation occurring once.
Conversely, a rare deviation may still be critical where its consequence is catastrophic.
Deviation Materiality
Deviation magnitude alone does not determine materiality.
Conceptually:
Deviation Materiality
may depend upon:
Magnitude + Context + Frequency + Consequence + Scenario + Reliance Purpose.
A two-percent difference may be immaterial in one simulation and mission-critical in another.
Materiality Classification
Possible implementation states may include:
Negligible
Minor
Material
Major
Critical
or:
Materiality Undetermined.
These classifications are implementation-dependent rather than universal SIMULOS® thresholds.
Threshold Deviation
Where correlation criteria establish acceptable thresholds, SDMM should distinguish:
Within Correlation Boundary
from:
Outside Correlation Boundary.
However, passing a threshold does not prove universal simulation-to-reality equivalence.
Deviation Clustering
Individual deviations may reveal little when viewed separately.
SDMM may therefore identify:
Deviation Clusters
where multiple differences occur around: one subsystem, one scenario family, one operating condition, one environment state, one parameter region, or one behavioral pattern.
Clusters can expose simulation weaknesses hidden by aggregate metrics.
Deviation Propagation
A deviation in one simulated element may propagate through the simulation.
For example:

Sensor Timing Deviation
↓
State Estimation Deviation
↓
Decision Deviation
↓
Trajectory Deviation
↓
Outcome Deviation
SDMM should preserve known propagation relationships rather than treating each downstream difference as independent.
Deviation Dependency
Some deviations exist only when multiple conditions combine.
For example:
Low Visibility Sensor Noise High Speed
↓
Material Simulation-Reality Deviation
Each factor independently may show acceptable correlation.
The combination may not.
Deviation Attribution
Where sufficient evidence exists, a deviation may be associated with a probable basis such as: Reality Representation, assumption, model structure, environment configuration, parameterization, input data, scenario design, execution condition, measurement limitation, Operational Reality change, or unknown cause.
Attribution Must Not Be Invented
SIMULOS® establishes:
Observed deviation does not by itself establish the cause of deviation.
Where causation is not sufficiently supported, the status should remain:
Deviation Cause Undetermined.
This is preferable to false explanation.
Unresolved Deviation
A deviation may remain unresolved when: its cause is unknown, observations are incomplete, measurements conflict, reproduction fails, the real-world basis is uncertain, or multiple explanations remain plausible.
Unresolved deviations remain part of the governed correlation record.
No Average-Washing Principle
A critical SIMULOS® rule is:

Material Simulation-Reality Deviations must not disappear merely because aggregate averages remain acceptable.
A simulation could perform extremely well across 99% of conditions while failing in the 1% that matters most operationally.
No Selective Correlation Principle
Simulation-reality analysis should not preserve only those comparisons that demonstrate strong correspondence.
Material negative correlation evidence must remain visible.
Reality Change
A deviation may emerge because reality changed rather than because the simulation changed.
Therefore SDMM should preserve where possible:
Simulation Version
and:
Operational Reality State / Time Basis.
This allows later analysis to distinguish:
Simulation Drift
from:
Reality Drift
or:
Combined Drift.
Deviation Across Versions
Simulation versions may be compared against the same or equivalent reality basis.
For example:
Simulation v1 → Reality → Deviation Set A
Simulation v2 → Reality → Deviation Set B
This can reveal whether changes improved or worsened the correlation relationship.
Deviation Trend
Across repeated comparisons, deviations may:
Decrease
Remain Stable
Increase
Shift Location
Change Direction
or:
Become Uncertain.
Deviation trend can become an important governance signal for SRAM.
Deviation Record
A governed deviation record may contain:
Deviation ID
Simulation ID / Version
Reality Reference
Scenario / Condition
Correlation Criterion
Simulation Observation
Reality Observation
Deviation Measure
Deviation Direction

Deviation Magnitude
Deviation Classification
Materiality
Frequency
Affected Element
Known Dependencies
Probable Basis where supported
Uncertainty
Status
Required Follow-Up Relationship to SRCM
SRCM establishes:
what simulation observation and reality observation may legitimately be compared.
SDMM governs:
the material difference revealed by that comparison.
Without SRCM, a deviation may be based on incomparable observations.
Relationship to SCCM
SCCM establishes the correlation criteria and thresholds.
SDMM applies those criteria to structure and classify observed differences.
Therefore:
Correlation Criterion → Comparison → Deviation.
Relationship to SRAM
SDMM identifies where the simulation-reality relationship differs materially.
SRAM uses that governed deviation basis to determine where and how Reality Alignment should be examined.
Therefore:
Deviation Discovery precedes Alignment Action.
Relationship to SCUM
Some deviation measurements remain uncertain.
SCUM governs uncertainty in the broader simulation-to-reality correlation relationship.
SDMM must therefore preserve uncertainty rather than converting uncertain deviation into false precision.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.
SDMM does not redefine reality.
It consumes sufficiently governed reality observations or descriptions and governs the deviation relationship between those observations and the simulation.
Relationship to VALIDOS®

SDMM does not determine whether the simulation is valid for a particular Validation Purpose.
It produces structured Simulation-Reality Deviation evidence that VALIDOS® may subsequently use.
Relationship to INTEGROS®
SDMM does not own general integrity governance.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of the observations, measurements, records, or artifacts used in deviation analysis.
Autonomous Systems Application
For autonomous systems, SDMM can identify where simulated autonomous behavior diverges from operational behavior.
Material deviation regions may include: perception under degraded conditions, agent interaction, human response, recovery behavior, escalation, decision timing, unexpected environmental conditions, and long-horizon autonomous behavior.
This matters because a system can demonstrate excellent average simulation performance while diverging precisely in the operational conditions where autonomous governance is most important.
Space and Mission Simulation Application
Space systems often depend heavily on simulation because many mission conditions cannot be repeatedly reproduced in Operational Reality.
SDMM can govern differences revealed through: hardware tests, flight data, telemetry, prior missions, environmental measurements, subsystem tests, and operational mission observations.

A simulation may correlate strongly for nominal trajectory behavior while materially deviating in: thermal extremes, radiation response, communication degradation, sensor behavior, propulsion anomalies, subsystem interactions, or autonomous recovery.
The deviation record makes those limits explicit rather than allowing nominal correlation to represent the entire mission envelope.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Comparison Basis
Use governed simulation-reality comparisons from SRCM. 2. Apply Correlation Criteria
Determine which SCCM criteria govern the comparison. 3. Identify Deviations
Detect materially relevant differences. 4. Measure the Difference
Determine magnitude, direction, timing, distribution, or another applicable deviation measure. 5. Localize the Deviation
Identify the affected: condition, scenario, component, state, interaction, environment, or output.
6. Classify the Deviation
Determine whether it is: systematic, conditional, intermittent, localized, cumulative, or another relevant type.
7. Determine Materiality
Assess whether the deviation materially affects the intended simulation-reality relationship. 8. Identify Dependencies and Propagation
Determine whether other deviations or conditions contribute to or result from it. 9. Assess Attribution
Identify probable causes only where supported.
Otherwise preserve:
Cause Undetermined. 10. Preserve Uncertainty

Do not express deviation more precisely than the evidence permits. 11. Document the Deviation
Create a governed Simulation-Reality Deviation Record. 12. Transfer to Reality Alignment
Provide the structured deviation basis to SRAM.
Governance Outputs
SDMM may produce: Simulation-Reality Deviation ID, Simulation-Reality Deviation Record, Deviation Measurement Record, Deviation Magnitude Assessment, Deviation Direction Assessment, Deviation Localization Record, Temporal Deviation Record, Spatial Deviation Record, Behavioral Deviation Record, Environmental Deviation Record, Interaction Deviation Record, Trajectory Deviation Record, Systematic Deviation Record, Conditional Deviation Record, Intermittent Deviation Record, Deviation Frequency Assessment, Deviation Materiality Assessment, Threshold Deviation Record, Deviation Cluster Record, Deviation Dependency Map, Deviation Propagation Map, Deviation Attribution Record, Unresolved Deviation Record, Reality Change Record, Cross-Version Deviation Comparison, Deviation Trend Record, and Governed Simulation-Reality Deviation Basis.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
An autonomous driving system performs strongly in simulation and demonstrates high aggregate correspondence with road testing.
SDMM reveals, however, that under the combined conditions of:
heavy rain + low illumination + partially obscured road markings
the simulated perception stack consistently identifies lane boundaries earlier than the real system.

The deviation is classified as:
Conditional + Systematic + Material.
Instead of concluding that the entire simulation is inaccurate, SDMM localizes the problem to a specific operational region and transfers the governed deviation to Reality Alignment. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Autonomous Recovery
A spacecraft simulation predicts successful autonomous recovery from temporary communication loss across a broad mission scenario set.
Operational telemetry from comparable subsystem and mission conditions shows that real recovery begins materially later when:
low power state + communication degradation + thermal constraint
occur simultaneously.
SDMM identifies a conditional temporal and behavioral deviation that is largely invisible in nominal mission correlation statistics.
The deviation becomes a governed input to SRAM without prematurely declaring either the simulation or mission system invalid.
Architectural Position
SDMM is the third module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
The internal progression is:
SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison
↓
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria
↓
SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation
↓
SRAM — Reality Alignment
↓
SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty
SDMM occupies the critical point where:
observed correspondence becomes structured knowledge about non-correspondence.
Foundational Principle

Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence, and aggregate correlation must never conceal the specific conditions under which simulation and reality materially diverge.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation-Reality Deviation Module (SDMM) governs how material differences between simulation and Operational Reality are identified, measured, localized, classified, contextualized, traced, and preserved. By distinguishing deviation from failure, global correlation from local divergence, magnitude from materiality, observation from attribution, and simulation change from reality change, SDMM prevents strong aggregate performance from concealing the operational regions where simulation correspondence weakens or fails. It transforms simulation-reality difference from an informal observation into a governed deviation basis capable of supporting Reality Alignment, correlation uncertainty governance, validation, audit, and future simulation improvement without falsely treating simulation similarity as reality equivalence.

OOF™ Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM)
Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Depth & Precision
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 16 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Depth & Precision
Canonical Definition
Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM) defines the governance conditions under which the required analytical depth, representational precision, temporal and spatial granularity, parameter resolution, interaction detail, scenario intensity, uncertainty treatment, and consequence-proportionate simulation rigor are established for a defined Simulation Purpose, Scope, Exclusions, and Applicability Context.

SDPM determines how deeply and precisely the governed simulation inquiry must examine the Simulation Object without prescribing a particular simulation model, technology, numerical method, software platform, or validation methodology.
It prevents a simulation from being treated as sufficiently informative merely because the correct object and scope were selected.
Operational Role
SDPM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The preceding modules establish:
SPM — Why is the simulation being performed?
SSCM — What must the simulation cover?
SEXM — What remains outside the governed Simulation Scope?
SACM — Within which contexts is the simulation inquiry intended to apply?
SDPM asks:
At what depth and precision must the simulation inquiry operate to be adequate for its intended purpose and consequence?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Required Simulation Depth & Precision
SDPM therefore completes the simulation inquiry definition before the architecture proceeds into governance of how reality is represented inside the simulation.
Module Operational Space

SDPM governs: Simulation Depth, Simulation Precision, required simulation rigor, inquiry granularity, abstraction-depth requirements, parameter precision, temporal granularity, spatial granularity, behavioral detail, interaction detail, dependency detail, state resolution, event resolution, scenario intensity, scenario granularity, edge-condition depth, failure-condition depth, uncertainty-treatment depth, sensitivity-analysis depth, consequence-proportionate rigor, depth differentiation, precision differentiation, minimum acceptable depth, minimum acceptable precision, depth sufficiency, precision sufficiency, depth limitations, precision limitations, depth escalation, precision escalation, depth reduction, precision reduction, depth change, precision change, and Simulation Depth & Precision traceability.
Module Function
A simulation may have: the correct Simulation Object, a legitimate Simulation Purpose, a properly bounded Simulation Scope, explicit exclusions, and an appropriate Applicability Context,
while still being incapable of answering the simulation question with sufficient depth.
For example:
Purpose: Assess collision behavior.
Scope: Vehicle frontal collision.
Applicability: Defined vehicle configuration and impact conditions.
But the simulation represents the event only at a level sufficient for approximate structural deformation.
That simulation may be appropriate for early design exploration while being insufficient for detailed occupant-injury analysis.

SDPM prevents:
Correct Simulation Question → Insufficient Simulation Depth → Apparently Precise Output → Overstated Simulation Meaning
Its function is therefore to establish the required level of examination before apparent numerical precision is mistaken for methodological sufficiency.
Simulation Depth
Simulation Depth defines how extensively the simulation inquiry must examine the relevant characteristics, relationships, behaviors, interactions, dependencies, states, scenarios, and consequences within the governed Simulation Scope.
Depth answers:
How far must the simulation inquiry go?
Simulation Depth may determine whether the inquiry requires examination of: primary behavior only, secondary effects, interaction effects, cascading effects, dependencies, failure modes, edge conditions, rare conditions, recovery behavior, long-duration effects, or consequence propagation.
Simulation Precision
Simulation Precision defines the required degree of differentiation and granularity with which simulation-relevant variables, states, relationships, events, parameters, and outputs must be represented for the Simulation Purpose.
Precision answers:
How finely must the simulation distinguish simulation-relevant differences?
Precision may involve: parameter resolution, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, state resolution, behavioral resolution, event resolution, measurement granularity, interaction granularity, or output granularity.
Depth ≠ Precision

Depth and precision are related but not interchangeable.
A simulation may be:
deep but low-precision
or:
narrow but high-precision.
For example, a simulation may examine many interacting system dependencies while representing each through coarse parameter ranges.
Another simulation may represent one narrowly bounded physical process at extremely fine numerical resolution.
SDPM therefore governs both dimensions independently where necessary. Precision ≠ Accuracy
SDPM establishes an important distinction:
Simulation Precision does not itself establish Simulation Accuracy.
A simulation may produce highly precise numerical outputs from an inadequate model, incorrect assumptions, unsuitable inputs, or insufficient reality representation.
Therefore:
More decimal places ≠ Better simulation.
Precision must be justified by the simulation inquiry. Depth ≠ Fidelity
Simulation Depth governs how extensively the inquiry must examine the problem.
Representation Fidelity, governed subsequently within the Reality Representation Standard (RRS), concerns how faithfully selected aspects of reality are represented inside the simulation.
A simulation may therefore require high analytical depth while legitimately using different fidelity levels across different represented elements.
Purpose-Proportionate Depth
Required Simulation Depth should derive from the Simulation Purpose.
A simulation intended for:
early conceptual exploration
may legitimately require less depth than one intended for:

engineering qualification,
safety-critical analysis,
or:
high-consequence operational decision support.
SDPM does not establish one universal depth requirement.
It establishes that depth must be purpose-proportionate.
Consequence-Proportionate Rigor
Where simulation outputs may influence high-consequence decisions, the required depth and precision may need to increase.
Conceptually:
Higher Consequence → Stronger Justification for Required Simulation Rigor
This does not mean every high-consequence simulation must always maximize every form of precision.
It means that reductions in depth or precision require stronger justification where their consequences are material.
Minimum Sufficient Depth
The objective of SDPM is not maximum simulation complexity.
The objective is:
sufficient simulation depth for the governed purpose.
Unnecessary depth may: increase computational cost, increase modeling complexity, introduce additional assumptions, increase data requirements, obscure material relationships, and reduce operational usability.
SDPM therefore supports the minimum sufficient depth principle.
Minimum Sufficient Precision
Likewise, simulation precision should be sufficient to distinguish differences that materially affect the simulation inquiry.
Precision beyond what the purpose can meaningfully use may create: false confidence, unnecessary computational burden, misleading apparent certainty, or complexity without additional decision value.
The governing question is not:

How precise can the simulation become?
It is:
How precise must the simulation be for the intended purpose?
Depth Dimensions
Simulation Depth may be decomposed into relevant dimensions.
These may include: Structural Depth
How extensively must internal structures and relationships be examined?
Behavioral Depth
How extensively must behavior, behavioral variation, and behavioral transitions be represented?
Interaction Depth
How extensively must interactions among simulated entities be examined?
Dependency Depth
How deeply must external and internal dependencies be represented?
Failure Depth
Which failure conditions, degraded states, and failure combinations must be examined?
Consequence Depth
How far must downstream effects and consequence propagation be followed?
Scenario Depth
How broad and intensive must scenario exploration become?
Temporal Depth
How far through time must simulation behavior be examined?
Different dimensions may legitimately require different levels of depth.
Precision Dimensions
Precision may similarly be multidimensional.
Relevant dimensions may include:
Spatial Precision
Temporal Precision
Parameter Precision
State Precision
Behavioral Precision
Interaction Precision
Event Precision
Output Precision
A simulation does not need identical precision across all dimensions.
Differentiated Depth Rule
SDPM permits different components of the same simulation inquiry to operate at different depths where justified.
For example:
Primary safety mechanism → High Depth

Secondary cosmetic behavior → Low Depth
This allows simulation resources to concentrate on what materially affects the Simulation Purpose.
Differentiated Precision Rule
Different simulation variables may require different precision.
For example:
Collision timing → millisecond-level resolution
while:
ambient temperature → broader interval representation
may be sufficient for the same simulation.
Precision should follow materiality rather than uniformity.
Materiality Principle
A simulation characteristic is depth- or precision-material where insufficient treatment could materially alter: simulation behavior, simulation outputs, interpretation, decision relevance, scenario outcome, consequence assessment, or downstream reliance.
Material dimensions should receive explicit depth and precision requirements.
Temporal Granularity
Temporal granularity determines how finely simulation time must be represented.
Insufficient temporal granularity may conceal: rapid transitions, control instability, collisions, short-duration failures, timing dependencies, cascading events, or synchronization problems.
Excessive temporal granularity may create unnecessary computational burden without improving the governed inquiry.
Spatial Granularity
Spatial granularity determines how finely physical or virtual space must be represented.
The required level depends upon the simulation purpose.

A regional traffic-flow simulation and a vehicle collision simulation legitimately require radically different spatial precision.
Parameter Precision
Simulation parameters should have precision appropriate to their material influence.
Parameter precision should not exceed the defensible precision of the underlying information merely to make the simulation appear more exact.
Input Precision Constraint
Where an input is known only within a broad range, the simulation should not silently convert that uncertainty into artificial precision.
Conceptually:
Input Knowledge Precision → Limits Defensible Simulation Precision
unless additional modeling explicitly governs the uncertainty.
State Resolution
Simulation states should be differentiated sufficiently to capture state transitions material to the inquiry.
For example:
Operational / Failed
may be sufficient for one simulation.
Another may require:
Nominal → Degraded → Critical → Failed → Recovering → Restored
SDPM governs whether the chosen resolution is sufficient for the intended inquiry.
Interaction Resolution
Where outcomes depend upon interactions, the simulation must distinguish interaction characteristics at sufficient depth.
This may include: timing, sequencing, dependency, coordination, conflict, feedback, communication, or emergent interaction effects.
Scenario Depth
Scenario Depth establishes how extensively the simulation inquiry must explore the relevant scenario space.
This may include:
Nominal Conditions

Expected Variations
Edge Conditions
Failure Conditions
Rare Events
Adversarial Conditions
Compound Conditions
The required scenario depth derives from the Simulation Purpose and consequence context.
Detailed Scenario Design itself remains governed by the dedicated downstream SIMULOS® scenario governance space.
Edge-Condition Depth
Where boundary conditions materially influence simulation meaning, SDPM may require explicit examination near or beyond expected operating boundaries.
A simulation intended for robust safety analysis should not necessarily stop at average conditions.
Failure-Condition Depth
Failure-condition depth establishes how extensively failure modes and combinations must be examined.
Possible levels may include:
Single Failure
Multiple Independent Failures
Dependent Failures
Cascading Failures
Recovery Failure
The appropriate level depends upon purpose and consequence.
Uncertainty-Treatment Depth
Simulation Depth may require uncertainty to be examined rather than represented as a single deterministic value.
This may involve: ranges, distributions, sensitivity, confidence bounds, scenario variation, parameter uncertainty, or structural uncertainty.
SDPM establishes the required depth of uncertainty treatment.
It does not replace specialized validation or integrity governance.
Sensitivity Depth
Where simulation outcomes are highly sensitive to particular assumptions or parameters, greater depth may be required around those variables.

A parameter with negligible effect does not necessarily require the same precision as one capable of reversing the simulation conclusion.
Depth Sufficiency
Simulation Depth Sufficiency asks:
Is the established depth sufficient to address the Simulation Purpose within the governed Scope and Applicability Context?
Possible outcomes may include:
Sufficient
Conditionally Sufficient
Partially Sufficient
Insufficient
or:
Undetermined Precision Sufficiency
Simulation Precision Sufficiency asks:
Is the established precision sufficient to distinguish the simulation-relevant differences material to the governed inquiry?
Possible outcomes may include:
Sufficient
Conditionally Sufficient
Partially Sufficient
Insufficient
or:
Undetermined Depth–Precision Alignment
Depth and precision should remain mutually coherent.
A simulation should not use extreme numerical precision to disguise shallow analytical coverage.
Likewise, extensive analytical coverage should not rely upon resolution too coarse to distinguish material behavior.
SDPM therefore supports:
Required Depth ↔ Required Precision ↔ Simulation Purpose Depth–Purpose Alignment
Every material depth requirement should be traceable to the Simulation Purpose, Scope, Applicability Context, or consequence.
This prevents complexity from becoming arbitrary. Precision–Purpose Alignment
Precision should likewise remain connected to the actual simulation question.

A precision requirement without a meaningful simulation purpose may create computational cost without methodological value.
Depth Limitation
Where the required Simulation Depth cannot be achieved, the limitation should be explicit.
The simulation may still proceed where appropriate, but downstream interpretation must remain bounded by the achieved depth.
Precision Limitation
Where required precision cannot be achieved, the resulting limitation should remain visible.
The simulation should not silently present lower-resolution analysis as satisfying a higher-resolution requirement.
No False Precision Rule
Simulation outputs must not imply a level of precision materially stronger than the governed simulation basis can support.
No Complexity Substitution Rule
Greater model complexity must not be treated as automatic evidence of sufficient Simulation Depth.
Complexity and methodological adequacy are not equivalent.
No Computational-Scale Substitution Rule
A simulation does not become methodologically stronger merely because it uses: more compute, more parameters, more iterations, larger models, more agents, or longer execution.
Computational scale must serve the simulation inquiry.
No Uniform Precision Rule
A simulation need not apply maximum or identical precision to every simulated element.
Precision should be allocated according to materiality.
No Depth Inflation Rule
A simulation must not claim deeper analytical coverage than was actually established and executed.

No Precision Inflation Rule
A simulation must not represent outputs as more precise than the underlying simulation conditions legitimately support.
No Purpose Transfer Rule
Depth sufficient for one Simulation Purpose must not automatically be considered sufficient for another purpose.
For example:
Depth sufficient for concept exploration
does not automatically become:
Depth sufficient for operational safety authorization.
Depth Escalation
Required depth may increase when: Simulation Purpose changes, consequence increases, new failure modes emerge, new dependencies become material, new operational environments are introduced, new autonomy is added, new interactions emerge, uncertainty increases, or downstream use becomes more demanding.
Precision Escalation
Required precision may increase where: smaller differences become decision-relevant, timing becomes more critical, spatial relationships become more consequential, new thresholds emerge, control behavior changes, or output interpretation requires finer differentiation.
Depth Reduction
Depth may legitimately be reduced where: the Simulation Purpose narrows, consequence decreases, irrelevant dimensions are removed, sensitivity analysis demonstrates low materiality, or a previously complex inquiry becomes bounded to a simpler question.
Reduction should be justified rather than assumed.
Precision Reduction

Precision may also be reduced where additional granularity produces no material improvement to the governed simulation inquiry.
This supports computational and methodological proportionality.
Simulation Resource Proportionality
SDPM recognizes that depth and precision consume resources.
These may include: computational capacity, energy, time, data, engineering effort, expert review, infrastructure, and financial resources.
The objective is not unlimited consumption.
The objective is:
sufficient governed simulation capability proportional to the purpose and consequence.
Resource-efficiency governance may be addressed by complementary OOF® architectures where applicable.
Depth & Precision Change
Material changes to: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, exclusions, Applicability Context, Simulation Object, consequence, operational environment, or intended downstream use
may require reassessment of Simulation Depth & Precision.
Depth & Precision Traceability
A reviewer should be capable of determining:
Why was this depth selected?
Why was this precision selected?
Which dimensions received greater or lower treatment?
Which limitations remained?
and:
Was the achieved depth and precision sufficient for the original Simulation Purpose?
Simulation Depth & Precision Record

A governed record may preserve: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, exclusions, Applicability Context, consequence context, material simulation dimensions, required depth by dimension, required precision by dimension, temporal granularity, spatial granularity, parameter precision, state resolution, interaction resolution, scenario depth, uncertainty-treatment depth, sensitivity requirements, depth limitations, precision limitations, sufficiency status, change triggers, and traceability.
Failure Conditions
SDPM governance failure may exist where: required Simulation Depth is undefined, required precision is undefined where materially necessary, depth does not correspond to Simulation Purpose, precision does not correspond to material simulation differences, high-consequence use relies upon unjustifiably shallow simulation, false numerical precision is presented, insufficient input precision is hidden, model complexity is substituted for methodological depth, computational scale is treated as evidence of adequacy, material failure conditions are omitted, material interactions are represented too coarsely, scenario depth is insufficient for the stated purpose, uncertainty treatment is materially insufficient, depth limitations are hidden, precision limitations are hidden, achieved depth is represented as stronger than it is, or simulation outputs are used for a purpose requiring materially greater depth or precision than was established.
Minimum Implementation Framework

1. Identify Material Depth & Precision Dimensions
Determine which structural, behavioral, temporal, spatial, parameter, interaction, scenario, failure, consequence, and uncertainty dimensions materially affect the Simulation Purpose. 2. Establish Required Simulation Depth
Define how extensively each material dimension must be examined. 3. Establish Required Simulation Precision
Define the granularity and resolution necessary to distinguish simulation-relevant differences. 4. Assess Sufficiency and Limitations
Determine whether the planned or achieved depth and precision are sufficient and explicitly preserve material limitations. 5. Preserve Traceability and Change Control
Maintain the Simulation Depth & Precision Record and reassess requirements when purpose, scope, applicability, consequence, or other material simulation conditions change.
Governance Outputs

SDPM may produce: Simulation Depth Requirement, Simulation Precision Requirement, Simulation Depth & Precision Record, Simulation Rigor Profile, Depth Dimension Map, Precision Dimension Map, Structural Depth Requirement, Behavioral Depth Requirement, Interaction Depth Requirement, Dependency Depth Requirement, Failure Depth Requirement, Consequence Depth Requirement, Scenario Depth Requirement, Temporal Depth Requirement, Spatial Precision Requirement, Temporal Precision Requirement, Parameter Precision Requirement, State Resolution Requirement, Interaction Resolution Requirement, Event Resolution Requirement, Output Precision Requirement, Uncertainty-Treatment Requirement, Sensitivity Depth Requirement, Minimum Sufficient Depth Record, Minimum Sufficient Precision Record, Depth Sufficiency Assessment, Precision Sufficiency Assessment, Depth–Precision Alignment Record, Depth Limitation Record, Precision Limitation Record, Depth Escalation Record, Precision Escalation Record, Depth Reduction Record, Precision Reduction Record, Simulation Rigor Change Record, and Simulation Depth & Precision Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Safety Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous industrial robot is simulated before deployment around human workers.
The Simulation Purpose is to examine collision avoidance and emergency stopping.

A coarse simulation is sufficient to examine general navigation efficiency but not the timing and distance relationships relevant to human safety. Application
SDPM identifies safety-critical dimensions requiring greater depth and precision:
human–robot interaction,
sensor-to-action latency,
stopping distance,
human movement variation,
failure response,
and:
emergency-state transitions.
The simulation may retain lower precision for dimensions that do not materially affect the safety inquiry. Result
Simulation resources are concentrated on the dimensions capable of changing the safety conclusion.
The simulation does not need maximum fidelity everywhere, but it must achieve sufficient depth and precision where the Simulation Purpose materially depends upon them. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft mission simulation is used first for early mission architecture exploration and later proposed as part of a higher-consequence mission-planning process.
The original simulation uses broad parameter ranges and relatively coarse temporal resolution. Application
SDPM identifies that the new Simulation Purpose requires increased depth in:
propulsion behavior,
orbital interactions,
failure conditions,
navigation dependencies,
and:
mission-phase transitions.
Temporal and parameter precision requirements are also increased where small deviations materially affect mission outcomes. Result

The original simulation is not treated as automatically sufficient merely because the Simulation Object remains the same.
The changed purpose creates a new Simulation Depth & Precision requirement proportionate to the new decision context.
Architectural Position
Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM) is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The complete SPSS progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Simulation Depth & Precision
Together, these five modules establish:
why the simulation exists,
what it must examine,
what it does not cover,
where and under which conditions it is intended to apply,
and:
how deeply and precisely the inquiry must operate.
SDPM ends the Simulation Purpose & Scope governance space.
The architecture can then proceed to the Reality Representation Standard (RRS), which governs which aspects of reality must be represented inside the simulation and at what abstraction, fidelity, resolution, and limitation.
SDPM does not govern general Validation Depth under VALIDOS®.
The distinction is:
VALIDOS® Validation Depth: How strong and extensive must the validation inquiry be?
SIMULOS® Simulation Depth: How deeply must the simulation inquiry examine the simulated problem?
SDPM also does not govern actual Operational Reality under ORA™, general integrity under INTEGROS®, or computational efficiency itself.

Its governed object is specifically:
the required depth and precision of the simulation inquiry.
Foundational Principle
A simulation should be neither shallower than its purpose permits nor more precise than its underlying simulation basis can legitimately support; depth and precision must remain proportional to what the simulation is intended to determine.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM) completes the Simulation Purpose & Scope governance layer by establishing how deeply and precisely a simulation inquiry must examine the Simulation Object within its governed purpose, scope, exclusions, applicability context, and consequence environment. Through differentiated depth and precision requirements, materiality, temporal and spatial granularity, parameter and state resolution, scenario and failure depth, uncertainty treatment, sufficiency assessment, anti-inflation rules, proportionality, change governance, and lifecycle traceability, SDPM prevents simulation complexity, computational scale, or apparent numerical precision from being mistaken for methodological adequacy. By requiring simulation rigor to remain proportional to the actual inquiry, SDPM establishes the final governance condition necessary before SIMULOS® proceeds from defining the simulation question to governing how reality itself is represented within the simulation.

OOF™ Simulation Data Representativeness Module (SDRM)
Simulation Data Representativeness Module (SDRM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Data Representativeness
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Data Representativeness
Canonical Definition
Simulation Data Representativeness Module (SDRM) defines the governance framework through which identified Simulation Inputs and datasets are assessed to determine whether they sufficiently represent the populations, environments, operating states, behaviors, distributions, conditions, variations, and other materially relevant characteristics of the reality that a defined simulation intends to represent.

SDRM establishes the representativeness layer of SIDS by determining whether available information is sufficiently aligned with the Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and intended simulation context before that information is relied upon as a representative basis for simulation activity.
Operational Role
SDRM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The preceding module, SIIM — Simulation Input Identification Module, establishes what the material Simulation Inputs are, where they originate, how they are classified, and what simulation roles they may influence.
SDRM asks:
Does the identified information sufficiently represent the reality, population, environment, state, behavior, distribution, or condition that the simulation intends it to represent?
The governed progression is:
Identified Simulation Input → Representation Target → Representativeness Dimensions → Coverage Assessment → Gap Identification → Materiality Assessment → Representativeness Status → Representativeness Conditions & Restrictions
SDRM therefore prevents identified data from being treated as representative merely because it is available, accurate within its original context, technically compatible, or large in volume.
Module Operational Space

SDRM governs: representation target identification, population representativeness, environmental representativeness, geographic representativeness, operational-state representativeness, behavioral representativeness, system-state representativeness, configuration representativeness, distributional representativeness, range representativeness, variation representativeness, rare-condition representation, subgroup representation, class representation, boundary-condition representation, sampling coverage, representation imbalance, representation gaps, overrepresentation, underrepresentation, proxy representation, cross-context applicability, representativeness materiality, representativeness uncertainty, representativeness restrictions, representativeness status, representativeness change, and representativeness traceability.
Module Function

SDRM exists to prevent: available data being assumed representative by default, large datasets being confused with representative datasets, one population being silently generalized to another, normal-operation data being generalized to failure conditions, one geographic environment being generalized globally, one system version being treated as representative of materially different versions, averages concealing relevant distributions, majority populations hiding minority or rare cases, proxy data being treated as direct representation, historical operating conditions being generalized to structurally different environments, missing representation being interpreted as absence of the represented phenomenon, and simulation outputs appearing broadly applicable when the input basis supports only a narrower context.
Representativeness
Simulation Data Representativeness is the degree to which an identified Simulation Input or Input Set sufficiently reflects the materially relevant characteristics of the reality segment it is intended to represent within a defined simulation.
Representativeness is not an intrinsic universal property of data.
It is relational.
Conceptually:
Data + Representation Target + Simulation Context → Representativeness Assessment Representation Target
A Representation Target defines what the input is expected to represent.

The target may be: population, environment, geographic region, operating state, system configuration, behavior, physical condition, temporal condition, distribution, event class, failure state, or another materially relevant reality segment.
Without a defined Representation Target, the statement:
“The data is representative.”
is incomplete.
Representativeness Is Purpose-Relative
SIMULOS® establishes:
No dataset is representative in the abstract; it is representative only relative to a defined simulation inquiry and representation target.
The same dataset may therefore be:
Representative
for one simulation,
and:
Non-Representative
for another. Representativeness ≠ Accuracy
Data may be highly accurate and still be unrepresentative.
For example:
a perfectly measured dataset from dry-road driving may accurately describe dry-road conditions while being unsuitable as the sole representative basis for snow-road simulation.
Therefore:
Accuracy asks whether the recorded information is correct.
Representativeness asks whether the information sufficiently reflects what the simulation needs to represent. Representativeness ≠ Volume
A billion observations from one narrow operating condition may provide less representative coverage than a much smaller dataset covering materially different relevant conditions.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Data volume cannot compensate for missing representation of materially relevant reality.
Population Representativeness

Where a simulation represents a population, SDRM determines whether materially relevant population characteristics are sufficiently represented.
Population may include: humans, vehicles, machines, organizations, infrastructure assets, biological entities, software systems, autonomous agents, devices, or other classes of objects.
Relevant dimensions may include: subgroup, capability, age, configuration, size, performance class, technical generation, behavioral profile, or another simulation-relevant distinction.
Subgroup Representation
A population-level dataset may conceal weak coverage of materially relevant subgroups.
SDRM therefore asks:
Which subgroups materially affect simulation behavior, and are they sufficiently represented?
Overall population coverage does not automatically establish subgroup coverage.
Environmental Representativeness
Environmental data should represent the environments within which simulated behavior is expected to be examined.
Relevant environmental dimensions may include: weather, terrain, temperature, lighting, infrastructure, electromagnetic conditions, network conditions, traffic density, physical obstacles, or other environmental factors.
Geographic Representativeness
Data obtained in one geographic region may not sufficiently represent another where material differences exist.
Possible differences include: infrastructure, climate, terrain, regulation, traffic behavior, architecture, population characteristics, or environmental conditions.

Geographic transfer should therefore remain explicit where material.
Operational-State Representativeness
Data from one operational state should not automatically represent another.
Relevant states may include:
Normal
Degraded
Failure
Emergency
Recovery
Maintenance
Startup
Shutdown
or another defined operating state.
A simulation intended to explore failures may require data that represents more than normal operation.
System-Version Representativeness
Simulation data may originate from a different version or configuration of the represented system.
SDRM asks whether differences between:
Data-Origin System
and:
Simulation-Represented System
are material to simulation behavior.
Behavioral Representativeness
Where behavior affects simulation outcomes, input data should sufficiently represent materially relevant behavioral variation.
This may include: human behavior, autonomous behavior, organizational behavior, market behavior, system response, interaction behavior, or adversarial behavior.
Distributional Representativeness
Representativeness includes more than averages.
Relevant characteristics may include: mean, variance, distribution shape, tails, correlations, clusters, multimodality, extremes, and conditional distributions.
Average ≠ Representative Distribution
SIMULOS® establishes:
A representative average does not establish a representative distribution.
Two populations may have the same average while producing materially different simulation behavior.

Range Representativeness
The observed range of an input should be compared with the range relevant to the simulation.
For example:
Training / observed temperature range: 0°C–30°C
Simulation scope: −30°C–50°C
The input basis does not fully represent the simulation range.
Variation Representativeness
Simulation behavior may depend upon variation rather than absolute values alone.
SDRM therefore evaluates whether material variation patterns are sufficiently represented.
This may include: rapid changes, cyclic changes, random variation, seasonal variation, load variation, behavioral variation, or environmental variation.
Rare-Condition Representation
Rare events may have low frequency but high simulation importance.
Examples include: catastrophic failures, extreme weather, unusual human behavior, collision conditions, cascading infrastructure failures, unusual system interactions, or low-frequency safety events.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Low frequency does not imply low representational importance.
Consequence-Weighted Representativeness
The required representation of a condition may increase where failure to represent it could materially affect a high-consequence simulation conclusion.
This does not mean every rare condition must always be included.
It means representativeness decisions should reflect the purpose and consequence of the simulation.
Boundary-Condition Representativeness
Simulation behavior may change near operational boundaries.

Data concentrated in the center of an operating range may therefore fail to represent behavior near: maximum load, minimum load, speed limits, thermal limits, stability limits, communication limits, control limits, or other material boundaries.
Representation Coverage
Representation Coverage describes how much of the materially relevant Representation Target is sufficiently represented by the available input basis.
Coverage may be assessed across multiple dimensions rather than reduced to one percentage.
Multidimensional Representativeness
A dataset may be representative along one dimension and weak along another.
For example:
Population Coverage — Strong
Geographic Coverage — Strong
Failure-State Coverage — Weak
Extreme-Weather Coverage — Missing
SDRM preserves these distinctions.
No Single-Score Requirement
SDRM does not require representativeness to be compressed into one numerical score.
A single score may hide material gaps.
Representativeness may instead be represented through: dimensional assessments, coverage maps, statuses, conditions, restrictions, and gap records.
Representation Gap
A Simulation Data Representativeness Gap exists where available information does not sufficiently represent a materially relevant part of the Representation Target.
Examples include: missing population, missing environment, missing state, missing behavior, missing distribution tail, missing failure condition, missing configuration, or insufficient range.
Representation Gap Classification

A gap may be classified as:
Non-Material
The gap is not expected to materially affect the defined simulation inquiry.
Material but Bounded
The gap matters but its effect can be sufficiently restricted or isolated.
Conditional
Simulation use remains possible only under explicit conditions.
Material and Unresolved
The gap materially weakens the simulation basis and has not been sufficiently addressed.
Representativeness Undetermined
Available information is insufficient to determine materiality or coverage. Underrepresentation
Underrepresentation occurs where a relevant condition exists in the target reality but appears insufficiently in the simulation input basis.
Underrepresentation can produce artificially weak exposure to that condition. Overrepresentation
Overrepresentation occurs where a condition appears disproportionately in the input basis relative to the Representation Target.
This may distort simulation behavior if the simulation interprets the data as naturally distributed.
Representation Imbalance
A dataset may contain all required classes while still representing them in proportions inconsistent with the intended simulation context.
SDRM therefore distinguishes:
Presence
from:
Representative Proportion.
Intentional Oversampling
Overrepresentation is not always a defect.
Rare or high-consequence conditions may intentionally be oversampled for testing.
Where intentional, the difference between:
Natural Representation
and:
Test Amplification
should remain explicit.

Proxy Representation
A Proxy Input represents a target indirectly because direct data is unavailable or impractical.
For example:
data from one machine type may be used as a proxy for another similar machine.
Proxy use may be legitimate.
SDRM requires the representational relationship to remain explicit. Proxy ≠ Target
SIMULOS® establishes:
Similarity between a proxy and a target does not establish representational equivalence.
Material differences must remain visible.
Cross-Context Transfer
Data may be transferred from one context to another.
Conceptually:
Source Context → Transfer Basis → Target Simulation Context
SDRM governs whether the transfer preserves sufficient representativeness.
Cross-Context Representativeness Conditions
Transfer may depend upon similarities in: population, environment, system configuration, behavior, operating range, physical properties, or causal structure.
Where differences matter, restrictions should follow the transferred data.
Synthetic Representation
Synthetic data may intentionally fill representativeness gaps.
For example:
real-world datasets may contain too few critical failure events.
Synthetic data may increase coverage.
SDRM asks:
Does the synthetic information sufficiently represent the intended condition?
Its synthetic origin remains governed under SIIM. Synthetic Coverage ≠ Real-World Frequency
Synthetic datasets may deliberately alter frequencies.
Therefore:
Synthetic Scenario Coverage
should not automatically be interpreted as:

Observed Real-World Distribution.
Representativeness and Simulation Assumptions
Simulation Assumptions may influence representativeness requirements.
For example:
if the simulation assumes operation only within a narrow environmental range, data outside that range may not be required.
If the scope expands, the representativeness requirement may change.
Representativeness and Reality Representation
RRS — Reality Representation Standard determines which aspects of reality the simulation must represent.
SDRM determines whether the input basis sufficiently represents those selected aspects.
The relationship is:
Selected Reality → Representation Requirement → Input Representation Target → Representativeness Assessment Representativeness and Scenario Design
SDRM does not determine which scenarios must be executed.
However, representativeness gaps may become important inputs to SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard.
For example:
a weakly represented rare failure may justify deliberate scenario coverage.
Representativeness Materiality
Not every representational difference matters.
Materiality depends upon whether the difference could reasonably affect: simulation behavior, simulation outputs, scenario conclusions, downstream validation, or operational reliance.
Materiality Assessment
A representativeness gap should be evaluated relative to:
Simulation Object
Simulation Purpose
Simulation Scope
Reality Representation
Simulation Assumptions
Model & Environment
and where relevant:

intended downstream reliance.
Representativeness Restriction
An input may remain usable despite limited representativeness if its use is explicitly restricted.
For example:
Representative only for dry-road daytime operation.
The restriction should propagate to downstream simulation interpretation.
Representativeness Condition
A Simulation Input may receive a condition such as:
Suitable only when ambient temperature remains between 0°C and 30°C.
Conditional representativeness should not become unconditional merely because simulation execution succeeds.
Representativeness Status
A material Simulation Input or Input Set may receive a status such as:
Representative
Conditionally Representative
Partially Representative
Non-Representative
or:
Representativeness Undetermined
The status is always relative to a defined Representation Target and simulation context.
No Universal Representative Status
SIMULOS® establishes:
Representative for one simulation does not mean representative for all simulations.
Representativeness status must therefore remain context-bound.
Input-Level vs Input-Set Representativeness
Individual inputs may be representative while the complete Input Set is not.
Conversely, several individually incomplete datasets may together provide sufficient representation.
SDRM therefore supports assessment at:
Individual Input Level
and:
Simulation Input Set Level.
Complementary Representation
Multiple datasets may complement one another.
For example:

Dataset A — Normal Operation Dataset B — Failure Operation Dataset C — Extreme Weather
may collectively provide stronger representation than any dataset alone.
Representativeness Conflict
Different datasets may imply materially different representations of the same target.
For example:
Dataset A: failure frequency 0.1%
Dataset B: failure frequency 2.5%
The conflict should remain visible rather than being silently averaged away.
Representation Basis
A Simulation Representation Basis records why an input or Input Set is considered sufficiently representative for a defined simulation context.
It may reference: target definition, coverage, gaps, materiality, restrictions, conditions, proxies, synthetic supplementation, and unresolved uncertainty.
Representativeness Traceability
SDRM establishes:
Simulation Input
↓
Representation Target
↓
Relevant Representation Dimensions
↓
Coverage
↓
Gap
↓
Materiality
↓
Representativeness Status
↓
Conditions / Restrictions
↓
Simulation Use
This enables downstream users to determine what the data actually supports.
Representativeness Change
Representativeness may change even when the dataset itself does not.
For example:
the Simulation Scope may expand.
A new environment may be introduced.
A new population may be added.
The represented system may change configuration.
The same data may therefore become less representative because the target changed.
Representativeness Reassessment Trigger

Reassessment may be required when there is material change in: Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model, Environment, target population, operational conditions, system configuration, or available input basis.
No Representativeness Inheritance Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Representativeness must not be inherited automatically from a previous simulation when the Representation Target or simulation context has materially changed.
No Availability-to-Representativeness Principle
Available data is not representative data by default.
No Size-to-Representativeness Principle
More data does not resolve a missing reality dimension if the additional data comes from the same unrepresentative condition.
No Majority-to-Whole Principle
Strong representation of the majority does not establish representation of every materially relevant subgroup or condition.
No Normal-to-Extreme Principle
Data representative of normal operation does not automatically represent degraded, failure, emergency, boundary, or extreme conditions.
No Proxy Equivalence Principle
Proxy data must not silently acquire the identity or representativeness status of the target it approximates.
No Successful-Execution Principle
A simulation running successfully with an input does not establish that the input was representative of the reality being simulated.
Representativeness Limitation Propagation
Material representativeness limitations should propagate downstream.
Conceptually:

Representativeness Gap → Scenario / Execution Limitation → Output Interpretation Limitation → Downstream Reliance Limitation
The relevant downstream Parent Standards govern those later stages.
SDRM ensures the original limitation remains visible.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify the Representation Target
Define what each material Simulation Input or Input Set is expected to represent. 2. Identify Material Representation Dimensions
Determine which dimensions matter, such as: population, environment, geography, operating state, behavior, configuration, distribution, range, variation, or rare conditions.
3. Assess Representation Coverage
Determine which materially relevant portions of the target are sufficiently represented. 4. Identify Representation Gaps
Record missing, weak, imbalanced, proxy-based, or uncertain representation. 5. Assess Gap Materiality
Determine whether each gap could materially affect the defined simulation inquiry. 6. Assess Distribution and Range
Determine whether averages, ranges, tails, variation, and dependencies are sufficiently represented where material. 7. Assess Rare and Boundary Conditions
Determine whether low-frequency or boundary conditions require representation because of their simulation relevance or consequence. 8. Govern Proxy and Cross-Context Use
Document the basis and limitations where information is transferred from another population, environment, configuration, or context. 9. Assess Synthetic Supplementation

Where synthetic information fills representation gaps, preserve its role and the limits of what it represents. 10. Establish Conditions and Restrictions
Bound simulation use where representativeness is incomplete but sufficiently manageable. 11. Assign Representativeness Status
Determine whether the input basis is: Representative, Conditionally Representative, Partially Representative, Non-Representative, or Representativeness Undetermined.
12. Preserve Representativeness Traceability
Maintain the relationship between target, coverage, gaps, materiality, status, restrictions, and simulation use.
Governance Outputs

SDRM may produce: Representation Target Record, Representation Dimension Map, Population Representativeness Assessment, Subgroup Representation Record, Environmental Representativeness Assessment, Geographic Representativeness Assessment, Operational-State Representativeness Assessment, System-Version Representativeness Assessment, Behavioral Representativeness Assessment, Distributional Representativeness Assessment, Range Representativeness Record, Variation Representativeness Record, Rare-Condition Representation Record, Boundary-Condition Representation Record, Representation Coverage Map, Representation Imbalance Record, Underrepresentation Record, Overrepresentation Record, Representation Gap Record, Representation Gap Materiality Assessment, Proxy Representation Record, Cross-Context Transfer Record, Synthetic Representation Record, Complementary Representation Record, Representativeness Conflict Record, Representativeness Condition Record, Representativeness Restriction Record, Representativeness Status, Simulation Representation Basis, Representativeness Reassessment Trigger, Representativeness Change Record, and Simulation Data Representativeness Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle simulation is intended to assess operation across: daytime and nighttime, dry and wet roads, urban and rural environments, normal traffic, emergency braking, and pedestrian interactions.

The available driving dataset contains millions of kilometers of data.
However, almost all observations come from:
daytime + dry roads + urban operation. Application
SDRM does not treat dataset size as proof of representativeness.
It identifies material gaps in: nighttime conditions, wet-road behavior, rural environments, emergency braking, and uncommon pedestrian interactions.
Result
The dataset receives:
Partially Representative
status for the declared simulation scope.
Its use may remain legitimate for defined urban dry-road scenarios while additional real or synthetic information is required for broader scenario coverage. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Landing Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft landing simulation relies upon atmospheric and terrain information derived primarily from previously observed regions.
The planned landing zone contains terrain and atmospheric conditions that are only partially represented by those observations. Application
SDRM establishes:
Observed Region ≠ Landing Target Region
and evaluates: terrain coverage, atmospheric ranges, geographic transfer, boundary conditions, and proxy assumptions.
Result
The available input basis may be classified:
Conditionally Representative
with explicit limitations requiring additional synthetic or model-derived coverage for materially underrepresented landing conditions.
Architectural Position
Simulation Data Representativeness is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).

The complete SIDS progression is:
Simulation Input Identification
↓
Simulation Data Representativeness
↓
Simulation Data Transformation
↓
Simulation Temporal Data
↓
Simulation Input Uncertainty
SIIM determines:
What information is entering the simulation?
SDRM determines:
What reality can that information legitimately represent?
The next module, SDTM — Simulation Data Transformation Module, governs what happens when that identified and representationally understood information must be transformed before simulation use.
Foundational Principle
Simulation data becomes representative only relative to a defined representation target, and no simulation may legitimately generalize its input basis beyond the populations, environments, states, behaviors, distributions, conditions, and boundaries that the available information can sufficiently represent.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Data Representativeness Module establishes the representational governance layer of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by determining whether identified Simulation Inputs and Input Sets sufficiently represent the populations, environments, geographic contexts, operating states, behaviors, configurations, distributions, ranges, variations, rare events, and boundary conditions required by a defined simulation inquiry. Through explicit Representation Targets, multidimensional coverage assessment, gap and materiality analysis, proxy governance, synthetic supplementation, conditional applicability, restrictions, reassessment triggers, and representativeness traceability, SDRM prevents data availability, volume, accuracy, technical compatibility, or successful execution from being mistaken for sufficient representation of the reality a simulation is intended to examine.
