Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Data Transformation
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Data Transformation
Canonical Definition
Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM) defines the governance framework through which identified Simulation Inputs may be cleaned, filtered, normalized, converted, aggregated, disaggregated, interpolated, extrapolated, encoded, imputed, derived, synthesized, resampled, aligned, or otherwise transformed before or during simulation use while preserving the traceability, meaning, limitations, uncertainty, provenance, and material consequences of those transformations.
SDTM establishes the transformation layer of SIDS by governing the transition:

Source Information → Transformation → Simulation-Usable Input
so that transformed information cannot silently acquire properties, precision, representativeness, certainty, or observational status that the transformation process did not legitimately establish.
Operational Role
SDTM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The preceding modules establish:
SIIM — What information is entering the simulation?
SDRM — What reality can that information legitimately represent?
SDTM asks:
What has been done to that information before the simulation consumes it, why was the transformation necessary, and what did the transformation materially change?
The governed progression is:
Identified Input → Transformation Need → Transformation Method → Transformation Execution → Transformed Input → Transformation Effect Assessment → Transformation Status → Simulation-Usable Input
Module Operational Space

SDTM governs: transformation identification, transformation purpose, transformation necessity, transformation methods, transformation rules, transformation parameters, data cleaning, filtering, normalization, standardization, unit conversion, format conversion, aggregation, disaggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, resampling, encoding, decoding, feature derivation, imputation, synthetic supplementation, dimensional transformation, temporal alignment transformation, spatial transformation, coordinate transformation, data fusion, data reduction, outlier treatment, missing-value treatment, transformation sequencing, transformation dependencies, transformation reproducibility, transformation reversibility where relevant, information loss, transformation-induced bias, transformation-induced uncertainty, transformation limitations, transformation validation references, transformation versioning, transformation change, transformed-input identity, and transformation traceability.
Module Function

SDTM exists to prevent: transformed information being treated as raw information, cleaning decisions disappearing from the simulation record, filtering silently removing material observations, normalization changing meaning without disclosure, unit conversion errors, aggregation hiding material variation, interpolation being represented as observation, extrapolation being represented as measured reality, imputed values appearing as recorded values, synthetic supplementation appearing as empirical data, transformations introducing hidden bias, precision being artificially increased, information loss becoming invisible, multiple transformation stages becoming unreconstructable, changed transformation logic being applied under an unchanged identity, and simulation outputs becoming impossible to trace back to the information basis from which they were produced.
Simulation Data Transformation
A Simulation Data Transformation is any governed operation that materially changes the: representation, structure, scale, format, resolution, composition, value, distribution, temporal organization, spatial organization, completeness, or interpretation
of information before or during simulation use.
Conceptually:
Input A → Transformation T → Input B
Input B may remain related to Input A, but it is not necessarily methodologically identical to it.
Transformation Need
Every material transformation should have an identifiable reason.

A Transformation Need may arise because: the simulation requires another unit, sources use incompatible formats, sampling frequencies differ, missing information must be treated, data contains technical noise, model interfaces require normalization, multiple sources must be aligned, resolution must change, derived variables are required, or information must be adapted to the simulation representation.
Transformation Purpose
The transformation purpose should explain:
Why must this information be changed before simulation use?
Examples include:
Compatibility
Alignment
Noise Reduction
Feature Construction
Missing-Value Treatment
Resolution Adjustment
Unit Harmonization
Data Fusion
or:
Simulation Interface Preparation Transformation Necessity
SDTM distinguishes:
Necessary Transformation
from:
Convenience Transformation.
A transformation may be technically convenient without being methodologically justified.
Where a transformation materially affects simulation behavior, convenience alone should not establish its legitimacy.
Transformation Method
A Transformation Method defines how the original information is converted into the transformed Simulation Input.
It may specify: operation, algorithm, formula, rule, threshold, parameter, model, software process, sequence, or another transformation mechanism.
Transformation Rule
A transformation should be sufficiently explicit that the relationship between:
Input Before Transformation
and:
Input After Transformation

can be understood and, where required, reconstructed.
Transformation Parameters
Material parameters should remain traceable.
For example:
a smoothing filter may require: window size, threshold, frequency, kernel, or another parameter.
Changing these parameters may materially change the resulting Simulation Input.
Data Cleaning
Cleaning may include: invalid-record removal, duplicate removal, formatting correction, impossible-value treatment, corrupted-record treatment, or consistency correction.
Cleaning should not become an invisible mechanism for removing inconvenient data. Cleaning ≠ Evidence Removal
SIMULOS® establishes:
Data should not be removed merely because it produces undesirable simulation behavior.
Where materially relevant records are excluded, the basis for exclusion should remain identifiable. Filtering
Filtering may remove: noise, frequencies, observations, events, values, or records.
SDTM requires material filtering logic to remain visible.
Filter Effect
A filter may improve usability while reducing information.
Therefore:
Cleaner Data ≠ More Complete Data
The effect of filtering should be assessed where material. Normalization
Normalization may transform values into a common range or representation.
For example:
0–100 → 0–1
The normalized value should remain connected to: original scale, transformation rule, and semantic meaning.
Standardization
Standardization may express values relative to a distribution.

The underlying basis should remain identifiable where the transformed values affect simulation interpretation.
Unit Conversion
Unit transformations must preserve the relationship:
Original Value + Original Unit → Conversion Rule → Converted Value + Target Unit
SDTM prevents converted values from becoming detached from their original measurement basis.
Format Conversion
Data may move between: structured formats, numerical representations, image formats, coordinate systems, encoding systems, categorical structures, or simulation-specific schemas.
Technical conversion should preserve materially relevant meaning.
Semantic Preservation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A transformation that preserves technical readability but changes material meaning is not semantically neutral. Aggregation
Aggregation combines multiple observations into a reduced representation.
Examples include:
second → minute
individual → group
sensor points → regional average
Aggregation may simplify simulation input while hiding: variation, extremes, sequences, correlations, or rare events.
Aggregation Loss
Where aggregation removes materially relevant information, the loss should remain visible.
For example:
an average temperature may hide short thermal spikes capable of affecting system failure. Disaggregation
Disaggregation converts aggregated information into a more granular representation.

Where the original information does not contain that granularity, disaggregated values may depend upon assumptions or models.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Disaggregation must not be represented as direct observation where the additional granularity was inferred. Interpolation
Interpolation estimates values between known observations.
Conceptually:
Observed A → Estimated Intermediate Value → Observed B
Interpolated values should remain distinguishable from direct observations where material. Extrapolation
Extrapolation estimates information beyond the observed range.
Because extrapolation extends beyond available observation, its methodological basis and limitations should remain visible.
No Extrapolation-as-Observation Principle
A value generated beyond the observed data range does not become observed reality merely because it is numerically precise. Resampling
Resampling changes the frequency, density, or structure of observations.
Examples include:
100 Hz → 10 Hz
or:
hourly → minute-level representation
Resampling may: remove information, introduce estimated information, alter signal behavior, or change temporal relationships.
Encoding
Information may be encoded into representations required by simulation systems.
For example:
Category → Numerical Vector
The encoded representation should remain traceable to the original semantic category.
Derived Input
A Derived Simulation Input is produced from one or more existing inputs.
Conceptually:
Input A + Input B + Rule → Derived Input C

The derivation relationship should remain preserved. Derived ≠ Observed
SIMULOS® establishes:
A calculated value must not silently acquire the status of a directly observed value.
Feature Derivation
Simulation models may require derived features.
Examples include: velocity from position changes, acceleration from velocity, risk indicator from multiple variables, density from count and area, or another constructed feature.
The derivation method should remain traceable where material.
Missing-Value Treatment
Missing information may be treated through: exclusion, substitution, interpolation, imputation, default value, synthetic replacement, or another governed method.
SDTM requires the treatment to remain explicit. Missing ≠ Zero
SIMULOS® establishes:
Absence of information must not automatically become a zero-valued observation. Imputation
Imputation replaces missing information with an estimated value.
An imputed value should remain identifiable as:
Imputed
rather than:
Observed
or:
Measured.
Imputation Basis
The basis may include: statistical estimate, neighboring observations, historical values, model output, population average, or another method.
The selected basis may materially influence simulation behavior.
Default Values
A simulation may technically require a value where none is available.
A default value may be used where methodologically justified.
The default should remain identifiable as a default rather than being silently treated as source data.

Synthetic Supplementation
Synthetic information may be introduced during transformation to supplement missing or weak data.
SDTM governs the transformation process that introduces it.
SIIM preserves its synthetic identity.
SDRM governs what reality it can legitimately represent.
Outlier Treatment
Outliers may be: retained, excluded, capped, transformed, separately modeled, or investigated.
Outlier treatment should depend upon the simulation purpose and data basis. Outlier ≠ Error
SIMULOS® establishes:
An unusual observation is not automatically an invalid observation.
Rare values may represent precisely the conditions a simulation needs to examine.
Data Fusion
Multiple information sources may be combined into one Simulation Input.
Conceptually:
Source A + Source B + Fusion Method → Fused Input
The fusion process should preserve materially relevant source relationships and transformation logic. Fusion ≠ Independent Confirmation
Two sources combined into one input do not necessarily constitute independent evidence.
Their dependencies may remain relevant.
Spatial Transformation
Spatial information may require: coordinate conversion, map projection, spatial aggregation, interpolation, alignment, or resolution change.
Material spatial transformation should remain traceable where it can influence simulated relationships.
Coordinate Transformation
Coordinate-system changes must preserve the applicable reference system and transformation basis.

Errors in coordinate conversion can produce apparently valid but physically incorrect simulation inputs.
Dimensional Transformation
Information may be reduced or expanded across dimensions.
For example:
3D Reality → 2D Representation
or:
Multiple Variables → Composite Index
Such transformations may intentionally simplify reality.
The simplification should remain connected to the simulation's Reality Representation under RRS.
Transformation Sequence
Simulation data may undergo multiple transformations.
For example:
Raw Sensor Data
↓
Cleaning
↓
Filtering
↓
Unit Conversion
↓
Resampling
↓
Normalization
↓
Simulation Input
SDTM requires material sequence to remain reconstructable.
Transformation Order Matters
Transformations may not be commutative.
Conceptually:
Filter → Aggregate
may produce a different result from:
Aggregate → Filter
Where order materially affects the resulting input, transformation sequence becomes a governed property.
Transformation Dependency
One transformation may depend upon the output of another.
These dependencies should remain visible where they affect reproducibility or interpretation.
Transformation Chain
A Simulation Transformation Chain records the material progression:
Original Input → T1 → Intermediate Input → T2 → Intermediate Input → T3 → Simulation-Usable Input Transformation Identity
Each material transformation may receive an identifiable reference.
For example:
SDT-0042

This allows simulation records to reference the exact transformation logic used.
Transformation Version
Transformation logic may change.
For example:
Filter v1
may become:
Filter v2
A simulation executed under v1 should remain distinguishable from one executed under v2.
No Silent Transformation Update Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Materially changing transformation logic must not silently rewrite the transformation basis of previous simulation executions.
Transformation Reproducibility
Where required by the simulation purpose, a transformation should be sufficiently documented to allow an authorized independent implementation to reproduce the transformed input from the same original basis.
Reproducibility may require: method, parameters, software version, transformation sequence, source input version, and relevant execution conditions.
Transformation Reversibility
Not every transformation is reversible.
For example:
aggregation may permanently discard detail.
SDTM therefore distinguishes:
Reproducibility
from:
Reversibility.
A transformation may be reproducible while information loss makes reversal impossible.
Information Loss
Transformation may remove information.
Loss may be:
Intentional
Incidental
Necessary
or:
Unrecognized
SDTM requires material information loss to remain visible.
Transformation Gain
Some transformations create additional information representations.
For example:
interpolation may create additional values.
But:
More values ≠ More observations.

Generated resolution should not be confused with additional empirical evidence.
Precision Inflation
Transformation may produce numerically precise outputs from imprecise inputs.
For example:
an estimated value may mathematically produce:
17.384729
This numerical precision does not establish equivalent informational certainty.
No Precision Inflation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Transformation must not create an appearance of certainty or observational precision unsupported by the underlying information basis.
Transformation-Induced Bias
Transformation logic may systematically alter the information basis.
Examples include: selective filtering, biased imputation, asymmetric clipping, population-dependent normalization, or model-based reconstruction.
Material transformation-induced bias should be identified and carried forward.
Transformation-Induced Uncertainty
A transformation may introduce additional uncertainty.
For example: interpolation uncertainty, extrapolation uncertainty, imputation uncertainty, fusion uncertainty, conversion uncertainty, or model-derived uncertainty.
The subsequent SIUM — Simulation Input Uncertainty Module governs the consolidated input uncertainty.
SDTM identifies transformation-induced contributions to that uncertainty.
Transformation Effect Assessment

After transformation, the resulting input should be assessed for material changes in: meaning, range, distribution, resolution, completeness, representativeness, uncertainty, and simulation influence.
Representativeness Reassessment
Transformation may change representativeness.
For example:
aggressive filtering may remove rare conditions that SDRM previously considered represented.
Where transformation materially affects representation:
SDRM reassessment may be required.
Transformation Cannot Launder Weak Input
SIMULOS® establishes:
Transformation does not automatically cure an unrepresentative, uncertain, ambiguous, or otherwise limited input basis.
A weak source input may remain weak after sophisticated processing.
Transformation Limitation
A Transformation Limitation identifies a material restriction introduced or preserved by transformation.
Examples include: lost high-frequency behavior, inferred missing values, reduced spatial resolution, extrapolation beyond observed range, or uncertain source alignment.
Transformation Condition
A transformed input may be suitable only under explicit conditions.
For example:
Interpolated values suitable only where gaps do not exceed 5 seconds.
The condition should remain attached to downstream simulation use.
Transformation Status
A material transformation may receive a status such as:
Transformation Accepted
Conditionally Accepted
Transformation Restricted
Transformation Rejected
or:
Transformation Undetermined

The status applies to the transformation's suitability for the defined simulation use.
Transformed Input Status
The resulting Simulation Input may be classified as:
Simulation-Usable
Conditionally Simulation-Usable
Restricted
Not Simulation-Usable
or:
Suitability Undetermined
This status does not replace subsequent temporal or uncertainty governance.
Transformation Change
A material change may occur in: transformation method, parameters, software, source mapping, sequence, threshold, imputation rule, fusion logic, or another transformation property.
Material changes should trigger reassessment of affected transformed inputs.
Transformation Impact Propagation
Where transformation materially affects downstream simulation use, the effect should propagate.
Conceptually:
Transformation Change → Transformed Input Change → Scenario / Execution Effect → Output Effect → Reliance Effect
The later SIMULOS® Parent Standards govern those downstream consequences.
Point-in-Time Transformation Reconstruction
SDTM supports questions such as:
Which transformation was used for this execution?
Which parameters were active?
Which source input version entered it?
Which values were imputed?
Which observations were removed?
Which transformations introduced additional uncertainty?

Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Material Transformations
Determine which input changes can materially affect simulation behavior or interpretation. 2. Establish Transformation Purpose
Record why each material transformation is required. 3. Define Transformation Method
Specify the applicable: operation, rule, algorithm, formula, parameters, or processing method.
4. Preserve Source Input Identity
Bind every material transformation to the exact input version from which it originates. 5. Execute and Record the Transformation
Preserve the material transformation sequence and resulting input state. 6. Identify Generated, Removed, or Modified Information
Determine whether the transformation: removes information, generates inferred information, changes resolution, changes distribution, changes meaning, or changes simulation influence.
7. Assess Transformation Effects
Evaluate material effects upon: representativeness, uncertainty, completeness, precision, semantics, and simulation applicability.
8. Govern Missing Values, Outliers, and Synthetic Supplementation
Ensure treatment remains explicit and traceable. 9. Assess Transformation Limitations
Identify information loss, extrapolation, imputation, bias, uncertainty, or other material restrictions. 10. Assign Transformation Status
Determine whether the transformation is: Accepted, Conditionally Accepted, Restricted, Rejected, or Undetermined.

11. Establish Transformed Input Status
Determine whether the resulting input may proceed to subsequent SIDS governance. 12. Preserve Transformation Traceability
Maintain the complete relationship:
Source Input → Transformation → Transformed Input → Transformation Effect → Simulation Use

Foundational Principle
A transformed Simulation Input remains legitimate only when the path from its original information basis to its simulation-usable form remains sufficiently identifiable, justified, reproducible, limitation-aware, and traceable, without allowing transformation to manufacture unsupported meaning, representativeness, observational status, precision, or certainty.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Data Transformation Module establishes the transformation governance layer of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing how identified Simulation Inputs are cleaned, filtered, normalized, converted, aggregated, interpolated, extrapolated, resampled, encoded, derived, imputed, fused, supplemented, aligned, or otherwise transformed for simulation use. Through explicit transformation purpose, method, parameters, sequencing, source binding, versioning, information-loss assessment, generated-information distinction, bias and uncertainty identification, representativeness reassessment, conditions, limitations, status, and complete transformation traceability, SDTM ensures that simulation-ready information remains methodologically connected to the information from which it originated and that preprocessing cannot silently manufacture properties the underlying data never possessed.

Simulation Execution Control
Canonical Definition
Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM) defines the governance framework through which an instantiated Simulation Execution is initiated, progressed, constrained, synchronized, monitored, intervened in where permitted, paused, resumed, terminated, and completed while preserving the execution conditions necessary to determine what actually occurred during the run.
SECM establishes the active-control layer of Simulation Execution.
Its purpose is to ensure that a simulation does not become an uncontrolled computational process once execution begins and that material runtime changes cannot occur without remaining visible within the execution record.
Operational Role

SECM is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES).
The preceding module:
SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module
establishes:
What exact simulation configuration has been instantiated for execution?
SECM asks:
How must that instantiated simulation remain governed while it is actually running?
The governed progression is:
Instantiated Simulation → Execution Authorization → Execution Initiation → Runtime Control → State Monitoring → Intervention / Deviation Handling → Pause / Resume / Termination → Execution Completion Status
Module Operational Space
SECM governs: execution authorization, execution initiation, execution start conditions, runtime control, execution sequencing, control-state management, runtime constraints, temporal control, synchronization control, resource control, execution-state transitions, intervention permissions, intervention execution, runtime modification, runtime deviation, anomaly response, pause, resume, restart, cancellation, termination, emergency termination, timeout, dependency failure response, execution boundary enforcement, control loss, control recovery, execution completion, and execution-control traceability.
Execution Authorization
A Simulation Execution may require an explicit authorization before it begins.

Authorization may define: who or what may initiate execution, which Scenario may run, which configuration may be used, which resources may be consumed, which interventions are permitted, which external connections may be active, which control limits apply, and who or what may terminate the run.
Execution Authorization ≠ Simulation Validity
Authorization means the simulation is permitted to run under defined conditions.
It does not establish that: the model is correct, the scenario is sufficient, the output will be valid, or the simulated system is safe.
Execution Initiation
Execution Initiation marks the transition:
Instantiated
↓
Running
A governed initiation may require that: the intended Simulation Instance exists, required dependencies are available, applicable inputs are loaded, runtime conditions are satisfied, control mechanisms are active, and authorization is confirmed.
Start Condition
A Simulation Start Condition establishes the requirements that must exist before execution may begin.
Possible start conditions may include: environment ready, input set available, scenario loaded, parameter configuration applied, required services active, simulation clock synchronized, required hardware connected, required participant ready, or execution authority confirmed.
No Unverified Start Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation should not be assumed to have started under its intended configuration merely because the execution engine reports that a run began.

Material start conditions should be verifiable where necessary.
Execution State
A Simulation Execution should maintain an identifiable current state.
Possible states may include:
Prepared
Initialized
Running
Paused
Waiting
Degraded
Interrupted
Restarting
Terminating
Completed
Failed
or:
Execution State Unknown
depending upon implementation.
Execution State Transition
Material changes between execution states should remain identifiable.
Conceptually:
Initialized → Running → Paused → Running → Completed
or:
Running → Degraded → Failed
The execution history should preserve the actual path.
Runtime Control
Runtime Control governs how the active Simulation Execution remains aligned with the conditions under which it was instantiated.
This may include: state progression, event sequencing, clock progression, resource allocation, scenario progression, environmental updates, external inputs, actor activation, dependency use, and termination criteria.
Execution Control ≠ Outcome Control
SIMULOS® establishes:
Execution Control must govern how the simulation runs, not manipulate the simulation merely to force a preferred output.
Unexpected results should remain observable.
Unfavorable system behavior must not become a reason to silently alter the run.
Runtime Constraint
A Runtime Constraint defines a condition that must remain satisfied during execution.

Examples may include: allowed resource consumption, allowed scenario bounds, permitted external interfaces, maximum execution duration, parameter locks, environmental limits, intervention permissions, or synchronization requirements.
Constraint Violation
A Constraint Violation occurs when actual execution moves outside a materially relevant runtime condition.
The response may include:
Continue with Record
Pause
Restrict
Reconfigure
Restart
Terminate
or:
Escalate
depending upon the Simulation Purpose.
Execution Boundary
The Execution Boundary defines what the active simulation is permitted to do.
It may govern: accessible resources, connected systems, external actions, scenario range, execution duration, control authority, or other material runtime limits.
Boundary Enforcement
A simulation should not silently operate outside the execution boundary merely because the underlying technology permits it.
Execution Sequence
Some simulations require governed sequencing.
For example:
Initialize
↓
Activate Environment
↓
Activate Agents
↓
Introduce Scenario Event
↓
Observe Response
↓
Terminate
Changing sequence may materially change the simulation.
SECM therefore governs sequence where order matters.
No Sequence Substitution Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A materially different execution sequence should not be represented as the same controlled execution merely because the same components were eventually activated.
Temporal Control

Simulation execution may rely upon: simulation time, wall-clock time, event time, mission time, synchronized system time, or accelerated / slowed simulation time.
SECM governs the execution-control side of these timing conditions.
Clock Control
Where the simulation clock materially affects behavior, relevant clock state should remain controlled.
This may include: clock start, clock rate, time acceleration, time pause, synchronization, reset, and clock discontinuities.
Synchronization Control
Distributed simulations may require multiple: agents, models, services, hardware systems, sensors, or environments
to remain synchronized.
Synchronization failure may create behavior that reflects infrastructure error rather than the intended scenario.
Synchronization Deviation
A material synchronization deviation should remain identifiable.
Possible treatment may include: tolerance-based continuation, pause, resynchronization, partial restart, run invalidation, or termination.
Resource Control
Execution may require controlled access to: compute, memory, storage, network bandwidth, energy, hardware, external services, or human participants.
Resource constraints may materially alter simulation behavior.
Resource Exhaustion
A simulation may terminate or degrade because computational or infrastructural resources are exhausted.
This should remain distinguishable from:
failure of the simulated system itself.
No Infrastructure-Failure-as-System-Failure Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Failure of the simulation infrastructure must not automatically be interpreted as failure of the Simulation Object.
Dependency Control
Simulation execution may depend upon: APIs, external models, databases, hardware, external services, or distributed infrastructure.
Dependency state should remain visible where changes can materially affect execution.
Dependency Failure
Possible responses to dependency failure may include:
Fallback
Pause
Substitute
Continue Degraded
Restart
or:
Terminate.
The selected response should remain traceable.
Runtime Intervention
A Runtime Intervention is a deliberate action that materially changes an active Simulation Execution.
Examples include: parameter modification, scenario injection, human command, failure injection, environment modification, control transfer, agent override, pause, or forced state transition.
Intervention Authority
Where interventions are allowed, SECM should identify who or what may perform them.
Possible intervention authorities include:
Human Operator
Simulation Controller
Automated Control Logic
AI Controller
Autonomous Simulation Agent
or another governed execution actor.
No Invisible Intervention Principle
A material runtime intervention must remain visible in the execution history.
Planned Intervention
Some interventions are part of Scenario Design.
Examples include: injecting a failure at time T, reducing communication availability, triggering handover, or introducing an environmental event.

Such interventions remain governed actions even where planned.
Unplanned Intervention
An intervention may occur unexpectedly because: simulation instability develops, infrastructure fails, safety boundaries are crossed, an operator acts, or an execution anomaly requires control.
Unplanned interventions should be distinguished from planned scenario events.
Runtime Modification
A simulation may permit certain configuration changes during execution.
Material modifications may include: parameter adjustment, model switching, environment changes, agent activation, dependency replacement, or runtime configuration change.
Where permitted, the modification should remain identifiable.
No Silent Configuration Mutation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A materially changed runtime configuration must not continue to be represented as if the original execution configuration remained unchanged.
Execution Deviation
An Execution Deviation is a material difference between:
intended controlled execution
and:
actual runtime behavior or condition.
Possible deviations include: wrong sequence, unexpected delay, missing dependency, incorrect configuration, intervention, resource exhaustion, synchronization failure, runtime exception, timing deviation, or control-state mismatch.
Deviation Classification
A deviation may be classified as:
Minor
Material
Critical
Execution-Limiting
Execution-Invalidating
or:
Undetermined
depending upon the simulation context. Deviation ≠ Automatic Failure

A deviation does not necessarily invalidate a simulation.
The module requires the deviation to remain explicit so its consequence can later be assessed.
Execution Anomaly
An Execution Anomaly is an unexpected runtime event or state that differs materially from expected execution behavior.
An anomaly may originate from: the Simulation Object, the Simulation Model, the environment, infrastructure, external dependencies, configuration, or control logic.
SECM does not determine the cause automatically.
It ensures the event remains governable.
Control Response
A material anomaly may trigger a controlled response such as:
Observe
Continue
Restrict
Pause
Escalate
Recover
Restart
or:
Terminate. Pause
A Simulation Execution may enter a controlled Paused State.
Pause should preserve sufficient execution state to determine: when the pause occurred, why it occurred, what state existed, what changed while paused, and whether resume remains comparable to uninterrupted execution.
Pause ≠ No Change
The simulation may be paused while: external services continue changing, hardware state changes, humans act, external clocks advance, or dependencies change.
Therefore the assumption that a paused simulation preserves identical execution conditions may require verification. Resume
Resume returns a paused Simulation Execution to active execution.
Material changes occurring during the pause should remain visible. Restart

A Restart begins execution again after: interruption, failure, modification, or control decision.
Restart may occur:
from initial state
or:
from checkpoint.
These are materially different execution paths. Checkpoint
A simulation may preserve a checkpoint from which execution can later resume.
A checkpoint should remain connected to: Execution ID, execution state, simulation clock, configuration, relevant memory/state, environment, and applicable dependencies.
Checkpoint ≠ Original Execution
Restart from checkpoint may preserve continuity, but it should not automatically be represented as identical to uninterrupted execution.
Execution Interruption
An interruption occurs when active execution stops before intended completion.
Possible causes include: infrastructure failure, external dependency failure, operator intervention, resource exhaustion, software failure, or emergency control.
Interruption Status
An interrupted run may become:
Resumable
Restart Required
Terminated
Failed
or:
Status Undetermined.
Execution Termination
Termination deliberately ends an execution.
Termination may be:
Normal
Conditional
Early
Failure-Based
Safety-Based
Resource-Based
Operator-Initiated
Automatically Triggered
or:
Emergency
where relevant.
Termination Criteria
Termination criteria should be established where materially relevant.

Examples include: scenario complete, target state reached, maximum duration reached, failure state reached, invalid simulation region entered, resource limit exceeded, safety boundary crossed, or information objective achieved.
Early Termination
An execution may terminate before planned completion because the simulation has already reached a state that satisfies or invalidates the execution purpose.
Early termination should remain explicit.
Emergency Termination
Emergency Termination may be required when continuing execution could: damage hardware, affect external systems, violate resource constraints, create unsafe human interaction, or move beyond authorized simulation boundaries.
Timeout
A Timeout occurs when execution exceeds a predefined temporal or processing condition.
Timeout should remain distinguishable from: simulated-system failure, execution infrastructure failure, or intentional termination.
Execution Completion
Execution Completion occurs when the Simulation Execution reaches an accepted terminal state.
Completion may be:
Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
Failed
or:
Completion Undetermined. Completion ≠ Positive Result
SIMULOS® establishes:
A fully completed simulation may show complete system failure, while an incomplete simulation may appear to show a positive result.
Execution completion and simulation outcome must remain distinct.
Control Loss

A Simulation Execution Control Loss occurs where the execution can no longer be governed according to its required runtime controls.
Examples include: inability to pause, inability to terminate, lost synchronization, uncontrolled parameter change, uncontrolled external interaction, controller failure, or execution-state uncertainty.
Control Loss Response
Where control loss is material, the execution may require:
Containment
Emergency Termination
Isolation
Restart
or:
Execution Invalidity Assessment.
Control Recovery
Where control is restored, the execution should preserve: when control was lost, how long control was absent, what occurred during the gap, how control was recovered, and whether execution continuity remains acceptable.
Autonomous Execution Control
Simulation campaigns may increasingly be controlled by autonomous orchestration systems.
An autonomous controller may: launch runs, select scenarios, modify configurations, detect anomalies, stop executions, allocate resources, or generate follow-up runs.
SECM remains applicable.
The controller's execution authority and actions should remain governable.
No Autonomous Control Opacity Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Autonomous execution control must not remove visibility into why materially relevant runtime actions occurred.
Adaptive Execution Control
Some simulations adapt during execution.
The simulation may:
Observe Behavior
↓
Change Runtime Condition
↓
Continue Execution
↓
Observe New Behavior
This may be legitimate.

However, the adaptive path should remain explicit.
Execution-Control Traceability
SECM should support reconstruction of:
Who / What Controlled the Run
↓
Which Controls Applied
↓
What Execution State Existed
↓
What Interventions Occurred
↓
What Deviations Occurred
↓
How the Run Ended Simulation Campaign Control
For large simulation campaigns, execution control may occur at two levels:
Campaign-Level Control
and:
Run-Level Control.
Campaign-level rules may establish: permitted scenarios, run counts, resource allocations, stopping criteria, failure handling, retry logic, and exception treatment.
Individual runs may still require their own execution-state history.
Retry Governance
Automated campaigns may retry failed runs.
A retry should remain distinguishable from the original execution.
Conceptually:
Run 001 — Failed
↓
Retry 001A
Rather than:
Run 001 — Successful
where the first failure disappears.
No Failure Erasure by Retry Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A successful retry must not erase the existence of the execution failure that triggered it.
Execution Selection Bias
Large campaigns may automatically discard runs classified as: failed, anomalous, incomplete, or outlying.
SECM requires material execution-control exclusions to remain visible.
No Success-Only Preservation Principle
Execution governance must not preserve only completed or desirable runs where failed, interrupted, anomalous, or deviating executions are materially relevant to understanding the simulation.

Space and Mission Execution Control
Mission simulations may include: spacecraft dynamics, communication delay, autonomous response, hardware-in-the-loop systems, ground-control simulation, navigation systems, power simulation, and environmental models.
A runtime deviation may originate from:
the simulated spacecraft
or:
the simulation infrastructure.
SECM preserves this distinction.
A mission run showing loss of navigation cannot automatically be interpreted as spacecraft navigation failure if synchronization loss inside the simulator caused the event.
Autonomous Systems
For autonomous systems, execution control may need to preserve: autonomy mode, human override, permission state, fallback state, communication state, external-agent interaction, and runtime authority transitions.
This becomes particularly important where the simulation itself allows dynamic changes in authority.
Industrial Systems
A digital-twin or industrial simulation may interact with: real hardware, production data, live sensor feeds, or control systems.
SECM provides the control layer needed to prevent simulation execution from becoming an unbounded interaction with operational infrastructure.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Execution Authorization
Identify who or what may initiate, control, intervene in, and terminate the Simulation Execution. 2. Verify Start Conditions

Confirm the materially required configuration, dependencies, controls, and runtime conditions before execution begins. 3. Initiate the Execution
Create the active execution state and preserve the execution start record. 4. Maintain Runtime Control
Govern: sequence, timing, synchronization, resources, dependencies, state transitions, and applicable runtime boundaries.
5. Govern Interventions
Record and classify planned and unplanned runtime interventions. 6. Govern Deviations and Anomalies
Identify material differences between intended and actual execution. 7. Govern Pause, Resume, Restart, and Retry
Preserve execution continuity and distinguish interrupted or repeated execution paths. 8. Govern Termination
Apply explicit termination criteria and preserve the reason and state at termination. 9. Determine Completion Status
Classify execution as: Complete, Conditionally Complete, Partially Complete, Incomplete, Failed, or Undetermined.
10. Preserve Execution-Control Traceability
Maintain the runtime control history required for subsequent observation, repetition, and execution documentation.

Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Campaign
Scenario
A large autonomous-driving simulation campaign runs thousands of scenarios.
One execution shows unexpected failure of collision avoidance.
The run was automatically retried and the second execution completed successfully. Application
SECM preserves:
Original Run — Failure

Runtime Conditions
Execution Deviation
Retry Trigger
Retry Execution
Differences Between Runs
rather than replacing the failed run with the successful retry. Result
Engineers can determine whether the original behavior came from: the autonomous system, simulation infrastructure, timing, synchronization, runtime configuration, or another execution condition.
The failed execution remains part of the governed simulation history. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft autonomy simulation is connected to flight-like hardware and communication subsystems.
During an autonomous recovery scenario, synchronization between the simulation environment and hardware begins to drift. Application
SECM identifies a material Synchronization Deviation.
Execution enters:
Paused
rather than silently continuing.
The synchronization state is restored and the execution is resumed from an identified checkpoint. Result
The mission team can distinguish:
behavior of the spacecraft autonomy logic
from:
behavior produced by simulation-infrastructure timing error.
The resumed execution remains traceable to the synchronization deviation and checkpoint rather than being represented as an uninterrupted nominal run.

The complete SES progression is:
Simulation Instantiation
↓
Simulation Execution Control
↓

Simulation Observation
↓
Simulation Repetition
↓

What exactly has been instantiated?

How does that instantiated simulation remain controlled while running?
The next module, SOM — Simulation Observation Module, governs what materially relevant states, events, transitions, anomalies, and runtime behavior must be observed and preserved during execution.
Foundational Principle
A simulation execution remains governable only while the conditions controlling how it starts, progresses, changes, pauses, resumes, deviates, and terminates remain explicit and traceable.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Execution Control Module establishes the runtime governance layer of the Simulation Execution Standard by governing authorization, start conditions, execution states, sequencing, timing, synchronization, resource and dependency control, interventions, deviations, anomalies, pause and resume, restart, retry, termination, control loss, recovery, and completion. SECM ensures that active simulation execution cannot silently diverge from its instantiated basis, that infrastructure failures remain distinguishable from simulated-system failures, that retries do not erase failed runs, and that every materially relevant runtime control event remains reconstructable as part of the governed Simulation Execution history.

Simulation Execution Documentation
Canonical Definition
Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM) defines the governance framework through which materially relevant information about Simulation Execution is captured, structured, linked, preserved, version-bounded, and made sufficiently reconstructable to establish what was actually executed, under which configuration and conditions, what occurred during execution, which interventions and deviations arose, how repetitions were related, whether execution was completed, and which Simulation Outputs originated from that execution.

SEDM converts distributed execution information into a governed:
Simulation Execution Record.
Its purpose is not to require documentation for documentation's sake.
Its purpose is to ensure that material Simulation Outputs and downstream claims do not become detached from the execution history required to understand how they were produced.
Operational Role
SEDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES).
The preceding modules establish:
SIM — What exact simulation instance was instantiated?
SECM — How was active execution controlled?
SOM — What materially relevant events and behaviors occurred during execution?
SRPM — How were executions repeated, related, varied, and compared?
SEDM asks:
Can the complete materially relevant execution history now be reconstructed sufficiently to determine what actually ran, what occurred, how the execution changed, and which outputs it produced?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Instantiation Record
↓
Execution Control Record
↓
Simulation Observation Record
↓
Simulation Repetition Record
↓
Execution Documentation Assembly
↓
Execution Traceability
↓
Execution Provenance
↓
Execution Lineage
↓
Execution Completeness Documentation
↓
Execution-to-Output Linkage
↓
Governed Simulation Execution Record
Module Operational Space

SEDM governs: execution documentation requirements, Execution Record identity, documentation scope, documentation granularity, documentation timing, execution metadata, configuration documentation, model-version documentation, environment-version documentation, scenario documentation, input documentation, parameter documentation, initialization documentation, authorization documentation, execution-state documentation, runtime-condition documentation, control-action documentation, intervention documentation, deviation documentation, observation documentation, anomaly documentation, interruption documentation, restart documentation, termination documentation, failure documentation, completion documentation, repetition documentation, randomization documentation, seed documentation where applicable, execution provenance, execution lineage, campaign documentation, run-to-campaign relationships, documentation completeness, documentation gaps, documentation uncertainty, execution reconstruction, point-in-time reconstruction, execution-to-output traceability, record retention, record continuity, and formation of the Governed Simulation Execution Record.
Module Function

SEDM exists to prevent: simulation outputs with no identifiable originating execution, intended configurations being substituted for actual executed configurations, model versions becoming detached from execution records, undocumented runtime interventions, execution deviations disappearing after completion, failed and interrupted runs being removed from history, observations losing their execution context, repetitions becoming indistinguishable, seeds or stochastic conditions becoming untraceable, simulation campaigns becoming collections of anonymous output files, later reconstruction depending upon individual memory, partial documentation being represented as complete documentation, and downstream validation or audit being forced to infer what happened during execution.
Simulation Execution Record
A Simulation Execution Record is the governed documentation structure representing a specific Simulation Execution and its materially relevant execution history.
Conceptually:
Execution Identity Instantiated Configuration Execution Conditions Execution Controls Observed Events Interventions Deviations Execution State History Repetition Context Completion Status Output Linkage
=
Governed Simulation Execution Record Execution Record Identity
Every materially relevant Execution Record should be bound to an identifiable Simulation Execution.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID → Simulation Execution Record

The record should not exist merely as an anonymous log file or output directory.
Documentation Scope
Documentation requirements should correspond to the Simulation Purpose, consequence, complexity, execution environment, and downstream reliance.
SEDM does not require every technical event to be permanently recorded.
It requires:
materially relevant execution information to remain sufficiently available for the intended governance purpose.
Documentation Granularity
Documentation may operate at different levels:
Run Level
Episode Level
Batch Level
Scenario Level
Campaign Level
or another defined execution unit.
Large-scale simulation may combine these levels.
Run-Level Documentation
Run-level documentation may preserve: Execution ID, configuration, inputs, parameters, seed, execution state, interventions, deviations, observations, completion status, and outputs.
Campaign-Level Documentation
Campaign-level documentation may preserve shared conditions across large populations of executions.
For example:
Campaign C-001
may define: model version, environment version, common scenario family, infrastructure, orchestration configuration, repetition rules, and shared execution controls.
Individual runs then document material differences from that common basis.
No Duplicate Documentation Requirement
SEDM does not require identical information to be copied into every run record where a governed shared Campaign Record already establishes that information.
The requirement is:

traceable inheritance.
Documentation Inheritance
A run may inherit documented conditions from a Campaign Record where: the inherited condition is explicitly linked, the relevant version is stable, exceptions remain visible, and the run can be reconstructed without ambiguity.
No Assumed Inheritance Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A run must not be assumed to inherit campaign conditions where material evidence shows that its actual execution differed.
Actual execution takes precedence over intended campaign configuration.
Actual Configuration Documentation
SEDM should preserve the materially relevant configuration that actually entered execution.
This may include: Simulation Object version, model version, environment version, scenario version, Input Set, parameter set, software build, hardware configuration, dependencies, randomization basis, and initialization state.
Intended vs Executed Configuration
SEDM distinguishes:
Intended Configuration
from:
Executed Configuration.
Where these differ, the difference becomes part of the Execution Record.
Configuration Delta Record
A Configuration Delta Record may identify:
Expected Configuration → Actual Configuration → Material Difference
This supports later interpretation of unexpected behavior.
Execution State History
SEDM may preserve state transitions such as:
Prepared
↓
Initialized
↓
Running
↓
Paused
↓
Restarted
↓
Running
↓
Completed
This is materially different from a record that merely states:
Completed.
Execution Timeline

Where timing is material, SEDM may preserve an Execution Timeline connecting:
Initialization
Start
Control Events
Observations
Interventions
Anomalies
Interruptions
Restarts
Termination
and:
Completion.
Event Ordering
The order of execution events may itself be material.
SEDM should therefore preserve event ordering where causal interpretation depends upon sequence.
Timestamp Governance
Where timestamps are used, the record should preserve sufficient context to determine what they represent.
This may include: simulation time, wall-clock time, mission time, relative execution time, or another defined temporal reference.
Simulation Time ≠ Wall-Clock Time
A simulation may represent:
24 hours of operational behavior
while executing in:
12 minutes of wall-clock time.
SEDM preserves which temporal frame an event belongs to.
Execution Control Documentation
Material execution-control actions should remain linked to the execution.
Examples include: pause, resume, termination, resource restriction, synchronization, scenario progression, injected event, controlled failure, recovery command, or another runtime control.
Intervention Documentation
A material intervention should document where applicable:
Who or what intervened
When
Under which authority
What changed
Why
and:
Which part of execution may have been affected.
Human Intervention
Where humans intervene during execution, SEDM may preserve: role, intervention type, decision point, timing, authority, and resulting execution effect.

AI or Autonomous Intervention
Where an AI or autonomous system modifies simulation execution, SEDM may preserve: initiating system, decision basis where available, authorized capability, action performed, affected parameters or scenario state, and resulting execution path.
No Invisible Intervention Principle
A material intervention capable of changing Simulation Execution must not disappear from the execution history.
Deviation Documentation
A material Execution Deviation should remain connected to: the expected condition, actual condition, time or execution stage, affected execution component, response, and resulting execution status.
Deviation Resolution
A deviation may be:
Resolved During Execution
Accepted
Conditionally Accepted
Unresolved
Execution-Limiting
or:
Execution-Terminating.
SEDM documents the status.
It does not independently determine downstream validity.
Observation Documentation
Material observations produced under SOM should remain linked to the execution context in which they occurred.
An observation should not become:
Behavior X occurred
without sufficient ability to determine:
during which execution, scenario, state, configuration, and conditions Behavior X occurred.
Observation Context Preservation
Where material:
Observation → Execution ID → Execution State → Scenario → Configuration → Time Context
should remain traceable.
Observation Limitation Documentation

If portions of execution were not observable, that limitation should remain part of the Execution Record.
Examples include: telemetry loss, missing internal state, insufficient sampling, sensor dropout, logging failure, or inaccessible agent state.
No Full-Observation Assumption
SIMULOS® establishes:
Absence of a recorded event does not establish absence of the event where the relevant execution region was not sufficiently observable.
Anomaly Documentation
Material anomalies should remain visible even where the execution ultimately completes successfully.
Anomaly records may include: anomaly identity, observation time, affected component, execution context, response, persistence, and relationship to resulting outputs.
Failure Documentation
Failed Simulation Executions remain part of the governed execution history where material.
A failure record may preserve: failure state, failure point, observed cause where known, affected scenario, affected configuration, recovery attempt, and output status.
Failure Cause ≠ Failure Observation
SEDM distinguishes:
Observed Failure
from:
Determined Cause of Failure.
The execution record should not present an unverified causal explanation as established fact.
Interrupted Execution
An interrupted execution should remain distinguishable from:
Completed Execution
and:
Failed Execution.
An interruption may later be restarted or abandoned.
Restart Documentation

Where execution restarts, SEDM should preserve whether the restart: resumed from prior state, restored from checkpoint, restarted from initialization, changed configuration, changed input, changed seed, or created a new Execution ID.
Execution Continuity
A restarted execution should not automatically be treated as continuous with the original run.
The continuity relationship should be explicitly governed.
Termination Documentation
Termination may be:
Normal
Rule-Based
Human-Initiated
AI-Initiated
Safety-Initiated
Failure-Induced
or another defined condition.
Where material, the termination basis should remain visible.
Execution Completion Documentation
SEDM preserves the Execution Completeness status established under SES.
Possible statuses may include:
Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
Failed
or:
Undetermined. Completion ≠ Success
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Execution may be completely executed while the simulated system fails catastrophically.
Execution completion describes execution status.
It does not describe desirability of the simulated outcome.
Repetition Documentation
SEDM preserves the repetition structure established by SRPM.
This may include: Repetition Set ID, Reference Execution, controlled constants, permitted variation, seed relationship, execution order, run dependency, repetition drift, comparability status, and repetition sufficiency.
Repetition Lineage
A repetition history may be represented:
Run R001
↓

Unexpected Divergence
↓
Focused Repeat R002
↓
Focused Repeat R003
↓
Rare Behavior Reproduced
↓
New Scenario Requirement
SEDM preserves this lineage so that the discovery pathway remains reconstructable.
Randomization Documentation
Where randomness materially affects execution, SEDM may preserve: randomization method, random seed, sampling configuration, stochastic parameter state, and relationship between randomization and execution.
No Seed-Only Reconstruction Principle
A seed should not be treated as a complete execution record.
Reconstruction may also depend upon: model version, environment version, dependencies, initialization, inputs, hardware, software, timing, and execution controls.
Execution Provenance
Execution Provenance establishes the origin of the Simulation Execution Record and its material components.
It may connect:
Execution Record
to: simulation system, execution engine, orchestration platform, infrastructure, configuration source, input source, scenario source, observation source, and responsible execution authority where applicable.
Provenance ≠ Integrity
SEDM governs execution-specific provenance relationships.
General integrity properties remain governed under INTEGROS®.
Execution Lineage
Execution Lineage establishes relationships between Simulation Executions over time.
Examples include:
Baseline → Repeat
Baseline → Modified Parameter Run
Failure → Recovery Run
Scenario → Stress Escalation
Model v1 Run → Model v2 Comparative Run

Initial Campaign → Follow-Up Campaign Why Lineage Matters
Without lineage, a simulation repository may contain millions of outputs while losing the reasoning path that explains:
why later executions were performed.
SEDM preserves that relationship.
Execution Reconstruction
Execution Reconstruction is the ability to recover the materially relevant execution basis after the original execution has ended.
A reconstruction should answer, where applicable:
What was executed?
Which versions were used?
Which scenario ran?
Which inputs entered?
Which parameters were active?
Which randomization conditions applied?
What occurred during execution?
Which interventions occurred?
Which deviations occurred?
Was the execution interrupted or restarted?
Was it part of a Repetition Set?
Was execution complete?
Which outputs came from it? Reconstruction ≠ Reproduction
A simulation may be sufficiently documented for reconstruction even where exact technical reproduction is impossible.
For example, external dependencies may no longer exist.
SEDM distinguishes:
Can we determine what happened?
from:
Can we execute exactly the same run again?
Point-in-Time Reconstruction
SEDM should support reconstruction of the execution state at a materially relevant point in time.
For example:
What was the active parameter configuration when the anomaly occurred?
or:
Had the human intervention already occurred when the autonomous recovery behavior began?
Causal Sequence Preservation

SEDM does not determine causality.
However, it should preserve sufficient temporal and execution relationships to allow downstream analysis to investigate causality.
Documentation Completeness
Documentation Completeness asks:
Does the Execution Record contain the materially required information necessary for its intended governance and downstream use?
Possible statuses may include:
Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
or:
Completeness Undetermined. Documentation Completeness ≠ Execution Completeness
These are separate conditions.
A simulation may be:
Execution Complete + Documentation Incomplete
or:
Execution Failed + Documentation Complete.
This distinction is critical.
Documentation Gap
A Documentation Gap exists where materially relevant execution information is missing, inaccessible, ambiguous, or insufficiently linked.
Examples include: unknown model version, missing seed, unknown intervention, missing runtime log, unidentified scenario revision, missing input version, unknown restart state, or orphan output.
Documentation Gap Classification
A gap may be:
Minor
Material
Critical
or:
Undetermined
relative to the intended downstream use.
No Documentation Inflation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A partially documented execution must not be represented as fully reconstructable merely because large volumes of technical logs exist.
Volume of logging is not equivalent to documentation sufficiency. Machine Logs ≠ Governed Documentation

Raw logs may be important evidence.
But a collection of logs does not automatically establish: execution identity, configuration binding, lineage, material event classification, completion status, or output linkage.
SEDM provides the governance structure around technical records.
Documentation Uncertainty
Where documentation cannot establish a material fact with sufficient confidence, the uncertainty should remain visible.
Possible representation:
Known
Conditionally Known
Inferred
Unknown
or another governed classification.
No Retrospective Certainty Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Missing execution information must not later be converted into certainty merely because a downstream conclusion requires it.
Execution-to-Output Traceability
Every material Simulation Output should remain traceable to the Simulation Execution or governed execution population that produced it.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID
↓
Output ID
or:
Simulation Campaign / Repetition Set
↓
Aggregated Output ID Output Origin
SEDM establishes the execution-side provenance of an output.
SOGS then governs:
what the output is, how it is classified, how it is bounded, and what may legitimately be inferred from it.
No Orphan Output Principle
A material Simulation Output should not become detached from the execution basis that produced it.
Aggregated Output Traceability
An aggregated result may represent: multiple runs, a Repetition Set, a Scenario Set, or a complete Simulation Campaign.

SEDM should preserve the population of executions contributing to the aggregate where material.
No Anonymous Aggregation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
An aggregate Simulation Output should not conceal which materially relevant executions were included, excluded, failed, or unavailable.
Excluded Execution Documentation
Where runs are excluded from aggregation or analysis, the exclusion may itself require documentation.
This can prevent: cherry-picking, survivor bias, silent removal of failed runs, and post hoc population manipulation.
Campaign Documentation
Large Simulation Campaigns may require hierarchical documentation:
Campaign Record
↓
Scenario Families
↓
Repetition Sets
↓
Individual Executions
↓
Outputs
This structure allows governance at scale without losing material run-level traceability.
Large-Scale Execution Documentation
A campaign containing millions or billions of runs cannot always preserve every technical artifact indefinitely.
SEDM therefore supports risk- and purpose-appropriate documentation strategies while protecting material reconstructability.
Possible approaches include: structured metadata, hierarchical records, exception-focused retention, representative execution preservation, aggregate lineage, checkpoint preservation, reproducibility packages, and selective high-resolution logging.
Selective Retention
Selective retention may be legitimate where the selection logic itself is governed.

For example, an organization may preserve: all failed runs, all anomalous runs, all rare-event runs, representative successful runs, complete metadata for every run, and aggregated technical logs.
No Selective Success Preservation Principle
Retention policy must not systematically preserve favorable executions while eliminating materially relevant unfavorable executions.
Record Retention
Retention periods may depend upon: simulation purpose, consequence, regulatory context, contractual requirements, validation use, audit requirements, operational reliance, incident exposure, and reproducibility needs.
SEDM does not prescribe one universal retention period.
Documentation Continuity
Documentation should remain sufficiently interpretable across: software changes, model changes, environment changes, personnel changes, organizational changes, storage migrations, and simulation-platform replacement.
Format Obsolescence
Long-lived simulation programs may lose access to historical records because: proprietary formats disappear, software versions become unavailable, dependencies expire, or storage systems change.
SEDM treats continued interpretability as part of documentation continuity where materially required.
Documentation Versioning
Execution documentation structures may evolve.
Where schema changes affect interpretation, the applicable documentation version should remain identifiable.
AI-Readable Execution Records

Where technically appropriate, SEDM supports machine-readable records capable of connecting:
Object → Model → Environment → Scenario → Input → Execution → Observation → Repetition → Output
This can support automated: simulation governance, anomaly investigation, validation, audit, comparison, and future simulation planning.
Automated Documentation
Simulation platforms may automatically generate substantial portions of the Execution Record.
Automation is encouraged where appropriate.
However:
Automated capture ≠ automatically sufficient governance.
The record still needs to capture the materially relevant relationships required by SEDM.
AI-Generated Documentation
AI systems may summarize execution histories, classify anomalies, or construct documentation records.
Where AI-generated documentation introduces interpretation rather than direct observation, that distinction should remain visible.
Observed Fact vs Generated Summary
SEDM should preserve the difference between:
Machine-Captured Execution Event
and:
AI-Generated Description of the Event.
This prevents generated summaries from silently replacing source execution evidence.
Autonomous Simulation Campaigns
Future autonomous systems may: generate scenarios, launch simulations, analyze observations, select follow-up runs, terminate low-value branches, and generate new campaigns
without continuous human direction.
SEDM becomes particularly important because the execution pathway itself may be machine-generated.

Autonomous Execution Lineage
For autonomous campaigns, documentation should preserve where material:
Trigger
↓
Simulation Selection
↓
Execution
↓
Observation
↓
Machine Decision
↓
Follow-Up Execution
↓
Result
This allows later reconstruction of why the simulation system chose to execute what it did.
No Hidden Autonomous Path Principle
When an autonomous system materially determines the simulation path, that path should remain reconstructable rather than appearing as an unexplained collection of simulation outputs.
Space and Mission Simulation
Space agencies and aerospace organizations may run enormous simulation campaigns before: launch, docking, landing, autonomous navigation, recovery, fault response, or mission-critical maneuvers.
The challenge may not be generating simulation data.
The challenge may be answering months later:
Which exact spacecraft configuration produced this anomaly?
Which environmental assumptions applied?
Which run first revealed the failure mode?
Was the anomaly reproduced?
Which software version was running?
Was that run included in the final aggregate?
Which follow-up simulations were triggered by it?
SEDM provides the documentation structure required to preserve these relationships.
Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
An autonomous-vehicle organization may execute hundreds of millions of simulated driving episodes.
A later incident may require comparison with historical simulation.

SEDM allows the organization to determine: whether the relevant condition had been simulated, which execution population contained it, what system version was tested, what behavior occurred, whether anomalous runs existed, and whether those runs were included in downstream analysis.
Simulation Documentation Bottleneck
At simulation scale, the bottleneck may shift from:
Can we run enough simulations?
to:
Can we reconstruct why the simulations produced what they produced?
Organizations may possess enormous computational capacity while lacking governed relationships between: execution, configuration, observation, repetition, anomaly, and output.
SEDM defines that relationship as a governable space.

The relationship is:

Use Case 1 — Autonomous Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario

A space organization runs a large pre-mission simulation campaign for autonomous spacecraft recovery.
Several months later, engineers discover an unusual recovery behavior and need to determine whether it had appeared during simulation. Application
SEDM connects the relevant historical execution to: spacecraft software version, simulation model version, environment version, scenario, navigation inputs, power state, random seed, execution observations, runtime interventions, and follow-up repetitions.

The organization discovers that similar behavior occurred in several historical runs, but some of those executions had been excluded from an aggregate because they were classified as incomplete. Result
