Canonical Definition
Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM) is the first Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SEQM governs the transformation of simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, and governed inferences into explicitly qualified Simulation Evidence for a defined evidential purpose.

The Module establishes whether a simulation-derived information object is sufficiently identified, traceable, context-bound, purpose-linked, condition-aware, and methodologically interpretable to be treated as governed evidence within the SIMULOS® lifecycle.
SEQM does not determine the ultimate strength, sufficiency, or validation consequence of that evidence.
Its task is narrower and foundational:
to determine whether simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence at all, and to define the evidential basis under which that qualification is valid.
Core Question
What simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence, and for what evidential purpose?
Architectural Position
SEQM is the first module within SERBS.
It receives governed information from:
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS)
and
Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
It precedes:
SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module.
Its architectural role is therefore to establish the evidence object before any attempt is made to assign evidential weight, define reliance boundaries, impose use limitations, or transfer the evidence into broader validation governance.
Internal Flow Position

Governed Simulation Output Governed Inference Basis Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis → Evidence Candidate Identification → Evidential Purpose Definition → Simulation Basis Traceability → Qualification Condition Assessment → Applicability Definition → Uncertainty Preservation → Evidence Qualification State → Qualified Simulation Evidence → SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module
Operational Space
SEQM governs the point at which simulation-derived information crosses from:
simulation result
into:
qualified simulation evidence.
This operational space includes: evidence candidate identification; evidential purpose definition; proposition linkage; simulation basis traceability; output provenance; inference provenance; correlation basis linkage; contextual qualification; applicability definition; qualification conditions; uncertainty preservation; temporal applicability; version applicability; scenario applicability; configuration applicability; evidence qualification state; evidence disqualification where the required basis is absent.
Operational Scope
SEQM applies to any simulation-derived information that an organization intends to use as evidence.

Such information may include: numerical outputs; state transitions; observed simulated behavior; event frequencies; failure patterns; scenario outcomes; threshold crossings; sensitivity results; comparative results; stochastic distributions; trajectory results; predicted behaviors; simulated interactions; failure modes; anomaly patterns; scenario coverage observations; simulation-to-reality comparisons; governed simulation inferences.
The Module applies equally to: a single simulation execution; repeated runs; scenario portfolios; Monte Carlo campaigns; high-performance simulation campaigns; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; mission simulations; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies.
Evidence Candidate Principle
A simulation-derived result must first be identified as an Evidence Candidate before it can be qualified.
An Evidence Candidate is:
a defined simulation-derived information object proposed for use in supporting, challenging, comparing, informing, or constraining a specific proposition, question, assessment, or decision context.
An Evidence Candidate may originate from: one execution; multiple executions; one scenario; a scenario set; a simulation campaign; a correlation result; a pattern across outputs; a governed inference.
But existence alone does not establish evidential status. Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence

SEQM enforces the distinction:
Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence
A result becomes governed evidence only when the relationship between that result and an explicit evidential purpose is established.
For example:
“The simulator produced a maximum temperature of 912°C.”
is an output statement.
“Under Scenario S-47, Configuration C-3, and the governed assumptions of Simulation Model M-12, the simulation produced a maximum temperature of 912°C, supporting evidence concerning thermal behavior under those represented conditions.”
is an evidentially qualified statement.
The difference is governance context.
Evidential Purpose Principle
Every qualified Simulation Evidence object must have a defined Evidential Purpose.
The Evidential Purpose specifies what the evidence is intended to inform.
It may relate to: a hypothesis; a design question; a performance question; a safety proposition; a comparative assessment; a mission condition; a failure hypothesis; a scenario question; a behavioral proposition; a threshold condition; an engineering claim; a validation input; an operational question.
Evidence without a defined evidential purpose remains analytically informative but methodologically underqualified.
Evidence-to-Proposition Relationship
SEQM requires a defined relationship between:
Simulation Evidence and the proposition or question the evidence is intended to inform.

The relationship may be: supporting; challenging; contradicting; comparative; conditional; exclusionary; sensitivity-based; exploratory.
This distinction matters because the same simulation result may legitimately serve different evidential functions in different contexts.
A failure result may weaken one proposition while strongly supporting another.
Simulation Basis Traceability
Qualified Simulation Evidence must remain traceable, where materially relevant, to the governed simulation basis from which it originated.
The traceability chain may include:
Simulation Evidence → Simulation Output → Execution Record → Scenario → Input Basis → Model & Environment → Assumptions → Reality Representation → Purpose & Scope → Simulation Object
Where SRCS applies:
Simulation Evidence → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis
This chain ensures that evidential meaning cannot become detached from the conditions that created it.
Evidence Context Principle
Simulation evidence is inherently context-dependent.
SEQM therefore requires relevant evidential context to remain visible.
Context may include: Simulation Object identity; object version; configuration; purpose; scope; excluded conditions; reality representation; abstraction level; fidelity level; assumptions; model version; environment version; input set; temporal basis; scenario; parameter range; execution conditions; output type; correlation basis; uncertainty.
Context is not metadata decoration.
It is part of the evidential meaning.

Qualification Conditions
An Evidence Candidate may be qualified only where the minimum material conditions necessary to interpret it are established.
Qualification conditions may require: identifiable evidence object; identifiable originating output; defined evidential purpose; traceable simulation basis; known Simulation Object; known object version or configuration; known scenario basis; known execution source; known material assumptions; known output meaning; known correlation basis where reality claims are involved; known uncertainty affecting interpretation; known applicability conditions; known material exclusions.
The precise combination depends on the evidential purpose.
SEQM therefore does not impose unnecessary uniformity.
It requires sufficient contextual definition for legitimate evidential interpretation.
Evidence Qualification State
SEQM establishes explicit qualification states.
A Simulation Evidence Candidate may be classified as: 1. Unqualified
The simulation-derived information exists but lacks sufficient evidential context or purpose definition. 2. Conditionally Qualified
The information may function as evidence only under explicitly defined conditions or limitations. 3. Qualified
The information has sufficient simulation-specific basis, traceability, purpose alignment, and contextual definition to function as governed Simulation Evidence. 4. Qualification Suspended

A previously qualified evidence object has encountered a material change, unresolved discrepancy, missing provenance, or other condition requiring reassessment. 5. Disqualified
The information cannot legitimately function as Simulation Evidence for the stated evidential purpose.
Qualification state must remain distinguishable from evidential weight.
Qualified ≠ strong evidence.
Qualification determines whether the object may enter evidence governance.
SEWM determines how much simulation-specific evidential weight it may carry.
Conditional Qualification
Many simulation results can be evidentially valid only under specified conditions.
SEQM therefore permits conditional qualification.
Example:
Qualified only for Object Version V4, environmental range E2–E5, Scenario Family S3, and model configuration M7.
Such evidence remains legitimate.
Its qualification is simply bounded.
Conditional qualification must not be silently transformed into universal qualification downstream.
Negative Evidence Qualification
SEQM explicitly allows negative, failed, anomalous, unstable, or contradictory results to qualify as evidence.
Evidence qualification must not depend upon whether the result supports the preferred hypothesis.
Examples include: failure to achieve mission objectives; model divergence; repeated instability; scenario-specific failure; unexpected collision; thermal exceedance; non-convergence; behavioral anomaly; disagreement with operational data; unexpected sensitivity.

If the result is relevant, traceable, and contextually interpretable, it may qualify as evidence.
Inference Qualification
Some simulation evidence is directly observed in simulation outputs.
Other evidence is derived through inference.
SEQM requires this distinction to remain visible.
Direct Simulation Observation ≠ Derived Simulation Inference
Where evidence depends upon an inference, the qualification basis must identify: originating outputs; inference method; inferential assumptions; transformation or aggregation; inference scope; uncertainty introduced by inference.
The existence of a governed inference does not automatically increase or decrease evidence weight.
It simply changes the evidential pathway that must remain traceable.
Aggregated Evidence Qualification
Simulation campaigns frequently aggregate outputs across large numbers of runs.
SEQM requires aggregated evidence to identify: aggregation basis; included executions; excluded executions; scenario composition; common assumptions; common model dependencies; statistical method; aggregation transformation; treatment of failed runs; treatment of anomalous runs; dependence structure where known.
An aggregate metric must not obscure the evidence objects from which it was created.
Evidence Independence Awareness
SEQM does not determine final evidential weight, but it must preserve information relevant to later assessment of evidence dependence.

Examples include: repeated use of the same model; shared assumptions; identical input generation; common scenario design; shared execution infrastructure; common data transformations; common correlation basis.
This enables SEWM to distinguish between:
many evidence objects
and
many independently informative evidence objects.
Applicability Definition
Every qualified evidence object should identify the context within which its evidential meaning applies.
Applicability may be defined by: object; configuration; scenario; environment; parameter range; temporal interval; operational condition; mission phase; behavior class; model state; input family; uncertainty range.
Applicability defines where the evidence may meaningfully enter subsequent governance.
It does not yet define the maximum reliance boundary; that is owned by SRBM.
Temporal Qualification
Evidence qualification may depend upon time.
Evidence can become underqualified where: the Simulation Object changes; a model is replaced; assumptions become obsolete; new operational data appears; reality correlation changes; input distributions materially shift; scenario relevance changes.
SEQM must therefore support:
Qualification Review and Qualification Reassessment.
This creates the interface to SLRS lifecycle governance.
Evidence Provenance
SEQM requires simulation evidence to preserve sufficient provenance to identify how the evidence came into existence.

Provenance may include: originating simulation; originating execution ID; simulation campaign ID; scenario ID; model version; environment version; object version; input package; output reference; transformation history; inference history; aggregation history; qualification record.
SEQM governs the simulation-specific evidential provenance relationship.
General provenance integrity and audit assurance remain outside its boundary where governed by INTEGROS® or ADIT®.
Qualification Failure Conditions
An Evidence Candidate should not qualify where material information necessary to understand its evidential meaning is absent.
Examples include: unknown originating execution; unknown Simulation Object version; missing scenario basis; unclear evidential purpose; untraceable transformed output; unidentified material assumption; unknown model configuration; missing relationship to the proposition being supported; output used outside its represented context; correlation claim without a governed correlation basis; aggregation that conceals materially relevant failures; evidence whose meaning cannot be reconstructed.
Qualification failure does not necessarily mean the underlying simulation is invalid.
It means the information cannot currently function as governed Simulation Evidence for the intended purpose.
SEQM Boundary with SOGS
SOGS governs: what the simulation produced; output identity; output classification; inference; output limitation; output documentation.

SEQM governs: whether that governed output or inference may legitimately function as evidence; for what evidential purpose; under what qualification conditions; with what simulation basis.
Therefore:
Governed Output ≠ Qualified Evidence.
SEQM Boundary with SRCS
SRCS governs the correlation relationship between simulation and reality.
SEQM may use that governed correlation relationship as part of an evidence qualification basis.
It does not recalculate or redefine correlation.
Therefore:
Correlation Result → Evidence Qualification Input
not
Evidence Qualification → Correlation Determination.
SEQM Boundary with SEWM
SEQM determines whether simulation-derived information qualifies as evidence.
SEWM determines the simulation-specific evidential weight of that qualified evidence.
Therefore:
Qualification ≠ Weight.
A result may be fully qualified yet carry weak evidential weight.
A result may also be conditionally qualified yet carry strong evidential weight within a narrow context.
SEQM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SEQM does not determine whether evidence is sufficient for a broader Validation Determination.
It governs only the qualification of simulation-derived information as Simulation Evidence.
The boundary is:
SEQM: Does this simulation-derived information legitimately qualify as evidence for this defined evidential purpose?
VALIDOS®: Does the total validation evidence basis sufficiently support the Validation Determination and intended reliance?
SEQM Boundary with INTEGROS®

SEQM does not own general evidence integrity.
It may require evidence provenance, traceability, and contextual completeness as conditions of qualification.
INTEGROS® governs broader integrity properties of the evidence and its supporting structures.
SEQM Boundary with ADIT®
SEQM may require a reconstructable evidential basis.
ADIT® may audit whether records, evidence, observations, and execution traces are sufficiently preserved and verifiable.
SEQM does not own auditability governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SEQM implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Candidate Identification
Identify the exact simulation-derived information proposed as evidence. 2. Evidential Purpose Definition
Define the proposition, question, comparison, or decision context the evidence is intended to inform. 3. Evidence Source Identification
Identify the originating outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, or inferences. 4. Simulation Basis Traceability
Link the Evidence Candidate to the relevant governed simulation lifecycle elements. 5. Context Definition
Identify object, version, configuration, scenario, model, environment, assumptions, inputs, and other materially relevant conditions. 6. Applicability Definition
Define where the evidential meaning applies. 7. Uncertainty Preservation
Preserve material uncertainty affecting interpretation. 8. Qualification Condition Assessment

Determine whether the minimum required conditions for legitimate evidential interpretation are satisfied. 9. Qualification State Assignment
Assign the Evidence Candidate a governed qualification state. 10. Qualification Record Creation
Document the basis supporting the qualification decision.
Governance Outputs
SEQM may produce: Simulation Evidence Candidate Record Simulation Evidential Purpose Statement Simulation Evidence Source Record Simulation Evidence Traceability Chain Simulation Evidence Context Record Simulation Evidence Applicability Statement Simulation Evidence Qualification Condition Record Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Link Simulation Evidence Qualification State Simulation Evidence Disqualification Record Simulation Evidence Qualification Record Qualified Simulation Evidence Object
These outputs provide the input basis for SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module.
Enterprise Application
SEQM enables organizations to prevent a common simulation governance failure:
treating every technically generated result as evidence.

An organization may use SEQM to determine: whether a particular simulation result legitimately supports a stated proposition; whether the result remains connected to the correct Simulation Object version; whether scenario and execution context are preserved; whether a derived inference is traceable to its source outputs; whether failed and anomalous outcomes remain evidentially visible; whether aggregated campaign results conceal material dependencies; whether evidence is still applicable after material change; whether an output should remain unqualified, become conditionally qualified, become fully qualified, or be disqualified; whether simulation-derived information is ready to proceed into evidential weight assessment.
This becomes especially important in very large simulation programs where millions or billions of outputs may exist but only a subset may legitimately function as evidence for a particular claim.
SEQM therefore creates an explicit methodological gate between simulation production and simulation evidence governance.
Foundational Principles
Simulation output is not automatically simulation evidence.
Evidence qualification requires an explicit evidential purpose.
Evidence must remain connected to the simulation basis that gives it meaning.
Qualification is contextual, not universal.
Qualified evidence may still carry weak evidential weight.
Conditional evidence must remain conditional.
Negative simulation results may qualify as evidence.

Aggregated evidence must not erase its originating simulation basis.
Evidence provenance is part of evidential qualification.
A simulation result that cannot be meaningfully traced, contextualized, and interpreted should not be treated as governed Simulation Evidence.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Evidence Qualification Module establishes the first evidential control point within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by transforming simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, and governed inferences into explicitly identified, purpose-linked, traceable, context-bound, applicability-defined, uncertainty-aware, and qualification-state-controlled Simulation Evidence. Through governance of Evidence Candidates, evidential purpose, proposition relationships, simulation basis traceability, contextual conditions, provenance, inference pathways, aggregation, applicability, qualification states, temporal relevance, and qualification failure, SEQM prevents simulation results from acquiring evidential status merely because they were computationally produced or analytically persuasive. By separating evidence qualification from evidential weight, reliance, validation sufficiency, integrity, and auditability, SEQM preserves the architectural boundaries of SIMULOS®, VALIDOS®, INTEGROS®, and ADIT® while creating the governed evidence object required for downstream evidence assessment. No simulation-derived result should legitimately enter broader evidential reliance until the conditions under which it becomes evidence have first been made explicit.

Simulation Environment Versioning
Canonical Definition
Simulation Environment Versioning Module (SEVM) defines the governance framework for identifying, establishing, distinguishing, freezing, changing, comparing, preserving, restoring, and reconstructing the versions and materially relevant configuration states of a governed Simulation Environment.

SEVM establishes the version-control layer through which simulation executions remain bound to the exact environmental configuration under which they occurred, preventing materially different Simulation Environments from being treated as if they were the same simulation context.
Operational Role
SEVM is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
The preceding modules establish:
SMMM — What is the Simulation Model structurally composed of?
SECM — Within what configured Simulation Environment does that model operate?
SBIM — How do the model, environment, and connected domains interact across their boundaries?
SPHM — Which controlled parameters configure the model and environment for simulation activity?
SEVM asks:
Which exact version of the Simulation Environment existed for a particular simulation execution, what changed between environment versions, and can the environment state relevant to that execution later be reconstructed?
The governed progression is:
Model Structure → Environment Configuration → Boundary Interaction → Parameterization → Environment Version Identification → Version Baseline → Change Control → Execution Binding → Version Reconstruction → Governed Simulation Environment Version
Module Operational Space

SEVM governs: Simulation Environment version identity, environment version identifiers, environment configuration states, environment baselines, environment snapshots, version composition, version lineage, version ancestry, version succession, version differentiation, version equivalence, version compatibility, version activation, version deactivation, version supersession, version freezing, version restoration, version rollback, environment forks, environment branches, environment merges, environment change, material change classification, environment configuration drift, dependency version change, boundary configuration change, parameter configuration change references, environment release states, execution-to-version binding, output-to-version traceability, version comparability, historical environment preservation, point-in-time environment reconstruction, and environment-version lifecycle continuity.
Module Operational Scope
SEVM applies wherever a change in the Simulation Environment may materially alter simulation behavior, execution conditions, comparability, repeatability, interpretation, or resulting Simulation Outputs.

It may apply across: engineering simulations, robotics simulations, autonomous-system simulations, AI simulations, digital twins, scientific simulations, industrial simulations, infrastructure simulations, transportation simulations, aerospace simulations, mission simulations, financial simulations, environmental simulations, cyber-physical simulations, multi-agent simulations, distributed simulations, federated simulations, software-in-the-loop environments, hardware-in-the-loop environments, cloud-based simulation platforms, live-system-connected simulations, and future simulation environments.
Governance depth should remain proportional to the material effect environment change may have upon the simulation inquiry.
Module Function
A simulation environment is rarely static.
Software changes.
Libraries change.
Dependencies change.
External services change.
Hardware changes.
Boundary configurations change.
Environmental assets change.
Parameter baselines change.
Models connected to the environment change.
If these changes are not version-governed, two executions may appear to use the same simulation while actually operating under materially different conditions.

SEVM exists to prevent: unidentified environment versions, silent environment updates, loss of historical configurations, execution against unknown environment states, uncontrolled dependency changes, environment drift, inappropriate comparison across materially different versions, loss of reproducibility, ambiguous rollback, and inability to reconstruct the environment that produced a simulation result.
Simulation Environment Version
A Simulation Environment Version is an identifiable governed state of the Simulation Environment representing a materially distinguishable configuration applicable during a defined simulation context.
Conceptually:
Simulation Environment + Governed Configuration State + Version Identity = Simulation Environment Version Version Identity
Each materially relevant Simulation Environment Version should be distinguishable.
A Version Identity may include: Environment Identifier, Version Identifier, configuration reference, release identifier, activation date, dependency state, parameter baseline reference, boundary configuration reference, and applicable model compatibility.
Version Identifier
A Version Identifier provides a persistent reference to a specific governed environment state.
For example:
SEV-1.0
SEV-1.1
SEV-2.0
The numbering mechanism may differ by implementation.
The governance requirement is not a particular numbering convention.
The requirement is:
materially distinguishable environment states must remain distinguishable.

Environment Version Composition
A Simulation Environment Version may be composed of multiple governed components.
Conceptually:
Environment Version = Environment Configuration + Dependencies + Boundary Configuration + Parameter Baseline + Relevant Runtime State
Where these components have independent versions, their relationships should remain traceable.
Composite Version Identity
Complex Simulation Environments may require a Composite Version Identity.
For example:
Environment Version 4.2
may consist of:
Simulation Engine 7.1
Physics Library 3.4
Sensor Package 2.8
Weather Model 5.0
Boundary Configuration B12
Parameter Baseline P17
The composite relationship should remain reconstructable where material.
Environment Baseline
An Environment Baseline establishes an approved reference state of the Simulation Environment.
The baseline provides a controlled point against which subsequent change may be evaluated.
Conceptually:
Baseline Environment → Change → Successor Environment Version Baseline Content
A material Environment Baseline may identify: environment structure, software components, dependency versions, relevant hardware, environmental assets, interfaces, boundary configurations, parameter references, runtime configuration, external service dependencies, and other materially relevant environment properties.
Baseline ≠ Permanent Environment
A baseline is a governed reference state.
It does not prohibit change.
It makes change visible.
Environment Snapshot

An Environment Snapshot captures the materially relevant environment state at a defined point in time or execution context.
Snapshots may support: forensic reconstruction, repeatability, rollback, comparison, incident analysis, and execution traceability.
Snapshot ≠ Version
A snapshot records a state.
A version represents a governed environment identity.
Multiple snapshots may exist within one version where transient runtime state differs without constituting a new governed version.
Version Lineage
SEVM should preserve the lineage between environment versions.
Conceptually:
Version 1.0 → Version 1.1 → Version 1.2 → Version 2.0
Lineage allows later determination of: predecessor, successor, change path, branching, rollback, and historical dependency.
Version Ancestry
Where environments are derived from earlier configurations, ancestry should remain visible.
For example:
Environment B v1.0 derived from Environment A v3.2
This may be important where assumptions, dependencies, or configuration defects propagate between versions.
Environment Version Change
An Environment Version Change occurs when a materially relevant property of the governed Simulation Environment changes.

Possible changes include: simulation engine update, dependency update, library update, hardware replacement, environment asset change, boundary configuration change, external service change, parameter baseline change, timing-system change, synchronization change, network configuration change, or runtime architecture change.
Material Version Change
Not every technical modification requires a new governed environment version.
The governing question is:
Could the change materially affect simulation behavior, execution conditions, repeatability, comparability, interpretation, or reconstruction?
If yes, the change should be visible to environment-version governance.
Version Change Classification
Environment changes may be classified as:
Non-Material
Minor
Material
Major
Critical
or another implementation-specific classification.
Classification should reflect simulation consequence rather than software-release terminology alone.
No Silent Version Change Principle
A materially changed Simulation Environment must not continue to be represented as the same governed environment version merely because the technical system retained the same name or deployment location.
Version Differentiation
Two environment states should be considered materially different where their differences can materially alter simulation behavior or interpretation.

Version differentiation may depend upon: changed dependencies, changed interaction behavior, changed parameterization, changed timing, changed physical components, changed external services, changed environmental assets, or changed runtime conditions.
Version Equivalence
Two technical environment instances may be treated as version-equivalent only where their materially relevant configuration states are sufficiently equivalent for the simulation inquiry.
Technical duplication does not automatically establish governance equivalence.
Environment Compatibility
A Simulation Environment Version may be compatible only with certain: Simulation Model versions, parameter configurations, boundary configurations, scenario structures, execution engines, hardware, or dependencies.
Compatibility should remain identifiable where incompatibility could materially alter execution. Model–Environment Version Compatibility
A Simulation Model Version should not be assumed compatible with every Simulation Environment Version.
Conceptually:
Model Version + Environment Version → Compatibility Status
Possible statuses may include:
Compatible
Conditionally Compatible
Incompatible
Compatibility Undetermined Dependency Versioning
A Simulation Environment may rely upon external or internal dependencies.
Examples include: software libraries, physics engines, databases, AI models, APIs, external services, hardware firmware, operating systems, middleware, or communication infrastructure.

Material dependency versions should remain identifiable.
Dependency Change
A dependency change may create a new environment state even where the primary Simulation Environment software remains unchanged.
For example:
Same Simulation Platform + New Physics Engine = Potentially Different Simulation Environment External Service Version Change
External services may change outside direct simulation control.
Where such change materially affects simulation behavior, the affected environment state should not remain invisible.
SEVM may preserve:
External Service Identity → Previous State → Changed State → Affected Environment Version Boundary Configuration Version Relationship
SBIM governs Simulation Boundary Interaction.
SEVM preserves which governed boundary configuration applied to a particular Simulation Environment Version.
Conceptually:
Environment Version → Boundary Configuration Reference
A material boundary change may therefore require environment-version reassessment.
Parameter Configuration Version Relationship
SPHM governs Simulation Parameterization.
SEVM preserves the applicable Parameter Baseline or configuration relationship where it forms part of the environment version.
Conceptually:
Environment Version → Parameter Baseline Reference
Not every parameter change requires a new Environment Version.
But a material baseline-level configuration change may.
Version Activation
A Simulation Environment Version should have an identifiable activation point where necessary.

This allows determination of which version was operational for a specific simulation execution.
Version Deactivation
When an environment version is no longer approved for new execution, its deactivation should remain distinguishable from deletion.
Historical versions may still be required for reconstruction.
Version Supersession
A new environment version may supersede a prior version.
Conceptually:
SEV-1.0 → Superseded by → SEV-1.1
Supersession does not erase the historical environment state.
Version Freeze
A Version Freeze prevents material changes to an environment configuration during a defined simulation campaign, controlled comparison, benchmark, investigation, or validation activity.
The purpose is to maintain stable execution conditions.
Frozen Environment Principle
A frozen Simulation Environment Version must not materially change during the governed freeze period without creating an explicit exception or successor version.
Environment Release State
An environment version may hold a governed release state such as:
Draft
Test
Approved
Active
Frozen
Deprecated
Superseded
Archived
or another implementation-specific state.
Release state should not be confused with validation status. Environment Version ≠ Validation State
SEVM identifies and governs Simulation Environment Versions.
VALIDOS® governs validation conclusions and Validation States.
Therefore:
Environment Version 3.0
does not mean:
Validated Environment Version 3.0

unless a separate validation process establishes that state.
Environment Version Fork
A Version Fork occurs when one governed environment state develops into multiple successor configurations.
For example:
Environment 2.0
↓
Environment 2.1-A
and
Environment 2.1-B
Forks should preserve common ancestry.
Environment Branch
Branches may support: experimental environments, alternative configurations, hardware variants, regional configurations, different scenario families, or research variants.
A branch should not silently replace the primary environment baseline.
Environment Merge
Where branches are recombined, the resulting environment should identify the material configuration inherited from each branch.
Merge complexity should not destroy version traceability.
Environment Rollback
A Rollback restores a previous governed environment configuration.
Rollback should identify: current version, target version, reason, affected executions, activation point, and any retained changes.
Rollback ≠ Erasure
A rollback does not erase the intervening version history.
Conceptually:
V1 → V2 → Rollback to V1-derived state
should preserve the existence and use of V2.
Environment Restoration
Restoration may reconstruct a historical environment for: repeat execution, forensic analysis, validation, comparison, or incident investigation.
The restored environment should remain distinguishable from the historical original where differences remain.
Restoration Fidelity
A restored environment may be:

Exact
Functionally Equivalent
Partially Reconstructed
or:
Reconstruction Uncertain
depending upon what can actually be restored.
This distinction should remain explicit.
Environment Configuration Drift
Environment Configuration Drift occurs where the actual Simulation Environment progressively departs from its governed version or baseline without corresponding version governance.
Examples include: silent dependency updates, changed runtime settings, modified hardware, external service changes, unrecorded configuration changes, parameter baseline changes, or altered boundary behavior.
Drift Detection
SEVM should support detection of material divergence between:
Declared Environment Version
and:
Actual Environment State Declared–Actual Version Consistency
A simulation execution should not claim:
Environment Version X
when the actual materially relevant environment state no longer corresponds to Version X.
Version Integrity Interface
SEVM does not own general integrity governance.
Where preservation, tamper resistance, authenticity, or record integrity requires dedicated controls, INTEGROS® may apply.
SEVM governs:
which version existed and what it contained.
INTEGROS® may govern:
whether the relevant version records and artifacts preserved their required integrity.
Execution-to-Version Binding
Every material Simulation Execution should be bindable to the Simulation Environment Version under which it occurred.
Conceptually:

Simulation Execution ID → Simulation Environment Version ID
This relationship is fundamental to repeatability and interpretation.
Execution Environment Record
An execution record may preserve: Execution Identifier, Environment Version Identifier, Model Version reference, Parameter Configuration reference, Boundary Configuration reference, dependency state, execution time, and relevant environment snapshot.
No Unbound Execution Principle
A material Simulation Execution should not produce governable Simulation Output without an identifiable relationship to the Simulation Environment Version under which that execution occurred.
Output-to-Version Traceability
Downstream Simulation Output should remain traceable to the environment version that contributed to its production.
Conceptually:
Environment Version → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output
SEVM establishes the environment-version side of this chain.
Version Comparability
Two simulation executions should not be assumed comparable merely because they used the same Simulation Model.
Their environment versions may differ.
SEVM therefore asks:
Are the materially relevant environment conditions sufficiently equivalent for the intended comparison?
Version Comparison
A Version Comparison may identify: common components, changed components, changed dependencies, changed boundaries, changed parameter baselines, changed runtime conditions, and expected behavioral consequences.
Comparability Status
Possible statuses may include:

Environment-Comparable
Conditionally Environment-Comparable
Partially Environment-Comparable
Not Environment-Comparable
or:
Environment Comparability Undetermined Version Delta
A Version Delta represents the material differences between two Simulation Environment Versions.
Conceptually:
Version B − Version A = Environment Version Delta
The delta may identify: added components, removed components, updated components, dependency changes, boundary changes, parameter baseline changes, runtime changes, and configuration changes.
Version Delta Propagation
A material Environment Version Delta may affect later SIMULOS® governance spaces.
Conceptually:
Environment Version Change
↓
Input / Scenario Conditions
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output
↓
Reality Correlation
↓
Simulation Evidence
SEVM preserves the version change.
Downstream Parent Standards govern their respective consequences.
Environment Version Continuity
SEVM should preserve the lifecycle:
Environment Creation → Baseline → Active Version → Change → Successor Version → Supersession / Branch / Rollback → Archive
This allows the environment to remain governable across repeated simulation activity.
Historical Environment Preservation
Historical environment versions may be necessary to answer:
Which environment produced this result?
What changed afterward?
Could the execution be repeated?
Did a later environment update alter behavior?
Was the relevant defect present at the time of execution?

Point-in-Time Environment State
SEVM should support determination of the environment state applicable at a specific point in time.
This is particularly important for: incident reconstruction, scientific reproducibility, regulatory review, certification support, validation, dispute resolution, and audit.
Point-in-Time Reconstruction
A Point-in-Time Reconstruction should establish, where possible:
Environment Identity
Environment Version
Configuration State
Dependencies
Boundary Configuration
Parameter Baseline
Runtime State
and:
Execution Relationship
for the relevant time.
Environment Version Reconstruction
SEVM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer:
Which environment version was active?
What did that version contain?
Which dependencies were present?
Which boundary configuration applied?
Which parameter baseline applied?
What changed from the previous version?
Was the version frozen, active, deprecated, or superseded?
Which executions used it?
Can the relevant state be restored?
Version Traceability
A complete version traceability path may be represented as:
Simulation Environment
↓
Environment Baseline
↓
Environment Version
↓
Environment Configuration
↓
Dependency State
↓
Boundary Configuration
↓
Parameter Baseline
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify the Simulation Environment
Establish the governed environment whose versions require control. 2. Establish Environment Version Identity

Assign distinguishable version references to materially different environment states. 3. Establish the Environment Baseline
Define the controlled reference configuration. 4. Capture Material Version Composition
Preserve materially relevant components, dependencies, boundaries, and parameter references. 5. Govern Environment Change
Determine whether changes require a successor version or other governed treatment. 6. Preserve Version Lineage
Maintain predecessor, successor, branch, merge, rollback, and ancestry relationships. 7. Control Activation, Freeze, Supersession, and Restoration
Ensure environment lifecycle states remain explicit. 8. Detect Material Configuration Drift
Identify divergence between the declared version and actual environment state. 9. Bind Simulation Execution to Environment Version
Preserve the exact environment-version relationship for material executions. 10. Preserve Historical Reconstruction
Maintain sufficient information to compare, restore, and reconstruct materially relevant environment states.
Governance Outputs

SEVM may produce: Simulation Environment Version Identifier, Environment Version Record, Environment Baseline, Environment Snapshot, Environment Version Composition Record, Composite Version Identity, Version Lineage Record, Version Ancestry Record, Environment Version Change Record, Material Change Classification, Environment Version Delta, Environment Version Comparison, Environment Comparability Status, Model–Environment Compatibility Record, Dependency Version Record, External Service Version Record, Boundary Configuration Version Reference, Parameter Baseline Version Reference, Environment Activation Record, Environment Deactivation Record, Version Supersession Record, Version Freeze Record, Environment Release State, Environment Fork Record, Environment Branch Record, Environment Merge Record, Environment Rollback Record, Environment Restoration Record, Restoration Fidelity Record, Environment Configuration Drift Record, Declared–Actual Version Consistency Record, Execution Environment Record, Execution-to-Version Binding, Output-to-Version Traceability Reference, Point-in-Time Environment State, Environment Version Reconstruction Record, Historical Environment Record, and Simulation Environment Version Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Platform
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle simulation is executed using:
Environment Version 4.2

containing a defined physics engine, road environment, sensor emulation system, weather model, dependency set, boundary configuration, and parameter baseline.
The physics engine is later updated. Application
SEVM evaluates the change as material because vehicle behavior may change.
A successor environment becomes:
Environment Version 4.3
rather than silently retaining Version 4.2. Result
Results generated under 4.2 and 4.3 remain distinguishable, and any comparison can account for the environment change. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation
Scenario
A mission simulation produces a critical navigation result.
Months later, a defect is discovered in a communication-model dependency. Application
SEVM traces the affected dependency across environment-version lineage and identifies which executions used the defective version.
The historical environment is reconstructed. Result
Investigators can determine whether the critical simulation result was produced under the affected environment rather than rerunning the mission unknowingly under a corrected configuration. Use Case 3 — Scientific Climate Simulation
Scenario
A long-running scientific simulation program produces results across several years.
During that period: libraries change, computational infrastructure changes, parameter baselines evolve, and external datasets are updated.
Application
SEVM preserves distinct governed Simulation Environment Versions and binds each execution to its corresponding environment state. Result

Researchers can distinguish scientific differences caused by changed simulation assumptions or scenarios from differences potentially introduced by changes in the Simulation Environment itself.
Architectural Position
Simulation Environment Versioning is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
The complete SMES progression is:
Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning
Together, the five modules establish:
what the Simulation Model contains,
where it operates,
how it interacts across its boundaries,
how its configurable properties are instantiated,
and:
which exact governed environment version exists for simulation execution.
Within the broader SIMULOS® lifecycle:
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence → Validation Interface → Operational Reliance → Drift / Resimulation / Retirement
SEVM closes the Simulation Model & Environment governance space and establishes the controlled versioned configuration required before the architecture proceeds into simulation inputs, data, scenarios, and execution.
Foundational Principle

A simulation result cannot be fully reconstructed or meaningfully compared unless the materially relevant Simulation Environment Version that produced it remains identifiable.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Environment Versioning Module completes the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by establishing the governed version-control layer through which materially distinct Simulation Environment states remain identifiable across simulation activity. Through environment baselines, version identity, composition, dependency tracking, lineage, change classification, compatibility, activation, freezing, branching, rollback, drift detection, execution binding, comparability, historical preservation, and point-in-time reconstruction, SEVM ensures that changes to the environment cannot silently alter simulation behavior while historical and current executions continue to be represented as if they occurred under the same governed simulation conditions.

Canonical Definition
Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM) is the second Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SEWM governs the simulation-specific evidential weight assigned to qualified Simulation Evidence by determining how strongly that evidence may legitimately support, challenge, constrain, compare, or inform a defined evidential proposition within its governed simulation context.

The Module evaluates the material factors that strengthen, weaken, condition, narrow, or qualify evidential significance, including reality representation, assumption dependence, model applicability, input representativeness, scenario relevance, execution basis, repetition structure, output meaning, inference distance, simulation-to-reality correlation, uncertainty, evidence dependence, and temporal relevance.
SEWM does not determine whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient for a Validation Determination.
Its task is narrower:
to determine how much simulation-specific evidential significance qualified Simulation Evidence may legitimately carry before reliance boundaries and broader validation sufficiency are considered.
Core Question
How much evidential significance may qualified simulation evidence legitimately carry within its defined context?
Architectural Position
SEWM is the second module within SERBS.
It follows:
SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module
and precedes:
SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module.
SEQM establishes:
what legitimately qualifies as Simulation Evidence.
SEWM then establishes:
how much simulation-specific evidential weight that qualified evidence may carry.
SRBM subsequently determines:
how far reliance upon that evidence may legitimately extend.
The sequence is therefore:
Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary.
Internal Flow Position

Qualified Simulation Evidence → Evidential Proposition Alignment → Evidence Strength Factor Identification → Evidence Weakness Factor Identification → Dependence Assessment → Uncertainty Effect Assessment → Correlation Contribution Assessment → Contextual Weight Determination → Simulation Evidence Weight State → Weighted Simulation Evidence → SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module Operational Space
SEWM governs the space between:
qualified evidence
and
the evidential significance attributed to that evidence.
This operational space includes: evidence-to-proposition strength; representational contribution; assumption dependence; model applicability; environmental applicability; input representativeness; scenario relevance; scenario coverage relevance; execution consistency; repetition value; evidence independence; common-mode weakness; output directness; inference distance; correlation contribution; uncertainty effects; contradictory evidence; evidence convergence; evidence divergence; temporal relevance; evidence degradation; contextual weight assignment.
Operational Scope
SEWM applies whenever qualified simulation evidence is expected to carry evidential significance beyond mere existence.

It may govern evidence derived from: individual simulation runs; repeated simulations; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; large simulation campaigns; comparative simulations; sensitivity studies; failure simulations; mission simulations; engineering simulations; safety simulations; scientific simulations; digital twins; infrastructure simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; future simulation technologies.
The Module remains technology-neutral.
Its concern is not computational sophistication.
Its concern is:
how much evidential meaning the governed simulation basis can legitimately support. Evidence Qualification ≠ Evidence Weight
SEWM enforces the distinction:
Qualified Evidence ≠ Strong Evidence
SEQM may determine that an evidence object is:
Qualified
because it is sufficiently identified, traceable, contextualized, and interpretable.
SEWM may nevertheless determine that the evidence carries:
low evidential weight
because it depends heavily upon uncertain assumptions, weak reality representation, narrow scenarios, limited correlation, or other material constraints.
Conversely, conditionally qualified evidence may carry substantial evidential weight within a narrow context.
Qualification answers:
May this information function as evidence?
Weight answers:
How strongly may this evidence support the defined proposition?
Evidence Weight Is Proposition-Specific

Evidential weight does not exist in isolation.
The same simulation evidence may carry different weight for different propositions.
For example, a simulation may provide:
high evidential weight
for the proposition:
“Configuration A performs more efficiently than Configuration B under Scenario Set S.”
while providing:
low evidential weight
for the proposition:
“Configuration A will outperform Configuration B across unrestricted operational reality.”
SEWM therefore requires evidence weight to remain linked to the specific proposition being considered.
Representational Strength
SEWM evaluates how the governed reality representation affects evidential weight.
Relevant factors may include: whether materially relevant aspects of reality were represented; abstraction level; fidelity; resolution; excluded phenomena; proxy use; simplified interactions; representation limitations.
High representational sophistication does not automatically produce high evidential weight.
The relevant question is:
Was the reality necessary for this evidential proposition represented sufficiently?
Assumption Dependence
Simulation evidence may depend materially upon assumptions.
SEWM therefore evaluates: number of material assumptions; consequence of assumption failure; sensitivity to assumption variation; dependencies between assumptions; uncertainty surrounding assumptions; whether assumptions are empirically supported; whether results remain stable when assumptions change.

Evidence whose conclusion disappears under plausible assumption variation may legitimately carry less weight.
Model Applicability
A simulation model may be technically valid within one range while poorly suited to another.
SEWM therefore considers whether: the model was used within its intended applicability; extrapolation occurred; relevant behaviors are represented; model simplifications affect the proposition; parameter ranges remain supported; model structure creates known systematic limitations.
Model sophistication ≠ model applicability.
Input Representativeness
Qualified evidence may still carry limited weight where its input basis poorly represents the evidential context.
SEWM may consider: source relevance; distribution representativeness; temporal representativeness; environmental representativeness; population representativeness; transformation effects; synthetic-data dependence; input uncertainty; missing input conditions.
The relevant question is:
Do the inputs support the evidential proposition being made?
Scenario Relevance
Evidence weight depends partly upon whether the simulated scenarios materially address the proposition.
SEWM evaluates: relevance of scenarios to the evidential question; coverage of expected conditions; representation of material variations; edge-case inclusion; stress-condition inclusion; uncertainty coverage; scenario omission; scenario overconcentration.

A very large simulation campaign may carry little weight for a specific proposition if the decisive scenario was never simulated.
Execution Basis
SEWM may consider whether evidential weight is strengthened or weakened by the execution basis.
Relevant factors may include: controlled execution; configuration consistency; execution reproducibility; runtime intervention; failed executions; execution anomalies; incomplete runs; execution drift; campaign consistency; reconstructability.
SEWM does not govern execution itself.
That remains under SES.
It uses governed execution information as an input into evidential weight assessment.
Repetition Value Principle
Repeated simulation may increase evidential weight.
But repetition does not automatically do so.
SEWM distinguishes:
Repeated Evidence from Independent Evidential Support.
Repeated runs may increase weight where they legitimately test: stochastic variation; uncertainty; parameter variation; scenario diversity; sensitivity; reproducibility; robustness.
Repeated runs may add little weight where every execution reproduces the same material weakness.
Evidence Independence
SEWM requires evidence dependence to remain visible.
Evidence objects may share: the same model; the same assumptions; the same input source; the same scenario design; the same reality representation; the same execution infrastructure; the same correlation basis; the same transformation methodology.

Ten thousand evidence objects sharing one material weakness may not provide ten thousand independent confirmations.
Therefore:
Evidence Count ≠ Evidence Independence.
Common-Mode Weakness
A common-mode weakness is a material limitation shared across multiple evidence objects.
Examples include: one incorrect assumption; one omitted physical phenomenon; one unrepresentative dataset; one systematic sensor model error; one missing scenario class; one correlation deficiency; one shared transformation error.
SEWM requires common-mode weaknesses to reduce the apparent independence of aggregated evidence where materially relevant.
Output Directness
Evidence may carry different weight depending on how directly it arises from governed outputs.
SEWM distinguishes between:
Directly Observed Simulation Evidence
and
Derived or Inferred Simulation Evidence.
Direct evidence may include: observed state; threshold crossing; collision event; simulated failure; measured simulated parameter.
Derived evidence may require: aggregation; transformation; inference; statistical interpretation; causal interpretation; model-based extrapolation.
Derived evidence is not automatically weaker.
But the inferential pathway must be included when assessing weight.
Inference Distance
SEWM introduces Inference Distance as the methodological distance between:
what the simulation directly produced
and
what the evidence is being used to claim.
Short inference distance may occur where:

output → directly corresponding proposition.
Long inference distance may occur where:
output → transformation → aggregation → statistical inference → causal interpretation → real-world claim.
Greater inference distance may introduce additional dependence, assumptions, and uncertainty.
It must therefore remain visible in evidence-weight determination.
Correlation Contribution
Simulation-to-reality correlation established through SRCS may materially influence evidential weight.
SEWM may consider: strength of observed correlation; number of reality comparison points; diversity of comparison conditions; correlation uncertainty; known deviations; systematic discrepancies; temporal stability; correlation applicability to the evidential proposition.
However:
Correlation Strength ≠ Reality Equivalence.
Strong correlation may strengthen evidence.
It does not remove all remaining limitations.
Uncertainty Effect
SEWM requires material uncertainty to influence evidence weight.
Relevant uncertainty may arise from: inputs; assumptions; parameters; model structure; scenario selection; execution variability; outputs; inference; correlation; represented reality.
Uncertainty need not make evidence unusable.
It must make evidential weight more realistic.
Sensitivity Principle
Evidence weight should reflect the sensitivity of the evidential conclusion to material changes in the simulation basis.

Where small changes in: assumptions; inputs; parameters; scenarios; environmental conditions; model structure
produce major changes in the conclusion, evidence may require lower or more conditional weight.
Where the conclusion remains stable across materially relevant variation, evidence weight may be strengthened.
Evidence Convergence
Multiple evidence objects may increase evidential weight where they converge upon the same proposition through meaningfully different evidential pathways.
Convergence may be stronger where evidence differs across: models; assumptions; input sources; scenarios; methods; environmental configurations; execution structures; correlation sources.
SEWM therefore distinguishes:
Repeated Agreement
from
Independent Convergence.
Contradictory Evidence
SEWM must preserve material contradictory simulation evidence.
Evidence weight cannot legitimately be determined only from evidence supporting the preferred proposition.
Contradictory evidence may include: different model results; scenario-specific failures; alternative parameter outcomes; inconsistent repeated runs; operational disagreement; correlation failures; unexpected sensitivities.
Contradiction may: reduce evidential weight; narrow applicability; require conditional weighting; trigger further simulation; require separate evidence classes.
Evidence Weight States
SEWM may assign a governed evidence-weight state.
A minimum state model may include: 1. Indeterminate Weight

Evidence is qualified, but the simulation basis is insufficiently characterized to assign meaningful evidential weight. 2. Limited Weight
Evidence legitimately informs the proposition but is materially constrained by uncertainty, representation, assumptions, scenarios, correlation, dependence, or other weaknesses. 3. Moderate Weight
Evidence provides meaningful support within a defined context, while material limitations remain. 4. Substantial Weight
Evidence provides strong simulation-specific support for the defined proposition under the governed conditions. 5. Conditional Weight
Evidence may carry substantial or moderate weight only within explicitly defined conditions. 6. Degraded Weight
Previously assigned weight has materially weakened because of new information, reality change, model change, evidence contradiction, correlation deterioration, or another material change.
The states are not universal scientific truth categories.
They are governance states requiring defined organizational criteria. Weight State ≠ Validation Status
An evidence object with Substantial Weight is not automatically sufficient for validation.
Likewise, multiple substantial-weight evidence objects do not automatically establish validation sufficiency.
SEWM governs:
simulation-specific evidential significance.
VALIDOS® governs:
the sufficiency of the total validation basis.
Quantitative and Qualitative Weighting

SEWM may support: qualitative weighting; ordinal weighting; numerical weighting; probabilistic weighting; multi-factor weighting; evidence matrices; structured expert assessment; hybrid approaches.
SIMULOS® does not require one universal scoring method.
The weighting method must remain: explicit; interpretable; proposition-linked; context-aware; reproducible where appropriate; transparent about uncertainty; bounded by its intended use.
A numerical score must not create false precision.
Weight Calibration
Organizations may establish evidence-weight criteria appropriate to their context.
Calibration should consider: consequence of reliance; simulation type; evidential purpose; available reality data; expected uncertainty; model maturity; scenario criticality; safety relevance; operational significance.
SEWM governs the simulation-specific structure of weighting.
It does not establish organization-wide risk appetite or accountability.
Temporal Weight
Evidence weight may change over time.
Weight may increase where: new real-world correlation becomes available; additional independent evidence converges; model limitations are reduced; relevant scenario coverage expands.
Weight may decrease where: reality changes; the Simulation Object changes; assumptions become obsolete; contradictory evidence emerges; correlation deteriorates; new failure modes are discovered.
Evidence weight must therefore be reviewable rather than permanently fixed.
SEWM Boundary with SEQM

SEQM determines whether simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence.
SEWM determines how much evidential weight the qualified evidence may carry.
Therefore:
Qualification ≠ Weight.
SEWM must not retroactively redefine evidence qualification except where weight assessment reveals missing information that requires SEQM reassessment.
SEWM Boundary with SRBM
SEWM determines:
how strong the evidence is within its governed context.
SRBM determines:
how far reliance upon that evidence may extend.
A strong evidence object may still have a narrow reliance boundary.
Therefore:
High Weight ≠ Broad Reliance.
SEWM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SEWM does not determine: total evidence sufficiency; validation criteria satisfaction; Validation Determination; operational reliance authorization.
VALIDOS® remains responsible for broader validation governance.
The boundary is:
SEWM: How much simulation-specific evidential significance may this evidence carry?
VALIDOS®: Is the total evidence basis sufficient for the relevant validation claim and intended reliance?
SEWM Boundary with SRCS
SRCS determines the governed correlation relationship between simulation and reality.
SEWM may use correlation as one evidential-strength factor.
SEWM does not establish correlation independently.
SEWM Boundary with SSS
SSS governs scenario design and scenario coverage.
SEWM may assess how scenario relevance and coverage affect evidential weight.

It does not redesign or retroactively redefine the scenario space.
SEWM Boundary with SAS
SAS governs simulation assumptions.
SEWM evaluates how dependence upon those governed assumptions affects evidential weight.
It does not determine the universal validity of the assumptions.
SEWM Boundary with SIDS
SIDS governs simulation inputs and data at the simulation-input boundary.
SEWM evaluates how input representativeness and uncertainty affect evidential significance.
It does not become a general data-quality framework.
SEWM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SEWM does not determine general evidence integrity.
It assumes governed integrity information may be relevant to evidence-weight assessment where supplied by INTEGROS®.
Integrity and evidential weight remain distinct governance questions.
SEWM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may determine whether evidential records and execution evidence are sufficiently observable, preserved, verifiable, or auditable.
SEWM determines the simulation-specific evidential weight those governed records may support.
Auditability ≠ Evidential Weight.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SEWM implementation should establish: 1. Qualified Evidence Input
Receive a qualified Simulation Evidence object from SEQM. 2. Evidential Proposition
Confirm the specific proposition or question against which weight is being assessed. 3. Strength Factor Identification
Identify material factors strengthening evidential meaning. 4. Weakness Factor Identification

Identify material factors weakening or constraining evidential meaning. 5. Dependence Assessment
Identify dependencies across evidence objects and common-mode weaknesses. 6. Uncertainty Assessment
Determine how material uncertainty affects evidential significance. 7. Correlation Contribution
Determine how governed simulation-to-reality correlation affects evidence weight where relevant. 8. Contradictory Evidence Review
Identify materially conflicting or divergent evidence. 9. Weight Determination
Assign a governed simulation-specific evidence-weight state or value. 10. Weight Basis Record
Document the basis, conditions, uncertainty, dependencies, and factors supporting the determination.
Governance Outputs
SEWM may produce: Simulation Evidence Weight Assessment Evidence Strength Factor Record Evidence Weakness Factor Record Assumption Dependence Record Scenario Relevance Assessment Evidence Independence Assessment Common-Mode Weakness Record Inference Distance Record Correlation Contribution Record Evidence Uncertainty Effect Record Contradictory Evidence Record Evidence Convergence Record Simulation Evidence Weight State Simulation Evidence Weight Basis Weighted Simulation Evidence Object
These outputs provide the governed basis for:
SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module.
Enterprise Application
SEWM enables organizations to solve a problem that appears repeatedly in large-scale simulation programs:

a simulation may generate enormous quantities of qualified evidence without all of that evidence carrying equal significance.
An organization may use SEWM to determine: whether repeated simulations provide genuinely new evidence; whether millions of runs share one common model weakness; whether evidence depends critically upon one assumption; whether scenario coverage actually addresses the proposition being supported; whether correlation with reality meaningfully strengthens evidence; whether an aggregate success rate conceals important failures; whether multiple models independently converge; whether inference from output to real-world claim is short or extensive; whether uncertainty materially weakens the evidential conclusion; whether previously strong evidence has degraded after reality change; whether evidence should carry limited, moderate, substantial, conditional, indeterminate, or degraded weight.
SEWM therefore prevents organizations from equating:
more simulations
with
more proof.
A billion simulations using the same incomplete representation may provide less evidential strength than a smaller body of independently convergent simulations supported by strong reality correlation and materially different evidential pathways.
The Module gives organizations a method for distinguishing evidence volume from evidence strength.
Foundational Principles
Qualified evidence is not automatically strong evidence.
Evidence weight is proposition-specific.

Evidence volume is not evidential strength.
Repeated evidence is not automatically independent evidence.
Common assumptions create common evidential dependencies.
Simulation sophistication does not determine evidence weight.
Numerical precision does not create evidential certainty.
Scenario relevance matters more than scenario count.
Correlation may strengthen evidence without creating reality equivalence.
Independent convergence may carry greater evidential significance than repeated agreement generated through one common pathway.
High evidential weight does not automatically create broad reliance.
Simulation evidence should carry only the weight that its governed representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, execution basis, outputs, correlation, dependencies, and uncertainty can legitimately support.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Evidence Weight Module establishes the evidential significance layer within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by determining how strongly qualified Simulation Evidence may legitimately support, challenge, constrain, compare, or inform a defined proposition within its governed simulation context. Through governance of representational strength, assumption dependence, model applicability, input representativeness, scenario relevance, execution basis, repetition value, evidence independence, common-mode weakness, output directness, inference distance, correlation contribution, uncertainty, sensitivity, convergence, contradiction, temporal relevance, and evidence-weight states, SEWM prevents simulation evidence from acquiring strength merely through scale, repetition, complexity, numerical precision, or apparent sophistication. By separating evidence qualification from evidential weight, and evidential weight from reliance boundaries and validation sufficiency, SEWM preserves the methodological boundaries of SERBS and VALIDOS® while creating the governed basis required for downstream reliance control. Simulation evidence should carry neither more nor less evidential significance than the governed simulation conditions can legitimately support.
