chunks.text:
OOF™ Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM)
Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Exclusions
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 16 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Exclusions
Canonical Definition
Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) defines the governance conditions under which simulation-relevant objects, functions, behaviors, interactions, conditions, environments, populations, scenarios, temporal periods, failure modes, capabilities, variables, dependencies, and other material elements are explicitly identified as outside the governed Simulation Scope and preserved as visible limitations of the simulation inquiry.

SEXM establishes the formal negative boundary of a simulation: not merely what the simulation covers, but what it does not cover and therefore cannot legitimately be assumed to have simulated.
Operational Role
SEXM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The preceding modules establish:
SPM — Why is the simulation being performed?
SSCM — What exactly must the simulation cover?
SEXM asks:
What remains outside that scope, why is it excluded, and what consequences does the exclusion create for simulation interpretation?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Candidate Exclusions → Exclusion Classification → Exclusion Justification → Materiality Assessment → Exclusion Consequence → Governed Simulation Exclusions
SEXM prevents absence from becoming invisible.
Module Operational Space

SEXM governs: Simulation Exclusion identification, explicit exclusions, implicit-exclusion detection, object exclusions, component exclusions, functional exclusions, behavioral exclusions, interaction exclusions, environmental exclusions, operational-condition exclusions, spatial exclusions, temporal exclusions, population exclusions, capability exclusions, autonomy exclusions, scenario exclusions, event exclusions, failure-mode exclusions, variable exclusions, dependency exclusions, boundary-condition exclusions, data-related scope exclusions, excluded uncertainty domains, exclusion rationale, exclusion classification, exclusion materiality, exclusion dependencies, exclusion consequences, exclusion conflicts, exclusion change, exclusion traceability, and Simulation Exclusion status.
Module Function
A simulation can appear broader than it actually is when omitted elements remain undocumented.
SEXM exists to prevent:
Not Simulated → Not Mentioned → Assumed Covered
from becoming an acceptable simulation-governance pathway.
Its function is to transform material absence into governed information.
The required relationship becomes:
Excluded Element → Reason for Exclusion → Materiality → Affected Scope → Interpretive Consequence
An exclusion does not automatically make a simulation inadequate.
An undisclosed material exclusion may.
Simulation Exclusion

A Simulation Exclusion is an identifiable simulation-relevant element intentionally or necessarily maintained outside the governed Simulation Scope.
An exclusion may concern: part of the Simulation Object, a system function, a behavior, an interaction, an environment, an operating condition, a population, a time period, a scenario, a failure mode, a dependency, or another materially relevant dimension.
Positive and Negative Simulation Boundaries
SSCM establishes the positive boundary:
What is inside the simulation inquiry?
SEXM establishes the negative boundary:
What is outside the simulation inquiry?
Together they create a more complete scope structure:
Included Space | Governed Boundary | Excluded Space
A simulation boundary is methodologically stronger when both sides are visible.
Explicit Exclusion Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material element outside Simulation Scope should remain explicitly identifiable where its absence could affect interpretation of the simulation or its outputs.
Silence is not a sufficient exclusion mechanism.
Exclusion Does Not Mean Irrelevance
An excluded element may remain operationally important.
For example:
Snow conditions
may be excluded from an autonomous-vehicle simulation because the current simulation campaign addresses dry and rainy environments.
This does not establish:
Snow is irrelevant.
It establishes:
Snow is outside the current governed Simulation Scope.
Exclusion Classification

Simulation Exclusions may be classified according to why they exist.
Possible classes include: Purpose-Based Exclusion
The element is not required for the governed Simulation Purpose.
Scope-Based Exclusion
The element falls outside the explicitly approved Simulation Scope.
Capability-Based Exclusion
The available simulation environment cannot adequately represent the element.
Evidence-Based Exclusion
Required inputs or supporting information are insufficient.
Methodological Exclusion
The simulation methodology is not suitable for representing the element.
Resource-Based Exclusion
The element is omitted because of time, computational, financial, infrastructure, or other resource constraints.
Dependency-Based Exclusion
The element cannot be simulated because a required dependency is unavailable or unresolved.
Uncertainty-Based Exclusion
The element cannot be represented with sufficient confidence for the intended inquiry.
Regulatory or Governance Exclusion
Applicable governance conditions prevent or constrain its inclusion.
Deferred Exclusion
The element is intentionally reserved for a later simulation cycle.
The classification should make clear why the exclusion exists.
Intentional Exclusion
An Intentional Exclusion is deliberately established before or during simulation planning.
Intentional exclusions should remain traceable to their rationale.
A deliberate exclusion may be completely legitimate where it is compatible with the Simulation Purpose.
Necessary Exclusion

A Necessary Exclusion exists where an element cannot reasonably be included under the current simulation conditions.
For example: unavailable data, unavailable model capability, unresolved physics, unavailable environmental representation, inaccessible dependencies, or insufficient computational capability.
Necessary exclusions remain limitations even when unavoidable.
Deferred Exclusion
A material element may be excluded from one simulation cycle because it will be addressed separately.
For example:
Nominal Operation Simulation
may precede:
Failure & Recovery Simulation
The first simulation must not be represented as having covered the deferred failure conditions.
Object Exclusion
Parts of the Simulation Object may remain outside scope.
For example:
A spacecraft simulation may include:
Guidance + Navigation + Propulsion
while excluding:
Crew Life-Support Dynamics
SEXM preserves that distinction.
Functional Exclusion
A system may possess functions not examined by the simulation.
These functions should remain identifiable where their omission affects interpretation.
Behavioral Exclusion
Behavioral modes may be excluded.
Examples include: degraded behavior, emergency behavior, adversarial behavior, adaptive behavior, rare behavior, or human intervention.
Simulation of nominal behavior does not imply simulation of excluded behaviors.
Interaction Exclusion
A simulation may represent multiple actors while excluding certain interactions among them.
This distinction matters because:

Objects Represented ≠ All Interactions Represented
For example, two autonomous agents may both exist in a simulation while agent-to-agent negotiation remains excluded.
Environmental Exclusion
Environmental conditions may materially affect simulation outcomes.
Possible exclusions include: extreme temperature, rain, snow, radiation, low visibility, high wind, electromagnetic interference, network degradation, terrain classes, or other operational environments.
Environmental exclusions should remain connected to output applicability.
Operational Condition Exclusion
A simulation may cover:
Normal Operation
while excluding:
Emergency Operation
or:
Maximum Load Conditions
Such exclusions must remain visible wherever simulation outputs could otherwise be interpreted more broadly.
Spatial Exclusion
Simulation applicability may exclude specific geographic, physical, or logical regions.
A simulation performed for one operating region must not silently imply coverage of excluded regions.
Temporal Exclusion
A simulation may exclude: startup periods, long-term degradation, seasonal variation, future system states, specific mission phases, or extended operating durations.
A simulation covering short-term behavior cannot establish long-term behavior where long-term dynamics remain excluded.
Population Exclusion
Where humans, users, agents, organizations, or other populations are relevant, specific groups may remain outside scope.
For example:
Adult Population Included

Pediatric Population Excluded
The exclusion must remain visible wherever outputs could otherwise be generalized.
Capability Exclusion
A simulation of an AI or autonomous system may intentionally exclude capabilities.
For example:
Navigation Included
Autonomous Tool Execution Excluded
Simulation results must remain bounded accordingly.
Autonomy Exclusion
A simulation may examine a system under:
Human Supervision
while excluding:
Fully Autonomous Operation
The system's broader technical capability does not remove this exclusion.
Scenario Exclusion
Not every possible scenario must be simulated.
SEXM governs which materially relevant scenario classes remain outside the simulation campaign.
Examples may include: rare events, edge cases, adversarial scenarios, extreme-load scenarios, cascading failures, or multi-system emergencies.
Failure-Mode Exclusion
Failure modes may be excluded from a simulation.
Where safety, resilience, recovery, or reliability conclusions are intended, such exclusions may become highly material.
SEXM does not determine whether a failure mode must be simulated.
It ensures that exclusion remains visible and interpretable.
Dependency Exclusion
A simulation may exclude a dependency or simplify its role.
Examples include: external infrastructure, third-party systems, communications networks, human operators, supply dependencies, external AI services, or environmental dependencies.
The excluded dependency may still materially influence real-world behavior.

Variable Exclusion
Some variables may be held constant, omitted, or intentionally removed from the simulation inquiry.
Where the excluded variable could materially affect outcomes, the exclusion should remain explicit.
Excluded Uncertainty
A simulation may deliberately avoid or defer uncertainty domains that cannot yet be sufficiently represented.
SEXM requires such uncertainty exclusions to remain visible rather than being converted into artificial certainty.
Implicit Exclusion
An Implicit Exclusion exists where an element is outside actual simulation coverage but has not been formally declared outside scope.
Implicit exclusions are methodologically dangerous because they can create false assumptions of coverage.
Implicit-Exclusion Detection
SEXM should support comparison between:
Simulation Purpose
Governed Simulation Scope
Planned Representation
Scenario Coverage
and:
Actual Simulation Coverage
to identify material elements that have disappeared without explicit exclusion.
Unknown Exclusion
Some relevant conditions may not be known when Simulation Scope is established.
Where later analysis identifies a previously unknown omitted condition, it should become a governed exclusion, scope gap, or scope-change question rather than remaining invisible.
Exclusion Justification
Material exclusions should have a documented basis.

Possible justifications include: not relevant to current purpose, outside approved scope, separately simulated, technically unavailable, insufficient evidence, insufficient model capability, unacceptable uncertainty, deferred to future simulation, or resource limitation.
A justification explains the exclusion.
It does not automatically make the exclusion acceptable for every intended interpretation.
Exclusion Materiality
Not all exclusions have equal significance.
An exclusion is material where its absence could reasonably affect: simulation design, output interpretation, comparison, applicability, decision relevance, safety relevance, reliance, or downstream validation.
Materiality should be assessed relative to the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope.
Material Exclusion
A Material Simulation Exclusion is an exclusion capable of changing the meaning, applicability, or interpretation of simulation outputs.
Material exclusions should propagate downstream.
Non-Material Exclusion
An exclusion may be non-material where its absence cannot reasonably affect the governed inquiry.
Non-materiality should not be inferred merely because an excluded element produced no observed problem.
Exclusion Consequence
Each material exclusion should identify the consequence it creates.
Possible consequences include:
No Material Consequence
Interpretation Limitation
Applicability Limitation
Scenario Limitation
Coverage Limitation
Representation Limitation
Output Qualification Required

Additional Simulation Required
or:
Consequence Undetermined Exclusion Propagation
Material exclusions should remain available to downstream SIMULOS® governance.
Conceptually:
Exclusion → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Reality Correlation
This prevents an exclusion declared early in the lifecycle from disappearing before outputs are interpreted.
Exclusion Dependency
One exclusion may create additional exclusions.
For example:
External Communication Network Excluded
may also require exclusion of:
Network-Failure Recovery Behavior
where that behavior depends upon representation of the network.
SEXM should preserve such dependency chains.
Compound Exclusions
Several individually limited exclusions may collectively become material.
For example:
Night Excluded
Rain Excluded
High-Speed Operation Excluded
Emergency Braking Excluded
may collectively make a broad claim of:
Urban Autonomous Driving Simulation
methodologically misleading.
SEXM therefore permits cumulative exclusion assessment. Exclusion–Purpose Conflict
An Exclusion–Purpose Conflict exists where an excluded element is materially required to answer the governed Simulation Purpose.
Example:
Simulation Purpose: Evaluate emergency landing safety.
Exclusion: Hydraulic failure conditions.
If hydraulic failure is materially relevant to emergency landing safety, the exclusion creates a direct purpose conflict. Exclusion–Scope Conflict

An exclusion conflicts with Simulation Scope where an element is simultaneously represented as:
inside governed scope
and:
excluded from actual simulation coverage.
Such a conflict must be resolved or preserved explicitly as a scope gap.
Exclusion Cannot Be Hidden by Abstraction
Simplifying a material element through abstraction is not necessarily equivalent to excluding it.
However, where abstraction removes the material behavior the inquiry depends upon, the architecture should prevent the simplification from being used to disguise functional exclusion.
Reality Representation governance addresses the quality of representation.
SEXM governs whether the relevant element is actually inside or outside the simulation inquiry.
Exclusion Cannot Become Assumption by Default
An excluded element and an assumed condition are not the same governance concept.
For example:
Wind Excluded
is different from:
Wind Assumed Constant at 5 m/s
The first removes wind dynamics from scope.
The second represents wind through an assumption.
SEXM preserves this distinction while later Assumption governance governs the assumption itself.
Exclusion Cannot Become Validation
The fact that an excluded condition was not simulated cannot support a positive conclusion about that condition.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Not Simulated ≠ Successfully Simulated
and:
Excluded ≠ Validated No Silent Exclusion Rule

A material simulation element must not disappear from the governed inquiry without becoming either explicitly excluded, represented as a scope gap, or returned for scope reassessment.
No Exclusion Concealment Rule
An exclusion must not be hidden because disclosure would weaken the perceived completeness of a simulation.
No Convenience Relevance Rule
An element must not be declared irrelevant solely because: it is difficult to model, data are unavailable, computation is expensive, the current tool cannot represent it, or its inclusion produces unfavorable outcomes.
These conditions may justify exclusion.
They do not establish irrelevance.
No Exclusion-to-Coverage Conversion Rule
A collection of successfully simulated conditions cannot convert excluded conditions into covered conditions.
Covered Scope + Excluded Scope ≠ Complete Scope
unless the exclusions are genuinely outside the required inquiry.
No Retrospective Exclusion Rule
A condition must not be retrospectively declared excluded merely because its simulation produced undesirable results.
Where a condition was within the governed Simulation Scope during execution, removing it after results are known constitutes a material scope change and must be governed accordingly.
No Exclusion Generalization Rule
Results obtained inside included conditions must not automatically be generalized to excluded conditions.
Exclusion Change
Simulation Exclusions may change.
An element may move:
Excluded → Included
or:
Included → Excluded

Such changes can alter downstream simulation requirements.
Exclusion Removal
When an excluded element becomes included, its removal from the exclusion set should trigger assessment of whether new: representation, assumptions, model capability, inputs, scenarios, execution, or output interpretation
are required.
New Exclusion
A new exclusion introduced after simulation planning may materially narrow the inquiry.
The resulting scope and downstream applicability should be reassessed.
Exclusion Status
Possible statuses may include:
Established Exclusion
Conditionally Excluded
Deferred
Temporarily Excluded
Exclusion Under Review
Exclusion Conflicted
or:
Exclusion Undetermined Exclusion Register
A governed simulation may maintain a Simulation Exclusion Register.
The register may identify: Exclusion ID, excluded element, exclusion class, rationale, affected scope, materiality, dependencies, downstream consequences, status, effective point, and change history.
Exclusion Traceability
Material exclusions should remain traceable through simulation outputs.
A reviewer examining an output should be capable of determining whether a relevant condition was:
Included
Excluded
Not Represented
or:
Undetermined
where that distinction materially affects interpretation.
Failure Conditions

SEXM governance failure may exist where: material exclusions are undocumented, excluded conditions are represented as simulated, absence is treated as successful coverage, an exclusion conflicts with the Simulation Purpose without disclosure, exclusions conflict with declared Simulation Scope, technical inability is presented as irrelevance, resource constraints are hidden, material excluded dependencies remain invisible, cumulative exclusions materially narrow the simulation without disclosure, excluded populations are generalized into represented populations, excluded operating conditions are treated as covered, retrospective exclusions remove unfavorable results, excluded uncertainty is converted into apparent certainty, exclusions fail to propagate to downstream interpretation, or simulation claims extend into explicitly excluded space.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Excluded Simulation Elements
Determine which materially relevant objects, functions, behaviors, conditions, interactions, environments, populations, scenarios, dependencies, and other elements remain outside the governed Simulation Scope. 2. Classify and Justify Exclusions
Establish why each material exclusion exists and distinguish purpose-based, capability-based, methodological, resource-based, deferred, dependency-based, and other applicable exclusion classes. 3. Assess Materiality and Consequence

Determine whether each exclusion affects simulation coverage, representation, interpretation, applicability, downstream validation, or required additional simulation. 4. Govern Exclusion Dependencies and Change
Preserve cumulative exclusions, dependency effects, inclusion/exclusion transitions, conflicts, and material changes. 5. Preserve Exclusion Traceability
Maintain a Simulation Exclusion Register and propagate material exclusions into downstream simulation design, execution, outputs, and interpretation.
Governance Outputs

SEXM may produce: Simulation Exclusion Definition, Simulation Exclusion Register, Simulation Exclusion Record, Exclusion Classification Record, Exclusion Rationale Record, Exclusion Materiality Assessment, Exclusion Consequence Record, Purpose-Based Exclusion Record, Scope-Based Exclusion Record, Capability-Based Exclusion Record, Methodological Exclusion Record, Resource-Based Exclusion Record, Evidence-Based Exclusion Record, Dependency-Based Exclusion Record, Uncertainty-Based Exclusion Record, Deferred Exclusion Record, Object Exclusion Record, Functional Exclusion Record, Behavioral Exclusion Record, Interaction Exclusion Record, Environmental Exclusion Record, Operational Condition Exclusion Record, Spatial Exclusion Record, Temporal Exclusion Record, Population Exclusion Record, Capability Exclusion Record, Autonomy Exclusion Record, Scenario Exclusion Record, Failure-Mode Exclusion Record, Dependency Exclusion Record, Variable Exclusion Record, Implicit Exclusion Record, Unknown Exclusion Record, Compound Exclusion Assessment, Exclusion–Purpose Conflict Record, Exclusion–Scope Conflict Record, Exclusion Change Record, Exclusion Removal Record, New Exclusion Record, Simulation Exclusion Status, and Simulation Exclusion Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Safety Simulation
Scenario
A mobile industrial robot is simulated to examine collision avoidance within a warehouse.
The simulation covers:
normal warehouse traffic,
human workers,
standard lighting,
and:

defined operating speeds.
It does not represent emergency power loss, smoke-obscured sensors, or operation outside the warehouse. Application
SEXM formally establishes these as Simulation Exclusions.
Emergency power loss is classified as a Deferred Exclusion scheduled for a separate safety simulation.
Smoke-obscured perception is classified as a Capability-Based Exclusion because the current environment cannot adequately represent the sensor degradation.
Outdoor operation is a Purpose-Based Exclusion because it falls outside the governed Simulation Purpose. Result
The simulation may support interpretation within its governed warehouse conditions.
It cannot legitimately be presented as comprehensive simulation of the robot across emergency, degraded-visibility, and outdoor environments. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft simulation examines orbital insertion and autonomous navigation.
Solar radiation effects are simplified, crew behavior is excluded, and one rare propulsion-failure mode is not represented because the required physical model is unavailable. Application
SEXM distinguishes the three conditions.
Simplified solar radiation remains inside the simulation and is governed through Reality Representation and Assumption governance.
Crew behavior is an explicit Scope Exclusion.
The propulsion failure becomes a Capability-Based Material Exclusion because the simulation environment cannot currently represent it. Result

The architecture prevents all three conditions from being treated identically.
The simulation record can distinguish:
represented through simplification,
explicitly excluded,
and:
materially excluded because simulation capability is insufficient.
This distinction remains available when simulation outputs are later interpreted.
Architectural Position
Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The internal progression is:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Simulation Depth & Precision
SPM establishes why the simulation exists.
SSCM establishes what the simulation must cover.
SEXM establishes what remains outside that governed inquiry and what consequences follow from that absence.
The subsequent modules determine where the resulting simulation is contextually applicable and how deeply and precisely the simulation must represent the intended inquiry.
SEXM does not govern general integrity under INTEGROS®, Validation Scope under VALIDOS®, actual Operational Reality under ORA™, or the fidelity of Reality Representation under RRS.
It governs specifically:
the explicit negative boundary of the simulation inquiry.
Foundational Principle
A simulation is governed not only by what it includes, but by whether everything materially excluded from the inquiry remains visible wherever that absence can affect the meaning of its results.

Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) establishes the negative boundary of governed simulation by identifying, classifying, justifying, assessing, and preserving the objects, functions, behaviors, interactions, environments, populations, scenarios, failure modes, dependencies, uncertainties, and other material elements that remain outside Simulation Scope. Through explicit exclusion governance, materiality assessment, dependency mapping, anti-concealment rules, change control, exclusion propagation, and complete traceability, SEXM prevents unmodeled conditions from becoming invisible assumptions of coverage and prevents simulation results from expanding into conditions that were never simulated. By making absence itself governable, SEXM ensures that the limitations of a simulation remain as structurally visible as the conditions it successfully represents.

OOF™ Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM)
Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Input Identification
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Input Identification
Canonical Definition
Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM) defines the governance framework through which every materially relevant data object, value, signal, measurement, state, distribution, event, record, synthetic input, derived input, human-supplied input, model-generated input, or other information capable of influencing a simulation is identified, classified, distinguished, source-referenced, bound to its simulation role, and maintained as a traceable Simulation Input.

SIIM establishes the first internal governance space of SIDS by determining what is entering the simulation before questions of representativeness, transformation, temporal applicability, and uncertainty are evaluated.
Operational Role
SIIM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The preceding Parent Standard, Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES), establishes the controlled model and environment through which simulation occurs.
SIIM asks:
What information is proposed to enter that governed simulation structure, what exactly is each input, where does it originate, and what role can it influence?
The governed progression is:
Governed Simulation Model & Environment → Input Requirement → Proposed Input → Input Identification → Input Classification → Origin Reference → Simulation Role Binding → Simulation Input Register
The resulting identified input basis becomes available to the subsequent SIDS modules for representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty governance.
Module Operational Space

SIIM governs: simulation input discovery, input identification, input naming, input distinction, input classification, input origin reference, source association, input type, input format, input unit, input semantics, input state, input role, input ownership reference where relevant, observed inputs, measured inputs, historical inputs, live inputs, derived inputs, estimated inputs, synthetic inputs, human-supplied inputs, externally supplied inputs, model-generated inputs, scenario-specified inputs, input-to-object binding, input-to-model binding, input-to-environment binding, input-to-configuration binding, input-to-scenario reference, input dependencies, composite inputs, duplicate inputs, ambiguous inputs, unidentified inputs, input substitution visibility, input-set membership, input identifiers, and input traceability.
Module Function
SIIM exists to prevent a simulation from consuming materially influential information whose identity or role is unclear.

It prevents: unidentified inputs entering simulation execution, ambiguous variables being treated as equivalent, different data objects sharing an indistinguishable identity, source origin disappearing after ingestion, synthetic information appearing as observed information, derived information appearing as directly measured information, historical information appearing as live information, units or semantics becoming detached from values, input roles becoming unclear, substitutions occurring invisibly, input dependencies being hidden, and simulation outputs becoming impossible to reconstruct because the actual consumed inputs cannot be determined.
Simulation Input
A Simulation Input is any identifiable information object capable of materially influencing: simulation initialization, model behavior, environmental state, actor behavior, state transitions, simulation progression, scenario conditions, or simulation outputs.
A Simulation Input may be:
Data
Value
Signal
Measurement
State
Event
Distribution
Record
Sequence
Instruction
External Observation
Synthetic Information
or another governed information object consumed by the simulation.
Material Input
SIIM focuses on material Simulation Inputs.
An input is material where changing, removing, substituting, or misidentifying it could materially affect: simulation configuration, simulation behavior, scenario conditions, execution, output, interpretation, or downstream reliance.

Not every technical field requires equal governance depth.
Input Requirement
Before an input is identified, the simulation may establish an Input Requirement.
An Input Requirement defines what information the simulation needs without presupposing which specific data object will satisfy that need.
For example:
Requirement: Current external temperature
may later be satisfied by:
Sensor TEMP-04 measurement
This distinction prevents the required information from being confused with the particular source selected to provide it.
Input Identification
Every material Simulation Input should be sufficiently identifiable before governed simulation use.
Identification may establish: Simulation Input Identifier, input name, input description, input type, input origin, source reference, unit, format, semantic meaning, temporal reference where known, transformation state, applicable Simulation Object, applicable model or environment element, and intended simulation role.
Simulation Input Identifier
A Simulation Input Identifier provides a persistent reference through which a material input can remain distinguishable throughout the simulation lifecycle.
Conceptually:
SI-0001
may identify one governed input object.
The identifier should remain connected to the actual input rather than merely to a display label. Identity ≠ Variable Name
SIMULOS® establishes:
A variable name is not sufficient input identity where materially different information can exist under that same name.
For example:

Temperature
could refer to: external temperature, engine temperature, battery temperature, historical average temperature, predicted temperature, or synthetic scenario temperature.
SIIM requires sufficient distinction.
Input Naming
Input names should communicate the represented information with enough specificity to prevent material ambiguity.
Where necessary:
Temperature
should become:
External Ambient Temperature
or another sufficiently precise representation.
Naming alone does not establish full identity, but poor naming can weaken traceability.
Input Semantics
SIIM governs what the input means, not only how it is technically encoded.
For example:
0.75
may represent: 75% probability, normalized sensor output, friction coefficient, model confidence, actuator position, or another quantity.
The numerical value alone is insufficient.
Input Units
Where units materially affect interpretation, they must remain associated with the input.
For example:
50
is not a sufficiently defined physical input if it could mean:
50 km/h
50 mph
50 °C
or:
50 milliseconds.
Input Format
Input format may include: scalar, vector, matrix, categorical value, time series, event stream, image, audio, text, geospatial data, structured record, distribution, or another machine- or human-readable form.
Format should remain identifiable where it affects simulation interpretation.
Input Classification
SIIM classifies Simulation Inputs according to their material origin and role.

Possible classes include: Observed Input
Information obtained through observation of represented reality.
Measured Input
Information produced through a measurement process.
Historical Input
Information originating from a previous period.
Live Input
Information supplied from an active operational environment during or near simulation execution.
Estimated Input
Information established through estimation where direct measurement or observation is unavailable.
Derived Input
Information calculated from other information objects.
Synthetic Input
Information generated rather than directly observed from the represented reality.
Human-Supplied Input
Information introduced by a human participant or operator.
Externally Supplied Input
Information supplied by an external organization, system, service, or data provider.
Model-Generated Input
Information produced by another model and consumed by the simulation.
Scenario-Specified Input
Information deliberately introduced to establish a scenario condition.
One input may require multiple classifications where its provenance or role is composite.
Classification Must Follow Reality
SIMULOS® establishes:
Input classification must describe how the information was actually produced, not how the simulation wishes to interpret it.
A model-generated estimate does not become a measured input merely because it is formatted like sensor data.
Input Origin
Input Origin identifies the point from which the information entered the governed simulation chain.

Origin may refer to: sensor, database, organization, person, operational system, AI system, external model, simulator, scientific instrument, historical dataset, synthetic generator, or another identifiable origin.
Origin ≠ Reliability
SIIM identifies origin.
It does not establish that the origin is reliable.
Source reliability may require governance under VALIDOS® or another applicable architecture.
The distinction is important:
Known Origin ≠ Trusted Origin Origin Preservation
Where materially relevant, origin should remain attached throughout:
Origin → Input → Transformation → Simulation Use
Subsequent transformation should not silently erase the origin of the information.
Source Reference
An input may maintain a reference to the source object or system from which it originates.
The source reference may include: source identifier, system identifier, dataset identifier, sensor identifier, provider identifier, model identifier, or another persistent reference.
Input State
An input may exist in different states.
For example:
Raw
Cleaned
Normalized
Aggregated
Derived
Imputed
Synthetic
or:
Transformed
SIIM identifies the state.
SDTM — Simulation Data Transformation Module governs the transformation itself.
Raw Input
A Raw Simulation Input is information before simulation-specific transformation.
Raw does not mean: correct, reliable, representative, complete, or suitable.
It only describes its position relative to subsequent processing.
Derived Input

A Derived Input should preserve the relationship:
Source Input(s) → Derivation → Derived Input
SIIM identifies the resulting object as derived.
SDTM governs the methodological transformation.
Synthetic Input Identification
Synthetic inputs must remain distinguishable from directly observed or measured information.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Synthetic information must never acquire an observed-data identity merely because it is technically indistinguishable in format.
Estimated Input Identification
Estimated values should remain identifiable as estimates.
For example:
Estimated Vehicle Mass = 1,850 kg
should not silently become:
Measured Vehicle Mass = 1,850 kg
after ingestion.
Live vs Historical Input
SIIM distinguishes whether information originates from:
current or near-current operational conditions
or:
historical records.
Detailed temporal suitability is governed by STDM — Simulation Temporal Data Module.
SIIM preserves the initial classification required for that assessment.
Input Role
An input should remain connected to the role it performs in the simulation.
Possible roles include: initialization, state update, environmental condition, actor condition, control signal, disturbance, behavioral input, scenario condition, external event, calibration reference, or another defined simulation function.
Input-to-Simulation Object Binding
Where relevant:
Simulation Input → Simulation Object
should remain identifiable.

This prevents inputs associated with one Simulation Object from being silently applied to another.
Input-to-Model Binding
Where an input affects a specific model component:
Simulation Input → Model Component
should remain traceable.
This supports later analysis of which information could have influenced which simulated behavior.
Input-to-Environment Binding
Inputs affecting environmental conditions should preserve:
Simulation Input → Environment Element / State
For example:
Rainfall Input → Road Surface Environment State Input-to-Configuration Binding
Where an input is valid only under a particular simulation configuration, that relationship should remain visible.
Input-to-Scenario Reference
An input may be associated with one or more scenarios.
SIIM records the association where known.
SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard governs scenario design and coverage.
Input Dependency
One input may depend upon another.
For example:
Vehicle Speed
may contribute to:
Calculated Braking Distance Input
The dependency should remain visible where it materially affects traceability.
Composite Input
A Composite Input combines multiple information objects into one simulation-consumed input.
Conceptually:
Input A + Input B + Input C → Composite Input D
The composite should not erase the identities of its materially relevant components.
Duplicate Input
Two technically separate inputs may represent the same underlying information.

Duplicate inputs can create: double counting, unintended weighting, correlated influence, or false independence.
SIIM identifies material duplication for subsequent treatment.
Ambiguous Input
An Ambiguous Simulation Input exists where the available information is insufficient to determine exactly: what the input represents, where it originated, which unit applies, which object it describes, or which role it performs.
Material ambiguity should be resolved or explicitly preserved before simulation use.
Unidentified Input
An Unidentified Simulation Input is a materially influential input whose identity cannot be sufficiently established.
Possible treatment may include:
Resolve
Restrict
Exclude
or:
Escalate for further assessment
depending upon the simulation context.
No Anonymous Material Input Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A materially influential input should not enter governed simulation execution anonymously.
Input Equivalence
Two inputs should not be considered equivalent merely because: their values match, their names match, their formats match, or they occupy the same software field.
Input equivalence may depend upon: semantics, origin, unit, population, environment, time, transformation, and simulation role.
Input Substitution
An identified input may later be substituted.
For example:
Live Sensor Input
may be replaced with:
Historical Replay Input
The replacement should receive its own identity and classification.
The simulation record should preserve:

Original Intended Input → Substitution → Actual Consumed Input Actual Consumed Input
SIIM distinguishes:
Planned Input
from:
Actual Consumed Input.
This distinction becomes critical when execution does not consume exactly what was originally configured.
Input Set Membership
Each material Simulation Input may belong to one or more governed Simulation Input Sets.
Conceptually:
Simulation Input Set SIS-001
may contain:
SI-001 + SI-002 + SI-003 + SI-004
Input-set governance enables reconstruction of the complete information basis of an execution.
Input Set Identifier
A Simulation Input Set may receive a persistent identifier.
This allows:
Execution → Input Set → Individual Inputs
to remain traceable.
Input Set Composition
The composition of an Input Set should identify materially relevant: inputs, input versions, classifications, states, source references, and applicable simulation configuration.
Input Version Distinction
Where materially changed information exists under the same logical input identity, versions should remain distinguishable.
For example:
Weather Dataset v3
should not silently overwrite:
Weather Dataset v2
where previous executions relied upon v2.
Input Change
A material input may change because: source data changes, values change, origin changes, classification changes, format changes, unit changes, derivation changes, or its simulation role changes.
The changed input should remain distinguishable from the previous state where required for reconstruction.

Input Identity Continuity
Input Identity Continuity preserves the relationship between successive states or versions of the same logical input.
Conceptually:
SI-001 v1 → SI-001 v2 → SI-001 v3
while preventing materially different objects from being falsely treated as one unchanged input.
Point-in-Time Input Identity
SIIM supports reconstruction of:
Which exact input existed at the time of a particular simulation execution?
This is essential where input data changes after execution.
No Retrospective Input Replacement Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Updating an input must not silently rewrite the historical input identity of completed simulation executions.
Input Traceability
SIIM establishes the traceability foundation:
Input Requirement
↓
Simulation Input
↓
Origin / Source Reference
↓
Classification
↓
Simulation Role
↓
Model / Environment / Scenario Binding
↓
Input Set
↓
Simulation Execution Reference
This chain enables later governance of simulation behavior and outputs.
Input Identification Status
A material Simulation Input may receive an identification status such as:
Identified
Conditionally Identified
Ambiguous
Unidentified
Superseded
or:
Excluded
The status concerns input identity.
It does not establish representativeness, temporal suitability, uncertainty, or general validity.
Identification Sufficiency
Input identification is sufficient when the information necessary to distinguish and trace the material input is adequate for its intended simulation role.

The required identification depth may vary with: simulation consequence, input influence, system complexity, simulation purpose, and downstream reliance.
Identification Failure
An Input Identification Failure occurs where a material input cannot be sufficiently distinguished or traced for governed use.
Possible causes include: missing origin, ambiguous semantics, unknown units, indistinguishable versions, undocumented substitution, unknown derivation, or inability to determine the actual consumed input.
Identification Failure ≠ Data Invalidity
Failure to identify an input sufficiently does not prove the underlying information is false.
It establishes that the information cannot currently support the required level of governed simulation traceability.
Simulation Input Register
SIIM may maintain a Simulation Input Register containing material Simulation Inputs and their governance attributes.
A register entry may contain: Simulation Input Identifier, input name, description, classification, origin, source reference, unit, format, semantic definition, input state, simulation role, applicable object, model binding, environment binding, scenario reference, input-set membership, version, and identification status.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Input Requirements
Determine which information the governed simulation requires. 2. Discover Material Proposed Inputs

Identify all materially influential information proposed for simulation use. 3. Assign Simulation Input Identity
Create a persistent identifier for each material input where appropriate. 4. Define Input Meaning
Record sufficient: name, semantics, unit, format, and represented quantity or state.
5. Classify Input Origin and Type
Determine whether the input is: observed, measured, historical, live, estimated, derived, synthetic, human-supplied, externally supplied, model-generated, scenario-specified, or another defined class.
6. Preserve Origin and Source Reference
Bind the input to its identifiable origin and source where available. 7. Bind the Input to Simulation Role
Establish which: Simulation Object, model component, environment element, configuration, or scenario context
the input may influence. 8. Identify Dependencies and Composite Inputs
Preserve material relationships between inputs. 9. Detect Ambiguity, Duplication, and Substitution
Identify materially unclear, duplicated, replaced, or unexpectedly consumed inputs. 10. Establish Input Set Membership
Bind the identified inputs to the applicable Simulation Input Set. 11. Assign Identification Status
Determine whether each material input is sufficiently identified for further SIDS governance. 12. Preserve Input Traceability
Maintain the chain from input requirement and origin through simulation role and eventual execution use.

The module prevents:

Architectural Position
Simulation Input Identification is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The complete SIDS progression is:
Simulation Input Identification
↓
Simulation Data Representativeness
↓
Simulation Data Transformation
↓
Simulation Temporal Data
↓
Simulation Input Uncertainty
SIIM therefore establishes the identity layer upon which all subsequent SIDS governance depends.

Representativeness cannot be meaningfully assessed until the input being assessed is known.
Transformation cannot be governed unless the source and resulting input can be distinguished.
Temporal applicability cannot be evaluated without an identifiable information object.
Input uncertainty cannot remain attached to an input whose identity is unstable.
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot govern the suitability of information it cannot first identify, distinguish, classify, and trace to the role through which that information can influence simulated behavior.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Input Identification Module establishes the identity and traceability foundation of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing how materially influential data, values, signals, measurements, states, distributions, events, synthetic information, derived information, and other simulation inputs are discovered, identified, classified, source-referenced, distinguished, versioned, bound to their simulation roles, assembled into controlled Input Sets, and preserved across execution history. Through explicit separation of observed, measured, estimated, derived, synthetic, historical, live, human-supplied, externally supplied, model-generated, and scenario-specified information, SIIM prevents anonymous, ambiguous, substituted, or semantically unclear inputs from silently entering governed simulation activity and establishes the traceability basis required for representativeness, transformation, temporal, uncertainty, execution, and downstream simulation governance.

Canonical Definition
Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM) defines the governance framework through which a governed simulation specification is transformed into a specific executable Simulation Instance by binding the applicable Simulation Object, object version, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, dependencies, randomization state, execution infrastructure, and other materially relevant conditions into an identifiable execution configuration before simulation activity begins.
SIM establishes the first internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES).
Its purpose is to ensure that:

what was designed to be simulated
can be distinguished from:
what was actually assembled for execution.
SIM therefore establishes the exact governed starting configuration from which subsequent Simulation Execution Control, Observation, Repetition, and Documentation proceed.
Operational Role
The preceding Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) establishes:
which materially relevant conditions should be simulated.
SIM receives that governed scenario basis and asks:
What exact executable simulation instance has now been assembled from the approved simulation components and conditions?

↓

↓

↓

↓
Instantiation Verification
↓
Executable Simulation Instance
↓

Module Function
SIM exists because a simulation may be perfectly designed at the architectural level while the actual executable instance differs materially from that design.

Possible causes include: wrong model version, wrong environment version, outdated Scenario Set, wrong Input Set, missing dependency, incorrect parameter baseline, unexpected default values, changed software library, changed hardware, unavailable external service, wrong randomization configuration, incorrect initial state, different agent population, unrecorded infrastructure change, or manual configuration error.
SIM prevents those differences from remaining invisible. Simulation Specification ≠ Simulation Instance
SIMULOS® establishes a fundamental distinction:
Simulation Specification
describes the governed simulation that is intended to be executable.
Simulation Instance
represents the exact materially relevant configuration actually assembled for a particular execution.
Therefore:
Intended Configuration ≠ Instantiated Configuration by default.
The relationship must be established.
Simulation Instance
A Simulation Instance is the identifiable and execution-ready realization of a governed simulation configuration assembled for one Simulation Execution or defined group of executions.
Conceptually:
Simulation Object Model Environment Scenario Inputs Parameters Dependencies Initial State Execution Infrastructure
=
Simulation Instance Simulation Instance Identity
Every materially relevant Simulation Instance should be sufficiently identifiable.

The identity may include: Simulation Instance ID, planned Execution ID, Simulation Object ID, object version, model version, environment version, Scenario ID, Scenario Set version, Input Set ID, parameter baseline, randomization configuration, dependency state, execution infrastructure, instantiation timestamp, and instantiation status.
Instance Identity ≠ Scenario Identity
A Scenario identifies the condition intended for examination.
A Simulation Instance identifies the complete executable realization of that Scenario under a particular technical and governed configuration.
One Scenario may therefore produce many Simulation Instances.
For example:
Scenario S-021
may be instantiated as:
Instance I-021-A
Instance I-021-B
Instance I-021-C
under different: model versions, random seeds, Input Sets, environments, or execution infrastructures.
Execution Requirement
Instantiation should begin from an identifiable Execution Requirement.
The requirement may originate from: Scenario Set, simulation campaign plan, validation requirement, engineering inquiry, autonomous follow-up simulation, incident analysis, stress escalation, scenario discovery, or another governed simulation need.
The requirement should make clear:
Why is this simulation instance being created?
Instantiation Requirement
An Instantiation Requirement defines which governed components must be assembled before execution can begin.

This may include mandatory: object version, model version, environment version, scenario, Input Set, parameters, dependencies, initial conditions, and runtime conditions.
Object Binding
Every Simulation Instance should remain bound to the exact Simulation Object it represents.
Conceptually:
Simulation Instance → Simulation Object ID → Object Version
This prevents an execution associated with one object version from later being interpreted as if it represented another.
Object-Version Binding
Where the Simulation Object changes materially, the applicable instance should identify which object version was instantiated.
For example:
Spacecraft Configuration v4.2
must remain distinguishable from:
Spacecraft Configuration v4.3.
No Object Substitution Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation execution must not silently substitute a materially different Simulation Object version while preserving the identity of the original execution basis.
Model Binding
A Simulation Instance should identify the exact Simulation Model configuration used.
This may include: model identifier, model version, component versions, active model modules, enabled capabilities, model configuration, and relevant model dependencies.
Model-Version Binding
Where multiple model versions exist, a Simulation Instance should not rely solely upon the statement:
“Latest model used.”
It should preserve the exact version instantiated.
No Latest-Version Ambiguity Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

A dynamically changing reference such as “latest” is insufficient where exact model identity materially affects execution reconstruction.
Environment Binding
The Simulation Instance should identify the exact governed Simulation Environment in which the execution is instantiated.
This includes the environment version established under SMES.
Conceptually:
Simulation Instance → Simulation Environment Version Environment Configuration Binding
Materially relevant environment attributes may include: environment version, simulation engine, runtime configuration, physics engine, network model, terrain state, environmental model, agent environment, external interfaces, and dependency state.
Scenario Binding
Every Simulation Instance should bind to the Scenario or Scenario Configuration it is intended to execute.
Conceptually:
Simulation Instance → Scenario ID → Scenario Version Scenario Configuration Binding
Where the Scenario contains variation, edge-case, or stress configurations, the instance should preserve the exact applicable configuration.
For example:
Scenario: Autonomous Recovery
Variation: Communication Delay = 8 s
Edge: Power near autonomy-transition threshold
Stress: Navigation uncertainty elevated
These are materially different from the generic Scenario identity alone.
No Generic-Scenario Binding Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Binding an execution only to a broad Scenario name is insufficient where materially relevant Scenario Variation, Edge, or Stress conditions determine execution behavior.
Input Set Binding
Every materially relevant Simulation Instance should identify the Input Set it will consume.
Conceptually:
Simulation Instance → Input Set ID → Input Versions
This preserves the SIDS governance basis established before execution.
Input Version Binding
Where inputs change over time, the instance should preserve the exact versions selected.
A new dataset must not silently replace the dataset originally intended for a historical execution.
Input Availability Check
Instantiation may identify whether required inputs are:
Available
Conditionally Available
Substituted
Missing
or:
Unavailable.
Material input absence should be resolved before execution or preserved as an explicit Instantiation Deviation.
Input Substitution at Instantiation
Where an intended input is unavailable and another is substituted, the relationship should remain visible.
Conceptually:
Required Input A
↓
Unavailable
↓
Substituted Input B
↓
Instantiation Deviation / Approved Substitution
The substitute does not become the originally required input merely because execution proceeds successfully.
Parameter Binding
A Simulation Instance should preserve the applicable parameter configuration established under SMES and the relevant Scenario Variation.

Parameter binding may include: baseline parameters, Scenario parameters, control parameters, runtime limits, threshold values, physical constants, behavioral parameters, and configuration switches.
Default Parameter Governance
Simulation software may contain default values.
SIM establishes:
A default value is still part of the instantiated configuration where it can materially influence execution.
Material defaults should not disappear merely because they were not manually entered.
No Invisible Default Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation must not treat materially influential default configuration as if no configuration decision existed.
Assumption Reference Binding
SAS governs Simulation Assumptions.
SIM does not re-govern those assumptions.
Where an assumption materially conditions execution, however, the Simulation Instance may preserve a reference to the applicable assumption basis.
Dependency Binding
Simulation execution may depend upon external or internal systems including: libraries, APIs, databases, AI models, services, operating systems, middleware, simulation engines, communication services, external models, or hardware.
SIM should bind material dependencies to the Simulation Instance.
Dependency State
A dependency may be:
Available
Degraded
Restricted
Emulated
Substituted
Unavailable
or:
Dependency State Undetermined.
The instantiated state may materially affect execution.
External Service Binding

Where execution depends upon an external service, SIM may preserve: service identity, version where available, configuration, API state, endpoint behavior, availability, and relevant execution conditions.
No External-Service Assumption Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
An external dependency must not be assumed materially unchanged merely because the simulation configuration itself was not modified.
Software Binding
A Simulation Instance may preserve materially relevant: software build, simulator version, compiler, libraries, runtime, container image, orchestration layer, operating system, or another technical state.
SIM does not prescribe how deeply every software component must be recorded.
Governance depth should reflect materiality.
Hardware Binding
Where hardware may materially influence execution, SIM may bind: processor type, accelerator, embedded hardware, sensor emulator, actuator hardware, hardware-in-the-loop component, firmware version, or other physical components.
Execution Infrastructure Binding
Simulation behavior may depend upon execution infrastructure.
Relevant infrastructure may include: workstation, cloud environment, HPC cluster, distributed simulation environment, hardware-in-the-loop bench, robotic test platform, mission simulator, or another execution environment.
Infrastructure Identity
SIM may preserve:
Simulation Instance → Execution Infrastructure ID
where infrastructure materially affects timing, performance, determinism, or execution behavior.

Randomization Binding
Where execution uses randomness, the Simulation Instance should identify the applicable randomization basis where material.
This may include: randomization method, seed, sampling distribution, agent initialization, stochastic environment, random event schedule, or other stochastic configuration.
Seed Binding
Where applicable:
Simulation Instance → Random Seed
may support later repeatability or diagnostic analysis.
Seed governance does not imply that execution will necessarily be perfectly reproducible.
Initial-State Binding
Simulation behavior frequently depends strongly upon the initial state.
SIM therefore governs the explicit binding of materially relevant initial conditions.
These may include: system state, environment state, agent state, position, velocity, resource levels, memory state, mission phase, authority state, sensor state, or active dependencies.
No Initial-State Neutrality Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Two executions using the same Scenario and Model are not necessarily comparable if their materially relevant initial states differ.
Agent-Population Binding
Multi-agent simulations may require identification of: number of agents, agent types, agent versions, roles, goals, behavioral configurations, authority relationships, and initial positions or states.
Autonomous-Agent State Binding

Where autonomous agents contain persistent or adaptive state, the Simulation Instance may need to preserve: memory state, policy version, permission state, tool availability, authority level, active goals, or previous interaction history.
This becomes particularly important where nominally identical runs can diverge because agent state differs.
Temporal Starting State
SIM may establish the temporal position from which the simulation begins.
Examples include: mission time, operational time, historical timestamp, relative simulation time, system lifecycle state, or event position.
Instantiation Time
The time at which the Simulation Instance was created may itself be relevant where: dependencies change, external services change, data update, model versions change, or execution infrastructure is dynamic.
Planned vs Actual Instantiation
SIM distinguishes:
Planned Configuration
from:
Instantiated Configuration.
The two should be compared before execution where material.
Instantiation Delta
An Instantiation Delta represents the material difference between the intended simulation configuration and the configuration actually assembled.
Conceptually:
Actual Instantiated Configuration − Intended Configuration = Instantiation Delta Instantiation Delta Examples

A delta may include: different model version, changed environment, substituted Input Set, parameter difference, missing dependency, different seed, infrastructure change, altered agent population, different initial state, or unexpected software version.
Instantiation Delta Status
A material Instantiation Delta may be:
Accepted
Conditionally Accepted
Requires Correction
Requires Reauthorization
Execution-Blocking
or:
Undetermined.
No Silent Delta Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material difference between intended and instantiated configuration must not disappear merely because the simulation is technically capable of running.
Configuration Conflict
A Configuration Conflict exists where two required simulation components impose incompatible conditions.
Examples include: Scenario requires Model v4 but environment supports only Model v3, Input Set uses units incompatible with the selected model, parameter configuration violates environment limits, hardware version does not support the required execution state, or scenario assumes a dependency that is unavailable.
Conflict Resolution
A Configuration Conflict may be:
Resolved
Conditionally Resolved
Accepted as Limitation
Execution-Blocking
or:
Unresolved.
The resolution should remain traceable where material.
Missing Instantiation Component
A required component may be absent.
Examples include: missing input, missing parameter, unavailable dependency, absent model module, missing environment element, or unresolved initial state.

No Missing-to-Default Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A required but missing instantiation component must not silently become a default configuration unless that substitution is itself governed.
Unexpected Instantiation Component
A component may appear in the assembled Simulation Instance despite not being part of the intended basis.
Examples include: automatically loaded library, inherited configuration, persistent agent memory, cached state, environment plugin, external tool, or additional subsystem.
Where materially influential, it should remain visible.
Configuration Inheritance
Simulation systems may inherit configuration from: templates, previous runs, campaign defaults, environment defaults, user profiles, persistent state, or parent configurations.
SIM requires material inherited configuration to remain traceable.
No Hidden Inheritance Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Inherited configuration is part of the Simulation Instance where it materially influences execution, even if it was not explicitly selected for the current run.
Simulation Instance Completeness
Instantiation Completeness asks:
Have all materially required components of the intended simulation been sufficiently assembled and identified for execution?
Possible statuses may include:
Instantiation Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
or:
Instantiation Completeness Undetermined. Instantiation Completeness ≠ Execution Readiness

An instance may contain every required component while unresolved: conflicts, authorization, compatibility problems, or blocking deviations
still prevent execution.
Simulation Instance Readiness
A Simulation Instance may receive a readiness status such as:
Execution Ready
Conditionally Execution Ready
Execution Restricted
Not Execution Ready
or:
Execution Readiness Undetermined.
Instantiation Verification
Before transfer to Simulation Execution Control, SIM should verify that the instantiated configuration sufficiently corresponds to the governed Execution Requirement.
Verification may examine: identity, version, compatibility, completeness, dependencies, inputs, parameters, initial state, infrastructure, randomization, and material deltas.
Instantiation Verification ≠ Validation
Instantiation Verification confirms the consistency of the executable configuration with the governed simulation basis.
It does not establish that: the model is valid, the simulation is accurate, the output will be correct, or the system is safe.
Instance Freeze
Where required, an instantiated configuration may be frozen before execution.
An Instance Freeze prevents material configuration change between:
Instantiation Verification
and:
Execution Initiation
unless the change is explicitly governed.
No Pre-Execution Drift Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

A verified Simulation Instance should not materially change before execution without creating an identifiable configuration change or successor instance.
Successor Instance
Where a material change occurs before execution, the system may create a successor instance.

Instance I-001
↓
Material Configuration Change
↓
Instance I-002
rather than silently modifying I-001.
Simulation Instance Versioning
A logical Simulation Instance may require version distinction where configuration changes before execution or across campaign preparation.
Campaign Instantiation
Large-scale Simulation Campaigns may instantiate thousands or millions of related executions.
SIM may govern these through:
Campaign Configuration Run-Specific Configuration
The campaign basis can define common configuration while individual runs preserve material differences.
Campaign Template
A Simulation Campaign may establish a common template including: model version, environment version, infrastructure, common Input Set, scenario family, parameter ranges, randomization strategy, and logging requirements.
Run-Specific Instantiation
Each run may then instantiate its own: Scenario configuration, random seed, parameter values, actor population, initial state, or other run-specific attributes.
No Campaign-Level Identity Substitution

A Campaign ID must not replace run-level identity where materially different execution configurations exist inside the campaign.

↓

↓

Where material, the instantiation record should preserve: initiating actor/system, selection basis, generated configuration, authorization state, and parent execution relationship.

Autonomous Agent
Simulation Orchestrator
or another authorized actor.

A new Simulation Instance may derive from: baseline run, previous execution, failed run, edge-case discovery, stress escalation, scenario expansion, or incident investigation.
SIM may preserve:

where this relationship materially explains why the new simulation exists.
