OOF™ Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS)
Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) is the Parent Standard within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture that governs what simulation-derived information may legitimately become evidence, what evidential meaning and weight that evidence may carry, how far reliance upon it may extend, which uses must remain limited or prohibited, and how simulation-derived evidence must interface with broader validation governance.
SERBS establishes the methodological boundary between simulation output, simulation-derived evidence, and validation reliance.
It requires simulation evidence to remain connected to the Simulation Object, simulation purpose and scope, represented reality, assumptions, model and environment, input basis, scenario conditions, execution record, governed outputs, and simulation-to-reality correlation from which its evidential meaning originates.
SERBS does not determine whether an object, system, claim, process, or operational proposition is validated. It governs the simulation-specific evidential basis that may legitimately be transferred into broader validation processes.
Core Question
What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary?

Architectural Position
SERBS occupies the eleventh governed space of the SIMULOS® simulation governance lifecycle.
It follows:
Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS)
and precedes:
Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS).
The preceding standards establish:
what is simulated → why it is simulated → how reality is represented → what assumptions are used → how the model and environment are constituted → what inputs enter → what scenarios are tested → how execution occurs → what outputs are produced → how those outputs correlate with reality.
SERBS then asks the next methodological question:
What may those governed simulation results legitimately support as evidence?
The purpose of SERBS is therefore not to produce additional simulation results, but to establish the legitimate evidential meaning and reliance boundary of results already produced and governed through the preceding SIMULOS® lifecycle.
Governance Flow Position
Governed Simulation Outputs + Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence Qualification → Simulation Evidence Weight → Simulation Reliance Boundary → Simulation Use Limitation → Simulation Validation Interface → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation
Where broader validation is required:
Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → VALIDOS® Validation Governance
Operational Space

SERBS governs the operational space between simulation-derived information and legitimate reliance upon that information.
Its governed space includes: simulation evidence identification; simulation evidence qualification; evidence-purpose alignment; evidence provenance; simulation-specific evidential weight; conditional evidential meaning; evidence applicability; uncertainty affecting evidential meaning; aggregation of evidence across runs or campaigns; reliance boundaries; unsupported reliance; use limitations; prohibited interpretations; temporal applicability of simulation evidence; evidence transfer into broader validation processes; preservation of simulation-specific qualifications during downstream use.
SERBS transforms simulation-derived information from an unbounded analytical product into an explicitly governed evidential basis.
Operational Scope
SERBS applies whenever simulation results are expected to support or influence a material claim, assessment, comparison, engineering judgment, scientific conclusion, design decision, safety argument, mission decision, operational decision, validation process, deployment decision, or other form of reliance.

It applies across: individual simulation runs; repeated simulations; scenario portfolios; large-scale simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; physical simulations; digital simulations; hybrid simulations; digital twins; infrastructure simulations; safety simulations; mission simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies.
SERBS remains technology-neutral.
Its concern is not how sophisticated the simulation technology is, but what evidential meaning its results can legitimately support. Core Governance Distinctions Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence
A simulation output is information produced by simulation execution.
Simulation evidence is simulation-derived information that has been explicitly qualified for a defined evidential purpose.
The existence of an output does not automatically create an evidential basis. Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination
Simulation evidence may contribute materially to validation.
It does not automatically establish validation.
A Validation Determination may require simulation evidence together with empirical, operational, observational, experimental, documentary, or other evidence governed through VALIDOS®. Evidence Availability ≠ Evidence Sufficiency
Large quantities of simulation evidence do not necessarily create sufficient evidence.

A million executions based upon the same inaccurate representation, assumption, model limitation, or missing scenario may reproduce the same weakness one million times. Evidence Weight ≠ Evidence Volume
The amount of simulation data is not equivalent to the strength of its evidential meaning.
Evidence weight depends on the governed relationship between the evidence and the proposition it is intended to support. Correlation ≠ Equivalence
Even strong simulation-to-reality correlation does not establish that the simulation and reality are equivalent.
The evidential meaning of a simulation result remains bounded by the conditions under which the correlation was established. Reliance ≠ Unlimited Generalization
Evidence legitimately applicable to one scenario, configuration, operational condition, time period, or purpose must not automatically be generalized to another.
Simulation Evidence Qualification
Simulation-derived information may be treated as governed simulation evidence only where its evidential basis is sufficiently identifiable.

Qualification should establish, where materially relevant: the simulation-derived information being relied upon; the evidential question or proposition; originating Simulation Object; relevant Simulation Object version and configuration; simulation purpose and scope; applicable exclusions; reality representation; material assumptions; model and environment; input and data basis; relevant scenario or scenario set; execution basis; output identity and classification; inference basis; simulation-to-reality correlation; material uncertainty; temporal applicability; known limitations.
Evidence qualification therefore creates an explicit relationship between:
Evidence → Simulation Basis → Evidential Meaning.
Simulation Evidence Weight
SERBS requires the evidential weight of simulation-derived evidence to remain distinct from the mere existence of the evidence.
Evidence weight may be influenced by: strength of reality representation; representational fidelity; model applicability; assumption dependence; input representativeness; scenario relevance; scenario coverage; execution consistency; repetition results; output classification; inference distance; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; known limitations; temporal relevance; dependence between evidence sources.
Evidence weight must not be inferred merely from: computational scale; simulation sophistication; graphical realism; institutional prestige; number of runs; number of generated outputs; apparent precision.

Precision of simulation output does not itself establish strength of simulation evidence.
Simulation Evidence Aggregation
SERBS recognizes that simulation campaigns may create evidence across thousands, millions, or more individual executions.
Evidence aggregation must therefore distinguish between:
More executions
and
More independent evidential support.
Repeated executions may strengthen evidence where repetition legitimately tests variability, uncertainty, stochastic behavior, scenario diversity, or reproducibility.
They may add little evidential strength where all executions share the same material: assumption; model weakness; representation error; input deficiency; scenario omission; correlation limitation.
Common-mode weaknesses must therefore remain visible when simulation evidence is aggregated.
Simulation Reliance Boundary
The Simulation Reliance Boundary establishes the maximum simulation-specific reliance that may legitimately be placed upon qualified evidence.
A reliance boundary may be constrained by: Simulation Object; object version; object configuration; purpose; scope; exclusion; represented reality; abstraction; fidelity; assumption; parameter range; model applicability; environmental configuration; input basis; scenario; execution condition; output class; inference; correlation; uncertainty; temporal validity.
Reliance outside these boundaries requires a new governed basis.
SERBS therefore prevents the transformation:

Evidence valid under Condition A → claim assumed valid everywhere.
Simulation Use Limitation
Every material limitation affecting legitimate use of simulation-derived evidence must remain attached to that evidence.
Use limitations may establish that evidence: supports only a defined proposition; applies only to specified scenarios; applies only to a defined Simulation Object configuration; applies only within a defined parameter range; depends upon identified assumptions; excludes particular conditions; does not represent specified real-world phenomena; cannot support specified decisions; cannot independently establish operational performance; requires additional evidence; cannot be generalized beyond a stated environment; expires or requires review after material change; may support comparison but not absolute prediction; may support exploration but not validation; may support validation only together with additional evidence.
A limitation that is separated from the evidence it constrains is no longer an effective governance control.
Unsupported Reliance
SERBS requires unsupported reliance to be identifiable.

Unsupported reliance may arise where simulation evidence is used: outside its simulation purpose; beyond its scope; for an excluded condition; for a different Simulation Object version; beyond tested parameter ranges; outside represented reality; outside scenario coverage; beyond established correlation; beyond temporal applicability; after material change; contrary to a documented limitation; as sole validation evidence where broader evidence is required.
Unsupported reliance must not become legitimate merely because it becomes organizational practice.
Negative Evidence Principle
SERBS recognizes that failed, anomalous, contradictory, unstable, divergent, or unexpected simulation results may carry significant evidential meaning.
Simulation campaigns must therefore not treat only favorable or successful outcomes as evidence.
Governable simulation evidence may include: failure; non-convergence; instability; unexpected behavior; threshold violation; scenario failure; sensitivity; disagreement between models; divergence from observed reality; unexpected variance; evidence against an intended claim.
An unwanted simulation result does not cease to be evidentially relevant because it is inconvenient.
Temporal Evidence Principle
Simulation evidence has a temporal dimension.

Evidence qualified at one point in time may become less relevant where: the Simulation Object changes; operating conditions change; reality changes; new observations become available; assumptions become obsolete; models are replaced; inputs change materially; new scenarios become relevant; correlation deteriorates.
SERBS therefore connects directly to Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS).
Evidence whose simulation basis has materially changed must not retain an unchanged reliance status automatically.
Validation Interface Principle
SERBS establishes the methodological interface between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS®.
The boundary is explicit:
SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean.
VALIDOS® determines whether that evidence is sufficient, alone or together with other evidence, to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance.
SERBS may therefore qualify: what evidence exists; what proposition it supports; what weight it may carry; under what conditions it applies; what uncertainties affect it; what limitations govern its use.
SERBS does not decide: whether the complete Validation Object is valid; whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient; whether validation criteria have been satisfied; whether a Validation Determination may be issued; whether operational reliance is justified by the total validation basis.
Cross-Architecture Boundaries SERBS ↔ VALIDOS®

SIMULOS® / SERBS governs simulation-derived evidence and the legitimate boundary of simulation-specific reliance.
VALIDOS® governs the sufficiency of the complete validation basis and formal Validation Determination.
Simulation evidence qualification ≠ validation sufficiency. SERBS ↔ INTEGROS®
SERBS governs the simulation-specific meaning and use of simulation-derived evidence.
INTEGROS® governs broader integrity properties affecting objects, processes, states, information, and evidence.
SERBS must therefore not redefine general evidence integrity. SERBS ↔ ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SIMULOS® may use governed Operational Reality and SRCS correlation relationships when establishing simulation evidential meaning.
SERBS does not determine what operational reality is. SERBS ↔ ADIT®
ADIT® may govern auditability, preservation, evidential observation, verification, and examination of what occurred.
SERBS governs the simulation-specific meaning and reliance boundary of simulation-derived evidence.
Auditability of evidence ≠ evidential meaning of simulation evidence. SERBS ↔ AGA™
AGA™ governs who holds authority, responsibility, accountability, and attribution for decisions involving simulation evidence.
SERBS governs what the evidence can legitimately support. SERBS ↔ AIG® / ASGA™
SIMULOS® may generate evidence concerning AI or autonomous systems.
SERBS governs that simulation-derived evidence.

AIG® and ASGA™ continue to govern the actual behavior, authority, autonomy, constraints, and operation of the systems themselves. Parent Standard Modules 1. SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module
Governs the transformation of simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, and inferences into explicitly qualified simulation evidence.
SEQM establishes: evidence identity; evidential purpose; simulation basis; provenance; qualification conditions; applicability; uncertainty; evidential qualification state.
Its core question is:
What simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence, and for what evidential purpose? 2. SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module
Governs the simulation-specific evidential weight assigned to qualified simulation evidence.
SEWM evaluates factors that materially strengthen, weaken, condition, or constrain evidential meaning.
Its core question is:
How much evidential significance may qualified simulation evidence legitimately carry within its defined context? 3. SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module
Governs the maximum legitimate reliance that may be placed upon simulation-derived evidence within the simulation governance context.
Its core question is:
How far may reliance upon this simulation evidence legitimately extend before the evidence is being used beyond its governed basis? 4. SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module

Governs conditions, exclusions, restrictions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses attached to simulation evidence.
Its core question is:
What must simulation-derived evidence not be used to claim, infer, justify, or support? 5. SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module
Governs the transfer boundary between SIMULOS® simulation evidence governance and VALIDOS® validation governance.
SVIM ensures that evidence entering validation retains its: identity; provenance; qualification; evidential weight; applicability; uncertainty; reliance boundary; limitations.
Its core question is:
How must simulation-derived evidence enter broader validation governance without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning?
Internal Module Flow
Governed Simulation Outputs + Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module → SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module → SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record
The internal logic is:
What qualifies as evidence → what weight it carries → how far reliance may extend → what uses remain prohibited or constrained → how evidence may enter broader validation governance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SERBS implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Object

Identify the precise simulation-derived information proposed for evidential use. 2. Evidential Purpose
Define the proposition, question, decision, or claim the evidence is intended to inform. 3. Simulation Basis
Trace the evidence to its originating Simulation Object, purpose, scope, representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, and correlation basis where relevant. 4. Evidence Qualification
Determine whether the simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence for the stated purpose. 5. Evidence Weight
Determine the simulation-specific weight that the evidence may legitimately carry. 6. Reliance Boundary
Establish the maximum context in which reliance remains supported. 7. Use Limitations
Record material exclusions, restrictions, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses. 8. Uncertainty
Preserve uncertainty affecting evidential meaning. 9. Validation Interface
Preserve all relevant evidence conditions when evidence enters VALIDOS® or another downstream validation process. 10. Lifecycle Sensitivity
Identify changes capable of invalidating or weakening the current evidential basis and triggering review or resimulation.
Governance Outputs

SERBS may generate: Simulation Evidence Qualification Record Simulation Evidence Basis Record Simulation Evidence Weight Assessment Simulation Evidence Provenance Record Simulation Evidence Applicability Statement Simulation Reliance Boundary Statement Simulation Use Limitation Record Unsupported Reliance Register Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Record Simulation Evidence Aggregation Record Simulation Validation Interface Package Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record
Together, these outputs make the evidential meaning of simulation results explicit, transferable, reviewable, and bounded.
Enterprise Application
SERBS enables an organization to determine not merely whether a simulation has produced results, but what those results can legitimately support.
It can be used to govern simulation evidence used for: engineering decisions; design decisions; safety cases; scientific claims; infrastructure planning; mission preparation; product development; system qualification; operational planning; AI evaluation; autonomous-system evaluation; validation programs; regulatory submissions; investment decisions; risk analysis; scenario comparison.
SERBS is particularly relevant where simulation produces highly convincing, precise, or large-scale outputs that may create an appearance of certainty greater than their actual evidential basis.
A simulation may produce billions of data points without adequately supporting the real-world proposition for which those data are being used.

Equally, a narrowly designed simulation may provide strong evidence for a precisely bounded question even though it cannot support broader claims.
SERBS gives organizations the governance structure needed to distinguish between these situations.
Foundational Principles
Simulation output is not automatically simulation evidence.
Simulation evidence is not automatically validation evidence sufficient for a Validation Determination.
Evidence availability is not evidence sufficiency.
Evidence volume is not evidential strength.
Repeated simulation is not automatically independent evidence.
Simulation complexity is not evidential authority.
Numerical precision is not evidential certainty.
Correlation with reality does not establish equivalence with reality.
Evidence must remain bounded by the conditions that give it meaning.
Use limitations are part of the evidence itself.
Negative and anomalous simulation results may carry material evidential meaning.
Simulation-derived evidence must not be relied upon beyond the object, conditions, scenarios, assumptions, executions, outputs, correlations, and temporal context from which its evidential meaning was established.
SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean. VALIDOS® determines whether the total evidence basis is sufficient to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard establishes the evidential boundary layer of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture by transforming simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, and inferences into explicitly qualified, weighted, bounded, limitation-aware, and validation-interface-ready simulation evidence. Through governance of evidential purpose, qualification, provenance, weight, applicability, uncertainty, aggregation, reliance boundaries, use limitations, unsupported interpretations, temporal relevance, and validation transfer, SERBS prevents simulation results from acquiring greater authority, certainty, generality, or operational meaning than their governed simulation basis can legitimately support. By separating simulation evidence qualification from broader validation sufficiency, SERBS preserves the methodological boundary between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS® while enabling simulation-derived evidence to enter validation, engineering, scientific, safety, mission, operational, and decision processes without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning. SERBS therefore establishes the final evidential gateway of the active simulation process before lifecycle governance begins, ensuring that no simulation-derived evidence can legitimately be relied upon more broadly than the Simulation Object, purpose, reality representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, uncertainties, limitations, and

more broadly than the Simulation Object, purpose, reality representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, uncertainties, limitations, and temporal conditions from which that evidence was derived.

Module Architecture
→ Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM)
→ Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM)
→ Simulation Reliance Boundary Module (SRBM)
→ Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM)
→ Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM)
Related Documents
→ About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS)

OOF™ Simulation Execution Standard - (SES)
Simulation Execution Standard - (SES)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Simulation Execution Standard (SES) defines the governance conditions under which an approved Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumption Basis, Model & Environment, Input & Data Basis, and Scenario Set are instantiated into an actual simulation run or campaign, operationally controlled during execution, observed without losing material execution context, repeated where required, and documented as a traceable Simulation Execution Record.
SES governs the transition from:
Simulation Design
to:
Simulation Activity.
Its purpose is to ensure that a simulation does not become an undocumented computational event whose relationship to its intended configuration, inputs, scenarios, execution conditions, observations, repetitions, deviations, and resulting outputs can no longer be reconstructed.
SES does not determine whether the simulation result is valid, correct, reliable, or operationally applicable.
It governs:
what was actually executed, under which governed conditions, what occurred during execution, whether repetition was controlled, and whether the execution can later be reconstructed sufficiently for downstream governance.
Architectural Position
SES is the eighth Parent Standard of SIMULOS®.
It occupies the transition point between:
Simulation Scenario Governance
and:
Simulation Output Governance.

The architecture progresses:
Simulation Object
↓
Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model & Environment
↓
Simulation Inputs & Data
↓
Simulation Scenarios
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output Governance
↓
Downstream Simulation Lifecycle Governance
SES therefore represents the point at which the governed simulation specification becomes an executed simulation event.
Governance Flow Position
Upstream Input:
Governed Scenario Space + Governed Simulation Configuration + Governed Input Basis
↓
Simulation Instantiation
↓
Execution Control
↓
Simulation Observation
↓
Simulation Repetition
↓
Execution Documentation
↓
Governed Simulation Execution Record
↓
Downstream Output Governance
Operational Space

SES governs: simulation-run instantiation, simulation-campaign instantiation, execution identity, execution configuration, object-version binding, model-version binding, environment-version binding, scenario binding, input binding, parameter binding, assumption binding where material, execution authorization, execution initiation, execution state, execution sequencing, execution controls, runtime conditions, execution interventions, execution deviations, execution interruption, execution restart, execution termination, execution completion, simulation observation, observation context, observation timing, event capture, anomaly capture, state-transition capture, repeated execution, repetition conditions, randomization control, seed governance where applicable, repeatability conditions, reproducibility conditions, execution comparison, execution documentation, execution provenance, execution traceability, execution completeness, execution lineage, and formation of the Governed Simulation Execution Record.
Operational Scope

SES applies to simulation execution across environments including: AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, multi-agent systems, aerospace and space systems, industrial systems, digital twins, infrastructure systems, transportation systems, scientific and engineering simulations, financial and economic simulations, safety simulations, mission simulations, training simulations, synthetic environments, hardware-in-the-loop environments, software-in-the-loop environments, and future simulation systems.
SES is technology-neutral.
It does not prescribe a particular: simulator, simulation engine, programming language, computational infrastructure, numerical method, orchestration platform, or execution technology.
Execution Object
Every governed simulation execution should be distinguishable as an identifiable execution object.
Depending upon implementation, this may be:
Simulation Run
Simulation Episode
Simulation Trial
Simulation Batch
Simulation Campaign
or another defined execution unit.
The governing requirement is not terminology.
The governing requirement is:
the executed activity must be sufficiently identifiable to reconstruct what actually occurred.
Simulation Execution ID
A materially relevant simulation execution should have a stable identifier capable of connecting the execution to its governing basis.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID
↓
Simulation Object Version
Purpose & Scope
Reality Representation
Assumption Basis
Model Version
Environment Version
Input Set

Scenario ID
Parameter Configuration
Execution Conditions
Execution Record
Produced Outputs
This prevents simulation results from becoming detached from the execution that produced them.
Instantiation Principle
A simulation specification does not become an executed simulation merely because its components exist.
SES distinguishes:
Defined Simulation Configuration
from:
Instantiated Simulation Configuration.
Instantiation establishes which exact versions, parameters, inputs, scenarios, environments, and relevant conditions were assembled for a specific execution.
Configuration Binding
Before execution, materially relevant components should be bound to the execution instance.
This may include: Simulation Object version, model version, environment version, scenario version, input dataset, parameter set, software configuration, hardware configuration, random seed, dependency state, external service configuration, and execution timestamp.
No Assumed Configuration Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
The configuration intended to run must not automatically be treated as the configuration that actually ran.
Where material, execution records should establish the instantiated configuration rather than relying solely upon pre-execution intent.
Execution Authorization
Where organizational, technical, safety, financial, or regulatory consequence requires authorization, SES may require an identifiable authorization basis before execution.

Authorization may govern: permitted scenario classes, resource limits, execution environment, access permissions, external-system interaction, sensitive data, hardware use, operational interfaces, and termination authority.
Execution Initiation
Execution Initiation marks the transition from prepared simulation configuration to active simulation.
A governed initiation record may establish: execution identity, initiation time, configuration status, scenario, inputs, environment, authorization, and initial state.
Execution State
SES may distinguish execution states such as:
Prepared
Initialized
Running
Paused
Interrupted
Restarted
Completed
Terminated
Failed
or:
Execution State Unknown.
These states allow downstream users to distinguish a successfully completed simulation from a partial or interrupted execution.
Execution Control
Simulation Execution Control governs the mechanisms through which execution remains within the conditions established for the simulation.
Controls may concern: execution sequence, timing, resource use, synchronization, scenario progression, parameter application, dependency behavior, state transitions, interventions, runtime limits, termination criteria, and recovery behavior.
Execution Control ≠ Outcome Control
A critical SIMULOS® distinction is:
Execution Control governs how the simulation is performed. It must not become manipulation designed to force a preferred simulation outcome.

Unexpected or unfavorable behavior should remain observable rather than being silently corrected merely because it conflicts with expectations.
Runtime Intervention
A simulation may require intervention during execution.
Examples include: pause, parameter adjustment, injected failure, scenario escalation, external input, human intervention, recovery command, or controlled termination.
Where intervention can materially affect the result, it should remain traceable.
No Invisible Intervention Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material intervention during simulation execution must not disappear from the execution history.
Execution Deviation
An Execution Deviation exists where actual execution materially differs from the intended execution basis.
Examples include: wrong configuration, missing dependency, delayed input, unexpected environment state, parameter mismatch, runtime error, unscheduled intervention, timing failure, resource exhaustion, incomplete scenario execution, or execution-system failure.
Deviation Does Not Automatically Invalidate Execution
SES does not predetermine the consequence of a deviation.
Instead it requires the deviation to remain visible.
A deviation may be:
Immaterial
Material but Acceptable
Conditionally Acceptable
Execution-Limiting
Execution-Invalidating
or:
Undetermined
depending upon downstream assessment.
Execution Observation
Simulation Observation governs the structured capture of materially relevant events and states during execution.

Observation may concern: system state, environment state, agent behavior, transitions, failures, recoveries, interactions, timing, resource consumption, control events, interventions, anomalies, and emergent behavior.
Observation ≠ Interpretation
SES establishes a strong boundary:
Observation records what occurred during execution. Interpretation determines what that occurrence means.
The latter belongs primarily to downstream output and analytical governance.
Observation Context
An observation without sufficient context may become misleading.
Where material, observations should preserve:
What happened
When it happened
Where in the simulation it happened
Under which configuration
Under which scenario
Under which inputs
Under which execution state
and:
What preceded or followed the event.
Observation Resolution
Not every simulation requires identical observation resolution.
Observation may be: continuous, periodic, event-triggered, threshold-triggered, state-triggered, sampled, or selectively captured.
The appropriate resolution depends upon the Simulation Purpose and materially relevant execution phenomena.
Observation Blind Spots
SES should preserve known observation limitations.
Examples include: unlogged internal states, insufficient sampling frequency, unavailable telemetry, inaccessible agent reasoning, missing environment events, or data lost during execution.

A simulation should not later be represented as fully observed where material execution regions were not observable.
Execution Repetition
A simulation may be repeated to examine: consistency, variability, stochastic behavior, uncertainty, scenario sensitivity, parameter sensitivity, rare events, or distributional behavior.
SES governs how repetitions remain distinguishable and comparable. Repeatability
Repeatability concerns whether materially equivalent execution conditions can produce sufficiently comparable execution behavior when repetition is intended to preserve those conditions. Reproducibility
Where applicable, Reproducibility concerns whether another execution environment, actor, system, or implementation can recreate the materially relevant simulation execution basis sufficiently to examine comparable behavior.
SIMULOS® does not assume every simulation must be perfectly reproducible.
Some simulations contain: stochastic processes, nondeterministic hardware, external services, adaptive agents, distributed systems, real-time human interaction, or changing environments.
The requirement is to govern the conditions affecting reproducibility rather than falsely claim determinism.
Randomness Governance
Where randomness materially affects execution, SES may govern: randomization method, seed identity, seed generation, seed reuse, stochastic parameterization, sampling state, and relationship between randomization and repetitions.
Seed Traceability

Where technically applicable and materially relevant, preserving a random seed may allow an execution to be reconstructed.
However:
Seed preservation alone does not establish reproducibility
if other execution conditions have changed.
Repetition Identity
Every repeated execution should remain distinguishable.
For example:
Scenario S-104
may produce:
Run S-104-R001
Run S-104-R002
Run S-104-R003
and so forth.
The exact naming system is implementation-specific.
Controlled Repetition
SES distinguishes:
Controlled Repetition
from:
Uncontrolled Re-Running.
Controlled repetition preserves sufficient information to determine: what remained constant, what changed, why it changed, and whether resulting executions may legitimately be compared.
Repetition Variance
Repeated simulations may intentionally vary: seed, input, parameter, environment, agent population, timing, scenario condition, or another dimension.
Such variation should remain distinguishable from accidental execution drift.
Execution Drift
Execution Drift occurs where repeated simulations cease to represent materially comparable execution conditions without that change being sufficiently governed.
Possible causes include: software updates, infrastructure changes, model changes, environment updates, dependency changes, altered defaults, parameter changes, or orchestration changes.
Execution Comparability
Two simulation executions should not be treated as directly comparable merely because they share the same Scenario ID.

Comparability may also depend upon: model version, environment version, input basis, parameterization, randomization, execution controls, and material runtime conditions.
Simulation Campaign Governance
Large simulation programs may execute: thousands, millions, or billions
of simulation runs.
SES allows these runs to be governed as a Simulation Campaign while preserving sufficient run-level traceability where material.
Campaign Identity
A Simulation Campaign may bind:
Campaign ID
↓
Simulation Purpose
↓
Scenario Set
↓
Execution Configuration
↓
Run Population
↓
Repetition Logic
↓
Execution Controls
↓
Campaign Record Campaign-Level Control
Campaign-level governance may establish: permitted configurations, scenario population, execution infrastructure, resource limits, repetition rules, stopping conditions, logging requirements, exception handling, and documentation requirements.
Run-Level Exceptions
A campaign may be generally conformant while individual runs contain deviations.
SES should therefore preserve the distinction between:
Campaign Status
and:
Individual Execution Status.
Execution Completeness
Execution Completeness asks:
Was the simulation activity required by the instantiated execution basis actually completed sufficiently?
Possible states may include:
Complete
Conditionally Complete
Partially Complete
Incomplete
Failed
or:
Undetermined. Completion ≠ Successful Outcome
A simulation may execute completely and reveal catastrophic system failure.

That may still represent a fully completed simulation execution.
Likewise, a simulation producing an apparently desirable output may have been incompletely executed.
SIMULOS® therefore establishes:
Execution Completeness and Simulation Outcome are separate governable questions.
Execution Documentation
Simulation Execution Documentation preserves the execution history sufficiently for later reconstruction.
Documentation may include: Execution ID, Campaign ID, object version, model version, environment version, scenario, inputs, parameters, assumptions where material, authorization, start time, completion time, execution state, interventions, deviations, observations, repetition relationship, randomization basis, infrastructure state, completion status, and output references.
Execution Provenance
Execution Provenance establishes where a Simulation Execution Record came from and which technical and governance basis produced it.
Execution Lineage
Execution Lineage connects related runs.
For example:
Baseline Run
↓
Repeated Run
↓
Modified Parameter Run
↓
Stress Escalation Run
↓
Recovery Run
This allows simulation evolution to be reconstructed rather than viewed as disconnected output files.
Point-in-Time Reconstruction
SES should enable questions such as:
Which exact model version ran?
Which scenario version was instantiated?
Which inputs were used?
Which parameters were active?
Which environment version existed?
Was the execution interrupted?
Was there a runtime intervention?

Was the run repeated?
Which seed was used where applicable?
Were material anomalies observed?
Was the execution complete?
Which outputs originated from this execution?
No Orphan Output Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material Simulation Output should remain traceable to the Simulation Execution that produced it.
An output detached from its execution basis loses critical interpretive context.
No Successful-Run Selection Bias
Where a Simulation Campaign produces both expected and unexpected executions, SES should preserve material failed, interrupted, anomalous, and unfavorable runs.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation Execution governance must not preserve only the runs that support the preferred conclusion.
Failed Executions as Information
Failed executions may reveal: infrastructure weaknesses, scenario incompatibility, model instability, resource constraints, timing problems, or previously unknown simulation limitations.
SES therefore treats execution failure as governable information rather than disposable noise.
Autonomous Simulation Execution
AI and autonomous systems may increasingly: generate simulations, select scenarios, instantiate environments, modify parameters, execute campaigns, identify anomalies, and launch follow-up simulations automatically.
SES remains applicable.
The execution record should preserve where material:
Human-Initiated Execution
AI-Initiated Execution
Autonomously Triggered Execution
or another relevant execution authority state.

Adaptive Simulation
An adaptive simulation may alter future execution based upon earlier results.
For example:
Run
↓
Observation
↓
Adaptive Scenario Selection
↓
New Run
↓
New Observation
SES should preserve this causal execution chain.
No Hidden Adaptive Path Principle
Where prior simulation results materially determine subsequent execution selection, the adaptive path should remain reconstructable.
Otherwise the resulting campaign may appear predetermined when it was actually dynamically generated.
Human-in-the-Loop Simulation
Where humans participate during simulation, SES may preserve: participant role, intervention authority, intervention timing, decisions, response delay, override, and materially relevant human actions.
Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation
For hardware-in-the-loop environments, execution records may additionally preserve: hardware identity, hardware configuration, firmware version, calibration state, communication state, timing characteristics, and physical interface conditions.
Software-in-the-Loop Simulation
Software-in-the-loop execution may preserve: software build, dependencies, runtime environment, API versions, model versions, configuration, and orchestration state.
Space and Mission Simulation
Space and aerospace simulation programs may execute enormous campaigns across: trajectories, navigation uncertainty, environmental conditions, communication states, propulsion states, sensor states, subsystem failures, autonomy states, and recovery conditions.

SES governs not merely whether these simulations were launched but whether the execution history can establish:
which mission configuration actually ran under which conditions and what occurred during that run.
This becomes especially important when simulation campaigns are used to support decisions that cannot later be easily tested in operational reality.
Autonomous Systems
For autonomous systems, execution governance becomes particularly important where behavior can depend upon: internal state, prior actions, memory, stochasticity, environment changes, external agents, timing, permissions, and adaptive decision paths.
Two runs using nominally identical scenarios may diverge materially.
SES preserves the conditions necessary to understand that divergence.
Execution Bottleneck
In mature simulation programs, the bottleneck may not be computational capacity.
Organizations may already possess enormous simulation infrastructure.
The bottleneck may instead be:
execution traceability across millions of runs.
Typical questions become:
Which configuration produced this result?
Can we reproduce it?
Was this run interrupted?
Was there an intervention?
Which environment version was active?
Which outputs belong to which execution?
Did failed runs disappear from analysis?
Did execution conditions drift across the campaign?
SES turns these questions into an explicit governance space.
Relationship to Simulation Scenario Standard
SSS determines:

what should be simulated and whether materially relevant Scenario Space is sufficiently covered.
SES determines:
how those scenarios are actually instantiated and executed.
Therefore:
Scenario Coverage ≠ Execution Completion.
A scenario may exist in the governed Scenario Set without ever being successfully executed.
Relationship to Simulation Model & Environment Standard
SMES governs construction, configuration, boundaries, parameterization, and versioning of the simulation model and environment.
SES binds a specific governed model and environment configuration to an actual execution.
Relationship to Simulation Input & Data Standard
SIDS governs which data and inputs may enter the simulation and under which conditions.
SES records which governed inputs actually entered a specific execution.
Relationship to Simulation Assumption Standard
SAS governs the role of assumptions inside the simulation.
SES preserves the applicable assumption basis where it materially affects execution reconstruction.
Relationship to Simulation Output Governance Standard
SES ends by producing the governed execution basis from which simulation outputs emerge.
SOGS begins by asking:
What exactly did the simulation produce, how should those outputs be classified and bounded, and what may legitimately be inferred from them?
The handoff is therefore:
Governed Simulation Execution Record
↓
Simulation Output
↓
Simulation Output Governance Relationship to VALIDOS®

VALIDOS® may later determine whether simulation execution records and outputs are sufficient for a particular Validation Purpose.
SES does not make that Validation Determination.
This preserves the boundary:
Simulation Execution Governance ≠ Validation Governance.
Relationship to INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of execution records, artifacts, or related information.
SES does not duplicate general integrity governance.
SES governs the simulation-specific execution lifecycle.
Relationship to ADIT®
ADIT® may audit evidence and records produced by simulation execution.
SIMULOS® owns:
simulation execution itself.
ADIT® may subsequently ask whether the execution record is sufficiently auditable, evidenced, or reconstructable for an audit purpose.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SES governs activity occurring inside the simulation environment.
An execution that perfectly conforms to its simulation environment does not establish that the environment accurately represents operational reality.
Relationship to ASGA™
ASGA™ may define governance requirements concerning autonomous authority, permissions, override, escalation, coordination, and continuity.
SES may instantiate and observe scenarios exercising those conditions without taking ownership of autonomous-system governance itself.
Execution Governance Boundary

SES begins when the upstream simulation basis is sufficiently established for a scenario or simulation campaign to be instantiated.
SES ends when the required simulation activity has been: instantiated, executed, controlled, observed, repeated where required, documented, linked to material deviations, assigned an execution-completeness status, and preserved as a Governed Simulation Execution Record capable of supporting downstream Simulation Output Governance.
SES does not determine: whether the simulation model is universally valid, whether Reality Representation is sufficient, whether the resulting output is correct, whether an inference from the output is legitimate, whether operational deployment should occur, whether a Validation Object is valid, or whether a system is safe.
Parent Standard Modules 1. SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module
Governs how a defined simulation basis becomes a specific executable simulation instance.
It establishes the binding between:
Execution ID → Simulation Object → Model → Environment → Scenario → Inputs → Parameters → Applicable Conditions
Its primary question is:
What exactly is being instantiated for execution? 2. SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module
Governs how active simulation execution is initiated, controlled, progressed, interrupted, modified where permitted, terminated, and completed.
Its primary question is:
How must the simulation remain controlled while it is actually running? 3. SOM — Simulation Observation Module

Governs how materially relevant execution states, events, behaviors, transitions, anomalies, interventions, and runtime conditions are observed and preserved.
Its primary question is:
What materially relevant events occurred during execution, and under which execution context? 4. SRPM — Simulation Repetition Module
Governs repeated execution, randomization, repeatability, reproducibility conditions, comparison, execution variance, and controlled repetition.
Its primary question is:
When a simulation is repeated, what must remain constant, what may change, and how can repeated executions remain meaningfully comparable? 5. SEDM — Simulation Execution Documentation Module
Governs the documentation, provenance, lineage, completeness, traceability, and reconstructability of simulation execution.
Its primary question is:
Can the executed simulation later be reconstructed sufficiently to determine what actually ran and what occurred?

Governed Simulation Execution Record
This sequence transforms:
simulation intent
into:
traceable simulation execution. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Execution
Assign a Simulation Execution ID or equivalent stable execution identity. 2. Bind the Execution Configuration

Record the materially relevant: Simulation Object, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, versions, and conditions.
3. Establish Execution Authorization
Where required, establish who or what may initiate and control execution. 4. Instantiate the Simulation
Create the actual executable simulation instance. 5. Execute Under Defined Controls
Apply relevant runtime, sequencing, intervention, resource, and termination controls. 6. Observe Material Execution Events
Capture materially relevant states, transitions, anomalies, interventions, failures, and other execution events. 7. Govern Deviations
Identify differences between intended and actual execution. 8. Govern Repetition
Where execution is repeated, preserve what remained constant and what materially changed. 9. Assess Execution Completeness
Determine whether execution was: Complete, Conditionally Complete, Partially Complete, Incomplete, Failed, or Undetermined.
10. Preserve Execution Documentation
Create sufficient documentation to reconstruct the execution basis and history. 11. Link Execution to Outputs
Ensure resulting Simulation Outputs remain connected to the executions that produced them. 12. Establish the Governed Simulation Execution Record
Produce the controlled execution basis for downstream Simulation Output Governance.
Governance Outputs

SES may produce: Simulation Execution ID, Simulation Campaign ID, Simulation Instantiation Record, Execution Configuration Record, Object-Version Binding, Model-Version Binding, Environment-Version Binding, Scenario Binding Record, Input Binding Record, Parameter Binding Record, Execution Authorization Record, Execution Initiation Record, Execution State Record, Execution Control Record, Runtime Condition Record, Execution Intervention Record, Execution Deviation Record, Execution Interruption Record, Execution Restart Record, Execution Termination Record, Execution Completion Record, Simulation Observation Record, Event Observation Record, Anomaly Observation Record, State Transition Record, Observation Limitation Record, Simulation Repetition Record, Randomization Record, Seed Record, Repeatability Record, Reproducibility Condition Record, Repetition Variance Record, Execution Drift Record, Execution Comparability Record, Simulation Campaign Record, Campaign Exception Record, Execution Completeness Assessment, Execution Provenance Record, Execution Lineage Record, Execution Documentation Record, Execution-to-Output Traceability Record, and Governed Simulation Execution Record.
Enterprise Application
SES can be applied over an organization's existing simulation infrastructure without replacing the underlying simulator.

The organization may retain its: simulation engine, digital twin, HPC infrastructure, Monte Carlo platform, robotics simulator, mission simulator, AI evaluation environment, or proprietary simulation stack.
SES adds the governance layer that asks:
What actually ran?
Under which configuration?
Who or what initiated it?
What changed during execution?
What was observed?
Was it completed?
Was it repeated under comparable conditions?
Can the execution be reconstructed?
Can every material output be traced back to the execution that produced it?
This makes SES applicable as a simulation-execution governance and diagnostic framework without requiring organizations to abandon existing technical infrastructure.
Foundational Principle
A simulation result cannot be fully understood from its output alone; it must remain connected to the exact simulation configuration, execution conditions, observations, deviations, repetitions, and execution history that produced it.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Execution Standard (SES) governs the point at which the designed simulation becomes an actual simulation event. Through governed instantiation, configuration binding, execution control, runtime observation, deviation preservation, repetition governance, randomization traceability, execution-completeness assessment, campaign governance, provenance, lineage, and execution documentation, SES establishes the conditions under which simulation activity remains reconstructable across individual runs and large-scale simulation campaigns. It prevents intended configuration from being confused with executed configuration, successful outcomes from being confused with complete execution, repeated runs from being assumed comparable without evidence, and Simulation Outputs from becoming detached from the executions that produced them. SES therefore transforms Simulation Execution from a transient computational event into a governed, traceable, and reusable operational record capable of supporting downstream Simulation Output Governance, validation, audit, and future simulation analysis.

OOF™ Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) defines the governance conditions under which data, values, signals, measurements, states, distributions, records, synthetic inputs, externally supplied information, and other simulation inputs are identified, qualified for simulation use, assessed for representativeness, transformed under controlled conditions, temporally aligned, uncertainty-aware, and bound to the Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model, Environment, and applicable simulation configuration.
SIDS establishes the governed input boundary through which information becomes capable of materially influencing simulation behavior.
It ensures that information does not become simulation input merely because it is technically available or technically ingestible.
Core Governance Question
Which inputs and data may enter the simulation, and under what representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions?
Purpose

A simulation may be structurally well designed and correctly configured while still producing misleading behavior because the information entering it is: irrelevant, unrepresentative, temporally misaligned, incorrectly transformed, incompletely sourced, improperly aggregated, synthetically generated without disclosure, stale, overly precise, uncertain, or inconsistent with the simulation conditions it is intended to represent.
SIDS exists to govern that problem.
The standard separates:
having data
from:
having data suitable to enter this simulation under these conditions.
Operational Role
SIDS is the sixth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The preceding standards establish:
1. Simulation Object — What exactly is being simulated?
2. Simulation Purpose & Scope — Why is it being simulated and what must it cover?
3. Reality Representation — Which aspects of reality must be represented and how?
4. Simulation Assumptions — Which premises are required and what limitations do they introduce?
5. Simulation Model & Environment — Through which controlled model and environment will the simulation operate?
SIDS asks:
Which information may now enter that governed model and environment, and under what conditions is that information suitable to shape simulation behavior?
It therefore establishes the input basis required before governed Scenario Design.

Operational Space
SIDS governs simulation-specific conditions surrounding: input identification, input classification, input origin, input provenance references, data representativeness, population representativeness, environmental representativeness, state representativeness, distributional representativeness, temporal representativeness, input transformation, normalization, conversion, aggregation, disaggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, filtering, encoding, synthetic-data use, derived inputs, temporal alignment, timestamp relevance, input currency, temporal windows, sequence, synchronization, uncertainty attached to input, input ranges, missing information, conflicting inputs, input substitution, input restrictions, and input-to-simulation traceability.
Operational Scope
SIDS applies only where data or other information becomes an input into a simulation.

It may govern inputs originating from: sensors, operational systems, historical records, scientific measurements, engineering systems, external databases, third-party providers, human operators, AI systems, autonomous systems, previous simulations, synthetic-data generators, probabilistic models, statistical models, digital twins, live operational feeds, batch datasets, scenario specifications, or manually supplied values.
SIDS is not a general-purpose Data Governance Architecture.
It does not attempt to govern the complete lifecycle of data across an organization.
Its boundary is narrower:
the point at which information is proposed for use as simulation input and the conditions under which that use remains methodologically governable.
Simulation Input
A Simulation Input is any governed information, value, state, signal, event, distribution, condition, record, or data object introduced into the simulation and capable of influencing its configuration, behavior, progression, or outputs.
Simulation Inputs may include: measured values, observed states, environmental values, actor states, initial conditions, time-series data, event streams, probability distributions, behavioral data, control signals, geographic information, scientific measurements, operational records, system telemetry, or synthetic values.
Input ≠ Parameter
SIDS distinguishes Simulation Input from Simulation Parameter.
A parameter configures the model or environment.

An input supplies information consumed by the simulation.
For example:
Vehicle Mass = 1,800 kg
may be a parameter.
Current Vehicle Position = X, Y
may be an input.
The distinction should follow simulation function rather than software implementation. Input ≠ Assumption
A Simulation Assumption establishes a premise.
A Simulation Input supplies information.
For example:
Assumption: Network latency remains within normal operating range.
Input: Current network latency = 47 ms.
An assumption may influence interpretation of an input, but the governance objects remain distinct. Input ≠ Evidence by Default
A Simulation Input may later contribute to simulation evidence.
However:
Input into a simulation is not automatically validation evidence merely because the simulation consumed it.
VALIDOS® governs formal Validation Evidence Fitness where such evidence is used for validation.
Input Identification
Every material Simulation Input should be sufficiently identifiable.
Where relevant, identification should establish: input identity, input type, source reference, applicable Simulation Object, applicable model or environment element, temporal context, unit or representation, transformation status, uncertainty status, and simulation configuration.
Input Classification
Simulation Inputs may be classified as:
Observed
Measured
Derived
Estimated
Synthetic
Historical
Live
External
Human-Supplied
Model-Generated
Scenario-Specified
or another simulation-specific class.

Classification supports different governance treatment without assuming one class is universally superior.
Input Origin
Input Origin identifies where the Simulation Input came from.
The origin may include: instrument, system, dataset, organization, individual, model, simulator, external service, AI system, or synthetic-generation process.
SIDS preserves origin visibility.
It does not replace general Source Reliability governance under VALIDOS® where formal source qualification is required. Representativeness
A Simulation Input may be factually correct yet still be unsuitable for the simulation because it does not adequately represent the relevant simulation conditions.
SIDS therefore governs Simulation Data Representativeness.
Representativeness asks:
Does this input sufficiently represent the population, environment, state, distribution, time, behavior, or condition that the simulation intends to model?
Representativeness Is Purpose-Relative
No dataset is universally representative.
Representativeness depends upon:
Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Scenario Context
A dataset suitable for one simulation inquiry may be materially unsuitable for another.
Population Representativeness
Where simulation data represents humans, systems, assets, organizations, biological entities, or other populations, SIDS asks whether the input captures materially relevant population characteristics.

This may include: subgroup differences, distribution differences, behavior, demographic characteristics, technical classes, system variants, or operating profiles.
Environmental Representativeness
Input data may represent only certain environments.
For example:
dry-road vehicle data
may not sufficiently represent:
snow-covered road conditions.
Environmental applicability should remain explicit.
Operational-State Representativeness
Data from normal operation may not represent: degraded operation, failure, emergency states, recovery states, or extreme conditions.
The operating state from which input data originates should therefore remain relevant to simulation-input governance.
Distributional Representativeness
Average values may conceal: variance, tails, multimodality, extreme events, correlations, clusters, or rare conditions.
Where these properties materially affect simulation behavior, SIDS requires their representativeness to remain visible.
Representativeness Gap
A Simulation Data Representativeness Gap exists where the available input data does not sufficiently represent a material part of the simulation inquiry.
A gap may be:
Non-Material
Material but Bounded
Conditional
Material and Unresolved
or:
Representativeness Undetermined Input Transformation
Simulation data frequently cannot enter a simulation in its original form.

It may require: cleaning, filtering, normalization, scaling, unit conversion, coordinate conversion, encoding, aggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, feature derivation, compression, imputation, or another transformation.
SIDS requires material transformations to remain visible.
Transformation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A transformed simulation input is not methodologically identical to its source data merely because the transformation is technically routine.
Transformations may: remove information, introduce assumptions, create synthetic values, change distributions, alter temporal meaning, suppress outliers, or reshape dependencies.
Transformation Traceability
Where material:
Source Input → Transformation → Transformed Input → Simulation Use
should remain reconstructable.
Transformation Loss
A transformation may remove information.
Examples include: aggregation, compression, filtering, dimensional reduction, categorization, or rounding.
Material information loss should remain visible where it can affect simulation behavior. Transformation Gain ≠ New Reality
Interpolation, extrapolation, synthetic extension, or statistical reconstruction may create additional values.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Generated or inferred values must not silently become treated as directly observed reality.
Synthetic Simulation Input
A Synthetic Simulation Input is generated rather than directly observed from the represented reality.
Synthetic inputs may be legitimate and highly useful.

Their synthetic origin must remain identifiable.
Examples include: synthetic populations, generated weather, simulated sensor streams, artificial failure sequences, generated network traffic, synthetic user behavior, or AI-generated input data.
Synthetic ≠ Inferior by Default
SIDS does not assume synthetic input is methodologically weaker.
It requires that its role and generation basis remain visible.
In some simulation contexts synthetic data may be required specifically to test conditions that real-world datasets do not sufficiently contain.
Derived Input
A Derived Input is calculated from one or more existing data objects.
Conceptually:
Input A + Input B + Derivation Method → Derived Input C
The derivation should remain traceable where C materially affects the simulation.
Temporal Data Governance
Simulation data has a temporal relationship to the reality it represents.
SIDS governs: when the data was generated, when it was observed, which period it represents, whether it remains current, whether sequence matters, whether synchronization is required, and whether temporal aggregation changes meaning.
Data Currency
Recent data is not automatically better data.
Historical data is not automatically unsuitable.
The correct question is:
Is the temporal context of this input appropriate for the simulation inquiry?
Temporal Applicability
An input should remain connected to the period or temporal condition it represents where material.
Data from:
System Version 1 in 2022

may not represent:
System Version 4 in 2026.
Temporal Alignment
Multiple input streams may originate from different times.
Where the simulation assumes they represent the same state, temporal alignment must be sufficiently governed.
Temporal Misalignment
A Temporal Misalignment exists where inputs treated as simultaneous or causally connected actually represent materially different time states.
This can create simulation behavior that never existed in the represented reality.
Temporal Sequence
Some simulation behavior depends not only upon values but upon their order.
SIDS therefore preserves sequence where:
A → B → C
is materially different from:
C → A → B.
Temporal Aggregation
Data aggregated across long periods may hide: transient events, peaks, seasonality, failures, transitions, or rapid variability.
Where these phenomena matter, temporal aggregation may create an input limitation.
Input Uncertainty
A Simulation Input may contain uncertainty arising from: measurement, estimation, missing values, transformation, sampling, temporal mismatch, synthetic generation, incomplete representativeness, sensor limits, model derivation, or another source.
SIDS requires material input uncertainty to remain visible. Input Uncertainty ≠ Simulation Assumption Uncertainty
SAUM governs uncertainty attached to assumptions.
SIDS governs uncertainty attached to simulation inputs and data.
The two may interact but remain distinct governance spaces.
Measurement Uncertainty

Measured values may include: tolerance, error range, confidence interval, noise, or calibration limitation.
Simulation use should not imply greater certainty than the measurement supports.
Estimated Input
Estimated inputs may be necessary where direct measurement is unavailable.
Where material, the simulation should distinguish:
Measured Input
from:
Estimated Input.
Missing Input
A Missing Simulation Input exists where the simulation requires information that is not available.
Missing data should not silently become zero, average, default, or synthetic replacement without an identifiable treatment.
Missing Input Treatment
Possible treatments may include:
Exclude
Impute
Substitute
Generate Synthetic Input
Restrict Scenario
Proceed Conditionally
or:
Input Unresolved
depending upon the simulation context.
No Missing-to-Zero Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
Missing information must not automatically be interpreted as a zero value unless zero is itself a governed and justified input.
Conflicting Inputs
Multiple input sources may provide materially inconsistent values.
For example:
Sensor A = 50
Sensor B = 75
Where both are materially credible, the conflict should remain visible.
SIDS does not require one universal conflict-resolution method.
It requires the resolution basis to remain governable.
Input Precedence
Where multiple data sources exist, the simulation may establish rules determining which source takes precedence.

Such precedence should not be arbitrary where it materially affects simulation behavior.
Input Substitution
A planned Simulation Input may be replaced by another.
Example:
Live Sensor Feed → Historical Replay Data
or:
Measured Dataset → Synthetic Dataset
Material substitution should remain visible.
Input Equivalence
Two input sources should not be treated as equivalent merely because they share the same variable name or data format.
Equivalence depends upon materially relevant: meaning, population, environment, time, precision, transformation, uncertainty, and origin.
Input Compatibility
Simulation Inputs should remain compatible with: Simulation Model, Simulation Environment, parameter configuration, units, temporal structure, spatial structure, expected data type, state representation, and applicable scenario conditions.
Technical ingestion alone does not establish compatibility.
No Technical Ingestibility Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
The fact that a simulation can ingest data does not establish that the data is suitable to influence the simulation.
Input Acceptance
A proposed input may receive a simulation-specific status such as:
Accepted
Conditionally Accepted
Accepted with Limitation
Rejected
Substituted
or:
Input Status Undetermined
The status applies to its role within the simulation.
It is not a universal judgment about the data itself.
Input Restriction

A Simulation Input may be suitable only for defined: scenarios, environments, populations, model versions, temporal periods, geographic regions, system states, or analysis purposes.
Restrictions should remain bound to the affected input.
Input-to-Model Binding
Material inputs should remain traceable to the model components they influence.
Conceptually:
Simulation Input → Model Component → Simulation Behavior Input-to-Environment Binding
Some inputs configure or update the Simulation Environment.
Conceptually:
Simulation Input → Environmental Element / State
This relationship should remain visible where material.
Input-to-Scenario Binding
Some inputs may apply only within particular scenarios.
SIDS preserves the input relationship.
SSS governs scenario design itself.
Input-to-Execution Binding
A simulation execution should be capable of identifying the materially relevant input set it consumed.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID → Simulation Input Set ID Simulation Input Set
A Simulation Input Set is the governed collection of materially relevant inputs used for a defined simulation execution or scenario.
The set may identify: input identities, values, origin, transformation state, temporal state, uncertainty, restrictions, and applicable execution.
Input Set Versioning
Where materially different input sets can produce materially different behavior, they should remain distinguishable.

A later update to input data should not silently rewrite the historical input basis of a previous execution.
Point-in-Time Input Reconstruction
SIDS should support questions such as:
Which data entered this simulation run?
What did those inputs represent?
What transformations had occurred?
Which time periods did they represent?
What uncertainty was attached?
Which inputs were synthetic or estimated?
Which inputs were missing, substituted, or restricted?
No Input Laundering Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation input must not acquire greater representativeness, certainty, currency, or evidentiary strength merely because it has passed through a simulation.
No Representativeness Inflation Principle
A dataset representative of:
Population A
must not silently become representative of:
Population A + B + C
simply because the simulation contains all three populations.
No Temporal Inflation Principle
Historical data must not silently become current-state data merely because it is replayed inside a current simulation environment.
No Transformation Concealment Principle
A materially transformed input should not be represented as if it were the original data object.
No Synthetic-to-Observed Conversion Principle
Synthetic data must not become labeled or interpreted as observed reality merely because simulation execution used it successfully.
Input Change

Simulation input conditions may change when: new data arrives, source systems change, transformations change, temporal windows change, data is corrected, additional populations are included, uncertainty changes, or new representativeness gaps are discovered.
Material changes should remain traceable.
Input Change Propagation
A material input change may affect:
Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output → Reality Correlation → downstream Simulation Evidence
SIDS identifies the input change.
Subsequent Parent Standards govern their respective downstream consequences.
Input Drift
Input Drift occurs where the statistical, behavioral, environmental, temporal, or semantic characteristics of incoming Simulation Inputs materially change relative to the input basis under which the simulation was designed.
Drift may be: population drift, distribution drift, environment drift, temporal drift, source drift, measurement drift, or semantic drift.
SIDS governs drift at the simulation-input boundary.
Broader lifecycle drift and resimulation governance remain with the later SIMULOS® lifecycle space.
Input Reassessment Trigger
Material changes in: Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model, Environment, scenario context, source data, transformation process, or time
may require input reassessment.
Governed Simulation Input & Data Basis

At completion of SIDS, the simulation should possess a sufficiently governed Simulation Input & Data Basis establishing: which inputs may enter, what they represent, where they originate, how they were transformed, which temporal conditions apply, what uncertainty remains, where restrictions exist, and which simulation configuration may use them.
This basis supports Scenario Design.
Governance Boundary
SIDS begins when a governed Simulation Model & Environment requires information, data, states, values, signals, or other inputs capable of influencing simulation activity.
SIDS ends when the materially relevant inputs have been sufficiently identified, assessed for representativeness, transformation-governed, temporally qualified, uncertainty-aware, restricted where necessary, and assembled into a governed Simulation Input & Data Basis suitable for Simulation Scenario Design.
Architectural Boundary
SIDS does not govern: enterprise-wide data governance, universal data quality, general database governance, complete data lifecycle management, general source reliability, formal validation of data, model parameterization, Simulation Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output, or operational reliance.
Where those questions arise, the appropriate SIMULOS® Parent Standard or complementary OOF® architecture applies.
Minimum Governance Requirements
