Reality Correlation Governance Governed Output Object
SOGS introduces the governed concept:
Simulation Output Object
A Simulation Output Object is an identifiable output or governed output collection produced from one or more Simulation Executions and preserved with sufficient execution context, classification, inference boundaries, limitations, and documentation to support legitimate downstream examination.
A Simulation Output Object may include: numerical result, state trajectory, event sequence, simulated failure, behavioral trace, probability distribution, performance measure, optimization result, agent action, decision path, generated scenario outcome, Monte Carlo distribution, visualization, aggregated execution result, statistical summary, or another identifiable product of Simulation Execution.
Direct Output
A Direct Simulation Output is produced directly by the Simulation Execution.
Examples include:
collision occurred
trajectory reached state X
temperature exceeded threshold Y
agent selected action Z
18 of 250,000 executions entered recovery failure
These are execution-derived outputs.
Derived Output
A Derived Simulation Output results from processing one or more Direct Simulation Outputs.

Examples include: averages, distributions, percentiles, rankings, aggregate failure rates, confidence estimates, transformed metrics, comparative measures, and post-processed visualizations.
Derived Outputs should remain traceable to their contributing Simulation Outputs and executions where material. Inference
An Inference is a conclusion drawn from one or more Simulation Outputs.
For example:
Output: 18 of 250,000 simulated executions entered recovery failure.
Inference: Recovery failure appears concentrated under a particular combination of simulated conditions.
These are not the same object. Output ≠ Inference Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Output is what the simulation produced. An inference is what an actor concludes from that output.
The two must remain distinguishable. Inference ≠ Reality Principle
SIMULOS® further establishes:
An inference supported inside a simulation does not by itself establish that the same relationship exists in Operational Reality.
That transition belongs to downstream governance.
Output Context Binding
A Simulation Output should remain sufficiently connected to the execution basis that produced it.
Where material, this includes:
Simulation Object
↓
Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Assumptions
↓
Model & Environment
↓
Inputs & Data
↓
Scenario
↓
Execution
↓
Output
Without this context, an output may remain computationally correct while becoming methodologically misleading.
No Context-Free Output Principle

Simulation Outputs must not acquire broader meaning merely because their originating simulation context has been removed.
Output Classification
Outputs may require classification according to characteristics such as:
Direct / Derived
Individual / Aggregated
Deterministic / Stochastic
Expected / Unexpected
Nominal / Edge-Case / Stress
Complete / Partial
Final / Intermediate
Observed / Calculated
Comparative / Standalone
Execution-Specific / Campaign-Level
Classification enables downstream users to understand what type of Simulation Output they are examining.
Aggregated Simulation Output
An aggregated output may combine many executions.
For example:
2,000,000 Monte Carlo runs → Failure Probability Estimate
SOGS requires the aggregate to remain sufficiently connected to: contributing execution population, relevant exclusions, failed runs, scenario population, repetition structure, and aggregation method.
No Aggregation Concealment Principle
Aggregation must not erase materially relevant execution behavior that changes interpretation of the aggregated result.
Output Population
A Simulation Output may represent:
one execution
one Repetition Set
one Scenario
multiple scenarios
one campaign
or:
multiple simulation populations.
The population basis should remain identifiable.
Output Exclusion
Where executions or results are excluded from an output population, material exclusions should remain visible.

This prevents: silent failed-run removal, cherry-picking, survivor-only reporting, post hoc filtering, and misleading aggregate construction.
Output Limitation
Every materially relevant Simulation Output may carry limitations arising from: assumptions, abstraction, fidelity, model boundaries, environment boundaries, input uncertainty, data representativeness, scenario coverage, execution conditions, repetition sufficiency, observation limitations, output processing, or unresolved simulation behavior.
SOGS does not require all limitations to invalidate the output.
It requires them to remain visible where they materially constrain interpretation.
Inherited Limitation Principle
A Simulation Output inherits materially relevant limitations from the simulation conditions upon which it depends.
Post-processing does not erase those limitations.
No Precision Inflation Principle
A highly precise numerical output does not establish equivalent certainty about reality.
For example:
Failure Probability = 0.003742%
may be computationally precise while remaining highly sensitive to: assumptions, scenario selection, model fidelity, data quality, and representation boundaries.
Computational Precision ≠ Epistemic Certainty
SIMULOS® establishes:
The numerical precision of a Simulation Output must not be confused with the strength of what that output legitimately establishes.
Unexpected Output
A Simulation Output may reveal behavior not anticipated by the Simulation Purpose or Scenario Design.

Unexpected output should not automatically be: deleted, classified as error, excluded, or normalized away.
It may reveal: hidden interaction, model instability, unmodeled dependency, scenario insufficiency, rare behavior, or a new simulation question.
Output-to-Scenario Feedback
A materially unexpected output may therefore create:
New Scenario Requirement
or:
Scenario Expansion Requirement
under SSS.
SIMULOS® is therefore capable of recursive simulation learning.
Output-to-Assumption Feedback
An output may expose sensitivity to an assumption.
This may create:
Assumption Reassessment
under SAS.
Output-to-Model Feedback
Unexpected or unstable outputs may create a need to reassess:
Simulation Model & Environment
under SMES.
Output-to-Input Feedback
Output behavior may expose input sensitivity, missing data regions, or representativeness problems requiring reassessment under SIDS.
Output-to-Execution Feedback
An output anomaly may originate from: execution deviation, hidden state, incomplete run, control intervention, or repetition drift.
SOGS therefore preserves backward traceability into SES.
No Automatic Failure Attribution
An unexpected Simulation Output does not establish that the simulated system failed, the simulation failed, or Operational Reality would fail.
Those remain separate questions requiring appropriate governance.
Inference Boundary

An inference should remain bounded by: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, represented reality, assumptions, model and environment, inputs, scenario population, execution population, output population, uncertainty, and known limitations.
Inference Escalation
SOGS distinguishes between increasingly strong claims.
For example:
Level 1 — Execution Observation
“Failure occurred in Run 184.”
Level 2 — Repetition Observation
“Failure occurred in 18 of 250,000 repetitions.”
Level 3 — Simulation Pattern Inference
“Failure is associated with simulated low-power recovery conditions.”
Level 4 — Reality-Oriented Claim
“The real spacecraft will fail under low-power recovery conditions.”
The first three may potentially be governed within simulation output analysis.
The fourth crosses toward:
Reality Correlation
and cannot be established by SOGS alone.
No Reality Leap Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Output must not move directly from simulated behavior to a claim about Operational Reality without passing through the appropriate reality-correlation and validation governance.
Output Documentation
A governed Simulation Output should preserve, where material: Output ID, Output Type, originating Execution ID, Repetition Set, Scenario ID, model version, environment version, Input Set, relevant parameters, output population, aggregation method, processing history, inference status, limitations, uncertainty context, exclusions, and downstream use.
Output Lineage

Output lineage may follow:
Execution
↓
Direct Output
↓
Derived Output
↓
Aggregated Output
↓
Inference
↓
Downstream Assessment
This allows later reconstruction of how a conclusion emerged from Simulation Execution.
No Output Laundering Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Derived Output or inference must not acquire stronger methodological status merely because its relationship to the original Simulation Execution has become less visible.
Output Transformation
Outputs may undergo: filtering, normalization, aggregation, smoothing, dimensional reduction, statistical transformation, visualization, AI summarization, or other processing.
Material transformations should remain traceable where they affect interpretation.
AI Interpretation of Simulation Outputs
AI systems may analyze enormous Simulation Output populations.
They may: identify patterns, detect anomalies, cluster failures, generate summaries, propose causal hypotheses, or identify new scenarios.
SOGS distinguishes:
Simulation Output
from:
AI-Generated Interpretation of Simulation Output.
AI-Generated Inference Principle
An AI-generated interpretation does not become a Simulation Output merely because it was generated automatically from Simulation Outputs.
Its interpretive status should remain visible.
Output Conflict
Different executions or Simulation Output populations may support conflicting interpretations.
SOGS preserves conflict rather than forcing artificial agreement.
Possible status:
Output Consistent

Output Conditionally Consistent
Output Mixed
Output Conflicted
Output Relationship Undetermined Output Uncertainty
Output uncertainty may arise from multiple sources.
SOGS may preserve:
Input Uncertainty
Parameter Uncertainty
Stochastic Uncertainty
Model Uncertainty
Scenario Uncertainty
Execution Uncertainty
Observation Uncertainty
and:
Inference Uncertainty.
These should not automatically be collapsed into one generic uncertainty number.
Output Sufficiency
A Simulation Output may be technically valid as an output while still insufficient for a particular downstream inference.
Therefore:
Output Existence ≠ Inference Sufficiency.
Simulation Campaign Bottleneck
Modern simulation systems can produce more outputs than organizations can meaningfully interpret.
The governance bottleneck may therefore shift from:
Can we generate simulation results?
to:
Can we determine what those results actually mean, what they do not mean, and which decisions they may legitimately support?
SOGS governs this transition.
Space & Mission Simulation Application
A space organization may run millions of mission simulations producing: trajectory distributions, navigation errors, failure modes, communication losses, recovery outcomes, fuel margins, and mission-success estimates.
The critical governance question is not merely:
What percentage succeeded?
It is also:
Which execution population produced that percentage?
Which scenarios were included?
Which failed executions were excluded?

Which assumptions materially shaped the result?
What does the output directly establish?
Which conclusions are interpretations?
Which conclusions require correlation with Operational Reality?
SOGS provides the structure required to answer these questions.
Autonomous Systems Application
An autonomous robot may complete:
99.97% of simulated tasks successfully.
SOGS prevents this result from automatically becoming:
The robot is 99.97% safe in reality.
The simulation output may legitimately establish a performance property within the governed simulation conditions.
Moving from that result toward real-world safety requires downstream governance.
Relationship to SES
SES governs:
how Simulation Execution occurs.
SOGS governs:
what emerges from that execution and how that output may be interpreted.
The formal handoff is:
Governed Simulation Execution Record
↓
Simulation Output Object Relationship to RRS
RRS governs how reality is represented inside the simulation.
SOGS preserves relevant representation limitations when interpreting outputs.
Relationship to SAS
SAS governs Simulation Assumptions.
SOGS ensures materially relevant assumption limitations propagate into output interpretation.
Relationship to SSS
SSS governs Scenario Design and Coverage.
SOGS ensures outputs are not interpreted beyond the scenario population that produced them.
Relationship to ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SOGS does not determine whether a Simulation Output corresponds to reality.

That question belongs to the downstream reality-correlation governance space.
Relationship to VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® determines whether a Simulation Output, inference, correlation claim, simulation methodology, or other Validation Object can legitimately support a formal validation claim.
SOGS governs the Simulation Output before that validation determination.
Relationship to INTEGROS®
SOGS deliberately does not govern general Output Integrity.
General integrity remains under INTEGROS®.
SOGS governs:
identification, classification, inference, limitation, and documentation of Simulation Outputs.
Relationship to ADIT®
ADIT® may audit Simulation Output records, inference pathways, exclusions, and traceability.
SOGS governs the output space itself.
Governance Boundary
SOGS begins when one or more identifiable outputs emerge from a governed Simulation Execution.
SOGS ends when those outputs have been sufficiently: identified, execution-bound, classified, population-bounded, inference-bounded, limitation-bound, transformation-traced, and documented
to form a Governed Simulation Output suitable for downstream Reality Correlation.
SOGS does not determine: whether the simulation accurately represents Operational Reality, whether a Simulation Output is externally valid, whether the simulated behavior will occur in reality, whether a system is operationally safe, whether a Simulation Output constitutes sufficient Validation Evidence, or whether operational reliance is justified.

Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Simulation Output
Assign a stable Output ID and establish what exactly was produced. 2. Bind the Output to Execution
Connect the output to its originating Simulation Execution, Repetition Set, or Campaign. 3. Classify the Output
Determine whether the output is: direct, derived, aggregated, deterministic, stochastic, intermediate, final, or another governed class.
4. Establish the Output Population
Identify which executions and scenarios contribute to the output. 5. Preserve Material Exclusions
Document excluded executions, failed runs, filtered results, and other material population changes. 6. Trace Material Transformations
Preserve transformations affecting output interpretation. 7. Separate Output From Inference
Distinguish what the simulation produced from conclusions subsequently drawn from it. 8. Bound the Inference
Ensure inference does not exceed the simulation conditions supporting it. 9. Propagate Material Limitations
Carry forward relevant limitations from upstream simulation governance. 10. Assess Output Uncertainty Context
Identify material uncertainty affecting interpretation. 11. Establish Output Documentation
Preserve the context, lineage, inference, limitations, and downstream relationships. 12. Establish the Governed Simulation Output
Create the formal output object suitable for Reality Correlation and downstream validation.
Governance Outputs

SOGS may produce: Simulation Output ID, Simulation Output Object, Direct Simulation Output Record, Derived Simulation Output Record, Aggregated Simulation Output Record, Output Classification, Output Population Record, Output Exclusion Record, Output Transformation Record, Output-to-Execution Traceability Record, Output Lineage Record, Simulation Inference Record, Inference Classification, Inference Boundary, Inference Limitation Record, Output Limitation Record, Inherited Limitation Record, Output Uncertainty Record, Output Conflict Record, Output Sufficiency Assessment, AI-Generated Interpretation Record, Output Documentation Record, Reality-Correlation Handoff Record, and Governed Simulation Output.
Architectural Position
Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) is the ninth Parent Standard of SIMULOS®.
Its position is:
8. Simulation Execution Standard (SES)
↓

↓

SOGS therefore forms the critical boundary between:
what happened inside the simulation
and:
what that simulated result may legitimately tell us about something beyond the simulation.
Foundational Principle
A Simulation Output becomes governable only when what the simulation directly produced remains distinguishable from how that output was processed, interpreted, limited, aggregated, and ultimately used to support claims beyond the execution that produced it.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Output Governance Standard establishes the governed transition from Simulation Execution to interpretable Simulation Output by defining how outputs are identified, classified, execution-bound, population-bounded, transformed, inferred from, limitation-bound, uncertainty-contextualized, and documented. Through explicit separation of direct output, derived output, aggregation, and inference, SOGS prevents computational precision from becoming false certainty, simulation behavior from becoming an unsupported claim about Operational Reality, and large-scale simulation results from losing the execution context and limitations necessary for legitimate interpretation. SOGS therefore creates the governed Simulation Output Object that can move forward into Reality Correlation and downstream validation without exceeding what the simulation itself actually established.

Simulation Purpose & Scope
Canonical Definition
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a simulation, the questions the simulation is intended to address, the portions of the governed Simulation Object to which it applies, the conditions and contexts included within the simulation inquiry, the material exclusions and limitations surrounding that inquiry, and the required simulation depth and precision are formally established before downstream simulation representation begins.
SPSS ensures that a technically successful simulation cannot silently acquire a broader purpose, scope, applicability, or interpretive meaning than was actually established before simulation design and execution.
Core Question

Why is the simulation being performed, what exactly must it examine, what remains outside its governed scope, and at what depth and precision must the simulation operate for its intended purpose?
Purpose
The purpose of SPSS is to transform a governed Simulation Object into a governed simulation inquiry.
SOS establishes:
What exactly is being simulated?
SPSS establishes:
Why is it being simulated and what must the simulation actually cover?
The distinction is fundamental.
The same Simulation Object may be simulated for radically different purposes.
A spacecraft may be simulated for: thermal behavior, navigation, structural stress, docking, autonomous control, communication loss, mission failure, or complete mission performance.
The Simulation Object may remain the same while the required simulation scope, depth, precision, conditions, and exclusions change substantially.
SPSS governs those differences.
Operational Role
SPSS is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
It receives the governed Simulation Object produced by SOS and establishes the simulation-specific purpose and scope required before the object can be represented inside a simulation.

Its role is to prevent: undefined simulation purpose, purpose substitution, scope ambiguity, hidden scope expansion, hidden scope contraction, partial simulation represented as whole-object simulation, excluded conditions being treated as simulated, inappropriate generalization of simulation outputs, insufficient simulation depth, unjustified precision, and downstream simulation design becoming detached from the question the simulation was originally intended to answer.
Governance Flow
Governed Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Questions → Simulation Scope → Scope Inclusions → Scope Exclusions → Applicability Context → Simulation Depth → Simulation Precision → Purpose & Scope Record → Governed Simulation Inquiry
The governed Simulation Purpose & Scope becomes the input to:
Reality Representation Governance Simulation Purpose
Simulation Purpose defines why simulation is being performed and what decision, inquiry, exploration, comparison, investigation, design activity, operational question, or knowledge requirement it is intended to support.
A Simulation Purpose may include: design exploration, performance assessment, behavior analysis, mission planning, safety investigation, failure exploration, scenario examination, stress assessment, training, operational preparation, comparative analysis, system optimization, autonomous-system testing, policy exploration, scientific inquiry, forecasting support, or another explicitly governed simulation objective.

The purpose must be sufficiently explicit to guide downstream simulation governance.
Purpose Must Be Object-Bound
The Simulation Purpose must remain connected to the governed Simulation Object.
A simulation purpose should therefore answer:
What are we trying to learn, examine, reproduce, compare, explore, or understand about this Simulation Object?
A purpose that cannot be connected to the governed object is not sufficiently established.
Primary and Secondary Purpose
A simulation may have more than one legitimate purpose.
SPSS may distinguish:
Primary Simulation Purpose
from:
Secondary Simulation Purposes
where necessary.
Secondary purposes must not silently become equivalent to the primary purpose if they require different representation, scenarios, depth, or precision.
Purpose Substitution
Purpose Substitution occurs when a simulation performed for one purpose is later treated as though it had been performed for another materially different purpose.
For example:
Design Exploration
must not automatically become:
Operational Safety Demonstration
and:
Training Simulation
must not automatically become:
Real-World Performance Evidence
without a governed basis.
SPSS prohibits silent purpose substitution.
Simulation Question
A Simulation Purpose should be translated into one or more sufficiently clear Simulation Questions.
Examples may include:
How does the system behave under condition X?
What happens if component Y fails?
How does the object respond across operating range Z?

Which scenario produces the greatest system stress?
How does autonomous behavior change when communication is lost?
The Simulation Question provides a bridge between broad purpose and concrete simulation scope.
Simulation Scope
Simulation Scope defines the governed extent of the simulation inquiry.
It determines which portions, characteristics, behaviors, conditions, interactions, operating modes, temporal periods, environments, populations, scenarios, and relationships are intended to be examined.
Simulation Scope establishes:
what the simulation covers
and:
what it does not cover. Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Scope
SIMULOS® establishes an important distinction:
Simulation Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Scope
SOS may define an entire aircraft as the Simulation Object.
SPSS may define the simulation scope as:
Landing Behavior Under Crosswind Conditions
The object remains the aircraft.
The simulation does not automatically cover every possible aircraft behavior.
Scope Inclusion
Material inclusions should be sufficiently explicit.
Depending upon the simulation, scope may include: specific components, functions, behaviors, operating modes, mission phases, environmental conditions, failure conditions, populations, interactions, geographic regions, temporal periods, or consequence pathways.
Scope Exclusion
Material exclusions must remain visible.

An exclusion identifies a condition, characteristic, behavior, environment, population, operating mode, component, or interaction intentionally outside the governed simulation inquiry.
SPSS establishes:
Excluded from Simulation Scope ≠ Demonstrated by Simulation
This distinction must remain preserved throughout downstream interpretation.
No Hidden Scope Expansion Rule
A simulation must not acquire broader scope after execution merely because the resulting outputs appear useful beyond the original inquiry.
For example:
Simulated urban daytime driving
must not silently become:
simulated autonomous driving under all operational conditions.
Any material expansion requires explicit reassessment of Simulation Purpose & Scope and affected downstream SIMULOS® spaces.
No Hidden Scope Contraction Rule
Likewise, difficult, adverse, or inconvenient conditions must not be silently removed from the Simulation Scope after they were established as materially relevant.
Scope contraction must remain explicit and its effect on downstream simulation claims must be preserved.
Scope Inflation
Scope Inflation occurs when a narrow simulation inquiry becomes represented as supporting a substantially broader conclusion.
Examples include:
Single Scenario → Complete Scenario Coverage
One Environment → All Environments
One Operating Mode → Complete Operational Envelope
One Population → General Population
One Mission Phase → Entire Mission
SPSS prohibits scope inflation without a governed basis.

Scope Fragmentation
A complex Simulation Scope may be divided into smaller governed simulation scopes.
This may be appropriate where different: environments, operating modes, components, scenarios, populations, or mission stages
require different simulation methods or representations.
Fragmentation must preserve the relationship between each partial scope and the complete intended inquiry.
Partial Simulation Scope
A partial scope is legitimate.
SIMULOS® does not require every simulation to cover the complete Simulation Object or complete operational reality.
It requires partial scope to remain explicit.
Therefore:
Partial Simulation ≠ Incomplete Governance
provided the boundary of the partial inquiry is clearly established.
Simulation Applicability Context
Simulation Applicability Context defines the conditions within which the simulation is intended to have meaning.
It may include: operational environment, geographic context, user population, mission phase, deployment condition, system state, autonomy level, interaction pattern, resource condition, consequence context, or another relevant domain.
Applicability Context is not equivalent to later validation or operational authorization.
It defines the context the simulation itself is intended to examine.
Simulation Purpose vs Operational Reliance
SPSS does not determine whether simulation outputs may be relied upon operationally.
It may record an intended downstream use where that use influences the required simulation design.

However:
Intended Use ≠ Authorized Reliance
Formal validation and reliance questions belong to VALIDOS® and other applicable governance layers.
Simulation Purpose vs Validation Purpose
SIMULOS® and VALIDOS® must remain separate.
SPSS asks:
Why are we performing this simulation and what must it cover?
VALIDOS® VPSS asks:
Why are we validating this Validation Object and what must that validation establish?
A simulation may later become: validation evidence, a Validation Object, part of a Validation Method, or one input into a broader validation determination.
The purposes may interact, but they are not the same governance question.
Simulation Depth
Simulation Depth defines how deeply the governed simulation inquiry must examine the selected Simulation Object characteristics and conditions.
Depth may increase where the simulation purpose involves: high consequence, high complexity, high uncertainty, autonomous behavior, significant interaction effects, rare failure conditions, safety-critical operations, irreversible decisions, or broad downstream dependence.
Simulation Depth should remain proportional to the purpose. Simulation Depth ≠ Validation Depth
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation Depth ≠ Validation Depth
Simulation Depth governs the required depth of the simulation inquiry.
Validation Depth under VALIDOS® governs the strength and assurance level required to establish a validation conclusion.
One may influence the other without becoming the same concept.
Simulation Precision

Simulation Precision defines the level of detail, granularity, resolution, or quantitative specificity required to satisfy the Simulation Purpose.
Precision may concern: temporal resolution, spatial resolution, behavioral granularity, component detail, parameter resolution, scenario resolution, measurement granularity, or output specificity.
Greater precision is not automatically better.
No False Precision Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation precision must not exceed what the simulation purpose, object definition, representation basis, assumptions, inputs, and model structure can meaningfully support.
A highly precise numerical output does not automatically imply highly precise representation of reality.
Purpose-Depth Alignment
Simulation Depth should be sufficient for the Simulation Purpose.
A mismatch may occur where:
High-Consequence Purpose → Low Simulation Depth
or:
Exploratory Purpose → Excessive Simulation Burden
SPSS governs alignment rather than maximum complexity.
Purpose-Precision Alignment
Simulation Precision should also be appropriate to purpose.
A simulation intended only to identify broad directional behavior may not require the same precision as one intended to examine a narrow engineering tolerance.
Scope-Depth Alignment
Depth must apply to the actual Simulation Scope.
A simulation cannot compensate for missing scope merely by examining the included portion in extreme detail.
Therefore:

Deep Simulation of Narrow Scope ≠ Broad Simulation Coverage Scope-Precision Alignment
High precision within one narrow scope does not justify claims concerning excluded conditions.
This prevents precise outputs from creating artificial scope credibility.
Consequence Context
The consequence attached to the intended simulation use may influence required: depth, precision, scenario breadth, representation fidelity, documentation, or later validation.
SPSS may therefore record a Simulation Consequence Context where materially relevant.
It does not replace general risk governance.
Exploratory Simulation
An exploratory simulation may intentionally operate with: broader uncertainty, lower precision, incomplete knowledge, wider hypothesis space, or provisional assumptions.
This is legitimate if the Simulation Purpose clearly identifies the exploratory nature of the inquiry.
Exploratory results must not silently become high-assurance conclusions.
Decision-Support Simulation
Where simulation is intended to support a decision, the decision context should be sufficiently described to establish the required scope, depth, and precision.
SPSS does not govern the decision itself.
It governs the simulation inquiry supporting that decision.
High-Consequence Simulation
Where simulation may materially influence: safety, critical infrastructure, autonomous operation, medical decisions, aerospace operations, mission-critical systems, financial stability, or other high-consequence environments,

SPSS should require correspondingly explicit purpose, scope, exclusions, depth, and applicability.
Simulation Purpose Change
The Simulation Purpose may change during the lifecycle.
A Material Purpose Change occurs where the new purpose would require materially different: representation, assumptions, model structure, inputs, scenarios, execution, outputs, or correlation requirements.
Material purpose change requires downstream reassessment.
Simulation Scope Change
Simulation Scope may also change.
Relevant changes include:
Scope Expansion
Scope Contraction
Scope Recomposition
Scope Extension
Scope Restriction
or:
Applicability Change
Material scope change must remain traceable.
Purpose & Scope Change Propagation
SIMULOS® establishes:
A material change to Simulation Purpose or Scope must propagate to every downstream simulation governance space materially dependent upon that purpose or scope.
Potentially affected spaces include: Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output Governance, Simulation-to-Reality Correlation, Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary, and Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation.
No Retrospective Purpose Redefinition Rule
A Simulation Purpose must not be materially redefined after results become known merely to make those results appear more successful or relevant.
Material change must be explicitly documented and affected simulation governance reconsidered.

No Retrospective Scope Redefinition Rule
Likewise, the scope must not be silently changed after execution so that failed or unmodeled conditions disappear from the represented inquiry.
Purpose & Scope Traceability
The simulation lifecycle should remain traceable to:
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Questions → Simulation Scope → Inclusions → Exclusions → Applicability → Depth → Precision
This relationship allows later reviewers to determine what the simulation was actually designed to establish.
Simulation Purpose & Scope Record
SPSS should produce a persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record sufficient to reconstruct: why the simulation was performed, which questions it addressed, what was included, what was excluded, where the simulation applied, how deeply it was intended to examine the object, and what level of precision was required.
Operational Space
SPSS governs: Simulation Purpose, primary and secondary purposes, Simulation Questions, Simulation Scope, scope inclusions, scope exclusions, applicability context, partial scope, scope fragmentation, Simulation Depth, Simulation Precision, consequence context, intended simulation use, purpose changes, scope changes, scope limitations, purpose and scope traceability, and the persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record.
Governance Boundary
SPSS begins when:
a governed Simulation Object exists and requires a defined reason, inquiry boundary, and simulation extent.
SPSS ends when:

Simulation Purpose, Simulation Questions, Scope, material inclusions and exclusions, Applicability Context, Simulation Depth, and required Simulation Precision are sufficiently established to support governed Reality Representation.
Governance Scope
SPSS governs only the purpose and scope of simulation.
It does not govern: Simulation Object identity, Simulation Object boundary itself, reality-representation fidelity, simulation assumptions, model construction, simulation environment construction, input-data suitability, scenario design, execution, outputs, simulation-to-reality correlation, formal validation, Validation State, operational reliance authorization, general integrity, risk governance, accountability, or audit execution.
These responsibilities belong to other SIMULOS® Parent Standards or adjacent OOF® architectures.
Minimum Governance Requirements
A conforming application of SPSS should establish:

1. an explicit Simulation Purpose, 2. a clear relationship between purpose and the governed Simulation Object, 3. one or more identifiable Simulation Questions, 4. a bounded Simulation Scope, 5. explicit material scope inclusions, 6. explicit material scope exclusions, 7. a defined Simulation Applicability Context, 8. sufficient Simulation Depth relative to purpose, 9. appropriate Simulation Precision, 10. visibility of intended downstream use where materially relevant, 11. prevention of purpose substitution, 12. prevention of scope inflation, 13. prevention of retrospective purpose or scope redefinition, 14. traceability of material purpose and scope changes, 15. and a persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record.
Governance Outputs
SPSS may produce: Simulation Purpose Statement, Primary Simulation Purpose, Secondary Simulation Purpose Record, Simulation Question Set, Simulation Scope Definition, Simulation Scope Map, Scope Inclusion Record, Scope Exclusion Record, Partial Scope Record, Scope Fragmentation Map, Simulation Applicability Context, Simulation Depth Requirement, Simulation Precision Requirement, Simulation Consequence Context, Intended Simulation Use Record, Purpose Limitation Record, Scope Limitation Record, Purpose Change Record, Scope Expansion Record, Scope Contraction Record, Scope Recomposition Record, Purpose & Scope Change Assessment, Purpose & Scope Traceability Map, and Simulation Purpose & Scope Record.
Operational Applications

Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotics, aerospace, space missions, aviation, autonomous vehicles, manufacturing, digital twins, scientific simulation, engineering simulation, healthcare, financial systems, critical infrastructure, environmental systems, mission planning, system-of-systems simulation, policy simulation, organizational simulation, population simulation, training environments, safety analysis, failure analysis, and future operational ecosystems.

Architectural Position
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The architecture begins:
Simulation Object
↓
Simulation Purpose & Scope
SOS establishes:
What exactly is being simulated?
SPSS establishes:
Why is it being simulated, what must the simulation cover, what is excluded, and how deeply must the inquiry operate?
Once those conditions are sufficiently established, the next architectural question becomes:
Which aspects of reality must now be represented inside the simulation, and at what level of abstraction and fidelity?
This transition leads directly into:
Reality Representation Governance
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot legitimately answer a broader question than the purpose and scope for which it was actually designed.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) establishes the inquiry boundary of SIMULOS® by governing why a simulation is performed, which questions it is intended to answer, what portions of the Simulation Object and surrounding conditions it covers, what remains explicitly excluded, where its applicability begins and ends, and what depth and precision are required for the intended simulation purpose. Through purpose definition, scope governance, inclusion and exclusion control, applicability bounding, depth and precision alignment, anti-inflation rules, change propagation, and persistent traceability, SPSS prevents technically successful simulations from acquiring purposes, meanings, or coverage that they were never designed to support. By transforming a governed Simulation Object into a bounded simulation inquiry, SPSS establishes the second methodological foundation of the SIMULOS® lifecycle and prepares that inquiry for governed representation of reality.

OOF™ Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation scenarios are identified, selected, structured, varied, bounded, stressed, combined, prioritized, documented, and assessed for sufficient coverage so that a governed simulation examines not only expected operating conditions but also materially relevant variations, edge cases, stress conditions, uncertainty ranges, alternative states, transitions, failures, interactions, and plausible combinations capable of affecting simulation outcomes.
SSS establishes the scenario-governance layer through which the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and Input & Data Basis are transformed into an explicit set of conditions that the simulation will actually examine.
It ensures that a technically capable simulation cannot create an appearance of adequate examination merely because it executes many runs while materially relevant scenarios remain absent.
Core Governance Question
Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives?
Purpose

A simulation can possess: a correctly identified Simulation Object, a clear purpose and scope, a strong representation of reality, governed assumptions, a well-constructed model and environment, and suitable input data,
and still fail to provide useful simulation insight because the wrong scenarios were selected.
A simulation may test only:
normal conditions
while the real risk exists in:
degraded conditions.
It may test:
individual failures
while the critical problem arises from:
combined failures.
It may test:
average behavior
while material consequences occur at:
distribution tails.
It may test:
steady-state operation
while the dangerous condition appears only during:
transition.
SSS exists to govern this problem.
Operational Role
SSS is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
The preceding Parent Standards establish:
1. Simulation Object — What exactly is being simulated?
2. Simulation Purpose & Scope — Why is the simulation being performed and what must it cover?
3. Reality Representation — Which aspects of reality must be represented and at what abstraction and fidelity?
4. Simulation Assumptions — Which premises enable the simulation and under what limitations?
5. Simulation Model & Environment — Through which controlled model and environment will the simulation operate?
6. Simulation Inputs & Data — Which information may enter and influence the simulation?
SSS asks:

Which governed combinations of conditions must that simulation actually examine?
It therefore establishes the scenario basis required before governed Simulation Execution begins.

Operational Space

SSS governs simulation-specific conditions relating to: scenario identification, scenario purpose, scenario identity, scenario classification, baseline scenarios, nominal scenarios, expected-condition scenarios, alternative scenarios, scenario variation, parameter variation, input variation, environmental variation, behavioral variation, uncertainty-driven scenarios, boundary scenarios, edge cases, rare conditions, failure scenarios, degraded-state scenarios, transition scenarios, recovery scenarios, stress conditions, extreme conditions, combined conditions, correlated conditions, multi-factor scenarios, cascading scenarios, sequential scenarios, scenario interaction, scenario dependency, scenario prioritization, scenario exclusion, scenario sufficiency, scenario coverage, scenario gaps, scenario redundancy, scenario comparability, scenario change, scenario versioning, and scenario-to-execution traceability.
Operational Scope
SSS applies wherever a simulation must intentionally determine which conditions are to be examined.

It may govern scenario design for: AI systems, autonomous systems, autonomous agents, robotics, aerospace systems, spacecraft, mission systems, industrial systems, manufacturing, critical infrastructure, transportation, digital twins, financial systems, energy systems, healthcare systems, scientific models, climate and environmental systems, cyber systems, defense systems, emergency systems, organizational processes, human-machine systems, multi-agent environments, and future operational ecosystems.
SSS does not prescribe which domain-specific scenarios are universally correct.
It governs how a simulation establishes that the scenarios selected for its specific purpose are sufficiently structured and sufficiently complete.
Simulation Scenario
A Simulation Scenario is a governed configuration of materially relevant conditions, states, inputs, parameters, events, behaviors, interactions, constraints, or transitions under which a Simulation Object is examined through simulation.
Conceptually:
Scenario = Defined Simulation Conditions + Applicable Configuration + Relevant Variation + Execution Intent
A scenario may describe: one operating condition, one failure, one environmental state, one behavior pattern, one combination of conditions, one transition, one stress state, or a complete event sequence.
Scenario Identity
Every material scenario should be sufficiently identifiable.

A Scenario Identity may establish: Scenario Identifier, scenario name, scenario purpose, relevant Simulation Object, applicable Simulation Scope, model and environment configuration, relevant Input Set, parameter configuration, environmental conditions, assumptions, scenario state, intended variation, and scenario version.
Scenario Requirement
Before scenarios are selected, SSS establishes Scenario Requirements.
A Scenario Requirement answers:
What condition, variation, boundary, uncertainty, interaction, or potential failure must the simulation be capable of examining?
The requirement exists independently of the exact technical scenario used to satisfy it.
This distinction supports traceability:
Scenario Requirement → Designed Scenario → Simulation Execution Baseline Scenario
A Baseline Scenario represents the governed reference condition against which materially different scenarios may be compared.
Baseline does not mean:
correct reality
or:
most likely future.
It establishes a controlled reference.
Nominal Scenario
A Nominal Scenario represents expected or intended operating conditions.
Nominal conditions may be important for: normal behavior, expected performance, baseline comparison, and operational-state understanding.
But nominal scenarios alone rarely establish sufficient scenario coverage for complex or high-consequence systems.
No Nominal-Only Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Successful simulation under nominal conditions does not demonstrate adequate simulation coverage when materially relevant non-nominal conditions exist.
Expected-Condition Scenario
Expected-condition scenarios represent conditions reasonably anticipated within the intended Simulation Scope.
They may include variation within: normal operating ranges, known environments, expected populations, expected loads, routine disturbances, or normal operational transitions.
Scenario Variation
Scenario Variation governs deliberate changes to one or more materially relevant simulation conditions.
Variation may involve: parameters, inputs, environmental conditions, system states, actor behavior, timing, resource availability, communication conditions, failures, or dependencies.
Controlled Scenario Variation
Where comparative interpretation matters, the simulation should identify which conditions are intentionally changed and which remain controlled.
Conceptually:
Baseline Scenario
↓
Change X
↓
Variation Scenario
This supports determination of whether differences in behavior are associated with the intended variation rather than hidden scenario changes.
Single-Factor Variation
A scenario may vary one material factor while maintaining other conditions.
This may help isolate sensitivity or causal contribution within the simulation.
Multi-Factor Variation
Some behavior emerges only when several factors change simultaneously.
SSS therefore allows scenarios involving:
Factor A + Factor B + Factor C

where combined conditions are materially relevant.
No Single-Failure Sufficiency Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Testing individual failures does not establish coverage of combinations of failures where combined failures can produce materially different system behavior.
Edge Case
An Edge Case is a scenario representing conditions near or beyond the normal operating distribution, common expectation, typical configuration, or frequently observed state where simulation behavior may materially differ from nominal behavior.
An edge case may arise from: unusual inputs, rare environmental conditions, uncommon interactions, boundary values, atypical behavior, unusual sequencing, unexpected combinations, or low-frequency events.
Edge ≠ Impossible
A condition should not be excluded merely because it is rare.
The relevant governance question is:
Is the condition materially plausible and consequential within the Simulation Purpose & Scope?
Rare Scenario
A Rare Scenario may have low occurrence probability while retaining high consequence.
SSS therefore distinguishes:
Frequency
from:
Scenario Importance.
Consequence-Weighted Scenario Selection
Scenario selection should consider not only:
How likely is this condition?
but also:
What happens if it occurs?
A low-frequency catastrophic condition may warrant stronger scenario coverage than a high-frequency trivial variation.
Boundary Scenario

A Boundary Scenario examines behavior close to an applicable operating, environmental, physical, behavioral, or governance boundary.
Examples may involve: maximum load, minimum power, communication limits, environmental tolerance, control limits, resource exhaustion, operational envelopes, or response thresholds.
Boundary Crossing Scenario
Where materially relevant, scenarios should examine not only operation near a boundary but also what occurs when the boundary is crossed.
Conceptually:
Inside Boundary → Boundary Reached → Boundary Exceeded
The system may behave differently at each state.
Stress Scenario
A Stress Scenario intentionally subjects the simulated system to conditions beyond ordinary operating variation to determine how behavior changes under increased pressure or constraint.
Stress may involve: load, resource scarcity, environmental extremes, communication degradation, timing pressure, component degradation, information loss, actor density, adversarial behavior, or other system-specific stressors.
Stress Does Not Mean Arbitrary Extremity
Stress scenarios should remain relevant to the Simulation Purpose.
SSS does not require testing arbitrary impossible conditions merely to maximize scenario count.
Extreme Scenario
An Extreme Scenario represents a materially severe condition at or beyond ordinary expectations where system behavior or consequences may change significantly.

Extreme scenarios may be appropriate where: consequence is high, operational resilience matters, safety margins matter, rare-event behavior matters, or failure containment is being examined.
Failure Scenario
A Failure Scenario represents the failure of a component, dependency, capability, resource, interface, actor, process, or environmental condition relevant to the Simulation Object.
Failures may be:
Single
Multiple
Sequential
Simultaneous
Dependent
Cascading
or:
Common-Cause
where those distinctions matter.
Common-Cause Scenario
Multiple failures may arise from one common underlying cause.
For example:
Power Loss
may simultaneously affect:
Communications + Sensors + Cooling + Control
Treating the failures as statistically independent may miss the actual scenario structure.
Cascading Scenario
A Cascading Scenario examines a sequence in which one material event causes or enables another.
Conceptually:
Failure A → Degradation B → Resource Loss C → Failure D
Complex systems may fail through chains rather than isolated events.
Sequential Scenario
The order of conditions may materially change the outcome.
Therefore:
A → B → C
may require separate examination from:
C → B → A.
Transition Scenario
A system may behave safely in State A and safely in State B while becoming vulnerable during the transition between them.

A Transition Scenario therefore examines changes such as: startup, shutdown, mode change, handover, control transfer, autonomy escalation, environment transition, recovery, docking, landing, or state switching.
No Stable-State-Only Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Testing stable states alone does not establish coverage of transitions between those states where transition behavior may materially affect outcomes.
Degraded-State Scenario
A Degraded-State Scenario examines operation where the system remains functional but one or more capabilities, resources, dependencies, or operating conditions are reduced.
Examples may involve: reduced sensing, reduced communication, degraded power, limited computation, partial actuator availability, incomplete information, reduced human support, or degraded infrastructure.
Recovery Scenario
A Recovery Scenario examines behavior after disruption or failure.
It may address: restoration, restart, failover, fallback, state reconstruction, resource recovery, human intervention, or return to nominal operation.
SSS governs selection of the scenario.
ORA™ may govern actual Operational Recovery in real-world operation.
Uncertainty-Driven Scenario
Uncertainty identified in upstream SIMULOS® spaces may require deliberate scenario representation.
For example:
Input Uncertainty Range
may generate:
Low → Central → High
scenario conditions.
Uncertainty should not remain documented while scenario design tests only one convenient point estimate.

Unresolved-Uncertainty Scenario
Where uncertainty cannot be sufficiently quantified, scenario design may require alternative plausible states rather than one probabilistic representation.
Scenario Interaction
Scenarios may interact with: Simulation Assumptions, Input Sets, Environment Configurations, Parameters, actor behavior, dependencies, and execution conditions.
These relationships should remain explicit.
Scenario Dependency
A scenario may depend upon another condition being active.
For example:
Emergency Power Failure Scenario
may become relevant only after:
Primary Power Failure.
Scenario dependencies should remain traceable where material.
Scenario Combination
Individual scenario elements may need to be combined.
Conceptually:
Extreme Weather + Sensor Degradation + Communication Delay
may produce behavior not observable when each condition is simulated separately.
Combination Explosion
Complex systems can generate an enormous number of possible scenario combinations.
SSS does not require brute-force simulation of every mathematically possible combination.
It requires governed determination of which combinations are materially relevant.
Scenario Prioritization
Where exhaustive simulation is impractical, scenarios may be prioritized according to factors such as: materiality, consequence, probability, uncertainty, boundary proximity, dependency concentration, scenario novelty, known failure history, operational importance, and unresolved governance gaps.

Prioritization must not silently erase excluded material scenarios.
Scenario Selection Basis
Each material scenario or scenario family should have an identifiable selection basis.
This may include: Simulation Purpose, Reality Representation, Assumptions, uncertainty, input limitations, model sensitivities, operational states, known failure modes, boundary conditions, historical events, or defined exploratory objectives.
Scenario Exclusion
A potential scenario may be excluded where it is: outside Simulation Scope, materially impossible, non-relevant, duplicative, already sufficiently covered, or otherwise methodologically unnecessary.
Material exclusions should remain visible where omission could later be misunderstood as coverage.
No Convenience Exclusion Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A materially relevant scenario must not be excluded solely because it is difficult, computationally expensive, inconvenient, or likely to produce an undesirable result.
Scenario Feasibility
Scenario feasibility may involve: computational constraints, model capability, data availability, environment capability, time, physical interface limitations, or other constraints.
Where a materially required scenario cannot be simulated, the resulting Scenario Coverage Gap should remain visible.
Scenario Coverage
Scenario Coverage describes the extent to which the governed Scenario Set examines the materially relevant conditions required by the Simulation Purpose & Scope.

Coverage may include: normal conditions, variation, populations, environments, boundaries, uncertainty ranges, failure states, transitions, stresses, rare events, combinations, and recovery conditions.
Scenario Coverage ≠ Scenario Count
SIMULOS® establishes:
A large number of simulation scenarios does not establish adequate scenario coverage.
Ten thousand scenarios concentrated in one narrow region may provide weaker coverage than a smaller scenario set deliberately spanning all materially relevant condition classes.
Scenario Coverage Dimension
Coverage may be evaluated across multiple dimensions, such as:
Operating State
Environment
Population
Input Range
Uncertainty
Failure Mode
Transition
Stress
Interaction
Dependency
Recovery
or another simulation-specific dimension.
Coverage Matrix
Where useful, scenario coverage may be represented through a multidimensional matrix connecting:
Scenario Requirement × Condition Class × Scenario × Coverage Status
This allows gaps to become visible without reducing scenario completeness to one numerical count.
Scenario Coverage Status
A scenario requirement may receive a status such as:
Covered
Conditionally Covered
Partially Covered
Not Covered
or:
Coverage Undetermined Scenario Coverage Gap
A Scenario Coverage Gap exists where a materially relevant condition required by the Simulation Purpose & Scope is not sufficiently examined by the governed Scenario Set.

A gap may arise from: missing data, model limitation, environment limitation, computational constraints, unrecognized scenario need, excluded edge cases, missing combinations, or incomplete uncertainty coverage.
Coverage Gap Materiality
Scenario gaps should be assessed according to whether the omitted condition could materially affect: system behavior, outputs, risk understanding, failure understanding, operational decisions, or downstream validation and reliance.
Coverage Sufficiency
Scenario Coverage Sufficiency asks:
Does the Scenario Set provide enough governed variation and condition coverage to support the Simulation Purpose without claiming broader examination than was actually performed?
No Full-Coverage Claim Without Basis
SIMULOS® establishes:
Scenario coverage must not be represented as comprehensive where materially relevant scenario classes remain unexamined.
Scenario Redundancy
Multiple scenarios may examine substantially the same condition.
Redundancy may be useful for: repeatability, uncertainty exploration, random variation, or sensitivity testing.
But scenario count should not be inflated through redundant scenarios while important gaps remain.
Scenario Independence
Two scenarios should not be assumed independent where they depend upon the same: Input Set, Assumption, environment, failure source, behavioral model, or dependency.
This may matter when scenario results appear to provide independent confirmation.
Scenario Equivalence

Two scenarios may be scenario-equivalent where material differences do not alter the simulation inquiry.
Equivalence should be established rather than presumed.
Scenario Family
Related scenarios may be grouped into a Scenario Family.
Examples may include:
Communication Degradation Family
Power Failure Family
Extreme Environment Family
Autonomous Interaction Family
Scenario families may support systematic coverage without eliminating scenario-level identity.
Scenario Set
A Governed Simulation Scenario Set is the complete collection of scenarios approved for a defined simulation campaign or inquiry.
It may identify: scenario identities, scenario families, requirements, configurations, applicable inputs, variation dimensions, edge conditions, stress conditions, coverage relationships, exclusions, gaps, priorities, and execution status.
Scenario Set Version
Scenario design may evolve.
A new Scenario Set Version should be distinguishable where materially relevant scenarios are: added, removed, modified, combined, reprioritized, or reclassified.
Scenario Change
Scenario change may be triggered by: new evidence, new input uncertainty, model change, environment change, discovered failure mode, changed Simulation Scope, new operational condition, changed assumptions, incident, or new system capability.
Scenario Reassessment
Material upstream change should trigger reassessment of whether existing scenario coverage remains sufficient.
No Static Scenario Set Principle

SIMULOS® establishes:
A Scenario Set that was sufficient for one simulation configuration or lifecycle state must not automatically be treated as sufficient after material change.
Scenario-to-Input Traceability
Scenarios should remain traceable to the input conditions they consume where material.
Conceptually:
Scenario → Simulation Input Set Scenario-to-Parameter Traceability
Where scenarios differ through parameter configuration:
Scenario → Parameter Configuration
should remain traceable.
Scenario-to-Assumption Traceability
A scenario may exist specifically to test an assumption boundary or uncertainty.
Conceptually:
Simulation Assumption → Relevant Scenario Requirement → Scenario Scenario-to-Environment Traceability
Environment-specific scenarios should remain connected to the Simulation Environment Configuration they require.
Scenario-to-Execution Binding
Every Simulation Execution should be bindable to the scenario under which it occurred.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID → Scenario ID
This allows outputs to remain traceable to the exact conditions examined.
Scenario Reproducibility
Where required, a scenario should be defined sufficiently to permit reconstruction of the materially relevant conditions under which it was executed.
Not every stochastic simulation will reproduce the identical output.
But the governed scenario configuration should remain reconstructable.
Scenario Comparability

Two scenario executions may be compared only where materially relevant differences are understood.
Scenario comparison should distinguish:
Intended Variation
from:
Unintended Configuration Difference.
Scenario Escalation
Scenario execution may reveal a condition that requires stronger or broader scenario coverage.
For example:
a nominal stress scenario may unexpectedly expose a cascading dependency.
Scenario governance should allow:
Observed Simulation Behavior → New Scenario Requirement → Scenario Set Expansion
without altering completed historical records.
Scenario Discovery
Not every relevant scenario is known before simulation begins.
SIMULOS® therefore permits scenario discovery during the lifecycle.
Discovered scenarios should enter governance rather than remain informal observations.
Emergent Scenario
An Emergent Scenario is a materially relevant condition discovered through simulation interaction, execution behavior, external events, incident analysis, or new knowledge that was not part of the original Scenario Set.
Scenario Discovery Does Not Erase Earlier Gap
When an important scenario is discovered later, the architecture should preserve that earlier simulations did not examine it.
This distinction matters for historical reliance and reconstruction.
Scenario Selection Bias
Scenario design may become biased toward: expected successful behavior, easy-to-model conditions, familiar failure modes, available data, or scenarios supporting a desired conclusion.

SSS requires material selection logic to remain visible.
No Outcome-Seeking Scenario Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Scenario design must not be structured solely to produce the desired simulation outcome.
The Scenario Set should remain capable of exposing unfavorable, unexpected, or contradictory behavior relevant to the Simulation Purpose.
No Data-Convenience Scenario Principle
Scenario selection should not be limited exclusively to conditions for which convenient datasets already exist where material conditions outside those datasets remain within Simulation Scope.
No Model-Convenience Scenario Principle
A scenario does not cease to matter merely because the current Simulation Model cannot represent it sufficiently.
The result may instead be:
Scenario Required — Current Simulation Capability Insufficient Scenario Capability Gap
A Scenario Capability Gap exists where the simulation architecture identifies a materially required scenario that cannot currently be represented or executed with sufficient governance.
The gap should remain explicit.
Scenario Readiness
A Scenario Set may receive a readiness status such as:
Scenario Ready
Conditionally Scenario Ready
Partially Scenario Ready
Scenario Not Ready
or:
Scenario Readiness Undetermined
Readiness applies to progression into governed Simulation Execution. Scenario Readiness ≠ Simulation Validity
A Scenario Ready status means the scenario basis is sufficiently governed for execution.

It does not establish: correct execution, valid outputs, reality correlation, or legitimate operational reliance.
Those questions belong to downstream SIMULOS® spaces and VALIDOS® where applicable.
Governance Boundary
SSS begins when the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and Input & Data Basis are sufficiently established to determine which conditions the simulation should examine.
SSS ends when materially relevant scenarios have been sufficiently identified, varied, bounded, stressed, combined, prioritized, coverage-assessed, gap-documented, versioned, and assembled into a governed Simulation Scenario Set suitable for controlled Simulation Execution.
Architectural Boundary
SSS does not govern: general operational scenario planning, enterprise risk management, actual Operational Reality, general validation methodology, general integrity governance, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output governance, Reality Correlation, final simulation validation, or operational reliance.
SSS governs specifically:
the design and coverage of the conditions that SIMULOS® will ask the simulation to examine.
Minimum Governance Requirements
A conforming application of SSS should establish:

1. identifiable Scenario Requirements, 2. identifiable Simulation Scenarios, 3. baseline or reference scenarios where relevant, 4. expected-condition coverage, 5. material scenario variation, 6. edge-case identification, 7. boundary-condition coverage, 8. materially relevant stress conditions, 9. failure and degraded-state scenarios where applicable, 10. transition and recovery scenarios where applicable, 11. uncertainty-driven scenario treatment, 12. materially relevant scenario combinations, 13. scenario prioritization where exhaustive coverage is impractical, 14. explicit material scenario exclusions, 15. multidimensional Scenario Coverage assessment, 16. Scenario Coverage Gaps, 17. scenario-to-input/configuration traceability, 18. scenario versioning and change visibility, 19. Scenario Readiness, 20. and sufficient scenario-to-execution traceability for reconstruction.
Governance Outputs

SSS may produce: Scenario Requirement Register, Simulation Scenario Identifier, Simulation Scenario Record, Scenario Classification, Baseline Scenario, Nominal Scenario, Expected-Condition Scenario, Scenario Variation Record, Single-Factor Variation Record, Multi-Factor Variation Record, Edge-Case Scenario Record, Rare Scenario Record, Boundary Scenario Record, Boundary-Crossing Scenario Record, Stress Scenario Record, Extreme Scenario Record, Failure Scenario Record, Common-Cause Scenario Record, Cascading Scenario Record, Sequential Scenario Record, Transition Scenario Record, Degraded-State Scenario Record, Recovery Scenario Record, Uncertainty-Driven Scenario Record, Scenario Interaction Map, Scenario Dependency Map, Scenario Combination Record, Scenario Priority Record, Scenario Selection Basis, Scenario Exclusion Record, Scenario Capability Gap, Scenario Family, Scenario Coverage Matrix, Scenario Coverage Assessment, Scenario Coverage Status, Scenario Coverage Gap, Scenario Coverage Gap Materiality Assessment, Scenario Coverage Sufficiency Assessment, Scenario Set, Scenario Set Identifier, Scenario Set Version, Scenario Change Record, Scenario Reassessment Trigger, Scenario Discovery Record, Emergent Scenario Record, Scenario-to-Assumption Traceability Reference, Scenario-to-Input Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Environment Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Execution Binding Requirement, Scenario Readiness Status, and Governed Simulatio
Map, Scenario-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Environment Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Execution Binding Requirement, Scenario Readiness Status, and Governed Simulation Scenario Set.

Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures
SSS remains bounded to simulation-specific Scenario Design.
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SSS may use operational conditions as scenario references but does not govern real-world operational states themselves.
VALIDOS® governs validation. Scenario coverage produced under SSS may later become evidence relevant to validation, but SSS does not itself determine whether the simulation or its results satisfy a formal Validation Determination.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity of scenario definitions, records, configurations, and preserved scenario history.
ADIT® may preserve evidence of scenario design, selection, change, execution, and coverage.
AGA™ may govern accountability for material scenario selection, exclusion, prioritization, or approval decisions.
ASGA™ may define autonomous-system governance conditions that become scenario requirements when autonomous systems are simulated.
AIG® may contribute AI behavioral conditions that require scenario representation.
SSS does not replace those architectures.
It governs specifically which simulation conditions must be deliberately constructed and examined before simulation execution can claim meaningful scenario coverage.
Architectural Position
Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
Its position in the 12-Parent-Standard architecture is:
1. Simulation Object
↓
2. Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓

3. Reality Representation
↓
4. Simulation Assumptions
↓
5. Simulation Model & Environment
↓
6. Simulation Inputs & Data
↓
7. Simulation Scenario Design
↓
8. Simulation Execution
↓
9–12. Downstream SIMULOS® lifecycle governance
SSS occupies the point where the previously governed simulation foundation becomes an explicit testable condition space.
Before SSS, SIMULOS® establishes:
what is being simulated, why, how reality is represented, what is assumed, through which model and environment the simulation operates, and which information may enter it.
SSS then determines:
which materially relevant conditions that governed simulation must actually examine.
Only after that scenario basis exists should the architecture proceed into controlled Simulation Execution.
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot claim meaningful coverage merely because it executes successfully; it must deliberately examine the materially relevant conditions, variations, boundaries, uncertainties, failures, stresses, interactions, and alternatives capable of changing the behavior or conclusions of the simulation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Scenario Standard establishes the scenario-design governance layer of SIMULOS® by defining how materially relevant simulation conditions are identified, structured, varied, combined, stressed, bounded, prioritized, coverage-assessed, and preserved before execution. By governing nominal conditions, expected variation, edge cases, boundary conditions, rare events, degraded and failure states, transitions, cascading interactions, uncertainty-driven scenarios, stress conditions, scenario exclusions, coverage gaps, scenario readiness, versioning, and complete scenario-to-execution traceability, SSS prevents simulation volume from being mistaken for simulation coverage and ensures that a simulation cannot appear comprehensively examined while the conditions most capable of changing its behavior remain outside the governed Scenario Set.
Module Architecture
→ Scenario Identification Module (SCIM)
→ Scenario Variation Module (SCVM)
→ Scenario Edge-Case Module (SECM)
→ Scenario Stress-Condition Module (SSCM)
→ Scenario Coverage Module (SCCM)
Related Documents
→ About Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS)
