chunks.text:
OOF™ Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM)
Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Input Uncertainty
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Input Uncertainty
Canonical Definition
Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM) defines the governance framework through which uncertainty associated with Simulation Inputs is identified, classified, bounded, quantified or qualitatively characterized where appropriate, propagated into simulation execution, and preserved through downstream interpretation so that uncertainty in the input basis cannot disappear merely because the simulation produces precise outputs.
SIUM establishes the final internal governance layer of SIDS by governing the transition:

Identified + Representative + Transformed + Temporally Governed Inputs → Input Uncertainty Identification → Uncertainty Characterization → Dependency Assessment → Uncertainty Propagation Requirements → Simulation Input Uncertainty Status
Its purpose is not to eliminate uncertainty.
Its purpose is to ensure that uncertainty remains visible, attributable, bounded, and operationally consequential wherever it can materially affect simulation behavior or conclusions.
Operational Role
SIUM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The preceding modules establish:
SIIM — What information is entering the simulation?
SDRM — What reality can that information legitimately represent?
SDTM — What happened to that information before simulation use?
STDM — Is that information temporally appropriate for the reality and dynamics being simulated?
SIUM asks:
What uncertainty remains in the complete Simulation Input basis, where does that uncertainty originate, how may uncertainties interact, and what must remain visible when the simulation uses those inputs?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Input Basis → Uncertainty Sources → Uncertainty Classification → Uncertainty Magnitude / Character → Dependency → Materiality → Propagation Requirement → Input Uncertainty Status → Simulation Use
Module Operational Space

SIUM governs: input uncertainty identification, uncertainty source attribution, measurement uncertainty, observational uncertainty, sampling uncertainty, representativeness uncertainty, transformation-induced uncertainty, temporal uncertainty, estimation uncertainty, interpolation uncertainty, extrapolation uncertainty, imputation uncertainty, synthetic-input uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, classification uncertainty, source-dependent uncertainty, missing-information uncertainty, uncertainty range, uncertainty distribution, uncertainty bounds, qualitative uncertainty, quantitative uncertainty, known uncertainty, partially characterized uncertainty, unknown or unresolved uncertainty, uncertainty dependency, correlated uncertainty, compounded uncertainty, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty sensitivity, uncertainty propagation requirements, uncertainty aggregation, uncertainty conditions, uncertainty limitations, uncertainty status, uncertainty reassessment, and uncertainty traceability.
Module Function

SIUM exists to prevent: uncertain inputs being represented as certain, estimated values being treated as observations, measurement uncertainty disappearing during ingestion, transformation-induced uncertainty being ignored, temporal uncertainty being lost, multiple uncertainties being assumed independent without basis, uncertainty being hidden by numerical precision, uncertainty ranges being collapsed into single values without justification, incomplete information being interpreted as certainty, uncertainty being averaged away, model inputs being presented as exact merely because the simulation requires exact numerical values, simulation outputs appearing more certain than their input basis legitimately supports, and downstream users losing visibility into material uncertainty inherited from Simulation Inputs.
Simulation Input Uncertainty
Simulation Input Uncertainty is the material uncertainty associated with the identity, value, state, origin, representation, transformation, timing, completeness, or applicability of information entering a simulation.
It may concern:
What the value is
Whether the value is correct
Whether the value represents the intended reality
When the value applies
How the value was produced
How complete the information is
or:
How confidently the input may be relied upon within the simulation context.
Uncertainty Is Not Error
SIMULOS® establishes:
Uncertainty does not necessarily mean that an input is wrong.

An input may be the best available representation while still containing material uncertainty.
For example:
Temperature = 20°C ± 1°C
does not mean the measurement is invalid.
It means the information basis contains a bounded uncertainty.
Error vs Uncertainty
SIUM distinguishes:
Known Error
from:
Uncertainty.
A known incorrect value may require correction.
An uncertain value may remain legitimate if the uncertainty is sufficiently understood and governed.
Uncertainty Source
Every material uncertainty should be attributable, where possible, to an identifiable source.
Possible sources include: measurement process, sensor precision, sampling, source reliability, missing information, estimation, transformation, interpolation, extrapolation, temporal misalignment, synthetic generation, model-derived inputs, classification, environmental variability, or unresolved knowledge limitations.
Measurement Uncertainty
Measurement systems have finite accuracy and precision.
A measured value may therefore represent:
Observed Value ± Measurement Uncertainty
rather than an exact physical state.
Where material, the uncertainty should remain connected to the input.
Observational Uncertainty
Some phenomena cannot be observed perfectly.
Observational uncertainty may arise from: incomplete visibility, ambiguous detection, limited sensor coverage, human observation, environmental interference, or indirect observation.
Sampling Uncertainty

A sample represents only part of a broader population, period, environment, or state space.
Sampling uncertainty asks:
How uncertain is the inference from the observed sample to the reality the simulation intends to represent?
SDRM governs representativeness.
SIUM governs the uncertainty remaining within that representation.
Representativeness Uncertainty
A dataset may be accepted as sufficiently representative while still containing uncertainty about how completely it captures: rare conditions, subpopulations, environmental variation, extreme behavior, or future conditions.
Acceptance under SDRM does not eliminate that uncertainty.
Transformation-Induced Uncertainty
SDTM may introduce uncertainty through: filtering, aggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, imputation, normalization, data fusion, synthetic supplementation, or derived-variable construction.
SIUM consolidates these uncertainty contributions into the governed Simulation Input basis.
Temporal Uncertainty
STDM may identify uncertainty involving: timestamps, synchronization, latency, event timing, temporal alignment, applicability periods, drift, or regime transition.
SIUM ensures material temporal uncertainty remains part of the complete uncertainty basis.
Estimation Uncertainty
Estimated inputs should preserve uncertainty associated with the estimation method.
Conceptually:
Observed Basis + Estimation Method → Estimated Input + Estimation Uncertainty Interpolation Uncertainty

Values generated between observations may contain uncertainty dependent upon: distance between observations, variability, interpolation method, system dynamics, and missing-data structure.
Extrapolation Uncertainty
Extrapolation extends beyond observed information.
Uncertainty may increase as extrapolation moves further from the observed basis.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Numerical continuation beyond observed data does not establish equivalent informational confidence.
Imputation Uncertainty
An imputed value may be necessary for simulation execution.
But the simulation should preserve that:
Imputed Value ≠ Observed Value
and that the imputation carries uncertainty derived from its method and basis.
Synthetic Input Uncertainty
Synthetic information may represent plausible conditions without being direct observation.
Where synthetic inputs are used, SIUM governs uncertainty associated with: generation assumptions, generator limitations, distribution fit, scenario coverage, and divergence from observed reality.
Parameter Uncertainty
Simulation Inputs may include parameters whose exact values are unknown.
A parameter may therefore be represented as:
Fixed Estimate
Range
Distribution
Scenario Set
or:
Unknown within defined bounds.
The representation should reflect the available basis rather than artificial precision.
Classification Uncertainty
Some inputs depend upon classification.
For example:
an object may be classified as:
Pedestrian
with:
92% confidence.

Where classification uncertainty can materially affect simulation behavior, it should remain visible.
Missing-Information Uncertainty
Missing information creates uncertainty even where no substitute value is inserted.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Unknown does not become known merely because the simulation can execute without the missing information.
Known Uncertainty
A Known Uncertainty has an identifiable source and sufficiently characterized effect or range.
Example:
Sensor accuracy ±0.5°C Partially Characterized Uncertainty
A Partially Characterized Uncertainty is known to exist but cannot be fully quantified or bounded.
It should remain explicitly represented.
Unresolved Uncertainty
An Unresolved Uncertainty exists where material uncertainty is known but its magnitude, distribution, or consequences cannot yet be sufficiently established.
Unresolved uncertainty may require: restriction, sensitivity analysis, scenario expansion, additional evidence, or downstream limitation.
Unknown Uncertainty
Not every uncertainty can be anticipated.
SIUM does not claim to identify unknowable conditions.
It requires that known limitations in the ability to characterize uncertainty remain visible.
Quantitative Uncertainty
Where appropriate, uncertainty may be expressed through: range, interval, probability distribution, confidence interval, variance, standard deviation, tolerance, error bound, or another justified quantitative representation.
Qualitative Uncertainty

Not all uncertainty should be forced into numerical form.
Qualitative states may include:
Low
Moderate
High
Material but Unquantified
Unresolved
or another governed classification.
No False Quantification Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Uncertainty should not be assigned artificial numerical precision where the available information cannot legitimately support it.
Uncertainty Bounds
Where uncertainty can be bounded, the relevant range should be identified.
For example:
Input X ∈ [8.5, 10.2]
A bounded range should reflect the available evidence rather than an arbitrary convenience range.
Unbounded or Open Uncertainty
Some uncertainty may not have a defensible upper or lower bound.
Such uncertainty should not be converted into a narrow interval merely to satisfy a simulation interface.
Point Estimate Governance
A simulation may technically require a single value.
Where a point estimate represents an uncertain quantity, the record should preserve:
Point Estimate + Uncertainty Basis
rather than allowing the estimate to become indistinguishable from exact observation.
No Point-Estimate Certainty Principle
A single numerical input does not become certain merely because the simulation engine accepts only one number.
Uncertainty Dependency
Uncertainties may be dependent.
For example:
multiple inputs derived from the same sensor may share the same measurement uncertainty.
Treating them as independent may underestimate total uncertainty.
Correlated Uncertainty

Where uncertainty in one input is materially correlated with another, the relationship should be preserved where feasible.
Conceptually:
Uncertainty A ↔ Uncertainty B
rather than:
Uncertainty A + Independent Uncertainty B Shared-Source Uncertainty
Multiple inputs may inherit uncertainty from a common source.
For example:
Input A
Input B
and:
Input C
may all depend upon:
Sensor S
A failure or bias in Sensor S may therefore affect all three inputs simultaneously.
No Independence-by-Default Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Input uncertainties must not be assumed independent merely because they are represented as separate variables.
Compounded Uncertainty
Multiple uncertainties may interact.
Conceptually:
Measurement Uncertainty + Transformation Uncertainty + Temporal Uncertainty + Parameter Uncertainty
may create a broader uncertainty condition than any individual contribution alone.
Uncertainty Aggregation
Where multiple uncertainty contributions are aggregated, the aggregation method should be: identifiable, appropriate, reproducible where required, and bounded by known dependencies.
No Simple Addition Rule
Uncertainty components should not automatically be added, averaged, or multiplied without a justified methodological basis.
Uncertainty Materiality
Not every uncertainty requires the same governance intensity.

An uncertainty is material where it could reasonably affect: simulation behavior, scenario outcome, output interpretation, validation, operational decision, or reliance.
Materiality Is Context-Dependent
An uncertainty of:
±1 mm
may be irrelevant in one simulation and critical in another.
Therefore:
Uncertainty Magnitude ≠ Uncertainty Materiality
Materiality depends upon the Simulation Purpose and the sensitivity of the simulated system.
Uncertainty Sensitivity
A simulation may respond differently to uncertainty across inputs.
Some inputs may have little effect.
Others may produce major output changes.
SIUM therefore supports identification of:
Uncertainty-Sensitive Inputs
where uncertainty requires stronger downstream attention.
Sensitivity Requirement
Where material uncertainty exists, downstream simulation design may require sensitivity analysis.
The relevant later SIMULOS® governance spaces determine how that analysis is executed.
SIUM establishes that the uncertainty requiring examination must not disappear before reaching them.
Uncertainty Propagation
Input uncertainty may propagate through:
Simulation Inputs
↓
Simulation Model
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Outputs
↓
Simulation Interpretation
↓
Operational Reliance
SIUM governs the input-side uncertainty basis and establishes propagation requirements for later SIMULOS® stages.
Uncertainty Does Not End at Input Boundary
SIMULOS® establishes:

Material uncertainty attached to an input remains relevant until a governed downstream process demonstrates why it no longer materially affects the simulation result.
No Uncertainty Erasure Principle
A transformation, model, or simulation execution must not silently erase material uncertainty merely because the downstream output is deterministic. Deterministic Model ≠ Certain Result
A deterministic simulation may produce exactly the same output from exactly the same input.
That does not mean the simulated result is certain where the input itself is uncertain.
Precision vs Certainty
A simulation may produce:
0.87346192
from uncertain input data.
The number of decimal places does not determine the certainty of the result.
No Precision-to-Certainty Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Computational precision must not be represented as evidentiary certainty.
Uncertainty Scenario Representation
Where uncertainty cannot be adequately represented through a single input, the simulation may require multiple input conditions.
For example:
Low Estimate
Central Estimate
High Estimate
or:
Multiple Probability-Based Samples
SIUM establishes the uncertainty basis requiring such treatment.
Boundary Conditions
Uncertain inputs may require simulation at boundary values.
This can reveal whether conclusions remain stable across plausible input ranges.
Worst-Credible Input Condition
Where consequence is high, the simulation may need to examine credible adverse input combinations.

SIUM identifies the uncertainty basis.
Scenario governance determines how those conditions are represented.
Uncertainty Interaction With Scenario Design
SIUM connects directly to the subsequent Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS).
Uncertainty may require scenarios that explore: plausible ranges, adverse combinations, edge conditions, uncertainty distributions, alternative input states, and unresolved input assumptions.
SIUM does not design those scenarios.
It establishes what uncertainty the scenario design must be capable of addressing.
Uncertainty Register
Material input uncertainties should be capable of being preserved within a Simulation Input Uncertainty Register.
The register may identify: uncertainty identifier, affected input, uncertainty source, uncertainty type, magnitude or characterization, dependency, materiality, downstream relevance, condition, and current status.
Uncertainty Identifier
A material uncertainty may receive a persistent identifier.
For example:
SIU-0047
This allows later simulation records to reference the same uncertainty across: scenario design, execution, output interpretation, validation, and reliance.
Uncertainty Status
Possible uncertainty statuses may include:
Characterized
Partially Characterized
Bounded
Conditionally Bounded
Unresolved
Material Unquantified
or:
Not Material for Defined Simulation Use Uncertainty Acceptance

An uncertainty may be accepted for simulation use where: it is sufficiently understood, its effect is bounded, required downstream treatment exists, and the Simulation Purpose permits reliance upon that uncertainty level.
Acceptance does not mean the uncertainty disappears.
Conditional Uncertainty Acceptance
A Simulation Input may remain usable subject to conditions.
For example:
Input accepted only if sensitivity testing covers ±10% variation.
Uncertainty Restriction
An input may be restricted where uncertainty prevents broader use.
For example:
Suitable for exploratory simulation only.
but:
Not suitable for safety-critical operational reliance.
Uncertainty Rejection
Where uncertainty is too great or too poorly understood for the intended simulation purpose, the input may be rejected.
Uncertainty Undetermined
Where the available information is insufficient to assess uncertainty, the correct state may be:
Uncertainty Undetermined
rather than an assumed acceptable level.
Uncertainty Threshold
A simulation may define thresholds beyond which input uncertainty requires: additional evidence, broader scenarios, stronger sensitivity testing, restriction, or rejection.
Thresholds should derive from the Simulation Purpose and consequence rather than convenience.
Uncertainty Budget
Where appropriate, a simulation may establish an Input Uncertainty Budget defining how much uncertainty can be tolerated across material input categories.

The budget should not permit one uncertainty to disappear merely because another input is highly precise.
No Precision Compensation Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
High certainty in one Simulation Input cannot automatically compensate for material uncertainty in another input upon which the simulated outcome critically depends.
Uncertainty Concentration
A simulation may contain many high-quality inputs but depend critically upon one highly uncertain variable.
SIUM therefore assesses uncertainty according to influence, not merely average input quality.
Weakest Critical Input Principle
Where an outcome materially depends upon a highly uncertain critical input, the simulation conclusion should remain bounded by that uncertainty.
Uncertainty Change
Input uncertainty may change when: new evidence becomes available, sensors are recalibrated, source reliability changes, transformation logic changes, temporal distance increases, missing values increase, new environments are introduced, or Simulation Scope changes.
Uncertainty Reassessment Trigger
Material changes should trigger reassessment of the affected uncertainty basis.
Scope Expansion and Uncertainty
Expanding Simulation Scope may expose uncertainty that was immaterial under the original scope.
For example:
an input sufficiently certain for:
normal operating conditions
may be insufficiently characterized for:
extreme operating conditions.
Version Change and Uncertainty

A new input version should not automatically inherit the uncertainty characterization of its predecessor.
The new version may require reassessment where: source, measurement, transformation, temporal basis, or distribution
has materially changed.
Uncertainty Traceability
SIUM establishes:
Simulation Input
↓
Uncertainty Source
↓
Uncertainty Type
↓
Magnitude / Characterization
↓
Dependency
↓
Materiality
↓
Propagation Requirement
↓
Condition / Restriction
↓
Uncertainty Status
↓
Simulation Use Input Uncertainty Basis
The final SIUM result should establish a coherent Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis for the complete Simulation Input Set.
This basis should identify: material uncertainties, their origins, their relationships, their characterization, unresolved uncertainty, downstream treatment requirements, and limitations upon simulation use.
Input-Set Uncertainty
Individual inputs may each have acceptable uncertainty while their combination creates material uncertainty.
SIUM therefore distinguishes:
Input-Level Uncertainty
from:
Input-Set Uncertainty.
Input-Set Uncertainty Coherence
The complete uncertainty basis should account for: shared sources, dependencies, correlations, transformation chains, temporal relationships, and interacting uncertainty.
Simulation Input Readiness
After SIUM, the complete SIDS input basis may receive an overall readiness status such as:
Simulation Input Ready
Conditionally Simulation Input Ready
Partially Simulation Input Ready

Simulation Input Not Ready
or:
Simulation Input Readiness Undetermined
This status represents completion of the SIDS input-governance sequence.
Input Readiness Does Not Mean Simulation Validity
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation Input Readiness confirms only that the input basis is sufficiently governed for its defined simulation use. It does not establish that the model, scenarios, execution, outputs, or simulation itself are valid.
Those questions belong to subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Material Input Uncertainties
Determine which Simulation Inputs contain uncertainty capable of materially affecting simulation behavior or interpretation. 2. Identify Uncertainty Sources
Bind each material uncertainty to its known or suspected origin. 3. Classify Uncertainty
Determine whether uncertainty is associated with: measurement, observation, sampling, representativeness, transformation, time, estimation, interpolation, extrapolation, imputation, synthetic generation, parameterization, classification, or another relevant source.
4. Characterize Uncertainty
Use justified: quantitative bounds, distributions, qualitative classifications, or explicit unresolved status.
5. Assess Dependencies
Determine whether material uncertainties are: independent, correlated, shared-source, sequentially dependent, or otherwise linked.
6. Assess Materiality

Determine whether each uncertainty can materially affect the Simulation Purpose, behavior, outputs, or downstream reliance. 7. Establish Propagation Requirements
Identify which uncertainties must remain visible through subsequent simulation stages. 8. Establish Conditions and Restrictions
Define limitations upon simulation use where uncertainty remains material. 9. Assign Uncertainty Status
Classify material uncertainties as: Characterized, Partially Characterized, Bounded, Conditionally Bounded, Unresolved, Material Unquantified, or Not Material for Defined Simulation Use.
10. Assess Input-Set Uncertainty
Evaluate interactions across the complete Simulation Input basis. 11. Determine Simulation Input Readiness
Establish whether the governed input basis is: Ready, Conditionally Ready, Partially Ready, Not Ready, or Readiness Undetermined.
12. Preserve Uncertainty Traceability
Maintain:
Input → Uncertainty → Source → Characterization → Dependency → Materiality → Propagation → Condition → Status → Simulation Use
Governance Outputs

SIUM may produce: Simulation Input Uncertainty Register, Input Uncertainty Identifier, Uncertainty Source Record, Measurement Uncertainty Record, Observational Uncertainty Record, Sampling Uncertainty Record, Representativeness Uncertainty Record, Transformation-Induced Uncertainty Record, Temporal Uncertainty Record, Estimation Uncertainty Record, Interpolation Uncertainty Record, Extrapolation Uncertainty Record, Imputation Uncertainty Record, Synthetic Input Uncertainty Record, Parameter Uncertainty Record, Classification Uncertainty Record, Missing-Information Uncertainty Record, Quantitative Uncertainty Assessment, Qualitative Uncertainty Assessment, Uncertainty Bound, Uncertainty Distribution Record, Unresolved Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Dependency Map, Correlated Uncertainty Record, Shared-Source Uncertainty Record, Compounded Uncertainty Assessment, Uncertainty Materiality Assessment, Uncertainty Sensitivity Signal, Uncertainty Propagation Requirement, Input Uncertainty Budget, Uncertainty Condition Record, Uncertainty Restriction Record, Uncertainty Status, Input-Set Uncertainty Assessment, Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis, Simulation Input Readiness Status, Uncertainty Reassessment Trigger, and Simulation Input Uncertainty Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Simulation
Scenario

A robot-navigation simulation receives: object-position measurements with sensor error, estimated surface-friction values, partially observed pedestrian movement, and interpolated localization data.
Each input is technically usable.
However, each contains a different uncertainty basis. Application
SIUM identifies: measurement uncertainty in object position, estimation uncertainty in surface friction, observational uncertainty in pedestrian movement, and interpolation uncertainty in localization.
Dependencies between localization and object-position measurements are also identified because both depend partly upon the same sensor system. Result
The input basis becomes:
Conditionally Simulation Input Ready
with a requirement that material uncertainty be propagated into subsequent scenario and execution governance rather than treating the nominal input values as exact reality. Use Case 2 — Energy Infrastructure Simulation
Scenario
A long-term energy simulation uses: historical demand, future population projections, weather forecasts, estimated technology adoption, and assumed future industrial demand.
The simulation produces precise annual energy-demand figures. Application
SIUM distinguishes:
Observed Historical Inputs
from:
Projected Inputs
Estimated Inputs
and:
Assumed Inputs.
The largest material uncertainty is found in future industrial demand.
Sensitivity to this input is high. Result

The simulation may continue, but the uncertainty basis requires downstream scenarios covering materially different industrial-demand conditions.
The final simulation cannot legitimately present the central numerical trajectory as a certain future state.
Architectural Position
Simulation Input Uncertainty is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The complete SIDS progression is:
Simulation Input Identification
↓
Simulation Data Representativeness
↓
Simulation Data Transformation
↓
Simulation Temporal Data
↓
Simulation Input Uncertainty
Together, the five modules answer:
What information is entering the simulation?
↓
What reality can it legitimately represent?
↓
What happened to it before simulation use?
↓
Is it temporally appropriate?
↓
What uncertainty remains in the complete input basis?
The resulting:
Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis
and:
Simulation Input Readiness Status
provide the governed input foundation required by subsequent SIMULOS® lifecycle spaces.
The next Parent Standard, Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS), governs which scenarios must be designed to examine expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives.
Foundational Principle

Simulation Inputs become uncertainty-governed only when material uncertainty remains identifiable from its source through its characterization, dependencies, conditions, and downstream propagation requirements, so that computational precision cannot transform uncertain information into an appearance of certain reality.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Input Uncertainty Module completes the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing the uncertainty that remains after Simulation Inputs have been identified, assessed for representativeness, transformed, and temporally governed. Through uncertainty-source attribution, classification, quantitative and qualitative characterization, dependency and correlation assessment, materiality, sensitivity, propagation requirements, conditions, restrictions, reassessment, Input-Set Uncertainty, readiness determination, and complete uncertainty traceability, SIUM ensures that uncertainty entering a simulation cannot disappear merely because the simulation can process the data or produce precise numerical outputs. The module establishes the final governed Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis from which subsequent SIMULOS® scenario design and simulation execution can legitimately proceed.

OOF™ Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM)
Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS)
Module: SLMM — Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module
Operational Layer: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring
Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SLMM-012.1
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 20 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM) is the first Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SLMM governs the continuing observation of conditions capable of materially affecting the relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, or continued use of an existing simulation and its governed results.

The Module establishes a structured relationship between the simulation basis that existed when simulation evidence was produced and the conditions that exist as the simulation continues through its lifecycle.
SLMM does not determine whether observed change constitutes Simulation Drift, nor whether resimulation is required.
Its task is foundational:
to ensure that material changes capable of affecting simulation relevance can become visible rather than allowing a simulation to remain operationally influential after its governing basis has silently changed.
Core Question
Which conditions must remain monitored so that material changes affecting simulation relevance can be detected throughout the simulation lifecycle?
Architectural Position
SLMM is the first module within SLRS.
It follows the completed active simulation lifecycle:
Simulation Object → Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary
and begins lifecycle governance.
SLMM precedes:
SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module.
The relationship is:
Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition.
SLMM observes and structures relevant change.
SDRM determines whether that change creates a material divergence between the existing simulation basis and the conditions to which that simulation remains applied.
Internal Flow Position

Governed Simulation Lifecycle Basis → Monitoring Context Definition → Change-Sensitive Condition Identification → Lifecycle Observation → Change Signal Detection → Material Change Candidate Registration → Simulation Relevance Review Input → SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module Operational Space
SLMM governs the space between:
an established governed simulation basis
and
subsequent changes capable of affecting that basis.
This includes monitoring relevant change affecting: Simulation Object identity; object version; object configuration; object state; simulation purpose; simulation scope; represented reality; abstraction; fidelity requirements; assumptions; model applicability; model version; simulation environment; parameterization; inputs; data distributions; temporal data relevance; input uncertainty; scenario relevance; scenario coverage; observed operational conditions; simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence applicability; evidence weight; reliance conditions; known limitations; previously unknown conditions.
Operational Scope
SLMM applies wherever simulation results, evidence, models, scenarios, or simulation-derived conclusions continue to be retained, reused, referenced, compared, relied upon, or maintained after their initial production.

It may govern lifecycle monitoring for: individual simulations; simulation models; repeated simulation programs; scenario portfolios; Monte Carlo studies; digital twins; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; infrastructure simulations; mission simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; large-scale simulation campaigns; long-duration simulation programs; future simulation technologies.
The Module remains technology-neutral.
Its concern is not how frequently a simulator executes.
Its concern is whether the conditions supporting simulation relevance remain sufficiently observable over time. Simulation Completion ≠ Lifecycle Completion
SLMM establishes the distinction:
Simulation Execution Completion ≠ Simulation Lifecycle Completion
A simulation run may end.
A simulation campaign may end.
The simulator may be switched off.
But the simulation results may continue influencing: engineering; design; planning; scientific reasoning; safety assessment; mission preparation; system development; validation; operational decisions; deployment; future simulation campaigns.
Lifecycle governance therefore continues for as long as simulation-derived information remains materially relevant or relied upon.
Lifecycle Monitoring Basis
SLMM requires a Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Basis to identify which parts of the governed simulation lifecycle are capable of materially affecting continuing relevance.

The monitoring basis may reference:
Simulation Object → what was simulated.
Purpose & Scope → why and within what boundaries it was simulated.
Reality Representation → which reality was represented and how.
Assumptions → what conditions were presumed.
Model & Environment → which model and simulation environment generated the behavior.
Inputs & Data → which information basis entered the simulation.
Scenarios → which conditions were tested.
Execution → how the simulation was actually executed.
Outputs → what was produced.
Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → what relationship with reality was established.
Evidence & Reliance Boundary → what the simulation-derived evidence was permitted to support.
Lifecycle monitoring does not require every element to be monitored equally.
It requires monitoring to remain proportionate to the conditions capable of materially changing simulation relevance.
Change-Sensitive Condition Principle
Not every characteristic of a simulation requires continuous monitoring.
SLMM identifies Change-Sensitive Conditions:
conditions whose material change could alter the relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, or legitimate reliance of an existing simulation.

Examples may include: object redesign; software update; hardware replacement; environmental change; changed operational profile; new observed behavior; changed data distribution; new failure mode; revised assumption; model discovery; changed mission condition; new regulatory operating constraint; new physical observation; changed scenario prevalence; newly discovered edge case; degraded simulation-to-reality correlation.
The monitoring burden should therefore follow material relevance, not indiscriminate observation.
Reality Change Monitoring
A simulation may remain unchanged while reality changes around it.
SLMM therefore requires relevant changes in represented or relied-upon reality to remain observable where those changes can affect simulation relevance.
Examples may include: environmental change; infrastructure change; human behavioral change; operational practice change; traffic pattern change; climate condition change; market structure change; mission environment update; newly observed physical behavior; new operational interactions.
ORA™ continues to govern Operational Reality itself.
SLMM governs whether changes in relevant reality are being observed for their potential effect on simulation relevance.
Simulation Object Change Monitoring
A simulation may become stale because the Simulation Object itself changes.

SLMM may monitor: new object versions; configuration changes; component replacement; software changes; hardware changes; changed interfaces; changed capabilities; changed constraints; changed operational modes; changed dependencies.
A simulation of Object Version V3 does not automatically remain representative of Object Version V7.
Object evolution must therefore remain connected to lifecycle monitoring.
Assumption Change Monitoring
Assumptions that were reasonable when a simulation was constructed may later become questionable, obsolete, contradicted, or unnecessary.
SLMM may therefore monitor: newly available evidence affecting assumptions; observed contradiction; changed uncertainty; revised scientific understanding; changed operational conditions; dependence on assumptions no longer applicable.
SLMM does not govern the assumptions themselves.
That remains under SAS — Simulation Assumption Standard.
It monitors changes capable of affecting their continued applicability.
Model and Environment Change Monitoring
Simulation models and environments may evolve independently of the simulation evidence already produced.
SLMM may monitor: model replacement; model revision; environment updates; parameterization changes; discovered model defects; corrected physical relationships; changed solver behavior; updated simulation infrastructure; changed environmental representations.
A newer model does not automatically invalidate earlier simulations.

But material differences must become visible for lifecycle assessment.
Input and Data Change Monitoring
Simulation relevance may degrade when the distributions or conditions represented by simulation inputs materially change.
SLMM may monitor: new operational data; changed distributions; changed populations; changed environmental data; temporal shifts; new sensor characteristics; newly available empirical data; changed uncertainty; changed input-generation methods.
SIDS continues to govern simulation inputs and data at the simulation-input boundary.
SLMM monitors subsequent changes that may affect the relevance of previously generated simulation results.
Scenario Relevance Monitoring
Scenario sets may become incomplete over time.
SLMM may identify changes such as: new operational scenarios; newly observed edge cases; changed scenario frequency; emerging stress conditions; newly relevant interactions; previously unknown failure combinations; changed environmental combinations.
The discovery of a new scenario does not automatically invalidate existing simulations.
It may, however, reveal that existing scenario coverage no longer represents the relevant problem space sufficiently.
Correlation Change Monitoring
Simulation-to-reality correlation is not necessarily permanent.
New real-world observations may show: stronger correlation; weaker correlation; systematic deviation; condition-specific divergence; temporal degradation; newly discovered mismatch.

SLMM therefore monitors information capable of changing the existing correlation basis established through SRCS.
It does not recalculate correlation.
That remains within Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
Evidence Relevance Monitoring
Simulation-derived evidence may remain technically unchanged while its relevance changes.
SLMM may monitor conditions capable of affecting: evidence qualification; evidential weight; applicability; reliance boundaries; use limitations; temporal relevance.
Where a material lifecycle change affects simulation evidence, the relevant SERBS governance may require reassessment.
SLMM does not independently redefine evidential weight or reliance.
Change Signal
SLMM introduces the Simulation Lifecycle Change Signal.
A Change Signal is:
an observed or reported change that may materially affect the continuing relevance of a governed simulation basis.
A Change Signal is not yet Simulation Drift.
It is an input for further assessment.
Possible sources include: operational observations; engineering change records; new measurements; updated datasets; new scientific findings; system version changes; mission updates; incident findings; model corrections; new scenario discoveries; changed environmental conditions; changed correlation results.
Material Change Candidate
Where a Change Signal has a plausible relationship to simulation relevance, SLMM may register it as a Material Change Candidate.
The distinction is:
Change Signal → something changed.

Material Change Candidate → the change may matter to the simulation.
Simulation Drift → the change has produced a material divergence affecting the governed simulation basis.
The final determination of Simulation Drift belongs to SDRM.
Monitoring by Dependency
Simulation relevance may be affected indirectly.
For example:
Component Change → changes system behavior → changes object configuration → affects scenario behavior → changes simulation applicability.
SLMM therefore permits lifecycle monitoring across material dependency chains rather than monitoring only direct changes to the simulator.
This is especially important for complex systems where a seemingly small change may propagate into a simulation-relevant difference.
Event-Driven Monitoring
Lifecycle monitoring may be event-driven.
Relevant events may include: object update; software release; hardware change; new operational dataset; incident; newly observed failure; mission redesign; environmental change; assumption challenge; model correction; correlation deterioration; regulatory operating change.
An event may initiate a simulation relevance review without waiting for a scheduled lifecycle review.
Periodic Monitoring
Where simulation relevance may degrade gradually or where material change is not tied to a discrete event, organizations may use periodic monitoring.

The appropriate interval may depend upon: rate of object change; rate of environmental change; consequence of stale simulation reliance; simulation purpose; operational volatility; evidence importance; availability of new reality information.
SLMM does not impose one universal review interval.
Continuous Monitoring
Certain simulation contexts may justify continuous or near-continuous lifecycle monitoring.
Examples include: digital twins; rapidly changing autonomous systems; high-frequency operational environments; continuously updated models; adaptive systems; dynamic infrastructure environments.
Continuous monitoring does not imply continuous resimulation.
It provides a higher-frequency basis for detecting potentially material change.
Monitoring Proportionality Principle
SLMM rejects the assumption that all simulations require identical monitoring intensity.
Monitoring should be proportionate to: rate of relevant change; consequence of outdated reliance; simulation reuse; operational importance; uncertainty; dependence on volatile assumptions; dependence on changing reality; expected lifecycle duration.
A one-time exploratory simulation may require minimal lifecycle monitoring.
A simulation supporting years of safety-critical operational reliance may require substantially stronger monitoring.
Dormant Simulation Principle
A simulation may remain unused for a period and later return to active use.
Dormancy must not create an assumption of continuing relevance.

Before material reuse, the simulation may require review against accumulated lifecycle changes.
Therefore:
Stored Simulation ≠ Current Simulation Basis.
Monitoring at Scale
Large organizations may maintain thousands or millions of simulation artifacts and evidence objects.
SLMM must therefore support lifecycle monitoring at scale.
Monitoring may operate through: simulation families; object families; model versions; scenario families; evidence classes; dependency relationships; change-event propagation; lifecycle status registers.
A material change affecting one shared model may therefore identify many dependent simulation results requiring review.
Lifecycle Monitoring State
SLMM may assign a lifecycle monitoring state such as: 1. Active Monitoring
Relevant lifecycle conditions are currently monitored. 2. Reduced Monitoring
Monitoring continues at a reduced level because active reliance or change exposure is limited. 3. Dormant
The simulation is retained but not currently subject to active reliance. 4. Review Required
A material Change Signal or accumulated lifecycle change requires assessment. 5. Monitoring Suspended
Required monitoring cannot currently be performed sufficiently. 6. Lifecycle Exit Candidate
The simulation may no longer justify continued monitoring and may require retirement assessment.
These are governance states rather than universal technical classifications.
Lifecycle Traceability

SLMM requires material lifecycle changes to remain traceable to the simulation assets potentially affected by them.
A lifecycle trace may connect:
Change Event → Affected Reality Condition → Affected Simulation Basis Element → Affected Simulation → Affected Outputs → Affected Evidence → Potential Reliance Impact
This relationship enables downstream drift recognition and proportionate resimulation decisions.
SLMM Boundary with SDRM
SLMM identifies and structures potentially relevant lifecycle change.
SDRM determines whether the change constitutes material Simulation Drift.
Therefore:
Monitoring Signal ≠ Drift Determination.
SLMM Boundary with SRGM
SLMM does not determine whether resimulation must occur.
That decision belongs to:
SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module.
The lifecycle sequence is:
Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Trigger Determination.
SLMM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality.
SLMM may consume relevant reality-change information to determine whether simulation relevance requires review.
It does not redefine, reconstruct, or govern Operational Reality itself.
SLMM Boundary with SERBS
SERBS governs simulation-derived evidence, evidential weight, reliance boundaries, and use limitations.
SLMM monitors changes capable of affecting those governed evidence conditions.
It does not independently redefine evidence qualification, weight, or permitted reliance.
SLMM Boundary with VALIDOS®
VALIDOS® governs validation and revalidation.

SLMM governs simulation lifecycle monitoring.
A lifecycle change detected by SLMM may eventually contribute to revalidation processes, but:
Simulation Lifecycle Review ≠ Validation Reassessment.
SLMM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SLMM does not govern general lifecycle integrity.
INTEGROS® continues to govern integrity properties of objects, states, evidence, and processes.
SLMM governs only lifecycle monitoring specifically required to preserve the continuing relevance of simulation.
SLMM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether lifecycle records, change evidence, and monitoring activities are observable, preserved, and verifiable.
SLMM owns the simulation-specific monitoring logic.
Lifecycle Monitoring ≠ Lifecycle Audit.
Governance Outputs
SLMM may produce: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Basis Change-Sensitive Condition Register Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Profile Simulation Lifecycle Change Signal Material Change Candidate Record Simulation Object Change Link Reality Change Link Assumption Change Link Model & Environment Change Link Input & Data Change Link Scenario Relevance Change Link Correlation Change Link Evidence Relevance Change Link Simulation Dependency Change Record Lifecycle Monitoring State Simulation Relevance Review Input Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Record
These outputs provide the governed input basis for:
SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module.
Enterprise Application

SLMM enables organizations to answer a lifecycle question that conventional simulation programs frequently leave implicit:
How will we know when the simulation we trusted yesterday no longer represents the problem we face today?
An organization may use SLMM to detect when: a simulated product has changed configuration; new operational behavior has emerged; a mission environment has been revised; new physical measurements challenge earlier assumptions; an autonomous system receives a significant software update; operational data distributions change; new edge cases appear; a model defect is discovered; simulation-to-reality correlation deteriorates; simulation evidence remains in organizational use long after its original basis has changed.
SLMM does not force the organization to rerun every simulation whenever something changes.
Instead, it creates the governed observation layer necessary to determine whether the change matters at all.
This allows later modules to distinguish between:
irrelevant change, material drift, targeted resimulation, broad resimulation, replacement, and retirement.
Foundational Principles
Simulation completion is not simulation lifecycle completion.
A simulation may remain computationally unchanged while becoming operationally stale.
Lifecycle monitoring must follow the conditions that give simulation results their meaning.
Not every change is material to simulation relevance.
A detected change is not automatically Simulation Drift.

Monitoring intensity should be proportional to the consequence and likelihood of simulation obsolescence.
Stored simulation results do not automatically remain current simulation evidence.
Reality change, object change, assumption change, model change, data change, scenario change, and correlation change may all affect continuing simulation relevance.
Continuous monitoring does not require continuous resimulation.
A simulation cannot remain governably relevant over time if material changes to the basis supporting its relevance are allowed to remain invisible.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module establishes the lifecycle observation layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by maintaining structured visibility over changes capable of affecting the continuing relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, and legitimate use of governed simulations. Through governance of monitoring bases, change-sensitive conditions, object change, reality change, assumption change, model and environment change, input and data change, scenario relevance, correlation change, evidence relevance, dependency propagation, change signals, material change candidates, monitoring states, and lifecycle traceability, SLMM prevents simulation results from remaining operationally influential merely because the conditions that once supported them are no longer being examined. By separating lifecycle observation from Simulation Drift recognition and resimulation decisions, SLMM creates the first governed control point of the recursive SIMULOS® lifecycle and provides the structured change basis required by SDRM. A simulation can remain governably relevant over time only when material changes capable of altering its meaning can first become visible.

OOF™ Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM)
Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES)
Operational Layer: Simulation Model & Environment Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Model Structure
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Model Structure
Canonical Definition
Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM) defines the governance framework for identifying, constructing, decomposing, organizing, documenting, and controlling the structural composition of a Simulation Model so that its components, relationships, dependencies, interfaces, internal states, interaction pathways, and structural boundaries remain explicit, traceable, and consistent with the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, and Simulation Assumptions.

SMMM establishes the structural foundation through which a simulation representation becomes an identifiable executable model rather than an opaque technical implementation.
Operational Role
SMMM is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
It answers:
What is the Simulation Model structurally composed of, how are its components related, and what structural arrangement actually produces the behavior being simulated?
The governed progression is:
Governed Reality Representation → Governed Simulation Assumptions → Model Structure Definition → Component Identification → Relationship & Dependency Mapping → Interface Definition → Structural Boundary Establishment → Governed Simulation Model Structure
SMMM establishes the model structure upon which the remaining SMES governance spaces can operate.
Module Operational Space

SMMM governs: Simulation Model identification, model structural definition, model decomposition, model composition, component identification, component classification, component roles, component relationships, structural dependencies, model hierarchy, model topology, interaction pathways, internal interfaces, external model interfaces, state relationships, structural constraints, model coupling, model composition rules, structural abstraction, structural completeness, structural consistency, structural change visibility, model-structure version binding, representation-to-model traceability, assumption-to-model traceability, and structural reconstruction.
Module Operational Scope
SMMM applies to any Simulation Model whose internal structure materially affects simulation behavior, interpretation, reproducibility, comparability, or downstream reliance.
The module may govern: mathematical models, computational models, physics-based models, statistical models, behavioral models, agent-based models, AI-based simulation models, autonomous-system models, digital twins, system-of-systems models, discrete-event models, continuous models, hybrid models, multi-model simulations, coupled models, scientific models, industrial models, infrastructure models, economic models, biological models, and future simulation-model structures.
The required governance depth should remain proportional to the Simulation Purpose, Scope, complexity, and consequence.
Module Function

SMMM exists to prevent the Simulation Model from becoming a technical black box whose structural composition cannot be connected back to the simulation inquiry it is intended to represent.
Its function is to ensure that material model structure remains sufficiently explicit to determine:
what components exist,
what each component represents,
how components interact,
which components depend upon others,
where structural boundaries exist,
which interfaces connect the structure,
and:
how the complete model structure relates to the governed representation of reality.
Simulation Model Structure
A Simulation Model Structure is the governed arrangement of model components and the relationships through which those components collectively represent and execute the modeled behavior of the Simulation Object or relevant represented reality.
The structure may be:
Monolithic
Modular
Hierarchical
Distributed
Networked
Layered
Coupled
Composite
Agent-Based
or:
Hybrid
provided that its material structural properties remain governable.
Model Structure Identification
Every governed Simulation Model should have a sufficiently identifiable structural representation.
At minimum, where materially relevant, the structure should establish: model identity, model version, structural architecture, primary components, component relationships, material dependencies, interfaces, state relationships, structural boundaries, and relevant external dependencies.

A model name alone does not establish model structure.
Model Decomposition
Complex Simulation Models may require decomposition into governable components.
Conceptually:
Simulation Model
↓
Subsystem
↓
Component
↓
Subcomponent
↓
Relevant Structural Element
Decomposition should continue only to the level necessary for the intended simulation governance purpose.
SMMM does not require unnecessary decomposition where additional structural detail would not materially improve governance.
Model Component
A Model Component is an identifiable structural element performing a distinguishable function within the Simulation Model.
A component may represent: an object, actor, subsystem, process, rule system, behavior, physical mechanism, computational mechanism, AI model, controller, population, resource, network, or another modeled element.
Component Identity
Material components should remain distinguishable from one another.
Where two components perform materially different simulation functions, their identities should not be collapsed merely because they share the same technical implementation.
Component Role
Each material component should have an identifiable role within the model.
A Component Role may establish: what the component represents, what behavior it produces, which inputs it receives, which outputs it generates, which states it maintains, and which other components depend upon it.
Component Relationship
SMMM governs material relationships between model components.

Relationships may include:
Input → Processing
Cause → Effect
Parent → Child
Controller → Controlled Component
Producer → Consumer
Agent → Agent
System → Subsystem
State → Transition
or other simulation-specific relationships.
Structural Dependency
A Structural Dependency exists where the function, state, behavior, or interpretation of one model component materially depends upon another model component or structural element.
Dependencies should remain visible where their failure or modification could materially affect simulation behavior.
Dependency Direction
Where relevant, dependency direction should be identifiable.
For example:
Component B depends upon Component A
does not necessarily mean:
Component A depends upon Component B.
Bidirectional dependencies should be represented explicitly where they exist.
Model Hierarchy
Where a model contains hierarchical relationships, SMMM should preserve the hierarchy sufficiently to understand how lower-level behavior contributes to higher-level simulation behavior.
Conceptually:
System Model
↓
Subsystem Model
↓
Component Model
↓
Behavioral Element
Hierarchy should support governance, not merely documentation.
Model Topology
Where interaction structure materially affects simulation behavior, the topology of the model should remain identifiable.
This may include: networks, graphs, communication pathways, resource pathways, causal pathways, control pathways, or spatial relationships.
Interaction Pathways

A Simulation Model may produce behavior through sequences of interactions.
Material pathways should be traceable where necessary.
For example:
Input → Sensor Model → Interpretation Model → Decision Model → Action Model → Environment Interaction
If a material pathway cannot be reconstructed, simulation behavior may become difficult to explain or compare.
Internal Interfaces
An Internal Model Interface connects two or more components within the Simulation Model.
Where materially relevant, an interface should establish: connected components, exchanged information or state, direction, format or representation, timing conditions, interaction rules, and applicable constraints.
External Model Interfaces
A model may also interact with elements outside its structural boundary.
External interfaces may connect the model to: Simulation Environment, input sources, external models, live systems, humans, AI systems, hardware, external services, or other simulation environments.
SMMM identifies the structural interface.
Governance of the broader simulation boundary interaction remains within the appropriate SMES governance space.
State Structure
Where a model contains states, the structural relationship between those states should remain sufficiently defined.
Examples:
Operational → Degraded → Failed
Idle → Active → Terminated
Untrained → Trained → Adapted
State transitions may materially alter model behavior.
Structural Constraints

Some model relationships are subject to structural constraints.
Examples may include: prohibited interactions, maximum connectivity, required component presence, dependency ordering, synchronization conditions, or topology restrictions.
Material structural constraints should remain explicit.
Model Coupling
Where multiple models or components influence one another, their coupling should be identifiable.
Coupling may be:
Loose
Tight
Unidirectional
Bidirectional
Synchronous
Asynchronous
Static
or:
Dynamic
where such distinctions materially affect simulation behavior.
Composite Simulation Models
A simulation may combine several models into a composite structure.
Conceptually:
Model A + Model B + Model C → Composite Simulation Model
SMMM requires the composition to preserve sufficient visibility into: constituent models, their identities, versions, roles, interfaces, dependencies, and interaction logic.
Composition must not erase material differences between constituent models.
Model-of-Models Structure
Some simulations contain models that themselves govern or invoke other models.
Where this occurs, SMMM should preserve:
Model → Submodel → Invoked Model → External Model
relationships sufficiently for structural reconstruction.
Structural Abstraction
Not every real-world element requires a separate model component.
SMMM permits structural abstraction where consistent with the governed Reality Representation.
However:

Structural simplification must not silently remove a material element that the governed Reality Representation requires the simulation to represent.
Representation-to-Structure Binding
The model structure should remain connected to the Reality Representation from which it was constructed.
Conceptually:
Reality Element → Represented Element → Model Component
This enables later determination of where a relevant aspect of reality appears within the executable model.
Assumption-to-Structure Binding
Material Simulation Assumptions may affect: component existence, component behavior, component relationships, dependencies, interfaces, state transitions, or structural constraints.
Where material, the relationship should remain traceable:
Simulation Assumption → Structural Element
An assumption should not become invisible merely because it has been encoded into model architecture.
Structural Completeness
Structural Completeness asks:
Does the governed model structure contain the material elements required by the approved Reality Representation and Simulation Purpose & Scope?
Completeness is relative to the governed simulation inquiry.
It does not require complete representation of reality.
Structural Consistency
Structural Consistency asks whether the components and relationships of the model remain mutually compatible with the intended structural design.

Examples of structural inconsistency may include: incompatible interfaces, contradictory dependencies, missing required components, invalid component relationships, incompatible state transitions, or broken composition rules.
Structural Coherence
A structurally complete model may still be incoherent if its elements cannot operate together as intended.
SMMM therefore distinguishes:
Structural Presence
from:
Structural Coherence.
No Hidden Component Principle
A material model component must not influence simulation behavior while remaining outside the governed model structure merely because it is technically embedded, externally invoked, or automatically generated.
No Hidden Dependency Principle
A material dependency must not be treated as irrelevant merely because it exists below the visible simulation interface.
No Structural Substitution Principle
A materially different structural implementation should not be treated as the same governed Simulation Model without assessing whether the change affects: representation, assumptions, dependencies, interfaces, states, execution behavior, or downstream interpretation.
Model Structure Change
A Model Structure Change may include: component addition, component removal, component replacement, hierarchy change, topology change, dependency change, interface change, state-model change, coupling change, or structural constraint change.
Material changes should remain identifiable.
Structural Change Classification

A change may be classified as:
Non-Material
Material
Critical
or:
Undetermined
relative to the Simulation Purpose & Scope.
Structural Change Propagation
A structural change may affect other SIMULOS® governance spaces.
For example:
Component Replacement
may affect:
Assumptions → Parameters → Inputs → Scenarios → Execution → Outputs
SMMM identifies the structural change.
Affected downstream spaces govern their respective consequences.
Model Structure Version Binding
The governed structure should remain connected to the applicable Simulation Model Version.
A simulation execution should therefore be capable of identifying which governed structural version was active.
Structural Reconstruction
SMMM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer:
What was the model structurally composed of at the relevant time?
Which components existed?
How were they connected?
Which dependencies were active?
Which interfaces existed?
Which structural assumptions applied?
Which model version contained this structure?
Structural Traceability
The complete structural traceability path may be represented as:
Simulation Object
↓
Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model
↓
Model Components
↓
Relationships & Dependencies
↓
Interfaces
↓
Structural Boundaries
↓
Model Structure Version
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify the Simulation Model
Establish the model identity and applicable model version. 2. Define the Structural Architecture

Determine the material organization of the model. 3. Identify Material Components
Establish the components required for the governed simulation inquiry. 4. Map Relationships and Dependencies
Identify how material components interact and depend upon one another. 5. Establish Interfaces
Document material internal and external structural interfaces. 6. Bind Structure to Representation and Assumptions
Preserve traceability from governed representation and assumptions into the model structure. 7. Establish Structural Boundaries
Determine which elements belong to the model structure and which remain external. 8. Assess Structural Completeness and Consistency
Determine whether required structural elements are present and mutually coherent. 9. Bind Structure to Model Version
Ensure the governed structure can be associated with the correct model version. 10. Preserve Structural Reconstruction
Maintain sufficient records to reconstruct the relevant model structure later.
Governance Outputs

SMMM may produce: Simulation Model Structure Record, Model Component Register, Model Component Identity Record, Component Role Map, Model Hierarchy Map, Model Topology Record, Component Relationship Map, Structural Dependency Map, Interaction Pathway Map, Internal Interface Record, External Model Interface Reference, State Structure Record, Structural Constraint Record, Model Coupling Record, Composite Model Structure Record, Reality Representation-to-Model Map, Assumption-to-Structure Map, Structural Completeness Assessment, Structural Consistency Assessment, Structural Coherence Assessment, Model Structure Change Record, Structural Change Classification, Structural Change Propagation Record, Model Structure Version Binding, Structural Reconstruction Record, and Simulation Model Structure Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
A vehicle simulation contains separate models for:
Perception → Planning → Control → Vehicle Dynamics
SMMM identifies each as a material model component and governs their interfaces and dependencies.
If the planning component is replaced by a new AI model, the change cannot remain hidden merely because the rest of the simulation remains unchanged.
The new structural relationship and affected dependencies become visible for downstream governance. Use Case 2 — Multi-Agent Financial Market Simulation
A financial simulation contains thousands of autonomous trading agents interacting through a simulated market.

SMMM governs the structural classes of agents, market mechanism, interaction topology, information pathways, and dependencies required to understand how collective market behavior emerges.
The module does not determine whether the simulated market accurately predicts the real market.
It establishes whether the model structure producing the simulated behavior is identifiable and governable. Use Case 3 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
A spacecraft simulation combines:
Flight Dynamics Model + Guidance Model + Propulsion Model + Thermal Model + Communication Model
SMMM preserves the identity, role, dependencies, interfaces, and version relationships of the constituent models.
If the propulsion model changes, the simulation can identify which structural pathways and dependent components may be affected before subsequent simulation execution.
Architectural Position
Simulation Model Structure is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
The complete SMES progression is:
Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning
SMMM establishes the structural model basis required by the remaining SMES modules.
Within the broader SIMULOS® lifecycle:
Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → downstream simulation governance

SMMM therefore governs the first internal transition from the conceptual representation of the simulation into the controlled executable structure through which simulation behavior will later be produced.
Foundational Principle
A simulation model cannot be structurally governed when the components, relationships, dependencies, interfaces, and assumptions producing its behavior cannot be identified and reconstructed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Model Structure Module establishes the structural governance foundation of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by making the internal composition of a Simulation Model explicit, bounded, traceable, and reconstructable. Through component identification, decomposition, relationship and dependency mapping, hierarchy, topology, interface governance, state structure, coupling, structural abstraction, representation and assumption binding, change visibility, version binding, completeness, consistency, and reconstruction, SMMM ensures that simulation behavior cannot emerge from an invisible model structure whose relationship to the governed Simulation Object, Reality Representation, and Simulation Assumptions cannot be demonstrated.
