OOF™ Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM)
Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Object Boundary
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 15 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Object Boundary
Canonical Definition
Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) defines the governance conditions under which the limits of an identified Simulation Object are formally established, distinguished from surrounding systems, environments, dependencies, actors, processes, interfaces, and external conditions, and maintained as a traceable Simulation Object Boundary throughout downstream simulation governance.
SOBM ensures that a simulation cannot silently expand, contract, or redefine what belongs to the Simulation Object after its identity has been established.
Operational Role

SOBM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
SOIM establishes:
What exactly is the Simulation Object?
SOBM asks:
Where does that Simulation Object begin and end, and what lies outside it?
The governed progression is:
Identified Simulation Object → Boundary Context → Included Elements → Excluded Elements → Interfaces & Dependencies → Boundary Conditions → Boundary Status → Governed Simulation Object Boundary
SOBM establishes the structural perimeter within which subsequent object version, configuration, representation, assumptions, modeling, scenario, execution, and output governance can operate.
Module Operational Space
SOBM governs: Simulation Object boundary establishment, object inclusion, object exclusion, internal elements, external elements, system boundaries, subsystem boundaries, component boundaries, process boundaries, behavioral boundaries, organizational boundaries, spatial boundaries, temporal boundaries, functional boundaries, operational boundaries, environmental interfaces, external actors, external systems, dependencies, boundary-crossing interactions, boundary conditions, boundary assumptions, boundary ambiguity, boundary conflicts, boundary change, boundary expansion, boundary contraction, boundary inheritance, boundary traceability, and Simulation Object Boundary status.
Module Function
SOBM exists to prevent an identified Simulation Object from becoming structurally ambiguous once simulation design begins.

Its function is to establish which elements are:
Inside the Simulation Object
Outside the Simulation Object
and:
Connected Across the Simulation Object Boundary
This distinction matters because simulation conclusions may change materially depending upon what the simulation treats as part of the object itself versus part of its external environment.
SOBM therefore prevents: hidden boundary expansion, hidden boundary contraction, omitted material components, uncontrolled inclusion of external systems, environmental conditions being mistaken for object properties, dependencies being absorbed into the object without disclosure, object behavior being confused with external interaction, and simulation findings being generalized beyond the established object boundary.
Simulation Object Boundary
A Simulation Object Boundary is the governed perimeter separating the Simulation Object from the external conditions, entities, systems, processes, actors, and environments with which it may interact.
The boundary may be: physical, digital, logical, functional, organizational, behavioral, spatial, temporal, operational, or composite.
A single Simulation Object may therefore require several mutually consistent boundary dimensions.
Boundary Establishment
Once the Simulation Object has been identified through SOIM, its relevant boundaries must be established before downstream simulation structures depend upon them.
Boundary establishment should answer:
What belongs to the object?

What does not belong to the object?
Which external elements materially interact with it?
Through which interfaces do those interactions occur?
Which boundary conditions materially affect simulation behavior?
The required precision depends upon the intended simulation.
Included Elements
An Included Element is an element treated as part of the Simulation Object for the governed simulation.
Included elements may consist of: components, subsystems, software, hardware, internal processes, internal actors, internal control mechanisms, internal data structures, internal resources, or other constituent elements.
Inclusion must be sufficiently explicit where the element could materially affect simulation interpretation.
Excluded Elements
An Excluded Element is an element intentionally outside the Simulation Object Boundary.
Exclusion does not mean irrelevance.
An excluded element may still influence the object through an external interaction or dependency.
SOBM therefore distinguishes:
Outside the Object
from:
Irrelevant to the Simulation
These are not equivalent.
Boundary Interfaces
A Boundary Interface is a governed point through which the Simulation Object interacts with something outside its boundary.
Interfaces may include: data interfaces, physical connections, control interfaces, communication channels, human interactions, resource inputs, energy flows, sensor inputs, actuator outputs, organizational interactions, or environmental interactions.

Boundary interfaces should remain identifiable where their behavior materially affects simulation.
External Dependencies
A Simulation Object may depend upon entities that remain outside its boundary.
Examples may include: cloud infrastructure, navigation systems, external databases, communication networks, human operators, power systems, supply chains, regulatory inputs, external AI services, or supporting infrastructure.
SOBM requires these dependencies to remain distinguishable from the Simulation Object itself.
The existence of dependency does not automatically justify boundary inclusion.
Object Boundary vs Simulation Environment
SIMULOS® establishes a critical distinction:
Simulation Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Environment Boundary
The Simulation Object defines what is being simulated as the target.
The Simulation Environment defines the conditions within which simulation activity occurs.
For example:
Autonomous Drone
may be the Simulation Object.
Urban Airspace + Weather + Navigation Infrastructure + Other Aircraft
may form part of the simulated environment.
Those concepts must not be collapsed merely because they interact during simulation.
Object Boundary vs Reality Representation
SOBM establishes the boundary of the target object.
It does not determine whether that boundary has been represented accurately inside the simulation.
That later question belongs to the appropriate SIMULOS® Reality Representation governance space.
Therefore:

Object Boundary = What belongs to the target
while:
Representation Boundary = What the simulation representation actually models
A difference between the two may become a material simulation-governance issue.
Functional Boundary
A Simulation Object may require a functional boundary specifying which functions belong to the object being simulated.
For example, an autonomous vehicle simulation may include:
Perception
Planning
Decision
Vehicle Control
while an external navigation service remains outside the object.
The boundary should preserve this distinction even where the systems operate as one practical service.
Spatial Boundary
Where location or physical extent matters, the object may require a spatial boundary.
This may define: physical dimensions, geographic area, infrastructure extent, operational zone, or another spatial perimeter.
Spatial boundaries should not be confused with the wider simulation environment.
Temporal Boundary
A Simulation Object may also require a temporal boundary.
The object represented at:
Time T1
may not be materially equivalent to the same nominal object at:
Time T2
where its relevant characteristics have changed.
Detailed version governance belongs to the appropriate SOS module, but SOBM preserves the temporal perimeter relevant to the object definition.
Operational Boundary
An operational boundary identifies which operational functions, modes, states, or interactions belong to the Simulation Object for the particular simulation.

An object may have broader real-world capability than the operational portion included within a simulation.
SOBM requires this difference to remain explicit.
Composite Object Boundary
Composite Simulation Objects require governance over the relationship between:
Composite Boundary
and:
Constituent Boundaries
For example:
Autonomous Warehouse System
may contain:
Robots + Control System + Internal Network + Charging Infrastructure
while:
External Electrical Grid
remains outside the object boundary.
SOBM preserves both the composite perimeter and relevant internal constituent boundaries.
Nested Boundaries
Simulation Objects may contain nested boundaries.
Conceptually:
System Boundary
↓
Subsystem Boundary
↓
Component Boundary
↓
Functional Boundary
SOBM allows these boundaries to coexist where needed.
A lower-level simulation claim must not automatically be represented as applying to every higher-level boundary.
Boundary-Crossing Interaction
A Boundary-Crossing Interaction occurs whenever information, resources, commands, forces, signals, behaviors, or effects pass between the Simulation Object and an external element.
Such interactions may materially influence simulation behavior even though the external element remains outside the Simulation Object.
SOBM therefore requires material boundary-crossing interactions to remain visible.
Boundary Conditions

A Simulation Object Boundary Condition defines a governed condition applying at the interface between the object and its surroundings.
Examples may include: incoming data characteristics, resource availability, communication latency, physical forces, environmental exposure, human commands, external control signals, or other interface conditions.
Boundary conditions must not silently become assumed constants where variability is material.
Boundary Assumptions
Where a boundary cannot be fully established from known information, a boundary assumption may be necessary.
SOBM requires such assumptions to remain explicit.
Detailed governance of the assumption itself belongs to the SIMULOS® assumption-governance space.
SOBM preserves the fact that the object boundary depends upon that assumption.
Boundary Ambiguity
Simulation Object Boundary Ambiguity exists where it is unclear whether a materially relevant element belongs inside or outside the Simulation Object.
Ambiguity may arise from: incomplete architecture records, unclear ownership, dynamic system composition, external services, shared infrastructure, distributed control, unclear subsystem relationships, or evolving operational configurations.
Material ambiguity should not be silently resolved.
Boundary Conflict
A Boundary Conflict exists where credible sources define materially different boundaries for the same Simulation Object.
For example:

one system architecture may include an external decision service within the system boundary,
while another treats it as an external dependency.
Where the difference can affect simulation design or interpretation, the conflict must remain visible until governed.
No Silent Boundary Expansion Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Object Boundary must not be expanded after simulation activity begins without explicit governance of the change.
Adding new components, functions, populations, dependencies, or operational modes may materially change the Simulation Object.
No Silent Boundary Contraction Rule
Likewise:
Material elements may not be removed from the Simulation Object Boundary without explicit governance of the exclusion.
A simulation must not obtain more favorable results by quietly removing difficult or high-risk portions of the object.
No Environment Absorption Rule
An environmental element does not become part of the Simulation Object merely because it materially affects object behavior.
This rule protects the distinction between:
Object
and:
Environment
throughout the simulation lifecycle.
No Dependency Absorption Rule
A dependency does not automatically become part of the Simulation Object merely because the object cannot operate without it.
Dependency relationships must be visible.
Boundary inclusion requires an explicit basis.
No Boundary Inflation Rule

A simulation result established within one object boundary must not automatically be represented as applying to a broader boundary.
Therefore:
Subsystem Simulation ≠ Whole-System Simulation
Component Simulation ≠ Product Simulation
Single Operational Mode ≠ Complete Operational Capability
unless a governed basis supports the broader claim.
Boundary Change
A Simulation Object Boundary Change occurs when the governed perimeter of the object changes materially.
Possible changes include:
Expansion
Contraction
Recomposition
Interface Change
Dependency Change
or:
Boundary Reclassification
A boundary change may require downstream simulation governance to be reassessed.
Boundary Change Propagation
A material boundary change may affect: object version, configuration, reality representation, assumptions, model structure, input requirements, scenarios, execution, outputs, reality correlation, or simulation reliance.
SOBM therefore preserves boundary-change information for downstream governance rather than determining all downstream consequences itself.
Boundary Continuity
Where the Simulation Object remains in use across multiple simulations, its boundary should remain traceable between simulation cycles.
This enables comparison between:
Previous Simulation Object Boundary
and:
Current Simulation Object Boundary
and prevents materially different simulation scopes from being treated as equivalent.
Boundary Equivalence

Two simulations may use different technical representations while still concern the same Simulation Object Boundary.
Conversely, two simulations using the same model may concern materially different object boundaries.
SOBM therefore does not infer boundary equivalence from model similarity alone.
Simulation Object Boundary Status
Possible boundary statuses may include:
Established
Conditionally Established
Partially Established
Boundary Conflicted
Boundary Ambiguous
or:
Boundary Undetermined
Boundary status describes the strength of the object-boundary basis.
It does not establish simulation validity or operational reliance.
Simulation Object Boundary Record
SOBM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Boundary Record sufficient to reconstruct what was considered inside, outside, and connected to the Simulation Object when downstream simulation governance occurred.
The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, boundary definition, boundary dimensions, included elements, excluded elements, constituent boundaries, external dependencies, boundary interfaces, boundary-crossing interactions, boundary conditions, boundary assumptions, ambiguity, conflicts, boundary status, boundary changes, and boundary traceability.
Failure Conditions

SOBM governance failure may exist where: the Simulation Object has no sufficiently defined boundary, material included elements are unidentified, material exclusions remain hidden, object and environment are improperly collapsed, dependencies are silently absorbed, material interfaces remain unidentified, boundary-crossing interactions are omitted, boundary assumptions remain hidden, conflicting boundaries are ignored, the object boundary is silently expanded or contracted, subsystem results are represented as whole-system results without sufficient basis, or downstream simulation activity cannot be traced to the boundary under which it was performed.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Candidate Object Boundary
Determine the physical, digital, logical, functional, spatial, temporal, operational, organizational, or composite perimeter required for the identified Simulation Object. 2. Classify Included, Excluded, and External Elements
Establish which material elements belong inside the object, which are explicitly excluded, and which remain external but relevant. 3. Identify Interfaces, Dependencies, and Boundary Conditions
Map material relationships crossing the Simulation Object Boundary and preserve conditions capable of affecting simulation behavior. 4. Resolve or Record Boundary Ambiguity

Identify conflicts, assumptions, uncertain inclusions, exclusions, and boundary limitations and assign the appropriate Simulation Object Boundary Status. 5. Establish the Simulation Object Boundary Record
Preserve the governed boundary, material elements, interfaces, dependencies, conditions, limitations, status, changes, and traceability required for downstream simulation governance.
Governance Outputs
SOBM may produce: Simulation Object Boundary Record, Object Boundary Definition, Boundary Dimension Record, Included Element Register, Excluded Element Register, External Element Register, Composite Object Boundary Record, Constituent Boundary Map, Boundary Interface Register, External Dependency Register, Boundary-Crossing Interaction Map, Boundary Condition Record, Boundary Assumption Reference, Boundary Ambiguity Record, Boundary Conflict Record, Simulation Object Boundary Status, Boundary Change Record, Boundary Expansion Record, Boundary Contraction Record, Boundary Continuity Record, Boundary Equivalence Assessment, and Simulation Object Boundary Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario
A space institution simulates a spacecraft operating during a lunar mission.
The spacecraft depends upon: ground-control infrastructure, navigation data, communication networks, and mission-support systems.
Application
SOBM establishes the spacecraft and its defined onboard systems as the Simulation Object.

Ground control, external communication infrastructure, lunar environment, and navigation services remain outside the Simulation Object Boundary while their material interfaces and dependencies remain explicitly represented. Result
Simulation findings cannot silently treat the entire mission ecosystem as if it were part of the spacecraft itself.
The distinction between:
Spacecraft
External Infrastructure
and:
Simulation Environment
remains traceable throughout downstream SIMULOS® governance. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Facility
Scenario
An organization simulates an autonomous warehouse containing robots, control software, internal communications, charging systems, human workers, and external cloud services. Application
SOBM establishes which elements form the governed Simulation Object.
The autonomous warehouse control system and designated robotic fleet may fall inside the object boundary.
Human workers and external cloud services may remain outside the boundary while their interactions with the system remain material simulation inputs and interfaces. Result
The simulation cannot later be represented as covering the complete warehouse ecosystem if only the autonomous control system and robotic fleet were actually within the governed Simulation Object Boundary.
Architectural Position
Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The internal progression begins:

Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary
SOIM establishes:
Which object is being simulated?
SOBM establishes:
What belongs to that object, what remains outside it, and where does the object end?
Subsequent SOS modules may then govern the object's version, configuration, and documentation against a sufficiently identified and bounded Simulation Object.
SOBM does not replace governance of general governance boundaries under GOA™, operational boundaries under ORA™, validation scope under VALIDOS®, integrity under INTEGROS®, or autonomous-system constraints under ASGA™.
It governs specifically:
the boundary of the object that a simulation claims to represent.
Foundational Principle
A simulation claim cannot legitimately extend beyond the Simulation Object Boundary under which the simulation was governed and executed.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) establishes the structural perimeter of the Simulation Object by governing what belongs to the object, what remains outside it, and how material interfaces, dependencies, interactions, conditions, ambiguities, and boundary changes remain visible throughout the simulation lifecycle. Through explicit inclusion and exclusion, object-environment separation, interface and dependency mapping, anti-expansion and anti-contraction rules, boundary-status governance, change propagation, continuity, and traceability, SOBM prevents simulation results from acquiring broader object coverage than the boundary actually represented. By establishing a persistent Simulation Object Boundary before downstream version, configuration, representation, modeling, scenario, execution, and output governance proceeds, SOBM provides the second foundational object-governance mechanism of SIMULOS®.

Governed Space
Simulation Object Configuration
Canonical Definition
Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) defines the governance conditions under which the specific configuration of a Simulation Object is identified, bounded, recorded, differentiated, changed, and maintained as a traceable simulation-governance state.

SOCM ensures that simulation activity remains bound not merely to the correct Simulation Object and version, but to the specific arrangement of components, settings, parameters, options, dependencies, interfaces, capabilities, and operational features that materially define the object state represented by the simulation.
Operational Role
SOCM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The preceding modules establish:
SOIM — What exactly is the Simulation Object?
SOBM — Where does the Simulation Object begin and end?
SOVM — Which materially distinguishable version of that object is being simulated?
SOCM asks:
What exact configuration of that Simulation Object Version is represented by the simulation?
The governed progression is:
Identified Object → Bounded Object → Object Version → Configuration Basis → Configuration Identification → Material Configuration State → Configuration Change → Simulation Binding → Governed Simulation Object Configuration
Module Operational Space

SOCM governs: Simulation Object configuration identity, configuration basis, configuration parameters, configuration components, configuration settings, configuration options, configuration dependencies, configuration interfaces, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational modes, feature states, component combinations, configuration baselines, configuration variants, configuration relationships, configuration changes, configuration materiality, temporary configurations, experimental configurations, configuration ambiguity, configuration conflict, configuration equivalence, configuration divergence, configuration applicability, configuration status, configuration history, configuration-to-simulation binding, configuration-to-output binding, cross-configuration applicability, and configuration traceability.
Module Function
A Simulation Object Version may exist in multiple configurations.
Those configurations may behave differently even though they belong to the same version.
An autonomous vehicle may operate with different sensor packages.
A robot may operate with different payloads.
An AI system may have different tools enabled.
A spacecraft may use different subsystem arrangements.
An industrial system may operate under different control settings.
A digital system may expose different capabilities depending upon deployment configuration.
Therefore:
Object Identity + Version Identity alone may be insufficient to establish what was actually simulated.

SOCM prevents: undefined configurations, silent configuration substitution, materially different configurations being treated as equivalent, configuration-dependent results being represented as version-wide results, configuration changes being hidden, outputs being detached from the configuration that produced them, temporary settings being mistaken for baseline configuration, and simulation conclusions being transferred between configurations without a governed basis.
Simulation Object Configuration
A Simulation Object Configuration is the defined arrangement of simulation-relevant characteristics within a Simulation Object Version at a particular governed state.
A configuration may include: installed components, activated components, disabled components, software settings, control parameters, operational modes, feature flags, interfaces, connected subsystems, dependency states, tool permissions, sensor arrangements, actuator arrangements, hardware options, safety mechanisms, or other simulation-relevant object characteristics.
Configuration Basis
The Configuration Basis establishes which object characteristics must be known to distinguish one simulation-relevant configuration from another.
The Configuration Basis should focus on characteristics capable of materially affecting: object behavior, available capabilities, interactions, assumptions, scenario response, simulation execution, outputs, reality correlation, or interpretation of simulation results.

Configuration Identity
Where configuration differences can materially affect simulation outcomes, the represented configuration should possess sufficient identity to distinguish it from other configurations.
Conceptually:
Simulation Object → Version → Configuration
For example:
Robot R1 → Version 4.2 → Configuration C7
The configuration identifier may be internally assigned or derived from another controlled configuration system.
SIMULOS® does not require a particular naming convention.
Configuration Baseline
A Simulation Object Configuration Baseline establishes the reference configuration represented by the simulation.
The baseline may identify: Simulation Object, object version, configuration identifier, material components, material settings, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational mode, material dependencies, relevant interfaces, effective state, and known configuration limitations.
Material Configuration Element
A Material Configuration Element is any configurable characteristic capable of materially affecting the simulation or interpretation of its results.
Materiality is simulation-relative.
A setting irrelevant to one simulation may be critical to another.
Therefore:
Configuration Materiality must be evaluated relative to the Simulation Purpose and the behavior being represented.
Configuration Completeness
Configuration Completeness asks:

Are all materially relevant configurable characteristics sufficiently identified to know which object state was actually represented?
Configuration completeness does not require documentation of every technically possible parameter.
It requires sufficient representation of the configuration characteristics material to the governed simulation.
Configuration Variants
One Simulation Object Version may contain multiple valid configurations.
For example:
Version 5.0
may exist as:
Configuration A — Standard
Configuration B — Extended Capability
Configuration C — Restricted Safety Mode
Configuration D — Experimental
These remain configurations of the same version unless the underlying change satisfies the governed conditions for a new version.
Parallel Configurations
Multiple configurations may exist simultaneously.
SOCM preserves their distinction where simulation results could differ materially between them.
Parallel configurations must not be collapsed into one generic object state merely because they share the same version.
Temporary Configuration
A Simulation Object may temporarily enter a configuration used only for: testing, maintenance, emergency operation, degraded operation, experimentation, calibration, or another temporary purpose.
Where that configuration is simulated, its temporary nature should remain explicit.
Experimental Configuration
An experimental configuration should remain distinguishable from the approved or operational baseline configuration.

Simulation findings from an experimental configuration must not silently become findings about the operational configuration.
Configuration Change
A Configuration Change occurs when one or more configuration characteristics change while the underlying Simulation Object identity remains continuous.
Conceptually:
Version V1 / Configuration A → Configuration Change → Version V1 / Configuration B
A configuration change may or may not create a new Simulation Object Version.
Configuration Change Materiality
A configuration change is material where it can materially affect: simulated behavior, available capabilities, scenario response, system interaction, expected outputs, reality representation, or interpretation of simulation results.
Material configuration changes should remain explicitly traceable.
Configuration Change vs Version Change
SIMULOS® distinguishes:
Configuration Change ≠ Version Change
A configuration change modifies the arrangement or state of configurable characteristics.
A version change establishes a materially distinguishable object generation or state requiring separate version identity.
For example:
Version 3.0 / Sensor Package A
and:
Version 3.0 / Sensor Package B
may represent two configurations of the same version.
A fundamental redesign of the sensing architecture may instead require:
Version 4.0
SOVM governs version identity.
SOCM governs configuration identity.
Configuration Change Escalation

A configuration change may become sufficiently significant that the existing version classification should be reconsidered.
SOCM should therefore be capable of generating a:
Version Reassessment Signal
where configuration change appears to exceed the current version boundary.
SOVM determines the resulting version consequence.
Configuration-to-Simulation Binding
Every governed simulation should be capable of answering:
Which configuration of the Simulation Object Version was represented?
The relationship becomes:
Simulation Object → Version → Configuration → Simulation Activity
This binding prevents simulation results from becoming detached from the actual configured state represented during simulation.
Configuration-to-Output Binding
Where outputs depend materially upon configuration, the relationship should remain reconstructable:
Object Configuration → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output
SOCM governs the configuration relationship.
It does not govern the substantive Simulation Output.
No Silent Configuration Substitution Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A materially different Simulation Object Configuration must not replace the configuration represented by a simulation without explicit governance of the change.
If a simulation begins against Configuration A and execution materially shifts to Configuration B, the change must remain visible.
No Configuration-Wide Assumption Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:

Results established for one configuration must not automatically be represented as applicable to every configuration of the same Simulation Object Version.
Shared version identity does not establish configuration equivalence.
Cross-Configuration Applicability
A result established for Configuration A may remain applicable to Configuration B where the changed configuration characteristics do not materially affect the simulation question.
Possible applicability states may include:
Fully Applicable
Conditionally Applicable
Partially Applicable
Not Applicable
or:
Applicability Undetermined
The basis should remain explicit.
Configuration Equivalence
Two configurations may be treated as simulation-equivalent for a specific simulation purpose where their differences do not materially affect the characteristics being simulated.
Therefore:
Technical Configuration Difference ≠ Automatic Simulation Difference
but equally:
Shared Version ≠ Automatic Simulation Equivalence Configuration Divergence
Configuration Divergence exists where configurations differ sufficiently that simulation findings cannot legitimately be transferred between them without additional governance.
Divergence may result from differences in: components, capabilities, permissions, control settings, operational modes, dependencies, interfaces, safety mechanisms, or other material configuration elements.
Configuration Ambiguity

Configuration Ambiguity exists where the exact configuration represented by the simulation cannot be established with sufficient confidence.
Material ambiguity should remain visible.
It must not be silently converted into an assumed configuration.
Configuration Conflict
A Configuration Conflict exists where credible records indicate materially different configurations for the same Simulation Object during the same relevant simulation state.
The conflict should be resolved or explicitly preserved before configuration-dependent conclusions are relied upon.
Configuration Status
A configuration may have a governed status such as:
Baseline
Operational
Alternative
Temporary
Experimental
Degraded
Emergency
Superseded
Retired
Ambiguous
or:
Undetermined
Configuration Status describes the relationship of the configuration to the Simulation Object.
It does not determine simulation validity.
Configuration History
SOCM should preserve material configuration history where configuration changes affect interpretation of simulation activity.
Conceptually:
Configuration A → Change → Configuration B → Change → Configuration C
This allows later reconstruction of which configuration existed at each relevant simulation point.
Configuration Freeze
For some simulations, the represented configuration may need to remain fixed during execution.
A Configuration Freeze identifies the configuration state that must remain stable for the governed simulation activity.

Where a material change occurs during a freeze, the change should produce a governance signal rather than being silently incorporated.
Dynamic Configuration
Some Simulation Objects legitimately change configuration during operation.
Examples include: adaptive robots, reconfigurable spacecraft, autonomous systems, modular industrial systems, dynamically provisioned computing systems, and AI systems with changing tool availability.
In such cases, SOCM should not artificially freeze the object.
Instead, it governs the allowed configuration state space and the transitions occurring within it.
Configuration State Transition
For dynamically configurable objects, a simulation may intentionally represent:
Configuration A → Configuration B → Configuration C
The transition itself may be part of the simulated behavior.
SOCM preserves which configuration states existed and when transitions occurred.
Allowed Configuration State Space
Where dynamic configuration is expected, an Allowed Configuration State Space may define which configurations or configuration transitions belong to the intended simulation representation.
A transition outside that space may generate a configuration deviation signal.
Configuration Deviation
A Configuration Deviation exists where the represented or executed configuration differs materially from the approved Simulation Object Configuration Basis.
Possible outcomes include:
Accepted Deviation
Conditional Deviation
Material Deviation
Configuration Conflict
or:

Deviation Undetermined
SOCM records the deviation.
Downstream simulation governance determines its consequences.
Configuration Dependency
Some configuration characteristics depend upon external or internal components.
SOCM records the configuration relationship where necessary to know the actual object state.
It does not assume governance ownership over the external dependency itself.
Configuration vs Environment
SOCM governs characteristics belonging to the Simulation Object.
It does not govern the simulated environment surrounding the object.
For example:
Robot Sensor Package
belongs to:
Simulation Object Configuration
while:
Warehouse Lighting Conditions
belong to the relevant simulation environment governance space.
The distinction preserves the object/environment boundary established by SOBM.
Configuration vs Simulation Inputs
Configuration characteristics define the state of the object.
Simulation inputs are values, data, stimuli, or conditions supplied to simulation execution.
Therefore:
Object Configuration ≠ Simulation Input
A parameter may appear technically similar in both contexts, but its governance role determines its architectural location.
Configuration vs Scenario
A configuration describes:
what state the Simulation Object is in.
A scenario describes:
what governed situation the simulation subjects that object to.
SOCM does not govern scenario design.
Configuration vs Reality Representation

SOCM identifies the actual object configuration claimed to be represented.
It does not determine whether the simulation model accurately represents that configuration.
That question belongs to the later Reality Representation governance space of SIMULOS®.
Configuration vs Integrity
SOCM does not govern the general integrity of configuration records, components, or configuration processes.
That belongs to INTEGROS® where applicable.
SOCM governs specifically:
which configuration is relevant to the Simulation Object and how that configuration remains identifiable and traceable throughout simulation governance.
Configuration vs Validation
SOCM does not determine whether a configuration has been validated for operational reliance.
That belongs to VALIDOS® where formal validation is required.
SOCM supplies the configuration identity and change information that validation may consume.
Configuration Change Propagation
A material configuration change may affect downstream SIMULOS® governance, including: reality representation, assumptions, model and environment, inputs and data, scenario design, execution, outputs, reality correlation, simulation evidence, and operational reliance.
SOCM identifies the change and preserves its traceability.
It does not replace those downstream governance spaces.
Simulation Object Configuration Record
SOCM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Configuration Record sufficient to reconstruct the configuration represented by the simulation.

The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, Simulation Object Version Identifier, Simulation Object Configuration Identifier, Configuration Basis, Configuration Baseline, material components, material settings, material parameters, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational modes, dependencies, interfaces, configuration status, configuration variants, temporary states, experimental states, configuration changes, configuration deviations, configuration ambiguity, configuration conflicts, configuration equivalence, cross-configuration applicability, configuration history, simulation bindings, output references, and configuration traceability.
Failure Conditions

SOCM governance failure may exist where: the Simulation Object Configuration cannot be identified, material configuration elements remain unknown, simulation activity cannot be bound to the configuration represented, materially different configurations are treated as equivalent without basis, configuration changes occur silently, configuration-dependent findings are represented as version-wide findings, temporary or experimental configurations are confused with operational configurations, configuration ambiguity is hidden, conflicting configuration records remain undisclosed, configuration transitions cannot be reconstructed, configuration changes are confused with version changes, object configuration is confused with environmental conditions, or downstream simulation conclusions cannot be traced to the configuration from which they originated.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Configuration Basis
Identify which configurable characteristics are material to the governed simulation. 2. Establish the Configuration Baseline
Record the material components, settings, capabilities, modes, interfaces, dependencies, and other configuration characteristics represented. 3. Bind Configuration to Object Version
Establish:
Simulation Object → Version → Configuration
and preserve sufficient identity to distinguish materially different configurations. 4. Govern Configuration Change

Detect material configuration changes, preserve transitions and deviations, and trigger version reassessment where configuration change may exceed the current version boundary. 5. Preserve Simulation Traceability
Bind the relevant configuration to simulation activity and preserve sufficient history to determine which configuration produced or influenced downstream simulation outputs.
Governance Outputs
SOCM may produce: Simulation Object Configuration Identifier, Simulation Object Configuration Record, Configuration Basis Record, Configuration Baseline, Material Configuration Element Record, Configuration Completeness Assessment, Configuration Variant Record, Parallel Configuration Record, Temporary Configuration Record, Experimental Configuration Record, Configuration Change Record, Configuration Materiality Assessment, Configuration Transition Record, Configuration Freeze Record, Allowed Configuration State Space, Configuration Deviation Record, Configuration Equivalence Assessment, Cross-Configuration Applicability Assessment, Configuration Divergence Record, Configuration Ambiguity Record, Configuration Conflict Record, Configuration Status, Configuration History Record, Version Reassessment Signal, Configuration-to-Simulation Binding, Configuration-to-Output Reference, and Simulation Object Configuration Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Tool Configuration
Scenario

An autonomous industrial robot operates under the same software and hardware version but may use different tools:
Configuration A — Welding Tool
Configuration B — Cutting Tool
The control system version remains unchanged. Application
SOCM preserves the two configurations as distinct object states.
A simulation executed against the welding configuration remains bound to:
Robot R1 → Version 5.2 → Welding Configuration
Simulation findings dependent upon tool geometry, payload, motion, or operational capability are not automatically transferred to the cutting configuration. Result
Shared version identity does not erase material configuration differences. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Operational Configuration
Scenario
A spacecraft operates in multiple governed configurations:
Launch Configuration
Orbital Configuration
Docking Configuration
The spacecraft remains the same object and version. Application
SOCM identifies each configuration and the permitted transitions between them.
A simulation evaluating docking behavior remains bound to the Docking Configuration rather than being represented generically as a simulation of the spacecraft in every operational state. Result
Simulation conclusions remain attached to the configuration actually represented.
Architectural Position
Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The internal progression is:

Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary → Simulation Object Versioning → Simulation Object Configuration
SOIM establishes:
What is being simulated?
SOBM establishes:
Where does the object begin and end?
SOVM establishes:
Which version of the object is being simulated?
SOCM establishes:
What exact configuration of that version is being simulated?
The next internal governance space, SODM — Simulation Object Documentation Module, governs the persistent documentation necessary to preserve the complete governed Simulation Object definition.
Foundational Principle
A simulation of the correct object and correct version may still represent the wrong operational reality if the configuration actually simulated is not the configuration to which its conclusions are applied.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) establishes the configuration-governance layer of the Simulation Object by ensuring that the specific arrangement of components, settings, parameters, capabilities, interfaces, dependencies, and operational modes represented by simulation remains explicitly identifiable and traceable. Through configuration baselines, materiality assessment, configuration variants, controlled change, dynamic configuration transitions, equivalence, divergence, deviation governance, cross-configuration applicability, and explicit simulation binding, SOCM prevents shared object or version identity from concealing materially different configured states. By preserving the relationship between Simulation Object identity, version, configuration, simulation activity, and downstream outputs, SOCM provides the fourth foundational object-governance mechanism of SIMULOS®.

Governed Space
Simulation Object Documentation
Canonical Definition
Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) defines the governance conditions under which the identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, changes, limitations, and simulation-relevant state of a Simulation Object are consolidated into a persistent, traceable, reconstructable, and operationally usable governed record.
SODM ensures that the Simulation Object established through the preceding SOS modules does not remain distributed across disconnected definitions, assumptions, records, systems, or undocumented knowledge.

It creates the persistent documentary representation through which the exact object intended for simulation can be reconstructed and referenced throughout the SIMULOS® lifecycle.
Operational Role
SODM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The preceding modules establish:
SOIM — What exactly is the Simulation Object?
SOBM — Where does the Simulation Object begin and end?
SOVM — Which materially distinguishable version of the Simulation Object is being simulated?
SOCM — What exact configuration of that version is being simulated?
SODM asks:
How must the complete governed definition of that Simulation Object be documented and preserved so that every downstream simulation activity refers to the same reconstructable object basis?
The governed progression is:
Object Identity → Object Boundary → Object Version → Object Configuration → Documentation Basis → Object Record Formation → Documentation Qualification → Simulation Object Reference → Documentation Change → Persistent Simulation Object Record
Module Operational Space

SODM governs: Simulation Object documentation basis, object record formation, object definition consolidation, object identity documentation, object boundary documentation, version documentation, configuration documentation, material characteristic documentation, inclusion documentation, exclusion documentation, object-state documentation, object limitation documentation, object dependency references, object relationship references, object documentation completeness, object documentation consistency, object documentation currency, object documentation ambiguity, object documentation conflict, object documentation gaps, object documentation change, object documentation supersession, object record status, simulation-object reference, downstream object referencing, point-in-time reconstruction, historical object documentation, documentation continuity, and Simulation Object record traceability.
Module Function
A Simulation Object may be correctly identified, bounded, versioned, and configured while still remaining operationally unusable for governed simulation if those characteristics cannot be reconstructed from a coherent record.
Material information may otherwise exist across: engineering documents, software repositories, configuration systems, model inventories, technical specifications, databases, operational records, human knowledge, external documentation, or temporary simulation records.

SODM prevents: undocumented Simulation Objects, fragmented object definitions, downstream use of inconsistent object descriptions, loss of object boundaries, undocumented version or configuration state, obsolete object records being treated as current, silent modification of the documented object, historical object states being overwritten, object limitations disappearing from downstream simulation activity, and simulation findings becoming detached from the object definition on which they were based.
Simulation Object Documentation Basis
The Simulation Object Documentation Basis is the governed set of information required to establish a sufficiently complete documentary representation of the Simulation Object.
It may draw from: SOS governance records, technical documentation, controlled object records, configuration records, authoritative specifications, system descriptions, engineering records, object inventories, operational records, or other identifiable sources.
SODM does not require all information to exist in one technical system.
It requires the governed Simulation Object definition to remain reconstructable.
Simulation Object Record
A Simulation Object Record is the persistent governed representation of the Simulation Object used throughout the SIMULOS® lifecycle.

At minimum, where applicable, it should establish: Simulation Object Identifier, object name or designation, object type, object description, object boundary, material inclusions, material exclusions, object version, object configuration, material characteristics, relevant operational state, known limitations, material dependencies, relevant relationships, documentation status, effective point, historical references, and sufficient traceability to the underlying SOS governance basis.
Documentation Consolidation
SODM does not require duplication of every underlying document.
Instead, it establishes a governed documentary layer capable of connecting distributed object information into one coherent Simulation Object definition.
Conceptually:
Identity Record + Boundary Record + Version Record + Configuration Record + Material Object Information
↓
Simulation Object Record
The record may therefore operate as a controlled reference layer rather than a duplicate technical repository.
Authoritative Object Reference
A governed simulation should have an identifiable Authoritative Simulation Object Reference.
This reference establishes which Simulation Object Record governs the simulation.
Where multiple object descriptions exist, the authoritative reference prevents downstream simulation activities from selecting incompatible object definitions without visibility.
Documentation Completeness
Documentation Completeness asks:

Is sufficient information available to reconstruct the Simulation Object relevant to the intended simulation?
Completeness is relative to the Simulation Object and the material information required to distinguish it.
It does not require documentation of every technically knowable characteristic.
Material Documentation Requirement
A characteristic should be documented where its omission could materially affect: object identification, object distinction, object boundary, version identification, configuration identification, downstream simulation design, interpretation of simulation results, or later reconstruction of what was simulated.
Documentation Consistency
Documentation Consistency asks whether material Simulation Object records describe a mutually compatible object state.
For example:
Version Record: V4.2
and:
Configuration Record: only valid for V5.0
would create a documentation inconsistency requiring resolution.
Documentation Currency
A Simulation Object Record should indicate the object state and effective period it represents.
A record may remain historically valid while no longer being current.
Therefore:
Historically Accurate ≠ Currently Applicable Current Documentation State
Where the Simulation Object changes, SODM should make it possible to distinguish:
Current Object Record
from:
Historical Object Record
and:
Superseded Object Record
This prevents documentation history from being mistaken for present object reality.
Documentation Ambiguity

Documentation Ambiguity exists where the available records permit multiple materially different interpretations of the Simulation Object.
Examples include uncertainty regarding: object identity, boundary, version, configuration, included components, excluded components, or relevant operational state.
Material ambiguity should remain explicit until resolved.
Documentation Conflict
A Documentation Conflict exists where credible object records materially contradict one another.
For example:
Record A → Configuration C4
Record B → Configuration C7
for the same relevant object state.
SODM requires the conflict to remain visible.
It must not be silently resolved through undocumented preference.
Documentation Gap
A Documentation Gap exists where information necessary to reconstruct a material characteristic of the Simulation Object is absent.
Possible statuses may include:
Non-Material Gap
Conditionally Acceptable Gap
Material Gap
or:
Gap Materiality Undetermined
The gap itself does not determine simulation validity.
It becomes an explicit input to downstream simulation governance.
Documentation Qualification
Before the Simulation Object Record becomes the governing object reference, its documentation basis should be sufficiently qualified for: completeness, consistency, currency, applicability, ambiguity, conflict, and material gaps.
SODM does not perform general evidence validation.

It determines whether the Simulation Object has a sufficiently usable governed documentary representation.
No Undocumented Object Substitution Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Object materially different from the documented governing object must not be substituted without explicit change to the Simulation Object Record.
The simulation cannot silently move from:
Object A
to:
Object A′
while preserving the original object reference.
No Documentation Override Rule
An informal description, label, filename, or operational shorthand must not silently override a materially different governed Simulation Object Record.
Where disagreement exists, the difference should be resolved or preserved as a conflict.
Documentation Change
A Documentation Change occurs when information within the Simulation Object Record is modified.
A documentation change may represent: correction, clarification, additional information, object change, version change, configuration change, boundary change, status change, or removal of obsolete information.
The reason for material changes should remain traceable. Documentation Change ≠ Object Change
SIMULOS® distinguishes:
Documentation Change
from:
Simulation Object Change
Correcting an incorrectly recorded serial number may change documentation without changing the object.
Changing the physical subsystem represented may change the object itself.
SODM records the documentary consequence.

The appropriate preceding SOS module determines the underlying object-governance consequence.
Material Documentation Change
A documentation change is material where it changes how the Simulation Object would be: identified, bounded, versioned, configured, interpreted, distinguished, or represented in downstream simulation activity.
Material documentation changes should generate downstream reassessment where necessary.
Documentation Supersession
Where a new Simulation Object Record replaces a previous record, the previous record should not disappear.
The relationship should remain reconstructable:
Previous Record → Supersession Event → Successor Record Historical Preservation
Historical Simulation Object Records should remain available where required to reconstruct previous simulations.
This enables questions such as:
What object definition governed Simulation Run SR-104?
Which version and configuration were documented at that time?
Which boundaries were applicable?
Which limitations were known?
Point-in-Time Reconstruction
SODM should support reconstruction of the Simulation Object as it was documented at a specific relevant point.
This is particularly important where: the object evolves, configuration changes, multiple simulations occur over time, simulation outputs are later reused, incidents occur, or historical simulation conclusions are reviewed.
Object Documentation Continuity
Documentation Continuity preserves the relationship:
Object Identity
↓
Boundary
↓
Version
↓

Configuration
↓
Simulation Object Record
↓
Simulation Activity
↓
Subsequent Object Change
↓
Successor Object Record
This ensures that object evolution does not erase the basis of earlier simulation activity.
Simulation Object Reference
Once sufficiently established, the Simulation Object Record becomes the controlled reference consumed by subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards.
Downstream simulation governance should reference the governed object rather than independently redefining it.
Downstream Reference Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A downstream simulation activity should not silently redefine the Simulation Object established by SOS.
Where a downstream requirement demonstrates that the object definition is insufficient or incorrect, the issue should return to the appropriate SOS governance space.
Documentation and Purpose & Scope
SODM establishes the object documentation basis.
It does not determine: why the simulation is being performed, what the simulation must evaluate, what reliance is intended, or how broad the simulation inquiry should be.
Those questions belong to the subsequent Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard.
Documentation and Reality Representation
SODM documents the real or conceptual object claimed to be represented.
It does not determine whether a simulation model accurately represents that object.
That belongs to the later Reality Representation governance space.
Documentation and Simulation Model
A Simulation Object Record is not the Simulation Model.

The distinction is:
Simulation Object Record → What is intended to be represented
Simulation Model → How that object is represented for simulation
Confusing these two layers can cause a model description to replace the actual object definition.
Documentation and Environment
SODM governs documentation of the Simulation Object.
It does not govern the complete simulated environment surrounding that object.
Environmental characteristics belong to the relevant SIMULOS® environment governance space.
Documentation and Evidence
A Simulation Object Record may later become part of a validation or audit evidence basis.
SODM does not determine its general evidential fitness.
Where formal validation is required, VALIDOS® governs validation evidence fitness.
Where audit evidence is required, ADIT® governs the relevant audit-evidence lifecycle.
Documentation and Integrity
SODM does not replace INTEGROS®.
INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of: records, data, documentation structures, storage, change history, or other integrity-relevant elements.
SODM governs specifically whether the Simulation Object possesses a sufficiently persistent and reconstructable documentary representation for simulation governance.
Documentation and Identity
SODM does not replace broader identity governance.
Where identity, origin, ownership, provenance, or transfer require independent governance, complementary OOF® identity architectures may apply.

SODM consumes the identity necessary to maintain the Simulation Object as a stable simulation reference.
Documentation and Auditability
SODM creates traceability necessary for later reconstruction.
It does not govern the complete audit lifecycle.
ADIT® may consume SODM records where continuous or retrospective audit is required.
Documentation Change Propagation
A material change to the Simulation Object Record may affect downstream governance.
Potentially affected spaces may include: Simulation Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output, Reality Correlation, Simulation Evidence, Operational Reliance, and Resimulation.
SODM identifies the documentary change.
The affected downstream governance spaces determine its consequence.
Documentation Reassessment Signal
Where a material documentation change may invalidate the current object basis, SODM should generate a Simulation Object Reassessment Signal.
Possible causes include: corrected object identity, changed boundary, new version information, configuration discovery, previously unknown material component, corrected exclusion, newly identified limitation, or resolved documentation conflict.
Documentation Status
A Simulation Object Record may carry a status such as:
Draft
Qualified
Current
Conditionally Current
Superseded
Historical
Conflicted
Incomplete
or:
Undetermined
Status indicates documentary condition.

It does not establish simulation validity.
Persistent Simulation Object Record
The complete SOS lifecycle should result in a persistent record capable of preserving: object identity, object boundary, object version, object configuration, material characteristics, relevant limitations, dependencies, documentation basis, documentation qualification, conflicts, gaps, changes, status, effective period, supersession, historical continuity, and downstream references.
SOS Completion Gate
SODM establishes the final internal completion gate of SOS.
The key question is:
Is the Simulation Object sufficiently identified, bounded, versioned, configured, documented, and reconstructable to enter governed Simulation Purpose & Scope?
Possible outcomes may include:
SOS Complete
SOS Conditionally Complete
SOS Incomplete
or:
SOS Completion Undetermined
A conditional or incomplete status should remain visible downstream.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Documentation Basis
Identify the records necessary to reconstruct the Simulation Object. 2. Consolidate the Governed Object Definition
Connect identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, limitations, and relevant references into the Simulation Object Record. 3. Qualify the Documentation
Assess completeness, consistency, currency, applicability, ambiguity, conflict, and material gaps. 4. Establish the Authoritative Object Reference

Identify the Simulation Object Record that governs downstream simulation activity. 5. Preserve Change and Historical Continuity
Record material documentation changes, supersession, prior object states, and point-in-time applicability. 6. Bind the Record to Downstream Simulation Governance
Ensure subsequent SIMULOS® spaces reference the established Simulation Object rather than silently redefining it. 7. Generate Reassessment Signals
Where new information materially changes the object basis, return the issue to the relevant SOS governance space and propagate the resulting change downstream. 8. Determine SOS Completion
Establish whether the Simulation Object is sufficiently governed to proceed into Simulation Purpose & Scope.
Governance Outputs

SODM may produce: Simulation Object Documentation Basis, Simulation Object Record, Authoritative Simulation Object Reference, Object Definition Consolidation Record, Object Documentation Completeness Assessment, Object Documentation Consistency Assessment, Object Documentation Currency Assessment, Object Documentation Applicability Record, Object Documentation Ambiguity Record, Object Documentation Conflict Record, Object Documentation Gap Record, Material Documentation Change Record, Object Documentation Supersession Record, Historical Simulation Object Record, Point-in-Time Object Reconstruction Record, Object Documentation Status, Simulation Object Reassessment Signal, Downstream Object Reference, Simulation Object Documentation Traceability Map, SOS Completion Record, and Persistent Simulation Object Record.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle platform is represented across: engineering specifications, sensor configuration records, software version records, and operational configuration databases.
No single record identifies the complete object state used by the simulation. Application
SODM consolidates the relevant governed references into:
Vehicle AV-17 → Version 6.3 → Configuration C12
The Simulation Object Record identifies the applicable sensor package, control software, material boundaries, exclusions, and known object limitations. Result

The simulation no longer depends upon an informal assumption about which vehicle configuration is being represented.
Every downstream SIMULOS® space can reference the same governed Simulation Object. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Simulation History
Scenario
A spacecraft undergoes configuration changes during its operational lifecycle.
A simulation performed two years earlier becomes relevant after an operational anomaly. Application
SODM reconstructs the historical Simulation Object Record applicable to the earlier simulation.
The record establishes:
Object Identity → Historical Version → Historical Configuration → Applicable Boundary → Known Limitations → Simulation Reference Result
Investigators can determine exactly which spacecraft state the historical simulation represented rather than applying current spacecraft documentation retrospectively.
Architectural Position
Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The complete SOS progression is:
Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary → Simulation Object Versioning → Simulation Object Configuration → Simulation Object Documentation
Together, these five modules establish the governed Simulation Object before simulation purpose, representation, assumptions, models, data, scenarios, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence, reliance, or lifecycle governance begins.

SOS therefore answers one foundational architectural question:
What exactly is being simulated?
Once SODM establishes a sufficiently persistent and reconstructable Simulation Object Record, the object may proceed to the next SIMULOS® Parent Standard:
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard.
Foundational Principle
A Simulation Object is not sufficiently governed merely because its identity is known; the complete object basis must remain reconstructable so that every simulation activity can demonstrate exactly what object it represented.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) completes the Simulation Object Standard by consolidating object identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, limitations, changes, and historical continuity into a persistent and reconstructable Simulation Object Record. Through documentation qualification, authoritative referencing, ambiguity and conflict preservation, change governance, supersession, point-in-time reconstruction, downstream binding, and SOS completion control, SODM prevents simulation activity from becoming detached from the exact object it claims to represent. By establishing a stable documentary bridge between Simulation Object governance and every subsequent SIMULOS® lifecycle space, SODM completes the foundational answer to the first question of Simulation Governance Architecture: exactly what is being simulated.
