OOF™ Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM)
Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Object Versioning
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 15 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Object Versioning
Canonical Definition
Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM) defines the governance conditions under which materially distinguishable versions of a Simulation Object are identified, differentiated, related, transitioned, and maintained as traceable simulation-governance objects throughout the simulation lifecycle.
SOVM ensures that simulation activity, evidence, outputs, findings, and downstream reliance remain bound to the version of the Simulation Object to which they actually apply.
Operational Role
SOVM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).

The preceding modules establish:
SOIM — What exactly is the Simulation Object?
SOBM — Where does the Simulation Object begin and end?
SOVM asks:
Which version of that Simulation Object is being simulated, and when does change create a materially different version?
The governed progression is:
Identified & Bounded Simulation Object → Version Basis → Version Identity → Material Change Assessment → Version Relationship → Version Status → Version Traceability → Governed Simulation Object Version
SOVM prevents simulation conclusions established for one object version from silently migrating to another.
Module Operational Space
SOVM governs: Simulation Object version identity, version designation, version basis, version differentiation, version chronology, version relationships, predecessor versions, successor versions, parallel versions, derived versions, version baselines, version transitions, material version change, minor change, major change, version ambiguity, version conflict, version equivalence, version applicability, version status, version lineage, version continuity, version supersession, version retirement, historical version preservation, version-to-simulation binding, version-to-output binding, cross-version applicability, and version traceability.
Module Function
SOVM exists because identifying a Simulation Object once is insufficient.
Objects change.
Software is updated.
Hardware is modified.
AI models evolve.
Control logic changes.
Processes are redesigned.

Components are replaced.
Operational capabilities expand or contract.
A simulation result produced against an earlier version may therefore cease to represent the object that exists later.
SOVM prevents: unknown object versions, version ambiguity, silent version substitution, uncontrolled inheritance of simulation findings, simulation outputs being detached from their object version, materially changed objects being represented as unchanged, different versions being aggregated without disclosure, superseded versions being confused with current versions, and historical simulation conclusions being represented as current without a governed basis.
Simulation Object Version
A Simulation Object Version is a distinguishable state of a Simulation Object defined by a set of characteristics sufficient to determine which object state was represented by a simulation.
Version identity may depend upon: design revision, software release, model release, hardware revision, structural modification, capability change, process revision, control-logic change, operational change, or another materially relevant object change.
A version does not require a particular commercial or technical versioning convention.
SOVM governs methodological distinguishability.
Version Basis
A Version Basis establishes which characteristics determine whether two states of a Simulation Object should be treated as:
the same version
or:
different versions
for simulation-governance purposes.

The Version Basis should reflect characteristics capable of materially changing: simulated behavior, simulation assumptions, applicable scenarios, interactions, expected outputs, reality correlation, or interpretation of simulation results.
Technical Version ≠ Governed Simulation Version
SIMULOS® establishes:
Technical Version Identity ≠ Simulation Governance Version Identity
A vendor may label two builds:
v3.1.1
and:
v3.1.2
while the difference is immaterial to a particular simulation.
Conversely, an operational change may materially alter simulation relevance even where no formal software version number changes.
SOVM therefore does not depend exclusively upon external version labels.
Version Identification
Every simulation should be sufficiently bound to an identifiable Simulation Object Version where version differences could materially affect the simulation.
Version identification may include: version identifier, release identifier, revision identifier, build identifier, object state, effective date, material characteristics, predecessor relationship, or other distinguishing information.
Material Version Change
A Material Version Change is a change capable of affecting the validity, applicability, interpretation, or transferability of simulation activity or simulation-derived results.

Possible examples include: changed system behavior, changed physical characteristics, changed algorithms, changed decision logic, changed interfaces, changed capabilities, changed autonomy, changed safety mechanisms, changed operating modes, or changed material dependencies.
A material change should create either:
a new governed Simulation Object Version
or:
an explicit determination explaining why version continuity remains justified.
Minor Change
A change may be classified as minor where it does not materially affect the simulation-relevant characteristics of the Simulation Object.
Minor changes should not automatically require creation of a new governed simulation version.
However, the basis for treating a potentially relevant change as minor should remain reconstructable.
Major Change
A major change materially alters one or more characteristics relevant to simulation behavior or interpretation.
A major change normally requires a distinguishable Simulation Object Version.
Version Significance Is Simulation-Relative
The significance of a change may depend upon the simulation purpose.
A modification irrelevant to one simulation may be material to another.
For example:
a cosmetic physical change may be irrelevant to a software-behavior simulation,
but material to an aerodynamic simulation.
Therefore:
Version Materiality must be evaluated relative to the governed simulation context.
Version Baseline

A Simulation Object Version Baseline establishes the reference version against which relevant changes are evaluated.
The baseline may identify: object identity, boundary, version identifier, material characteristics, effective state, known limitations, and applicable simulation relationship.
Version Transition
A Version Transition occurs when the Simulation Object moves from one governed version to another.
Conceptually:
Version A → Material Change → Version B
The transition should preserve the relationship between predecessor and successor.
Version Lineage
Version Lineage establishes how Simulation Object Versions relate across time.
For example:
V1 → V2 → V3
or:
V1 → V2A
V1 → V2B
where parallel development produces divergent versions.
Version lineage allows simulation evidence and findings to remain attached to the correct historical object state.
Parallel Versions
Multiple versions of the same Simulation Object may exist simultaneously.
For example: production version, experimental version, regional version, safety-modified version, prototype version, or alternative design version.
SOVM requires each materially distinguishable version to remain identifiable.
Derived Version
A Derived Version originates from an existing Simulation Object Version but contains changes sufficient to require independent version identity.
Its relationship to the originating version should remain traceable.
Version-to-Simulation Binding
Every governed simulation should be capable of answering:

Which Simulation Object Version did this simulation represent?
This creates the relationship:
Simulation Object → Object Version → Simulation Activity
Without this binding, later interpretation may incorrectly apply simulation findings to another version.
Version-to-Output Binding
Simulation outputs should remain traceable to the Simulation Object Version from which they were generated.
Conceptually:
Object Version → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output
SOVM governs the version relationship.
It does not govern the substantive output itself, which belongs to the relevant downstream SIMULOS® governance space.
No Silent Version Substitution Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation Object Version must not be replaced by another materially different version without explicit governance of the change.
A simulation started against Version A must not silently become represented as a simulation of Version B.
No Automatic Result Inheritance Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation results established for one Simulation Object Version do not automatically apply to another version.
Cross-version applicability requires a governed basis.
Cross-Version Applicability
A simulation result from Version A may remain relevant to Version B where the changed characteristics do not materially affect the simulation question.
SOVM permits such applicability, but requires the relationship to be explicit.
Possible statuses may include:
Fully Applicable
Conditionally Applicable
Partially Applicable

Not Applicable
or:
Applicability Undetermined Version Equivalence
Two formally different versions may be simulation-equivalent for a specific simulation purpose.
Version equivalence should not be assumed merely because the versions are similar.
It should be based upon the characteristics relevant to the simulation.
Version Divergence
Version Divergence exists where two versions become sufficiently different that simulation findings can no longer be safely treated as mutually applicable.
Divergence may result from: capability expansion, architecture change, behavior change, interface change, physical redesign, changed autonomy, or accumulated modifications.
Version Ambiguity
Version Ambiguity exists where the exact Simulation Object Version represented by a simulation cannot be established with sufficient confidence.
Material version ambiguity should remain visible.
It must not be silently converted into a specific version assignment.
Version Conflict
A Version Conflict exists where credible records identify materially different versions as the object represented by the same simulation activity.
The conflict should be resolved or explicitly preserved before downstream conclusions depend upon version identity.
Version Supersession
A newer Simulation Object Version may supersede an earlier version.
Supersession does not erase the earlier version.
Historical simulation records must continue to identify the version to which they originally applied.
Historical Version Preservation

SOVM preserves historical Simulation Object Versions because later questions may require reconstruction of: what object existed, which version was simulated, which findings applied, what changed afterward, and whether later reliance crossed a version boundary.
Version Retirement
A Simulation Object Version may be retired when it is no longer active or relevant for current operation.
Retirement does not delete: version identity, simulation history, outputs, lineage, or previous applicability.
Version Status
A Simulation Object Version may hold statuses such as:
Current
Active
Experimental
Parallel
Superseded
Retired
Ambiguous
or:
Undetermined
Status identifies the lifecycle position of the version.
It does not determine simulation validity.
Version Change Propagation
A material version change may affect downstream SIMULOS® governance, including: reality representation, assumptions, model and environment, inputs and data, scenario design, execution, outputs, reality correlation, simulation evidence, or operational reliance.
SOVM identifies and propagates the version change.
It does not replace the downstream governance spaces responsible for determining the consequences.
Version Change vs Configuration Change
SOVM distinguishes:
Version Change
from:
Configuration Change
A version identifies a materially distinguishable state or generation of the Simulation Object.

A configuration identifies the specific arrangement of relevant components, settings, parameters, options, dependencies, or operational features associated with that object.
A configuration change does not necessarily create a new version.
A version change may contain multiple configurations.
Detailed configuration governance belongs to SOCM — Simulation Object Configuration Module.
Version Change vs Boundary Change
A version change does not necessarily change the Simulation Object Boundary.
Likewise, a boundary change may be material enough to require a new version.
SOBM governs the boundary.
SOVM governs version identity and continuity.
Where both change, the relationship should remain traceable.
Version Change vs Validation
SOVM does not determine whether a changed object remains valid for operational reliance.
That question belongs to VALIDOS® where formal validation or revalidation is required.
SOVM provides the version-change basis that VALIDOS® may consume.
Version Change vs Integrity
SOVM does not determine whether the object has preserved integrity through change.
That governance belongs to INTEGROS®.
SOVM determines whether the change creates or affects a distinguishable Simulation Object Version.
Simulation Object Version Record
SOVM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Version Record sufficient to reconstruct which object version existed and which simulations were bound to it.

The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, Simulation Object Version Identifier, Version Basis, version designation, effective period, material characteristics, predecessor version, successor version, parallel versions, derived-version relationships, material changes, minor changes, version status, version ambiguity, version conflicts, cross-version applicability, version lineage, supersession, retirement, simulation bindings, output references, and version traceability.
Failure Conditions
SOVM governance failure may exist where: a materially relevant Simulation Object Version is unidentified, simulations cannot be bound to the object version represented, materially different versions are treated as equivalent without basis, version changes occur silently, historical simulation results are automatically transferred to successor versions, version ambiguity is hidden, conflicting version records are ignored, superseded versions are represented as current, version lineage cannot be reconstructed, version changes are confused with configuration changes, or downstream simulation conclusions cannot be traced to the version from which they originated.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Version Basis
Define which characteristics are relevant for distinguishing Simulation Object Versions within the governed simulation context. 2. Identify the Simulation Object Version

Assign or preserve sufficient version identity and bind it to the identified and bounded Simulation Object. 3. Assess Material Change
Determine whether relevant changes preserve the current version, create a new version, or leave version status unresolved. 4. Establish Version Relationships
Preserve predecessor, successor, parallel, derived, superseded, and applicable cross-version relationships where relevant. 5. Preserve Version Traceability
Bind simulation activity and resulting outputs to the applicable Simulation Object Version and maintain the historical version lineage.
Governance Outputs
SOVM may produce: Simulation Object Version Record, Simulation Object Version Identifier, Version Basis Record, Version Baseline, Version Materiality Assessment, Minor Change Record, Material Version Change Record, Version Transition Record, Version Relationship Map, Version Lineage Record, Predecessor Version Reference, Successor Version Reference, Parallel Version Record, Derived Version Record, Version Equivalence Assessment, Cross-Version Applicability Assessment, Version Divergence Record, Version Ambiguity Record, Version Conflict Record, Version Status, Version Supersession Record, Version Retirement Record, Version-to-Simulation Binding, Version-to-Output Reference, and Simulation Object Version Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Software Upgrade
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle has been simulated using:
Autonomous Driving System Version 7.2

A later release changes perception and decision logic.
The manufacturer labels the successor:
Version 7.3 Application
SOVM assesses whether the changes affect characteristics material to the simulations previously performed against Version 7.2.
Because perception and decision logic materially affect simulated driving behavior, Version 7.3 is maintained as a distinguishable Simulation Object Version.
Existing Version 7.2 simulation results remain historically valid records but do not automatically transfer to Version 7.3. Result
The relationship remains explicit:
Version 7.2 → Material Change → Version 7.3
Downstream SIMULOS® governance can determine which simulation activities must be repeated or reassessed. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Hardware Revision
Scenario
A spacecraft component undergoes a hardware revision before launch.
The change affects thermal behavior but does not affect navigation software. Application
SOVM records the new Simulation Object Version and identifies the thermal modification as the material change.
Previous navigation simulations may remain applicable where version equivalence is sufficiently established for that simulation purpose.
Previous thermal simulations are not automatically inherited. Result
SOVM prevents an all-or-nothing interpretation.
The new spacecraft version remains historically connected to the previous version while simulation applicability is bounded according to the characteristics actually affected by the change.

Architectural Position
Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM) is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS).
The internal progression is:
Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary → Simulation Object Versioning
SOIM establishes:
What is being simulated?
SOBM establishes:
Where does that object begin and end?
SOVM establishes:
Which materially distinguishable version of that object is being simulated?
The next internal governance space, SOCM — Simulation Object Configuration Module, governs the specific configuration of that version.
SOVM does not replace configuration governance, reality-representation governance, integrity governance, validation governance, or operational-reality governance.
It governs specifically:
the identity, differentiation, continuity, lineage, and simulation applicability of Simulation Object Versions.
Foundational Principle
A simulation result belongs first to the Simulation Object Version that was actually simulated; applicability to another version must be governed, not assumed.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM) establishes the version-governance layer of the Simulation Object by ensuring that materially distinguishable object states remain identified, differentiated, historically related, and traceable throughout the simulation lifecycle. Through version baselines, material-change assessment, version transitions, lineage, cross-version applicability, equivalence, divergence, supersession, historical preservation, and explicit simulation binding, SOVM prevents simulation findings established for one object version from silently becoming findings about another. By preserving the relationship between Simulation Object identity, object change, version history, simulation activity, and downstream outputs, SOVM provides the third foundational object-governance mechanism of SIMULOS®.

OOF™ Simulation Purpose Definition Module (SPDM)
Simulation Purpose Definition Module (SPDM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Purpose Definition
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · AGA™ · ADIT®
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Purpose Definition
Canonical Definition
Simulation Purpose Definition Module (SPDM) defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a simulation is explicitly identified, justified, bounded, documented, and connected to the Simulation Object and the question the simulation is intended to investigate.
SPDM establishes the purpose basis from which simulation scope, applicability, required depth, precision, reality representation, assumptions, scenarios, and downstream simulation design can legitimately be derived.
Operational Role
SPDM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).

The preceding Simulation Object Standard establishes:
What exactly is being simulated?
SPDM asks:
Why is this Simulation Object being simulated, and what legitimate inquiry is the simulation intended to support?
The governed progression begins:
Simulation Object → Simulation Need → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Question → Intended Outcome → Purpose Boundary
A simulation should not proceed into detailed representation or design before this purpose basis is sufficiently established.
Module Operational Space
SPDM governs: Simulation Purpose identification, Simulation Need, purpose justification, Simulation Question formation, intended simulation outcome, intended analytical use, intended decision-support role, exploratory versus confirmatory purpose, design-support purpose, testing purpose, comparison purpose, safety-related purpose, training purpose, predictive or scenario-exploration purpose, pre-deployment simulation purpose, purpose hierarchy, multiple-purpose simulations, purpose compatibility, purpose conflicts, purpose changes, purpose expansion, purpose substitution, purpose traceability, and Purpose Definition Records.
Module Function
The function of SPDM is to ensure that simulation begins from an explicit governed purpose rather than from available technology, an existing model, available data, organizational habit, or an undefined desire to “simulate the system.”

SPDM prevents: simulations without a defined reason, technical capability determining purpose retrospectively, vague simulation objectives, hidden secondary purposes, conflicting purposes being treated as one inquiry, exploratory simulations being represented as confirmatory, simulation results being used for decisions the simulation was never designed to support, purpose expansion after results are known, and downstream simulation architecture being constructed before the intended inquiry is understood.
Simulation Need
Before defining purpose, an organization should establish why simulation is an appropriate activity.
A Simulation Need exists where examination of a Simulation Object through governed simulated representation can materially contribute to understanding, testing, comparison, exploration, preparation, design, or decision support.
The existence of a Simulation Object does not itself establish a need to simulate it.
Simulation Purpose
Simulation Purpose defines the primary reason the simulation is being performed.
Examples may include:
Exploration — understanding possible behaviors or outcomes.
Testing — examining behavior against defined conditions.
Comparison — comparing configurations, strategies, systems, or alternatives.
Design Support — informing development or engineering decisions.
Safety Investigation — examining behavior under potentially hazardous conditions.
Operational Preparation — studying expected operational situations before deployment.

Training — reproducing governed situations for human or system preparation.
Scenario Analysis — examining alternative future or hypothetical conditions.
Decision Support — producing simulation-derived information relevant to a defined decision.
These purposes may coexist, but they must remain distinguishable where their governance requirements differ.
Purpose Must Precede Simulation Design
SIMULOS® establishes:
The simulation purpose should determine the simulation design; the available simulation design should not silently determine the purpose.
An organization may already possess a model, digital twin, simulator, dataset, environment, or simulation platform.
Their availability does not establish that they are appropriate for the new purpose.
Simulation Question
Every material Simulation Purpose should be translated into one or more explicit Simulation Questions.
For example:
Purpose:
Evaluate autonomous robot behavior before deployment.
Simulation Question:
How does the defined robot configuration behave under the specified operating conditions and disturbance scenarios?
The Simulation Question creates a bridge between general purpose and governable scope.
Question Specificity
A Simulation Question should be sufficiently specific to determine what downstream simulation design must investigate.
A question such as:
“Is the system good?”
is not sufficiently governed.
A question such as:

“Can the specified robotic configuration complete the defined material-handling task within the modeled operating envelope while remaining within the specified operational constraints?”
creates a substantially stronger simulation basis.
Intended Outcome
SPDM should identify what type of outcome the simulation is expected to produce.
The intended outcome may include: behavioral understanding, comparative information, performance observations, scenario outcomes, design information, failure observations, boundary observations, sensitivity information, operational preparation, or decision-support information.
The intended outcome should not predetermine the substantive result. Purpose ≠ Desired Result
A simulation may have a legitimate intended purpose.
It must not have a predetermined required conclusion.
For example:
Purpose: Determine whether Configuration A performs better than Configuration B
is legitimate.
Purpose: Demonstrate that Configuration A is better than Configuration B
may create methodological bias if the simulation is structurally expected to confirm that conclusion.
SPDM therefore separates:
What the simulation should investigate
from:
What the organization wants the simulation to conclude.
Exploratory Simulation
An exploratory simulation investigates possibilities without necessarily testing a predetermined proposition.

It may be appropriate for: discovery, sensitivity exploration, scenario generation, early design, emerging-risk investigation, or behavior mapping.
Exploratory results should remain identified as exploratory when downstream reliance is considered.
Confirmatory Simulation
A confirmatory simulation evaluates a defined proposition, requirement, expectation, configuration, or hypothesis against governed conditions.
Its purpose should identify what is being examined and against which intended question.
Confirmatory simulation normally requires stronger control over: scope, assumptions, scenarios, representation, inputs, execution, and interpretation.
Decision-Support Simulation
Where simulation is intended to support a decision, SPDM should identify the decision context.
The record should distinguish between:
Simulation informs the decision
and:
Simulation determines the decision.
These are materially different governance conditions.
High-Consequence Purpose
Where simulation may materially influence: human safety, critical infrastructure, autonomous deployment, healthcare, financial exposure, regulatory decisions, public systems, or other high-consequence environments,
the purpose should explicitly identify that consequence context.
This information may affect downstream Simulation Depth and governance requirements.
Pre-Deployment Purpose
SIMULOS® may be used to examine systems before real-world deployment.

For pre-deployment simulation, the purpose should identify what the organization seeks to understand before exposure to operational reality.
Examples include: behavioral boundaries, failure conditions, environmental response, interaction behavior, autonomous decisions, performance limitations, or scenario response.
SPDM does not determine whether simulation alone is sufficient for deployment authorization.
Multiple Simulation Purposes
One simulation may support multiple purposes.
For example:
Design Optimization + Safety Exploration + Operator Training
These purposes should not automatically be merged into one undifferentiated purpose.
Each may require different: scope, representation, assumptions, scenarios, precision, outputs, and downstream reliance boundaries.
Purpose Hierarchy
Where several purposes exist, SPDM may establish:
Primary Purpose
Secondary Purpose
Supporting Purpose
This helps prevent a secondary use from silently becoming the primary justification for the simulation.
Purpose Compatibility
Multiple purposes may share one simulation only where their requirements are sufficiently compatible.
If one purpose requires substantially different representation, precision, scenarios, or operating conditions, separate simulation pathways may be necessary.
Purpose Conflict
A Purpose Conflict exists where two or more simulation purposes create incompatible methodological requirements.
For example:

A simulation optimized for rapid exploratory iteration may not simultaneously satisfy the conditions required for a high-consequence confirmatory simulation.
Purpose conflicts should be resolved or explicitly separated before downstream simulation design.
Purpose Boundary
Every Simulation Purpose should establish a boundary around what the simulation is intended to investigate.
The purpose boundary prevents the simulation from later being interpreted as having addressed questions that were never part of the original inquiry.
Conceptually:
Legitimate Simulation Interpretation ≤ Governed Simulation Purpose Purpose Expansion
A Simulation Purpose may legitimately expand during a project.
However:
Purpose expansion requires governance reassessment.
A broader purpose may require changes to: scope, representation, assumptions, inputs, scenarios, depth, precision, execution, or downstream interpretation.
Existing simulation work should not automatically be presumed sufficient for the expanded purpose.
Purpose Reduction
Purpose may also narrow.
Where this occurs, downstream simulation activities may be simplified only where the reduced purpose no longer requires them.
Historical purpose should remain traceable.
Purpose Substitution
Purpose Substitution occurs when simulation results generated for one purpose are later represented as supporting a materially different purpose.
Example:
Original Purpose: Early Engineering Exploration
later becomes:

Claimed Purpose: Deployment Safety Demonstration
without corresponding simulation redesign or reassessment.
SIMULOS® treats this as a material governance issue.
Purpose Change
A material change in purpose should create a Purpose Reassessment Trigger.
The reassessment should determine whether existing: scope, assumptions, representations, scenarios, data, execution, and outputs
remain suitable.
Purpose Traceability
SPDM should preserve the relationship:
Simulation Object → Simulation Need → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Question → Intended Outcome
This relationship should remain traceable throughout the simulation lifecycle.
Downstream simulation outputs should therefore be interpretable against the purpose that originally justified their production.
Purpose and Reality Representation
SPDM does not determine how reality should be represented.
It establishes why reality must be represented and what inquiry that representation must support.
The downstream Reality Representation governance space determines how the relevant aspects of reality are represented for that purpose.
Purpose and Validation
SPDM does not validate the simulation.
VALIDOS® governs general validation methodology where validation is required.
SIMULOS® establishes the simulation-specific purpose that may later become part of a validation inquiry.
This preserves the boundary:
SIMULOS® governs the simulation.
VALIDOS® governs validation of the relevant object or claim.
Purpose and Integrity

SPDM does not govern general integrity.
INTEGROS® governs integrity where applicable.
SPDM governs whether the simulation purpose itself remains explicit, bounded, stable, and traceable.
Failure Conditions
SPDM should identify a governance failure where: no explicit Simulation Purpose exists, purpose cannot be connected to the Simulation Object, the Simulation Question remains materially ambiguous, the intended outcome is undefined, purpose is defined retrospectively from available results, a desired result is disguised as simulation purpose, materially different purposes are silently merged, incompatible purposes are not resolved, purpose expands without reassessment, purpose substitution occurs, high-consequence use is not reflected in the purpose, or downstream simulation use materially exceeds the governed purpose.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify the Simulation Need
Document why simulation is being used for the defined Simulation Object. 2. Define the Simulation Purpose
State the primary reason for performing the simulation and distinguish secondary purposes where applicable. 3. Establish the Simulation Question
Translate the purpose into a sufficiently explicit question or set of questions that downstream simulation design can address. 4. Define the Intended Outcome and Purpose Boundary
Identify what type of information the simulation is expected to produce and what the simulation is not intended to establish. 5. Approve and Preserve Purpose Traceability

Record the governed purpose basis and maintain its connection to downstream scope, representation, design, execution, outputs, and any subsequent purpose changes.
Governance Outputs
SPDM may produce: Simulation Need Record, Simulation Purpose Statement, Primary Simulation Purpose, Secondary Simulation Purpose Record, Simulation Question Set, Intended Simulation Outcome, Decision-Support Context Record, Consequence Context Record, Purpose Hierarchy, Purpose Compatibility Assessment, Purpose Conflict Record, Purpose Boundary, Purpose Change Record, Purpose Expansion Record, Purpose Substitution Record, Purpose Reassessment Trigger, and Simulation Purpose Traceability Record.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Pre-Deployment Simulation
Scenario
An industrial organization intends to deploy an autonomous mobile robot within a production facility.
The organization creates a simulation before physical deployment. Application
SPDM establishes the primary purpose as:
Pre-deployment investigation of autonomous robot behavior within defined production operating conditions.
The governed Simulation Questions include whether the robot can: navigate the intended environment, respond to defined obstacles, operate within specified boundaries, and respond to selected abnormal conditions.
SPDM explicitly prevents the simulation from being represented as universal proof of safety across environments not included in the purpose. Result

The downstream simulation architecture receives a defined inquiry basis from which scope, reality representation, assumptions, scenarios, depth, and precision can be established. Use Case 2 — Aerospace Design Comparison
Scenario
An aerospace engineering team uses simulation to compare two proposed component configurations before physical prototyping. Application
SPDM defines:
Primary Purpose: Comparative engineering evaluation.
Simulation Question: How do Configurations A and B differ under the defined modeled operating conditions?
Intended Outcome: Comparative performance and behavior information supporting design selection.
The purpose does not state that Configuration A must outperform Configuration B. Result
Both configurations can be simulated against a common governed purpose without predetermining the result, while later use of the simulation for unrelated certification or deployment claims would require separate governance assessment.
Architectural Position
Simulation Purpose Definition is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
It follows the establishment of the Simulation Object and precedes detailed governance of Simulation Scope and downstream Reality Representation.
The architectural progression is:
Simulation Object → Simulation Need → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Question → Intended Outcome → Purpose Boundary → Simulation Scope → Reality Representation

SPDM therefore establishes the reason from which the remainder of the simulation governance lifecycle begins.
Foundational Principle
A simulation can legitimately support only the inquiry for which its purpose was explicitly defined and governed.
Canonical Closing Statement
Simulation Purpose Definition Module establishes the governed purpose foundation of SIMULOS® by defining why a Simulation Object is being simulated, which questions the simulation is intended to investigate, what type of outcome it is expected to produce, and where the legitimate purpose boundary ends. Through governance of simulation need, purpose definition, question formation, intended outcomes, multiple-purpose compatibility, purpose conflict, purpose change, expansion, substitution, consequence context, and complete purpose traceability, SPDM ensures that simulation design begins from a defined inquiry and that simulation results cannot legitimately acquire a broader purpose merely because downstream users wish to apply them beyond the reason for which the simulation was originally created.

resources.title: OOF™ Simulation Parameterization Module (SPHM)
topics: Same Model + Different Parameters = Different Simulation Behavior

chunks.text:
OOF™ Simulation Parameterization Module (SPHM)
Simulation Parameterization Module (SPHM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES)
Operational Layer: Simulation Model & Environment Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Parameterization
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 17 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Parameterization
Canonical Definition
Simulation Parameterization Module (SPHM) defines the governance framework for identifying, defining, assigning, constraining, documenting, controlling, changing, and reconstructing the parameters through which a governed Simulation Model and Simulation Environment are configured for simulation execution.
SPHM establishes the controlled parameter layer between the structural design of the simulation and the specific configured conditions under which simulation behavior is produced.
Operational Role

SPHM is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
The preceding modules establish:
SMMM — What is the Simulation Model structurally composed of?
SECM — Within what configured Simulation Environment does that model operate?
SBIM — How do the model, environment, and connected domains interact across their boundaries?
SPHM asks:
Which configurable values govern the behavior of the model and environment, why were those values selected, what ranges and constraints apply, and which parameter configuration produced a particular simulation execution?
The governed progression is:
Model Structure → Environment Configuration → Boundary Interaction → Parameter Identification → Parameter Definition → Value Assignment → Constraint & Range Control → Parameter Configuration → Execution Binding → Governed Simulation Parameterization
Module Operational Space

SPHM governs: Simulation Parameter identification, parameter identity, parameter definition, parameter classification, parameter ownership, parameter source, parameter basis, parameter units, parameter types, parameter values, parameter ranges, parameter distributions, parameter constraints, parameter dependencies, parameter relationships, parameter inheritance, parameter overrides, default parameters, fixed parameters, variable parameters, dynamic parameters, stochastic parameters, derived parameters, calibrated parameters, externally supplied parameters, model parameters, environment parameters, boundary parameters, parameter sets, parameter configurations, parameter baselines, parameter sensitivity, parameter change, parameter substitution, parameter uncertainty references, parameter traceability, execution binding, and parameter reconstruction.
Module Operational Scope
SPHM applies wherever configurable values materially influence simulation behavior.

This may include: computational simulations, engineering simulations, robotics simulations, autonomous-system simulations, AI simulations, digital twins, scientific models, climate and environmental simulations, industrial simulations, infrastructure simulations, financial simulations, economic simulations, biological simulations, healthcare simulations, transportation simulations, aerospace simulations, mission simulations, multi-agent simulations, software-in-the-loop environments, hardware-in-the-loop environments, and hybrid physical-digital simulations.
Governance depth should remain proportional to the material influence of parameterization upon the simulation inquiry.
Module Function
A correctly structured model can produce materially different behavior depending upon how it is parameterized.
For example:
Same Model + Different Parameters = Different Simulation Behavior
A simulation may therefore fail methodologically even when its model structure is correct if: material parameters are undocumented, default values are silently inherited, parameter values lack an identifiable basis, permissible ranges are undefined, incompatible parameters are combined, units are inconsistent, values change during execution without visibility, parameter dependencies are ignored, or the parameter set used for a result cannot later be reconstructed.
SPHM prevents parameterization from becoming an invisible technical configuration layer.
Simulation Parameter

A Simulation Parameter is a governed configurable property whose assigned value, range, distribution, rule, or state may materially influence the behavior of a Simulation Model, Simulation Environment, Simulation Boundary, or simulation execution.
A parameter may represent: physical property, behavioral property, environmental condition, system capability, timing property, probability, threshold, tolerance, resource quantity, interaction property, control value, or another configurable simulation characteristic.
Parameter Identity
Each material parameter should be sufficiently identifiable.
Where relevant, Parameter Identity may establish: parameter name, parameter identifier, parameter type, governed component, unit, source, basis, permissible range, current value, and applicable configuration.
Parameter names alone may be insufficient where multiple components use similarly named variables.
Parameter Definition
A parameter should have a sufficiently precise definition to establish what the value actually represents.
For example:
Reaction Time = 0.8
is incomplete if the simulation record does not establish: whose reaction time, measured in which unit, under which conditions, applied to which model component, and whether the value is fixed, variable, or distributed.
Parameter Classification
Parameters may be classified according to their simulation role.
Possible classifications include:
Model Parameter
Environment Parameter
Boundary Parameter
Control Parameter

Initial-State Parameter
Behavioral Parameter
Physical Parameter
Timing Parameter
Resource Parameter
Stochastic Parameter
or another simulation-specific class.
Model Parameter
A Model Parameter configures a property of the Simulation Model without changing its underlying structural identity unless the change becomes structurally material.
Examples may include: mass, acceleration limit, control threshold, sensor range, decision threshold, response rate, or behavioral coefficient.
Environment Parameter
An Environment Parameter configures a governed property of the Simulation Environment.
Examples may include: temperature, traffic density, visibility, network latency, market liquidity, resource availability, or environmental response rate.
SECM establishes the environment and its configuration structure.
SPHM governs the controlled values through which configurable environmental properties are instantiated.
Boundary Parameter
A Boundary Parameter configures a property of a governed Simulation Boundary or interaction mechanism.
Examples may include: interface latency, transmission frequency, timeout, conversion tolerance, synchronization interval, or signal range.
SBIM governs the boundary interaction.
SPHM governs its configurable parameter values.
Parameter Type
A parameter may be:
Fixed
Variable
Dynamic
Stochastic
Derived
Calibrated
Externally Supplied
Scenario-Controlled
or:
Execution-Controlled
where the distinction materially affects simulation behavior.
Fixed Parameter

A Fixed Parameter is intended to remain unchanged during the applicable simulation execution or governed simulation configuration.
Its fixed status should not imply that its value requires no basis.
Variable Parameter
A Variable Parameter may take different governed values between simulation runs or configurations.
The permissible variation should remain bounded where material.
Dynamic Parameter
A Dynamic Parameter may change during simulation execution according to defined logic, state, events, or external conditions.
Its governing rule may be as important as its initial value.
Stochastic Parameter
A Stochastic Parameter is governed through a probability distribution or stochastic mechanism rather than one fixed value.
Relevant governance may include: distribution type, parameters of the distribution, permitted range, sampling rule, correlation, and seed relationship where material.
Derived Parameter
A Derived Parameter is calculated from other governed values.
Conceptually:
Parameter A + Parameter B + Derivation Rule → Derived Parameter C
The derivation should remain traceable where the resulting parameter materially affects simulation behavior.
Calibrated Parameter
A Calibrated Parameter receives its value through a calibration process.
SPHM governs the parameterization role and resulting value.
It does not replace broader validation governance over whether the calibration evidence is sufficient for an intended validation claim.
Externally Supplied Parameter

Some parameters originate outside the simulation.
Examples include: operational measurements, external datasets, sensor values, market values, environmental feeds, engineering specifications, or third-party model outputs.
Their external origin should remain identifiable.
Parameter Basis
Every material parameter should have an identifiable basis where practicable.
A Parameter Basis may derive from: measured reality, scientific literature, engineering specification, historical data, expert judgment, Simulation Assumption, calibration, scenario design, operational data, regulatory requirement, or explicit experimental selection.
Parameter Basis ≠ Parameter Validity
SPHM governs:
Why was this parameter value selected and how is it represented inside the simulation?
VALIDOS® may separately govern:
Is the evidentiary and methodological basis sufficient to validate reliance upon the resulting simulation evidence?
This separation protects the architectural boundary between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS®.
Assumption-to-Parameter Traceability
Simulation Assumptions may become parameter values.
Conceptually:
Simulation Assumption → Parameter Definition → Parameter Value
For example:
Assumption: Average Human Reaction Time = 1 second
may become:
Reaction_Time = 1.0 s
Where material, the relationship should remain traceable.
Reality-Representation-to-Parameter Traceability
Reality Representation requirements may also determine parameterization.
Conceptually:

Represented Reality Property → Simulation Variable → Parameter Definition → Parameter Value / Distribution
This establishes continuity between what the simulation claims to represent and how that representation is configured.
Parameter Value
A Parameter Value is the assigned value or state applied to a parameter within a defined Simulation Configuration.
A value should remain interpretable together with: parameter identity, unit, applicable range, source or basis, configuration, and execution context.
Parameter Units
Where parameters represent measurable quantities, units should be explicit.
Examples:
Velocity = 30 m/s
Latency = 120 ms
Temperature = 25 °C
Mass = 1,500 kg
Unit ambiguity can materially alter simulation behavior.
Unit Compatibility
Parameters participating in shared calculations or interactions should use compatible units or governed conversion.
Silent unit conversion should not create an invisible simulation transformation.
Parameter Range
A Parameter Range establishes the values within which a parameter may legitimately operate for a defined simulation configuration.
Conceptually:
Minimum ≤ Parameter ≤ Maximum
Ranges may be: physical, methodological, empirical, scenario-defined, operational, safety-related, or technically imposed.
Parameter Range Violation
A parameter value outside its governed range should not silently enter simulation execution.
Possible treatments may include:
Reject
Flag
Constrain
Require Authorization
Create Exception

or another governed response.
Parameter Constraint
A Parameter Constraint defines a condition restricting permissible parameter values or combinations.
Constraints may include: minimum, maximum, allowed states, prohibited combinations, conditional ranges, dependency conditions, or cross-parameter relationships.
Cross-Parameter Constraint
Some values may be legitimate individually but illegitimate together.
For example:
Payload Mass = Valid
and:
Fuel Level = Valid
may nevertheless create an impossible combined configuration.
SPHM therefore governs parameter relationships as well as individual values.
Parameter Dependency
A Parameter Dependency exists where the value, range, interpretation, or effect of one parameter depends materially upon another parameter or governed simulation condition.
Conceptually:
Parameter A → constrains / determines / modifies → Parameter B Parameter Dependency Map
Where dependencies are material, SPHM should support:
Parameter → Dependency → Dependent Parameter → Effect
This becomes particularly important in complex models containing hundreds or thousands of configurable variables.
Parameter Distribution
Some simulation properties are more appropriately represented by distributions than single values.
Examples include: human reaction times, equipment failure rates, weather variation, demand behavior, network latency, biological variability, or market behavior.
The distribution itself becomes a governed parameterization object.
Distribution Governance

Where material, governance may establish: distribution type, central tendency, dispersion, bounds, truncation, correlation, sampling method, and applicable population or condition.
Parameter Correlation
Parameters may be statistically or structurally related.
Treating correlated parameters as independent may create unrealistic simulation states.
Material correlation assumptions should therefore remain visible.
Default Parameter
A Default Parameter is a parameter value automatically applied when no alternative value is explicitly selected.
Defaults are not methodologically neutral.
A default can materially shape simulation behavior.
No Invisible Default Principle
A material parameter must not escape governance merely because its value was supplied automatically by software, inherited from a template, or left unchanged from a previous configuration.
Parameter Inheritance
Parameters may be inherited from: parent configurations, templates, model defaults, environment defaults, prior simulation versions, or scenario configurations.
Material inheritance should remain traceable.
Parameter Override
A Parameter Override occurs when an inherited, default, or previously established value is replaced for a specific configuration or execution.
An override should identify: affected parameter, previous value, new value, reason, applicable scope, and execution relationship
where material.
Parameter Set
A Parameter Set is a governed collection of parameters intended to operate together.

Examples:
Baseline Parameter Set
Adverse Weather Parameter Set
High-Load Parameter Set
Failure Parameter Set
Experimental Parameter Set Parameter Configuration
A Parameter Configuration is the complete materially relevant combination of parameter values, distributions, constraints, dependencies, and overrides applicable to a defined simulation execution or group of executions.
Conceptually:
Simulation Parameter Configuration = Parameter Set + Values + Ranges + Constraints + Dependencies + Overrides Parameter Configuration Identifier
Material parameter configurations should be uniquely distinguishable where different configurations may produce different simulation behavior.
This enables:
Simulation Result → Simulation Execution → Parameter Configuration Parameter Baseline
A Parameter Baseline establishes the approved reference parameter configuration against which changes may be identified.
The baseline may support: repeatability, comparability, sensitivity analysis, scenario variation, configuration control, and change detection.
Baseline ≠ Universal Correctness
A baseline establishes a controlled reference.
It does not establish that the baseline perfectly represents reality.
Parameter Variation
Parameter Variation may be intentional.
Examples include: sensitivity testing, stress testing, scenario exploration, uncertainty exploration, optimization, robustness testing, or boundary testing.
SPHM governs the variation itself.

Scenario Design governance determines how parameter variation is organized into governed scenarios.
Parameter Variation Range
Where parameter variation is intentional, the tested range should remain identifiable.
For example:
Wind Speed: 0–150 km/h
rather than simply:
Wind varied.
Parameter Sweep
A Parameter Sweep systematically varies one or more parameters across defined values or ranges.
SPHM may govern: parameter identity, variation range, step, distribution, combinations, exclusions, and resulting configuration identifiers.
Parameter Sensitivity
Parameter Sensitivity describes the degree to which changes in a parameter materially alter simulation behavior or outputs.
SPHM governs the identification and configuration relevance of sensitivity.
It does not replace the downstream interpretation or validation of simulation outputs.
High-Sensitivity Parameter
A parameter may be classified as high-sensitivity where small changes can materially alter simulation behavior.
Such parameters may justify stronger: basis documentation, range control, change control, traceability, and execution binding.
Parameter Sensitivity ≠ Uncertainty Governance
Sensitivity asks:
How strongly does simulation behavior respond when this parameter changes?
Uncertainty asks:
How uncertain are we about the parameter or its basis?
Simulation Assumption governance and other relevant spaces may govern uncertainty.
SPHM preserves the parameterization relationship without duplicating those spaces.

Parameter Substitution
A parameter may be substituted when the originally intended value or source is unavailable.
For example:
Measured Wind Data → Synthetic Wind Distribution
The substitution should remain visible where material.
Parameter Change
A Parameter Change may involve: value change, range change, distribution change, unit change, constraint change, dependency change, source change, basis change, inheritance change, override, or parameter removal.
Parameter Change Record
Material changes should preserve:
Previous Parameter State → Change → New Parameter State → Applicable Configuration Parameter Drift
Parameter Drift occurs where parameter values or parameterization behavior progressively depart from the governed configuration without an equivalent governed decision.
Drift may arise through: automated adaptation, external feeds, configuration changes, software updates, calibration updates, environment changes, or inherited defaults.
Dynamic Parameter Change
A parameter changing during execution according to its governed rule is not necessarily drift.
The distinction is:
Governed Dynamic Change
versus:
Uncontrolled Parameter Change Parameter Lock
A parameter may be locked where its value must not change during a defined execution or comparison set.
Locking may be important for: repeatability, controlled experimentation, comparative simulation, benchmark execution, or forensic reconstruction.
Parameter Freeze

A Parameter Freeze may preserve a complete parameter configuration for a defined simulation execution campaign.
This creates a stable configuration reference.
Parameterization and Scenario Design
SPHM governs:
Which parameters exist and how their values may be configured.
Scenario Design governs:
Which combinations of conditions and parameter configurations are intentionally selected as scenarios for simulation.
Therefore:
Parameterization ≠ Scenario Design
This boundary prevents duplication between Parent Standards.
Parameterization and Input Data
A parameter should also remain distinguishable from Input Data.
A parameter configures the simulation.
Input Data supplies data consumed during simulation execution.
In some systems the distinction may be technically blurred.
The governance classification should follow operational function rather than software implementation.
Parameterization and Assumptions
Simulation Assumptions may justify or constrain parameter values.
However:
Assumption Governance ≠ Parameter Governance
SAS governs the assumption and its role.
SPHM governs how that assumption becomes an operational simulation configuration.
Parameterization and Environment Configuration
SECM establishes:
what environmental configuration exists.
SPHM establishes:
which configurable values instantiate or control material properties of that environment.
Parameterization and Boundary Interaction
SBIM establishes:

what may cross a Simulation Boundary and under which interaction conditions.
SPHM governs:
the configurable values controlling those interaction properties.
Parameter Configuration Completeness
Parameter Configuration Completeness asks:
Have all material parameters required to reconstruct the governed simulation execution been identified and preserved?
Completeness does not require documenting every technically available setting.
It requires visibility over settings capable of materially affecting the simulation inquiry.
Parameter Configuration Consistency
Parameter Configuration Consistency asks whether: units are compatible, values fall within applicable ranges, dependencies are satisfied, constraints are respected, inherited values remain applicable, and combined values form a coherent simulation configuration.
Parameter Configuration Coherence
A parameter configuration may contain individually valid values while producing an incoherent overall simulation state.
SPHM therefore evaluates configuration-level coherence rather than only individual parameter validity.
Parameter Comparability
Two simulation executions should not be treated as parameter-equivalent unless their materially relevant parameter configurations are sufficiently aligned.
Differences should remain visible where they affect interpretation.
Controlled Comparison
For controlled comparative simulation:

Compared Executions should differ only in the variables intentionally changed or otherwise explicitly disclosed.
This enables parameter-level causal interpretation without assuming broader methodological validation.
Parameter Change Propagation
A material parameter change may propagate through later SIMULOS® spaces.
Conceptually:
Parameter Change
↓
Scenario Configuration
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Output
↓
Reality Correlation
↓
Simulation Evidence
SPHM preserves the parameter change.
The downstream spaces govern their respective consequences.
Parameter-to-Execution Binding
Every material simulation execution should be bindable to the Parameter Configuration under which it occurred.
Conceptually:
Simulation Execution ID → Parameter Configuration ID
Without this relationship, repeatability and reconstruction may become impossible.
Parameter-to-Output Traceability
Where material, simulation outputs should remain traceable to the parameter configuration that contributed to their production.
Conceptually:
Parameter Configuration → Execution → Simulation Output
SPHM establishes the parameter side of that traceability chain.
Parameter Reconstruction
SPHM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer:
Which parameters were active?
Which values were assigned?
Which units applied?
Which ranges and constraints applied?
Which values were inherited or overridden?
Which parameters were dynamic or stochastic?
Which dependencies existed?

Which parameter configuration produced the execution?
Did any material parameter change during execution?
Parameterization Traceability
A complete parameterization traceability path may be represented as:
Simulation Purpose & Scope
↓
Reality Representation
↓
Simulation Assumptions
↓
Simulation Model & Environment
↓
Simulation Parameter
↓
Parameter Basis
↓
Parameter Value / Distribution
↓
Parameter Configuration
↓
Simulation Execution
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Identify Material Simulation Parameters
Determine which configurable properties may materially influence simulation behavior. 2. Define and Classify Parameters
Establish meaning, type, unit, role, and governed component. 3. Establish Parameter Basis
Identify the basis supporting material parameter values or distributions. 4. Establish Values, Ranges, and Distributions
Define applicable values and permissible variation. 5. Govern Constraints and Dependencies
Identify relationships that limit or modify parameter configuration. 6. Control Defaults, Inheritance, and Overrides
Prevent invisible parameterization through technical defaults or inherited configurations. 7. Establish Parameter Sets and Baselines
Create controlled parameter configurations for simulation activity. 8. Govern Material Parameter Change
Preserve changes, substitutions, drift, and dynamic behavior. 9. Bind Parameter Configuration to Execution

Ensure each material execution can identify its applicable parameter configuration. 10. Preserve Parameter Reconstruction
Maintain sufficient traceability to reconstruct the parameterization that produced simulation behavior.
Governance Outputs
SPHM may produce: Simulation Parameter Register, Simulation Parameter Identifier, Parameter Definition Record, Parameter Classification Record, Parameter Basis Record, Parameter Source Record, Parameter Unit Record, Parameter Value Record, Parameter Range Record, Parameter Distribution Record, Parameter Constraint Record, Cross-Parameter Constraint Record, Parameter Dependency Map, Parameter Correlation Record, Default Parameter Record, Parameter Inheritance Record, Parameter Override Record, Parameter Set, Parameter Configuration, Parameter Configuration Identifier, Parameter Baseline, Parameter Variation Record, Parameter Sweep Record, Parameter Sensitivity Record, High-Sensitivity Parameter Record, Parameter Substitution Record, Parameter Change Record, Parameter Drift Record, Parameter Lock Record, Parameter Freeze Record, Assumption-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Reality-Representation-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Parameter Configuration Completeness Assessment, Parameter Configuration Consistency Assessment, Parameter Configuration Coherence Assessment, Parameter-to-Execution Binding, Parameter Reconstruction Record, and Simulation Parameterization Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
Scenario

An autonomous vehicle simulation uses configurable values for:
Vehicle Mass + Sensor Range + Reaction Delay + Road Friction + Visibility + Traffic Density Application
SPHM identifies each material parameter, establishes units and ranges, preserves the source or assumption supporting each value, and binds the resulting Parameter Configuration to the simulation execution.
A change from:
Road Friction = 0.8
to:
Road Friction = 0.3
creates a materially different parameter configuration. Result
The resulting vehicle behavior can be traced to the exact parameter configuration under which it was produced. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation
Scenario
A spacecraft simulation includes:
Vehicle Mass + Fuel Load + Engine Performance + Communication Delay + Thermal Conditions + Orbital Parameters Application
SPHM governs the values, units, permissible ranges, dependencies, and parameter sets.
If spacecraft mass changes, dependent fuel and propulsion parameters can be identified rather than remaining silently inconsistent. Result
Mission simulation executions remain reconstructable and parameter-comparable. Use Case 3 — Financial Stress Simulation
Scenario
A financial simulation varies:
Interest Rate + Default Probability + Liquidity + Asset Correlation + Market Volatility Application
SPHM governs parameter ranges, distributions, correlations, parameter sweeps, and the specific configuration applied to each execution. Result

A stress result can be distinguished from a baseline result through its governed Parameter Configuration rather than only through its final output.
Architectural Position
Simulation Parameterization is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES).
The complete SMES progression is:
Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning
SPHM receives: the governed Simulation Model Structure from SMMM, the governed Simulation Environment Configuration from SECM, and the governed Simulation Boundary Interaction structure from SBIM.
It then establishes the controlled parameter configuration required to determine which specific configuration of the model and environment is actually prepared for simulation activity.
The resulting governed configuration becomes an input to Simulation Environment Versioning and later SIMULOS® lifecycle spaces.
Foundational Principle
A simulation cannot be meaningfully reconstructed, compared, or governed when the material parameters shaping its behavior are unknown, uncontrolled, or detached from the execution they produced.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Parameterization Module establishes the parameter governance layer of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by transforming configurable model, environment, and boundary properties into explicit, bounded, traceable, and reconstructable Simulation Parameter Configurations. Through parameter identification, definition, classification, basis, units, values, ranges, distributions, constraints, dependencies, defaults, inheritance, overrides, sensitivity, controlled variation, change governance, configuration baselines, and execution binding, SPHM ensures that materially different simulation behavior cannot be produced by invisible parameter choices while being represented as if it arose from the same governed simulation configuration.
