OOF™ Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance
Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS)
Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation-Reality Comparison
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 19 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation-Reality Comparison
Canonical Definition
Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance conditions under which simulated conditions, states, behaviors, events, relationships, trajectories, and outputs are systematically compared with corresponding observations from Operational Reality so that similarities, differences, missing correspondence, and unavailable comparison evidence remain explicitly identifiable and traceable.
SRCM establishes the first governed comparison layer between:
what occurred in simulation
and:
what occurred in reality.

It does not assume that similarity establishes equivalence, nor does it determine whether the observed level of correlation is sufficient for a particular reliance or validation purpose.
Operational Role
SRCM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
The module asks:
What exactly can be compared between the simulation and Operational Reality, and what does that comparison actually show?
The governed progression begins:
Simulation Evidence + Operational Reality Evidence → Comparison Basis → Correspondence Mapping → Difference Identification → Comparison Record
The resulting comparison basis becomes an input to:
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module.
Module Operational Space

SRCM governs: simulation-reality comparison objects, comparison purpose, comparison scope, simulation-side evidence, reality-side evidence, comparable variables, comparable states, comparable behaviors, comparable events, comparable trajectories, comparable conditions, comparable outputs, temporal alignment, spatial alignment, state alignment, unit alignment, resolution alignment, abstraction alignment, correspondence mapping, comparison windows, baseline comparison, event comparison, behavioral comparison, trajectory comparison, distributional comparison, sequence comparison, comparison gaps, unavailable reality evidence, unavailable simulation evidence, incomparable elements, observed similarity, observed difference, and complete comparison traceability.
Module Function
SRCM prevents organizations from moving directly from:
“the simulation looks realistic”
to:
“the simulation represents reality.”
Its function is to create an explicit comparison basis before correlation strength, deviations, alignment, or uncertainty are evaluated.
The module separates:
Simulation Evidence
from:
Operational Reality Evidence
and then establishes which elements can legitimately be compared.
Simulation-Reality Comparison Object
Every governed comparison should identify the exact phenomenon being compared.

A Comparison Object may include: system behavior, autonomous decision, physical trajectory, sensor response, thermal behavior, structural response, failure sequence, communication behavior, resource consumption, human-system interaction, environmental response, recovery behavior, or another materially relevant phenomenon.
Comparison Pair
SRCM establishes a basic relationship:
Simulation Observation
↕
Corresponding Reality Observation
A comparison is meaningful only where the relationship between the two sides is sufficiently defined.
Comparison Identity
A materially relevant comparison should be distinguishable through a stable Comparison ID or equivalent mechanism.
Conceptually:
Comparison ID
↓
Simulation Execution
↓
Simulation Observation / Output
↓
Reality Observation
↓
Comparison Object
↓
Comparison Conditions
↓
Comparison Result
This preserves the provenance of the comparison.
Comparison Purpose
Before comparison, the organization should establish why the comparison is being performed.
Examples include: behavioral correspondence, model calibration support, mission reconstruction, failure investigation, autonomous-system assessment, performance comparison, environmental correspondence, or post-deployment simulation review.
Different purposes may require different comparison depth.
Comparison Scope
SRCM requires the comparison boundary to remain explicit.
The comparison may concern:
Entire System
Subsystem
Specific Behavior
Specific Scenario
Specific Operating Region

Specific Failure Mode
Specific Time Window
or another bounded domain.
No Whole-Simulation Inference from Partial Comparison
SIMULOS® establishes:
Correlation observed within one bounded comparison region must not automatically be represented as correlation across the entire simulation.
A simulation may correspond strongly to reality in one region and poorly in another.
Simulation-Side Basis
The simulation side of the comparison should remain connected to the governed execution that produced it.
Where material, this may include: Simulation Execution ID, model version, environment version, scenario, inputs, parameters, assumptions, runtime conditions, observations, and Simulation Outputs.
Reality-Side Basis
The reality side should identify the Operational Reality evidence against which simulation is compared.
This may include: physical measurements, sensor records, operational telemetry, observed system behavior, incident records, mission data, environmental observations, human observations, field-test results, production-system records, or another sufficiently identifiable reality source.
ORA™ Relationship
ORA™ governs Operational Reality itself.
SRCM does not redefine Operational Reality.
SRCM consumes or references sufficiently governed reality observations and governs the comparison relationship between those observations and the simulation.
Therefore:
ORA™ → Operational Reality
SIMULOS® SRCM → Simulation ↔ Reality Comparison Comparison Correspondence Mapping

Before numerical or qualitative comparison occurs, SRCM should establish which simulation element corresponds to which reality element.
Conceptually:
Simulation Variable A ↔ Reality Variable A
Simulation Event B ↔ Reality Event B
Simulation State C ↔ Reality State C
Simulation Trajectory D ↔ Reality Trajectory D
This prevents comparison between superficially similar but materially different phenomena.
Semantic Correspondence
Two variables carrying similar names may not represent the same underlying phenomenon.
SRCM therefore distinguishes:
Label Similarity
from:
Semantic Correspondence.
Unit Alignment
Where quantitative comparison is performed, units must be sufficiently aligned.
For example:
meters ↔ meters
seconds ↔ seconds
degrees Celsius ↔ degrees Celsius
or converted through an explicit transformation.
Temporal Alignment
Simulation time and Operational Reality time may not correspond directly.
SRCM may require alignment of: timestamps, event sequence, elapsed time, phase, cycle, mission stage, or relative temporal position.
Temporal Distortion
A simulation may reproduce the correct event sequence but at materially different timing.
That difference should remain visible.
For example:
Simulation failure occurs after 120 seconds
while:
Operational failure occurs after 37 seconds.
The presence of the same failure does not establish temporal correspondence.
Spatial Alignment

Physical and spatial simulations may require alignment of: position, coordinate system, orientation, altitude, distance, geometry, or reference frame.
Resolution Alignment
Reality observations and simulation observations may exist at different resolutions.
For example:
Simulation sampling: 1 millisecond
Reality telemetry: 1 second
A direct point-by-point comparison may therefore be misleading.
SRCM requires resolution differences to remain explicit.
Abstraction Alignment
Simulation may represent reality at a higher abstraction level.
For example:
Operational Reality may contain:
hundreds of interacting physical components
while simulation represents them as:
one aggregated subsystem.
SRCM does not prohibit this abstraction.
It requires the comparison to recognize it.
Condition Alignment
Simulation and reality should not be treated as directly comparable merely because they concern the same system.
Relevant conditions may include: environment, load, temperature, velocity, system configuration, software version, hardware version, autonomy state, population, external actors, weather, communication state, or mission phase.
Comparable Condition Set
SRCM may establish a:
Comparable Condition Set
representing the conditions sufficiently aligned for comparison.
Condition Mismatch
Where material conditions differ, the comparison should preserve the mismatch.
A condition mismatch does not necessarily make comparison useless.
It limits what may legitimately be inferred from it.

Behavioral Comparison
SRCM may compare how a simulated system behaves relative to the real system.
Examples include: decision sequence, control response, navigation behavior, obstacle avoidance, recovery behavior, failure response, resource allocation, or human interaction.
Event Comparison
Events may be compared according to:
Occurrence
Non-Occurrence
Timing
Order
Frequency
Duration
Magnitude
and:
Context.
Trajectory Comparison
Trajectory comparison may apply to: spacecraft, aircraft, robots, vehicles, physical processes, economic states, system states, or other evolving phenomena.
A trajectory should not be reduced to final-state similarity where the path itself is materially relevant.
Sequence Comparison
Some simulations must reproduce not merely events but their ordering.
For example:
Sensor degradation → Navigation error → Recovery attempt → Safe-state transition
may differ materially from:
Navigation error → Sensor degradation → System shutdown.
Even if both end in a safe state, the underlying behavior is different.
Distributional Comparison
For stochastic systems, individual-run comparison may be insufficient.
SRCM may compare:
Simulation Distribution
with:
Observed Reality Distribution.
This can include: frequency, variance, tails, rare events, failure rates, response ranges, or other statistical characteristics.
Population Comparison

Where simulation represents populations, SRCM may govern comparison across: demographic groups, system fleets, agent populations, operating environments, geographic regions, or other relevant populations.
Baseline Comparison
A baseline may be established to determine whether later simulation versions move:
closer to
or:
further from
observed reality.
Observed Similarity
SRCM may record areas where simulation and reality correspond.
However:
Observed Similarity is an observation, not a declaration of reality equivalence.
Observed Difference
Differences should be preserved even where overall correspondence appears strong.
Differences may concern: magnitude, timing, sequence, frequency, direction, state, behavior, distribution, or occurrence.
No Selective Similarity Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A Simulation-Reality Comparison must not preserve only the dimensions in which simulation performs well while silently excluding materially relevant dimensions in which correspondence is weak.
Comparison Gap
A Comparison Gap exists where a materially relevant simulation phenomenon cannot currently be compared with Operational Reality.
Reasons may include: reality has not yet occurred, measurement is unavailable, telemetry is missing, the phenomenon cannot be safely tested, reality evidence is inaccessible, the simulation contains an abstract construct with no direct physical equivalent, or the comparison method is insufficient.
No Reality Evidence ≠ Simulation Confirmation

A foundational SRCM rule is:
The absence of contradictory reality evidence does not establish that the simulation corresponds to reality.
Where Operational Reality evidence does not exist, the comparison status should remain appropriately bounded.
Comparison Availability States
SRCM may classify comparison availability as:
Directly Comparable
Conditionally Comparable
Partially Comparable
Indirectly Comparable
Not Currently Comparable
or:
Comparability Undetermined.
Incomparable Elements
Some simulation elements may legitimately have no direct reality counterpart.
These should remain identifiable rather than being forced into artificial comparison.
Comparison Evidence Quality
SRCM does not own general validation of evidence quality.
However, it should preserve whether the comparison basis depends upon: incomplete measurements, sparse observations, uncertain telemetry, transformed data, indirect observations, or another material limitation.
These limitations propagate downstream.
Point-in-Time Comparison
SRCM may support reconstruction of questions such as:
Which simulation version was compared?
Which real system version was observed?
Which scenario was used?
Which operational conditions existed?
Which variables were compared?
Which variables were unavailable?
Which transformations were applied?
Which differences were observed?
Comparison Matrix
A practical SRCM implementation may establish a Simulation-Reality Comparison Matrix.
Example structure:

Phenomenon → Simulation Representation → Reality Observation → Alignment Conditions → Comparison Availability → Observed Relationship → Limitation
This creates a structured basis for downstream correlation assessment.
Space and Mission Simulation
For space missions, direct Operational Reality evidence may be expensive, sparse, delayed, or available only after deployment.
SRCM can compare: simulated trajectories with mission trajectories, predicted thermal states with flight telemetry, simulated communication loss with actual communication behavior, simulated navigation uncertainty with observed navigation error, simulated subsystem failures with mission anomalies, and simulated autonomous recovery with actual recovery behavior.
This allows every mission to become a potential source of evidence for improving the simulation-reality relationship.
Autonomous Systems
For autonomous systems, comparison may extend beyond final performance.
SRCM can compare: decisions, action sequences, recovery paths, timing, interaction patterns, environmental responses, failure behavior, and emergent system behavior.
This matters because two systems may achieve the same final outcome through materially different behavioral paths.
Digital Twins
A digital twin may appear visually or numerically close to its physical counterpart while diverging in specific operational regions.
SRCM provides a structured basis for comparing:
Digital Representation
against:
Physical Operational Reality

without presuming that the existence of the digital twin establishes correspondence.
Comparison at Scale
Organizations may possess millions of simulation runs but only limited Operational Reality observations.
SRCM allows reality evidence to be mapped against relevant subsets of the simulation population rather than treating the complete simulation corpus as equally correlated.
Reality Evidence Accumulation
Simulation-to-Reality Comparison may improve over time as Operational Reality produces additional evidence.
The comparison relationship is therefore potentially dynamic.
A previously:
Not Currently Comparable
simulation phenomenon may later become:
Directly Comparable
when operational evidence becomes available.
Historical Comparison Preservation
New Operational Reality evidence should not erase earlier comparison states.
Historical comparison records may reveal whether simulation correspondence is: improving, degrading, stable, condition-dependent, or previously misunderstood.
Comparison Does Not Equal Correlation Determination
SRCM establishes the comparison basis.
It does not determine:
how much similarity is sufficient.
That question moves to:
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module.
Comparison Does Not Equal Deviation Governance
SRCM identifies observed differences.
Detailed governance of material simulation-reality deviations belongs to:
SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module.
Comparison Does Not Equal Reality Alignment

SRCM identifies correspondence and difference.
Governance of how the simulation may be brought into better alignment with reality belongs to:
SRAM — Reality Alignment Module.
Comparison Does Not Resolve Correlation Uncertainty
Uncertainty surrounding the simulation-reality relationship belongs to:
SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module.
Internal SRCS Flow
SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison
↓
SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria
↓
SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation
↓
SRAM — Reality Alignment
↓
SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty
SRCM therefore creates the empirical comparison foundation upon which the remainder of SRCS operates.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Define the Comparison Object
Identify exactly which simulated and real phenomenon is being compared. 2. Establish Comparison Purpose
Define why the comparison is required. 3. Establish Comparison Scope
Identify included and excluded regions, conditions, variables, behaviors, and time periods. 4. Bind Simulation Evidence
Connect the comparison to the applicable Simulation Execution and outputs. 5. Bind Operational Reality Evidence
Identify the corresponding real-world observations. 6. Establish Correspondence Mapping
Map simulation variables, states, events, behaviors, and outputs to their reality counterparts. 7. Align Comparison Conditions
Assess temporal, spatial, unit, resolution, abstraction, state, and environmental alignment. 8. Perform the Comparison

Compare the materially relevant phenomena. 9. Preserve Similarities and Differences
Do not selectively retain favorable correspondence. 10. Identify Comparison Gaps
Record unavailable, incomplete, indirect, or incomparable elements. 11. Establish Comparison Availability Status
Classify the degree to which meaningful comparison is currently possible. 12. Produce the Simulation-Reality Comparison Record
Create the governed comparison basis for downstream correlation criteria and deviation governance.
Governance Outputs
SRCM may produce: Simulation-Reality Comparison ID, Comparison Object Record, Comparison Purpose Record, Comparison Scope Record, Simulation Evidence Binding, Operational Reality Evidence Binding, Correspondence Map, Comparable Variable Set, Comparable State Set, Comparable Event Set, Comparable Behavior Set, Comparable Condition Set, Temporal Alignment Record, Spatial Alignment Record, Unit Alignment Record, Resolution Alignment Record, Abstraction Alignment Record, Condition Mismatch Record, Behavioral Comparison Record, Event Comparison Record, Trajectory Comparison Record, Sequence Comparison Record, Distributional Comparison Record, Population Comparison Record, Observed Similarity Record, Observed Difference Record, Comparison Gap Record, Incomparable Element Record, Comparison Availability Status, Simulation-Reality Comparison Matrix, and Governed Simulation-Reality Comparison Record.
Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation vs Flight Reality

A space agency executes extensive pre-mission simulations covering trajectory, thermal behavior, navigation, communication, subsystem failure, and autonomous recovery.
After launch, SRCM maps actual mission telemetry against the corresponding simulation conditions.
The comparison reveals that trajectory and thermal behavior correspond closely within tested regions, while communication degradation begins materially earlier in Operational Reality than in simulation.
SRCM does not declare the simulation valid or invalid.
It establishes exactly:
where correspondence exists, where difference exists, under which conditions, and where reality evidence remains insufficient.
The resulting comparison record provides the basis for correlation criteria, deviation analysis, and future reality alignment. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot Simulation vs Deployment Behavior
An autonomous mobile robot performs reliably across millions of simulated warehouse scenarios.
After deployment, operational records show that its obstacle-avoidance behavior differs when reflective surfaces, human movement, and temporary sensor degradation occur simultaneously.
SRCM compares the relevant simulated behaviors with the corresponding Operational Reality observations across: decision sequence, sensor state, response timing, trajectory, recovery behavior, and environmental conditions.

The organization can then distinguish between simulation regions that correspond strongly to deployment reality and regions where the simulation-reality relationship remains weak or insufficiently observed.
Architectural Position
SRCM is the first module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS).
It transforms:
Simulation Evidence + Operational Reality Evidence
into:
Governed Simulation-Reality Comparison Record.
That record becomes the foundation for determining correlation criteria, identifying deviations, governing reality alignment, and expressing correlation uncertainty.
Foundational Principle
Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation-Reality Comparison Module establishes the governed empirical bridge between simulation and Operational Reality by identifying what can legitimately be compared, binding simulation evidence to corresponding reality observations, aligning materially relevant conditions, preserving both similarities and differences, exposing comparison gaps, and maintaining complete comparison traceability. SRCM prevents visual similarity, isolated matching outcomes, or the absence of contradictory evidence from being transformed into unsupported claims of reality correspondence. By establishing a structured Simulation-Reality Comparison Record before correlation is judged, deviation is interpreted, alignment is attempted, or uncertainty is bounded, SRCM provides the foundational comparison layer through which SIMULOS® can determine what simulation actually demonstrates about the reality it claims to represent.

OOF™ Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM)
Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS)
Module: SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module
Operational Layer: Resimulation Trigger Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Resimulation Trigger Governance
Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SRGM-012.3
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 20 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM) is the third Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.

SRGM governs the determination of when recognized Simulation Drift, material change, new evidence, changed simulation conditions, changed reality relationships, or other simulation-relevant lifecycle developments require a simulation to be executed again, updated before execution, partially repeated, comprehensively repeated, reconsidered, or escalated toward replacement or retirement assessment.
The Module transforms recognized lifecycle divergence into an explicit Resimulation Trigger State.
SRGM does not determine the detailed scope of the required resimulation. That responsibility belongs to SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module.
Its task is narrower and foundational:
to determine whether the existing governed simulation basis remains sufficient for continued simulation-specific use or whether a new simulation cycle must be initiated.
Architectural Position
SRGM is the third module within SLRS.
It follows:
SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module
and precedes:
SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module.
The sequence is:
Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope.
SLMM identifies materially relevant lifecycle changes.
SDRM determines whether those changes constitute Simulation Drift.
SRGM determines whether the resulting condition requires a new simulation cycle.
SRSM then determines what must actually be resimulated.
Internal Flow Position

Governed Simulation Drift Record Material Change Evidence Current Simulation Use Context → Trigger Candidate Identification → Trigger Relevance Assessment → Materiality Assessment → Existing Simulation Sufficiency Assessment → Continued-Use Consequence Assessment → Trigger Threshold Evaluation → Resimulation Trigger State → Governed Resimulation Trigger Record → SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module
Operational Space
SRGM governs the space between:
recognized simulation-relevant change or drift
and
the formal initiation of a new simulation cycle.
This operational space includes: trigger candidate identification; trigger source classification; drift-trigger relationships; material-change triggers; threshold-based triggers; event-based triggers; cumulative triggers; temporal triggers; evidence-based triggers; uncertainty-driven triggers; scenario emergence triggers; object-change triggers; model-change triggers; input-change triggers; correlation-change triggers; reliance-change triggers; trigger materiality; trigger urgency; trigger state; trigger escalation; trigger deferral conditions; trigger documentation.
Operational Scope
SRGM applies wherever previously governed simulations continue to be referenced, reused, compared, interpreted, relied upon, or incorporated into subsequent simulation, evidential, validation, engineering, scientific, mission, safety, or operational processes.

It may govern resimulation triggers for: individual simulation runs; repeated simulation programs; scenario portfolios; simulation campaigns; digital twins; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; mission simulations; safety simulations; infrastructure simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; continuously updated simulations; long-lived simulation programs; future simulation technologies.
The Module remains technology-neutral.
Its concern is not how expensive or computationally difficult resimulation may be.
Its concern is whether continued use of the existing simulation basis remains methodologically supportable without a new simulation cycle. Drift Recognition ≠ Automatic Resimulation
SRGM establishes the fundamental distinction:
Recognized Simulation Drift ≠ Automatic Resimulation
Not every recognized divergence requires another simulation.
A drift condition may be: immaterial to the current use; outside the applicable scope; confined to an unused configuration; limited to an irrelevant scenario family; already bounded by an existing limitation; insufficiently developed to justify immediate resimulation; appropriate for continued monitoring.
Conversely, relatively small drift may require immediate resimulation where it affects a highly sensitive or consequential simulation condition.
The trigger must therefore be determined from the relationship between the change and the continuing use of the simulation.

Trigger Candidate Principle
Any lifecycle development capable of materially affecting the legitimate continuing use of a simulation may become a Resimulation Trigger Candidate .
Trigger Candidates may originate from: Simulation Object change; configuration change; reality change; representation change; assumption change; model change; simulation environment change; input or data change; scenario change; execution anomaly; output anomaly; correlation change; evidence degradation; changed reliance context; temporal expiration; newly discovered uncertainty; newly discovered failure mode; new operational observations; cumulative minor changes; compound Simulation Drift.
A Trigger Candidate is not yet a Resimulation Trigger.
It must first be assessed.
Trigger Source Classification
SRGM requires the source of a potential trigger to remain explicit.
A trigger may be classified as:
Object Trigger A material change to the Simulation Object.
Reality Trigger A material change in the reality represented by the simulation.
Representation Trigger A material deficiency or change in how reality is represented.
Assumption Trigger A material assumption has changed, weakened, failed, or become uncertain.
Model Trigger The simulation model has materially changed or become insufficient for continued use.
Environment Trigger The simulation environment or relevant simulation dependencies have materially changed.
Input Trigger The input basis or relevant data distribution has materially changed.

Scenario Trigger A new materially relevant scenario, edge case, stress condition, or scenario class has emerged.
Execution Trigger Execution behavior reveals anomalies, instability, drift, or conditions requiring renewed simulation.
Output Trigger Outputs reveal unexpected or materially unresolved behavior.
Correlation Trigger Simulation-to-reality correlation materially changes or deteriorates.
Evidence Trigger Simulation-derived evidence loses qualification, weight, applicability, or relevance.
Temporal Trigger A defined review period or simulation applicability period has expired.
Multiple trigger sources may coexist.
Material Change Trigger
A material change may require resimulation where it alters one or more conditions upon which the existing simulation results materially depend.
Examples include: new hardware configuration; software revision; changed physical component; changed environmental range; altered operating conditions; changed mission profile; changed behavioral logic; changed sensor characteristics; changed parameter range; changed infrastructure dependency.
The relevant question is not:
Did the object change?
It is:
Does the change materially affect the simulation basis upon which continued use depends?
Scenario Emergence Trigger
A new real-world or anticipated scenario may create a Resimulation Trigger even where the Simulation Object itself has not changed.

Examples include: newly observed failure combinations; new environmental extremes; new interaction patterns; new adversarial conditions; newly relevant edge cases; expanded operational domains; new mission phases; new human-system interactions.
Where the new scenario lies outside previously governed scenario coverage and materially affects the intended use of the simulation evidence, resimulation may be required.
Correlation Trigger
A previously acceptable simulation may require resimulation where new reality observations materially alter the established simulation-to-reality relationship.
Examples include: systematic real-world deviation; unexpected operational behavior; repeated prediction mismatch; degraded physical correspondence; changed environmental relationship; new empirical measurements.
SRCS governs the correlation relationship.
SRGM determines whether a material change in that relationship activates a new simulation cycle.
Evidence Degradation Trigger
Simulation evidence may become weaker even where the original simulation remains technically reproducible.
SERBS or lifecycle monitoring may identify: degraded evidential weight; reduced applicability; expired temporal relevance; new contradictory evidence; changed reliance conditions; weakened correlation; invalidated assumptions.
SRGM may treat such developments as Trigger Candidates.
Reproducible Simulation ≠ Permanently Sufficient Evidence.
Cumulative Trigger Principle

A series of individually non-triggering changes may collectively require resimulation.
Therefore:
No Single Trigger ≠ No Resimulation Requirement
SRGM must permit cumulative trigger assessment.
For example:
Minor Object Revision Small Input Distribution Shift New Edge Cases Moderate Correlation Deterioration
may collectively cross a resimulation threshold even though none independently would do so.
Compound Trigger Principle
Trigger conditions may interact non-linearly.
A changed assumption may become material only after a model update.
A new scenario may become critical only after an operational-domain expansion.
A modest correlation decline may become significant after reliance expands.
SRGM therefore evaluates both:
individual Trigger Candidates
and
combined Trigger Conditions.
Trigger Threshold
Organizations may define explicit Resimulation Trigger Thresholds.
Thresholds may be: qualitative; quantitative; probabilistic; event-based; consequence-based; sensitivity-based; time-based; configuration-based; evidence-based; hybrid.
SIMULOS® does not prescribe one universal numerical threshold.
The threshold must instead remain: explicit; relevant to the simulation purpose; connected to materiality; sensitive to the consequence of continued use; reviewable; traceable to its governance basis.
Trigger Sensitivity
Different simulation contexts may legitimately require different trigger sensitivity.

A minor change may justify resimulation where: simulation evidence supports safety-critical decisions; the model is highly sensitive to the changed variable; the simulation governs narrow tolerance conditions; correlation is already uncertain; consequences of unsupported reliance are severe.
The same change may not justify immediate resimulation for: exploratory analysis; historical comparison; broad conceptual modeling; an unaffected scenario family.
Therefore:
Trigger Sensitivity Must Follow Simulation Relevance, Not Change Magnitude Alone.
Trigger Urgency
SRGM distinguishes whether resimulation is:
Non-Urgent Resimulation is required but continued bounded use remains temporarily acceptable.
Scheduled Resimulation must occur within a defined lifecycle or review window.
Priority Resimulation should occur before specified further reliance or decision activity.
Immediate Existing simulation reliance should not continue for the affected use until resimulation or another governed response occurs.
Urgency does not determine scope.
SRSM determines the required resimulation scope.
Resimulation Trigger States
SRGM may assign a governed Resimulation Trigger State. 1. No Trigger
Available change or drift does not require a new simulation cycle for the defined use. 2. Monitor
A Trigger Candidate exists, but current evidence does not justify resimulation.
The condition remains under lifecycle monitoring. 3. Conditional Trigger

Resimulation becomes required if a defined condition, threshold, event, use expansion, or additional change occurs. 4. Triggered
A governed basis exists for initiating resimulation. 5. Priority Trigger
Resimulation is required before specified further reliance, use, or lifecycle progression. 6. Immediate Trigger
The affected simulation basis should not continue to support the relevant use without immediate resimulation or another governed lifecycle response. 7. Indeterminate
Available information is insufficient to determine whether resimulation is required.
An Indeterminate state must not silently become No Trigger.
Trigger Deferral
A valid trigger may sometimes be deferred.
Deferral may occur where: required data are temporarily unavailable; a replacement model is being prepared; the affected simulation use has been suspended; the relevant operational condition will not occur before resimulation; another controlled mitigation temporarily bounds reliance.
Deferral must identify: reason; affected simulation; affected use; temporary limitations; expiration condition; review point.
Deferred Trigger ≠ Cancelled Trigger.
Trigger Closure
A Trigger Candidate or Trigger State must eventually reach a governed disposition.
Possible dispositions include: no resimulation required; continue monitoring; conditional trigger retained; resimulation initiated; trigger superseded; simulation replaced; simulation retired.

Unresolved Trigger Candidates must not disappear merely because time passes. Resimulation Trigger ≠ Resimulation Scope
SRGM determines whether a new simulation cycle is required.
It does not determine whether the response requires: one repeated run; one scenario; one parameter region; one subsystem; one configuration; a partial campaign; a complete campaign; model reconstruction; simulation replacement.
That determination belongs to:
SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module.
Therefore:
Trigger ≠ Scope. Resimulation Trigger ≠ Validation Trigger
A Simulation Resimulation Trigger concerns the need to re-enter the simulation lifecycle.
A Validation Trigger concerns broader validation governance.
A change may trigger: resimulation only; revalidation only; both; neither.
VALIDOS® remains responsible for broader validation lifecycle governance.
Negative Results as Trigger Inputs
Failed or anomalous simulations may themselves generate Trigger Candidates.
Examples include: unexpected instability; unexplained divergence; inconsistent repetitions; previously unseen failure; unexplained sensitivity; execution-specific anomalies; output patterns inconsistent with prior campaigns.
A failed execution does not automatically require resimulation.
But failure must remain available to trigger governance rather than being discarded as computational noise without assessment.
Traceability of Trigger Decisions
Every material trigger determination should remain traceable through:

Change Signal → Simulation Drift Record → Trigger Candidate → Affected Simulation Basis → Current Use Context → Materiality → Threshold → Trigger State → Urgency → Disposition → Resimulation Scope Assessment
This enables organizations to reconstruct not merely that resimulation occurred, but why it became necessary.
SRGM Boundary with SLMM
SLMM identifies lifecycle change.
SRGM does not independently replace lifecycle monitoring.
It receives relevant lifecycle information as trigger inputs.
Monitoring Signal ≠ Resimulation Trigger.
SRGM Boundary with SDRM
SDRM determines whether lifecycle change constitutes Simulation Drift.
SRGM determines whether that recognized drift requires a new simulation cycle.
Therefore:
Simulation Drift ≠ Automatic Resimulation.
SRGM Boundary with SRSM
SRGM determines whether resimulation is required.
SRSM determines what portion of the simulation lifecycle, scenario space, configuration space, or simulation campaign must be repeated or reconstructed.
Therefore:
Trigger Decision ≠ Scope Decision.
SRGM Boundary with SERBS
SERBS may identify degraded evidence, changed applicability, reduced evidential weight, or changed reliance boundaries.
SRGM may consume these conditions as Trigger Candidates.
It does not independently redefine simulation evidence qualification, weight, or reliance.
SRGM Boundary with SRCS
SRCS governs simulation-to-reality correlation.
SRGM may consume material correlation change as a trigger input.

It does not determine correlation itself.
SRGM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SRGM does not determine whether broader revalidation is required.
Its decision is simulation-specific:
Must a new simulation cycle be initiated?
VALIDOS® governs whether a Validation Object requires revalidation and what validation lifecycle response is necessary.
SRGM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.
Changes in Operational Reality may create Trigger Candidates where they affect the simulation basis.
SRGM does not determine or govern Operational Reality itself.
SRGM Boundary with INTEGROS®
INTEGROS® governs integrity properties.
An integrity issue may become a Trigger Candidate where it materially affects simulation relevance, but SRGM does not replace integrity governance.
SRGM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether trigger evidence, decisions, thresholds, records, and lifecycle actions are preserved and verifiable.
SRGM governs the simulation-specific trigger determination itself.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SRGM implementation should establish: 1. Trigger Candidate Intake
Receive recognized Simulation Drift, material changes, new evidence, anomalies, correlation changes, and other simulation-relevant lifecycle signals. 2. Affected Simulation Identification
Identify the simulation, campaign, configuration, scenario family, evidence basis, or other simulation asset potentially affected. 3. Current Use Context

Determine how the existing simulation is currently being used, interpreted, or relied upon. 4. Trigger Relevance Assessment
Determine whether the Trigger Candidate can materially affect that continuing use. 5. Materiality Assessment
Assess the significance of the change relative to the simulation basis and intended reliance. 6. Cumulative and Compound Assessment
Evaluate whether multiple changes collectively create a trigger condition. 7. Trigger Threshold Evaluation
Compare the condition against the applicable qualitative, quantitative, event-based, temporal, or hybrid trigger criteria. 8. Trigger State Assignment
Assign an explicit Resimulation Trigger State. 9. Urgency and Deferral Control
Determine urgency and document any controlled trigger deferral. 10. Trigger Record Creation
Create a traceable record linking the trigger determination to its originating lifecycle conditions and downstream scope assessment. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Mission Configuration Changes After Qualification Campaign
A spacecraft mission completes an extensive simulation campaign covering guidance, navigation, propulsion, thermal behavior, landing sequences, communication loss, contingency procedures, and mission-critical failure conditions.
The simulation evidence supports a defined mission configuration.

Months later, before launch, several changes occur: a flight-software update modifies guidance behavior; spacecraft mass distribution changes; a component is replaced; new environmental observations alter part of the landing-condition model; mission planners modify one phase of the descent profile.
None of these changes automatically proves that the previous simulation campaign is unusable.
Equally, the organization cannot safely assume that millions of previously successful simulation executions still represent the modified mission configuration.
SRGM receives the recognized drift conditions and determines whether they cross a governed Resimulation Trigger.
The Module asks:
Which changes materially affect the basis upon which the existing mission simulations continue to be relied upon?
A guidance-software modification affecting descent control may create a Priority Trigger.
A component change outside the simulated behavioral pathway may create No Trigger.
Updated environmental observations may create a Conditional Trigger pending assessment of whether the new conditions fall outside previous scenario coverage.
The result is not automatic repetition of the entire mission campaign.
It is a governed determination that establishes whether resimulation is required before deciding what must be resimulated.
This prevents two costly failures:
continuing to rely on stale mission simulations
and

repeating enormous simulation campaigns after changes that do not materially affect their basis. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: New Real-World Failure Pattern After Deployment
An autonomous vehicle or mobile robot has completed millions of simulated scenarios before deployment.
After limited real-world operation, a previously rare interaction pattern begins appearing:
a combination of unusual lighting, partial sensor obstruction, human movement, and environmental geometry causes behavior that was not adequately represented in the original scenario portfolio.
The individual real-world events are uncommon.
However, they reveal: a new scenario class; changed understanding of sensor behavior; possible representation limitations; weakened simulation-to-reality correlation in the affected conditions; reduced evidential applicability of the original simulation campaign.
SRGM does not automatically order a complete rerun of millions of simulations.
Instead, it evaluates whether the new evidence creates a Resimulation Trigger.
If the condition affects a safety-relevant operational domain and lies outside previously governed scenario coverage, SRGM may assign an Immediate Trigger or Priority Trigger for the affected simulation basis.
The decision then passes to SRSM, which may determine that only:
the affected sensor conditions + scenario family + environmental range + related autonomous behaviors
require targeted resimulation.
The governance advantage is substantial.

Without a trigger framework, an organization may either dismiss rare real-world failures because the system passed millions of simulations or repeatedly rerun huge campaigns without knowing which part actually requires renewed testing.
SRGM creates the decision layer between those extremes:
new real-world evidence does not automatically invalidate all previous simulation, but material evidence must be capable of forcing simulation back into the lifecycle when the existing basis is no longer sufficient.
Governance Outputs
SRGM may produce: Resimulation Trigger Candidate Record Trigger Source Classification Affected Simulation Basis Record Current Simulation Use Context Record Trigger Relevance Assessment Trigger Materiality Assessment Cumulative Trigger Assessment Compound Trigger Assessment Trigger Threshold Record Resimulation Trigger State Trigger Urgency Classification Trigger Deferral Record Trigger Disposition Record Governed Resimulation Trigger Record Resimulation Scope Assessment Input
These outputs provide the governed basis for:
SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module.
Enterprise Application
SRGM gives organizations a systematic method for deciding when simulation must be performed again.
This becomes increasingly important as simulation programs grow larger, more expensive, more continuous, and more deeply connected to operational decisions.
Without explicit trigger governance, organizations risk two opposite failures:

under-resimulation — continuing to rely upon simulation after material conditions have changed;
and
over-resimulation — repeatedly executing expensive simulation campaigns after changes that do not materially affect the relevant simulation basis.
SRGM enables organizations to establish trigger logic around: product revisions; software updates; hardware changes; environmental changes; newly discovered edge cases; changed data distributions; model updates; new operational observations; degraded simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence degradation; changed reliance contexts; accumulated lifecycle drift.
For very large simulation campaigns, this can materially reduce unnecessary computational effort while ensuring that genuinely consequential change forces the simulation lifecycle to reopen.
SRGM therefore transforms resimulation from an ad hoc organizational judgment into a traceable governance decision.
Foundational Principles
Simulation Drift does not automatically require resimulation.
Absence of one decisive change does not mean absence of a cumulative trigger.
A Resimulation Trigger must be connected to the continuing use of the simulation.
Trigger sensitivity should reflect simulation relevance and consequence, not change magnitude alone.
New scenarios can trigger resimulation even when the Simulation Object has not changed.
New reality evidence can trigger resimulation even when the simulation remains technically reproducible.

Deferred resimulation is not cancelled resimulation.
An indeterminate trigger must not silently become No Trigger.
Trigger determination and resimulation scope are separate governance decisions.
The purpose of trigger governance is neither to maximize nor minimize resimulation, but to ensure that resimulation occurs when the existing simulation basis can no longer legitimately support continued use.
Canonical Closing Statement

Resimulation Trigger Module establishes the lifecycle decision layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by transforming recognized Simulation Drift, material change, emerging scenarios, new evidence, correlation change, uncertainty, anomalies, temporal conditions, and cumulative or compound lifecycle developments into explicit and traceable Resimulation Trigger States. Through governance of Trigger Candidates, trigger sources, materiality, thresholds, sensitivity, cumulative and compound conditions, urgency, deferral, disposition, and traceability, SRGM prevents simulations from being repeated merely because change occurred while also preventing materially stale simulation bases from remaining in use because no single change appeared sufficient to force reconsideration. By separating lifecycle monitoring from drift recognition, drift recognition from trigger determination, trigger determination from resimulation scope, and resimulation from broader validation governance, SRGM creates the controlled decision point through which a governed simulation lifecycle may legitimately reopen. A simulation should be performed again not simply because reality changed, but because the change materially affects the basis upon which continued simulation use depends.

Simulation Repetition
Canonical Definition
Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) defines the governance framework through which Simulation Executions are deliberately repeated under controlled, traceable, and sufficiently comparable conditions so that repeated runs can reveal stochastic variation, consistency, instability, sensitivity, rare behavior, execution divergence, and other materially relevant differences without allowing repetition volume to be mistaken for independent evidence or methodological strength.
SRPM governs:

what must remain constant, what may deliberately vary, why repetition is required, how repeated executions are related, and under which conditions their results may legitimately be compared or aggregated.
Its purpose is to transform repeated simulation from:
“run it again”
into:
a governed repetition process.
Operational Role
SRPM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES).
The preceding modules establish:
SIM — What exact simulation instance was instantiated?
SECM — How was active execution controlled?
SOM — What materially relevant behavior and events were observed during execution?
SRPM asks:
When the simulation is repeated, which execution conditions must remain fixed, which may change, and how can the resulting runs remain meaningfully distinguishable and comparable?
The governed progression is:
Completed / Repeatable Simulation Execution
↓
Repetition Requirement
↓
Reference Execution
↓
Controlled Constant Conditions
↓
Permitted Variation
↓
Repetition Identity
↓
Repeated Simulation Executions
↓
Repetition Comparability
↓
Repetition Variance & Divergence
↓
Repetition Sufficiency

Governed Simulation Repetition Set
↓
Execution Documentation
Module Operational Space

SRPM governs: repetition requirements, repetition purpose, repetition identity, reference executions, repetition sets, repeat-run configuration, controlled constants, permitted variation, intentional variation, accidental variation, repeated execution binding, repeatability, reproducibility conditions, stochastic repetition, deterministic repetition, randomization, random seed governance, seed variation, initialization variation, execution-order variation, repetition sequencing, repetition independence, repetition dependence, repeated-run comparability, repeated-run equivalence, repetition divergence, repetition variance, rare-event emergence, convergence signals, repetition saturation, repetition sufficiency, repetition gaps, repetition failure, repetition drift, repetition versioning, repetition lineage, and repetition traceability.
Module Function

SRPM exists to prevent: repeated runs being treated as independent when they are not, identical runs being counted as broad simulation evidence, hidden parameter changes across repetitions, changed model or environment versions being treated as repetition of the same simulation, random seed changes disappearing, uncontrolled execution drift being mistaken for stochastic behavior, deterministic divergence being ignored, stochastic consistency being overstated, rare events being dismissed as anomalies without governance, successful repetitions being retained while failed repetitions disappear, arbitrary repetition counts being represented as methodological sufficiency, and large Monte Carlo campaigns being treated as meaningful merely because the run count is large.
Simulation Repetition
A Simulation Repetition is a subsequent governed Simulation Execution intentionally related to one or more prior executions for the purpose of examining behavior under materially equivalent or deliberately modified execution conditions.
Conceptually:
Reference Execution → Governed Repetition Conditions → Repeated Execution Repetition Requirement
A Repetition Requirement establishes why simulation repetition is necessary.

Possible purposes include: examining stochastic variability, assessing consistency, determining execution stability, exploring uncertainty, evaluating sensitivity, identifying rare behavior, comparing alternative seeds, confirming unexpected observations, examining nondeterminism, evaluating distributional behavior, or supporting a broader simulation campaign.
No Repetition-for-Volume Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation should not be repeated merely to inflate execution count where additional repetitions do not materially improve the governed simulation inquiry.
Reference Execution
A Reference Execution provides a defined execution basis against which subsequent repetitions may be compared.
It should remain traceable to: Execution ID, Simulation Object, model version, environment version, scenario, Input Set, parameter configuration, randomization state, execution controls, and relevant runtime conditions.
Reference Execution ≠ Correct Execution
A Reference Execution establishes comparison context.
It does not establish that the reference behavior was valid, expected, correct, or desirable.
Controlled Constants
A repetition process should identify which materially relevant execution conditions are intended to remain constant.

These may include: Simulation Object version, model version, environment version, Scenario ID, Input Set, parameter configuration, hardware state, software state, execution-control rules, initialization conditions, external dependencies, or other materially relevant conditions.
Controlled Constant Principle
A condition cannot support repetition comparability if the repetition process does not know whether that condition remained unchanged.
Permitted Variation
Some repetition dimensions may deliberately change.
Possible examples include: random seed, stochastic sampling, initial state, timing, actor behavior, uncertain parameter values, external-event ordering, or another explicitly governed variable.
Permitted variation should remain distinguishable from uncontrolled deviation.
Intentional vs Accidental Variation
SRPM establishes:
Intentional Variation → deliberately introduced to examine a defined simulation question.
Accidental Variation → arises without governed design or adequate control.
These two conditions must not be conflated.
Repetition Identity
Every repeated execution should retain its own execution identity while remaining connected to its repetition family.
Conceptually:
Repetition Set RS-001
may include:
Execution E-001
Execution E-002
Execution E-003
and:
Execution E-004
Each run remains independently traceable.
Repetition Set

A Simulation Repetition Set is a governed collection of related Simulation Executions performed under explicitly defined repetition conditions.
The set may identify: Reference Execution, repetition purpose, controlled constants, permitted variation, number of executions, randomization basis, comparability conditions, and resulting execution statuses.
Repetition Set ≠ Scenario Set
A Scenario Set defines which conditions should be simulated.
A Repetition Set defines how one or more scenario executions are repeated.
Therefore:
Scenario diversity ≠ Repetition
and:
Repetition volume ≠ Scenario Coverage.
Deterministic Repetition
A deterministic simulation is expected to produce materially equivalent behavior when materially equivalent execution conditions are reproduced.
Where materially different behavior emerges, SRPM may identify:
Unexpected Execution Divergence.
No Determinism Assumption
A simulation should not be classified as deterministic merely because its design intends determinism.
Actual execution behavior must remain governable.
Stochastic Repetition
A stochastic simulation intentionally permits variability.
SRPM governs: randomization mechanism, random seed, distribution sampling, number of repetitions, relation between repetitions, and whether observed variation is consistent with the intended stochastic structure.
Random Seed
A random seed may determine a stochastic execution path.
Where material, SRPM preserves:
Seed Identity → Execution ID

This supports reconstruction and comparison.
Seed Reuse
Seed reuse may be deliberate.
For example, the same stochastic path may be replayed while one parameter changes.
This can strengthen controlled comparison.
The reuse should remain explicit.
Seed Variation
Different seeds may be used to explore distributional behavior.
The simulation record should preserve which execution used which seed where technically applicable. Seed ≠ Reproducibility
SIMULOS® establishes:
Preserving the random seed does not establish reproducibility when other materially relevant execution conditions differ.
Initialization Variation
Repeated simulations may vary initial states.
Examples include: actor placement, resource state, environmental state, memory state, system state, mission phase, or another initialization condition.
Where initialization varies intentionally, it should remain part of the repetition design.
Execution-Order Effects
Some simulation systems may behave differently depending upon execution order because of: shared state, cache behavior, external dependencies, persistent environment state, adaptive models, memory, or resource contention.
SRPM should identify materially relevant execution-order effects.
No Independent-Run Assumption
SIMULOS® establishes:
Separate execution IDs do not prove statistical or operational independence.

Runs may remain dependent through: shared initialization, shared randomization, shared data, shared adaptive state, shared infrastructure, previous-run state, or common external services.
Repetition Independence
Where independence matters, the repetition process should identify whether executions are:
Independent
Conditionally Independent
Dependent
or:
Independence Undetermined.
Shared-State Repetition
Repeated simulations may unintentionally inherit state from earlier runs.
Examples include: memory, cache, learned model state, environment state, persistent agent state, database state, or external service state.
This can make apparently repeated executions materially non-equivalent.
No Hidden State Carryover Principle
A repetition must not be represented as a fresh execution where material state from earlier executions persists invisibly. Repeatability
Repeatability concerns whether materially equivalent executions performed under sufficiently equivalent conditions produce behavior consistent with the simulation's expected execution characteristics.
Repeatability does not necessarily require identical outputs.
The required equivalence depends upon whether the simulation is deterministic, stochastic, adaptive, distributed, or human-in-the-loop.
Repeatability Conditions

Repeatability may depend upon: identical model version, identical environment, identical inputs, identical parameters, identical seed, equivalent hardware, equivalent software dependencies, equivalent timing, and absence of hidden state.
Repeatability Failure
A Repeatability Failure occurs where executions expected to be materially equivalent produce unexplained materially different behavior.
The result should not immediately be treated as simulation invalidity.
It creates a governed question requiring explanation. Reproducibility
Reproducibility concerns whether materially comparable simulation behavior can be recreated under another suitably controlled execution context.
This may involve: another machine, another environment, another organization, another implementation, or a later point in time.
Repeatability ≠ Reproducibility
A simulation may be repeatable on one platform while not reproducible elsewhere.
These remain distinct properties.
Repetition Comparability
Two repeated executions should be treated as comparable only where their materially relevant similarities and differences are known.
Comparability may be:
Fully Comparable
Conditionally Comparable
Partially Comparable
Not Comparable
or:
Comparability Undetermined.
No Same-Scenario Comparability Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Sharing the same Scenario ID does not establish that two Simulation Executions are sufficiently comparable.

Material differences may exist in: inputs, parameters, environment version, model version, timing, infrastructure, randomization, or runtime intervention.
Repetition Equivalence
A repeated execution may be considered materially equivalent to another where relevant differences do not materially affect the repetition purpose.
Equivalence should remain tied to the specific comparison question.
Repetition Variance
Repetition Variance describes materially relevant differences across repeated executions.
Variance may be expected.
For example, stochastic simulations may deliberately generate different outcomes.
SRPM asks:
Is the variance expected, explainable, bounded, and traceable to governed repetition conditions?
Execution Divergence
Execution Divergence occurs where repeated executions move into materially different behavior.
Divergence may arise from: stochasticity, chaotic system behavior, timing, hidden state, model instability, adaptive behavior, environment differences, or uncontrolled execution drift.
Expected vs Unexpected Divergence
SRPM distinguishes:
Expected Divergence
from:
Unexpected Divergence.
Expected divergence follows from the simulation design.
Unexpected divergence requires investigation because materially equivalent execution conditions were expected to behave differently only within known bounds.
Divergence Trigger

A material divergence may create: additional observation requirements, new repetition requirements, new scenario requirements, edge-case discovery, stress-condition requirements, or execution-control review.
Rare-Event Emergence
Repeated simulation may reveal low-frequency behavior absent from earlier runs.
A rare event should not automatically be discarded as:
simulation noise.
SRPM preserves:
Rare Observed Behavior → Execution Identity → Repetition Context
so the condition can be evaluated by downstream governance. Rare Event ≠ Error
SIMULOS® establishes:
Low-frequency behavior must not be classified as execution error solely because it occurred rarely.
Rare-Event Confirmation
A newly observed rare condition may justify additional repetition to determine whether it: recurs, depends upon specific conditions, represents stochastic variation, reflects hidden instability, or reveals a new scenario requirement.
Repetition Convergence
Some simulation campaigns seek evidence that repeated results have stabilized sufficiently for the Simulation Purpose.
A Convergence Signal may indicate that additional repetitions produce diminishing material changes in the relevant result distribution or observed behavior. Convergence ≠ Truth
SIMULOS® establishes:
Stable repeated output does not establish that the simulation correctly represents reality.
It establishes only a property of repeated simulation behavior.
Reality correlation and validation remain separate governance questions.

Repetition Saturation
A Repetition Set may reach Repetition Saturation where additional repeated runs provide little additional information for the defined repetition purpose.
This can prevent wasteful run-volume growth.
No Fixed Run-Count Principle
SIMULOS® does not establish that:
10 runs
1,000 runs
or:
1,000,000 runs
are universally sufficient.
Repetition sufficiency depends upon: purpose, stochasticity, uncertainty, variability, rarity, sensitivity, consequence, and the simulation question being examined.
Repetition Sufficiency
Repetition Sufficiency asks:
Have enough controlled repetitions been performed to support the repetition purpose without claiming more than the resulting execution set can demonstrate?
Possible statuses may include:
Sufficient
Conditionally Sufficient
Partially Sufficient
Insufficient
or:
Undetermined.
Repetition Gap
A Repetition Gap exists where additional governed repetition is materially required but has not been completed.
A gap may arise because of: insufficient run count, rare-event uncertainty, unexplained divergence, inadequate stochastic sampling, resource limitations, interrupted campaign, or missing repeatability analysis.
Repetition Failure
A repeated execution may itself fail.
Failed repetitions should remain visible.
A simulation campaign should not preserve:
successful runs only
while removing failures from the repetition basis.
No Survivor-Only Repetition Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:

Repetition governance must preserve materially relevant failed, interrupted, anomalous, and divergent executions rather than allowing only successful repetitions to define the observed simulation behavior.
Repetition Drift
Repetition Drift occurs where repeated executions gradually cease to share the material conditions required for the intended comparison.
Possible causes include: model updates, environment updates, configuration changes, dependency updates, hardware changes, data refresh, adaptive state, or altered execution controls.
Repetition Drift vs Intended Evolution
Not every change is drift.
A repetition campaign may deliberately evolve.
The distinction is:
Governed Change
versus:
Uncontrolled Change affecting repetition comparability.
Version-Bounded Repetition
Repetition Sets should remain bounded to relevant: model versions, environment versions, scenario versions, input versions, and execution-control versions
where changes materially affect comparability.
Cross-Version Repetition
Cross-version comparison may be legitimate where the purpose is explicitly to evaluate change.
For example:
Model Version 1 vs Model Version 2
However, this is not repetition under equivalent conditions.
It is a governed comparative repetition structure.
Baseline Replay
A prior execution may be replayed as a baseline against a changed system version.
This can help isolate the effect of a change where other materially relevant conditions remain controlled.
Repetition Lineage

SRPM preserves lineage such as:
Reference Execution
↓
Repeat 1
↓
Repeat 2
↓
Rare Behavior Detected
↓
Focused Repeat Set
↓
Controlled Reproduction
↓
New Scenario Requirement
This allows repeated simulation to become a source of structured discovery.
Adaptive Repetition
An execution campaign may adapt repetition based on observed results.
For example:
Initial 100 Runs
↓
Rare Divergence Detected
↓
Additional 1,000 Targeted Runs
↓
Behavior Region Identified
The adaptive decision should remain traceable.
No Hidden Adaptive Sampling Principle
Where observed simulation results materially determine which additional repetitions occur, the selection logic should remain visible.
Otherwise the final repetition population may appear unbiased when it was adaptively selected.
Monte Carlo Repetition
Monte Carlo simulation is a major application of SRPM.
SRPM may govern: run identity, seed generation, sampling distributions, sample dependence, repeated configuration, randomization logic, execution failures, coverage of relevant probability regions, and relation between run volume and actual repetition purpose.
Monte Carlo Volume ≠ Evidence Sufficiency
SIMULOS® establishes:
Millions of Monte Carlo runs do not establish methodological sufficiency if the sampling model, scenario basis, execution conditions, or materially relevant low-probability regions remain poorly governed.
Stochastic Tail Repetition
High-consequence behavior may occur in distribution tails.

Random sampling may generate too few such executions for meaningful examination.
SRPM may therefore identify a need for: targeted tail repetition, stratified repetition, controlled seed selection, scenario injection, or another deliberate method.
Scenario design remains governed under SSS.
SRPM governs the repetition structure.
Repeated Edge Cases
An Edge Case identified under SSS may require repetition to determine whether observed behavior is: deterministic, stochastic, unstable, timing-dependent, or conditional upon another execution variable.
Repeated Stress Conditions
Stress scenarios may require repeated execution because system behavior near a failure or degradation boundary may vary.
SRPM can support examination of whether:
Failure always occurs
Failure sometimes occurs
or:
Failure depends upon specific stochastic conditions.
Autonomous-System Repetition
Autonomous systems may produce different behaviors under apparently similar conditions because of: nondeterministic decision processes, adaptive state, memory, multi-agent interaction, environment timing, or stochastic components.
SRPM preserves the distinction between:
same scenario
and:
same execution path.
AI Agent Repetition
An AI agent may be executed repeatedly on the same task while producing materially different: plans, tool calls, escalation behavior, recovery behavior, or final actions.

SRPM can govern: prompt or task identity, model version, tool state, permissions, memory state, environment state, temperature or sampling configuration, and repetition results.
This helps reveal behavioral dispersion that a single successful run cannot expose.
Space and Mission Simulation
Space simulation programs frequently rely upon large repeated campaigns to examine uncertainty in: trajectory, navigation, component behavior, environment, communication, timing, power, sensor error, and mission recovery.
SRPM asks:
Are these repetitions actually controlled enough to interpret their differences?
For example, if a spacecraft recovery simulation fails in:
7 of 100,000 runs
the relevant questions include:
Which seven?
Which seeds?
Which input combinations?
Did those runs share a dependency state?
Can the behavior be reproduced?
Was the same environment version used?
Did any run contain an execution deviation?
The value lies not in the number:
100,000
but in the governed ability to understand what the repetitions collectively demonstrate.
Industrial Autonomous Systems
A manufacturing robot may pass:
999 of 1,000 repetitions
of one scenario.
The remaining execution may reveal a rare coordination failure.
SRPM prevents that execution from being discarded merely because:
99.9% succeeded.
Instead the rare behavior can be: reconstructed, repeated, isolated, and transferred to Scenario Design if a new material condition is discovered.
Repetition Campaign Diagnostic

SRPM can be used on an existing simulation program to ask:
Why are these runs repeated?
Which variables remain constant?
Which variables intentionally change?
Which variables changed unintentionally?
Are the runs independent?
Are seeds traceable?
Are failed runs preserved?
Are repeated executions actually comparable?
What variance is expected?
What divergence is unexplained?
Has repetition reached saturation?
Are millions of executions producing materially new information?
This can expose substantial inefficiency and weak execution governance without changing the simulation engine itself.
Relationship to SIM
SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module establishes the exact simulation instance.
SRPM depends upon that execution identity to determine whether a later run is sufficiently comparable to a prior one.
Relationship to SECM
SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module governs the active control conditions applied during each run.
SRPM determines whether those execution controls remained sufficiently equivalent across repetitions.
Relationship to SOM
SOM — Simulation Observation Module captures materially relevant behavior during each execution.
SRPM compares the resulting observations across a Repetition Set.
Relationship to SEDM
SEDM — Simulation Execution Documentation Module preserves the repetition records, lineage, differences, and resulting execution history.
SRPM establishes the repetition governance logic.

SEDM ensures that logic and its execution record remain reconstructable.
Relationship to SSS
SSS governs:
which scenarios and condition spaces should be examined.
SRPM governs:
how an execution of those scenarios is repeated.
Therefore:
Scenario Coverage ≠ Repetition Sufficiency.
Both may be required, but they govern different methodological questions.
Relationship to SIDS
SIDS governs the suitability of Simulation Inputs.
SRPM preserves which exact Input Set or input variations applied across repeated executions.
Relationship to SMES
SMES governs the Simulation Model & Environment.
SRPM relies upon model and environment version binding to determine whether repeated runs remain comparable.
Relationship to SOGS
SOGS governs the outputs produced by repeated executions.
SRPM establishes the repetition basis needed to determine whether outputs represent: one run, one Repetition Set, a distribution, a rare execution, an aggregated result, or another repetition-derived output structure.
Relationship to VALIDOS®
Repeated simulation may later become part of a Validation Evidence Basis.
VALIDOS® determines what that repetition evidence can legitimately support.
SRPM does not establish formal validation.
Relationship to ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether repetition records, run populations, seed usage, execution failures, and comparability claims are sufficiently supported.
SRPM governs repetition itself.
Governance Boundary

SRPM begins when one or more governed Simulation Executions require deliberate repetition for a defined simulation purpose.
SRPM ends when repeated executions have been sufficiently: identified, related, controlled, differentiated, compared, variance-assessed, divergence-assessed, sufficiency-assessed, and preserved as a governed Repetition Set
for downstream Execution Documentation and Output Governance.
SRPM does not determine: general Scenario Coverage, model validity, output interpretation, formal validation, or operational reliance.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish the Repetition Requirement
Define why repeated execution is required. 2. Identify the Reference Execution
Bind the repetition process to a sufficiently defined execution basis. 3. Define Controlled Constants
Identify the materially relevant conditions intended to remain unchanged. 4. Define Permitted Variation
Identify which conditions may intentionally change across repetitions. 5. Establish Repetition Identity
Assign distinct Execution IDs and a common Repetition Set relationship. 6. Govern Randomization
Where applicable, preserve: randomization method, seed, distribution, and relevant stochastic configuration.
7. Execute Controlled Repetitions
Perform repeated runs while preserving intended constants and permitted variation. 8. Detect Repetition Drift
Identify material unintended changes affecting comparability. 9. Assess Variance and Divergence

Distinguish expected stochastic variation from unexplained execution divergence. 10. Preserve Failed and Rare Executions
Ensure materially relevant anomalous, failed, interrupted, and low-frequency runs remain part of the repetition record. 11. Assess Repetition Sufficiency
Determine whether additional repetition would materially improve the defined simulation inquiry. 12. Establish the Governed Repetition Set
Preserve the complete repetition basis for Execution Documentation and downstream Output Governance.
Governance Outputs
