Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Autonomous Recovery Monte Carlo Campaign
Scenario
A spacecraft autonomous-recovery simulation executes 250,000 repeated runs under uncertainty in: navigation error, communication delay, power state, sensor noise, and recovery timing.
A small number of executions fail to recover correctly. Application

SRPM preserves: Repetition Set identity, individual Execution IDs, seeds, input and parameter combinations, environment version, controlled constants, permitted stochastic variation, and failed-run lineage.
The failed executions are compared with successful repetitions.
A common pattern is discovered:
high navigation uncertainty + delayed communication + low remaining power at recovery initiation. Result
The organization can move beyond:
249,982 successful / 18 unsuccessful runs
to determine:
which governed conditions are associated with the rare failure behavior and whether that behavior can be deliberately reproduced.
The 18 executions may then create new Scenario or Stress-Condition requirements rather than disappearing inside aggregate statistics. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot Repetition Divergence
Scenario
An industrial autonomous robot is simulated repeatedly under what is intended to be the same degraded-sensor scenario.
Most runs behave consistently.
A small subset produces different fallback behavior. Application
SRPM compares: model version, environment version, input basis, parameterization, randomization, memory state, and prior execution state.
The analysis discovers that persistent agent state was not reset between some repetitions. Result
The behavior is not incorrectly classified as inherent stochastic variation.
It is identified as:
Hidden State Carryover → Repetition Comparability Failure.

The simulation program can correct the repetition process and rerun the affected executions under controlled conditions.
Architectural Position
Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES).
The complete SES progression is:
Simulation Instantiation
↓
Simulation Execution Control
↓
Simulation Observation
↓
Simulation Repetition
↓
Simulation Execution Documentation
SIM establishes what exact simulation instance enters execution.
SECM governs how that instance is controlled while running.
SOM governs what materially relevant behavior occurs during execution.
SRPM governs how executions are deliberately repeated and meaningfully compared.
SEDM then preserves the complete execution and repetition history as a reconstructable governed record.
Foundational Principle
Repeated simulation creates methodological value only when the conditions that remained constant, the conditions that changed, the dependencies between runs, and the reasons for observed variance remain sufficiently governed to distinguish meaningful repetition from mere execution volume.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Repetition Module establishes the repetition governance layer of the Simulation Execution Standard by defining how governed Simulation Executions are repeated, related, randomized, compared, and assessed for repeatability, reproducibility conditions, variance, divergence, rare behavior, convergence, saturation, and sufficiency. Through controlled constants, permitted variation, run identity, seed governance, independence assessment, hidden-state detection, repetition drift control, preservation of failed and anomalous runs, adaptive repetition, and complete repetition lineage, SRPM prevents high execution counts from being mistaken for methodological strength and ensures that repeated simulations remain interpretable as a governed body of execution evidence rather than an undifferentiated collection of runs.

Canonical Definition
Resimulation Scope Module (SRSM) is the fourth Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SRSM governs the determination of what must be resimulated after a governed Resimulation Trigger has been established.
The Module determines the minimum sufficient and methodologically justified resimulation boundary across affected Simulation Objects, configurations, representations, assumptions, models, environments, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, and simulation-derived evidence.

SRSM prevents two opposite governance failures:
insufficient resimulation, where the renewed simulation scope fails to cover materially affected dependencies;
and
unnecessary resimulation, where unaffected simulation spaces are repeated without a methodological reason.
Its task is therefore:
to translate a Resimulation Trigger into an explicit, dependency-aware, traceable, and proportionate Resimulation Scope.
Architectural Position
SRSM is the fourth module within SLRS.
It follows:
SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module
and precedes:
SRTM — Simulation Retirement & Transition Module.
The sequence is:
Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Retirement & Transition.
SRGM establishes:
whether resimulation is required.
SRSM establishes:
what must be resimulated.
SRTM subsequently governs whether a simulation should continue through its lifecycle, transition toward a replacement, or be retired.
Internal Flow Position

Governed Resimulation Trigger Record → Affected Simulation Basis Identification → Dependency Propagation Analysis → Affected Object / Configuration Identification → Affected Scenario Space Identification → Affected Model / Environment Identification → Affected Input Basis Identification → Affected Execution Requirements → Affected Output / Correlation / Evidence Identification → Scope Sufficiency Assessment → Resimulation Scope Determination → Governed Resimulation Scope Record → Resimulation Lifecycle Re-Entry / SRTM Operational Space
SRSM governs the space between:
a confirmed need to resimulate
and
the definition of the simulation lifecycle elements that must be reopened, updated, repeated, reconstructed, or reassessed.
This operational space includes: resimulation scope identification; affected simulation component identification; dependency propagation; impact boundaries; scenario re-entry; configuration re-entry; model re-entry; input re-entry; assumption re-entry; representation re-entry; execution re-entry; output reassessment; correlation reassessment; evidence consequence identification; partial resimulation; targeted resimulation; campaign resimulation; comprehensive resimulation; scope expansion; scope reduction; unaffected-space preservation; scope sufficiency; scope documentation.
Operational Scope
SRSM applies whenever a Resimulation Trigger requires some portion of an existing simulation basis to be reconsidered or executed again.

It may govern: one simulation run; one parameter range; one scenario; one scenario family; one Simulation Object configuration; one subsystem; one model component; one environmental condition; one input distribution; one failure mode; one mission phase; one behavioral domain; one simulation campaign; multiple interconnected campaigns; the complete simulation lifecycle.
It applies across engineering, scientific, physical, digital, hybrid, mission, safety, infrastructure, economic, AI, autonomous-system, digital-twin, and future simulation environments.
SRSM remains technology-neutral. Trigger ≠ Scope
SRSM establishes the fundamental distinction:
Resimulation Trigger ≠ Resimulation Scope
A trigger establishes that the existing simulation basis requires renewed simulation activity.
It does not establish how much must be repeated.
A material change in one subsystem may require:
targeted resimulation
rather than:
complete campaign repetition.
Conversely, a seemingly localized change may propagate through dependencies and require much broader resimulation than its initial location suggests.
Therefore:
The size of the originating change does not determine the size of the required resimulation scope.
Minimum Sufficient Scope Principle
SRSM seeks the Minimum Sufficient Resimulation Scope.
This means:
the smallest resimulation boundary that fully captures all materially affected simulation dependencies necessary to restore the governed simulation basis for the intended use.

“Minimum” prevents unnecessary repetition.
“Sufficient” prevents under-scoping.
The objective is not computational minimization at any cost.
The objective is methodologically justified proportionality.
Affected Simulation Basis
Every Resimulation Trigger must be mapped to the simulation basis it potentially affects.
The affected basis may include: Simulation Object; object version; object configuration; simulation purpose; scope; exclusions; reality representation; abstraction; fidelity; assumptions; model structure; environment; parameters; inputs; data; temporal conditions; scenarios; scenario coverage; execution configuration; outputs; correlation relationships; evidence objects.
The scope cannot be determined reliably until these dependencies are visible.
Dependency Propagation Principle
A change may propagate beyond the simulation element where it originated.
For example:
Input Change → affects Model Behavior → affects Scenario Outcomes → affects Outputs → affects Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → affects Simulation Evidence.
Or:
Object Configuration Change → affects Reality Representation → affects Assumptions → affects Model Parameterization → affects Scenario Relevance → affects Execution → affects Outputs.
SRSM therefore requires dependency-aware scope determination. Local Change ≠ Local Scope
A localized technical change does not guarantee a localized resimulation requirement.

A single changed parameter may influence: multiple model components; multiple scenario families; downstream control behavior; interaction effects; failure thresholds; evidence already derived from previous executions.
Conversely, a large physical modification may have no material effect on a narrowly defined simulation question.
Scope must follow material simulation dependency, not superficial change size.
Resimulation Scope Levels
SRSM may classify scope into governed levels. 1. Execution-Level Resimulation
Repeat one or more executions without materially changing the upstream simulation basis.
Appropriate where the issue concerns: execution anomaly; stochastic repetition; failed run; incomplete execution; runtime instability.
2. Scenario-Level Resimulation
Repeat or expand specific scenarios or scenario families.
Appropriate where: new edge cases emerge; scenario conditions change; coverage gaps are discovered; one scenario class becomes materially relevant.
3. Input-Level Resimulation
Renew simulation where input or data conditions materially change.
This may require: new datasets; updated distributions; changed temporal inputs; changed uncertainty ranges.
4. Configuration-Level Resimulation
Repeat simulations for affected Simulation Object, model, or environment configurations. 5. Model-Level Resimulation
Reopen the simulation model or environment basis before execution.

Appropriate where: model structure changes; model limitations are discovered; environment behavior changes; parameterization must be reconstructed.
6. Representation-Level Resimulation
Reopen the representation of reality itself.
Appropriate where previously simplified, excluded, or inaccurately represented reality becomes materially relevant. 7. Comprehensive Resimulation
Re-enter multiple or all materially relevant simulation lifecycle stages.
This may be necessary where change is systemic, dependencies are extensive, or the previous simulation basis can no longer support meaningful partial reuse.
These levels may overlap.
They are governance classifications, not rigid technical implementation categories.
Partial Resimulation
SRSM permits partial resimulation where the unaffected simulation basis remains legitimate.
A partial scope should establish: what remains unchanged; why it remains reusable; what must be updated; what must be repeated; what downstream results become affected; what previous evidence remains applicable; what evidence requires reassessment.
Partial resimulation must not become an assumption of convenience.
Its sufficiency must be demonstrable.
Targeted Resimulation
Targeted resimulation may focus computational and analytical resources upon the specific conditions affected by the Trigger.

Examples include: one failure mode; one sensor condition; one mission phase; one environmental range; one scenario family; one subsystem interaction; one parameter region.
Targeted resimulation can dramatically reduce unnecessary simulation effort while preserving methodological sufficiency.
Comprehensive Resimulation
Comprehensive resimulation may be required where: Simulation Object identity materially changes; reality representation becomes structurally insufficient; foundational assumptions fail; model architecture changes substantially; multiple scenario families become affected; dependencies cannot be reliably isolated; correlation deteriorates broadly; accumulated drift becomes systemic; previous evidence can no longer be cleanly separated from the affected basis.
Comprehensive resimulation should result from governed scope analysis rather than default organizational habit.
Scope Expansion Principle
An initially narrow Resimulation Scope may need to expand.
During renewed simulation activity, organizations may discover: additional affected dependencies; new failure modes; broader scenario impact; unexpected sensitivity; new model interactions; wider correlation deterioration; additional evidence consequences.
SRSM therefore allows:
Initial Scope → New Information → Scope Reassessment → Expanded Scope.
A scope determination must not become immutable when new material information emerges.
Scope Reduction Principle

A provisional scope may also be reduced where evidence establishes that suspected dependencies are not materially affected.
Reduction must be justified.
It should identify: the excluded simulation space; the evidence supporting exclusion; the dependency analysis; remaining uncertainty.
Scope Reduction ≠ Convenience-Based Exclusion.
Unchanged Basis Preservation
SRSM should preserve simulation components that remain legitimately reusable.
This may include: unaffected scenarios; unchanged input sets; unaffected model components; stable environmental configurations; previous execution records; unaffected outputs; still-applicable correlation evidence.
This prevents simulation governance from creating unnecessary computational waste.
However, reuse requires a governed basis.
Previously Simulated ≠ Automatically Reusable.
Scenario Scope
Where the Trigger affects scenario coverage, SRSM determines which scenario space must be reopened.
This may include: expected conditions; variations; edge cases; stress conditions; uncertainty conditions; interaction scenarios; newly observed scenarios; previously excluded scenarios.
SSS continues to govern scenario design.
SRSM determines which scenario governance must be re-entered because of the Trigger.
Model & Environment Scope
Where the Trigger affects the simulation model or environment, SRSM determines which model or environmental elements require renewed governance.

Possible consequences include: model component revision; parameterization revision; environment reconfiguration; boundary interaction reassessment; version change; dependency reconstruction.
SMES governs these elements when re-entered.
SRSM governs the requirement to reopen them.
Input & Data Scope
Where simulation inputs are affected, SRSM determines which input basis must be reconsidered.
Possible scope may include: one variable; one dataset; one distribution; one time period; one environmental source; one uncertainty range; the complete input basis.
SIDS governs the renewed input and data conditions.
SRSM defines the affected boundary.
Assumption Scope
A changed assumption may propagate through many simulation layers.
SRSM must determine: which assumption changed; which model components depend upon it; which scenarios rely upon it; which executions used it; which outputs were affected; which correlation conclusions depend upon it; which evidence objects inherit the dependency.
SAS governs the assumption itself.
SRSM governs the lifecycle scope affected by its change.
Output and Evidence Consequence Scope
Resimulation scope does not stop at new execution.
Where prior outputs or simulation-derived evidence depend upon the affected simulation basis, SRSM should identify them for downstream reconsideration.
This may require renewed governance through:
SOGS → SRCS → SERBS.

A new simulation execution may therefore invalidate, supersede, narrow, strengthen, or leave unchanged different portions of the previous evidence basis.
Scope Sufficiency Assessment
Before a Resimulation Scope is accepted, SRSM should determine whether the proposed scope is sufficient to address the Trigger.
The assessment may ask: Have all material dependencies been identified? Are affected scenarios included? Are changed assumptions covered? Are model consequences captured? Are affected inputs reconsidered? Are downstream outputs identified? Is correlation reassessment required? Is existing evidence affected? Are excluded simulation spaces demonstrably unaffected? Could residual uncertainty materially undermine the intended use?
The purpose is to prevent a technically completed resimulation from remaining methodologically incomplete.
Scope Uncertainty
Sometimes the required scope cannot initially be determined with confidence.
SRSM may therefore establish:
Provisional Resimulation Scope
where uncertainty remains.
The provisional scope may be expanded or reduced as evidence emerges.
Uncertainty about scope should be documented rather than hidden through arbitrary boundary selection.
Resimulation Re-Entry Principle
SRSM does not require every Resimulation Trigger to restart SIMULOS® from Standard 1.
Instead, it determines the earliest materially affected governance point.
Examples:
Execution anomaly → re-enter at SES.
New scenario → re-enter at SSS.

Input distribution shift → re-enter at SIDS.
Model revision → re-enter at SMES.
Assumption failure → re-enter at SAS.
Reality representation deficiency → re-enter at RRS.
Simulation Object material change → potentially re-enter at SOS.
This enables SIMULOS® to operate recursively without forcing unnecessary full-lifecycle repetition.
Lifecycle Propagation
Once the re-entry point is established, downstream governance should be reconsidered wherever materially affected.
For example:
SAS Re-Entry → SMES → SIDS where affected → SSS → SES → SOGS → SRCS → SERBS.
Not every downstream element must necessarily change.
But every materially dependent downstream element must be considered.
SRSM Boundary with SRGM
SRGM determines:
whether resimulation is required.
SRSM determines:
what must be resimulated.
Therefore:
Trigger ≠ Scope.
SRSM must not redefine the original Trigger merely to reduce or expand workload.
SRSM Boundary with SSS
SRSM may determine that a scenario space must be reopened.
SSS governs the actual identification, variation, edge-case design, stress conditions, and coverage of those scenarios.
SRSM Boundary with SMES
SRSM may determine that the model or environment must be reopened.
SMES governs model structure, environmental configuration, boundary interactions, parameterization, and environment versioning.
SRSM Boundary with SIDS
SRSM may identify affected input and data spaces.
SIDS governs those inputs once simulation governance re-enters that layer.

SRSM Boundary with SES
SRSM determines which executions must occur again.
SES governs how those simulations are instantiated, controlled, observed, repeated, and documented.
SRSM Boundary with SOGS
SRSM may determine which prior or newly produced outputs require renewed governance.
SOGS governs output identification, classification, inference, limitations, and documentation.
SRSM Boundary with SRCS
SRSM may determine that simulation-to-reality correlation must be reassessed because the simulation basis has materially changed.
SRCS governs the actual correlation process.
SRSM Boundary with SERBS
SRSM identifies simulation-derived evidence potentially affected by resimulation.
SERBS determines the qualification, weight, reliance boundary, limitations, and validation interface of that evidence.
SRSM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SRSM determines the simulation-specific scope of resimulation.
It does not determine the broader scope of revalidation.
A VALIDOS® revalidation process may require additional evidence or activities outside simulation.
SRSM Boundary with ORA™
Operational Reality may provide changes that influence scope determination.
ORA™ continues to govern Operational Reality itself.
SRSM governs only the resulting simulation lifecycle re-entry boundary.
SRSM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SRSM does not govern general integrity.
Integrity issues may create dependencies affecting resimulation scope, but integrity governance remains under INTEGROS®.
SRSM Boundary with ADIT®

ADIT® may audit whether the basis, exclusions, dependency analysis, scope determination, and resulting resimulation records are preserved and verifiable.
SRSM governs the scope determination itself.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SRSM implementation should establish: 1. Trigger Intake
Receive the governed Resimulation Trigger and its supporting basis. 2. Affected Basis Identification
Identify the simulation lifecycle elements directly affected by the Trigger. 3. Dependency Mapping
Determine material upstream, downstream, and cross-component dependencies. 4. Re-Entry Point Determination
Identify the earliest materially affected SIMULOS® governance layer. 5. Scope Classification
Determine whether execution-level, scenario-level, input-level, configuration-level, model-level, representation-level, or comprehensive resimulation is required. 6. Unaffected Basis Assessment
Identify previous simulation elements that remain legitimately reusable. 7. Downstream Consequence Assessment
Identify outputs, correlation relationships, evidence objects, and reliance boundaries requiring reconsideration. 8. Scope Sufficiency Assessment
Determine whether the proposed boundary captures all material consequences of the Trigger. 9. Scope Adjustment Control
Permit governed expansion or reduction where new information materially changes the required boundary. 10. Resimulation Scope Record

Document the final or provisional Resimulation Scope, exclusions, dependencies, re-entry point, and downstream consequences. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Flight Software Change Before Launch
A spacecraft has completed a very large pre-launch simulation campaign covering: ascent; navigation; orbital operations; descent; landing; communication failures; propulsion anomalies; contingency scenarios.
A late flight-software update modifies the guidance algorithm used during descent.
SRGM has already established a Priority Resimulation Trigger.
The organization now faces a major practical question:
Must the complete mission simulation campaign be repeated?
SRSM maps the change through the simulation dependency structure.
The updated guidance algorithm affects:
Descent Control → Navigation Interaction → Propulsion Commands → Landing Trajectory → Fuel Consumption → Landing-Site Dispersion → Failure and Contingency Scenarios → Mission Outputs → Relevant Simulation Evidence.
But the change may have no material relationship to unrelated orbital communication scenarios or other unaffected mission phases.
SRSM therefore establishes a targeted but dependency-complete Resimulation Scope.
The organization re-enters the simulation lifecycle at the affected model/configuration layer, reconstructs the relevant scenario space, repeats the affected execution campaign, regenerates governed outputs, and reassesses relevant simulation-to-reality correlation and evidence.

This avoids both extremes:
repeating the entire mission campaign unnecessarily
and
testing only the modified algorithm while missing its downstream mission interactions.
The governing principle is:
Resimulate the dependency chain affected by the change, not merely the component where the change originated. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot: Rare Failure Reveals a Missing Scenario Domain
A mobile autonomous robot has successfully completed millions of simulations before deployment.
Operational observation later reveals failures occurring when three conditions combine:
low-angle sunlight + partially contaminated sensor surface + unusual pedestrian movement.
SRGM determines that the new failure pattern creates a Resimulation Trigger.
SRSM must now determine the required scope.
Repeating the complete historical campaign may consume enormous computational resources while adding little information.
Repeating only the exact failed event may be too narrow because the failure could belong to a broader interaction domain.
SRSM therefore traces the affected dependencies:
New Reality Condition → Reality Representation → Sensor Model → Environmental Inputs → Scenario Family → Autonomous Behavior → Execution → Outputs → Sim-to-Real Correlation → Existing Evidence.

The resulting scope may require: updating the representation of contaminated sensors; expanding relevant lighting ranges; creating variations of human movement; testing combinations rather than isolated conditions; rerunning the affected behavioral scenario family; reassessing outputs; recalculating relevant correlation; reconsidering simulation evidence previously used for that operational domain.
Unaffected simulation domains remain reusable where their independence is established.
The organization therefore avoids the misleading choice between:
rerun everything
and
rerun only the failure.
SRSM establishes the third option:
rerun everything materially connected to the failure, and preserve everything demonstrably unaffected.
Governance Outputs
SRSM may produce: Resimulation Scope Assessment Affected Simulation Basis Map Simulation Dependency Map Resimulation Re-Entry Point Resimulation Scope Classification Affected Scenario Scope Affected Input Scope Affected Model & Environment Scope Affected Configuration Scope Required Execution Scope Downstream Output Reassessment Scope Correlation Reassessment Requirement Affected Simulation Evidence Register Unaffected Simulation Basis Statement Scope Exclusion Record Scope Sufficiency Assessment Provisional Resimulation Scope Final Resimulation Scope Governed Resimulation Scope Record
Enterprise Application
SRSM gives organizations a method for answering one of the most expensive questions in simulation lifecycle management:

When something changes, how much simulation must actually be repeated?
Without governed scope determination, organizations may either repeat massive simulation campaigns unnecessarily or perform narrow retesting that fails to capture downstream dependencies.
SRSM enables simulation-intensive organizations to determine: the earliest lifecycle point requiring re-entry; which scenarios must be repeated; which model components require revision; which inputs must be updated; which configurations are affected; which executions must be repeated; which previous outputs remain usable; which correlation relationships require reassessment; which simulation-derived evidence has become affected; which unaffected simulation assets may legitimately be preserved.
This becomes especially important where simulation campaigns contain millions or billions of executions.
The objective is not simply to reduce simulation cost.
It is to ensure that computational effort follows methodological necessity .
Foundational Principles
Resimulation Trigger does not determine Resimulation Scope.
The size of a change does not determine the size of its simulation consequence.
Local change does not necessarily imply local resimulation.
Resimulation scope must follow material dependency.
The minimum scope must still be sufficient.
Unaffected simulation assets should not be discarded merely because another part of the simulation changed.
Previously simulated does not mean automatically reusable.

A resimulation may re-enter SIMULOS® at any materially affected lifecycle layer.
Downstream outputs and evidence must be reconsidered where their simulation basis has changed.
Scope may expand or contract when new information changes the known dependency boundary.
Resimulation should repeat neither less nor more than the materially affected simulation basis requires.
Canonical Closing Statement

Resimulation Scope Module establishes the scope-determination layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by transforming a governed Resimulation Trigger into an explicit, dependency-aware, proportionate, sufficient, and traceable Resimulation Scope. Through governance of affected simulation bases, dependency propagation, lifecycle re-entry points, scenario scope, input scope, model and environment scope, configuration scope, execution requirements, downstream output consequences, correlation reassessment, evidence consequences, unaffected-basis preservation, scope sufficiency, and scope adjustment, SRSM prevents both insufficient resimulation and unnecessary repetition of unaffected simulation spaces. By separating the decision that resimulation is required from the decision concerning what must be resimulated, SRSM enables SIMULOS® to operate recursively across individual executions, targeted scenario families, model revisions, configuration changes, large simulation campaigns, and complete lifecycle reconstruction. Resimulation should not restart more of the simulation lifecycle than necessary, but it must reopen every materially affected dependency required to restore a legitimate governed simulation basis.

OOF™ Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM)
Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS)
Module: SRTM — Simulation Retirement & Transition Module
Operational Layer: Simulation Retirement & Transition Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Simulation Retirement & Transition
Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SRTM-012.5
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 20 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM) is the fifth and final Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SRTM governs the controlled retirement, supersession, replacement, transition, archival disposition, and residual-use status of simulations that can no longer legitimately continue under their existing lifecycle state.

The Module establishes when a simulation should cease active use, when its governed role should transfer to a successor simulation, how dependencies and simulation-derived evidence must be treated during transition, and what historical simulation assets may remain available for explicitly bounded purposes.
SRTM prevents obsolete, superseded, materially drifted, unsupported, or retired simulations from continuing to influence decisions merely because they remain technically accessible.
Its task is:
to ensure that the end of active simulation use becomes a governed lifecycle state rather than an informal disappearance, silent replacement, or uncontrolled continuation.
Architectural Position
SRTM is the fifth and final module within SLRS.
It follows:
SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module.
The complete SLRS module sequence is:
SLMM — Lifecycle Monitoring → SDRM — Drift Recognition → SRGM — Resimulation Trigger → SRSM — Resimulation Scope → SRTM — Retirement & Transition
SRTM closes the active lifecycle where continued resimulation is no longer the appropriate response.
It may produce three principal lifecycle directions:
Continue → existing governed simulation remains active.
Transition / Replace → simulation responsibility moves toward a successor simulation basis.
Retire → simulation ceases active governed use.
Internal Flow Position

Lifecycle Monitoring Record Recognized Simulation Drift Resimulation Trigger Resimulation Scope Determination → Continuation Feasibility Assessment → Retirement / Transition Condition Assessment → Dependency Identification → Successor Simulation Identification where applicable → Transition Boundary Definition → Residual Use Determination → Evidence Consequence Identification → Lifecycle State Assignment → Retirement / Transition Record → Archived / Superseded / Retired Simulation State
Where a successor simulation is established:
Retired or Superseded Simulation → Successor Simulation Basis → Applicable SIMULOS® Lifecycle Re-Entry Operational Space
SRTM governs the lifecycle space where a simulation can no longer simply be assumed to remain current.
This includes: simulation retirement; simulation supersession; simulation replacement; simulation transition; successor simulation identification; transition boundaries; residual simulation use; historical simulation use; retirement conditions; retirement state; supersession state; transition state; dependency transfer; simulation lineage; evidence consequences; unresolved limitation preservation; archive status; lifecycle closure; controlled reactivation where justified.
Operational Scope

SRTM applies where continued use of an existing simulation requires explicit reconsideration because of: material reality change; Simulation Object change; accumulated simulation drift; model obsolescence; environment obsolescence; unsupported assumptions; unavailable dependencies; obsolete input basis; inadequate scenario coverage; technological replacement; architecture change; unresolved correlation deterioration; inability to resimulate sufficiently; excessive reconstruction requirement; successor simulation introduction; termination of the original simulation purpose; loss of support or reproducibility; end of relevant operational lifecycle.
SRTM applies to individual simulation models, simulation environments, digital twins, scenario systems, simulation platforms, integrated simulation systems, mission simulations, engineering simulations, scientific simulations, safety simulations, AI simulations, autonomous-system simulations, large simulation campaigns, and future simulation technologies. Resimulation ≠ Indefinite Continuation
SLRS must not assume that every lifecycle problem can or should be solved through another simulation run.
Repeated resimulation may become inappropriate where the underlying simulation basis itself has become obsolete.
Therefore:
Resimulation Capability ≠ Continued Simulation Legitimacy
A simulation may remain technically executable while no longer being methodologically appropriate for its original purpose.
Retirement Principle

Simulation retirement occurs when a simulation ceases to hold an active governed role for its defined purpose.
Retirement may occur because: its Simulation Object no longer exists in the represented form; the object has materially changed; the original purpose has ended; its representation has become materially obsolete; assumptions can no longer be supported; the model can no longer represent relevant behavior; the environment has become obsolete; required inputs are unavailable; scenario space has changed beyond practical adaptation; correlation with reality has materially deteriorated; a successor simulation has replaced it; the simulation cannot be reconstructed sufficiently; continued use would exceed legitimate reliance boundaries.
Retirement should be explicit.
Non-use ≠ Governed Retirement.
Retirement State
SRTM establishes a formal Retired Simulation State.
A retired simulation should be distinguishable from: active simulation; temporarily suspended simulation; simulation under review; simulation undergoing resimulation; superseded simulation; archived simulation; successor simulation.
The state should indicate: retirement date; retirement basis; affected purpose; affected Simulation Object; final applicable configuration; successor where applicable; residual permitted uses; prohibited uses; evidence consequences; archival disposition.
Transition Principle
Not every simulation lifecycle ends through simple retirement.

Many simulations transition into: updated simulation versions; successor models; replacement environments; new digital twins; new mission simulators; new system configurations; redesigned simulation architectures.
SRTM governs the transition relationship between:
Outgoing Simulation Basis and Incoming Simulation Basis.
Transition must not create an unexamined assumption that the successor inherits the legitimacy of the predecessor.
Successor Simulation Principle
A successor simulation must be identifiable as a distinct governed simulation basis where material changes justify that distinction.
The relationship may be:
Version Successor
Configuration Successor
Model Successor
Environment Successor
Representation Successor
Purpose Successor
Complete Simulation Replacement
SRTM preserves lineage between predecessor and successor without treating them as methodologically identical.
Simulation Lineage ≠ Simulation Equivalence.
Transition Boundary
A transition must identify what crosses from the predecessor into the successor.
Potentially transferable elements include: Simulation Object definitions; purpose definitions; scope structures; reality representations; assumptions; model components; environmental configurations; parameter structures; input datasets; scenario libraries; execution procedures; historical outputs; correlation records; simulation evidence; known limitations; unresolved anomalies; lifecycle records.
Transferability must be assessed rather than assumed.

Inherited Basis Principle
A successor simulation may inherit parts of an earlier simulation basis.
But inherited elements must remain identifiable as:
Inherited and Reconfirmed
Inherited with Modification
Inherited Conditionally
Not Transferable
Replaced
This prevents simulation modernization from silently carrying obsolete assumptions, limitations, scenarios, or evidence into a new simulation generation. Retirement ≠ Deletion
SRTM establishes a critical distinction:
Simulation Retirement ≠ Simulation Deletion
A retired simulation may remain valuable for: historical comparison; research; incident reconstruction; longitudinal analysis; methodological analysis; regression comparison; training; audit support; understanding previous decisions; comparison with successor simulations.
Retirement governs active legitimacy, not necessarily physical existence.
Residual Use
A retired simulation may retain explicitly bounded residual uses.
Examples include: historical reconstruction; comparison with past system versions; educational use; research; regression analysis; archival reference; legacy incident analysis.
Residual use must not recreate active reliance implicitly.
A simulation retired from operational decision support should not regain that role merely because someone can still execute it.
Residual Use Limitation

Where residual use is permitted, SRTM should define: permitted purpose; prohibited purpose; applicable object version; applicable temporal period; known limitations; successor status; warning that the simulation is retired; whether new execution is permitted; whether outputs may enter current evidence processes.
This creates a governed distinction between:
historically useful
and
currently authoritative.
Supersession Principle
A simulation becomes Superseded where another governed simulation basis has formally replaced its active role.
Supersession should identify:
Predecessor Simulation → Successor Simulation
together with: transition date; transferred elements; non-transferred elements; changed assumptions; changed representation; changed models; changed scenarios; changed inputs; evidence consequences; residual predecessor use.
Supersession must not erase methodological history.
Transition Completeness
A transition is not complete merely because the successor simulation can execute.

Transition completeness may require confirmation that: successor identity is established; purpose and scope are established; transferred elements are known; non-transferable elements are identified; relevant assumptions are reconsidered; model and environment changes are governed; inputs remain appropriate; scenario space is sufficient; execution basis is established; outputs are distinguishable from predecessor outputs; correlation relationships are reconsidered where necessary; simulation evidence is not improperly inherited; predecessor status is updated.
Evidence Transition Principle
Simulation-derived evidence from a predecessor simulation must not automatically become evidence of the successor simulation.
A successor may materially change: representation; assumptions; model; environment; input basis; scenario structure; execution behavior; output meaning; reality correlation.
SRTM therefore requires inherited evidence to be identified for reassessment where the successor basis materially differs.
SERBS continues to govern the evidential meaning and reliance boundary.
SRTM governs the lifecycle consequence of the transition.
Historical Evidence Preservation
Retirement does not erase the historical evidential meaning that a simulation legitimately possessed at the time it was active.
Historical evidence may remain relevant to: historical decisions; previous system configurations; prior mission states; earlier operational periods; longitudinal comparison.
However:

Historically Legitimate Evidence ≠ Currently Applicable Evidence.
Retirement Due to Reality Change
A simulation may require retirement where Operational Reality has moved beyond the representational space the simulation can reasonably maintain.
Examples may include: fundamentally changed operating environments; new physical conditions; redesigned infrastructure; new system architecture; changed human behavior; changed regulatory or operational constraints; newly discovered phenomena; previously unknown interactions.
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.
SRTM governs whether the resulting change makes continued simulation use inappropriate.
Retirement Due to Model Obsolescence
A simulation may become obsolete because its underlying model no longer represents the relevant system sufficiently.
Model obsolescence may result from: new scientific knowledge; better physical models; discovered model deficiencies; unsupported software; changed system architecture; unavailable dependencies; inability to reproduce historical execution conditions.
SRTM does not determine general model quality.
It governs the lifecycle consequence where model obsolescence makes continued simulation use inappropriate.
Retirement Due to Accumulated Drift
Individual drift events may initially remain tolerable.
Over time, however:
Small Reality Changes Object Changes Input Changes Scenario Changes Model Limitations Correlation Degradation → Accumulated Simulation Drift

Accumulated drift may eventually make incremental resimulation insufficient.
SRTM provides the governance point at which the organization may determine:
stop adapting the old simulation and establish a new simulation basis.
Replacement Threshold
Organizations may define a Replacement Threshold representing the point at which continued modification of an existing simulation becomes methodologically inappropriate relative to replacement.
The threshold may consider: extent of structural change; number of affected lifecycle layers; accumulated assumptions; representation divergence; model modification burden; dependency obsolescence; scenario reconstruction requirements; correlation deterioration; inability to preserve traceability; evidence discontinuity.
The threshold should not be based solely upon economic convenience.
It is a simulation lifecycle governance decision.
Retirement with Unresolved Issues
A simulation may be retired while unresolved anomalies, limitations, discrepancies, or evidence questions remain.
These should not disappear with retirement.
SRTM requires material unresolved issues to remain attached to the retired simulation record where relevant.
This prevents retirement from functioning as a mechanism for eliminating inconvenient simulation history.
Reactivation Principle
A retired simulation may sometimes need to be reactivated.
Examples include: historical incident reconstruction; comparison against a successor; renewed research; legacy-system analysis.

Reactivation does not automatically restore the simulation's former active status.
SRTM requires the intended reactivation purpose to be explicit.
Where the simulation is intended to return to active current use, the relevant SIMULOS® lifecycle layers must be reconsidered.
Technical Reactivation ≠ Governance Reinstatement.
Simulation Lineage
SRTM requires meaningful predecessor-successor relationships to remain traceable.
A lineage may appear as:
Simulation V1 → Simulation V2 → Simulation V3 → Replacement Simulation R1 → Replacement Simulation R2
Each transition should preserve enough information to understand: what changed; why it changed; what was inherited; what was replaced; what evidence remained applicable; what evidence required reassessment; when active authority transferred.
This creates a governed simulation history rather than disconnected simulation versions.
Lifecycle Closure
A simulation lifecycle reaches governed closure when: active status has ended; retirement or supersession basis is documented; successor relationship is identified where applicable; residual use is defined; prohibited use is defined; evidence consequences are identified; unresolved material issues are preserved; archival disposition is established; lifecycle status is traceable.
Lifecycle closure does not mean that all simulation information disappears.
It means its governance state is explicit.
SRTM Boundary with SRSM
SRSM determines:
what must be resimulated.
SRTM determines:

whether continued resimulation remains appropriate, whether transition is required, or whether the simulation should retire.
Therefore:
Resimulation Scope ≠ Lifecycle Continuation Decision.
SRTM Boundary with SOS
SRTM may identify that a successor Simulation Object version or configuration requires a new simulation basis.
SOS governs the identity, boundary, version, configuration, and documentation of the Simulation Object.
SRTM governs the lifecycle transition between simulation generations.
SRTM Boundary with SMES
SRTM may determine that model or environment obsolescence requires replacement.
SMES governs the successor model and simulation environment when the lifecycle re-enters that layer.
SRTM Boundary with SES
SRTM may terminate active execution authority for a retired simulation.
SES governs simulation execution itself.
SRTM does not govern execution procedures.
SRTM Boundary with SERBS
SRTM identifies evidence potentially affected by retirement, supersession, replacement, or transition.
SERBS governs the qualification, weight, reliance boundary, use limitations, and validation interface of simulation-derived evidence.
Therefore:
Retirement does not automatically invalidate historical evidence, and transition does not automatically transfer evidential legitimacy.
SRTM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality and changes occurring within it.

SRTM governs the simulation lifecycle consequences arising when those changes make continued simulation use inappropriate.
SRTM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SRTM does not determine whether an operational system remains validated.
A simulation's retirement may affect a validation evidence basis, but VALIDOS® determines the resulting validation consequences.
SRTM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SRTM does not govern general integrity.
INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of archived simulation objects, records, evidence, states, and transition information.
SRTM governs the simulation-specific lifecycle status and transition.
SRTM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit or verify retirement records, transition evidence, predecessor-successor relationships, and historical execution records.
SRTM governs the retirement and transition process itself.
SRTM Boundary with AGA™
SRTM does not determine organizational accountability for approving retirement, replacement, or continued use.
AGA™ governs authority, responsibility, accountability, and attribution.
SRTM defines the simulation-governance conditions that the lifecycle decision must address.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SRTM implementation should establish: 1. Lifecycle State Review
Determine whether the simulation remains active, requires transition, is superseded, or should retire. 2. Retirement / Transition Basis
Document the simulation-specific conditions supporting the lifecycle change. 3. Continuation Feasibility

Determine whether resimulation or modification remains methodologically appropriate. 4. Successor Identification
Identify a successor simulation where replacement or transition occurs. 5. Transferability Assessment
Determine which simulation elements may legitimately transfer to the successor and which require renewed governance. 6. Evidence Consequence Assessment
Identify simulation-derived evidence affected by retirement or transition. 7. Residual Use Definition
Define any permitted historical, analytical, research, training, or reconstruction uses. 8. Prohibited Use Definition
Identify uses that must cease after retirement or supersession. 9. Lineage & Transition Record
Preserve predecessor-successor relationships, transferred elements, material changes, and transition state. 10. Lifecycle Closure Record
Assign and document the final governed lifecycle state. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Transition to a New Spacecraft Configuration
A space organization maintains a high-fidelity mission simulator for a spacecraft architecture used across several mission cycles.
Over time, the next spacecraft generation introduces: redesigned propulsion; new navigation hardware; different thermal behavior; modified flight software; new landing systems; changed mission phases.
The existing simulator can technically be modified again.

But accumulated changes now affect the Simulation Object, reality representation, assumptions, model structure, environment, inputs, scenarios, and previous simulation-to-reality correlations.
SRTM asks whether continuing to modify the legacy simulator remains methodologically legitimate.
The organization determines that the old simulator should become Superseded and a successor simulation basis should be established.
SRTM governs:
Legacy Simulation → Transferability Assessment → Reusable Scenario Assets → Reconfirmed Assumptions → Rejected Legacy Assumptions → New Model Components → New Correlation Requirements → Successor Simulation → Legacy Simulation Retirement.
Historical mission outputs remain available for previous mission analysis.
But they are not automatically treated as evidence for the new spacecraft generation.
The critical principle is:
A successor mission simulator may inherit knowledge from its predecessor without inheriting its legitimacy automatically. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot: Legacy Simulator After Major Platform Redesign
An autonomous mobile robot was originally developed and tested using a simulation environment representing its first-generation sensors, actuators, perception stack, physical dimensions, and control architecture.
Several years later, the robot platform is redesigned.

The new generation introduces: different cameras; new depth sensors; changed wheel geometry; new actuator behavior; different latency; redesigned perception software; new autonomous planning behavior.
The organization still possesses millions of historical simulation scenarios and results.
Simply continuing to use the old simulator would be computationally convenient.
But the represented robot no longer corresponds sufficiently to the new operational platform.
SRTM establishes a transition from:
Legacy Robot Simulation → Successor Robot Simulation.
Scenario libraries may remain partially transferable.
Historical failure scenarios may remain highly valuable.
Some environmental representations may remain reusable.
But sensor models, dynamics, assumptions, configurations, outputs, correlation relationships, and simulation evidence require renewed governance.
The legacy simulator is retained for historical comparison and regression research but is prohibited from serving as the current primary simulation basis for the redesigned robot.
This prevents a common lifecycle failure:
the operational system evolves, while the simulation quietly remains anchored to yesterday's system.
Governance Outputs

SRTM may produce: Simulation Lifecycle State Record Simulation Retirement Assessment Simulation Retirement Decision Record Simulation Supersession Record Simulation Transition Plan Successor Simulation Identification Record Simulation Transferability Assessment Inherited Simulation Basis Record Non-Transferable Element Record Simulation Residual Use Statement Simulation Prohibited Use Record Simulation Evidence Transition Record Historical Evidence Applicability Record Simulation Lineage Record Unresolved Issue Preservation Record Simulation Archive Disposition Simulation Reactivation Record Simulation Lifecycle Closure Record
Enterprise Application
SRTM enables organizations to govern a simulation problem that becomes increasingly important as simulation systems persist for years or decades:
When should an existing simulation stop being treated as the current simulation basis?
Without lifecycle retirement governance, organizations may continue using models, environments, assumptions, scenarios, and evidence long after the systems or realities they represent have materially changed.

SRTM enables organizations to: distinguish active, superseded, transitioned, archived, and retired simulations; determine when incremental resimulation is no longer sufficient; replace obsolete simulation foundations deliberately; preserve useful historical simulation assets; prevent obsolete simulations from supporting current decisions; establish predecessor-successor lineage; determine what can transfer into a successor; prevent obsolete assumptions from silently migrating into new simulations; preserve unresolved failures and limitations; control historical and residual use; identify evidence affected by transition; close simulation lifecycles explicitly.
This is especially important for long-lived engineering programs, mission systems, digital twins, autonomous systems, infrastructure, scientific models, and simulation platforms that evolve across multiple technological generations.
SRTM ensures that simulation governance does not end when execution stops.
It ends only when the simulation's lifecycle status, successor relationship, residual use, evidential consequences, and historical position are explicitly governed.
Foundational Principles
Resimulation does not imply indefinite continuation.
A simulation may remain executable after it ceases to be methodologically current.
Non-use is not governed retirement.
Retirement is not deletion.
Simulation lineage is not simulation equivalence.

A successor simulation does not automatically inherit the legitimacy of its predecessor.
Transferable simulation assets must be distinguished from transferable simulation authority.
Historically legitimate evidence is not automatically currently applicable evidence.
Accumulated drift may require replacement rather than another incremental update.
Technical reactivation does not automatically restore governance status.
Obsolete simulations must not remain operationally authoritative merely because they remain accessible.
The end of a simulation lifecycle must be governed as explicitly as its beginning.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Retirement & Transition Module establishes the final lifecycle-control layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by governing when simulations cease active use, become superseded, transition into successor simulation bases, retain bounded residual uses, or reach formal lifecycle closure. Through governance of retirement conditions, continuation feasibility, supersession, successor identification, transferability, inherited simulation bases, residual and prohibited uses, evidence consequences, historical applicability, unresolved issues, reactivation, archival disposition, and simulation lineage, SRTM prevents obsolete or superseded simulations from retaining methodological authority merely because they remain technically available. By distinguishing retirement from deletion, lineage from equivalence, historical evidence from current applicability, and technical reactivation from governance reinstatement, SRTM closes the recursive SIMULOS® lifecycle while preserving the knowledge necessary for future simulation generations. A governed simulation lifecycle is complete only when not merely its creation and execution, but also its transition, supersession, residual use, and retirement have become explicit, traceable, and methodologically bounded.
