OOF™ Simulation Scope Module (SSCM)
Simulation Scope Module (SSCM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Scope
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 16 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Scope
Canonical Definition
Simulation Scope Module (SSCM) defines the governance conditions under which the exact extent of a simulation inquiry is established, bounded, decomposed, maintained, changed, and documented relative to the governed Simulation Object and Simulation Purpose.
SSCM determines which object characteristics, functions, behaviors, interactions, operating conditions, temporal ranges, spatial ranges, system states, and inquiry dimensions are included within the simulation and prevents simulation outputs from being interpreted beyond the scope actually governed and executed.
Operational Role

SSCM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The preceding Simulation Purpose governance establishes:
Why is the simulation being performed?
SSCM asks:
What exactly must the simulation cover in order to address that purpose?
The governed progression is:
Governed Simulation Purpose → Scope Requirement → Scope Dimensions → Scope Inclusion → Scope Boundary → Scope Structure → Scope Status → Governed Simulation Scope
SSCM transforms simulation purpose into a concrete inquiry perimeter capable of guiding downstream Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Execution, and Output Governance.
Module Operational Space
SSCM governs: Simulation Scope definition, scope dimensions, functional scope, behavioral scope, component scope, system scope, interaction scope, operational scope, environmental scope relevance, spatial scope, temporal scope, population scope, mission-phase scope, condition scope, operating-mode scope, failure-mode scope, capability scope, autonomy scope, scope hierarchy, partial scope, composite scope, scope decomposition, scope aggregation, scope dependencies, scope interfaces, scope expansion, scope contraction, scope recomposition, scope change, scope ambiguity, scope conflict, scope status, scope continuity, and Simulation Scope traceability.
Module Function

SSCM exists because knowing why a simulation is being performed does not establish what the simulation actually covers.
A simulation can have a legitimate purpose and still fail methodologically because its scope is: undefined, too narrow, unintentionally broad, fragmented, internally inconsistent, misaligned with purpose, silently expanded, silently contracted, or represented more broadly than what was actually simulated.
SSCM therefore creates the governed relationship:
Simulation Purpose → Required Simulation Coverage
Its function is to ensure that downstream simulation design addresses the intended inquiry without allowing omitted or unmodeled conditions to disappear from visibility.
Simulation Scope
Simulation Scope is the governed extent of the simulation inquiry.
It defines which portions of the Simulation Object and which simulation-relevant dimensions are intended to be represented and examined.
Simulation Scope may be defined across several dimensions simultaneously.
For example:
Object: Autonomous vehicle Functional Scope: Perception and braking Operational Scope: Urban low-speed driving Environmental Scope: Daylight and rain Temporal Scope: Single maneuver sequence Interaction Scope: Vehicle–pedestrian interaction
These dimensions together form the governed Simulation Scope.
Scope Must Derive From Purpose
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation Scope should be derived from the governed Simulation Purpose rather than from whatever the available model happens to support.

Existing simulation tools may influence implementation feasibility.
They must not silently redefine the inquiry. Purpose–Scope Alignment
A Simulation Scope should be sufficiently broad and sufficiently detailed to address the governed Simulation Purpose.
A Purpose–Scope Gap exists where the purpose requires investigation of conditions not covered by the Simulation Scope.
For example:
Purpose: Evaluate autonomous-system behavior across emergency conditions.
Scope: Normal operating conditions only.
The scope is structurally insufficient for the stated purpose.
Scope Dimensions
Simulation Scope may include several independent dimensions.
These may include:
Object Dimension — which object components or systems are covered.
Functional Dimension — which functions are examined.
Behavioral Dimension — which behaviors are represented.
Operational Dimension — which operating modes or conditions apply.
Environmental Dimension — which surrounding conditions matter to the inquiry.
Spatial Dimension — where the simulation applies.
Temporal Dimension — when or for how long the simulation applies.
Population Dimension — which populations, users, actors, or entities are represented.
Interaction Dimension — which interactions among systems or actors are included.
Capability Dimension — which capabilities are covered.
A governed Simulation Scope may require several of these dimensions to be combined.
Functional Scope

Functional Scope identifies which functions of the Simulation Object are included in the inquiry.
A system may contain many functions while only a subset is simulated.
For example:
Aircraft Simulation Object
may have scope limited to:
Landing Guidance + Braking
rather than:
Complete Aircraft Operation
SSCM requires this distinction to remain visible.
Behavioral Scope
Behavioral Scope identifies which object behaviors are included.
This may include: nominal behavior, degraded behavior, failure behavior, autonomous behavior, human interaction, recovery behavior, emergency behavior, or selected adaptive behavior.
A simulation of normal behavior does not automatically establish behavior under abnormal conditions.
Component Scope
Complex systems may require explicit component-level scope.
A simulation may include:
Subsystems A, B, and C
while excluding:
Subsystem D
Even where the complete system remains the Simulation Object, the inquiry itself may be partial.
Interaction Scope
Many simulation outcomes depend upon interaction among multiple components, actors, systems, or environments.
Interaction Scope establishes which relationships are included.
Examples may include: robot–human interaction, vehicle–vehicle interaction, spacecraft–ground interaction, AI-agent–tool interaction, system–infrastructure interaction, or subsystem–subsystem interaction.
Omitting a material interaction may create a scope limitation even where both participating objects are individually represented.

Operational Scope
Operational Scope identifies the operating conditions or modes within which the simulation applies.
Examples include: normal operation, startup, shutdown, emergency mode, autonomous mode, supervised mode, degraded mode, high-load operation, low-resource operation, maintenance mode, or mission-specific operation.
Operating Envelope
Where applicable, SSCM may establish a governed Simulation Operating Envelope.
This defines the range of operating conditions covered by the simulation.
A simulation result established within one operating envelope must not automatically be generalized beyond it.
Spatial Scope
Spatial Scope defines the geographic, physical, or logical area covered by the simulation.
Examples may include: one manufacturing cell, one warehouse, one city, one orbital region, one network segment, one infrastructure zone, or one defined physical volume.
Temporal Scope
Temporal Scope establishes the relevant time dimension.
A simulation may examine: milliseconds, one operational cycle, one mission phase, one day, one year, long-term system evolution, or another governed period.
A short-duration simulation must not automatically support conclusions about long-term behavior.
Population Scope
Where simulation concerns humans, users, agents, organizations, or populations, SSCM may define which population is included.

Population Scope may distinguish: age groups, user classes, geographic groups, operator classes, expertise levels, organizational roles, behavioral profiles, or other simulation-relevant populations.
Capability Scope
A complex AI or autonomous system may possess multiple capabilities.
Simulation Scope may include only defined capabilities.
For example:
Perception + Navigation
may be included while:
Autonomous Tool Execution
remains outside scope.
This distinction must remain explicit.
Autonomy Scope
Where autonomy is material, Simulation Scope should identify the autonomy level represented.
A simulation of:
Human-Supervised Operation
must not automatically be treated as simulation of:
Fully Autonomous Operation
where system behavior materially differs.
Failure and Abnormal Condition Scope
Failure conditions may be inside or outside Simulation Scope.
Where the Simulation Purpose includes safety, robustness, resilience, or failure analysis, applicable failure modes should be explicitly governed.
The absence of failure scenarios cannot later be interpreted as successful simulation of failure behavior.
Partial Simulation Scope
SIMULOS® permits partial simulation.
A simulation does not need to model the complete object or every possible condition.
However:
Partial Simulation Scope must remain explicitly partial.
A narrow but correctly governed simulation may be methodologically stronger than an apparently comprehensive simulation with undefined boundaries.
Scope Hierarchy

Complex simulation programs may require hierarchical scope:
Program Scope
↓
System Scope
↓
Subsystem Scope
↓
Scenario Scope
↓
Execution Scope
SSCM preserves the relationship among these levels.
Lower-level scope must remain traceable to the higher-level inquiry it supports.
Scope Decomposition
A broad Simulation Scope may be decomposed into manageable subscopes.
For example:
Complete Mission Scope
may be decomposed into:
Launch
Transit
Orbital Operation
Docking
Return
Decomposition is legitimate when the relationship among the subscopes remains governed.
Scope Aggregation
Multiple partial simulations may later contribute to a broader simulation inquiry.
However:
Aggregation of partial scopes does not automatically establish complete scope coverage.
The combined scope must be assessed for: missing areas, overlaps, incompatible assumptions, boundary gaps, interaction gaps, and uncovered transitions.
Scope Coverage
Scope Coverage describes the extent to which planned or completed simulation activity addresses the governed Simulation Scope.
Possible coverage states may include:
Complete
Substantially Complete
Partial
Fragmented
Insufficient
or:
Undetermined
Coverage does not determine simulation validity.
It determines whether the intended inquiry has actually been represented across its defined scope.
Scope Gap
A Simulation Scope Gap exists where a material part of the governed Simulation Scope is not covered by planned or completed simulation activity.

Examples may include: unrepresented operating mode, missing interaction, missing population, missing mission phase, missing failure condition, missing capability, or missing temporal range.
Scope gaps must remain visible.
Scope Overlap
Multiple simulation activities may cover the same portion of scope.
Overlap is not inherently problematic.
It may provide: redundancy, comparative analysis, sensitivity testing, or independent representation.
However, duplicated coverage should not be confused with broader coverage.
Scope Dependency
One portion of Simulation Scope may depend upon another.
For example:
Emergency Recovery Scope
may depend upon behavior established during:
Failure Initiation Scope
SSCM preserves material scope dependencies to prevent isolated simulation fragments from being interpreted without required context.
Scope Interface
A Scope Interface exists where two separately governed scope regions meet.
Interfaces may occur between: mission phases, subsystem simulations, model domains, populations, operating modes, or sequential simulation stages.
Where interface behavior is material, SSCM should prevent it from falling between separately governed scope segments.
No Scope Inflation Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulation claim must not extend beyond the Simulation Scope actually governed and covered.
Therefore:
One Function ≠ Complete System
One Scenario ≠ Complete Operational Envelope
One Environment ≠ All Environments
One Population ≠ Universal Population

One Mission Phase ≠ Complete Mission
unless a governed basis establishes broader applicability.
No Precision-for-Scope Substitution Rule
A highly detailed simulation of one narrow domain does not compensate for missing scope elsewhere.
SIMULOS® establishes:
Simulation Depth and Precision cannot substitute for missing Simulation Scope.
No Execution-for-Scope Substitution Rule
Repeating the same simulation many times does not expand its scope.
More Runs ≠ Broader Scope
unless new governed conditions are actually introduced.
No Model-Capability Scope Rule
The capabilities of an available simulation model must not silently determine the governed Simulation Scope.
If the purpose requires conditions the model cannot represent, that limitation must remain visible.
Scope Expansion
Scope Expansion occurs when new material functions, conditions, objects, populations, environments, capabilities, interactions, or periods are added to the Simulation Scope.
Expansion may require reassessment of: Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Execution, Output Governance, and Reality Correlation.
Scope Contraction
Scope Contraction removes material portions of the previously governed Simulation Scope.
Contraction may be legitimate where: purpose changes, constraints emerge, simulation is decomposed, or a narrower inquiry is intentionally adopted.
It must remain explicit.
Scope Recomposition

Scope Recomposition changes the structure of scope without necessarily making it strictly broader or narrower.
For example:
several subsystem scopes may be reorganized into interaction-based scopes.
The relationship to the original Simulation Purpose must remain traceable.
Scope Change Materiality
A change is material where it could alter: simulation meaning, representation requirements, assumptions, scenario requirements, outputs, interpretation, or downstream applicability.
Material changes should trigger downstream reassessment.
No Silent Scope Change Rule
Material Simulation Scope must not change without explicit governance.
This applies both before and after execution.
No Retrospective Scope Adjustment Rule
Simulation Scope must not be narrowed after results are known merely to remove failed or inconvenient conditions from the represented inquiry.
Likewise, it must not be expanded retrospectively to make favorable results appear more widely applicable.
Scope Ambiguity
Scope Ambiguity exists where it is unclear whether a material dimension belongs inside or outside the simulation inquiry.
Ambiguity may concern: functions, conditions, populations, interactions, operating modes, environments, or time periods.
Material ambiguity must remain explicit until resolved.
Scope Conflict
A Scope Conflict exists where credible simulation records or stakeholders define materially different intended scopes for the same simulation activity.
For example:

engineering may treat a simulation as:
Component Evaluation
while management presents it as:
System Safety Simulation
Such conflict must be resolved or explicitly preserved.
Scope Status
Possible Simulation Scope statuses may include:
Established
Conditionally Established
Partially Established
Scope Ambiguous
Scope Conflicted
or:
Scope Undetermined
Status describes the quality of scope definition, not the quality of simulation execution.
Scope Continuity
Simulation Scope should remain traceable through the full simulation lifecycle.
Conceptually:
Simulation Purpose → Governed Scope → Representation → Scenarios → Execution → Outputs
This allows later determination of whether a simulation output actually corresponds to the scope claimed for it.
Simulation Scope Record
SSCM should establish a persistent Simulation Scope Record capable of reconstructing: scope basis, scope dimensions, inclusions, functional coverage, behavioral coverage, operational conditions, environmental relevance, spatial range, temporal range, population, interactions, capabilities, partial scopes, dependencies, gaps, changes, and current scope status.
Failure Conditions

SSCM governance failure may exist where: Simulation Scope is not explicitly established, scope cannot be connected to the Simulation Purpose, material scope dimensions remain undefined, the scope is insufficient for the stated purpose, partial simulation is represented as complete coverage, material scope gaps are hidden, different scopes are aggregated without coverage analysis, scope interfaces remain ungoverned, scope is determined solely by available model capability, scope expands or contracts silently, retrospective scope adjustment occurs, materially different scopes are treated as equivalent, or simulation outputs are represented beyond the scope under which they were produced.
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Derive Scope from the Simulation Purpose
Translate the governed Simulation Purpose and Simulation Questions into the required simulation coverage. 2. Define Material Scope Dimensions
Establish the relevant functional, behavioral, component, operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population, interaction, capability, and other applicable scope dimensions. 3. Structure and Bound the Scope
Define complete, partial, composite, or decomposed scope and identify material dependencies, interfaces, and known gaps. 4. Govern Scope Change and Status
Record scope expansion, contraction, recomposition, ambiguity, conflict, and current Simulation Scope Status. 5. Preserve Scope Traceability

Create the Simulation Scope Record and maintain the relationship between purpose, scope, downstream simulation design, execution, and resulting outputs.
Governance Outputs
SSCM may produce: Simulation Scope Definition, Simulation Scope Record, Purpose–Scope Alignment Record, Simulation Scope Map, Scope Dimension Record, Functional Scope Record, Behavioral Scope Record, Component Scope Record, Interaction Scope Record, Operational Scope Record, Simulation Operating Envelope, Spatial Scope Record, Temporal Scope Record, Population Scope Record, Capability Scope Record, Autonomy Scope Record, Failure Condition Scope Record, Partial Scope Record, Composite Scope Record, Scope Hierarchy, Scope Decomposition Map, Scope Aggregation Assessment, Scope Coverage Assessment, Simulation Scope Gap Record, Scope Overlap Record, Scope Dependency Map, Scope Interface Record, Scope Expansion Record, Scope Contraction Record, Scope Recomposition Record, Scope Change Assessment, Scope Ambiguity Record, Scope Conflict Record, Simulation Scope Status, and Simulation Scope Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Operational Scope
Scenario
An autonomous vehicle developer intends to simulate pedestrian avoidance before urban deployment.
The Simulation Object is already identified and the purpose is:
Evaluate pedestrian-avoidance behavior under selected urban operating conditions. Application
SSCM establishes scope across:
Functional Scope: Perception, prediction, path planning, and braking.

Operational Scope: Urban driving below the defined speed threshold.
Environmental Scope: Daylight, dry conditions, and selected rain conditions.
Interaction Scope: Vehicle–pedestrian interaction.
Population Scope: Defined pedestrian behavior profiles.
Night-time operation, snow, highway driving, and vehicle-to-vehicle collision scenarios remain outside the governed Simulation Scope. Result
Successful simulation results cannot later be represented as evidence that the vehicle has been simulated across its complete autonomous-driving operational envelope. Use Case 2 — Integrated Space Mission Simulation
Scenario
A space organization intends to simulate an integrated mission from launch through orbital operation.
The initial mission program contains separate simulation environments for:
Launch
Orbital Insertion
Navigation
and:
Docking Application
SSCM decomposes the broader mission scope into controlled subscopes while identifying the interfaces between mission phases.
The architecture detects that the transition between:
Orbital Insertion
and:
Navigation
is not covered by either simulation environment.
This becomes a documented Simulation Scope Gap. Result
The organization cannot claim complete mission simulation merely because each major mission phase has an individual simulation.
The uncovered transition remains visible until governed simulation coverage is established.
Architectural Position

Simulation Scope Module (SSCM) is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS).
The internal progression begins:
Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope
The preceding purpose module establishes:
Why is the simulation being performed?
SSCM establishes:
What exactly must that simulation cover?
The next SPSS governance spaces separately govern:
what must be explicitly excluded,
where the simulation is contextually applicable,
and:
how much simulation depth and precision the intended inquiry requires.
SSCM does not replace Validation Scope under VALIDOS®, Operational Reality governance under ORA™, Simulation Object Boundary governance under SOS, or Reality Representation governance under RRS.
It governs specifically:
the extent of the simulation inquiry itself.
Foundational Principle
A simulation can legitimately support only the portion of the intended inquiry that falls within the scope actually governed and covered by simulation.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Scope Module (SSCM) establishes the governed extent of the simulation inquiry by translating Simulation Purpose into explicit functional, behavioral, component, interaction, operational, spatial, temporal, population, capability, and other materially relevant scope dimensions. Through purpose–scope alignment, partial-scope governance, decomposition, aggregation control, coverage assessment, gap detection, interface governance, anti-inflation rules, change control, scope status, and complete traceability, SSCM prevents narrow or fragmented simulation activity from being represented as broader coverage than was actually established. By defining exactly what the simulation must cover before downstream representation, assumptions, modeling, scenario design, execution, and output interpretation proceed, SSCM provides the second internal governance mechanism of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard.

Simulation Object Standard (SOS)
Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard governs the contextual environment within which an observed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is situated before it proceeds through tax-relevant event governance, and establishes the methodological basis for identifying, scoping, relating, and maintaining the context necessary for subsequent event interpretation without determining event recognition, taxability, jurisdiction, or legal tax consequence.
An occurrence becomes legitimately context-ready only when the materially relevant conditions required to interpret it are sufficiently identified, scoped, related, and maintainable without predetermining whether a Tax-Relevant Event exists or whether any tax is legally due.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance

Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard governs how a sufficiently contextualized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is evaluated and recognized as a legitimate candidate for further tax-relevant event governance, while preserving the boundary between occurrence recognition, Event Formation, and jurisdiction-specific tax determination.
An occurrence becomes legitimately recognized only when sufficient governed context and recognition conditions establish that it warrants progression into Event Formation; technical detection, economic relevance, machine execution, or potential tax relevance do not by themselves establish a governed Tax-Relevant Event or legal taxability.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard governs how a sufficiently recognized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is transformed into a coherent governed event structure through governed formation of materially relevant components, assembly, dependencies, operational root association, and formation integrity, while preserving the boundaries between Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Determination, and jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.

A recognized occurrence becomes a legitimate Governed Formed Event only when its materially relevant formation structure is sufficiently established, coherent, traceable, and structurally fit to proceed into Event Boundary governance without allowing formation itself to determine legal taxability.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard governs how a sufficiently formed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is bounded as a distinct governed event by establishing its legitimate structural extent, including what belongs within the event, what remains outside it, and where separation from adjacent or overlapping activity is required, while preserving the boundaries between Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Determination, and jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
A Governed Formed Event becomes a legitimate Governed Bounded Event only when its structural extent is sufficiently established, explicit, coherent, traceable, and capable of distinguishing event membership from surrounding or related activity without allowing Event Boundary governance to determine legal taxability or Tax Jurisdiction.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance

Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard governs how a sufficiently bounded real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is temporally situated through governed identification of its operational time, start, completion, duration, and temporal order, while preserving the distinction between operational Event Timing and jurisdiction-specific legal tax timing, including Legal Tax Point and Tax Period Determination.
Tax-Relevant Event Timing Governance Flow: Real-World / Digital Event → Event Context → Event Recognition → Event Formation & Root Association → Event Boundary → Event Timing → Event Location → Event Participation → Value Association → Event Relationships → Event Determination → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → Event Continuity & Lifecycle → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine → Tax Determination Reporting / Compliance A Governed Bounded Event becomes a legitimate Governed Temporally Situated Event only when its operational temporal position is sufficiently identified, coherent, traceable, and appropriately qualified without allowing Event Timing to determine a Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, legal taxability, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance

The Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) governs how a temporally situated real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, distributed, or value-affecting event is spatially situated through governed identification and representation of its physical, digital, distributed, and correlated operational locations, while preserving the distinction between Event Location and jurisdiction-specific Tax Jurisdiction.
Tax-Relevant Event Location Governance Flow: Real-World / Digital Event → Event Context → Event Recognition → Event Formation & Root Association → Event Boundary → Event Timing → Event Location → Event Participation → Value Association → Event Relationships → Event Determination → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → Event Continuity & Lifecycle → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine → Tax Determination Reporting / Compliance A Governed Temporally Situated Event becomes a legitimate Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event only when its operational location is sufficiently identified, represented, traceable, and appropriately qualified without allowing Event Location to determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, legal taxability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard (TREPS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance

The Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard (TREPS) governs how human, organizational, digital, machine, autonomous, and other materially relevant actors participate in a governed Tax-Relevant Event, including their operational roles, actor-event associations, and participation continuity, without converting operational participation into taxpayer status or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Participation Governance Flow: Real-World / Digital Event → Event Context → Event Recognition → Event Formation & Root Association → Event Boundary → Event Timing → Event Location → Event Participation → Value Association → Event Relationships → Event Determination → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → Event Continuity & Lifecycle → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine → Tax Determination Reporting / Compliance A spatially and temporally governed event becomes a legitimate Governed Participatory Event only when materially relevant actors and their participation relationships are sufficiently governed without allowing participant identification or participation to determine taxpayer status, liability, tax jurisdiction, or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence.
→ View Standard

Tax-Relevant Event Participation Governance Flow: Real-World / Digital Event → Event Context → Event Recognition → Event Formation & Root Association → Event Boundary → Event Timing → Event Location → Event Participation → Value Association → Event Relationships → Event Determination → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → Event Continuity & Lifecycle → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine → Tax Determination Reporting / Compliance A spatially and temporally governed event becomes a legitimate Governed Participatory Event only when materially relevant actors and their participation relationships are sufficiently governed without allowing participant identification or participation to determine taxpayer status, liability, tax jurisdiction, or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence. → View Standard
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard (TRVAS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
TRVAS governs how governed value references, Value States, Value Changes, and other governed value results are materially associated with a Tax-Relevant Event without redefining the Value Lifecycle or determining jurisdiction-specific taxable value.
Tax-Relevant Value Association Governance Flow: Event Participation → Value Association Event Relationships Foundational Principle: VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ governs which governed value result belongs to the event.
→ View Standard

Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard (TRERLS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
TRERLS governs how already-governed Tax-Relevant Events are related, distinguished, sequenced, dependent, grouped, merged, split, or otherwise structurally associated without allowing technical workflows, shared records, or downstream tax interpretation to redefine Event Identity.
Tax-Relevant Event Relationships Governance Flow: Value Association → Event Relationships → Event Determination Foundational Principle: Event Relationship ≠ Event Identity.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard (TREDS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
TREDS governs how a fully structured and relationship-governed event is formally evaluated to determine whether it is sufficiently complete, coherent, attributable, bounded, and reconstructable to become a Tax-Relevant Event for downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis without determining the tax itself. Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Determination Governance Flow: Event Relationships → Event Determination Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Foundational Principle: Event Determination ≠ Taxability Determination.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Determination Governance Flow: Event Relationships → Event Determination Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Foundational Principle: Event Determination ≠ Taxability Determination. → View Standard
→ View Standard

Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard (TREGS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
The Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard (TREGS) governs how a Determined Tax-Relevant Event is transformed into a canonical, identifiable, structured, linked, traceable, and interoperable governed Event Record suitable for persistent representation, system exchange, downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis, and subsequent lifecycle governance. Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Governance Flow: TRECS → TRERS → TREFS → TREBS → TRETS → TRELS → TREPS → TRVAS → TRERLS → TREDS → TREGS ← CURRENT TRECLS A Determined Tax-Relevant Event becomes operationally reusable only when its governed meaning can persist across records, systems, organizations, and downstream tax environments without being redefined.
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Governance Flow: TRECS → TRERS → TREFS → TREBS → TRETS → TRELS → TREPS → TRVAS → TRERLS → TREDS → TREGS ← CURRENT TRECLS A Determined Tax-Relevant Event becomes operationally reusable only when its governed meaning can persist across records, systems, organizations, and downstream tax environments without being redefined. → View Standard
→ View Standard
Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard (TRECLS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance

The Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard (TRECLS) governs how a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record remains methodologically continuous, historically reconstructable, and governably current as the Event is amended, corrected, superseded, maintained, closed, or referred for new Event Formation when continuity can no longer legitimately be preserved.
Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance Flow: TRECS → TRERS → TREFS → TREBS → TRETS → TRELS → TREPS → TRVAS → TRERLS → TREDS → TREGS TRECLS ← CURRENT A Tax-Relevant Event becomes jurisdiction-ready only when its current state, historical continuity, corrections, supersessions, and closure status remain governable without erasing prior Event reality or converting lifecycle governance into tax-law administration.
→ View Standard
Simulation Object Standard (SOS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Defines the governance conditions under which the object, system, process,
environment, behavior, phenomenon, or other target proposed for simulation is
formally identified, bounded, distinguished, versioned, configured, and
documented as a governed Simulation Object throughout the simulation lifecycle.
SOS governs the Simulation Object. It establishes the object foundation required
before simulation purpose, representation, assumptions, modeling, execution,
outputs, evidence use, or lifecycle resimulation can be governed.

A simulation can only meaningfully represent reality when the exact object
being simulated is explicitly identified and bounded.
→ View Standard
Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a
simulation, the questions it must address, the governed portions of the
Simulation Object, its exclusions, applicability context, and required depth
and precision are formally established before representation begins.
SPSS governs Simulation Purpose & Scope. It prevents a technically successful
simulation from silently acquiring a broader purpose, scope, applicability, or
interpretive meaning than was actually established.
A simulation cannot legitimately answer a broader question than the
question for which it was governed.
→ View Standard
Reality Representation Standard (RRS)
Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Defines the governance conditions under which the aspects of reality relevant to
a governed Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Applicability Context, and required

Simulation Temporal Data Module (STDM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS)
Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Parent Standard Module
Governed Space: Simulation Temporal Data
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Module
Effective Date: 18 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
Canonical Language: English (UCL™)
Governed Space
Simulation Temporal Data
Canonical Definition
Simulation Temporal Data Module (STDM) defines the governance framework through which the temporal properties of Simulation Inputs are identified, aligned, bounded, assessed, and preserved so that information entering a simulation remains temporally appropriate for the reality period, sequence, frequency, duration, synchronization, and dynamic behavior the simulation is intended to represent.

STDM establishes the temporal-input layer of SIDS by governing whether data is not merely available and technically usable, but temporally fit for the simulation context in which it is relied upon.
It governs the transition:
Simulation-Usable Input → Temporal Context → Temporal Alignment → Temporal Fitness Assessment → Temporal Conditions & Limitations → Temporally Governed Simulation Input
Operational Role
STDM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The preceding modules establish:
SIIM — What information is entering the simulation?
SDRM — What reality can that information legitimately represent?
SDTM — What happened to that information before simulation use?
STDM asks:
Does the information represent the correct time, temporal sequence, frequency, duration, synchronization, and dynamic context required by the simulation?
The governed progression is:
Simulation Input → Temporal Identity → Temporal Reference → Temporal Alignment → Temporal Coverage → Temporal Gap & Distortion Assessment → Temporal Fitness Status → Simulation Use
Module Operational Space

STDM governs: temporal input identification, observation time, collection time, event time, processing time, effective time, simulation reference time, temporal provenance, temporal currency, temporal applicability, temporal alignment, temporal synchronization, temporal sequence, temporal ordering, temporal resolution, sampling frequency, temporal granularity, temporal coverage, duration coverage, temporal gaps, temporal discontinuities, stale data, delayed data, asynchronous data, temporal interpolation, temporal extrapolation, time-window selection, historical-period selection, seasonal coverage, cyclic behavior, trend representation, regime change, temporal drift, temporal dependencies, latency, temporal distortion, temporal uncertainty, temporal limitations, temporal status, temporal reassessment, and temporal traceability.
Module Function

STDM exists to prevent: old data being treated as current without assessment, current data being assumed relevant to historical conditions, observations from different periods being combined as if simultaneous, temporal order being lost during preprocessing, sampling frequency hiding fast system behavior, short observation periods being generalized to long-term dynamics, seasonal data being generalized across the entire year, temporal gaps disappearing during interpolation, asynchronous sensors appearing synchronized, delayed information being treated as real-time information, historical relationships being assumed stable after regime change, future extrapolation being represented as observation, and simulations producing precise outputs from temporally inappropriate input foundations.
Temporal Identity
Every material temporal Simulation Input should preserve sufficient information to determine when the represented information applies.
Temporal identity may include: timestamp, observation period, collection period, effective period, duration, sequence position, sampling interval, temporal resolution, or another relevant temporal reference.
Temporal Reference
A Temporal Reference establishes the time basis against which an input is interpreted.
Examples include:
UTC
Local Time
Mission Time
System Runtime
Relative Simulation Time
Event Time
Historical Period
or another defined reference system.
Where multiple references are used, their relationship should remain explicit.

Observation Time
Observation Time identifies when the represented phenomenon actually occurred or was observed.
This may differ from:
Collection Time
Processing Time
Transmission Time
or:
Simulation Consumption Time.
These distinctions may materially affect dynamic simulations.
Event Time vs Processing Time
SIMULOS® establishes:
When information was processed is not necessarily when the represented event occurred.
For real-time and event-driven simulations, confusing these temporal properties may distort causal or sequential relationships.
Temporal Currency
Temporal Currency asks:
Is the input sufficiently current for the simulation inquiry?
Currency is context-dependent.
Data from ten years ago may be suitable for one simulation and materially obsolete for another.
No Universal Freshness Rule
SIMULOS® establishes:
Temporal fitness cannot be determined from data age alone.
The relevant question is whether material properties of the represented reality have changed since the data was produced.
Temporal Applicability
An input may be temporally applicable only to a defined period.
For example:
Applicable: 2024–2026 operating configuration
does not automatically establish:
Applicable: 2030 projected configuration.
Temporal applicability should therefore remain bounded.
Temporal Alignment
Temporal Alignment establishes whether multiple Simulation Inputs refer to sufficiently compatible time periods or temporal states.
Conceptually:

Input A Time Basis + Input B Time Basis + Simulation Time Basis → Temporal Alignment Assessment Cross-Source Temporal Alignment
Different sources may contain observations from different periods.
For example:
Traffic Data — 2025
Road Infrastructure Data — 2022
Vehicle Population Data — 2026
Combining them may be legitimate, but the temporal differences should be assessed where they can materially affect simulation behavior.
Temporal Synchronization
Synchronization governs whether inputs that interact dynamically are sufficiently aligned in time.
This is particularly important for: sensor simulations, robotics, autonomous systems, control systems, industrial systems, communication systems, financial simulations, and real-time digital twins.
Synchronization Tolerance
Perfect synchronization may not always be required.
A simulation may define an acceptable temporal tolerance.
For example:
Maximum Sensor Alignment Difference: ±20 ms
The tolerance should reflect the dynamics of the simulated system rather than technical convenience alone.
Temporal Sequence
Some simulation behavior depends upon the order of events.
Conceptually:
A → B → C
may produce a materially different outcome from:
B → A → C
STDM therefore preserves sequence where sequence affects simulated causality or behavior.
No Sequence Neutrality Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Temporal order must not be treated as irrelevant where changing event order can materially change the simulated outcome.
Temporal Resolution

Temporal Resolution defines the smallest meaningful time interval represented by an input.
Examples include: milliseconds, seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, or years.
The required resolution depends upon the dynamics being simulated.
Resolution Fitness
A simulation of millisecond control behavior may not legitimately rely solely upon hourly averages.
Conversely, millisecond data may be unnecessary for a multi-decade infrastructure simulation.
STDM therefore asks:
Is temporal resolution sufficient for the simulation question?
Sampling Frequency
Sampling Frequency defines how often observations are captured.
For example:
100 Hz
means:
100 observations per second.
Sampling frequency may determine whether fast behavior is visible or lost.
Sampling Adequacy
Where relevant system dynamics occur faster than the available sampling interval, material behavior may remain unobserved.
Therefore:
Available Frequency ≠ Sufficient Frequency Temporal Granularity
Temporal granularity describes the level at which information is temporally grouped.
For example:
individual transactions
may be aggregated into:
hourly totals
or:
daily averages.
Granularity changes may hide important temporal patterns.
Temporal Coverage
Temporal Coverage describes the period represented by the available input.
Examples:
One Hour
Three Months
Five Years
Complete Operational Lifecycle
Coverage should be evaluated relative to the Simulation Purpose and Scope.
Duration Sufficiency

A dataset may contain high-frequency observations while covering only a very short period.
High sampling density does not automatically establish sufficient duration coverage.
SIMULOS® therefore distinguishes:
Observation Density
from:
Observation Duration.
Seasonal Coverage
Where seasonal variation matters, the input basis should sufficiently represent relevant seasonal conditions.
For example:
data collected only during summer may not sufficiently support simulation of winter energy demand.
Cyclic Behavior
Relevant temporal cycles may include: daily, weekly, monthly, seasonal, annual, maintenance, production, economic, biological, or operational cycles.
STDM determines whether required cycles are sufficiently represented.
Temporal Variation
Simulation behavior may depend upon changes over time rather than static values.
Relevant patterns may include: acceleration, degradation, growth, decay, oscillation, accumulation, recovery, fatigue, adaptation, or escalation.
Trend Representation
Historical data may contain a trend.
The simulation should determine whether that trend: remains relevant, has stabilized, has reversed, has structurally changed, or should not be extrapolated.
Regime Change
A Temporal Regime Change occurs where relationships represented by historical information materially change.
Examples include: new regulation, new technology, infrastructure redesign, market restructuring, environmental change, system upgrade, behavioral shift, or operational-policy change.

Pre-Change ≠ Post-Change
SIMULOS® establishes:
Data representative of one temporal regime must not automatically be treated as representative of a materially different regime.
Temporal Drift
Temporal Drift occurs where the relationship between the input basis and current or target reality gradually changes over time.
Drift may affect: distributions, behaviors, environmental conditions, system performance, populations, or dependencies.
Temporal Gap
A Temporal Gap exists where required time periods contain insufficient or missing information.
Examples include: missing sensor intervals, absent seasonal periods, incomplete historical records, missing transition periods, or unobserved operational phases.
Temporal Gap Materiality
Not every gap matters.
A temporal gap becomes material where it could affect: simulated dynamics, scenario behavior, output interpretation, validation, or downstream reliance.
Temporal Discontinuity
A discontinuity occurs where a time series changes abruptly because of: missing data, sensor replacement, system change, measurement-method change, configuration change, or actual physical change.
The cause should remain distinguishable where material.
Stale Data
Stale Data is information whose temporal distance from the simulation context may materially weaken its applicability.
Staleness is not determined solely by age.
It depends upon the rate at which the represented reality changes.
Stability-Relative Currency

A stable physical constant may remain temporally applicable indefinitely.
A rapidly changing market variable may become stale within minutes.
Therefore:
Required Currency ∝ Rate of Material Change
This relationship is conceptual, not numerical.
Delayed Data
Data may describe a current event but arrive after a delay.
Relevant delay may include: sensing delay, transmission delay, processing delay, aggregation delay, publication delay, or ingestion delay.
Latency
Temporal Latency is the difference between a relevant event time and the time at which the information becomes available to the simulation.
Latency may materially affect simulations involving: control, reaction, coordination, autonomous decision-making, or real-time operation.
Latency Must Not Disappear
SIMULOS® establishes:
Information available after an event must not be represented as information that was available before the event where availability timing affects simulated behavior.
Asynchronous Data
Inputs may arrive or be observed at different temporal frequencies.
Asynchronous information may require: alignment, buffering, interpolation, resampling, or explicit asynchronous modeling.
SDTM governs the transformation.
STDM governs whether the resulting temporal relationship is suitable.
Temporal Interpolation
Interpolation may fill values between known temporal observations.
STDM governs the temporal consequence of using those values.

Interpolated time points should remain distinguishable from direct observations where material.
Temporal Extrapolation
Temporal extrapolation estimates values beyond the observed period.
Extrapolated values should not silently acquire the temporal status of observations.
Historical Input
Historical information may be used to represent: prior conditions, baseline behavior, long-term patterns, rare events, or model calibration.
Historical status should remain explicit. Historical ≠ Current
SIMULOS® establishes:
Historical relevance must be demonstrated where historical information is used to represent current or future conditions.
Future-Oriented Simulation Inputs
Future simulations may depend upon: forecasts, projections, assumptions, synthetic trajectories, planned configurations, or predicted environmental conditions.
Such information should remain distinguishable from historical observations.
Observed Time vs Projected Time
The simulation record should preserve whether a temporal input is:
Observed
Estimated
Projected
Forecast
Assumed
or:
Synthetic
where the distinction is material.
Temporal Dependency
One input may depend upon the temporal state of another.
For example:
Battery Temperature at Time t
may depend upon:
Load during t−1 through t−n.
Static treatment may therefore fail to represent the actual dependency.
Lag Relationship
Some effects occur after a delay.

Examples include: thermal response, economic response, biological response, fatigue, infrastructure degradation, or control-system delay.
Where material, lag relationships should remain represented.
Lead Relationship
Some information may act as an advance indicator of another condition.
Where such relationships are used in simulation, their temporal basis should remain explicit.
Temporal Causality
STDM does not establish universal causal truth.
It ensures that temporal relationships relied upon by the simulation do not become detached from the sequence and timing assumptions upon which they depend.
Temporal Distortion
A Temporal Distortion occurs where processing or input construction materially changes the timing characteristics of the represented phenomenon.
Examples include: smoothing away rapid events, shifting timestamps, averaging across event boundaries, resampling beyond adequate resolution, or synchronizing sources through unsupported assumptions.
Transformation-Induced Temporal Distortion
SDTM may identify the transformation.
STDM evaluates its temporal consequence.
This separation preserves the boundary:
SDTM → What transformation occurred?
STDM → Is the resulting temporal representation still fit for simulation use?
Temporal Uncertainty
Temporal information may itself be uncertain.
Examples include: approximate event time, clock error, synchronization uncertainty, uncertain historical dating, variable latency, or estimated temporal alignment.

STDM identifies temporal uncertainty as a distinct contribution to the broader Simulation Input Uncertainty governed by SIUM.
Clock and Reference Uncertainty
Different systems may use: different clocks, different synchronization mechanisms, different time zones, or imperfect timestamp precision.
Where material, these differences should be governed.
Temporal Boundary
A simulation may define explicit temporal boundaries.
For example:
Simulation Period: 2026–2030
Input applicability outside or inside that period should be assessed accordingly.
Temporal Scope Expansion
If the simulation period expands materially, previously accepted data may require reassessment.
For example:
Original Scope: 2026
becoming:
Expanded Scope: 2026–2040
may materially change the required temporal basis.
Temporal Fitness
Temporal Fitness describes whether an input is sufficiently appropriate for the temporal conditions of its intended simulation use.
Possible statuses may include:
Temporally Fit
Conditionally Temporally Fit
Partially Temporally Fit
Temporally Unfit
or:
Temporal Fitness Undetermined Temporal Fitness Is Context-Bound
A dataset may be temporally fit for one simulation and unfit for another.
Therefore:
Temporal Fitness = Input Time Basis relative to Simulation Time Requirement Temporal Condition
An input may remain usable under explicit temporal conditions.
For example:
Applicable only to system configuration before 1 January 2027.
or:
Suitable only where input latency remains below 50 ms.

Temporal Restriction
A temporal restriction narrows where or when the information may legitimately be used.
Restrictions should propagate downstream where they materially affect simulation interpretation.
Temporal Limitation
A Temporal Limitation may include: insufficient duration, stale information, missing seasonal coverage, uncertain synchronization, unresolved regime change, excessive latency, inadequate sampling frequency, temporal gaps, or projected rather than observed values.
Temporal Reassessment Trigger
Reassessment may be required when: the Simulation Scope changes, the target time period changes, system dynamics change, a new regime begins, new data becomes available, sampling requirements change, latency changes, synchronization changes, a new system version is introduced, or temporal assumptions are materially revised.
No Temporal Inheritance Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
Temporal fitness must not be inherited automatically from a previous simulation when the relevant time context has materially changed.
No Recency-to-Fitness Principle
Newer data is not automatically better data if it represents the wrong temporal condition.
No Historical-to-Current Principle
Historical data does not automatically represent current reality.
No Current-to-Future Principle
Current data does not automatically represent future reality.
No Density-to-Duration Principle
A large number of observations collected over a short period does not establish long-duration temporal coverage.

No Synchronization-by-Assumption Principle
Inputs from different clocks, systems, or periods must not be treated as synchronized merely because the simulation can technically combine them.
No Interpolation-to-Observation Principle
A temporally interpolated value remains generated information, not a direct observation.
No Latency Erasure Principle
A simulation must not silently give an actor, model, or system information earlier than that information would legitimately have been available in the represented reality.
Temporal Information Leakage
A particularly important failure occurs when future information is inadvertently introduced into an earlier simulated decision point.
Conceptually:
Information from t+1 → used at decision t
when the represented actor could not have known it.
This creates Temporal Information Leakage.
No Future Knowledge Principle
SIMULOS® establishes:
A simulated actor must not receive future information unless the Simulation Purpose explicitly requires and identifies that condition.
This is especially important for: financial simulations, predictive systems, autonomous decision systems, policy simulations, operational decision models, and historical counterfactual analysis.
Temporal Leakage Control
Where decision-making is simulated, the information available at each decision point should remain bounded by what would legitimately have been available at that time.
Conceptually:
Decision at t ≤ Information Available at t

unless the scenario explicitly introduces another information condition.
Temporal Snapshot Integrity
Where a simulation reconstructs a historical state, inputs should reflect a coherent temporal snapshot or explicitly governed multi-period reconstruction.
A historical simulation should not silently combine:
2022 knowledge + 2024 infrastructure + 2026 policy
and represent the result as:
Reality in 2022.
Temporal Input Set Coherence
Individual inputs may each be temporally acceptable while the complete Input Set is temporally incoherent.
STDM therefore assesses both:
Input-Level Temporal Fitness
and:
Input-Set Temporal Coherence.
Temporal Coherence
A Simulation Input Set is temporally coherent where material inputs can legitimately coexist within the represented simulation time context.
Temporal Conflict
A Temporal Conflict exists where two or more material inputs imply incompatible temporal states.
For example:
Infrastructure Version A active until June
while another input assumes:
Infrastructure Version B active since March.
The conflict should be resolved, bounded, or preserved explicitly.
Temporal Fitness Propagation
Material temporal limitations should propagate downstream.
Conceptually:
Temporal Limitation → Scenario / Execution Constraint → Output Interpretation Limitation → Reliance Limitation
Later SIMULOS® Parent Standards govern those downstream stages.
STDM ensures the original temporal limitation remains visible.
Point-in-Time Reconstruction

STDM should enable questions such as:
What data was available at this simulated moment?
Which system version did the data represent?
Were the sources synchronized?
Which values were observed and which were interpolated?
Did the simulation use information from the future?
Was the input still temporally applicable?
Temporal Traceability
STDM establishes:
Simulation Input
↓
Temporal Identity
↓
Temporal Reference
↓
Temporal Coverage
↓
Temporal Alignment & Synchronization
↓
Temporal Gaps / Drift / Regime Change
↓
Temporal Fitness
↓
Conditions / Restrictions
↓
Simulation Use
Minimum Implementation Framework
1. Establish Temporal Identity
Identify the material temporal properties of each Simulation Input. 2. Define Simulation Temporal Requirements
Determine the: relevant period, resolution, frequency, duration, sequence, and synchronization requirements.
3. Assess Temporal Applicability
Determine whether each input represents the required time context. 4. Assess Temporal Alignment
Evaluate whether material inputs refer to sufficiently compatible temporal states. 5. Assess Resolution and Sampling
Determine whether the available temporal resolution and sampling frequency can represent materially relevant dynamics. 6. Assess Duration and Coverage
Determine whether the observation period covers required: cycles, seasons, transitions, operating phases, and long-term behavior.
7. Identify Temporal Gaps and Distortions

Record: missing periods, discontinuities, stale data, latency, asynchronous inputs, interpolation, extrapolation, and transformation-induced temporal effects.
8. Assess Drift and Regime Change
Determine whether historical temporal relationships remain applicable to the simulation context. 9. Control Temporal Information Leakage
Ensure simulated actors and systems receive only information legitimately available at the represented decision time unless explicitly governed otherwise. 10. Establish Temporal Conditions and Restrictions
Bound input use where temporal fitness is incomplete but manageable. 11. Assign Temporal Fitness Status
Determine whether the input or Input Set is: Temporally Fit, Conditionally Temporally Fit, Partially Temporally Fit, Temporally Unfit, or Temporal Fitness Undetermined.
12. Preserve Temporal Traceability
Maintain:
Input → Time Basis → Alignment → Coverage → Limitation → Temporal Fitness → Simulation Use
Governance Outputs

STDM may produce: Simulation Temporal Requirement, Temporal Input Identity Record, Temporal Reference Record, Observation-Time Record, Event-Time Record, Effective-Time Record, Simulation Reference-Time Record, Temporal Applicability Record, Temporal Currency Assessment, Temporal Alignment Assessment, Cross-Source Temporal Alignment Record, Synchronization Assessment, Synchronization Tolerance, Temporal Sequence Record, Temporal Resolution Assessment, Sampling Frequency Assessment, Temporal Granularity Record, Temporal Coverage Assessment, Duration Sufficiency Assessment, Seasonal Coverage Record, Cyclic Behavior Coverage Record, Trend Applicability Record, Regime Change Record, Temporal Drift Record, Temporal Gap Record, Temporal Discontinuity Record, Stale Data Record, Latency Record, Asynchronous Data Record, Temporal Interpolation Record, Temporal Extrapolation Record, Temporal Dependency Record, Lag Relationship Record, Temporal Distortion Record, Temporal Uncertainty Record, Temporal Information Leakage Record, Temporal Snapshot Record, Temporal Conflict Record, Temporal Input Set Coherence Assessment, Temporal Condition Record, Temporal Restriction Record, Temporal Limitation Record, Temporal Fitness Status, Temporal Reassessment Trigger, and Simulation Temporal Data Traceability Map.
Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Simulation
Scenario

An autonomous-driving simulation combines: camera data captured at 30 Hz, radar data captured at 20 Hz, vehicle telemetry captured at 100 Hz, and pedestrian-location information updated every second.
The system being simulated makes control decisions every 50 milliseconds. Application
STDM evaluates: sampling adequacy, synchronization, latency, event-time alignment, interpolation, and what information would actually have been available at each decision point.
The simulation is prohibited from using a pedestrian position update before that update would have been available to the vehicle. Result
The Input Set receives a governed Temporal Fitness Status with explicit synchronization tolerances and latency conditions.
The simulation can reconstruct the information state available to the autonomous system at every material decision point. Use Case 2 — Energy Demand Simulation
Scenario
A simulation estimates future electricity demand using three years of historical consumption data.
The available dataset contains: strong summer coverage, incomplete winter observations, a major industrial-demand shift in the final year, and no data after a significant energy-pricing reform.
Application
STDM identifies: seasonal coverage weakness, a temporal regime change, incomplete historical applicability, and limitations on projecting historical relationships forward.
Result
The data may remain:
Conditionally Temporally Fit

for defined baseline analysis but insufficient for unrestricted future-demand representation without additional temporal evidence or explicitly governed assumptions.
Architectural Position
Simulation Temporal Data is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS).
The complete SIDS progression is:
Simulation Input Identification
↓
Simulation Data Representativeness
↓
Simulation Data Transformation
↓
Simulation Temporal Data
↓
Simulation Input Uncertainty
SIIM establishes:
What information is entering the simulation?
SDRM establishes:
What reality can it legitimately represent?
SDTM establishes:
What happened to it before simulation use?
STDM establishes:
Is it temporally appropriate for the reality and dynamics being simulated?
The next module, SIUM — Simulation Input Uncertainty Module, governs the uncertainty carried by the complete Simulation Input basis after identification, representativeness, transformation, and temporal conditions have been established.
Foundational Principle
Simulation data becomes temporally legitimate only when its time basis, sequence, resolution, coverage, synchronization, latency, applicability, and limitations remain aligned with the temporal reality the simulation is intended to represent.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Temporal Data Module establishes the temporal governance layer of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing when Simulation Inputs apply, how their temporal references and sequences relate, whether their resolution, sampling frequency, duration, synchronization, and coverage are sufficient, and how temporal gaps, latency, drift, regime change, interpolation, extrapolation, temporal conflict, and future-information leakage affect simulation use. Through explicit temporal identity, applicability, alignment, coherence, conditions, restrictions, fitness status, reassessment triggers, and complete temporal traceability, STDM prevents technically usable information from being treated as temporally legitimate when its timing, age, sequence, availability, or dynamic context cannot support the reality the simulation claims to represent.
