chunks.text:
OOF™ Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM)
Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture
Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS)
Module: SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module
Operational Layer: Simulation Use Limitation Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Simulation Governance
Type: Core Module
Governed Space: Simulation Evidence Use Limitation
Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SUM-011.4
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 20 August 2026
Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM) is the fourth Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SUM governs the explicit restrictions, exclusions, conditions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, prohibited uses, and dependency conditions that must remain attached to simulation-derived evidence when that evidence is interpreted, communicated, transferred, or used.

The Module translates the governed reliance boundary established by SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module into explicit controls over what simulation evidence may not legitimately be used to claim, infer, justify, demonstrate, predict, authorize, or support.
SUM does not determine whether simulation evidence qualifies as evidence, how much evidential weight it carries, or whether the complete validation basis is sufficient.
Its task is narrower:
to ensure that the limitations governing simulation-derived evidence remain explicit, persistent, interpretable, transferable, and inseparable from downstream use of that evidence.
Core Question
What must simulation-derived evidence not be used to claim, infer, justify, or support?
Architectural Position
SUM is the fourth module within SERBS.
It follows:
SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module
→ establishes what qualifies as Simulation Evidence;
SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module
→ establishes how much simulation-specific evidential significance the evidence may carry;
SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module
→ establishes how far legitimate reliance may extend.
SUM then converts those boundaries into explicit use controls.
It precedes:
SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module
which governs transfer of simulation-derived evidence into broader validation governance under VALIDOS®.
The sequence is therefore:
Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary → Use Limitation → Validation Interface.

Internal Flow Position
Weighted Simulation Evidence Governed Simulation Reliance Boundary → Intended Use Identification → Limitation Source Identification → Use Condition Definition → Restriction Definition → Exclusion Definition → Unsupported Interpretation Identification → Prohibited Use Definition → Limitation Persistence Requirements → Use Limitation State → Governed Simulation Use Limitation Record → SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module
Operational Space
SUM governs the space between:
where legitimate simulation reliance ends
and
how that boundary must constrain actual evidence use.
This operational space includes: intended evidence use; permitted-use conditions; conditional use; restricted use; excluded use; unsupported interpretation; prohibited inference; prohibited generalization; prohibited extrapolation; decision-class limitation; configuration limitation; scenario limitation; parameter limitation; environmental limitation; temporal limitation; uncertainty limitation; correlation limitation; dependency limitation; communication limitation; transfer limitation; limitation persistence; limitation review; limitation withdrawal following material change.
Operational Scope

SUM applies whenever simulation-derived evidence is: interpreted; summarized; aggregated; communicated; transferred; presented; cited; compared; used in engineering; used in scientific analysis; used in safety arguments; used in mission planning; used in design decisions; used in system qualification; used in regulatory submissions; used in validation processes; used in operational preparation; used in deployment decisions; used in AI or autonomous-system evaluation; used in consequential organizational decisions.
It applies to evidence derived from: individual simulation runs; repeated executions; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; mission simulations; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies.
SUM remains technology-neutral. Reliance Boundary ≠ Use Limitation
SUM enforces the distinction:
Reliance Boundary ≠ Use Limitation
SRBM determines:
where legitimate reliance stops.
SUM determines:
what restrictions must govern use because that boundary exists.
For example, SRBM may establish that evidence applies only to:
Object Version V4 + Scenario Family S3 + Parameter Range P2 + Environment E1.
SUM may translate this into explicit controls:
Do not apply this evidence to Object Version V5.
Do not generalize this evidence beyond Scenario Family S3.

Do not use this evidence to support performance outside Parameter Range P2.
Do not represent this evidence as demonstrating performance in environments materially different from E1.
SRBM defines the boundary.
SUM operationalizes it.
Use Limitation Principle
A Simulation Use Limitation is:
an explicit governance condition constraining how simulation-derived evidence may be interpreted, communicated, transferred, generalized, or relied upon.
A limitation may arise from: simulation purpose; simulation scope; exclusions; reality representation; abstraction; fidelity; assumptions; model applicability; environmental configuration; input basis; scenario coverage; execution conditions; output classification; inference basis; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; evidence weight; reliance boundary; temporal relevance.
Use limitations must remain linked to their source.
Limitations Are Part of the Evidence
SUM establishes a central principle:
A material limitation is part of the governed evidential meaning, not optional commentary attached to it.
Removing a material limitation while preserving the evidence can materially change the meaning of the evidence.
Therefore:
Evidence − Material Limitation ≠ Same Evidence Meaning.
Where a limitation materially determines legitimate interpretation, the limitation must travel with the evidence.
Intended Use Identification
SUM requires the intended use of simulation evidence to be explicit.

An Intended Use may include: exploration; comparison; screening; engineering design; optimization; hypothesis support; safety analysis; scenario planning; mission planning; training; system qualification; validation input; operational preparation; deployment support; regulatory evidence; predictive analysis.
The same evidence may have different limitations for different intended uses.
Permitted Use Conditions
SUM may establish conditions under which evidence remains legitimately usable.
Examples include:
Permitted only for comparative analysis.
Permitted only for the governed Simulation Object configuration.
Permitted only within represented environmental conditions.
Permitted only within Parameter Range P.
Permitted only while Assumption Set A remains applicable.
Permitted only as one input to a broader validation process.
Conditional use must remain distinguishable from unrestricted use. Restriction
A restriction narrows how evidence may be used without completely prohibiting its use.
Restrictions may concern: purpose; object; configuration; scenario; environment; parameter range; decision type; temporal period; inference class; communication context.
For example:
Evidence may support comparative design selection but must not be used as independent evidence of operational safety. Exclusion
An exclusion identifies a condition or domain that the evidence does not cover.

Examples include: weather conditions not represented; hardware versions not simulated; excluded failure modes; populations not modeled; untested terrain; unrepresented physical phenomena; mission phases outside simulation scope; operating conditions outside parameter limits.
An exclusion must not disappear merely because downstream users are unaware of it.
Unsupported Interpretation
An Unsupported Interpretation occurs where the evidence is described as meaning more than its governed basis supports.
Examples include:
Simulation demonstrated safe behavior
when the evidence only establishes:
no unsafe behavior was observed within the simulated scenario set.
Or:
The system performs reliably in reality
when the evidence establishes only:
high simulated performance within represented conditions.
SUM requires unsupported interpretations to be identifiable and preventable. Observed Absence ≠ Demonstrated Impossibility
Simulation campaigns frequently produce no instance of a particular failure.
SUM establishes:
Failure Not Observed ≠ Failure Impossible
The absence of an event within a simulated scenario space may provide evidence concerning that tested space.
It does not automatically establish impossibility outside that space.
This distinction is especially important in: rare-event simulation; safety analysis; autonomous systems; mission simulation; infrastructure failure analysis; high-consequence engineering.
Simulation Success ≠ Operational Safety

A simulation campaign may demonstrate extensive successful simulated behavior.
That does not independently establish operational safety.
Therefore:
Simulation Success ≠ Operational Safety Determination.
SUM must prevent simulation success metrics from being communicated as broader safety determinations where the evidence basis does not support that interpretation. Scenario Success ≠ Universal Performance
Successful performance across all executed scenarios means:
successful performance across those governed executed scenarios.
It does not mean:
successful performance across every possible condition.
SUM therefore preserves:
Tested Scenario Space ≠ Total Possible Reality Space. Comparative Evidence ≠ Absolute Evidence
Evidence demonstrating that:
Configuration A outperformed Configuration B
does not necessarily establish:
Configuration A meets an absolute operational performance requirement.
SUM requires comparative claims and absolute claims to remain distinct. Simulation Prediction ≠ Guaranteed Outcome
Where simulation evidence supports prediction, SUM requires the distinction:
Predicted Outcome ≠ Guaranteed Outcome.
Predictive simulation evidence may legitimately inform planning and decision-making.
It must not acquire deterministic meaning merely because the simulation produces precise numerical outputs.
Precision Limitation
Highly precise simulation outputs may create false confidence.
SUM therefore establishes:
Numerical Precision ≠ Evidential Certainty.
An output of:

0.003721 failure probability
does not necessarily mean the real-world probability is known to six significant digits.
The precision communicated must remain compatible with: model uncertainty; input uncertainty; scenario uncertainty; representation limits; correlation uncertainty; inference uncertainty.
Extrapolation Limitation
Where evidence is extrapolated beyond directly simulated conditions, the extrapolation must remain explicitly identified.
SUM may require statements such as:
This conclusion includes extrapolation beyond the directly simulated parameter range.
or:
This evidence does not independently support performance beyond the simulated environmental domain.
Unidentified extrapolation is a use-governance failure.
Decision-Class Limitation
Simulation evidence may legitimately inform one decision class while remaining insufficient for another.
For example:
Exploratory Design Decision
may require less evidential support than:
Safety-Critical Deployment Decision.
SUM may therefore assign different use limitations based upon the intended decision class.
It does not define organizational decision authority.
Configuration Limitation
Evidence associated with one Simulation Object configuration must retain limitations concerning materially different configurations.
Changes may include: hardware; software; architecture; sensor suite; actuator system; material; payload; model configuration; operating mode.
Evidence transfer across configurations requires a governed basis.

Scenario Limitation
SUM requires scenario limitations to remain visible.
Evidence may be limited to: expected scenarios; edge cases; stress conditions; specified scenario families; defined uncertainty ranges; specific failure combinations.
A scenario limitation should identify both:
what was represented
and, where material:
what was not represented.
Environmental Limitation
Evidence may be valid only under specified represented environments.
Limitations may concern: weather; terrain; lighting; atmosphere; gravity; thermal conditions; traffic; infrastructure; communication availability; human interaction; electromagnetic conditions.
Environmental limitations are especially important where simulation-to-reality transfer is material.
Temporal Limitation
Simulation evidence may have a temporal use boundary.
A limitation may require review when: the Simulation Object changes; the operational environment changes; new reality data becomes available; model versions change; assumptions become obsolete; new failure modes emerge; input distributions shift; correlation deteriorates.
Evidence should not retain permanent unrestricted use merely because it was once appropriately qualified.
Uncertainty Limitation
Material uncertainty must constrain interpretation where relevant.
SUM may require: confidence qualification; uncertainty ranges; conditional language; restricted extrapolation; additional evidence; prohibition of deterministic claims.

Uncertainty is not a reason to discard useful evidence.
It is a reason to govern how strongly that evidence is expressed and used.
Dependency Limitation
Where evidence objects share material dependencies, downstream users must not interpret their quantity as equivalent independent confirmation.
SUM may therefore require disclosure that: runs share the same model; evidence shares the same assumptions; outputs share the same input source; models share a common representation; scenario sets share common omissions; evidence shares one correlation basis.
Multiple dependent evidence objects must not be presented as independent confirmation.
Aggregation Limitation
Aggregated simulation metrics must not erase material information.
An aggregate success rate may conceal: rare failures; scenario-specific failures; environmental clusters; configuration-specific weaknesses; anomalous executions; distribution tails; common-mode failures.
SUM may therefore require that material underlying limitations remain attached to aggregate evidence.
Communication Limitation
Simulation evidence can be methodologically distorted through communication even when the underlying evidence remains unchanged.
SUM therefore applies to: reports; dashboards; executive summaries; regulatory submissions; presentations; scientific communication; engineering documentation; automated AI-generated summaries; machine-readable evidence transfers.

A summary must not remove limitations necessary to interpret the evidence correctly.
Human-Readable and Machine-Readable Limitations
Because simulation evidence may move through automated systems, limitations should be capable of being represented in both:
human-readable form
and
machine-readable form.
Machine-readable limitation fields may include: permitted use; restricted use; prohibited use; applicable object; applicable version; applicable configuration; scenario domain; parameter domain; environmental domain; temporal validity; uncertainty condition; correlation condition; review trigger.
This allows limitations to survive automated evidence pipelines.
Limitation Persistence Principle
SUM establishes:
A limitation must travel at least as far as the evidence it limits.
If evidence is: copied; exported; aggregated; summarized; transferred; transformed; entered into another system; entered into validation; reused in another analysis,
material limitations must remain discoverable and linked.
Limitation Detachment
Limitation Detachment occurs when evidence continues downstream while its governing limitations are lost, hidden, omitted, weakened, or separated.

Examples include: copying a simulation metric without its scenario boundary; presenting a success percentage without excluded failures; transferring evidence without uncertainty; using a graph without its parameter range; citing a simulation conclusion after the Simulation Object configuration changed; removing caveats from an executive summary.
SUM treats material limitation detachment as a simulation governance failure.
Limitation Conflict
Different evidence objects may carry conflicting use limitations.
One evidence object may support a proposition under one condition while another constrains it under another.
SUM requires such conflicts to remain visible rather than collapsing them into one apparently unrestricted conclusion.
Use Limitation States
SUM may assign a governed Use Limitation State.
A minimum state model may include: 1. Undefined Limitation
Evidence exists, but material use limitations have not yet been explicitly established. 2. Conditional Use
Evidence may be used only while defined conditions remain satisfied. 3. Restricted Use
Evidence may be used only for specified purposes, contexts, objects, scenarios, or decision classes. 4. Prohibited Use
A specified use, interpretation, inference, or decision application is not supported by the governed simulation evidence. 5. Review Required
Material change or new information requires reassessment before continued use. 6. Limitation Superseded

A previous limitation has been replaced by a newly governed limitation basis.
These states govern evidence use rather than overall validation status.
Prohibited Use
A Prohibited Use is a use that exceeds the legitimate simulation-specific evidential basis sufficiently that it should not proceed without a new governed basis.
Examples may include: claiming universal behavior from bounded scenarios; claiming real-world equivalence from simulation alone; claiming operational safety solely from simulated success; applying evidence to a materially different object configuration; concealing known scenario exclusions; treating correlated simulations as independent evidence; presenting inferred results as directly observed results; using stale evidence after material reality change; treating extrapolation as direct simulation evidence; representing simulation evidence as a formal Validation Determination.
Prohibited Use ≠ Organizational Prohibition
SUM defines methodological prohibited use within simulation evidence governance.
It does not itself impose legal, regulatory, corporate, or disciplinary sanctions.
Other governance structures may use SUM outputs to establish such controls.
Limitation Review Trigger
Use limitations should be reassessed when materially relevant changes occur.

Triggers may include: Simulation Object change; configuration change; new simulation results; new scenarios; new model; new input basis; new correlation evidence; operational observations; newly discovered failure; changed intended use; changed decision class; changed environment; expired temporal applicability.
Review may result in:
limitation retained → limitation narrowed → limitation expanded → limitation replaced → additional simulation required.
SUM Boundary with SRBM
SRBM determines the maximum legitimate reliance boundary.
SUM operationalizes that boundary through explicit restrictions and prohibited uses.
Therefore:
SRBM = Where reliance stops.
SUM = What use must be constrained because it stops there.
SUM Boundary with SVIM
SUM establishes the limitations.
SVIM ensures that those limitations remain attached when evidence crosses into broader validation governance.
SUM therefore provides a critical input to SVIM.
SUM Boundary with VALIDOS®
SUM does not determine validation sufficiency.
It may establish that simulation evidence:
must not independently be used to support a Validation Determination.
VALIDOS® then determines whether the total evidence basis is sufficient.
Therefore:
Simulation Use Limitation ≠ Validation Determination.
SUM Boundary with SOGS
SOGS governs limitations associated with what simulation outputs themselves mean.
SUM governs limitations on evidential use after those outputs have become qualified Simulation Evidence.
Therefore:

Output Limitation ≠ Evidence Use Limitation.
An output limitation may become an input into SUM, but the governed spaces remain distinct.
SUM Boundary with SRCS
SRCS governs simulation-to-reality correlation.
SUM may impose use limitations based upon the correlation conditions established by SRCS.
It does not determine correlation itself.
SUM Boundary with ORA™
ORA™ governs Operational Reality.
SUM may prohibit or restrict claims about Operational Reality where simulation evidence does not support them.
It does not define Operational Reality.
SUM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SUM does not govern general evidence integrity.
INTEGROS® may govern whether evidence and limitations retain integrity through processing or transfer.
SUM governs what limitations must exist and remain associated with simulation evidence.
SUM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit whether limitations were preserved, communicated, or followed.
SUM defines the simulation-specific limitations that should govern evidence use.
SUM Boundary with AGA™
AGA™ governs who holds responsibility and accountability for decisions involving evidence.
SUM governs what simulation evidence may legitimately be used to support.
It does not assign accountability for violating a limitation. SUM Boundary with AIG® / ASGA™
SUM may constrain claims derived from simulations of AI or autonomous systems.
It does not govern the actual deployed system's behavior, autonomy, authority, permissions, or operational constraints.

Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SUM implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Input
Receive qualified, weighted, reliance-bounded Simulation Evidence. 2. Intended Use Identification
Define how the evidence is intended to be interpreted or used. 3. Limitation Source Identification
Identify the simulation conditions creating material use limitations. 4. Permitted Use Conditions
Define conditions under which use remains legitimate. 5. Restriction Definition
Identify materially restricted uses. 6. Exclusion Definition
Identify contexts, conditions, objects, scenarios, or claims outside the evidence basis. 7. Unsupported Interpretation Assessment
Identify interpretations that exceed the governed meaning. 8. Prohibited Use Definition
Define uses that cannot legitimately proceed on the existing simulation evidence basis. 9. Persistence Control
Ensure material limitations remain linked to evidence through communication, aggregation, transformation, and transfer. 10. Limitation State and Review
Assign a governed limitation state and identify conditions requiring reassessment.
Governance Outputs

SUM may produce: Simulation Intended Use Record Simulation Permitted Use Condition Simulation Evidence Restriction Record Simulation Evidence Exclusion Record Unsupported Interpretation Record Prohibited Simulation Evidence Use Record Simulation Extrapolation Limitation Simulation Decision-Class Limitation Simulation Configuration Limitation Simulation Scenario Limitation Simulation Environmental Limitation Simulation Temporal Limitation Simulation Uncertainty Limitation Simulation Evidence Dependency Limitation Simulation Limitation Persistence Record Simulation Use Limitation State Governed Simulation Use Limitation Record
These outputs provide the limitation basis required by:
SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module.
Enterprise Application
SUM enables organizations to solve a critical problem that occurs after simulation evidence has already been produced correctly:
the evidence may be governed correctly at its source but used incorrectly downstream.
A simulation team may clearly understand that a result applies only to: one configuration; one scenario family; one environment; one parameter range; one model version; one uncertainty range.
But after the result enters a dashboard, management report, validation package, regulatory submission, engineering decision, or automated evidence pipeline, those qualifications may disappear.
The result may remain numerically identical while its organizational meaning becomes distorted.
SUM prevents that separation.

For a spacecraft simulation, evidence concerning a defined landing envelope must not silently become evidence for all landing conditions.
For an autonomous vehicle, millions of successful simulated scenarios must not be represented as proving unrestricted real-world safety where the simulation did not represent all materially relevant conditions.
For a robot, evidence produced for one sensor, actuator, payload, software, and environmental configuration must not automatically transfer to another configuration.
For engineering simulation, results generated within defined physical assumptions and parameter ranges must not be presented as universal physical behavior.
SUM therefore ensures that organizations preserve not only:
the simulation result
but also:
the rules governing what that result may legitimately be used to mean.
Foundational Principles
A material use limitation is part of the evidential meaning.
Reliance boundaries must become operational use controls.
Evidence must not travel without the limitations that govern it.
Failure not observed does not mean failure impossible.
Simulation success does not independently establish operational safety.
Scenario success does not establish universal performance.
Comparative evidence does not automatically establish absolute performance.
Simulation prediction does not guarantee outcome.
Numerical precision does not create evidential certainty.
Extrapolation must remain identifiable as extrapolation.

Multiple dependent evidence objects must not be represented as independent confirmation.
Summarization must not remove limitations necessary for legitimate interpretation.
A limitation must travel at least as far as the evidence it limits.
Simulation-derived evidence must never become more general, certain, transferable, or authoritative merely because the limitations that originally constrained it have been forgotten.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Use Limitation Module establishes the explicit evidence-use control layer within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by transforming governed reliance boundaries into persistent conditions, restrictions, exclusions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, prohibited uses, and review requirements attached to simulation-derived evidence. Through governance of intended use, permitted-use conditions, configuration, scenario, environmental, parameter, temporal, uncertainty, dependency, extrapolation, decision-class, communication, aggregation, and transfer limitations, SUM prevents simulation evidence from acquiring broader meaning merely through reuse, summarization, organizational transfer, automation, or loss of context. By distinguishing reliance boundaries from use limitations, output limitations from evidential limitations, and simulation-specific restrictions from broader validation determinations, SUM preserves the architectural boundaries of SIMULOS®, VALIDOS®, ORA™, INTEGROS®, ADIT®, AGA™, AIG®, and ASGA™. A simulation limitation is therefore not peripheral commentary: where it materially constrains evidential meaning, it is part of the governed evidence itself and must remain attached for as long and as far as that evidence is used.

Canonical Definition
Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM) is the fifth Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture.
SVIM governs the methodological transfer boundary through which qualified simulation-derived evidence leaves simulation-specific evidence governance and enters broader validation governance.

The Module ensures that Simulation Evidence transferred beyond SIMULOS® retains the identity, provenance, evidential purpose, qualification state, evidential weight, applicability, reliance boundary, uncertainty, dependencies, use limitations, and simulation basis necessary to preserve its legitimate meaning.
SVIM does not determine whether the transferred evidence is sufficient for validation, whether validation criteria have been satisfied, whether a Validation Determination may be issued, or whether operational reliance is justified.
Those questions belong to VALIDOS®.
Its task is narrower and architecturally critical:
to ensure that simulation-derived evidence crosses into broader validation governance without becoming detached from the conditions that define what that evidence legitimately means.
Core Question
How must simulation-derived evidence enter broader validation governance without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning?
Architectural Position
SVIM is the fifth and final module within SERBS.
It follows:
SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → determines what simulation-derived information qualifies as evidence.
SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → determines how much simulation-specific evidential significance it may carry.
SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module → determines how far reliance may legitimately extend.

SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module → determines what uses, claims, interpretations, or generalizations must remain constrained or prohibited.
SVIM then governs the controlled transfer of this complete simulation-specific evidential meaning into broader validation governance.
The sequence is:
Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary → Use Limitation → Validation Interface.
SVIM therefore represents the final simulation-evidence gateway before validation governance begins.
Internal Flow Position
Qualified Simulation Evidence Simulation Evidence Weight Simulation Reliance Boundary Simulation Use Limitations Simulation Evidence Provenance Material Uncertainty → Validation Transfer Purpose Identification → Evidence Package Assembly → Simulation Basis Preservation → Qualification Preservation → Weight Preservation → Boundary Preservation → Limitation Preservation → Uncertainty Preservation → Transfer Completeness Assessment → Validation Interface State → Simulation Validation Interface Package → VALIDOS® Validation Governance
Operational Space
SVIM governs the space between:
completed simulation-specific evidence governance
and
entry into broader validation governance.

This operational space includes: validation transfer purpose; evidence package identity; transferred evidence identity; simulation evidence provenance; originating Simulation Object linkage; simulation lifecycle traceability; evidential purpose preservation; qualification-state preservation; evidence-weight preservation; applicability preservation; reliance-boundary preservation; use-limitation preservation; uncertainty preservation; dependency disclosure; inference disclosure; correlation-basis preservation; negative-evidence preservation; contradictory-evidence preservation; transfer completeness; transfer versioning; evidence-package status; receiving validation context; validation-interface state; re-entry following evidence change.
Operational Scope
SVIM applies whenever simulation-derived evidence is transferred into a broader process intended to determine, support, challenge, reconsider, or inform: validation; system qualification; engineering acceptance; scientific validation; safety validation; mission validation; performance validation; deployment validation; operational readiness; regulatory validation; design validation; infrastructure validation; AI validation; autonomous-system validation; other governed validation processes.

It applies regardless of whether the transferred evidence originates from: one simulation; repeated simulations; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; large simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; mission simulations; safety simulations; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies.
SVIM remains technology-neutral. Simulation Evidence Governance ≠ Validation Governance
SVIM enforces the architectural distinction:
Simulation Evidence Governance ≠ Validation Governance
SIMULOS® may establish: what evidence exists; what proposition it addresses; how it was produced; what it legitimately means; what simulation-specific weight it carries; where reliance upon it stops; what limitations constrain its use.
SIMULOS® must not then make the separate determination:
Is the complete validation basis sufficient?
That question belongs to VALIDOS®.
The interface exists precisely because these are different governance spaces.
Interface Principle
SVIM establishes:
A validation interface must transfer evidential meaning, not merely evidence content.
A simulation result copied into a validation package without its governing conditions is not methodologically equivalent to the governed evidence object from which it originated.
Therefore:
Transferred Result ≠ Transferred Evidential Meaning
unless the material simulation-specific evidence conditions are preserved.

Validation Transfer Purpose
Every SVIM transfer should identify why simulation evidence is entering validation governance.
The transfer purpose may include: supporting a validation criterion; challenging a validation proposition; supplementing empirical evidence; supporting comparative validation; identifying unresolved uncertainty; demonstrating bounded simulated behavior; documenting failure conditions; contributing to a safety argument; supporting mission readiness evaluation; informing operational readiness; supporting a broader validation determination.
The transfer purpose must not silently expand the evidential purpose originally established under SEQM.
Simulation Validation Interface Package
SVIM establishes the Simulation Validation Interface Package as the governed transfer object between SIMULOS® and broader validation governance.
A package may contain one or multiple Simulation Evidence objects.
At minimum, where materially relevant, the package should preserve:
Evidence Identity → What simulation-derived evidence is being transferred?
Evidential Purpose → What proposition was the evidence qualified to address?
Simulation Basis → From which governed simulation conditions did the evidence originate?
Provenance → Which outputs, executions, scenarios, models, inputs, assumptions, and object configurations produced it?
Qualification State → Is the evidence Qualified, Conditionally Qualified, Suspended, or otherwise governed?

Evidence Weight → What simulation-specific evidential significance was assigned?
Applicability → Where does the evidence apply?
Reliance Boundary → How far may simulation-specific reliance legitimately extend?
Use Limitations → What uses, interpretations, claims, or generalizations remain constrained?
Uncertainty → What uncertainty materially affects evidential meaning?
Correlation Basis → What simulation-to-reality relationship supports or constrains the evidence?
Dependencies → Which common models, assumptions, inputs, scenarios, or other dependencies affect independence?
Temporal Applicability → When does the evidence remain applicable? Evidence Content ≠ Evidence Context
SVIM establishes:
Evidence Content ≠ Evidence Context
A numerical value, chart, probability, trajectory, success rate, failure rate, confidence interval, comparison, or simulation conclusion may be correctly copied while its evidential meaning is incorrectly transferred.
For example:
99.97% simulated success
without: scenario domain; model basis; environmental representation; excluded conditions; failure treatment; uncertainty; object configuration; correlation basis;
does not preserve the original governed evidential meaning.
SVIM therefore treats contextual preservation as part of transfer governance.
Provenance Preservation
Simulation evidence entering validation must remain traceable to its originating simulation basis.
Where materially relevant, SVIM preserves:

Simulation Evidence → Simulation Output → Execution Record → Scenario → Input Basis → Model & Environment → Assumptions → Reality Representation → Purpose & Scope → Simulation Object
and, where applicable:
Simulation Evidence → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis
SVIM does not replace general provenance or integrity governance.
It ensures that the simulation-specific provenance required to understand the evidence remains available at the interface.
Qualification Preservation
An evidence object must not acquire a stronger qualification state merely because it enters validation.
Therefore:
Conditionally Qualified Simulation Evidence must not become Unconditionally Qualified Validation Evidence
through transfer alone.
Likewise:
Qualification Suspended
must remain visible to the receiving validation process.
Transfer does not repair qualification deficiencies.
Evidence Weight Preservation
SVIM requires simulation-specific evidential weight to remain visible during transfer.
A validation process may subsequently evaluate the evidence differently within the complete validation basis.
But it must be able to identify the simulation-specific weight established under SEWM and the basis supporting that determination.
Therefore:
Validation Entry ≠ Automatic Evidence Weight Increase.
Reliance Boundary Preservation
The reliance boundary established under SRBM must remain attached to the evidence entering validation.
If evidence applies only to:

Object Version V3 + Scenario Family S7 + Environment E4 + Parameter Range P2
the validation process must receive that boundary.
The transfer must not silently convert it into evidence applicable to:
all object versions + all scenarios + all environments + unrestricted parameter ranges.
Use Limitation Preservation
All material SUM limitations must remain available at the validation interface.
These may include: prohibited generalization; prohibited extrapolation; configuration restriction; scenario restriction; environmental restriction; temporal restriction; uncertainty limitation; decision-class limitation; comparative-only use; prohibition against independent safety claims; requirement for additional empirical evidence.
SVIM establishes:
A limitation omitted at transfer is a limitation no longer capable of governing downstream interpretation.
Uncertainty Preservation
Simulation evidence must not become artificially more certain when transferred.
SVIM therefore requires material uncertainty to remain visible.
This may include uncertainty originating from: reality representation; assumptions; model structure; parameters; inputs; scenarios; execution; outputs; inference; simulation-to-reality correlation.
Validation transfer must not convert bounded uncertainty into apparent certainty.
Dependency Preservation
Large simulation campaigns may generate many evidence objects sharing common dependencies.

SVIM requires relevant dependencies to accompany evidence where they affect interpretation.
Examples include: common model; common assumption set; common input source; common scenario generator; common environment model; common transformation; common inference methodology; common correlation basis.
This allows validation governance to distinguish:
multiple evidence objects
from
multiple independent evidence sources.
Negative Evidence Preservation
SVIM must preserve materially relevant negative evidence.
A validation interface must not transfer only: successful runs; favorable outputs; confirming evidence; preferred scenarios.
Material: failures; anomalies; contradictions; divergence; instability; non-convergence; threshold violations; correlation failures;
must remain visible where relevant to the validation proposition.
Validation transfer must not become evidence selection.
Contradictory Evidence Preservation
Where simulation evidence objects materially disagree, the disagreement must cross the interface.
SVIM must not resolve contradiction by simply transferring the preferred evidence object.
The validation process may need to determine the significance of the contradiction.
SVIM's responsibility is to preserve it.
Inference Preservation
Where evidence is derived through inference rather than direct simulation observation, the validation interface must identify that inferential pathway.
The receiving validation process should be able to distinguish:

Direct Simulation Observation
from
Simulation-Derived Inference.
Where materially relevant, the transfer should preserve: originating outputs; inference methodology; transformations; assumptions; aggregation; inference uncertainty; inference limitations.
Correlation Basis Preservation
Where evidence makes or supports claims concerning reality, the relevant SRCS correlation basis should remain available.
This may include: reality reference; comparison conditions; correlation criteria; observed deviations; alignment basis; correlation uncertainty; applicability boundary.
SVIM does not determine whether correlation is sufficient.
It preserves the governed correlation information necessary for the receiving validation process.
Transfer Completeness
SVIM requires assessment of whether the evidence package is sufficiently complete for transfer.
Completeness is purpose-specific.
A package may be incomplete where it lacks materially necessary: evidence identity; evidential purpose; simulation provenance; qualification state; evidence-weight basis; applicability; reliance boundary; limitation; uncertainty; correlation basis; dependency disclosure; negative evidence; temporal applicability.
An incomplete package should not be represented as a complete simulation evidence transfer. Transfer Completeness ≠ Validation Sufficiency
SVIM establishes an important distinction:
Complete Transfer ≠ Sufficient Validation Basis

A perfectly constructed Simulation Validation Interface Package may still provide only a small part of the evidence needed for validation.
Conversely, a validation process may ultimately have sufficient evidence from multiple sources even where simulation evidence contributes only limited weight.
SVIM governs transfer quality.
VALIDOS® governs validation sufficiency.
Validation Interface States
SVIM may assign a governed interface state.
A minimum state model may include: 1. Interface Not Ready
Material evidence conditions required for transfer remain unresolved. 2. Conditionally Transferable
Evidence may enter validation only with explicit unresolved conditions or restrictions. 3. Transfer Ready
The simulation evidence package contains the material simulation-specific information required for governed transfer. 4. Transferred
The governed evidence package has entered the designated validation process. 5. Transfer Review Required
A material change has occurred that may affect evidence meaning after transfer. 6. Transfer Superseded
A newer governed evidence package replaces the previous transfer basis.
These states describe the simulation-validation interface.
They are not validation states. Validation Interface State ≠ Validation State
SVIM must not create a parallel validation determination.
Therefore:
Transfer Ready ≠ Validated
Transferred ≠ Validated
Conditionally Transferable ≠ Conditionally Validated
The interface state answers only:

Is the simulation evidence appropriately constituted for transfer into validation governance?
Versioned Evidence Transfer
Simulation evidence may evolve after: additional executions; model updates; new scenarios; revised assumptions; new reality data; new correlation analysis; evidence requalification; changed evidence weight; revised reliance boundaries; new use limitations.
SVIM should therefore support versioned Simulation Validation Interface Packages.
A new package should not silently overwrite the evidential basis of an earlier validation process.
Evidence Change After Transfer
Where evidence changes materially after transfer, SVIM should support notification or re-entry into the validation interface.
Possible triggers include: qualification suspension; evidence disqualification; degraded weight; changed reliance boundary; newly discovered limitation; contradictory evidence; new simulation failure; new correlation deviation; object change; reality change; resimulation.
The downstream validation basis may need reassessment.
SVIM identifies the interface condition.
VALIDOS® determines the validation consequence.
Interface Re-Entry
Evidence may cross the interface more than once.
The lifecycle may therefore become:
Simulation Evidence → Validation Interface → Validation Governance → New Simulation Evidence / Material Change → Interface Re-Entry → Validation Reassessment
This supports recursive governance rather than one-time evidence transfer.

Machine-Readable Validation Interface
SVIM should support machine-readable evidence transfer where simulation and validation pipelines are automated.
Machine-readable interface fields may include: evidence ID; simulation object ID; object version; evidence version; evidential purpose; qualification state; evidence-weight state; applicability; reliance boundary; use limitations; uncertainty; dependency references; scenario references; execution references; output references; correlation references; temporal applicability; transfer state; supersession relationship.
This allows automated validation systems to ingest simulation evidence without stripping away governance context.
Human-Readable Validation Interface
Machine-readable transfer does not eliminate the need for understandable human interpretation.
SVIM therefore supports human-readable statements such as:
What the evidence shows.
What it does not show.
Under which conditions it applies.
What uncertainty remains.
How strongly the simulation evidence supports the proposition.
Where reliance must stop.
What additional validation may be necessary.
SVIM Boundary with SEQM
SEQM qualifies simulation-derived information as evidence.
SVIM transfers that qualified evidence into validation governance.
SVIM must not independently requalify evidence except where transfer review identifies a condition requiring return to SEQM.
SVIM Boundary with SEWM
SEWM determines simulation-specific evidential weight.

SVIM preserves that weight and its basis during transfer.
It does not determine validation-level evidence weight within the total validation basis.
SVIM Boundary with SRBM
SRBM establishes the simulation reliance boundary.
SVIM preserves that boundary when evidence enters validation.
It does not broaden the boundary.
SVIM Boundary with SUM
SUM establishes evidence-use limitations.
SVIM ensures those limitations survive transfer.
Therefore:
SUM defines the limitation.
SVIM preserves the limitation across the validation boundary.
SVIM Boundary with VALIDOS®
This is the primary architectural boundary governed by SVIM.
SVIM / SIMULOS®: packages simulation-derived evidence; preserves simulation-specific meaning; preserves qualification; preserves evidence weight; preserves applicability; preserves uncertainty; preserves reliance boundaries; preserves limitations; preserves provenance; transfers the evidence.
VALIDOS®: identifies the Validation Object; establishes Validation Purpose & Scope; applies validation criteria; governs validation methodology; evaluates validation evidence fitness; evaluates source reliability; executes validation; issues Validation Determinations; governs Validation States; governs reliance and revalidation.
The boundary is:
SIMULOS® prepares and transfers simulation-derived evidence.
VALIDOS® determines what that evidence means within the complete validation basis.
SVIM Boundary with INTEGROS®
SVIM does not establish general evidence integrity.

INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of the evidence package, records, transformations, and transfer mechanisms.
SVIM governs which simulation-specific evidential conditions must survive the transfer.
SVIM Boundary with ADIT®
ADIT® may audit: whether the transfer occurred; what package was transferred; whether records were preserved; whether evidence conditions were omitted or altered; whether transfer history is reconstructable.
SVIM defines the simulation-specific transfer structure.
It does not own audit governance.
SVIM Boundary with ORA™
Operational Reality information may become relevant to validation.
SVIM does not determine Operational Reality.
It preserves the simulation-specific relationship to reality established through SRCS where that relationship is material to transferred evidence.
SVIM Boundary with AGA™
AGA™ governs responsibility, authority, accountability, and attribution for validation-related decisions.
SVIM does not determine who may approve validation, accept evidence, authorize deployment, or assume operational risk. SVIM Boundary with AIG® / ASGA™
Where simulation evidence concerns AI or autonomous systems, SVIM may transfer that evidence into validation governance.
It does not govern the behavior, authority, autonomy, permissions, constraints, or deployment of the actual AI or autonomous system.
Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum SVIM implementation should establish: 1. Transfer Purpose Identification

Define why the Simulation Evidence is entering broader validation governance. 2. Evidence Package Identification
Identify the precise evidence object or evidence set being transferred. 3. Simulation Basis Preservation
Preserve traceability to the governed simulation lifecycle that produced the evidence. 4. Qualification Preservation
Transfer the current evidence qualification state and qualification basis. 5. Evidence Weight Preservation
Transfer the simulation-specific evidence weight and material factors supporting or constraining it. 6. Reliance Boundary Preservation
Transfer the maximum simulation-specific reliance boundary. 7. Use Limitation Preservation
Transfer material restrictions, exclusions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses. 8. Uncertainty and Dependency Preservation
Transfer material uncertainty and evidence dependencies relevant to interpretation. 9. Transfer Completeness Assessment
Determine whether the package contains the simulation-specific information necessary for governed validation entry. 10. Interface State Assignment
Assign and document the current Validation Interface State. 11. Transfer Record
Record the evidence package version, receiving validation context, transfer state, and material interface conditions. 12. Change and Re-Entry Control
Define conditions requiring updated transfer, supersession, or validation-interface re-entry.
Governance Outputs

SVIM may produce: Simulation Validation Transfer Purpose Statement Simulation Validation Evidence Package Simulation Evidence Transfer Manifest Simulation Basis Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Qualification Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Weight Transfer Record Simulation Reliance Boundary Transfer Statement Simulation Use Limitation Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Dependency Disclosure Simulation Negative Evidence Disclosure Simulation Correlation Basis Transfer Record Simulation Validation Interface State Simulation Validation Interface Package Simulation Evidence Transfer Record Simulation Validation Interface Re-Entry Record
Together these outputs form the governed interface between:
SIMULOS® Simulation Evidence Governance
and
VALIDOS® Validation Governance.
Enterprise Application
SVIM solves a major organizational problem:
simulation teams and validation teams frequently work with the same results but not necessarily with the same evidential meaning.
A simulation team may know that a result: applies only to one configuration; depends upon specific assumptions; covers a defined scenario family; excludes particular environmental conditions; contains significant uncertainty; derives from dependent simulations; has limited reality correlation; supports comparison rather than absolute prediction.
Yet the downstream validation package may contain only:
the final number, graph, success percentage, or conclusion.

At that point the result has crossed organizational boundaries while its governance context has not.
SVIM prevents this loss.
For a space mission, a simulation package transferred into mission validation can retain the exact mission configuration, represented environment, scenario coverage, assumptions, correlation basis, uncertainty, failures, and permitted evidential meaning.
For an autonomous vehicle or robot, millions of simulated scenarios can enter validation together with their shared model dependencies, unrepresented conditions, sim-to-real limitations, failure distributions, scenario boundaries, and evidence-weight assessment.
For engineering systems, simulation-derived structural, thermal, aerodynamic, mechanical, electrical, or reliability evidence can enter validation without becoming detached from the model, parameter range, configuration, assumptions, and conditions that produced it.
SVIM therefore creates a governed handover protocol for evidential meaning .
It enables organizations to use simulation aggressively while preventing the organizational transfer process from silently converting bounded simulation evidence into apparently unrestricted validation evidence.
Foundational Principles
Simulation evidence governance and validation governance are distinct governance spaces.
A validation interface must transfer evidential meaning, not merely evidence content.
Evidence content without evidence context is an incomplete evidential transfer.

Conditional qualification must remain conditional after transfer.
Simulation-specific evidence weight must not increase merely because evidence enters validation.
Reliance boundaries must survive validation transfer.
Use limitations must survive validation transfer.
Material uncertainty must survive validation transfer.
Evidence dependencies must survive validation transfer.
Negative and contradictory evidence must not disappear at the validation boundary.
Transfer completeness is not validation sufficiency.
Transfer Ready does not mean Validated.
A simulation result must not acquire greater certainty, generality, applicability, independence, or authority merely by crossing from simulation governance into validation governance.
SIMULOS® governs the legitimate simulation-specific evidential meaning carried to the boundary; VALIDOS® governs what the complete validation basis can legitimately determine beyond that boundary.
Canonical Closing Statement

Simulation Validation Interface Module establishes the final evidential transfer layer of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by governing how qualified simulation-derived evidence crosses from SIMULOS® simulation governance into broader validation governance without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning. Through preservation of evidence identity, evidential purpose, simulation basis, provenance, qualification state, evidential weight, applicability, reliance boundaries, use limitations, uncertainty, dependencies, inference pathways, correlation basis, negative evidence, contradictory evidence, temporal applicability, transfer state, versioning, and interface re-entry, SVIM prevents bounded simulation evidence from becoming artificially broader, stronger, more certain, or more authoritative through organizational, methodological, or automated transfer. By separating transfer completeness from validation sufficiency and Validation Interface States from Validation States, SVIM preserves the architectural boundary between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS® while enabling simulation-derived evidence to enter validation as a fully contextualized and governable evidential object. The simulation lifecycle therefore reaches the validation boundary not with an isolated result, but with a reconstructable statement of what the evidence is, where it came from, what it supports, how strongly it supports it, where reliance stops, what uncertainty remains, and what th

a reconstructable statement of what the evidence is, where it came from, what it supports, how strongly it supports it, where reliance stops, what uncertainty remains, and what the evidence must never be used to claim.
