OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard - (TRELS)
Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard - (TRELS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard
Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Location Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Location
Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-006
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP®
Canonical Language: English ------------------------------
Canonical Definition
The Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) governs how a temporally situated real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, distributed, or value-affecting event is spatially situated through the identification, differentiation, association, correlation, qualification, and governance of the physical, digital, distributed, and operational locations relevant to that event.
TRELS establishes a governed location representation for the Tax-Relevant Event before jurisdiction-specific taxation rules are applied.

The Standard determines how location information becomes legitimately associated with the governed event, how multiple or conflicting location signals are differentiated, how physical and digital locations coexist, how distributed events are spatially represented, and how location uncertainty, ambiguity, change, and correlation are governed.
TRELS does not determine which country, state, municipality, tax authority, or other legal jurisdiction has the legal right to tax the event.
Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
A governed operational location may subsequently become an input into one or more jurisdiction-specific tax determinations, but TRELS itself does not make that legal determination. ------------------------------ 1. Purpose
The purpose of TRELS is to establish a consistent, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral governance structure for determining where a Tax-Relevant Event occurred operationally.
Modern events frequently cannot be represented by a single physical location.
An event may involve: a buyer in one country, a seller in another, a digital platform operated elsewhere, a payment processor in another jurisdiction, cloud infrastructure distributed across multiple regions, an autonomous agent operating without a meaningful human operating location, physical goods moving between locations, digital services consumed remotely, machines communicating across industrial networks, or distributed infrastructure executing different components of the same event.

Without governed Event Location, downstream taxation systems may consume inconsistent, incomplete, technically incidental, or contextually misleading location signals.
TRELS therefore establishes the governed spatial representation of the event before tax law determines whether any particular location creates jurisdictional significance. ------------------------------ 2. Core Question
Where did the governed event occur operationally, and how can its physical, digital, distributed, and correlated locations be represented without converting Event Location into Tax Jurisdiction? ------------------------------ 3. Governance Objective
TRELS shall ensure that Event Location is: operationally grounded, associated with the governed event, distinguishable by location type, sufficiently bounded, traceable to its relevant source, capable of representing multiple locations, capable of representing distributed events, appropriately qualified where uncertain, preserved when conflicting location signals exist, compatible with machine and autonomous activity, and suitable for downstream jurisdiction-specific evaluation.
The Standard shall prevent location information from being prematurely transformed into a legal conclusion regarding taxation authority. ------------------------------ 4. TREGA™ Architecture Governance Flow
TRELS operates as the sixth Parent Standard within the complete TREGA™ Tax-Relevant Event Governance lifecycle:

Real-World / Digital Event ↓ 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard Event Context ↓ 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard Event Recognition ↓ 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard Event Formation & Root Association ↓ 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard Event Boundary ↓ 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard Event Timing ↓ 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard EVENT LOCATION — CURRENT STANDARD ↓ 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Event Participation ↓ 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Value Association ↓ 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Event Relationships ↓ 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Event Determination ↓ 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Event Continuity & Lifecycle ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance
TRELS occupies the governance transition:
Event Timing
↓
EVENT LOCATION
↓
Event Participation
TRETS establishes when the governed event occurred operationally.
TRELS establishes where the governed event occurred operationally.
TREPS subsequently establishes who or what participated in that governed event. ------------------------------ 5. Governed Transition
TRELS governs the transition:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
↓

Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
The incoming event has already been: contextualized, recognized, formed, bounded, and temporally situated.
TRELS adds governed spatial representation without reopening those prior governance determinations unless material evidence requires escalation to the responsible upstream standard.
The output shall be sufficiently spatially governed for Event Participation and later TREGA™ stages. ------------------------------ 6. Event Location Governance
Event Location represents the operational spatial relationship between the governed event and the locations materially relevant to its occurrence.
Location governance may include: physical location, digital location, infrastructure location, execution location, service location, asset location, transaction location, device location, machine location, network-associated location, distributed location, origin or destination location where operationally relevant, and correlated location structures.
A location becomes part of the governed event only where its association with that event can be operationally justified.
Location Availability ≠ Event-Location Relevance.
The mere presence of a location signal does not make that location part of the governed Event Location. ------------------------------ 7. Physical Event Location
TRELS governs physical location where the event or a materially relevant component of the event occurs in physical space.

Physical location may relate to: people, goods, machinery, facilities, infrastructure, assets, operational activities, delivery, production, storage, movement, or physical execution.
Physical Event Location shall be distinguished from addresses or geographic information that are merely administratively associated with an actor.
Registered Address ≠ Physical Event Location by Default.
Participant Residence ≠ Event Location by Default.
Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location by Default.
A location must be connected to the operational reality of the governed event. ------------------------------ 8. Digital Event Location
Digital events may occur without a single meaningful physical event location.
TRELS therefore governs digital location as a distinct spatial representation.
Digital location may include materially relevant: platform environments, service environments, application environments, logical infrastructure regions, cloud regions, digital execution environments, network environments, system domains, virtual operational spaces, or other digitally bounded locations.
Digital location shall not automatically inherit the physical location of the infrastructure on which the digital operation is technically executed.
Server Location ≠ Digital Event Location by Default.
IP Address ≠ Event Location by Default.
Cloud Region ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.

Technical infrastructure may provide location evidence, but its relevance must be governed in relation to the event. ------------------------------ 9. Distributed Event Location
A single governed event may legitimately involve multiple operational locations.
TRELS shall therefore support distributed spatial representation.
A distributed event may involve:
Location A + Location B + Location C
↓
One Governed Distributed Event Location Structure
The Standard shall not force distributed events into an artificial single-location representation where operational reality does not support one.
Distributed Event Location may include: simultaneous locations, sequential locations, complementary locations, origin and destination locations, execution and consumption locations, machine-to-machine locations, physical-digital combinations, and infrastructure-spanning locations.
Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default.
Whether multiple operational activities constitute one event or several events remains governed by TREGA™ Event Formation and Event Boundary rules. ------------------------------ 10. Location Signal Governance
TRELS may receive location signals from multiple sources.

Examples include: GPS data, device location, IP-derived location, network information, platform records, logistics records, facility records, machine telemetry, cloud infrastructure metadata, payment records, shipping information, delivery information, user-declared location, contractual information, asset records, and operational system data.
Each location signal shall be evaluated according to its relationship to the governed event.
Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Location.
A technically precise signal may still be operationally irrelevant.
A less technically precise signal may be operationally material.
TRELS therefore governs relevance before location is incorporated into the governed event representation. ------------------------------ 11. Location Source Differentiation
Location sources shall remain distinguishable where their meaning, origin, precision, or operational function differs.
The governed representation should preserve, where materially relevant: source type, source origin, observed location, declared location, inferred location, derived location, correlated location, precision, confidence, temporal applicability, and relevant qualification.
Location normalization shall not destroy materially relevant source distinctions.
Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence. ------------------------------ 12. Event Location Correlation
Some Event Locations cannot be established through one direct location signal.
TRELS therefore governs location correlation.

Location correlation may combine multiple operational signals to establish a coherent spatial representation.
For example:
Device Location + Operational Record + Asset Position + Network Signal + Delivery Record
↓
Correlated Event Location
Correlation shall not create unsupported spatial certainty.
Where correlation remains probabilistic or incomplete, the governed Event Location shall preserve that qualification.
Location Correlation ≠ Permission to Manufacture Precision. ------------------------------ 13. Location Precision
Event Location shall be represented at the level of spatial precision justified by the available operational information.
Possible levels may include: exact coordinate, facility, site, building, city, region, country, digital environment, infrastructure region, distributed spatial structure, or another operationally appropriate representation.
TRELS shall not require artificial precision.
Technical Location Precision ≠ Operational Location Precision.
If the event can legitimately be located only to a region, the governed record shall not manufacture a specific address or coordinate. ------------------------------ 14. Location Ambiguity
Location ambiguity exists where multiple spatial interpretations remain operationally plausible.
TRELS shall preserve ambiguity where it cannot legitimately be resolved.
A governed Event Location may therefore be: established, qualified, distributed, conflicting, uncertain, or unresolved.

Location Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Location Selection.
Downstream systems shall be able to distinguish established spatial facts from qualified or unresolved spatial interpretations. ------------------------------ 15. Conflicting Location Signals
Different systems may produce conflicting location information.
Examples include: device location conflicting with declared location, shipping origin conflicting with transaction records, platform location conflicting with infrastructure metadata, machine telemetry conflicting with facility records, or digital service records indicating multiple execution regions.
TRELS shall require conflicts to be identified rather than silently collapsed.
Conflict resolution shall be based on governed operational relevance, not convenience for downstream taxation.
Location Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Tax-Advantageous Location. ------------------------------ 16. Location Change
Events may move through space during their lifecycle.
Examples include: transported goods, mobile machinery, autonomous vehicles, moving devices, distributed computing workloads, migrating cloud processes, or services executed across changing infrastructure environments.
TRELS shall preserve materially relevant location change where required to represent the event accurately.
A changing location does not automatically create a new event.
Location Change ≠ New Event by Default.

Event identity and boundary remain governed by the relevant upstream TREGA™ standards. ------------------------------ 17. Machine and Autonomous Event Location
Machine-generated and autonomous events may produce complex spatial structures.
A machine or autonomous agent may: initiate activity in one environment, execute through another, interact with physical infrastructure elsewhere, consume digital services across distributed infrastructure, and complete an operational event without a directly involved human actor.
TRELS shall distinguish between: machine physical location, machine operational location, autonomous execution environment, infrastructure location, network location, digital service location, and other materially relevant spatial signals.
Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Autonomous Execution Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
The governed Event Location shall represent operational reality rather than assuming that the physical position of a server, robot, device, or autonomous agent independently determines the event's legal jurisdiction. ------------------------------ 18. Physical-Digital Hybrid Events
Many modern events cross physical and digital spaces.
Examples include: e-commerce, digitally controlled manufacturing, autonomous logistics, smart infrastructure, remote professional services, IoT transactions, digital asset operations linked to physical assets, and AI-mediated commercial activity.

TRELS shall allow both physical and digital location dimensions to coexist within the same governed Event Location.
Physical Location ≠ Digital Location.
Neither dimension shall automatically override the other.
Their operational relevance depends on the structure of the governed event. ------------------------------ 19. Event Location States
TRELS may assign governance states including: Location Ready
Sufficient location information exists to begin location governance.
Location Under Governance
Location signals are being identified, differentiated, associated, or correlated.
Location Qualified
A location representation exists but requires explicit qualification.
Location Distributed
The event legitimately occupies multiple relevant locations.
Location Conflicted
Material location signals remain inconsistent.
Location Unresolved
Available information is insufficient to establish a legitimate spatial representation.
Location Established
The event has a sufficiently governed operational location representation.
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
The event has completed TRELS sufficiently to proceed to Event Participation governance. ------------------------------ 20. Event Location and Tax Jurisdiction
TRELS establishes operational spatial facts.
Tax jurisdiction is a legal determination performed outside TRELS.

A jurisdiction may later consider: event location, participant location, establishment, residence, destination, origin, place of supply, asset location, consumption location, permanent establishment, economic nexus, statutory sourcing rules, treaty rules, or other jurisdiction-specific legal criteria.
TRELS does not decide how those rules apply.
The same governed Event Location may legitimately be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions.
One Governed Event Location
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
This is a core design principle of TREGA™. ------------------------------ 21. Jurisdiction Readiness
TRELS contributes spatial information required for eventual jurisdiction-specific evaluation.
However:
Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined.
TRELS may establish that an event has: a physical location, multiple physical locations, a digital location, distributed locations, origin and destination locations, correlated locations, or unresolved location components.
It shall not conclude that any location creates legal taxing authority. ------------------------------ 22. Cross-Architecture Governance
TRELS shall preserve architecture ownership boundaries. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture
May establish operational reality from which location facts are derived. OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture
Governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, and provenance associated with relevant actors or objects.

TRELS does not redefine identity through location. ADIT®
Governs evidence and auditability structures supporting location claims.
TRELS consumes relevant evidence without taking ownership of evidence governance. VALIDOS™
May validate relevant location information or methods.
TRELS consumes validation results without taking ownership of validation governance. INTEGROS®
May govern integrity conditions affecting location information.
TRELS does not replace integrity governance. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism
Governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle.
TRELS does not infer value location merely from Event Location. TREGA™
TRELS owns the operational spatial representation of the Tax-Relevant Event. ------------------------------ 23. Governance Requirements
A TRELS-conformant implementation shall:

1. identify location information potentially relevant to the governed event; 2. distinguish physical, digital, distributed, and other operational location types; 3. associate location signals with the governed event; 4. preserve materially relevant location-source distinctions; 5. assess operational relevance before accepting location signals; 6. support multiple legitimate Event Locations; 7. support distributed Event Location; 8. preserve location precision honestly; 9. identify uncertainty and ambiguity; 10. identify materially conflicting location signals; 11. support location correlation where direct location evidence is insufficient; 12. preserve materially relevant location change; 13. support machine-generated and autonomous Event Locations; 14. distinguish technical infrastructure location from operational Event Location; 15. preserve traceability of governed location representations; 16. prevent Event Location from being represented as Tax Jurisdiction; 17. prevent location governance from determining legal taxability; 18. produce a sufficiently governed spatial representation for downstream TREGA™ governance.
------------------------------ 24. Governance Logic
TRELS applies the following canonical logic:
IF a Governed Temporally Situated Event exists AND location signals relevant to that event can be identified THEN those signals shall be differentiated and associated according to their operational role.

IF multiple locations are materially relevant THEN the event shall support a distributed or multi-location representation rather than forcing artificial singularity.
IF location signals conflict THEN the conflict shall be governed, qualified, or preserved rather than silently resolved.
IF location precision exceeds what operational evidence supports THEN the representation shall be reduced to the justified level of precision.
IF an operational Event Location is sufficiently governed THEN TRELS may produce a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event.
TRELS SHALL NOT infer Tax Jurisdiction solely from Event Location. ------------------------------ 25. Minimum Implementation Framework
A minimum TRELS implementation should provide: 1. Location Signal Register
Identifies candidate spatial information. 2. Location Type Classification
Distinguishes physical, digital, distributed, technical, inferred, and other location roles. 3. Event-Location Association
Connects legitimate location information to the governed event. 4. Location Source Record
Preserves materially relevant source information. 5. Location Precision Record
Defines justified spatial precision. 6. Location Conflict and Ambiguity Record
Preserves unresolved or conflicting spatial information. 7. Distributed Location Structure
Represents events spanning multiple locations. 8. Location Correlation Structure
Documents legitimate correlation between spatial signals. 9. Location Governance State

Records the current governance status. 10. Event Location Output
Produces the governed spatial representation passed downstream. ------------------------------ 26. Governance Outputs
TRELS may produce: Governed Event Location, Governed Physical Event Location, Governed Digital Event Location, Governed Distributed Event Location, Event Location Association Record, Location Source Structure, Location Precision State, Location Correlation Record, Location Ambiguity State, Location Conflict Record, Location Change Record, Machine / Autonomous Event Location Structure, Event Location Governance State, and Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event.
These outputs remain operational governance artifacts.
They are not legal tax determinations. ------------------------------ 27. Critical Distinctions
Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Location
Location Availability ≠ Event-Location Relevance
Physical Location ≠ Digital Location
Registered Address ≠ Physical Event Location by Default
Participant Residence ≠ Event Location by Default
Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location by Default
Server Location ≠ Digital Event Location by Default
IP Address ≠ Event Location by Default
Cloud Region ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default
Autonomous Execution Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction
Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default
Location Change ≠ New Event by Default
Technical Location Precision ≠ Operational Location Precision

Location Correlation ≠ Permission to Manufacture Precision
Location Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Location Selection
Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence
Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined
Event Location ≠ Place of Supply Determination
Event Location ≠ Permanent Establishment Determination
Event Location ≠ Tax Nexus Determination
Event Location ≠ Legal Taxability ------------------------------ 28. Enterprise and Infrastructure Application
TRELS may operate as a jurisdiction-neutral Event Location layer between operational systems and taxation infrastructure.
Example architecture:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Digital Platform / AI Agent / Machine System ↓ TREGA™ Event Layer ↓ TRELS — Governed Event Location ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ Country A Tax Engine / Country B Tax Engine / Country C Tax Engine ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Determination
This allows multiple tax systems to consume the same governed operational event without requiring each system to reconstruct spatial reality independently. ------------------------------ 29. Parent Standard Internal Module Flow
TRELS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1. ELIM — Event Location Identification Module
Identifies location information potentially relevant to the governed event. 2. ELPM — Event Physical Location Module
Governs materially relevant physical Event Locations. 3. ELDM — Event Digital Location Module

Governs materially relevant digital Event Locations. 4. ELDSM — Event Distributed Location Module
Governs events whose legitimate spatial representation spans multiple locations. 5. ELCM — Event Location Correlation Module
Correlates relevant location information into a coherent governed spatial representation.
Internal Module Progression
ELIM — What location information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — Where did the event occur in physical operational space? ↓ ELDM — Where did the event occur in digital operational space? ↓ ELDSM — How is the event represented when it spans multiple legitimate locations? ↓ ELCM — How are relevant location dimensions correlated into a coherent governed Event Location? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
The modules shall preserve the distinction between operational spatial governance and jurisdiction-specific legal interpretation. ------------------------------ 30. Relationship to the Next Parent Standard
TRELS passes its governed output to:
TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard
The transition is:
Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ TRELS — Event Location Governance ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ TREPS — Event Participation Governance
TRELS answers:
Where did the event occur operationally?
TREPS subsequently answers:
Who or what participated in the event, and in what operational role?

TREPS does not convert Event Location into participant identity, and TRELS does not infer Event Participation merely from spatial presence. ------------------------------ 31. Canonical Boundary
TRELS owns the governance of the operational spatial representation of a Tax-Relevant Event, including: Event Location identification, physical Event Location, digital Event Location, distributed Event Location, location-source differentiation, location association, location correlation, spatial precision, location ambiguity, location conflict, materially relevant location change, machine and autonomous Event Location, and readiness for Event Participation governance.
TRELS does not own: Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Root Association, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, participant identity, taxpayer determination, value lifecycle governance, final Value Association, Event Relationships, final Event Determination, tax jurisdiction, tax nexus, place-of-supply determination, permanent-establishment determination, legal tax point, tax period, tax base, tax rate, exemptions, deductions, legal taxability, tax liability, filing obligations, reporting obligations, collection, payment, or enforcement.
Those responsibilities remain with their respective TREGA™ standards, other OOF® architectures, or jurisdiction-specific legal and taxation systems. ------------------------------
Canonical Closing Statement

TRELS governs where the event occurred as governed operational reality — not which jurisdiction has the legal authority to tax it.
Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard (TREPS) governs how human, organizational, digital, machine, autonomous, infrastructural, and other materially relevant actors are represented as participants in a spatially and temporally governed Tax-Relevant Event. TREPS establishes the governance conditions under which an actor may legitimately be associated with the event, distinguished from other actors, represented according to its operational participation, and maintained as part of the governed event representation. TREPS governs participation in the event. It does not determine whether a participant is legally a taxpayer, taxable person, liable party, beneficial owner, permanent establishment, tax representative, withholding agent, employer, employee, supplier, customer, or any other jurisdiction-specific legal or tax status.
The foundational distinction is: Participant ≠ Taxpayer TREPS establishes the governed participation layer required before downstream tax systems determine what legal significance, if any, attaches to that participation. Purpose The purpose of TREPS is to ensure that materially relevant participation in a Tax-Relevant Event can be represented consistently across human, organizational, digital, autonomous, and machine-mediated economies.

Modern events may involve: individuals; companies; public organizations; platforms; intermediaries; service providers; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machines; software services; digital infrastructure; and combinations of these actors. The existence of an actor near, inside, connected to, recorded by, or technically involved with an event does not by itself establish governed participation.
TREPS therefore establishes the methodological layer between: Actor Association → Governed Event Participation → Jurisdiction-Specific Legal Interpretation Its purpose is to preserve operational participation before legal systems assign jurisdiction-specific meaning to it. Core Question Who or what materially participated in the governed event, and how can that participation be represented without converting operational participation into taxpayer status, legal identity, tax residence, liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion? Governance Objective

TREPS shall ensure that Event Participation is: attributable to the governed event; operationally justified; distinguishable by participant; capable of representing different participation roles; compatible with human and non-human actors; capable of representing multiple participants; compatible with distributed and autonomous activity; traceable; continuity-aware; uncertainty-aware; jurisdiction-neutral; and suitable for subsequent Value Association governance. TREPS shall prevent participation data from being prematurely converted into legal tax conclusions. TREGA™ Architecture Governance Flow TREPS occupies the seventh Parent Standard position within the complete

TREGA™ governance lifecycle: Real-World / Digital Event → 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard — CURRENT → 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard → 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard → 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard → 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine → Tax Determination → Reporting / Compliance
TREPS therefore occupies the canonical position: Event Location → Event Participation → Value Association TRELS governs where the event occurred. TREPS governs who or what participated in that event. TRVAS subsequently governs which governed value results are associated with the event. Governed Transition
TREPS receives: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event from TRELS.
TREPS governs participation within that event and produces: Governed Participatory Event

The canonical transition is: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event → Governed Participatory Event The resulting event has sufficient governed participation structure to proceed to TRVAS.
Governed Space
TREPS governs Tax-Relevant Event Participation as an architecture-level space.
This includes governance of: participant presence within the event; participant identification requirements; participation differentiation; participation roles; actor-event association; multiple-participant structures; human participation; organizational participation; digital participation; machine participation; autonomous participation; participation continuity; participation change; participation uncertainty; participation conflict; and participation traceability.
The detailed operational mechanisms for these areas belong to TREPS Core Modules.
Participation Principle
An actor becomes a governed Event Participant only where its relationship to the bounded event is sufficiently supported to justify participation representation.
Mere association is insufficient.
Therefore:
Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Examples of insufficient standalone indicators may include: appearing in a database; receiving a notification; being geographically present; owning infrastructure; owning a participating machine; operating a platform; appearing on a payment record; holding an account; being named in a contract; or being technically connected to an event.

Such information may support participation governance.
It does not automatically establish participation.
Participant Diversity
TREPS shall remain neutral to the nature of the participant.
A participant may be:
Human
Organization
Digital System
Software Service
Platform
AI Agent
Autonomous System
Robot
Machine
Infrastructure System
Machine-to-Machine Actor
Other Governable Actor
TREPS shall not require human participation for an event to possess governed participation.
This is essential for autonomous and machine economies.
Economic Participation ≠ Human Participation by Default.
Multi-Participant Events
A single Tax-Relevant Event may contain multiple participants.
TREPS shall support:
One Event
↓
Multiple Governed Participants
without assuming that every participant has the same operational role, legal status, economic interest, responsibility, or downstream tax significance.
Likewise:
Multiple Participants ≠ Multiple Events by Default.
Event multiplicity remains governed through Event Formation and Event Boundary.
Participation Roles
Participants may perform materially different operational functions within the same event.
TREPS shall require participation to be capable of role differentiation where such differentiation is necessary to represent the event faithfully.
However, operational participation roles shall remain separate from jurisdiction-specific legal classifications.
Operational Participation Role ≠ Legal Tax Role.

A role governed by TREPS does not automatically establish that an actor is legally: seller; buyer; taxpayer; employer; employee; principal; agent under law; permanent establishment; taxable person; beneficial owner; withholding agent; importer; exporter; or another legally defined party.
Such legal classifications remain downstream.
Participation and Identity
Participation requires sufficient actor differentiation to preserve the integrity of the event.
TREPS does not, however, own the complete governance of identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, or provenance.
Those governance spaces remain with OBIDENITY® where applicable.
The canonical distinction is:
Participation ≠ Identity Governance.
TREPS governs:
which actor participates in the event and in what operational participation relationship.
OBIDENITY® governs:
the governed identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance structures associated with that actor.
TREPS may consume governed identity information without redefining it.
Participation and Location
TRELS establishes where the event occurred.
TREPS shall not infer participation merely because an actor is located at or near an Event Location.
Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation by Default.
Likewise, remote participation may be legitimate even where the participant is physically located elsewhere.
Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default.

Spatial proximity is evidence of possible association, not automatic proof of participation.
Participation and Event Timing
Participation may begin, change, pause, resume, or end during the governed event.
TREPS shall support participation structures that remain compatible with Event Timing governed under TRETS.
However:
Participation Timing ≠ Event Timing Governance.
TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing.
TREPS governs only the relationship between participation and that governed temporal structure.
Participation and Event Boundary
Only participation materially associated with the bounded event may become part of the TREPS representation.
TREPS shall not expand Event Boundary merely because additional actors can be technically or commercially associated with the event.
Actor Association ≠ Event Boundary Expansion.
TREBS remains authoritative for Event Boundary.
Machine and Autonomous Participation
TREPS shall support events in which machines or autonomous systems materially participate without contemporaneous human action.
Examples may include: autonomous purchasing; machine-to-machine contracting workflows; automated resource acquisition; autonomous logistics; robotic production; AI-mediated service execution; automated financial operations; autonomous infrastructure; and future machine economies.
TREPS shall preserve the operational reality of such participation.

It shall not automatically substitute the machine owner, developer, operator, manufacturer, supervising person, or organization as the operational participant merely because a human or organization exists somewhere in the control or ownership structure.
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner.
Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by Default.
Questions of authority, ownership, accountability, responsibility, and legal attribution remain governed elsewhere.
Participation Continuity
Participation may evolve while the same governed event continues.
Participants may: enter; leave; change operational roles; become inactive; be replaced; act sequentially; act simultaneously; or participate through delegated or automated systems.
TREPS shall preserve materially relevant participation continuity.
Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default.
Whether a new event exists remains governed through Event Formation and Event Boundary.
Participation Uncertainty
TREPS shall permit participation to remain qualified where available evidence does not support complete certainty.
Possible architecture-level participation conditions may include: established; qualified; partial; disputed; conflicted; unresolved; or unknown.
Participation Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Invent a Participant.
Where participation cannot legitimately be established, uncertainty shall remain visible.
Participation Conflict
Different evidence sources may identify incompatible participants or participation roles.

TREPS shall preserve material conflict rather than silently selecting whichever representation best supports a downstream tax outcome.
Participation Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Participant Selection.
Conflict resolution mechanisms are operationalized through the relevant TREPS modules and supporting evidence-governance architectures.
Participation Traceability
Governed Event Participation shall remain reconstructable.
A downstream system should be able to determine: which participants were represented; why their participation was accepted; what operational role was governed; what evidence supported the association; what uncertainty existed; what material changes occurred; and what governance state applied.
TREPS establishes this requirement at Parent Standard level.
Detailed participant-record mechanics belong to the Core Modules.
Participation and Value
Participation alone does not determine which participant owns, receives, creates, transfers, controls, consumes, or benefits from value.
Those questions require separate governance.
The next Parent Standard, TRVAS, governs association of governed value results with the event.
Therefore:
Event Participation ≠ Value Association.
Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default.
Participation Role ≠ Value Entitlement.
VFM® remains authoritative for the Value Lifecycle itself.
Participation and Accountability
Operational participation does not automatically establish responsibility, accountability, fault, or liability.
Therefore:

Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default.
Participation ≠ Accountability.
Participation ≠ Liability.
AGA™ governs accountability structures where applicable.
HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability where applicable.
TREPS preserves participation as an operational fact without converting it into a conclusion about blame or legal responsibility.
Participation and Taxpayer Status
TREPS shall preserve a strict separation between Event Participation and jurisdiction-specific taxpayer determination.
A participant may later be evaluated by a jurisdiction as: taxpayer; taxable person; supplier; customer; employer; employee; withholding party; intermediary; marketplace operator; permanent establishment; reporting party; or another legally defined actor.
TREPS does not make that determination.
The canonical boundary is: Participant ≠ Taxpayer
Likewise:
Participation ≠ Tax Residence.
Participation ≠ Permanent Establishment.
Participation ≠ Tax Nexus.
Participation ≠ Legal Liability.
Participation ≠ Filing Obligation.
Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness
A governed participant structure shall remain reusable across jurisdiction-specific evaluations.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Event
↓
One Governed Participation Structure
↓
Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations
Jurisdiction A may legally classify Participant X one way.
Jurisdiction B may classify the same participant differently.
Jurisdiction C may determine that another participant has the relevant legal obligation.

TREPS preserves the underlying participation reality.
Jurisdictions determine its legal significance.
Governance States
At Parent Standard level, TREPS recognizes participation governance states including:
Participation Ready
Participation Under Governance
Participation Established
Participation Multi-Actor
Participation Machine / Autonomous
Participation Qualified
Participation Conflicted
Participation Unresolved
Governed Participatory Event
Detailed state transitions and operational conditions belong to the Core Modules.
Governance Requirements

TREPS implementations shall ensure that: participation belongs to a governed event; participants are sufficiently distinguishable; actor-event association is operationally justified; participant roles can be differentiated where necessary; multiple participants can be represented; human and non-human participants can be represented; machine and autonomous participation can be governed; participation can change without automatic Event reformation; participation uncertainty can remain visible; participation conflicts can remain visible; participation remains traceable; participant location is not substituted for Event Location; participation does not redefine Event Boundary; identity governance remains distinct from participation governance; participation does not automatically establish accountability or liability; participation does not automatically establish Value Association; participation does not determine taxpayer status; jurisdiction-specific legal classifications remain downstream; and the resulting participation structure is suitable for subsequent TREGA™ governance.
Governance Logic
TREPS applies the following architecture-level logic:
IF a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event exists, THEN materially relevant actors may be evaluated for Event Participation.
IF an actor's relationship to the event is sufficiently governed, THEN the actor may be represented as a Governed Event Participant.

IF multiple actors materially participate, THEN TREPS shall preserve the multi-participant structure rather than force a single-participant representation.
IF a machine, AI agent, or autonomous system materially participates, THEN non-human participation may be represented without substituting a human participant by default.
IF participation remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN that state shall remain visible.
IF participation is sufficiently governed, THEN TREPS may produce a Governed Participatory Event.
TREPS SHALL NOT convert Event Participation into taxpayer status or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion.
Governance Outputs
TREPS may produce architecture-level outputs including: Governed Event Participation; Governed Participant Structure; Governed Multi-Participant Structure; Governed Participation Role Structure; Governed Human Participation; Governed Organizational Participation; Governed Machine Participation; Governed Autonomous Participation; Governed Participation Continuity; Participation Uncertainty State; Participation Conflict State; Participation Governance State; and the principal Parent Standard output:
Governed Participatory Event
The Governed Participatory Event becomes the input to: TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Critical Distinctions
Participant ≠ Taxpayer
Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default
Economic Participation ≠ Human Participation by Default
Multiple Participants ≠ Multiple Events by Default

Operational Participation Role ≠ Legal Tax Role
Participation ≠ Identity Governance
Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation by Default
Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default
Participation Timing ≠ Event Timing Governance
Actor Association ≠ Event Boundary Expansion
Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner
Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by Default
Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default
Participation Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Invent a Participant
Participation Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Participant Selection
Event Participation ≠ Value Association
Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default
Participation Role ≠ Value Entitlement
Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default
Participation ≠ Accountability
Participation ≠ Liability
Participation ≠ Tax Residence
Participation ≠ Permanent Establishment
Participation ≠ Tax Nexus
Participation ≠ Legal Liability
Participation ≠ Filing Obligation Cross-Architecture Governance Boundaries
TREGA™ Owns Event Participation within the Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle.
ORA™ Governs what actually occurred in operational reality.
OBIDENITY® Governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, and related identity structures.
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle.
AGA™ Governs accountability structures.
HALIA™ Governs the lifecycle of harm and liability.
ADIT® Governs evidence and auditability.
VALIDOS™ Governs validation.
INTEGROS® Governs integrity.

TREPS may consume governed outputs from these spaces where required.
It shall not redefine them.
Enterprise Application
TREPS provides a jurisdiction-neutral participation layer between governed operational events and downstream tax systems.
A generalized enterprise flow is:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Autonomous System / Machine Network
→ TREGA™ Event Layer
→ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
→ TREPS
→ Governed Participatory Event
→ TRVAS — Value Association
→ Remaining TREGA™ Governance
→ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event
→ Country A / Country B / Country C Tax Engines
This architecture allows a single governed representation of who or what actually participated in an event to support multiple legal tax interpretations without embedding one jurisdiction's legal assumptions into the event itself.
Internal Module Architecture
TREPS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1. EPIM — Event Participant Identification Module
Governs identification and differentiation of actors that may legitimately become Event Participants. 2. EPRM — Event Participation Role Module
Governs the operational participation roles through which identified participants act within the event. 3. EPAM — Event Actor Association Module
Governs the association between participants, their governed roles, and the bounded Tax-Relevant Event. 4. EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module

Governs participation structures involving machines, AI agents, autonomous systems, robots, and other non-human operational actors. 5. EPCM — Event Participation Continuity Module
Governs continuity, change, entry, exit, replacement, and material evolution of participation during the event.
The canonical internal module flow is:
EPIM — Participant Identification
↓
EPRM — Participation Role
↓
EPAM — Actor Association
↓
EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance
↓
EPCM — Participation Continuity
↓
Governed Participatory Event Relationship to the Previous Parent Standard
TRELS produces:
Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event
TREPS receives that event and establishes:
Governed Event Participation
The relationship is:
TRELS — Where did the event occur?
→
TREPS — Who or what participated in the event?
Location does not determine participation.
Spatial Presence ≠ Participation by Default.
Relationship to the Next Parent Standard
TREPS produces: Governed Participatory Event
TRVAS subsequently determines which governed value results legitimately associate with that event.
The relationship is:
TREPS — Who or what participated?
→
TRVAS — Which governed value result belongs to the event?
TREPS shall not pre-assign value ownership, value entitlement, tax base, consideration, revenue, benefit, or other downstream value conclusions merely because participation has been established.
Canonical Boundary

TREPS owns the governance of participation within a Tax-Relevant Event, including the architecture-level requirements for participant identification, participation-role differentiation, actor-event association, multi-participant representation, human and non-human participation, machine and autonomous participation, participation continuity, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability.
TREPS does not own Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Root Association, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, Value Lifecycle governance, final Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Event Record Governance, or Event Lifecycle Governance.
TREPS does not determine complete identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, accountability, responsibility, fault, liability, taxpayer status, taxable-person status, tax residence, permanent establishment, tax nexus, place of supply, source jurisdiction, legal situs, Tax Jurisdiction, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, tax base, deduction, exemption, filing obligation, reporting obligation, collection, payment, or enforcement.
Those governance and legal spaces remain outside TREPS.
Canonical Closing Statement
TREPS establishes who or what materially participated in the governed event without allowing operational participation to become legal identity, taxpayer status, responsibility, liability, or tax jurisdiction by default.

Participation establishes involvement in the event. It does not establish the legal tax consequence of that involvement.
Participant ≠ Taxpayer.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard - (TRERS)
Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard - (TRERS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS)
Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition
Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-002
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 29 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection
Canonical Language: English
Canonical Definition
Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) is the Parent Standard within TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ that governs how an observed and sufficiently contextualized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is evaluated and recognized as a legitimate candidate for further tax-relevant event governance.

TRERS establishes the governance conditions through which an occurrence is distinguished from background activity, screened for potential tax-event relevance, evaluated against governed recognition criteria, assigned an appropriate recognition confidence or uncertainty condition, and either advanced, withheld, rejected, or escalated for further governance.
Recognition under TRERS does not establish that a Tax-Relevant Event has been fully formed.
It does not establish that the occurrence is legally taxable.
It does not determine jurisdiction, taxpayer status, tax nexus, tax base, tax rate, liability, reporting obligation, or any other jurisdiction-specific legal tax consequence.
Its task is narrower and foundational:
to determine whether an occurrence is sufficiently relevant and sufficiently established to legitimately proceed into Tax-Relevant Event Formation.
Core Question
When should an observed and contextualized occurrence be legitimately recognized as a candidate for further tax-relevant event governance?
Architectural Position
TRERS is the second Parent Standard of TREGA™.
It operates after TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard has established the governed contextual environment surrounding an occurrence and before TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard determines how recognized occurrence components are assembled into a governed event structure.
The architectural transition is:
Governed Event Context
↓
Event Recognition
↓
Candidate Tax-Relevant Occurrence

↓
Event Formation
TRECS establishes the environment necessary to understand the occurrence.
TRERS determines whether that occurrence warrants progression through the architecture.
TREFS subsequently determines what governed event structure can legitimately be formed from it.
This separation is fundamental.
Context-Ready ≠ Event-Recognized.
Event-Recognized ≠ Event-Formed.
Event-Recognized ≠ Legally Taxable.
Governance Flow Position
Within the complete TREGA™ governance flow:
Real-World / Digital Event
↓
Event Context
↓
Event Recognition
↓
Event Formation & Root Association
↓
Event Boundary
↓
Event Timing
↓
Event Location
↓
Event Participation
↓
Value Association
↓
Event Relationships
↓
Event Determination
↓
Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
↓
Event Continuity & Lifecycle
↓
Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event
↓
Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine
↓
Tax Determination
↓
Reporting / Compliance
TRERS owns:
Contextualized Occurrence
↓
Event Recognition
It does not own:
Event Recognition
↓
Event Formation
and it does not own any downstream legal taxation determination.
Operational Space
TRERS governs Tax-Relevant Event Recognition.

Its operational space includes: occurrence recognition; occurrence differentiation; signal-to-occurrence qualification; potential tax-event relevance screening; recognition criteria; recognition rules; recognition thresholds where methodologically appropriate; recognition confidence; recognition uncertainty; ambiguous occurrence treatment; duplicate recognition risk; machine-generated occurrence recognition; autonomous occurrence recognition; distributed occurrence recognition; recognition escalation; recognition rejection; recognition reconsideration; recognition traceability.
TRERS establishes whether something observed in governed context should legitimately become a candidate input to Event Formation.
Operational Scope
TRERS may apply to occurrences originating from: commercial transactions; financial activity; payments; transfers; production processes; supply chains; service delivery; digital platforms; marketplaces; APIs; software systems; digital assets; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; machine-to-machine activity; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; infrastructure operations; hybrid physical-digital environments; future machine economies.
TRERS remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral.
An occurrence does not require a human initiator to become recognizable.
Nor does machine generation make an occurrence tax-relevant by default.
Occurrence Recognition Principle

Operational systems generate signals continuously.
But:
Signal ≠ Occurrence.
A database update may be a technical signal.
A sensor message may be a technical signal.
An API retry may be a technical signal.
A ledger entry may be a technical signal.
A payment notification may be a technical signal.
TRERS requires that an occurrence be sufficiently distinguishable from the technical or informational signals through which it becomes observable.
This prevents taxation infrastructure from treating every generated record as an independent real-world or economic occurrence. Occurrence ≠ Tax-Relevant Event
Even where an occurrence is sufficiently established, it has not yet necessarily become a governed Tax-Relevant Event.
Recognition is an architectural gateway.
It establishes that the occurrence warrants further governance.
Therefore:
Occurrence Recognized
↓
Eligible for Event Formation
not:
Occurrence Recognized
↓
Tax-Relevant Event Fully Established
and never:
Occurrence Recognized
↓
Tax Legally Due.
Recognition Relevance
TRERS determines whether an occurrence has sufficient potential relevance to the tax-event lifecycle to justify further governance.

Potential relevance may arise from materially relevant: economic activity; exchange; transfer; provision of goods or services; value movement; value change; ownership-related activity; operational activity; digital activity; platform activity; autonomous economic execution; machine-to-machine activity; resource consumption or provision; distributed commercial activity; other occurrences capable of requiring downstream taxation evaluation.
Potential relevance is deliberately broader than legal taxability.
The purpose is to avoid making tax-law conclusions at the recognition stage.
Recognition Criteria
Recognition should be based upon governed criteria rather than arbitrary system behavior.
Relevant criteria may consider whether: an occurrence can be sufficiently distinguished; materially relevant context exists; the occurrence represents more than technical noise; the occurrence has plausible economic, operational, transactional, digital, value-related, or other tax-event relevance; sufficient information exists for further governance; duplicate representation risk has been considered; material uncertainty is identified; the occurrence can be referenced through subsequent stages.
Recognition criteria may vary by implementation environment while remaining governed by the methodological boundaries of TRERS.
Recognition Rules
Organizations and systems may implement recognition rules to identify occurrences requiring TREGA™ processing.

Such rules may be deterministic, probabilistic, AI-assisted, manually governed, or hybrid.
However:
Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule.
A recognition rule determines whether an occurrence should proceed through event governance.
A tax rule determines a legal taxation consequence under a jurisdiction.
The two must remain architecturally separated.
Recognition Confidence
Not every occurrence can be recognized with equal certainty.
TRERS therefore permits Recognition Confidence to express the strength of the governed basis supporting recognition.
Confidence may reflect: source reliability; contextual completeness; signal consistency; corroborating records; occurrence distinguishability; recognition-rule strength; unresolved contradictions.
Recognition Confidence does not represent probability that tax is legally due.
Therefore:
Recognition Confidence ≠ Taxability Probability.
Recognition Uncertainty
Where evidence or context is insufficient, TRERS must preserve uncertainty rather than manufacture recognition certainty.
An occurrence may remain:
Recognition Unresolved
where the available information cannot legitimately support either recognition or rejection.
This is particularly important in fragmented, distributed, autonomous, or cross-border systems where complete information may not be immediately available.
Recognition States
A TREGA™ implementation may represent recognition through governance states such as:

1. Occurrence Observed 2. Occurrence Under Recognition 3. Recognition Unresolved 4. Occurrence Recognized 5. Occurrence Not Recognized 6. Recognition Escalated 7. Recognition Reconsidered
These states represent governance status.
They do not represent legal tax status.
Recognition Rejection
TRERS must permit an occurrence to be rejected from further event governance where it does not satisfy legitimate recognition conditions.
Examples may include: technical noise; duplicate signals; system retries; internal telemetry without relevant economic meaning; corrupted records; irrelevant operational activity; insufficiently established occurrences.
Rejection prevents unnecessary Event Formation.
However:
Recognition Rejection ≠ Legal Non-Taxability Determination.
It means only that the occurrence, as currently represented, does not legitimately proceed through TREGA™ recognition.
Duplicate Recognition Risk
One real-world activity may generate many records.
For example:
Order Created
↓
API Call
↓
Payment Authorization
↓
Payment Confirmation
↓
ERP Entry
↓
Warehouse Signal
↓
Invoice Record
TRERS must avoid assuming that every observable record represents a separate occurrence requiring independent Event Formation.
Conversely, several genuinely distinct occurrences must not be collapsed merely because they share identifiers or systems.
Therefore:
Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Occurrences.
and:
Shared Identifier ≠ Single Occurrence by Default.
Machine-Generated Recognition

Machine environments create recognition challenges because they can generate operational records at volumes far beyond human economic activity.
An autonomous system may produce thousands or millions of: API calls; state transitions; resource allocations; machine instructions; settlement messages; automated purchases; service invocations.
TRERS must distinguish technical execution activity from occurrences that plausibly require further tax-event governance.
Therefore:
Machine Activity ≠ Tax-Relevant Occurrence by Default.
Autonomous Recognition
An occurrence may originate without immediate human intervention.
TREGA™ must therefore permit recognition of activity initiated by: AI agents; autonomous software; robots; automated marketplaces; autonomous infrastructure; machine coordination systems.
TRERS does not determine legal personhood, identity, responsibility, taxpayer status, or liability of those systems.
It determines only whether an occurrence produced through such an environment warrants further event governance.
Distributed Occurrence Recognition
One occurrence may become visible through several systems or locations.
No single record may contain the complete representation.
TRERS must therefore support recognition where evidence of an occurrence is distributed across:
Platform A
↓
Payment System B
↓
Infrastructure C
↓
Enterprise System D
Recognition may legitimately depend upon governed combination of contextualized signals.
However:

Distributed Evidence ≠ Multiple Events.
Recognition Escalation
Some occurrences cannot be legitimately recognized or rejected automatically.
TRERS must permit escalation where: evidence conflicts; contextual ambiguity remains material; recognition criteria produce inconsistent results; machine-generated activity cannot be reliably interpreted; duplicate occurrence risk cannot be resolved; the potential significance of incorrect recognition is material.
Escalation may involve additional evidence, another governance mechanism, human review, validation, audit, or another appropriate process.
Escalation exists to preserve methodological legitimacy under uncertainty.
Recognition Reconsideration
Recognition may later require reconsideration where: new evidence becomes available; context is corrected; duplicate records are discovered; a previously unresolved occurrence becomes sufficiently established; the original recognition basis is shown to be materially incorrect.
Reconsideration must remain traceable.
A changed recognition outcome should not silently erase the earlier governance state.
Recognition Traceability
A recognized occurrence should remain traceable to the basis upon which recognition occurred.
Where materially required, the system should preserve: relevant context; recognition criteria; recognition rule or method; supporting evidence references; uncertainty; confidence; escalation; reconsideration.

This allows later stages to understand why the occurrence entered Event Formation.
Recognition Independence from Tax Rules
TRERS must remain capable of recognizing an occurrence independently of the jurisdiction-specific tax rule eventually applied to it.
This is essential because the same governed occurrence may later be evaluated by different taxation systems.
The recognition layer should not have to reconstruct operational reality whenever tax legislation changes.
Therefore:
Tax Rule Change ≠ Occurrence Recognition Change by Default.
Jurisdiction-Neutral Recognition
An occurrence may have characteristics relevant to several jurisdictions.
TRERS may preserve those characteristics.
It does not decide which jurisdiction has legal authority to tax.
Therefore:
Cross-Border Recognition ≠ Jurisdiction Determination.
A single recognized occurrence may later support multiple legitimate jurisdictional evaluations.
Recognition Readiness
An occurrence becomes recognition-ready when sufficient context and information exist to evaluate whether it should proceed through TRERS.
Recognition readiness does not itself establish recognition.
Therefore:
Recognition-Ready ≠ Recognized.
Similarly:
Recognized ≠ Formed.
and:
Formed ≠ Taxable.
These distinctions preserve the sequential integrity of TREGA™.
Governance Boundary with TRECS
TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard governs the environment necessary to understand the occurrence.
TRERS consumes that governed context.
TRECS asks:

What surrounding conditions are necessary to understand what happened?
TRERS asks:
Does the contextualized occurrence legitimately warrant further tax-relevant event governance?
Therefore:
Event Context ≠ Event Recognition.
Governance Boundary with TREFS
TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard begins after legitimate recognition.
TRERS does not determine the complete components, root association, dependencies, or structural composition of the governed event.
TRERS determines whether Event Formation should begin.
Therefore:
Recognition ≠ Formation.
Governance Boundary with TREDS
TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard later determines whether the fully governed structure is sufficiently established as a Tax-Relevant Event suitable for downstream taxation analysis.
TRERS performs a much earlier gateway function.
Therefore:
Event Recognition ≠ Event Determination.
Recognition means:
this occurrence warrants further governance.
Determination may later establish:
a sufficiently governed Tax-Relevant Event exists.
Neither statement means:
tax is legally due.
Cross-Architecture Boundary
TRERS may consume governed results from other OOF® architectures where available.
ORA™ may establish what actually occurred operationally.
ASGA™ may govern autonomous-system operation and execution.
OBIDENITY® may govern identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance.
VFM® may govern what happened to value.
CLA® may provide governed classification.

INTEGROS® may govern integrity.
ADIT® may govern evidence and auditability.
VALIDOS™ may validate relevant claims, methods, or results.
AGA™ may govern accountability.
TRERS does not absorb these governed spaces.
Its responsibility remains:
recognition of the contextualized occurrence for progression through TREGA™.
Foundational Principles
Signal ≠ Occurrence.
Occurrence ≠ Tax-Relevant Event.
Context-Ready ≠ Event-Recognized.
Recognition-Ready ≠ Recognized.
Recognized ≠ Formed.
Recognition ≠ Event Determination.
Event Recognition ≠ Taxability Determination.
Potential Tax Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability.
Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule.
Recognition Confidence ≠ Taxability Probability.
Recognition Rejection ≠ Legal Non-Taxability.
Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Occurrences.
Shared Identifier ≠ Single Occurrence by Default.
Machine Activity ≠ Tax-Relevant Occurrence by Default.
Autonomous Execution ≠ Taxability.
Distributed Evidence ≠ Multiple Events.
Correlation ≠ Independent Occurrence.
Recognition Escalation ≠ Recognition Failure.
Recognition Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure.
Cross-Border Recognition ≠ Tax Jurisdiction.
Tax Rule Change ≠ Recognition Change by Default.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
Canonical Closing Statement

Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard establishes the recognition governance layer of TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ by determining when a sufficiently contextualized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence legitimately warrants progression into Tax-Relevant Event Formation. Through governance of occurrence recognition, relevance screening, recognition criteria, recognition rules, confidence, uncertainty, duplicate-recognition risk, machine-generated activity, distributed occurrences, escalation, rejection, reconsideration, and traceability, TRERS prevents raw signals, technical records, system retries, platform activity, autonomous execution, or isolated transactional data from being automatically elevated into governed Tax-Relevant Events. The Standard preserves the architectural distinctions between Signal and Occurrence, Context and Recognition, Recognition and Formation, Recognition and Event Determination, potential tax relevance and legal taxability, and cross-border occurrence characteristics and Tax Jurisdiction. By creating a jurisdiction-neutral recognition gateway between governed operational context and formal Event Formation, TRERS enables human, enterprise, digital, and autonomous economic activity to enter the TREGA™ lifecycle through a consistent methodological process without allowing recognition itself to determine whether tax is legally due.

Module Architecture
→ Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM)
→ Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM)
→ Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM)
→ Event Recognition Confidence Module (ERCM)
→ Event Recognition Escalation Module (EREM)
Related Documents
→ About Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS)
