OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard - (TRETS)
Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard - (TRETS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)
Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Timing
Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-005
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 31 August 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection

Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) governs how a sufficiently bounded real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is temporally situated through governed identification of its operational time, start, completion, duration, and temporal order. TRETS establishes the governance conditions through which a Governed Bounded Event becomes a Governed Temporally Situated Event capable of progressing through subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. It governs the temporal representation of what happened operationally without determining the legal tax point, tax period, filing period, recognition date under tax law, legal timing of tax liability, or any other jurisdiction-specific taxation consequence.
The principal transition governed by TRETS is: Governed Bounded Event → Governed Temporally Situated Event TRETS governs when the event occurred as governed operational reality — not when a jurisdiction decides that the event becomes relevant for taxation under law. ------------------------------ Operational Role
TREBS establishes: What belongs within the governed event and where its structural Event Boundary lies.
TRETS establishes: When that bounded event occurred, began, completed, persisted, and how it is temporally ordered relative to other relevant events.

Its narrow task is: to establish a sufficiently explicit, coherent, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral temporal representation of a Governed Bounded Event so that subsequent TREGA™ governance can operate on an event whose operational temporal position is known without allowing Event Timing itself to determine a legal tax point or tax period. TRETS therefore creates the governed temporal layer between Event Boundary and Event Location. ------------------------------ Core Question When did a Governed Bounded Event occur operationally, and how can its temporal position be governed without converting operational time into a jurisdiction-specific legal tax point? ------------------------------ Governance Flow Governed Bounded Event ↓ Event Time Identification ↓ Event Start Governance ↓ Event Completion Governance ↓ Event Duration Governance ↓ Event Temporal Order Governance ↓ Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------
Governed Space
TRETS governs:
Tax-Relevant Event Timing
This governed space includes the temporal structures necessary to situate an already bounded event within operational reality.

TRETS governs: Event Time identification temporal signal differentiation temporal source association Event Start Event Completion Event Duration temporal sequence temporal order temporal uncertainty temporal conflict temporal qualification distributed event timing machine-generated timing autonomous event timing multi-stage event timing temporal continuity temporal traceability readiness for Event Location governance
TRETS does not determine the legal taxation consequence of any temporal state. ------------------------------ Event Timing Principle
Operational events require temporal representation.
However, different systems may record different times for the same underlying activity.
Examples may include: order creation authorization execution shipment delivery acceptance settlement invoice creation database entry ledger posting API execution machine initiation machine completion system synchronization human confirmation
These timestamps do not automatically represent the governed Event Time.
Therefore:
Recorded Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default.
TRETS determines which temporal information legitimately represents the operational event within the governed event lifecycle. ------------------------------ Operational Event Time
An Operational Event Time represents the governed temporal position of an event within operational reality.

Depending on the event structure, this may require: a single temporal point, multiple temporal points, a start and completion, an interval, a duration, an ordered sequence, or a qualified temporal representation.
TRETS must preserve the temporal structure actually required by the event rather than forcing every event into a single timestamp.
Therefore:
Event Time ≠ Single Timestamp by Default. ------------------------------ Temporal Source Principle
Temporal information may originate from multiple sources.
These may include: physical observations enterprise systems transaction systems payment infrastructure distributed systems digital platforms sensors machines autonomous agents human records external systems synchronized clocks asynchronous logs
A temporal source may provide evidence about Event Timing.
It does not automatically determine Event Timing.
Therefore:
Source Timestamp ≠ Authoritative Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ Event Time Identification
Before Start, Completion, Duration, or Temporal Order can be governed, the relevant temporal representation of the event must be identified.
This requires distinguishing temporal signals associated with the event from timestamps that merely describe: system processing, record creation, synchronization, reporting, later correction, downstream settlement, unrelated activity.
Detailed Event Time Identification belongs to:
ETIM — Event Time Identification Module. ------------------------------ Event Start

Where the event has a meaningful operational beginning, TRETS must govern the Event Start.
Event Start must be grounded in the event's operational structure.
It must not be inferred automatically from: earliest database record, earliest technical log, first associated communication, contract creation, first payment record, or earliest dependency.
Therefore:
Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default.
Detailed Event Start governance belongs to:
ETSM — Event Start Module. ------------------------------ Event Completion
Where the event has a meaningful operational completion, TRETS must establish when the event became operationally complete.
Completion may differ from: payment, invoicing, accounting posting, system closure, reporting, legal acceptance, tax recognition.
Therefore:
Operational Completion ≠ Legal Tax Recognition.
Detailed Event Completion governance belongs to:
ETCM — Event Completion Module. ------------------------------ Event Duration
Some events cannot be represented legitimately by a single temporal point.
They may persist across: seconds, hours, days, months, continuous service periods, production cycles, distributed operations, autonomous execution periods.
TRETS must therefore support governed Event Duration where duration is structurally relevant.
Therefore:
Event Duration ≠ Tax Period.
Detailed Event Duration governance belongs to:
ETDM — Event Duration Module. ------------------------------ Temporal Order

Events may exist within chains, sequences, dependencies, or broader operational structures.
TRETS must support governed temporal ordering where relative order matters.
Examples may include:
Event A
↓
Event B
↓
Event C
or:
Event A ∥ Event B
↓
Event C
Temporal order must distinguish chronological relationship from other relationships.
Therefore:
Temporal Order ≠ Causal Relationship by Default.
Detailed Temporal Order governance belongs to:
ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module. ------------------------------ Point Events
Some events may legitimately be represented by a sufficiently precise operational temporal point.
TRETS permits point representation where the underlying event structure supports it.
However:
Technical Timestamp Precision ≠ Operational Temporal Precision.
A system capable of recording microseconds does not establish that the event itself can legitimately be governed at microsecond precision. ------------------------------ Interval Events
Some events have a meaningful start and completion and must therefore be represented as temporal intervals.
Conceptually:
Event Start
↓
Event Activity
↓
Event Completion
The interval belongs to the operational event representation.
It must not automatically be converted into a jurisdiction-specific taxation period. ------------------------------ Open Events
An event may begin without having reached operational completion.
Such an event may remain:
Temporally Open
until sufficient operational conditions establish completion.

TRETS must not manufacture a completion point merely because downstream systems require one.
Therefore:
Missing Completion ≠ Permission to Invent Completion. ------------------------------ Continuous Events
Certain governed events may represent continuous operational activity rather than discrete instantaneous occurrence.
Examples may include: continuing digital services infrastructure operation continuous machine activity ongoing resource provision autonomous service execution
TRETS must preserve legitimate temporal continuity without automatically dividing the event according to accounting or tax periods.
Therefore:
Continuous Operational Event ≠ Periodic Tax Event by Default. ------------------------------ Multi-Stage Events
A bounded event may contain multiple operational stages.
For example:
Initiation
↓
Processing
↓
Fulfilment
↓
Completion
The existence of multiple temporal stages does not automatically create multiple governed events.
That distinction belongs to prior Event Boundary governance.
Therefore:
Multiple Temporal Stages ≠ Multiple Events by Default. ------------------------------ Distributed Event Timing
A distributed event may occur across systems operating: asynchronously, in different time zones, with different clock precision, with synchronization delays, across multiple infrastructure layers.
TRETS must allow these temporal representations to be reconciled without assuming that one system clock defines the event.
Therefore:

System Clock ≠ Event Clock by Default. ------------------------------ Machine-Generated Event Timing
Machines may produce extremely granular timestamp streams.
One autonomous industrial event may generate thousands or millions of machine timestamps.
TRETS must distinguish machine telemetry from governed Event Timing.
Therefore:
Machine Timestamp ≠ Independent Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ Autonomous Event Timing
Autonomous systems may initiate, execute, modify, and complete activities without direct human temporal intervention.
TRETS applies the same governance principle:
the temporal structure must represent the governed operational event rather than merely the internal execution cycle of the autonomous system.
Therefore:
Autonomous Execution Cycle ≠ Governed Event Timing by Default. ------------------------------ Time-Zone Governance
Operational events may involve systems and participants operating across different time zones.
TRETS must preserve sufficient information to distinguish: recorded local time, normalized time, source time zone, temporal conversion, operational temporal context.
Time-zone normalization must not destroy the original temporal representation.
Therefore:
Normalized Time ≠ Original Recorded Time.
Both may need to remain reconstructable. ------------------------------ Temporal Precision
Event Timing must be represented only at a precision legitimately supported by the governed information.

Possible precision may include: date hour minute second sub-second bounded interval approximate interval qualified temporal range
TRETS must not manufacture false temporal precision.
Therefore:
Available Clock Precision ≠ Justified Event-Time Precision. ------------------------------ Temporal Ambiguity
Multiple plausible temporal interpretations may exist.
TRETS must represent temporal ambiguity explicitly where the available governed information does not support one legitimate interpretation.
Therefore:
Temporal Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Timestamp Selection. ------------------------------ Temporal Conflict
Sources may disagree.
For example: payment system says 23:59, marketplace says 00:01, logistics system says 00:04, autonomous agent log says 23:58.
TRETS must preserve material temporal conflict rather than silently selecting the timestamp most convenient for downstream taxation.
Possible state:
Temporal Conflict ------------------------------ Temporal Uncertainty
Event Timing may be known only within a range.
For example:
14:00–14:10
may be more legitimate than an unsupported claim of:
14:03:27
Therefore:
Qualified Temporal Range > False Temporal Precision.
TRETS permits explicit temporal uncertainty where operational reality requires it. ------------------------------ Temporal Correction
Later information may establish that a temporal representation was incorrect.
Correction must preserve traceability between previous and corrected temporal states.
Therefore:

Event Time Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Temporal correction must not silently rewrite the governed event history. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Event Boundary
TRETS receives a Governed Bounded Event.
It does not use timing information to silently redefine Event Boundary.
If temporal information reveals a material structural problem in the existing boundary, the issue may require governed reconsideration through TREBS.
Therefore:
Event Timing ≠ Event Boundary Governance. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Event Location
Knowing when an event occurred does not establish where it occurred.
A digital event may have precise temporal information while its operational location remains distributed or unresolved.
Therefore:
Event Time ≠ Event Location.
Event Location belongs to:
TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Participation
A timestamp may identify when an actor performed an action.
It does not establish the actor's governed participation role.
Therefore:
Temporal Association ≠ Event Participation Determination.
Participation belongs to TREPS. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Value
A change in value may occur at or around a particular time.
TRETS may preserve the temporal relationship but does not govern the value lifecycle or final Event-to-Value Association.
Therefore:
Event Time ≠ Value Recognition Determination.
VFM® governs the value lifecycle.

TRVAS governs Event-to-Value Association within TREGA™. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Event Relationships
Chronological order may inform later relationship governance.
However:
Earlier Event ≠ Cause of Later Event by Default.
Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship by Default.
Final Event Relationship governance belongs to TRERLS. ------------------------------ Operational Event Time ≠ Legal Tax Point
This is a foundational TRETS boundary.
A jurisdiction may legally define a taxation point according to: supply delivery payment invoice transfer settlement acceptance realization accrual statutory deeming rule another jurisdiction-specific condition
TRETS does not choose among these legal rules.
TRETS establishes the governed operational temporal reality upon which such rules may subsequently operate.
Therefore:
Operational Event Time ≠ Legal Tax Point. ------------------------------ Event Timing ≠ Tax Period Determination
An event occurring on a particular date does not by itself determine the legal tax period to which a jurisdiction assigns the event.
Tax period determination belongs to jurisdiction-specific taxation systems.
Therefore:
Event Timing ≠ Tax Period Determination. ------------------------------ Jurisdiction-Neutral Timing
TRETS must remain jurisdiction-neutral.
The same Governed Temporally Situated Event may subsequently be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions.
Conceptually:
One Governed Event
↓

One Governed Operational Temporal Representation
↓
Jurisdiction A
↓
Legal Tax Timing Rule A
Jurisdiction B
↓
Legal Tax Timing Rule B
Jurisdiction C
↓
Legal Tax Timing Rule C
The operational temporal representation remains stable unless the underlying governed event information itself changes. ------------------------------ Temporal Governance States
TRETS may represent Event Timing through states including:
1.
Timing Ready 2.
Timing Under Governance 3.
Timing Qualified 4.
Timing Conflicted 5.
Timing Unresolved 6.
Timing Established 7.
Governed Temporally Situated Event
These states allow downstream systems to distinguish established timing from qualified or unresolved timing. ------------------------------ Cross-Architecture Boundary
TRETS may consume or interact with governed outputs from other OOF® architectures.
ORA™ may establish operational reality from which temporal information originates.
ADIT® may govern evidence and auditability associated with temporal records.
VALIDOS™ may govern validation of relevant temporal claims or methods.
INTEGROS® may govern broader integrity conditions.
OBIDENITY® may govern identity and origin associated with temporal sources.
VFM® may govern temporal states within the value lifecycle.
TRETS remains responsible specifically for:
the temporal governance of the Tax-Relevant Event within TREGA™. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements
TRETS requires that:
1.
Event Timing begins from a Governed Bounded Event. 2.

relevant temporal signals are distinguished from unrelated system timestamps. 3.
recorded timestamps are not automatically treated as governed Event Time. 4.
temporal sources remain traceable. 5.
Event Start is governed where structurally relevant. 6.
Event Completion is governed where structurally relevant. 7.
Event Duration is governed where structurally relevant. 8.
temporal order is established where materially relevant. 9.
point events and interval events remain distinguishable. 10.
open events may remain temporally open where completion is not established. 11.
continuous events are not automatically divided according to tax or accounting periods. 12.
multi-stage timing does not automatically create multiple events. 13.
distributed-system timestamps are reconciled without allowing one system clock to silently define operational reality. 14.
machine-generated timestamp volume does not determine event multiplicity. 15.
autonomous execution cycles do not automatically determine Event Timing. 16.
original time-zone information remains traceable where relevant. 17.
normalized time does not erase source temporal representation. 18.
temporal precision does not exceed the governed information supporting it. 19.
temporal ambiguity remains explicit. 20.
temporal conflict remains explicit. 21.
temporal uncertainty may be represented as a qualified range. 22.
temporal correction preserves historical traceability. 23.
Event Timing does not silently redefine Event Boundary. 24.

Event Timing does not determine Event Location. 25.
Event Timing does not determine Event Participation. 26.
Event Timing does not govern value lifecycle. 27.
chronological order does not automatically establish Event Relationships. 28.
Operational Event Time remains distinct from Legal Tax Point. 29.
Event Timing remains distinct from Tax Period Determination. 30.
jurisdiction-specific taxation rules do not redefine operational Event Timing by default. 31.
the resulting temporal representation is sufficiently governed before transfer to TRELS.
------------------------------ Governance Logic
TRETS applies the following architecture-level logic:
Has a Governed Bounded Event been established?
If no:
→ Event Timing governance is not ready.
If yes:
→ identify relevant temporal information.
Can operational Event Time be sufficiently distinguished from technical, administrative, reporting, or downstream timestamps?
If no:
→ preserve Timing Qualified, Conflicted, or Unresolved state.
If yes:
→ establish the relevant temporal representation.
Does the event require a governed Start?
If yes:
→ govern Event Start.
Does the event require a governed Completion?
If yes:
→ govern Event Completion.
Is duration materially relevant?
If yes:
→ govern Event Duration.
Is relative temporal order materially relevant?
If yes:
→ govern Event Temporal Order.
Are material temporal conflicts or uncertainties unresolved?
If yes:
→ preserve the appropriate qualified state.
If no:

→ establish the governed temporal representation.
Is the event sufficiently temporally situated for subsequent TREGA™ governance?
If yes:
→ produce Governed Temporally Situated Event.
If no:
→ preserve the appropriate unresolved or qualified state. ------------------------------ Core Modules
TRETS is operationalized through five Core Modules. 1. ETIM — Event Time Identification Module
Governs identification and differentiation of temporal information relevant to the Governed Bounded Event.
Primary question owned by the module: Which temporal signals legitimately describe the operational time of this event? ------------------------------ 2. ETSM — Event Start Module
Governs establishment of the operational beginning of an event where a meaningful Event Start exists.
Primary responsibility: Event Start governance. ------------------------------ 3. ETCM — Event Completion Module
Governs establishment of the operational completion of an event where a meaningful completion state exists.
Primary responsibility: Event Completion governance. ------------------------------ 4. ETDM — Event Duration Module
Governs the temporal interval or duration of events for which duration is materially relevant.
Primary responsibility: Event Duration governance. ------------------------------ 5. ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module
Governs relative temporal ordering of the event against materially relevant events or operational structures.

Primary responsibility: Event Temporal Order governance. ------------------------------ Internal Module Progression
ETIM — What temporal information legitimately belongs to the event?
↓
ETSM — When did the event operationally begin?
↓
ETCM — When did the event operationally complete?
↓
ETDM — What governed temporal duration did the event occupy?
↓
ETOM — Where does the event stand in relevant temporal order?
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event ------------------------------ Transition from TREBS
TREBS provides:
Governed Bounded Event
TRETS receives that bounded event and governs its temporal representation.
The architectural transition is:
Event Boundary
↓
Event Timing
TRETS must not reopen Event Boundary merely because multiple timestamps exist.
Where temporal governance reveals a material structural defect in the Event Boundary, the issue must be returned to the appropriate TREBS governance process. ------------------------------ Transition to TRELS
TRETS produces:
Governed Temporally Situated Event
This becomes the input to:
TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard
The transition is:
Governed Bounded Event
↓
TRETS — Event Timing
↓
Governed Temporally Situated Event
↓
TRELS — Event Location
The next governance question becomes:
Where did the temporally situated event occur operationally?
Not:
Which jurisdiction has the legal right to tax it? ------------------------------
Foundational Principles
Recorded Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default.

Event Time ≠ Single Timestamp by Default.
Source Timestamp ≠ Authoritative Event Time by Default.
Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default.
Operational Completion ≠ Legal Tax Recognition.
Event Duration ≠ Tax Period.
Temporal Order ≠ Causal Relationship by Default.
Technical Timestamp Precision ≠ Operational Temporal Precision.
System Clock ≠ Event Clock by Default.
Machine Timestamp ≠ Independent Event Time by Default.
Autonomous Execution Cycle ≠ Governed Event Timing by Default.
Normalized Time ≠ Original Recorded Time.
Temporal Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Timestamp Selection.
Event Time Correction ≠ Historical Erasure.
Event Timing ≠ Event Boundary Governance.
Event Time ≠ Event Location.
Temporal Association ≠ Event Participation Determination.
Event Time ≠ Value Recognition Determination.
Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship by Default.
Operational Event Time ≠ Legal Tax Point.
Event Timing ≠ Tax Period Determination. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary
TRETS governs the operational temporal representation of a Governed Bounded Event, including Event Time identification, Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, Event Temporal Order, temporal precision, ambiguity, conflict, uncertainty, distributed timing, machine-generated timing, autonomous timing, temporal correction, and readiness for subsequent Event Location governance.

TRETS does not govern: Event Context Event Recognition Event Formation Event Boundary Event Location Tax Jurisdiction Event Participation taxpayer determination value lifecycle final Event-to-Value Association Event Relationship determination final Event Determination legal tax point tax period determination legal taxability tax base tax rate exemptions deductions tax liability reporting obligations payment collection enforcement
TRETS begins with:
Governed Bounded Event
and ends with:
Governed Temporally Situated Event ------------------------------
Canonical Closing Statement
The Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard establishes a governed temporal representation of operational reality before jurisdiction-specific taxation rules interpret that reality.
It ensures that timestamps, system clocks, accounting dates, settlement records, machine logs, autonomous execution cycles, and downstream tax assumptions do not silently become authoritative definitions of when an event occurred.
A governed event may have a point in time, an interval, a duration, multiple temporal stages, distributed timing, or qualified temporal uncertainty. TRETS preserves the representation that operational reality legitimately supports.
TRETS governs when the event occurred as governed operational reality — not when tax law decides that the event becomes taxable.
TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
Module Architecture
→ Event Time Identification Module (ETIM)

→ Event Start Module (ETSM)
→ Event Completion Module (ETCM)
→ Event Duration Module (ETDM)
→ Event Temporal Order Module (ETOM)
Related Documents
→ About Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS)

OOF™ Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard - (TRVAS)
Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard - (TRVAS)
OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™
Independent Methodological Authority
Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™
Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™
Parent Standard: TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard
Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Value Association Governance Layer
Category: Governance & Enforcement
Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance
Type: Parent Standard
Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Value Association
Origin ID: TREGA-TRVAS-008
Version: 1.0
Status: Canonical · Open Standard
Effective Date: 1 September 2026
AI-Readable: Yes
Authority: OOF®
Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection

Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard (TRVAS) governs how value references, value states, value changes, and other governed value results are associated with a Governed Participatory Event so that the event can carry a sufficiently structured representation of value into subsequent Tax-Relevant Event governance. TRVAS establishes which governed value information legitimately belongs to the event, how that relationship is represented, how multiple value associations are distinguished, how value states and changes are connected to the event, and how those associations remain traceable. TRVAS does not determine the origin, emergence, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, extinction, ownership, economic meaning, or complete lifecycle of value. Those questions belong to VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism and other appropriate governance architectures. TRVAS also does not determine taxable value, Tax Base, consideration under law, customs value, transfer-pricing value, market value under a jurisdiction-specific rule, deductible amount, taxable income, taxable gain, tax rate, or Tax Liability.
The foundational boundary is: VFM® determines what happened to value. TREGA™ determines which governed value result belongs to the event. Purpose Tax-relevant events frequently interact with value.

An event may: create value; transfer value; exchange value; consume value; transform value; increase value; decrease value; temporarily hold value; redistribute value; destroy value; restore value; or affect several different values simultaneously. Yet the existence of value somewhere in an operational system does not establish that the value belongs to the specific event being governed. Likewise, a monetary amount appearing in a transaction record does not automatically represent the complete value structure of the event.
TRVAS exists to establish a governed association layer between: Governed Participatory Event
and: Governed Value Information without converting that association into a legal tax valuation. Core Question Which governed value results materially belong to the Tax-Relevant Event, and how can those relationships be represented without determining the jurisdiction-specific taxable value, Tax Base, ownership, entitlement, or legal tax consequence of that value? TREGA™ Governance Flow

The complete TREGA™ Parent Standard governance sequence is: 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard → 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard ← CURRENT STANDARD → 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard → 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard → 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Position Within TREGA™ TRVAS operates after Event Participation has been governed and before relationships between multiple events are governed.
Its architectural position is: Event Participation → Value Association → Event Relationships
TREPS establishes: Who or what materially participated in the event?
TRVAS establishes: Which governed value results materially belong to the event?
TRERLS subsequently establishes: How does the event relate to other governed events? Governed Transition
TRVAS receives: Governed Participatory Event
together with relevant governed value information and produces: Governed Value-Associated Event

The canonical transition is: Governed Participatory Event + Governed Value Results → TRVAS — Value Association Governance → Governed Value-Associated Event This output proceeds to TRERLS.
Governed Space
TRVAS governs the architecture-level space through which value is legitimately associated with a Tax-Relevant Event.
This includes governance of: value-association identification; value references; event-value relationships; value-state association; value-change association; multiple value associations; participant-value-event distinctions; direct and indirect value association; value-association qualification; value-association uncertainty; value-association conflict; value-association traceability; and value-association readiness for downstream TREGA™ governance.
TRVAS does not govern the internal lifecycle of the value itself.
Value Association
A Value Association represents the governed relationship between a value result and the specific Tax-Relevant Event.
The existence of value does not automatically establish this relationship.
Therefore: Value Existence ≠ Event Value Association
A governed association requires sufficient support that the value information materially belongs to the event.
Governed Value Result
TRVAS may consume governed value results from VFM® or another legitimate upstream value-governance source.

Such results may describe: value reference; value state; value change; value development; value degradation; value nullification; value restoration; or another governed value condition.
TRVAS does not recalculate or redefine those results.
Its question is narrower:
Does this governed value result materially belong to this governed event?
Value Reference
A value associated with an event must be sufficiently referenceable so that the relationship can remain stable and reconstructable.
A Value Reference may connect the event to an upstream governed value object or value result.
The reference does not itself establish the association.
Value Reference ≠ Value Association by Default.
Monetary and Non-Monetary Value
TRVAS shall not assume that relevant value must be expressed as money.
Governed events may involve: monetary value; goods; services; digital assets; rights; access; resources; productive capacity; data-related value; computational resources; energy; economic benefits; obligations; or other governed forms of value.
Therefore: Value ≠ Monetary Amount by Default
TRVAS must remain capable of representing value associations before a jurisdiction determines which forms of value matter for taxation.
Recorded Amount Versus Governed Value
Operational systems frequently contain prices, balances, invoices, settlement amounts, accounting amounts, estimated values, and other numeric representations.
These records may support Value Association.

They are not automatically authoritative representations of governed value.
Therefore:
Recorded Amount ≠ Governed Value by Default.
And:
Invoice Amount ≠ Taxable Value by Default.
Value Association Identification
TRVAS shall establish whether available governed value information potentially belongs to the event.
The purpose is to distinguish:
Value information relevant to this event
from:
Value information merely present in surrounding operational systems.
A value reference may enter association governance only where a plausible event relationship exists.
Direct Value Association
A governed value result may directly correspond to the event.
For example, an event may directly produce, transfer, consume, or transform a governed value.
Where sufficient support exists, TRVAS may establish a direct Value Association.
However:
Direct Value Association ≠ Taxable Consideration.
The legal meaning remains downstream.
Indirect Value Association
Some value relationships may exist through intermediate operational structures.
TRVAS may preserve indirect association where materially relevant.
An indirect relationship shall not automatically be excluded merely because the value does not move directly between two participants.
Therefore:
Indirect Value Association ≠ Irrelevant Value by Default.
Multiple Value Associations
One event may legitimately interact with multiple values.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Event
↓
Value A + Value B + Value C + Value N

Examples may include: goods and payment; service and digital entitlement; asset and consideration; energy and computational output; several currencies; multiple digital assets; or multiple value changes.
Therefore: One Event ≠ One Value by Default
TRVAS shall preserve materially distinct value relationships rather than forcing the event into one value field.
One Value Across Multiple Events
The same governed value may also relate to multiple events over time.
TRVAS shall not assume that a value belongs exclusively to one event merely because an association exists.
Therefore:
Value Association ≠ Exclusive Event Ownership of Value.
TRERLS may subsequently govern relationships among events where necessary.
VFM® remains authoritative for the Value Lifecycle.
Value State Association
An event may be materially associated with a particular governed state of value.
TRVAS shall preserve that relationship where relevant.
However:
Value State Association ≠ Value State Determination.
VFM® governs the value state itself.
TRVAS only establishes its relationship to the event.
Value Change Association
A governed event may be associated with a change in value.
This may include increase, decrease, transfer, transformation, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or another governed change.
TRVAS shall establish whether the governed change materially belongs to the event.
The boundary is:
VFM® governs the Value Change.
TRVAS governs the Event ↔ Value Change relationship.

Therefore: Value Change Association ≠ Value Change Governance Value Without Transfer
Value may be associated with an event even where no conventional transfer occurs.
An event may: create value; consume value; destroy value; improve value; impair value; unlock value; restrict value; or transform value.
Therefore:
No Value Transfer ≠ No Value Association.
This distinction is particularly important for digital, machine, infrastructure, and autonomous economies.
Transfer Without Ownership Determination
Where value is transferred, TRVAS may represent the relationship between the transfer result and the event.
It does not determine legal ownership before or after the transfer.
Therefore:
Value Transfer Association ≠ Ownership Determination.
OBIDENITY® remains authoritative for governed ownership where applicable.
Participant and Value Association
TREPS establishes Event Participation.
TRVAS shall not assume that every participant owns, receives, supplies, controls, or benefits from every value associated with the event.
Therefore: Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default
and: Participation Role ≠ Value Entitlement
An actor may materially participate without owning the associated value. Participant–Value Relationship
Where materially relevant, TRVAS may preserve which value relationship is associated with which participant structure.
However, such representation remains an event-value association structure.

It shall not independently determine: legal ownership; beneficial ownership; legal entitlement; contractual entitlement; economic ownership under tax law; or liability for the value.
Those conclusions remain outside TRVAS.
Gross and Component Value Structures
A single event may contain several value components.
A total recorded amount may conceal materially different governed value relationships.
TRVAS shall permit component-level associations where operationally justified.
However:
Total Recorded Amount ≠ Single Governed Value by Default.
TRVAS does not prescribe a jurisdiction-specific gross/net or taxable/non-taxable decomposition. Positive, Negative, and Null Value Conditions
Value association shall not be limited to positive economic amounts.
A governed event may involve: positive value; negative value; zero-value state; value loss; value degradation; liability-like economic burden; or value nullification.
TRVAS may associate such governed results with the event without determining their tax treatment.
Zero Monetary Amount ≠ No Tax-Relevant Value Association by Default.
Currency and Unit Representation
Value may be expressed in different currencies, units, quantities, measures, or governed representations.
TRVAS shall preserve the relevant upstream representation without assuming that one currency or unit constitutes the legally required tax measurement.
Value Unit ≠ Tax Measurement Rule.

Currency conversion, valuation methodology, and jurisdiction-specific tax measurement remain downstream unless governed by another appropriate architecture.
Estimated Value
Some operational events may contain estimated rather than directly observed value.
TRVAS may associate a governed estimated value result where its status is clearly preserved.
Therefore:
Estimated Value ≠ Established Value.
and:
Estimated Value Association ≠ Tax Valuation.
Value Association Confidence
Value associations may possess different levels of support.
TRVAS shall permit qualification where necessary.
A Value Association may be:
Established
Qualified
Partial
Ambiguous
Conflicted
Unresolved
A downstream requirement for a numeric amount shall not justify artificial certainty.
Value Association Uncertainty
Where it is unclear whether a governed value result belongs to the event, uncertainty shall remain visible.
Therefore:
Value Association Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assign Convenient Value.
The association shall not be created or rejected merely because one outcome produces a preferred tax result.
Value Association Conflict
Different operational or governed sources may associate different value results with the same event.
TRVAS shall preserve material conflicts until sufficiently resolved.
Therefore:
Value Association Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Valuation Selection.
TRVAS governs the conflict in association.
It does not determine jurisdiction-specific legal valuation.

Value Association Traceability
Every material Value Association should remain sufficiently reconstructable.
The governance structure should permit determination of: which event the value relates to; which governed value reference was used; which upstream value source produced the value result; which value state or change is associated; what basis supports the association; whether the association is direct or indirect; whether uncertainty existed; whether conflicting associations existed; and what governance state was assigned.
Traceability must preserve the distinction between the value result and its association with the event.
Value Association and Event Boundary
TRVAS operates within the Event Boundary already governed by TREBS.
Value information shall not silently expand the Event Boundary.
Therefore: Value Association ≠ Event Boundary Expansion
If value evidence indicates that the existing Event Boundary may be incorrect, the matter shall be referred to the appropriate upstream TREGA™ governance layer.
TRVAS shall not redefine the Event Boundary independently.
Value Association and Event Formation
The presence of additional value does not automatically create another event.
Likewise, multiple value changes may belong to one formed event.
Therefore:
Multiple Values ≠ Multiple Events by Default.
If materially distinct event formation may exist, TREFS remains authoritative.
Value Association and Event Timing

A value may be recorded, recognized, transferred, settled, measured, or updated at a time different from the governed operational Event Timing.
Therefore:
Value Timestamp ≠ Event Time by Default.
TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing.
TRVAS shall preserve relevant value timing only as part of the association where necessary.
Value Association and Event Location
A value may be recorded, stored, transferred, or represented in a location different from the governed Event Location.
Therefore:
Value Location ≠ Event Location by Default.
Asset Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction by Default.
TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location.
Value Association and Event Participation
TRVAS receives the Governed Participatory Event from TREPS.
It shall preserve participant structures without redefining them.
A value relationship may provide additional evidence relevant to participation, but TRVAS shall not independently create or remove participants.
Therefore:
Value Association ≠ Participation Determination.
TREPS remains authoritative for Event Participation.
Value Association and Event Relationships
The same value may appear across several related events.
TRVAS shall preserve the association within the current event.
TRERLS subsequently governs relationships among those events.
Therefore:
Shared Value Reference ≠ Same Event by Default. Relationship to VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism
VFM® owns the governance of the Value Lifecycle.
Its governed space includes what happens to value across:

Value Context
↓
Value Origin
↓
Value Emergence
↓
Value Recognition
↓
Value State
↓
Value Change
↓
Value Development / Value Degradation
↓
Value Nullification
↓
Value Restoration / Value Extinction
TRVAS shall not reproduce this lifecycle.
The architectural boundary is: VFM® governs what happened to value. TRVAS governs which governed value result belongs to the Tax-Relevant Event.
This separation allows TREGA™ to consume governed value information without becoming a second value-governance architecture.
Relationship to OBIDENITY®
TRVAS does not determine ownership merely because value is associated with an actor or event.
OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, continuity, and related identity-governance structures where applicable.
Therefore:
Value Association ≠ Ownership Governance.
Relationship to Accountability and Liability
Value association does not establish who is responsible for value creation, loss, transfer, degradation, or another outcome.
Therefore:
Value Association ≠ Accountability.
Value Loss Association ≠ Liability Determination.
AGA™ and HALIA™ remain authoritative for their respective governance spaces.
Relationship to Tax Law
TRVAS deliberately stops before jurisdiction-specific tax valuation.

A jurisdiction may later determine whether an associated value constitutes: taxable consideration; taxable income; taxable gain; taxable benefit; customs value; transfer-pricing value; deductible amount; tax base; exempt value; or another legally defined amount.
TRVAS does not make those determinations.
Therefore: Governed Event Value ≠ Taxable Value
and: Value Association ≠ Tax Base Determination Multi-Jurisdiction Governance
One governed Value Association may legitimately support different tax interpretations across jurisdictions.
The canonical model is:
One Governed Event
→ One Governed Value Association Structure
→ Jurisdiction A Evaluation
→ Jurisdiction B Evaluation
→ Jurisdiction C Evaluation
TRVAS shall therefore preserve operational value association independently from any single jurisdiction's valuation rules.
Machine and Autonomous Economy
Machine and autonomous events may produce value structures that do not resemble traditional human transactions.
An AI agent may: allocate computational capacity; obtain a digital service; exchange digital assets; consume energy; generate operational output; trigger resource use; optimize production; or initiate another value-affecting action.
TRVAS shall permit these governed value results to associate with the event without requiring a conventional invoice, human buyer, human seller, or monetary payment.
Therefore:
No Human Transaction ≠ No Value Association.
Value Association States

TRVAS may represent architecture-level states including:
Value Association Ready
Value Association Under Governance
Value Association Established
Multi-Value Association
Direct Value Association
Indirect Value Association
Value State Associated
Value Change Associated
Value Association Qualified
Value Association Ambiguous
Value Association Conflicted
Value Association Unresolved
Governed Value-Associated Event
These states describe Value Association only.
They do not determine legal tax valuation.
Governance Requirements

A TRVAS-conformant implementation shall ensure that: value information is associated only where materially relevant to the governed event; governed value references remain distinguishable; monetary and non-monetary value can be represented; multiple values can be associated with one event; one value can remain associated with multiple events where legitimate; Value States can be associated without being redefined; Value Changes can be associated without being re-governed; direct and indirect associations can remain distinguishable; participant identity does not automatically determine value ownership; Participation Role does not automatically determine value entitlement; recorded amounts are not automatically treated as governed value; invoice amounts are not automatically treated as taxable value; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; association traceability remains reconstructable; Value Association does not silently redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary; VFM® ownership of the Value Lifecycle remains preserved; ownership governance remains separate; tax valuation remains downstream; and Value Association does not determine Tax Base or Tax Liability.
Governance Logic
IF a Governed Participatory Event exists, THEN relevant governed value information may enter Value Association governance.
IF a governed value result materially belongs to the event, THEN a Governed Value Association may be established.

IF multiple materially distinct value results belong to the same event, THEN multiple Value Associations shall be preserved where necessary.
IF a Value State or Value Change is governed upstream, THEN TRVAS may associate that result without redefining it.
IF a value reference is merely present in surrounding operational data, THEN association shall not be established solely from that presence.
IF Value Association remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the relevant governance state shall remain visible.
IF additional value information suggests that Event Formation or Event Boundary may be incorrect, THEN TRVAS shall refer the issue upstream rather than independently redefining the event.
IF the event's value associations are sufficiently governed, THEN TRVAS may produce a Governed Value-Associated Event.
TRVAS SHALL NOT convert Governed Event Value into jurisdiction-specific taxable value, Tax Base, or Tax Liability.
Governance Outputs

TRVAS may produce architecture-level outputs including: Governed Value Association; Governed Value Reference Structure; Governed Multi-Value Association Structure; Governed Direct Value Association; Governed Indirect Value Association; Governed Value State Association; Governed Value Change Association; Governed Participant–Value Relationship Reference; Value Association Confidence State; Value Association Ambiguity State; Value Association Conflict State; Value Association Traceability Structure; Value Association Governance State; and the principal output:
Governed Value-Associated Event
This output becomes the governed input to:
TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Critical Distinctions
Value Existence ≠ Event Value Association
Value Reference ≠ Value Association by Default
Value ≠ Monetary Amount by Default
Recorded Amount ≠ Governed Value by Default
Invoice Amount ≠ Taxable Value by Default
Direct Value Association ≠ Taxable Consideration
Indirect Value Association ≠ Irrelevant Value by Default
One Event ≠ One Value by Default
Value Association ≠ Exclusive Event Ownership of Value
Value State Association ≠ Value State Determination
Value Change Association ≠ Value Change Governance
No Value Transfer ≠ No Value Association
Value Transfer Association ≠ Ownership Determination
Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default
Participation Role ≠ Value Entitlement
Total Recorded Amount ≠ Single Governed Value by Default

Zero Monetary Amount ≠ No Tax-Relevant Value Association by Default
Estimated Value ≠ Established Value
Estimated Value Association ≠ Tax Valuation
Value Association ≠ Event Boundary Expansion
Multiple Values ≠ Multiple Events by Default
Value Timestamp ≠ Event Time by Default
Value Location ≠ Event Location by Default
Value Association ≠ Participation Determination
Shared Value Reference ≠ Same Event by Default
Value Association ≠ Ownership Governance
Value Association ≠ Accountability
Value Loss Association ≠ Liability Determination
Governed Event Value ≠ Taxable Value
Value Association ≠ Tax Base Determination
Enterprise Application
TRVAS provides the value-association layer between governed participation and subsequent Event Relationship governance:
ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System
→ Governed Operational Event
→ TREPS — Governed Participatory Event VFM® / Governed Value Information
→ TRVAS — Governed Value-Associated Event
→ TRERLS — Event Relationship Governance
→ TREDS — Event Determination
→ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record
→ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine
This structure allows taxation systems to consume governed event-value relationships without requiring TREGA™ to determine the tax treatment of the value.
Internal Module Architecture
TRVAS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1. VAIM — Value Association Identification Module

Identifies governed value information that may materially belong to the event and determines which value references should enter Value Association governance. 2. VARM — Value Reference Module
Establishes stable and traceable references between the governed event and relevant governed value objects or results. 3. VACM — Value Change Association Module
Governs the association between the event and governed changes affecting value without re-governing the Value Change itself. 4. VASM — Value State Association Module
Governs the association between the event and relevant governed Value States without determining those states independently. 5. VATM — Value Association Traceability Module
Preserves reconstructable provenance, qualification, uncertainty, conflict, and history of the event-value association structure.
Internal Module Flow
VAIM — Value Association Identification
→ VARM — Value Reference
→ VACM — Value Change Association
→ VASM — Value State Association
→ VATM — Value Association Traceability
→ Governed Value-Associated Event Cross-Architecture Boundaries
VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Owns the Value Lifecycle and determines what happened to value.
OBIDENITY® Owns governed identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, and related structures.
TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Owns who or what materially participated in the event.

TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Owns which governed value results materially belong to the event.
TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Owns relationships among governed events.
AGA™ Owns accountability governance.
HALIA™ Owns the lifecycle of harm and liability.
Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Systems Own legal tax classification, taxable value, Tax Base, Tax Liability, tax rates, exemptions, deductions, reporting, payment, collection, and enforcement.
Canonical Boundary
TRVAS governs the association of governed value references, Value States, Value Changes, and other legitimate governed value results with a specific Tax-Relevant Event.
It does not govern the complete Value Lifecycle, determine the origin or ownership of value, redefine upstream governed Value States or Value Changes, determine Event Participation, redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary, establish accountability or liability, or determine jurisdiction-specific taxable value, Tax Base, taxable income, taxable gain, consideration, customs value, transfer-pricing value, tax rate, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing obligation, collection, payment, or enforcement.
TRVAS ends when the event possesses a sufficiently governed, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral Value Association structure for subsequent TREGA™ governance.
Canonical Closing Statement

TRVAS establishes which governed value results belong to the event without allowing Event Value Association to become Value Lifecycle governance, ownership determination, or tax valuation.
What happened to value and which part of that governed value reality belongs to an event are separate governance questions. What tax law subsequently does with that value is a third. VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ governs which governed value result belongs to the event. Governed Event Value ≠ Taxable Value. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
Module Architecture
→ Value Association Identification Module (VAIM)
→ Value Reference Module (VARM)
→ Value Change Association Module (VACM)
→ Value State Association Module (VASM)
→ Value Association Traceability Module (VATM)
Related Documents
→ About Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard (TRVAS)
